1. The Chapter on Steadfastness

[151] 1. Rājovādajātakavaṇṇanā

[151] 1. The Commentary on the Rājovāda Jātaka

Daḷhaṃ [V 2.0001][M 2.0001][P 2.0001] daḷhassa khipatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto rājovādaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So tesakuṇajātake (jā. 2.17.1 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Ekasmiṃ pana divase kosalarājā ekaṃ agatigataṃ dubbinicchayaṃ aḍḍaṃ vinicchinitvā bhuttapātarāso allahatthova alaṅkatarathaṃ abhiruyha satthu santikaṃ gantvā phullapadumasassirikesu pādesu nipatitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ satthā etadavoca – “handa kuto nu tvaṃ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti. “Bhante, ajja ekaṃ agatigataṃ dubbinicchayaṃ aḍḍaṃ vinicchinanto [V 2.0002] okāsaṃ alabhitvā idāni taṃ tīretvā bhuñjitvā allahatthova tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgatomhī”ti. Satthā “mahārāja, dhammena samena aḍḍavinicchayaṃ nāma kusalaṃ, saggamaggo esa. Anacchariyaṃ kho panetaṃ, yaṃ tumhe mādisassa sabbaññubuddhassa santikā ovādaṃ labhamānā dhammena samena aḍḍaṃ vinicchineyyātha. Etadeva acchariyaṃ, yaṃ pubbe rājāno asabbaññūnampi paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā dhammena samena [M 2.0002] aḍḍaṃ vinicchinantā cattāri agatigamanāni vajjetvā dasa rājadhamme akopetvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā saggapuraṃ pūrayamānā agamiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“He hurls the hard against the hard.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning advice to kings. This will become clear in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka. On one occasion, the King of Kosala, having decided a biased and perplexing case, and having eaten his breakfast, with hands still wet, mounted his decorated chariot and went to the Teacher. Having prostrated himself at the Teacher's feet, which had the splendor of full-blown lotuses, he paid homage and sat down to one side. The Teacher then said to him: “Well now, great king, where are you coming from so late in the day?” “Venerable sir, today, while deciding a biased and perplexing case, I did not get an opportunity earlier; having now settled it, eaten, and with my hands still wet, I have come to attend upon you.” The Teacher said: “Great king, to decide cases with Dhamma and equity is indeed meritorious; it is the path to heaven. It is not astonishing that you, receiving instruction from an All-knowing Buddha like me, should decide cases with Dhamma and equity. But this is truly astonishing: that formerly, kings, hearing the words of wise men who were not all-knowing, decided cases with Dhamma and equity, avoiding the four wrong courses of conduct, without violating the ten royal virtues, ruling righteously, and having filled the city of the gods, passed away.” Being asked by him, the Teacher told a story of the past.

Atīte [P 2.0002] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā laddhagabbhaparihāro sotthinā mātukucchimhā nikkhami. Nāmaggahaṇadivase panassa “brahmadattakumāro”tveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So anupubbena vayappatto soḷasavassakāle takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāresi, chandādivasena agantvā vinicchayaṃ anusāsi. Tasmiṃ evaṃ dhammena rajjaṃ kārente amaccāpi dhammeneva vohāraṃ vinicchiniṃsu. Vohāresu dhammena vinicchayamānesu kūṭaḍḍakārakā nāma nāhesuṃ, tesaṃ abhāvā aḍḍatthāya rājaṅgaṇe uparavo pacchijji. Amaccā divasampi vinicchayaṭṭhāne nisīditvā kañci vinicchayatthāya āgacchantaṃ adisvā uṭṭhāya pakkamanti, vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ chaḍḍetabbabhāvaṃ pāpuṇi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of his chief queen. Having received the care due to a pregnancy, he safely emerged from his mother's womb. On the naming day, they gave him the name 'Prince Brahmadatta.' Gradually coming of age, at sixteen years old, he went to Takkasilā and attained perfection in all the arts. Upon his father's death, he was established on the throne and ruled righteously and equitably, administering justice without being led by desire and the other wrong courses. While he ruled thus righteously, his ministers also decided cases justly. Since cases were decided righteously, there were no bringers of false suits. Due to their absence, the clamor of litigants in the royal courtyard ceased. The ministers, though sitting in the judgment hall for the entire day, would see no one coming for a judgment, and so would rise and depart. The judgment hall reached a state where it was to be abandoned.

Bodhisatto cintesi – “mayi dhammena rajjaṃ kārente vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantā nāma natthi, uparavo pacchijji, vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ chaḍḍetabbabhāvaṃ pattaṃ, idāni mayā attano aguṇaṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭati ‘ayaṃ nāma me aguṇo’ti sutvā taṃ pahāya guṇesuyeva vattissāmī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya “atthi nu kho me koci aguṇavādī”ti pariggaṇhanto antovaḷañjakānaṃ antare kañci aguṇavādiṃ adisvā attano guṇakathameva sutvā “ete mayhaṃ bhayenāpi aguṇaṃ avatvā guṇameva vadeyyu”nti bahivaḷañjanake pariggaṇhanto tatthāpi adisvā antonagare pariggaṇhi. Bahinagare catūsu dvāresu catugāmake pariggaṇhi. Tatthāpi kañci aguṇavādiṃ adisvā attano guṇakathameva sutvā “janapadaṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti amacce rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā rathaṃ āruyha sārathimeva gahetvā aññātakavesena nagarā nikkhamitvā janapadaṃ pariggaṇhamāno yāva paccantabhūmiṃ gantvā kañci aguṇavādiṃ [P 2.0003] adisvā attano guṇakathameva sutvā paccantasīmato mahāmaggena nagarābhimukhoyeva nivatti.

The Bodhisatta thought: "As I rule righteously, there are none coming to the court of justice; the clamor has ceased, and the court of justice has reached the state of being abandoned. Now I should seek out my own faults. Having heard, 'This is my fault,' I shall abandon it and conduct myself only in virtues." From then on, while investigating, "Is there anyone who speaks of my faults?" he found no fault-finder among the inner attendants, hearing only praise of his virtues. Thinking, "These people, even out of fear of me, might speak only of my virtues without mentioning my faults," he investigated among the outer attendants; finding none there either, he investigated within the city. Outside the city, he investigated at the four gates and in the four suburban villages. There too, finding no fault-finder and hearing only praise of his virtues, he thought, "I shall investigate the countryside." Entrusting the kingdom to his ministers, he mounted a chariot, taking only the charioteer, and left the city in disguise. Investigating the countryside, he went as far as the borderlands. Finding no fault-finder and hearing only praise of his virtues, he turned back from the border limit along the high road, heading towards the city.

Tasmiṃ [V 2.0003][M 2.0003] pana kāle balliko nāma kosalarājāpi dhammena rajjaṃ kārento aguṇakathaṃ gavesanto hutvā antovaḷañjakādīsu aguṇavādiṃ adisvā attano guṇakathameva sutvā janapadaṃ pariggaṇhanto taṃ padesaṃ agamāsi. Te ubhopi ekasmiṃ ninnaṭṭhāne sakaṭamagge abhimukhā ahesuṃ, rathassa ukkamanaṭṭhānaṃ natthi. Atha ballikarañño sārathi bārāṇasirañño sārathiṃ “tava rathaṃ ukkamāpehī”ti āha. Sopi “ambho sārathi, tava rathaṃ ukkamāpehi, imasmiṃ rathe bārāṇasirajjasāmiko brahmadattamahārājā nisinno”ti āha. Itaropi naṃ “ambho sārathi, imasmiṃ rathe kosalarajjasāmiko ballikamahārājā nisinno, tava rathaṃ ukkamāpetvā amhākaṃ rañño rathassa okāsaṃ dehī”ti āha. Bārāṇasirañño sārathi “ayampi kira rājāyeva, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti cintento “attheso upāyo”ti vayaṃ pucchitvā “daharassa rathaṃ ukkamāpetvā mahallakassa okāsaṃ dāpessāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā taṃ sārathiṃ kosalarañño vayaṃ pucchitvā pariggaṇhanto ubhinnampi samānavayabhāvaṃ ñatvā rajjaparimāṇaṃ balaṃ dhanaṃ yasaṃ jātiṃ gottaṃ kulapadesanti sabbaṃ pucchitvā “ubhopi tiyojanasatikassa rajjassa sāmino samānabaladhanayasajātigottakulapadesā”ti ñatvā “sīlavantassa okāsaṃ dassāmī”ti cintetvā “bho sārathi, tumhākaṃ rañño sīlācāro kīdiso”ti pucchi. So “ayañca ayañca amhākaṃ rañño sīlācāro”ti attano rañño aguṇameva guṇato pakāsento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, King Ballika of Kosala, also ruling righteously and searching for any talk of his faults, finding no one who spoke of his faults among his attendants and so forth, and hearing only praise of his own virtues, was inspecting the countryside and arrived at that region. Both of them met face to face on a cart track in a low-lying place; there was no room for a chariot to turn aside. Then the charioteer of King Ballika said to the charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī, "Make your chariot move aside." The other replied, "Friend charioteer, move your chariot aside. In this chariot sits the lord of the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, the Great King Brahmadatta." The first also said to him, "Friend charioteer, in this chariot sits the lord of the kingdom of Kosala, the Great King Ballika. Move your chariot aside and give way to our king's chariot." The charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "This one, it seems, is also a king. What is to be done?" considered, "There is a way." He decided, "I will ask their age, have the younger one's chariot moved aside, and give way to the elder." He then asked that charioteer the age of the King of Kosala. While investigating, he realized that both were of the same age. He then asked everything: the extent of their kingdoms, their power, wealth, fame, birth, lineage, and family origin. Realizing that both were lords of kingdoms of three hundred leagues, and were equal in power, wealth, fame, birth, lineage, and family origin, he thought, "I will give way to the more virtuous one." He then asked, "Friend charioteer, what is your king's conduct and virtue like?" The other, proclaiming his own king's faults as virtues, recited the first verse: "This and this is our king's conduct and virtue."

1.

1.

“Daḷhaṃ daḷhassa khipati, balliko mudunā muduṃ;

Sādhumpi sādhunā jeti, asādhumpi asādhunā;

Etādiso ayaṃ rājā, maggā uyyāhi sārathī”ti.

"Ballika hurls harshness against the harsh, and treats the gentle with gentleness; he conquers even the good with goodness, and even the wicked with wickedness. Such is this king! O charioteer, move aside from the path!"

Tattha [P 2.0004] daḷhaṃ daḷhassa khipatīti yo daḷho hoti balavadaḷhena pahārena vā vacanena vā jinitabbo, tassa daḷhameva pahāraṃ vā vacanaṃ vā khipati. Evaṃ daḷhova hutvā taṃ jinātīti dasseti. Ballikoti tassa rañño nāmaṃ. Mudunā mudunti mudupuggalaṃ sayampi mudu hutvā mudunāva upāyena jināti. Sādhumpi sādhunā jetīti ye sādhū sappurisā, te sayampi sādhu hutvā sādhunāva [M 2.0004] upāyena jināti. Asādhumpi asādhunāti ye pana asādhū, te sayampi asādhu hutvā asādhunāva upāyena jinātīti dasseti. Etādiso ayaṃ rājāti ayaṃ amhākaṃ kosalarājā sīlācārena evarūpo. Maggā uyyāhi sārathīti attano rathaṃ maggā ukkamāpetvā uyyāhi, uppathena yāhi, amhākaṃ rañño maggaṃ dehīti vadati.

In that verse, 'he hurls harshness against the harsh' means that for one who is harsh and must be conquered by a strong, harsh blow or word, he hurls a harsh blow or word. Thus, it shows that being harsh himself, he conquers him. 'Ballika' is the name of that king. 'The gentle with gentleness' means that being gentle himself, he conquers a gentle person by gentle means. 'He conquers even the good with goodness' means that with regard to those who are good and virtuous, he, being good himself, conquers them by good means. 'And even the wicked with wickedness' shows that with regard to those who are wicked, he, being wicked himself, conquers them by wicked means. 'Such is this king' means this king of ours, the King of Kosala, is of such a nature in conduct and character. 'Move aside from the path, charioteer' means he says, 'Having made your own chariot move aside from the path, go away, take a side path, and give way to our king.'

Atha [V 2.0004] naṃ bārāṇasirañño sārathi “ambho, kiṃ pana tayā attano rañño guṇakathā kathitā”ti vatvā “āmā”ti vutte “yadi pana ete guṇāti vadasi, aguṇā pana kīdisī”ti vatvā “ete tāva aguṇā hontu, tumhākaṃ pana rañño kīdiso guṇo”ti vutte “tena hi suṇāhī”ti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī said to him, "Friend, have you just spoken of the virtues of your own king?" When he replied "Yes," the other said, "If you call these virtues, what then would the faults be like?" and continued, "Let these be faults for now, but what is your king's virtue like?" When asked this, the charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī said, "Well then, listen," and spoke the second verse:

2.

2.

“Akkodhena jine kodhaṃ, asādhuṃ sādhunā jine;

Jine kadariyaṃ dānena, saccenālikavādinaṃ;

Etādiso ayaṃ rājā, maggā uyyāhi sārathī”ti.

"With non-anger one should conquer anger; with goodness one should conquer the wicked. One should conquer the stingy with a gift, and the speaker of falsehood with truth. Such is this king! O charioteer, move aside from the path!"

Tattha etādisoti etehi “akkodhena jine kodha”ntiādivasena vuttehi guṇehi samannāgato. Ayañhi kuddhaṃ puggalaṃ sayaṃ akkodho hutvā akkodhena jināti, asādhuṃ pana sayaṃ sādhu hutvā sādhunāva upāyena jināti, kadariyaṃ thaddhamacchariṃ sayaṃ dāyako hutvā dānena jināti. Saccenālikavādinanti musāvādiṃ sayaṃ saccavādī hutvā saccena jināti. Maggā uyyāhi sārathīti, samma sārathi, maggato apagaccha. Evaṃvidhasīlācāraguṇayuttassa amhākaṃ rañño maggaṃ dehi, amhākaṃ rājā maggassa anucchavikoti.

In that verse, 'Such is this' means he is endowed with the virtues mentioned, beginning with 'conquer anger with non-anger.' For he, being without anger himself, conquers an angry person with non-anger; he conquers a wicked person by being good himself, by good means indeed; he conquers the stingy and stubbornly avaricious by being a giver himself, with generosity. 'And the speaker of falsehood with truth' means that he, being a speaker of truth himself, conquers a liar with truth. 'Move aside from the path, charioteer' means, 'Friend charioteer, depart from the path. Give way to our king who is endowed with such virtues of conduct, for our king is worthy of the path.'

Evaṃ vutte ballikarājā ca sārathi ca ubhopi rathā otaritvā asse mocetvā rathaṃ apanetvā bārāṇasirañño maggaṃ adaṃsu. Bārāṇasirājā ballikarañño “raññā nāma idañcidañca kātuṃ [P 2.0005] vaṭṭatī”ti ovādaṃ datvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā dānādīni puññāni katvā jīvitapariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūresi. Ballikarājāpi tassa ovādaṃ gahetvā janapadaṃ pariggahetvā attano aguṇavādiṃ adisvāva sakanagaraṃ gantvā dānādīni puññāni katvā jīvitapariyosāne saggapurameva pūresi.

When this was said, both King Ballika and his charioteer descended from the chariot, unyoked the horses, moved the chariot aside, and gave way to the King of Bārāṇasī. The King of Bārāṇasī gave King Ballika the advice: 'It is proper for a king to do such and such,' then went to Bārāṇasī, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and at the end of his life, filled the city of the gods. King Ballika also, having accepted that advice, inspected the countryside, and without finding anyone to speak of his faults, went to his own city, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and at the end of his life, also filled the city of the gods.

Satthā [M 2.0005] kosalarājassa ovādatthāya imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ballikarañño sārathi moggallāno ahosi, ballikarājā ānando, bārāṇasirañño sārathi sāriputto, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, for the sake of advising the King of Kosala, brought forth this Dhamma discourse and identified the birth-story: "At that time, the charioteer of King Ballika was Moggallāna, King Ballika was Ānanda, the charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī was Sāriputta, and the King of Bārāṇasī was I myself."

Rājovādajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Rājovāda Jātaka, the first.

[152] 2. Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā

[152] 2. The Commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka

Asamekkhitakammantanti [V 2.0005] idaṃ satthā kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ viharanto vesālivāsikaṃ ekaṃ nhāpitaputtaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa kira pitā rājūnaṃ rājorodhānaṃ rājakumārānaṃ rājakumārikānañca massukaraṇakesasaṇṭhapanaaṭṭhapadaṭṭhapanādīni sabbakiccāni karoti saddho pasanno tisaraṇagato samādinnapañcasīlo, antarantare satthu dhammaṃ suṇanto kālaṃ vītināmeti. So ekasmiṃ divase rājanivesane kammaṃ kātuṃ gacchanto attano puttaṃ gahetvā gato. So tattha ekaṃ devaccharāpaṭibhāgaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ licchavikumārikaṃ disvā kilesavasena paṭibaddhacitto hutvā pitarā saddhiṃ rājanivesanā nikkhamitvā “etaṃ kumārikaṃ labhamāno jīvissāmi, alabhamānassa me ettheva maraṇa”nti āhārupacchedaṃ katvā mañcakaṃ parissajitvā nipajji.

"One whose actions are unconsidered..." This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Kūṭāgāra Hall concerning a certain barber's son from Vesālī. His father, it is said, performed all duties for kings, royal consorts, princes, and princesses, such as shaving beards, arranging hair, and styling it in square patterns, and so forth. He was faithful, confident, had gone to the Three Refuges, and had undertaken the five precepts, and he passed his time listening to the Teacher's Dhamma from time to time. One day, while going to the royal residence to perform his work, he took his son with him. There, seeing a Licchavi princess, adorned and prepared, who was like a celestial nymph, his mind became bound by the power of defilement. Leaving the royal residence with his father, he said, "If I obtain this princess, I will live; if I do not obtain her, my death will be right here." Then, having cut off food, he embraced his bed and lay down.

Atha naṃ pitā upasaṅkamitvā “tāta, avatthumhi chandarāgaṃ mā kari, hīnajacco tvaṃ nhāpitaputto, licchavikumārikā khattiyadhītā jātisampannā, na sā tuyhaṃ anucchavikā, aññaṃ te jātigottehi sadisaṃ kumārikaṃ ānessāmī”ti āha. So pitu kathaṃ na gaṇhi. Atha naṃ mātā bhātā bhaginī cūḷapitā cūḷamātāti sabbepi ñātakā ceva mittasuhajjā ca sannipatitvā saññāpentāpi saññāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. So tattheva sussitvā parisussitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Athassa pitā sarīrakiccapetakiccāni katvā tanusoko [P 2.0006] “satthāraṃ vandissāmī”ti bahuṃ gandhamālāvilepanaṃ gahetvā mahāvanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno “kiṃ nu kho, upāsaka, bahūni divasāni na dissasī”ti vutte tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, upāsaka, idāneva tava putto avatthusmiṃ [M 2.0006] chandarāgaṃ uppādetvā vināsaṃ pāpuṇi, pubbepi pattoyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then his father approached him and said, "Dear son, do not create desire and passion for an unsuitable object. You are of low birth, a barber's son, while the Licchavi maiden is a Khattiya's daughter, endowed with high birth. She is not suitable for you. I will bring you another maiden equal in birth and clan." But he did not accept his father's words. Then his mother, brother, sister, paternal uncle, and maternal aunt—all his relatives and close friends—gathered and, though they tried to make him understand, were unable to do so. Right there he wasted away, became utterly emaciated, and reached the end of his life. After performing the bodily rites and funeral duties for the deceased, his father, his grief having been somewhat alleviated, thought, "I will pay homage to the Teacher." Taking many perfumes, garlands, and ointments, he went to the Great Forest, paid homage to the Teacher with them, and sat to one side. When asked, "Lay follower, why have you not been seen for many days?" he related the matter. The Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not only now that your son, having aroused desire for an unsuitable object, has met with destruction. In the past, too, he did so." And, being requested by him, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese sīhayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Tassa cha kaniṭṭhabhātaro ekā ca bhaginī ahosi, sabbepi kañcanaguhāyaṃ vasanti. Tassā pana guhāya avidūre rajatapabbate ekā phalikaguhā atthi, tattheko siṅgālo vasati. Aparabhāge sīhānaṃ mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. Te bhaginiṃ sīhapotikaṃ kañcanaguhāyaṃ ṭhapetvā gocarāya pakkamitvā maṃsaṃ āharitvā tassā denti. So siṅgālo taṃ sīhapotikaṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto ahosi. Tassā pana mātāpitūnaṃ dharamānakāle okāsaṃ nālattha, so sattannampi tesaṃ gocarāya pakkantakāle phalikaguhāya otaritvā kañcanaguhāya dvāraṃ gantvā sīhapotikāya [V 2.0006] purato lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ evarūpaṃ rahassakathaṃ kathesi – “sīhapotike, ahampi catuppado, tvampi catuppadā, tvaṃ me pajāpatī hohi, ahaṃ te pati bhavissāmi, te mayaṃ samaggā sammodamānā vasissāma, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya maṃ kilesavasena saṅgaṇhāhī”ti. Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi – “ayaṃ siṅgālo catuppadānaṃ antare hīno paṭikuṭṭho caṇḍālasadiso, mayaṃ uttamarājakulasammatā, esa kho mayā saddhiṃ asabbhiṃ ananucchavikaṃ kathaṃ katheti, ahaṃ evarūpaṃ kathaṃ sutvā jīvitena kiṃ karissāmi, nāsāvātaṃ sannirujjhitvā marissāmī”ti. Athassā etadahosi – “mayhaṃ evameva maraṇaṃ ayuttaṃ, bhātikā tāva me āgacchantu, tesaṃ kathetvā [P 2.0007] marissāmī”ti. Siṅgālopi tassā santikā paṭivacanaṃ alabhitvā “idāni esā mayhaṃ kujjhatī”ti domanassappatto phalikaguhāyaṃ pavisitvā nipajji.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a lion in the Himālaya region. He had six younger brothers and one sister, and they all lived in a golden cave. Not far from that cave, on a silver mountain, there was a crystal cave where a jackal lived. In time, the parents of the lions died. Leaving their sister, the young lioness, in the golden cave, the brothers went out to seek food, brought back meat, and gave it to her. That jackal, seeing the young lioness, became infatuated with her. But while her parents were alive, he found no opportunity. Then, when all seven of those brothers had gone out for food, he descended from the crystal cave, went to the door of the golden cave, and before the young lioness, he spoke these secret words connected with worldly allurements: “O young lioness, I too am a quadruped, and you too are a quadruped. Be my wife, and I shall be your husband. We shall live together in harmony and contentment. From this day forth, support me out of passion.” She, hearing his words, thought: “This jackal is low and despised among quadrupeds, like an outcaste. We are considered to be of the highest royal lineage. This fellow is speaking to me in an unseemly and unsuitable manner. Having heard such words, what is the use of my life? I shall hold my breath and die!” Then it occurred to her: “For me to die in this way is not right. Let my brothers first return. I shall tell them, and then I shall die.” And the jackal, receiving no reply from her, thought, “Now she is angry with me,” and, overcome with sadness, entered the crystal cave and lay down.

Atheko sīhapotako mahiṃsavāraṇādīsu aññataraṃ vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā bhaginiyā bhāgaṃ āharitvā “amma, maṃsaṃ khādassū”ti āha. “Bhātika, nāhaṃ maṃsaṃ khādāmi, marissāmī”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? Sā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. “Idāni kahaṃ so siṅgālo”ti ca vutte phalikaguhāyaṃ nipannaṃ siṅgālaṃ “ākāse nipanno”ti maññamānā “bhātika, kiṃ na passasi, eso rajatapabbate ākāse nipanno”ti. Sīhapotako tassa phalikaguhāyaṃ nipannabhāvaṃ ajānanto “ākāse nipanno”ti saññī [M 2.0007] hutvā “māressāmi na”nti sīhavegena pakkhanditvā phalikaguhaṃ hadayeneva pahari. So hadayena phalitena tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patvā pabbatapāde pati. Athāparo āgacchi, sā tassapi tatheva kathesi. Sopi tatheva katvā jīvitakkhayaṃ patvā pabbatapāde pati.

Then one young lion, having killed a buffalo, elephant, or some other animal, ate the meat and brought a portion for his sister, saying, “Dear sister, eat this meat.” “Brother, I will not eat meat; I am going to die,” she replied. “For what reason?” he asked. She told him what had happened. And when he asked, “Where is that jackal now?” she, thinking the jackal lying in the crystal cave was lying in the sky, said, “Brother, do you not see? There he is, lying in the sky on the silver mountain.” The young lion, not knowing that he was lying in the crystal cave and perceiving him to be lying in the sky, thought, “I will kill him!” and leaping with the speed of a lion, he struck the crystal cave with his chest. With his heart shattered, he met his end right there and fell at the foot of the mountain. Then another brother came, and she told him the same. He also did the same and, meeting his end, fell at the foot of the mountain.

Evaṃ chasupi bhātikesu matesu sabbapacchā bodhisatto āgacchi. Sā tassapi taṃ kāraṇaṃ ārocetvā “idāni so kuhi”nti vutte “eso rajatapabbatamatthake ākāse nipanno”ti āha. Bodhisatto cintesi – “siṅgālānaṃ ākāse patiṭṭhā nāma natthi, phalikaguhāyaṃ nipannako bhavissatī”ti. So pabbatapādaṃ otaritvā cha bhātike mate disvā “ime attano bālatāya pariggaṇhanapaññāya abhāvena phalikaguhabhāvaṃ ajānitvā hadayena paharitvā matā bhavissanti, asamekkhitvā atituritaṃ karontānaṃ kammaṃ nāma evarūpaṃ hotī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In this way, when all six brothers were dead, the Bodhisatta arrived last of all. She told him the reason as well, and when he asked, 'Where is that jackal now?' she replied, 'Dear brother, he is lying in the sky on the summit of the silver mountain.' The Bodhisatta thought, 'There is no such thing as a jackal's standing-place in the sky; he must be lying in a crystal cave.' Having thought so, he descended to the foot of the mountain and, seeing his six brothers dead, he said, 'These lions must have died because, through their own foolishness and lack of discerning wisdom, they did not realize it was a crystal cave and struck it with their chests. Such indeed is the nature of actions for those who act with excessive haste without consideration.' Having said this, he spoke the first verse:

3.

3.

“Asamekkhitakammantaṃ, turitābhinipātinaṃ;

Sāni kammāni tappenti, uṇhaṃvajjhohitaṃ mukhe”ti.

3. For one whose actions are unconsidered, who rushes forward with excessive haste, their own deeds cause them torment, like something hot put into the mouth.

Tattha [V 2.0007][P 2.0008] asamekkhitakammantaṃ, turitābhinipātinanti yo puggalo yaṃ kammaṃ kattukāmo hoti, tattha dosaṃ asamekkhitvā anupadhāretvā turito hutvā vegeneva taṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ abhinipatati pakkhandati paṭipajjati, taṃ asamekkhitakammantaṃ turitābhinipātinaṃ evaṃ sāni kammāni tappenti, socenti kilamenti. Yathā kiṃ? Uṇhaṃvajjhohitaṃ mukheti, yathā bhuñjantena “idaṃ sītalaṃ idaṃ uṇha”nti anupadhāretvā uṇhaṃ ajjhoharaṇīyaṃ mukhe ajjhoharitaṃ ṭhapitaṃ mukhampi kaṇṭhampi kucchimpi dahati soceti kilameti, evaṃ tathārūpaṃ puggalaṃ sāni kammāni tappenti.

In that verse, 'asamekkhitakammantaṃ, turitābhinipātinaṃ' means a person who, wishing to perform some action, without examining or considering the faults therein, becomes hasty and rushes, leaps, and proceeds to perform that action with speed. Such a person, whose actions are unconsidered and who rushes forward hastily, is tormented, grieved, and afflicted by their own deeds. Like what? 'Uṇhaṃvajjhohitaṃ mukhe' means: just as when someone is eating, if without considering 'this is cool, this is hot,' they put a hot edible item in their mouth, it burns the mouth, the throat, and the stomach, causing grief and affliction; so too do their own deeds torment such a person.

Iti so sīho imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā “mama bhātikā anupāyakusalatāya ‘siṅgālaṃ māressāmā’ti ativegena pakkhanditvā sayaṃ matā, ahaṃ pana evarūpaṃ akatvā siṅgālassa phalikaguhāyaṃ nipannasseva hadayaṃ phālessāmī”ti siṅgālassa ārohanaorohanamaggaṃ sallakkhetvā tadabhimukho hutvā tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ nadi, pathaviyā saddhiṃ ākāsaṃ ekaninnādaṃ ahosi. Siṅgālassa phalikaguhāyaṃ nipannasseva sītatasitassa hadayaṃ phali, so tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi.

Thus, the lion, having spoken this verse, thought: 'My brothers, being unskillful in means, rushed with excessive speed thinking, "We will kill the jackal," and died themselves. But I, for my part, will not act as my brothers did, but will cause the jackal's heart to burst while he is lying in the crystal cave.' Observing the jackal's path of ascent and descent, he faced in that direction and roared his lion’s roar three times. The earth and the sky became a single echo. While the jackal was lying in the crystal cave, his heart burst from extreme terror. That jackal met his end right there in that cave.

Satthā [M 2.0008] “evaṃ so siṅgālo sīhanādaṃ sutvā jīvitakkhayaṃ patto”ti vatvā abhisambuddho hutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, saying, 'Thus that jackal, having heard the lion’s roar, met his end,' as the Perfectly Enlightened One, spoke this verse completing the pair:

4.

4.

“Sīho ca sīhanādena, daddaraṃ abhinādayi;

Sutvā sīhassa nigghosaṃ, siṅgālo daddare vasaṃ;

Bhīto santāsamāpādi, hadayañcassa apphalī”ti.

4. The lion with his lion’s roar made Mount Daddara resound;

Hearing the lion’s resounding cry, the jackal dwelling on Daddara,

Frightened, fell into terror, and his heart burst apart.

Tattha sīhoti cattāro sīhā – tiṇasīho, paṇḍusīho, kāḷasīho, surattahatthapādo kesarasīhoti. Tesu kesarasīho idha adhippeto. Daddaraṃ abhinādayīti tena asanipātasaddasadisena bheravatarena sīhanādena taṃ rajatapabbataṃ abhinādayi ekaninnādaṃ akāsi. Daddare vasanti phalikamissake rajatapabbate vasanto. Bhīto santāsamāpādīti maraṇabhayena bhīto cittutrāsaṃ āpādi. Hadayañcassa apphalīti tena cassa bhayena hadayaṃ phalīti.

In that verse, 'sīho' refers to the king of lions, the master of all beasts. 'Sīhanādena' means with the lion's roar which is like the sound of a thunderbolt. 'Daddaraṃ abhinādayi' means he made the silver mountain resound with a single echo. 'Daddare vasaṃ' means dwelling on the summit of the silver mountain mixed with crystal. 'Bhīto santāsamāpādi' means, being afraid of death, he reached the state of terror. 'Hadayañcassa apphalī' means that because of that extreme fear, the heart of that jackal burst.

Evaṃ [V 2.0008][P 2.0009] sīho siṅgālaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā bhātaro ekasmiṃ ṭhāne paṭicchādetvā tesaṃ matabhāvaṃ bhaginiyā ācikkhitvā taṃ samassāsetvā yāvajīvaṃ kañcanaguhāyaṃ vasitvā yathākammaṃ gato.

In the manner described, the king of lions, having brought the jackal to his end, buried his six brothers in one place, informed his sister of their death, and consoled her. He lived in the golden cave for the rest of his life and then passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne upāsako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā siṅgālo nhāpitaputto ahosi, sīhapotikā licchavikumārikā, cha kaniṭṭhabhātaro aññataratherā ahesuṃ, jeṭṭhabhātikasīho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, explained the Truths and made the connection in the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the explanation of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry. How did he connect the Jātaka? 'At that time, the barber's son was the jackal, the young Licchavi maiden was the young lioness, the six undistinguished elders were the six younger brothers, and I myself was the eldest brother, the lion.' Thus he connected the Jātaka.

Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

Seeking what is beyond one's station, one will perish through attachment.

The Siṅgāla Jātaka is finished.

[153] 3. Sūkarajātakavaṇṇanā

[153] 3. 3. Sūkara Jātaka

The Hog and the Lion

Catuppado ahaṃ, sammāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ mahallakattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi divase rattiṃ dhammassavane vattamāne satthari gandhakuṭidvāre ramaṇīye sopānaphalake ṭhatvā bhikkhusaṅghassa sugatovādaṃ datvā gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhe dhammasenāpati satthāraṃ vanditvā attano pariveṇaṃ agamāsi. Mahāmoggallānopi pariveṇameva gantvā [M 2.0009] muhuttaṃ vissamitvā therassa santikaṃ āgantvā pañhaṃ pucchi, pucchitapucchitaṃ dhammasenāpati gaganatale puṇṇacandaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya vissajjetvā pākaṭamakāsi. Catassopi parisā dhammaṃ suṇamānā nisīdiṃsu. Tattheko mahallakatthero cintesi – “sacāhaṃ imissā parisāya majjhe sāriputtaṃ āluḷento pañhaṃ pucchissāmi, ayaṃ me parisā ‘bahussuto aya’nti ñatvā sakkārasammānaṃ karissatī”ti parisantarā uṭṭhāya theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā “āvuso sāriputta, mayampi taṃ ekaṃ pañhaṃ pucchāma, amhākampi okāsaṃ karohi, dehi me vinicchayaṃ āvedhikāya vā nivedhikāya vā niggahe vā paggahe vā visese vā paṭivisese vā”ti āha. Thero taṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ mahallako icchācāre ṭhito tuccho na kiñci jānātī”ti tena saddhiṃ akathetvāva lajjamāno bījaniṃ ṭhapetvā āsanā otaritvā pariveṇaṃ [P 2.0010] pāvisi, moggallānattheropi attano pariveṇameva agamāsi.

3. 'I am four-footed, friend.' The Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, spoke this Sūkara Jātaka adorned with this verse while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain elderly monk. To elaborate: one day, when a Dhamma discourse was taking place at night, after the Teacher had stood on the delightful stair-platform at the door of the perfumed chamber, given the Buddha's advice to the community of monks, and entered the perfumed chamber, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, who was the chief of the assembly through wisdom, paid homage to the Teacher and went to his own dwelling. Venerable Moggallāna also went to his dwelling, and having relieved his fatigue, came to the presence of Venerable Sāriputta and asked questions. To every question asked, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, answered and made it clear, as if making the full moon appear in the sky. The four assemblies sat listening to the Dhamma. Among those four assemblies, an elderly monk thought: 'If I, in the midst of the assembly listening to the Dhamma, ask Sāriputta a question while confounding him, this assembly, if they know that this elderly monk is very learned, will properly prepare offerings and show great respect.' Having thought so, he rose from the midst of the assembly, approached the elder, stood in a suitable place, and said: 'Friend Sāriputta, we too would ask you one question. Grant us the opportunity. Give me your decision, whether it be in answering directly, in answering without remainder, in refutation, in establishment, in making distinctions, or in further distinctions.' The Elder Sāriputta looked at the elderly monk and thought, 'This elderly monk is practicing under the influence of greed; he is empty and knows nothing.' Without speaking even a word to him, feeling ashamed, he put down his fan, descended from his seat, and entered his dwelling. Venerable Moggallāna also went to his own dwelling.

Manussā uṭṭhāya “gaṇhathetaṃ tucchamahallakaṃ, madhuradhammassavanaṃ no sotuṃ na adāsī”ti anubandhiṃsu. So palāyanto vihārapaccante bhinnapadarāya vaccakuṭiyā patitvā gūthamakkhito aṭṭhāsi. Manussā taṃ disvā vippaṭisārino hutvā satthu santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Satthā te disvā “kiṃ [V 2.0009] upāsakā avelāya āgatatthā”ti pucchi, manussā tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā “na kho upāsakā idānevesa mahallako uppilāvito hutvā attano balaṃ ajānitvā mahābalehi saddhiṃ payojetvā gūthamakkhito jāto, pubbepesa uppilāvito hutvā attano balaṃ ajānitvā mahābalehi saddhiṃ payojetvā gūthamakkhito ahosī”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The people, rising up, said, "Seize this worthless old monk! He did not allow us to listen to the sweet Dhamma!" and pursued him. Fleeing, he fell into a latrine with a broken plank at the edge of the monastery and stood there smeared with excrement. Seeing this, the people became displeased and went to the Teacher. The Teacher, seeing them, asked, "Why have you come at this unseasonable hour, lay followers?" The people explained the matter. The Teacher said, "Lay followers, not only now has this old monk, being frivolous and unaware of his own strength, contended with the powerful and become smeared with excrement. In the past too, he was frivolous, unaware of his own strength, contended with the powerful, and became smeared with excrement." Having spoken thus, at their request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sīho hutvā himavantapadese pabbataguhāya vāsaṃ kappesi. Tassā avidūre ekaṃ saraṃ nissāya bahū sūkarā nivāsaṃ kappesuṃ. Tameva saraṃ nissāya tāpasāpi paṇṇasālāsu vāsaṃ kappesuṃ. Athekadivasaṃ sīho mahiṃsavāraṇādīsu aññataraṃ vadhitvā yāvadatthaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditvā taṃ saraṃ otaritvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā uttari. Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko thūlasūkaro taṃ saraṃ nissāya gocaraṃ gaṇhāti. Sīho taṃ disvā “aññaṃ ekadivasaṃ [M 2.0010] imaṃ khādissāmi, maṃ kho pana disvā puna na āgaccheyyā”ti tassa anāgamanabhayena sarato uttaritvā ekena passena gantuṃ ārabhi. Sūkaro oloketvā “esa maṃ disvā mama bhayena upagantuṃ asakkonto bhayena palāyati, ajja mayā iminā sīhena saddhiṃ payojetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā taṃ yuddhatthāya avhayanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta became a lion and lived in a mountain cave in the Himalayan region. Not far from there, many boars made their dwelling near a certain lake. Near that same lake, ascetics also lived in leaf huts. One day, the lion killed one of the animals like a buffalo or an elephant, ate as much meat as he wanted, then descended to the lake to drink water before emerging. At that moment, a certain impudent boar was searching for food near that lake. Seeing him, the lion thought, "I will eat this one another day. But if he sees me, he might not come again." Fearing his non-return, the lion emerged from the lake and began to walk to one side. The boar, observing this, thought, "This lion, seeing me and being unable to approach for fear of me, is fleeing in terror. Today I should engage in a fight with this lion!" Lifting his head, he challenged him to a battle and first spoke this verse:

5.

5.

“Catuppado ahaṃ samma, tvampi samma catuppado;

Ehi samma nivattassu, kiṃ nu bhīto palāyasī”ti.

"I am four-footed, friend, and you too, friend, are four-footed. Come, friend, turn back! Why do you flee, frightened?"

Sīho [P 2.0011] tassa kathaṃ sutvā “samma sūkara, ajja amhākaṃ tayā saddhiṃ saṅgāmo natthi, ito pana sattame divase imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne saṅgāmo hotū”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Sūkaro “sīhena saddhiṃ saṅgāmessāmī”ti haṭṭhapahaṭṭho taṃ pavattiṃ ñātakānaṃ ārocesi. Te tassa kathaṃ sutvā bhītatasitā “idāni tvaṃ sabbepi amhe nāsessasi, attano balaṃ ajānitvā sīhena saddhiṃ saṅgāmaṃ kattukāmoti, sīho āgantvā sabbepi amhe jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessati, sāhasikakammaṃ mā karī”ti āhaṃsu. Sopi bhītatasito “idāni kiṃ karomī”ti pucchi. Sūkarā “samma, tvaṃ etesaṃ tāpasānaṃ uccārabhūmiṃ gantvā pūtigūthe satta divasāni sarīraṃ parivaṭṭetvā sukkhāpetvā sattame divase sarīraṃ ussāvabindūhi temetvā sīhassa āgamanato purimataraṃ gantvā vātayogaṃ ñatvā uparivāte tiṭṭha, sucijātiko sīho tava sarīragandhaṃ ghāyitvā tuyhaṃ jayaṃ datvā gamissatī”ti āhaṃsu. So tathā katvā sattame divase tattha aṭṭhāsi. Sīho tassa sarīragandhaṃ ghāyitvā gūthamakkhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “samma sūkara, sundaro te leso [V 2.0010] cintito, sace tvaṃ gūthamakkhito nābhavissa, idheva taṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ apāpessaṃ, idāni pana te sarīraṃ neva mukhena ḍaṃsituṃ, na pādena paharituṃ sakkā, jayaṃ te dammī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The lion, hearing his words, said, "Friend boar, today there is no battle between us; but on the seventh day from now, let the battle take place in this very spot." Having said this, he departed. The boar, thrilled at the thought, "I will fight with the lion," reported the news to his relatives. Hearing his words, they were terrified and said, "Now you will destroy us all! Not knowing your own strength, you wish to fight with a lion. When the lion comes, he will bring us all to the end of our lives. Do not act so recklessly!" He, too, became terrified and asked, "What should I do now?" The boars said, "Friend, go to the latrine area of those ascetics and roll your body in rotting excrement for seven days, let it dry, and on the seventh day, moisten your body with dew drops. Then, arriving before the lion does, determine the wind direction and stand upwind. The lion, being of a cleanly nature, will smell the stench of your body, grant you victory, and depart." He did as instructed and stood there on the seventh day. The lion, smelling the stench of his body and realizing he was smeared with excrement, said, "Friend boar, a clever trick has been devised by you. If you were not smeared with excrement, I would have ended your life right here. But now, it is impossible to bite your body with my mouth or strike it with my foot. I grant you victory." Then he spoke a second verse:

6.

6.

“Asuci pūtilomosi, duggandho vāsi sūkara;

Sace yujjitukāmosi, jayaṃ samma dadāmi te”ti.

"You are impure, foul-haired, and you emit a foul smell, O boar. If you wish to fight, friend, I grant you victory."

Tattha [M 2.0011] pūtilomoti mīḷhamakkhitattā duggandhalomo. Duggandho vāsīti aniṭṭhajegucchapaṭikūlagandho hutvā vāyasi. Jayaṃ, samma, dadāmi teti “tuyhaṃ jayaṃ demi, ahaṃ parājito, gaccha tva”nti vatvā sīho tatova nivattitvā gocaraṃ gahetvā sare pānīyaṃ pivitvā pabbataguhameva gato. Sūkaropi “sīho me jito”ti ñātakānaṃ ārocesi[P 2.0012]. Te bhītatasitā “puna ekadivasaṃ āgacchanto sīho sabbeva amhe jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessatī”ti palāyitvā aññattha agamaṃsu.

In this context, 'foul-haired' (pūtilomo) means having hair that smells bad due to being smeared with dung. 'You emit a foul smell' (duggandho vāsi) means you give off a smell that is unpleasant, disgusting, and repulsive. 'I grant you victory, friend,' means, 'I give you victory; I am defeated; you may go.' Having said this, the lion turned back from that very place, and after taking his food and drinking water at the lake, he returned to his mountain cave. The boar also announced to his relatives, "The lion was defeated by me!" They, terrified, said, "If the lion returns another day, he will bring all of us to the end of our lives," and they fled elsewhere.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sūkaro mahallako ahosi, sīho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having related this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the boar was the old monk, and the lion was I myself."

Sūkarajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Sūkarajātaka, the third.

[154] 4. Uragajātakavaṇṇanā

[154] 4. The Commentary on the Uraga Jātaka.

Idhūragānaṃ pavaro paviṭṭhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto seṇibhaṇḍanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kosalarañño kira sevakā seṇipamukhā dve mahāmattā aññamaññaṃ diṭṭhaṭṭhāne kalahaṃ karonti, tesaṃ veribhāvo sakalanagare pākaṭo jāto. Te neva rājā, na ñātimittā samagge kātuṃ sakkhiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ satthā paccūsasamaye bodhaneyyabandhave olokento tesaṃ ubhinnampi sotāpattimaggassa upanissayaṃ disvā punadivase ekakova sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā tesu ekassa gehadvāre aṭṭhāsi. So nikkhamitvā pattaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ antonivesanaṃ pavesetvā āsanaṃ paññapetvā nisīdāpesi. Satthā nisīditvā tassa mettābhāvanāya ānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā kallacittataṃ ñatvā saccāni pakāsesi, so saccapariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

Here, "The chief of the Uragas entered..." This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a quarrel between two generals. It is said that two great ministers of the Kosala king, who were generals, quarreled with each other wherever they met, and their enmity became evident throughout the entire city. Neither the king nor their relatives and friends were able to reconcile them. Then one day, at dawn, the Teacher, surveying those worthy of being awakened, saw in both of them the potential for the path of stream-entry. The next day, he entered Sāvatthī alone for alms and stood at the door of one of their houses. That man came out, took the bowl, led the Teacher inside his home, prepared a seat, and invited him to sit. After sitting, the Teacher spoke of the benefits of developing loving-kindness and, perceiving the readiness of his mind, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, that man became established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Satthā [V 2.0011] tassa sotāpannabhāvaṃ ñatvā tameva pattaṃ gāhāpetvā uṭṭhāya itarassa gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. Sopi nikkhamitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā “pavisatha, bhante”ti gharaṃ pavesetvā nisīdāpesi. Itaropi pattaṃ gahetvā satthārā saddhiṃyeva pāvisi. Satthā tassa ekādasa mettānisaṃse vaṇṇetvā kallacittataṃ ñatvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne sopi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Iti te ubhopi sotāpannā [M 2.0012] hutvā aññamaññaṃ accayaṃ dassetvā khamāpetvā samaggā sammodamānā ekajjhāsayā ahesuṃ. Taṃ divasaññeva ca bhagavato sammukhāva ekato bhuñjiṃsu. Satthā bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Te bahūni mālāgandhavilepanāni ceva sappimadhuphāṇitādīni ca ādāya satthārā saddhiṃyeva nikkhamiṃsu. Satthā bhikkhusaṅghena vatte [P 2.0013] dassite sugatovādaṃ datvā gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi.

The Teacher, knowing he had attained stream-entry, had that same man take the bowl, then rose and went to the door of the other's house. The other too came out, paid homage to the Teacher, and saying, "Enter, Venerable Sir," led him inside and seated him. The first one, taking the bowl, also entered together with the Teacher. The Teacher praised the eleven benefits of loving-kindness to the second man and, perceiving the readiness of his mind, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, he too became established in the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, both became stream-enterers, acknowledged their transgressions to each other, asked for forgiveness, and became harmonious, rejoicing together with a common purpose. That very day, they ate together in the presence of the Blessed One. The Teacher, having finished his meal, returned to the monastery. They took many flowers, perfumes, and unguents, as well as ghee, honey, and molasses, and departed together with the Teacher. When the community of monks had performed their duties, the Teacher gave the advice of the Well-Gone One and entered the Fragrant Chamber.

Bhikkhū sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhāyaṃ satthu guṇakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, satthā adantadamako, ye nāma dve mahāmatte ciraṃ vāyamamānopi neva rājā samagge kātuṃ sakkhi, na ñātimittādayo sakkhiṃsu, te ekadivaseneva tathāgatena damitā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevāhaṃ ime dve jane samagge akāsiṃ, pubbepete mayā samaggā katāyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

In the evening, the monks in the Dhamma hall raised a discussion praising the virtues of the Teacher: 'Friends, the Teacher is a tamer of the untamed. Indeed, these two great ministers, whom even the king was unable to reconcile despite striving for a long time, nor were their relatives and friends able, have been tamed by the Tathāgata in a single day.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?' When they replied, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that I have reconciled these two persons; in the past, too, they were reconciled by me,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasiyaṃ ussave ghosite mahāsamajjaṃ ahosi. Bahū manussā ceva devanāgasupaṇṇādayo ca samajjadassanatthaṃ sannipatiṃsu. Tatrekasmiṃ ṭhāne eko nāgo ca supaṇṇo ca samajjaṃ passamānā ekato aṭṭhaṃsu. Nāgo supaṇṇassa supaṇṇabhāvaṃ ajānanto aṃse hatthaṃ ṭhapesi. Supaṇṇo “kena me aṃse hattho ṭhapito”ti nivattitvā olokento nāgaṃ sañjāni. Nāgopi olokento supaṇṇaṃ sañjānitvā maraṇabhayatajjito nagarā nikkhamitvā nadīpiṭṭhena palāyi. Supaṇṇopi “taṃ gahessāmī”ti anubandhi. Tasmiṃ samaye bodhisatto tāpaso hutvā tassā nadiyā tīre paṇṇasālāya vasamāno divā darathapaṭippassambhanatthaṃ udakasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvā vakkalaṃ bahi ṭhapetvā nadiṃ otaritvā nhāyati. Nāgo “imaṃ pabbajitaṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ labhissāmī”ti pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā maṇikkhandhavaṇṇaṃ māpetvā vakkalantaraṃ pāvisi. Supaṇṇo anubandhamāno taṃ tattha paviṭṭhaṃ disvā vakkale garubhāvena aggahetvā bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “bhante, ahaṃ chāto, tumhākaṃ vakkalaṃ gaṇhatha, imaṃ nāgaṃ khādissāmī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, a great festival was proclaimed, and there was a large gathering. Many people, along with gods, nāgas, garuḍas, and others, assembled to see the spectacle. In one spot, a nāga and a garuḍa stood together watching the gathering. The nāga, unaware that the other was a garuḍa, placed a hand on his shoulder. The garuḍa, wondering, "Who has placed a hand on my shoulder?" turned around and recognized the nāga. The nāga, also looking, recognized the garuḍa and, terrified of death, fled the city and escaped along the riverbank. The garuḍa, thinking, "I will catch him," gave chase. At that time, the Bodhisatta was living as an ascetic in a leaf hut on the bank of that river. To alleviate the heat at midday, he donned a bathing cloth, left his bark garment outside, and entered the river to bathe. The nāga, thinking, "I will save my life by relying on this renunciant," shed his natural form, took on the appearance of a gemstone, and slipped inside the bark garment. The garuḍa, pursuing, saw him enter there but, out of respect for the bark garment, did not seize it. Instead, he addressed the Bodhisatta: "Venerable sir, I am hungry. Please take your bark garment; I will devour this nāga." To explain this matter, he spoke the first verse:

7.

7.

“Idhūragānaṃ [V 2.0012][P 2.0014][M 2.0013] pavaro paviṭṭho, selassa vaṇṇena pamokkhamicchaṃ;

Brahmañca vaṇṇaṃ apacāyamāno, bubhukkhito no vitarāmi bhottu”nti.

“The best of serpents has entered here, seeking release in the guise of a gemstone; but respecting the holy garb, though hungry, I do not venture to eat.”

Tattha idhūragānaṃ pavaro paviṭṭhoti imasmiṃ vakkale uragānaṃ pavaro nāgarājā paviṭṭho. Selassa vaṇṇenāti maṇivaṇṇena, maṇikkhandho hutvā paviṭṭhoti attho. Pamokkhamicchanti mama santikā mokkhaṃ icchamāno. Brahmañca vaṇṇaṃ apacāyamānoti ahaṃ pana tumhākaṃ brahmavaṇṇaṃ seṭṭhavaṇṇaṃ pūjento garuṃ karonto. Bubhukkhito no vitarāmi bhottunti etaṃ nāgaṃ vakkalantaraṃ paviṭṭhaṃ chātopi samāno bhakkhituṃ na sakkomīti.

In that verse, "The best of serpents has entered here" means that into this bark garment, the best of serpents, the nāga king, has entered. "In the guise of a gemstone" means with the appearance of a jewel; the meaning is that he entered having transformed into a mass of jewels. "Seeking release" means desiring to be freed from me. "Respecting the holy garb" means "but I, honoring and respecting your noble garb, your superior appearance." "Though hungry, I do not venture to eat" means that even though I am hungry, I am not able to devour this nāga that has entered within the bark garment.

Bodhisatto udake ṭhitoyeva supaṇṇarājassa thutiṃ katvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, while still standing in the water, praised the garuḍa king and spoke the second verse:

8.

8.

“So brahmagutto cirameva jīva, dibyā ca te pātubhavantu bhakkhā;

Yo brahmavaṇṇaṃ apacāyamāno, bubhukkhito no vitarāsi bhottu”nti.

“May you, protected by the holy garb, live for a long time, and may divine foods appear for you; you who, respecting the noble appearance, though hungry, do not venture to eat.”

Tattha so brahmaguttoti so tvaṃ brahmagopito brahmarakkhito hutvā. Dibyā ca te pātubhavantu bhakkhāti devatānaṃ paribhogārahā bhakkhā ca tava pātubhavantu, mā pāṇātipātaṃ katvā nāgamaṃsakhādako ahosi.

In that verse, "protected by the holy garb" means you, being guarded and protected by the holy power of the bark garment. "May divine foods appear for you" means may foods worthy of the consumption of gods appear to you; do not become a consumer of nāga flesh by destroying life.

Iti bodhisatto udake ṭhitova anumodanaṃ katvā uttaritvā vakkalaṃ nivāsetvā te ubhopi gahetvā assamapadaṃ gantvā mettābhāvanāya vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā dvepi jane samagge akāsi. Te tato paṭṭhāya samaggā sammodamānā sukhaṃ vasiṃsu.

Thus the Bodhisatta, while still standing in the water, gave words of appreciation, came out, put on the bark garment, took both of them, went to the hermitage, spoke in praise of the development of loving-kindness, and reconciled the two. From then on, they lived together in harmony, rejoicing and happy.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā nāgo ca supaṇṇo ca ime dve mahāmattā ahesuṃ, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher made the connection in the Jātaka: "At that time, the nāga and the garuḍa were these two great ministers, and the ascetic was none other than myself."

Uragajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Uraga Jātaka, the Fourth.

[155] 5. Bhaggajātakavaṇṇanā

[155] 5. Commentary on the Bhagga Jātaka

Jīva [V 2.0013][P 2.0015][M 2.0014] vassasataṃ bhaggāti idaṃ satthā jetavanasamīpe pasenadikosalena raññā kārite rājakārāme viharanto attano khipitakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi divase satthā rājakārāme catuparisamajjhe nisīditvā dhammaṃ desento khipi. Bhikkhū “jīvatu, bhante bhagavā, jīvatu, sugato”ti uccāsaddaṃ mahāsaddaṃ akaṃsu, tena saddena dhammakathāya antarāyo ahosi. Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “api nu kho, bhikkhave, khipite ‘jīvā’ti vutto tappaccayā jīveyya vā mareyya vā”ti? “No hetaṃ bhante”ti. “Na, bhikkhave, khipite ‘jīvā’ti vattabbo, yo vadeyya āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (cūḷava. 288). Tena kho pana samayena manussā bhikkhūnaṃ khipite “jīvatha, bhante”ti vadanti, bhikkhū kukkuccāyantā nālapanti. Manussā ujjhāyanti – “kathañhi nāma samaṇā sakyaputtiyā ‘jīvatha, bhante’ti vuccamānā nālapissantī”ti. Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Gihī, bhikkhave, maṅgalikā, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gihīnaṃ “jīvatha, bhante”ti vuccamānena “ciraṃ jīvā”ti vattunti. Bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ pucchiṃsu – “bhante, jīvapaṭijīvaṃ nāma kadā uppanna”nti? Satthā “bhikkhave, jīvapaṭijīvaṃ nāma porāṇakāle uppanna”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“May you live a hundred years, Bhagga!” – the Teacher said this while dwelling near Jetavana in the royal monastery built by King Pasenadi of Kosala, concerning his own sneezing. For one day, the Teacher was seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly in the royal monastery, teaching the Dhamma, when he sneezed. The monks made a loud and great noise, crying, “May the Blessed One live, venerable sir, may the Well-farer live!” Because of that noise, the Dhamma talk was interrupted. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, if when one sneezes, one is told ‘Live!’, would one live or die on account of that?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Monks, one should not say ‘Live!’ when someone sneezes. Whoever should say so commits an offense of wrong-doing.” (Cūḷavagga 288) Now at that time, people would say to the monks when they sneezed, “May you live, venerable sirs,” but the monks, being scrupulous, did not respond. The people complained, “How is it that these Sakyan ascetics do not reply when told, ‘May you live, venerable sirs’?” They reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks, householders are fond of auspicious sayings. I allow you, monks, when told by householders, ‘May you live, venerable sirs,’ to respond with, ‘May you live long.’” The monks asked the Blessed One, “Venerable sir, when did this practice of exchanging wishes for life and responding to them arise?” The Teacher replied, “Monks, the practice of wishing for life and responding to it arose in ancient times,” and then recounted a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Tassa pitā vohāraṃ katvā jīvikaṃ kappeti, so soḷasavassuddesikaṃ bodhisattaṃ maṇikabhaṇḍaṃ ukkhipāpetvā gāmanigamādīsu caranto bārāṇasiṃ patvā dovārikassa ghare bhattaṃ pacāpetvā bhuñjitvā nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ alabhanto “avelāya āgatā āgantukā kattha vasantī”ti pucchi. Atha naṃ manussā “bahinagare ekā sālā atthi, sā pana amanussapariggahitā. Sace icchatha, tattha vasathā”ti āhaṃsu. Bodhisatto “etha, tāta, gacchāma, mā yakkhassa bhāyittha, ahaṃ taṃ dametvā tumhākaṃ pādesu pātessāmī”ti [P 2.0016] pitaraṃ gahetvā tattha gato. Athassa pitā phalake nipajji, sayaṃ pitu pāde sambāhanto nisīdi. Tattha adhivattho yakkho dvādasa vassāni vessavaṇaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā taṃ sālaṃ labhanto “imaṃ sālaṃ paviṭṭhamanussesu yo khipite ‘jīvā’ti vadati, yo ca ‘jīvā’ti vutte ‘paṭijīvā’ti vadati, te jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino [M 2.0015] ṭhapetvā avasese khādeyyāsī”ti labhi. So piṭṭhivaṃsathūṇāya vasati. So “bodhisattassa pitaraṃ khipāpessāmī”ti attano ānubhāvena sukhumacuṇṇaṃ vissajjesi, cuṇṇo āgantvā tassa nāsapuṭe pāvisi. So phalake nipannakova khipi, bodhisatto na “jīvā”ti [V 2.0014] āha. Yakkho taṃ khādituṃ thūṇāya otarati. Bodhisatto taṃ otarantaṃ disvā “iminā me pitā khipāpito bhavissati, ayaṃ so khipite ‘jīvā’ti avadantaṃ khādakayakkho bhavissatī”ti pitaraṃ ārabbha paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. His father made a living by trade. When the Bodhisatta was about sixteen years old, his father had him carry a stock of jewels and, while traveling through villages and towns, reached Bārāṇasī. There, he had a meal prepared at the gatekeeper’s house. After eating, being unable to find a place to stay, he asked, “Where do travelers who arrive at an untimely hour stay?” The people told him, “There is a hall outside the city, but it is possessed by a non-human being. If you wish, you may stay there.” The Bodhisatta said, “Come, father, let us go. Do not fear the yakkha; I will subdue him and make him fall at your feet.” Taking his father, he went there. His father lay down on a plank, while he himself sat massaging his father’s feet. The yakkha who dwelt there had served Vessavaṇa for twelve years and had obtained that hall with the boon: “Among the humans who enter this hall, excepting those who say ‘Live!’ when someone sneezes, and those who, when told ‘Live!’, reply ‘May you also live!’, you may devour the rest.” He lived in a pillar supporting the main beam. Thinking, “I will make the Bodhisatta’s father sneeze,” he sent forth fine dust by his power. The dust went and entered his nostrils. As he was lying on the plank, he sneezed, but the Bodhisatta did not say, “Live!” The yakkha descended from the pillar to devour him. Seeing him descending, the Bodhisatta thought, “It must have been he who made my father sneeze. This must be the yakkha who devours one who does not say ‘Live!’ when someone sneezes.” Then, concerning his father, he spoke the first verse:

9.

9.

“Jīva vassasataṃ bhagga, aparāni ca vīsatiṃ;

Mā maṃ pisācā khādantu, jīva tvaṃ saradosata”nti.

“Live a hundred years, O Bhagga, and another twenty more; may the ghouls not devour me, may you live a hundred autumns.”

Tattha bhaggāti pitaraṃ nāmenālapati. Aparāni ca vīsatinti aparāni ca vīsati vassāni jīva. Mā maṃ pisācā khādantūti maṃ pisācā mā khādantu. Jīva tvaṃ saradosatanti tvaṃ pana vīsuttaraṃ vassasataṃ jīvāti. Saradosatañhi gaṇiyamānaṃ vassasatameva hoti, taṃ purimehi vīsāya saddhiṃ vīsuttaraṃ idha adhippetaṃ.

Therein, “Bhagga” is how he addresses his father by name. “And another twenty” means ‘live for another twenty years.’ “May the ghouls not devour me” means, “may the ghouls not devour me.” “May you live a hundred autumns” means, ‘may you live for one hundred and twenty years.’ For “a hundred autumns,” when counted, is just one hundred years, but here, that hundred combined with the previous twenty is intended to mean one hundred and twenty.

Yakkho bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā “imaṃ tāva māṇavaṃ ‘jīvā’ti vuttattā khādituṃ na sakkā, pitaraṃ panassa khādissāmī”ti pitu santikaṃ agamāsi. So taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā cintesi – “ayaṃ so ‘paṭijīvā’ti abhaṇantānaṃ khādakayakkho bhavissati, paṭijīvaṃ karissāmī”ti. So puttaṃ ārabbha dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The yakkha, hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, thought, “I cannot devour this young man, because he has said ‘Live!’, but I will devour his father.” So he approached the father. Seeing him coming, the father thought, “This must be the yakkha who devours those who do not say ‘May you also live!’ I will say it.” Then, concerning his son, he spoke the second verse:

10.

10.

“Tvampi vassasataṃ jīvaṃ, aparāni ca vīsatiṃ;

Visaṃ pisācā khādantu, jīva tvaṃ saradosata”nti.

“May you, too, live a hundred years, and another twenty more; may the ghouls eat poison, may you live a hundred autumns.”

Tattha [P 2.0017] visaṃ pisācā khādantūti pisācā halāhalavisaṃ khādantu.

Therein, “may the ghouls eat poison” means, “may the ghouls eat the halāhala poison.”

Yakkho tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ubhopi me na sakkā khāditu”nti paṭinivatti. Atha naṃ bodhisatto pucchi – “bho yakkha, kasmā tvaṃ imaṃ sālaṃ paviṭṭhamanusse khādasī”ti? “Dvādasa vassāni vessavaṇaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā laddhattā”ti. “Kiṃ pana sabbeva khādituṃ labhasī”ti? “Jīvapaṭijīvabhāṇino ṭhapetvā avasese khādāmī”ti. “Yakkha, tvaṃ pubbepi akusalaṃ katvā kakkhaḷo [M 2.0016] pharuso paravihiṃsako hutvā nibbatto, idānipi tādisaṃ kammaṃ katvā tamo tamaparāyaṇo bhavissati, tasmā ito paṭṭhāya pāṇātipātādīhi viramassū”ti taṃ yakkhaṃ dametvā nirayabhayena tajjetvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā yakkhaṃ pesanakārakaṃ viya akāsi.

Hearing his words, the yakkha turned back, thinking, “I cannot eat either of them.” Then the Bodhisatta asked him, “Ho, yakkha, why do you devour the people who enter this hall?” “Because I obtained it after serving Vessavaṇa for twelve years.” “But are you allowed to eat everyone?” “Excepting the speakers of ‘Live!’ and ‘May you also live!’, I eat the rest.” “Yakkha, in a past life you did unwholesome deeds and were reborn harsh, cruel, and harmful to others. Now, too, by doing such deeds, you will go from darkness to deeper darkness. Therefore, from this day forward, abstain from the destruction of life and other such things.” Having thus tamed the yakkha, threatening him with the fear of hell, he established him in the five precepts and made the yakkha like his attendant.

Punadivase [V 2.0015] sañcarantā manussā yakkhaṃ disvā bodhisattena cassa damitabhāvaṃ ñatvā rañño ārocesuṃ – “deva, eko māṇavo taṃ yakkhaṃ dametvā pesanakārakaṃ viya katvā ṭhito”ti. Rājā bodhisattaṃ pakkosāpetvā senāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi, pitu cassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi. So yakkhaṃ balipaṭiggāhakaṃ katvā bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggapuraṃ pūresi.

The next day, people traveling about saw the yakkha and, realizing he had been tamed by the Bodhisatta, reported to the king: “Your Majesty, a young man has tamed that yakkha and made him like his attendant.” The king summoned the Bodhisatta and appointed him to the position of commander-in-chief, and he bestowed great glory upon his father. The king made the yakkha a receiver of offerings, and he himself, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and was reborn in the city of the devas.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “jīvapaṭijīvaṃ nāma tasmiṃ kāle uppanna”nti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā yakkho aṅgulimālo ahosi, rājā ānando, pitā kassapo, putto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, “The practice of saying ‘Live!’ and responding with ‘Live!’ arose at that time,” and then connected the birth story: “At that time, the yakkha was Aṅgulimāla, the king was Ānanda, the father was Kassapa, and the son was I myself.”

Bhaggajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Bhagga Jātaka, the Fifth.

[156] 6. Alīnacittajātakavaṇṇanā

[156] 6. The Commentary on the Alīnacitta Jātaka.

Alīnacittaṃ nissāyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu ekādasanipāte saṃvarajātake (jā. 1.11.97 ādayo) āvibhavissati. So pana bhikkhu satthārā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, vīriyaṃ ossajī”ti vutte “saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti [P 2.0018] āha. Atha naṃ satthā “nanu tvaṃ, bhikkhu, pubbe vīriyaṃ avissajjetvā maṃsapesisadisassa daharakumārassa dvādasayojanike bārāṇasinagare rajjaṃ gahetvā adāsi, idāni kasmā evarūpe sāsane pabbajitvā vīriyaṃ ossajasī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Relying on a mind that is not indolent,” this the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who had abandoned effort. The story will be found in the eleventh section, in the Saṃvara Jātaka. When the Teacher asked him, “Is it true, monk, that you have given up effort?” he replied, “It is true, Blessed One.” Then the Teacher said to him, “Monk, did you not formerly, without abandoning effort, after taking the kingdom in the city of Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent, give it to a young prince resembling a lump of flesh? Why now, having gone forth in such a Dispensation, do you give up effort?” And so he brought forth the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasito avidūre vaḍḍhakīgāmo ahosi, tattha pañcasatā vaḍḍhakī vasanti. Te nāvāya [M 2.0017] uparisotaṃ gantvā araññe gehasambhāradārūni koṭṭetvā tattheva ekabhūmikadvibhūmikādibhede gehasambhāre sajjetvā thambhato paṭṭhāya sabbadārūsu saññaṃ katvā nadītīraṃ netvā nāvaṃ āropetvā anusotena nagaraṃ āgantvā ye yādisāni gehāni ākaṅkhanti, tesaṃ tādisāni katvā kahāpaṇe gahetvā puna tattheva gantvā gehasambhāre āharanti. Evaṃ tesaṃ jīvikaṃ kappentānaṃ ekasmiṃ kāle khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā dārūni koṭṭentānaṃ avidūre eko hatthī khadirakhāṇukaṃ akkami. Tassa so khāṇuko pādaṃ vijjhi, balavavedanā vattanti, pādo uddhumāyitvā pubbaṃ gaṇhi. So vedanāppatto [V 2.0016] tesaṃ dārukoṭṭanasaddaṃ sutvā “ime vaḍḍhakī nissāya mayhaṃ sotthi bhavissatī”ti maññamāno tīhi pādehi tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā avidūre nipajji, vaḍḍhakī taṃ uddhumātapādaṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā pāde khāṇukaṃ disvā tikhiṇavāsiyā khāṇukassa samantato odhiṃ datvā rajjuyā bandhitvā ākaḍḍhantā khāṇuṃ nīharitvā pubbaṃ mocetvā uṇhodakena dhovitvā tadanurūpehi bhesajjehi makkhetvā nacirasseva vaṇaṃ phāsukaṃ kariṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, not far from Bārāṇasī there was a village of carpenters where five hundred carpenters lived. They would go upstream by boat, enter the forest to cut timber for house-building, prepare the house components there—classifying them as for single-story, two-story, and so on—mark all the logs starting from the posts, bring them to the riverbank, load them onto the boat, return downstream to the city, and build houses as desired by their clients, taking payment in coins. Then they would go back to the same place to fetch more building materials. While they were making a living in this way, on one occasion, as they were setting up camp and cutting logs, an elephant nearby stepped on an acacia stump. The stump pierced its foot, causing severe pain; the foot swelled up and formed pus. The elephant, afflicted by pain, heard the sound of the carpenters cutting wood and, thinking, ‘My well-being will come from these carpenters,’ approached them on three legs and lay down nearby. The carpenters saw its swollen foot and went closer. Seeing the stump in its foot, they made an incision around the stump with a sharp adze, tied it with a rope, and pulled the stump out. They then drained the pus, washed the wound with warm water, and applied suitable medicines. Before long, they had healed the wound.

Hatthī arogo hutvā cintesi – “mayā ime vaḍḍhakī nissāya jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ, idāni tesaṃ mayā upakāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya vaḍḍhakīhi saddhiṃ [P 2.0019] rukkhe nīharati, tacchentānaṃ parivattetvā deti, vāsiādīni upasaṃharati, soṇḍāya veṭhetvā kāḷasuttakoṭiyaṃ gaṇhāti. Vaḍḍhakīpissa bhojanavelāya ekekaṃ piṇḍaṃ dentā pañca piṇḍasatāni denti. Tassa pana hatthissa putto sabbaseto hatthājānīyapotako atthi, tenassa etadahosi – “ahaṃ etarahi mahallako. Idāni mayā imesaṃ vaḍḍhakīnaṃ kammakaraṇattāya puttaṃ datvā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So vaḍḍhakīnaṃ anācikkhitvāva araññaṃ pavisitvā puttaṃ ānetvā “ayaṃ hatthipotako mama putto, tumhehi mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ dinnaṃ, ahaṃ vo vejjavetanatthāya imaṃ dammi, ayaṃ tumhākaṃ ito paṭṭhāya kammāni karissatī”ti vatvā “ito paṭṭhāya, puttaka, yaṃ mayā kattabbaṃ kammaṃ, taṃ tvaṃ karohī”ti puttaṃ ovaditvā vaḍḍhakīnaṃ datvā sayaṃ araññaṃ pāvisi.

The elephant, having become well, thought: “I have received my life because of these carpenters; now it is right for me to render them a service.” From then on, he would haul logs with the carpenters, turn them over for those who were shaping the wood, and bring them tools such as adzes. He would wrap his trunk around the end of the marking-line and hold it. The carpenters, for their part, at mealtime, would give him one ball of food each, amounting to five hundred balls of food. Now, this elephant had a son, an all-white young elephant of noble breed. It occurred to him: “I am now old. It is right for me to give my son to these carpenters to do their work and then depart.” Without informing the carpenters, he entered the forest, brought his son, and said: “This young elephant is my son. You gave me my life; I give him to you as payment for my treatment. From now on, he will do your work.” Then, advising his son, “From now on, my child, whatever work was to be done by me, you must do,” he handed him over to the carpenters and himself entered the forest.

Tato paṭṭhāya hatthipotako vaḍḍhakīnaṃ vacanakaro ovādakkhamo hutvā sabbakiccāni karoti. Tepi taṃ pañcahi piṇḍasatehi posenti, so [M 2.0018] kammaṃ katvā nadiṃ otaritvā nhatvā kīḷitvā āgacchati, vaḍḍhakīdārakāpi taṃ soṇḍādīsu gahetvā udakepi thalepi tena saddhiṃ kīḷanti. Ājānīyā pana hatthinopi assāpi purisāpi udake uccāraṃ vā passāvaṃ vā na karonti, tasmā sopi udake uccārapassāvaṃ akatvā bahinadītīreyeva karoti. Athekasmiṃ divase uparinadiyā devo vassi, atha sukkhaṃ hatthilaṇḍaṃ udakena nadiṃ otaritvā gacchantaṃ bārāṇasīnagaratitthe ekasmiṃ gumbe laggetvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha rañño hatthigopakā “hatthī nhāpessāmā”ti pañca hatthisatāni nayiṃsu. Ājānīyalaṇḍassa gandhaṃ ghāyitvā ekopi hatthī nadiṃ otarituṃ na ussahi. Sabbepi naṅguṭṭhaṃ ukkhipitvā palāyituṃ ārabhiṃsu, hatthigopakā hatthācariyānaṃ ārocesuṃ. Te “udake paripanthena bhavitabba”nti udakaṃ sodhāpetvā tasmiṃ [P 2.0020] gumbe taṃ ājānīyalaṇḍaṃ disvā “idamettha kāraṇa”nti ñatvā cāṭiṃ āharāpetvā udakassa pūretvā taṃ tattha madditvā hatthīnaṃ sarīre siñcāpesuṃ, sarīrāni sugandhāni ahesuṃ. Tasmiṃ kāle te nadiṃ otaritvā nhāyiṃsu.

From that time onward, the young elephant, obedient to the carpenters' words and receptive to their advice, performed all his duties. They, in turn, provided for him with five hundred balls of food. Having done his work, he would descend to the river, bathe, play, and return. The carpenters' children would also take him by the trunk and so forth, and play with him, both in the water and on land. Now, noble beings—elephants, horses, and men—do not defecate or urinate in the water. Therefore, he too, not defecating or urinating in the water, would do so only on the riverbank. Then one day, it rained upstream. Dry elephant dung was carried down the river by the water and, lodging in a bush at the bathing ford of the city of Bārāṇasī, it remained there. The king’s elephant keepers, intending to bathe the elephants, led five hundred elephants to the river. But upon smelling the scent of the dung of the noble-bred elephant, not a single elephant dared to enter the water. They all lifted their tails and began to flee. The elephant keepers reported this to the elephant trainers. The trainers said, "There must be an obstacle in the water." After having the water cleared, they saw the noble-bred elephant's dung on that bush and, realizing, "This is the cause," they had a pot brought, filled it with water, crumbled the dung in it, and had the mixture sprinkled over the elephants' bodies. Their bodies became fragrant. At that moment, they descended into the river and bathed.

Hatthācariyā [V 2.0017] rañño taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “taṃ hatthājānīyaṃ pariyesitvā ānetuṃ vaṭṭati, devā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā nāvāsaṅghāṭehi nadiṃ pakkhanditvā uddhaṃgāmīhi nāvāsaṅghāṭehi vaḍḍhakīnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sampāpuṇi. Hatthipotako nadiyaṃ kīḷanto bherisaddaṃ sutvā gantvā vaḍḍhakīnaṃ santike aṭṭhāsi. Vaḍḍhakī rañño paccuggamanaṃ katvā “deva, sace dārūhi attho, kiṃ kāraṇā āgatattha, kiṃ pesetvā āharāpetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti āhaṃsu. “Nāhaṃ, bhaṇe, dārūnaṃ atthāya āgato, imassa pana hatthissa atthāya āgatomhī”ti. “Gāhāpetvā gacchatha, devā”ti. Hatthipotako gantuṃ na icchi. “Kiṃ kārāpeti, bhaṇe, hatthī”ti? “Vaḍḍhakīnaṃ posāvanikaṃ āharāpeti, devā”ti. “Sādhu, bhaṇe”ti rājā hatthissa catunnaṃ pādānaṃ soṇḍāya naṅguṭṭhassa ca santike satasahassasatasahassakahāpaṇe ṭhapāpesi. Hatthī ettakenāpi agantvā sabbavaḍḍhakīnaṃ dussayugesu vaḍḍhakībhariyānaṃ nivāsanasāṭakesu dinnesu saddhiṃkīḷitānaṃ dārakānañca dārakaparihāre kate nivattitvā vaḍḍhakī ca itthiyo ca dārake ca oloketvā raññā saddhiṃ agamāsi.

The elephant trainers informed the king of that matter and said, 'Your Majesty, it is fitting to search for that noble elephant and bring him back.' The king, embarking on rafts, entered the river and, traveling upstream by means of the rafts, reached the dwelling place of the carpenters. The young elephant, while playing in the river, heard the sound of drums and went to stand near the carpenters. The carpenters went out to meet the king and said, 'Your Majesty, if you have need of timber, for what reason have you come? Is it not fitting to send a message to have it brought?' The king replied, 'I have not come for timber, sirs, but I have come for the sake of this elephant.' 'Take him and go, Your Majesty,' they said. But the young elephant did not wish to go. 'What does the elephant want, sirs?' the king asked. 'He wants the rearing-fee to be given to the carpenters, Your Majesty,' they replied. 'Very well, sirs,' the king said, and he had one hundred thousand kahapanas placed near each of the elephant’s four feet, his trunk, and his tail. Even with this much, the elephant would not go. Only when pairs of garments had been given to all the carpenters, wearing-cloths to the carpenters’ wives, and gifts were made to the children with whom he had played, did he look back at the carpenters, the women, and the children, and then depart together with the king.

Rājā [M 2.0019] taṃ ādāya nagaraṃ gantvā nagarañca hatthisālañca alaṅkārāpetvā hatthiṃ nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ kāretvā hatthisālaṃ pavesetvā sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā abhisekaṃ datvā opavayhaṃ katvā attano sahāyaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā upaḍḍharajjaṃ hatthissa [P 2.0021] datvā attanā samānaparihāraṃ akāsi. Hatthissa āgatakālato paṭṭhāya rañño sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ hatthagatameva ahosi. Evaṃ kāle gacchante bodhisatto tassa rañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassā gabbhaparipākakāle rājā kālamakāsi. Hatthī pana sace rañño kālakatabhāvaṃ jāneyya, tatthevassa hadayaṃ phaleyya, tasmā hatthiṃ rañño kālakatabhāvaṃ ajānāpetvāva upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Rañño pana kālakatabhāvaṃ sutvā “tucchaṃ kira rajja”nti anantarasāmantakosalarājā mahatiyā senāya āgantvā nagaraṃ parivāresi. Nagaravāsino dvārāni pidahitvā kosalarañño sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu – “amhākaṃ rañño aggamahesī paripuṇṇagabbhā ‘ito kira sattame divase puttaṃ vijāyissatī’ti aṅgavijjāpāṭhakā āhaṃsu. Sace sā puttaṃ vijāyissati, mayaṃ sattame divase yuddhaṃ dassāma, na rajjaṃ, ettakaṃ kālaṃ āgamethā”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

The king, taking him, went to the city. He had the city and the elephant stable decorated, then had the elephant circumambulate the city and led him into the stable. Adorned with all ornaments, he was consecrated, made the royal mount, and established in the position of his friend. He granted the elephant half the kingdom and accorded him the same honors as himself. From the time the elephant arrived, the king's rule over the entire Jambudīpa was firmly in his grasp. As time passed, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the king's chief queen. When her pregnancy reached full term, the king passed away. Now, if the elephant were to learn of the king's death, its heart would burst on the spot. Therefore, they continued to attend to the elephant without letting it know of the king's death. Upon hearing of the king's death, the neighboring king of Kosala, thinking, 'The kingdom is indeed vacant,' arrived with a great army and surrounded the city. The inhabitants of the city shut the gates and sent a message to the king of Kosala: 'Our king’s chief queen is with child at full term; the interpreters of bodily signs have stated that she will give birth to a son on the seventh day from now. If she gives birth to a son, we shall give battle on the seventh day, not the kingdom; please wait for this length of time.' The king agreed, saying, 'Very well.'

Devī sattame divase puttaṃ vijāyi. Tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase pana mahājanassa alīnacittaṃ paggaṇhanto jātoti “alīnacittakumāro”tvevassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Jātadivasatoyeva panassa paṭṭhāya nāgarā kosalaraññā saddhiṃ yujjhiṃsu. Ninnāyakattā saṅgāmassa mahantampi balaṃ yujjhamānaṃ thokaṃ thokaṃ osakkati. Amaccā deviyā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “mayaṃ [V 2.0018] evaṃ osakkamāne bale parājayabhāvassa bhāyāma, amhākaṃ pana rañño kālakatabhāvaṃ, puttassa jātabhāvaṃ, kosalarañño āgantvā yujjhānabhāvañca rañño sahāyako maṅgalahatthī na jānāti, jānāpema na”nti pucchiṃsu. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā puttaṃ alaṅkaritvā dukūlacumbaṭake nipajjāpetvā pāsādā oruyha amaccagaṇaparivutā hatthisālaṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ hatthissa pādamūle [P 2.0022] nipajjāpetvā “sāmi, sahāyo te kālakato, mayaṃ tuyhaṃ hadayaphālanabhayena nārocayimha, ayaṃ te sahāyassa putto, kosalarājā āgantvā nagaraṃ [M 2.0020] parivāretvā tava puttena saddhiṃ yujjhati, balaṃ osakkati, tava puttaṃ tvaññeva vā mārehi, rajjaṃ vāssa gaṇhitvā dehī”ti āha.

On the seventh day, the queen gave birth to a son. On the day of his naming ceremony, because he was born uplifting the unslothful spirit of the great populace, they gave him the name 'Prince Alīnacitta.' From the very day of his birth, the citizens began to fight with the King of Kosala. Due to the lack of a leader for the battle, even the great army, while fighting, gradually retreated. The ministers informed the queen of this matter, saying, 'As our forces thus retreat, we fear defeat. The king’s companion, the state elephant, does not know that our king has died, that a son has been born, and that the King of Kosala has come and is fighting. Shall we inform him?' She agreed, saying, 'Very well.' Having adorned her son and laid him on a cushion of fine cloth, she descended from the palace, and surrounded by a host of ministers, went to the elephant stable. She had the Bodhisatta laid at the elephant's feet and said, 'Lord, your companion has died. We did not inform you for fear that your heart would break. This is your companion’s son. The King of Kosala has come, besieged the city, and is fighting against your son. The army is retreating. Either kill your son yourself, or win the kingdom and give it to him.'

Tasmiṃ kāle hatthī bodhisattaṃ soṇḍāya parāmasitvā ukkhipitvā kumbhe ṭhapetvā roditvā bodhisattaṃ otāretvā deviyā hatthe nipajjāpetvā “kosalarājaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti hatthisālato nikkhami. Athassa amaccā vammaṃ paṭimuñcitvā alaṅkaritvā nagaradvāraṃ avāpuritvā taṃ parivāretvā nikkhamiṃsu. Hatthī nagarā nikkhamitvā koñcanādaṃ katvā mahājanaṃ santāsetvā palāpetvā balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā kosalarājānaṃ cūḷāya gahetvā ānetvā bodhisattassa pādamūle nipajjāpetvā māraṇatthāyassa uṭṭhite vāretvā “ito paṭṭhāya appamatto hohi, ‘kumāro daharo’ti saññaṃ mā karī”ti ovaditvā uyyojesi. Tato paṭṭhāya sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ bodhisattassa hatthagatameva jātaṃ, añño paṭisattu nāma uṭṭhahituṃ samattho nāhosi. Bodhisatto sattavassikakāle abhisekaṃ katvā alīnacittarājā nāma hutvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā jīvitapariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūresi.

At that moment, the elephant caressed the Bodhisatta with its trunk, lifted him up, placed him on its forehead, and wept. Then it lowered the Bodhisatta and had him laid in the queen’s hands. Declaring, 'I shall capture the King of Kosala!' it left the elephant stable. Then the ministers, having put on their armor and adorned the elephant, opened the city gates and went forth, surrounding him. The elephant, having emerged from the city, trumpeted like a crane, terrifying the great crowd and putting them to flight. It broke through the army's ranks, seized the King of Kosala by his top-knot, brought him back, and laid him at the Bodhisatta’s feet.
