When people rose up to kill him, the elephant restrained them, advising the king, 'Henceforth be heedful; do not think, "The prince is young!"' Then it released him. From that day on, sovereignty over all Jambudīpa came into the Bodhisatta’s possession, and no other rival was able to arise. At the age of seven years, the Bodhisatta was consecrated and became the king named Alīnacitta. He ruled according to the Dhamma and, at the end of his life, filled the city of the gods.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

Having related this story of the past, the Teacher, after becoming fully awakened, spoke these two verses:

11.

11.

“Alīnacittaṃ nissāya, pahaṭṭhā mahatī camū;

Kosalaṃ senāsantuṭṭhaṃ, jīvaggāhaṃ agāhayi.

Relying on Alīnacitta, the great and joyful army caused the Kosala king, who was discontent with his kingdom, to be captured alive.

12.

12.

“Evaṃ nissayasampanno, bhikkhu āraddhavīriyo;

Bhāvayaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, yogakkhemassa pattiyā;

Pāpuṇe anupubbena, sabbasaṃyojanakkhaya”nti.

Thus, a bhikkhu endowed with support, with effort aroused, developing the wholesome Dhamma for the attainment of security from the yokes, may gradually reach the destruction of all fetters.

Tattha [P 2.0023] alīnacittaṃ nissāyāti alīnacittaṃ rājakumāraṃ nissāya. Pahaṭṭhā mahatī camūti “paveṇīrajjaṃ no diṭṭha”nti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā mahatī senā. Kosalaṃ senāsantuṭṭhanti kosalarājānaṃ [V 2.0019] sena rajjena asantuṭṭhaṃ pararajjalobhena āgataṃ. Jīvaggāhaṃ agāhayīti amāretvāva sā camū taṃ rājānaṃ hatthinā jīvaggāhaṃ gaṇhāpesi. Evaṃ nissayasampannoti yathā sā camū, evaṃ aññopi kulaputto nissayasampanno kalyāṇamittaṃ [M 2.0021] buddhaṃ vā buddhasāvakaṃ vā nissayaṃ labhitvā. Bhikkhūti parisuddhādhivacanametaṃ. Āraddhavīriyoti paggahitavīriyo catudosāpagatena vīriyena samannāgato. Bhāvayaṃ kusalaṃ dhammanti kusalaṃ niravajjaṃ sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvento. Yogakkhemassa pattiyāti catūhi yogehi khemassa nibbānassa pāpuṇanatthāya taṃ dhammaṃ bhāvento. Pāpuṇe anupubbena, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayanti evaṃ vipassanato paṭṭhāya imaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvento so kalyāṇamittupanissayasampanno bhikkhu anupubbena vipassanāñāṇāni ca heṭṭhimamaggaphalāni ca pāpuṇanto pariyosāne dasannampi saṃyojanānaṃ khayante uppannattā sabbasaṃyojanakkhayasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Yasmā vā nibbānaṃ āgamma sabbasaṃyojanāni khīyanti, tasmā tampi sabbasaṃyojanakkhayameva, evaṃ anupubbena nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ sabbasaṃyojanakkhayaṃ pāpuṇātīti attho.

There, 'relying on Alīnacitta' means relying on Prince Alīnacitta. 'A great and joyful army' means the great army was happy and pleased, thinking, 'Our hereditary kingdom has been secured!' 'The Kosala king, discontent with his kingdom' means the King of Kosala who was discontented with his own kingdom and came out of greed for another's kingdom. 'Caused to be captured alive' means that army, without killing him, had that king captured alive by the elephant. 'Thus endowed with support' means just as that army was, so too another person of good family, endowed with support, having gained the support of a good friend, whether the Buddha or a disciple of the Buddha. 'Bhikkhu' is a designation for one of pure virtue. 'With effort aroused' means one who has exerted effort, endowed with energy free from the four faults. 'Developing the wholesome Dhamma' means developing the wholesome, blameless Dhamma known as the thirty-seven factors of awakening. 'For the attainment of security from the yokes' means developing that Dhamma for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, which is security from the four yokes. 'May gradually reach the destruction of all fetters' means thus, beginning with insight, that bhikkhu, endowed with the support of a good friend, developing this wholesome Dhamma, gradually attaining the insight knowledges and the lower paths and fruits, in the end attains Arahantship, which is called 'the destruction of all fetters' because it arises upon the destruction of all ten fetters. Or, since all fetters are destroyed by reaching Nibbāna, Nibbāna itself is 'the destruction of all fetters.' Thus, the meaning is that one gradually attains the destruction of all fetters, which is Nibbāna.

Iti bhagavā amatamahānibbānena dhammadesanāya kūṭaṃ gahetvā uttaripi saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā mātā mahāmāyā, pitā suddhodanamahārājā ahosi, rajjaṃ gahetvā dinnahatthī ayaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu, hatthissa pitā sāriputto, sāmantakosalarājā moggallāno, alīnacittakumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Blessed One brought the Dhamma discourse to its climax with the deathless, great Nibbāna, explained the Truths, and connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the bhikkhu who had given up his effort was established in Arahantship. 'At that time, the mother was Mahāmāyā, the father was King Suddhodana. The elephant who won the kingdom and gave it was this bhikkhu who had given up his effort. The elephant's father was Sāriputta. The neighboring King of Kosala was Moggallāna. And I myself was Prince Alīnacitta.'

Alīnacittajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Alīnacitta Jātaka, the sixth.

[157] 7. Guṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[157] 7. The Commentary on the Guṇa Jātaka.

Yena kāmaṃ paṇāmetīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ānandattherassa sāṭakasahassalābhaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Therassa kosalarañño antepure dhammavācanavatthu heṭṭhā mahāsārajātake (jā. 1.1.92) āgatameva. Iti there rañño antepure dhammaṃ vācente rañño [P 2.0024] sahassagghanikānaṃ sāṭakānaṃ sahassaṃ āhariyittha. Rājā tato pañca sāṭakasatāni pañcannaṃ devīsatānaṃ adāsi. Tā sabbāpi te sāṭake ṭhapetvā punadivase ānandattherassa datvā sayaṃ purāṇasāṭakeyeva pārupitvā rañño pātarāsaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher spoke this Guna Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Yena kāmaṃ paṇāmeti', concerning the receiving of a thousand robes by the Venerable Ānanda. The account of the Venerable teaching the Dhamma in the inner palace of the King of Kosala has already appeared earlier in the Mahāsāra Jātaka. Thus, as the Venerable was teaching the Dhamma in the king’s inner palace, a thousand garments, each worth a thousand pieces, were brought to the king. From these, the king gave five hundred garments to his five hundred queens. All of them set those garments aside and, having given them to the Venerable Ānanda the next day, they themselves wore only their old garments and went to the king's breakfast chamber.

Rājā [V 2.0020][M 2.0022] “mayā tumhākaṃ sahassagghanikā sāṭakā dāpitā, kasmā tumhe te apārupitvāva āgatā”ti pucchi. “Deva, amhehi te ānandattherassa dinnā”ti. “Ānandattherena sabbe gahitā”ti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Sammāsambuddhena ticīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ, ānandatthero dussavaṇijjaṃ maññe karissati, atibahū tena sāṭakā gahitā”ti therassa kujjhitvā bhuttapātarāso vihāraṃ gantvā therassa pariveṇaṃ pavisitvā theraṃ vanditvā nisinno pucchi – “api, bhante, amhākaṃ ghare itthiyo tumhākaṃ santike dhammaṃ uggaṇhanti vā suṇanti vā”ti? “Āma, mahārāja, gahetabbayuttakaṃ gaṇhanti, sotabbayuttakaṃ suṇantī”ti. “Kiṃ tā suṇantiyeva, udāhu tumhākaṃ nivāsanaṃ vā pārupanaṃ vā dadantī”ti? “Tā ajja, mahārāja, sahassagghanikāni pañca sāṭakasatāni adaṃsū”ti. “Tumhehi gahitāni tāni, bhante”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Nanu, bhante, satthārā ticīvarameva anuññāta”nti? “Āma, mahārāja, bhagavatā ekassa bhikkhuno ticīvarameva paribhogasīsena anuññātaṃ, paṭiggahaṇaṃ pana avāritaṃ, tasmā mayāpi aññesaṃ jiṇṇacīvarikānaṃ dātuṃ te sāṭakā paṭiggahitā”ti. “Te pana bhikkhū tumhākaṃ santikā sāṭake labhitvā porāṇacīvarāni kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Porāṇasaṅghāṭiṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karissantī”ti? “Porāṇauttarāsaṅgaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Antaravāsakaṃ karissantī”ti. “Porāṇaantaravāsakaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Paccattharaṇaṃ karissantī”ti. “Porāṇapaccattharaṇaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Bhummattharaṇaṃ karissantī”ti. “Porāṇabhummattharaṇaṃ [P 2.0025] kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Pādapuñchanaṃ karissantī”ti. “Porāṇapādapuñchanaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Mahārāja, saddhādeyyaṃ nāma vinipātetuṃ na labbhati, tasmā porāṇapādapuñchanaṃ vāsiyā koṭṭetvā mattikāya makkhetvā senāsanesu mattikālepanaṃ karissantī”ti. “Bhante, tumhākaṃ dinnaṃ yāva pādapuñchanāpi nassituṃ na labbhatī”ti? “Āma, mahārāja, amhākaṃ dinnaṃ nassituṃ na labbhati, paribhogameva hotī”ti.

The king asked, "I had garments worth a thousand each given to you; why have you come without wearing those new ones?" "Your Majesty, we have given them to the Venerable Ānanda." "Did the Venerable Ānanda take them all?" "Yes, Your Majesty." The king, thinking, "The Fully Enlightened One has allowed only three robes; I suppose the Venerable Ānanda will engage in the cloth trade since he has taken so many garments," became angry with the Elder. After breakfast, he went to the monastery, entered the Elder’s dwelling, paid homage to the Elder, and while sitting, asked: "Venerable sir, do the women in our palace learn or listen to the Dhamma in your presence?" "Yes, Great King, they learn what is worthy to be learned and listen to what is worthy to be heard." "Do they only listen, or do they also give you inner or outer garments?" "Today, Great King, they gave me five hundred garments worth a thousand each." "Did you accept them, Venerable sir?" "Yes, Great King." "But, Venerable sir, did the Teacher not allow only three robes?" "Yes, Great King, the Blessed One allowed only three robes for a single monk for the purpose of personal use, but the acceptance of gifts is not prohibited. Therefore, I accepted them to give to other monks whose robes are worn out." "But when those monks receive the garments from you, what will they do with their old robes?" "They will make their old outer robes into upper robes." "What will they do with the old upper robes?" "They will make them into inner robes." "What will they do with the old inner robes?" "They will make them into bedspreads." "What will they do with the old bedspreads?" "They will make them into floor rugs." "What will they do with the old floor rugs?" "They will make them into foot-wipers." "What will they do with the old foot-wipers?" "Great King, that which is given in faith should not be wasted. Therefore, they will shred the old foot-wipers with an adze, mix them with clay, and use the mixture to plaster the lodgings." "Venerable sir, then what is given to you does not go to waste even down to the foot-wiper?" "Yes, Great King, what is given to us does not go to waste; it is indeed used to its full capacity."

Rājā tuṭṭho somanassappatto hutvā itarānipi gehe ṭhapitāni pañca sāṭakasatāni āharāpetvā therassa datvā anumodanaṃ sutvā theraṃ vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Thero paṭhamaladdhāni pañca sāṭakasatāni jiṇṇacīvarikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ adāsi. Therassa pana pañcamattāni saddhivihārikasatāni[M 2.0023], tesu eko daharabhikkhu therassa bahūpakāro pariveṇaṃ sammajjati, pānīyaparibhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhapeti, dantakaṭṭhaṃ mukhodakaṃ nhānodakaṃ deti, vaccakuṭijantāgharasenāsanāni paṭijaggati, hatthaparikammapādaparikammapiṭṭhiparikammādīni karoti. Thero pacchā laddhāni pañca sāṭakasatāni “ayaṃ me bahūpakāro”ti yuttavasena sabbāni tasseva adāsi. Sopi sabbe te sāṭake bhājetvā attano samānupajjhāyānaṃ adāsi.

The king, being pleased and full of joy, had the other five hundred garments that were kept in the palace brought and gave them to the Elder. After listening to the words of appreciation, he paid homage to the Elder, performed the circumambulation, and departed. The Elder gave the first five hundred garments he had received to the monks with worn-out robes. Now, the Elder had about five hundred resident pupils. Among them, one young monk was very helpful to the Elder; he swept the dwelling, prepared drinking and washing water, provided tooth-wood, water for the face, and bathing water, looked after the toilet, the hot room, and the lodgings, and performed services such as massaging the hands, feet, and back. The Elder, considering, 'This one is very helpful to me,' gave all five hundred garments received later to that monk alone, as was fitting. That monk then distributed all those garments and gave them to his fellow disciples who shared the same preceptor.

Evaṃ [V 2.0021] sabbepi te laddhasāṭakā bhikkhū sāṭake chinditvā rajitvā kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇāni kāsāyāni nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā evamāhaṃsu – “bhante, sotāpannassa ariyasāvakassa mukholokanadānaṃ nāma atthī”ti. “Na, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakānaṃ mukholokanadānaṃ nāma atthī”ti. “Bhante, amhākaṃ upajjhāyena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikattherena sahassagghanikānaṃ sāṭakānaṃ pañca satāni ekasseva daharabhikkhuno dinnāni, so pana attanā laddhe bhājetvā amhākaṃ adāsī”ti. “Na, bhikkhave, ānando mukholokanabhikkhaṃ deti[P 2.0026], so panassa bhikkhu bahūpakāro, tasmā attano upakārassa upakāravasena guṇavasena yuttavasena ‘upakārassa nāma paccupakāro kātuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti kataññukatavedibhāvena adāsi. Porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi hi attano upakārānaññeva paccupakāraṃ kariṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Thus, all those monks who received the garments cut and dyed them, and having put on and wrapped themselves in the saffron-colored robes which were the color of the kaṇikāra flower, they approached the Teacher. After paying homage and sitting to one side, they said: "Venerable sir, is there such a thing as a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer giving a gift out of partiality?" "No, monks, there is no such thing as noble disciples giving out of partiality." "Venerable sir, our preceptor, the Elder who is the Treasurer of the Dhamma, gave five hundred garments worth a thousand each to a single young monk. That monk then divided what he received and gave them to us." "Monks, Ānanda did not give out of partiality. That monk was very helpful to him. Therefore, he gave them with a heart of gratitude and appreciation, recognizing the help received and thinking, 'It is proper to repay a kindness.' For even the wise of old repaid the kindness of those who helped them." Having said this, and being requested by the monks, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sīho hutvā pabbataguhāyaṃ vasati. So ekadivasaṃ guhāya nikkhamitvā pabbatapādaṃ olokesi, taṃ pana pabbatapādaṃ parikkhipitvā mahāsaro ahosi. Tassa ekasmiṃ unnataṭṭhāne uparithaddhakaddamapiṭṭhe mudūni haritatiṇāni jāyiṃsu. Sasakā ceva hariṇādayo ca sallahukamigā kaddamamatthake vicarantā tāni khādanti. Taṃ divasampi eko migo tāni khādanto vicarati. Sīho “taṃ migaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti pabbatamatthakā uppatitvā sīhavegena pakkhandi, migo maraṇabhayatajjito viravanto palāyi. Sīho vegaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto kalalapiṭṭhe nipatitvā [M 2.0024] osīditvā uggantuṃ asakkonto cattāro pādā thambhā viya osīditvā sattāhaṃ nirāhāro aṭṭhāsi.

Once upon a time, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a lion living in a mountain cave. One day, he came out of the cave and surveyed the foot of the mountain, which was encircled by a great lake. At one elevated spot, on the surface of the mud which was hard on top, soft green grass grew. Hares, deer, and other light-footed animals wandered about on the surface of the mud, eating them. On that very day, a certain deer was also wandering about eating them. The lion, thinking, 'I will seize that deer,' sprang from the mountaintop and charged with the speed of a lion. The deer, terrified by the fear of death, cried out and fled. The lion, unable to restrain his momentum, fell onto the surface of the mud and sank; being unable to rise, his four legs sank in like pillars, and he remained without food for seven days.

Atha naṃ eko siṅgālo gocarappasuto taṃ disvā bhayena palāyi. Sīho taṃ pakkositvā “bho siṅgāla, mā palāyi, ahaṃ kalale laggo, jīvitaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Siṅgālo tassa santikaṃ gantvā “ahaṃ taṃ uddhareyyaṃ, uddhaṭo pana maṃ khādeyyāsīti bhāyāmī”ti āha. “Mā bhāyi, nāhaṃ taṃ khādissāmi, mahantaṃ pana te guṇaṃ karissāmi, ekenupāyena maṃ uddharāhī”ti. Siṅgālo tassa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā catunnaṃ pādānaṃ samantā kalale apanetvā catunnampi pādānaṃ catasso mātikā khaṇitvā [P 2.0027] udakābhimukhaṃ akāsi, udakaṃ pavisitvā kalalaṃ muduṃ akāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe siṅgālo sīhassa udarantaraṃ attano sīsaṃ pavesetvā “vāyāmaṃ karohi, sāmī”ti uccāsaddaṃ karonto sīsena udaraṃ pahari. Sīho vegaṃ janetvā kalalā uggantvā pakkhanditvā thale aṭṭhāsi. So muhuttaṃ vissamitvā saraṃ oruyha kaddamaṃ dhovitvā nhāyitvā darathaṃ paṭippassambhetvā ekaṃ mahiṃsaṃ vadhitvā dāṭhāhi ovijjhitvā maṃsaṃ [V 2.0022] ubbattetvā “khāda, sammā”ti siṅgālassa purato ṭhapetvā tena khādite pacchā attanā khādi. Puna siṅgālo ekaṃ maṃsapesiṃ ḍaṃsitvā gaṇhi. “Idaṃ kimatthāya, sammā”ti ca vutte “tumhākaṃ dāsī atthi, tassā bhāgo bhavissatī”ti āha. Sīho “gaṇhāhī”ti vatvā sayampi sīhiyā atthāya maṃsaṃ gaṇhitvā “ehi, samma, amhākaṃ pabbatamuddhani ṭhatvā sakhiyā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmā”ti vatvā tattha gantvā maṃsaṃ khādāpetvā siṅgālañca siṅgāliñca assāsetvā “ito paṭṭhāya idāni ahaṃ tumhe paṭijaggissāmī”ti attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ netvā guhāya dvāre aññissā guhāya vasāpesi. Te tato paṭṭhāya gocarāya gacchantā sīhiñca siṅgāliñca ṭhapetvā siṅgālena saddhiṃ gantvā nānāmige vadhitvā ubhopi tattheva maṃsaṃ khāditvā itarāsampi dvinnaṃ āharitvā denti.

Then a certain jackal, intent on foraging, seeing him, fled in fear. The lion called out to him, saying, 'Friend jackal, do not flee! I am stuck in the mud; grant me my life!' The jackal approached him and said, 'I could pull you out, but I fear that once freed, you might eat me.' 'Do not fear; I will not eat you. Rather, I shall do you a great service. Pull me out by some means.' The jackal, having accepted his promise, removed the mud from around his four paws and dug four channels for all four paws towards the water. The water flowed in and softened the mud. At that moment, the jackal thrust his head under the lion’s belly and, crying out loudly, 'Exert yourself, my lord!' struck the belly with his head. The lion, exerting himself, burst free from the mud, sprang forth, and stood on dry land. After resting a moment, he went down to the lake, washed off the mud, bathed, relieved his weariness, killed a buffalo, pierced it with his fangs, tore out the meat, and placing it before the jackal, said, 'Eat, friend.' After the jackal had eaten, the lion ate it himself. Again, the jackal bit off a piece of meat and took it. When asked, 'What is this for, friend?' he replied, 'You have a female servant; this will be her share.' The lion said, 'Take it.' He then took meat for his own lioness. 'Come, friend,' he said, 'let us go to our mountain peak and then to your mate’s dwelling.' Going there, he had them eat the meat, reassured the jackal and his mate, and said, 'From now on, I shall look after you.' He led them to his own dwelling and settled them in another cave near his own cave's entrance. From then on, when they went foraging, they left the lioness and the she-jackal behind. The lion and the jackal went together, killed various animals, ate the meat on the spot, and brought portions back for the other two as well.

Evaṃ kāle gacchante sīhī dve putte vijāyi, siṅgālīpi dve putte vijāyi. Te sabbepi samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ sīhiyā etadahosi – “ayaṃ sīho siṅgālañca siṅgāliñca siṅgālapotake ca ativiya piyāyati, nūnamassa siṅgāliyā saddhiṃ santhavo atthi, tasmā evaṃ sinehaṃ karoti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ pīḷetvā tajjetvā ito palāpeyya”nti[M 2.0025]. Sā sīhassa siṅgālaṃ gahetvā gocarāya gatakāle siṅgāliṃ pīḷesi tajjesi “kiṃkāraṇā imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasati[P 2.0028], na palāyasī”ti? Puttāpissā siṅgāliputte tatheva tajjayiṃsu. Siṅgālī tamatthaṃ siṅgālassa kathetvā “sīhassa vacanena etāya evaṃ katabhāvampi na jānāma, ciraṃ vasimhā, nāsāpeyyāpi no, amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānameva gacchāmā”ti āha. Siṅgālo tassā vacanaṃ sutvā sīhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha – “sāmi, ciraṃ amhehi tumhākaṃ santike nivutthaṃ, aticiraṃ vasantā nāma appiyā honti, amhākaṃ gocarāya pakkantakāle sīhī siṅgāliṃ viheṭheti ‘imasmiṃ ṭhāne kasmā vasatha, palāyathā’ti tajjeti, sīhapotakāpi siṅgālapotake tajjenti. Yo nāma yassa attano santike vāsaṃ na roceti, tena so ‘yāhī’ti nīharitabbova, viheṭhanaṃ nāma kimatthiya”nti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

As time passed, the lioness gave birth to two cubs, and the she-jackal also gave birth to two cubs. They all lived together in harmony. Then one day, the lioness thought: 'This lion shows excessive affection towards the jackal, the she-jackal, and the jackal cubs. Surely, he must have an intimacy with the she-jackal; that is why he shows such fondness. What if I were to harass and threaten her and drive her away from here?' When the lion went out to hunt, taking the jackal with him, she harassed and threatened the she-jackal, saying, 'For what reason do you stay in this place? Why do you not flee?' Her cubs also similarly threatened the jackal cubs. The she-jackal, after telling this to the jackal, said, 'We do not even know if this behavior of hers is due to the lion’s words. We have lived here for a long time; perhaps we are no longer cared for. Let us go to our own dwelling place.' Hearing her words, the jackal approached the lion and said: 'Master, we have lived near you for a long time. Those who stay too long become unwelcome. When we go out to hunt, the lioness harasses the she-jackal, saying, "Why do you stay here? Leave!" and threatens her. The lion cubs also threaten the jackal cubs. If someone does not wish for another to live near them, they should simply be told, "Go!" and be turned out. What is the use of harassment?' Having spoken thus, he uttered the first verse:

13.

13.

“Yena kāmaṃ paṇāmeti, dhammo balavataṃ migī;

Unnadantī vijānāhi, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

“The powerful drive away whom they please; that is their way, O lioness. O roaring one, understand: fear has arisen from what was our refuge.”

Tattha yena kāmaṃ paṇāmeti, dhammo balavatanti balavā nāma issaro attano sevakaṃ yena disābhāgena icchati, tena disābhāgena so paṇāmeti nīharati. Esa dhammo balavataṃ ayaṃ issarānaṃ sabhāvo paveṇidhammova, tasmā sace amhākaṃ vāsaṃ na rocetha, ujukameva no nīharatha[V 2.0023], viheṭhanena ko atthoti dīpento evamāha. Migīti sīhaṃ ālapati. So hi migarājatāya migā assa atthīti migī. Unnadantītipi tameva ālapati. So hi unnatānaṃ dantānaṃ atthitāya unnatā dantā assa atthīti unnadantī. “Unnatadantī”tipi pāṭhoyeva. Vijānāhīti “esa issarānaṃ dhammo”ti evaṃ jānāhi. Jātaṃ saraṇato bhayanti amhākaṃ tumhe patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena saraṇaṃ, tumhākaññeva santikā bhayaṃ jātaṃ, tasmā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gamissāmāti dīpeti.

There, 'To drive away at will is the way of the powerful' means that the powerful one, a lord, sends away or removes his servant in whatever direction he wishes. This is the way of the powerful; this is the nature of lords, indeed a traditional custom. Therefore, if our dwelling does not please you, simply remove us straightforwardly—what is the use of harassment? Thus he explains. 'Migī' addresses the lion. For he is the king of beasts, and since he has beasts, he is called 'migī'. 'Unnadantī' also addresses him. For he is called 'Unnadantī' because he possesses upturned teeth. The reading 'Unnatadantī' is also found. 'Understand' means know thus: 'This is the way of lords.' 'Fear has arisen from refuge' means: you are our refuge in the sense of protection, yet fear has arisen from you yourself. Therefore, we will go to our own place of dwelling. Thus he explains.

Aparo nayo – tava migī sīhī unnadantīmama puttadāraṃ tajjentī yena kāmaṃ paṇāmeti, yena yenākārena icchati, tena paṇāmeti pavattati, viheṭhetipi [P 2.0029] palāpetipi, evaṃ tvaṃ vijānāhi, tattha kiṃ sakkā amhehi kātuṃ. Dhammo balavataṃ esa balavantānaṃ sabhāvo, idāni mayaṃ gamissāma. Kasmā? Jātaṃ saraṇato bhayanti.

Another interpretation: 'Your lioness, roaring fiercely, threatens my children and mate, driving them away as she pleases, in whatever manner she desires. She harasses and makes them flee. Thus, you should understand—what can we possibly do about it?' This is the way of the powerful; this is the nature of the strong. Now we shall depart. Why? Because fear arises from refuge.

Tassa [M 2.0026] vacanaṃ sutvā sīho sīhiṃ āha – “bhadde, asukasmiṃ nāma kāle mama gocaratthāya gantvā sattame divase iminā siṅgālena imāya ca siṅgāliyā saddhiṃ āgatabhāvaṃ sarasī”ti. “Āma, sarāmī”ti. “Jānāsi pana mayhaṃ sattāhaṃ anāgamanassa kāraṇa”nti? “Na jānāmi, sāmī”ti. “Bhadde, ahaṃ ‘ekaṃ migaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti virajjhitvā kalale laggo, tato nikkhamituṃ asakkonto sattāhaṃ nirāhāro aṭṭhāsiṃ, svāhaṃ imaṃ siṅgālaṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ labhiṃ, ayaṃ me jīvitadāyako sahāyo. Mittadhamme ṭhātuṃ samattho hi mitto dubbalo nāma natthi, ito paṭṭhāya mayhaṃ sahāyassa ca sahāyikāya ca puttakānañca evarūpaṃ avamānaṃ mā akāsī”ti vatvā sīho dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, the lion spoke to the lioness: "Dear one, do you recall that at such and such a time, when I went out for sustenance, I arrived on the seventh day with this jackal and this she-jackal?" "Yes, I remember," she replied. "But do you know the reason for my seven-day absence?" "No, my lord," she said. "Dear one, having failed in my attempt to catch a beast, I slipped and became stuck in the mud. Unable to extricate myself, I remained without food for seven days. I gained my life through relying on this jackal; he is my life-giving friend. For a friend who is able to stand firm in the duty of friendship, there is no such thing as a weak friend. From now on, do not show such disrespect toward my friend, his mate, or their children." Having spoken thus, the lion uttered the second verse:

14.

14.

“Api cepi dubbalo mitto, mittadhammesu tiṭṭhati;

So ñātako ca bandhu ca, so mitto so ca me sakhā;

Dāṭhini mātimaññittho, siṅgālo mama pāṇado”ti.

“Even if a friend is weak, if he stands firm in the laws of friendship, he is a relative and a kinsman, he is a friend, and he is my companion. O tusked one, do not despise this jackal, my life-giver.”

Tattha api cepīti eko apisaddo anuggahattho, eko sambhāvanattho. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – dubbalopi ce mitto mittadhammesu api tiṭṭhati, sace ṭhātuṃ sakkoti, so ñātako ca bandhu ca, so mettacittatāya mitto, so ca me sahāyaṭṭhena sakhā. Dāṭhini mātimaññitthoti, bhadde, dāṭhāsampanne sīhi mā mayhaṃ sahāyaṃ vā sahāyiṃ vā atimaññi, ayañhi siṅgālo mama pāṇadoti.

Here, in 'api cepi,' one 'api' signifies concession and the other signifies possibility. The construction is as follows: even if a friend is weak, yet he stands firm in the laws of friendship; if he is able to stand firm, he is a relative and a kinsman; through his kindly disposition, he is a friend; and through his role as a companion, he is my friend. 'O tusked one, do not despise' means: Good lady, O lioness possessed of tusks, do not disdain my companion or his mate, for this jackal is my life-giver.

Sā [V 2.0024] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā siṅgāliṃ khamāpetvā tato paṭṭhāya saputtāya tāya saddhiṃ samaggavāsaṃ vasi. Sīhapotakāpi siṅgālapotakehi saddhiṃ kīḷamānā sammodamānā mātāpitūnaṃ atikkantakālepi [P 2.0030] mittabhāvaṃ abhinditvā sammodamānā vasiṃsu. Tesaṃ kira sattakulaparivaṭṭe abhijjamānā metti agamāsi.

Hearing his words, she asked for the she-jackal's forgiveness, and from then on, she lived harmoniously with her and her children. The lion cubs also, playing joyfully and amicably with the jackal cubs, lived in harmony, maintaining their friendship unbroken even after their parents had passed away. It is said that their friendship continued unbroken through seven generations.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – saccapariyosāne keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahanto ahesuṃ. “Tadā siṅgālo ānando ahosi, sīho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka: At the conclusion of the Truths, some monks became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some became arahants. "At that time, the jackal was Ānanda, and the lion was I myself."

Guṇajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Guṇa Jātaka is finished.

[158] 8. Suhanujātakavaṇṇanā

[158] 8. 8. Suhanu Jātaka: The Two Rogue Horses

Nayidaṃ [M 2.0027] visamasīlenāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dve caṇḍabhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi samaye jetavanepi eko bhikkhu caṇḍo ahosi pharuso sāhasiko janapadepi. Athekadivasaṃ jānapado bhikkhu kenacideva karaṇīyena jetavanaṃ agamāsi, sāmaṇerā ceva daharabhikkhū ca tassa caṇḍabhāvaṃ jānanti. “Tesaṃ dvinnaṃ caṇḍānaṃ kalahaṃ passissāmā”ti kutūhalena taṃ bhikkhuṃ jetavanavāsikassa pariveṇaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Te ubhopi caṇḍā aññamaññaṃ disvāva piyasaṃvāsaṃ saṃsandiṃsu samiṃsu, hatthapādapiṭṭhisambāhanādīni akaṃsu. Dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, caṇḍā bhikkhū aññesaṃ upari caṇḍā pharusā sāhasikā, aññamaññaṃ pana ubhopi samaggā sammodamānā piyasaṃvāsā jātā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepete aññesaṃ caṇḍā pharusā sāhasikā, aññamaññaṃ pana samaggā sammodamānā piyasaṃvāsā ca ahesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This is not with one of dissimilar character…” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning two fierce monks. At that time, there was a monk in Jetavana who was fierce, harsh, and reckless, and there was also one in the countryside. One day, the country monk came to Jetavana for some business. The novices and young monks, knowing his fierce nature, thought, "We will see a quarrel between these two fierce ones," and out of curiosity, they sent that monk to the dwelling of the Jetavana resident. When the two fierce monks saw each other, they immediately became friendly, conversed amiably, and associated, and they massaged each other's hands, feet, and backs. In the Dhamma hall, the monks started a discussion: "Friends, these fierce monks are fierce, harsh, and reckless toward others, but with each other, they have become united, harmonious, and affectionate." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" and when they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now have they been fierce, harsh, and reckless toward others while being united and harmonious with each other; in the past also, they were fierce, harsh, and reckless toward others, yet united and affectionate with each other." Then he related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa sabbatthasādhako atthadhammānusāsako amacco ahosi. So pana rājā thokaṃ dhanalobhapakatiko, tassa [P 2.0031] mahāsoṇo nāma kūṭaasso atthi. Atha uttarāpathakā assavāṇijā pañca assasatāni ānesuṃ, assānaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Tato pubbe pana bodhisatto asse agghāpetvā [V 2.0025] mūlaṃ aparihāpetvā dāpesi. Rājā taṃ parihāyamāno aññaṃ amaccaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, asse agghāpehi, agghāpento ca paṭhamaṃ mahāsoṇaṃ yathā tesaṃ assānaṃ antaraṃ pavisati, tathā vissajjetvā asse ḍaṃsāpetvā vaṇite kārāpetvā dubbalakāle mūlaṃ hāpetvā asse agghāpeyyāsī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tathā akāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister, one who accomplished all affairs and was an advisor on matters of welfare and Dhamma. But that king was by nature somewhat greedy for wealth, and he had a rogue horse named Mahāsoṇa. Then, horse traders from the northern region brought five hundred horses and informed the king of their arrival. Previously, the Bodhisatta had the horses appraised and paid for without reducing their original price. The king, seeking to avoid paying the full price, summoned another minister and said, "My dear, appraise the horses. While appraising them, first release Mahāsoṇa so that he enters among those horses. Then, have him bite and wound them, and when they are weakened, reduce the original price and appraise the horses." The minister agreed, saying, "Very well," and did as instructed.

Assavāṇijā anattamanā hutvā tena katakiriyaṃ bodhisattassa ārocesuṃ. Bodhisatto “kiṃ pana tumhākaṃ nagare kūṭaasso natthī”ti pucchi. “Atthi sāmi, suhanu nāma kūṭaasso caṇḍo pharuso”ti. “Tena [M 2.0028] hi puna āgacchantā taṃ assaṃ āneyyāthā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā puna āgacchantā taṃ kūṭassaṃ gāhāpetvā āgacchiṃsu. Rājā “assavāṇijā āgatā”ti sutvā sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā asse oloketvā mahāsoṇaṃ vissajjāpesi. Assavāṇijāpi mahāsoṇaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā suhanuṃ vissajjāpesuṃ. Te aññamaññaṃ patvā sarīrāni lehantā sammodamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Rājā bodhisattaṃ pucchi – “passasi ime dve kūṭassā aññesaṃ caṇḍā pharusā sāhasikā, aññe asse ḍaṃsitvā gelaññaṃ pāpenti, idāni aññamaññaṃ pana sarīraṃ lehantā sammodamānā aṭṭhaṃsu, kiṃ nāmeta”nti? Bodhisatto “nayime, mahārāja, visamasīlā, samasīlā samadhātukā ca ete”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

The horse traders, being displeased, reported the king's actions to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta asked, "Is there no rogue horse in your city?" They replied, "There is, lord, a fierce and harsh rogue horse named Suhaṇu." "In that case, when you come again, bring that horse Suhaṇu with you," said the Bodhisatta. They agreed, and upon their return, they brought the rogue horse Suhaṇu. Hearing that the horse traders had arrived, the king opened the lion-window and, looking at the horses, had Mahāsoṇa released. The horse traders, seeing Mahāsoṇa approaching, released Suhaṇu. The two horses, having reached each other, stood there licking one another's bodies in friendship. The king asked the Bodhisatta, "Do you see these two rogue horses? They are fierce, harsh, and reckless toward others; they bite other horses and cause them to fall ill. Yet now they stand together joyfully licking each other's bodies. Why is this so?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great king, these two horses are not of dissimilar character, nor are they of dissimilar nature. These two are of similar character and similar nature," and spoke these two verses:

15.

15.

“Nayidaṃ visamasīlena, soṇena suhanū saha;

Suhanūpi tādisoyeva, yo soṇassa sagocaro.

This association of Suhaṇu with Soṇa is not between those of dissimilar character; Suhaṇu too is just like him, one who shares the same range as Soṇa.

16.

16.

“Pakkhandinā [P 2.0032] pagabbhena, niccaṃ sandānakhādinā;

Sameti pāpaṃ pāpena, sameti asatā asa”nti.

With the aggressive and the audacious, who constantly gnaws at the tether; evil meets with evil, and the ignoble meets with the ignoble.

Tattha nayidaṃ visamasīlena, soṇena suhanū sahāti yaṃ idaṃ suhanu kūṭasso soṇena saddhiṃ pemaṃ karoti, idaṃ na attano visamasīlena, atha kho attano samasīleneva saddhiṃ karoti. Ubhopi hete attano anācāratāya dussīlatāya samasīlā samadhātukā. Suhanūpi tādisoyeva, yo soṇassa sagocaroti yādiso soṇo, suhanupi tādisoyeva, yo soṇassa sagocaro yaṃgocaro soṇo, sopi taṃgocaroyeva. Yatheva hi soṇo assagocaro asse ḍaṃsentova carati, tathā suhanupi. Iminā nesaṃ samānagocarataṃ dasseti.

In those verses, 'this association of Suhaṇu with Soṇa is not between those of dissimilar character' means that the affection this rogue horse Suhaṇu shows for Soṇa is not based on a character unlike his own, but rather it is formed with one of similar character. For both of them are alike in their character and disposition due to their misconduct and immorality. 'Suhaṇu too is just like him, one who shares the same range as Soṇa' means that Suhaṇu is exactly as Soṇa is; whatever range Soṇa has, he too has the same. Just as Soṇa's range consists of other horses, as he goes about biting them, so too does Suhaṇu. By this, the teacher shows that they share a common range.

Te [V 2.0026] pana ācāragocare ekato katvā dassetuṃ “pakkhandinā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pakkhandināti assānaṃ upari pakkhandanasīlena pakkhandanagocarena. Pagabbhenāti kāyapāgabbhiyādisamannāgatena dussīlena. Niccaṃ sandānakhādināti sadā attano bandhanayottaṃ khādanasīlena khādanagocarena ca. Sameti pāpaṃ pāpenāti etesu aññatarena pāpena saddhiṃ aññatarassa [M 2.0029] pāpaṃ dussīlyaṃ sameti. Asatā asanti etesu aññatarena asatā anācāragocarasampannena saha itarassa asaṃ asādhukammaṃ sameti, gūthādīni viya gūthādīhi ekato saṃsandati sadisaṃ nibbisesameva hotīti.

Furthermore, combining their conduct and range to show them as one, the verse beginning with 'pakkhandinā' was spoken. There, 'with the aggressive' refers to the habit and range of leaping upon other horses. 'With the audacious' means being immoral and endowed with bodily insolence and the like. 'Who constantly gnaws at the tether' means the habit and range of always gnawing at his own binding-ropes. 'Evil meets with evil' means the evil or immorality of one of these horses corresponds with the evil of the other. 'The ignoble meets with the ignoble' means the unwholesome deeds of one who is ignoble due to bad conduct and range correspond with those of the other; just as filth mixes with filth, they are similar and entirely without distinction.

Evaṃ vatvā ca pana bodhisatto “mahārāja, raññā nāma atiluddhena na bhavitabbaṃ, parassa santakaṃ nāma nāsetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti rājānaṃ ovaditvā asse agghāpetvā bhūtameva mūlaṃ dāpesi. Assavāṇijā yathāsabhāvameva mūlaṃ labhitvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā agamaṃsu. Rājāpi bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta admonished the king, saying, "Great king, a king should not be overly greedy; it is not right to destroy another’s property." He then had the horses appraised and made the king pay the true price. The horse traders, receiving a price that was fair to their nature, departed delighted and joyful. The king, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, passed away to fare according to his deeds.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dve assā ime dve duṭṭhabhikkhū ahesuṃ, rājā ānando, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, connected the Jātaka: "At that time, those two fierce horses were these two corrupt monks, the king was Ānanda, and I myself was the wise minister."

Suhanujātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Suhaṇu Jātaka, the eighth.

[159] 9. Morajātakavaṇṇanā

[159] 9. 9. Mora Jātaka: The Golden Peacock and the Snare

Udetayaṃ [P 2.0033] cakkhumā ekarājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi bhikkhu bhikkhūhi satthu santikaṃ nīto “saccaṃ kira, tvaṃ bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhito”ti vutte “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vatvā “kiṃ disvā”ti vutte “ekaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattasarīraṃ mātugāmaṃ oloketvā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “bhikkhu mātugāmo nāma kasmā tumhādisānaṃ cittaṃ nāluḷessati, porāṇakapaṇḍitānampi hi mātugāmassa saddaṃ sutvā satta vassasatāni asamudāciṇṇakilesā okāsaṃ labhitvā khaṇeneva samudācariṃsu. Visuddhāpi sattā saṃkilissanti, uttamayasasamaṅginopi āyasakyaṃ pāpuṇanti, pageva aparisuddhā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this Mora Jātaka concerning a monk who was discontented in the Dispensation, beginning with the verse, 'Udetayaṃ cakkhumā ekarājā.' Indeed, that discontented monk was brought by his fellow monks to the Teacher's presence. When the Teacher asked, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' he replied, 'It is true, Venerable Sir.' When asked, 'What did you see to become discontented?' he said, 'Venerable Sir, I became discontented upon seeing a woman in fine adornments.' Then the Teacher said, 'Monk, why would a woman not agitate the minds of those like you? They certainly do. Even for the wise ones of old, defilements that had not arisen for seven hundred years found an opportunity and were stirred up in a single moment upon hearing a woman's voice. Even pure beings become defiled, and even those endowed with supreme glory fall into ignominy; what need is there to mention those who are not pure?' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto morayoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā aṇḍakālepi [V 2.0027] kaṇikāramakuḷavaṇṇaaṇḍakoso hutvā aṇḍaṃ bhinditvā nikkhanto suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ahosi dassanīyo pāsādiko pakkhānaṃ antare surattarājivirājito, so attano [M 2.0030] jīvitaṃ rakkhanto tisso pabbatarājiyo atikkamma catutthāya pabbatarājiyā ekasmiṃ daṇḍakahiraññapabbatatale vāsaṃ kappesi. So pabhātāya rattiyā pabbatamatthake nisinno sūriyaṃ uggacchantaṃ oloketvā attano gocarabhūmiyaṃ rakkhāvaraṇatthāya brahmamantaṃ bandhanto “udetaya”ntiādimāha.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta took conception in a peacock's womb. During his time as an egg, the shell was the color of a kaṇikāra bud, and when he broke the shell and emerged, he was golden-hued, lovely, and pleasing to behold, adorned with deep crimson streaks between his wings. To protect his life, he crossed three mountain ranges and made his home on the fourth range, on a plateau of the golden mountain named Daṇḍaka. When the night had turned to dawn, he would sit on the mountain peak and, looking at the rising sun, would recite a sublime mantra to establish protection and a safeguard for his feeding grounds, saying:

17.

17.

“Udetayaṃ cakkhumā ekarājā,

Harissavaṇṇo pathavippabhāso;

Taṃ taṃ namassāmi harissavaṇṇaṃ pathavippabhāsaṃ,

Tayājja guttā viharemu divasa”nti.

“This one with the eye, the sole king, arises, golden-hued, illuminating the earth. To you, to you I pay homage—golden-hued, illuminating the earth. Protected by you today, may we dwell safely through the day.”

Tattha [P 2.0034] udetīti pācīnalokadhātuto uggacchati. Cakkhumāti sakalacakkavāḷavāsīnaṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā cakkhupaṭilābhakaraṇena yaṃ tena tesaṃ dinnaṃ cakkhu, tena cakkhunā cakkhumā. Ekarājāti sakalacakkavāḷe ālokakarānaṃ antare seṭṭhavisiṭṭhaṭṭhena ekarājā. Harissavaṇṇoti harisamānavaṇṇo, suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti attho. Pathavippabhāsoti pathaviyā pabhāso. Taṃ taṃ namassāmīti tasmā taṃ evarūpaṃ bhavantaṃ namassāmi vandāmi. Tayājja guttā viharemu divasanti tayā ajja rakkhitā gopitā hutvā imaṃ divasaṃ catuiriyāpathavihārena sukhaṃ vihareyyāma.

Herein, 'rises' (udeti) means it ascends from the eastern world-system. 'Cakkhumā' (the one with sight) means that by dispelling the darkness for all inhabitants of the entire world-system, it grants them the gift of sight; it is 'the one with sight' because of the sight it gives them. 'Ekarājā' (sole king) means it is the foremost and most distinguished among all light-givers in the entire world-system. 'Harissavaṇṇo' means having a color like gold, that is, golden-hued. 'Pathavippabhāso' means the radiance of the earth. 'Taṃ taṃ namassāmi' means: 'Therefore, I pay homage and venerate you of such a nature.' 'Tayājja guttā viharemu divasaṃ' means: 'Protected and guarded by you today, may we dwell happily this day in the four postures.'

Evaṃ bodhisatto imāya gāthāya sūriyaṃ namassitvā dutiyagāthāya atīte parinibbute buddhe ceva buddhaguṇe ca namassati.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having paid homage to the sun with this verse, with the second verse pays homage to the Buddhas of the past who have attained final Nibbāna, and to the virtues of the Buddhas.

“Ye brāhmaṇā vedagū sabbadhamme, te me namo te ca maṃ pālayantu;

Namatthu buddhānaṃ namatthu bodhiyā, namo vimuttānaṃ namo vimuttiyā;

Imaṃ so parittaṃ katvā, moro carati esanā”ti.

“To those brahmins who are knowers of all phenomena, be my homage; and may they protect me. Homage be to the Buddhas, homage to enlightenment; homage to the liberated ones, homage to liberation. Having made this protection, the peacock goes about its quest.”

Tattha ye brāhmaṇāti ye bāhitapāpā visuddhibrāhmaṇā. Vedagūti vedānaṃ pāraṃ gatātipi vedagū, vedehi pāraṃ gatātipi vedagū. Idha pana sabbe saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhamme vidite pākaṭe katvā gatāti vedagū. Tenevāha [M 2.0031] “sabbadhamme”ti. Sabbe khandhāyatanadhātudhamme salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇavasena [V 2.0028] attano ñāṇassa vidite pākaṭe katvā gatā, tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ matthakaṃ madditvā dasasahassilokadhātuṃ unnādetvā bodhitale sammāsambodhiṃ patvā saṃsāraṃ vā atikkantāti attho. Te me namoti te mama imaṃ namakkāraṃ paṭicchantu. Te ca maṃ pālayantūti evaṃ mayā namassitā ca te bhagavanto maṃ pālentu rakkhantu gopentu. Namatthu buddhānaṃ namatthu bodhiyā, namo vimuttānaṃ namo vimuttiyāti ayaṃ mama namakkāro [P 2.0035] atītānaṃ parinibbutānaṃ buddhānaṃ atthu, tesaññeva catūsu ca maggesu catūsu phalesu ñāṇasaṅkhātāya bodhiyā atthu, tathā tesaññeva arahattaphalavimuttiyā vimuttānaṃ atthu, yā ca nesaṃ tadaṅgavimutti vikkhambhanavimutti samucchedavimutti paṭippassaddhivimutti nissaraṇavimuttīti pañcavidhā vimutti, tassā nesaṃ vimuttiyāpi ayaṃ mayhaṃ namakkāro atthūti. “Imaṃ so parittaṃ katvā, moro carati esanā”ti idaṃ pana padadvayaṃ satthā abhisambuddho hutvā āha. Tassattho – bhikkhave, so moro imaṃ parittaṃ imaṃ rakkhaṃ katvā attano gocarabhūmiyaṃ pupphaphalādīnaṃ atthāya nānappakārāya esanāya carati.

There, 'those brahmins' refers to those who have cast out evil, the purified brahmins. 'Vedagū' means one who has gone to the far shore of the Vedas, or one who has gone beyond by means of the Vedas. Here, however, it means those who have gone having known and made manifest all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. Therefore, it is said, 'all phenomena.' This means having made known and manifest to one's own knowledge all phenomena—the aggregates, sense bases, and elements—through their specific and general characteristics; having crushed the heads of the three Māras; having made the ten-thousand-world-system resound; having attained perfect full enlightenment at the seat of awakening; or having transcended saṃsāra. 'Te me namo' means: 'May they accept this homage of mine.' 'Te ca maṃ pālayantu' means: 'And may those Blessed Ones, thus venerated by me, protect, guard, and preserve me.' 'Namatthu buddhānaṃ... vimuttiyā' means: 'May this homage of mine be for the past Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna; may it be for their enlightenment, which is the knowledge in the four paths and four fruits; likewise, may it be for the liberated ones through their liberation of the Arahant fruit; and may this homage of mine also be for their fivefold liberation, namely: liberation by substitution, liberation by suppression, liberation by eradication, liberation by tranquillization, and liberation by escape.' 'Imaṃ so parittaṃ katvā, moro carati esanā'—these two lines, however, the Teacher spoke after becoming fully enlightened. The meaning is: 'Monks, that peacock, having made this protection, this safeguard, roams in its feeding ground on its diverse quest for the sake of flowers, fruits, and so on.'

Evaṃ divasaṃ caritvā sāyaṃ pabbatamatthake nisīditvā atthaṅgataṃ sūriyaṃ olokento buddhaguṇe āvajjetvā nivāsaṭṭhāne rakkhāvaraṇatthāya puna brahmamantaṃ bandhanto “apetaya”ntiādimāha.

Having wandered thus for the day, in the evening he sat on the mountaintop and, watching the setting sun, reflected on the virtues of the Buddhas. For the protection and safeguarding of his dwelling place, he again bound the Brahma charm, beginning with 'Apetayaṃ'.

18.

18.

“Apetayaṃ cakkhumā ekarājā, harissavaṇṇo pathavippabhāso;

Taṃ taṃ namassāmi harissavaṇṇaṃ pathavippabhāsaṃ, tayājja guttā viharemu rattiṃ.

“This one with the eye, the sole king, departs, golden-hued, illuminating the earth. To you, to you I pay homage, golden-hued, illuminating the earth. By you protected today, may we dwell through the night.”

“Ye brāhmaṇā vedagū sabbadhamme, te me namo te ca maṃ pālayantu;

Namatthu buddhānaṃ namatthu bodhiyā, namo vimuttānaṃ namo vimuttiyā;

Imaṃ so parittaṃ katvā, moro vāsamakappayī”ti.

“To those brahmins who are knowers of all phenomena, be my homage; and may they protect me. Homage be to the Buddhas, homage to enlightenment; homage to the liberated ones, homage to liberation. Having made this protection, the peacock arranged its dwelling.”

Tattha apetīti apayāti atthaṃ gacchati. Imaṃ so parittaṃ katvā, moro vāsamakappayīti idampi abhisambuddho hutvā āha. Tassattho – bhikkhave[M 2.0032], so moro imaṃ parittaṃ imaṃ rakkhaṃ katvā attano nivāsaṭṭhāne vāsaṃ kappayittha, tassa rattiṃ vā divā vā imassa parittassānubhāvena neva bhayaṃ, na lomahaṃso ahosi.

There, 'apeti' means 'goes away,' 'goes to its setting.' 'Having made this protection, the peacock arranged its dwelling'—this too the Teacher spoke, having become fully enlightened. Its meaning is: 'Monks, that peacock, having made this protection, this safeguard, arranged its dwelling in its own living place. By the power of this protection, neither fear nor horripilation arose in him, either by night or by day.'

Atheko [P 2.0036] bārāṇasiyā avidūre nesādagāmavāsī nesādo himavantapadese vicaranto tasmiṃ [V 2.0029] daṇḍakahiraññapabbatamatthake nisinnaṃ bodhisattaṃ disvā āgantvā puttassa ārocesi. Athekadivasaṃ khemā nāma bārāṇasirañño devī supinena suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ moraṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ disvā pabuddhakāle rañño ārocesi – “ahaṃ, deva, suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa morassa dhammaṃ sotukāmā”ti. Rājā amacce pucchi. Amaccā “brāhmaṇā jānissantī”ti āhaṃsu. Brāhmaṇā taṃ sutvā “suvaṇṇavaṇṇā morā nāma hontī”ti vatvā “kattha hontī”ti vutte “nesādā jānissantī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā nesāde sannipātetvā pucchi. Atha so nesādaputto “āma, mahārāja, daṇḍakahiraññapabbato nāma atthi, tattha suvaṇṇavaṇṇo moro vasatī”ti āha. “Tena hi taṃ moraṃ amāretvā bandhitvāva ānehī”ti. Nesādo gantvā tassa gocarabhūmiyaṃ pāse oḍḍesi. Morena akkantaṭṭhānepi pāso na sañcarati. Nesādo gaṇhituṃ asakkonto satta vassāni vicaritvā tattheva kālamakāsi. Khemāpi devī patthitaṃ alabhamānā kālamakāsi.

Now, a certain hunter, living in a hunter's village not far from Bārāṇasī, while wandering in the Himalayan region, saw the Bodhisatta seated on the summit of Mount Daṇḍaka-Hirañña. Upon returning, he informed his son. Then one day, Queen Khemā, the consort of the King of Bārāṇasī, having seen in a dream a golden-colored peacock teaching the Dhamma, reported it to the king upon waking: 'O king, I wish to hear the Dhamma from a golden-colored peacock.' The king asked his ministers. The ministers said, 'The brahmins will know.' The brahmins, hearing this, said, 'There are indeed golden-colored peacocks,' and when asked where they are, replied, 'The hunters will know.' The king assembled the hunters and questioned them. Then that hunter's son said, 'Yes, great king, there is a mountain called Mount Daṇḍaka-Hirañña, where a golden-colored peacock dwells.' 'Then go, without killing that peacock, bind it and bring it here.' The hunter went and set a snare in its feeding ground. But even when the peacock stepped on the snare, it did not spring. Unable to capture it, the hunter wandered for seven years and died there. Queen Khemā, too, not obtaining what she desired, passed away.

Rājā “moraṃ me nissāya devī kālakatā”ti kujjhitvā “himavantapadese daṇḍakahiraññapabbato nāma atthi, tattha suvaṇṇavaṇṇo moro vasati, ye tassa maṃsaṃ khādanti, te ajarā amarā hontī”ti akkharaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhāpetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ mañjūsāya nikkhipāpesi. Tasmiṃ kālakate añño rājā rajjaṃ patvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ vācetvā “ajaro amaro bhavissāmī”ti aññaṃ nesādaṃ pesesi. Sopi gantvā bodhisattaṃ gahetuṃ asakkonto tattheva kālamakāsi. Eteneva niyāmena cha rājaparivaṭṭā gatā. Atha sattamo rājā rajjaṃ patvā ekaṃ nesādaṃ pahiṇi. So gantvā bodhisattena akkantaṭṭhānepi pāsassa asañcaraṇabhāvaṃ, attano [P 2.0037] parittaṃ katvā gocarabhūmigamanabhāvañcassa ñatvā paccantaṃ otaritvā ekaṃ moriṃ gahetvā yathā hatthatāḷasaddena naccati, accharāsaddena ca vassati, evaṃ sikkhāpetvā taṃ ādāya gantvā morena paritte [M 2.0033] akate pātoyeva pāsayaṭṭhiyo ropetvā pāse oḍḍetvā moriṃ vassāpesi. Moro visabhāgaṃ mātugāmasaddaṃ sutvā kilesāturo hutvā parittaṃ kātuṃ asakkuṇitvā gantvā pāse bajjhi. Atha naṃ nesādo gahetvā gantvā bārāṇasirañño adāsi.

The king, angry that 'the queen has died on account of the peacock,' had an inscription written on a golden plate: 'In the Himalayan region, there is a mountain called Daṇḍakahirañña. There lives a golden-colored peacock. Those who eat its flesh become ageless and immortal.' He had the golden plate placed in a casket. When that king died, another king attained the throne. Having had the golden plate read and, thinking, 'I shall become ageless and immortal,' he sent another hunter. That hunter also went but, being unable to capture the Bodhisatta, he died right there. In this same manner, six successions of kings passed. Then the seventh king attained the throne and sent a hunter. He went and, having realized the snare's failure to spring even in the place stepped upon by the Bodhisatta, and knowing of his practice of making a protection for himself before going to his feeding ground, he descended to a border region. There he captured a peahen and trained her to dance at the sound of clapping hands and to cry out at the sound of snapping fingers. Taking her, he went and, early in the morning before the peacock had made his protection, he planted the snare-sticks, set the snares, and made the peahen cry out. The peacock, hearing the sound of a female which was of the opposite nature, became afflicted by defilement. Unable to perform his protection, he went and was caught in the snare. Then the hunter seized him, took him away, and presented him to the king of Bārāṇasī.

Rājā tassa rūpasampattiṃ disvā tuṭṭhamānaso āsanaṃ dāpesi. Bodhisatto paññattāsane nisīditvā “mahārāja, kasmā maṃ gaṇhāpesī”ti pucchi. “Ye kira tava maṃsaṃ khādanti, te ajarā amarā honti, svāhaṃ tava maṃsaṃ khāditvā ajaro amaro hotukāmo taṃ gaṇhāpesi”nti. “Mahārāja, mama tāva maṃsaṃ khādantā ajarā amarā hontu, ahaṃ pana marissāmī”ti[V 2.0030]? “Āma, marissasī”ti. “Mayi marante pana mama maṃsameva khāditvā kinti katvā na marissantī”ti? “Tvaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, tasmā kira tava maṃsaṃ khādakā ajarā amarā bhavissantī”ti. “Mahārāja, ahaṃ pana na akāraṇā suvaṇṇavaṇṇo jāto, pubbe panāhaṃ imasmiṃyeva nagare cakkavattī rājā hutvā sayampi pañca sīlāni rakkhiṃ, sakalacakkavāḷavāsinopi rakkhāpesiṃ, svāhaṃ kālaṃ karitvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatto, tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto aññassa akusalassa nissandena morayoniyaṃ nibbattitvāpi porāṇasīlānubhāvena suvaṇṇavaṇṇo jāto”ti. “‘Tvaṃ cakkavattī rājā hutvā sīlaṃ rakkhitvā sīlaphalena suvaṇṇavaṇṇo jāto’ti kathamidaṃ amhehi saddhātabbaṃ. Atthi no koci sakkhī”ti[P 2.0038]? “Atthi, mahārājā”ti. “Ko nāmā”ti? “Mahārāja, ahaṃ cakkavattikāle ratanamaye rathe nisīditvā ākāse vicariṃ, so me ratho maṅgalapokkharaṇiyā antobhūmiyaṃ nidahāpito, taṃ maṅgalapokkharaṇito ukkhipāpehi, so me sakkhi bhavissatī”ti.

The king, seeing his physical perfection, was pleased in heart and had a seat offered. The Bodhisatta sat on the prepared seat and asked, 'Great king, why did you have me captured?' 'It is said that those who eat your flesh become ageless and immortal. Thus, wishing to become ageless and immortal by eating your flesh, I had you captured.' 'Great king, granted that those who eat my flesh may become ageless and immortal, but shall I myself die?' 'Yes, you will die.' 'But if I die, how will they, by eating my very flesh, not die?' 'You are golden-colored; therefore it is said that those who eat your flesh will become ageless and immortal.' 'Great king, I was not born golden-colored without a cause. In a former time, I was a wheel-turning monarch in this very city. I myself observed the five precepts and had the inhabitants of the entire world-system observe them as well. When I passed away, I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Having stayed there for the full lifespan, I passed away from there and, as a result of another unwholesome deed, was reborn in a peacock's womb. Yet, by the power of my former virtue, I was born golden-colored.' 'That you were a wheel-turning monarch who observed the precepts, and by the fruit of that virtue you were born golden-colored—how is this to be believed by us? Is there any witness?' 'There is, great king.' 'Who is it?' 'Great king, when I was a wheel-turning monarch, I sat in a jeweled chariot and traveled through the sky. That chariot of mine was caused to be buried in the earth beneath the royal lotus pond. Have it raised up from the royal lotus pond; it will be my witness.'

Rājā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā pokkharaṇito udakaṃ harāpetvā rathaṃ nīharāpetvā bodhisattassa saddahi. Bodhisatto “mahārāja, ṭhapetvā amatamahānibbānaṃ avasesā sabbe saṅkhatadhammā hutvā abhāvino aniccā khayavayadhammāyevā”ti rañño dhammaṃ desetvā rājānaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Rājā pasanno bodhisattaṃ rajjena pūjetvā mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ akāsi. So rajjaṃ tasseva paṭiniyyādetvā katipāhaṃ vasitvā “appamatto hohi, mahārājā”ti ovaditvā ākāse [M 2.0034] uppatitvā daṇḍakahiraññapabbatameva agamāsi. Rājāpi bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

The king, saying 'Excellent,' consented, and having had the water removed from the lotus pond and the chariot brought out, he believed the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to the king, saying: 'Great king, with the exception of the deathless, great Nibbāna, all remaining conditioned things, having come to be, are subject to non-existence; they are impermanent, and have the nature of decay and dissolution.' He then established the king in the five precepts. The king, being pleased, honored the Bodhisatta with the kingdom and paid him great respect. The Bodhisatta, having returned the kingdom to that same king, stayed for some days. Then, after advising him, 'Be heedful, great king,' he rose into the sky and went back to Mount Daṇḍakahirañña. The king, abiding by the Bodhisatta's advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and went according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, suvaṇṇamoro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in Arahantship. 'At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the golden peacock was I myself.'

Morajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The ninth, the commentary on the Mora Birth Story.

[160] 10. Vinīlajātakavaṇṇanā

[160] 10. The commentary on the Vinīla Birth Story.

Evameva nūna rājānanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa sugatālayaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadatte hi gayāsīsagatānaṃ dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ sugatālayaṃ dassetvā nipanne ubhopi therā [V 2.0031] dhammaṃ desetvā attano nissitake ādāya veḷuvanaṃ agamiṃsu. Te satthārā “sāriputta, devadatto tumhe disvā kiṃ [P 2.0039] akāsī”ti puṭṭhā “bhante, sugatālayaṃ dassetvā mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇī”ti ārocesuṃ. Satthā “na kho, sāriputta, devadatto idāneva mama anukiriyaṃ karonto vināsaṃ patto, pubbepi pāpuṇiyevā”ti vatvā therehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'Even so, indeed, O king'—this the Teacher told while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta's imitation of the Sugata. For when Devadatta had shown the imitation of the Sugata to the two chief disciples who had gone to Gayāsīsa, and then lay down, both elders preached the Dhamma, and taking their own followers, went to the Bamboo Grove. When they were asked by the Teacher, 'Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do when he saw you?' they reported, 'Venerable sir, after showing the imitation of the Sugata, he came to great ruin.' The Teacher said, 'Sāriputta, not only now has Devadatta come to ruin while imitating me; he came to ruin in the past as well.' Having been requested by the elders, he related a story of the past.

Atīte videharaṭṭhe mithilāyaṃ videharāje rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāsi. Tadā ekassa suvaṇṇahaṃsarājassa gocarabhūmiyaṃ kākiyā saddhiṃ saṃvāso ahosi. Sā puttaṃ vijāyi. So neva mātupatirūpako ahosi, na pitu. Athassa vinīlakadhātukattā “vinīlako”tveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Haṃsarājā abhiṇhaṃ gantvā puttaṃ passati. Apare panassa dve haṃsapotakā puttā ahesuṃ. Te pitaraṃ abhiṇhaṃ manussapathaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pucchiṃsu – “tāta, tumhe kasmā abhiṇhaṃ manussapathaṃ gacchathā”ti? “Tātā, ekāya me kākiyā saddhiṃ saṃvāsamanvāya eko putto jāto, ‘vinīlako’tissa nāmaṃ, tamahaṃ daṭṭhuṃ gacchāmī”ti. “Kahaṃ panete [M 2.0035] vasantī”ti? “Videharaṭṭhe mithilāya avidūre asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne ekasmiṃ tālagge vasantī”ti. “Tāta, manussapatho nāma sāsaṅko sappaṭibhayo, tumhe mā gacchatha, mayaṃ gantvā taṃ ānessāmā”ti dve haṃsapotakā pitarā ācikkhitasaññāya tattha gantvā taṃ vinīlakaṃ ekasmiṃ daṇḍake nisīdāpetvā mukhatuṇḍakena daṇḍakoṭiyaṃ ḍaṃsitvā mithilānagaramatthakena pāyiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe videharājā sabbasetacatusindhavayuttarathavare nisīditvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karoti. Vinīlako taṃ disvā cintesi – “mayhaṃ videharaññā kiṃ nānākāraṇaṃ, esa catusindhavayuttarathe nisīditvā nagaraṃ anusañcarati, ahaṃ pana haṃsayuttarathe nisīditvā gacchāmī”ti. So ākāsena gacchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, in the kingdom of Videha, while the King of Videha was reigning in Mithilā, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When he reached maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and, on his father's death, was established in the kingdom. At that time, a golden mallard king had a union with a crow in his feeding ground. She gave birth to a son. He resembled neither his mother nor his father. Because of his dark-blue complexion, they named him 'Vinīlaka'. The mallard king went frequently to see his son. He had two other sons who were young mallards. Seeing their father frequently going to the human world, they asked: 'Father, why do you frequently go to the human world?' 'My sons, a son was born to me from a union with a crow; his name is Vinīlaka. I go to see him.' 'But where do they live?' 'In the kingdom of Videha, not far from Mithilā, at a certain place, he lives on the top of a palm tree.' 'Father, the human world is full of suspicion and danger; you should not go. We will go and bring him back.' Guided by their father's description, the two young mallards went there, seated Vinīlaka on a stick, and, gripping the ends of the stick with their beaks, they flew over the city of Mithilā. At that moment, the king of Videha, seated in a magnificent chariot yoked with four all-white Sindh horses, was making a ceremonial circuit of the city. Vinīlaka saw him and thought: 'What is the difference between the king of Videha and me? This king of Videha is traveling about the city seated in a chariot yoked with four Sindh horses, but I am traveling seated in a chariot yoked with mallards.' As he was flying through the air, he spoke the first verse:

19.

19.

“Evameva [P 2.0040] nūna rājānaṃ, vedehaṃ mithilaggahaṃ;

Assā vahanti ājaññā, yathā haṃsā vinīlaka”nti.

"Even so, surely, the noble steeds carry the king of Videha, the lord of Mithilā, just as the mallards carry Vinīlaka."

Tattha evamevāti evaṃ eva, nūnāti parivitakke nipāto. Ekaṃsepi vaṭṭatiyeva. Vedehanti videharaṭṭhasāmikaṃ. Mithilaggahanti mithilagehaṃ, mithilāyaṃ gharaṃ pariggahetvā vasamānanti attho. Ājaññāti kāraṇākāraṇājānanakā. Yathā haṃsā vinīlakanti yathā ime haṃsā maṃ vinīlakaṃ vahanti, evameva vahantīti.

Here, 'evamevāti' means 'even so'. 'Nūnāti' is a particle of deliberation; it is also used in the sense of certainty. 'Vedehanti' refers to the lord of the kingdom of Videha. 'Mithilaggahanti' means 'possessing a house in Mithilā', that is, one who lives having taken up a residence in Mithilā. 'Ājaññāti' means those who know what is appropriate and what is not. 'Yathā haṃsā vinīlakanti' means 'just as these mallards carry me, Vinīlaka, so do they carry him'.

Haṃsapotakā [V 2.0032] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā kujjhitvā “idheva naṃ pātetvā gamissāmā”ti cittaṃ uppādetvāpi “evaṃ kate pitā no kiṃ vakkhatī”ti garahabhayena pitu santikaṃ netvā tena katakiriyaṃ pitu ācikkhiṃsu. Atha naṃ pitā kujjhitvā “kiṃ tvaṃ mama puttehi adhikatarosi, yo mama putte abhibhavitvā rathe yuttasindhave viya karosi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsi. Imaṃ ṭhānaṃ tava agocaro, attano mātu vasanaṭṭhānameva gacchāhī”ti tajjetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, the young mallards became angry and thought, 'We will drop him right here and go.' But then they thought, 'If we do this, what will our father say?' and fearing a rebuke, they took him to their father and reported what he had done. Then the father, enraged, scolded him: 'Are you superior to my sons, you who treat my sons as if they were Sindh horses yoked to a chariot? You do not know your own measure. This place is not your feeding ground. Go to your mother’s dwelling place,' and then spoke the second verse:

20.

20.

“Vinīla duggaṃ bhajasi, abhūmiṃ tāta sevasi;

Gāmantakāni sevassu, etaṃ mātālayaṃ tavā”ti.

"Vinīla, you frequent a difficult place, you resort to a place that is not your ground, dear one; resort to the village outskirts, for that is your mother’s home."

Tattha vinīlāti taṃ nāmenālapati. Duggaṃ bhajasīti imesaṃ vasena giriduggaṃ bhajasi. Abhūmiṃ, tāta, sevasīti, tāta, girivisamaṃ nāma tava abhūmi[M 2.0036], taṃ sevasi upagacchasi. Etaṃ mātālayaṃ tavāti etaṃ gāmantaṃ ukkāraṭṭhānaṃ āmakasusānaṭṭhānañca tava mātu ālayaṃ gehaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha gacchāhīti. Evaṃ taṃ tajjetvā “gacchatha, naṃ mithilanagarassa ukkārabhūmiyaññeva otāretvā ethā”ti putte āṇāpesi, te tathā akaṃsu.

Here, 'vinīlāti' is addressing him by name. 'Duggaṃ bhajasīti' means 'you frequent a mountain-gorge' by means of these mallards. 'Abhūmiṃ, tāta, sevasīti' means, 'dear one, the uneven mountain terrain is not your ground, yet you frequent it, you approach it.' 'Etaṃ mātālayaṃ tavāti' means 'this village outskirts, the refuse dump, and the charnel ground is the home of your mother, her dwelling place; go there.' Having thus rebuked him, he ordered his sons: 'Go, drop him at the refuse dump of the city of Mithilā and then return.' They did so.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vinīlako devadatto ahosi, dve haṃsapotakā dve aggasāvakā ahesuṃ, pitā ānando ahosi, videharājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, Vinīlaka was Devadatta, the two young mallards were the two chief disciples, the father was Ānanda, and the King of Videha was I myself.'

Vinīlajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The tenth: The Explanation of the Vinīla Jātaka.

Daḷhavaggo paṭhamo.

The first chapter: The Daḷhavagga (The Chapter on Firmness).

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary is:

Rājovādañca siṅgālaṃ, sūkaraṃ uragaṃ bhaggaṃ;

Alīnacittaguṇañca, suhanu moravinīlaṃ.

Royal Counsel, Jackal, Pig, Snake, Bhagga; Alīnacitta, Guṇa, Suhanu, Mora, and Vinīla.

2. Santhavavaggo

2. The Intimacy Chapter

[161] 1. Indasamānagottajātakavaṇṇanā

[161] 1. The Explanation of the Indasamānagotta Jātaka

Na [V 2.0033][P 2.0041] santhavaṃ kāpurisena kayirāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dubbacajātikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa vatthu navakanipāte gijjhajātake (jā. 1.9.1 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ “pubbepi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, dubbacatāya paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā mattahatthipādehi sañcuṇṇito”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“One should not associate with a base person”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was difficult to admonish. The story of this will appear in the Gijjha Jātaka of the Ninth Nipāta. The Teacher then said to that monk: 'In the past too, monk, because of your obstinacy, not heeding the words of the wise, you were crushed to pieces by the feet of a rutting elephant,' and he related the past incident.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vuḍḍhippatto gharāvāsaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcannaṃ isisatānaṃ gaṇasatthā hutvā himavantapadese vāsaṃ kappesi. Tadā tesu tāpasesu indasamānagotto nāmeko tāpaso [M 2.0037] ahosi dubbaco anovādako. So ekaṃ hatthipotakaṃ posesi. Bodhisatto sutvā taṃ pakkositvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ hatthipotakaṃ posesī”ti pucchi. “Saccaṃ, ācariya, matamātikaṃ ekaṃ hatthipotakaṃ posemī”ti. “Hatthino nāma vuḍḍhippattā posakeyeva mārenti, mā taṃ posehī”ti. “Tena vinā vattituṃ na sakkomi ācariyā”ti. “Tena hi paññāyissasī”ti. So tena posiyamāno aparabhāge mahāsarīro ahosi.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. Having reached maturity, he gave up the household life, took up the ascetic life of a seer, and became the leader of a group of five hundred ascetics, living in the Himalayan region. At that time, among those ascetics was one named Indasamānagotta, who was difficult to admonish and unteachable. He raised a young elephant. Hearing of this, the Bodhisatta summoned him and asked: 'Is it true, as they say, that you are raising a young elephant?' 'It is true, teacher; I am raising a young elephant whose mother had died.' 'Elephants, when they reach maturity, kill even those who raise them; do not raise it.' 'I cannot live without it, teacher.' 'Then it will become known to you.' As it was being raised by him, in due course it became large in body.

Athekasmiṃ kāle te isayo vanamūlaphalāphalatthāya dūraṃ gantvā tattheva katipāhaṃ vasiṃsu. Hatthīpi aggadakkhiṇavāte pabhinnamado hutvā tassa paṇṇasālaṃ viddhaṃsetvā pānīyaghaṭaṃ bhinditvā pāsāṇaphalakaṃ khipitvā ālambanaphalakaṃ luñcitvā “taṃ tāpasaṃ māretvāva gamissāmī”ti ekaṃ gahanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā tassa āgamanamaggaṃ olokento aṭṭhāsi. Indasamānagotto tassa gocaraṃ [P 2.0042] gahetvā sabbesaṃ puratova āgacchanto taṃ disvā pakatisaññāyevassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ so hatthī gahanaṭṭhānā nikkhamitvā soṇḍāya parāmasitvā bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā sīsaṃ pādena akkamitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā madditvā koñcanādaṃ katvā araññaṃ pāvisi. Sesatāpasā taṃ pavattiṃ bodhisattassa ārocesuṃ[V 2.0034]. Bodhisatto “kāpurisehi nāma saddhiṃ saṃsaggo na kātabbo”ti vatvā imā gāthā āha –

Once, the 178 ascetics went far away to gather wild roots and fruits and stayed there for two or three days. The elephant, whose temporal fluid began to flow due to the early southern wind, entered Indasamānagotta's leaf hut, broke the water pot, threw aside the stone slab, and tore down the support plank. Thinking, “I will kill that ascetic and then leave,” he entered a dense thicket and stood watching the path for his return. Indasamānagotta, having gathered food for the elephant and returning ahead of all the others, saw the elephant and approached it with his usual familiarity. Then the elephant, emerging from the thicket, grabbed him firmly with its trunk, threw him to the ground, trampled his head with its foot, crushed him to death, trumpeted a cry like a crane, and entered the forest. The remaining ascetics reported the incident to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta said, “One should not associate with a base person,” and spoke these verses:

21.

21.

“Na santhavaṃ kāpurisena kayirā, ariyo anariyena pajānamatthaṃ;

Cirānuvutthopi karoti pāpaṃ, gajo yathā indasamānagottaṃ.

“A noble person, knowing what is beneficial, should not associate with an ignoble, base person. Even after living together for a long time, an ignoble person does evil, just as the elephant did to Indasamānagotta.”

22.

22.

“Yaṃ tveva jaññā sadiso mamanti, sīlena paññāya sutena cāpi;

Teneva mettiṃ kayirātha saddhiṃ, sukho have sappurisena saṅgamo”ti.

“One should cultivate friendship with only that person whom one knows to be one’s equal in virtue, wisdom, and learning; for association with a good person is indeed pleasant.”

Tattha na santhavaṃ kāpurisena kayirāti kucchitena kodhapurisena saddhiṃ taṇhāsanthavaṃ vā mittasanthavaṃ vā na kayirātha. Ariyo anariyena pajānamatthanti [M 2.0038] ariyoti cattāro ariyā ācāraariyo liṅgaariyo dassanaariyo paṭivedhaariyoti. Tesu ācāraariyo idha adhippeto. So pajānamatthaṃ atthaṃ pajānanto atthānatthakusalo ācāre ṭhito ariyapuggalo anariyena nillajjena dussīlena saddhiṃ santhavaṃ na kareyyāti attho. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Cirānuvutthopi karoti pāpanti, yasmā anariyo ciraṃ ekato anuvutthopi taṃ ekato nivāsaṃ agaṇetvā karoti pāpaṃ lāmakakammaṃ karotiyeva. Yathā kiṃ? Gajo yathā indasamānagottanti, yathā so gajo indasamānagottaṃ mārento pāpaṃ akāsīti attho. Yaṃ tveva jaññā sadiso mamantiādīsu yaṃ tveva puggalaṃ “ayaṃ mama sīlādīhi sadiso”ti jāneyya, teneva saddhiṃ mettiṃ kayirātha, sappurisena saddhiṃ samāgamo sukhāvahoti.

There, “one should not associate with a base person” means one should not form a bond of craving or a bond of friendship with a contemptible, angry person. “A noble one, knowing what is beneficial” refers to four types of noble ones: noble in conduct, noble in outward signs, noble in vision, and noble in realization. Among these, the one noble in conduct is intended here. The meaning is that a noble person, who understands what is beneficial, is skilled in discerning benefit and harm, and is established in good conduct, should not form an association with a shameless, immoral, ignoble person. Why? “Because even after long association, he does evil”—because an ignoble person, even after living together for a long time, disregarding that shared living, commits evil, performing base deeds. “Just as the elephant did to Indasamānagotta” means just as that elephant, by killing Indasamānagotta, committed a wicked act. In the lines beginning “If one should know someone to be one’s equal,” it means that if one recognizes a person, “This one is like me in virtue and so forth,” one should cultivate friendship with that person alone, for association with a good person brings happiness.

Evaṃ [P 2.0043] bodhisatto “anovādakena nāma na bhavitabbaṃ, susikkhitena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti isigaṇaṃ ovaditvā indasamānagottassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus the Bodhisatta, advising the group of ascetics, “One should not be unteachable; one should be well-behaved according to the instructions of the wise,” and after having the funeral rites performed for Indasamānagotta, cultivated the divine abidings and was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā indasamānagotto ayaṃ dubbaco ahosi, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, this unteachable monk was Indasamānagotta, and I myself was the teacher of the group of ascetics.”

Indasamānagottajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Indasamānagotta Jātaka is finished.

[162] 2. Santhavajātakavaṇṇanā

[162] 2. 2. Santhava Jātaka

The Ascetic and the Fire

Na [V 2.0035] santhavasmā paramatthi pāpiyoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aggijuhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā naṅguṭṭhajātake (jā. 1.1.144 ādayo) kathitasadisameva. Bhikkhū te aggiṃ juhante disvā “bhante, jaṭilā nānappakāraṃ micchātapaṃ karonti, atthi nu kho ettha vuḍḍhī”ti bhagavantaṃ pucchiṃsu. “Na, bhikkhave, etthakāci vuḍḍhi nāma atthi, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi aggijuhane vuḍḍhi atthīti saññāya ciraṃ aggiṃ juhitvā tasmiṃ kamme avuḍḍhimeva disvā [M 2.0039] aggiṃ udakena nibbāpetvā sākhādīhi pothetvā puna nivattitvāpi na olokesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“There is no greater evil than intimacy”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the fire sacrifice. The story is just as it was told below in the Naṅguṭṭha Jātaka of the Eka-Nipāta. The monks, seeing those matted-hair ascetics offering the fire sacrifice, asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, these ascetics practice various kinds of false asceticism. Is there any benefit in this?” The Blessed One replied: “Monks, there is no benefit whatsoever in false asceticism. In the past, wise men also offered fire for a long time, thinking there was benefit in the fire sacrifice. But seeing only the lack of benefit in that action, they extinguished the fire with water, beat it with branches and so forth, and never looked back at it.” Having said this, he related the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Mātāpitaro tassa jātaggiṃ gahetvā taṃ soḷasavassuddese ṭhitaṃ āhaṃsu – “kiṃ, tāta, jātaggiṃ gahetvā araññe aggiṃ paricarissasi, udāhu tayo vede uggaṇhitvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā gharāvāsaṃ vasissasī”ti. So “na me gharāvāsena attho, araññe aggiṃ paricaritvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo bhavissāmī”ti jātaggiṃ gahetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā araññaṃ pavisitvā paṇṇasālāya vāsaṃ kappetvā aggiṃ paricari. So ekadivasaṃ nimantitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā sappinā pāyāsaṃ labhitvā “imaṃ pāyāsaṃ mahābrahmuno yajissāmī”ti taṃ pāyāsaṃ [P 2.0044] āharitvā aggiṃ jāletvā “aggiṃ tāva bhavantaṃ sappiyuttaṃ pāyāsaṃ pāyemī”ti pāyāsaṃ aggimhi pakkhipi. Bahusinehe pāyāse aggimhi pakkhittamatteyeva aggi jalitvā paccuggatāhi accīhi paṇṇasālaṃ jhāpesi. Brāhmaṇo bhītatasito palāyitvā bahi ṭhatvā “kāpurisehi nāma santhavo na kātabbo, idāni me iminā agginā kicchena katā paṇṇasālā jhāpitā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. On the day of his birth, his parents lit a birth-fire, and when he was sixteen years old, they said to him: “Dear son, will you take the birth-fire and tend it in the forest, or will you learn the three Vedas, establish a household, and live the life of a householder?” He replied, “I have no desire for the householder’s life. I will take the birth-fire, tend it in the forest, and be destined for the Brahma world.” Taking the birth-fire, he paid homage to his parents and entered the forest, where he lived in a leaf-hut and tended the fire. One day, after going to a place where he was invited for a meal, he received milk-rice mixed with ghee. Thinking, “I will offer this milk-rice to the Great Brahma,” he brought it back, lit the fire, and said, “Honorable Fire-King, first I will let you drink this milk-rice mixed with ghee,” and he placed the milk-rice in the fire. As soon as the milk-rice, which contained much ghee, was placed in the fire, the flames blazed up and reached high, burning down his leaf-hut. The brahmin was terrified and fled, and standing outside, he said, “One should not associate with base people. Now this fire has burned down my leaf-hut that was built with such difficulty!” Then he spoke this first stanza:

23.

23.

“Na santhavasmā paramatthi pāpiyo, yo santhavo kāpurisena hoti;

Santappito sappinā pāyasena, kicchākataṃ paṇṇakuṭiṃ adayhī”ti.

“There is no evil greater than intimacy with a base person. Though sated with ghee and milk-rice, he burned down the leaf-hut made with such effort.”

Tattha na santhavasmāti taṇhāsanthavāpi ca mittasanthavāpi cāti duvidhāpi etasmā santhavā paraṃ uttari aññaṃ pāpataraṃ natthi, lāmakataraṃ nāma natthīti attho. Yo santhavo kāpurisenāti yo pāpakena kāpurisena saddhiṃ duvidhopi santhavo, tato pāpataraṃ aññaṃ natthi. Kasmā? Santappito [V 2.0036] …pe…adayhīti, yasmā sappinā ca pāyāsena ca santappitopi ayaṃ aggi mayā kicchena kataṃ paṇṇasālaṃ jhāpesīti attho.

Here, “There is no evil greater than intimacy” means that there is no other association more inferior or wretched than these two types of intimacy: intimacy based on craving and intimacy based on friendship. “Intimacy with a base person” means any association of either of these two types with an evil, base person; there is nothing worse than that. Why? “Though sated with ghee and milk-rice, he burned down” means that even though this fire was gratified with ghee and milk-rice, it burned down the leaf-hut I had built with difficulty. This is the meaning.

So evaṃ vatvā “na me tayā mittadubbhinā attho”ti taṃ aggiṃ udakena nibbāpetvā sākhāhi pothetvā antohimavantaṃ pavisitvā ekaṃ sāmamigiṃ sīhassa ca byagghassa ca dīpino ca mukhaṃ lehantiṃ disvā [M 2.0040] “sappurisehi saddhiṃ santhavā paraṃ seyyo nāma natthī”ti cintetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, he said, “I have no need of you, a friend who betrays,” and extinguished that fire with water, beat it with branches, and entered the Himalayas. There he saw a doe named Sāmā—so called because she was golden-colored—licking the mouths of a lion, a tiger, and a leopard. Reflecting, “There is truly no better intimacy than with good people,” he uttered the second verse:

24.

24.

“Na santhavasmā paramatthi seyyo, yo santhavo sappurisena hoti;
