Sīhassa [P 2.0045] byagghassa ca dīpino ca, sāmā mukhaṃ lehati santhavenā”ti.

“Nothing is better than intimacy, that is, intimacy with a good person; Sāmā licks the mouths of a lion, a tiger, and a leopard through intimacy.”

Tattha sāmā mukhaṃ lehati santhavenāti sāmā nāma migī imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ santhavena sinehena mukhaṃ lehatīti.

There, “Sāmā licks the mouths through intimacy” means that the doe named Sāmā licks the mouths of these three animals with affection and fondness because of their intimacy.

Evaṃ vatvā bodhisatto antohimavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā jīvitapariyosāne brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Having said this, the Bodhisatta entered the Himalayas, took up the ascetic life of a sage, developed the higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments, and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tena samayena tāpaso ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the ascetic was indeed myself.”

Santhavajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Santhava Jātaka: The Second.

[163] 3. Susīmajātakavaṇṇanā

[163] 3. The Commentary on the Susīma Jātaka

Kāḷā migā setadantā tavīmeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto chandakadānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi kadāci ekameva kulaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ deti, kadāci aññatitthiyānaṃ deti, kadāci gaṇabandhanena bahū ekato hutvā denti, kadāci vīthisabhāgena, kadāci sakalanagaravāsino chandakaṃ saṃharitvā dānaṃ denti. Imasmiṃ pana kāle sakalanagaravāsino chandakaṃ saṃharitvā sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ sajjetvā dve koṭṭhāsā hutvā ekacce “imaṃ sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ dassāmā”ti āhaṃsu, ekacce “buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassā”ti. Evaṃ punappunaṃ kathāya vattamānāya aññatitthiyasāvakehi aññatitthiyānaññeva[V 2.0037], buddhasāvakehi “‘buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassevā’ti vutte sambahulaṃ karisāmā”ti sambahulāya kathāya “buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dassāmā”ti vadantāyeva bahukā jātā, tesaññeva kathā patiṭṭhāsi[M 2.0041]. Aññatitthiyasāvakā buddhānaṃ dātabbadānassa antarāyaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Nāgarā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā sattame divase sabbaparikkhāre adaṃsu. Satthā anumodanaṃ katvā mahājanaṃ maggaphalehi [P 2.0046] pabodhetvā jetavanavihārameva gantvā bhikkhusaṅghena vatte dassite gandhakuṭippamukhe ṭhatvā sugatovādaṃ datvā gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi.

“These black deer with white tusks are yours”—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a voluntary subscription. In Sāvatthī, sometimes a single family would give alms to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, sometimes to followers of other sects, sometimes many would gather together by association to give, sometimes by street section, and sometimes all the city-dwellers would collect a voluntary subscription and give alms. At this time, all the city-dwellers collected a voluntary subscription and prepared a gift of all requisites, dividing into two groups. Some said, 'We will give this gift of all requisites to the followers of other sects,' while others said, 'To the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.' As this discussion went on repeatedly, the disciples of other sects argued for the followers of other sects alone, while the disciples of the Buddha said, 'If it is said, “To the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha,” we will follow the majority.' Through the majority opinion, those who said, 'We will give to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha,' became the majority, and their word prevailed. The disciples of other sects could not obstruct the offering to be given to the Buddha. The citizens invited the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and held a great almsgiving for seven days. On the seventh day, they presented all the requisites. The Teacher gave a discourse of appreciation, awakened the people to the paths and their fruits, and then returned to Jetavana Monastery. After the Sangha of bhikkhus had performed their duties, he stood at the entrance to the Perfumed Chamber, gave an exhortation of the Sugata, and then entered the Perfumed Chamber.

Sāyanhasamaye bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitvā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, aññatitthiyasāvakā buddhānaṃ dātabbadānassa antarāyakaraṇatthāya vāyamantāpi antarāyaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, taṃ sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ buddhānaṃyeva pādamūlaṃ āgataṃ, aho buddhabalaṃ nāma mahanta”nti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, ete aññatitthiyasāvakā idāneva mayhaṃ dātabbadānassa antarāyakaraṇatthāya vāyamanti, pubbepi vāyamiṃsu, so pana parikkhāro sabbakālepi mameva pādamūlaṃ āgacchatī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

In the evening, the bhikkhus gathered in the Hall of Dhamma and raised a topic of conversation: 'Friends, even though the disciples of other sects strove to create an obstacle to the offering to be given to the Buddha, they were unable to do so. That offering of all requisites came to the very feet of the Buddha. Ah, indeed, the power of the Buddha is great!' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Bhikkhus, for what topic of conversation are you now assembled here?' When they replied, 'For this one,' he said, 'Bhikkhus, it is not only now that these disciples of other sects strive to create an obstacle to the offering to be given to me. They strove in the past as well. But that offering has, at all times, come to my feet alone.' Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ susīmo nāma rājā ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto tassa purohitassa brāhmaṇiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, tassa soḷasavassikakāle pitā kālamakāsi. So pana dharamānakāle rañño hatthimaṅgalakārako ahosi. Hatthīnaṃ maṅgalakaraṇaṭṭhāne ābhataupakaraṇabhaṇḍañca hatthālaṅkārañca sabbaṃ soyeva alattha. Evamassa ekekasmiṃ maṅgale koṭimattaṃ dhanaṃ uppajjati. Atha tasmiṃ kāle hatthimaṅgalachaṇo sampāpuṇi. Sesā brāhmaṇā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mahārāja, hatthimaṅgalachaṇo sampatto, maṅgalaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Purohitabrāhmaṇassa pana putto atidaharo, neva tayo vede jānāti, na hatthisuttaṃ, mayaṃ hatthimaṅgalaṃ karissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Brāhmaṇā purohitaputtassa hatthimaṅgalaṃ kātuṃ adatvā “hatthimaṅgalaṃ katvā mayaṃ dhanaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā vicaranti. Atha “catutthe divase hatthimaṅgalaṃ bhavissatī”ti bodhisattassa mātā [P 2.0047] taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “hatthimaṅgalakaraṇaṃ nāma yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā amhākaṃ vaṃso, vaṃso ca no osakkissati, dhanā ca parihāyissāmā”ti anusocamānā parodi.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Susīma reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the brahmin wife of the king's royal priest. When he was sixteen years old, his father passed away. During his lifetime, the father had been the performer of the elephant festival for the king. Whatever equipment and elephant ornaments were brought to the place of the elephant festival, he alone received them all. Thus, from each festival, wealth amounting to a crore arose for him. Then, a time for the elephant festival arrived. The other brahmins approached the king and said, 'Great king, the elephant festival has arrived; the ceremony should be performed. But the royal priest's son is very young; he knows neither the three Vedas nor the elephant lore. We will perform the elephant festival.' The king agreed, saying, 'Very well.' The brahmins, not allowing the royal priest's son to perform the elephant festival, went about joyful and delighted, thinking, 'Having performed the elephant festival, we will take the wealth.' When the Bodhisatta's mother heard that the elephant festival would take place on the fourth day, she wept in sorrow, saying, 'The performance of the elephant festival has been our family tradition for seven generations. Our lineage will now be broken, and we will lose our wealth.'

Bodhisatto [V 2.0038][M 2.0042] “kasmā, amma, rodasī”ti vatvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā “nanu, amma, ahaṃ maṅgalaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. “Tāta, tvaṃ neva tayo vede jānāsi, na hatthisuttaṃ, kathaṃ maṅgalaṃ karissasī”ti. “Amma, kadā pana hatthimaṅgalaṃ karissatī”ti? “Ito catutthe divase, tātā”ti. “Amma, tayo pana vede paguṇe katvā hatthisuttaṃ jānanakaācariyo kahaṃ vasatī”ti? “Tāta, evarūpo disāpāmokkho ācariyo ito vīsayojanasatamatthake gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilāyaṃ vasatī”ti. “Amma, amhākaṃ vaṃsaṃ na nāsessāmi, ahaṃ sve ekadivaseneva takkasilaṃ gantvā ekaratteneva tayo vede ca hatthisuttañca uggaṇhitvā punadivase āgantvā catutthe divase hatthimaṅgalaṃ karissāmi, mā rodī”ti mātaraṃ samassāsetvā punadivase bodhisatto pātova bhuñjitvā ekakova nikkhamitvā ekadivaseneva takkasilaṃ gantvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

The Bodhisatta asked, 'Why are you weeping, mother?' and after hearing the reason, he said, 'Mother, will I not perform the festival?' 'Dear son, you know neither the three Vedas nor the elephant lore; how will you perform the festival?' 'Mother, when will the elephant festival be performed?' 'On the fourth day from now, dear son.' 'Mother, where lives the teacher who has mastered the three Vedas and knows the elephant lore?' 'Dear son, such a world-renowned teacher lives in Takkasilā, in the Gandhāra country, one hundred and twenty leagues from here.' 'Mother, I will not let our lineage be destroyed. Tomorrow, I will go to Takkasilā in a single day, learn the three Vedas and the elephant lore in one night, return the following day, and perform the elephant festival on the fourth day. Do not weep.' Having consoled his mother, the Bodhisatta ate early the next morning and set out alone. By the power of the Bodhisatta, and because the deities shortened the earth, he reached Takkasilā in a single day. He paid homage to the teacher and sat down to one side.

Atha naṃ ācariyo “kuto āgatosi, tātā”ti pucchi. “Bārāṇasito, ācariyā”ti. “Kenatthenā”ti? “Tumhākaṃ santike tayo vede ca hatthisuttañca uggaṇhanatthāyā”ti. “Sādhu, tāta, uggaṇhā”ti. Bodhisatto “ācariya, mayhaṃ kammaṃ accāyika”nti sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “ahaṃ ekadivaseneva vīsayojanasataṃ āgato, ajjevekarattiṃ mayhameva okāsaṃ karotha, ito tatiyadivase hatthimaṅgalaṃ bhavissati, ahaṃ ekeneva uddesamaggena sabbaṃ uggaṇhissāmī”ti vatvā ācariyaṃ okāsaṃ kāretvā ācariyassa bhuttakāle sayaṃ bhuñjitvā ācariyassa pāde dhovitvā sahassatthavikaṃ purato ṭhapetvā [P 2.0048] vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno pariyattiṃ paṭṭhapetvā aruṇe uggacchante tayo vede ca hatthisuttañca niṭṭhapetvā “aññopi atthi, ācariyā”ti pucchitvā “natthi tāta, sabbaṃ niṭṭhita”nti vutte “ācariya, imasmiṃ ganthe ettakaṃ padapaccābhaṭṭhaṃ, ettakaṃ sajjhāyasammohaṭṭhānaṃ, ito paṭṭhāya tumhe antevāsike evaṃ vāceyyāthā”ti ācariyassa sippaṃ sodhetvā pātova bhuñjitvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā ekadivaseneva bārāṇasiṃ paccāgantvā mātaraṃ vanditvā “uggahitaṃ te, tāta, sippa”nti vutte “āma, ammā”ti vatvā mātaraṃ paritosesi.

Then the teacher asked him, 'From where have you come, dear son?' 'From Bārāṇasī, teacher.' 'For what purpose?' 'To learn the three Vedas and the elephant lore from you.' 'Very well, dear son, learn them.' The Bodhisatta explained that his business was urgent and told him everything, saying, 'Teacher, I have traveled one hundred and twenty leagues in a single day. Please give me an opportunity tonight alone. The elephant festival will be on the third day from now. I will learn everything in a single course of instruction.' Having obtained the teacher's permission, he ate after the teacher had finished, washed the teacher's feet, placed a purse of a thousand pieces before him, paid homage, and, sitting to one side, began his studies. By dawn, through the power of his wisdom, he had completed the three Vedas and the elephant lore. He asked, 'Is there anything else, teacher?' When told, 'No, dear son, all is finished,' he said, 'Teacher, in this text, there are this many misapplied words and this many points of confusion in recitation. From now on, do not teach your pupils in this way.' Having thus corrected the teacher's craft, he ate early, paid homage to the teacher, and returned to Bārāṇasī in a single day. When his mother asked, 'Have you learned the craft, dear son?' he replied, 'Yes, mother,' and made her happy.

Punadivase [M 2.0043] hatthimaṅgalachaṇo paṭiyādiyittha. Satamatte hatthisoṇḍālaṅkāre ca suvaṇṇaddhaje hemajālasañchanne katvā ṭhapesuṃ, rājaṅgaṇaṃ alaṅkariṃsu. Brāhmaṇā “mayaṃ hatthimaṅgalaṃ karissāma, mayaṃ karissāmā”ti maṇḍitapasādhitā aṭṭhaṃsu. Susīmopi rājā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito upakaraṇabhaṇḍaṃ gāhāpetvā maṅgalaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Bodhisattopi kumāraparihārena alaṅkato attano parisāya purakkhataparivārito rañño santikaṃ gantvā “saccaṃ kira, mahārāja, tumhe amhākaṃ [V 2.0039] vaṃsañca attano vaṃsañca nāsetvā ‘aññehi brāhmaṇehi hatthimaṅgalaṃ kāretvā hatthālaṅkārañca upakaraṇāni ca tesaṃ dassāmā’ti avacutthā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The next day, preparations for the elephant festival were made. About a hundred elephant-trunk ornaments and golden banners covered with golden nets were prepared; the palace courtyard was decorated. The brahmins, adorned and embellished, stood there saying, 'We will perform the elephant festival, we will perform it!' King Susīma, adorned with all ornaments, had the ceremonial equipment brought and went to the festival grounds. The Bodhisatta, adorned with the attendance of a prince and surrounded by his retinue, went to the king and said, 'Is it true, great king, that you, destroying both our lineage and your own, have said, "Having other brahmins perform the elephant festival, I will give the elephant ornaments and equipment to them"?' and he spoke the first verse:

25.

25.

“Kāḷā migā setadantā tavīme, parosataṃ hemajālābhichannā;

Te te dadāmīti susīma brūsi, anussaraṃ pettipitāmahāna”nti.

‘These black elephants of yours with white tusks, more than a hundred, covered with golden nets; "These I give to you," so you say, Susīma, while recalling the tradition of your fathers and grandfathers.’

Tattha te te dadāmīti susīma brūsīti te ete tava santake “kāḷā migā setadantā”ti evaṃ gate parosataṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍite [P 2.0049] hatthī aññesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ dadāmīti saccaṃ kira, bho susīma, evaṃ brūsīti attho. Anussaraṃ pettipitāmahānanti amhākañca attano ca vaṃse pitupitāmahānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ sarantoyeva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, yāva sattamakulaparivaṭṭā tumhākaṃ pettipitāmahānaṃ amhākaṃ pettipitāmahā ca hatthimaṅgalaṃ karonti, so tvaṃ evaṃ anussarantopi amhākañca attano ca vaṃsaṃ nāsetvā saccaṃ kira evaṃ brūsīti.

Therein, ‘I am giving them, so you say, Susīma’ means: ‘Is it true, good Susīma, that you say you are giving these elephants of yours—described as “black beasts with white tusks,” more than a hundred of them, adorned with all ornaments—to other brahmins?’ This is the meaning. ‘While recalling your fathers and grandfathers’ means recalling the custom of the fathers and grandfathers in both our lineage and your own. This is what is said: ‘Great king, is it true that even while recalling that for seven generations our ancestors have performed the elephant ceremony for your ancestors, you, by destroying both our lineage and your own, speak thus?’

Susīmo rājā bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

King Susīma, having heard the Bodhisatta's words, spoke the second verse:

26.

26.

“Kāḷā migā setadantā mamīme, parosataṃ hemajālābhichannā;

Te te dadāmīti vadāmi māṇava, anussaraṃ pettipitāmahāna”nti.

“These black beasts with white tusks are mine, more than a hundred, covered with golden nets; ‘I give them,’ I say, young man, while recalling my fathers and grandfathers.”

Tattha [M 2.0044] te te dadāmīti te ete hatthī aññesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ dadāmīti saccameva māṇava vadāmi, neva hatthī brāhmaṇānaṃ dadāmīti attho. Anussaranti pettipitāmahānaṃ kiriyaṃ anussarāmiyeva, no nānussarāmi, amhākaṃ pettipitāmahānaṃ hatthimaṅgalaṃ tumhākaṃ pettipitāmahā karontīti pana anussarantopi evaṃ vadāmiyevāti adhippāyenevamāha.

Therein, regarding ‘I give them,’ he means: ‘I truly say, young man, that I am giving these elephants to other brahmins; the meaning is that I am not giving the elephants to [your family of] brahmins.’ As for ‘while recalling,’ he means: ‘I do indeed recall the deeds of my fathers and grandfathers; it is not that I do not recall. However, even while recalling that your ancestors performed the elephant ceremony for our ancestors, I still speak thus.’ With this intention he spoke.

Atha naṃ bodhisatto etadavoca – “mahārāja, amhākañca attano ca vaṃsaṃ anussarantoyeva kasmā maṃ ṭhapetvā aññehi hatthimaṅgalaṃ kārāpethā”ti. “Tvaṃ kira, tāta, tayo vede hatthisuttañca na jānāsī”ti mayhaṃ ārocesuṃ, tenāhaṃ aññehi brāhmaṇehi kārāpemīti. “Tena hi, mahārāja, ettakesu brāhmaṇesu ekabrāhmaṇopi tīsu vedesu vā hatthisuttesu vā ekadesampi yadi mayā saddhiṃ kathetuṃ samatto atthi, uṭṭhahatu, tayopi vede hatthisuttañca saddhiṃ hatthimaṅgalakaraṇena maṃ ṭhapetvā añño sakalajambudīpepi jānanto nāma [P 2.0050] natthī”ti [V 2.0040] sīhanādaṃ nadi. Ekabrāhmaṇopi tassa paṭisattu hutvā uṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi. Bodhisatto attano kulavaṃsaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā maṅgalaṃ katvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ ādāya attano nivesanaṃ agamāsi.

Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “Great king, while recalling both our lineage and your own, why do you, excluding me, have the elephant ceremony performed by others?” “They informed me, dear one, that you do not know the three Vedas nor the elephant lore, which is why I am having it performed by other brahmins.” “Well then, great king, if among all these brahmins even a single one is capable of discussing with me even a portion of the three Vedas or the elephant lore, let him stand up. Apart from me, there is no one in all of Jambudīpa who knows the three Vedas and the elephant lore along with the performance of the elephant ceremony!” he roared a lion's roar. Not a single brahmin was able to rise and be his adversary. The Bodhisatta, having established his family lineage, performed the ceremony, received much wealth, and returned to his dwelling.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne keci sotāpannā ahesuṃ, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. “Tadā mātā mahāmāyā ahosi, pitā suddhodanamahārājā, susīmo rājā ānando, disāpāmokkho ācariyo sāriputto, māṇavo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the truths, connected the Jātaka. At the end of the truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some attained arahantship. “At that time, the mother was Mahāmāyā, the father was King Suddhodana, King Susīma was Ānanda, the world-renowned teacher was Sāriputta, and I myself was the young brahmin.”

Susīmajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The commentary on the Susīma Jātaka, the third.

[164] 4. Gijjhajātakavaṇṇanā

[164] 4. Commentary on the Gijjha Jātaka

Yaṃ [M 2.0045] nu gijjho yojanasatanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ mātuposakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu sāmajātake (jā. 2.22.296 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, gihī posesī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte “kiṃ pana te hontī”ti pucchitvā “mātāpitaro me, bhante”ti vutte “sādhu sādhū”ti tassa sādhukāraṃ datvā “mā, bhikkhave, imaṃ bhikkhuṃ ujjhāyittha, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi guṇavasena aññātakānampi upakāraṃ akaṃsu, imassa pana mātāpitūnaṃ upakārakaraṇaṃ bhāroyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The vulture for a hundred leagues…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a monk who supported his mother. The story will be made clear in the Sāma Jātaka. The Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you support a layperson?” When he replied, “It is true,” the Teacher asked, “And who are they to you?” When he said, “They are my parents, venerable sir,” the Teacher gave his approval, saying, “Good, good!” He then said to the monks, “Monks, do not find fault with this monk. Even the wise of old, on account of virtue, helped those unrelated to them. For this monk, helping his parents is truly his responsibility.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gijjhakūṭapabbate gijjhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā mātāpitaro poseti. Athekasmiṃ kāle mahatī vātavuṭṭhi ahosi. Gijjhā vātavuṭṭhiṃ sahituṃ asakkontā sītabhayena bārāṇasiṃ gantvā pākārasamīpe ca parikhāsamīpe ca sītena kampamānā nisīdiṃsu. Tadā bārāṇasiseṭṭhi nagarā nikkhamitvā nhāyituṃ gacchanto te gijjhe kilamante disvā ekasmiṃ anovassakaṭṭhāne sannipātetvā aggiṃ kārāpetvā gosusānaṃ pesetvā gomaṃsaṃ āharāpetvā tesaṃ dāpetvā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Gijjhā vūpasantāya vātavuṭṭhiyā [P 2.0051] kallasarīrā hutvā pabbatameva agamaṃsu. Te tattheva sannipatitvā evaṃ mantayiṃsu – “bārāṇasiseṭṭhinā amhākaṃ upakāro kato, katūpakārassa ca nāma paccupakāraṃ kātuṃ [V 2.0041] vaṭṭati, tasmā ito paṭṭhāya tumhesu yo yaṃ vatthaṃ vā ābharaṇaṃ vā labhati, tena taṃ bārāṇasiseṭṭhissa gehe ākāsaṅgaṇe pātetabba”nti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into the vulture species on Vulture Peak Mountain and supported his parents. At one time, a great storm of wind and rain arose. Unable to endure the storm, and fearing the cold, the vultures went to Bārāṇasī and sat trembling with cold near the city walls and the moat. At that time, the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī, leaving the city to bathe, saw the vultures suffering. He gathered them in a place sheltered from the rain, had a fire lit, sent to the cattle charnel ground to have cow meat brought, and had it given to them, stationing a guard for their protection. When the storm had subsided, the vultures, their bodies restored, returned to the mountain. There they gathered and conferred, saying: “The chief merchant of Bārāṇasī has done us a kindness, and it is right to repay a kindness that has been done. Therefore, from now on, whoever among you obtains any cloth or ornament should drop it into the courtyard of the chief merchant’s house.”

Tato paṭṭhāya gijjhā manussānaṃ vatthābharaṇāni ātape sukkhāpentānaṃ pamādaṃ oloketvā senā viya maṃsapesiṃ sahasā gahetvā bārāṇasiseṭṭhissa gehe ākāsaṅgaṇe pātenti. So gijjhānaṃ āharaṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā sabbāni tāni visuṃyeva ṭhapesi. “Gijjhā nagaraṃ vilumpantī”ti rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “ekaṃ gijjhampi tāva gaṇhatha, sabbaṃ āharāpessāmī”ti tattha tattha pāse ceva jālāni ca oḍḍāpesi. Mātuposakagijjho [M 2.0046] pāse bajjhi, taṃ gahetvā “rañño dassessāmā”ti nenti. Bārāṇasiseṭṭhi rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto te manusse gijjhaṃ gahetvā gacchante disvā “mā imaṃ gijjhaṃ bādhayiṃsū”ti saddhiññeva agamāsi. Gijjhaṃ rañño dassesuṃ. Atha naṃ rājā pucchi – “tumhe nagaraṃ vilumpitvā vatthādīni gaṇhathā”ti. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Kassa tāni dinnānī”ti? “Bārāṇasiseṭṭhissā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Amhākaṃ tena jīvitaṃ dvinnaṃ, upakārassa nāma paccupakāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā adamhā”ti. Atha naṃ rājā “gijjhā kira yojanasatamatthake ṭhatvā kuṇapaṃ passanti, kasmā tvaṃ attano oḍḍitaṃ pāsaṃ na passasī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

From that time onward, the vultures, observing the carelessness of people drying their clothes and ornaments in the sun, would swiftly snatch them, like a hawk snatching a piece of meat, and drop them in the courtyard of the wealthy merchant of Bārāṇasī. Knowing that the vultures were bringing these things, he kept all those items separately. “The vultures are plundering the city!” they reported to the king. The king ordered, “First, capture just one vulture; I will make them bring everything back.” So snares and nets were set up here and there. The vulture who supported his mother was caught in a snare. Seizing him, they said, “We will show him to the king,” and took him away. As the wealthy merchant of Bārāṇasī was going to attend upon the king, he saw those men carrying the vulture. Saying, “Do not harm this vulture,” he went along with them. They presented the vulture to the king. Then the king questioned him: “Do you plunder the city and take clothes and other things?” “Yes, great king.” “To whom were those things given?” “To the wealthy merchant of Bārāṇasī.” “For what reason?” “He gave life to the two of us. It is proper to return a favor to one who has been helpful, therefore we gave them.” Then the king said to him, “They say vultures can spot a carcass from a hundred leagues away. Why did you not see the snare set for your own undoing?” And he spoke the first verse:

27.

27.

“Yaṃ nu gijjho yojanasataṃ, kuṇapāni avekkhati;

Kasmā jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhasī”ti.

“If a vulture can see a carcass from a hundred leagues away, why, having encountered a net and a snare, do you not perceive it?”

Tattha [P 2.0052] yanti nipātamattaṃ, nūti nāmatthe nipāto. Gijjho nāma yojanasataṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitāni kuṇapāni avekkhati, passatīti attho. Āsajjāpīti āsādetvāpi, sampāpuṇitvāpīti attho. “Tvaṃ attano atthāya oḍḍitaṃ jālañca pāsañca patvāpi kasmā na bujjhasī”ti pucchi.

Herein, ‘yaṃ’ is merely a particle; ‘nu’ is a particle in the sense of ‘nāma’ (indeed). ‘Gijjho… avekkhati’ means: a vulture observes, that is, it sees, carcasses situated a hundred leagues away. ‘Āsajjāpi’ means: even having encountered, even having reached. He asked: “Why, even after coming upon the net and the snare set for your own undoing, do you not perceive it?”

Gijjho tassa vacanaṃ sutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, the vulture spoke a second verse:

28.

28.

“Yadā parābhavo hoti, poso jīvitasaṅkhaye;

Atha jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhatī”ti.

“When ruin befalls a person at the end of their life, then, even when encountering a net and a snare, they do not perceive it.”

Tattha [V 2.0042] parābhavoti vināso. Posoti satto.

Herein, ‘parābhava’ means destruction. ‘Posa’ means a being.

Gijjhassa vacanaṃ sutvā rājā seṭṭhiṃ pucchi – “saccaṃ kira, mahāseṭṭhi, gijjhehi tumhākaṃ gehe vatthādīni ābhatānī”ti. “Saccaṃ, devā”ti. “Kahaṃ tānī”ti? “Deva, mayā tāni sabbāni visuṃ ṭhapitāni, yaṃ yesaṃ santakaṃ, taṃ tesaṃ dassāmi, imaṃ gijjhaṃ vissajjethā”ti gijjhaṃ vissajjāpetvā mahāseṭṭhiṃ sabbesaṃ santakāni dāpesi.

Hearing the vulture’s words, the king asked the merchant, “Is it true, great merchant, that vultures have brought clothes and other things to your house?” “It is true, Your Majesty.” “Where are they?” “Your Majesty, I have set them all aside separately, thinking, ‘I will give the property to its rightful owners.’ Please release this vulture.” Having the vulture released, the king then had the great merchant give everyone their property.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne mātuposakabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi[M 2.0047]. “Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi sāriputto, mātuposakagijjho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, the merchant of Bārāṇasī was Sāriputta, and the vulture who supported his mother was I myself.”

Gijjhajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The commentary on the Gijjha Jātaka, the fourth.

[165] 5. Nakulajātakavaṇṇanā

[165] 5. The Commentary on the Nakula Jātaka

Saddhiṃ katvā amittenāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto seṇibhaṇḍanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā uragajātake (jā. 1.2.7-8) kathitasadisameva. Idhāpi satthā “na, bhikkhave, ime dve mahāmattā idāneva mayā samaggā katā, pubbepāhaṃ ime samagge akāsiṃyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Having made an alliance with an enemy”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a quarrel between two ministers. The story is similar to the one told before in the Uraga Jātaka (Jā. 1.2.7-8). Here too, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that I have reconciled these two ministers; in the past, too, I reconciled them.” Having said this, he related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ gāmake brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ [P 2.0053] sabbasippāni uggahetvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā uñchācariyāya vanamūlaphalāhāro himavantapadese vāsaṃ kappesi. Tassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ekasmiṃ vammike nakulo, tasseva santike ekasmiṃ rukkhabile sappo ca vāsaṃ kappesi. Te ubhopi ahinakulā niccakālaṃ kalahaṃ karonti. Bodhisatto tesaṃ kalahe ādīnavañca mettābhāvanāya ca ānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā “kalahaṃ nāma akatvā samaggavāsaṃ vasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ovaditvā ubhopi te samagge akāsi. Atha sappassa bahinikkhantakāle nakulo caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ vammikassa biladvāre sīsaṃ nīharitvā mukhaṃ vivaritvā nipanno assasanto passasanto niddaṃ upagañchi. Bodhisatto taṃ tathā [V 2.0043] niddāyamānaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho te nissāya bhayaṃ uppanna”nti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain village. Having come of age and mastered all the crafts at Takkasilā, he renounced the household life and went forth as a hermit. Having developed the supernormal powers and meditative attainments, he took up residence in the Himalayan region, living on wild roots and fruits. At the end of his walking path, a mongoose lived in an anthill, and near that very same anthill, a snake lived in the hollow of a tree. Those two, a snake and a mongoose, were constantly quarreling. The Bodhisatta, explaining to them the danger in quarreling and the benefit of developing loving-kindness, advised them, “It is proper to live in harmony without quarreling,” and he reconciled them both. Then, when the snake had gone out, the mongoose, at the end of the walking path at the entrance of the anthill hole, put its head out, opened its mouth, and lay down, breathing in and out as it fell asleep. Seeing it sleeping thus, the Bodhisatta, wishing to ask, “From what has fear arisen for you?” spoke the first verse:

29.

29.

“Sandhiṃ katvā amittena, aṇḍajena jalābuja;

Vivariya dāṭhaṃ sesi, kuto te bhayamāgata”nti.

“Having made a truce with your enemy, the egg-born, O womb-born one, you lie with your mouth open. From where has fear come to you?”

Tattha [M 2.0048] sandhiṃ katvāti mittabhāvaṃ karitvā. Aṇḍajenāti aṇḍakose nibbattena nāgena. Jalābujāti nakulaṃ ālapati. So hi jalābumhi jātattā “jalābujo”ti vuccati. Vivariyāti vivaritvā.

Herein, ‘sandhiṃ katvā’ means having made friends. ‘Aṇḍajena’ means with the snake, born from an egg-shell. ‘Jalābuja’ is a term of address for the mongoose. For it is called ‘jalābuja’ (womb-born) because it is born from a womb. ‘Vivariya’ means having opened.

Evaṃ bodhisattena vutto nakulo “ayya, paccāmitto nāma na avajānitabbo āsaṅkitabboyevā”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus addressed by the Bodhisatta, the mongoose said, “Venerable sir, one should not underestimate an enemy; he should indeed be suspected,” and spoke the second verse:

30.

30.

“Saṅketheva amittasmiṃ, mittasmimpi na vissase;

Abhayā bhayamuppannaṃ, api mūlāni kantatī”ti.

“One should be suspicious of an enemy, and not trust even a friend. Fear that arises from a source of safety cuts one down even to the roots.”

Tattha abhayā bhayamuppannanti na ito te bhayamuppannanti abhayo, ko so? Mitto. Yañhi mittasmimpi vissāse sati tato bhayaṃ uppajjati, taṃ mūlānipi kantati, mittassa sabbarandhānaṃ viditattā mūlaghaccāya saṃvattatīti attho.

Herein, 'abhayā bhayamuppannaṃ' means: 'abhaya' (a source of safety) is that from which one thinks, 'no fear will arise from this.' Who is that? A friend. For when fear arises from a friend in whom one has placed trust, it cuts one down to the very roots. The meaning is that because all of a friend’s weaknesses are known, it leads to utter destruction.

Atha [P 2.0054] naṃ bodhisatto “mā bhāyi, yathā sappo tayi na dubbhati, evamahaṃ karissāmi, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya tasmiṃ āsaṅkaṃ mā karī”ti ovaditvā cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi. Tepi yathākammaṃ gatā.

Then the Bodhisatta advised him, saying, “Do not be afraid. I will ensure that the snake does not harm you. From now on, do not be suspicious of him.” Having given this advice, he developed the four divine abidings and was reborn in the Brahma world. They too passed away according to their kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sappo ca nakulo ca ime dve mahāmattā ahesuṃ, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the snake and the mongoose were these two chief ministers, and the ascetic was I myself.”

Nakulajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The explanation of the Nakula Jātaka, the fifth.

[166] 6. Upasāḷakajātakavaṇṇanā

[166] 6. The Explanation of the Upasāḷaka Jātaka

Upasāḷakanāmānīti [V 2.0044] idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ekaṃ upasāḷakaṃ nāma susānasuddhikaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira aḍḍho ahosi mahaddhano, diṭṭhigatikattā pana dhuravihāre vasantānampi buddhānaṃ saṅgahaṃ nāma na akāsi. Putto panassa paṇḍito ahosi ñāṇasampanno. So mahallakakāle puttaṃ āha – “mā kho maṃ, tāta, aññassa vasalassa jhāpitasusāne jhāpehi, ekasmiṃ pana anucchiṭṭhasusāneyeva maṃ [M 2.0049] jhāpeyyāsī”ti. “Tāta, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ jhāpetabbayuttakaṃ ṭhānaṃ na jānāmi, sādhu vata maṃ ādāya gantvā ‘imasmiṃ ṭhāne maṃ jhāpeyyāsī’ti tumheva ācikkhathā”ti. Brāhmaṇo “sādhu, tātā”ti taṃ ādāya nagarā nikkhamitvā gijjhakūṭamatthakaṃ abhiruhitvā “tāta, idaṃ aññassa vasalassa ajhāpitaṭṭhānaṃ, ettha maṃ jhāpeyyāsī”ti vatvā puttena saddhiṃ pabbatā otarituṃ ārabhi.

“Upasāḷakanāmāni” – the Teacher told this story while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning a brahmin named Upasāḷaka who was fastidious about the purity of cemeteries. He was very wealthy, but because of his adherence to wrong views, he never offered support even to the Buddhas living in the monastery nearby. His son, however, was wise and endowed with insight. In his old age, the brahmin said to his son: “Dear son, do not cremate me in a cemetery where some outcaste has been cremated. Instead, cremate me only in a cemetery that has not been used before.” The son replied: “Father, I do not know a suitable place for your cremation. Please take me and show me the place, saying, ‘Cremate me here.’” The brahmin agreed, saying, “Very well, my son.” Taking him, he left the city, climbed to the top of Vulture Peak, and said, “Dear son, this is a place where no other outcaste has been cremated. Cremate me here.” Then, with his son, he began to descend the mountain.

Satthā pana taṃ divasaṃ paccūsakāle bodhaneyyabandhave olokento tesaṃ pitāputtānaṃ sotāpattimaggassa upanissayaṃ addasa. Tasmā maggaṃ gahetvā ṭhitaluddako viya pabbatapādaṃ gantvā tesaṃ pabbatamatthakā otarantānaṃ āgamayamāno nisīdi, te otarantā satthāraṃ addasaṃsu. Satthā paṭisanthāraṃ karonto “kahaṃ gamissatha brāhmaṇā”ti pucchi. Māṇavo tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “tena hi ehi, tava pitarā ācikkhitaṭṭhānaṃ gacchāmā”ti ubho pitāputte gahetvā pabbatamatthakaṃ āruyha “kataraṃ ṭhāna”nti pucchi. Māṇavo “imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pabbatānaṃ antaraṃ ācikkhi, bhante”ti [P 2.0055] āha. Satthā “na kho, māṇava, tava pitā idāneva susānasuddhiko, pubbepi susānasuddhikova, na cesa idāneva ‘imasmiṃ ṭhāne maṃ jhāpeyyāsī’ti tava ācikkhati, pubbepi imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne attano jhāpitabhāvaṃ ācikkhī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

At dawn that day, the Teacher, surveying those who were ready to be awakened, saw the supporting condition for the path of stream-entry in the father and son. Therefore, like a hunter lying in wait on a path for deer, he went to the foot of the mountain and sat down, waiting for them as they descended from the mountain top. As they were descending, they saw the Teacher. The Teacher greeted them politely, asking, “Where are you going, brahmins?” The young man explained the matter. The Teacher said, “In that case, come, let us go to the place your father pointed out.” Taking both father and son, he ascended to the top of the mountain and asked, “Which place is it?” The young man replied, “Venerable sir, he pointed out the area between these three mountains.” The Teacher said, “Young man, your father is not obsessed with the purity of cemeteries only now—he was so in the past as well. And not only now does he tell you, ‘Cremate me in this place’—in the past as well he pointed out this very place for his own cremation.” Then, at the youth’s request, he related the past.

Atīte imasmiññeva rājagahe ayameva upasāḷako brāhmaṇo ayamevassa putto ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto magadharaṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā paripuṇṇasippo isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto himavantapadese ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya gijjhakūṭe paṇṇasālāyaṃ vihāsi. Tadā so brāhmaṇo imināva niyāmena puttaṃ vatvā puttena “tumheyeva me tathārūpaṃ ṭhānaṃ ācikkhathā”ti vutte “idameva ṭhāna”nti ācikkhitvā puttena saddhiṃ otaranto bodhisattaṃ disvā tassa santikaṃ upasaṅkami. Bodhisatto imināva niyāmena pucchitvā māṇavassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ehi, tava pitarā ācikkhitaṭṭhānassa [V 2.0045] ucchiṭṭhabhāvaṃ vā anucchiṭṭhabhāvaṃ vā jānissāmā”ti tehi saddhiṃ pabbatamatthakaṃ āruyha “idaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pabbatānaṃ antaraṃ [M 2.0050] anucchiṭṭhaṭṭhāna”nti māṇavena vutte “māṇava, imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne jhāpitakānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi, taveva pitā imasmiṃyeva rājagahe brāhmaṇakuleyeva nibbattitvā upasāḷakoyeva nāma hutvā imasmiṃyeva pabbatantare cuddasa jātisahassāni jhāpito. Pathaviyañhi ajhāpitaṭṭhānaṃ vā asusānaṭṭhānaṃ vā sīsānaṃ anivesitaṭṭhānaṃ vā laddhuṃ na sakkā”ti pubbenivāsañāṇena paricchinditvā imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

In the past, in this very city of Rājagaha, this same brahmin was Upasāḷaka, and this same youth was his son. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the country of Magadha. Having mastered all the arts, he went forth as an ascetic, attained the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and after living for a long time in the Himalayan region, delighting in the bliss of jhāna, he resided in a leaf-hut on Vulture Peak to obtain salt and sour foods. At that time, that brahmin spoke to his son in the same manner. When his son said, “You yourself show me such a place,” and the brahmin pointed out, “This is the very spot,” they met the Bodhisatta while descending. The Bodhisatta questioned them in the same way and, hearing the youth’s words, said, “Come, let us find out whether the place your father pointed out has been used or not.” Ascending the mountain summit with them, when the youth said, “This unused ground is between these three mountains,” the Bodhisatta replied, “Young man, there is no limit to those who have been cremated in this very spot. Your own father, having been born in a brahmin family in this very Rājagaha and named Upasāḷaka, was cremated in this very mountain cleft fourteen thousand times. Indeed, it is impossible to find a spot on earth that is not a cemetery, or a place where heads have not been laid.” Having discerned this through his knowledge of past lives, he spoke these two verses:

31.

31.

“Upasāḷakanāmāni[P 2.0056], sahassāni catuddasa;

Asmiṃ padese daḍḍhāni, natthi loke anāmataṃ.

“Fourteen thousand named Upasāḷaka have been burned in this region; in this world, there is no place untouched by death.”

32.

32.

“Yamhi saccañca dhammo ca, ahiṃsā saṃyamo damo;

Etaṃ ariyā sevanti, etaṃ loke anāmata”nti.

“That in which there is truth and Dhamma, non-violence, restraint, and self-control—this the Noble Ones frequent; this in the world is the deathless.”

Tattha anāmatanti mataṭṭhānaṃ. Tañhi upacāravasena “amata”nti vuccati, taṃ paṭisedhento “anāmata”nti āha. “Anamata”ntipi pāṭho, lokasmiñhi anamataṭṭhānaṃ asusānaṃ nāma natthīti attho. Yamhi saccañca dhammo cāti yasmiṃ puggale catusaccavatthukaṃ pubbabhāgasaccañāṇañca lokuttaradhammo ca atthi. Ahiṃsāti paresaṃ avihesā aviheṭhanā. Saṃyamoti sīlasaṃyamo. Damoti indriyadamanaṃ. Idañca guṇajātaṃ yamhi puggale atthi, etaṃ ariyā sevantīti, ariyā buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca etaṃ ṭhānaṃ sevanti, evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ upasaṅkamanti bhajantīti attho. Etaṃ loke anāmatanti etaṃ guṇajātaṃ loke amatabhāvasādhanato anāmataṃ nāma.

Therein, `anāmata` means a place where one has not died. For a place of death is figuratively called `amata`, and by negating that, he says `anāmata`. There is also the reading `anamata`; the meaning is that in the world there is no such thing as a place that is not a cemetery, that is, a place where no one has died. 'In whom there is truth and Dhamma' refers to a person in whom there is both the preliminary knowledge of the truth concerning the Four Noble Truths and the supramundane Dhamma. 'Non-violence' means not harming or harassing others. 'Restraint' is restraint by means of virtue. 'Self-control' is the taming of the sense faculties. 'The Noble Ones frequent this' means that where this collection of virtues is found in a person, the Noble Ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—frequent that state; that is, they approach and associate with such a person. 'This in the world is the deathless' means this collection of virtues is called `anāmata` (the deathless) in the world because it brings about the attainment of deathlessness.

Evaṃ bodhisatto pitāputtānaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, having taught the Dhamma to the father and son, the Bodhisatta cultivated the four divine abodes and was destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ubho pitāputtā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. “Tadā pitāputtāva etarahi pitāputtā ahesuṃ, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the truths, both father and son were established in the fruit of stream-entry. "The father and son of that time were this father and son of today, and the ascetic was I myself."

Upasāḷakajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Upasāḷaka Jātaka, the Sixth.

[167] 7. Samiddhijātakavaṇṇanā

[167] 7. The Commentary on the Samiddhi Jātaka

Abhutvā [V 2.0046][M 2.0051] bhikkhasi bhikkhūti idaṃ satthā rājagahaṃ upanissāya tapodārāme viharanto samiddhitheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi āyasmā samiddhi sabbarattiṃ padhānaṃ padahitvā aruṇuggamanavelāya nhatvā suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ attabhāvaṃ sukkhāpayamāno antaravāsakaṃ nivāsetvā uttarāsaṅgaṃ hatthena gahetvā aṭṭhāsi suparikammakatā viya suvaṇṇapaṭimā. Attabhāvasamiddhiyāyeva hissa [P 2.0057] “samiddhī”ti nāmaṃ ahosi. Athassa sarīrasobhaggaṃ disvā ekā devadhītā paṭibaddhacittā theraṃ evamāha – “tvaṃ khosi, bhikkhu, daharo yuvā susu kāḷakeso bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko, evarūpassa tava kāme aparibhuñjitvā ko attho pabbajjāya, kāme tāva paribhuñjassu, pacchā pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karissasī”ti. Atha naṃ thero āha – “devadhīte, ‘asukasmiṃ nāma vaye ṭhito marissāmī’ti mama maraṇakālaṃ na jānāmi, esa me kālo paṭicchanno, tasmā taruṇakāleyeva samaṇadhammaṃ katvā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī”ti. Sā therassa santikā paṭisanthāraṃ alabhitvā tattheva antaradhāyi. Thero satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, samiddhi, tvaññeva etarahi devadhītāya palobhito, pubbepi devadhītaro pabbajite palobhiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“You beg without having enjoyed, O monk”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling near Rājagaha in the Tapodārāme, concerning the Elder Samiddhi. For one day, the Venerable Samiddhi, having applied himself to striving all night, bathed at dawn and, drying his golden-hued body, donned his inner robe and stood holding his upper robe in his hand, like a well-polished golden statue. Indeed, it was because of the perfection of his physical form that his name was “Samiddhi.” Then, a divine maiden, seeing the splendor of his body, her mind became attached to the Elder and she said to him: “You, monk, are young, youthful, with black hair, endowed with the prime of youth, handsome, pleasing, and charming. What is the use of your going forth without enjoying such sensual pleasures? Enjoy sensual pleasures first, and afterwards, having gone forth, you can practice the ascetic life.” Then the Elder replied: “O divine maiden, I do not know the time of my death, thinking, ‘I will die at such and such an age.’ My time is hidden; therefore, while still young, I will practice the ascetic life and make an end of suffering.” Not receiving a friendly response from the Elder, she vanished then and there. The Elder approached the Teacher and reported this matter. The Teacher said, “Samiddhi, it is not only now that you have been tempted by a divine maiden; in the past too, divine maidens tempted those who had gone forth.” And being requested by him, he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ kāsigāmake brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā himavantapadese ekaṃ jātassaraṃ nissāya vāsaṃ kappesi. So sabbarattiṃ padhānaṃ padahitvā aruṇuggamanavelāya nhatvā ekaṃ vakkalaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ hatthena gahetvā sarīraṃ vodakaṃ karonto aṭṭhāsi. Athassa rūpasobhaggappattaṃ attabhāvaṃ oloketvā paṭibaddhacittā ekā devadhītā bodhisattaṃ palobhayamānā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family in a certain Kasi village. Having reached maturity and attained perfection in all the arts, he went forth into the ascetic life. Having developed supernormal powers and meditative attainments, he took up residence near a natural lake in the Himalayan region. He applied himself to striving the whole night. At the break of dawn, he bathed, put on one bark garment and, holding the other in his hand, stood drying his body. Then, a divine maiden, seeing the beauty of his form, her mind became attached and, seeking to tempt the Bodhisatta, she spoke the first verse:

33.

33.

“Abhutvā bhikkhasi bhikkhu, na hi bhutvāna bhikkhasi;

Bhutvāna bhikkhu bhikkhassu, mā taṃ kālo upaccagā”ti.

“You beg without having enjoyed, O monk; for you do not beg after having enjoyed. Having enjoyed, O monk, then you should beg; let not this time pass you by.”

Tattha [M 2.0052] abhutvā bhikkhasi bhikkhūti bhikkhu tvaṃ daharakāle kilesakāmavasena vatthukāme abhutvāva bhikkhāya carasi. Na hi bhutvāna bhikkhasīti nanu nāma pañca kāmaguṇe bhutvā bhikkhāya caritabbaṃ, kāme abhutvāva bhikkhācariyaṃ upagatosi. Bhutvāna bhikkhu bhikkhassūti bhikkhu [V 2.0047] daharakāle tāva kāme bhuñjitvā pacchā mahallakakāle bhikkhassu. Mā taṃ kālo upaccagāti ayaṃ kāme bhuñjanakālo daharakālo, taṃ mā atikkamatūti.

There, ‘You beg without having enjoyed, O monk’ means: O monk, in your youth, without having enjoyed material sensual pleasures on account of sensual desire, you wander for alms. ‘For you do not beg after having enjoyed’ means: Is it not the case that one should wander for alms only after having enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasure? But you have undertaken the alms-life without having enjoyed sensual pleasures. ‘Having enjoyed, O monk, then you should beg’ means: O monk, first enjoy sensual pleasures in your youth, and afterwards, in old age, you should beg. ‘Let not this time pass you by’ means: this time for enjoying sensual pleasures is your youth; do not let it pass you by.

Bodhisatto [P 2.0058] devatāya vacanaṃ sutvā attano ajjhāsayaṃ pakāsento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing the words of the divine maiden, the Bodhisatta, revealing his own intention, spoke the second verse:

34.

34.

“Kālaṃ vohaṃ na jānāmi, channo kālo na dissati;

Tasmā abhutvā bhikkhāmi, mā maṃ kālo upaccagā”ti.

“I do not know the time; the hidden time is not seen. Therefore, I beg without having enjoyed, lest time overtake me.”

Tattha kālaṃ vohaṃ na jānāmīti voti nipātamattaṃ. Ahaṃ pana “paṭhamavaye vā mayā maritabbaṃ majjhimavaye vā pacchimavaye vā”ti evaṃ attano maraṇakālaṃ na jānāmi. Paṇḍitena hi puggalena –

There, in ‘I do not know the time,’ ‘vo’ is merely a particle. I, however, do not know the time of my own death, thinking: ‘Must I die in the first stage of life, or the middle stage, or the final stage?’ For indeed, a wise person knows that—

“Jīvitaṃ byādhi kālo ca, dehanikkhepanaṃ gati;

Pañcete jīvalokasmiṃ, animittā na nāyare”ti.

“Life, disease, time, the laying down of the body, and destination—these five in the world of the living are signless, not to be known.”

Channo kālo na dissatīti yasmā “asukasmiṃ nāma vayakāle hemantādiutukāle vā mayā maritabba”nti mayhampesa channo hutvā kālo na dissati, suppaṭicchanno hutvā ṭhito na paññāyati. Tasmā abhutvā bhikkhāmīti tena kāraṇena pañca kāmaguṇe abhutvā bhikkhāmi. Mā maṃ kālo upaccagāti maṃ samaṇadhammakaraṇakālo mā atikkamatūti attho. Iminā kāraṇena daharova samāno pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karomīti. Devadhītā bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā tattheva antaradhāyi.

‘The hidden time is not seen’ means: because for me too, this time, being hidden, is not seen—that is, ‘I must die at such and such an age or in such and such a season as winter’—it stands well-concealed, it is not discerned. ‘Therefore, I live as a mendicant without having enjoyed’ means: for that reason, I live as a mendicant without having enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Lest time overtake me’ means: may the time for practicing the ascetic’s duty not pass me by. For this reason, being young, I went forth and am practicing the ascetic’s duty. Having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, the divine maiden vanished then and there.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā devadhītā ayaṃ devadhītā ahosi, ahameva tena samayena tāpaso ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, that divine maiden was this divine maiden, and I myself was the ascetic at that time.”

Samiddhijātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The commentary on the Samiddhi Jātaka is the seventh.

[168] 8. Sakuṇagghijātakavaṇṇanā

[168] 8. The Commentary on the Sakuṇagghi Jātaka

Seno [V 2.0048][M 2.0053] balasā patamānoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto attajjhāsayaṃ sakuṇovādasuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.372) ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi satthā bhikkhū āmantetvā “gocare, bhikkhave, caratha sake pettike visaye”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.372) imaṃ saṃyuttamahāvagge suttantaṃ kathento [P 2.0059] “tumhe tāva tiṭṭhatha, pubbe tiracchānagatāpi sakaṃ pettikavisayaṃ pahāya agocare carantā paccāmittānaṃ hatthapathaṃ gantvāpi attano paññāsampattiyā upāyakosallena paccāmittānaṃ hatthā mucciṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“A hawk swooping down with force”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, on his own initiative, concerning the Sakuṇovāda Sutta (Saṃ. Ni. 5.372). For one day, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, wander in your own ancestral domain, your own proper sphere” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.372). While relating this discourse from the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta, he said, “Let that be; even in the past, animals, having abandoned their own ancestral domain and wandering in an improper sphere, though they fell into the grasp of their enemies, were yet freed from their enemies’ hands by their attainment of wisdom and skill in means.” Thus, he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto lāpasakuṇayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇe leḍḍuṭṭhāne vāsaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ “sakavisaye gocaragahaṇaṃ pahāya paravisaye gocaraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti aṭavipariyantaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ tattha gocaraṃ gaṇhantaṃ disvā sakuṇagghi sahasā ajjhappattā aggahesi. So sakuṇagghiyā hariyamāno evaṃ paridevasi – “mayamevamha alakkhikā, mayaṃ appapuññā, ye mayaṃ agocare carimha paravisaye, sacejja mayaṃ gocare careyyāma sake pettike visaye, na myāyaṃ sakuṇagghi alaṃ abhavissa yadidaṃ yuddhāyā”ti. “Ko pana, te lāpa, gocaro sako pettiko visayo”ti? “Yadidaṃ naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇaṃ leḍḍuṭṭhāna”nti. Atha naṃ sakuṇagghi sake bale apatthaddhā amuñci – “gaccha kho, tvaṃ lāpa, tatrapi me gantvā na mokkhasī”ti. So tattha gantvā mahantaṃ leḍḍuṃ abhiruhitvā “ehi kho dāni sakuṇagghī”ti senaṃ avhayanto aṭṭhāsi. Sakuṇagghi sake bale apatthaddhā ubho pakkhe sannayha lāpasakuṇaṃ sahasā ajjhappattā. Yadā pana taṃ lāpo “bahuāgatā kho myāyaṃ sakuṇagghī”ti aññāsi, atha parivattitvā tasseva leḍḍussa antaraṃ paccāpādi. Sakuṇagghi vegaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontī tattheva uraṃ paccatāḷesi. Evaṃ sā bhinnena hadayena nikkhantehi akkhīhi jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a quail and took up residence in a place of clods in a field being plowed. One day, thinking, “Having abandoned foraging in my own domain, I will forage in another’s domain,” he went to the edge of the forest. There, a hawk, seeing him foraging, suddenly swooped down and seized him. As he was being carried off by the hawk, he lamented thus: “We are indeed unfortunate, we are lacking in merit, for we wandered in an improper sphere, in another’s domain. If today we had wandered in our own ancestral domain, this hawk would not have been a match for me in battle.” “What, then, O quail, is your own ancestral domain?” “It is this place of clods in a field being plowed.” The hawk, overconfident in its own strength, released him, saying, “Go, O quail, but even if you go there, you will not escape me.” He went there, climbed onto a large clod of earth, and stood there, calling out to the hawk, “Come now, hawk!” The hawk, overconfident in its own strength, preparing both its wings, suddenly swooped down upon the quail. But when the quail realized, “This hawk is indeed coming with great speed,” he turned around and slipped into the space within that very clod of earth. Unable to check its speed, the hawk struck its breast against that very clod. Thus, with its heart shattered and its eyes dislodged, it met its end.

Satthā [P 2.0060] imaṃ atītaṃ dassetvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatāpi agocare carantā sapattahatthaṃ gacchanti, gocare pana sake pettike visaye carantā sapatte niggaṇhanti, tasmā tumhepi mā agocare caratha paravisaye. Agocare[M 2.0054], bhikkhave, carataṃ paravisaye lacchati māro otāraṃ, lacchati māro ārammaṇaṃ. Ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo? Yadidaṃ pañca kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā…pe… ayaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno agocaro paravisayo”ti vatvā abhisambuddho hutvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having shown this past event, said: “Thus, bhikkhus, even animals, wandering in an improper sphere, fall into the hands of their enemies, but wandering in their own ancestral domain, they subdue their enemies. Therefore, you too should not wander in an improper sphere, in another’s domain. Bhikkhus, for one wandering in an improper sphere, in another’s domain, Māra finds an opportunity, Māra finds a foothold. And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s improper sphere, another’s domain? It is the five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye… This, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s improper sphere, another’s domain.” Having spoken thus, as the Fully Enlightened One, he spoke the first verse:

35.

35.

“Seno [V 2.0049] balasā patamāno, lāpaṃ gocaraṭhāyinaṃ;

Sahasā ajjhappattova, maraṇaṃ tenupāgamī”ti.

“The hawk, rushing with force, suddenly attacked the quail dwelling in its feeding ground, and thereby met its own death.”

Tattha balasā patamānoti “lāpaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti balena thāmena patamāno. Gocaraṭhāyinanti sakavisayā nikkhamitvā gocaratthāya aṭavipariyante ṭhitaṃ. Ajjhappattoti sampatto. Maraṇaṃ tenupāgamīti tena kāraṇena maraṇaṃ patto.

In that verse, `balasā patamāno` means rushing with strength and power, thinking, ‘I will seize the quail.’ `Gocaraṭhāyinaṃ` means the one that, having left its own territory, stood at the edge of the forest for the purpose of foraging. `Ajjhappatto` means having reached. `Maraṇaṃ tenupāgamī` means it met death due to that cause.

Tasmiṃ pana maraṇaṃ patte lāpo nikkhamitvā “diṭṭhā vata me paccāmittassa piṭṭhī”ti tassa hadaye ṭhatvā udānaṃ udānento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

However, when the hawk had met its death, the quail came out and, thinking, “Indeed, I have seen the back of my enemy!” stood on the hawk's breast and, uttering an inspired utterance, spoke the second verse:

36.

36.

“Sohaṃ nayena sampanno, pettike gocare rato;

Apetasattu modāmi, sampassaṃ atthamattano”ti.

“I, endowed with strategy, delighting in my ancestral pasture, with my enemy gone, rejoice, beholding my own well-being.”

Tattha nayenāti upāyena. Atthamattanoti attano arogabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ.

Here, `nayena` means by strategy. `Atthamattano` means one's own welfare, that is, the prosperity known as the state of being unafflicted.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū bhikkhū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu. “Tadā seno devadatto ahosi, lāpo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, many bhikkhus attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth. “At that time, the hawk was Devadatta, but the quail was I myself.”

Sakuṇagghijātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The eighth, the commentary on the Sakuṇagghijātaka.

[169] 9. Arakajātakavaṇṇanā

[169] 9. The Commentary on the Arakajātaka.

Yo [M 2.0055] ve mettena cittenāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mettasuttaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye satthā bhikkhū āmantesi – “mettāya, bhikkhave, cetovimuttiyā āsevitāya bhāvitāya [P 2.0061] bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya ekādasānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā. Katame ekādasa? Sukhaṃ supati, sukhaṃ paṭibujjhati, na pāpakaṃ supinaṃ passati, manussānaṃ piyo hoti, amanussānaṃ piyo hoti, devatā rakkhanti, nāssa aggi vā visaṃ vā satthaṃ vā kamati, tuvaṭaṃ cittaṃ samādhiyati, mukhavaṇṇo vippasīdati, asammūḷho kālaṃ karoti, uttari appaṭivijjhanto brahmalokūpago hoti. Mettāya, bhikkhave, cetovimuttiyā āsevitāya…pe… susamāraddhāya ime ekādasānisaṃsā [V 2.0050] pāṭikaṅkhā”ti (a. ni. 11.15). Ime ekādasānisaṃse gahetvā ṭhitaṃ mettābhāvanaṃ vaṇṇetvā “bhikkhave, bhikkhunā nāma sabbasattesu odissakānodissakavasena mettā bhāvetabbā, hitopi hitena pharitabbo, ahitopi hitena pharitabbo, majjhattopi hitena pharitabbo. Evaṃ sabbasattesu odissakānodissakavasena mettā bhāvetabbā, karuṇā muditā upekkhā bhāvetabbā, catūsu brahmavihāresu kammaṃ kātabbameva. Evaṃ karonto hi maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā alabhantopi brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi satta vassāni mettaṃ bhāvetvā satta saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe brahmalokasmiṃyeva vasiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“He who with a mind of loving-kindness”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Mettasutta. On one occasion, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness is cultivated, developed, frequently practiced, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, familiarized, and well undertaken, eleven benefits can be expected. What are the eleven? One sleeps happily, wakes happily, sees no evil dreams, is dear to humans, is dear to non-humans, deities protect one, neither fire nor poison nor weapons affect one, the mind quickly becomes concentrated, the facial complexion brightens, one dies unconfused, and if one does not penetrate further, one is reborn in the Brahma-world. Bhikkhus, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness is cultivated... and well undertaken, these eleven benefits can be expected.” Having praised the cultivation of loving-kindness endowed with these eleven benefits, he said: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should indeed develop loving-kindness toward all beings, both specifically and non-specifically. The friendly should be pervaded with goodwill, the unfriendly should be pervaded with goodwill, and the neutral should be pervaded with goodwill. In this way, loving-kindness should be developed toward all beings, specifically and non-specifically. Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity should be developed. One should certainly practice in the four divine abidings. For one who does so, even without attaining the path or its fruit, is destined for the Brahma-world. The wise ones of old also cultivated loving-kindness for seven years and dwelt in the Brahma-world for seven aeons of contraction and expansion.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte ekasmiṃ kappe bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā catunnaṃ brahmavihārānaṃ lābhī arako nāma satthā hutvā himavantapadese vāsaṃ kappesi, tassa mahā parivāro ahosi. So isigaṇaṃ ovadanto “pabbajitena nāma mettā bhāvetabbā, karuṇā muditā upekkhā bhāvetabbā. Mettacittañhi nāmetaṃ appanāppattaṃ brahmalokaparāyaṇataṃ sādhetī”ti mettāya ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsento imā gāthā āha –

In a past aeon, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he came of age, he renounced sensual pleasures and went forth into the ascetic life, becoming a teacher named Araka, an obtainer of the four divine abidings. He dwelled in the Himalayan region and had a large following. While instructing the community of ascetics, he said: “One who has gone forth should cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. For this mind of loving-kindness, having reached absorption, accomplishes the destiny of the Brahma-world.” Expounding the benefits of loving-kindness, he spoke these verses:

37.

37.

“Yo [M 2.0056] ve mettena cittena, sabbalokānukampati;

Uddhaṃ adho ca tiriyaṃ, appamāṇena sabbaso.

“He who with a mind of loving-kindness, is compassionate towards the entire world, above, below, and across, immeasurably, in every way.”

38.

38.

“Appamāṇaṃ hitaṃ cittaṃ, paripuṇṇaṃ subhāvitaṃ;

Yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ, na taṃ tatrāvasissatī”ti.

“With a mind that is immeasurable, beneficent, complete, and well-developed, whatever limited action has been done, none of that remains therein.”

Tattha [P 2.0062] yo ve mettena cittena, sabbalokānukampatīti khattiyādīsu vā samaṇabrāhmaṇesu vā yo koci appamāṇena mettena cittena sakalaṃ sattalokaṃ anukampati. Uddhanti pathavito yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanabrahmalokā. Adhoti pathaviyā heṭṭhā ussade mahāniraye. Tiriyanti manussaloke, yattakāni cakkavāḷāni ca tesu sabbesu ettake ṭhāne nibbattā sabbe sattā averā hontu, abyāpajjhā anīghā, sukhī attānaṃ pariharantūti evaṃ bhāvitena mettena cittenāti attho. Appamāṇenāti appamāṇasattānaṃ appamāṇārammaṇattā appamāṇena. Sabbasoti sabbākārena, uddhaṃ adho tiriyanti evaṃ sabbasugatiduggativasenāti attho.

Here, ‘yo ve mettena cittena, sabbalokānukampatīti’ means whoever, whether among warriors and so forth or among ascetics and brahmins, with an immeasurable mind of loving-kindness has compassion for the entire world of beings. ‘Uddhaṃ’ means from the earth up to the Brahma-world of the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. ‘Adho’ means beneath the earth, down to the great Ussada hell. ‘Tiriyaṃ’ means in the human world, and in all the world-systems that exist, in all those places may all beings be free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness—thus, this is the meaning of a mind so developed with loving-kindness. ‘Appamāṇena’ means immeasurable because of having immeasurable beings as an immeasurable object. ‘Sabbaso’ means in every way; ‘uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ’—thus, in terms of all happy and unhappy destinies, this is the meaning.

Appamāṇaṃ hitaṃ cittanti appamāṇaṃ katvā bhāvitaṃ sabbasattesu hitacittaṃ. Paripuṇṇanti avikalaṃ. Subhāvitanti suvaḍḍhitaṃ, appanācittassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammanti yaṃ “appamāṇaṃ [V 2.0051] appamāṇārammaṇa”nti evaṃ ārammaṇattikavasena ca vasībhāvappattivasena ca avaḍḍhitvā kataṃ parittaṃ kāmāvacarakammaṃ. Na taṃ tatrāvasissatīti taṃ parittaṃ kammaṃ yaṃ taṃ “appamāṇaṃ hitaṃ citta”nti saṅkhagataṃ rūpāvacarakammaṃ, tatra na avasissati. Yathā nāma mahoghena ajjhotthaṭaṃ parittodakaṃ oghassa abbhantare tena asaṃhīramānaṃ nāvasissati na tiṭṭhati, atha kho mahoghova taṃ ajjhottharitvā tiṭṭhati, evameva taṃ parittakammaṃ tassa mahaggatakammassa abbhantare tena mahaggatakammena acchinditvā aggahitavipākokāsaṃ hutvā na avasissati na tiṭṭhati, na sakkoti attano vipākaṃ dātuṃ, atha kho mahaggatakammameva taṃ ajjhottharitvā tiṭṭhati vipākaṃ detīti.

‘Appamāṇaṃ hitaṃ cittaṃ’ means a beneficial mind developed immeasurably for all beings. ‘Paripuṇṇaṃ’ means without deficiency. ‘Subhāvitaṃ’ means well-cultivated; this is a name for the absorption-mind. ‘Yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ’ refers to the limited action of the sense-sphere, which is performed without having been developed to be ‘immeasurable, with an immeasurable object’ by way of the threefold object and the attainment of mastery. ‘Na taṃ tatrāvasissatīti’ means that limited action will not remain there within the ‘appamāṇaṃ hitaṃ cittaṃ’, which is classified as action in the form sphere. Just as a small amount of water overwhelmed by a great flood does not remain or stand within the flood, being carried away unmixed, but rather the great flood itself, having overwhelmed it, stands; so too that limited action, within that exalted action, having no opportunity to give its result because it is overwhelmed by the exalted action, does not remain or stand; it cannot give its own result, but the exalted action overwhelms it and stands, giving its result.

Evaṃ bodhisatto antevāsikānaṃ mettābhāvanāya ānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke nibbattitvā satta saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe na imaṃ lokaṃ puna agamāsi.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having explained to his disciples the benefits of the development of loving-kindness, was reborn in the Brahma-world without his absorption having declined, and he did not return to this world for seven aeons of cosmic contraction and expansion.

Satthā [M 2.0057] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā isigaṇo buddhaparisā ahosi, arako pana satthā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the group of seers was the Buddha's assembly, but the Teacher Araka was I myself.”

Arakajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Araka Jātaka is the ninth.

[170] 10. Kakaṇṭakajātakavaṇṇanā

[170] 10. The Commentary on the Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka

Nāyaṃ [P 2.0063] pure uṇṇamatīti idaṃ kakaṇṭakajātakaṃ mahāumaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvibhavissati.

“This did not swell up before”—this Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka will become clear in the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.590 ff.).

Kakaṇṭakajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka is the tenth.

Santhavavaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter: The Chapter on Acquaintance

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of its contents:

Indasamānagottañca, santhavaṃ susīmaṃ gijjhaṃ;

Nakulaṃ upasāḷakaṃ, samiddhi ca sakuṇagghi;

Arakañca kakaṇṭakaṃ.

Indasamānagotta, Santhava, Susīma, Gijjha, Nakula, Upasāḷaka, Samiddhi, Sakuṇagghi, Araka, and Kakaṇṭaka.

3. Kalyāṇavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Wholesome

[171] 1. Kalyāṇadhammajātakavaṇṇanā

[171] 1. The Commentary on the Kalyāṇadhamma Jātaka

Kalyāṇadhammoti [V 2.0052] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ badhirasassuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi eko kuṭumbiko saddho pasanno tisaraṇagato pañcasīlena samannāgato. So ekadivasaṃ bahūni sappiādīni bhesajjāni ceva pupphagandhavatthādīni ca gahetvā “jetavane satthu santike dhammaṃ sossāmī”ti agamāsi. Tassa tattha gatakāle sassu khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ gahetvā dhītaraṃ daṭṭhukāmā taṃ gehaṃ agamāsi, sā ca thokaṃ badhiradhātukā hoti. Sā dhītarā saddhiṃ bhuttabhojanā [M 2.0058] bhattasammadaṃ vinodayamānā dhītaraṃ pucchi – “kiṃ, amma, bhattā te sammodamāno avivadamāno piyasaṃvāsaṃ vasatī”ti. “Kiṃ, amma, kathetha yādiso tumhākaṃ jāmātā sīlena ceva ācārasampadāya ca, tādiso pabbajitopi dullabho”ti. Upāsikā dhītu vacanaṃ sādhukaṃ asallakkhetvā “pabbajito”ti padameva gahetvā “amma, kasmā te bhattā pabbajito”ti mahāsaddaṃ akāsi. Taṃ sutvā sakalagehavāsino “amhākaṃ kira kuṭumbiko pabbajito”ti viraviṃsu. Tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā dvārena sañcarantā “kiṃ nāma kireta”nti pucchiṃsu. “Imasmiṃ kira gehe kuṭumbiko pabbajito”ti. Sopi kho kuṭumbiko dasabalassa dhammaṃ sutvā vihārā nikkhamma nagaraṃ pāvisi.

“The Wholesome Quality”—this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain deaf mother-in-law. In Sāvatthī, there was a certain householder, devout and confident, who had gone for refuge to the Triple Gem and was endowed with the five precepts. One day, he took many medicinal substances such as ghee, as well as flowers, scents, and cloths, thinking, “I will listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher at Jetavana,” and went. When he had gone there, his mother-in-law, wishing to see her daughter, took some hard and soft food and went to that house. She was somewhat hard of hearing. After eating with her daughter, while dispelling the drowsiness from the meal, the mother-in-law asked her daughter, “My dear, does your husband live with you in harmony, without quarreling, in pleasant companionship?” “What are you saying, Mother? A son-in-law like yours, so accomplished in virtue and good conduct, is rare even among those who have gone forth!” The laywoman, not properly grasping her daughter’s words, caught only the word “gone forth” and cried out loudly, “My dear, why has your husband gone forth?” Hearing this, all the household residents exclaimed, “Our householder has supposedly gone forth!” Hearing their noise, those passing by the door asked, “What is this, pray tell?” “In this house, the householder has supposedly gone forth!” That householder, having listened to the Dhamma of the Ten-Powered One, left the monastery and entered the city.

Atha naṃ antarāmaggeyeva eko puriso disvā “samma, tvaṃ kira pabbajitoti tava gehe puttadāraparijano paridevatī”ti āha. Athassa [P 2.0064] etadahosi – “ayaṃ apabbajitameva kira maṃ ‘pabbajito’ti vadati, uppanno kho pana me kalyāṇasaddo na antaradhāpetabbo, ajjeva mayā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tatova nivattitvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ nu kho, upāsaka, idāneva buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ katvā gantvā idāneva paccāgatosī”ti vutte tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “bhante, kalyāṇasaddo nāma uppanno na antaradhāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā pabbajitukāmo hutvā āgatomhī”ti āha. So pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhitvā sammā paṭipanno nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Idaṃ kira kāraṇaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko nāma kuṭumbiko ‘uppanno kalyāṇasaddo [V 2.0053] na antaradhāpetabbo’ti pabbajitvā idāni arahattaṃ patto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “bhikkhave, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi ‘uppanno kalyāṇasaddo virādhetuṃ na vaṭṭatī’ti pabbajiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then, on the way, a certain man saw him and said, “Friend, it seems you have gone forth; your children, wife, and family at home are grieving.” Then it occurred to him: “This man calls me ‘one who has gone forth’ though I have not gone forth. But a good report has arisen for me; it should not be allowed to disappear. Today itself I must go forth.” Turning back right there, he went to the Teacher. When asked, “Why, lay follower, having just attended upon the Buddha and left, have you now returned?” he explained the matter and said, “Venerable sir, a good report has arisen; it should not be allowed to disappear. Therefore, desiring to go forth, I have come.” He received the going forth and the higher ordination. Practicing rightly, he soon attained arahantship. This matter, it seems, became known in the community of monks. Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks started a discussion: “Friends, a certain householder, thinking ‘a good report that has arisen should not be allowed to disappear,’ went forth and has now attained arahantship.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the topic of your discussion as you are sitting here?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, even the wise of old, thinking ‘a good report that has arisen should not be forsaken,’ went forth.” And he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā vayappatto pitu accayena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi. So ekadivasaṃ nivesanā nikkhamitvā rājupaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Athassa sassu “dhītaraṃ passissāmī”ti taṃ gehaṃ agamāsi, sā thokaṃ badhiradhātukāti sabbaṃ [M 2.0059] paccuppannavatthusadisameva. Taṃ pana rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā attano gharaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā eko puriso “tumhe kira pabbajitāti tumhākaṃ gehe mahāparidevo pavattatī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “uppanno kalyāṇasaddo nāma na antaradhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tatova nivattitvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ, mahāseṭṭhi, idāneva gantvā puna āgatosī”ti vutte “deva, gehajano kira maṃ apabbajitameva ‘pabbajito’ti vatvā paridevati, uppanno kho pana kalyāṇasaddo na antaradhāpetabbo, pabbajissāmahaṃ, pabbajjaṃ me anujānāhī”ti etamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ imā gāthā āha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a merchant's family. Having come of age, upon his father’s death, he attained the position of chief merchant. One day, leaving his residence, he went to attend upon the king. Then his mother-in-law, thinking, "I will see my daughter," went to that house. She was somewhat deaf by nature—the whole incident is just like the present one. But when a certain man saw him, having gone to attend upon the king and returning to his own house, he said, "It is said that you have gone forth; there is great lamentation in your home." The Bodhisatta thought, "A good report has arisen; it should not be allowed to disappear." Turning back right there, he went to the king. When asked, "Great merchant, having just gone, why have you now returned?", he explained, "Sire, my household calls me 'one who has gone forth' and grieves, though I have not gone forth. But a good report has arisen; it should not be allowed to disappear. I will go forth; permit my going forth." And to explain this matter, he spoke these verses:

41.

41.

“Kalyāṇadhammoti [P 2.0065] yadā janinda, loke samaññaṃ anupāpuṇāti;

Tasmā na hiyyetha naro sapañño, hiriyāpi santo ghuramādiyanti.

"O lord of people, when in the world one gains the designation 'one of wholesome qualities,' a wise person should not fall away from it. Even the virtuous, through moral shame, undertake the burden."

42.

42.

“Sāyaṃ samaññā idha majja pattā, kalyāṇadhammoti janinda loke;

Tāhaṃ samekkhaṃ idha pabbajissaṃ, na hi matthi chando idha kāmabhoge”ti.

"This very designation, 'one of wholesome qualities,' O lord of people, has been attained by me here today in the world. Reflecting on that, I shall go forth here, for indeed, I have no desire for sensual pleasures here."

Tattha kalyāṇadhammoti sundaradhammo. Samaññaṃ anupāpuṇātīti yadā sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo pabbajitoti idaṃ paññattivohāraṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā na hiyyethāti tato sāmaññato na parihāyetha. Hiriyāpi santo dhuramādiyantīti, mahārāja, sappurisā nāma ajjhattasamuṭṭhitāya hiriyā bahiddhasamuṭṭhitena ottappenapi etaṃ pabbajitadhuraṃ gaṇhanti. Idha majja pattāti idha mayā ajja pattā. Tāhaṃ samekkhanti taṃ ahaṃ guṇavasena laddhasamaññaṃ samekkhanto passanto. Na hi matthi chandoti na hi me atthi chando. Idha kāmabhogeti imasmiṃ loke kilesakāmavatthukāmaparibhogehi.

In this context, `kalyāṇadhammo` means one of beautiful qualities. `Samaññaṃ anupāpuṇāti` means: when a virtuous person of wholesome qualities attains this conceptual designation, 'one who has gone forth.' Therefore, `na hiyyetha` means: one should not fall away from that designation. `Hiriyāpi santo dhuramādiyanti` means: Great king, truly good people, through inner-arisen moral shame and outer-arisen moral dread, undertake this burden of one who has gone forth. `Idha majja pattā` means: it has been attained by me here today. `Tāhaṃ samekkhaṃ` means: I, observing and seeing that designation gained by means of virtue... `Na hi matthi chando` means: indeed, I have no desire. `Idha kāmabhoge` means: in this world, for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures which are defilements and sensual pleasures which are objects.

Bodhisatto [V 2.0054] evaṃ vatvā rājānaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā himavantapadesaṃ gantvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta, having caused the king to permit his going forth, went to the Himalayan region, and having gone forth as an ascetic, he developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and became destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā [M 2.0060] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, connected the Jātaka: "At that time the king was Ānanda, but the merchant of Bārāṇasī was I myself."

Kalyāṇadhammajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kalyāṇadhamma Jātaka, the First.

[172] 2. Daddarajātakavaṇṇanā

[172] 2. The Commentary on the Daddara Jātaka

Ko nu saddena mahatāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kokālikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi kāle bahū bahussutā bhikkhū manosilātale nadamānā taruṇasīhā viya ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārentā [P 2.0066] viya saṅghamajjhe sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇanti. Kokāliko tesu sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇantesu attano tucchabhāvaṃ ajānitvāva “ahampi sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ antaraṃ pavisitvā “amhākaṃ sarabhāṇaṃ na pāpenti. Sace amhākampi pāpeyyuṃ, mayampi bhaṇeyyāmā”ti bhikkhusaṅghassa nāmaṃ aggahetvāva tattha tattha kathento āhiṇḍati. Tassa sā kathā bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭā jātā. Bhikkhū “vīmaṃsissāma tāva na”nti saññāya evamāhaṃsu – “āvuso kokālika, ajja saṅghassa sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti. So attano balaṃ ajānitvāva “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “ajja sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti attano sappāyaṃ yāguṃ pivi, khajjakaṃ khādi, sappāyeneva sūpena bhuñji.

"Who indeed with a loud sound...?" This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Kokālika. For at that time, many learned monks were reciting with intonation in the midst of the Saṅgha, like young lions roaring on a realgar terrace, or as if bringing down the celestial Ganges. While they were reciting with intonation, Kokālika, not realizing his own worthlessness, thought, "I too will recite with intonation." Entering among the monks, he went about speaking here and there without the Saṅgha's authorization, saying, "They do not grant me a turn to recite. If they were to grant it to me, I too would recite." This talk of his became well-known in the Saṅgha of monks. The monks, thinking "Let us test him first," said this: "Friend Kokālika, recite with intonation for the Saṅgha today." Not knowing his own ability, he agreed, saying, "Very well." Thinking, "Today I shall recite with intonation," he drank suitable gruel, ate solid food, and ate with suitable curry.

Sūriye atthaṅgate dhammassavanakāle ghosite bhikkhusaṅgho sannipati. So kaṇṭakuraṇḍakavaṇṇaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇaṃ cīvaraṃ pārupitvā saṅghamajjhaṃ pavisitvā there vanditvā alaṅkataratanamaṇḍape paññattavaradhammāsanaṃ abhiruhitvā citrabījaniṃ gahetvā “sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇissāmī”ti nisīdi, tāvadevassa sarīrā sedā mucciṃsu, sārajjaṃ okkami, pubbagāthāya paṭhamaṃ padaṃ udāharitvā anantaraṃ na passi. So kampamāno āsanā oruyha lajjito saṅghamajjhato apakkamma attano pariveṇaṃ agamāsi. Añño bahussuto bhikkhu sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇi. Tato paṭṭhāya bhikkhū tassa tucchabhāvaṃ jāniṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ [M 2.0061] dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, paṭhamaṃ kokālikassa tucchabhāvo dujjāno, idāni [V 2.0055] panesa sayaṃ naditvā pākaṭo jāto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, kokāliko idāneva naditvā pākaṭo jāto, pubbepi naditvā pākaṭo ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

When the sun had set and the time for hearing the Dhamma was announced, the Saṅgha of monks assembled.
