He put on an under-robe of the color of a yellow amaranth flower and draped an upper-robe of the color of a kaṇikāra flower. Entering the midst of the Saṅgha and paying homage to the elders, he ascended the excellent Dhamma-seat prepared in the decorated jewel-pavilion. Taking a painted fan, he sat down, thinking, "I will recite with intonation." Right then, sweat poured from his body and embarrassment overcame him. After uttering the first line of the introductory verse, he could not see the next part. Trembling, he descended from the seat and, ashamed, withdrew from the midst of the Saṅgha and went to his own cell. Another learned monk recited with intonation. From then on, the monks knew of his worthlessness. Then one day, a discussion arose among the monks in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, at first Kokālika’s worthlessness was hard to discern, but now he has become exposed by his own sound." The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" and when they told him, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has become exposed by his sound; he was exposed by his sound in the past as well," and he related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese sīhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā bahūnaṃ [P 2.0067] sīhānaṃ rājā ahosi. So anekasīhaparivāro rajataguhāyaṃ vāsaṃ kappesi. Tassa avidūre ekissāya guhāya eko siṅgālopi vasati. Athekadivasaṃ deve vassitvā vigate sabbe sīhā sīharājasseva guhadvāre sannipatitvā sīhanādaṃ nadantā sīhakīḷaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Tesaṃ evaṃ naditvā kīḷanakāle sopi siṅgālo nadati. Sīhā tassa saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ siṅgālo amhehi saddhiṃ nadatī”ti lajjitā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ tuṇhībhūtakāle bodhisattassa putto sīhapotako “tāta, ime sīhā naditvā sīhakīḷaṃ kīḷantā etassa saddaṃ sutvā lajjāya tuṇhī jātā, ko nāmesa attano saddena attānaṃ jānāpetī”ti pitaraṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the lion species in the Himalayan region and became the king of many lions. Accompanied by a retinue of many lions, he lived in a silver cave. Not far from him, a jackal also lived in a certain cave. Then one day, after the rain had stopped, all the lions gathered at the entrance of the lion king’s cave and, roaring with a lion’s roar, played the lions’ sport. While they were roaring and playing, that jackal also howled. The lions, hearing his sound, were ashamed, thinking, "This jackal is howling along with us," and they became silent. While they were silent, the Bodhisatta’s son, a lion cub, asked his father, "Father, while these lions were roaring and playing the lions’ sport, they heard this creature's sound and became silent out of shame. Who is this that makes himself known by his own sound?" and asking his father, he spoke the first verse:

43.

43.

“Ko nu saddena mahatā, abhinādeti daddaraṃ;

Taṃ sīhā nappaṭinadanti, ko nāmeso migādhibhū”ti.

"Who indeed with a loud sound makes Mount Daddara resound? At whom the lions do not roar back? Who is this, O Lord of Beasts?"

Tattha abhinādeti daddaranti daddaraṃ rajatapabbataṃ ekanādaṃ karoti. Migādhibhūti pitaraṃ ālapati. Ayañhettha attho – migādhibhū migajeṭṭhaka sīharāja pucchāmi taṃ “ko nāmeso”ti.

There, "makes Daddara resound" means he makes Mount Daddara, the silver mountain, a single roar. "Lord of Beasts" is an address to his father. The meaning here is: "O Lord of Beasts, O chief of beasts, O lion king, I ask you, 'Who is this?'"

Athassa vacanaṃ sutvā pitā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having heard his words, the father spoke the second verse:

44.

44.

“Adhamo migajātānaṃ, siṅgālo tāta vassati;

Jātimassa jigucchantā, tuṇhī sīhā samaccare”ti.

"It is the lowest of beasts, my son, a jackal that is howling; loathing his species, the lions remain silent."

Tattha samaccareti santi upasaggamattaṃ, accantīti attho, tuṇhī hutvā nisīdantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Potthakesu pana “samacchare”ti likhanti.

There, regarding "samaccare": the "saṃ" is just a prefix; the meaning is "accanti" (they remain/continue). It is said that they sit in silence. However, in manuscripts, they write "samacchare".

Satthā [V 2.0056][M 2.0062] “na, bhikkhave, kokāliko idāneva attano nādena attānaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti, pubbepi akāsiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo kokāliko ahosi, sīhapotako rāhulo, sīharājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika makes himself known by his own noise; he did so in the past as well." Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, he connected the Jātaka: "At that time the jackal was Kokālika, the young lion was Rāhula, and the lion king was indeed myself."

Daddarajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Daddara Jātaka, the Second.

[173] 3. Makkaṭajātakavaṇṇanā

[173] 3. The Commentary on the Makkaṭa Jātaka

Tātamāṇavako [P 2.0068] esoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pakiṇṇakanipāte uddālakajātake (jā. 1.14.62 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Tadā pana satthā “bhikkhave, nāyaṃ bhikkhu idāneva kuhako, pubbepi makkaṭo hutvā aggissa kāraṇā kohaññaṃ akāsiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"This is a young man, father..." This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a deceitful monk. The story will become clear in the Uddālaka Jātaka in the Pakiṇṇaka Nipāta. At that time, the Teacher said, "Monks, this monk is not deceitful only now; in the past too, as a monkey, he practiced deceit for the sake of fire." Having said this, he related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ kāsigāmake brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapesi. Athassa brāhmaṇī ekaṃ puttaṃ vijāyitvā puttassa ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle kālamakāsi. Bodhisatto tassā petakiccaṃ katvā “kiṃ me dāni gharāvāsena, puttaṃ gahetvā pabbajissāmī”ti assumukhaṃ ñātimittavaggaṃ pahāya puttaṃ ādāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tattha vanamūlaphalāhāro vāsaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ vassānakāle deve vassante sāradārūni aggiṃ jāletvā visibbanto phalakatthare nipajji, puttopissa tāpasakumārako pitu pāde sambāhantova nisīdi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a village of Kāsi. Having come of age, he learned the arts at Takkasilā and established a household. Then his brahmin wife gave birth to a son, and she passed away when the son had reached the age of running and playing about. The Bodhisatta performed her funeral rites and thought, “What use is household life to me now? I will take my son and go forth.” Leaving his weeping relatives and friends, he took his son and entered the Himalayas, where he became an ascetic. There, he lived on forest roots and fruits. One day during the rainy season, while it was raining, he lit a fire with heartwood and lay down on a wooden plank, warming himself. His son, the young ascetic, sat massaging his father’s feet.

Atheko vanamakkaṭo sītena pīḷiyamāno tassa paṇṇasālāya taṃ aggiṃ disvā “sacāhaṃ ettha pavisissāmi, ‘makkaṭo makkaṭo’ti maṃ pothetvā nīharissanti, aggiṃ visibbetuṃ na labhissāmi, atthi dāni me upāyo, tāpasavesaṃ gahetvā kohaññaṃ katvā pavisissāmī”ti cintetvā ekassa matatāpasassa vakkalāni nivāsetvā pacchiñca aṅkusayaṭṭhiñca [M 2.0063] gahetvā paṇṇasāladvāre ekaṃ tālarukkhaṃ nissāya saṃkuṭito aṭṭhāsi. Tāpasakumārako taṃ disvā makkaṭabhāvaṃ ajānanto “eko mahallakatāpaso sītena pīḷito aggiṃ visibbetuṃ āgato [P 2.0069] bhavissatī”ti pitu tāpasassa kathetvā “etaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ pavesetvā visibbāpessāmī”ti cintetvā pitaraṃ ālapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then a certain forest monkey, tormented by the cold, saw the fire in the leaf-hut and thought, “If I enter there, they will strike me, saying, ‘Monkey, monkey,’ and drive me out; I will not get to warm myself by the fire. Now I have a plan: I will take on the guise of an ascetic and enter by practicing deceit.” Having thought this, he put on the bark garments of a deceased ascetic, took a basket and a hooked staff, and stood hunched, leaning against a palm tree near the door of the leaf-hut. Seeing him, the young ascetic, not knowing he was a monkey, thought, “An elderly ascetic, tormented by the cold, must have come to warm himself by the fire.” He told his father, the ascetic, and thinking, “I will let him into this leaf-hut to warm himself,” he addressed his father and spoke the first verse:

45.

45.

“Tāta [V 2.0057] māṇavako eso, tālamūlaṃ apassito;

Agārakañcidaṃ atthi, handa demassagāraka”nti.

“Father, this young man is leaning against the foot of the palm tree; we have a small hut here, come, let us give him shelter.”

Tattha māṇavakoti sattādhivacanaṃ. Tena “tāta, eso eko māṇavako satto eko tāpaso”ti dīpeti. Tālamūlaṃ apassitoti tālakkhandhaṃ nissāya ṭhito. Agārakañcidaṃ atthīti idañca amhākaṃ pabbajitāgāraṃ atthi, paṇṇasālaṃ sandhāya vadati. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Demassagārakanti etassa ekamante vasanatthāya agārakaṃ dema.

Herein, 'māṇavaka' is a designation for a being. By this, he shows, 'Father, this is a young man, a being, an ascetic.' 'Leaning against the foot of the palm tree' means he stood relying on the trunk of the palm tree. 'We have a dwelling here' means 'this renunciant’s hut of ours exists,' speaking with reference to the leaf-hut. 'Handa' is a particle in the sense of urging. 'Let us give him a dwelling' means 'let us give him a place to stay in one corner of the hut.'

Bodhisatto puttassa vacanaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāya paṇṇasāladvāre ṭhatvā olokento tassa makkaṭabhāvaṃ ñatvā “tāta, manussānaṃ nāma na evarūpaṃ mukhaṃ hoti, makkaṭo esa, nayidha pakkositabbo”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, hearing his son’s words, rose and stood at the door of the leaf-hut. Looking out and recognizing that it was a monkey, he said, “My dear son, the faces of humans are not like this. This is a monkey; he should not be invited in here.” Then he spoke the second verse:

46.

46.

“Mā kho tvaṃ tāta pakkosi, dūseyya no agārakaṃ;

Netādisaṃ mukhaṃ hoti, brāhmaṇassa susīlino”ti.

“My dear son, do not invite him, he would defile our hut; a virtuous brahmin does not have such a face.”

Tattha dūseyya no agārakanti ayañhi idha paviṭṭho samāno imaṃ kicchena kataṃ paṇṇasālaṃ agginā vā jhāpento uccārādīni vā karonto dūseyya. Netādisanti “etādisaṃ brāhmaṇassa susīlino mukhaṃ na hoti, makkaṭo eso”ti vatvā bodhisatto ekaṃ ummukaṃ gahetvā “kiṃ ettha tiṭṭhasī”ti khipitvā taṃ palāpesi. Makkaṭo vakkalāni chaḍḍetvā rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā vanasaṇḍaṃ pāvisi. Bodhisatto cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Herein, 'he would defile our hut' means that if he were to enter here, he would defile this leaf-hut, made with such difficulty, either by burning it with fire or by voiding excrement and so on. 'Not such a face' means: saying, 'A virtuous brahmin does not have such a face; this is a monkey,' the Bodhisatta took a firebrand and, throwing it at him, said 'Why do you stand here?' and made him flee. The monkey, discarding the bark garments, climbed a tree and entered the forest thicket. The Bodhisatta, having developed the four divine abidings, was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā [M 2.0064] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā makkaṭo ayaṃ kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, tāpasakumāro rāhulo, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, connected the birth story: “At that time, the monkey was this deceitful monk, the young ascetic was Rāhula, and the ascetic was indeed myself.”

Makkaṭajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Explanation of the Makkaṭa Jātaka is the third.

[174] 4. Dubbhiyamakkaṭajātakaṇṇanā

[174] 4. The Explanation of the Dubbhiya-makkaṭa Jātaka

Adamha [V 2.0058][P 2.0070] te vāri pahūtarūpanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū devadattassa akataññumittadubbhibhāvaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva akataññū mittadubbhī, pubbepi evarūpo ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“We gave you water in plenty...” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Veluvana, concerning Devadatta. For one day, the monks sat in the Dhamma hall discussing Devadatta’s ingratitude and treachery toward friends. The Teacher arrived and said, “Monks, not only now is Devadatta ungrateful and treacherous toward friends; in the past, too, he was of such a nature.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ kāsigāmake brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapesi. Tasmiṃ pana samaye kāsiraṭṭhe vattanimahāmagge eko gambhīro udapāno hoti anotaraṇīyo tiracchānānaṃ, maggappaṭipannā puññatthikā manussā dīgharajjukena vārakena udakaṃ ussiñcitvā ekissā doṇiyā pūretvā tiracchānānaṃ pānīyaṃ denti. Tassa sāmantato mahantaṃ araññaṃ, tattha bahū makkaṭā vasanti. Atha tasmiṃ magge dve tīṇi divasāni manussasañcāro pacchijji, tiracchānā pānīyaṃ na labhiṃsu. Eko makkaṭo pipāsāturo hutvā pānīyaṃ pariyesanto udapānassa santike vicarati. Bodhisatto kenacideva karaṇīyena taṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā tattha gacchanto pānīyaṃ uttāretvā pivitvā hatthapāde dhovitvā ṭhito taṃ makkaṭaṃ addasa. Athassa pipāsitabhāvaṃ ñatvā pānīyaṃ ussiñcitvā doṇiyaṃ ākiritvā adāsi, datvā ca pana “vissamissāmī”ti ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle nipajji. Makkaṭo pānīyaṃ pivitvā avidūre nisīditvā mukhamakkaṭikaṃ karonto bodhisattaṃ bhiṃsāpesi. Bodhisatto tassa taṃ kiriyaṃ disvā “are duṭṭhamakkaṭa, ahaṃ tava pipāsitassa kilantassa bahuṃ [P 2.0071] pānīyaṃ adāsiṃ, idāni tvaṃ mayhaṃ mukhamakkaṭikaṃ karosi, aho pāpajanassa nāma kato upakāro niratthako”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain village of Kāsi. When he came of age, he established a household. At that time, along the main highway in the country of Kāsi, there was a deep well from which animals could not descend to drink. Travelers seeking merit would draw water with a vessel attached to a long rope and fill a trough to provide drinking water for the animals. Nearby was a great forest where many monkeys lived. Then, for two or three days, the passage of people along that road ceased, and the animals could not get any water. One monkey, afflicted by thirst, wandered near the well in search of water. The Bodhisatta, traveling along that road on some business, arrived there, drew water, drank, and washed his hands and feet. While standing there, he saw that monkey. Realizing its thirst, he drew water, poured it into the trough, and gave it to the monkey. After giving it, thinking, “I will rest,” he lay down at the foot of a tree. The monkey drank the water and, sitting not far away, made monkey-faces to frighten the Bodhisatta. Seeing this behavior, the Bodhisatta said, “You wicked monkey! I gave you plenty of water when you were thirsty and weary, and now you make monkey-faces at me. Alas, a favor done for a wicked person is truly fruitless!” and spoke the first verse:

47.

47.

“Adamha [M 2.0065] te vāri pahūtarūpaṃ, ghammābhitattassa pipāsitassa;

So dāni pitvāna kiriṅkarosi, asaṅgamo pāpajanena seyyo”ti.

“We gave you plenty of water when you were scorched by the heat and thirsty; now having drunk it, you make the sound ‘kiri kiri.’ Better is non-association with a wicked person.”

Tattha so dāni pitvāna kiriṅkarosīti so idāni tvaṃ mayā dinnapānīyaṃ pivitvā mukhamakkaṭikaṃ karonto “kiri kirī”ti saddaṃ karosi. Asaṅgamo pāpajanena seyyoti pāpajanena saddhiṃ saṅgamo na seyyo, asaṅgamova seyyoti.

Therein, ‘so dāni pitvāna kiriṅkarosi’ means: now, having drunk the water given by me, you make monkey-faces and make the sound ‘kiri kiri.’ ‘Asaṅgamo pāpajanena seyyo’ means: association with a wicked person is not good; indeed, non-association is better.

Taṃ [V 2.0059] sutvā so mittadubbhī makkaṭo “tvaṃ ‘ettakenavetaṃ niṭṭhita’nti saññaṃ karosi, idāni te sīse vaccaṃ pātetvā gamissāmī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the treacherous monkey thought, “You think this matter is finished with just this much, but now I will drop excrement on your head before I go.” And he spoke the second verse:

48.

48.

“Ko te suto vā diṭṭho vā, sīlavā nāma makkaṭo;

Idāni kho taṃ ohacchaṃ, esā asmāka dhammatā”ti.

“Where have you heard or seen a monkey that is virtuous? Now I shall defecate upon you; for such is our nature.”

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – bho brāhmaṇa, “makkaṭo kataguṇajānanako ācārasampanno sīlavā nāma atthī”ti kahaṃ tayā suto vā diṭṭho vā, idāni kho ahaṃ taṃ ohacchaṃ vaccaṃ te sīse katvā pakkamissāmi, asmākañhi makkaṭānaṃ nāma esā dhammatā ayaṃ jātisabhāvo, yadidaṃ upakārakassa sīse vaccaṃ kātabbanti.

Here is the summary of the meaning: O brahmin, where have you heard or seen that there is such a thing as a virtuous monkey who is grateful and well-behaved? Now I shall defecate upon you, leaving excrement on your head before I depart. For this is indeed the nature of us monkeys, our innate disposition, namely, that we should defecate on the head of a benefactor.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto uṭṭhāya gantuṃ ārabhi. Makkaṭo taṅkhaṇaññeva uppatitvā sākhāyaṃ nisīditvā olambakaṃ otaranto viya tassa sīse vaccaṃ pātetvā viravanto vanasaṇḍaṃ pāvisi. Bodhisatto nhatvā agamāsi.

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta got up and prepared to leave. At that very moment, the monkey leaped up and sat on a branch, and as if dangling down, he dropped excrement on the Bodhisatta's head, then entered the forest thicket while screeching. The Bodhisatta bathed and went on his way.

Satthā [P 2.0072] “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto, pubbepi mayā kataguṇaṃ na jānāsiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā makkaṭo devadatto ahosi, brāhmaṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta failed to acknowledge a favor done by me; he failed to do so in the past as well.” Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the monkey was Devadatta, and the brahmin was I myself.”

Dubbhiyamakkaṭajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Dubbhiyamakkaṭa Jātaka is the fourth.

[175] 5. Ādiccupaṭṭhānajātakavaṇṇanā

[175] 5. The Commentary on the Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka

Sabbesu [M 2.0066] kira bhūtesūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā kathitasadisameva.

“Sabbesu kira bhūtesu”: The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain deceitful monk. The story is just as was told before.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā mahāparivāro gaṇasatthā hutvā himavante vāsaṃ kappesi. So tattha ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya pabbatā oruyha paccante ekaṃ gāmaṃ nissāya [V 2.0060] paṇṇasālāyaṃ vāsaṃ upagañchi. Atheko lolamakkaṭo isigaṇe bhikkhācāraṃ gate assamapadaṃ āgantvā paṇṇasālā uttiṇṇā karoti, pānīyaghaṭesu udakaṃ chaḍḍeti, kuṇḍikaṃ bhindati, aggisālāyaṃ vaccaṃ karoti. Tāpasā vassaṃ vasitvā “idāni himavanto pupphaphalasamiddho ramaṇīyo, tattheva gamissāmā”ti paccantagāmavāsike āpucchiṃsu. Manussā “sve, bhante, mayaṃ bhikkhaṃ gahetvā assamapadaṃ āgamissāma, taṃ paribhuñjitvāva gamissathā”ti vatvā dutiyadivase pahūtaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ gahetvā tattha agamaṃsu. Taṃ disvā so makkaṭo cintesi – “kohaññaṃ katvā manusse ārādhetvā mayhampi khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ āharāpessāmī”ti. So tāpasacaraṇaṃ caranto viya sīlavā viya ca hutvā tāpasānaṃ [P 2.0073] avidūre sūriyaṃ namassamāno aṭṭhāsi. Manussā taṃ disvā “sīlavantānaṃ santike vasantā sīlavantā hontī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the country of Kāsi. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā, was ordained as an ascetic, attained the supernormal powers and meditative attainments, and having become the teacher of a large group of ascetics, lived in the Himalayas. After living there for a long time, he descended from the mountains to consume salt and sour foods and took up residence in a leaf hut near a border village. At that time, a certain fickle monkey would come to the hermitage when the group of ascetics had gone out for alms, and would play and run about on the roof of the leaf hut, spill water from the water pots, break the water jar, and defecate in the fire hall. After the ascetics had spent the rainy season there, they took leave of the border villagers, saying, “Now the Himalayas are delightful and rich in flowers and fruits; we shall go there.” The people said, “Venerable sirs, tomorrow we shall bring food to the hermitage; please depart only after partaking of it.” On the following day, they brought plenty of hard and soft food and arrived there. Seeing this, the monkey thought, “I will perform some marvel to please these people so that they will give me hard and soft food too.” Then, pretending to practice the conduct of an ascetic and appearing virtuous, he stood not far from the ascetics, paying homage to the sun. Seeing him, the people said, “Those who live near the virtuous become virtuous,” and spoke the first verse:

49.

49.

“Sabbesu kira bhūtesu, santi sīlasamāhitā;

Passa sākhamigaṃ jammaṃ, ādiccamupatiṭṭhatī”ti.

“Indeed, among all beings, there are those established in virtue. Look at this wretched monkey, worshipping the sun!”

Tattha santi sīlasamāhitāti sīlena samannāgatā saṃvijjanti, sīlavantā ca samāhitā ca ekaggacittā saṃvijjantītipi attho. Jammanti lāmakaṃ. Ādiccamupatiṭṭhatīti sūriyaṃ namassamāno tiṭṭhati.

Here, 'santi sīlasamāhitā' means those who are endowed with virtue are present; the meaning is also that both the virtuous and the concentrated, with one-pointed minds, are present. 'Jammaṃ' means base. 'Ādiccamupatiṭṭhati' means he stands paying homage to the sun.

Evaṃ te manusse tassa guṇaṃ kathente disvā bodhisatto “tumhe imassa lolamakkaṭassa sīlācāraṃ ajānitvā avatthusmiṃyeva pasannā”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing those people speaking of his virtue, the Bodhisatta said, "You, not knowing the conduct of this fickle monkey, are pleased with what is groundless." Then he spoke the second verse:

50.

50.

“Nāssa [M 2.0067] sīlaṃ vijānātha, anaññāya pasaṃsatha;

Aggihuttañca uhannaṃ, dve ca bhinnā kamaṇḍalū”ti.

"You do not know his virtue; you praise him without understanding. The fire-hut has been defecated upon, and two water pots have been broken."

Tattha anaññāyāti ajānitvā. Uhannanti iminā pāpamakkaṭena ūhadaṃ. Kamaṇḍalūti kuṇḍikā. “Dve ca kuṇḍikā tena bhinnā”ti evamassa aguṇaṃ kathesi.

Here, 'anaññāya' means 'without knowing.' 'Uhannaṃ' means 'defecated upon by this wicked monkey.' 'Kamaṇḍalū' means a water pot. Thus he spoke of his fault: "And two water pots were broken by him."

Manussā makkaṭassa kuhakabhāvaṃ ñatvā leḍḍuñca yaṭṭhiñca gahetvā pothetvā palāpetvā isigaṇassa bhikkhaṃ adaṃsu. Isayopi himavantameva gantvā aparihīnajjhānā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

The people, recognizing the monkey’s deceitful nature, took clods and sticks, beat him and chased him away, and gave alms to the company of ascetics. The ascetics, too, went to the Himalayas and, without falling away from their meditation, were destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā [V 2.0061] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā makkaṭo ayaṃ kuhako bhikkhu ahosi, isigaṇo buddhaparisā, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the monkey was this deceitful monk, the company of ascetics was the Buddha's assembly, and the leader of the company was indeed myself."

Ādiccupaṭṭhānajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka is the fifth.

[176] 6. Kaḷāyamuṭṭhijātakavaṇṇanā

[176] 6. The Commentary on the Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi Jātaka

Bālo [P 2.0074] vatāyaṃ dumasākhagocaroti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarājānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye vassakāle kosalarañño paccanto kupi. Tattha ṭhitā yodhā dve tīṇi yuddhāni katvā paccatthike abhibhavituṃ asakkontā rañño sāsanaṃ pesesuṃ. Rājā akāle vassāneyeva nikkhamitvā jetavanasamīpe khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā cintesi – “ahaṃ akāle nikkhanto, kandarapadarādayo udakapūrā, duggamo maggo, satthāraṃ upasaṅkamissāmi, so maṃ ‘kahaṃ gacchasi, mahārājā’ti pucchissati, athāhaṃ etamatthaṃ ārocessāmi, na kho pana maṃ satthā samparāyikenevatthena anuggaṇhāti, diṭṭhadhammikenāpi anuggaṇhātiyeva, tasmiṃ sace me gamanena avuḍḍhi bhavissati, ‘akālo, mahārājā’ti vakkhati. Sace pana vuḍḍi bhavissati, tuṇhī bhavissatī”ti. So jetavanaṃ pavisitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā “handa kuto nu tvaṃ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti pucchi. “Bhante, ahaṃ paccantaṃ vūpasametuṃ nikkhanto ‘tumhe vanditvā gamissāmī’ti āgatomhī”ti[M 2.0068]. Satthā “pubbepi, mahārāja, rājāno senāya abbhuggacchamānāya paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā akāle abbhuggamanaṃ nāma na gamiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"Bālo vatāyaṃ dumasākhagocaro": The Teacher told this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the king of Kosala. On one occasion, during the rainy season, the border of the Kosalan king was in turmoil. The soldiers stationed there, after fighting two or three battles and being unable to defeat the enemy, sent a message to the king. The king set out unseasonably during the rains and encamped near Jetavana. He thought, “I have set out at the wrong time; the mountain caves and chasms are full of water, the road is difficult to travel. I will approach the Teacher. He will ask me, ‘Where are you going, great king?’ Then I will explain the matter. The Teacher does not assist me only with matters pertaining to the next life; he also assists with matters pertaining to this life. In that case, if my journey will bring no success, he will say, ‘It is the wrong time, great king.’ But if it will bring success, he will remain silent.” So he entered Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat to one side. The Teacher asked, “Well, great king, from where have you come in broad daylight?” “Venerable sir, I have set out to pacify the border and have come to pay homage to you before going.” The Teacher said, “Great king, in the past too, kings, when their army was setting out, having heard the words of the wise, did not undertake a departure at the wrong time.” Being asked by the king, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako sabbatthakaamacco ahosi. Atha rañño paccante kupite paccantayodhā paṇṇaṃ pesesuṃ. Rājā vassakāle nikkhamitvā uyyāne khandhāvāraṃ bandhi, bodhisatto rañño santike aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe assānaṃ kaḷāye sedetvā āharitvā doṇiyaṃ pakkhipiṃsu. Uyyāne makkaṭesu eko makkaṭo rukkhā otaritvā tato kaḷāye gahetvā mukhaṃ pūretvā hatthehipi gahetvā uppatitvā rukkhe nisīditvā khādituṃ ārabhi, athassa khādamānassa hatthako eko kaḷāyo bhūmiyaṃ pati. So mukhena ca hatthehi ca gahite sabbe [P 2.0075] kaḷāye chaḍḍetvā rukkhā oruyha tameva kaḷāyaṃ olokento taṃ kaḷāyaṃ adisvāva puna rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā aḍḍe sahassaparājito viya socamāno dummukho rukkhasākhāyaṃ nisīdi. Rājā makkaṭassa kiriyaṃ disvā bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā [V 2.0062] “passatha, kiṃ nāmetaṃ makkaṭena kata”nti pucchi. Bodhisatto “mahārāja, bahuṃ anavaloketvā appaṃ oloketvā dubbuddhino bālā evarūpaṃ karontiyevā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his advisor on matters of welfare and righteousness, and his chief minister in all affairs. Once, when the border provinces revolted, the border guards sent a message. The king set out during the rainy season and established his camp in a garden, while the Bodhisatta remained by the king’s side. At that moment, they brought boiled peas for the horses and placed them in the troughs. In the garden, a monkey descended from a tree, took some peas, filled its mouth, and grabbed some with its hands. Then it leaped up, sat on the tree, and began to eat. While it was eating, one pea fell from its hand to the ground. Letting go of all the peas held in its mouth and hands, the monkey climbed down from the tree, looking for that single pea. Not finding that pea, it climbed back up the tree and, grieving like one who had lost a thousand pieces in a lawsuit, sat on a branch with a sorrowful face. The king, seeing the monkey’s behavior, called the Bodhisatta and asked, “See what this monkey has done?” The Bodhisatta replied, “Great king, fools of poor understanding, overlooking much and looking at little, act in just this way.” Then he spoke the first verse:

51.

51.

“Bālo vatāyaṃ dumasākhagocaro, paññā janinda nayimassa vijjati;

Kaḷāyamuṭṭhiṃ avakiriya kevalaṃ, ekaṃ kaḷāyaṃ patitaṃ gavesatī”ti.

“Foolish indeed is this one whose pasture is the branches of a tree. O lord of people, wisdom is not found in him. Having scattered an entire handful of peas, he searches for a single pea that has fallen.”

Tattha dumasākhagocaroti makkaṭo. So hi dumasākhāsu gocaraṃ gaṇhāti, sāva assa gocaro sañcaraṇabhūmibhūtā, tasmā “dumasākhagocaro”ti vuccati. Janindāti rājānaṃ ālapati. Rājā hi paramissarabhāvena janassa indoti janindo. Kaḷāyamuṭṭhinti caṇakamuṭṭhiṃ. “Kāḷarājamāsamuṭṭhi”ntipi vadantiyeva. Avakiriyāti avakiritvā. Kevalanti sabbaṃ. Gavesatīti bhūmiyaṃ patitaṃ ekameva pariyesati.

There, ‘whose pasture is the branches of a tree’ refers to a monkey. For it takes its food from the branches of trees, and they are its pasture and roaming ground; therefore, it is called ‘one whose pasture is the branches of a tree’. ‘Lord of people’ addresses the king. For the king, by virtue of being the supreme lord, is the ‘lord’ of the people, hence ‘lord of people’. ‘A handful of peas’ means a handful of chickpeas. Some also say ‘a handful of black beans’. ‘Having scattered’ means having scattered. ‘Entire’ means all. ‘He searches’ means he searches for the single one fallen on the ground.

Evaṃ [M 2.0069] vatvā puna bodhisatto taṃ upasaṅkamitvā rājānaṃ āmantetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, the Bodhisatta approached the king again, and addressing him, spoke a second verse:

52.

52.

“Evameva mayaṃ rāja, ye caññe atilobhino;

Appena bahuṃ jiyyāma, kaḷāyeneva vānaro”ti.

“Just so, O king, we and other overly greedy ones, for a little we lose much, like the monkey with the pea.”

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – mahārāja, evameva mayañca ye caññe lobhābhibhūtā janā sabbepi appena bahuṃ jiyyāma. Mayañhi etarahi akāle vassānasamaye maggaṃ gacchantā appakassa atthassa kāraṇā bahukā atthā parihāyāma. Kaḷāyeneva vānaroti yathā ayaṃ vānaro ekaṃ kaḷāyaṃ pariyesamāno tenekena kaḷāyena sabbakaḷāyehi parihīno, evaṃ mayampi [P 2.0076] akālena kandarapadarādīsu pūresu gacchamānā appamattakaṃ atthaṃ pariyesamānā bahūhi hatthivāhanaassavāhanādīhi ceva balakāyena ca parihāyissāma. Tasmā akāle gantuṃ na vaṭṭatīti rañño ovādaṃ adāsi.

Here is the summary of the meaning—O great king, just so, we and all other people overcome by greed lose much for the sake of a little. For now, traveling on the road out of season during the rainy season, for the sake of a small benefit, we lose many benefits. ‘Like the monkey with the pea’ means: just as this monkey, searching for one pea, was deprived of all the peas because of that one pea, so too we, going out of season through flooded caves and mountain passes, seeking a small benefit, will lose many things—elephant mounts, horse mounts, and even our forces. Therefore, it is not proper to go out of season. Thus he gave this advice to the king.

Rājā tassa kathaṃ sutvā tato nivattitvā bārāṇasimeva pāvisi. Corāpi “rājā kira coramaddanaṃ karissāmīti nagarā nikkhanto”ti sutvā paccantato palāyiṃsu. Paccuppannepi corā “kosalarājā kira nikkhanto”ti sutvā palāyiṃsu. Rājā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā sāvatthimeva pāvisi.

Having heard his words, the king turned back from there and entered Benares itself. The thieves, hearing that ‘the king, it seems, has left the city to suppress the thieves,’ fled from the border regions. In the present time as well, the thieves, hearing that ‘the Kosala king, it seems, has set out,’ fled. Having heard the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, the king rose from his seat, paid homage, performed the circumambulation, and entered Sāvatthī itself.

Satthā [V 2.0063] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher identified the Birth-story: ‘At that time, the king was Ānanda, but the wise advisor was indeed myself.’

Kaḷāyamuṭṭhijātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Explanation of the Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi Jātaka, the Sixth.

[177] 7. Tindukajātakavaṇṇanā

[177] 7. 7. Tinduka Jātaka (The Wise Monkey)

Dhanuhatthakalāpehīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Satthā hi mahābodhijātake (jā. 2.18.124 ādayo) viya umaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) viya ca attano paññāya vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ sutvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva tathāgato paññavā, pubbepi paññavā upāyakusaloyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘With bows and quivers in hand’—The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the perfection of wisdom. For the Teacher, having heard praise of his own wisdom, as in the Mahābodhi Jātaka and the Umaṅga Jātaka, said, ‘Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is wise; in the past too, he was wise and skilled in means,’ and then he brought forth the past story.

Atīte [M 2.0070] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto vānarayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā asītisahassavānaragaṇaparivāro himavantapadese vāsaṃ kappesi. Tassāsanne eko paccantagāmako kadāci vasati, kadāci ubbasati. Tassa pana gāmassa majjhe sākhāviṭapasampanno madhuraphalo eko tindukarukkho atthi, vānaragaṇo ubbasitakāle āgantvā tassa phalāni khādati. Athāparasmiṃ phalavāre so gāmo puna āvāso ahosi daḷhaparikkhitto dvārayutto, sopi rukkho phalabhāranamitasākho [P 2.0077] aṭṭhāsi. Vānaragaṇo cintesi – “mayaṃ pubbe asukagāme tindukaphalāni khādāma, phalito nu kho so etarahi rukkho, udāhu no, āvasito so gāmo, udāhu no”ti. Evañca pana cintetvā “gaccha imaṃ pavattiṃ jānāhī”ti ekaṃ vānaraṃ pesesi. So gantvā rukkhassa ca phalitabhāvaṃ gāmassa ca gāḷhavāsabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgantvā vānarānaṃ ārocesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a monkey's womb and lived in the Himalayan region with a retinue of eighty thousand monkeys. Nearby, there was a border village that was sometimes inhabited and sometimes deserted. In the middle of that village stood a tinduka tree, full of branches and bearing sweet fruit. When the village was deserted, the troop of monkeys would come and eat its fruit. Later, in another fruiting season, that village was once more inhabited, strongly fortified, and provided with a gate, and the tree stood there with its branches bent low with the weight of fruit. The troop of monkeys thought, ‘Previously, we ate the tinduka fruits in such-and-such a village. Is that tree now bearing fruit, or not? Is that village inhabited, or not?’ Having thought thus, they sent one monkey, saying, ‘Go and find out the news.’ He went, and having ascertained that the tree was bearing fruit and that the village was densely inhabited, he returned and informed the monkeys.

Vānarā tassa phalitabhāvaṃ sutvā “madhurāni tindukaphalāni khādissāmā”ti ussāhajātā vānarindassa tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Vānarindo “gāmo āvāso anāvāso”ti pucchi. “Āvāso, devā”ti. “Tena hi na gantabbaṃ. Manussā hi bahumāyā hontī”ti. “Deva, manussānaṃ paṭisallānavelāya aḍḍharattasamaye khādissāmā”ti bahū gantvā vānarindaṃ sampaṭicchāpetvā himavantā otaritvā tassa gāmassa avidūre manussānaṃ paṭisallānakālaṃ āgamayamānā mahāpāsāṇapiṭṭhe sayitvā majjhimayāme manussesu niddaṃ okkamantesu rukkhaṃ āruyha phalāni khādiṃsu. Atheko puriso sarīrakiccena gehā nikkhamitvā gāmamajjhagato vānare [V 2.0064] disvā manussānaṃ ācikkhi. Bahū manussā dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā nānāvudhahatthā leḍḍudaṇḍādīni ādāya “pabhātāya rattiyā vānare gaṇhissāmā”ti rukkhaṃ parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Asītisahassavānarā manusse disvā maraṇabhayatajjitā “natthi no aññaṃ paṭissaraṇaṃ aññatra vānarindenā”ti tassa santikaṃ gantvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Hearing that it was bearing fruit, the monkeys, eager to eat the sweet tinduka fruits, informed the monkey king of the matter. The monkey king asked, ‘Is the village inhabited or uninhabited?’ ‘Inhabited, lord,’ they replied. ‘Then you should not go. Humans are full of deceit,’ he said. ‘Lord, we will eat at midnight, during the humans' rest time,’ they said. Having persuaded the monkey king, many went down from the Himalayas and, not far from that village, waited for the humans' rest time. They lay down on a large rock slab, and in the middle watch of the night when the humans had fallen asleep, they climbed the tree and ate the fruits. Then a man, having left his house for bodily functions, went into the middle of the village, saw the monkeys, and told the people. Many humans, equipping themselves with bows and quivers and taking up various weapons, clods, sticks, and the like, stood surrounding the tree, saying, ‘When the night has dawned, we will capture the monkeys.’ The eighty thousand monkeys, seeing the humans and terrified by the fear of death, thought, ‘We have no other refuge than the monkey king.’ They went to his presence and spoke the first verse:

53.

53.

“Dhanuhatthakalāpehi, nettiṃsavaradhāribhi;

Samantā parikiṇṇamha, kathaṃ mokkho bhavissatī”ti.

“With bows and quivers in hand, and bearing excellent swords, we are surrounded on all sides; how will our escape be?”

Tattha [M 2.0071] dhanuhatthakalāpehīti dhanukalāpahatthehi, dhanūni ceva sarakalāpe ca gahetvā ṭhitehīti attho. Nettiṃsavaradhāribhīti nettiṃsā vuccanti khaggā, uttamakhaggadhārīhīti attho. Parikiṇṇamhāti parivāritamha. Kathanti kena nu kho upāyena amhākaṃ mokkho bhavissatīti.

Therein, ‘dhanuhatthakalāpehīti’ means with bows and quivers in their hands; the meaning is standing holding both bows and quivers of arrows. Regarding ‘nettiṃsavaradhāribhīti,’ swords are called nettiṃsa; the meaning is by those bearing excellent swords. ‘Parikiṇṇamhāti’ means we are surrounded. ‘Kathanti’ means by what means will our escape be possible?

Tesaṃ [P 2.0078] kathaṃ sutvā vānarindo “mā bhāyittha, manussā nāma bahukiccā, ajjapi majjhimayāmo vattati, api nāma tesaṃ ‘amhe māressāmā’ti parivāritānaṃ imassa kiccassa antarāyakaraṃ aññaṃ kiccaṃ uppajjeyyā”ti vānare samassāsetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing their words, the monkey king said, ‘Do not be afraid. Humans are busy with many tasks. Even now the middle watch is passing. Perhaps for those who have surrounded us thinking, “We will kill them,” some other task might arise that interrupts this task.’ Reassuring the monkeys, he spoke the second verse:

54.

54.

“Appeva bahukiccānaṃ, attho jāyetha koci naṃ;

Atthi rukkhassa acchinnaṃ, khajjathaññeva tinduka”nti.

“Perhaps for those with many tasks, some other matter may arise for them; there is still unplucked fruit on the tree; just eat the tinduka fruit.”

Tattha nanti nipātamattaṃ, appeva bahukiccānaṃ manussānaṃ añño koci attho uppajjeyyāti ayamevettha attho. Atthi rukkhassa acchinnanti imassa rukkhassa phalānaṃ ākaḍḍhanaparikaḍḍhanavasena acchinnaṃ bahu ṭhānaṃ atthi. Khajjathaññeva tindukanti tindukaphalaṃ khajjathaññeva. Tumhe hi yāvatakena vo attho atthi, tattakaṃ khādatha, amhākaṃ paharaṇakālaṃ jānissāmāti.

Therein, ‘naṃ’ is merely a particle; the meaning here is this: ‘Perhaps some other purpose may arise for humans who have many tasks.’ ‘There is much on the tree that is unplucked’ means that on this tree, there are many places with fruit unplucked by way of pulling and dragging. ‘Just eat the tinduka’ means just eat the tinduka fruit. ‘You, for your part, eat as much as you need; we will know our time to strike.’

Evaṃ mahāsatto kapigaṇaṃ samassāsesi. Ettakañhi assāsaṃ alabhamānā sabbepi te phalitena hadayena jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇeyyuṃ. Mahāsatto pana evaṃ vānaragaṇaṃ assāsetvā “sabbe vānare samānethā”ti āha. Samānentā tassa bhāgineyyaṃ senakaṃ nāma vānaraṃ adisvā “senako nāgato”ti ārocesuṃ. “Sace senako nāgato, tumhe mā bhāyittha, idāni vo so [V 2.0065] sotthiṃ karissatī”ti. Senakopi kho vānaragaṇassa gamanakāle niddāyitvā pacchā pabuddho kañci adisvā padānupadiko hutvā āgacchanto manusse disvā “vānaragaṇassa bhayaṃ uppanna”nti ñatvā ekasmiṃ pariyante gehe aggiṃ jāletvā suttaṃ kantantiyā mahallakitthiyā santikaṃ gantvā khettaṃ gacchanto gāmadārako viya ekaṃ ummukaṃ gahetvā [P 2.0079] uparivāte ṭhatvā gāmaṃ padīpesi. Manussā makkaṭe chaḍḍetvā aggiṃ nibbāpetuṃ agamaṃsu. Vānarā palāyantā senakassatthāya ekekaṃ phalaṃ gahetvā palāyiṃsu.

Thus, the Great Being reassured the troop of monkeys. For without this much reassurance, all of them would have met their end with broken hearts. Having reassured the troop of monkeys in this way, the Great Being said, "Gather all the monkeys." While gathering them, they did not see his nephew, a monkey named Senaka, and reported, "Senaka has not come." "If Senaka has not come, do not fear; he will now ensure your safety," he said. Now, Senaka had fallen asleep when the troop of monkeys was leaving. Later, waking up and seeing no one, he followed their tracks. Upon seeing the humans, he realized, "Danger has arisen for the troop of monkeys." In a house at one edge of the village, he lit a fire. Then, approaching an old woman spinning thread, he took a burning brand like a village boy going to the fields. Standing on the upwind side, he set the village ablaze. The people, abandoning the monkeys, went to extinguish the fire. The monkeys, fleeing, each took a fruit for Senaka's sake and fled.

Satthā [M 2.0072] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bhāgineyyo senako mahānāmo sakko ahosi, vānaragaṇo buddhaparisā, vānarindo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher made the connection to the Jātaka: "At that time, the nephew Senaka was Mahānāma the Sakyan, the troop of monkeys was the Buddha's assembly, and the monkey king was indeed I myself."

Tindukajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Tinduka Jātaka, the Seventh.

[178] 8. Kacchapajātakavaṇṇanā

[178] 8. The Commentary on the Kacchapa Jātaka

Janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ meti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ahivātakarogamuttaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira ekasmiṃ kule ahivātakarogo uppajji. Mātāpitaro puttaṃ āhaṃsu – “tāta, mā imasmiṃ gehe vasa, bhittiṃ bhinditvā palāyitvā yattha katthaci gantvā jīvitaṃ rakkha, pacchā āgantvā imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne mahānidhānaṃ atthi, taṃ uddharitvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā sukhena jīveyyāsī”ti. Putto tesaṃ vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā bhittiṃ bhinditvā palāyitvā attano roge vūpasante āgantvā mahānidhānaṃ uddharitvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā gharāvāsaṃ vasi. So ekadivasaṃ sappitelādīni ceva vatthacchādanādīni ca gāhāpetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisīdi. Satthā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “tumhākaṃ gehe ahivātakarogo uppannoti assumha, kinti katvā muttosī”ti pucchi, so taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Satthā “pubbepi kho, upāsaka, bhaye uppanne attano vasanaṭṭhāne ālayaṃ katvā aññattha agatā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, anālayaṃ pana katvā aññattha gatā jīvitaṃ labhiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“My birthplace, my place of being…”: this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning one who had recovered from the snake-wind disease. It seems that in a certain household at Sāvatthī, the snake-wind disease arose. The parents said to their son: "Dear one, do not stay in this house. Break through the wall and flee; go wherever you can to save your life. Later, return, and in such-and-such a place there is a great treasure. Dig it up, establish the household, and live happily." The son accepted their words, broke through the wall, and fled. When his illness had subsided, he returned, dug up the great treasure, established the household, and lived the household life. One day, having had ghee, oil, and so on, as well as clothes and coverings, brought to him, he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. The Teacher exchanged pleasantries with him and asked, "We heard that the snake-wind disease arose in your household. How were you freed from it?" He explained what had happened. The Teacher said, "In the past too, lay follower, when danger arose, those who, having an attachment to their dwelling place, did not go elsewhere met with the destruction of their lives, while those who had no attachment and went elsewhere obtained life." Being requested by him, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsigāmake kumbhakārakule nibbattitvā kumbhakārakammaṃ katvā puttadāraṃ posesi. Tadā pana bārāṇasiyaṃ mahānadiyā saddhiṃ ekābaddho mahājātassaro ahosi. So bahuudakakāle nadiyā saddhiṃ ekodako hoti, udake mandībhūte [V 2.0066] visuṃ hoti. Macchakacchapā [P 2.0080] pana “imasmiṃ saṃvacchare suvuṭṭhikā bhavissati, imasmiṃ saṃvacchare dubbuṭṭhikā”ti jānanti. Atha tasmiṃ sare nibbattamacchakacchapā “imasmiṃ saṃvacchare dubbuṭṭhikā bhavissatī”ti ñatvā udakassa ekābaddhakāleyeva tamhā sarā nikkhamitvā [M 2.0073] nadiṃ agamiṃsu. Eko pana kacchapo “idaṃ me jātaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhitaṭṭhānaṃ, mātāpitūhi vasitaṭṭhānaṃ, na sakkomi imaṃ jahitu”nti nadiṃ na agamāsi. Atha nidāghasamaye tattha udakaṃ chijji, so kacchapo bodhisattassa mattikagahaṇaṭṭhāne bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā pāvisi. Bodhisatto “mattikaṃ gahessāmī”ti tattha gantvā mahākuddālena bhūmiṃ khaṇanto kacchapassa piṭṭhiṃ bhinditvā mattikapiṇḍaṃ viya kuddāleneva naṃ uddharitvā thale pātesi. So vedanāppatto hutvā “vasanaṭṭhāne ālayaṃ jahituṃ asakkonto evaṃ vināsaṃ pāpuṇi”nti vatvā paridevamāno imā gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a potter’s family in a Kasi village. He worked as a potter and supported his wife and children. At that time, near Benares, there was a large natural lake connected to the great river. When the water was high, it became one with the river, but when the water receded, it became separate. The fish and turtles, however, knew, “This year there will be good rain,” or, “This year there will be a drought.” Then, the fish and turtles born in that lake, realizing, “This year there will be a drought,” left that lake while the water was still connected and went to the river. But one turtle thought, “This is my birthplace, the place where I grew up, the place where my parents lived—I cannot abandon it,” and did not go to the river. Then, in the hot season, the water there dried up. That turtle dug into the ground at the Bodhisatta’s clay-gathering place and entered it. The Bodhisatta, thinking, “I will get clay,” went there and, while digging the ground with a large hoe, broke the turtle’s back. Lifting it up with the hoe itself as though it were a lump of clay, he threw it onto the dry land. Overcome with pain, the turtle lamented, “Being unable to abandon my attachment to my dwelling place, I have thus met with destruction,” and uttered these verses:

55.

55.

“Janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ me, iti paṅke avassayiṃ;

Taṃ maṃ paṅko ajjhabhavi, yathā dubbalakaṃ tathā;

Taṃ taṃ vadāmi bhaggava, suṇohi vacanaṃ mama.

“‘This is my birthplace, this is my place of being,’ thus I dwelt in the mud. That mud overwhelmed me, as it would a weakling. Therefore, Bhaggava, I say this to you, listen to my words.

56.

56.

“Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, sukhaṃ yatrādhigacchati;

Taṃ janittaṃ bhavittañca, purisassa pajānato;

Yamhi jīve tamhi gacche, na niketahato siyā”ti.

“Whether in a village or in a forest, wherever one attains happiness, that is the birthplace and place of being for a discerning person. Wherever one can live, there one should go; one should not be slain by attachment to one's home.”

Tattha janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ meti idaṃ mama jātaṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ mama vaḍḍhitaṭṭhānaṃ. Iti paṅke avassayinti iminā kāraṇenāhaṃ imasmiṃ kaddame avassayiṃ nipajjiṃ, vāsaṃ kappesinti attho. Ajjhabhavīti adhiabhavi vināsaṃ pāpesi. Bhaggavāti kumbhakāraṃ ālapati. Kumbhakārānañhi nāmagottapaññatti esā, yadidaṃ bhaggavāti. Sukhanti kāyikacetasikassādaṃ. Taṃ [P 2.0081] janittaṃ bhavittañcāti taṃ jātaṭṭhānañca vaḍḍhitaṭṭhānañca. “Jānittaṃ bhāvitta”nti dīghavasenapi pāṭho, soyevattho. Pajānatoti atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ jānantassa. Na niketahato siyāti nikete ālayaṃ katvā aññattha agantvā niketena hato, evarūpaṃ maraṇadukkhaṃ pāpito na bhaveyyāti.

Therein, 'janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ me' means: this is my birthplace, this is my place of growth. 'Iti paṅke avassayiṃ' means: for this reason, I settled in this mud, I lay down, I made my dwelling—that is the meaning. 'Ajjhabhavi' means: he overpowered, he brought to destruction. 'Bhaggavā' is an address to the potter. For this is a designation of name and clan for potters, that is, 'Bhaggavā.' 'Sukhaṃ' refers to bodily and mental pleasure. 'Taṃ janittaṃ bhavittañcāti' means: that birthplace and place of growth. The reading 'jānittaṃ bhāvittaṃ' with long vowels is also found, and the meaning is the same. 'Pajānato' means: of one who knows what is beneficial and not beneficial, the cause and the non-cause. 'Na niketahato siyā' means: one should not be struck down by one's dwelling—that is, having formed an attachment to a dwelling and not going elsewhere, one should not be brought to the suffering of death caused by that dwelling.

Evaṃ so bodhisattena saddhiṃ kathento kālamakāsi. Bodhisatto taṃ gahetvā sakalagāmavāsino sannipātāpetvā te manusse ovadanto evamāha – “passatha imaṃ kacchapaṃ, ayaṃ [V 2.0067] aññesaṃ macchakacchapānaṃ mahānadiṃ gamanakāle attano vasanaṭṭhāne ālayaṃ chindituṃ asakkonto [M 2.0074] tehi saddhiṃ agantvā mama mattikagahaṇaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā nipajji. Athassāhaṃ mattikaṃ gaṇhanto mahākuddālena piṭṭhiṃ bhinditvā mattikapiṇḍaṃ viya naṃ thale pātesiṃ, ayaṃ attanā katakammaṃ saritvā dvīhi gāthāhi paridevitvā kālamakāsi. Evamesa attano vasanaṭṭhāne ālayaṃ katvā maraṇaṃ patto, tumhepi mā iminā kacchapena sadisā ahuvattha, ito paṭṭhāya ‘mayhaṃ rūpaṃ mayhaṃ saddo mayhaṃ gandho mayhaṃ raso mayhaṃ phoṭṭhabbo mayhaṃ putto mayhaṃ dhītā mayhaṃ dāsadāsiparicchedo mayhaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇa’nti taṇhāvasena upabhogavasena mā gaṇhittha, ekakovesa satto tīsu bhavesu parivattatī”ti. Evaṃ buddhalīlāya mahājanassa ovādamadāsi, so ovādo sakalajambudīpaṃ pattharitvā saṭṭhimattāni vassasahassāni aṭṭhāsi. Mahājano bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā āyupariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūresi, bodhisattopi tatheva puññāni katvā saggapuraṃ pūresi.

Thus, while conversing with the Bodhisatta, the turtle died. The Bodhisatta, taking it, gathered all the villagers and admonished those people, saying: 'Behold this turtle. When other fish and turtles were going to the great river, it, being unable to sever its attachment to its own dwelling place, did not go with them but entered the place where I was gathering clay and lay down. Then, as I was taking the clay, I struck its back with a great spade, breaking it, and cast it onto the shore like a lump of clay. Remembering the deed it had done, it lamented with two verses and died. Thus, having formed an attachment to its dwelling place, it met death. You too must not be like this turtle. From now on, do not grasp by way of craving and by way of enjoyment, thinking: “My form, my sound, my smell, my taste, my touch, my son, my daughter, my retinue of male and female slaves, my gold and silver.” This single being wanders through the three realms of existence.' Thus, with the majesty of a Buddha, he gave this counsel to the great multitude. That counsel spread throughout all of Jambudīpa and endured for sixty thousand years. The great multitude, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s counsel, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and, at the end of their lives, filled the heavenly city. The Bodhisatta also, having performed meritorious deeds in the same way, filled the heavenly city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so kulaputto sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. “Tadā kacchapo ānando ahosi, kumbhakāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that clansman was established in the fruit of stream-entry. 'At that time, the tortoise was Ānanda, and the potter was I myself.'

Kacchapajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kacchapa Jātaka, the Eighth.

[179] 9. Satadhammajātakavaṇṇanā

[179] 9. The Commentary on the Satadhamma Jātaka.

Tañca [P 2.0082] appanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekavīsatividhaṃ anesanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi kāle bahū bhikkhū vejjakammena dūtakammena pahiṇakammena jaṅghapesanikena piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍenāti evarūpāya ekavīsatividhāya anesanāya jīvikaṃ kappesuṃ. Sā sāketajātake (jā. 1.2.173-174) āvibhavissati. Satthā tesaṃ tathā jīvikakappanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “etarahi kho bahū bhikkhū anesanāya jīvikaṃ kappenti, te pana evaṃ jīvikaṃ kappetvā yakkhattabhāvā petattabhāvā na muccissanti, dhuragoṇā hutvāva nibbattissanti, niraye paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhissanti, etesaṃ hitatthāya sukhatthāya [M 2.0075] attajjhāsayaṃ sakapaṭibhānaṃ ekaṃ dhammadesanaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā “na, bhikkhave, ekavīsatividhāya anesanāya paccayā uppādetabbā. Anesanāya hi uppanno piṇḍapāto ādittalohaguḷasadiso halāhalavisūpamo. Anesanā hi nāmesā buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakehi garahitabbā paṭikuṭṭhā. Anesanāya [V 2.0068] uppannaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjantassa hi hāso vā somanassaṃ vā natthi. Evaṃ uppanno hi piṇḍapāto mama sāsane caṇḍālassa ucchiṭṭhabhojanasadiso, tassa paribhogo satadhammamāṇavassa caṇḍālucchiṭṭhabhattaparibhogo viya hotī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Tañca appaṃ'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the twenty-one kinds of improper livelihood. For at one time, many monks were sustaining their lives through the twenty-one kinds of improper livelihood, such as practicing medicine, acting as messengers, running errands, serving as foot-messengers, and barter of alms-food. This will be made clear in the Sāketa Jātaka. The Teacher, knowing that they were sustaining their lives in this way, thought: 'At present, many monks sustain their lives through improper livelihood. By doing so, they will not be freed from the state of yakshas or pretas; they will be reborn as oxen at the yoke; they will take rebirth in hell. For their welfare and happiness, it is fitting that I deliver a Dhamma discourse from my own inclination and insight.' Having assembled the community of monks, he said: 'Monks, requisites should not be acquired through the twenty-one kinds of improper livelihood. Alms-food obtained through improper livelihood is like a blazing iron ball, like the deadly halāhala poison. This improper livelihood is indeed censured and condemned by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples. For one who eats alms-food obtained through improper livelihood, there is no mirth or gladness. Alms-food obtained in this way is, in my Dispensation, like the leftover food of a caṇḍāla. Consuming it is like the consumption of a caṇḍāla's leftovers by the brahmin youth Satadhamma.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto caṇḍālayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto kenacideva karaṇīyena pātheyyataṇḍule ca bhattapuṭañca gahetvā maggaṃ paṭipajji. Tasmiñhi kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ eko māṇavo atthi satadhammo nāma udiccabrāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbatto. Sopi kenacideva karaṇīyena taṇḍule ca bhattapuṭañca agahetvāva maggaṃ paṭipajji, te ubhopi mahāmagge samāgacchiṃsu. Māṇavo bodhisattaṃ “kiṃjātikosī”ti pucchi. So “ahaṃ caṇḍālo”ti vatvā “tvaṃ kiṃjātikosī”ti māṇavaṃ pucchi[P 2.0083]. “Udiccabrāhmaṇo aha”nti. “Sādhu gacchāmā”ti te ubhopi maggaṃ agamaṃsu. Bodhisatto pātarāsavelāya udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne nisīditvā hatthe dhovitvā bhattapuṭaṃ mocetvā “māṇava, bhattaṃ bhuñjāhī”ti āha. “Natthi, are caṇḍāla, mama bhattena attho”ti. Bodhisatto “sādhū”ti puṭakabhattaṃ ucchiṭṭhaṃ akatvāva attano yāpanamattaṃ aññasmiṃ paṇṇe pakkhipitvā puṭakabhattaṃ bandhitvā ekamante ṭhapetvā bhuñjitvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā dhotahatthapādo taṇḍule ca sesabhattañca ādāya “gacchāma, māṇavā”ti maggaṃ paṭipajji.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a caṇḍāla family. Having come of age, for a certain purpose he took some rice for the journey and a packet of food and set out on the road. At that time in Bārāṇasī, there was a young man named Satadhamma, born into a great family of Udicca brahmins. He too, for a certain purpose, set out on the road without taking any rice or packet of food. Both of them met on the highway. The young man asked the Bodhisatta, 'Of what birth are you?' He replied, 'I am a caṇḍāla,' and asked the youth, 'And of what birth are you?' 'I am an Udicca brahmin.' 'Very well, let us go,' they said, and both proceeded on the road together. At the time of the morning meal, the Bodhisatta sat down at a convenient place with water, washed his hands, opened his packet of food, and said, 'Young man, eat some food.' 'Away, you caṇḍāla! I have no need for your food.' The Bodhisatta said, 'Very well,' and without making the food in the packet into leftovers, he placed only enough for his own sustenance on another leaf, tied up the packet of food, set it aside, ate, drank water, washed his hands and feet, took the rice and the remaining food, and saying, 'Let us go, young man,' he proceeded on the road.

Te sakaladivasaṃ gantvā sāyaṃ ubhopi ekasmiṃ udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne nhatvā paccuttariṃsu. Bodhisatto phāsukaṭṭhāne nisīditvā bhattapuṭaṃ mocetvā māṇavaṃ anāpucchitvā bhuñjituṃ ārabhi. Māṇavo sakaladivasaṃ maggagamanena kilanto chātajjhatto “sace me bhattaṃ dassati, bhuñjissāmī”ti olokento aṭṭhāsi. Itaro kiñci avatvā bhuñjateva. Māṇavo cintesi – “ayaṃ caṇḍālo mayhaṃ avatvāva sabbaṃ bhuñjati [M 2.0076] nippīḷetvāpi taṃ gahetvā upari ucchiṭṭhabhattaṃ chaḍḍetvā sesaṃ bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tathā katvā ucchiṭṭhabhattaṃ bhuñji. Athassa bhuttamattasseva “mayā attano jātigottakulapadesānaṃ ananucchavikaṃ kataṃ, caṇḍālassa nāma me ucchiṭṭhabhattaṃ bhutta”nti balavavippaṭisāro uppajji, tāvadevassa salohitaṃ bhattaṃ mukhato uggacchi. So “appamattakassa vata me kāraṇā ananucchavikaṃ kammaṃ kata”nti uppannabalavasokatāya paridevamāno paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having traveled the whole day, in the evening they both bathed at a convenient place with water and came out. The Bodhisatta sat down in a comfortable spot, opened his packet of food, and began to eat without inviting the young man. The youth, weary from walking all day and overcome by hunger, stood watching, thinking, 'If he offers me food, I will eat.' The other simply ate without saying anything. The youth thought: 'This caṇḍāla is eating everything without speaking to me. I should seize it, even by force, discard the leftover food from the top, and eat the rest.' Having done so, he ate the leftover food. As soon as he had eaten, a powerful remorse arose in him: 'I have done something unbecoming of my birth, lineage, and family! I have eaten the leftovers of a caṇḍāla!' Immediately, the food, together with blood, gushed from his mouth. Lamenting with powerful sorrow, thinking, 'Alas, for such a trivial reason I have done an unbecoming deed!', he spoke the first verse:

57.

57.

“Tañca [P 2.0084] appañca ucchiṭṭhaṃ, tañca kicchena no adā;

Sohaṃ brāhmaṇajātiko, yaṃ bhuttaṃ tampi uggata”nti.

That little bit of leftover food, he did not give it willingly, but only with difficulty. I, though of brahmin birth—even what was eaten has come up.

Tatrāyaṃ [V 2.0069] saṅkhepattho – yaṃ mayā bhuttaṃ, taṃ appañca ucchiṭṭhañca, tañca so caṇḍālo na attano ruciyā maṃ adāsi, atha kho nippīḷiyamāno kicchena kasirena adāsi, sohaṃ parisuddhabrāhmaṇajātiko, teneva me yaṃ bhuttaṃ, tampi saddhiṃ lohitena uggatanti.

The summary meaning is: What I have eaten was little and leftovers, and the caṇḍāla did not give it to me of his own will, but being pressed, gave it with difficulty and hardship. I am of pure brahmin birth; for that very reason, even what I have eaten has come up together with blood.

Evaṃ māṇavo paridevitvā “kiṃ dāni me evarūpaṃ ananucchavikaṃ kammaṃ katvā jīvitenā”ti araññaṃ pavisitvā kassaci attānaṃ adassetvāva anāthamaraṇaṃ patto.

Thus the young man lamented, thinking, 'Of what use now is life to me, having done such an unsuitable deed?' He entered the forest and, without showing himself to anyone, met a helpless death.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ dassetvā “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, satadhammamāṇavassa taṃ caṇḍālucchiṭṭhakaṃ bhuñjitvā attano ayuttabhojanassa bhuttattā neva hāso, na somanassaṃ uppajji, evameva yo imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajito anesanāya jīvikaṃ kappento tathāladdhapaccayaṃ paribhuñjati, tassa buddhapaṭikuṭṭhagarahitajīvitabhāvato neva hāso, na somanassaṃ uppajjatī”ti vatvā abhisambuddho hutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having related this past story, said: 'Monks, just as the young man Satadhamma, after eating the caṇḍāla's leftovers, felt neither joy nor satisfaction because he had eaten food unsuitable for himself; even so, for one who has gone forth in this Dispensation and maintains his life by improper means, using the requisites so obtained, neither joy nor satisfaction arises because his livelihood is despised and censured by the Buddha.' Having said this, as the Fully Enlightened One, he spoke the second verse:

58.

58.

“Evaṃ dhammaṃ niraṃkatvā, yo adhammena jīvati;

Satadhammova lābhena, laddhenapi na nandatī”ti.

Having thus rejected the Dhamma, one who lives by unrighteousness, like Satadhamma, finds no joy even in the gain acquired.

Tattha dhammanti ājīvapārisuddhisīladhammaṃ. Niraṃkatvāti nīharitvā chaḍḍetvā. Adhammenāti ekavīsatiyā anesanasaṅkhātena micchājīvena. Satadhammoti tassa nāmaṃ, “santadhammo”tipi pāṭho. Na nandatīti yathā satadhammo māṇavo “caṇḍālucchiṭṭhakaṃ me laddha”nti tena lābhena na [M 2.0077] nandati, evaṃ imasmimpi sāsane pabbajito kulaputto anesanāya laddhalābhaṃ paribhuñjanto na nandati na tussati, “buddhagarahitajīvikāya jīvāmī”ti domanassappatto hoti. Tasmā anesanāya jīvikaṃ kappentassa satadhammamāṇavasseva araññaṃ pavisitvā anāthamaraṇaṃ marituṃ varanti.

Therein, 'dhamma' means the virtue of purity of livelihood. 'Niraṃkatvā' means having removed and discarded. 'Adhammena' means by wrong livelihood, reckoned as the twenty-one kinds of improper seeking. 'Satadhammo' is his name. 'Na nandati' means: just as the young man Satadhamma did not rejoice in that gain, thinking, 'I have received the leftovers of a caṇḍāla,' so too a clansman gone forth in this Dispensation, using a gain obtained by improper means, does not rejoice or find satisfaction. He becomes afflicted with grief, thinking, 'I live by a livelihood censured by the Buddha.' Therefore, for one who maintains a livelihood by improper means, it is better to enter the forest and die a helpless death, just like the young man Satadhamma.

Evaṃ [P 2.0085] satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ desetvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū bhikkhū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu. “Tadā māṇavo ānando ahosi, ahameva caṇḍālaputto ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, many monks attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth. 'At that time, the young man was Ānanda, and I myself was the son of the outcaste.'

Satadhammajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Satadhamma Jātaka, the ninth.

[180] 10. Duddadajātakavaṇṇanā

[180] 10. The Commentary on the Duddada Jātaka

Duddadaṃ [V 2.0070] dadamānānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto gaṇadānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira dve sahāyakā kuṭumbiyaputtā chandakaṃ saṃharitvā sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ sajjetvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā sattame divase sabbaparikkhāre adaṃsu. Tesu gaṇajeṭṭhako satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā “bhante, imasmiṃ dāne bahudāyakāpi atthi appadāyakāpi, tesaṃ sabbesampi ‘idaṃ dānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hotū’”ti dānaṃ niyyādesi. Satthā “tumhehi kho upāsakā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ datvā evaṃ niyyādentehi mahākammaṃ kataṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi dānaṃ datvā evameva niyyādiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Giving what is hard to give... — this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a group offering. It is said that in Sāvatthī, two friends, sons of householders, collected contributions, prepared a gift of all requisites, invited the community of monks with the Buddha at its head, and held a great almsgiving for seven days. On the seventh day, they gave all the requisites. The leader of their group paid homage to the Teacher, sat down to one side, and dedicated the gift, saying: 'Venerable sir, in this offering there are both great donors and small donors; may this gift be of great fruit for all of them.' The Teacher said: 'Lay followers, in giving a gift to the community of monks headed by the Buddha and dedicating it thus, you have performed a great deed. The wise of old also gave gifts and dedicated them in just this way.' And being requested by him, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā gaṇasatthā hutvā himavantapadese ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadacārikaṃ caramāno bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase dvāragāme saparivāro bhikkhāya cari. Manussā bhikkhaṃ adaṃsu. Punadivase bārāṇasiyaṃ cari, manussā sampiyāyamānā bhikkhaṃ datvā gaṇabandhanena chandakaṃ [M 2.0078] saṃharitvā dānaṃ sajjetvā isigaṇassa mahādānaṃ pavattayiṃsu. Dānapariyosāne gaṇajeṭṭhako evameva vatvā imināva niyāmena dānaṃ niyyādesi. Bodhisatto “āvuso, cittappasāde sati appakaṃ nāma dānaṃ natthī”ti vatvā anumodanaṃ karonto imā gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kāsī kingdom. Having come of age and learned all the arts at Takkasilā, he renounced the household life and went forth as an ascetic. Becoming the teacher of a group, he lived for a long time in the Himalayan region. Then, for the sake of salt and sour food, he wandered through the country and came to Bārāṇasī, where he stayed in the royal park. The next day, he went for alms with his retinue in a village at the city gate. The people gave him alms. The day after, he went for alms in Bārāṇasī. The people, feeling affection for him, gave alms and, forming an association, they collected contributions, prepared a gift, and held a great almsgiving for the group of ascetics. At the conclusion of the almsgiving, the leader of the group spoke in the same way and dedicated the gift in this very manner. The Bodhisatta said, 'Friends, when the mind is serene, there is no such thing as a small gift.' Then, giving his blessing, he spoke these verses:

59.

59.

“Duddadaṃ [P 2.0086] dadamānānaṃ, dukkaraṃ kamma kubbataṃ;

Asanto nānukubbanti, sataṃ dhammo durannayo.

Those who give what is hard to give, who do what is hard to do—the unworthy do not imitate them; the nature of the good is hard to follow.

60.

60.

“Tasmā satañca asataṃ, nānā hoti ito gati;

Asanto nirayaṃ yanti, santo saggaparāyaṇā”ti.

Therefore, the destinations of the virtuous and the unworthy are different hereafter. The unworthy go to hell, while the virtuous are bound for heaven.

Tattha duddadanti dānaṃ nāma lobhadosavasikehi apaṇḍitehi dātuṃ na sakkā, tasmā “duddada”nti vuccati. Taṃ dadamānānaṃ. Dukkaraṃ kamma kubbatanti tadeva dānakammaṃ sabbehi kātuṃ na sakkāti dukkaraṃ. Taṃ kurumānānaṃ. Asantoti apaṇḍitā bālā. Nānukubbantīti taṃ [V 2.0071] kammaṃ nānukaronti. Sataṃ dhammoti paṇḍitānaṃ sabhāvo. Dānaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Durannayoti phalasambandhavasena dujjāno, evarūpassa dānassa evarūpo phalavipāko hotīti duranubodho. Apica durannayoti duradhigamo, apaṇḍitehi dānaṃ datvā dānaphalaṃ nāma laddhuṃ na sakkātipi attho. Nānā hoti ito gatīti ito cavitvā paralokaṃ gacchantānaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇaṃ nānā hoti. Asanto nirayaṃ yantīti apaṇḍitā dussīlā dānaṃ adatvā sīlaṃ arakkhitvā nirayaṃ gacchanti. Santo saggaparāyaṇāti paṇḍitā pana dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ rakkhitvā uposathakammaṃ karitvā tīṇi sucaritāni pūretvā saggaparāyaṇā honti, mahantaṃ saggasukhasampattiṃ anubhavantīti.

Herein, 'duddada' (hard to give) means that a gift cannot be given by the unwise who are under the sway of greed and hatred; therefore it is called 'hard to give.' This is said of those who give it. 'Dukkaraṃ kamma kubbataṃ' (doing a deed that is hard to do) means that very act of giving is difficult because it cannot be done by all. This is said of those who do it. 'Asanto' (the unworthy) means the unwise, the foolish. 'Nānukubbanti' (they do not emulate) means they do not imitate that deed. 'Sataṃ dhammo' (the way of the good) is the nature of the wise. This is said with reference to giving. 'Durannayo' (difficult to follow) means difficult to know in terms of its connection to the result; it is hard to understand that such a gift has such a result and ripening. Moreover, 'durannayo' also means 'difficult to attain'; that is, the unwise, even if they give a gift, cannot obtain the fruit of giving. 'Nānā hoti ito gati' (different is the destination hereafter) means that for those who pass away from here and go to the next world, the taking of rebirth is different. 'Asanto nirayaṃ yanti' (the unworthy go to hell) means the unwise and immoral, not having given gifts or protected their virtue, go to hell. 'Santo saggaparāyaṇā' (the virtuous are bound for heaven) means that the wise, having given gifts, protected their virtue, performed the Uposatha observance, and fulfilled the three kinds of good conduct, are bound for heaven and experience the great bliss and fortune of heaven.

Evaṃ bodhisatto anumodanaṃ katvā cattāro vassike māse tattheva vasitvā vassātikkame himavantaṃ gantvā jhānaṃ nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having given his blessing, dwelt right there for the four months of the rainy season. When the rains were over, he went to the Himalayas, developed the meditative absorptions, and, with his absorption undiminished, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā isigaṇo buddhaparisā ahosi, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the group of ascetics was the Buddha's assembly, and the teacher of the group was I myself.'

Duddadajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Duddada Jātaka, the tenth.

Kalyāṇavaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter on the Virtuous, the Third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Kalyāṇadhammaṃ [M 2.0079] daddaraṃ, makkaṭi dubbhimakkaṭaṃ;

Ādiccupaṭṭhānañceva, kaḷāyamuṭṭhi tindukaṃ;

Kacchapaṃ satadhammañca, duddadanti ca te dasa.

The Kalyāṇadhamma, the Daddara, the Monkey, the Treacherous Monkey, and the Ādiccupaṭṭhāna; the Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi, the Tinduka, the Kacchapa, the Satadhamma, and the Duddada—these are the ten.

4. Asadisavaggo

4. The Chapter of the Incomparable

[181] 1. Asadisajātakavaṇṇanā

[181] 1. The Commentary on the Asadisa Jātaka

Dhanuggaho [V 2.0072] asadisoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā bhagavato mahānikkhamapāramiṃ vaṇṇentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto, pubbepi setacchattaṃ pahāya nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The archer is unequalled: This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation. For one day, monks were sitting together in the Dhamma Hall, extolling the perfection of the Great Renunciation of the Blessed One. The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Concerning what discussion are you assembled here now, monks?' When they replied, 'Concerning this,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has gone forth in the Great Renunciation; in the past too, having abandoned the white parasol, he went forth.' Then he related a past story.

Atīte [P 2.0087] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, tassa sotthinā jātassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “asadisakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Athassa ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle añño puññavā satto deviyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, tassa sotthinā jātassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “brahmadattakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tesu bodhisatto soḷasavassakāle takkasilaṃ gantvā disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike tayo vede aṭṭhārasa ca sippāni uggaṇhitvā tesu issāsasippe asadiso hutvā bārāṇasiṃ paccāgami. Rājā kālaṃ karonto “asadisakumārassa rajjaṃ datvā brahmadattassa oparajjaṃ dethā”ti vatvā kālamakāsi. Tasmiṃ kālakate bodhisatto attano rajje dīyamāne “na mayhaṃ rajjenattho”ti paṭikkhipi, brahmadattaṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu. Bodhisatto “mayhaṃ rajjena attho natthī”ti kiñcipi na icchi, kaniṭṭhe rajjaṃ kārente pakatiyā vasanākāreneva vasi. Rājapādamūlikā “asadisakumāro [M 2.0080] rajjaṃ patthetī”ti vatvā rañño santike bodhisattaṃ paribhindiṃsu. Sopi tesaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā paribhinnacitto “bhātaraṃ me gaṇhathā”ti manusse payojesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When he was born safely, on the day of his naming, they gave him the name 'Prince Asadisa.' Later, when he reached the age of being able to run to and fro, another virtuous being was conceived in the queen's womb. When he was born safely, on the naming day, they gave him the name 'Prince Brahmadatta.' When the Bodhisatta was sixteen years old, he went to Takkasilā and studied the three Vedas and the eighteen arts under a world-renowned teacher. Becoming peerless in the art of archery, he returned to Benares. The king, upon his death, said, 'Give the kingdom to Prince Asadisa and the viceroyalty to Brahmadatta,' and then passed away. When the king died and the kingdom was offered to the Bodhisatta, he refused, saying, 'I have no need for a kingdom,' and they anointed Brahmadatta as king. Even though the Bodhisatta did not desire the kingship, while his younger brother ruled, he lived in his usual manner. The courtiers slandered the Bodhisatta to the king, saying, 'Prince Asadisa aspires to the kingdom.' The king, believing their words and having his heart turned against his brother, sent men, saying, 'Seize my brother.'

Atheko bodhisattassa atthacarako taṃ kāraṇaṃ bodhisattassa ārocesi. Bodhisatto kaniṭṭhabhātikassa kujjhitvā nagarā nikkhamitvā aññaṃ raṭṭhaṃ gantvā “eko dhanuggaho āgantvā rājadvāre ṭhito”ti rañño ārocāpesi. Rājā “kittakaṃ bhogaṃ icchasī”ti pucchi[V 2.0073]. “Ekasaṃvaccharena satasahassa”nti. “Sādhu āgacchatū”ti. Atha naṃ āgantvā samīpe ṭhitaṃ pucchi – “tvaṃ dhanaggahosī”ti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Sādhu maṃ upaṭṭhahassū”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahi. Tassa paribbayaṃ dīyamānaṃ [P 2.0088] disvā “atibahuṃ labhatī”ti porāṇakadhanuggahā ujjhāyiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ rājā uyyānaṃ gantvā maṅgalasilāpaṭṭasamīpe sāṇipākāraṃ parikkhipāpetvā ambarukkhamūle mahāsayane nipanno uddhaṃ olokento rukkhagge ekaṃ ambapiṇḍiṃ disvā “imaṃ na sakkā abhiruhitvā gaṇhitu”nti dhanuggahe pakkosāpetvā “imaṃ ambapiṇḍiṃ sarena chinditvā pātetuṃ sakkhissathā”ti āha. Na taṃ, deva, amhākaṃ garu, devena pana no bahuvāre kammaṃ diṭṭhapubbaṃ, adhunāgato dhanuggaho amhehi bahutaraṃ labhati, taṃ pātāpethāti.

Then an attendant of the Bodhisatta, who sought his welfare, informed the Bodhisatta of this matter. The Bodhisatta, instead of being angry with his younger brother, left the city and went to another kingdom, where he had it announced to the king: 'An archer has arrived and is standing at the royal gate.' The king asked, 'How much wealth do you desire?' He replied, 'One hundred thousand per year.' The king said, 'Very well, let him come.' Then, when he had come and stood nearby, the king asked him, 'Are you an archer?' 'Yes, O King,' he replied. 'Good, you shall serve me.' From then on, he served the king. Seeing the allowance given to him, the old archers grumbled, 'He receives too much.' One day, the king went to the park and, having had a cloth screen set up near the auspicious stone slab, lay down on a grand couch at the foot of a mango tree. Looking upwards, he saw a cluster of mangoes at the top of the tree and, thinking, 'It is impossible to climb up and pick this,' he summoned the archers and asked, 'Can you cut this mango cluster with an arrow and make it fall?' They replied, 'O King, that is not difficult for us. However, your majesty has seen our work many times before. This newly arrived archer receives much more than we do; let him make it fall.'

Rājā bodhisattaṃ pakkosāpetvā “sakkhissasi, tāta, etaṃ pātetu”nti pucchi. “Āma, mahārāja, ekaṃ okāsaṃ labhamāno sakkhissāmī”ti. “Katarokāsa”nti? “Tumhākaṃ sayanassa antokāsa”nti. Rājā sayanaṃ harāpetvā okāsaṃ kāresi. Bodhisattassa hatthe dhanu natthi, nivāsanantare dhanuṃ sannayhitvā vicarati, tasmā “sāṇiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Rājā “sādhū”ti sāṇiṃ āharāpetvā parikkhipāpesi. Bodhisatto antosāṇiṃ pavisitvā uparinivatthaṃ setavatthaṃ haritvā ekaṃ rattapaṭaṃ nivāsetvā kacchaṃ bandhitvā ekaṃ rattapaṭaṃ udare bandhitvā pasibbakato sandhiyuttaṃ khaggaṃ nīharitvā vāmapasse sannayhitvā suvaṇṇakañcukaṃ paṭimuñcitvā cāpanāḷiṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ sannayhitvā sandhiyuttameṇḍakamahādhanuṃ ādāya pavāḷavaṇṇaṃ jiyaṃ āropetvā uṇhīsaṃ sīse paṭimuñcitvā tikhiṇakhurappaṃ nakhehi parivattayamāno sāṇiṃ dvidhā katvā pathaviṃ phāletvā alaṅkatanāgakumāro viya nikkhamitvā sarakhipanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā khurappaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ āha – “kiṃ, mahārāja, etaṃ ambapiṇḍiṃ uddhaṃ ārohanakaṇḍena pātemi, udāhu [M 2.0081] adho orohanakaṇḍenā”ti[P 2.0089]. “Tāta, bahū mayā ārohanakaṇḍena pātentā diṭṭhapubbā, orohanakaṇḍena pana pātentā mayā na diṭṭhapubbā, orohanakaṇḍena pātehī”ti. “Mahārāja, idaṃ kaṇḍaṃ dūraṃ ārohissati, yāva cātumahārājikabhavanaṃ, tāva gantvā sayaṃ orohissati, yāvassa orohanaṃ, tāva tumhehi adhivāsetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

The king summoned the Bodhisatta and asked, 'Dear son, can you make this fall?' 'Yes, great king, if I am given a space, I can,' he replied. 'What space?' 'The space inside your majesty's couch area.' The king had the couch removed and the space prepared. The Bodhisatta had no bow in his hand, for he traveled with his bow fastened within his inner garment; therefore, he said, 'I need to obtain a screen.' The king agreed and had a screen set up. The Bodhisatta entered the screen, removed the white cloth he wore on top, and put on a red garment. He tied one red cloth around his loins and another around his belly. Then, he drew out a well-fitted sword from its scabbard and fastened it to his left side. He put on a golden jacket, slung the quiver on his back, and taking up his great bow made of ram's horn with fitted joints, he strung it with a coral-colored string. He placed a diadem on his head and, turning a sharp razor-arrow with his nails, he split the screen in two and emerged like an adorned Naga prince splitting the earth. He went to the shooting spot, nocked the razor-arrow, and asked the king, 'Great king, shall I make this mango cluster fall with an ascending arrow or a descending arrow?' 'Dear son, I have often seen it fallen by an ascending arrow, but I have never seen it fallen by a descending arrow. Make it fall with a descending arrow.' 'Great king, this arrow will ascend far, even to the realm of the Four Great Kings; it will go that far and then descend by itself. You must have patience until it descends.' The king agreed, saying, 'Very well.'
