Atha naṃ puna āha – “mahārāja, idaṃ kaṇḍaṃ pana ārohamānaṃ ambapiṇḍivaṇṭaṃ yāvamajjhaṃ kantamānaṃ ārohissati, orohamānaṃ kesaggamattampi ito vā etto vā agantvā ujuññeva patitvā ambapiṇḍiṃ gahetvā otarissati, passa, mahārājā”ti vegaṃ janetvā kaṇḍaṃ [V 2.0074] khipi. Taṃ kaṇḍaṃ ambapiṇḍivaṇṭaṃ yāvamajjhaṃ kantamānaṃ abhiruhi. Bodhisatto “idāni taṃ kaṇḍaṃ yāva cātumahārājikabhavanaṃ gataṃ bhavissatī”ti ñatvā paṭhamaṃ khittakaṇḍato adhikataraṃ vegaṃ janetvā aññaṃ kaṇḍaṃ khipi, taṃ gantvā purimakaṇḍapuṅkhe paharitvā nivattitvā sayaṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ abhiruhi. Tattha naṃ devatā aggahesuṃ, nivattanakaṇḍassa vātachinnasaddo asanisaddo viya ahosi. Mahājanena “kiṃ eso saddo”ti vutte bodhisatto “nivattanakaṇḍassa saddo”ti vatvā attano attano sarīre kaṇḍassa patanabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhītatasitaṃ mahājanaṃ “mā bhāyitthā”ti samassāsetvā “kaṇḍassa bhūmiyaṃ patituṃ na dassāmī”ti āha. Kaṇḍaṃ otaramānaṃ kesaggamattampi ito vā etto vā agantvā ujuññeva patitvā ambapiṇḍiṃ chindi. Bodhisatto ambapiṇḍiyā ca kaṇḍassa ca bhūmiyaṃ patituṃ adatvā ākāseyeva sampaṭicchanto ekena hatthena ambapiṇḍiṃ, ekena hatthena kaṇḍaṃ aggahesi. Mahājano taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā “na no evarūpaṃ diṭṭhapubba”nti mahāpurisaṃ pasaṃsati [P 2.0090] unnadati apphoṭeti aṅguliyo vidhūnati, celukkhepasahassāni pavatteti. Rājaparisāya tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhāya bodhisattassa dinnadhanaṃ koṭimattaṃ ahosi. Rājāpissa dhanavassaṃ vassento viya bahuṃ dhanaṃ mahantañca yasaṃ adāsi.

Then he spoke to him again: 'Great king, this arrow, as it ascends, will cut the stalk of the mango cluster right through the middle; as it descends, without veering even a hair’s breadth to this side or that, it will fall straight down, take the mango cluster, and descend. Look, great king!' And generating speed, he shot the arrow. That arrow ascended, cutting the stalk of the mango cluster right through the middle. The Bodhisatta, knowing, 'Now that arrow will have reached as far as the realm of the Four Great Kings,' generated even greater speed than for the first arrow and shot another arrow. That arrow went and struck the nock of the first arrow, turning it back, while it itself ascended to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. There, the deities received it. The sound of the returning arrow cutting through the wind was like a peal of thunder. When the people asked, 'What is that sound?' the Bodhisatta replied, 'It is the sound of the returning arrow.' Seeing the people frightened and trembling with the fear that the arrow would fall upon their own bodies, he reassured them, saying, 'Do not be afraid,' and declared, 'I will not let the arrow fall to the ground.' As the arrow descended, without veering even a hair’s breadth to this side or that, it fell straight down and cut the mango cluster. The Bodhisatta, not allowing either the mango cluster or the arrow to fall to the ground, caught them in mid-air, taking the mango cluster with one hand and the arrow with the other. Seeing this marvel, the people praised the Great Being, shouting, clapping their hands, snapping their fingers, and waving thousands of garments, saying, 'We have never seen anything like this before!' The wealth given to the Bodhisatta by the delighted and joyful royal assembly amounted to a crore. The king, as if pouring down a rain of wealth, bestowed upon him much wealth and great fame.

Evaṃ bodhisatte tena raññā sakkate garukate tattha vasante “asadisakumāro kira bārāṇasiyaṃ natthī”ti satta rājāno āgantvā bārāṇasinagaraṃ [M 2.0082] parivāretvā “rajjaṃ vā detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti rañño paṇṇaṃ pesesuṃ. Rājā maraṇabhayabhīto “kuhiṃ me bhātā vasatī”ti pucchitvā “ekaṃ sāmantarājānaṃ upaṭṭhahatī”ti sutvā “mama bhātike anāgacchante mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ natthi, gacchatha tassa mama vacanena pāde vanditvā khamāpetvā gaṇhitvā āgacchathā”ti dūte pāhesi. Te gantvā bodhisattassa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Bodhisatto taṃ rājānaṃ āpucchitvā bārāṇasiṃ paccāgantvā rājānaṃ “mā bhāyī”ti samassāsetvā kaṇḍe akkharāni chinditvā “ahaṃ asadisakumāro āgato, aññaṃ ekakaṇḍaṃ khipanto sabbesaṃ vo jīvitaṃ harissāmi, jīvitena atthikā palāyantū”ti aṭṭālake ṭhatvā sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ bhuñjantānaṃ kañcanapātimakuleyeva kaṇḍaṃ pātesi. Te akkharāni disvā maraṇabhayabhītā sabbeva palāyiṃsu. Evaṃ mahāsatto khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitaṃ anuppādetvā satta rājāno palāpetvā kaniṭṭhabhātaraṃ apaloketvā kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā jīvitapariyosāne brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus, while the Bodhisatta lived there honored and respected by that king, seven kings, hearing that Prince Asadisa was not in Bārāṇasī, came and surrounded the city of Bārāṇasī, sending a message to the king: 'Either give up the kingdom or give battle.' The king, terrified by the fear of death, asked, 'Where is my brother living?' and hearing that he was serving a neighboring king, he said, 'If my brother does not come, I shall not live. Go, and in my name, bow at his feet, ask his forgiveness, and bring him back.' He sent messengers. They went and told the Bodhisatta the news. The Bodhisatta, having taken leave of that king, returned to Bārāṇasī and reassured the king, saying, 'Do not be afraid.' Then, writing letters on an arrow: 'I, Prince Asadisa, have come. By shooting one other arrow, I will take all of your lives. Let those who desire life flee!' Standing on a watchtower, as the seven kings were eating, he made the arrow fall right on the lid of their golden dish. Seeing the letters, they all fled, terrified of death. Thus the Great Being, without causing blood to flow even as much as a small fly could drink, put the seven kings to flight. Then, having taken leave of his younger brother, he renounced sensual pleasures and went forth as an ascetic, developing the higher knowledges and meditative attainments. At the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā [V 2.0075][P 2.0091] “evaṃ, bhikkhave, asadisakumāro satta rājāno palāpetvā vijitasaṅgāmo isipabbajjaṃ pabbajito”ti abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

The Teacher, having become fully enlightened, spoke these verses: 'Thus, monks, Prince Asadisa, having put seven kings to flight and being victorious in battle, went forth into the ascetic life.'

61.

61.

“Dhanuggaho asadiso, rājaputto mahabbalo;

Dūrepātī akkhaṇavedhī, mahākāyappadālano.

An archer unequaled, a royal prince of mighty strength; a far-shooter, an unerring marksman, a shatterer of great bodies.

62.

62.

“Sabbāmitte raṇaṃ katvā, na ca kañci viheṭhayi;

Bhātaraṃ sotthiṃ katvāna, saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamī”ti.

Having fought all enemies, he harmed not a single one; having brought his brother to safety, he entered upon a life of restraint.

Tattha asadisoti na kevalaṃ nāmeneva, balavīriyapaññāhipi asadisova. Mahabbaloti kāyabalenapi paññābalenapi mahabbalo. Dūrepātīti yāva cātumahārājikabhavanā tāvatiṃsabhavanā ca kaṇḍaṃ pesetuṃ samatthatāya dūrepātī. Akkhaṇavedhīti avirādhitavedhī. Atha vā akkhaṇā vuccati vijju, yāva ekā vijju niccharati, tāva tenobhāsena sattaṭṭha [M 2.0083] vāre kaṇḍāni gahetvā vijjhatīti akkhaṇavedhī. Mahākāyappadālanoti mahante kāye padāleti. Cammakāyo, dārukāyo, lohakāyo, ayokāyo, vālikakāyo, udakakāyo, phalakakāyoti ime satta mahākāyā nāma. Tattha añño cammakāyapadālano mahiṃsacammaṃ vinivijjhati, so pana satampi mahiṃsacammānaṃ vinivijjhatiyeva. Añño aṭṭhaṅgulabahalaṃ udumbarapadaraṃ, caturaṅgulabahalaṃ asanapadaraṃ vinivijjhati, so pana phalakasatampi ekato baddhaṃ vinivijjhati, tathā dvaṅgulabahalaṃ tambalohapaṭṭaṃ, aṅgulabahalaṃ ayapaṭṭaṃ. Vālikasakaṭassa badarasakaṭassa palālasakaṭassa vā pacchābhāgena kaṇḍaṃ pavesetvā purebhāgena atipāteti, pakatiyā udake catuusabhaṭṭhānaṃ kaṇḍaṃ peseti, thale aṭṭhausabhanti evaṃ imesaṃ sattannaṃ mahākāyānaṃ padālanato mahākāyappadālano. Sabbāmitteti sabbe amitte. Raṇaṃ katvāti yuddhaṃ katvā palāpesīti attho. Na ca kañci viheṭhayīti ekampi na viheṭhesi. Aviheṭhayantoyeva pana tehi saddhiṃ kaṇḍapesaneneva raṇaṃ katvā. Saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamīti sīlasaṃyamaṃ pabbajjaṃ upagato.

Therein, 'Asadisa' (Unequaled) means he is unequaled not only in name, but also in strength, energy, and wisdom. 'Mahabbala' (Of Mighty Strength) means he is of mighty strength both in bodily strength and in wisdom-strength. 'Dūrepātī' (Far-shooter) means he is a far-shooter because of his ability to shoot an arrow as far as the realm of the Four Great Kings and the realm of Tāvatiṃsa. 'Akkhaṇavedhī' (Unerring Marksman) means one who shoots without missing. Alternatively, 'akkhaṇā' is called lightning; in the time a single flash of lightning is emitted, he can take and shoot arrows seven or eight times by that light, thus he is an 'akkhaṇavedhī'. 'Mahākāyappadālano' (Shatterer of Great Bodies) means he shatters great bodies. The hide-body, the wood-body, the bronze-body, the iron-body, the sand-body, the water-body, and the plank-body—these seven are called great bodies. Among these, another shatterer of hide-bodies might pierce a buffalo hide, but he could pierce even a hundred buffalo hides. Another might pierce an udumbara plank eight finger-breadths thick, or an asana plank four finger-breadths thick, but he could pierce even a hundred planks bound together; likewise a copper-bronze plate two finger-breadths thick, or an iron plate one finger-breadth thick. He could shoot an arrow through the back of a cart of sand, a cart of jujubes, or a cart of straw, and make it pass out through the front. In water, he could shoot an arrow a distance of four usabhas; on land, eight usabhas. Thus, by shattering these seven great bodies, he is a 'shatterer of great bodies'. 'All enemies' means all foes. 'Having made war' means having fought a battle and put them to flight. 'And he harmed not a single one' means he did not harm even one. For without harming them, he made war with them merely by sending his arrows. 'He undertook restraint' means he entered upon the restraint of virtue, the going forth into the homeless life.

Evaṃ [P 2.0092] satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kaniṭṭhabhātā ānando ahosi, asadisakumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, having brought forward this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: 'At that time, the younger brother was Ānanda, but Prince Asadisa was I myself.'

Asadisajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The First Explanation, that of the Asadisa Jātaka.

[182] 2. Saṅgāmāvacarajātakavaṇṇanā

[182] 2. The Explanation of the Saṅgāmāvacara Jātaka.

Saṅgāmāvacaro [V 2.0076] sūroti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto nandattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Satthari hi paṭhamagamanena kapilapuraṃ gantvā kaniṭṭhabhātikaṃ nandarājakumāraṃ pabbājetvā kapilapurā nikkhamma anupubbena sāvatthiṃ gantvā viharante āyasmā nando bhagavato pattaṃ ādāya tathāgatena saddhiṃ gehā nikkhamanakāle “nandakumāro kira satthārā saddhiṃ gacchatī”ti sutvā aḍḍhullikhitehi kesehi vātapānantarena oloketvā “tuvaṭaṃ kho, ayyaputta, āgaccheyyāsī”ti idaṃ janapadakalyāṇiyā vuttavacanaṃ anussaranto ukkaṇṭhito anabhirato uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto dhamanisanthatagatto [M 2.0084] ahosi. Satthā tassa taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā “yaṃnūnāhaṃ nandaṃ arahatte patiṭṭhāpeyya”nti cintetvā tassa vasanapariveṇaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisinno “kacci, nanda, imasmiṃ sāsane abhiramasī”ti pucchi. “Bhante, janapadakalyāṇiyā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā nābhiramāmī”ti. “Himavantacārikaṃ gatapubbosi nandā”ti? “Na gatapubbo, bhante”ti. “Tena hi gacchāmā”ti. “Natthi me, bhante, iddhi, katāhaṃ gamissāmī”ti. Satthā “ahaṃ taṃ, nanda, mama iddhibalena nessāmī”ti theraṃ hatthe gahetvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandanto antarāmagge ekasmiṃ jhāmakhette jhāmakhāṇuke nisinnaṃ chinnakaṇṇanāsanaṅguṭṭhaṃ jhāmalomaṃ chinnachaviṃ cammamattaṃ lohitapaliguṇṭhitaṃ ekaṃ paluṭṭhamakkaṭiṃ dassesi – “passasi, nanda, etaṃ makkaṭi”nti. “Āma, bhante”ti. “Suṭṭhu paccakkhaṃ karohī”ti.

The hero who is proficient in battle—this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Nanda. For when the Teacher, on his first journey, went to the city of Kapila and ordained his younger brother, Prince Nanda, and having left Kapilapura reached Sāvatthī in due course and was dwelling there, the Venerable Nanda, taking the Blessed One’s bowl, was leaving the house with the Tathāgata. Hearing that 'Prince Nanda is reportedly going with the Teacher,' Janapadakalyāṇī, with her hair half-combed, looked out through a window and said, 'Come back quickly, noble sir!' Remembering these words spoken by Janapadakalyāṇī, he became weary of the monk's life, dissatisfied, pale and wan, with the veins standing out on his body. The Teacher, knowing his condition, thought, 'What if I were to establish Nanda in the fruit of Arahantship?' So he went to his living quarters, sat down on the prepared seat, and asked, 'Nanda, are you finding delight in this Dispensation?' 'Venerable sir, with my mind bound to Janapadakalyāṇī, I am not finding delight.' 'Nanda, have you ever gone on a journey to the Himalayas?' 'I have not, venerable sir.' 'Then let us go.' 'Venerable sir, I have no psychic power; how shall I go?' The Teacher said, 'Nanda, I will take you by my psychic power,' and taking the elder by the hand, he soared into the air. On the way, in a burnt field, he showed him a singed she-monkey with its ears, nose, and tail cut off, its fur burnt, its skin torn, being a mere frame of skin smeared with blood, sitting on a burnt stump, and said, 'Nanda, do you see that she-monkey?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'Observe her well.'

Atha naṃ gahetvā saṭṭhiyojanikaṃ manosilātalaṃ, anotattadahādayo satta mahāsare, pañca mahānadiyo, suvaṇṇapabbatarajatapabbatamaṇipabbatapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ anekasatarāmaṇeyyakaṃ himavantapabbatañca dassetvā “tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ te, nanda, diṭṭhapubba”nti pucchitvā “na[P 2.0093], diṭṭhapubbaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “ehi, nanda, tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ te dassayissāmī”ti tattha netvā paṇḍukambalasilāsane nisīdi. Sakko devarājā dvīsu devalokesu devasaṅghena saddhiṃ āgantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Aḍḍhatiyakoṭisaṅkhā tassa paricārikā pañcasatā kakuṭapādā devaccharāyopi āgantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ tā pañcasatā accharā kilesavasena punappunaṃ olokāpesi. “Passasi, nanda, imā kakuṭapādiniyo accharāyo”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ nu kho etā sobhanti, udāhu janapadakalyāṇī”ti. “Seyyathāpi, bhante, janapadakalyāṇiṃ upanidhāya sā paluṭṭhamakkaṭī, evameva imā upanidhāya janapadakalyāṇī”ti. “Idāni kiṃ karissasi nandā”ti? “Kiṃ kammaṃ katvā, bhante, imā accharā labhantī”ti? “Samaṇadhammaṃ katvā”ti. “Sace me, bhante, imāsaṃ [V 2.0077] paṭilābhatthāya bhagavā pāṭibhogo hoti, ahaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti. “Karohi, nanda, ahaṃ te pāṭibhogo”ti. Evaṃ thero devasaṅghassa majjhe tathāgataṃ pāṭibhogaṃ gahetvā “mā, bhante, atipapañcaṃ karotha, etha gacchāma, ahaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Satthā [M 2.0085] taṃ ādāya jetavanameva paccāgami. Thero samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ ārabhi.

Then, taking him, he showed the sixty-league Manosilā stone surface, the seven great lakes including Anotatta, the five great rivers, and the Himalayas, adorned with golden, silver, and jeweled mountains, and many hundreds of delightful spots. He asked, 'Nanda, have you ever seen the Tāvatiṃsa heaven before?' When Nanda replied, 'No, venerable sir,' the Teacher said, 'Come, Nanda, I will show you the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.' Taking him there, he sat down on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat. Sakka, the king of the devas, arrived with the assembly of devas from the two deva worlds, paid homage, and sat to one side. His attendants, numbering two and a half crores, along with five hundred pigeon-footed celestial nymphs, also arrived, paid homage, and sat to one side. The Teacher repeatedly made the Venerable Nanda look at those five hundred nymphs with a mind of desire. 'Nanda, do you see these pigeon-footed nymphs?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'Who then is more beautiful, these nymphs or Janapadakalyāṇī?' 'Venerable sir, compared to these nymphs, Janapadakalyāṇī is like that singed she-monkey.' 'What will you do now, Nanda?' 'By performing what deed, venerable sir, can one obtain these nymphs?' 'By practicing the monastic life.' 'If the Blessed One is my guarantor for obtaining them, venerable sir, I will practice the monastic life.' 'Exert yourself, Nanda, I am your guarantor.' Thus, in the midst of the assembly of devas, the elder took the Tathāgata as his guarantor and said, 'Venerable sir, do not make any further delay; let us go. I will practice the monastic life.' The Teacher brought him back to Jetavana. The elder then began to practice the monastic life.

Satthā dhammasenāpatiṃ āmantetvā “sāriputta, mayhaṃ kaniṭṭhabhātā nando tāvatiṃsadevaloke devasaṅghassa majjhe devaccharānaṃ kāraṇā maṃ pāṭibhogaṃ aggahesī”ti tassa ācikkhi. Etenupāyena mahāmoggallānattherassa mahākassapattherassa anuruddhattherassa dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaānandattherassāti asītiyā mahāsāvakānaṃ yebhuyyena ca sesabhikkhūnaṃ ācikkhi. Dhammasenāpati sāriputtatthero nandattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, āvuso nanda, tāvatiṃsadevaloke devasaṅghassa majjhe ‘devaccharā labhanto samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī’ti dasabalaṃ pāṭibhogaṃ gaṇhī”ti vatvā “nanu evaṃ sante tava brahmacariyavāso mātugāmasannissito kilesasannissito, tassa te itthīnaṃ atthāya samaṇadhammaṃ karontassa bhatiyā kammaṃ karontena kammakārakena saddhiṃ [P 2.0094] kiṃ nānākaraṇa”nti theraṃ lajjāpesi nittejaṃ akāsi. Etenupāyena sabbepi asītimahāsāvakā avasesabhikkhū ca taṃ āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ lajjāpayiṃsu.

The Teacher addressed the General of the Dhamma, saying, 'Sāriputta, my younger brother Nanda took me as a guarantor in the midst of the assembly of devas in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for the sake of celestial nymphs.' He informed him of this, and in the same way, he informed the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Anuruddha, the Elder Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, and likewise the eighty great disciples and most of the remaining monks. The General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, approached the Elder Nanda and said, 'Is it true, friend Nanda, that in the midst of the assembly of devas in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, you took the Ten-Powered One as a guarantor, saying, "I will practice the monastic life to obtain celestial nymphs"?' He then shamed the elder and deprived him of his pride, saying, 'If that is so, your holy life is dependent on women, dependent on defilements. For you, who are practicing the monastic life for the sake of women, what is the difference between you and a hired laborer working for wages?' In the same way, all the eighty great disciples and the remaining monks also shamed the Venerable Nanda.

So “ayuttaṃ vata me kata”nti hiriyā ca ottappena ca vīriyaṃ daḷhaṃ paggaṇhitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ patvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavato paṭissavaṃ muñcāmī”ti āha. Satthāpi “yadā tvaṃ, nanda, arahattaṃ patto, tadāyevāhaṃ paṭissavā mutto”ti āha. Etamatthaṃ viditvā dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “yāva ovādakkhamo cāyaṃ, āvuso, nandatthero ekovādeneva hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā samaṇadhammaṃ katvā arahattaṃ patto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi nando ovādakkhamoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Thinking, 'Indeed, I have done something improper,' he, through moral shame and dread, firmly exerted energy, developed insight, and attained arahantship. Then he approached the Teacher and said, 'Venerable sir, I release the Blessed One from his pledge.' The Teacher said, 'Nanda, at the very moment you attained arahantship, I was released from the pledge.' Having known this matter, the monks in the Dhamma hall started a discussion: 'Friends, how receptive to advice is the Elder Nanda! With just a single admonition, he established moral shame and dread, practiced the monastic life, and attained arahantship.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, what discussion are you gathered for now?' When they said, 'This one,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now; in the past too, Nanda was receptive to advice,' and he brought forth the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto hatthācariyakule nibbattitvā vayappatto hatthācariyasippe nipphattiṃ patto ekaṃ bārāṇasirañño sapattarājānaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. So tassa maṅgalahatthiṃ susikkhitaṃ katvā sikkhāpesi. So rājā “bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti bodhisattaṃ gahetvā maṅgalahatthiṃ āruyha mahatiyā senāya bārāṇasiṃ [M 2.0086] gantvā parivāretvā “rajjaṃ vā detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti rañño paṇṇaṃ pesesi. Brahmadatto “yuddhaṃ dassāmī”ti [V 2.0078] pākāradvāraṭṭālakagopuresu balakāyaṃ āropetvā yuddhaṃ adāsi. Sapattarājā maṅgalahatthiṃ vammena chādetvā sayampi vammaṃ paṭimuñcitvā hattikkhandhavaragato tikhiṇaṃ aṅkusaṃ ādāya “nagaraṃ bhinditvā paccāmittaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā rajjaṃ hatthagataṃ karissāmī”ti hatthiṃ nagarābhimukhaṃ pesesi. So uṇhakalalāni ceva yantapāsāṇe ca nānappakārāni ca paharaṇāni vissajjente disvā maraṇabhayabhīto upasaṅkamituṃ asakkonto paṭikkami. Atha naṃ hatthācariyo upasaṅkamitvā “tāta, tvaṃ sūro saṅgāmāvacaro, evarūpe ṭhāne paṭikkamanaṃ [P 2.0095] nāma tuyhaṃ nānucchavika”nti vatvā hatthiṃ ovadanto imā gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in a family of elephant trainers. When he reached maturity, he attained mastery in the elephant trainer's art and served a rival king of the king of Benares. He thoroughly trained that king's state elephant. That king, intending to seize the kingdom of Benares, took the Bodhisatta, mounted the state elephant, and went to Benares with a great army. Having surrounded it, he sent a letter to the king: 'Surrender the kingdom or fight.' Brahmadatta replied, 'I will fight,' and stationed his forces on the walls, gates, towers, and gate-houses, and gave battle. The rival king covered the state elephant with armor, put on armor himself, and mounted the elephant's back. Taking a sharp goad, he urged the elephant toward the city, thinking, 'I will break into the city, bring the enemy to his end, and take the kingdom into my hands.' But the elephant, seeing the boiling mud, catapulted stones, and various types of weapons being discharged, became terrified of death and retreated, unable to advance. Then the elephant trainer approached him and said, 'Dear one, you are a hero, a veteran of battle; retreating in such a place is not fitting for you.' Advising the elephant, he spoke these verses:

63.

63.

“Saṅgāmāvacaro sūro, balavā iti vissuto;

Kiṃ nu toraṇamāsajja, paṭikkamasi kuñjara.

"Accustomed to battle, a hero, renowned as strong; why, having reached the gateway, do you retreat, O elephant?"

64.

64.

“Omadda khippaṃ palighaṃ, esikāni ca abbaha;

Toraṇāni ca madditvā, khippaṃ pavisa kuñjarā”ti.

"Quickly crush the crossbar, and tear out the posts; having trampled the gateways, quickly enter, O elephant!"

Tattha iti vissutoti, tāta, tvaṃ pavattasampahāraṃ saṅgāmaṃ madditvā avacaraṇato saṅgāmāvacaro, thirahadayatāya sūro, thāmasampattiyā balavāti evaṃ vissuto paññāto pākaṭo. Toraṇamāsajjāti nagaradvārasaṅkhātaṃ toraṇaṃ patvā. Paṭikkamasīti kiṃ nu kho osakkasi, kena kāraṇena nivattasīti vadati. Omaddāti avamadda adho pātaya. Esikāni ca abbahāti nagaradvāre soḷasaratanaṃ aṭṭharatanaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pavesetvā niccalaṃ katvā nikhātā esikatthambhā honti, te khippaṃ uddhara luñcāhīti āṇāpeti. Toraṇāni ca madditvāti nagaradvārassa piṭṭhasaṅghāṭe madditvā. Khippaṃ pavisāti sīghaṃ nagaraṃ pavisa. Kuñjarāti nāgaṃ ālapati.

Here, 'renowned' means: 'My dear, you are one accustomed to battle because you move about after crushing the conflict, hence you are one accustomed to battle; you are a hero due to a steadfast heart, and powerful due to the possession of strength'—thus you are renowned, known, and manifest. 'Having reached the gateway' means having arrived at the gate designated as the city gate. 'Why do you retreat?' means 'Why indeed do you withdraw? For what reason do you turn back?' he says. 'Crush' means trample down or cast down. 'And tear out the posts' refers to the pillar-posts, sixteen or eighteen cubits long, which are fixed firmly and immovably in the ground at the city gate; he commands, 'Quickly uproot them, tear them out!' 'Having trampled the gateways' means having crushed the doorposts of the city gate. 'Quickly enter' means to swiftly enter the city. 'O elephant' is addressing the noble elephant.

Taṃ sutvā nāgo bodhisattassa ekovādeneva nivattitvā esikatthambhe soṇḍāya paliveṭhetvā ahicchattakāni viya luñcitvā toraṇaṃ madditvā palighaṃ otāretvā nagaradvāraṃ bhinditvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā rajjaṃ gahetvā adāsi.

Hearing that, the noble elephant, turning back at the Bodhisatta's single admonition, wrapped its trunk around the pillar-posts and, tearing them out as if they were mushrooms, trampled the gateway, brought down the crossbar, broke down the city gate, entered the city, and having seized the kingdom, gave it to his master.

Satthā [M 2.0087] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā hatthī nando ahosi, rājā ānando, hatthācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the elephant was Nanda, the king was Ānanda, but the elephant trainer was I myself.'

Saṅgāmāvacarajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Saṅgāmāvacara Jātaka, the second.

[183] 3. Vālodakajātakavaṇṇanā

[183] 3. The Commentary on the Vālodaka Jātaka

Vālodakaṃ [V 2.0079] apparasaṃ nihīnanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto pañcasate vighāsāde ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira pañcasatā upāsakā gharāvāsapalibodhaṃ puttadārassa niyyādetvā satthu [P 2.0096] dhammadesanaṃ suṇantā ekatova vicaranti. Tesu keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, ekopi puthujjano nāma natthi, satthāraṃ nimantentāpi te upāsake antokaritvāva nimantenti. Tesaṃ pana dantakaṭṭhamukhodakavatthagandhamāladāyakā pañcasatā cūḷupaṭṭhākā vighāsādā hutvā vasanti. Te bhuttapātarāsā niddāyitvā uṭṭhāya aciravatiṃ gantvā nadītīre unnadantā mallayuddhaṃ yujjhanti. Te pana pañcasatā upāsakā appasaddā appanigghosā paṭisallānamanuyuñjanti. Satthā tesaṃ vighāsādānaṃ uccāsaddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ eso, ānanda, saddo”ti theraṃ pucchitvā “vighāsādasaddo, bhante”ti vutte “na kho, ānanda, ime vighāsādā idāneva vighāsaṃ khāditvā unnadanti, pubbepi unnadantiyeva, imepi upāsakā na idāneva sannisinnā, pubbepi sannisinnāyevā”ti vatvā therena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Vālodaka Jātaka concerning five hundred eaters of scraps, beginning with the words: 'Dreg-water, of little taste and inferior.' It is said that in Sāvatthī, five hundred lay devotees, having entrusted the impediments of household life to their sons and wives, went about together listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching. Among them, some were stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners—not a single one was an ordinary person. Even when inviting the Teacher to a meal, they would include these lay devotees in the invitation. For them, five hundred minor attendants, who provided tooth-sticks, face-water, cloth, perfumes, and garlands, lived as eaters of scraps. After eating their morning meal, they would sleep, and upon rising, they would go to the Aciravatī River, where they would shout loudly and engage in wrestling matches. But those five hundred lay devotees remained quiet and without clamor, devoted to the attainment of the fruits. Hearing the loud noise of those eaters of scraps, the Teacher asked the Elder, 'Ānanda, what is this noise?' When the Elder replied, 'It is the noise of the eaters of scraps, Venerable Sir,' the Teacher said, 'Ānanda, it is not only now that these eaters of scraps shout after eating leftovers—they were noisy in the past as well. And it is not only now that these lay devotees are composed—they were composed in the past as well.' Requested by the Elder, he then related the account of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto amaccakule nibbattitvā vayappatto rañño atthadhammānusāsako ahosi. Athekasmiṃ kāle so rājā “paccanto kupito”ti sutvā pañcasate sindhave kappāpetvā caturaṅginiyā senāya gantvā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā bārāṇasimeva paccāgantvā “sindhavā kilantā allarasameva nesaṃ muddikapānaṃ dethā”ti āṇāpesi. Sindhavā gandhapānaṃ pivitvā assasālaṃ gantvā attano attano ṭhānesu aṭṭhaṃsu. Tesaṃ pana [M 2.0088] dinnāvasiṭṭhakaṃ apparasaṃ bahukasaṭaṃ ahosi. Manussā “idaṃ kiṃ karomā”ti rājānaṃ pucchiṃsu. Rājā udakena madditvā makacipilotikāhi parissāvetvā “ye gadrabhā sindhavānaṃ nivāpaṃ pahiṃsu, tesaṃ dāpethā”ti dāpesi. Gadrabhā kasaṭaudakaṃ pivitvā mattā hutvā viravantā rājaṅgaṇe vicariṃsu. Rājā mahāvātapānaṃ vivaritvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ olokayamāno samīpe ṭhitaṃ bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “passa, ime [P 2.0097] gadrabhā kasaṭodakaṃ pivitvā mattā hutvā viravantā uppatantā vicaranti, sindhavakule jātasindhavā pana gandhapānaṃ pivitvā nissaddā sannisinnā na uppilavanti, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a minister’s family. When he came of age, he became the king’s advisor in matters of welfare and righteousness. At one time, the king heard that 'the border region is being destroyed by thieves.' He had five hundred thoroughbred Sindhu horses prepared and set out with his fourfold army. After pacifying the border region, he returned to Bārāṇasī and ordered, 'The Sindhu horses are weary—give them fresh grape juice to drink.' The Sindhu horses drank the fragrant drink and went to the stable, standing in their respective places. However, the remainder of what was given to them was of little juice and much dregs. The men asked the king, 'What should we do with this remnant?' The king had it mixed with water, strained through coarse rags, and ordered, 'Give it to the donkeys who carried the Sindhu horses’ fodder.' The donkeys drank the dreg-water, became intoxicated, and braying and prancing about, they wandered in the royal courtyard. The king opened a large window and, looking over the royal courtyard, addressed the Bodhisatta standing nearby, saying, 'Minister, do you see? These donkeys, having drunk the dreg-water, are intoxicated and wander about braying and prancing. But the Sindhu horses, born of thoroughbred stock, having drunk the fragrant drink, remain silent and composed, and do not prance about. What is the reason for this?' As he asked, he spoke the first verse:

65.

65.

“Vālodakaṃ apparasaṃ nihīnaṃ, pitvā mado jāyati gadrabhānaṃ;

Imañca pitvāna rasaṃ paṇītaṃ, mado na sañjāyati sindhavāna”nti.

"Drinking dreg-water, of little taste and inferior, intoxication arises in donkeys; but having drunk this exquisite juice, intoxication does not arise in the Sindhu horses."

Tattha [V 2.0080] vālodakanti makacivālehi parissāvitaudakaṃ. “Vāludaka”ntipi pāṭho. Nihīnanti nihīnarasabhāvena nihīnaṃ. Na sañjāyatīti sindhavānaṃ mado na jāyati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇanti pucchi.

Here, 'vālodaka' means water strained through coarse fibers. There is also a reading 'vāludaka'. 'Inferior' means inferior due to its lack of taste. 'Does not arise' means the intoxication of the Sindhu horses does not arise; he asked, 'What then is the reason?'

Athassa kāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, explaining the reason to King Brahmadatta, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

66.

66.

“Appaṃ pivitvāna nihīnajacco, so majjatī tena janinda puṭṭho;

Dhorayhasīlī ca kulamhi jāto, na majjatī aggarasaṃ pivitvā”ti.

"Having drunk but a little, one of low birth becomes intoxicated, O ruler of men, being nourished by that; but one whose nature is to bear the yoke, born in a noble family, does not become intoxicated even after drinking the finest juice."

Tattha tena janinda puṭṭhoti janinda uttamarāja yo nihīnajacco, tena nihīnajaccabhāvena puṭṭho majjati pamajjati. Dhorayhasīlīti dhorayhasīlo dhuravahanakaācārena sampanno jātisindhavo. Aggarasanti sabbapaṭhamaṃ gahitaṃ muddikarasaṃ pivitvāpi na majjati.

There, 'being nourished by that, O ruler of men' means: O king, foremost of men, the donkeys of low birth, being nourished by that state of low birth, become intoxicated and heedless. 'Of the nature to bear the yoke' refers to a thoroughbred Sindhu horse endowed with the conduct of bearing a burden. 'The finest juice' means the grape juice taken first; even having drunk that, they do not become intoxicated.

Rājā bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā gadrabhe rājaṅgaṇā nīharāpetvā tasseva ovāde ṭhito dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

The king, having heard the Bodhisatta's words, had the donkeys removed from the royal courtyard, and abiding by that advice, performing meritorious deeds such as giving, he passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā pañcasatā [M 2.0089] gadrabhā ime vighāsādā ahesuṃ, pañcasatā sindhavā ime upāsakā, rājā ānando, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka thus: "At that time, the five hundred donkeys were these monks who lived on scraps, the five hundred Sindhu horses were these lay followers, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was myself."

Vālodakajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Vālodaka Jātaka: The Third.

[184] 4. Giridattajātakavaṇṇanā

[184] 4. The Commentary on the Giridatta Jātaka

Dūsito [P 2.0098] giridattenāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ekaṃ vipakkhaseviṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā mahiḷāmukhajātake (jā. 1.1.26) kathitameva. Satthā pana “na, bhikkhave, ayaṃ bhikkhu idāneva vipakkhaṃ sevati, pubbepesa vipakkhasevakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Regarding the verse beginning 'Dūsito giridattena,' the Teacher, while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove, spoke this concerning a certain monk who associated with an opposing faction. The story is the same as that told previously in the Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka (Jā. 1.1.26). But the Teacher said: 'Monks, this monk associates with an opposing faction not only now; formerly too he was one who associated with an opposing faction,' and related a tale of the past.

Atīte [V 2.0081] bārāṇasiyaṃ sāmarājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto amaccakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako ahosi. Rañño pana paṇḍavo nāma maṅgalasso, tassa giridatto nāma assabandho, so khañjo ahosi. Asso mukharajjuke gahetvā taṃ purato purato gacchantaṃ disvā “maṃ esa sikkhāpetī”ti saññāya tassa anusikkhanto khañjo ahosi. Tassa assassa khañjabhāvaṃ rañño ārocesuṃ, rājā vejje pesesi. Te gantvā assassa sarīre rogaṃ apassantā “rogamassa na passāmā”ti rañño kathayiṃsu. Rājā bodhisattaṃ pesesi – “gaccha vayassa, ettha kāraṇaṃ jānāhī”ti. So gantvā khañjaassabandhasaṃsaggena tassa khañjabhūtabhāvaṃ ñatvā rañño tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “saṃsaggadosena nāma evaṃ hotī”ti dassento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –-

In the past, in Benares, King Sāma ruled. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a minister's family and, having come of age, became his advisor in matters of welfare and righteousness. Now, the king had an auspicious horse named Paṇḍava, and its groom was named Giridatta, who was lame. The horse saw him walking ahead and, thinking, "He is teaching me," imitated him and became lame. They reported the horse's lameness to the king, who sent for veterinarians. They went, examined the horse's body, and, finding no illness, told the king, "We see no ailment in it." The king then sent the Bodhisatta, saying, "Go, friend, and find out the cause." He went and, realizing that the horse had become lame due to association with the lame groom, explained the matter to the king. To illustrate the harm of such association, he spoke the first verse:—

67.

67.

“Dūsito giridattena, hayo sāmassa paṇḍavo;

Porāṇaṃ pakatiṃ hitvā, tassevānuvidhiyyatī”ti.

"Corrupted by Giridatta, the horse Paṇḍava of Sāma, having abandoned its former nature, now follows his ways."

Tattha hayo sāmassāti sāmassa rañño maṅgalasso. Porāṇaṃ pakatiṃ hitvāti attano porāṇapakatiṃ siṅgārabhāvaṃ pahāya. Anuvidhiyyatīti anusikkhati.

There, 'hayo sāmassa' means the auspicious horse of King Sāma. 'Porāṇaṃ pakatiṃ hitvā' means having abandoned its own former nature, its graceful nature. 'Anuvidhiyyati' means it imitates.

Atha [M 2.0090] naṃ rājā “idāni vayassa kiṃ kattabba”nti pucchi. Bodhisatto “sundaraṃ assabandhaṃ labhitvā yathā porāṇo bhavissatī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king asked him, "Now, friend, what should be done?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Having obtained a good groom, he will become as he was before," and spoke the second verse:

68.

68.

“Sace [P 2.0099] ca tanujo poso, sikharākārakappito;

Ānane naṃ gahetvāna, maṇḍale parivattaye;

Khippameva pahantvāna, tassevānuvidhiyyatī”ti.

"If a well-matched person, with a fine appearance, taking him by the mouth, should lead him in a circle; quickly abandoning his lameness, he will follow his ways."

Tattha tanujoti tassa anujo. Anurūpaṃ jāto hi anujo, tassa anujo tanujo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace hi, mahārāja, tassa siṅgārassa ācārasampannassa assassa anurūpaṃ jāto siṅgāro ācārasampanno poso. Sikharākārakappitoti sikharena sundarena ākārena kappitakesamassu taṃ assaṃ ānane gahetvā assamaṇḍale parivatteyya, khippamevesa taṃ khañjabhāvaṃ pahāya “ayaṃ siṅgāro ācārasampanno assagopako maṃ sikkhāpetī”ti saññāya khippameva tassa anuvidhiyyati anusikkhissati, pakatibhāveyeva ṭhassatīti attho. Rājā tathā [V 2.0082] kāresi, asso pakatibhāve patiṭṭhāsi. Rājā “tiracchānānampi nāma āsayaṃ jānissatī”ti tuṭṭhacitto bodhisattassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi.

There, 'tanujo' means his counterpart. For one born suitably (anurūpaṃ jāto) is a counterpart (anujo); his counterpart is a 'tanujo'. This is what is meant: if, great king, a graceful and well-mannered person, born as a suitable match for that graceful and well-mannered horse... 'Sikharākārakappito' means with hair and beard arranged in a beautiful, crest-like manner; if such a person were to take that horse by the mouth and lead it around the horse enclosure, it would quickly abandon that lameness. Thinking, 'This graceful, well-mannered horse-keeper is training me,' it would quickly follow his ways and learn from him, and would be established in its natural state—this is the meaning. The king did so, and the horse was established in its natural state. The king, delighted, thinking, 'He knows the disposition even of animals!', bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā giridatto devadatto ahosi, asso vipakkhasevako bhikkhu, rājā ānando, amaccapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka thus: "At that time, Giridatta was Devadatta, the horse was the monk who associated with an opposing faction, the king was Ānanda, but the wise minister was indeed myself."

Giridattajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Giridatta Jātaka: The Fourth.

[185] 5. Anabhiratijātakavaṇṇanā

[185] 5. The Commentary on the Anabhirati Jātaka

Yathodake āvile appasanneti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ brāhmaṇakumāraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira eko brāhmaṇakumāro tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū bahū khattiyakumāre ca brāhmaṇakumāre ca mante vācesi. So aparabhāge gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vatthālaṅkāradāsadāsikhettavatthugomahiṃsaputtadārādīnaṃ [M 2.0091] atthāya cintayamāno rāgadosamohavasiko hutvā āvilacitto ahosi, mante paṭipāṭiyā parivattetuṃ nāsakkhi, ito cito ca mantā na paṭibhaṃsu. So ekadivasaṃ bahuṃ gandhamālādiṃ gahetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi[P 2.0100]. Satthā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kiṃ, māṇava, mante vācesi, paguṇā te mantā”ti pucchi. “Pubbe me, bhante, mantā paguṇā ahesuṃ, gharāvāsassa pana gahitakālato paṭṭhāya cittaṃ me āvilaṃ jātaṃ, tena me mantā na paguṇā”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “na kho, māṇava, idāneva, pubbepi te cittassa anāvilakāle tava mantā paguṇā ahesuṃ, rāgādīhi pana āvilakāle tava mantā na paṭibhaṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Regarding the verse beginning 'Yathodake āvile appasanne' (Just as in turbid, unclear water), the Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain brahmin youth. In Sāvatthī, it seems, a certain brahmin youth, having mastered the three Vedas, taught mantras to many young nobles and brahmins. Later, having settled into household life, he became preoccupied with thoughts for clothes, ornaments, male and female slaves, fields, lands, cattle, buffaloes, sons, wives, and so on. Overcome by lust, hatred, and delusion, his mind became turbid; he could not recite the mantras in order, nor did the mantras occur to him clearly. One day, taking many perfumes, garlands, and so on, he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat to one side. The Teacher exchanged pleasantries with him and asked, 'Well, young man, do you teach mantras? Are your mantras well-mastered?' 'Formerly, Venerable Sir, my mantras were well-mastered. But since taking up household life, my mind has become turbid, and now my mantras are no longer well-mastered.' Then the Teacher said to him, 'Not just now, young man—even in the past, when your mind was untroubled, your mantras were well-mastered. But when disturbed by lust and so forth, the mantras did not occur to you.' And being requested by him, he then related a tale of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ mante uggaṇhitvā disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā bārāṇasiyaṃ bahū khattiyakumāre ca brāhmaṇakumāre ca mante vācesi. Tassa santike eko brāhmaṇamāṇavo tayo vede paguṇe akāsi, ekapadepi nikkaṅkho piṭṭhiācariyo hutvā mante vācesi. So aparena samayena gharāvāsaṃ gahetvā gharāvāsacintāya āvilacitto mante parivattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ ācariyo attano santikaṃ āgataṃ “kiṃ, māṇava, paguṇā te mantā”ti pucchitvā “gharāvāsagahitakālato [V 2.0083] paṭṭhāya me cittaṃ āvilaṃ jātaṃ, mante parivattetuṃ na sakkomī”ti vutte “tāta, āvile cittamhi paguṇāpi mantā na paṭibhanti, anāvile pana citte appaṭibhāṇaṃ nāma natthī”ti vatvā imā gāthā āha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a great brahmin family. When he came of age, he mastered the Vedic hymns at Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher, instructing many young princes and brahmin youths in Benares in the Vedas. Among his students was a young brahmin who mastered the three Vedas and, becoming an assistant teacher without a single doubt in any word, also taught the hymns. Later on, this young man took up the household life and, with his mind disturbed by household concerns, was unable to recite the hymns. Then the teacher, seeing him come into his presence, asked him, "Young man, are your hymns well-mastered?" When he replied, "Teacher, ever since I took up the household life, my mind has become disturbed, and I am unable to recite the hymns," the teacher said, "My dear, when the mind is disturbed, even well-mastered hymns do not manifest; but when the mind is undisturbed, there is no such thing as non-manifestation." And he spoke these verses:

69.

69.

“Yathodake āvile appasanne, na passati sippikasambukañca;

Sakkharaṃ vālukaṃ macchagumbaṃ, evaṃ āvilamhi citte;

Na so passati attadatthaṃ paratthaṃ.

"Just as in water that is turbid and unclear, one cannot see shells and conches, pebbles, sand, and shoals of fish; so too, when the mind is turbid, one sees neither one's own benefit nor the benefit of others."

70.

70.

“Yathodake [M 2.0092] acche vippasanne, so passati sippikasambukañca;

Sakkharaṃ vālukaṃ macchagumbaṃ, evaṃ [P 2.0101] anāvilamhi citte;

So passati atthadatthaṃ parattha”nti.

"Just as in water that is clear and tranquil, one sees shells and conches, pebbles, sand, and shoals of fish; so too, when the mind is not turbid, one sees both one's own benefit and the benefit of others."

Tattha āvileti kaddamāluḷite. Appasanneti tāyeva āvilatāya avippasanne. Sippikasambukañcāti sippikañca sambukañca. Macchagumbanti macchaghaṭaṃ. Evaṃ āvilamhīti evameva rāgādīhi āvile citte. Attadatthaṃ paratthanti neva attadatthaṃ na paratthaṃ passatīti attho. So passatīti evameva anāvile citte so puriso attadatthaṃ paratthañca passatīti.

In those verses, 'turbid' (āvile) means stirred up with mud. 'Unclear' (appasanne) means not clear due to that very turbidity. 'Shells and conches' (sippikasambukañca) refers to both mussels and snails. 'A shoal of fish' (macchagumbaṃ) means a school of fish. 'Just so, when the mind is turbid' (evaṃ āvilamhī) means in a mind disturbed by lust and so on. 'One's own benefit and the benefit of others' (attadatthaṃ paratthaṃ) means that he sees neither his own benefit nor the benefit of others; this is the meaning. 'He sees' (so passati) means: just so, with an undisturbed mind, that person sees both his own benefit and the benefit of others.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne brāhmaṇakumāro sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā māṇavo ayameva māṇavo ahosi, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this story of the past, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the brahmin youth was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the young man was this very student, and the teacher was I myself."

Anabhiratijātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The fifth, the Exposition of the Anabhirati Jātaka, is finished.

[186] 6. Dadhivāhanajātakavaṇṇanā

[186] 6. The Exposition of the Dadhivāhana Jātaka.

Vaṇṇagandharasūpetoti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto vipakkhaseviṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā kathitameva. Satthā pana “bhikkhave, asādhusannivāso nāma pāpo anatthakaro, tattha manussabhūtānaṃ tāva pāpasannivāsassa anatthakaratāya kiṃ vattabbaṃ, pubbe pana asātena amadhurena nimbarukkhena saddhiṃ sannivāsamāgamma madhuraraso dibbarasapaṭibhāgo acetano ambarukkhopi amadhuro tittako jāto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Endowed with color, scent, and flavor'—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove, concerning a monk who associated with those in the opposing faction. The story has been told before. The Teacher then said, "Monks, association with the unrighteous is indeed evil and leads to ruin. This being so, what need is there to speak of the ruinous nature of unrighteous association among human beings? In the past, even an insentient mango tree, which possessed a sweet taste and partook of a divine flavor, became unsweet and bitter by coming into association with an unpleasant, non-sweet neem tree." Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 2.0084] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente kāsiraṭṭhe cattāro bhātaro brāhmaṇā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantapadese paṭipāṭiyā paṇṇasālā katvā vāsaṃ kappesuṃ. Tesaṃ jeṭṭhakabhātā kālaṃ katvā sakkattaṃ pāpuṇi. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā antarantarā sattaṭṭhadivasaccayena tesaṃ [M 2.0093] upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto ekadivasaṃ jeṭṭhakatāpasaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā [P 2.0102] – “bhante, kena te attho”ti pucchi. Paṇḍurogo tāpaso “agginā me attho”ti āha. So taṃ sutvā tassa vāsipharasukaṃ adāsi. Vāsipharasuko nāma daṇḍe pavesanavasena vāsipi hoti pharasupi. Tāpaso “ko me imaṃ ādāya dārūni āharissatī”ti āha. Atha naṃ sakko evamāha – “yadā te, bhante, dārūhi attho, imaṃ pharasuṃ hatthena paharitvā ‘dārūni me āharitvā aggiṃ karohī’ti vadeyyāsi, dārūni āharitvā aggiṃ katvā dassatī”ti. Tassa vāsipharasukaṃ datvā dutiyampi upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, kena te attho”ti pucchi. Tassa paṇṇasālāya hatthimaggo hoti, so hatthīhi upadduto “hatthīnaṃ me vasena dukkhaṃ uppajjati, te palāpehī”ti āha. Sakko tassa ekaṃ bheriṃ upanāmetvā “bhante, imasmiṃ tale pahaṭe tumhākaṃ paccāmittā palāyissanti, imasmiṃ tale pahaṭe mettacittā hutvā caturaṅginiyā senāya parivāressantī”ti vatvā taṃ bheriṃ datvā kaniṭṭhassa santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, kena te attho”ti pucchi. Sopi paṇḍurogadhātukova, tasmā “dadhinā me attho”ti āha. Sakko tassa ekaṃ dadhighaṭaṃ datvā “sace tumhe icchamānā imaṃ āsiñceyyātha, mahānadī hutvā mahoghaṃ pavattetvā tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ gahetvā dātuṃ samatthopi bhavissatī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Tato paṭṭhāya vāsipharasuko jeṭṭhabhātikassa aggiṃ karoti, itarena bheritale pahaṭe hatthī palāyanti, kaniṭṭho dadhiṃ paribhuñjati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, four brahmin brothers in the Kasi country went forth as ascetics. They built leaf huts in succession in the Himalayan region and took up residence there. Their eldest brother passed away and was reborn as Sakka. Knowing this, he would visit to attend on the other ascetics every seven or eight days. One day, after paying homage to the eldest ascetic and sitting to one side, he asked, 'Venerable sir, what do you need?' The ascetic, who suffered from jaundice, replied, 'I need fire.' Hearing this, Sakka gave him an axe-adze. An axe-adze is a tool that, depending on how it is fitted to the handle, serves as both an adze and an axe. The ascetic said, 'Who will fetch wood for me with this?' Then Sakka said to him, 'Venerable sir, whenever you need wood, strike this axe-adze with your hand and say, "Bring me wood and make a fire," and it will bring wood and make a fire for you.' After giving him the axe-adze, Sakka approached the middle brother and asked, 'Venerable sir, what do you need?' There was an elephant path near his leaf hut, and he was troubled by the elephants, so he said, 'I suffer because of the elephants; drive them away.' Sakka presented him with a drum and said, 'Venerable sir, when this side is struck, your enemies will flee; when this other side is struck, they will become friendly and surround you as a fourfold army.' After giving him the drum, Sakka went to the youngest brother and asked, 'Venerable sir, what do you need?' He too was of a jaundiced constitution, so he said, 'I need curds.' Sakka gave him a pot of curds and said, 'If you wish to pour this out, it will become a great river, flowing in a mighty flood, and it will even be capable of seizing a kingdom for you.' Having said this, he departed. From then on, the axe-adze made fire for the eldest brother; for the other, when he struck the side of the drum, the elephants fled; and the youngest brother enjoyed the curds.

Tasmiṃ kāle eko sūkaro ekasmiṃ purāṇagāmaṭṭhāne caranto ānubhāvasampannaṃ ekaṃ maṇikkhandhaṃ addasa. So taṃ maṇikkhandhaṃ mukhena ḍaṃsitvā tassānubhāvena ākāse uppatitvā samuddassa majjhe ekaṃ dīpakaṃ gantvā “ettha dāni mayā vasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti otaritvā phāsukaṭṭhāne ekassa udumbararukkhassa heṭṭhā [P 2.0103] vāsaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ rukkhamūle maṇikkhandhaṃ purato ṭhapetvā niddaṃ okkami. Atheko kāsiraṭṭhavāsī manusso “nirupakāro esa amhāka”nti mātāpitūhi gehā nikkaḍḍhito ekaṃ paṭṭanagāmaṃ gantvā nāvikānaṃ kammakāro hutvā nāvaṃ āruyha [M 2.0094] samuddamajjhe bhinnāya nāvāya phalake nipanno taṃ dīpakaṃ patvā phalāphalāni pariyesanto taṃ sūkaraṃ niddāyantaṃ disvā saṇikaṃ gantvā maṇikkhandhaṃ gaṇhitvā tassa ānubhāvena ākāse uppatitvā udumbararukkhe nisīditvā cintesi – “ayaṃ sūkaro [V 2.0085] imassa maṇikkhandhassa ānubhāvena ākāsacāriko hutvā idha vasati maññe, mayā paṭhamameva imaṃ sūkaraṃ māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā pacchā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So ekaṃ daṇḍakaṃ bhañjitvā tassa sīse pāteti. Sūkaro pabujjhitvā maṇiṃ apassanto ito cito ca kampamāno vidhāvati, rukkhe nisinnapuriso hasi. Sūkaro olokento taṃ disvā taṃ rukkhaṃ sīsena paharitvā tattheva mato.

At that time, a boar wandering in the site of an old village came upon a powerful jewel-block. Seizing the jewel-block with its snout, by its power, it soared into the sky and reached an island in the middle of the ocean. Thinking, 'Now it is suitable for me to live here,' it descended and settled in a comfortable spot under a fig tree. One day, having placed the jewel-block before it at the foot of that tree, the boar fell asleep. Now, a man from the Kasi country, who had been cast out from his home by his parents saying, 'He is of no use to us,' went to a port town and became a laborer for sailors. Having boarded a ship, when the ship was wrecked in the middle of the ocean, he clung to a plank and reached that island. While searching for fruits, he saw the sleeping boar. Approaching quietly, he took the jewel-block and, by its power, rose into the air and sat on the fig tree. He thought, 'This boar, I think, lives here by the power of this jewel-block, being able to travel through the sky. It is right that I first kill this boar, eat its flesh, and leave afterwards.' Breaking off a stick, he dropped it on its head. The boar, waking up and not seeing the jewel-block, ran about here and there, trembling. The man sitting in the tree laughed. The boar, looking up, saw him and, striking the tree with its head, died on that very spot.

So puriso otaritvā aggiṃ katvā tassa maṃsaṃ pacitvā khāditvā ākāse uppatitvā himavantamatthakena gacchanto assamapadaṃ disvā jeṭṭhabhātikassa tāpasassa assame otaritvā dvīhatīhaṃ vasitvā tāpasassa vattapaṭivattaṃ akāsi, vāsipharasukassa ānubhāvañca passi. So “imaṃ mayā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti maṇikkhandhassa ānubhāvaṃ tāpasassa dassetvā “bhante, imaṃ maṇiṃ gahetvā vāsipharasukaṃ dethā”ti āha. Tāpaso ākāsena caritukāmo taṃ gahetvā vāsipharasukaṃ adāsi. So taṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā vāsipharasukaṃ paharitvā “vāsipharasuka tāpasassa sīsaṃ chinditvā maṇikkhandhaṃ me āharā”ti āha. So gantvā tāpasassa sīsaṃ chinditvā maṇikkhandhaṃ āhari. So vāsipharasukaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā majjhimatāpasassa santikaṃ [P 2.0104] gantvā katipāhaṃ vasitvā bheriyā ānubhāvaṃ disvā maṇikkhandhaṃ datvā bheriṃ gaṇhitvā purimanayeneva tassapi sīsaṃ chindāpetvā kaniṭṭhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dadhighaṭassa ānubhāvaṃ disvā maṇikkhandhaṃ datvā dadhighaṭaṃ gahetvā purimanayeneva tassa sīsaṃ chindāpetvā maṇikkhandhañca vāsipharasukañca bheriñca dadhighaṭañca gahetvā ākāse uppatitvā bārāṇasiyā avidūre ṭhatvā bārāṇasirañño “yuddhaṃ vā me detu rajjaṃ vā”ti ekassa purisassa hatthe paṇṇaṃ pāhesi.

That man descended, made a fire, cooked the boar's flesh and ate it, then flew up into the sky. While traveling over the peak of the Himalayas, he saw a hermitage and descended into the hermitage of the eldest ascetic brother. He stayed for two or three days, performed the duties for the ascetic, and witnessed the power of the axe-adze. Thinking, 'It is right for me to take this,' he showed the power of the jewel-block to the ascetic and said, 'Venerable sir, take this jewel and give me the axe-adze.' The ascetic, desiring to travel through the air, took it and gave him the axe-adze. Taking it, he went a short distance, struck the axe-adze, and said, 'Axe-adze, cut off the ascetic's head and bring me the jewel-block.' It went, cut off the ascetic's head, and brought the jewel-block. He hid the axe-adze in a concealed place, went to the middle ascetic, and stayed for a few days. Having seen the power of the drum, he gave the jewel-block, took the drum, and in the same way as before, had his head cut off too. Then he approached the youngest, saw the power of the pot of curds, gave the jewel-block, took the pot of curds, and in the same way as before, had his head cut off. Taking the jewel-block, the axe-adze, the drum, and the pot of curds, he flew up into the sky, stood not far from Benares, and sent a message to the king of Benares by the hand of a man: 'Either give me battle or the kingdom.'

Rājā sāsanaṃ sutvāva “coraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti nikkhami. So ekaṃ bheritalaṃ pahari, caturaṅginī senā parivāresi. Rañño avattharaṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā dadhighaṭaṃ vissajjesi, mahānadī pavatti. Mahājano dadhimhi osīditvā nikkhamituṃ nāsakkhi. Vāsipharasukaṃ paharitvā “rañño sīsaṃ āharā”ti [M 2.0095] āha, vāsipharasuko gantvā rañño sīsaṃ āharitvā pādamūle nikkhipi. Ekopi āvudhaṃ ukkhipituṃ nāsakkhi. So mahantena balena parivuto nagaraṃ pavisitvā abhisekaṃ kāretvā dadhivāhano nāma rājā hutvā dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāresi.

The king, upon hearing the message, set out from the city, thinking, 'I will capture the thief.' The man struck one side of the drum, and a fourfold army surrounded him. Realizing he was being overwhelmed by the king, he poured out the pot of curds, and it became a great river. The multitude, sinking into the river of curds, was unable to escape. He struck the axe-adze and said, 'Bring the king’s head.' The axe-adze went, cut off the king’s head, and placed it at his feet. Not a single person was able to lift a weapon. Surrounded by a great retinue, he entered the city, had himself consecrated, and became king named Dadhivāhana. He ruled the kingdom justly and equitably.

Tassekadivasaṃ mahānadiyaṃ jālakaraṇḍake kīḷantassa kaṇṇamuṇḍadahato devaparibhogaṃ ekaṃ ambapakkaṃ āgantvā jāle laggi, jālaṃ ukkhipantā taṃ disvā rañño adaṃsu. Taṃ mahantaṃ ghaṭappamāṇaṃ [V 2.0086] parimaṇḍalaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ ahosi. Rājā “kissa phalaṃ nāmeta”nti vanacarake pucchitvā “ambaphala”nti sutvā paribhuñjitvā tassa aṭṭhiṃ attano uyyāne ropāpetvā khīrodakena siñcāpesi. Rukkho nibbattitvā tatiye saṃvacchare phalaṃ adāsi. Ambassa sakkāro mahā ahosi, khīrodakena siñcanti, gandhapañcaṅgulikaṃ denti, mālādāmāni parikkhipanti, gandhatelena dīpaṃ jālenti, parikkhepo panassa paṭasāṇiyā ahosi. Phalāni madhurāni suvaṇṇavaṇṇāni ahesuṃ. Dadhivāhanarājā aññesaṃ rājūnaṃ ambaphalaṃ pesento aṭṭhito rukkhanibbattanabhayena [P 2.0105] aṅkuranibbattanaṭṭhānaṃ maṇḍūkakaṇṭakena vijjhitvā pesesi. Tesaṃ ambaṃ khāditvā aṭṭhi ropitaṃ na sampajjati. Te “kiṃ nu kho ettha kāraṇa”nti pucchantā taṃ kāraṇaṃ jāniṃsu.

One day, while he was playing with a fishing net-trap in the great river, a ripe mango, fit for the enjoyment of the gods, floated down from the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa Lake and was caught in his net. Those lifting the net saw it and presented it to the king. It was as large as a water-pot, perfectly round, and golden in color. The king asked the forest-dwellers, 'What fruit is this?' and hearing it was a mango, he ate it and had its seed planted in his own garden, having it watered with milk-water. The tree grew and bore fruit in the third year. The mango tree received great honor: they watered it with milk-water, applied the five-fingered perfume mark, hung garlands, lit lamps with scented oil, and enclosed it with a cloth screen. The fruits were sweet and golden in color. King Dadhivāhana, when sending mangoes to other kings, fearing that trees might sprout from the seeds, pierced the sprouting point with a poisonous thorn before sending them. When those kings ate the mangoes and planted the seeds, they did not grow. Wondering, 'What could be the reason for this?' they discovered the cause.

Atheko rājā uyyānapālaṃ pakkositvā “dadhivāhanassa ambaphalānaṃ rasaṃ nāsetvā tittakabhāvaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissasī”ti pucchitvā “āma, devā”ti vutte “tena hi gacchāhī”ti sahassaṃ datvā pesesi. So bārāṇasiṃ gantvā “eko uyyānapālo āgato”ti rañño ārocāpetvā tena pakkosāpito pavisitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā “tvaṃ uyyānapālo”ti puṭṭho “āma, devā”ti vatvā attano ānubhāvaṃ vaṇṇesi. Rājā “gaccha amhākaṃ uyyānapālassa santike hohī”ti āha. Te tato paṭṭhāya dve janā uyyānaṃ paṭijagganti. Adhunāgato uyyānapālo akālapupphāni suṭṭhu pupphāpento akālaphalāni gaṇhāpento uyyānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ akāsi. Rājā tassa pasīditvā porāṇakauyyānapālaṃ nīharitvā tasseva uyyānaṃ adāsi. So uyyānassa attano hatthagatabhāvaṃ ñatvā ambarukkhaṃ parivāretvā nimbe ca phaggavavalliyo ca ropesi, anupubbena nimbā vaḍḍhiṃsu, mūlehi mūlāni, sākhāhi ca sākhā saṃsaṭṭhā onaddhavinaddhā ahesuṃ. Tena asātaamadhurasaṃsaggena tāvamadhuraphalo [M 2.0096] ambo tittako jāto nimbapaṇṇasadisaraso, ambaphalānaṃ tittakabhāvaṃ ñatvā uyyānapālo palāyi.

Then a certain king summoned a gardener and asked, "Can you destroy the taste of Dadhivāhana’s mango fruits and make them bitter?" When the gardener replied, "Yes, lord," the king said, "Then go," and sent him off with a thousand pieces of money. The gardener went to Bārāṇasī, and having it announced to the king, "A gardener has arrived," he was summoned. He entered, paid homage to the king, and when asked, "Are you a gardener?" he replied, "Yes, lord," and described his own skill. The king said, "Go and be with our gardener." From then on, the two men tended the garden. The newly arrived gardener made the garden delightful by causing unseasonal flowers to bloom and unseasonal fruits to be produced. Pleased with him, the king dismissed the former gardener and gave the garden to him alone. Realizing that the garden was now in his hands, he surrounded the mango tree with neem trees and planted phaggava vines. Gradually, the neem trees grew, their roots intertwined with the mango tree’s roots and their branches entwined and interlocked with its branches. Due to this association with the unpleasant and unsweet, the once-sweet mango fruit became bitter, its taste resembling that of neem leaves. Realizing the mango fruits had turned bitter, the gardener fled.

Dadhivāhano uyyānaṃ gantvā ambaphalaṃ khādanto mukhe paviṭṭhaṃ ambarasaṃ nimbakasaṭaṃ viya ajjhoharituṃ asakkonto kakkāretvā niṭṭhubhi. Tadā bodhisatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako amacco ahosi. Rājā bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “paṇḍita, imassa rukkhassa porāṇakaparihārato parihīnaṃ natthi, evaṃ santepissa phalaṃ tittakaṃ jātaṃ, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

King Dadhivāhana went to the garden and, while eating a mango, found the mango juice that entered his mouth to be like neem juice. Unable to swallow it, he hawked and spat it out. At that time, the Bodhisatta was his minister, an advisor on matters of benefit and Dhamma. The king addressed the Bodhisatta and asked, "Wise one, this tree has not declined from its former care, yet its fruit has become bitter. What could be the reason?" Then he spoke the first verse:

71.

71.

“Vaṇṇagandharasūpeto[V 2.0087][P 2.0106], amboyaṃ ahuvā pure;

Tameva pūjaṃ labhamāno, kenambo kaṭukapphalo”ti.

“Endowed with color, scent, and flavor, this mango was so before; receiving that very same homage, for what reason is the mango now bitter-fruited?”

Athassa kāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, explaining the reason to King Dadhivāhana, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

72.

72.

“Pucimandaparivāro, ambo te dadhivāhana;

Mūlaṃ mūlena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, sākhā sākhā nisevare;

Asātasannivāsena, tenambo kaṭukapphalo”ti.

“Surrounded by neem trees, Dadhivāhana, is your mango; root clings to root, branch consorts with branch. Through dwelling with the unpleasant, that mango’s fruit is bitter.”

Tattha pucimandaparivāroti nimbarukkhaparivāro. Sākhā sākhā nisevareti pucimandassa sākhāyo ambarukkhassa sākhāyo nisevanti. Asātasannivāsenāti amadhurehi pucimandehi saddhiṃ sannivāsena. Tenāti tena kāraṇena ayaṃ ambo kaṭukapphalo asātaphalo tittakaphalo jātoti.

Herein, 'surrounded by pucimanda' means surrounded by neem trees. 'Branch consorts with branch' means the branches of the neem trees associate with the branches of the mango tree. 'Through dwelling with the unpleasant' means by dwelling together with the unsweet neem trees. 'For that reason' means that because of this, this mango became bitter-fruited, unpleasant-fruited, and acrid-fruited.

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sabbepi pucimande ca phaggavavalliyo ca chindāpetvā mūlāni uddharāpetvā samantā amadhurapaṃsuṃ harāpetvā madhurapaṃsuṃ pakkhipāpetvā khīrodakasakkharodakagandhodakehi ambaṃ paṭijaggāpesi. So madhurasaṃsaggena puna madhurova ahosi. Rājā pakatiuyyānapālasseva uyyānaṃ niyyādetvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Hearing his words, the king ordered all the neem trees and phaggava vines to be cut down, their roots uprooted, the surrounding unsweet soil removed, and sweet soil put in its place. He then nurtured the mango tree with milk-water, sugar-water, and fragrant water. Through association with sweetness, it became sweet again. The king restored the garden to the original gardener and, having lived out his lifespan, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ahameva paṇḍitāmacco ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, I myself was the wise minister.”

Dadhivāhanajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The commentary on the Dadhivāhana Jātaka, the sixth.

[187] 7. Catumaṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā

[187] 7. The Commentary on the Catumaṭṭha Jātaka

Ucce [M 2.0097] viṭabhimāruyhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ mahallakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasaṃ kira dvīsu aggasāvakesu aññamaññaṃ pañhapucchanavissajjanakathāya nisinnesu eko mahallako bhikkhu tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā tatiyo hutvā nisīditvā [P 2.0107] “bhante, mayampi tumhe pañhaṃ pucchissāma, tumhepi attano kaṅkhaṃ amhe pucchathā”ti [V 2.0088] āha. Therā taṃ jigucchitvā uṭṭhāya pakkamiṃsu. Therānaṃ dhammaṃ sotuṃ nisinnaparisā samāgamassa bhinnakāle satthu santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ akāle āgatatthā”ti vutte taṃ kāraṇaṃ ārocayiṃsu. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva sāriputtamoggallānā etaṃ jigucchitvā akathetvā pakkamanti, pubbepi pakkamiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, told this story concerning a certain obscure elderly monk, beginning with 'Having climbed up on a high branch.' One day, it is said, while the two chief disciples were seated, engaged in a discussion of questions and answers with each other, an elderly monk approached them, sat down as a third, and said, 'Venerable Sirs, we too will ask you questions, and you may also ask us about your doubts.' The Elders, being repelled by him, rose and departed. The assembly that was seated to hear the Elders' teaching, when the gathering broke up, went to the Teacher. When asked, 'Why have you come at an unseasonable time?' they explained the reason. The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta and Moggallāna, being repelled by him, depart without speaking; they have done so in the past as well,' and he recounted a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññāyatane rukkhadevatā ahosi. Atha dve haṃsapotakā cittakūṭapabbatā nikkhamitvā tasmiṃ rukkhe nisīditvā gocarāya gantvā nivattantāpi tasmiṃyeva vissamitvā cittakūṭaṃ gacchanti. Gacchante gacchante kāle tesaṃ bodhisattena saddhiṃ vissāso ahosi. Gacchantā ca āgacchantā ca aññamaññaṃ sammoditvā dhammakathaṃ kathetvā pakkamiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ tesu rukkhagge nisīditvā bodhisattena saddhiṃ kathentesu eko siṅgālo tassa rukkhassa heṭṭhā ṭhatvā tehi haṃsapotakehi saddhiṃ mantento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in a forest region. Then two young geese, having departed from Cittakūṭa Mountain, sat on that tree. Going out to feed and returning, they would also rest there before going to Cittakūṭa. As time passed, they developed familiarity with the Bodhisatta. Coming and going, they would greet each other, discuss the Dhamma, and then depart. Then one day, while they were seated on the treetop conversing with the Bodhisatta, a jackal stood at the foot of that tree and, wishing to confer with those young geese, uttered the first verse:

73.

73.

“Ucce viṭabhimāruyha, mantayavho rahogatā;

Nīce oruyha mantavho, migarājāpi sossatī”ti.

“Having climbed a high branch, you two converse in private; descend and speak down low, for even the king of beasts will hear.”

Tattha ucce viṭabhimāruyhāti pakatiyā ca ucce imasmiṃ rukkhe uccataraṃ ekaṃ viṭapaṃ abhiruhitvā. Mantayavhoti mantetha kathetha. Nīce oruyhāti otaritvā nīce ṭhāne ṭhatvā mantetha. Migarājāpi sossatīti attānaṃ migarājānaṃ katvā āha. Haṃsapotakā jigucchitvā uṭṭhāya cittakūṭameva gatā.

Herein, 'having climbed a high branch' means having climbed to a higher branch on this naturally tall tree. 'Mantayavho' means 'confer, speak.' 'Nīce oruyha' means having descended, you should stand in a low place and confer. 'Even the king of beasts will hear' — he said this, making himself out to be the king of beasts. Being repelled, the young geese rose and went to Cittakūṭa itself.

Tesaṃ gatakāle bodhisatto siṅgālassa dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

After they had gone, the Bodhisatta uttered the second verse to the jackal:

74.

74.

“Yaṃ suvaṇṇo suvaṇṇena, devo devena mantaye;

Kiṃ tettha catumaṭṭhassa, bilaṃ pavisa jambukā”ti.

"When a golden one converses with a golden one, a god with a god, what is there for you, O four-fold polished one? Enter your hole, jackal!"

Tattha [M 2.0098] suvaṇṇoti sundaravaṇṇo. Suvaṇṇenāti dutiyena haṃsapotakena. Devo devenāti teyeva dve deve katvā katheti. Catumaṭṭhassāti sarīrena [P 2.0108] jātiyā sarena guṇenāti imehi catūhi maṭṭhassa suddhassāti akkharattho. Asuddhaṃyeva pana taṃ pasaṃsāvacanena nindanto evamāha, catūhi [V 2.0089] lāmakassa kiṃ te ettha siṅgālassāti ayamettha adhippāyo. “Bilaṃ pavisā”ti idaṃ bodhisatto bheravārammaṇaṃ dassetvā taṃ palāpento āha.

Here, 'suvaṇṇa' means 'of beautiful color.' 'By suvaṇṇa' refers to the second young goose. 'A god with a god'—here, he speaks, making them two gods. 'Catumaṭṭhassa'—the literal meaning of the word is 'polished' or 'pure' due to these four: body, birth, voice, and virtue. But in truth, he is impure, and by praising him, he criticizes him, saying, 'What is there for you, the lowly one in four ways, O jackal?' This is the intended meaning here. 'Enter your hole'—this the Bodhisatta said, showing a terrifying object to drive him away.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo mahallako ahosi, dve haṃsapotakā sāriputtamoggallānā, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the jackal was the elderly monk, the two young geese were Sāriputta and Moggallāna, and the tree-deity was none other than myself.'

Catumaṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Catumaṭṭha Jātaka, the seventh.

[188] 8. Sīhakotthujātakavaṇṇanā

[188] 8. The Commentary on the Sīhakotthu Jātaka.

Sīhaṅgulī sīhanakhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kokālikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasaṃ kira kokāliko aññesu bahussutesu dhammaṃ kathentesu sayampi kathetukāmo ahosīti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Taṃ pana pavattiṃ sutvā satthā “na, bhikkhave, kokāliko idāneva attano saddena pākaṭo jāto, pubbepi pākaṭo ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This story beginning with 'With lion's digits and lion's claws' the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Kokālika himself. One day, it seems, Kokālika, when other learned monks were teaching the Dhamma, wished to teach himself; the entire matter should be elaborated in the manner stated previously. Having heard of that occurrence, the Teacher said, 'Monks, Kokālika has not just now become conspicuous by his own voice; he was conspicuous before as well.' Having said this, he recounted a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese sīho hutvā ekāya siṅgāliyā saddhiṃ saṃvāsamanvāya puttaṃ paṭilabhi. So aṅgulīhi nakhehi kesarena vaṇṇena saṇṭhānenāti imehi ākārehi pitusadiso ahosi, saddena mātusadiso. Athekadivasaṃ deve vassitvā vigate sīhesu naditvā sīhakīḷaṃ kīḷantesu sopi tesaṃ antare naditukāmo hutvā siṅgālikaṃ nādaṃ nadi. Athassa saddaṃ sutvā sīhā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Tassa saddaṃ sutvā aparo bodhisattassa sajātiputto “tāta, ayaṃ sīho vaṇṇādīhi amhehi [M 2.0099] samāno, saddo panassa aññādiso, ko nāmeso”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having been reborn as a lion in the Himalayan region, lived with a she-jackal and obtained a son. He resembled his father in these aspects: digits, claws, mane, color, and form, but his voice was like his mother's. Then one day, when the rain had ceased and the lions were roaring and playing lion games, he too, desiring to roar among them, uttered a jackal's cry. Hearing his cry, the lions became silent. The Bodhisatta's own true-born son, hearing his cry, asked, 'Father, this lion is similar to us in color and so on, but his voice is different; what is he?' and uttered the first verse:

75.

75.

“Sīhaṅgulī sīhanakho, sīhapādapatiṭṭhito;

So sīho sīhasaṅghamhi, eko nadati aññathā”ti.

"With lion's digits and lion's claws, firmly placed on lion's feet; that lion in the lion's assembly, alone roars differently."

Tattha [P 2.0109] sīhapādapatiṭṭhitoti sīhapādeheva patiṭṭhito. Eko nadati aññathāti ekova avasesasīhehi asadisena siṅgālasaddena nadanto aññathā nadati.

Here, 'sīhapādapatiṭṭhito' means 'established on lion's feet.' 'Eko nadati aññathā' means roaring alone with a jackal-like sound, unlike the other lions; he roars differently.

Taṃ [V 2.0090] sutvā bodhisatto “tāta, esa tava bhātā siṅgāliyā putto, rūpena mayā sadiso, saddena mātarā sadiso”ti vatvā siṅgāliputtaṃ āmantetvā “tāta, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya idha vasanto appasaddo vasa, sace puna nadissasi, siṅgālabhāvaṃ te jānissantī”ti ovadanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said, 'My son, this is your brother, the son of the she-jackal. In form, he resembles me; in voice, he resembles his mother.' Then, addressing the jackal's son, advising him, 'My son, from now on, living here, live quietly. If you roar again, they will recognize your jackal-nature,' he uttered the second verse:

76.

76.

“Mā tvaṃ nadi rājaputta, appasaddo vane vasa;

Sarena kho taṃ jāneyyuṃ, na hi te pettiko saro”ti.

"Do not roar, prince, live quietly in the forest. Indeed, they would recognize you by your voice, for your voice is not that of your father."

Tattha rājaputtāti sīhassa migarañño putta. Imañca pana ovādaṃ sutvā puna so nadituṃ nāma na ussahi.

Here, 'rājaputta' means 'the son of the lion, the king of beasts.' Having heard this advice, he indeed did not dare to roar again.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo kokāliko ahosi, sajātiputto rāhulo, migarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the jackal was Kokālika, the true-born son was Rāhula, and the king of beasts was none other than myself.'

Sīhakotthujātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Sīhakotthu Jātaka, the eighth.

[189] 9. Sīhacammajātakavaṇṇanā

[189] 9. The Commentary on the Sīhacamma Jātaka.

Netaṃ sīhassa naditanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kokālikaññeva ārabbha kathesi. So imasmiṃ kāle sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇitukāmo ahosi. Satthā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā atītaṃ āhari.

This story beginning with 'This is not a lion's roar' the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Kokālika himself. At that time, he wished to recite a sarabhañña. The Teacher, hearing of that occurrence, recounted a past event.

Atīte [M 2.0100] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kassakakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kasikammena jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tasmiṃ kāle eko vāṇijo gadrabhabhārakena vohāraṃ karonto vicarati. So gatagataṭṭhāne gadrabhassa piṭṭhito bhaṇḍikaṃ otāretvā gadrabhaṃ sīhacammena pārupitvā sāliyavakhettesu [P 2.0110] vissajjeti. Khettarakkhakā taṃ disvā “sīho”ti saññāya upasaṅkamituṃ na sakkonti. Athekadivasaṃ so vāṇijo ekasmiṃ gāmadvāre nivāsaṃ gahetvā pātarāsaṃ pacāpento tato gadrabhaṃ sīhacammaṃ pārupitvā yavakhette vissajjesi. Khettarakkhakā “sīho”ti saññāya taṃ upasaṅkamituṃ asakkontā gehaṃ gantvā ārocesuṃ. Sakalagāmavāsino āvudhāni gahetvā saṅkhe dhamentā bheriyo vādentā khettasamīpaṃ gantvā unnadiṃsu, gadrabho maraṇabhayabhīto gadrabharavaṃ ravi. Athassa gadrabhabhāvaṃ ñatvā bodhisatto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having been reborn in a farmer’s family, when he reached maturity, made his living by farming. At that time, a merchant traveled, conducting trade with a donkey carrying his goods. At each place he went, he would unload the goods from the donkey’s back, cover the donkey with a lion’s skin, and let it loose in the rice and barley fields. The field guards, seeing it, with the perception 'it is a lion,' were unable to approach. Then one day, that merchant took up residence at a village gate, and while preparing his morning meal, he covered the donkey with the lion’s skin and let it loose in a barley field. The field guards, unable to approach it, with the perception 'it is a lion,' went home and reported it. All the villagers, taking up weapons, blowing conches, beating drums, went near the field and made a great noise. The donkey, terrified by the fear of death, brayed a donkey's bray. Then, realizing its donkey-nature, the Bodhisatta uttered the first verse:

77.

77.

“Netaṃ [V 2.0091] sīhassa naditaṃ, na byagghassa na dīpino;

Pāruto sīhacammena, jammo nadati gadrabho”ti.

"This is not a lion's roar, nor a tiger's, nor a leopard's; covered with a lion's skin, a wretched donkey brays."

Tattha jammoti lāmako. Gāmavāsinopi tassa gadrabhabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ aṭṭhīni bhañjantā pothetvā sīhacammaṃ ādāya agamaṃsu.

Here, 'jammo' means 'contemptible.' The villagers too, recognizing its donkey nature, broke its bones, beat it, took the lion’s skin, and departed.

Atha so vāṇijo āgantvā taṃ byasanabhāvappattaṃ gadrabhaṃ disvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the merchant, returning and seeing the donkey in such a wretched state, uttered the second verse:

78.

78.

“Cirampi kho taṃ khādeyya, gadrabho haritaṃ yavaṃ;

Pāruto sīhacammena, ravamānova dūsayī”ti.

"Indeed, for a long time might that donkey eat green barley, covered with a lion's skin; by braying, he ruined himself."

Tattha tanti nipātamattaṃ, ayaṃ gadrabho attano gadrabhabhāvaṃ ajānāpetvā sīhacammena pāruto cirampi kālaṃ haritaṃ yavaṃ khādeyyāti attho. Ravamānova dūsayīti attano pana gadrabharavaṃ ravamānovesa attānaṃ dūsayi, natthettha sīhacammassa dosoti. Tasmiṃ evaṃ kathenteyeva gadrabho tattheva nipanno mari, vāṇijopi taṃ pahāya pakkāmi.

Here, 'taṃ' is merely a particle. The meaning is that this donkey, without making known his donkey-nature, having been covered with a lion's skin, could have eaten green barley for a very long time. 'By braying, he ruined himself' means that by braying his own donkey's bray, he ruined himself; and there is no fault of the lion's skin in this. While he was speaking thus, the donkey lay down right there and died, and the merchant also abandoned him and departed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vāṇijo devadatto ahosi, gadrabho kokāliko, paṇḍitakassako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the merchant was Devadatta, the donkey was Kokālika, and the wise farmer was myself.”

Sīhacammajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Sīhacamma Jātaka is the ninth.

[190] 10. Sīlānisaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[190] 10. The Commentary on the Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka.

Passa [P 2.0111][M 2.0101] saddhāya sīlassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ saddhaṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira saddho pasanno ariyasāvako ekadivasaṃ jetavanaṃ gacchanto sāyaṃ aciravatinadītīraṃ gantvā nāvike nāvaṃ tīre ṭhapetvā dhammassavanatthāya gate titthe nāvaṃ adisvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā nadiṃ otari, pādā udakamhi na osīdiṃsu. So pathavītale gacchanto viya vemajjhaṃ gatakāle vīciṃ passi. Athassa buddhārammaṇā pīti mandā jātā, pādā osīdituṃ ārabhiṃsu, so puna buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā udakapiṭṭheneva gantvā jetavanaṃ pavisitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā [V 2.0092] “upāsaka, kacci maggaṃ āgacchanto appakilamathena āgatosī”ti pucchitvā “bhante, buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā udakapiṭṭhe patiṭṭhaṃ labhitvā pathaviṃ maddanto viya āgatomhī”ti vutte “na kho pana, upāsaka, tvaññeva buddhaguṇe anussaritvā patiṭṭhaṃ laddho, pubbepi upāsakā samuddamajjhe nāvāya bhinnāya buddhaguṇe anussarantā patiṭṭhaṃ labhiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Behold the faith and virtue!” The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain devout lay follower. It seems that this faithful and devoted noble disciple, one day while going to Jetavana, upon reaching the bank of the Aciravati River in the evening, when the boatmen had left their boats on the shore and gone to listen to the Dhamma, did not see a boat at the landing place.
