Generating joy with the Buddha as its object, he entered the river. His feet did not sink into the water. As he walked as if on solid ground, when he was midway he saw a wave. Then his joy with the Buddha as its object weakened, and his feet began to sink. He again firmly generated joy with the Buddha as its object and walked on the surface of the water until he entered Jetavana. He paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side. The Teacher exchanged friendly greetings with him and asked, ‐Lay follower, did you come along the road without much difficulty?‑ ‐Venerable sir, generating joy with the Buddha as its object, I gained a footing on the water’s surface and came as if treading the earth,‑ he replied. ‐But, lay follower, it is not only you who have gained a footing by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha. In the past too, lay followers whose boats broke in the middle of the ocean gained a footing by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha,‑ said the Teacher, and at his request, he brought forth a story of the past.

Atīte kassapasammāsambuddhakāle sotāpanno ariyasāvako ekena nhāpitakuṭumbikena saddhiṃ nāvaṃ abhiruhi, tassa nhāpitassa bhariyā “ayya, imassa sukhadukkhaṃ tava bhāro”ti nhāpitaṃ tassa upāsakassa hatthe nikkhipi. Atha sā nāvā sattame divase samuddamajjhe bhinnā, tepi dve janā ekasmiṃ phalake nipannā ekaṃ dīpakaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tattha so nhāpito sakuṇe māretvā pacitvā khādanto upāsakassapi deti. Upāsako “alaṃ mayha”nti na khādati. So cintesi – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne amhākaṃ ṭhapetvā tīṇi saraṇāni aññā patiṭṭhā natthī”ti. So tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇe anussari. Athassānusarantassa tasmiṃ dīpake nibbatto nāgarājā attano sarīraṃ mahānāvaṃ katvā māpesi, samuddadevatā [P 2.0112] niyāmako ahosi, nāvā sattahi ratanehi pūrayittha, tayo kūpakā indanīlamaṇimayā ahesuṃ, suvaṇṇamayo laṅkāro, rajatamayāni yottāni, suvaṇṇamayāni yaṭṭhiphiyāni.

In the time of the past Buddha Kassapa, a noble stream-entering disciple boarded a ship together with a barber householder. The barber’s wife said, ‐Sir, his happiness and suffering are your responsibility,‑ and placed the barber in the care of that lay follower. On the seventh day, the ship broke apart in the middle of the ocean, and the two of them, lying on a single plank, reached an island. There, the barber killed birds, cooked them, and ate, offering some to the lay follower as well. The lay follower said, ‐Enough for me,‑ and did not eat. He reflected, ‐In this place, apart from the Three Refuges, there is no other support for us.‑ He then recollected the virtues of the Triple Gem. As he was recollecting, a nāga king who had been reborn on that island magically fashioned his own body into a great ship. The ocean deity became the helmsman, and the ship was filled with seven kinds of jewels. There were three masts made of sapphire, golden ornaments, silver ropes, and golden poles and oars.

Samuddadevatā [M 2.0102] nāvāya ṭhatvā “atthi jambudīpagamikā”ti ghosesi. Upāsako “mayaṃ gamissāmā”ti āha. Tena hi ehi, nāvaṃ abhiruhāti. So nāvaṃ abhiruhitvā nhāpitaṃ pakkosi, samuddadevatā – “tuyhaññeva labbhati, na etassā”ti āha. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Etassa sīlaguṇācāro natthi, taṃ kāraṇaṃ. Ahañhi tuyhaṃ nāvaṃ āhariṃ, na etassā”ti. “Hotu, ahaṃ attanā dinnadānena rakkhitasīlena bhāvitabhāvanāya etassa pattiṃ dammī”ti. Nhāpito “anumodāmi, sāmī”ti āha. Devatā “idāni gaṇhissāmī”ti tampi āropetvā ubhopi jane samuddā nikkhāmetvā nadiyā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā attano ānubhāvena dvinnampi tesaṃ gehe dhanaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā “paṇḍiteheva saddhiṃ saṃsaggo nāma kātabbo. Sace hi imassa nhāpitassa iminā upāsakena saddhiṃ saṃsaggo nābhavissa, samuddamajjheyeva nassissā”ti paṇḍitasaṃsaggaguṇaṃ kathayamānā imā gāthā avoca –

The ocean deity, standing on the ship, proclaimed, ‐Are there any going to Jambudīpa?‑ The lay follower said, ‐We will go.‑ ‐Then come, board the ship.‑ He boarded the ship and called the barber, but the ocean deity said, ‐It is for you alone, not for him.‑ ‐For what reason?‑ ‐He has no virtue, good qualities, or good conduct—that is the reason. I brought this ship for you, not for him.‑ ‐So be it. Through my own generosity, guarded virtue, and developed meditation, I give him a share of this merit.‑ The barber said, ‐I rejoice, master.‑ The deity said, ‐Now I will take him,‑ and having him board as well, he brought both people out of the ocean and, traveling by river, went to Bārāṇasī. By his power, he established wealth in both their homes and said, ‐One should only associate with the wise. If this barber had not associated with this lay follower, he would have perished in the middle of the ocean.‑ Speaking of the benefit of associating with the wise, he uttered these verses:

79.

79.

“Passa saddhāya sīlassa, cāgassa ca ayaṃ phalaṃ;

Nāgo nāvāya vaṇṇena, saddhaṃ vahatupāsakaṃ.

“Behold the fruit of faith, of virtue, and of generosity! A nāga in the form of a ship carries the faithful lay follower.”

80.

80.

“Sabbhireva [V 2.0093] samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhavaṃ;

Satañhi sannivāsena, sotthiṃ gacchati nhāpito”ti.

“One should associate only with the good; with the good one should cultivate friendship. Through living with the virtuous, the barber attains well-being.”

Tattha passāti kañci aniyametvā passathāti ālapati. Saddhāyāti lokiyalokuttarāya saddhāya. Sīlepi eseva nayo. Cāgassāti deyyadhammapariccāgassa ceva kilesapariccāgassa ca. Ayaṃ phalanti idaṃ phalaṃ, guṇaṃ ānisaṃsanti attho. Atha vā cāgassa ca phalaṃ passa, ayaṃ nāgo nāvāya vaṇṇenāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Nāvāya vaṇṇenāti nāvāya saṇṭhānena. Saddhanti tīsu ratanesu patiṭṭhitasaddhaṃ. Sabbhirevāti paṇḍitehiyeva[P 2.0113]. Samāsethāti ekato āvaseyya, upavaseyyāti attho. Kubbethāti kareyya. Santhavanti mittasanthavaṃ. Taṇhāsanthavo pana kenacipi saddhiṃ na kātabbo. Nhāpitoti nhāpitakuṭumbiko. “Nahāpito”tipi pāṭho.

Therein, “Behold” is an address to someone unspecified, meaning “you all behold.” ‐Of faith‑ means of worldly and supramundane faith. The same method applies to ‐of virtue.‑ ‐Of generosity‑ means of the relinquishment of things to be given and the relinquishment of defilements. ‐This is the fruit‑ means this is the fruit, the quality, the benefit. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood thus: “Behold the fruit of generosity; this nāga is in the form of a ship.” ‐In the form of a ship‑ means in the shape of a ship. ‐The faithful‑ means one with faith established in the Three Jewels. ‐Only with the good‑ means only with the wise. ‐One should associate‑ means one should live together, one should dwell with. ‐One should cultivate‑ means one should make. ‐Friendship‑ means friendly intimacy. Intimacy based on craving, however, should not be made with anyone. ‐The barber‑ means the barber householder. There is also the variant reading, ‐Nahāpito.‑

Evaṃ samuddadevatā ākāse ṭhatvā dhammaṃ desetvā ovaditvā nāgarājānaṃ gaṇhitvā attano vimānameva agamāsi.

Thus the ocean deity, standing in the sky, having taught the Dhamma and given advice, took the nāga king and went to his own celestial mansion.

Satthā [M 2.0103] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – saccapariyosāne upāsako sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā sotāpannaupāsako parinibbāyi, nāgarājā sāriputto ahosi, samuddadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths, and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of Once-returning. “At that time, the stream-entering lay follower has since passed away into final Nibbāna, the nāga king was Sāriputta, and the ocean deity was myself.”

Sīlānisaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka is the tenth.

Asadisavaggo catuttho.

The Asadisa Chapter is the fourth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of it:

Asadisañca saṅgāmaṃ, vālodakaṃ giridattaṃ;

Nabhirati dadhivāhaṃ, catumaṭṭhaṃ sīhakoṭṭhaṃ;

Sīhacammaṃ sīlānisaṃsaṃ.

Asadisa, Saṅgāma, Vālodaka, Giridatta; Nabhirati, Dadhivāha, Catumaṭṭha, Sīhakoṭṭha; Sīhacamma, and Sīlānisaṃsa.

5. Ruhakavaggo

5. The Ruhaka Chapter

[191] 1. Ruhakajātakavaṇṇanā

[191] 1. The Commentary on the Ruhaka Jātaka

Api [V 2.0094] ruhaka chinnāpīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu aṭṭhakanipāte indriyajātake (jā. 1.8.60 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ “ayaṃ te bhikkhu itthī anatthakārikā, pubbepi te esā sarājikāya parisāya majjhe lajjāpetvā gehā nikkhamanākāraṃ kāresī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Even though cut off, Ruhaka…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the temptation by a former wife. The story will appear in the Indriya Jātaka of the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta. The Teacher, however, said to that monk, “This woman, monk, brings you harm. Even in the past, she caused you to be shamed in the midst of an assembly including the king and made you leave your home.” Having been requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā vayappatto pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa ruhako nāma purohito ahosi, tassa purāṇī nāma brāhmaṇī bhariyā. Rājā brāhmaṇassa assabhaṇḍakena alaṅkaritvā assaṃ adāsi. So taṃ assaṃ āruyha rañño upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati. Atha naṃ alaṅkataassassa piṭṭhe nisīditvā gacchantaṃ āgacchantañca disvā tahiṃ tahiṃ ṭhitā manussā “aho [M 2.0104] assassa rūpaṃ, aho asso sobhatī”ti assameva pasaṃsanti. So gehaṃ āgantvā pāsādaṃ abhiruyha bhariyaṃ āmantesi – “bhadde[P 2.0114], amhākaṃ asso ativiya sobhati, ubhosu passesu ṭhitā manussā amhākaṃ assameva vaṇṇentī”ti. Sā pana brāhmaṇī thokaṃ chinnikā dhuttikadhātukā, tena naṃ evamāha – “ayya, tvaṃ assassa sobhanakāraṇaṃ na jānāsi, ayaṃ asso attano alaṅkataṃ assabhaṇḍakaṃ nissāya sobhati, sace tvampi asso viya sobhitukāmo assabhaṇḍakaṃ piḷandhitvā antaravīthiṃ oruyha asso viya pāde koṭṭayamāno gantvā rājānaṃ passa, rājāpi taṃ vaṇṇayissati, manussāpi taññeva vaṇṇayissantī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When he came of age, after his father's passing, he was established on the throne and ruled righteously. He had a chaplain named Ruhaka, whose wife was a brahmin woman named Purāṇī. The king gave the brahmin a horse, having adorned it with horse-trappings. Riding that horse, the chaplain went to attend upon the king. Then people standing here and there, seeing him coming and going seated on the back of the adorned horse, praised only the horse, saying, 'Oh, the beauty of the horse! Oh, how splendid the horse is!' Returning home, he ascended to his mansion and addressed his wife: 'My dear, our horse is exceedingly splendid. People standing on both sides praise only our horse.' But that brahmin woman was somewhat wanton and of a deceitful nature, and so she said to him: 'Sir, you do not know the reason for the horse's splendor. This horse is splendid on account of the horse-trappings with which it is adorned. If you too wish to be splendid like the horse, put on the horse-trappings, go down into the street, and prancing with your feet like a horse, go see the king. The king will praise you, and the people will praise you as well.'

So ummattakajātiko brāhmaṇo tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “iminā nāma kāraṇena sā maṃ vadatī”ti ajānitvā tathāsaññī hutvā tathā akāsi. Ye ye passanti, te te parihāsaṃ karontā “sobhati ācariyo”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā pana naṃ “kiṃ, ācariya, pittaṃ te kupitaṃ[V 2.0095], ummattakosi jāto”tiādīni vatvā lajjāpesi. Tasmiṃ kāle brāhmaṇo “ayuttaṃ mayā kata”nti lajjito brāhmaṇiyā kujjhitvā “tāyamhi sarājikāya parisāya antare lajjāpito, pothetvā taṃ nikkaḍḍhissāmī”ti gehaṃ agamāsi. Dhuttikabrāhmaṇī tassa kujjhitvā āgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā puretaraññeva cūḷadvārena nikkhamitvā rājanivesanaṃ gantvā catūhapañcāhaṃ tattheva ahosi. Rājā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā purohitaṃ pakkosāpetvā “ācariya, mātugāmassa nāma doso hotiyeva, brāhmaṇiyā khamituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti khamāpanatthāya paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

That foolish brahmin heard her words, and without understanding her motive, took them to be true and acted accordingly. Whoever saw him mocked him, saying, 'The teacher looks splendid!' The king, however, shamed him by saying, 'What, teacher, is your bile disturbed? Have you gone mad?' and so on. At that time, the brahmin, feeling ashamed, thought, 'I have acted improperly,' and, angry with the brahmin woman, went home, resolving, 'She has shamed me in the midst of the royal assembly. I will beat her and throw her out!' The deceitful brahmin woman, knowing he was returning in anger, had already slipped out through a side door and gone to the king's palace, where she stayed for four or five days. The king, learning of the matter, summoned the chaplain and said, 'Teacher, faults are natural to womankind; you ought to forgive the brahmin woman.' To persuade him to forgive her, he then spoke the first verse:

81.

81.

“Api ruhaka chinnāpi, jiyā sandhīyate puna;

Sandhīyassu purāṇiyā, mā kodhassa vasaṃ gamī”ti.

“Even though cut off, Ruhaka, a bowstring can be joined again; Be reconciled with Purāṇī, do not come under the sway of anger.”

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – bho ruhaka, nanu chinnāpi dhanujiyā puna sandhīyati ghaṭīyati, evameva tvampi purāṇiyā saddhiṃ sandhīyassu, kodhassa vasaṃ mā gamīti.

Here is the summary of the meaning: 'O Ruhaka, is it not so that even a cut bowstring can be joined and fitted together again? In the same way, you too should be reconciled with Purāṇī. Do not fall under the sway of anger.'

Taṃ [P 2.0115][M 2.0105] sutvā ruhako dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Ruhaka spoke the second verse:

82.

82.

“Vijjamānesu vākesu, vijjamānesu kārisu;

Aññaṃ jiyaṃ karissāmi, alaññeva purāṇiyā”ti.

“While there are bark fibers, and while there are makers, I will make another bowstring; enough of this old one!”

Tassattho – mahārāja, dhanukāramuduvākesu ca jiyakārakesu ca manussesu vijjamānesu aññaṃ jiyaṃ karissāmi, imāya chinnāya purāṇiyā jiyāya alaṃ, natthi me koci atthoti. Evañca pana vatvā taṃ nīharitvā aññaṃ brāhmaṇiṃ ānesi.

The meaning is: 'Great king, while there are soft bark fibers for bow-making and men who make bowstrings, I will make another bowstring. Enough of this old, cut bowstring; it is of no use to me.' And having said this, he expelled her and brought another brahmin woman.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā, brāhmaṇī, purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, ruhako ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: 'At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. At that time, the brahmin woman was the former wife, Ruhaka was the discontented monk, and the King of Benares was I myself.'

Ruhakajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Ruhaka Jātaka is the first.

[192] 2. Sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakavaṇṇanā

[192] 2. The Commentary on the Sirikāḷakaṇṇī Jātaka

Itthī [V 2.0096] siyā rūpavatīti idaṃ sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakaṃ mahāumaṅgajātake āvibhavissati.

“A woman may be beautiful...” — this Sirikāḷakaṇṇī Jātaka will appear in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka.

Sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Sirikāḷakaṇṇī Jātaka is the second.

[193] 3. Cūḷapadumajātakavaṇṇanā

[193] 3. The Commentary on the Cūḷapaduma Jātaka

Ayameva sā ahamapi so anaññoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu ummādantījātake (jā. 2.20.57 ādayo) āvibhavissati. So pana bhikkhu satthārā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhito”ti vutte “saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti vatvā “kena pana tvaṃ ukkaṇṭhāpito”ti vutte [M 2.0106] “ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ mātugāmaṃ disvā kilesānuvattako hutvā ukkaṇṭhitomhī”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “bhikkhu, mātugāmo nāma akataññū mittadubbhī bahumāyā, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi attano dakkhiṇajāṇulohitaṃ pāyetvā yāvajīvitadānampi datvā mātugāmassa cittaṃ na labhiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'This is that very woman, and I am he, no other' — this the Teacher told while staying at Jetavana, concerning a monk who was dissatisfied with the holy life. (The story will be made clear in the Ummādantī Jātaka). When that monk was asked by the Teacher, 'Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?' he replied, 'It is true, Blessed One.' When asked, 'By whom were you made dissatisfied?' he said, 'Venerable Sir, I saw a woman elegantly dressed and adorned, and falling under the influence of defilements, I became dissatisfied.' Then the Teacher told him, 'Monk, womankind is ungrateful, treacherous to friends, and full of deceit. Even the wise men of old, though they gave their own blood from their right knee to drink and even gave the gift of life itself, could not win a woman's heart.' Having said this, he brought forth a story of the past.

Atīte [P 2.0116] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, nāmaggahaṇadivase cassa “padumakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tassa aparena cha kaniṭṭhabhātikā ahesuṃ. Te sattapi janā anupubbena vuḍḍhippattā gharāvāsaṃ gahetvā rañño sahāyā viya vicaranti. Athekadivasaṃ rājā rājaṅgaṇaṃ olokento ṭhito te mahāparivārena rājupaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchante disvā “ime maṃ vadhitvā rajjampi gaṇheyyu”nti āsaṅkaṃ uppādetvā te pakkosāpetvā – “tātā, tumhe imasmiṃ nagare vasituṃ na labhatha, aññattha gantvā mama accayena āgantvā kulasantakaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Te pitu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā roditvā kanditvā attano attano gharāni gantvā pajāpatiyo ādāya “yattha vā tattha vā gantvā jīvissāmā”ti nagarā nikkhamitvā maggaṃ gacchantā ekaṃ kantāraṃ patvā annapānaṃ alabhamānā khudaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkontā “mayaṃ jīvamānā itthiyo labhissāmā”ti kaniṭṭhassa bhariyaṃ māretvā terasa koṭṭhāse katvā maṃsaṃ khādiṃsu. Bodhisatto attano ca bhariyāya ca laddhakoṭṭhāsesu ekaṃ ṭhapetvā ekaṃ dvepi khādiṃsu. Evaṃ cha divase cha itthiyo māretvā maṃsaṃ khādiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. On his naming day, they gave him the name Prince Paduma. He had six younger brothers. In due course, all seven grew up, married, and lived as companions to the king. One day, the king, while looking out over the royal courtyard, saw them coming to wait upon him with a large retinue. Suspicion arose in him, 'These sons might kill me and seize the kingdom.' He summoned them and said, 'My sons, you cannot live in this city. Go elsewhere and return after my death to take the kingdom that belongs to our family.' Accepting their father’s words, they wept and lamented, went to their respective homes, took their wives, and left the city, thinking, 'We will live wherever we can.' As they were traveling, they reached a wilderness. Finding no food or drink and unable to endure their hunger, they thought, 'If we remain alive, we can get other wives.' So they killed the youngest brother's wife, divided the flesh into thirteen portions, and ate it. Out of the portions received by the Bodhisatta and his wife, they shared one portion and set the other aside. In this way, over six days, they killed six women and ate their flesh.

Bodhisatto [V 2.0097] pana divase divase ekekaṃ ṭhapetvā cha koṭṭhāse ṭhapesi. Sattame divase “bodhisattassa bhariyaṃ māressāmā”ti vutte bodhisatto te cha koṭṭhāse tesaṃ datvā “ajja tāva ime cha koṭṭhāse khādatha, sve jānissāmā”ti vatvā tesaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditvā niddāyanakāle bhariyaṃ gahetvā palāyi. Sā thokaṃ gantvā “gantuṃ na sakkomi, sāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ bodhisatto khandhenādāya aruṇuggamanavelāya kantārā nikkhami. Sā sūriye uggate “pipāsitāmhi, sāmī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “udakaṃ natthi, bhadde”ti vatvā punappunaṃ kathite khaggena [M 2.0107] dakkhiṇajāṇukaṃ paharitvā – “bhadde, pānīyaṃ natthi, idaṃ pana me dakkhiṇajāṇulohitaṃ pivamānā nisīdāhī”ti āha. Sā tathā akāsi. Te anupubbena mahāgaṅgaṃ patvā pivitvā ca nhatvā ca phalāphalaṃ khāditvā phāsukaṭṭhāne vissamitvā ekasmiṃ gaṅgānivattane assamapadaṃ māpetvā vāsaṃ kappesuṃ.

The Bodhisatta, however, had set aside one portion every day, thus keeping six portions. On the seventh day, when they said, 'We will kill the Bodhisatta's wife,' the Bodhisatta gave those six portions to them, saying, 'For today, eat these six portions; tomorrow we shall see.' While they were sleeping after eating the meat, he took his wife and fled. After going a short distance, she said, 'My lord, I cannot go on.' Then the Bodhisatta took her on his shoulders and emerged from the wilderness at dawn. When the sun had risen, she said, 'My lord, I am thirsty.' The Bodhisatta said, 'There is no water, dear lady.' But when she asked again and again, he struck his right knee with his sword and said, 'Dear lady, there is no drinking water; sit down and drink this blood from my right knee.' She did so. In due course, they reached the great Ganges, where they drank and bathed, ate various fruits, and after resting in a pleasant place, they built a hermitage at a bend in the river and took up residence.

Athekadivasaṃ uparigaṅgāya rājāparādhikaṃ coraṃ hatthapāde ca kaṇṇanāsañca chinditvā ekasmiṃ ambaṇake nipajjāpetvā mahāgaṅgāya pavāhesuṃ. So mahantaṃ aṭṭassaraṃ karonto taṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi. Bodhisatto tassa karuṇaṃ paridevitasaddaṃ sutvā “dukkhappatto satto mayi ṭhite mā nassī”ti gaṅgātīraṃ gantvā taṃ uttāretvā assamapadaṃ ānetvā kāsāvadhovanalepanādīhi vaṇapaṭikammaṃ akāsi. Bhariyā panassa “evarūpaṃ nāma dussīlaṃ kuṇṭhaṃ gaṅgāya āvāhetvā paṭijagganto vicaratī”ti vatvā taṃ kuṇṭhaṃ jigucchamānā niṭṭhubhantī vicarati. Bodhisatto tassa vaṇesu saṃviruḷhesu bhariyāya saddhiṃ taṃ assamapadeyeva ṭhapetvā aṭavito phalāphalāni āharitvā tañca bhariyañca posesi. Tesu evaṃ vasantesu sā itthī etasmiṃ kuṇṭhe paṭibaddhacittā hutvā tena saddhiṃ anācāraṃ caritvā ekenupāyena bodhisattaṃ māretukāmā hutvā evamāha – “sāmi, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ aṃse nisīditvā kantārā nikkhamamānā ekaṃ pabbataṃ oloketvā ayye pabbatamhi nibbattadevate ‘sace ahaṃ sāmikena saddhiṃ arogā jīvitaṃ labhissāmi, balikammaṃ te karissāmī’ti āyāciṃ, sā maṃ idāni uttāseti, karomassā balikamma”nti. Bodhisatto taṃ māyaṃ ajānanto “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā balikammaṃ sajjetvā tāya balibhājanaṃ gāhāpetvā pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruhi. Atha naṃ [P 2.0118] sā evamāha – “sāmi, devatāyapi tvaññeva uttamadevatā, paṭhamaṃ tāva taṃ vanapupphehi pūjetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā vanditvā pacchā devatāya balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti. Sā bodhisattaṃ papātābhimukhaṃ ṭhapetvā vanapupphehi pūjetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā vanditukāmā viya hutvā piṭṭhipasse ṭhatvā piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā papāte pātetvā “diṭṭhā me paccāmittassa piṭṭhī”ti tuṭṭhamānasā pabbatā orohitvā kuṇṭhassa santikaṃ agamāsi.

One day, on the upper Ganges, a thief who had committed an offense against the king had his hands, feet, ears, and nose cut off, and having been placed in a small boat, was set adrift on the great Ganges. He uttered a loud cry of distress as he reached that place. The Bodhisatta, hearing his pitiful wailing, thought, 'Let not a suffering being perish while I am here!' and went to the riverbank, rescued him, brought him to the hermitage, and treated his wounds by washing them with astringent water, applying ointments, and so forth. But his wife, disgusted, said, 'He goes about caring for such a wicked, mutilated wretch, having brought him from the Ganges,' and she went about spitting in contempt. When his wounds had healed, the Bodhisatta kept him in the hermitage and, bringing various fruits from the forest, supported both him and his wife. While they lived thus, the woman became infatuated with the cripple and, having committed misconduct with him, desired to kill the Bodhisatta by a trick. She said, 'Husband, while I was sitting on your shoulders as we were leaving the wilderness, I saw a certain mountain and prayed to the deity dwelling there, saying, "If I obtain my life and health along with my husband, I will offer a sacrifice to you." Now that deity alarms me; let us perform the sacrifice for her.' Unaware of her deceit, the Bodhisatta agreed, prepared the offering, and having her carry the sacrificial vessel, climbed to the mountaintop. Then she said to him, 'Husband, you are a supreme deity even to the gods. First, I will worship you with forest flowers, perform a circumambulation, and pay homage; afterwards, I will offer the sacrifice to the deity.' She positioned the Bodhisatta facing the precipice, worshipped him with forest flowers, and as if wishing to circumambulate and pay homage, she stood behind him, struck him on the back, and pushed him over the precipice. With a joyful heart, thinking, 'I have seen the back of my enemy!' she descended the mountain and went to the cripple.

Bodhisattopi [V 2.0098][M 2.0108] papātānusārena pabbatā patanto udumbararukkhamatthake ekasmiṃ akaṇṭake pattasañchanne gumbe laggi, heṭṭhāpabbataṃ pana orohituṃ na sakkā. So udumbaraphalāni khāditvā sākhantare nisīdi. Atheko mahāsarīro godharājā heṭṭhāpabbatapādato abhiruhitvā tasmiṃ udumbaraphalāni khādati. So taṃ divasaṃ bodhisattaṃ disvā palāyi, punadivase āgantvā ekasmiṃ passe phalāni khāditvā pakkāmi. So evaṃ punappunaṃ āgacchanto bodhisattena saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ āpajjitvā “tvaṃ imaṃ ṭhānaṃ kena kāraṇena āgatosī”ti pucchitvā “iminā nāma kāraṇenā”ti vutte “tena hi mā bhāyī”ti vatvā bodhisattaṃ attano piṭṭhiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā otāretvā araññato nikkhamitvā mahāmagge ṭhapetvā “tvaṃ iminā maggena gacchāhī”ti uyyojetvā araññameva pāvisi. Bodhisatto ekaṃ gāmakaṃ gantvā tattheva vasanto pitu kālakatabhāvaṃ sutvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā kulasantake rajje patiṭṭhāya padumarājā nāma hutvā dasa rājadhamme akopetvā dhammena rajjaṃ kārento catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāreti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ cha satasahassāni vissajjetvā dānaṃ adāsi.

The Bodhisatta, while falling from the mountain along the precipice, got caught in a thornless, leaf-covered thicket atop a fig tree, but he was unable to descend to the foot of the mountain. He lived among the branches, eating the fig fruits. Then a large-bodied king of monitor lizards climbed up from the base of the mountain and ate the fig fruits on that tree. That day, seeing the Bodhisatta, it fled. The next day it returned, ate fruits on one side, and left. Coming thus repeatedly, it became familiar with the Bodhisatta and asked, 'For what reason have you come to this place?' When told the reason, it said, 'In that case, do not fear,' and having the Bodhisatta lie on its back, it carried him down. Leaving the forest, it placed him on the highway and, after saying, 'Go by this road,' it returned to the forest. The Bodhisatta went to a small village and, while living there, heard of his father’s death. He then went to Bārāṇasī and, established in the kingship which was his family heritage, became known as King Paduma. Ruling righteously without violating the ten royal virtues, he had six alms halls built—at the four city gates, in the middle of the city, and at the palace gate—and gave alms, spending six hundred thousand coins daily.

Sāpi kho itthī taṃ kuṇṭhaṃ khandhe nisīdāpetvā araññā nikkhamitvā manussapathe bhikkhaṃ caramānā yāgubhattaṃ saṃharitvā taṃ kuṇṭhaṃ posesi. Manussā “ayaṃ te kiṃ hotī”ti [P 2.0119] pucchiyamānā “ahaṃ etassa mātuladhītā, pitucchāputto me eso, etasseva maṃ adaṃsu, sāhaṃ vajjhappattampi attano sāmikaṃ ukkhipitvā pariharantī bhikkhaṃ caritvā posemī”ti. Manussā “ayaṃ patibbatā”ti tato paṭṭhāya bahutaraṃ yāgubhattaṃ adaṃsu. Apare pana janā evamāhaṃsu – “tvaṃ mā evaṃ vicari, padumarājā bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ kāreti, sakalajambudīpaṃ saṅkhobhetvā dānaṃ deti, so taṃ disvā tussissati, tuṭṭho te bahuṃ dhanaṃ dassati, tava sāmikaṃ idheva nisīdāpetvā gacchā”ti thiraṃ katvā vettapacchiṃ adaṃsu. Sā anācārā taṃ kuṇṭhaṃ vettapacchiyaṃ nisīdāpetvā pacchiṃ ukkhipitvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā dānasālāsu bhuñjamānā vicarati. Bodhisatto alaṅkatahatthikkhandhavaragato dānaggaṃ gantvā aṭṭhannaṃ vā dasannaṃ vā sahatthā dānaṃ datvā puna gehaṃ gacchati[M 2.0109]. Sā anācārā taṃ kuṇṭhaṃ pacchiyaṃ nisīdāpetvā pacchiṃ ukkhipitvā tassa gamanamagge aṭṭhāsi.

That wicked woman, having seated the cripple on her shoulder, left the forest and wandered along the human paths seeking alms, supporting the cripple by collecting rice porridge and food. When people asked, 'What is he to you?' she replied, 'I am his maternal uncle's daughter, and he is my paternal aunt's son; my parents gave me to him. Even though he has met with the king's punishment, I carry my husband about, supporting him by wandering for alms.' People, thinking, 'This is a devoted wife,' gave her more rice porridge and food from then on. Other people said, 'Do not wander like this. King Paduma rules in Bārāṇasī and gives alms, having stirred all of Jambudīpa with his generosity. He will be pleased to see you and, being delighted, will give you much wealth. Seat your husband right here and go.' To make it secure, they gave her a wicker basket. That immoral woman seated the cripple in the wicker basket, lifted the basket, and went to Bārāṇasī, wandering and eating at the alms halls. The Bodhisatta, mounted on the back of a noble, decorated elephant, went to the hall of offerings and, having given gifts to eight or ten people with his own hands, was returning home. That immoral woman, having seated the cripple in the basket and lifted it, stood on the path where he was to pass.

Rājā disvā “kiṃ eta”nti pucchi. “Ekā, deva, patibbatā”ti. Atha naṃ pakkosāpetvā sañjānitvā kuṇṭhaṃ pacchiyā nīharāpetvā “ayaṃ te kiṃ hotī”ti pucchi. Sā “pitucchāputto me, deva, kuladattiko sāmiko”ti āha. Manussā taṃ antaraṃ ajānantā [V 2.0099] “aho patibbatā”tiādīni vatvā taṃ anācāritthiṃ vaṇṇayiṃsu. Puna rājā “ayaṃ te kuṇṭho kuladattiko sāmiko”ti pucchi. Sā rājānaṃ asañjānantī “āma, devā”ti sūrā hutvā kathesi. Atha naṃ rājā “kiṃ esa bārāṇasirañño putto, nanu tvaṃ padumakumārassa bhariyā asukarañño dhītā, asukā nāma mama jāṇulohitaṃ pivitvā imasmiṃ kuṇṭhe paṭibaddhacittā maṃ papāte pātesi. Sā idāni tvaṃ nalāṭena maccuṃ gahetvā maṃ ‘mato’ti maññamānā imaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgatā, nanu ahaṃ jīvāmī”ti [P 2.0120] vatvā amacce āmantetvā “bho, amaccā nanu cāhaṃ tumhehi puṭṭho evaṃ kathesiṃ ‘mama kaniṭṭhabhātikā cha itthiyo māretvā maṃsaṃ khādiṃsu, ahaṃ pana mayhaṃ bhariyaṃ arogaṃ katvā gaṅgātīraṃ netvā assamapade vasanto ekaṃ vajjhappattaṃ kuṇṭhaṃ uttāretvā paṭijaggiṃ. Sā itthī etasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā maṃ pabbatapāde pātesi. Ahaṃ attano mettacittatāya jīvitaṃ labhi’nti. Yāya ahaṃ pabbatā pātito, na sā aññā, esā dussīlā, sopi vajjhappatto kuṇṭho na añño, ayamevā”ti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –

The king, upon seeing this, asked, "What is this?" "A devoted wife, Your Majesty." Then, having her summoned, he recognized her. He had the cripple brought out from the basket and asked, "What is this man to you?" She said, "He is my paternal cousin, Your Majesty, my husband given by my family." The people, unaware of the truth, praised that immoral woman, saying such things as, "Ah, what a devoted wife!" Again the king asked, "Is this cripple your husband given by the family?" Not recognizing the king, she became bold and said, "Yes, Your Majesty." Then the king said to her, "Is this the son of the king of Benares? Are you not the wife of Prince Paduma, the daughter of a certain king, by the name of so-and-so? Did you not, after drinking the blood from my knee, become infatuated with this cripple and push me over a precipice? Now, carrying death on your forehead and thinking me dead, you have come to this place. Do I not still live?" Having spoken thus, he addressed his ministers, "Sirs, ministers, when asked by you, did I not say this: 'My six younger brothers killed their wives and ate their flesh, but I, having protected my wife from harm, took her to the bank of the Ganges and lived in a hermitage, where I rescued a condemned cripple and cared for him. That woman, infatuated with him, pushed me from the mountain precipice. But through my own mind of loving-kindness, I obtained my life.' The one by whom I was pushed from the mountain is none other than she, this immoral one, and that condemned cripple is none other than this very one." Having spoken thus, he uttered these verses:

85.

85.

“Ayameva sā ahamapi so anañño, ayameva so hatthacchinno anañño;

Yamāha ‘komārapatī mama’nti, vajjhitthiyo natthi itthīsu saccaṃ.

“This is indeed she, and I am indeed he, not another; this is indeed he with severed hands, not another. She of whom it was said, ‘He is my youthful husband’—women are worthy of death; there is no truth in women.”

86.

86.

“Imañca jammaṃ musalena hantvā, luddaṃ chavaṃ paradārūpaseviṃ;

Imissā ca naṃ pāpapatibbatāya, jīvantiyā chindatha kaṇṇanāsa”nti.

“Kill this wretch with a pestle—this cruel corpse who consorts with another’s wife—and of this woman of wicked fidelity, while she is still alive, cut off her ears and nose.”

Tattha yamāha komārapatī mamanti yaṃ esā “ayaṃ me, komārapati, kuladattiko sāmiko”ti āha, ayameva so, na añño. “Yamāhu[M 2.0110], komārapatī”tipi pāṭho. Ayameva hi potthakesu likhito, tassāpi ayamevattho, vacanavipallāso panettha veditabbo. Yañhi raññā vuttaṃ, tadeva idha āgataṃ. Vajjhitthiyoti itthiyo nāma vajjhā vadhitabbā eva. Natthi itthīsu saccanti etāsu sabhāvo nāmeko natthi. “Imañca jamma”ntiādi dvinnampi tesaṃ daṇḍāṇāpanavasena vuttaṃ. Tattha jammanti lāmakaṃ. Musalena hantvāti musalena hanitvā pothetvā aṭṭhīni bhañjitvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ katvā. Luddanti dāruṇaṃ. Chavanti guṇābhāvena nijjīvaṃ matasadisaṃ. Imissā [P 2.0121] ca nanti ettha nanti nipātamattaṃ, imissā ca pāpapatibbatāya anācārāya dussīlāya jīvantiyāva kaṇṇanāsaṃ chindathāti attho.

Therein, “She who said, ‘He is my youthful husband’” means what she said: “This is my husband, a youthful husband given by my family.” This is he, not another. There is also the reading, “Yamāhu, komārapatī.” This is indeed what is written in the manuscripts, and it has the same meaning; a verbal inversion should be understood here. For what was said by the king is what has come here. “Women are worthy of death” means that women are indeed worthy of punishment, worthy of being slain. “There is no truth in women” means that in them there is no single, constant nature. “And this wretch,” and so on, was said by way of ordering punishment for both of them. Therein, “wretch” means base. “Having killed with a pestle” means having struck with a pestle, crushed, broken the bones, and reduced them to powder. “Cruel” means harsh. “Corpse” means lifeless, like one who is dead, due to an absence of virtues. In “And of this woman,” the word “naṃ” is merely a particle. The meaning is: “and of this woman of wicked fidelity, this unchaste, immoral one, while she is still alive, cut off her ears and nose.”

Bodhisatto kodhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto evaṃ tesaṃ daṇḍaṃ āṇāpetvāpi na tathā kāresi[V 2.0100]. Kopaṃ pana mandaṃ katvā yathā sā pacchiṃ sīsato oropetuṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ gāḷhataraṃ bandhāpetvā kuṇṭhaṃ tattha pakkhipāpetvā attano vijitā nīharāpesi.

The Bodhisatta, though unable to suppress his anger and having thus ordered their punishment, did not have it carried out exactly so. Instead, having mitigated his anger, he had the basket bound so tightly to her that she was unable to lower it from her head, had the cripple placed in it, and had them driven out of his kingdom.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā cha bhātaro aññatarā therā ahesuṃ, bhariyā ciñcamāṇavikā, kuṇṭho devadatto, godharājā ānando, padumarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and explained the Truths, identified the Birth Story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the six brothers were certain elders, the wife was Ciñcamāṇavikā, the cripple was Devadatta, the iguana king was Ānanda, but King Paduma was I myself.”

Cūḷapadumajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The commentary on the Cūḷapaduma Jātaka is the third.

[194] 4. Maṇicorajātakavaṇṇanā

[194] 4. The Commentary on the Maṇicora Jātaka

Na santi devā pavasanti nūnāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto vadhāya parisakkantaṃ devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā pana satthā “devadatto vadhāya parisakkatī”ti sutvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkatiyeva, parisakkantopi pana maṃ vadhituṃ nāsakkhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The gods do not exist, surely they are absent.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta who was plotting to kill him. Then the Teacher, hearing that “Devadatta is plotting to kill him,” said, “Not only now, monks, but in the past too Devadatta plotted to kill me; yet though he plotted, he was not able to kill me,” and he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasito avidūre gāmake gahapatikule nibbatti. Athassa vayappattassa [M 2.0111] bārāṇasito kuladhītaraṃ ānesuṃ, sā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā ahosi abhirūpā dassanīyā devaccharā viya pupphalatā viya laḷamānā mattakinnarī viya ca sujātāti nāmena patibbatā sīlācārasampannā vattasampannā. Niccakālampissā pativattaṃ sassuvattaṃ sasuravattañca katameva hoti, sā bodhisattassa piyā ahosi manāpā. Iti ubhopi [P 2.0122] te sammodamānā ekacittā samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder’s family in a village not far from Benares. When he came of age, they brought him a bride of good family from Benares. She was of golden complexion, beautiful, lovely to behold, like a celestial nymph, like a flowering creeper in full bloom, and like an enraptured kinnarī. Named Sujātā, she was a devoted wife, endowed with virtue and good conduct, and fulfilled her duties. She always performed her duties to her husband, her mother-in-law, and her father-in-law. She was dear and pleasing to the Bodhisatta. Thus, rejoicing together, the two of them lived in harmony with a single mind.

Athekadivasaṃ sujātā “mātāpitaro daṭṭhukāmāmhī”ti bodhisattassa ārocesi. “Sādhu, bhadde, maggapātheyyaṃ pahonakaṃ paṭiyādehī”ti khajjavikatiṃ pacāpetvā khajjakādīni yānake ṭhapetvā yānakaṃ pājento yānakassa purato ahosi, itarā pacchato. Te nagarasamīpaṃ gantvā yānakaṃ mocetvā nhatvā bhuñjiṃsu. Puna bodhisatto yānakaṃ yojetvā purato nisīdi, sujātā vatthāni parivattetvā alaṅkaritvā pacchato nisīdi. Yānakassa antonagaraṃ paviṭṭhakāle bārāṇasirājā hatthikkhandhavaragato nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto taṃ padesaṃ agamāsi. Sujātā otaritvā [V 2.0101] yānakassa pacchato padasā pāyāsi. Rājā taṃ disvā tassā rūpasampattiyā ākaḍḍhiyamānalocano paṭibaddhacitto hutvā ekaṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi – “gaccha tvaṃ etissā sassāmikabhāvaṃ vā assāmikabhāvaṃ vā jānāhī”ti. So gantvā tassā sassāmikabhāvaṃ ñatvā “sassāmikā kira, deva, yānake nisinno puriso etissā sāmiko”ti āha.

One day, Sujātā said to the Bodhisatta, “I wish to see my parents.” He replied, “Very well, my dear, prepare sufficient provisions for the journey.” After having various kinds of delicacies prepared and placing cakes and other items in the carriage, the Bodhisatta, driving the carriage, sat at the front while she sat behind. When they reached the vicinity of the city, they unyoked the carriage, bathed, and ate. Then the Bodhisatta yoked the carriage again and sat in front, while Sujātā changed her clothes, adorned herself, and sat behind. As the carriage entered the city, the king of Benares, mounted on a splendid elephant and making a ceremonial circumambulation of the city, arrived at that spot. Sujātā alighted and walked behind the carriage on foot. When the king saw her, he was captivated by her beauty—his eyes drawn and his mind ensnared. He ordered a minister, “Go and find out whether she has a husband or is without one.” The minister went, learned she was married, and reported, “She is married, Your Majesty. The man seated in the carriage is her husband.”

Rājā paṭibaddhacittaṃ vinodetuṃ asakkonto kilesāturo hutvā “ekena naṃ upāyena mārāpetvā itthiṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā ekaṃ purisaṃ āmantetvā “gaccha, bho, imaṃ cūḷāmaṇiṃ vīthiṃ gacchanto viya hutvā etassa purisassa yānake pakkhipitvā ehī”ti cūḷāmaṇiṃ datvā uyyojesi. So “sādhū”ti taṃ gahetvā gantvā yānake ṭhapetvā “ṭhapito me, devā”ti āgantvā ārocesi. Rājā “cūḷāmaṇi me naṭṭho”ti āha, manussā ekakolāhalaṃ akaṃsu. Rājā “sabbadvārāni pidahitvā sañcāraṃ chinditvā coraṃ pariyesathā”ti āha, rājapurisā tathā akaṃsu, nagaraṃ ekasaṅkhobhaṃ ahosi. Itaro puriso manusse gahetvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “bho, yānakaṃ ṭhapehi, rañño cūḷāmaṇi [P 2.0123][M 2.0112] naṭṭho, yānakaṃ sodhessāmī”ti yānakaṃ sodhento attanā ṭhapitamaṇiṃ gahetvā bodhisattaṃ gahetvā “maṇicoro”ti hatthehi ca pādehi ca pothetvā pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā netvā “ayaṃ maṇicoro”ti rañño dassesi. Rājāpi “sīsamassa chindathā”ti āṇāpesi.

The king, unable to dispel his obsessive thoughts and overcome by defilements, thought, “By some means, I will have him killed and take the woman.” Summoning a man, he said, “Go, sir, pretend to be walking along the street. Place this crest-jewel in this man’s carriage and return.” Giving him the crest-jewel, he sent him off. The man, saying, “Very well,” took it and went. After placing it in the carriage, he returned and reported, “It has been placed, my lord.” The king said, “My crest-jewel is lost,” and the people raised a great uproar. The king ordered, “Close all the gates, stop all movement, and search for the thief.” The king’s men did so, and the city was thrown into chaos. The other man, taking people with him, went to the Bodhisatta and said, “Sir, stop the carriage. The king’s crest-jewel is lost. I will search the carriage.” While searching the carriage, he took the crest-jewel he had placed himself, seized the Bodhisatta, and cried, “Here is the jewel thief!” Beating him with hands and feet, he bound his hands behind his back and led him away, presenting him to the king, saying, “This is the jewel thief.” The king then commanded, “Cut off his head.”

Atha naṃ rājapurisā catukke catukke kasāhi tāḷentā dakkhiṇadvārena nagarā nikkhamāpesuṃ. Sujātāpi yānakaṃ pahāya bāhā paggayha paridevamānā “sāmi, maṃ nissāya imaṃ dukkhaṃ pattosī”ti paridevamānā pacchato pacchato agamāsi. Rājapurisā “sīsamassa chindissāmā”ti bodhisattaṃ uttānaṃ nipajjāpesuṃ. Taṃ disvā sujātā attano sīlaguṇaṃ āvajjetvā “natthi vata maññe imasmiṃ loke sīlavantānaṃ viheṭhake pāpasāhasikamanusse nisedhetuṃ samatthā devatā nāmā”tiādīni vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king’s men, beating him with whips at every crossroad, led him out of the city through the southern gate. Sujātā, too, abandoning her carriage and wailing with outstretched arms, followed behind, lamenting, “My lord, you have come to this suffering because of me.” The king’s men laid the Bodhisatta down on his back, intending to cut off his head. Seeing this, Sujātā reflected on her own virtuous qualities and, thinking, “Surely there are no deities in this world capable of restraining wicked and violent men who harm the virtuous!” she spoke the first verse:

87.

87.

“Na santi devā pavasanti nūna, na hi nūna santi idha lokapālā;

Sahasā karontānamasaññatānaṃ, na hi nūna santi paṭisedhitāro”ti.

“Surely there are no gods, they must be away; surely there are no world-protectors here. For those who act rashly and without restraint, surely there are none to restrain them.”

Tattha na santi, devāti imasmiṃ loke sīlavantānaṃ olokanakā pāpānañca nisedhakā na santi nūna devā. Pavasanti nūnāti evarūpesu vā kiccesu uppannesu nūna pavasanti pavāsaṃ gacchanti. Idha, lokapālāti imasmiṃ loke lokapālasammatā samaṇabrāhmaṇāpi sīlavantānaṃ [V 2.0102] anuggāhakā na hi nūna santi. Sahasā karontānamasaññatānanti sahasā avīmaṃsitvā sāhasikaṃ dāruṇaṃ kammaṃ karontānaṃ dussīlānaṃ. Paṭisedhitāroti evarūpaṃ kammaṃ mā karittha, na labbhā etaṃ kātunti paṭisedhentā natthīti attho.

Here, “there are no gods” means in this world there are no deities who watch over the virtuous or restrain the wicked. “They must be away” means that when such matters arise, they surely go away, they go into exile. “World-protectors” means those ascetics and brahmins esteemed as world-protectors in this world, who assist the virtuous—they surely do not exist. “For those unrestrained ones who act rashly” means for the immoral who commit cruel, reckless deeds without reflection. “Those who would restrain them” means those who would restrain them, saying, “Do not do such a deed, it is not allowable to do this,” are absent—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ tāya sīlasampannāya paridevamānāya sakkassa devarañño nisinnāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi, sakko “ko nu kho maṃ [P 2.0124] sakkattato cāvetukāmo”ti āvajjento imaṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “bārāṇasirājā atipharusakammaṃ karoti, sīlasampannaṃ sujātaṃ kilameti, gantuṃ dāni me vaṭṭatī”ti devalokā oruyha attano ānubhāvena hatthipiṭṭhe [M 2.0113] nisinnaṃ taṃ pāparājānaṃ hatthikkhandhato otāretvā dhammagaṇḍikāya uttānaṃ nipajjāpetvā bodhisattaṃ ukkhipitvā sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā rājavesaṃ gāhāpetvā hatthikkhandhe nisīdāpesi. Rājapurisā pharasuṃ ukkhipitvā sīsaṃ chindantā rañño sīsaṃ chindiṃsu, chinnakāleyeva cassa rañño sīsabhāvaṃ jāniṃsu. Sakko devarājā dissamānakasarīreneva bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā bodhisattassa rājābhisekaṃ katvā sujātāya ca aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ dāpesi. Amaccā ceva brāhmaṇagahapatikādayo ca sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ disvā “adhammikarājā mārito, idāni amhehi sakkadattiko dhammikarājā laddho”ti somanassappattā ahesuṃ.

Thus, as that virtuous woman lamented, the seat of Sakka, king of devas, showed signs of heat. Sakka, wondering, “Who now wishes to dislodge me from my position as Sakka?” reflected and, realizing the cause, thought, “The king of Bārāṇasī commits excessively harsh deeds, tormenting the virtuous Sujātā. Now it is time for me to go.” Descending from the heavenly realm by his own power, he brought the wicked king seated on an elephant down from the elephant's back, laid him supine on the execution block, and lifted up the Bodhisatta. Adorning him with all ornaments and having him assume the royal appearance, he seated him on the elephant’s back. The king’s men, raising their axes to behead, instead beheaded the king. The moment his head was severed, they recognized it as the king’s head. Sakka, the king of devas, in his visible form, went to the Bodhisatta, performed his royal consecration, and appointed Sujātā to the position of chief queen. The ministers, brahmins, householders, and others, seeing Sakka, the king of devas, rejoiced, thinking, “The unjust king has been slain; now we have obtained a righteous king given by Sakka.”

Sakkopi ākāse ṭhatvā “ayaṃ vo sakkadattiko rājā, ito paṭṭhāya dhammena rajjaṃ kāressati. Sace hi rājā adhammiko hoti, devo akāle vassati, kāle na vassati, chātabhayaṃ rogabhayaṃ satthabhayanti imāni tīṇi bhayāni upagatāneva hontī”ti ovadanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Sakka, standing in the sky, declared, "This is your king, given by Sakka. From now on, he will rule righteously. For if a king is unrighteous, it rains at the wrong time, it does not rain at the right time, and these three dangers—famine, disease, and violence—will surely befall." Then, advising them, he spoke the second verse:

88.

88.

“Akāle vassatī tassa, kāle tassa na vassati;

Saggā ca cavati ṭhānā, nanu so tāvatā hato”ti.

"For him, it rains at the wrong time; for him, it does not rain at the right time. He falls from his heavenly state—is he not destroyed by that much?"

Tattha akāleti adhammikarañño rajje ayuttakāle sassānaṃ pakkakāle vā lāyanamaddanādikāle vā devo vassati. Kāleti yuttapayuttakāle vapanakāle taruṇasassakāle gabbhaggahaṇakāle ca na vassati. Saggā ca cavati ṭhānāti saggasaṅkhātā ṭhānā devalokā cavatīti attho. Adhammikarājā hi appaṭilābhavasena devalokā cavati nāma, saggepi vā rajjaṃ kārento adhammikarājā tato cavatītipi attho. Nanu so tāvatā hatoti nanu so adhammiko rājā ettakena hato hoti. Atha [P 2.0125] vā ekaṃsavācī ettha nu-kāro, neso ekaṃsena ettāvatā [V 2.0103] hato, aṭṭhasu pana mahānirayesu soḷasasu ca ussadanirayesu dīgharattaṃ so haññissatīti ayamettha attho.

There, "at the wrong time" means rain falls at an improper time during the reign of an unrighteous king, such as when crops are ripe or at the time of reaping and threshing. "At the right time" means rain does not fall at the proper and suitable time, such as at the time of sowing, when crops are young, or when the grain is forming. "And he falls from his heavenly state" means he falls from the place called heaven, the celestial realm. For an unrighteous king is said to "fall from the celestial realm" by way of non-attainment of rebirth there; or it means even if an unrighteous king were ruling in heaven, he would fall from there—this is the meaning. "Is he not destroyed by that much?" means is that unrighteous king not ruined to this extent? Alternatively, the particle "nu" here expresses certainty, meaning he is not only destroyed to this extent, but for a long time he will be tormented in the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells—this is the meaning here.

Evaṃ [M 2.0114] sakko mahājanassa ovādaṃ datvā attano devaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Bodhisattopi dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā saggapuraṃ pūresi.

Having thus given advice to the people, Sakka went to his own divine abode. The Bodhisatta also ruled righteously and filled the city of heaven.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā adhammikarājā devadatto ahosi, sakko anuruddho, sujātā rāhulamātā, sakkadattiyarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the birth story: "At that time, the unrighteous king was Devadatta, Sakka was Anuruddha, Sujātā was Rāhula’s mother, but the king given by Sakka was indeed myself."

Maṇicorajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The commentary on the Maṇicora Jātaka, the fourth.

[195] 5. Pabbatūpattharajātakavaṇṇanā

[195] 5. The Commentary on the Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka

Pabbatūpatthare rammeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarājānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kosalarañño kira eko amacco antepure padussi. Rājāpi parivīmaṃsamāno taṃ tathato ñatvā “satthu ārocessāmī”ti jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā “bhante, amhākaṃ antepure eko amacco padussi, tassa kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pucchi. Atha naṃ satthā “upakārako te, mahārāja, so ca amacco sā ca itthī piyā”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante, ativiya upakārako sakalaṃ rājakulaṃ sandhāreti, sāpi me itthī piyā”ti vutte “mahārāja, ‘attano upakārakesu sevakesu piyāsu ca itthīsu dubbhituṃ na sakkā’ti pubbepi rājāno paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā majjhattāva ahesu”nti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"On a delightful mountain slope"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the King of Kosala. It is said that a certain minister of the King of Kosala misbehaved in the harem. The king, upon investigating and knowing the truth, thought, "I shall inform the Teacher," and went to Jetavana. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he asked, "Venerable Sir, a minister in our harem has misbehaved. What should be done about him?" Then the Teacher questioned him, "Great king, is that minister helpful to you, and is that woman dear?" When the king replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, he is extremely helpful, supporting the entire royal family, and that woman is dear to me," the Teacher said, "Great king, one cannot be treacherous toward one’s own helpful servants and beloved women. Even in the past, kings, hearing the words of the wise, remained impartial." Being thus entreated, he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto amaccakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako ahosi. Athassa rañño eko amacco antepure padussi. Rājā naṃ tathato ñatvā “amaccopi me bahūpakāro, ayaṃ itthīpi me piyā, dvepi ime nāsetuṃ na sakkā[P 2.0126], paṇḍitāmaccaṃ pañhaṃ pucchitvā sace sahitabbaṃ bhavissati, sahissāmi, no ce, na sahissāmī”ti bodhisattaṃ pakkosāpetvā āsanaṃ datvā “paṇḍita, pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti vatvā “pucchatha, mahārāja, vissajjessāmī”ti vutte pañhaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers. When he came of age, he became the king’s advisor in matters of welfare and Dhamma. Now, one of the king’s ministers misbehaved in the royal harem. The king, knowing this to be true, thought, "This minister has been of great service to me, and this woman is also dear to me. I cannot destroy them both. I will ask the wise minister a question, and if it is to be tolerated, I will tolerate it; if not, I will not." So he had the Bodhisatta summoned, offered him a seat, and said, "O wise one, I will ask you a question." When the Bodhisatta replied, "Ask, O great king, I will answer," the king, posing his question, spoke the first verse:

89.

89.

“Pabbatūpatthare [V 2.0104][M 2.0115] ramme, jātā pokkharaṇī sivā;

Taṃ siṅgālo apāpāyi, jānaṃ sīhena rakkhita”nti.

"On a delightful mountain slope, a lovely lotus pond arose; a jackal drank from it, knowing it was protected by a lion."

Tattha pabbatūpatthare rammeti himavantapabbatapāde pattharitvā ṭhite aṅgaṇaṭṭhāneti attho. Jātā pokkharaṇī sivāti sivā sītalā madhurodakā pokkharaṇī nibbattā, apica kho pokkharasañchannā nadīpi pokkharaṇīyeva. Apāpāyīti apa-iti upasaggo, apāyīti attho. Jānaṃ sīhena rakkhitanti sā pokkharaṇī sīhaparibhogā sīhena rakkhitā, sopi naṃ siṅgālo “sīhena rakkhitā aya”nti jānantova apāyi. Taṃ kiṃ maññati, bālo siṅgālo sīhassa abhāyitvā piveyya evarūpaṃ pokkharaṇinti ayametthādhippāyo.

There, "on a delightful mountain slope" means in a courtyard-like place spread out at the foot of the Himālaya mountains. "A lovely lotus pond arose" means a cool, sweet-watered lotus pond came into being; moreover, even a river covered with lotuses is called a lotus pond. "Drank" (apāpāyi): here "apa-" is a prefix; the meaning is "he drank". "Knowing it was protected by a lion" means that the pond was for the lion's use and was guarded by the lion, and that jackal drank from it even while knowing, "This is guarded by a lion." The implication here is: "What do you think? Would a foolish jackal drink from such a pond without fearing the lion?"

Bodhisatto “addhā etassa antepure eko amacco paduṭṭho bhavissatī”ti ñatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, realizing, "Surely, a minister in his harem must have misbehaved," spoke the second verse:

90.

90.

“Pivanti ce mahārāja, sāpadāni mahānadiṃ;

Na tena anadī hoti, khamassu yadi te piyā”ti.

"If, great king, wild animals drink from a great river, it does not thereby cease to be a river. Forgive, if she is dear to you."

Tattha sāpadānīti na kevalaṃ siṅgālova, avasesāni sunakhapasadabiḷāramigādīni sabbasāpadāni taṃ pokkharasañchannattā “pokkharaṇī”ti laddhanāmaṃ nadiṃ pivanti ce. Na tena anadī hotīti nadiyañhi dvipadacatuppadāpi ahimacchāpi sabbe pipāsitā pānīyaṃ pivanti, na sā tena kāraṇena anadī nāma hoti, nāpi ucchiṭṭhanadī. Kasmā? Sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇattā. Yathā nadī yena kenaci pītā na dussati, evaṃ itthīpi kilesavasena sāmikaṃ atikkamitvā aññena saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ gatā neva anitthī hoti. Kasmā? Sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvena. Nāpi ucchiṭṭhitthī. Kasmā? Odakantikatāya suddhabhāvena. Khamassu yadi te piyāti yadi pana te sā itthī piyā, so ca amacco bahūpakāro, tesaṃ ubhinnampi khamassu majjhattabhāvena tiṭṭhāhīti.

There, "wild animals" (sāpadāni) refers not only to the jackal, but to all other wild animals such as dogs, deer, cats, and so on—if they drink from the river which, being covered with lotuses, is called a "lotus pond." "It does not thereby cease to be a river" means that in a river, two-legged and four-legged creatures, as well as snakes and fish, all drink water when thirsty; for that reason, it does not become a non-river, nor is it called a defiled river. Why? Because it is common to all. Just as a river is not defiled by whoever drinks from it, so too a woman, even if she has transgressed against her husband due to defilements and cohabited with another, does not become a "non-woman." Why? Because of being common to all. Nor is she a "defiled woman." Why? Because of her pure nature, being like the water itself. "Forgive, if she is dear to you" means: if that woman is dear to you and that minister is of great service, then forgive both of them and remain impartial.

Evaṃ [P 2.0127] mahāsatto rañño ovādaṃ adāsi. Rājā tassa ovāde ṭhatvā “puna evarūpaṃ pāpakammaṃ mā karitthā”ti vatvā ubhinnampi khami. Tato paṭṭhāya [M 2.0116] te oramiṃsu. Rājāpi dānādīni puññāni katvā jīvitapariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūresi. Kosalarājāpi imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā tesaṃ ubhinnampi khamitvā majjhatto ahosi.

Thus the Great Being gave this counsel to the king. The king, abiding by his counsel, said, "Do not commit such an evil deed again," and forgave them both. From then on, they desisted. The king also performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and at the end of his life, he filled the city of heaven. The King of Kosala, too, having heard this Dhamma discourse, forgave them both and became equanimous.

Satthā [V 2.0105] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, but the wise minister was I myself."

Pabbatūpattharajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka, the fifth.

[196] 6. Valāhakassajātakavaṇṇanā

[196] 6. 6. Valāhaka Jātaka (The Commentary on the Valāhaka Jātaka)

Ye na kāhanti ovādanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi bhikkhu satthārā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti puṭṭho “sacca”nti vatvā “kiṃ kāraṇā”ti vutte “ekaṃ alaṅkataṃ mātugāmaṃ disvā kilesavasenā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “itthiyo nāmetā bhikkhu attano rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbehi ceva itthikuttavilāsehi ca purise palobhetvā attano vase katvā vasaṃ upagatabhāvaṃ ñatvā sīlavināsañceva dhanavināsañca pāpanaṭṭhena ‘yakkhiniyo’ti vuccanti. Pubbepi hi yakkhiniyo itthikuttena ekaṃ purisasatthaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vāṇije palobhetvā attano vase katvā puna aññe purise disvā te sabbepi jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā ubhohi hanukapassehi lohitena paggharantena mukhaṃ pūrāpetvā khādiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Those who will not do the bidding [follow the advice]..." This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who had become discontented. When that monk was asked by the Teacher, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?" he replied, "It is true, Bhante." When asked the reason, he said, "Bhante, having seen a beautifully adorned woman, I have become discontented through the power of defilement." Then the Teacher said to him, "Monk, these beings called women, by means of their own forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and touches, as well as by their feminine wiles, charms, and graces, entice men. Knowing that they have come under their control, they cause the destruction of both virtue and wealth; for this reason, they are called ‘yakkhinīs.’ For in the past, yakkhinīs, using feminine wiles, approached a caravan of men, enticed the merchants, brought them under their control, and then, seeing other men, they caused all the first group to reach the end of their lives, and filling their mouths with blood streaming from both sides of their jaws, they devoured them." Having said this, he related the story of the past.

Atīte tambapaṇṇidīpe sirīsavatthu nāma yakkhanagaraṃ ahosi, tattha yakkhiniyo vasiṃsu. Tā bhinnanāvānaṃ vāṇijānaṃ āgatakāle alaṅkatapaṭiyattā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ gāhāpetvā dāsigaṇaparivutā dārake aṅkenādāya vāṇije upasaṅkamanti. Tesaṃ [P 2.0128] “manussāvāsaṃ āgatamhā”ti sañjānanatthaṃ tattha tattha kasigorakkhādīni karonte manusse gogaṇe sunakheti evamādīni dassenti, vāṇijānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “imaṃ yāguṃ pivatha, bhattaṃ bhuñjatha, khādanīyaṃ khādathā”ti vadanti. Vāṇijā ajānantā tāhi dinnaṃ paribhuñjanti. Atha tesaṃ khāditvā bhuñjitvā pivitvā vissamitakāle [M 2.0117] paṭisanthāraṃ karonti, “tumhe kattha vāsikā, kuto āgatā, kahaṃ gacchissatha, kena kammena idhāgatatthā”ti pucchanti. “Bhinnanāvā hutvā idhāgatamhā”ti vutte “sādhu, ayyā, amhākampi sāmikānaṃ nāvaṃ abhiruhitvā gatānaṃ tīṇi saṃvaccharāni atikkantāni, te matā bhavissanti; tumhepi vāṇijāyeva, mayaṃ tumhākaṃ pādaparicārikā bhavissāmā”ti vatvā te vāṇije itthikuttahāvabhāvavilāsehi palobhetvā yakkhanagaraṃ netvā sace paṭhamagahitā manussā atthi, te devasaṅkhalikāya bandhitvā kāraṇaghare pakkhipanti[V 2.0106], attano vasanaṭṭhāne bhinnanāve manusse alabhantiyo pana parato kalyāṇiṃ orato nāgadīpanti evaṃ samuddatīraṃ anusañcaranti. Ayaṃ tāsaṃ dhammatā.

In the past, on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, there was a city of yakkhinīs named Sirīsavatthu; there the yakkhinīs lived. When merchants from shipwrecked vessels arrived, they would, adorned and prepared, have food and drink brought, and surrounded by a retinue of female servants and carrying children on their hips, they would approach the merchants. To make them think, "We have come to a human settlement," they would show them people in various places engaged in farming, cattle-herding, and so forth, along with herds of cattle, dogs, and such things. Approaching the merchants, they would say, "Drink this gruel, eat this rice, enjoy this food." The merchants, not knowing, would consume what was given by them. Then, when they had eaten, drunk, and rested, the yakkhinīs would make friendly conversation, asking, "Where do you live? Where have you come from? Where are you going? For what purpose have you come here?" When told, "We arrived here after our ship was wrecked," they would say, "Good, sirs. Three years have passed since our own husbands boarded a ship and departed; they must be dead. You too are merchants; we shall be your servants." Having said this, they would entice those merchants with feminine wiles, coquetry, and charms, and lead them to the city of the yakkhas. If there were any humans captured earlier, they would bind them with celestial chains and imprison them in a house of torture. If they did not find humans from a shipwreck in their own dwelling place, they would roam the seashore from Kalyāṇi on one side to Nāgadīpa on the other. This was their nature.

Athekadivasaṃ pañcasatā bhinnanāvā vāṇijā tāsaṃ nagarasamīpe uttariṃsu. Tā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā palobhetvā yakkhanagaraṃ netvā paṭhamaṃ gahite manusse devasaṅkhalikāya bandhitvā kāraṇaghare pakkhipitvā jeṭṭhayakkhinī jeṭṭhakavāṇijaṃ, sesā seseti tā pañcasatā yakkhiniyo te pañcasate vāṇije attano sāmike akaṃsu. Atha sā jeṭṭhayakkhinī rattibhāge vāṇije niddaṃ upagate uṭṭhāya gantvā kāraṇaghare manusse māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā āgacchati, sesāpi tatheva karonti. Jeṭṭhayakkhiniyā manussamaṃsaṃ khāditvā āgatakāle sarīraṃ sītalaṃ hoti. Jeṭṭhavāṇijo pariggaṇhanto tassā yakkhinibhāvaṃ ñatvā “imā pañcasatā yakkhiniyo [P 2.0129] bhavissanti, amhehi palāyituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti punadivase pātova mukhadhovanatthāya gantvā sesavāṇijānaṃ ārocesi – “imā yakkhiniyo, na manussitthiyo, aññesaṃ bhinnanāvānaṃ āgatakāle te sāmike katvā amhepi khādissanti, etha ito palāyissāmā”ti tesu pañcasatesu aḍḍhateyyasatā “na mayaṃ etā vijahituṃ sakkhissāma, tumhe gacchatha, mayaṃ na palāyissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Jeṭṭhavāṇijo attano vacanakāre aḍḍhateyyasate gahetvā tāsaṃ bhīto palāyi.

Then one day, five hundred shipwrecked merchants landed near their city. They went to those merchants, enticed them, and led them to the city of the yakkhas. Having bound the previously captured men with celestial chains and imprisoned them in the house of torture, the chief yakkhinī took the chief merchant, and the remaining yakkhinīs took the rest; thus those five hundred yakkhinīs made the five hundred merchants their husbands. Then, at nighttime, when the merchants had fallen asleep, the chief yakkhinī arose, went and killed the men in the house of torture, ate their flesh, and returned. The others did exactly the same. When the chief yakkhinī returned after eating human flesh, her body was cold. The chief merchant, upon investigating, realized her nature as a yakkhinī and thought, "These five hundred must be yakkhinīs. We ought to flee." The next day, early in the morning, he went as if to wash his face and informed the other merchants, "Friends, these are yakkhinīs, not human women. When other shipwrecked merchants arrive, they will make them their husbands and eat us too. Come, let us flee from here." Among those five hundred, two hundred and fifty said, "We cannot abandon these women. You go; we will not flee." The chief merchant, taking the two hundred and fifty who followed his word, fled in fear of those yakkhinīs.

Tasmiṃ pana kāle bodhisatto valāhakassayoniyaṃ nibbatti, sabbaseto kāḷasīso muñjakeso iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo ahosi. So [M 2.0118] himavantato ākāse uppatitvā tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ gantvā tattha tambapaṇṇisare pallale sayaṃjātasāliṃ khāditvā gacchati. Evaṃ gacchanto ca “janapadaṃ gantukāmā atthī”ti tikkhattuṃ karuṇāparibhāvitaṃ mānusiṃ vācaṃ bhāsati. Te bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā upasaṅkamitvā añjaliṃ paggayha “sāmi, mayaṃ janapadaṃ gamissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Tena hi mayhaṃ piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhathāti. Appekacce abhiruhiṃsu, tesu ekacce vāladhiṃ gaṇhiṃsu, ekacce añjaliṃ paggahetvā aṭṭhaṃsuyeva. Bodhisatto antamaso añjaliṃ paggahetvā ṭhite sabbepi te aḍḍhateyyasate vāṇije attano ānubhāvena janapadaṃ netvā sakasakaṭṭhānesu patiṭṭhapetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgamāsi. Tāpi kho yakkhiniyo aññesaṃ āgatakāle tattha ohīnake aḍḍhateyyasate manusse vadhitvā khādiṃsu.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was born in the breed of cloud horses; he was entirely white with a black head and hair like muñja grass, possessing psychic power and able to travel through the air. Rising into the sky from the Himalayas, he went to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, and after eating self-grown rice in the lakes and ponds of Tambapaṇṇi, he would depart. As he was traveling in this way, he spoke three times in a human voice, suffused with compassion: 'Is there anyone who wishes to go to the mainland?' Hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the merchants approached, and raising their joined palms, they said, 'Lord, we will go to the mainland.' 'Then climb upon my back,' he said. Some climbed on, some held onto his tail, and some stood merely with joined palms. The Bodhisatta, by his own power, took all those two hundred and fifty merchants—even those who stood merely with joined palms—to the mainland, established them in their respective places, and then returned to his own dwelling. As for those yakkhinīs, when other merchants arrived, they killed and devoured the two hundred and fifty men who had been left behind there.

Satthā bhikkhū āmantetvā “bhikkhave, yathā te yakkhinīnaṃ vasaṃ gatā vāṇijā jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā, valāhakassarājassa vacanakarā vāṇijā sakasakaṭṭhānesu patiṭṭhitā, evameva buddhānaṃ ovādaṃ akarontā bhikkhūpi bhikkhuniyopi upāsakāpi upāsikāyopi catūsu apāyesu [P 2.0130] pañcavidhabandhanakammakaraṇaṭṭhānādīsu [V 2.0107] mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇanti. Ovādakarā pana tisso kulasampattiyo ca cha kāmasagge vīsati brahmaloketi imāni ca ṭhānāni patvā amatamahānibbānaṃ sacchikatvā mahantaṃ sukhaṃ anubhavantī”ti vatvā abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

The Teacher addressed the monks: 'Monks, just as those merchants who fell under the power of the yakkhinīs met with the destruction of life, while the merchants who followed the word of the noble Valāhaka horse were established in their own places, even so, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who do not follow the advice of the Buddhas experience great suffering in the four woeful states, in places such as those where the fivefold bondage and punishment are carried out. But those who follow the advice reach these states—the three kinds of family prosperity, the six sensual heavens, and the twenty Brahma worlds—and having realized the deathless great Nibbāna, they experience supreme happiness.' Having become fully awakened, he spoke these verses:

91.

91.

“Ye na kāhanti ovādaṃ, narā buddhena desitaṃ;

Byasanaṃ te gamissanti, rakkhasīhiva vāṇijā.

“Those people who will not follow the advice taught by the Buddha will go to ruin, just like the merchants with the ogresses.”

92.

92.

“Ye ca kāhanti ovādaṃ, narā buddhena desitaṃ;

Sotthiṃ pāraṃ gamissanti, valāheneva vāṇijā”ti.

“And those people who will follow the advice taught by the Buddha will safely reach the far shore, just like the merchants with the cloud horse.”

Tattha ye na kāhantīti ye na karissanti. Byasanaṃ te gamissantīti te mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇissanti. Rakkhasīhiva vāṇijāti rakkhasīhi palobhitavāṇijā viya. Sotthiṃ pāraṃ gamissantīti anantarāyena nibbānaṃ pāpuṇissanti. Valāheneva vāṇijāti valāheneva “āgacchathā”ti [M 2.0119] vuttā tassa vacanakarā vāṇijā viya. Yathā hi te samuddapāraṃ gantvā sakasakaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu, evaṃ buddhānaṃ ovādakarā saṃsārapāraṃ nibbānaṃ gacchantīti amatamahānibbānena dhammadesanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhi.

In this context, 'those who will not follow' means those who will not act upon it. 'They will go to ruin' means they will meet with great destruction. 'Like the merchants with the ogresses' means like the merchants enticed by the ogresses. 'They will safely reach the far shore' means they will reach Nibbāna without obstacle. 'Like the merchants with the cloud horse' means like the merchants who followed the word of the cloud horse when he said, 'Come!' Just as those merchants, having reached the far shore of the ocean, went to their respective places, so those who follow the advice of the Buddhas go to Nibbāna, the far shore of saṃsāra. Thus, he reached the climax of the Dhamma teaching with the deathless great Nibbāna.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, aññepi bahū sotāpattiphalasakadāgāmiphalaanāgāmiphalaarahattaphalāni pāpuṇiṃsu. “Tadā valāhakassarājassa vacanakarā aḍḍhateyyasatā vāṇijā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, valāhakassarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the birth story: At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry; many other monks also reached the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship. 'At that time, the two hundred and fifty merchants who followed the word of the noble Valāhaka horse were the Buddha's assembly, and the noble Valāhaka horse was I myself.'

Valāhakassajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The explanation of the Valāhakassa Jātaka is the sixth.

[197] 7. Mittāmittajātakavaṇṇanā

[197] 7. Explanation of the Mittāmitta Jātaka

Na naṃ umhayate disvāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Aññataro bhikkhu “mayā gahite mayhaṃ upajjhāyo na kujjhissatī”ti upajjhāyena ṭhapitaṃ vissāsena ekaṃ vatthakhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā upāhanatthavikaṃ katvā pacchā upajjhāyaṃ āpucchi. Atha taṃ upajjhāyo [V 2.0108] “kiṃkāraṇā gaṇhī”ti [P 2.0131] vatvā “mayā gahite na kujjhissatīti tumhākaṃ vissāsenā”ti vutte “ko mayā saddhiṃ tuyhaṃ vissāso nāmā”ti vatvā kuddho uṭṭhahitvā pahari. Tassa sā kiriyā bhikkhūsu pākaṭā jātā. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko kira daharo upajjhāyassa vissāsena vatthakhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā upāhanatthavikaṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ upajjhāyo ‘ko mayā saddhiṃ tuyhaṃ vissāso nāmā’ti vatvā kuddho uṭṭhahitvā paharī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa bhikkhu attano saddhivihārikena saddhiṃ avissāsiko, pubbepi avissāsikoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Seeing him does not bring joy'—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk. A certain monk, thinking, 'My preceptor will not be angry if I take it,' took a piece of cloth left by his preceptor out of intimacy, made it into a bag for his sandals, and later asked his preceptor for permission. Then the preceptor said, 'Why did you take it?' When the monk replied, 'I took it out of intimacy with you, thinking you would not be angry,' the preceptor said, 'What is this thing called intimacy between you and me?' and becoming angry, he stood up and struck him. This behavior of his became known among the monks. Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, a certain young monk took a piece of cloth out of intimacy with his preceptor and made a bag for his sandals. Then the preceptor said, “What is this thing called intimacy between you and me?” and becoming angry, he stood up and struck him.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you sitting here now?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that this monk is untrusting toward his co-resident; he was untrusting in the past as well,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā [M 2.0120] ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā gaṇasatthā hutvā himavantapadese vāsaṃ kappesi. Tasmiṃ isigaṇe eko tāpaso bodhisattassa vacanaṃ akatvā ekaṃ matamātikaṃ hatthipotakaṃ paṭijaggi. Atha naṃ so vuddhippatto māretvā araññaṃ pāvisi. Tassa sarīrakiccaṃ katvā isigaṇo bodhisattaṃ parivāretvā – “bhante, kena nu ko kāraṇena mittabhāvo vā amittabhāvo vā sakkā jānitu”nti pucchi. Bodhisatto “iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenā”ti ācikkhanto imā gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kāsi country. Having come of age, he went forth as an ascetic, developed the supernormal knowledges and attainments, and becoming the leader of a group of ascetics, he lived in the Himālaya region. In that group of ascetics, one ascetic, not following the Bodhisatta's words, raised a young elephant whose mother had died. Then, when it reached maturity, it killed him and entered the forest. After performing the funeral rites for his body, the group of ascetics surrounded the Bodhisatta and asked, 'Venerable sir, by what means or cause can friendship or enmity be known?' Explaining to them, 'By this and that cause,' the Bodhisatta spoke these verses:

93.

93.

“Na naṃ umhayate disvā, na ca naṃ paṭinandati;

Cakkhūni cassa na dadāti, paṭilomañca vattati.

“He does not smile upon seeing him, nor does he welcome him; he does not look him in the eye, and he acts in opposition.”

94.

94.

“Ete bhavanti ākārā, amittasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā;

Yehi amittaṃ jāneyya, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito”ti.

“These are the signs found in an enemy; by these, seeing and hearing them, a wise person would recognize an enemy.”

Tattha na naṃ umhayate disvāti yo hi yassa amitto hoti, so taṃ puggalaṃ disvā na umhayate, hasitaṃ na karoti, pahaṭṭhākāraṃ na dasseti. Na [P 2.0132] ca naṃ paṭinandatīti tassa vacanaṃ sutvāpi taṃ puggalaṃ na paṭinandati, sādhu subhāsitanti na cānumodati. Cakkhūni cassa na dadātīti cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca paṭimukho hutvā na oloketi, aññato cakkhūni harati. Paṭilomañca vattatīti tassa kāyakammampi vacīkammampi na roceti, paṭilomagāhaṃ gaṇhāti paccanīkagāhaṃ. Ākārāti kāraṇāni. Yehi amittanti yehi kāraṇehi [V 2.0109] tāni kāraṇāni disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito puggalo “ayaṃ me amitto”ti jāneyya, tato viparītehi pana mittabhāvo jānitabboti.

Therein, “He does not smile upon seeing him” means that whoever is an enemy to another, upon seeing that person, he does not smile, he does not laugh, nor does he show a delighted expression. “Nor does he welcome him” means even upon hearing his words, he does not welcome that person, nor does he approve, saying, “Well spoken.” “He does not look him in the eye” means he does not look directly at him face-to-face, making eye contact, but turns his gaze elsewhere. “And he acts in opposition” means he does not approve of his bodily or verbal actions but takes a contrary and opposing stance. “Signs” means reasons. “By which an enemy” means that by seeing and hearing these reasons, a wise person would recognize, “This is my enemy.” Conversely, by the opposite signs, friendship should be known.

Evaṃ bodhisatto mittāmittabhāvakāraṇāni ācikkhitvā brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus, having explained the reasons for friendship and enmity, the Bodhisatta cultivated the divine abidings and was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā hatthiposakatāpaso saddhivihāriko ahosi, hatthī upajjhāyo, isigaṇo buddhaparisā, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the ascetic who cared for the elephant was the co-resident, the elephant was the preceptor, the group of ascetics was the Buddha’s assembly, and the teacher of the group was none other than myself.”

Mittāmittajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The seventh, the Commentarial Explanation of the Mittāmitta Jātaka.

[198] 8. Rādhajātakavaṇṇanā

[198] 8. The Commentarial Explanation of the Rādhā Jātaka

Pavāsā [M 2.0121] āgato tātāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira satthārā “saccaṃ kira, tvaṃ bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhito”ti puṭṭho “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vatvā “kiṃkāraṇā”ti vutte “ekaṃ alaṅkataitthiṃ disvā kilesavasenā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “mātugāmo nāma bhikkhu na sakkā rakkhituṃ, pubbepi dovārike ṭhapetvā rakkhantāpi rakkhituṃ na sakkhiṃsu, kiṃ te itthiyā, laddhāpi sā rakkhituṃ na sakkā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Father, returned from abroad”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain discontented monk. It is said that when the Teacher asked him, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” he replied, “It is true, Bhante.” When asked why, he said, “From seeing a beautifully adorned woman, by the power of defilements.” Then the Teacher told him, “Monk, a woman cannot be guarded. Even in the past, though they placed doorkeepers to guard them, they were unable to do so. What is that woman to you? Even if obtained, she cannot be guarded.” Having said this, he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto suvayoniyaṃ nibbatti, “rādho”tissa nāmaṃ, kaniṭṭhabhātā panassa poṭṭhapādo nāma. Te ubhopi taruṇakāleyeva eko luddako gahetvā bārāṇasiyaṃ aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa adāsi, brāhmaṇo te puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā paṭijaggi. Brāhmaṇassa [P 2.0133] pana brāhmaṇī arakkhitā dussīlā. So vohārakaraṇatthāya gacchanto te suvapotake āmantetvā “tātā, ahaṃ vohārakaraṇatthāya gacchāmi, kāle vā vikāle vā tumhākaṃ mātu karaṇakammaṃ olokeyyātha, aññassa purisassa gamanabhāvaṃ vā agamanabhāvaṃ vā jāneyyāthā”ti brāhmaṇiṃ suvapotakānaṃ paṭicchāpetvā agamāsi. Sā tassa nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya anācāraṃ cari, rattimpi divāpi āgacchantānañca gacchantānañca pamāṇaṃ natthi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a parrot, and his name was Rādhā. His younger brother was named Poṭṭhapāda. While they were still young, a hunter captured them both and gave them to a certain brahmin in Bārāṇasī. The brahmin placed them in the position of sons and cared for them. However, the brahmin’s wife was unguarded and unvirtuous. When he was leaving to conduct trade, he called the young parrots and said, “My dears, I am going away on business. At all times, observe your mother’s conduct. Find out whether any other man comes or does not come.” Having entrusted the brahmin woman to the young parrots, he departed. From the moment he left, she behaved improperly. There was no limit to the men coming and going, day and night.

Taṃ disvā poṭṭhapādo rādhaṃ pucchi – “brāhmaṇo imaṃ brāhmaṇiṃ amhākaṃ niyyādetvā gato, ayañca [V 2.0110] pāpakammaṃ karoti, vadāmi na”nti. Rādho “mā vadāhī”ti āha. So tassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā “amma, kiṃkāraṇā pāpakammaṃ karosī”ti āha.
