Sā taṃ māretukāmā hutvā “tāta, tvaṃ nāma mayhaṃ putto, ito paṭṭhāya na karissāmi, ehi, tāta, tāvā”ti piyāyamānā viya pakkositvā āgataṃ gahetvā “tvaṃ maṃ ovadasi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī”ti gīvaṃ parivattetvā māretvā uddhanantaresu pakkhipi. Brāhmaṇo āgantvā vissamitvā bodhisattaṃ “kiṃ, tāta rādha, mātā te anācāraṃ karoti, na karotī”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing this, Poṭṭhapāda asked Rādhā: “The brahmin entrusted this brahmin woman to us and left, and now she is doing evil. Shall I speak or not?” Rādhā replied, “Do not speak.” Not heeding his words, Poṭṭhapāda said, “Mother, why are you doing this evil deed?” Desiring to kill him, she called him as if with affection: “Dear child, you are my son. From now on, I will not do this. Come here, dear.” When he approached, she seized him and said, “You admonish me, yet you do not know your own measure!” Then she twisted his neck, killed him, and threw him between the stove-stones. When the brahmin returned and had rested, he asked the Bodhisatta, “Dear Rādhā, does your mother behave improperly or not?” and then spoke the first verse:

95.

95.

“Pavāsā [M 2.0122] āgato tāta, idāni nacirāgato;

Kaccinnu tāta te mātā, na aññamupasevatī”ti.

“Dear child, I have returned from abroad, just now arrived not long ago; I hope, dear child, your mother does not consort with another man?”

Tassattho – ahaṃ, tāta rādha, pavāsā āgato, so camhi idāneva āgato nacirāgato, tena pavattiṃ ajānanto taṃ pucchāmi – “kacci nu te, tāta, mātā aññaṃ purisaṃ na upasevatī”ti.

The meaning is: I, dear Rādhā, have come from abroad, and I have just now arrived, not long ago. Therefore, not knowing what has happened, I ask you: “I hope, dear child, your mother does not consort with another man?”

Rādho “tāta, paṇḍitā nāma bhūtaṃ vā abhūtaṃ vā aniyyānikaṃ nāma na kathesu”nti ñāpento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Rādhā, making it known that, “Father, the wise do not speak what is unbeneficial, whether it be true or untrue,” spoke the second verse:

96.

96.

“Na [P 2.0134] kho panetaṃ subhaṇaṃ, giraṃ saccupasaṃhitaṃ;

Sayetha poṭṭhapādova, mummure upakūthito”ti.

“Indeed, this is not a good thing to say, though it be a speech connected with truth; one might lie down like Poṭṭhapāda, scorched in the hot embers.”

Tattha giranti vacanaṃ. Tañhi yathā idāni girā, evaṃ tadā “gira”nti vuccati, so suvapotako liṅgaṃ anādiyitvā evamāha. Ayaṃ panettha attho – tāta, paṇḍitena nāma saccupasaṃhitaṃ yathābhūtaṃ atthayuttaṃ sabhāvavacanampi aniyyānikaṃ na subhaṇaṃ. Aniyyānikañca saccaṃ bhaṇanto sayetha poṭṭhapādova, mummure upakūthito, yathā poṭṭhapādo kukkuḷe jhāmo sayati, evaṃ sayeyyāti. “Upakūdhito”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho.

There, ‘gira’ means speech. For just as now the word is ‘girā,’ so then it was called ‘gira.’ That young parrot, disregarding the grammatical gender, spoke thus. The meaning here is: Father, by a wise person, even a factual, meaningful, and natural statement connected with truth should not be spoken if it is unbeneficial. For in speaking an unbeneficial truth, one might lie down like Poṭṭhapāda, scorched in the hot embers, just as Poṭṭhapāda lies scorched in the hot ashes. There is also a reading ‘upakūdhito,’ with the same meaning.

Evaṃ bodhisatto brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desetvā “mayāpi imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasituṃ na sakkā”ti brāhmaṇaṃ āpucchitvā araññameva pāvisi.

Thus, having taught the Dhamma to the brahmin, the Bodhisatta thought, “I too cannot stay in this place.” Taking leave of the brahmin, he entered the forest.

Satthā [V 2.0111] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā poṭṭhapādo ānando ahosi, rādho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and expounded the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, Poṭṭhapāda was Ānanda, but Rādhā was I myself.”

Rādhajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Explanation of the Rādhā Jātaka is the eighth.

[199] 9. Gahapatijātakavaṇṇanā

[199] 9. The Explanation of the Gahapati Jātaka

Ubhayaṃ [M 2.0123] me na khamatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitameva bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kathento ca “mātugāmo nāma arakkhito, pāpakammaṃ katvā yena kenaci upāyena sāmikaṃ vañcetiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Both are not agreeable to me”—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the same discontented bhikkhu. While speaking, he said, “Women indeed cannot be guarded; having done evil, they will certainly deceive their husbands by any means whatsoever,” and then he related the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe gahapatikule nibbattitvā vayappatto gharāvāsaṃ gaṇhi. Tassa bhariyā dussīlā gāmabhojakena saddhiṃ anācāraṃ carati. Bodhisatto taṃ ñatvā pariggaṇhanto carati[P 2.0135]. Tadā pana antovasse bījesu nīhaṭesu chātakaṃ ahosi, sassānaṃ gabbhagahaṇakālo jāto. Sakalagāmavāsino “ito māsadvayena sassāni uddharitvā vīhiṃ dassāmā”ti ekato hutvā gāmabhojakassa hatthato ekaṃ jaragoṇaṃ gahetvā maṃsaṃ khādiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a householder family in the Kāsi country. When he came of age, he took up the household life. His wife was immoral and engaged in misconduct with the village headman. The Bodhisatta, knowing this, kept watch. At that time, during the rainy season when the seeds had been sown, a famine occurred at the time when the crops were beginning to form grain. All the villagers, having come together and saying, “In two months from now, after harvesting the crops, we will give the paddy,” took an old ox from the village headman and ate its meat.

Athekadivasaṃ gāmabhājako khaṇaṃ oloketvā bodhisattassa bahigatavelāyaṃ gehaṃ pāvisi. Tesaṃ sukhanipannakkhaṇeyeva bodhisatto gāmadvārena pavisitvā gehābhimukho pāyāsi. Sā itthī gāmadvārābhimukhī taṃ disvā “ko nu kho eso”ti ummāre ṭhatvā olokentī “soyevā”ti ñatvā gāmabhojakassa ācikkhi, gāmabhojako bhīto pakampi. Atha naṃ sā “mā bhāyi, attheko upāyo, amhehi tava hatthato goṇamaṃsaṃ khāditaṃ, tvaṃ maṃsamūlaṃ sodhento viya hohi, ahaṃ koṭṭhaṃ āruyha koṭṭhadvāre ṭhatvā ‘vīhi natthī’ti vakkhāmi. Tvaṃ gehamajjhe ṭhatvā ‘amhākaṃ ghare dārakā chātā, maṃsamūlaṃ me dehī’ti punappunaṃ codeyyāsī”ti vatvā koṭṭhaṃ āruyha koṭṭhadvāre nisīdi. Itaro gehamajjhe ṭhatvā “maṃsamūlaṃ dehī”ti vadati. Sā koṭṭhadvāre nisinnā “koṭṭhe vīhi natthi, sasse uddharante dassāmi gacchāhī”ti āha.

One day, the village headman, watching for an opportunity, entered the house when the Bodhisatta had gone out. At the very moment they were enjoying themselves, the Bodhisatta entered through the village gate and headed towards the house. That woman, facing the village gate, saw him and, standing at the threshold, wondered, “Who could this be?” Recognizing him, she said, “It is he,” and informed the village headman. The village headman trembled in fear. Then she told him, “Do not be afraid, there is a way. We have eaten ox meat from you. You act as if you are collecting the price for the meat, while I will climb up to the granary and, standing at the granary door, say, ‘There is no paddy.’ You stand in the middle of the house and repeatedly demand, ‘Children in our house are hungry, give me the price for the meat!’” Having said this, she climbed up to the granary and sat at its door. The other man stood in the middle of the house, saying, “Give me the price for the meat!” Seated at the granary door, she said, “There is no paddy in the granary. I will give it when the crops are harvested. Go away!”

Bodhisatto gehaṃ pavisitvā tesaṃ kiriyaṃ disvā “imāya pāpāya kataupāyo esa bhavissatī”ti [V 2.0112] ñatvā gāmabhojakaṃ āmantetvā “so gāmabhojaka amhe tava jaragoṇassa maṃsaṃ khādantā ‘ito māsadvayena vīhiṃ dassāmā’ti khādimha, tvaṃ aḍḍhamāsampi anatikkamitvā idāneva [M 2.0124] kasmā āharāpesi, na tvaṃ iminā kāraṇena āgato, aññena kāraṇena āgato bhavissasi, mayhaṃ tava kiriyā na ruccati, ayampi anācārā pāpadhammā koṭṭhe vīhīnaṃ abhāvaṃ jānāti, sā dāni koṭṭhaṃ āruyha ‘vīhi natthī’ti [P 2.0136] vadati, tvampi ‘dehī’ti vadati, ubhinnampi vo karaṇaṃ mayhaṃ na ruccatī”ti etamatthaṃ pakāsento imā gāthā avoca –

The Bodhisatta entered the house and, seeing their behavior, knew, “This must be a scheme devised by this wicked woman.” Then, addressing the village headman, he said, “O village headman, when we ate the meat of your old ox, we ate it promising to give the paddy in two months. Why do you have it demanded now, when not even half a month has passed? You have not come for this reason; you must have come for another reason. I do not like your conduct. This woman, too, being immoral and wicked, knows of the lack of paddy in the granary. Now she climbs up to the granary and says, ‘There is no paddy,’ while you say, ‘Give it.’ I do not like the actions of both of you.” Explaining this matter, he spoke these verses:

97.

97.

“Ubhayaṃ me na khamati, ubhayaṃ me na ruccati;

Yācāyaṃ koṭṭhamotiṇṇā, nadassaṃ iti bhāsati.

“Both are not pleasing to me, both are not liked by me: this woman who has gone up to the granary and says, ‘I will not give.’”

98.

98.

“Taṃ taṃ gāmapati brūmi, kadare appasmi jīvite;

Dve māse saṅgaraṃ katvā, maṃsaṃ jaraggavaṃ kisaṃ;

Appattakāle codesi, tampi mayhaṃ na ruccatī”ti.

“O village headman, I say this to you: in this wretched and short life, having made an agreement for two months for the meat of a lean old ox, you demand it before the time has arrived. That, too, is not liked by me.”

Tattha taṃ taṃ gāmapati brūmīti, ambho gāmajeṭṭhaka, tena kāraṇena taṃ vadāmi. Kadare appasmi jīviteti amhākaṃ jīvitaṃ nāma kadarañceva thaddhaṃ lūkhaṃ kasiraṃ appañca mandaṃ parittaṃ, tasmiṃ no evarūpe jīvite vattamāne. Dve māse saṅgaraṃ katvā, maṃsaṃ jaraggavaṃ kisanti amhākaṃ maṃsaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ jaraggavaṃ kisaṃ dubbalaṃ jaragoṇaṃ dadamāno tvaṃ “dvīhi māsehi mūlaṃ dātabba”nti evaṃ dve māse saṅgaraṃ paricchedaṃ katvā. Appattakāle codesīti tasmiṃ kāle asampatte antarāva codesi. Tampi mayhaṃ na ruccatīti yā cāyaṃ pāpadhammā dussīlā antokoṭṭhe vīhīnaṃ natthibhāvaṃ jānamānāva ajānantī viya hutvā koṭṭhamotiṇṇā koṭṭhadvāre ṭhatvā na dassaṃ iti bhāsati, yañca tvaṃ akāle codesi, tampīti idaṃ ubhayampi mama neva khamati na ruccatīti.

Therein, ‘O village headman, I say this to you’ means: ‘O village chief, for that reason I speak to you.’ ‘In this wretched and short life’ means: our life is indeed miserable, hard, rough, difficult, short, feeble, and insignificant; such is the life we are living. ‘Having made an agreement for two months for the meat of a lean old ox’ means: to us who were taking the meat, you gave a lean, weak, old ox, saying, “The price must be paid in two months,” thus setting a two-month agreement as the limit. ‘You demand it before the time has arrived’ means: before that time had arrived, you demanded it in the meantime. ‘That, too, is not liked by me’ means: both this—that this wicked and immoral woman, knowing well the absence of paddy in the inner granary, pretending not to know, having gone up to the granary and standing at its door, says, “I will not give”; and that you demand at the wrong time—both of these are neither pleasing to me nor liked by me.

Evaṃ so kathentova gāmabhojakaṃ cūḷāya gahetvā kaḍḍhitvā gehamajjhe pātetvā “gāmabhojakomhīti parassa rakkhitagopitabhaṇḍe aparajjhasī”tiādīhi paribhāsitvā pothetvā dubbalaṃ katvā gīvāya gahetvā gehā nikkaḍḍhitvā tampi duṭṭhaitthiṃ kesesu gahetvā koṭṭhā otāretvā nippothetvā “sace puna evarūpaṃ karosi, jānissasī”ti santajjesi. Tato paṭṭhāya gāmabhojako taṃ gehaṃ oloketumpi na visahi, sāpi pāpā puna manasāpi aticarituṃ nāsakkhi.

Even as he was speaking, he grabbed the village headman by the hair, dragged him, threw him down in the middle of the house, and scolded him with words like, “While being a village headman, do you offend against the property guarded and protected by another?” He beat him until he was weak, then grabbed him by the neck and threw him out of the house. He also seized that wicked woman by the hair, brought her down from the granary, beat her, and threatened her, saying, “If you ever do such a thing again, you will find out!” From then on, the village headman did not even dare to look at that house, and that wicked woman was not able to transgress again, even in thought.

Satthā [P 2.0137][M 2.0125] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne [V 2.0113] ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā gāmabhojako devadatto, niggahakārako gahapati pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and expounded the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the village headman was Devadatta, but the householder who administered the punishment was I myself.”

Gahapatijātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Explanation of the Gahapati Jātaka is the ninth.

[200] 10. Sādhusīlajātakavaṇṇanā

[200] 10. The Explanation of the Sādhusīla Jātaka

Sarīradabyanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa kira catasso dhītaro ahesuṃ. Tā cattāro janā patthenti, tesu eko abhirūpo sarīrasampanno, eko vayappatto mahallako, eko jātisampanno, eko sīlavā. Brāhmaṇo cintesi – “dhītaro nivesentena patiṭṭhāpentena kassa nu kho dātabbā, kiṃ rūpasampannassa, udāhu vayappattassa, jātisampannasīlavantānaṃ aññatarassā”ti. So cintentopi ajānitvā “imaṃ kāraṇaṃ sammāsambuddho jānissati, taṃ pucchitvā etesaṃ antare anucchavikassa dassāmī”ti gandhamālādīni gāhāpetvā vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno ādito paṭṭhāya tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “bhante, imesu catūsu janesu kassa dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pucchi. Satthā “pubbepi paṇḍitā etaṃ pañhaṃ kathayiṃsu, bhavasaṅkhepagatattā pana sallakkhetuṃ na sakkosī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this teaching, which begins, “Sarīradabyaṃ,” concerning a certain brahmin. It is said that he had four daughters. Four men desired them: one was handsome and possessed of a fine physique, one was advanced in years and elderly, one was of noble birth, and one was virtuous. The brahmin thought: “When settling my daughters in marriage, to whom should they be given? Should it be to the one possessed of beauty, or to the one advanced in years, or to the one of noble birth, or to the virtuous one?” Even while thinking, he did not know, so he thought: “The Perfectly Enlightened One will know this matter. After asking him, I will give them to the one who is most suitable among these.” Having taken perfumes, garlands, and the like, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, sat down to one side, and from the beginning explained the matter, asking, “Venerable Sir, to which of these four men is it proper to give them?” The Teacher said: “In the past, wise men also discussed this question. But because you are caught in the round of existence, you are not able to discern it.” Then, being requested by him, he told a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā āgantvā bārāṇasiyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo ahosi. Athekassa brāhmaṇassa catasso dhītaro ahesuṃ, tā evameva cattāro janā patthayiṃsu. Brāhmaṇo “kassa nu kho dātabbā”ti ajānanto “ācariyaṃ pucchitvā dātabbayuttakassa dassāmī”ti tassa santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. Having come of age, he mastered the arts at Takkasilā, returned to Bārāṇasī, and became a world-renowned teacher. At that time, a certain brahmin had four daughters, and four men desired them in just this way. The brahmin, not knowing to whom he should give them, thought, “I shall ask the teacher and then give them to the one to whom it is appropriate to give.” Approaching him, he asked about this matter, first reciting this verse:

99.

99.

“Sarīradabyaṃ [M 2.0126] vuḍḍhabyaṃ, sojaccaṃ sādhusīliyaṃ;

Brāhmaṇaṃ teva pucchāma, kannu tesaṃ vanimhase”ti.

“Bodily excellence, age, noble birth, and virtuous conduct; O Brahmin, we ask you: among them, whom should we choose?”

Tattha [P 2.0138] “sarīradabya”ntiādīhi tesaṃ catunnaṃ vijjamāne guṇe pakāseti. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – dhītaro me cattāro janā patthenti, tesu ekassa sarīradabyamatthi, sarīrasampadā abhirūpabhāvo saṃvijjati. Ekassa vuḍḍhabyaṃ vuḍḍhibhāvo mahallakatā atthi. Ekassa sojaccaṃ sujātitā jātisampadā atthi. “Sujacca”ntipi pāṭho. Ekassa sādhusīliyaṃ sundarasīlabhāvo [V 2.0114] sīlasampadā atthi. Brāhmaṇaṃ teva pucchāmāti tesu asukassa nāmetā dātabbāti ajānantā mayaṃ bhavantaṃ brāhmaṇaññeva pucchāma. Kannu tesaṃ vanimhaseti tesaṃ catunnaṃ janānaṃ kaṃ vanimhase, kaṃ icchāma, kassa tā kumārikā dadāmāti pucchati.

Therein, by the words beginning with ‘bodily excellence,’ he indicates the qualities present in those four men. This is the meaning: “Four men desire my daughters. Among them, one has bodily excellence, that is, physical perfection and handsomeness. One has age, that is, the state of being advanced in years, of being elderly. One has noble birth, that is, good lineage, excellence of birth. (‘Sujacca’ is also a reading.) One has virtuous conduct, that is, the state of having fine character, excellence of morality. ‘O brahmin, we ask you’ means: not knowing to which one among them they should be given, we ask you, the brahmin. ‘Whom should we choose among them?’ means: ‘Among these four men, whom should we choose, whom do we desire, to whom should we give these maidens?’ he asks.

Taṃ sutvā ācariyo “rūpasampadādīsu vijjamānāsupi vipannasīlo gārayho, tasmā taṃ nappamāṇaṃ, amhākaṃ sīlavantabhāvo ruccatī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the teacher said, “Even if qualities such as beauty are present, one of ruined virtue is reprehensible; therefore, that is not the criterion. We prefer virtuous conduct.” To clarify this meaning, he spoke the second verse:

100.

100.

“Attho atthi sarīrasmiṃ, vuḍḍhabyassa namo kare;

Attho atthi sujātasmiṃ, sīlaṃ asmāka ruccatī”ti.

“There is purpose in the body; one should pay homage to old age! There is purpose in noble birth; virtue pleases us.”

Tattha attho atthi sarīrasminti rūpasampanne sarīrepi attho viseso vuddhi atthiyeva, “natthī”ti na vadāmi. Vuḍḍhabyassa namo kareti vuḍḍhabhāvassa pana namakkārameva karomi. Vuḍḍhabhāvo hi vandanamānanaṃ labhati. Attho atthi sujātasminti sujātepi purise vuḍḍhi atthi, jātisampattipi icchitabbāyeva. Sīlaṃ asmāka ruccatīti amhākaṃ pana sīlameva ruccati. Sīlavā hi ācārasampanno sarīradabyavirahitopi pujjo pāsaṃsoti. Brāhmaṇo tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sīlavantasseva dhītaro adāsi.

Here, “there is purpose in the body” means that even in a body endowed with beauty, there is indeed a special purpose, a growth; I do not say, “There is none.” “One should pay homage to old age” means I only offer reverence to old age. For old age receives honor and respect. “There is purpose in noble birth” means that even in a person of noble birth, there is growth, and noble birth is indeed desirable. “Virtue is what pleases us” means that for us, however, virtue alone is pleasing. For a virtuous person endowed with good conduct, though lacking physical beauty, is worthy of reverence and praise. Hearing his words, the brahmin gave his daughters to the virtuous one.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – saccapariyosāne brāhmaṇo sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā brāhmaṇo ayameva brāhmaṇo ahosi, disāpāmokkho ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, this very brahmin was the brahmin, but I myself was the world-renowned teacher.”

Sādhusīlajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Sādhusīla Jātaka: The Tenth.

Ruhakavaggo pañcamo.

The Ruhaka Chapter: The Fifth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its Summary:

Ruhakaṃ [M 2.0127] sirikāḷakaṃ, padumaṃ maṇicorakaṃ;

Pabbatūpattharavalāhaṃ, mittāmittañca rādhañca;

Gahapati sādhusīlaṃ.

Ruhaka, Sirikāḷaka, Paduma, Maṇicoraka, Pabbatūpatthara, Valāha, Mittāmitta, Rādha, Gahapati, Sādhusīla.

6. Nataṃdaḷhavaggo

6. The Na Taṃ Daḷha Chapter.

[201] 1. Bandhanāgārajātakavaṇṇanā

[201] 1. The Commentary on the Bandhanāgāra Jātaka.

Na [V 2.0115][P 2.0139] taṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto bandhanāgāraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiṃ kira kāle bahū sandhicchedakapanthaghātakacore ānetvā kosalarañño dassesuṃ. Te rājā addubandhanarajjubandhanasaṅkhalikabandhanehi bandhāpesi. Tiṃsamattā jānapadā bhikkhū satthāraṃ daṭṭhukāmā āgantvā disvā vanditvā punadivase piṇḍāya carantā bandhanāgāraṃ gantvā te core disvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā sāyanhasamaye tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, ajja amhehi piṇḍāya carantehi bandhanāgāre bahū corā addubandhanādīhi baddhā mahādukkhaṃ anubhavantā diṭṭhā, te tāni bandhanāni chinditvā palāyituṃ na sakkonti, atthi nu kho tehi bandhanehi thirataraṃ nāma aññaṃ bandhana”nti pucchiṃsu. Satthā “bhikkhave, kiṃ bandhanāni nāmetāni, yaṃ panetaṃ dhanadhaññaputtadārādīsu taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ kilesabandhanaṃ, etaṃ etehi bandhanehi sataguṇena sahassaguṇena thirataraṃ, evaṃ mahantampi panetaṃ ducchindaniyaṃ bandhanaṃ porāṇakapaṇḍitā chinditvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The wise do not call that a strong bond”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a prison. At that time, it seems, many burglars, highwaymen, and thieves were brought before the king of Kosala. The king had them bound with wooden fetters, rope bonds, and chain bonds. About thirty country monks, wishing to see the Teacher, came and, having seen him, paid homage. The next day, while wandering for alms, they went to the prison and saw those thieves. Returning from their alms round, they approached the Tathāgata in the evening and asked, “Venerable sir, today while we were wandering for alms, we saw many thieves in the prison, bound with wooden fetters and the like, experiencing great misery. They cannot cut those bonds and escape. Is there any other bond stronger than these?” The Teacher replied, “Monks, what are these things called bonds? That bond of defilements, which is the craving for wealth, grain, sons, wives, and so on—that is a hundredfold, a thousandfold stronger than these. Yet even this great bond, so difficult to break, was severed by the wise of old, who entered the Himalayas and went forth.” Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ duggatagahapatikule nibbatti, tassa vayappattassa pitā kālamakāsi. So bhatiṃ katvā mātaraṃ posesi, athassa mātā anicchamānasseva ekaṃ kuladhītaraṃ gehe katvā aparabhāge kālamakāsi. Bhariyāyapissa kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. So gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ajānanto “bhadde, tvaṃ bhatiṃ katvā jīvāhi, ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti āha[M 2.0128]. Sāpi “gabbho me patiṭṭhito, mayi [P 2.0140] vijātāya dārakaṃ disvā pabbajissasī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tassā vijātakāle “bhadde, tvaṃ sotthinā vijātā, idānāhaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti āpucchi. Atha naṃ sā “puttakassa tāva thanapānato apagamanakālaṃ āgamehī”ti vatvā puna gabbhaṃ gaṇhi.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor householder's family. When he came of age, his father died. He worked for wages and supported his mother. Then, even though he did not want it, his mother brought a girl from a good family into the house, and later her mother died. His wife became pregnant. Not knowing that she was pregnant, he said, “Dear, you can live by working for wages. I will go forth.” She replied, “I am pregnant. After I give birth and you see the child, then you may go forth.” He agreed. When she gave birth, he asked for her leave, saying, “Dear, you have given birth safely. Now I will go forth.” But she said, “Wait until the child is weaned from the breast,” and became pregnant again.

So cintesi – “imaṃ sampaṭicchāpetvā gantuṃ na sakkā, imissā anācikkhitvāva palāyitvā pabbajissāmī”ti. So tassā anācikkhitvā ratthibhāge uṭṭhāya palāyi. Atha naṃ [V 2.0116] nagaraguttikā aggahesuṃ. So “ahaṃ, sāmi, mātuposako nāma, vissajjetha ma”nti tehi attānaṃ vissajjāpetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasitvā aggadvāreneva nikkhamitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto vihāsi. So tattha vasanto “evarūpampi nāma me ducchindaniyaṃ puttadārabandhanaṃ kilesabandhanaṃ chindita”nti udānaṃ udānento imā gāthā avoca –

He thought: “It is not possible to go after getting her to agree. I will flee and go forth without telling her.” So without telling her, he rose in the night and fled. Then the city guards seized him. He said, “Sirs, I am one who supports his mother. Release me.” Having persuaded them to release him, he stayed in one place, then left through the main gate and entered the Himalayas. There, he adopted the ascetic life, developed psychic powers and meditative attainments, and dwelt delighting in the bliss of meditation. While dwelling there, thinking, “Even such a difficult-to-cut bond as this—the bondage of wife and children, the bondage of defilements—has been cut by me!” and uttering this inspired utterance, he spoke these verses:

101.

101.

“Na taṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrā, yadāyasaṃ dārujapabbajañca;

Sārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu, puttesu dāresu ca yā apekkhā.

“The wise do not call that a strong bond which is made of iron, wood, or fiber; but the impassioned attachment for jewels and earrings, and the longing for sons and wives—”

102.

102.

“Etaṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrā, ohārinaṃ sīthilaṃ duppamuñcaṃ;

Etampi chetvāna vajanti dhīrā, anapekkhino kāmasukhaṃ pahāyā”ti.

“This, say the wise, is a strong bond, dragging down, slack, and hard to release. Having cut this too, the wise go forth, without longing, having abandoned sensual pleasures.”

Tattha dhīrāti dhitimantā, dhikkatapāpāti dhīrā. Atha vā dhī vuccati paññā, tāya paññāya samannāgatāti dhīrā, buddhā paccekabuddhā buddhasāvakā [P 2.0141] bodhisattā ca ime dhīrā nāma. Yadāyasantiādīsu yaṃ saṅkhalikasaṅkhātaṃ ayasā nibbattaṃ āyasaṃ, yaṃ addubandhanasaṅkhātaṃ dārujaṃ, yañca pabbajatiṇehi vā aññehi vā vākādīhi rajjuṃ katvā katarajjubandhanaṃ, taṃ āyasādiṃ chindituṃ sakkuṇeyyabhāvena dhīrā daḷhaṃ thiranti nāhu na kathenti. Sārattarattāti sārattā hutvā rattā, balavarāgarattāti attho. Maṇikuṇḍalesūti maṇīsu ca kuṇḍalesu ca, maṇiyuttesu vā kuṇḍalesu.

Here, “the wise” (dhīrā) means the resolute; because they despise evil, they are called wise. Alternatively, ‘dhī’ means wisdom, and those endowed with that wisdom are “the wise”—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Buddha, and Bodhisattas; these are called “the wise.” Regarding “iron,” etc.: that which is made of iron, known as chains; that which is made of wood, known as wooden fetters; and whatever rope-bond is made by twisting pabbaja grass or other kinds of bark—the wise do not declare that bondage made of iron, etc., to be strong or firm, because it can be cut. “Deeply attached and impassioned” means being attached and impassioned, that is, impassioned with strong craving. “To jewels and earrings” means to jewels and to earrings, or to earrings adorned with jewels.

Etaṃ [M 2.0129] daḷhanti ye maṇikuṇḍalesu sārattarattā, tesaṃ yo ca sārāgo, yā ca tesaṃ puttadāresu apekkhā taṇhā, etaṃ kilesamayaṃ bandhanaṃ daḷhaṃ thiranti dhīrā āhu. Ohārinanti ākaḍḍhitvā catūsu apāyesu pātanato avaharati heṭṭhā haratīti ohārinaṃ. Sithilanti bandhanaṭṭhāne chavicammamaṃsāni na chindati, lohitaṃ na nīharati, bandhanabhāvampi na jānāpeti, thalapathajalapathādīsu kammāni kātuṃ detīti sithilaṃ. Duppamuñcanti taṇhālobhavasena hi ekavārampi uppannaṃ kilesabandhanaṃ daṭṭhaṭṭhānato kacchapo viya dummocayaṃ hotīti duppamuñcaṃ. Etampi chetvānāti etaṃ evaṃ daḷhampi kilesabandhanaṃ ñāṇakhaggena chinditvā ayadāmāni chinditvā mattavaravāraṇā viya pañjare chinditvā sīhapotakā viya ca dhīrā vatthukāmakilesakāme ukkārabhūmiṃ viya jigucchamānā anapekkhino hutvā kāmasukhaṃ pahāya vajanti pakkamanti, pakkamitvā ca pana himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānasukhena vītināmentīti.

“This, say the wise, is a strong bond.” For those who are deeply attached and impassioned for jewels and earrings, their passion and craving for sons and wives—this defilement-wrought bondage, the wise declare strong and firm. “Dragging down” (ohārinaṃ) means it drags one down, pulling them into the four states of misery; it carries them downwards. “Slack” (sithilaṃ) means that it does not cut skin, flesh, or blood at the point of bondage, nor does it reveal its nature as a fetter, and it allows one to perform tasks on land or water. “Hard to release” (duppamuñcaṃ) means that once it has arisen, this bondage of defilement, due to craving and greed, is hard to release, like a tortoise from the place it has bitten. “Having cut even this” means that having cut even this strong bondage of defilement with the sword of wisdom—like mighty elephants in rut cutting their iron chains, and like young lions breaking their cages—the wise, disgusted with sensual objects and sensual defilements as if they were a dung-heap, become unattached, abandon sensual joys, and depart. Having departed, they enter the Himalayas, embrace the ascetic life of sages, and pass their time in the bliss of meditation.

Evaṃ [V 2.0117] bodhisatto imaṃ udānaṃ udānetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having uttered this inspired utterance, without declining from jhāna, was destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahanto ahesuṃ. “Tadā mātā mahāmāyā ahosi, pitā suddhodanamahārājā, bhariyā rāhulamātā, putto rāhulo, puttadāraṃ pahāya nikkhamitvā pabbajito puriso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some arahants. “At that time, the mother was Mahāmāyā, the father was King Suddhodana, the wife was Rāhula's mother, the son was Rāhula, and the man who renounced wife and son to go forth was none other than myself.”

Bandhanāgārajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Bandhanāgāra Jātaka is finished.

[202] 2. Keḷisīlajātakavaṇṇanā

[202] 2. 2. Keḷisīla Jātaka

The King Fond of Play

Haṃsā [P 2.0142] koñcā mayūrā cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto āyasmantaṃ lakuṇḍakabhaddiyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kirāyasmā buddhasāsane pākaṭo ahosi paññāto madhurassaro madhuradhammakathiko paṭisambhidāppatto mahākhīṇāsavo asītiyā mahātherānaṃ antaro [M 2.0130] pamāṇena omako lakuṇḍako sāmaṇero viya, khuddako kīḷanatthāya kato viya. Tasmiṃ ekadivasaṃ tathāgataṃ vanditvā jetavanakoṭṭhakaṃ gate janapadā tiṃsamattā bhikkhū “dasabalaṃ vandissāmā”ti jetavanaṃ pavisantā vihārakoṭṭhake theraṃ disvā “sāmaṇero eso”ti saññāya theraṃ cīvarakaṇṇe gaṇhantā hatthe gaṇhantā sīsaṃ gaṇhantā nāsāya parāmasantā kaṇṇesu gahetvā cāletvā hatthakukkuccaṃ katvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā nisīditvā satthārā madhurapaṭisanthāre kate pucchiṃsu – “bhante, lakuṇḍakabhaddiyatthero kira nāmeko tumhākaṃ sāvako madhuradhammakathiko atthi, kahaṃ so idānī”ti. “Kiṃ pana, bhikkhave, daṭṭhukāmatthā”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, tumhe dvārakoṭṭhake disvā cīvarakaṇṇādīsu gaṇhantā hatthakukkuccaṃ katvā āgatā, esa so”ti. “Bhante, evarūpo patthitapatthano abhinīhārasampanno sāvako kiṃkāraṇā appesakkho jāto”ti? Satthā “attanā katapāpakammaṃ nissāyā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The swans, the herons, the peacocks—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya. Indeed, that venerable one was renowned in the Buddha’s dispensation, well-known, sweet-voiced, a speaker of sweet Dhamma, one who had attained the analytical knowledges, a great one whose taints were destroyed; yet among the eighty great elders, he was small in stature, like a stunted novice, as if made for play. One day, after paying homage to the Tathagata and going to the gate of Jetavana, about thirty monks from the countryside entered Jetavana, thinking, 'We will pay respects to the One of Ten Powers.' Seeing the elder at the monastery gate, they mistook him for a novice. They grabbed him by the edge of his robe, took his hand, seized his head, touched his nose, pulled his ears, and made mischief with their hands. Then, arranging their bowls and robes, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. After the Teacher had greeted them kindly, they asked, 'Venerable sir, we have heard that among your disciples there is one named the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, a speaker of sweet Dhamma. Where is he now?' 'What is it, monks, do you wish to see him?' 'Yes, Venerable sir.' 'The one you saw at the monastery gate, whom you grabbed by the edge of his robe and made mischief with—that was he.' 'Venerable sir, how is it that such a disciple, endowed with aspirations and resolve, came to be of such little majesty?' The Teacher replied, 'Due to evil deeds done by himself in the past,' and at their request, he recounted the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakko devarājā ahosi. Tadā brahmadattassa jiṇṇaṃ jarāppattaṃ hatthiṃ vā assaṃ vā goṇaṃ vā dassetuṃ na sakkā, keḷisīlo hutvā tathārūpaṃ disvāva anubandhāpeti, jiṇṇasakaṭampi disvā bhindāpeti, jiṇṇamātugāme disvā pakkosāpetvā udare paharāpetvā pātāpetvā puna uṭṭhāpetvā bhāyāpeti[V 2.0118], jiṇṇapurise disvā laṅghake viya bhūmiyaṃ saṃparivattakādikīḷaṃ kīḷāpeti, apassanto “asukaghare kira mahallako atthī”ti sutvāpi [P 2.0143] pakkosāpetvā kīḷati. Manussā lajjantā attano mātāpitaro tiroraṭṭhāni pesenti, mātupaṭṭhānadhammo pitupaṭṭhānadhammo pacchijji, rājasevakāpi keḷisīlāva ahesuṃ. Matamatā cattāro apāye pūrenti, devaparisā parihāyati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the king of the gods. At that time, Brahmadatta, being of a playful nature, could not bear to see any aged elephant, horse, or ox. Whenever he saw such a creature, he would have it chased. Seeing an old cart, he would have it smashed. Seeing an elderly woman, he would summon her, strike her in the belly, knock her down, then make her rise again and terrify her. Seeing an old man, he would have him perform games like tumbling or rolling about on the ground, as if he were an acrobat. Even if he did not see them, upon hearing, 'There is an old person in such-and-such house,' he would summon them and play. People, ashamed, sent their own parents to foreign lands. The duty of caring for mothers and the duty of caring for fathers was abandoned. Even the king’s servants became playful. Those who died filled the four lower realms, and the assembly of gods diminished.

Sakko abhinave devaputte apassanto “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “damessāmi na”nti mahallakavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā jiṇṇayānake dve takkacāṭiyo āropetvā dve jaragoṇe [M 2.0131] yojetvā ekasmiṃ chaṇadivase alaṅkatahatthiṃ abhiruhitvā brahmadatte alaṅkatanagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonte pilotikanivattho taṃ yānakaṃ pājento rañño abhimukho agamāsi. Rājā jiṇṇayānakaṃ disvā “etaṃ yānakaṃ apanethā”ti vadati. Manussā “kahaṃ, deva, na passāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Sakko attano ānubhāvena raññoyeva dassesi. Atha naṃ bahusampatte tasmiṃ tassa uparibhāgena pājento rañño matthake ekaṃ cāṭiṃ bhinditvā nivattāpento dutiyaṃ bhindi. Athassa sīsato paṭṭhāya ito cito ca takkaṃ paggharati, so tena aṭṭīyati harāyati jigucchati. Athassa taṃ upaddutabhāvaṃ ñatvā sakko yānakaṃ antaradhāpetvā sakkattabhāvaṃ māpetvā vajirahattho ākāse ṭhatvā “pāpa adhammikarāja, kiṃ tvaṃ mahallako na bhavissasi, tava sarīraṃ jarā na paharissati, keḷisīlo hutvā vuḍḍhe viheṭhanakammaṃ karosi, ekakaṃ taṃ nissāya etaṃ kammaṃ katvā matamatā apāye paripūrenti, manussā mātāpitaro paṭijaggituṃ na labhanti. Sace imamhā kammā na viramissasi, vajirena te sīsaṃ padālessāmi, mā ito paṭṭhāyetaṃ kammaṃ akatthā”ti santajjetvā mātāpitūnaṃ guṇaṃ kathetvā vuḍḍhāpacāyikakammassa ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsetvā ovaditvā sakaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Rājā tato paṭṭhāya tathārūpaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ cittampi na uppādesi.

Sakka, not seeing any new devas, wondered, 'What could be the reason?' Reflecting, he understood the reason and thought, 'I will tame him.' He created the appearance of an old man, placed two pots of buttermilk on a decrepit cart, yoked two old oxen to it, and on one of the festival days, while Brahmadatta was circling the adorned city, mounted on a beautifully adorned elephant, Sakka, wearing a rag, approached the king, driving that cart. The king, seeing the decrepit cart, said, 'Take this cart away.' The people replied, 'Where, lord? We do not see it.' Sakka, by his power, made it visible only to the king. Then, when he had arrived very close to him, driving it above him, he broke one pot above the king’s head and, turning back, broke the second. From the king’s head, buttermilk began to flow here and there; he was troubled, ashamed, and disgusted by it. Realizing the king’s distress, Sakka made the cart disappear, revealed his form as Sakka, and stood in the sky holding a thunderbolt. 'Wicked, unrighteous king! Will you not grow old? Will old age not strike your body? Being of a playful nature, you harass the elderly. Because of you alone, having done this deed, those who die fill the lower realms. People are not able to care for their parents. If you do not refrain from such actions, I will split your head with this thunderbolt. Do not commit such deeds from now on!' After threatening him, Sakka spoke of the virtues of parents, explained the benefits of honoring the elderly, advised him, and returned to his own abode. From then on, the king did not even entertain the thought of committing such deeds again.

Satthā [P 2.0144] imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

The Teacher, having related this past event, being fully enlightened, spoke these verses:

103.

103.

“Haṃsā koñcā mayūrā ca, hatthayo pasadā migā;

Sabbe sīhassa bhāyanti, natthi kāyasmi tulyatā.

"Swans, cranes, and peacocks, elephants and spotted deer, all fear the lion; there is no equality in body."

104.

104.

“Evameva [V 2.0119] manussesu, daharo cepi paññavā;

So hi tattha mahā hoti, neva bālo sarīravā”ti.

"Even so among humans, though young, if one is wise, he is indeed great there, and not the fool, even if large of body."

Tattha pasadā migāti pasadasaṅkhātā migā, pasadā migā ca avasesā migā cātipi attho. “Pasadamigā”tipi pāṭho, pasadā migāti attho. Natthi kāyasmi tulyatāti sarīre pamāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Yadi bhaveyya, mahāsarīrā hatthino ceva pasadamigā ca sīhaṃ māreyyuṃ, sīho haṃsādayo [M 2.0132] khuddakasarīreyeva māreyya, khuddakāyeva sīhassa bhāyeyyuṃ, na mahantā. Yasmā panetaṃ natthi, tasmā sabbepi te sīhassa bhāyanti. Sarīravāti bālo mahāsarīropi mahā nāma na hoti, tasmā lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo sarīrena khuddakopi mā taṃ ñāṇenapi khuddakoti maññitthāti attho.

Herein, 'pasadā migā' refers to deer known as pasadā; the meaning is both pasadā deer and other deer. The reading 'pasadamigā' is also found, meaning pasadā deer. 'There is no equality in body' means there is no fixed measure with respect to the body. If there were, large-bodied elephants and pasadā deer would kill a lion, while the lion would kill only small-bodied creatures like geese, and only the small ones would fear the lion, not the large ones. But since this is not so, all of them fear the lion. 'Sarīravā' means that even a fool with a large body is not truly great. Therefore, though Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya was small in body, do not think that he is also small in wisdom—this is the meaning.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne tesu bhikkhūsu keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahanto ahesuṃ. “Tadā rājā lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo ahosi, so tāya keḷisīlatāya paresaṃ keḷinissayo jāto, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, the Teacher connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, some of those monks became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some arahants. "At that time, the king was Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya; due to his playful nature in the past, he now became a source of amusement for others. But Sakka was none other than myself."

Keḷisīlajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The commentary on the Keḷisīla Jātaka, the second.

[203] 3. Khandhajātakavaṇṇanā

[203] 3. The Commentary on the Khandha Jātaka

Virūpakkhehi me mettanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ kira jantāgharadvāre kaṭṭhāni phālentaṃ pūtirukkhantarā nikkhamitvā eko sappo pādaṅguliyaṃ ḍaṃsi, so tattheva mato. Tassa matabhāvo sakalavihāre pākaṭo ahosi. Dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko kira bhikkhu jantāgharadvāre kaṭṭhāni phālento sappena daṭṭho tattheva mato”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya [P 2.0145] nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “sace so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cattāri ahirājakulāni ārabbha mettaṃ abhāvayissa, na naṃ sappo ḍaṃseyya. Porāṇakatāpasāpi anuppanne buddhe catūsu ahirājakulesu mettaṃ bhāvetvā tāni ahirājakulāni nissāya uppajjanakabhayato mucciṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'My loving-kindness is for the Virūpakkhas'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk. It is said that while this monk was splitting wood at the gate of the steam bath, a snake emerged from within a rotten tree and bit his toe, and he died on that very spot. The fact of his death became known throughout the monastery. In the Hall of Dhamma, the monks began a discussion: 'Venerable sirs, it is said that a certain monk, while splitting wood at the gate of the steam bath, was bitten by a snake and died right there.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'For what discussion are you now gathered here, monks?' When it was said, 'For this one,' he replied, 'Monks, if that monk had cultivated loving-kindness towards the four royal snake clans, a snake would not have bitten him. Even the ascetics of old, before a Buddha had arisen, cultivated loving-kindness towards the four royal snake clans and, by relying on those royal snake clans, were freed from the danger that could arise from them.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 2.0120][M 2.0133] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā himavantapadese ekasmiṃ gaṅgānivattane assamapadaṃ māpetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto isigaṇaparivuto vihāsi. Tadā gaṅgātīre nānappakārā dīghajātikā isīnaṃ paripanthaṃ karonti, yebhuyyena isayo jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇanti. Tāpasā tamatthaṃ bodhisattassa ārocesuṃ. Bodhisatto sabbe tāpase sannipātāpetvā “sace tumhe catūsu ahirājakulesu mettaṃ bhāveyyātha, na vo sappā ḍaṃseyyuṃ, tasmā ito paṭṭhāya catūsu ahirājakulesu evaṃ mettaṃ bhāvethā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kasi country. Having come of age, he renounced sensual pleasures and went forth into the ascetic life, producing the higher knowledges and meditative attainments. He dwelt in a hermitage he had made near a bend of the Ganges in the Himalayan region, delighting in the bliss of meditation, surrounded by a company of ascetics. At that time, various kinds of long-bodied creatures along the Ganges harassed the ascetics, and most of them met their end. The ascetics reported this matter to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta gathered all the ascetics and said, "If you cultivate loving-kindness toward the four royal snake clans, the snakes will not bite you. Therefore, from now on, cultivate loving-kindness toward these four royal snake clans in this way," and he spoke this verse:

105.

105.

“Virūpakkhehi me mettaṃ, mettaṃ erāpathehi me;

Chabyāputtehi me mettaṃ, mettaṃ kaṇhāgotamakehi cā”ti.

"My loving-kindness is for the Virūpakkhas, my loving-kindness is for the Erāpathas; my loving-kindness is for the Chabyāputtas, and my loving-kindness is for the Kaṇhāgotamakas as well."

Tattha virūpakkhehi me mettanti virūpakkhanāgarājakulehi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ mettaṃ. Erāpathādīsupi eseva nayo. Etānipi hi erāpathanāgarājakulaṃ chabyāputtanāgarājakulaṃ kaṇhāgotamakanāgarājakulanti nāgarājakulāneva.

Herein, 'My loving-kindness is for the Virūpakkhas' means my loving-kindness is with the Virūpakkha royal nāga clan. The same method applies to the Erāpathas and the others. For these too are royal nāga clans: the Erāpatha royal nāga clan, the Chabyāputta royal nāga clan, and the Kaṇhāgotamaka royal nāga clan.

Evaṃ cattāri nāgarājakulāni dassetvā “sace tumhe etesu mettaṃ bhāvetuṃ sakkhissatha, dīghajātikā vo na ḍaṃsissanti na viheṭhessantī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having thus pointed out the four royal nāga clans, he said: 'If you are able to cultivate loving-kindness towards these, the long-bodied creatures will neither bite you nor harass you.' Then he spoke the second verse:

“Apādakehi [P 2.0146] me mettaṃ, mettaṃ dvipādakehi me;

Catuppadehi me mettaṃ, mettaṃ bahuppadehi me”ti.

"My loving-kindness is for the footless, my loving-kindness for the two-footed; my loving-kindness for the four-footed, my loving-kindness for the many-footed."

Tattha paṭhamapadena odissakaṃ katvā sabbesu apādakesu dīghajātikesu ceva macchesu ca mettābhāvanā dassitā, dutiyapadena manussesu ceva pakkhijātesu ca, tatiyapadena hatthiassādīsu sabbacatuppadesu, catutthapadena vicchikasatapadiuccāliṅgapāṇakamakkaṭakādīsu.

Herein, by the first line, having made a specific reference, the cultivation of loving-kindness is shown towards all footless creatures, both the long-bodied ones and fish. By the second line, towards humans and birds. By the third line, towards elephants, horses, and all other quadrupeds. By the fourth line, towards scorpions, centipedes, insects, spiders, and the like.

Evaṃ sarūpena mettābhāvanaṃ dassetvā idāni āyācanavasena dassento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having thus shown the cultivation of loving-kindness in its specific form, now showing it by way of entreaty, he spoke this verse:

“Mā maṃ apādako hiṃsi, mā maṃ hiṃsi dvipādako;

Mā maṃ catuppado hiṃsi, mā maṃ hiṃsi bahuppado”ti.

"May no footless creature harm me, may no two-footed creature harm me; may no four-footed creature harm me, may no many-footed creature harm me."

Tattha [V 2.0121][M 2.0134] mā manti etesu apādakādīsu koci ekopi mā maṃ hiṃsatu, mā viheṭhetūti evaṃ āyācantā mettaṃ bhāvethāti attho.

Herein, 'May... not harm me' means: 'May not even a single one among these footless and other creatures harm me, may it not harass me.' The meaning is that you should cultivate loving-kindness while entreating in this way.

Idāni anodissakavasena mettābhāvanaṃ dassento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Now, demonstrating the cultivation of loving-kindness without specific direction, he spoke this verse:

“Sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā, sabbe bhūtā ca kevalā;

Sabbe bhadrāni passantu, mā kañci pāpamāgamā”ti.

"May all beings, all living things, all creatures without exception, see what is auspicious; may no evil whatsoever befall anyone."

Tattha taṇhādiṭṭhivasena vaṭṭe pañcasu khandhesu āsattā visattā laggā laggitāti sattā, assāsapassāsapavattanasaṅkhātena pāṇanavasena pāṇā, bhūtabhāvitanibbattanavasena bhūtāti evaṃ vacanamattaviseso veditabbo. Avisesena pana sabbānipetāni padāni sabbasattasaṅgāhakāneva. Kevalāti sakalā. Idaṃ sabbasaddasseva hi pariyāyavacanaṃ. Bhadrāni passantūti sabbepete sattā bhadrāni sādhūni kalyāṇāneva passantu. Mā kañci pāpamāgamāti etesu kañci ekaṃ sattampi pāpaṃ lāmakaṃ dukkhaṃ mā āgamā, mā āgacchatu mā pāpuṇātu, sabbe averā abyāpajjā sukhī niddukkhā hontūti.

Herein, beings are called 'sattā' because, by means of craving and wrong view, they are attached, clinging, stuck, and ensnared in the five aggregates within the round of existence. They are called 'pāṇā' by way of breathing, which is the process of inhalation and exhalation. They are called 'bhūtā' by way of having come into being, developed, and been produced. Thus, a mere verbal distinction should be understood. However, without distinction, all these terms are indeed inclusive of all beings. 'Kevalā' means 'entire.' This is indeed a synonym for the word 'sabba' (all). 'May they see what is auspicious' means: 'May all these beings see only what is auspicious, good, and wholesome.' 'May no evil whatsoever befall anyone' means: 'May no evil, wretchedness, or suffering come to even a single one among them; may it not come, may it not approach, may it not befall them. May all be without enmity, without affliction, happy, and free from suffering.'

Evaṃ [P 2.0147] “sabbasattesu anodissakavasena mettaṃ bhāvethā”ti vatvā puna tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇe anussarāpetuṃ –

Having thus said, 'Cultivate loving-kindness towards all beings without specific direction,' then again, to bring to mind the qualities of the Three Jewels:

106.

106.

“Appamāṇo buddho, appamāṇo dhammo;

Appamāṇo saṅgho”ti āha.

"Immeasurable is the Buddha, immeasurable is the Dhamma, immeasurable is the Saṅgha," he said.

Tattha pamāṇakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ abhāvena guṇānañca pamāṇābhāvena buddharatanaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Dhammoti navavidho lokuttaradhammo. Tassapi pamāṇaṃ kātuṃ na sakkāti appamāṇo. Tena appamāṇena dhammena samannāgatattā saṅghopi appamāṇo.

Herein, the Jewel of the Buddha is immeasurable due to the absence of the defilements that create measure, and due to the immeasurability of his virtues. The Dhamma is the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. It is not possible to measure it, thus it is immeasurable. Because the Saṅgha is endowed with that immeasurable Dhamma, the Saṅgha, too, is immeasurable.

Iti bodhisatto “imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇe anussarathā”ti vatvā tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ appamāṇaguṇataṃ dassetvā sappamāṇe satte dassetuṃ –

Thus the Bodhisatta, having said, 'Recollect the qualities of these three jewels,' and having shown the immeasurable qualities of the three jewels, then, in order to show beings who have measure—

“Pamāṇavantāni [V 2.0122][M 2.0135] sarīsapāni, ahi vicchika satapadī;

Uṇṇanābhi sarabū mūsikā”ti āha.

"Measurable are the creeping creatures: the snake, the scorpion, the centipede, the spider, the house lizard, and the mouse," he said.

Tattha sarīsapānīti sappadīghajātikānaṃ nāmaṃ. Te hi sarantā gacchanti, sirena vā sapantīti sarīsapā. “Ahī”tiādi tesaṃ sarūpato nidassanaṃ. Tattha uṇṇanābhīti makkaṭako. Tassa hi nābhito uṇṇāsadisaṃ suttaṃ nikkhamati, tasmā “uṇṇanābhī”ti vuccati. Sarabūti gharagoḷikā.

Herein, 'sarīsapāni' is a name for snakes and other long-bodied creatures. For they move by creeping, or they crawl on their front; therefore they are called 'sarīsapā'. 'Ahi' and so on are examples showing their specific forms. Herein, 'uṇṇanābhi' means a spider. For from its navel a thread resembling wool emerges, therefore it is called 'uṇṇanābhi'. 'Sarabū' means a house lizard.

Iti bodhisatto “yasmā etesaṃ antorāgādayo pamāṇakarā dhammā atthi, tasmā tāni sarīsapādīni pamāṇavantānī”ti dassetvā “appamāṇānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ ānubhāvena ime pamāṇavantā sattā rattindivaṃ parittakammaṃ karontūti evaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇe anussarathā”ti vatvā tato uttari kattabbaṃ dassetuṃ imaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus the Bodhisatta, having shown that 'because these creatures possess qualities like inner passion and the like that create measure, therefore these creeping creatures and so forth are measured beings,' and having said, 'By the power of the three immeasurable jewels, may these measured beings perform protective acts day and night—thus, recollect the virtues of the three jewels,' then, to further explain what should be done, spoke this verse:

“Katā me rakkhā katā me parittā, paṭikkamantu bhūtāni;

Sohaṃ namo bhagavato, namo sattannaṃ sammāsambuddhāna”nti.

My protection has been made, my safeguard has been made; may beings retreat. I pay homage to the Blessed One, homage to the seven Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones.

Tattha [P 2.0148] katā me rakkhāti mayā ratanattayaguṇe anussarantena attano rakkhā gutti katā. Katā me parittāti parittāṇampi me attano kataṃ. Paṭikkamantu bhūtānīti mayi ahitajjhāsayāni bhūtāni paṭikkamantu apagacchantu. Sohaṃ namo bhagavatoti so ahaṃ evaṃ kataparitto atītassa parinibbutassa sabbassapi buddhassa bhagavato namo karomi. Namo sattannaṃ sammāsambuddhānanti visesena pana atīte paṭipāṭiyā parinibbutānaṃ sattannaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ namo karomīti.

Here, 'My protection has been made' means that by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem, I have made protection and a guard for myself. 'My safeguard has been made' means that a safeguard has also been made by me for myself. 'May beings retreat' means: 'May beings with harmful intentions towards me retreat, may they go away.' 'I pay homage to the Blessed One' means: 'I, having thus made protection, pay homage to the Blessed One, to every Buddha who has attained final Nibbāna.' 'Homage to the seven Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones' means especially paying homage to the seven Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones who have attained final Nibbāna in succession in the past.

Evaṃ “namakkāraṃ karontāpi satta buddhe anussarathā”ti bodhisatto isigaṇassa imaṃ parittaṃ bandhitvā adāsi. Ādito pana paṭṭhāya dvīhi gāthāhi catūsu ahirājakulesu mettāya dīpitattā odissakānodissakavasena vā dvinnaṃ mettābhāvanānaṃ dīpitattā idaṃ parittaṃ idha vuttanti veditabbaṃ, aññaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya isigaṇo bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā mettaṃ bhāvesi, buddhaguṇe anussari. Evametesu [M 2.0136] buddhaguṇe anussarantesuyeva sabbe dīghajātikā paṭikkamiṃsu. Bodhisattopi brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, the Bodhisatta composed this protective chant and gave it to the group of sages, saying: 'Even while making salutations, recollect the seven Buddhas.' From then on, it should be understood that this protective chant was taught here because loving-kindness towards the four royal serpent families is illustrated through two verses, or because the two types of loving-kindness meditation—specifically and non-specifically—are illustrated. Alternatively, another reason should be sought. From then on, the group of sages, abiding by the Bodhisatta's advice, cultivated loving-kindness and recollected the qualities of the Buddha. While they were thus recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, all the long-bodied creatures retreated. The Bodhisatta, too, having cultivated the divine abidings, became destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā [V 2.0123] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā isigaṇo buddhaparisā ahosi, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the group of sages was the Buddha's assembly, and the teacher of the group was indeed I myself.'

Khandhajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Khandha Jātaka, the third.

[204] 4. Vīrakajātakavaṇṇanā

[204] 4. The Commentary on the Vīraka Jātaka

Api vīraka passesīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sugatālayaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadattassa parisaṃ gahetvā āgatesu hi theresu satthā “sāriputta, devadatto tumhe disvā kiṃ akāsī”ti pucchitvā “sugatālayaṃ, bhante, dassesī”ti vutte “na kho, sāriputta, idāneva devadatto mama anukiriyaṃ karonto vināsaṃ patto, pubbepi vināsaṃ pāpuṇī”ti vatvā therena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'O Vīraka, did you see?' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the imitation of the Sugata. When the elders arrived, having brought back Devadatta's following, the Teacher asked: 'Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do when he saw you?' Upon being told, 'Lord, he displayed an imitation of the Sugata,' the Teacher said: 'Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta has met destruction by imitating me; in the past too he met destruction.' Being entreated by the elder, he brought forth the past.

Atīte [P 2.0149] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese udakakākayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā ekaṃ saraṃ upanissāya vasi, “vīrako”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Tadā kāsiraṭṭhe dubbhikkhaṃ ahosi, manussā kākabhattaṃ vā dātuṃ yakkhanāgabalikammaṃ vā kātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Chātakaraṭṭhato kākā yebhuyyena araññaṃ pavisiṃsu. Tattheko bārāṇasivāsī saviṭṭhako nāma kāko kākiṃ ādāya vīrakassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ saraṃ nissāya ekamante vāsaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ sare gocaraṃ gaṇhanto vīrakaṃ saraṃ otaritvā macche khāditvā paccuttaritvā sarīraṃ sukkhāpentaṃ disvā “imaṃ udakakākaṃ nissāya sakkā bahū macche laddhuṃ, imaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ, sammā”ti vutte “icchāmi taṃ sāmi upaṭṭhahitu”nti vatvā “sādhū”ti tena sampaṭicchito tato paṭṭhāya upaṭṭhāsi. Vīrakopi tato paṭṭhāya attano yāpanamattaṃ khāditvā macche uddharitvā saviṭṭhakassa deti. Sopi attano yāpanamattaṃ khāditvā sesaṃ kākiyā deti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a water crow in the region of the Himalayas. He lived near a lake, and his name was Vīraka. At that time, there was a famine in the Kāsī kingdom, and people were unable to offer food to crows or perform sacrifices to yakkhas and nāgas. Most of the crows from the famine-stricken country fled into the forest. Among them was a crow named Saviṭṭhaka, a resident of Benares, who, taking his mate, went to the place where Vīraka lived. Settling near that lake, he made his home in a suitable spot. One day, while foraging in that lake, Saviṭṭhaka saw Vīraka dive into the lake, eat fish, come back up, and dry his body. Thinking, 'By depending on this water crow, it is possible to obtain many fish; I will serve him,' he approached Vīraka. When asked, 'What is it, friend?' Saviṭṭhaka replied, 'Master, I wish to serve you.' Vīraka agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and accepted him. From then on, Saviṭṭhaka served him. Vīraka, in turn, after eating just enough for his own sustenance, would catch fish and give them to Saviṭṭhaka. He too, after eating just enough for his own sustenance, would give the rest to his mate.

Tassa [M 2.0137] aparabhāge māno uppajji – “ayampi udakakāko kāḷako, ahampi kāḷako, akkhituṇḍapādehipi etassa ca mayhañca nānākaraṇaṃ natthi, ito paṭṭhāya iminā gahitamacchehi mayhaṃ kammaṃ natthi, ahameva gaṇhissāmī”ti. So vīrakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “samma, ito paṭṭhāya ahameva saraṃ otaritvā macche gaṇhissāmī”ti vatvā “na tvaṃ, samma, udakaṃ otaritvā macche gaṇhanakakule nibbatto, mā nassī”ti tena vāriyamānopi vacanaṃ anādiyitvā [V 2.0124] saraṃ oruyha udakaṃ pavisitvā ummujjamāno sevālaṃ chinditvā nikkhamituṃ nāsakkhi, sevālantare laggi, aggatuṇḍameva paññāyi. So nirassāso antoudakeyeva [P 2.0150] jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Athassa bhariyā āgamanaṃ apassamānā taṃ pavattiṃ jānanatthaṃ vīrakassa santikaṃ gantvā “sāmi, saviṭṭhako na paññāyati, kahaṃ nu kho so”ti pucchamānā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Later, pride arose in him: 'This water crow is black, and I am black. There is no difference between him and me in eyes, beak, and feet. From now on, I have no need for the fish caught by him; I myself will catch them.' Approaching Vīraka, he said, 'Friend, from now on I myself will dive into the lake and catch fish.' Though Vīraka warned him, 'Friend, you were not born into a family that catches fish by diving into the water; do not perish,' he disregarded the advice. Diving into the lake, he entered the water. As he tried to emerge, he was unable to break through the moss; he became entangled in the moss, and only the tip of his beak was visible. Breathless, he met his end right there in the water. Then, his mate, not seeing him return, went to Vīraka to find out what had happened. Asking, 'Master, Saviṭṭhaka is not to be seen; where could he be?' she spoke the first verse:

107.

107.

“Api vīraka passesi, sakuṇaṃ mañjubhāṇakaṃ;

Mayūragīvasaṅkāsaṃ, patiṃ mayhaṃ saviṭṭhaka”nti.

“Vīraka, did you see a sweet-voiced bird, resembling a peacock’s neck, my husband Saviṭṭhaka?”

Tattha api, vīraka, passesīti, sāmi vīraka, api passasi. Mañjubhāṇakanti mañjubhāṇinaṃ. Sā hi rāgavasena “madhurassaro me patī”ti maññati, tasmā evamāha. Mayūragīvasaṅkāsanti moragīvasamānavaṇṇaṃ.

Here, “Vīraka, do you see?” means “Master Vīraka, do you see?” “Sweet-voiced” means one who speaks sweetly. For she, through passion, thinks, “My husband has a sweet voice,” and therefore she says this. “Resembling a peacock’s neck” means having a color similar to a peacock’s neck.

Taṃ sutvā vīrako “āma, jānāmi te sāmikassa gataṭṭhāna”nti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Vīraka said, 'Yes, I know where your husband has gone,' and then spoke the second verse:

108.

108.

“Udakathalacarassa pakkhino, niccaṃ āmakamacchabhojino;

Tassānukaraṃ saviṭṭhako, sevāle paliguṇṭhito mato”ti.

“Saviṭṭhaka, imitating the bird that moves on water and land, which always feeds on raw fish, lies dead, entangled in moss.”

Tattha udakathalacarassāti udake ca thale ca carituṃ samatthassa. Pakkhinoti attānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tassānukaranti tassa anukaronto. Sevāle paliguṇṭhito matoti udakaṃ pavisitvā sevālaṃ chinditvā nikkhamituṃ asakkonto sevālapariyonaddho antoudakeyeva mato, passa, etassa tuṇḍaṃ dissatīti. Taṃ sutvā kākī paridevitvā bārāṇasimeva agamāsi.

Here, “of the bird that moves on water and land” means of one capable of moving both in water and on land. “Bird” he says referring to himself. “Imitating him” means imitating that one. “Entangled in moss, lies dead” means that after entering the water and being unable to break through the moss to come out, he became enveloped by moss and died right there in the water; “look, his beak is visible.” Hearing this, the female crow lamented and went back to Benares.

Satthā [M 2.0138] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā saviṭṭhako devadatto ahosi, vīrako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Saviṭṭhaka was Devadatta, and Vīraka was I myself.”

Vīrakajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Vīraka Jātaka, the fourth.

[205] 5. Gaṅgeyyajātakavaṇṇanā

[205] 5. The Commentary on the Gaṅgeyya Jātaka

Sobhati [V 2.0125][P 2.0151] maccho gaṅgeyyoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dve daharabhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Te kira sāvatthivāsino kulaputtā sāsane pabbajitvā asubhabhāvanaṃ anunuyuñjitvā rūpapasaṃsakā hutvā rūpaṃ upalāḷentā vicariṃsu. Te ekadivasaṃ “tvaṃ na sobhasi, ahaṃ sobhāmī”ti rūpaṃ nissāya uppannavivādā avidūre nisinnaṃ ekaṃ mahallakattheraṃ disvā “eso amhākaṃ sobhanabhāvaṃ vā asobhanabhāvaṃ vā jānissatī”ti taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, ko amhesu sobhano”ti pucchiṃsu. So “āvuso, tumhehi ahameva sobhanataro”ti āha. Daharā “ayaṃ mahallako amhehi pucchitaṃ akathetvā apucchitaṃ kathetī”ti taṃ paribhāsitvā pakkamiṃsu. Sā tesaṃ kiriyā bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭā jātā. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko mahallako thero kira te rūpanissitake dahare lajjāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, ime dve daharā idāneva rūpapasaṃsakā, pubbepete rūpameva upalāḷentā vicariṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story, beginning with “The Gaṅgeyya fish is beautiful,” concerning two young monks. It seems these two young men from Sāvatthī, having gone forth into the Dispensation, did not apply themselves to the meditation on foulness (asubhabhāvanā), but became praisers of beauty and went about cherishing their own appearance. One day, arguing based on their appearance, “You are not beautiful, I am beautiful,” they saw an elder monk sitting nearby and thought, “He will know whether we are beautiful or not.” Approaching him, they asked, “Venerable sir, who among us is beautiful?” He replied, “Friends, I am more beautiful than both of you.” The young monks, thinking, “This elder, instead of answering what we asked, says what we did not ask,” reviled him and departed. Their action became known in the Saṅgha. Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, a discussion arose: “Friends, that elder monk, it is said, shamed those two young monks who were attached to their appearance.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?” When told, he said, “Monks, it is not only now that these two young men are praisers of their own beauty; in the past, too, they went about cherishing their appearance.” Then he recounted a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gaṅgātīre rukkhadevatā ahosi. Tadā gaṅgāyamunānaṃ samāgamaṭṭhāne gaṅgeyyo ca yāmuneyyo ca dve macchā “ahaṃ sobhāmi, tvaṃ na sobhasī”ti rūpaṃ nissāya vivadamānā avidūre gaṅgātīre kacchapaṃ nipannaṃ disvā “eso amhākaṃ sobhanabhāvaṃ vā asobhanabhāvaṃ vā jānissatī”ti taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ nu kho, samma kacchapa, gaṅgeyyo sobhati, udāhu yāmuneyyo”ti pucchiṃsu. Kacchapo “gaṅgeyyopi sobhati[M 2.0139], yāmuneyyopi sobhati, tumhehi pana dvīhi ahameva atirekataraṃ sobhāmī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity on the bank of the Gaṅgā. At that time, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, two fish, a Gaṅgeyya and a Yāmuneyya, were arguing based on their appearance, “I am beautiful, you are not beautiful.” Not far from there, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, they saw a tortoise lying and thought, “This one will know whether we are beautiful or not.” Approaching it, they asked, “Friend tortoise, is the Gaṅgeyya fish beautiful, or is the Yāmuneyya fish beautiful?” The tortoise, intending to declare, “The Gaṅgeyya fish is beautiful, and the Yāmuneyya fish is also beautiful, but I am even more beautiful than you both,” spoke the first verse:

109.

109.

“Sobhati [P 2.0152] maccho gaṅgeyyo, atho sobhati yāmuno;

Catuppadoyaṃ puriso, nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo;

Īsakāyatagīvo ca, sabbeva atirocatī”ti.

“The Gaṅgeyya fish is beautiful, and the Yāmuneyya fish is also beautiful; but this four-footed person, well-proportioned like a banyan tree, with a neck as long as a chariot pole—he outshines everyone.”

Tattha catuppadoyanti catuppado ayaṃ. Purisoti attānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Nigrodhaparimaṇḍaloti sujāto nigrodho viya parimaṇḍalo. Īsakāyatagīvoti rathīsā viya āyatagīvo[V 2.0126]. Sabbeva atirocatīti evaṃ saṇṭhānasampanno kacchapo sabbeva atirocati, ahameva sabbe tumhe atikkamitvā sobhāmīti vadati.

Here, “this four-footed” (catuppadoyaṃ) means this one is four-footed. “Person” (puriso) he says referring to himself. “Well-proportioned like a banyan tree” (nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo) means well-proportioned like a well-grown banyan tree. “With a neck as long as a chariot pole” (īsā-āyata-gīvo) means its neck is long like a chariot pole. “He outshines everyone” means the tortoise, endowed with such a form, outshines all, saying, “Indeed, I myself surpass all of you and am beautiful.”

Macchā tassa kathaṃ hutvā “ambho! Pāpakacchapa amhehi pucchitaṃ akathetvā aññameva kathesī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The fish, hearing his words, said, “Hey, wicked tortoise! Instead of answering what we asked, you spoke of something else!” and spoke the second verse:

110.

110.

“Yaṃ pucchito na taṃ akkhāsi, aññaṃ akkhāsi pucchito;

Atthappasaṃsako poso, nāyaṃ asmāka ruccatī”ti.

“When asked, you did not explain that which was asked; you explained something else. A self-praising person—this one does not please us.”

Tattha attappasaṃsakoti attānaṃ pasaṃsanasīlo attukkaṃsako poso. Nāyaṃ asmāka ruccatīti ayaṃ pāpakacchapo amhākaṃ na ruccati na khamatīti kacchapassa upari udakaṃ khipitvā sakaṭṭhānameva gamiṃsu.

Here, “a self-praising person” means a person whose nature is to praise himself, one who exalts himself. “Such a one does not please us” means “this wicked tortoise does not please us, it is not acceptable to us.” Then, splashing water on the tortoise, they went back to their own place.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dve macchā dve daharabhikkhū ahesuṃ, kacchapo mahallako, imassa kāraṇassa paccakkhakārikā gaṅgātīre nibbattarukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the Jātaka thus: “At that time, the two fish were the two young monks, the tortoise was the elder monk, and the tree deity who was a direct witness to this matter, reborn on the bank of the Gaṅgā, was I myself.”

Gaṅgeyyajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Gaṅgeyya Jātaka is the fifth.

[206] 6. Kuruṅgamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[206] 6. The Commentary on the Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka

Iṅgha vaṭṭamayaṃ pāsanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “devadatto vadhāya parisakkatī”ti sutvā “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi parisakkiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Come, a circular leather snare”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta. For at that time, hearing that “Devadatta is striving for my destruction,” the Teacher said, “Monks, Devadatta is not striving for my destruction only now; he strove for it in the past as well,” and then he recounted a past event.

Atīte [M 2.0140][P 2.0153] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kuruṅgamigo hutvā araññe ekassa sarassa avidūre ekasmiṃ gumbe vāsaṃ kappesi. Tasseva sarassa avidūre ekasmiṃ rukkhagge satapatto, sarasmiṃ pana kacchapo vāsaṃ kappesi. Evaṃ te tayopi sahāyakā aññamaññaṃ piyasaṃvāsaṃ vasiṃsu. Atheko migaluddako araññe caranto pānīyatitthe bodhisattassa padavalañjaṃ disvā lohanigaḷasadisaṃ vaṭṭamayaṃ pāsaṃ oḍḍetvā agamāsi. Bodhisatto pānīyaṃ pātuṃ [V 2.0127] āgato paṭhamayāmeyeva pāse bajjhitvā baddharavaṃ ravi. Tassa tena saddena rukkhaggato satapatto udakato ca kacchapo āgantvā “kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti mantayiṃsu. Atha satapatto kacchapaṃ āmantetvā “samma, tava dantā atthi, tvaṃ imaṃ pāsaṃ chinda, ahaṃ gantvā yathā so nāgacchati, tathā karissāmi, evaṃ amhehi dvīhipi kataparakkamena sahāyo no jīvitaṃ labhissatī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was an antelope and lived in a thicket in a forest not far from a certain lake. Not far from that same lake, a woodpecker lived at the top of a tree, and a tortoise lived in the lake. Thus, the three of them lived together as friends in loving companionship. Then a certain deer hunter, wandering through the forest, saw the Bodhisatta’s footprints at a watering place. He set a circular leather snare, like an iron fetter, and left. The Bodhisatta, coming to drink water in the first watch of the night, was caught in the snare and cried out the cry of one who is caught. Hearing his cry, the woodpecker from the treetop and the tortoise from the water came, and they consulted, “What is to be done?” Then the woodpecker, addressing the tortoise, said, “Friend, you have teeth; you cut this snare. I will go and act in such a way that he will not come. Thus, through the effort made by both of us, our friend will receive his life.” To explain this matter, he spoke the first verse:

111.

111.

“Iṅgha vaṭṭamayaṃ pāsaṃ, chinda dantehi kacchapa;

Ahaṃ tathā karissāmi, yathā nehiti luddako”ti.

“Come now, Tortoise, cut this circular leather snare with your teeth; I will act so that the hunter will not come.”

Atha kacchapo cammavarattaṃ khādituṃ ārabhi, satapatto luddakassa vasanagāmaṃ gato avidūre rukkhe nisīdi. Luddako paccūsakāleyeva sattiṃ gahetvā nikkhami. Sakuṇo tassa nikkhamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā vassitvā pakkhe papphoṭetvā taṃ purimadvārena nikkhamantaṃ mukhe pahari. Luddo “kāḷakaṇṇinā sakuṇenamhi pahaṭo”ti nivattitvā thokaṃ sayitvā puna sattiṃ gahetvā uṭṭhāsi. Sakuṇo “ayaṃ paṭhamaṃ purimadvārena nikkhanto idāni pacchimadvārena nikkhamissatī”ti ñatvā gantvā pacchimagehe nisīdi. Luddopi [P 2.0154] “purimadvārena me nikkhantena kāḷakaṇṇī sakuṇo diṭṭho, idāni pacchimadvārena nikkhamissāmī”ti pacchimadvārena nikkhami, sakuṇo puna vassitvā gantvā mukhe pahari. Luddo “punapi kāḷakaṇṇīsakuṇena pahaṭo, na dāni me esa nikkhamituṃ detī”ti nivattitvā yāva aruṇuggamanā sayitvā aruṇuggamanavelāya sattiṃ gahetvā nikkhami. Sakuṇo vegena gantvā “luddo āgacchatī”ti bodhisattassa kathesi.

Then the tortoise began to chew on the leather strap, while the woodpecker went to the hunter’s village and perched on a tree not far away. The hunter, at dawn, took his spear and set out. The bird, knowing he was departing, cried out, flapped its wings, and struck the hunter on the face as he was leaving through the front door. The hunter thought, “I have been struck by an ill-omened bird,” and turned back. After resting a while, he took his spear again and rose. The bird, knowing, “This one first left through the front door; now he will leave through the back door,” went and perched at the back of the house. The hunter also thought, “When I left through the front door, I saw an ill-omened bird; now I will leave through the back door,” and so he left through the back door. The bird cried out again, flew, and struck him on the face. The hunter thought, “Again I have been struck by the ill-omened bird; it will not let me leave now,” and turned back. He lay down until dawn, and at the time of dawn, he took his spear and set out. The bird went swiftly and told the Bodhisatta, “The hunter is coming.”

Tasmiṃ [M 2.0141] khaṇe kacchapena ekameva cammavaddhaṃ ṭhapetvā sesavarattā khāditā honti. Dantā panassa patanākārappattā jātā, mukhato lohitaṃ paggharati. Bodhisatto luddaputtaṃ sattiṃ gahetvā asanivegena āgacchantaṃ disvā taṃ vaddhaṃ chinditvā vanaṃ pāvisi, sakuṇo rukkhagge nisīdi, kacchapo pana dubbalattā tattheva nipajji. Luddo kacchapaṃ gahetvā pasibbake pakkhipitvā ekasmiṃ khāṇuke laggesi. Bodhisatto nivattitvā olokento kacchapassa gahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “sahāyassa jīvitadānaṃ dassāmī”ti dubbalo viya hutvā luddassa attānaṃ dassesi. So “dubbalo esa bhavissati, māressāmi na”nti sattiṃ ādāya anubandhi. Bodhisatto nātidūre nāccāsanne gacchanto taṃ ādāya araññaṃ pāvisi, dūraṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā padaṃ vañcetvā aññena maggena vātavegena gantvā siṅgena pasibbakaṃ ukkhipitvā bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā [V 2.0128] phāletvā kacchapaṃ nīhari. Satapattopi rukkhā otari. Bodhisatto dvinnampi ovādaṃ dadamāno “ahaṃ tumhe nissāya jīvitaṃ labhiṃ, tumhehi sahāyakassa kattabbaṃ mayhaṃ kataṃ, idāni luddo āgantvā tumhe gaṇheyya, tasmā, samma satapatta, tvaṃ attano puttake gahetvā aññattha yāhi, tvampi, samma kacchapa, udakaṃ pavisāhī”ti āha. Te tathā akaṃsu.

At that moment, the tortoise had gnawed through the other thongs, leaving only one leather strap. His teeth were on the verge of falling out, and blood flowed from his mouth. The Bodhisatta, seeing the hunter approaching with a spear with the speed of a thunderbolt, broke that strap and entered the forest. The woodpecker perched on a treetop, while the tortoise, being weak, lay down right there. The hunter, seizing the tortoise, placed it in a sack and hung it on a stump. The Bodhisatta, turning back and looking, realized the tortoise had been captured and thought, 'I will give the gift of life to my friend.' Pretending to be weak, he revealed himself to the hunter. The hunter thought, 'This one must be weak; I will kill him,' and took his spear to follow. The Bodhisatta, going neither too far nor too close, led him into the forest. Once he knew they had gone far, he concealed his tracks and, taking another path with the speed of the wind, lifted the sack with his horns, threw it to the ground, broke it open, and freed the tortoise. The woodpecker also descended from the tree. The Bodhisatta, giving advice to both of them, said, 'I received my life because of you. You have performed the duty of a friend for me. Now the hunter will come and might capture you. Therefore, dear woodpecker, take your young and go elsewhere. And you, dear tortoise, enter the water.' They did as instructed.

Satthā abhisambuddho hutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having become fully awakened, the Teacher spoke the second verse:

112.

112.

“Kacchapo [P 2.0155] pāvisī vāriṃ, kuruṅgo pāvisī vanaṃ;

Satapatto dumaggamhā, dūre putte apānayī”ti.

Tattha apānayīti ānayi, gahetvā agamāsīti attho;

"The tortoise entered the water, the antelope entered the forest; the woodpecker from the treetop led its young far away." Here, 'led away' (apānayī) means 'brought' (ānayi); the meaning is that having taken them, he went away.

Luddopi taṃ ṭhānaṃ āgantvā kañci apassitvā chinnapasibbakaṃ gahetvā domanassappatto attano gehaṃ agamāsi. Te tayopi sahāyā yāvajīvaṃ vissāsaṃ acchinditvā yathākammaṃ gatā.

The hunter, having arrived at that place and seeing no one, took the torn sack and, filled with sorrow, went to his own home. And those three friends, without breaking their trust for as long as they lived, passed away according to their kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā luddako devadatto ahosi, satapatto sāriputto, kacchapo moggallāno, kuruṅgamigo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: "At that time the hunter was Devadatta, the woodpecker was Sāriputta, the tortoise was Moggallāna, but the antelope was indeed myself."

Kuruṅgamigajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Kuruṅga Antelope Jātaka, the Sixth.

[207] 7. Assakajātakavaṇṇanā

[207] 7. 7. The Commentary on the Assaka Jātaka (207)

Ayamassakarājenāti [M 2.0142] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi bhikkhu satthārā “saccaṃ kira, tvaṃ bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti puṭṭho “sacca”nti vatvā “kena ukkaṇṭhāpitosī”ti vutte “purāṇadutiyikāyā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “na idāneva tassā bhikkhu itthiyā tayi sineho atthi, pubbepi tvaṃ taṃ nissāya mahādukkhaṃ patto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Ayamassakarājenāti..." This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the allurement of a former wife. When that monk was asked by the Teacher, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?" he replied, "It is true." When asked, "By whom were you made discontented?" he said, "By my former wife." Then the Teacher said to him, "Not only now, monk, does this woman have affection for you; in the past too, because of her, you experienced great suffering," and he related a past story.

Atīte kāsiraṭṭhe pāṭalinagare assako nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa uparī nāma [V 2.0129] aggamahesī piyā ahosi manāpā abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā atikkantā mānusavaṇṇaṃ, apattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ. Sā kālamakāsi, tassā kālakiriyāya rājā sokābhibhūto ahosi dukkhī dummano. So tassā sarīraṃ doṇiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā telakalalaṃ pakkhipāpetvā heṭṭhāmañce ṭhapāpetvā nirāhāro rodamāno paridevamāno nipajji. Mātāpitaro [P 2.0156] avasesañātakā mittāmaccabrāhmaṇagahapatikādayopi “mā soci, mahārāja, aniccā saṅkhārā”tiādīni vadantā saññāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tassa vilapantasseva satta divasā atikkantā. Tadā bodhisatto pañcābhiññaaṭṭhasamāpattilābhī tāpaso hutvā himavantapadese viharanto ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbena cakkhunā jambudīpaṃ olokento taṃ rājānaṃ tathā paridevamānaṃ disvā “etassa mayā avassayena bhavitabba”nti iddhānubhāvena ākāse uppatitvā rañño uyyāne otaritvā maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe kañcanapaṭimā viya nisīdi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, in the city of Pāṭali, there reigned a king named Assaka. His chief queen, named Uparī, was dear, beloved, beautiful, lovely to see, and pleasing, surpassing human beauty, though not quite attaining divine beauty. She passed away, and upon her death, the king, overwhelmed by grief, became sorrowful and despondent. He had her body placed in a trough, filled it with oil, and set it beneath his bed.
