Fasting, weeping, and lamenting, he lay there. His parents, remaining relatives, friends, ministers, brahmins, householders, and others tried to console him, saying, "Do not grieve, great king. Conditioned things are impermanent," but they could not persuade him. Seven days passed while he continued lamenting. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a gainer of the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments, was living as an ascetic in the Himalayan region. Extending his light and surveying Jambudīpa with his divine eye, he saw the king grieving in this way. Thinking, "I must certainly help him," he rose into the air by his psychic power and descended into the king's park, where he sat on an auspicious stone slab like a golden statue.

Atheko pāṭalinagaravāsī brāhmaṇamāṇavo uyyānaṃ gato bodhisattaṃ disvā vanditvā nisīdi. Bodhisatto tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kiṃ, māṇava, rājā dhammiko”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante, dhammiko rājā, bhariyā panassa kālakatā, so tassā sarīraṃ doṇiyaṃ pakkhipāpetvā vilapamāno nipanno, ajja sattamo divaso, kissa tumhe rājānaṃ evarūpā dukkhā na mocetha, yuttaṃ nu kho tumhādisesu sīlavantesu saṃvijjamānesu rañño evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavitu”nti. “Na kho ahaṃ[M 2.0143], māṇava, rājānaṃ jānāmi, sace pana so āgantvā maṃ puccheyya, ahamevassa tassā nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā rañño santikeyeva taṃ kathāpeyya”nti. “Tena hi, bhante, yāva rājānaṃ ānemi, tāva imeva nisīdathā”ti māṇavo bodhisattassa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “tassa dibbacakkhukassa santikaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha.

Then a certain young brahmin who lived in the city of Pāṭali went to the park and, upon seeing the Bodhisatta, paid homage and sat down. The Bodhisatta greeted him and asked, "Young man, is the king righteous?" "Yes, venerable sir, the king is righteous, but his wife has died. He had her body placed in a trough and lies lamenting. Today is the seventh day. Why do you not free the king from such suffering? Is it fitting that the king should experience such sorrow while virtuous ones like you are present?" "I do not know the king, young man. But if he were to come and ask me, I would tell him where she has been reborn and even make her speak in the king’s presence." "Then, venerable sir, please sit right here until I bring the king." The young man, having received the Bodhisatta’s promise, went to the king and reported the matter, saying, "It is proper to go to that one with the divine eye."

Rājā “upariṃ kira daṭṭhuṃ labhissāmī”ti tuṭṭhamānaso rathaṃ abhiruhitvā tattha gantvā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno – “saccaṃ kira tumhe deviyā nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ jānāthā”ti pucchi. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Kattha nibbattā”ti? “Sā kho, mahārāja, rūpasmiṃyeva mattā pamādamāgamma kalyāṇakammaṃ akatvā imasmiṃyeva uyyāne gomayapāṇakayoniyaṃ nibbattā”ti[P 2.0157]. “Nāhaṃ saddahāmī”ti. “Tena hi te dassetvā kathāpemī”ti. “Sādhu kathāpethā”ti. Bodhisatto attano ānubhāvena “ubhopi gomayapiṇḍaṃ vaṭṭayamānā rañño purato āgacchantū”ti tesaṃ āgamanaṃ akāsi. Te tatheva āgamiṃsu. Bodhisatto taṃ dassento “ayaṃ te[V 2.0130], mahārāja, uparidevī, taṃ jahitvā gomayapāṇakassa pacchato pacchato gacchati, passatha na”nti āha. Bhante “‘uparī nāma gomayapāṇakayoniyaṃ nibbattissatī’ti na saddahāmaha”nti. “Kathāpemi naṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Kathāpetha, bhante”ti.

The king, thinking, "It seems I will get to see Uparī," joyfully mounted his chariot and went there. He paid homage to the Bodhisatta and sat down to one side, asking, "Is it true that you know where the queen has been reborn?" "Yes, great king." "Where has she been reborn?" "Great king, being intoxicated with her own beauty and having become negligent, she did not perform meritorious deeds and has been reborn right here in this park in the womb of a dung beetle." "I do not believe it." "Then I will show her to you and make her speak." "Good, please make her speak." By his own power, the Bodhisatta caused two dung beetles, male and female, to come before the king, rolling a ball of dung. They came just so. Pointing her out, the Bodhisatta said, "Great king, this female dung beetle is your queen Uparī. Having abandoned you, she follows behind the male dung beetle. Do you not see?" "Venerable sir, I do not believe that Uparī, being who she was, would be reborn in the womb of a dung beetle." "I will make her speak, great king." "Please make her speak, venerable sir."

Bodhisatto attano ānubhāvena taṃ kathāpento “uparī”ti āha. Sā manussabhāsāya “kiṃ, bhante”ti āha. “Tvaṃ atītabhave kā nāma ahosī”ti? “Bhante, assakarañño aggamahesī uparī nāma ahosi”nti. “Kiṃ pana te idāni assakarājā piyo, udāhu gomayapāṇako”ti? “Bhante, so mayhaṃ purimajātiyā sāmiko, tadā ahaṃ imasmiṃ uyyāne tena saddhiṃ rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbe anubhavamānā vicariṃ. Idāni pana me bhavasaṅkhepagatakālato paṭṭhāya so kiṃ hoti, ahañhi idāni assakarājānaṃ māretvā tassa galalohitena mayhaṃ sāmikassa gomayapāṇakassa pāde makkheyya”nti vatvā parisamajjhe manussabhāsāya imā gāthā avoca –

The Bodhisatta, by his own power, caused her to speak, calling her 'Uparī.' She, in human speech, replied, 'What is it, venerable sir?' 'What was your name in a past life?' 'Venerable sir, I was the chief queen of King Assaka, named Uparī.' 'But now, is King Assaka dear to you, or the male dung beetle?' 'Venerable sir, King Assaka was my husband in my previous life. At that time, I wandered in this garden with him, enjoying sights, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangible objects. But now, since that existence has ended, what is King Assaka to me? Indeed, I would now kill King Assaka and smear the feet of my husband, the male dung beetle, with the blood from his throat.' Having said this, in the midst of the assembly, she spoke these verses in human speech:

113.

113.

“Ayamassakarājena[M 2.0144], deso vicarito mayā;

Anukāmaya kāmena, piyena patinā saha.

13. "With King Assaka, my beloved husband, I traversed this land, in mutual desire."

114.

114.

“Navena sukhadukkhena, porāṇaṃ apidhīyati;

Tasmā assakaraññāva, kīṭo piyataro mamā”ti.

14. "By new happiness and suffering, the old is covered over; therefore, the beetle is dearer to me than even King Assaka."

Tattha ayamassakarājena, deso vicarito mayāti ayaṃ ramaṇīyo uyyānapadeso pubbe mayā assakarājena saddhiṃ vicarito. Anukāmaya kāmenāti anūti nipātamattaṃ, mayā taṃ kāmayamānāya tena maṃ kāmayamānena [P 2.0158] sahāti attho. Piyenāti tasmiṃ attabhāve piyena. Navena sukhadukkhena, porāṇaṃ apidhīyatīti, bhante, navena hi sukhena porāṇaṃ sukhaṃ, navena ca dukkhena porāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ pidhīyati paṭicchādīyati, esā lokassa dhammatāti dīpeti. Tasmā assakaraññāva, kīṭo piyataro mamāti yasmā navena porāṇaṃ pidhīyati, tasmā mama assakarājato sataguṇena sahassaguṇena kīṭova piyataroti.

Herein, 'With King Assaka, I traversed this land' means this delightful garden region was formerly traversed by me with King Assaka. 'In mutual desire'—'anu' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'with him desiring me as I was desiring him.' 'With my beloved' means beloved in that existence. 'By new happiness and suffering, the old is covered over'—venerable sir, by new happiness, old happiness is covered over, and by new suffering, old suffering is covered over, concealed; this shows that this is the nature of the world. 'Therefore, the beetle is dearer to me than even King Assaka'—because the new covers over the old, therefore the beetle is a hundredfold, a thousandfold dearer to me than King Assaka.

Taṃ sutvā assakarājā vippaṭisārī hutvā tattha ṭhitova kuṇapaṃ nīharāpetvā sīsaṃ nhatvā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā aññaṃ aggamahesiṃ katvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Bodhisattopi rājānaṃ ovaditvā nissokaṃ katvā himavantameva agamāsi.

Hearing this, King Assaka, filled with remorse, while standing right there, had the corpse removed, washed his head, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, entered the city, appointed another chief queen, and ruled the kingdom righteously. The Bodhisatta, having advised the king and freed him from sorrow, went to the Himalayas.

Satthā [V 2.0131] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā uparī purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, assakarājā ukkaṇṭhito bhikkhu, māṇavo sāriputto, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, illuminated the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the discourse on the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. 'At that time, Uparī was the former wife, King Assaka was the discontented monk, the young man was Sāriputta, and the ascetic was indeed I myself.'

Assakajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Assaka Jātaka, the Seventh.

[208] 8. Susumārajātakavaṇṇanā

[208] 8. 8. Susumāra Jātaka: The Monkey and the Crocodile

Alaṃ [M 2.0145] metehi ambehīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “devadatto vadhāya parisakkatī”ti sutvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi parisakkiyeva, santāsamattampi pana kātuṃ na sakkhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Enough with these mangoes!" This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Devadatta’s striving to murder him. At that time, the Teacher, hearing that "Devadatta is striving for my murder," said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta strives for my murder; he strove for it in the past as well. Yet he was not able to cause even the slightest fear." Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente himavantapadese bodhisatto kapiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā nāgabalo thāmasampanno mahāsarīro sobhaggappatto hutvā gaṅgānivattane araññāyatane vāsaṃ kappesi. Tadā gaṅgāya eko susumāro vasi. Athassa bhariyā bodhisattassa sarīraṃ disvā [P 2.0159] tassa hadayamaṃse dohaḷaṃ uppādetvā susumāraṃ āha – “ahaṃ sāmi, etassa kapirājassa hadayamaṃsaṃ khāditukāmā”ti. “Bhadde, mayaṃ jalagocarā, eso thalagocaro, kinti naṃ gaṇhituṃ sakkhissāmā”ti. “Yena kenaci upāyena gaṇha, sace na labhissāmi, marissāmī”ti. “Tena hi mā soci, attheko upāyo, khādāpessāmi taṃ tassa hadayamaṃsa”nti susumāriṃ samassāsetvā bodhisattassa gaṅgāya pānīyaṃ pivitvā gaṅgātīre nisinnakāle santikaṃ gantvā evamāha – “vānarinda, imasmiṃ padese kasāyaphalāni khādanto kiṃ tvaṃ niviṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva carasi, pāragaṅgāya ambalabujādīnaṃ madhuraphalānaṃ anto natthi, kiṃ te tattha gantvā phalāphalaṃ khādituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti? “Kumbhīlarāja, gaṅgā mahodakā vitthiṇṇā, kathaṃ tattha gamissāmī”ti? “Sace icchasi, ahaṃ taṃ mama piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā nessāmī”ti. So saddahitvā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. “Tena hi ehi piṭṭhiṃ me abhirūhā”ti ca vutte taṃ abhiruhi. Susumāro thokaṃ netvā udake osīdāpesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a monkey in the Himalayan region. Possessing the strength of an elephant, endowed with great power, having a massive body, and being of perfect beauty, he lived in a forest haunt at a bend of the Ganges. At that time, a certain crocodile lived in the Ganges. His wife, seeing the Bodhisatta’s body, conceived a craving for his heart-flesh and said to the crocodile, 'My lord, I wish to eat the heart-flesh of this monkey-king.' 'My dear, we are water-dwellers, while he is a land-dweller. How can we possibly catch him?' 'Catch him by any means whatsoever. If I do not get it, I shall die.' 'Then do not grieve; there is a way. I will have you eat his heart-flesh.' Having comforted his wife, the crocodile approached the Bodhisatta when he was sitting on the bank of the Ganges after drinking water and said, 'King of monkeys, why do you remain in this one place, eating astringent fruits in this region? On the other side of the Ganges, there is no end to sweet fruits such as mangoes and jackfruits. Is it not fitting for you to go there and eat various fruits?' 'King of crocodiles, the Ganges is full of water and wide; how shall I get there?' 'If you wish, I will carry you there on my back.' Trusting him, he agreed, saying, 'Very well.' When the crocodile said, 'Then come, climb onto my back,' he climbed on. The crocodile carried him a short distance and then began to sink him into the water.

Bodhisatto “samma, udake maṃ osīdāpesi, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti āha. “Nāhaṃ taṃ dhammasudhammatāya gahetvā gacchāmi, bhariyāya pana me tava hadayamaṃse dohaḷo uppanno, tamahaṃ tava [V 2.0132] hadayaṃ khādāpetukāmo”ti. “Samma, kathentena te sundaraṃ kataṃ. Sace hi amhākaṃ udare hadayaṃ bhaveyya, sākhaggesu carantānaṃ cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ bhaveyyā”ti. “Kahaṃ pana tumhe ṭhapethā”ti? Bodhisatto [M 2.0146] avidūre ekaṃ udumbaraṃ pakkaphalapiṇḍisañchannaṃ dassento “passetāni amhākaṃ hadayāni etasmiṃ udumbare olambantī”ti āha. “Sace me hadayaṃ [P 2.0160] dassasi, ahaṃ taṃ na māressāmī”ti. “Tena hi maṃ ettha nehi, ahaṃ te rukkhe olambantaṃ dassāmī”ti. So taṃ ādāya tattha agamāsi. Bodhisatto tassa piṭṭhito uppatitvā udumbararukkhe nisīditvā “samma, bāla susumāra, ‘imesaṃ sattānaṃ hadayaṃ nāma rukkhagge hotī’ti saññī ahosi, bālosi, ahaṃ taṃ vañcesiṃ, tava phalāphalaṃ taveva hotu, sarīrameva pana te mahantaṃ paññā pana natthī”ti vatvā imamatthaṃ pakāsento imā gāthā avoca –

The Bodhisatta said, 'Friend, you are making me sink in the water. What is the reason for this?' 'I am not carrying you out of pure righteousness. Rather, my wife has conceived a craving for your heart-flesh, and I want to have her eat your heart.' 'Friend, you have done well to speak of it. For if our hearts were in our bellies, they would be crushed to powder as we leap among the treetops.' 'Then where do you keep them?' The Bodhisatta, pointing to a nearby fig tree covered with clusters of ripe fruit, said, 'Behold, our hearts are hanging on that fig tree.' 'If you give me your heart, I will not kill you.' 'Then take me there, and I will give you the heart hanging on the tree.' The crocodile took him there. The Bodhisatta, leaping from his back, perched on the fig tree and said, 'Friend, foolish crocodile, you perceived that the hearts of these beings are in the treetops. You are a fool; I have deceived you. Your body is indeed large, but you have no wisdom.' Saying this to clarify the matter, he spoke these verses:

115.

115.

“Alaṃ metehi ambehi, jambūhi panasehi ca;

Yāni pāraṃ samuddassa, varaṃ mayhaṃ udumbaro.

"Enough for me are those mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits that are on the other side of the river; better for me is the fig tree."

116.

116.

“Mahatī vata te bondi, na ca paññā tadūpikā;

Susumāra vañcito mesi, gaccha dāni yathāsukha”nti.

"Great indeed is your body, but your wisdom is not its equal. O crocodile, you have been deceived by me; now go as you please."

Tattha alaṃ metehīti yāni tayā dīpake niddiṭṭhāni, etehi mayhaṃ alaṃ. Varaṃ mayhaṃ udumbaroti mayhaṃ ayameva udumbararukkho varaṃ. Bondīti sarīraṃ. Tadūpikāti paññā pana te tadūpikā tassa sarīrassa anucchavikā natthi. Gaccha dāni yathāsukhanti idāni yathāsukhaṃ gaccha, natthi te hadayamaṃsagahaṇūpāyoti attho. Susumāro sahassaṃ parājito viya dukkhī dummano pajjhāyantova attano nivāsaṭṭhānameva gato.

Herein, 'Enough with these' means: those fruits which you pointed out on the island, I have had enough of them. 'Better for me is the fig tree' means this very fig tree is better for me. 'Body' (bondi) means the body. 'Not its equal' (tadūpikā) means your wisdom is not commensurate with or suitable for that body. 'Now go as you please' means go now as you wish; the meaning is that you have no way to seize my heart-flesh. The crocodile, like one who has lost a thousand pieces of money, miserable and dejected, went back to his own dwelling place brooding.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā susumāro devadatto ahosi, susumārī ciñcamāṇavikā, kapirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the birth story: "At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, the female crocodile was Ciñcamāṇavikā, but the monkey-king was indeed myself."

Susumārajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Susumāra Jātaka, the eighth.

[209] 9. Kukkuṭajātakavaṇṇanā

[209] 9. The Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka

Diṭṭhā [V 2.0133][M 2.0147] mayā vane rukkhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherassa saddhivihārikaṃ daharabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira attano sarīrassa guttikamme cheko [P 2.0161] ahosi. “Sarīrassa me na sukhaṃ bhaveyyā”ti bhayena atisītaṃ accuṇhaṃ paribhogaṃ na karoti, “sītuṇhehi sarīraṃ kilameyyā”ti bhayena bahi na nikkhamati, atikilinnauttaṇḍulādīni na bhuñjati. Tassa sā sarīraguttikusalatā saṅghamajjhe pākaṭā jātā. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko daharo kira bhikkhu sarīraguttikamme cheko”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, ayaṃ daharo idāneva sarīraguttikamme cheko, pubbepi chekova ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“I have seen trees in the forest”—this the Teacher, dwelling in Jetavana, spoke concerning a young monk, a co-resident of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma. He was indeed skilled in the care of his own body. Fearing that his body might not be comfortable, he did not use things that were too cold or too hot; fearing that his body might be distressed by cold and heat, he did not go outside; he did not eat overly soggy or undercooked rice, and so forth. His skill in bodily care became well-known among the Saṅgha. The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, it seems that a certain young monk is skilled in bodily care.” When the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together?” and they replied, “About this matter,” he said, “Monks, this young one is not skilled in bodily care only now; he was skilled in the past as well,” and then he recounted the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññāyatane rukkhadevatā ahosi. Atheko sakuṇaluddako ekaṃ dīpakakukkuṭamādāya vālarajjuñca yaṭṭhiñca gahetvā araññe kukkuṭe bandhanto ekaṃ palāyitvā araññaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ porāṇakukkuṭaṃ bandhituṃ ārabhi. So vālapāse kusalatāya attānaṃ bandhituṃ na deti, uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya nilīyati. Luddako attānaṃ sākhāpallavehi paṭicchādetvā punappunaṃ yaṭṭhiñca pāsañca oḍḍeti. Kukkuṭo taṃ lajjāpetukāmo mānusiṃ vācaṃ nicchāretvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in a forest region. At that time, a bird-catcher, taking a decoy rooster, a hair-snare, and a rod, was in the forest snaring roosters. He began to try to catch an old rooster that had escaped and entered the forest. Skilled with hair-snares, it did not allow itself to be caught, but kept rising up and hiding. The hunter, concealing himself with branches and leaves, repeatedly set his rod and snare. Wishing to shame him, the rooster uttered human speech and spoke the first verse:

117.

117.

“Diṭṭhā mayā vane rukkhā, assakaṇṇā vibhīṭakā;

Na tāni evaṃ sakkanti, yathā tvaṃ rukkha sakkasī”ti.

“I have seen trees in the forest, assakaṇṇas and vibhīṭakas; they are not able to move about as you, O tree, are able to move about.”

Tassattho – samma luddaka, mayā imasmiṃ vane jātā bahū assakaṇṇā ca vibhīṭakā ca rukkhā diṭṭhapubbā, tāni pana rukkhāni yathā tvaṃ sakkasi saṅkamasi ito cito ca vicarasi, evaṃ na sakkanti na saṅkamanti na vicarantīti.

The meaning is: “Friend hunter, I have seen many assakaṇṇa and vibhīṭaka trees born in this forest before. But those trees are not able to move about, to shift, to wander here and there, as you are able to move about, to shift, and to wander here and there.”

Evaṃ vatvā ca pana so kukkuṭo palāyitvā aññattha agamāsi. Tassa palāyitvā gatakāle luddako dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, the rooster fled and went elsewhere. After it had fled and gone, the hunter spoke a second verse:

118.

118.

“Porāṇakukkuṭo [V 2.0134][P 2.0162][M 2.0148] ayaṃ, bhetvā pañjaramāgato;

Kusalo vālapāsānaṃ, apakkamati bhāsatī”ti.

“This is an old rooster; having broken its cage, it has come. Skilled with hair-snares, it departs while speaking.”

Tattha kusalo vālapāsānanti vālamayesu pāsesu kusalo attānaṃ bandhituṃ adatvā apakkamati ceva bhāsati ca, bhāsitvā ca pana palātoti evaṃ vatvā luddako araññe caritvā yathāladdhamādāya gehameva gato.

Therein, “skilled with hair-snares” means skilled with snares made of hair; not allowing itself to be caught, it departs and speaks, and having spoken, it fled. Thus saying, the hunter, having wandered in the forest and taken what he obtained, went home.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā luddako devadatto ahosi, kukkuṭo kāyaguttikusalo daharabhikkhu, tassa pana kāraṇassa paccakkhakārikā rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the birth story: “At that time, the hunter was Devadatta, the rooster was the young monk skilled in guarding himself, and the tree deity who witnessed that incident was none other than myself.”

Kukkuṭajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka, the ninth.

[210] 10. Kandagalakajātakavaṇṇanā

[210] 10. The Commentary on the Kandagalaka Jātaka

Ambho ko nāmayaṃ rukkhoti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto sugatālayaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “devadatto sugatālayaṃ akāsī”ti sutvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto mayhaṃ anukiriyaṃ karonto vināsaṃ patto, pubbepi pāpuṇiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Friend, what is this tree?”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning [Devadatta's] imitation of the Sugata. At that time, having heard that “Devadatta had imitated the Sugata,” the Teacher said, “Not only now, monks, has Devadatta met with ruin by imitating me; even in the past he met with it,” and he recounted a past incident.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese rukkhakoṭṭakasakuṇayoniyaṃ nibbatti, “khadiravaniyo”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So khadiravaneyeva gocaraṃ gaṇhi, tasseko kandagalako nāma sahāyo ahosi, so simbalipālibhaddakavane gocaraṃ gaṇhāti. So ekadivasaṃ khadiravaniyassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Khadiravaniyo “sahāyo me āgato”ti kandagalakaṃ gahetvā khadiravanaṃ pavisitvā khadirakhandhaṃ tuṇḍena paharitvā rukkhato pāṇake nīharitvā adāsi. Kandagalako dinne dinne madhurapūve viya chinditvā chinditvā khādi. Tassa khādantasseva māno uppajji – “ayampi [P 2.0163] rukkhakoṭṭakayoniyaṃ nibbatto, ahampi, kiṃ me etena dinnagocarena, sayameva khadiravane gocaraṃ [M 2.0149] gaṇhissāmī”ti. So khadiravaniyaṃ āha – “samma, mā tvaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavi, ahameva khadiravane gocaraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a woodpecker in the Himalayan region, and his name was Khadiravaniya. He took his feeding ground in the acacia forest itself. He had a friend named Kandagalaka, who took his feeding ground in the silk-cotton and coral tree forests. One day, Kandagalaka came to Khadiravaniya. Khadiravaniya, thinking, “My friend has come,” took Kandagalaka, entered the acacia forest, struck an acacia trunk with his beak, extracted insects from the tree, and gave them to him. Kandagalaka, as he ate what was given, broke it up bit by bit as if it were a sweet cake. As he was eating, pride arose in him: “He too is born as a woodpecker, and so am I. What need have I of this food given by him? I myself will take my feeding ground in the acacia forest.” So he said to Khadiravaniya, “Friend, do not trouble yourself; I myself will take my feeding ground in the acacia forest.”

Atha [V 2.0135] naṃ so “handa tvaṃ samma, simbalipālibhaddakādivane nissāre gocaraggahaṇakule jāto, khadirā nāma jātasārā thaddhā, mā te etaṃ ruccī”ti āha. Kandagalako “kiṃ dānāhaṃ na rukkhakoṭṭakayoniyaṃ nibbatto”ti tassa vacanaṃ anādiyitvā vegena gantvā khadirarukkhaṃ tuṇḍena pahari. Tāvadevassa tuṇḍaṃ bhijji, akkhīni nikkhamanākārappattāni jātāni, sīsaṃ phalitaṃ. So khandhe patiṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto bhūmiyaṃ patitvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then he said to him, “Come now, friend, you were born in a family that takes its feeding ground in sapless forests like those of the silk-cotton and coral tree. Acacia trees, however, have developed heartwood and are tough; this will not suit you.” Kandagalaka, disregarding his words, thinking, “Am I not also born as a woodpecker?” quickly went and struck an acacia tree with his beak. Immediately his beak broke, his eyes looked as if they were about to come out, and his head split. Unable to stand on the trunk, he fell to the ground and spoke the first verse:

119.

119.

“Ambho ko nāmayaṃ rukkho, sinnapatto sakaṇṭako;

Yattha ekappahārena, uttamaṅgaṃ vibhijjita”nti.

“Friend, what is this tree, with fine leaves and thorns, where with a single strike, my head is split apart?”

Tattha ambho ko nāmayaṃ rukkhoti, bho khadiravaniya, ko nāma ayaṃ rukkho. “Ko nāma so”tipi pāṭho. Sinnapattoti sukhumapatto. Yattha ekappahārenāti yasmiṃ rukkhe ekeneva pahārena. Uttamaṅgaṃ vibhijjitanti sīsaṃ bhinnaṃ, na kevalañca sīsaṃ, tuṇḍampi bhinnaṃ. So vedanāppattatāya khadirarukkhaṃ “kiṃ rukkho nāmeso”ti jānituṃ asakkonto vedanāppatto hutvā imāya gāthāya vippalapi.

Therein, “Friend, what is this tree?” means, “O Khadiravaniya, what is this tree?” “What is its name?” is also a reading. “With fine leaves” means with delicate leaves. “Where with a single strike” means “on which tree with just a single strike.” “The head is split apart” means “the head was broken,” and not only the head, but the beak was also broken. Overcome by pain, unable to recognize the acacia tree, he lamented with this verse in his suffering.

Taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā khadiravaniyo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing those words, Khadiravaniya spoke a second verse:

120.

120.

“Acāri vatāyaṃ vitudaṃ vanāni, kaṭṭhaṅgarukkhesu asārakesu;

Athāsadā khadiraṃ jātasāraṃ, yatthabbhidā garuḷo uttamaṅga”nti.

“Indeed, this one wandered, pecking in the forests among sapless trees that are mere wood; then he encountered the acacia, which has developed heartwood, where the bird smashed its head.”

Tattha [P 2.0164] acāri vatāyanti acari vata ayaṃ. Vitudaṃ vanānīti nissārasimbalipālibhaddakavanāni vitudanto vijjhanto. Kaṭṭhaṅgarukkhesūti vanakaṭṭhakoṭṭhāsesu rukkhesu. Asārakesūti nissāresu pālibhaddakasimbaliādīsu. Athāsadā khadiraṃ jātasāranti atha potakakālato paṭṭhāya jātasāraṃ khadiraṃ sampāpuṇi. Yatthabbhidā garuḷo uttamaṅganti yatthabbhidāti yasmiṃ khadire abhindi padālayi. Garuḷoti sakuṇo. Sabbasakuṇānañhetaṃ sagāravasappatissa vacanaṃ.

Herein, 'Indeed, this one wandered' (acāri vatāyaṃ) means this one roamed. 'Pecking in the forests' (vitudaṃ vanāni) means pecking and piercing through the pithless silk-cotton and coral-tree forests. 'Among trees that are mere wood' (kaṭṭhaṅgarukkhesu) means among trees that are just piles of forest wood. 'In the worthless ones' (asārakesu) means in the pithless coral-trees, silk-cottons, and so forth. 'Then he encountered the Khadira which has heartwood' (athāsadā khadiraṃ jātasāraṃ) means then, from the time it was a sapling, he reached a Khadira tree that had developed heartwood. 'Where the bird smashed its head' (yatthabbhidā garuḷo uttamaṅgaṃ): 'where he smashed' (yatthabbhidā) means on which Khadira tree he broke and shattered his head. 'The bird' (garuḷo) means a bird (sakuṇo); for this is a term of respect and deference used for all birds.

Iti [M 2.0150] naṃ khadiravaniyo vatvā “bho kandagalaka, yattha tvaṃ uttamaṅgaṃ abhindi, khadiro nāmeso sārarukkho”ti āha. So tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi.

Thus Khadiravaniya spoke to him, saying, 'Friend Kandagalaka, the tree where you broke your head is called the Khadira, a tree with heartwood.' He met the end of his life right there.

Satthā [V 2.0136] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kandagalako devadatto ahosi, khadiravaniyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, Kandagalaka was Devadatta, and Khadiravaniya was I myself.'

Kandagalakajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Kandagalaka Jātaka, the Tenth.

Nataṃdaḷhavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Nataṃdaḷha Chapter, the Sixth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Bandhanāgāraṃ keḷisīlaṃ, khaṇḍaṃ vīrakagaṅgeyyaṃ;

Kuruṅgamassakañceva, susumārañca kukkuṭaṃ;

Kandagalakanti te dasa.

The Prison, the Playful, the Fragment, Vīraka, Gaṅgeyya, Kuruṅga and Assaka, the Crocodile and the Rooster, and Kandagalaka—these are the ten.

7. Bīraṇathambhavaggo

7. The Chapter on the Clump of Bīraṇa Grass

[211] 1. Somadattajātakavaṇṇanā

[211] 1. The Commentary on the Somadatta Jātaka

Akāsi [V 2.0137] yogganti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lāḷudāyittheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ antare ekavacanampi sampādetvā kathesuṃ na sakkoti, sārajjabahulo “aññaṃ kathessāmī”ti aññameva kathesi. Tassa taṃ pavattiṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha[P 2.0165], bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, lāḷudāyī idāneva sārajjabahulo, pubbepi sārajjabahuloyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'He performed the training...' The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the elder Lāludāyī. For he was unable to complete even a single sentence in the presence of two or three people; being very timid, while intending to say one thing, he would say something else entirely. The monks were sitting in the Hall of Dhamma discussing this behavior of his. The Teacher arrived and asked, 'For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered together?' When it was said, 'Concerning this matter,' he replied, 'Monks, it is not only now that Lāludāyī is very timid; he was very timid in the past as well,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe aññatarasmiṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā puna gehaṃ āgantvā mātāpitūnaṃ duggatabhāvaṃ ñatvā “parihīnakulato seṭṭhikulaṃ patiṭṭhapessāmī”ti mātāpitaro āpucchitvā [M 2.0151] bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rājānaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. So raññā piyo ahosi manāpo. Athassa pituno “dvīhiyeva goṇehi kasiṃ katvā jīvikaṃ kappentassa eko goṇo mato. So bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tāta, eko goṇo mato, kasikammaṃ na pavattati, rājānaṃ ekaṃ goṇaṃ yācāhī”ti āha. “Tāta, nacirasseva me rājā diṭṭho, idāneva goṇaṃ yācituṃ na yuttaṃ, tumhe yācathā”ti. “Tāta, tvaṃ mayhaṃ sārajjabahulabhāvaṃ na jānāsi, ahañhi dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sammukhe kathaṃ sampādetuṃ na sakkomi. Sace ahaṃ rañño santikaṃ goṇaṃ yācituṃ gamissāmi, imampi datvā āgamissāmī”ti. “Tāta, yaṃ hoti, taṃ hotu, na sakkā mayā rājānaṃ yācituṃ, apica kho panāhaṃ tumhe yoggaṃ kāressāmī”ti. “Tena hi sādhu maṃ yoggaṃ kārehī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. Having come of age, he learned the arts at Takkasilā and then returned home. Realizing his parents' poverty, he thought, 'I will re-establish our fallen family as a wealthy one.' Taking leave of his parents, he went to Bārāṇasī and entered the king's service. He became dear and pleasing to the king. Now, his father, who made his living by farming with just two oxen, had one ox die. He approached the Bodhisatta and said, 'Son, one ox has died, and the farm work cannot proceed. Ask the king for an ox.' 'Father, I have only known the king for a short time; it is not proper to ask for an ox right now. You ask.' 'Son, you do not know how very timid I am. I cannot manage to complete a speech in front of two or three people. If I go to the king's presence to ask for an ox, I might even give away this remaining one and return.' 'Father, let it be as it may. I cannot ask the king, but I will train you.' 'In that case, very well, train me.'

Bodhisatto pitaraṃ ādāya bīraṇatthambhakasusānaṃ gantvā tattha tattha tiṇakalāpe bandhitvā “ayaṃ rājā, ayaṃ uparājā, ayaṃ senāpatī”ti nāmāni katvā paṭipāṭiyā pitu dassetvā “tāta, tvaṃ rañño santikaṃ gantvā ‘jayatu, mahārājā’ti evaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā goṇaṃ yāceyyāsī”ti gāthaṃ uggaṇhāpesi –

The Bodhisatta, taking his father, went to a cemetery named Bīraṇatthambaka. There he tied bundles of grass here and there and gave them names, saying, 'This is the king, this is the viceroy, this is the commander of the army,' and showed them in order to his father. He said, 'Father, you should go into the king's presence, say, "May the great king be victorious," and then ask for an ox by reciting this verse.' Then he had him learn the verse:

“Dve [V 2.0138] me goṇā mahārāja, yehi khettaṃ kasāmase;

Tesu eko mato deva, dutiyaṃ dehi khattiyā”ti.

“I have two oxen, O great king, with which we plow the field. Of those, one is dead, O Lord; give me a second, O Khattiya.”

Brāhmaṇo [P 2.0166] ekena saṃvaccharena imaṃ gāthaṃ paguṇaṃ katvā bodhisattaṃ āha – “tāta, somadatta, gāthā me paguṇā jātā, idāni ahaṃ yassa kassaci santike vattuṃ sakkomi, maṃ rañño santikaṃ nehī”ti. So “sādhu, tātā”ti tathārūpaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ gāhāpetvā pitaraṃ rañño santikaṃ nesi. Brāhmaṇo “jayatu, mahārājā”ti vatvā paṇṇākāraṃ adāsi. Rājā “ayaṃ te somadatta brāhmaṇo kiṃ hotī”ti āha. “Pitā me, mahārājā”ti. “Kenaṭṭhenāgato”ti? Tasmiṃ khaṇe brāhmaṇo goṇayācanatthāya gāthaṃ vadanto –

The brahmin, having mastered this verse over the course of a single year, said to the Bodhisatta, 'Son Somadatta, the verse has become fluent for me; now I am able to recite it in the presence of anyone at all. Take me to the king's presence.' He replied, 'Very well, father,' and having brought a suitable gift, he led his father to the king's presence. The brahmin, saying, 'May the great king be victorious,' presented the gift. The king asked, 'Somadatta, what is this brahmin to you?' 'He is my father, great king.' 'For what reason has he come?' At that moment, the brahmin, for the purpose of requesting an ox, spoke this verse:

“Dve me goṇā mahārāja, yehi khettaṃ kasāmase;

Tesu eko mato deva, dutiyaṃ gaṇha khattiyā”ti. – āha;

“I have two oxen, O great king, with which we plow the field. Of those, one has died, O Lord; take the second, O Khattiya.”

Rājā brāhmaṇena virajjhitvā kathitabhāvaṃ ñatvā sitaṃ katvā “somadatta, tumhākaṃ gehe bahū maññe goṇā”ti āha. “Tumhehi dinnā [M 2.0152] bhavissanti, mahārājā”ti. Rājā bodhisattassa tussitvā brāhmaṇassa soḷasa goṇe alaṅkārabhaṇḍake nivāsanagāmañcassa brahmadeyyaṃ datvā mahantena yasena brāhmaṇaṃ uyyojesi. Brāhmaṇo sabbasetasindhavayuttaṃ rathaṃ abhiruyha mahantena parivārena gāmaṃ agamāsi. Bodhisatto pitarā saddhiṃ rathe nisīditvā gacchanto “tāta, ahaṃ tumhe sakalasaṃvaccharaṃ yoggaṃ kāresiṃ, sanniṭṭhānakāle pana tumhākaṃ goṇaṃ rañño adatthā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, realizing that the brahmin had spoken in error, smiled and said, 'Somadatta, I suppose there are many oxen in your house.' 'They will be numerous, great king, being given by you,' Somadatta replied. The king, pleased with the Bodhisatta, gave the brahmin sixteen oxen, ornaments, and his place of residence as a royal grant, and sent the brahmin away with great honor. The brahmin, mounting a chariot yoked with all-white Sindh horses, went to the village with a large retinue. The Bodhisatta, seated with his father in the chariot as they were going, said, 'Father, I had you practice for a whole year; yet when the time came to conclude the request, you gave your ox to the king,' and he spoke this first verse:

121.

121.

“Akāsi yoggaṃ dhuvamappamatto, saṃvaccharaṃ bīraṇathambhakasmiṃ;

Byākāsi saññaṃ parisaṃ vigayha, na niyyamo tāyati appapañña”nti.

“Diligent and steadfast, you practiced the training for a year amidst the clumps of bīraṇa grass. Yet having entered the assembly, you confused the message; such discipline does not protect one of little wisdom.”

Tattha akāsi yoggaṃ dhuvamappamatto, saṃvaccharaṃ bīraṇathambhakasminti, tāta, tvaṃ niccaṃ appamatto bīraṇatthambhamaye susāne yoggaṃ akāsi[P 2.0167]. Byākāsi saññaṃ parisaṃ vigayhāti atha ca pana parisaṃ vigāhitvā taṃ saññaṃ viakāsi vikāraṃ āpādesi, parivattesīti attho. Na niyyamo tāyati appapaññanti appahaññaṃ nāma puggalaṃ niyyamo yoggāciṇṇaṃ caraṇaṃ na tāyati na rakkhatīti.

Therein, 'You undertook the training, steadfast and diligent, for a year amidst the clumps of bīraṇa grass' means: Son, you practiced the training constantly and diligently in the bīraṇa-thambhakas cemetery. 'Yet having plunged into the assembly, you altered your intention' means: and yet, having entered the assembly, you altered that perception, you produced a change, you transformed it—that is the meaning. 'Such practice does not protect one of little wisdom' means: the regular training, the conduct of that practice, does not save, does not protect, a person of little wisdom.

Athassa [V 2.0139] vacanaṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having heard the Bodhisatta's words, the brahmin spoke the second verse:

122.

122.

“Dvayaṃ yācanako tāta, somadatta nigacchati;

Alābhaṃ dhanalābhaṃ vā, evaṃdhammā hi yācanā”ti.

“A petitioner, my son Somadatta, meets with two outcomes: either the failure to gain wealth, or the gain of wealth. For such is the nature of asking.”

Tattha evaṃdhammā hi yācanāti yācanā hi evaṃsabhāvāti.

Therein, 'For such is the nature of asking' means: for asking is truly of such a nature.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, lāḷudāyī idāneva sārajjabahulo, pubbepi sārajjabahuloyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando, somadattassa pitā lāḷudāyī ahosi, somadatto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, saying, 'Monks, it is not only now that Lāḷudāyī is very timid; he was very timid in the past as well,' delivered this discourse on the Dhamma and connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the king was Ānanda, the father of Somadatta was Lāḷudāyī, and Somadatta was I myself.'

Somadattajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Somadatta Jātaka is finished.

[212] 2. Ucchiṭṭhabhattajātakavaṇṇanā

[212] 2. 2. Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka

(The Brahmin and the Leftover Food)

Añño [M 2.0153] uparimo vaṇṇoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi bhikkhu satthārā “saccaṃ kira, tvaṃ bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti puṭṭho “sacca”nti vatvā “ko taṃ ukkaṇṭhāpesī”ti vutte “purāṇadutiyikā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “bhikkhu ayaṃ te itthī anatthakārikā, pubbepi attano jārassa ucchiṭṭhakaṃ bhojesī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Another color above...' The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the enticement by a former wife. That monk, when asked by the Teacher, 'Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?' replied, 'It is true.' When he was asked, 'Who has caused you to be dissatisfied?' he said, 'My former wife.' Then the Teacher said to him, 'Monk, this woman is only a doer of harm for you. In the past, also, she fed you the leftovers of her lover,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ ṭhāne bhikkhaṃ caritvā jīvikakappake kapaṇe naṭakakule nibbattitvā vayappatto duggato durūpako hutvā bhikkhaṃ caritvā jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tadā kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ gāmake ekassa brāhmaṇassa brāhmaṇī dussīlā pāpadhammā aticāraṃ carati. Athekadivasaṃ brāhmaṇe kenacideva karaṇīyena [P 2.0168] bahi gate tassā jāro taṃ khaṇaṃ oloketvā taṃ gehaṃ pāvisi. Sā tena saddhiṃ aticaritvā “muhuttaṃ accha, bhuñjitvāva gamissasī”ti bhattaṃ sampādetvā sūpabyañjanasampannaṃ uṇhabhattaṃ vaḍḍhetvā “tvaṃ bhuñjā”ti tassa datvā sayaṃ brāhmaṇassa āgamanaṃ olokayamānā dvāre aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto brāhmaṇiyā jārassa bhuñjanaṭṭhāne piṇḍaṃ paccāsīsanto aṭṭhāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor, ugly family of dancers who made their living by begging. Having come of age, he was destitute and ill-favored, and made his living by wandering for food. At that time, in a small village in the Kāsi country, the wife of a certain brahmin was immoral. She committed adultery with a lover. One day, while the brahmin had gone out, she prepared a meal, served hot rice with curries and sauces, and gave it to her lover, saying, “Wait a moment, eat first.” While she herself stood at the door watching for the brahmin’s return, the Bodhisatta stood waiting for food at the place where the lover was eating.

Tasmiṃ [V 2.0140] khaṇe brāhmaṇo gehābhimukho āgacchati. Brāhmaṇī taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā vegena pavisitvā “uṭṭhehi, brāhmaṇo āgacchatī”ti jāraṃ koṭṭhe otāretvā brāhmaṇassa pavisitvā nisinnakāle phalakaṃ upanetvā hatthadhovanaṃ datvā itarena bhuttāvasiṭṭhassa sītabhattassa upari uṇhabhattaṃ vaḍḍhetvā brāhmaṇassa adāsi. So bhatte hatthaṃ otāretvā upari uṇhaṃ heṭṭhā ca bhattaṃ sītalaṃ disvā cintesi – “iminā aññassa bhuttādhikena ucchiṭṭhabhattena bhavitabba”nti. So brāhmaṇiṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, the brahmin was coming towards the house. Seeing him approaching, the brahmin’s wife quickly went inside and, saying, “Get up, the brahmin is coming!” made her lover hide in a granary. When the brahmin entered and sat down, she brought a vessel for water and gave him water for washing his hands, and served him hot rice on top of the cold rice left over from what the other man had eaten. The brahmin, putting his hand into the rice, noticed that the top was hot and the rice below was cold, and thought, “This must be the leftover food from someone else’s meal.” Wishing to question the brahmin’s wife, he spoke this first verse:

123.

123.

“Añño uparimo vaṇṇo, añño vaṇṇo ca heṭṭhimo;

Brāhmaṇī tveva pucchāmi, kiṃ heṭṭhā kiñca upparī”ti.

“The appearance above is one, and the appearance below is another; Brahmin woman, I ask you, what is below, and what is above?”

Tattha vaṇṇoti ākāro. Ayañhi uparimassa uṇhabhāvaṃ heṭṭhimassa ca sītabhāvaṃ pucchanto evamāha. Kiṃ heṭṭhā kiñca upparīti vuḍḍhitabhattena [M 2.0154] nāma upari sītalena, heṭṭhā uṇhena bhavitabbaṃ, idañca pana na tādisaṃ, tena taṃ pucchāmi – “kena kāraṇena upari bhattaṃ uṇhaṃ, heṭṭhimaṃ sītala”nti.

Therein, ‘appearance’ (vaṇṇa) means condition. For he, inquiring about the hotness of the upper part and the coolness of the lower part, speaks thus. As for ‘What is below and what is above?’, served rice should be cool on top and hot below, but this is not so; therefore I ask you: ‘For what reason is the rice on top hot and the part below cold?’”

Brāhmaṇī attanā katakammassa uttānabhāvabhayena brāhmaṇe punappunaṃ kathentepi tuṇhīyeva ahosi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe naṭaputtassa etadahosi – “koṭṭhe nisīdāpitapāpapurisena jārena bhavitabbaṃ, iminā gehassāmikena, brāhmaṇī pana attanā katakammassa pākaṭabhāvabhayena kiñci na katheti, handāhaṃ imissā katakammaṃ pakāsetvā jārassa koṭṭhake nisīdāpitabhāvaṃ brāhmaṇassa kathemī”ti. So brāhmaṇassa gehā nikkhantakālato [P 2.0169] paṭṭhāya itarassa gehapavesanaṃ aticaraṇaṃ aggabhattabhuñjanaṃ brāhmaṇiyā dvāre ṭhatvā maggaṃ olokanaṃ itarassa koṭṭhe otāritabhāvanti sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin woman, fearing the exposure of her deed, remained silent even when the brahmin repeatedly questioned her. At that moment, it occurred to the dancer: “This must be a lover, a wicked man, hidden in the granary. This one must be the master of the house. But the brahmin woman, fearing the revelation of her deed, says nothing. Come, I shall reveal her deed and tell the brahmin about the lover hidden in the granary.” So, from the time the brahmin left the house, he recounted the whole affair: the other man's entry, the adultery, the eating of the choice food, the brahmin woman standing at the door watching the road, and the other man hidden in the granary. Then he spoke the second verse:

124.

124.

“Ahaṃ naṭosmi bhaddante, bhikkhakosmi idhāgato;

Ayañhi koṭṭhamotiṇṇo, ayaṃ so yaṃ gavesasī”ti.

“I am a dancer, sir, a beggar who has come here; This one has descended into the granary; this is the one you seek.”

Tattha ahaṃ naṭosmi, bhaddanteti, sāmi, ahaṃ naṭajātiko. Bhikkhakosmi idhāgatoti svāhaṃ imaṃ ṭhānaṃ bhikkhako bhikkhaṃ pariyesamāno āgatosmi. Ayañhi koṭṭhamotiṇṇoti ayaṃ pana etissā jāro imaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjanto tava bhayena koṭṭhaṃ otiṇṇo. Ayaṃ so yaṃ gavesasīti yaṃ tvaṃ kassa nu kho iminā ucchiṭṭhakena bhavitabbanti gavesasi, ayaṃ so. Cūḷāya [V 2.0141] naṃ gahetvā koṭṭhā nīharitvā yathā na punevarūpaṃ pāpaṃ karoti, tathā assa satiṃ janehīti vatvā pakkāmi. Brāhmaṇo ubhopi te yathā naṃ na punevarūpaṃ pāpaṃ karonti, tajjanapothanehi tathā sikkhāpetvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Here, ‘I am an actor, venerable sir,’ means, ‘Sir, I am of the actor caste.’ ‘I have come here as a beggar,’ means, ‘I have come to this place as a beggar seeking alms.’ ‘For this one has descended into the granary,’ means, ‘This lover of hers, while eating this food, descended into the granary out of fear of you.’ ‘This is he whom you seek,’ means, ‘This is the one you are searching for, wondering, “Whose leftovers could these be?”’ Having said, ‘Seize him by his top-knot, drag him out of the granary, and teach him a lesson so that he does not commit such an evil deed again,’ he departed. The brahmin disciplined them both with threats and blows so that they would not commit such an evil deed again, and then went according to his karma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhito bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā brāhmaṇī purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, brāhmaṇo ukkaṇṭhito bhikkhu, naṭaputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the end of the teaching on the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. ‘At that time, the brahmin woman was the former wife, the brahmin was the discontented monk, but the actor’s son was none other than myself.’

Ucchiṭṭhabhattajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka, the second.

[213] 3. Bharujātakavaṇṇanā

[213] 3. The Commentary on the Bharu Jātaka

Isīnamantaraṃ [M 2.0155] katvāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarājānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Bhagavato hi bhikkhusaṅghassa ca lābhasakkāro mahā ahosi. Yathāha –

‘Having made an interval for the seers’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the King of Kosala. For the Blessed One and the Community of Monks received great gain and honor. As it is said:

“Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ. Bhikkhusaṅghopi kho sakkato hoti…pe… parikkhārānaṃ. Aññatitthiyā pana paribbājakā asakkatā honti…pe… parikkhārāna”nti (udā. 14).

‘At that time, the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The Saṅgha of monks was also honored... requisites. But the wandering ascetics of other sects were not honored... requisites’ (Udāna 14).

Te evaṃ parihīnalābhasakkārā ahorattaṃ guḷhasannipātaṃ katvā mantayanti “samaṇassa gotamassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya mayaṃ hatalābhasakkārā jātā[P 2.0170], samaṇo gotamo lābhaggayasaggappatto jāto, kena nu kho kāraṇenassa esā sampattī”ti. Tatreke evamāhaṃsu – “samaṇo gotamo sakalajambudīpassa uttamaṭṭhāne bhūmisīse vasati. Tenassa lābhasakkāro uppajjatī”ti, sesā “atthetaṃ kāraṇaṃ, mayampi jetavanapiṭṭhe titthiyārāmaṃ kāremu, evaṃ lābhino bhavissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Te sabbepi “evameta”nti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā “sacepi mayaṃ rañño anārocetvā ārāmaṃ kāressāma, bhikkhū vāressanti, lañjaṃ labhitvā abhijjanako nāma natthi, tasmā rañño lañjaṃ datvā ārāmaṭṭhānaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti sammantetvā upaṭṭhāke yācitvā rañño satasahassaṃ datvā “mahārāja, mayaṃ jetavanapiṭṭhiyaṃ titthiyārāmaṃ karissāma, sace [V 2.0142] bhikkhū ‘kātuṃ na dassāmā’ti tumhākaṃ ārocenti, nesaṃ paṭivacanaṃ na dātabba”nti āhaṃsu. Rājā lañjalobhena “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

Those who were thus deprived of gain and honor gathered in secret day and night and consulted: ‘Since the ascetic Gotama arose, we have been deprived of gain and honor, while the ascetic Gotama has attained the pinnacle of gain and fame. What could be the reason for his success?’ Some among them said: ‘The ascetic Gotama dwells in the foremost place, at the head of the earth in all of Jambudīpa. Therefore, gain and honor arise for him.’ Others said: ‘That is a reason. Let us also have a monastery for the sectarians built on the grounds of Jetavana. Thus we will become recipients of gain.’ They all came to the conclusion, ‘So be it,’ and decided: ‘If we build a monastery without informing the king, the monks will prevent it. There is no one who, having received a bribe, will not be swayed. Therefore, let us give a bribe to the king and obtain the site for the monastery.’ Having conferred thus, they begged from their supporters, gave the king a hundred thousand pieces, and said: ‘Great king, we will build a monastery for sectarians on the grounds of Jetavana. If the monks report to you, saying, “We will not allow it to be built,” you must not give them an audience.’ The king, out of greed for the bribe, consented, saying, ‘Very well.’

Titthiyā rājānaṃ saṅgaṇhitvā vaḍḍhakiṃ pakkosāpetvā kammaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ, mahāsaddo ahosi. Satthā “ke panete, ānanda, uccāsaddamahāsaddā”ti pucchi. “Aññatitthiyā, bhante, jetavanapiṭṭhiyaṃ titthiyārāmaṃ kārenti, tattheso saddo”ti. “Ānanda, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ titthiyārāmassa anucchavikaṃ, titthiyā uccāsaddakāmā, na sakkā tehi saddhiṃ [M 2.0156] vasitu”nti vatvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātetvā “gacchatha, bhikkhave, rañño ācikkhitvā titthiyārāmakaraṇaṃ nivārethā”ti āha. Bhikkhusaṅgho gantvā rañño nivesanadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Rājā saṅghassa āgatabhāvaṃ sutvāpi “titthiyārāmaṃ nissāya āgatā bhavissantī”ti lañjassa gahitattā “rājā gehe natthī”ti vadāpesi. Bhikkhū gantvā satthu ārocesuṃ. Satthā “lañjaṃ nissāya evaṃ karotī”ti dve aggasāvake pesesi. Rājā tesampi āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā tatheva vadāpesi. Tepi āgantvā satthu ārācesuṃ. Satthā “na idāni, sāriputta, rājā gehe nisīdituṃ labhissati, bahi nikkhamissatī”ti punadivase pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ rañño nivesanadvāraṃ agamāsi. Rājā sutvā pāsādā otaritvā pattaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ pavesetvā buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa yāgukhajjakaṃ datvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā rañño ekaṃ pariyāyadhammadesanaṃ ārabhanto “mahārāja, porāṇakarājāno lañjaṃ gahetvā sīlavante aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ kāretvā attano raṭṭhassa assāmino hutvā mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The sectarians, having won over the king, summoned a carpenter and began the work, creating a great uproar. The Teacher asked, ‘Ānanda, who is making such a loud and great noise?’ ‘Venerable sir, other sectarians are building a sectarian monastery on the grounds of Jetavana—that is the noise.’ ‘Ānanda, that place is not suitable for a sectarian monastery. Sectarians are fond of loud noise; it is impossible to live with them.’ Having said this, he assembled the Community of Monks and said, ‘Go, monks, inform the king and stop the construction of the sectarian monastery.’ The Community of Monks went and stood at the gate of the king’s residence. Although the king heard that the Saṅgha had arrived, thinking, ‘They must have come concerning the sectarian monastery,’ and because he had accepted the bribe, he had it said, ‘The king is not at home.’ The monks returned and reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher, knowing, ‘He acts thus because of the bribe,’ sent his two chief disciples. Hearing of their arrival, the king likewise had the same message given. They too returned and reported to the Teacher. The Teacher said, ‘Now, Sāriputta, the king will not be able to remain inside; he will come out.’ The next day, in the morning, the Teacher dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the gate of the king’s residence with five hundred monks. The king, hearing of it, descended from the palace, took the bowl, invited the Teacher inside, and offered rice gruel and food to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. After paying homage to the Teacher, he sat to one side. The Teacher, beginning a discourse to the king in a particular manner, said, ‘Great king, ancient kings, having taken bribes, caused virtuous persons to quarrel with one another, and becoming no longer masters of their own kingdoms, met with great ruin.’ Then, being entreated by the king, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 2.0171] bharuraṭṭhe bharurājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto pañcābhiñño aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī gaṇasatthā tāpaso hutvā himavantapadese ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya pañcasatatāpasaparivuto himavantā otaritvā anupubbena bharunagaraṃ patvā tattha piṇḍāya caritvā nagarā nikkhamitvā uttaradvāre sākhāviṭapasampannassa vaṭarukkhassa mūle nisīditvā bhattakiccaṃ katvā tattheva rukkhamūle vāsaṃ kappesi. Evaṃ tasmiṃ isigaṇe tattha vasante aḍḍhamāsaccayena añño gaṇasatthā pañcasataparivāro āgantvā nagare bhikkhāya caritvā nagarā nikkhamitvā dakkhiṇadvāre tādisasseva vaṭarukkhassa mūle nisīditvā bhattakiccaṃ katvā tattha rukkhamūle vāsaṃ kappesi. Iti te dvepi isigaṇā tattha yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā himavantameva agamaṃsu.

In the past, in the kingdom of Bharu, a king named Bharu ruled. At that time, the Bodhisatta, possessing the five higher knowledges and having attained the eight meditative attainments, became a teacher of a group of ascetics. After living for a long time in the Himalayan region, he descended from the Himalayas with a retinue of five hundred ascetics in order to obtain salt and sour foods. Gradually, he arrived at the city of Bharu, where he went for alms. Leaving the city, he sat at the foot of a banyan tree near the northern gate, which was endowed with branches and foliage. After completing his meal, he took up residence right there at the foot of the tree. While that group of sages was dwelling there, after half a month had passed, another teacher of a group, with a retinue of five hundred, arrived. He went for alms in the city and, upon leaving, sat at the foot of a similar banyan tree near the southern gate. After finishing his meal, he also took up residence at the foot of that tree. In this way, both groups of sages dwelt there as long as they pleased and then returned to the Himalayas.

Tesaṃ [V 2.0143] gatakāle dakkhiṇadvāre vaṭarukkho sukkho. Punavāre tesu āgacchantesu dakkhiṇadvāre vaṭarukkhavāsino paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā attano vaṭarukkhassa [M 2.0157] sukkhabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhikkhāya caritvā nagarā nikkhamitvā uttaradvāre vaṭarukkhamūlaṃ gantvā bhattakiccaṃ katvā tattha vāsaṃ kappesuṃ. Itare pana isayo pacchā āgantvā nagare bhikkhāya caritvā attano rukkhamūlameva gantvā bhattakiccaṃ katvā vāsaṃ kappesuṃ. Te “na so tumhākaṃ rukkho, amhākaṃ rukkho”ti rukkhaṃ nissāya aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ kariṃsu, kalaho mahā ahosi. Eke “amhākaṃ paṭhamaṃ vasitaṭṭhānaṃ tumhe na labhissathā”ti vadanti. Eke “mayaṃ imasmiṃ vāre paṭhamataraṃ idhāgatā, tumhe na labhissathā”ti vadanti. Iti te “mayaṃ sāmino, mayaṃ sāmino”ti kalahaṃ karontā rukkhamūlassatthāya rājakulaṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā paṭhamaṃ vutthaisigaṇaññeva sāmikaṃ akāsi[P 2.0172]. Itare “na dāni mayaṃ imehi parājitāti attānaṃ vadāpessāmā”ti dibbacakkhunā oloketvā ekaṃ cakkavattiparibhogaṃ rathapañjaraṃ disvā āharitvā rañño lañjaṃ datvā “mahārāja, amhepi sāmike karohī”ti āhaṃsu.

After they had departed, the banyan tree at the southern gate withered. On their next visit, the ascetics who had dwelt at the southern gate's banyan tree arrived first. Realizing their banyan tree had withered, they went for alms in the city, and after leaving the city, went to the foot of the banyan tree at the northern gate. After finishing their meal, they took up residence there. The other sages arrived later, went for alms in the city, and then went to the foot of their own tree. After finishing their meal, they also took up residence there. They argued, saying, 'That tree is not yours, it is ours,' and a great quarrel arose concerning the tree. Some said, 'This was our dwelling place first; you shall not have it.' Others said, 'We arrived here first this time; you shall not have it.' Thus, quarreling and claiming, 'We are the owners, we are the owners,' they went to the royal court over the matter of the tree's base. The king declared the group of sages who had dwelt there first to be the owners. The others, thinking, 'We will not let it be said that we were defeated by them,' looked around with their divine eye and, seeing a chariot frame that had been used by a wheel-turning monarch, brought it and gave it to the king as a bribe, saying, 'Great King, make us owners as well.'

Rājā lañjaṃ gahetvā “dvepi gaṇā vasantū”ti dvepi sāmike akāsi. Itare isayo tassa rathapañjarassa rathacakkāni nīharitvā lañjaṃ datvā “mahārāja, amheyeva sāmike karohī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā tathā akāsi. Isigaṇā “amhehi vatthukāme ca kilesakāme ca pahāya pabbajitehi rukkhamūlassa kāraṇā kalahaṃ karontehi lañjaṃ dadantehi ayuttaṃ kata”nti vippaṭisārino hutvā vegena palāyitvā himavantameva agamaṃsu. Sakalabharuraṭṭhavāsino devatā ekato hutvā “sīlavante kalahaṃ karontena raññā ayuttaṃ kata”nti bharurañño kujjhitvā tiyojanasatikaṃ bharuraṭṭhaṃ samuddaṃ ubbattetvā araṭṭhamakaṃsu. Iti ekaṃ bharurājānaṃ nissāya sakalaraṭṭhavāsinopi vināsaṃ pattāti.

The king, taking the bribe, declared, 'Let both groups stay,' and made both of them owners. The other sages then brought the wheels of that chariot frame, gave them as a bribe, and said, 'Great King, make us the sole owners.' The king did so. The groups of sages, becoming remorseful, thought: 'It is improper for us, who have gone forth having abandoned sensual pleasures related to objects and to defilements, to quarrel over the base of a tree and to give bribes.' Thus remorseful, they quickly fled and went back to the Himalayas. All the deities dwelling in the land of Bharu gathered together and, angered at the King of Bharu, said: 'An improper deed was done by the king in causing the virtuous to quarrel.' They caused the ocean to swell up and submerge the three-hundred-yojana land of Bharu, making it a non-country. Thus, on account of the one King of Bharu, all the inhabitants of the entire land met with destruction.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

The Teacher, having related this story of the past, as the Fully Enlightened One, spoke these verses:

125.

125.

“Isīnamantaraṃ katvā, bharurājāti me sutaṃ;

Ucchinno saha raṭṭhehi, sa rājā vibhavaṅgato.

'Having created a division among the sages, King Bharu, so I have heard, was uprooted along with his lands; that king went to ruin.'

126.

126.

“Tasmā hi chandāgamanaṃ, nappasaṃsanti paṇḍitā;

Aduṭṭhacitto bhāseyya, giraṃ saccupasaṃhita”nti.

'Therefore, the wise do not praise following a course of partiality; with a mind free from malice, one should speak words connected with truth.'

Tattha [V 2.0144][M 2.0158] antaraṃ katvāti chandāgativasena vivaraṃ katvā. Bharurājāti bharuraṭṭhe rājā. Iti me sutanti iti mayā pubbe etaṃ sutaṃ. Tasmā hi chandāgamananti yasmā hi chandāgamanaṃ gantvā bharurājā saha raṭṭhena ucchinno, tasmā chandāgamanaṃ paṇḍitā nappasaṃsanti. Aduṭṭhacittoti kilesehi adūsitacitto hutvā. Bhāseyya giraṃ saccupasaṃhitanti sabhāvanissitaṃ [P 2.0173] atthanissitaṃ kāraṇanissitameva giraṃ bhāseyya. Ye hi tattha bharurañño lañjaṃ gaṇhantassa ayuttaṃ etanti paṭikkosantā saccupasaṃhitaṃ giraṃ bhāsiṃsu, tesaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ nāḷikeradīpe ajjāpi dīpakasahassaṃ paññāyatīti.

Herein, 'having created a division' means having created a fissure by following a course of partiality. 'King Bharu' means the king in the land of Bharu. 'So I have heard' means this was heard by me in the past. 'Therefore... following a course of partiality': because King Bharu, having followed a course of partiality, was destroyed along with his kingdom, for that reason the wise do not praise following a course of partiality. 'With a mind free from malice' means having a mind undefiled by defilements. 'One should speak words connected with truth' means one should speak only words that are founded on reality, founded on meaning, and founded on reason. Indeed, as for those who, denouncing King Bharu's taking of a bribe as improper, spoke words connected with truth, the place where they stood, on Coconut Island, is still known today as the Thousand Isles.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “mahārāja, chandavasikena nāma na bhavitabbaṃ, dve pabbajitagaṇe kalahaṃ kāretuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “ahaṃ tena samayena jeṭṭhakaisi ahosi”nti, rājā tathāgatassa bhattakiccaṃ katvā gatakāle manusse pesetvā titthiyārāmaṃ viddhaṃsāpesi, titthiyā appatiṭṭhā ahesuṃ.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, 'Great King, one should not be under the influence of partiality; it is not proper to cause a quarrel between two groups of renunciants.' Then he made the connection in the Jātaka, saying, 'At that time, I was the elder sage.' After the king had served the meal to the Tathāgata and he had departed, he sent men and had the sectarians' monastery demolished. The sectarians were left without a place to stay.

Bharujātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Bharu Jātaka: The Third.

[214] 4. Puṇṇanadījātakavaṇṇanā

[214] 4. The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Full River

Puṇṇaṃ nadinti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi divase dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū tathāgatassa paññaṃ ārabbha kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, sammāsambuddho mahāpañño puthupañño hāsapañño javanapañño tikkhapañño gambhīrapañño nibbedhikapañño upāyapaññāya samannāgato”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato paññavā upāyakusaloyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The full river...”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Perfection of Wisdom. For one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised a discussion concerning the Tathāgata’s wisdom: 'Friends, the Fully Enlightened One is of great wisdom, wide wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, profound wisdom, and penetrative wisdom; he is endowed with wisdom in skillful means.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together?' When it was said, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, not only now, but in the past also the Tathāgata was wise and skilled in means,' and he brought forth the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto purohitakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena purohitaṭṭhānaṃ labhitvā bārāṇasirañño atthadhammānusāsako [M 2.0159] ahosi. Aparabhāge rājā paribhedakānaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā bodhisattassa kuddho “mā mama santike vasī”ti bodhisattaṃ bārāṇasito pabbājesi. Bodhisatto puttadāraṃ gahetvā ekasmiṃ kāsikagāmake vāsaṃ kappesi. Aparabhāge rājā tassa guṇaṃ saritvā “mayhaṃ kañci pesetvā ācariyaṃ pakkosituṃ na yuttaṃ, ekaṃ pana gāthaṃ bandhitvā paṇṇaṃ [V 2.0145][P 2.0174] likhitvā kākamaṃsaṃ pacāpetvā paṇṇañca maṃsañca setavatthena paliveṭhetvā rājamuddikāya lañchetvā pesessāmi. Yadi paṇḍito bhavissati, paṇṇaṃ vācetvā kākamaṃsabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgamissati, no ce, nāgamissatī”ti “puṇṇaṃ nadi”nti imaṃ gāthaṃ paṇṇe likhi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in the family of the royal chaplain. Having come of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, and upon his father’s passing, he attained the position of royal chaplain and became an advisor to the King of Benares on matters of welfare and righteousness. Later, the king, swayed by the words of slanderers, became angry with the Bodhisatta and banished him from Benares, saying, "Do not dwell in my presence!" The Bodhisatta took his wife and children and took up residence in a small village in the Kāsika country. Later, the king, remembering his virtues, thought, "It is not proper for me to send someone to summon the teacher. Instead, I will compose a verse, write it on a palm leaf, have crow’s meat cooked, wrap both the leaf and the meat in a white cloth, seal it with the royal seal, and send it. If he is wise, he will read the letter, realize it is crow's meat, and come. If not, he will not come." Thus, he wrote this verse on the leaf, beginning with 'Puṇṇaṃ nadiṃ':

127.

127.

“Puṇṇaṃ nadiṃ yena ca peyyamāhu, jātaṃ yavaṃ yena ca guyhamāhu;

Dūraṃ gataṃ yena ca avhayanti, so tyāgato handa ca bhuñja brāhmaṇā”ti.

"That by which they call a full river drinkable, and by which they call grown crops hidden; that by which they summon one gone far—that has come to you. Come now, Brahmin, and eat!"

Tattha puṇṇaṃ nadiṃ yena ca peyyamāhūti kākapeyyā nadīhi vadantā yena puṇṇaṃ nadiṃ kākapeyyamāhu, na hi apuṇṇā nadī “kākapeyyā”ti vuccati. Yadāpi nadītīre ṭhatvā gīvaṃ pasāretvā kākena pātuṃ sakkā hoti, tadā naṃ “kākapeyyā”ti vadanti. Jātaṃ yavaṃ yena ca guyhamāhūti yavanti desanāsīsamattaṃ, idha pana sabbampi jātaṃ uggataṃ sampannataruṇasassaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tañhi yadā anto paviṭṭhakākaṃ paṭicchādetuṃ sakkoti, tadā guyhatīti guyhaṃ. Kiṃ guyhati? Kākaṃ. Iti kākassa guyhaṃ kākaguyhanti taṃ vadamānā kākena guyhavacanassa kāraṇabhūtena “guyha”nti vadanti. Tena vuttaṃ “yena ca guyhamāhū”ti. Dūraṃ gataṃ yena ca avhayantīti dūraṃ gataṃ vippavutthaṃ piyapuggalaṃ yaṃ āgantvā nisinnaṃ disvā sace itthannāmo āgacchati, vassa kākāti vā vassantaññeva vā sutvā “yathā kāko vassati, itthannāmo āgamissatī”ti evaṃ vadantā yena ca avhayanti kathenti mantenti, udāharantīti attho. So tyāgatoti so te ānīto. Handa ca bhuñja, brāhmaṇāti gaṇha, brāhmaṇa, bhuñjassu naṃ, khāda idaṃ kākamaṃsanti attho.

Therein, 'That by which they call a full river drinkable' means: when speaking of rivers, they call a full river 'crow-drinkable' (kākapeyyā); for a river that is not full is not called 'crow-drinkable.' When a crow can stand on the riverbank, stretch its neck, and drink, then they call it 'crow-drinkable.' 'And by which they call grown barley hidden': 'barley' is merely a heading for the teaching; here, however, all grown, sprouted, and flourishing young crops are intended. For when the crop can conceal a crow that has entered it, it is 'hidden' (guyhaṃ). What does it hide? A crow. Thus, it is a crow's hiding place (kākaguyhaṃ), and in speaking of it, they say 'hidden' because the crow is the cause for the expression 'hidden.' Therefore it is said, 'by which they call it hidden.' 'That by which they summon one gone far': regarding a beloved person who has gone far away and is absent, upon seeing a crow that has come and alighted, or upon hearing it caw, they say, 'If so-and-so is coming, caw, O crow!' or 'Just as the crow caws, so-and-so will come.' Thus, 'by which they summon'—that is, speak, converse, or call out—this is the meaning. 'That has come to you' (so tyāgato) means it has been brought for you. 'Come now, Brahmin, and eat' means 'take it, Brahmin, eat it, consume this crow's meat.'

Iti [M 2.0160] rājā imaṃ gāthaṃ paṇṇe likhitvā bodhisattassa pesesi. So paṇṇaṃ vācetvā “rājā maṃ daṭṭhukāmo”ti ñatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus the king, having written this verse on a palm leaf, sent it to the Bodhisatta. Having read the letter and knowing, "The king wishes to see me," he spoke the second verse:

128.

128.

“Yato [P 2.0175] maṃ saratī rājā, vāyasampi pahetave;

Haṃsā koñcā mayūrā ca, asatīyeva pāpiyā”ti.

"Since the king remembers me, enough to send even a crow—what of geese, cranes, and peacocks? Not remembering is indeed a wretched thing."

Tattha yato maṃ saratī rājā, vāyasampi pahetaveti yadā rājā vāyasamaṃsaṃ labhitvā tampi pahetuṃ maṃ sarati. Haṃsā koñcā mayūrā cāti yadā panassa ete haṃsādayo upanītā bhavissanti, ekāni haṃsamaṃsādīni lacchati, tadā maṃ kasmā na sarissatīti attho? Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 2.0146] pana “haṃsakoñcamayūrāna”nti pāṭho. So sundaratarā, imesaṃ haṃsādīnaṃ maṃsaṃ labhitvā kasmā maṃ na sarissati, sarissatiyevāti attho. Asatīyeva pāpiyāti yaṃ vā taṃ vā labhitvā saraṇaṃ nāma sundaraṃ, lokasmiṃ pana asatiyeva pāpiyā, asatikaraṇaṃyeva hīnaṃ lāmakaṃ, tañca amhākaṃ rañño natthi. Sarati maṃ rājā, āgamanaṃ me paccāsīsati, tasmā gamissāmīti yānaṃ yojāpetvā gantvā rājānaṃ passi, rājā tussitvā purohitaṭṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhāpesi.

Therein, 'Since the king remembers me, enough to send even a crow' means: when the king obtains crow-meat, he remembers to send even that to me. 'Geese, cranes, and peacocks' means: when these geese and other birds are brought to him and he receives their meat, why would he then not remember me? In the commentary, however, the reading is 'haṃsakoñcamayūrānaṃ' (of geese, cranes, and peacocks). That is better, meaning: 'Having obtained the meat of these geese and others, why would he not remember me? Surely he will remember.' 'Not remembering is indeed a wretched thing' means: to remember someone upon receiving whatever it may be is beautiful, but in the world, not remembering is indeed wretched; the act of not remembering is low and contemptible, and our king is not like that. Thinking, 'The king remembers me; he expects my arrival, therefore I shall go,' he had his carriage harnessed, went, and saw the king. The king, being pleased, re-established him in the very position of royal priest.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, purohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth story: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the royal priest was I myself."

Puṇṇanadījātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Explanation of the Puṇṇanadī Jātaka, the fourth.

[215] 5. Kacchapajātakavaṇṇanā

[215] 5. Explanation of the Kacchapa Jātaka

Avadhī vata attānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kokālikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu mahātakkārijātake (jā. 1.13.104 ādayo) āvi-bhavissati. Tadā pana satthā “na, bhikkhave, kokāliko idāneva vācāya hato, pubbepi vācāya hatoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Alas, he has killed himself'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Kokālika. The story will be revealed in the Mahātakkāri Jātaka. At that time, however, the Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has been destroyed by his speech; in the past, too, he was destroyed by his speech,' and he related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto amaccakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako ahosi. So pana rājā bahubhāṇī ahosi, tasmiṃ kathente aññesaṃ [M 2.0161] vacanassa okāso nāma natthi. Bodhisatto [P 2.0176] tassa taṃ bahubhāṇitaṃ vāretukāmo ekaṃ upāyaṃ upadhārento vicarati. Tasmiñca kāle himavantapadese ekasmiṃ sare kacchapo vasati, dve haṃsapotakā gocarāya carantā tena saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ akaṃsu. Te daḷhavissāsikā hutvā ekadivasaṃ kacchapaṃ āhaṃsu – “samma kacchapa, amhākaṃ himavante cittakūṭapabbatatale kañcanaguhāyaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyo padeso, gacchasi amhākaṃ saddhi”nti. “Ahaṃ kinti katvā gamissāmī”ti? “Mayaṃ taṃ gahetvā gamissāma, sace tvaṃ mukhaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkhissasi, kassaci kiñci na kathessasī”ti. “Rakkhissāmi, sāmi, gahetvā maṃ gacchathā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti vatvā ekaṃ daṇḍakaṃ kacchapena ḍaṃsāpetvā sayaṃ [V 2.0147] tassa ubho koṭiyo ḍaṃsitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandiṃsu. Taṃ tathā haṃsehi nīyamānaṃ gāmadārakā disvā “dve haṃsā kacchapaṃ daṇḍakena harantī”ti āhaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers and, having come of age, became his advisor on matters of welfare and righteousness. Now, that king was very talkative; when he was speaking, there was no opportunity for others to speak. The Bodhisatta, wishing to check his excessive talkativeness, went about considering a stratagem. At that time, in a certain lake in the Himalayan region, there lived a tortoise. Two young swans, while searching for food, became friendly with him. Having become firm friends, one day they said to the tortoise, "Friend tortoise, our dwelling place in the Himalayas, at the foot of the Cittakūṭa mountain in the Golden Cave, is a delightful region. Will you go with us?" "How shall I go?" "We will take you, if you are able to guard your mouth and say nothing to anyone." "I will guard it, sirs; take me and go." Saying, "Good," they had the tortoise bite on a stick, and they themselves, biting the two ends, flew up into the sky. Seeing him being carried thus by the swans, some village boys cried out, "Two swans are carrying a tortoise with a stick!"

Kacchapo “yadi maṃ sahāyakā nenti, tumhākaṃ ettha kiṃ duṭṭhaceṭakā”ti vattukāmo haṃsānaṃ sīghavegatāya bārāṇasinagare rājanivesanassa uparibhāgaṃ sampattakāle daṭṭhaṭṭhānato daṇḍakaṃ vissajjetvā ākāsaṅgaṇe patitvā dvebhāgo ahosi, “kacchapo ākāsato patitvā dvedhā bhinno”ti ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Rājā bodhisattaṃ ādāya amaccagaṇaparivuto taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā kacchapaṃ disvā bodhisattaṃ pucchi – “paṇḍita, kinti katvā esa patito”ti? Bodhisatto “cirapaṭikaṅkhohaṃ rājānaṃ ovaditukāmo upāyaṃ upadhārento carāmi, iminā kacchapena haṃsehi saddhiṃ vissāso kato bhavissati, tehi imaṃ ‘himavantaṃ nessāmā'ti daṇḍakaṃ ḍaṃsāpetvā ākāsaṃ pakkhantehi bhavitabbaṃ, atha iminā kassaci vacanaṃ sutvā arakkhitamukhatāya kiñci vattukāmena daṇḍakā vissaṭṭho bhavissati, evaṃ [P 2.0177] ākāsato patitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ patteneva bhavitabba”nti cintetvā “āma mahārāja, atimukharā nāma apariyantavacanā evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ pāpuṇantiyevā”ti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –

The tortoise, wishing to say, 'If my friends are carrying me, what business is it of yours, you wicked rascals?'—due to the swift speed of the swans, when they reached the upper part of the royal palace in Benares, he let go of the stick from the place where he was biting, fell into the expanse of the sky, and split into two. 'The tortoise has fallen from the sky and broken in two!' There was a great uproar. The king, taking the Bodhisatta with him and surrounded by his retinue of ministers, went to that spot. Seeing the tortoise, he asked the Bodhisatta, 'O wise one, how did this one fall?' The Bodhisatta thought, 'For a long time I have wished to advise the king, seeking a means as I go about. This tortoise must have established trust with the swans. They must have made him bite the stick, thinking, 'We will take him to the Himalayas,' before flying into the sky. Then, upon hearing someone’s words, because he could not guard his mouth and wished to say something, he must have let go of the stick. Thus, falling from the sky, he must have met with the destruction of his life.' Reflecting thus, he said, 'Yes, great king, the overly talkative, those whose words are without limit, indeed meet with such suffering.' Then he spoke these verses:

129.

129.

“Avadhī vata attānaṃ, kacchapo byāharaṃ giraṃ;

Suggahītasmiṃ kaṭṭhasmiṃ, vācāya sakiyāvadhi.

"Indeed, the tortoise killed itself while uttering speech; although the stick was well-grasped, it slew itself with its own words."

130.

130.

“Etampi [M 2.0162] disvā naravīriyaseṭṭha, vācaṃ pamuñce kusalaṃ nātivelaṃ;

Passasi bahubhāṇena, kacchapaṃ byasanaṃ gata”nti.

"Seeing this, O best in heroic energy among men, one should utter skillful speech, and not excessively; you see how the tortoise, through much talk, met with disaster."

Tattha avadhī vatāti ghātesi vata. Byāharanti byāharanto. Suggahītasmiṃ kaṭṭhasminti mukhena suṭṭhu ḍaṃsitvā gahite daṇḍake. Vācāya sakiyāvadhīti atimukharatāya akāle vācaṃ nicchārento daṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā tāya sakāya vācāya attānaṃ avadhi ghātesi. Evamesa jīvitakkhayaṃ patto, na aññathāti. Etampi disvāti etampi kāraṇaṃ disvā. Naravīriyaseṭṭhāti naresu vīriyena seṭṭha uttamavīriya rājavara. Vācaṃ pamuñce kusalaṃ nātivelanti saccādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kusalameva paṇḍito puriso muñceyya nicchāreyya, tampi hitaṃ kālayuttaṃ, na ativelaṃ, atikkantakālaṃ apariyantavācaṃ na bhāseyya. Passasīti nanu paccakkhato passasi. Bahubhāṇenāti bahubhaṇanena. Kacchapaṃ byasanaṃ gatanti etaṃ kacchapaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pattanti.

Therein, 'indeed, he killed' means 'he indeed killed.' 'Uttering' means 'while uttering.' 'Though holding fast to the stick' means 'in the stick firmly bitten and grasped with the mouth.' 'By his own speech he killed' means that by excessive talkativeness, uttering speech at the wrong time, releasing his grip on the bitten spot, he killed himself by that very speech of his. Thus he met his end, not otherwise. 'Having seen this too' means 'having seen this reason as well.' 'Foremost in vigor among men' means 'foremost in effort among men, of supreme energy, O excellent king.' 'Utter skillful speech, not excessively' means that a wise person should utter only skillful speech connected with truth and the like, and that too should be beneficial and timely; one should not speak excessively, beyond the proper time, nor should one speak endless words. 'You see' means 'do you not see with your own eyes?' 'By much speaking' means 'by much speaking.' 'The tortoise met its ruin' means 'this tortoise met its end.'

Rājā [V 2.0148] “maṃ sandhāya bhāsatī”ti ñatvā “amhe sandhāya kathesi, paṇḍitā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “mahārāja, tvaṃ vā hohi añño vā, yo koci pamāṇātikkantaṃ bhāsanto evarūpaṃ byasanaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti pākaṭaṃ katvā kathesi. Rājā tato paṭṭhāya viramitvā mandabhāṇī ahosi.

The king, realizing, 'He is speaking with reference to me,' said, 'You spoke with reference to us, O wise one.' The Bodhisatta, making it clear, said, 'Great king, whether it be you or anyone else, whoever speaks beyond measure meets with such a disaster.' From that time on, the king refrained and became a man of few words.

Satthā [P 2.0178] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kacchapo kokāliko ahosi, dve haṃsapotakā dve mahātherā, rājā ānando, amaccapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the tortoise was Kokālika, the two young swans were the two great elders, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was I myself.'

Kacchapajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Kacchapa Jātaka, the fifth.

[216] 6. Macchajātakavaṇṇanā

[216] 6. Commentary on the Maccha Jātaka

Na māyamaggi tapatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchi. “Saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kena ukkaṇṭhāpitosī”ti puṭṭho “purāṇadutiyikāyā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “ayaṃ te bhikkhu itthī anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ etaṃ nissāya sūlena vijjhitvā [M 2.0163] aṅgāresu pacitvā khāditabbataṃ patto paṇḍite nissāya jīvitaṃ alatthā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'This fire does not burn me'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the enticement by a former wife. The Teacher asked that monk, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' When he replied, 'It is true, venerable sir,' he was asked, 'By whom were you made discontented?' He said, 'By my former wife.' Then the Teacher told him, 'Monk, this woman is a cause of harm to you. In the past, too, on account of her, you were pierced with a spit, cooked on embers, and reached a state where you were to be eaten. It was by relying on a wise one that you obtained your life.' And he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa purohito ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ kevaṭṭā jāle laggaṃ macchaṃ uddharitvā uṇhavālukāpiṭṭhe ṭhapetvā “aṅgāresu naṃ pacitvā khādissāmā”ti sūlaṃ tacchiṃsu. Maccho macchiṃ ārabbha paridevamāno imā gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his chaplain. Then one day, some fishermen, having pulled up a fish caught in their net, placed it on the hot sand and, saying, 'We will cook it on embers and eat it,' they sharpened a spit. The male fish, lamenting on account of the female fish, spoke these verses:

131.

131.

“Na māyamaggi tapati, na sūlo sādhutacchito;

Yañca maṃ maññate macchī, aññaṃ so ratiyā gato.

It is not this fire that burns me, nor the well-sharpened spit; but that my mate thinks of me, 'He has gone to another for delight'—that is what burns me.

132.

132.

“So maṃ dahati rāgaggi, cittaṃ cūpatapeti maṃ;
