Jālino muñcathāyirā maṃ, na kāme haññate kvacī”ti.

That fire of passion burns me, and it torments my mind. O net-wielders, sirs, release me! Nowhere is one slain on account of sensual desire.

Tattha [V 2.0149] na māyamaggi tapatīti na maṃ ayaṃ aggi tapati, na tāpaṃ janeti, na socayatīti attho. Na sūloti ayaṃ sūlopi sādhutacchito maṃ na tapati, na me sokaṃ uppādeti. Yañca maṃ maññateti yaṃ pana maṃ macchī evaṃ maññati “aññaṃ macchiṃ so pañcakāmaguṇaratiyā gato”ti, tadeva [P 2.0179] maṃ tapati socayati. So maṃ dahatīti yo panesa rāgaggi, so maṃ dahati jhāpeti. Cittaṃ cūpatapeti manti rāgasampayuttakaṃ mama cittameva ca maṃ upatāpeti kilameti viheṭheti. Jālinoti kevaṭṭe ālapati. Te hi jālassa atthitāya “jālino”ti vuccanti. Muñcathāyirā manti muñcatha maṃ sāminoti yācati. Na kāme haññate kvacīti kāme patiṭṭhito kāmena nīyamāno satto na kvaci haññati. Na hi taṃ tumhādisā hanituṃ anucchavikāti paridevati. Atha vā kāmeti hetuvacane bhummaṃ, kāmahetu macchiṃ anubandhamāno nāma na kvaci tumhādisehi haññatīti paridevati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bodhisatto nadītīraṃ gato tassa macchassa paridevitasaddaṃ sutvā kevaṭṭe upasaṅkamitvā taṃ macchaṃ mocesi.

Therein, 'It is not this fire that burns me' means: this fire does not burn me, it does not produce heat, it does not cause me to grieve. 'Nor the spit' means: this spit, though well-sharpened, does not burn me; it does not cause me sorrow. 'And what my mate thinks of me' means: what that female fish thinks of me, 'He has gone after another female fish for the delight of the five cords of sensual pleasure'—that indeed burns me, grieves me. 'That burns me' means: this fire of passion, it burns me, it scorches me. 'And it torments my mind' means: my mind, associated with passion, indeed torments me, exhausts me, afflicts me. 'O net-wielders' means: he addresses the fishermen. For they are called 'net-wielders' because they possess nets. 'Release me, sirs' means: he begs, 'Release me, O masters!' 'Nowhere is one slain on account of sensual desire' means: a being established in sensual pleasures, led by sensual pleasure, is not slain anywhere. 'For it is not fitting for the likes of you to slay such a one'—thus he laments. Or else, 'on account of desire' is a locative in the sense of cause, so he laments: 'One who is pursuing a female fish on account of desire is not slain anywhere by the likes of you.' At that moment, the Bodhisatta went to the riverbank and, hearing the lamenting cry of that fish, approached the fishermen and freed the fish.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi[M 2.0164]. “Tadā macchī purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, maccho ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, purohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. 'At that time, the female fish was the former wife, the male fish was the discontented monk, and the chaplain was I myself.'

Macchajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Maccha Jātaka, the sixth.

[217] 7. Seggujātakavaṇṇanā

[217] 7. The Commentary on the Seggu Jātaka

Sabbo lokoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ paṇṇikaupāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu ekakanipāte vitthāritameva. Idhāpi satthā taṃ “kiṃ, upāsaka, cirassaṃ āgatosī”ti pucchi. Paṇṇikaupāsako “dhītā me, bhante, niccaṃ pahaṃsitamukhī, tamahaṃ vīmaṃsitvā ekassa kuladārakassa adāsiṃ, tattha itikattabbatāya tumhākaṃ dassanāya āgantuṃ okāsaṃ na labhi”nti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “na kho, upāsaka, idānevesā sīlavatī, pubbepi sīlavatī, tvañca na idānevetaṃ vīmaṃsasi, pubbepi vīmaṃsiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'The whole world'—this the Teacher narrated while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain lay follower who was a greengrocer. The story is elaborated in the Ekakanipāta. Here too, the Teacher asked him, 'Why, lay follower, have you come after so long?' The greengrocer lay follower replied, 'Venerable sir, my daughter always has a smiling face. Having investigated this, I gave her in marriage to a certain young man of good family. Due to my duties there, I could not find an opportunity to come to see you.' Then the Teacher said to him, 'Lay follower, she is not virtuous only now; she was virtuous in the past as well. And you are not investigating this only now; you investigated it in the past as well.' Being requested by him, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto rukkhadevatā ahosi. Tadā ayameva [V 2.0150] paṇṇikaupāsako “dhītaraṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti araññaṃ netvā kilesavasena icchanto [P 2.0180] viya hatthe gaṇhi. Atha naṃ paridevamānaṃ paṭhamagāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity. At that time, this very lay follower who was a greengrocer, thinking, 'I will test my daughter,' took her to the forest and, as if desiring her due to defilement, took her by the hand. Then, as she lamented, he addressed her with the first verse:

133.

133.

“Sabbo loko attamano ahosi, akovidā gāmadhammassa seggu;

Komāri ko nāma tavajja dhammo, yaṃ tvaṃ gahitā pavane parodasī”ti.

'The whole world was delighted, O Seggu, unskilled in the ways of the village; Maiden, what indeed is your nature today, that you weep when taken in the forest?'

Tattha sabbo loko attamano ahosīti, amma, sakalopi sattaloko etissā kāmasevanāya attamano jāto. Akovidā gāmadhammassa seggūti seggūti tassā nāmaṃ. Tena tvaṃ pana, amma, seggu akovidā gāmadhammassa, imasmiṃ gāmadhamme vasaladhamme akusalāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Komāri ko nāma tavajja dhammoti, amma, kumāri ko nāmesa tava ajja sabhāvo. Yaṃ tvaṃ gahitā pavane parodasīti tvaṃ mayā imasmiṃ pavane santhavavasena hatthe gahitā parodasi [M 2.0165] na sampaṭicchasi, ko esa tava sabhāvo, kiṃ kumārikāyeva tvanti pucchati.

Here, 'the whole world was delighted' means, mother, all beings in the world were pleased by indulging in sensual pleasures. 'Seggu, unskilled in the village ways'—Seggu was her name. Therefore, you, mother, Seggu, are unskilled in the village ways, meaning you are unskilled in these base, vulgar customs. 'Maiden, what indeed is your nature today?'—mother, what indeed is your nature today? 'That you weep when taken in the forest'—you, taken by my hand in intimacy in this forest, weep and do not consent—what is this nature of yours? Are you still a maiden?—he asks.

Taṃ sutvā kumārikā “āma, tāta, kumārikāyevāhaṃ, nāhaṃ methunadhammaṃ nāma jānāmī”ti vatvā paridevamānā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the maiden said, 'Yes, father, I am indeed a maiden; I know nothing of sexual intercourse,' and lamenting, she spoke the second verse:

134.

134.

“Yo dukkhaphuṭṭhāya bhaveyya tāṇaṃ, so me pitā dubbhi vane karoti;

Sā kassa kandāmi vanassa majjhe, yo tāyitā so sahasaṃ karotī”ti.

'He who should have been my refuge when touched by suffering, my father, now does me harm in the forest; to whom shall I cry in the midst of the forest, since he who should protect me now acts violently?'

Sā heṭṭhā kathitāyeva. Iti so paṇṇiko tadā dhītaraṃ vīmaṃsitvā gehaṃ netvā kuladārakassa datvā yathākammaṃ gato.

The meaning of that verse is as previously explained. Thus, that greengrocer, having examined his daughter, took her home, gave her to a young man of good family, and went his way according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne paṇṇikaupāsako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā dhītā dhītāyeva, pitā pitāyeva ahosi, tassa kāraṇassa paccakkhakārikā rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry. 'At that time, the daughter was indeed the daughter, the father was indeed the father, and the tree deity who bore witness to that matter was I myself.'

Seggujātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Seggu Jātaka, the Seventh.

[218] 8. Kūṭavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā

[218] 8. The Commentary on the Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka

Saṭhassa [V 2.0151][P 2.0181] sāṭheyyamidanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kūṭavāṇijaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthivāsino hi kūṭavāṇijo ca paṇḍitavāṇijo ca dve vāṇijā mittikā hutvā pañca sakaṭasatāni bhaṇḍassa pūrāpetvā pubbantato aparantaṃ vicaramānā vohāraṃ katvā bahuṃ lābhaṃ labhitvā sāvatthiṃ paccāgamiṃsu. Paṇḍitavāṇijo kūṭavāṇijaṃ āha – “samma, bhaṇḍaṃ bhājemā”ti. Kūṭavāṇijo “ayaṃ dīgharattaṃ dukkhaseyyāya dubbhojanena kilanto attano ghare nānaggarasaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā ajīrakena marissati, atha sabbampetaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ mayhameva bhavissatī”ti cintetvā “nakkhattaṃ na manāpaṃ, divaso na manāpo, sve jānissāmi[M 2.0166], punadivase jānissāmī”ti kālaṃ khepeti. Atha naṃ paṇḍitavāṇijo nippīḷetvā bhājāpetvā gandhamālaṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā “kadā āgatosī”ti pucchitvā “aḍḍhamāsamatto me, bhante, āgatassā”ti vatvā “atha kasmā evaṃ papañcaṃ katvā buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ āgatosī”ti puṭṭho taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, upāsaka, idāneva, pubbepesa kūṭavāṇijoyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'Deceit against the deceitful...'—this the Teacher related while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain deceitful merchant. For in Sāvatthī, a deceitful merchant and a wise merchant, two merchants who had become friends, filled five hundred carts with goods and, traveling from the eastern end to the western end, conducted trade and gained much profit before returning to Sāvatthī. The wise merchant said to the deceitful merchant, 'Friend, let us divide the goods.' The deceitful merchant thought, 'This man, having long been afflicted by uncomfortable beds and poor food, will now eat various delicious foods at his own home and die from indigestion. Then all these goods will be mine alone.' So he said, 'The constellation is not auspicious, the day is not auspicious. I will see tomorrow, I will see the day after tomorrow,' thus delaying. Then the wise merchant pressed him and had the goods divided; then, taking perfumes and garlands, he went to the Teacher’s presence. Having honored and paid homage to the Teacher, he sat to one side. The Teacher asked, 'When did you arrive?' He replied, 'Venerable sir, it has been about half a month since I arrived.' Then, asked, 'Why then, after such a delay, have you come to attend upon the Buddha?' he related the incident. The Teacher said, 'Not only now, lay follower, but in the past, too, was this one a deceitful merchant.' Being requested, he then told of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto amaccakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tassa vinicchayāmacco ahosi. Tadā gāmavāsī ca nagaravāsī ca dve vāṇijā mittā ahesuṃ. Gāmavāsī nagaravāsissa santike pañca phālasatāni ṭhapesi. So te phāle vikkiṇitvā mūlaṃ gahetvā phālānaṃ ṭhapitaṭṭhāne mūsikavaccaṃ ākiritvā ṭhapesi. Aparabhāge gāmavāsī āgantvā “phāle me dehī”ti āha. Kūṭavāṇijo “phālā te mūsikāhi khāditā”ti mūsikavaccaṃ dassesi. Itaro “khāditāva hontu, mūsikāhi khādite kiṃ sakkā kātu”nti nhānatthāya tassa puttaṃ ādāya gacchanto ekassa sahāyakassa gehe “imassa katthaci gantuṃ mā adatthā”ti vatvā antogabbhe [P 2.0182] nisīdāpetvā sayaṃ nhāyitvā kūṭavāṇijassa gehaṃ agamāsi. So “putto me kaha”nti āha. “Samma, tava puttaṃ tīre ṭhapetvā mama udake nimuggakāle eko kulalo āgantvā tava puttaṃ nakhapañjarena gahetvā ākāsaṃ pakkhanto, ahaṃ pāṇiṃ paharitvā viravitvā vāyamantopi mocetuṃ nāsakkhi”nti. “Tvaṃ musā bhaṇasi, kulalā dārake gahetvā gantuṃ samatthā nāma natthī”ti. “Samma, hotu, ayuttepi honte ahaṃ kiṃ karomi, kulaleneva te putto nīto”ti. So taṃ santajjetvā “are duṭṭhacora manussamāraka[V 2.0152], idāni taṃ vinicchayaṃ gantvā kaḍḍhāpessāmī”ti nikkhami. So “mama ruccanakameva karosī”ti teneva saddhiṃ vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers and, having come of age, became his minister of justice. At that time, two merchants, one living in a village and the other in the city, were friends. The villager left five hundred ploughshares in the care of the city-dweller. He sold those ploughshares, took the money, and then scattered mouse droppings where the ploughshares had been stored. Later, when the villager returned and said, 'Give me my ploughshares,' the deceitful merchant replied, 'The mice have eaten your ploughshares,' and showed him the mouse droppings. The other thought, 'Let them be eaten—what can be done if mice have eaten them?' and, taking the merchant’s son to bathe, he went to a friend’s house, saying, 'Do not let this boy go anywhere,' and having made him sit in an inner chamber, he bathed himself and then went to the deceitful merchant’s house. The merchant asked, 'Where is my son?' He replied, 'Friend, I left your son on the bank, and while I was diving in the water, a kite came and, seizing your son with its talons, flew into the sky. Although I clapped my hands and shouted, striving to free him, I could not.' The merchant said, 'You lie! Kites are not capable of carrying off children.' The villager replied, 'Friend, so be it. Even if it is impossible, what can I do? Your son was taken by a kite.' Threatening him, the merchant said, 'You wicked thief, you murderer! Now I will take you to the court and have you dragged there!' and went out. The villager, thinking, 'You are doing just what I wish,' went with him to the place of judgment.

Kūṭavāṇijo bodhisattaṃ āha – “ayaṃ, sāmi, mama puttaṃ gahetvā nhāyituṃ gato, ‘kahaṃ me putto’ti vutte ‘kulalena haṭo’ti āha, vinicchinatha [M 2.0167] me aḍḍa”nti. Bodhisatto “saccaṃ bhaṇe”ti itaraṃ pucchi. So āha – “āma, sāmi, ahaṃ taṃ ādāya gato, senena pahaṭabhāvo saccameva, sāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana loke kulalā nāma dārake harantī”ti? “Sāmi, ahampi tumhe pucchāmi – “kulalā dārake gahetvā ākāse gantuṃ na sakkonti, mūsikā pana ayaphāle khādantī”ti. “Idaṃ kiṃ nāmā”ti? “Sāmi, mayā etassa ghare pañca phālasatāni ṭhapitāni, svāyaṃ ‘phālā te mūsikāhi khāditā’ti vatvā ‘idaṃ te phāle khāditamūsikānaṃ vacca’nti vaccaṃ dasseti, sāmi, mūsikā ce phāle khādanti, kulalāpi dārake harissanti. Sace na khādanti, senāpi taṃ na harissanti. Eso pana ‘phālā te mūsikāhi khāditā’ti vadati, tesaṃ khāditabhāvaṃ vā akhāditabhāvaṃ vā jānātha, aḍḍaṃ [P 2.0183] me vinicchinathā”ti. Bodhisatto “saṭhassa paṭisāṭheyyaṃ katvā jinissāmīti iminā cintitaṃ bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “suṭṭhu te cintita”nti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –

The deceitful merchant said to the Bodhisatta, 'Sir, this man took my son to bathe, and when I asked, "Where is my son?" he said, "A kite carried him away." Judge my case.' The Bodhisatta asked the other, 'Speak the truth.' He replied, 'Yes, sir, I did take him; it is true that he was seized by a hawk, my lord.' 'But do kites in this world carry away children?' 'Sir, I ask you in return: if kites cannot carry children and fly into the sky, can mice then eat iron ploughshares?' 'What is this about?' 'Sir, I stored five hundred ploughshares in this man's house. Now he says, "Mice have eaten your ploughshares," and shows me droppings, saying, "These are the droppings of the mice that ate your ploughshares." Sir, if mice can eat ploughshares, then kites can also carry away children. But if they do not eat them, then hawks will not carry him away either. This man, however, says, "Mice have eaten your ploughshares." You must determine whether they have been eaten or not. Judge my case.' The Bodhisatta, knowing that this one thought, 'By countering deceit with deceit, I shall win,' said, 'Well have you thought!' and spoke these verses:

135.

135.

“Saṭhassa sāṭheyyamiṃda sucintitaṃ, paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭaṃ;

Phālaṃ ce khādeyyuṃ mūsikā, kasmā kumāraṃ kulalā na hareyyuṃ.

'Deceit against the deceitful is this, well-conceived; a trick returned to the trickster. If mice were to eat a ploughshare, why would kites not carry away a young boy?'

136.

136.

“Kūṭassa hi santi kūṭakūṭā, bhavati cāpi nikatino nikatyā;

Dehi puttanaṭṭha phālanaṭṭhassa phālaṃ, mā te puttamahāsi phālanaṭṭho”ti.

'For the trickster, indeed, there are counter-tricks, and for the cheat, there is a counter-cheat. Give, O one who has lost a son, the ploughshare to the one who has lost a ploughshare; let not the one who has lost a ploughshare carry off your son.'

Tattha saṭhassāti saṭhabhāvena kerāṭikena “ekaṃ upāyaṃ katvā parasantakaṃ khādituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti saṭhassa. Sāṭheyyamidaṃ sucintitanti idaṃ paṭisāṭheyyaṃ cintentena tayā suṭṭhu cintitaṃ. Paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭanti kūṭassa puggalassa tayā paṭikūṭaṃ suṭṭhu paccoḍḍitaṃ, paṭibhāgaṃ katvā oḍḍitasadisameva katanti attho. Phālaṃ ce khādeyyuṃ mūsikāti yadi mūsikā phālaṃ khādeyyuṃ. Kasmā kumāraṃ kulalā na hareyyunti mūsikāsu phāle khādantīsu kulalā kiṃ kāraṇā kumāraṃ no hareyyuṃ.

Therein, 'of a cheat' means of one who is cunning by nature, a deceiver, thinking, 'Having devised a scheme, it is proper to consume another's property.' 'This deceit is well-conceived' means: this counter-deceit has been well thought out by you, who are pondering it. 'A trick has been set against the trickster' means: you have well set a counter-trick against the trickster, meaning it was made as a counterpart, just like a trap set in return. 'If mice were to eat the ploughshare' means: if mice were to gnaw the ploughshare. 'Why would hawks not carry off the boy?' means: while mice are gnawing the ploughshare, for what reason would hawks not carry off the boy?

Kūṭassa [V 2.0153][M 2.0168] hi santi kūṭakūṭāti tvaṃ “ahameva mūsikāhi phāle khādāpitapuriso kūṭo”ti maññasi, tādisassa pana kūṭassa imasmiṃ loke bahū kūṭā santi, kūṭassa kūṭāti kūṭapaṭikūṭānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ, kūṭassa paṭikūṭā nāma santīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhavati cāpi nikatino nikatyāti nikatino nekatikassa vañcanakapuggalassa nikatyā aparo nikatikārako vañcanakapuriso bhavatiyeva. Dehi puttanaṭṭha phālanaṭṭhassa phālanti ambho naṭṭhaputta purisa, etassa naṭṭhaphālassa phālaṃ dehi. Mā te puttamahāsi phālanaṭṭhoti sace hissa phālaṃ na dassasi, puttaṃ te harissati, taṃ te esa mā haratu, phālamassa dehīti. “Demi, sāmi, sace me puttaṃ detī”ti. “Demi, sāmi, sace me phāle detī”ti. Evaṃ [P 2.0184] naṭṭhaputto puttaṃ, naṭṭhaphālo ca phālaṃ paṭilabhitvā ubhopi yathākammaṃ gatā.

'For the deceitful, there are counter-tricks' means: you think, 'I alone am the trickster who caused the ploughshare to be eaten by mice,' but in this world, there are many tricksters like you. 'Kūṭassa kūṭā' is a name for tricks and counter-tricks, meaning there are indeed counter-tricks for the trickster. 'Moreover, for the cheat, there is a cheater' means: for a cheating, deceitful person, another cheating, deceitful person certainly arises. 'Give, O one who has lost a son, the ploughshare to the one who has lost a ploughshare' means: 'O man who has lost a son, give the ploughshare to this one who has lost a ploughshare!' 'Lest the one who has lost a ploughshare take away your son' means: 'If you do not give him his ploughshare, he will take your son. Let him not take him from you; give him his ploughshare!' 'I will give it, master, if he gives me my son.' 'I will give them, master, if he gives me my ploughshares.' Thus, the one who had lost his son recovered his son, and the one who had lost the ploughshare recovered his ploughshare, and both went according to their deeds.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kūṭavāṇijo idāni kūṭavāṇijova, paṇḍitavāṇijo paṇḍitavāṇijoyeva, vinicchayāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka thus: 'The deceitful merchant at that time is the deceitful merchant of today; the wise merchant at that time is the wise merchant of today; but the minister who gave the judgment was I myself.'

Kūṭavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka, the eighth.

[219] 9. Garahitajātakavaṇṇanā

[219] 9. Commentary on the Garahita Jātaka

Hiraññaṃ me suvaṇṇaṃ meti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ anabhiratiyā ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Etassa hi paccekaṃ gahitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi, anabhirativāsaṃ vasantaṃ pana taṃ satthu santikaṃ ānesuṃ. So satthārā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti puṭṭho “sacca”nti vatvā “kiṃkāraṇā”ti vutte “kilesavasenā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “ayaṃ, bhikkhu, kileso nāma pubbe tiracchānehipi garahito, tvaṃ evarūpe sāsane pabbajito kasmā tiracchānehipi garahitakilesavasena ukkaṇṭhito”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Silver is mine, gold is mine'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk agitated by discontent. For him, there was no specific object taken as a basis for his meditation, but as he lived in discontent, they brought him to the Teacher. When asked by the Teacher, 'Is it true, monk, that you are agitated?' he replied, 'It is true.' When asked further, 'For what reason?' he said, 'By the power of defilements.' Then the Teacher said to him, 'This defilement, monk, was criticized even by animals in the past. You, having gone forth into such a dispensation, why are you agitated because of defilements criticized even by animals?' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese vānarayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Tamenaṃ eko vanacarako gahetvā [M 2.0169] ānetvā rañño adāsi. So ciraṃ rājagehe vasamāno vattasampanno ahosi, manussaloke vattamānaṃ kiriyaṃ yebhuyyena aññāsi. Rājā tassa vatte pasīditvā vanacarakaṃ pakkosāpetvā “imaṃ vānaraṃ gahitaṭṭhāneyeva vissajjehī”ti āṇāpesi[V 2.0154], so tathā akāsi. Vānaragaṇo bodhisattassa āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā tassa dassanatthāya mahante pāsāṇapiṭṭhe sannipatitvā bodhisattena saddhiṃ sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ katvā “samma, kahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ vutthosī”ti āha. “Bārāṇasiyaṃ rājanivesane”ti. “Atha kathaṃ muttosī”ti? “Rājā maṃ keḷimakkaṭaṃ katvā mama vatte pasanno maṃ vissajjesī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Himalayan region in the womb of a monkey. A forest dweller caught him and brought him to the king. He lived in the king's palace for a long time and became accomplished in conduct, learning for the most part the activities current in the human world. The king, pleased with his conduct, summoned the forest dweller and ordered, 'Release this monkey in the very place you caught him.' He did so. The troop of monkeys, knowing of the Bodhisatta's arrival, gathered on a large flat rock to see him. After exchanging pleasantries with the Bodhisatta, they asked, 'Friend, where have you been living all this time?' 'In the royal residence at Benares,' he replied. 'Then how were you freed?' they asked. 'The king made me his play-monkey, and being pleased with his conduct, he released me,' he said.

Atha naṃ te vānarā “manussaloke vattamānakiriyaṃ nāma tumhe jānissatha[P 2.0185], amhākampi tāva kathetha, sotukāmamhā”ti āhaṃsu. “Mā maṃ manussānaṃ kiriyaṃ pucchathā”ti. “Kathetha sotukāmamhā”ti. Bodhisattopi “manussā nāma khattiyāpi brāhmaṇāpi ‘mayhaṃ mayha’nti vadanti, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccataṃ na jānanti, suṇātha dāni tesaṃ andhabālānaṃ kāraṇa”nti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –

Then those monkeys said to him, 'You must know about the ways of the human world. Please tell us, for we are eager to hear.' 'Do not ask me about the ways of humans,' he replied. 'Tell us, we are eager to hear,' they insisted. The Bodhisatta then said, 'Humans, whether nobles or brahmins, say, "Mine, mine." They do not understand impermanence through the fact of ceasing to be after having been. Now listen to the state of these blind fools,' and he spoke these verses:

137.

137.

“Hiraññaṃ me suvaṇṇaṃ me, esā rattiṃ divā kathā;

Dummedhānaṃ manussānaṃ, ariyadhammaṃ apassataṃ.

'Silver is mine, gold is mine,'—such is their talk night and day, of foolish humans who do not see the Noble Dhamma.

138.

138.

“Dve dve gahapatayo gehe, eko tattha amassuko;

Lambatthano veṇikato, atho aṅkitakaṇṇako;

Kīto dhanena bahunā, so taṃ vitudate jana”nti.

'Two householders are in the house; one of them is beardless, with pendulous breasts, with braided hair, and also with pierced ears. Bought with much wealth, that one torments the people.'

Tattha hiraññaṃ me suvaṇṇaṃ meti desanāsīsamattametaṃ, iminā pana padadvayena dasavidhampi ratanaṃ sabbaṃ, pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇaṃ khettavatthuṃ dvipadacatuppadañca sabbaṃ dassento “idaṃ me idaṃ me”ti āha. Esā rattiṃ divā kathāti esā manussānaṃ rattiñca divā ca niccakālaṃ kathā. Aññaṃ pana te “pañcakkhandhā aniccā”ti vā “hutvā na bhavantī”ti vā na jānanti, evameva paridevantā vicaranti. Dummedhānanti appapaññānaṃ. Ariyadhammaṃ apassatanti ariyānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ dhammaṃ, ariyaṃ vā niddosaṃ navavidhaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ apassantānaṃ esāva kathā. Aññā pana “aniccaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā”ti tesaṃ kathā nāma natthi.

Therein, 'Silver is mine, gold is mine'—this is merely the heading of the discourse. By these two words, however, he indicates all ten kinds of gems, all early and late grains, fields and land, bipeds and quadrupeds, declaring, 'This is mine, this is mine.' 'This is their talk night and day' means this is the constant talk of humans, night and day. But they do not know anything else, such as 'The five aggregates are impermanent,' or 'Having been, they are no more,' and so they wander about lamenting. 'Of the foolish' means of those of little wisdom. 'Of those not seeing the Noble Dhamma' means this is the only talk for those who do not see the Dhamma of the noble ones, the Buddhas and so on, or the noble, faultless, ninefold supramundane Dhamma. But for them there is no other talk, such as 'impermanence' or 'suffering.'

Gahapatayoti [M 2.0170] gehe adhipatibhūtā. Eko tatthāti tesu dvīsu gharasāmikesu “eko”ti mātugāmaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tattha veṇikatoti kataveṇī, nānappakārena saṇṭhāpitakesakalāpoti attho. Atho aṅkitakaṇṇakoti atha sveva viddhakaṇṇo chiddakaṇṇoti lambakaṇṇataṃ sandhāyāha. Kīto dhanena bahunāti so panesa amassuko lambatthano veṇikato aṅkitakaṇṇo mātāpitūnaṃ bahuṃ [V 2.0155] dhanaṃ datvā kīto, maṇḍetvā pasādhetvā yānaṃ āropetvā mahantena parivārena gharaṃ ānīto. So taṃ vitudate jananti so gahapati āgatakālato paṭṭhāya [P 2.0186] tasmiṃ gehe dāsakammakarādibhedaṃ janaṃ “are duṭṭhadāsa duṭṭhadāsi, imaṃ na karosī”ti mukhasattīhi vitudati, sāmiko viya hutvā mahājanaṃ vicāreti. Evaṃ tāva “manussaloke ativiya ayutta”nti manussalokaṃ garahi.

'Householders' means those who are masters in the house. 'One of them' means: among those two masters of the house, 'one' is said referring to the woman. In that context, 'with braided hair' means having made braids; the meaning is a mass of hair arranged in various ways. 'And also with pierced ears' means: and she has pierced ears, ears with holes; this is said referring to the long earlobes. 'Bought with much wealth' means: this beardless one with pendulous breasts, braided hair, and pierced ears was bought by giving much wealth to her parents, and was brought home adorned, beautified, placed in a vehicle, and accompanied by a great retinue. 'That one torments the people' means: that householder, from the time of her arrival, torments the people in that house—the various slaves, workers, and so on—with spears of the mouth, saying, 'Hey, wicked male slave, wicked female slave, why are you not doing this?' and she manages the people as if she were the master. Thus he first criticized the human world, saying, 'In the human world, this is exceedingly improper.'

Taṃ sutvā sabbe vānarā “mā kathetha, mā kathetha, asotabbayuttakaṃ assumhā”ti ubhohi hatthehi kaṇṇe daḷhaṃ pidahiṃsu. “Imasmiṃ ṭhāne amhehi idaṃ ayuttaṃ suta”nti taṃ ṭhānampi garahitvā aññattha agamaṃsu. So piṭṭhipāsāṇo garahitapiṭṭhipāsāṇoyeva kira nāma jāto.

Hearing that, all the monkeys said, "Do not speak, do not speak! We have heard what should not be heard!" and firmly covered their ears with both hands. "In this place, we have heard something improper," and condemning that place, they went elsewhere. That back-stone indeed came to be known as the 'Condemned Back-Stone'.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā vānaragaṇo buddhaparisā ahosi, vānarindo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths, and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the weary bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the troop of monkeys was the Buddha's assembly, and the monkey king was none other than myself."

Garahitajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Garahita Jātaka, the Ninth.

[220] 10. Dhammadhajajātakavaṇṇanā

[220] 10. The Commentary on the Dhammadhaja Jātaka

Sukhaṃ jīvitarūposīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkiyeva, santāsamattampi pana kātuṃ nāsakkhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove, spoke this Dhammadhaja Jātaka, beginning with 'Sukhaṃ jīvitarūposīti', concerning Devadatta's efforts to kill him. For at that time the Teacher said: "Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, Devadatta strove to kill me, yet he was not able to cause even the slightest terror." Having said this, he brought forth a story of the past.

Atīte [M 2.0171] bārāṇasiyaṃ yasapāṇi nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi, kāḷako nāmassa senāpati ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto tasseva purohito ahosi nāmena dhammadhajo nāma, rañño pana sīsappasādhanakappako chattapāṇi nāma. Rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāreti, senāpati panassa vinicchayaṃ karonto lañjaṃ khādati parapiṭṭhimaṃsiko, lañjaṃ gahetvā assāmike sāmike karoti. Athekadivasaṃ vinicchaye parājito manusso bāhā paggayha kandanto vinicchayā nikkhanto rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantaṃ [P 2.0187] bodhisattaṃ disvā tassa pādesu patitvā “tumhādisesu nāma, sāmi, rañño atthañca dhammañca anusāsantesu kāḷakasenāpati lañjaṃ gahetvā assāmike sāmike karotī”ti attano parājitabhāvaṃ bodhisattassa kathesi. Bodhisatto kāruññaṃ uppādetvā [V 2.0156] “ehi bhaṇe, aḍḍaṃ te vinicchinissāmī”ti taṃ gahetvā vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Mahājano sannipati, bodhisatto taṃ aḍḍaṃ paṭivinicchinitvā sāmikaññeva sāmikaṃ akāsi.

In the past, in Benares, a king named Yasapāṇi ruled, and his general was named Kāḷaka. At that time, the Bodhisatta was his chaplain, named Dhammadhaja, while the king's barber who adorned the king's head was named Chattapāṇi. The king ruled righteously, but his general, while judging cases, took bribes and was a backbiter; taking bribes, he made non-owners into owners. One day, a man who had lost his case, wailing with outstretched arms, left the court and saw the Bodhisatta going to attend upon the king. Falling at his feet, he said, "Sire, while noble ones like you advise the king on matters of welfare and righteousness, General Kāḷaka takes bribes and makes non-owners into owners!"—and he told the Bodhisatta about his defeat. Arousing compassion, the Bodhisatta said, "Come, friend, I will decide your case." Taking him, he went to the court. A great crowd gathered, and the Bodhisatta, re-examining the case, established the true owner as the owner.

Mahājano sādhukāraṃ adāsi, so saddo mahā ahosi. Rājā taṃ sutvā “kiṃ saddo nāmeso”ti pucchi. “Deva, dhammadhajapaṇḍitena dubbinicchito aḍḍo suvinicchito, tatresa sādhukārasaddo”ti. Rājā tuṭṭho bodhisattaṃ pakkosāpetvā “aḍḍo kira te ācariya vinicchito”ti pucchi. “Āma, mahārāja, kāḷakena dubbinicchitaṃ aḍḍaṃ vinicchini”nti vutte “ito dāni paṭṭhāya tumheva aḍḍaṃ vinicchinatha, mayhañca kaṇṇasukhaṃ bhavissati lokassa ca vuḍḍhī”ti vatvā anicchantampi taṃ “sattānuddayāya vinicchaye nisīdathā”ti yācitvā sampaṭicchāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya bodhisatto vinicchaye nisīdati, sāmikeyeva sāmike karoti.

The great crowd gave their applause, and the sound was immense. The king, hearing it, asked, "What is this sound?" "Your Majesty, a case that was poorly judged has been well-judged by Dhammadhaja the wise; that is the sound of applause in that place." The king, pleased, had the Bodhisatta summoned and asked, "Teacher, is it true you have judged the case?" "Yes, great king," he replied, "I have judged the case that was poorly judged by Kāḷaka." When this was said, the king declared, "From this day forward, you alone shall judge cases. This will be pleasing to my ear and will lead to the prosperity of the people." Though the Bodhisatta was unwilling, the king entreated him, saying, "Sit in judgment out of compassion for beings," and made him consent. From then on, the Bodhisatta sat in judgment, establishing the true owners as the owners.

Kāḷako tato paṭṭhāya lañjaṃ alabhanto lābhato parihāyitvā bodhisattassa āghātaṃ bandhitvā “mahārāja, dhammadhajapaṇḍito tava rajjaṃ patthetī”ti bodhisattaṃ rañño antare paribhindi. Rājā asaddahanto “mā evaṃ avacā”ti paṭikkhipitvā puna tena “sace me na saddahatha, tassāgamanakāle vātapānena oloketha. Athānena sakalanagarassa attano hatthe katabhāvaṃ passissathā”ti vutte rājā tassa aḍḍakārakaparisaṃ disvā “etasseva parisā”ti saññāya bhijjitvā “kiṃ karoma [M 2.0172] senāpatī”ti pucchi. “Deva, etaṃ māretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti[P 2.0188]. “Oḷārikadosaṃ apassantā kathaṃ māressāmā”ti? “Attheko upāyo”ti. “Katarūpāyo”ti. “Asayhamassa kammaṃ āropetvā taṃ kātuṃ asakkontaṃ taṃ tena dosena māressāmā”ti. “Kiṃ pana asayhakamma”nti? “Mahārāja, uyyānaṃ nāma sārabhūmiyaṃ ropitaṃ paṭijaggiyamānaṃ tīhi catūhi saṃvaccharehi phalaṃ deti. Tumhe taṃ pakkosāpetvā ‘sve uyyānaṃ kīḷissāma, uyyānaṃ me māpehī’ti vadatha, so māpetuṃ na sakkhissati. Atha naṃ tasmiṃ dose māressāmā”ti.

From that time on, Kāḷaka, receiving no bribes, declined in profit and harbored a grudge against the Bodhisatta. He slandered the Bodhisatta to the king, saying, "Great king, the wise Dhammadhaja covets your kingdom." The king, not believing him, dismissed it, saying, "Do not speak thus." But Kāḷaka persisted, "If you do not believe me, then watch through the window when he comes. Then you will see how he has brought the entire city into his own hands." When the king saw the crowd of litigants attending upon Dhammadhaja, he thought, "This is indeed his following," and, becoming alienated, asked, "What shall we do, general?" "Sire, he ought to be killed." "But without seeing any gross fault, how can we kill him?" "There is a way." "What kind of way?" "We will assign him an impossible task, and when he is unable to perform it, we will kill him for that fault." "And what is an impossible task?" "Great king, a park planted on fertile land, if carefully tended, bears fruit in three or four years. Summon him and say, 'Tomorrow we shall sport in the park; manifest a park for me.' He will not be able to manifest it, and then we can kill him for that fault."

Rājā bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “paṇḍita, mayhaṃ purāṇauyyāne ciraṃ kīḷimha, idāni navauyyāne kīḷitukāmamha, sve kīḷissāma, uyyānaṃ no māpehi, sace māpetuṃ na sakkhissasi, jīvitaṃ te natthī”ti. Bodhisatto “kāḷakena lañjaṃ alabhamānena rājā antare paribhinno bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “sakkonto jānissāmi, mahārājā”ti vatvā gehaṃ gantvā subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā cintayamāno sayane nipajji, sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko [V 2.0157] āvajjento bodhisattassa cittaṃ ñatvā vegenāgantvā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā ākāse ṭhatvā “kiṃ cintesi paṇḍitā”ti pucchi. “Kosi tva”nti? “Sakkohamasmī”ti. “Rājā maṃ ‘uyyānaṃ māpehī’ti āha, taṃ cintemī”ti. “Paṇḍita, mā cintayi, ahaṃ te nandanavanacittalatāvanasadisaṃ uyyānaṃ māpessāmi, katarasmiṃ ṭhāne māpemī”ti? “Asukaṭṭhāne māpehī”ti. Sakko māpetvā devapurameva gato.

The king summoned the Bodhisatta and said, "Wise one, we have long sported in the old park. Now we wish to sport in a new one. We shall play tomorrow, so have a park made for us. If you cannot have it made, you shall lose your life." The Bodhisatta, realizing that the king must have been turned against him by Kāḷaka, who was no longer receiving bribes, replied, "I shall see if it can be done, great king." He then went home, ate a fine meal, and lay down on his bed to ponder. This caused Sakka's abode to grow warm. Sakka, reflecting and perceiving the Bodhisatta’s thought, swiftly came, entered his bedchamber, stood in the air, and asked, "Wise one, what are you thinking?" "Who are you?" "I am Sakka." "The king has ordered me to have a park made, and I am thinking about that." "Wise one, do not worry. I will create for you a park like the Nandana and Cittalatā groves. Where shall I create it?" "Create it in such-and-such a place." Sakka created the park and returned to the city of the devas.

Punadivase bodhisatto uyyānaṃ paccakkhato disvā gantvā rañño ārocesi – “niṭṭhitaṃ te, mahārāja, uyyānaṃ, kīḷassū”ti. Rājā gantvā aṭṭhārasahatthena manosilāvaṇṇena pākārena parikkhittaṃ dvāraṭṭālakasampannaṃ pupphaphalabhārabharitanānārukkhapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ [P 2.0189] uyyānaṃ disvā kāḷakaṃ pucchi – “paṇḍitena amhākaṃ vacanaṃ kataṃ, idāni kiṃ karomā”ti. “Mahārāja, ekarattena uyyānaṃ māpetuṃ sakkonto rajjaṃ gahetuṃ kiṃ na sakkotī”ti? “Idāni kiṃ karomā”ti? “Aparampi naṃ asayhakammaṃ kāremā”ti. “Kiṃ kammaṃ nāmā”ti? “Sattaratanamayaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ māpemā”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “ācariya, uyyānaṃ tāva te māpitaṃ[M 2.0173], etassa pana anucchavikaṃ sattaratanamayaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ māpehi. Sace māpetuṃ na sakkhissasi, jīvitaṃ te natthī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “sādhu, mahārāja, sakkonto māpessāmī”ti āha. Athassa sakko pokkharaṇiṃ māpesi sobhaggappattaṃ satatitthaṃ sahassavaṅkaṃ pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchannaṃ nandanapokkharaṇisadisaṃ.

The next day, the Bodhisatta, having seen the park for himself, went and reported to the king: "Great king, your park is finished. You may now sport in it." The king went and saw the park, surrounded by a wall eighteen cubits high, the color of red arsenic, complete with gates and watchtowers, and adorned with various trees laden with an abundance of flowers and fruit. He then asked Kāḷaka, "The wise one has done as we commanded. What shall we do now?" "Great king, if he can have a park made in a single night, why could he not seize the kingdom?" "What should we do now?" "Let us have him perform another impossible task." "What task is that?" "Let us have him make a lotus pond of the seven precious gems." The king approved and summoned the Bodhisatta: "Teacher, you have had the park made. Now, have a fitting lotus pond of the seven gems made for it. If you cannot have it made, you shall lose your life." The Bodhisatta replied, "Very well, great king, if I am able, I will have it made." Then Sakka had the lotus pond made for him: splendid, with a hundred bathing places, a thousand curves, covered with five-colored lotuses, and resembling the Nandana pond.

Punadivase bodhisatto tampi paccakkhaṃ katvā rañño ārocesi – “māpitā, deva, pokkharaṇī”ti. Rājā tampi disvā “idāni kiṃ karomā”ti kāḷakaṃ pucchi. “Uyyānassa anucchavikaṃ gehaṃ māpetuṃ āṇāpehi, devā”ti. Rājā bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “idāni, ācariya, imassa uyyānassa ceva pokkharaṇiyā ca anucchavikaṃ sabbadantamayaṃ gehaṃ māpehi, no ce māpessasi, jīvitaṃ te natthī”ti āha. Athassa sakko gehampi māpesi. Bodhisatto punadivase tampi paccakkhaṃ katvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā tampi disvā “idāni kiṃ karomā”ti kāḷakaṃ pucchi. “Gehassa anucchavikaṃ maṇiṃ māpetuṃ āṇāpehi, mahārājā”ti āha. Rājā bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “paṇḍita, imassa dantamayagehassa anucchavikaṃ maṇiṃ māpehi, maṇiālokena vicarissāma. Sace māpetuṃ na sakkosi, jīvitaṃ te natthī”ti āha. Athassa sakko maṇimpi māpesi.

The next day, the Bodhisatta, having personally verified it, informed the king: "Your Majesty, the lotus pond is made." The king saw it and again asked Kāḷaka, "What shall we do now?" "Command the creation of a building suitable for the park, Your Majesty." The king summoned the Bodhisatta: "Now, teacher, build a building entirely of ivory, fitting for this park and pond. If you fail to make it, you will lose your life." And so, Sakka had the building made for him. The Bodhisatta personally verified it the next day and reported to the king. Seeing it, the king again asked Kāḷaka, "What shall we do now?" "Command the creation of a gem fitting for the building, great king." The king summoned the Bodhisatta: "Wise one, craft a gem suitable for this ivory building, so we may walk by the gem's light. If you fail to make it, you will lose your life." And so, Sakka had the gem fashioned for him.

Bodhisatto [V 2.0158] punadivase taṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā rañño ārocesi[P 2.0190]. Rājā tampi disvā “idāni kiṃ karissāmā”ti kāḷakaṃ pucchi. “Mahārāja, dhammadhajabrāhmaṇassa icchiticchitadāyikā devatā atthi maññe, idāni yaṃ devatāpi māpetuṃ na sakkoti, taṃ āṇāpehi. Caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ nāma manussaṃ devatāpi māpetuṃ na sakkoti, tasmā ‘caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ me uyyānapālaṃ māpehī’ti taṃ vadāhī”ti. Rājā bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “ācariya, tayā amhākaṃ uyyānaṃ, pokkharaṇī, dantamayapāsādo, tassa ālokakaraṇatthāya maṇiratanañca māpitaṃ, idāni me uyyānarakkhakaṃ caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ uyyānapālaṃ māpehi, no ce māpessasi, jīvitaṃ te natthī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “hotu, labhamāno jānissāmī”ti gehaṃ gantvā subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā nipanno paccūsakāle pabujjhitvā sayanapīṭhe nisinno cintesi – “sakko devarājā yaṃ attanā sakkā māpetuṃ, taṃ māpesi, caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ pana uyyānapālaṃ na sakkā māpetuṃ, evaṃ sante [M 2.0174] paresaṃ hatthe maraṇato araññe anāthamaraṇameva varatara”nti. So kassaci anārocetvā pāsādā otaritvā aggadvāreneva nagarā nikkhamitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle sataṃ dhammaṃ āvajjamāno nisīdi.

The Bodhisatta, having ascertained it the next day, reported it to the king. The king, seeing it too, asked Kāḷaka, "What shall we do now?" "Great king, I think the brahmin Dhammadhaja has a deity who grants every wish. Now, command something that even a deity cannot create. Even a deity cannot create a human being endowed with four qualities. Therefore, tell him, 'Create for me a park-keeper endowed with four qualities.'" The king summoned the Bodhisatta and said, "Teacher, you have created for us a park, a lotus pond, an ivory palace, and a jewel to illuminate it. Now, create for me a park-keeper endowed with four qualities to guard the park. If you do not create him, your life will be forfeit." The Bodhisatta replied, "So be it. I will know if one can be obtained." He returned home, ate a good meal, and lay down. At dawn, he awoke and sat on his couch, reflecting: "Sakka, the king of gods, creates what he himself can create, but it is not possible to create a park-keeper endowed with four qualities. In that case, dying a helpless death in the forest is better than death at the hands of others." Without informing anyone, he descended from the palace, left the city through the main gate, and entered the forest. Seating himself at the foot of a certain tree, he contemplated the Dhamma of the virtuous.

Sakko taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā vanacarako viya hutvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “brāhmaṇa, tvaṃ sukhumālo, adiṭṭhapubbadukkharūpo viya imaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā kiṃ karonto nisinnosī”ti imamatthaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Sakka, knowing that reason, approached the Bodhisatta in the guise of a forest dweller and asked him this question: "Brahmin, you are delicate, seemingly unaccustomed to suffering. Having entered this forest, what are you doing sitting here?" Thus, inquiring about this matter, he spoke the first verse:

136.

136.

“Sukhaṃ jīvitarūposi, raṭṭhā vivanamāgato;

So ekako rukkhamūle, kapaṇo viya jhāyasī”ti.

“You appear to live in comfort, having come from the kingdom to the wilderness; alone at the foot of a tree, you meditate like one who is wretched.”

Tattha sukhaṃ jīvitarūposīti tvaṃ sukhena jīvitasadiso sukhedhito sukhaparihato viya. Raṭṭhāti ākiṇṇamanussaṭṭhānā. Vivanamāgatoti nirudakaṭṭhānaṃ araññaṃ paviṭṭho. Rukkhamūleti rukkhasamīpe. Kapaṇo viya [P 2.0191] jhāyasīti kapaṇo viya ekako nisinno jhāyasi pajjhāyasi, kiṃ nāmetaṃ cintesīti pucchi.

Therein, ‘you appear to live in comfort’ means you are like one living in comfort, as if nurtured and protected by comfort. ‘From the kingdom’ means from a place crowded with people. ‘Having come to the wilderness’ means having entered a waterless forest. ‘At the foot of a tree’ means near a tree. ‘You meditate like one who is wretched’ means you sit alone, meditating and pondering like a wretched person. He asked, ‘What is it that you are thinking about?’

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

140.

140.

“Sukhaṃ [V 2.0159] jīvitarūposmi, raṭṭhā vivanamāgato;

So ekako rukkhamūle, kapaṇo viya jhāyāmi;

Sataṃ dhammaṃ anussara”nti.

“I appear to live in comfort, having come from the kingdom to the wilderness; alone at the foot of a tree, like one who is wretched, I meditate, recollecting the Dhamma of the virtuous.”

Tattha sataṃ dhammaṃ anussaranti, samma, saccametaṃ, ahaṃ sukhaṃ jīvitarūpo raṭṭhā ca vivanamāgato, sohaṃ ekakova imasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīditvā kapaṇo viya jhāyāmi. Yaṃ pana vadesi “kiṃ nāmetaṃ cintesī”ti, taṃ te pavedemi “sataṃ dhamma”nti. Ahañhi sataṃ dhammaṃ anussaranto idha nisinno. Sataṃ dhammanti buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ sataṃ sappurisānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ dhammaṃ. Lābho alābho yaso ayaso nindā pasaṃsā sukhaṃ dukkhanti ayañhi aṭṭhavidho lokadhammo. Iminā pana abbhāhatā santo na kampanti na pavedhenti, ayamettha akampanasaṅkhāto sataṃ dhammo imaṃ anussaranto nisinnomhīti dīpeti.

Therein, ‘recollecting the Dhamma of the virtuous’: ‘Friend, this is true. I appear to live in comfort, and I have come from the kingdom to the wilderness. Thus, sitting alone at the foot of this tree, I meditate like one who is wretched. But as to what you ask, “What is it that you are thinking about?” I will tell you: “the Dhamma of the virtuous.” For I sit here recollecting the Dhamma of the virtuous.’ The Dhamma of the virtuous means the Dhamma of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—the virtuous, the good, and the wise. Gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain—these are the eight worldly conditions. The virtuous, when struck by these, do not tremble or waver. This state, known as unshakeability, is called the Dhamma of the virtuous. He explains, ‘I sit recollecting this.’

Atha [M 2.0175] naṃ sakko “evaṃ sante, brāhmaṇa, imasmiṃ ṭhāne kasmā nisinnosī”ti. “Rājā caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ uyyānapālaṃ āharāpeti, tādisaṃ na sakkomi laddhuṃ, sohaṃ ‘kiṃ me parassa hatthe maraṇena, araññaṃ pavisitvā anāthamaraṇaṃ marissāmī’ti cintetvā idhāgantvā nisinno”ti. “Brāhmaṇa, ahaṃ sakko devarājā, mayā te uyyānādīni māpitāni, caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ uyyānapālaṃ māpetuṃ na sakkā, tumhākaṃ rañño sīsappasādhanakappako chattapāṇi nāma, so caturaṅgasamannāgato, caturaṅgasamannāgatena uyyānapālena atthe sati etaṃ kappakaṃ uyyānapālaṃ kātuṃ vadehī”ti. Iti sakko bodhisattassa ovādaṃ datvā “mā bhāyī”ti samassāsetvā attano devapurameva gato.

Then Sakka asked him, “If that is so, brahmin, why are you sitting in this place?” “The king has ordered me to bring a gardener endowed with four qualities. I am unable to find such a person. So I thought, ‘What is the use of dying at the hands of another? I will enter the forest and die a helpless death.’ Thinking thus, I came here and sat down.” “Brahmin, I am Sakka, king of the gods. It was I who created the park and other things for you. It is not possible to manifest a gardener endowed with four qualities. Your king has a barber named Chattapāṇi, who adorns his head, and he is endowed with four qualities. If there is a need for a gardener endowed with four qualities, you should tell the king to make this barber the gardener.” Having thus given advice to the Bodhisatta, Sakka reassured him, saying, “Do not fear,” and returned to his own celestial city.

Bodhisatto gehaṃ [P 2.0192] gantvā bhuttapātarāso rājadvāraṃ gantvā chattapāṇimpi tattheva disvā hatthe gahetvā “tvaṃ kira, samma chattapāṇi, caturaṅgasamannāgatosī”ti pucchitvā “ko te mayhaṃ caturaṅgasamannāgatabhāvaṃ ācikkhī”ti vutte “sakko, devarājā”ti vatvā “kiṃkāraṇā ācikkhī”ti puṭṭho “iminā nāma kāraṇenā”ti sabbaṃ ācikkhi. So “āma, ahaṃ caturaṅgasamannāgato”ti āha. Atha naṃ bodhisatto hatthe gahetvāva rañño santikaṃ gantvā “ayaṃ, mahārāja, chattapāṇi, caturaṅgasamannāgato, caturaṅgasamannāgatena uyyānapālena atthe sati imaṃ uyyānapālaṃ karothā”ti āha. Atha naṃ rājā “tvaṃ kira caturaṅgasamannāgatosī”ti pucchi. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Katamehi caturaṅgehi samannāgatosī”ti?

The Bodhisatta went home, ate his morning meal, and went to the king’s gate. Seeing Chattapāṇi there, he took him by the hand and asked, “Friend Chattapāṇi, is it true that you are endowed with four qualities?” When Chattapāṇi asked, “Who told you that I am endowed with four qualities?” he replied, “Sakka, the king of the gods.” Asked further, “For what reason did he tell you?” he explained the whole matter. Chattapāṇi then said, “Yes, I am endowed with four qualities.” Then the Bodhisatta, taking him by the hand, went to the king and said, “Great king, this Chattapāṇi is endowed with four qualities. If there is a need for a gardener endowed with four qualities, you should make him the gardener.” Then the king asked him, “Is it true that you are endowed with four qualities?” “Yes, great king.” “With which four qualities are you endowed?”

“Anusūyako [V 2.0160] ahaṃ deva, amajjapāyako ahaṃ;

Nisnehako ahaṃ deva, akkodhanaṃ adhiṭṭhito”ti.

“I am not envious, O king; I do not drink intoxicants; I am without personal affection, O king; and I am resolved on non-anger.”

“Mayhañhi, mahārāja, usūyā nāma natthi, majjaṃ me na pivitapubbaṃ, paresu me sneho vā kodho vā na bhūtapūbbo. Imehi catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatomhī”ti.

“Indeed, great king, I have no envy; I have never before drunk intoxicants; and neither affection nor anger towards others has ever occurred in me. I am endowed with these four qualities.”

Atha naṃ rājā, bho chattapāṇi, “anusūyakosmī”ti vadasīti. “Āma, deva, anusūyakomhī”ti. “Kiṃ ārammaṇaṃ disvā anusūyako jātosī”ti? “Suṇāhi devā”ti attano anusūyakakāraṇaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king said to him, “Ho, Chattapāṇi, you say, ‘I am not envious’?” “Yes, Your Majesty, I am not envious.” “Having seen what object did you become one who is not envious?” “Listen, Your Majesty,” he said, and explaining the reason for his lack of envy, he spoke this verse:

“Itthiyā [M 2.0176] kāraṇā rāja, bandhāpesiṃ purohitaṃ;

So maṃ atthe nivedesi, tasmāhaṃ anusūyako”ti.

“Because of a woman, O king, I had the chaplain imprisoned; he informed me of the truth; therefore, I am not envious.”

Tassattho – ahaṃ, deva, pubbe imasmiṃyeva bārāṇasinagare tādisova rājā hutvā itthiyā kāraṇā purohitaṃ bandhāpesiṃ.

The meaning is this: ‘O king, formerly, in this very city of Bārāṇasī, I myself was a king of that sort and, because of a woman, had the chaplain imprisoned.’

“Abaddhā tattha bajjhanti, yattha bālā pabhāsare;

Baddhāpi tattha muccanti, yattha dhīrā pabhāsare”ti. (jā. 1.1.120) –

“Where fools speak, the unbound are bound; where the wise speak, even the bound are freed.”

Imasmiñhi [P 2.0193] jātake āgatanayeneva ekasmiṃ kāle ayaṃ chattapāṇi rājā hutvā catusaṭṭhiyā pādamūlikehi saddhiṃ sampadussitvā bodhisattaṃ attano manorathaṃ apūrentaṃ nāsetukāmāya deviyā paribhinno bandhāpesi. Tadā naṃ bandhitvā ānīto bodhisatto yathābhūtaṃ deviyā dosaṃ āropetvā sayaṃ mutto raññā bandhāpite sabbepi te pādamūlike mocetvā “etesañca deviyā ca aparādhaṃ khamatha, mahārājā”ti ovadi. Sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva vitthārato veditabbaṃ. Taṃ sandhāyāha –

In the same manner as recounted in that Jātaka, at one time this Chattapāṇi, having become king, was offended together with sixty-four courtiers. Incited by the queen—who wished to destroy the Bodhisatta because he did not fulfill her desires—he had him imprisoned. Then, when the Bodhisatta was brought in bonds, he truthfully exposed the queen’s fault, was freed himself, and had all those courtiers who had been imprisoned by the king released, advising, ‘Forgive the offense of these courtiers and of the queen, O great king.’ The entire matter should be understood in detail in the manner stated previously. Referring to this, he said:

“Itthiyā kāraṇā rāja, bandhāpesiṃ purohitaṃ;

So maṃ atthe nivedesi, tasmāhaṃ anusūyako”ti.

“Because of a woman, O king, I had the chaplain imprisoned; he informed me of the truth; therefore, I am not envious.”

Tadā pana sohaṃ cintesiṃ – “ahaṃ soḷasa sahassaitthiyo pahāya etaṃ ekameva kilesavasena saṅgaṇhantopi santappetuṃ nāsakkhiṃ, evaṃ duppūraṇīyānaṃ itthīnaṃ kujjhanaṃ nāma nivatthavatthe [V 2.0161] kilissante ‘kasmā kilissasī’ti kujjhanasadisaṃ hoti, bhuttabhatte gūthabhāvaṃ āpajjante ‘kasmā etaṃ sabhāvaṃ āpajjasī’ti kujjhanasadisaṃ hoti. ‘Ito dāni paṭṭhāya yāva arahattaṃ na pāpuṇāmi, tāva kilesaṃ nissāya mayi usūyā mā uppajjatū’”ti adhiṭṭhahiṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya anusūyako jāto. Idaṃ sandhāya – “tasmāhaṃ anusūyako”ti āha.

At that time, I reflected: “Having abandoned sixteen thousand women, even though I supported only this one due to defilement, I was not able to satisfy her. Thus, anger towards women, who are so hard to satisfy, is like being angry at a garment being worn when it becomes soiled, asking, ‘Why are you stained?’ or like being angry at eaten food when it becomes excrement, asking, ‘Why have you taken on this nature?’ From now on, until I attain Arahantship, may no envy arise in me on account of defilement.” Thus I resolved. From that time on, I became free from envy. Referring to this, he said, “Therefore I am without envy.”

Atha naṃ rājā “samma chattapāṇi, kiṃ ārammaṇaṃ disvā amajjapo jātosī”ti pucchi. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king asked him, “Friend Chattapāṇi, seeing what object did you become a non-drinker of intoxicants?” Explaining that reason, he spoke this verse:

“Matto [M 2.0177] ahaṃ mahārāja, puttamaṃsāni khādayiṃ;

Tassa sokenahaṃ phuṭṭho, majjapānaṃ vivajjayi”nti.

“I was drunk, great king, when I ate the flesh of my son; touched by sorrow for that, I gave up drinking intoxicants.”

Ahaṃ, mahārāja, pubbe tādiso bārāṇasirājā hutvā majjena vinā vattituṃ nāsakkhiṃ, amaṃsakabhattampi bhuñjituṃ nāsakkhiṃ. Nagare uposathadivasesu māghāto hoti, bhattakārako pakkhassa terasiyaññeva maṃsaṃ gahetvā ṭhapesi, taṃ dunnikkhittaṃ sunakhā khādiṃsu. Bhattakārako uposathadivase maṃsaṃ alabhitvā rañño nānaggarasabhojanaṃ pacitvā pāsādaṃ āropetvā upanāmetuṃ asakkonto deviṃ upasaṅkamitvā “devi, ajja me maṃsaṃ na laddhaṃ, amaṃsakabhojanaṃ nāma upanāmetuṃ na sakkomi, kinti karomī”ti āha. “Tāta, mayhaṃ putto raññā piyo manāpo, puttaṃ me disvā rājā tameva cumbanto parissajanto attano [P 2.0194] atthibhāvampi na jānāti, ahaṃ puttaṃ maṇḍetvā rañño ūrumhi nisīdāpeyyaṃ, rañño puttena saddhiṃ kīḷanakāle tvaṃ bhattaṃ upaneyyāsī”ti. Sā evaṃ vatvā attano puttaṃ alaṅkatābharaṇaṃ maṇḍetvā rañño ūrumhi nisīdāpesi. Rañño puttena saddhiṃ kīḷanakāle bhattakārako bhattaṃ upanāmesi. Rājā surāmadamatto pātiyaṃ maṃsaṃ adisvā “maṃsaṃ kaha”nti pucchitvā “ajja, deva, uposathadivasaṃ māghātatāya maṃsaṃ na laddha”nti vutte “mayhaṃ maṃsaṃ nāma dullabha”nti vatvā ūrumhi nisinnassa piyaputtassa gīvaṃ vaṭṭetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā bhattakārakassa purato khipitvā “vegena sampādetvā āharā”ti āha. Bhattakārako tathā akāsi, rājā puttamaṃsena bhattaṃ bhuñji. Rañño bhayena ekopi kandituṃ vā rodituṃ vā kathetuṃ vā samattho nāma nāhosi.

Great king, in the past, when I was such a king of Bārāṇasī, I could not live without intoxicants, nor could I eat a meal without meat. In the city, on Uposatha days, there was a ban on slaughter. The cook would set aside meat on the thirteenth day of the fortnight, but it was poorly stored, and dogs ate it. On the Uposatha day, the cook, unable to obtain meat, prepared a meal of various excellent flavors for the king, but being unable to bring it up to the palace and serve it, he approached the queen and said, “My queen, today I could not get any meat. I cannot serve a meal without meat. What should I do?” “Dear one, my son is beloved and dear to the king. When the king sees my son, he kisses and embraces him, forgetting even his own existence. I will adorn my son and seat him on the king’s lap. While the king is playing with the child, you may serve the meal.” So saying, she adorned her son with ornaments and seated him on the king’s lap. While the king was playing with his son, the cook served the meal. The king, intoxicated with liquor, not seeing meat in his bowl, asked, “Where is the meat?” When told, “Today, lord, is the Uposatha day, and no meat was obtained due to the ban on slaughter,” he said, “Is meat really so hard to come by for me?” Then, twisting the neck of his beloved son seated on his lap, he ended the child’s life and threw him before the cook, saying, “Quickly prepare it and bring it here!” The cook did so, and the king ate his meal with his son’s flesh. Out of fear of the king, no one was able to weep, cry, or even speak a word.

Rājā bhuñjitvā sayanapiṭṭhe niddaṃ upagantvā paccūsakāle pabujjhitvā vigatamado “puttaṃ me ānethā”ti āha. Tasmiṃ kāle devī kandamānā pādamūle pati. “Kiṃ, bhadde”ti ca vutte[V 2.0162], “deva, hiyyo te puttaṃ māretvā puttamaṃsena bhattaṃ bhutta”nti āha. Rājā puttasokena roditvā kanditvā “idaṃ me dukkhaṃ surāpānaṃ nissāya uppanna”nti surāpāne dosaṃ disvā “ito paṭṭhāya yāva arahattaṃ na pāpuṇāmi, tāva evarūpaṃ vināsakārakaṃ [M 2.0178] suraṃ nāma na pivissāmī”ti paṃsuṃ gahetvā mukhaṃ puñchitvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya majjaṃ nāma na piviṃ. Imamatthaṃ sandhāya – “matto ahaṃ, mahārājā”ti imaṃ gāthamāha.

The king, having eaten, lay down on the bed and went to sleep. At dawn, he woke up, free from intoxication, and said, “Bring my son to me.” At that time, the queen, weeping, fell at his feet. When asked, “What is it, my lady?” she replied, “My lord, yesterday you killed your son and ate a meal with your son's flesh.” Overcome with grief for his son, the king wept and lamented. Seeing the fault in drinking liquor, he thought, “This suffering of mine has arisen because of drinking liquor,” and resolved, “From now on, until I attain Arahantship, I will not drink such a destructive liquor.” Taking dust, he wiped his face and made his resolution. From then on, I never drank liquor again. Referring to this matter, he spoke this verse: “I was intoxicated, great king.”

Atha naṃ rājā “kiṃ pana, samma chattapāṇi, ārammaṇaṃ disvā nisneho jātosī”ti pucchi. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king asked him, “But, friend Chattapāṇi, seeing what object have you become without affection?” He, explaining the reason, spoke this verse:

“Kitavāso nāmahaṃ rāja, putto paccekabodhi me;

Pattaṃ bhinditvā cavito, nisneho tassa kāraṇā”ti.

“O king, I was named Kitavāsa. My son, having broken the bowl of a Paccekabuddha, passed away. For that reason, I am without affection.”

Mahārāja, pubbe ahaṃ bārāṇasiyaṃyeva kitavāso nāma rājā. Tassa me putto vijāyi. Lakkhaṇapāṭhakā taṃ disvā “mahārāja, ayaṃ kumāro pānīyaṃ alabhitvā marissatī”ti āhaṃsu. “Duṭṭhakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto oparajjaṃ kāresi, rājā kumāraṃ purato vā pacchato vā katvā vicari, pānīyaṃ alabhitvā maraṇabhayena cassa catūsu dvāresu antonagaresu ca tattha tattha pokkharaṇiyo kāresi, catukkādīsu maṇḍape kāretvā pānīyacāṭiyo ṭhapāpesi. So ekadivase alaṅkatapaṭiyatto pātova uyyānaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge paccekabuddhaṃ passi. Mahājanopi paccekabuddhaṃ disvā tameva vandati [P 2.0195] pasaṃsati, añjaliñcassa paggaṇhāti.

Great king, in the past I was a king named Kitavāso in this very city of Bārāṇasī. A son was born to me. The readers of signs, upon seeing him, said, “Great king, this prince will die if he does not obtain water.” His name was Duṭṭhakumāra. When he reached maturity, he ruled as viceroy. The king, fearing the prince's death from lack of water, traveled with the prince either in front or behind him, and had ponds dug for him here and there at the four gates and within the inner city. He also had pavilions built at the crossroads and so forth, and had water jars placed there. One day, adorned and prepared early in the morning, while going to the park, on the way he saw a Paccekabuddha. The crowd, upon seeing the Paccekabuddha, paid homage to him, praised him, and raised their joined hands to him.

Kumāro cintesi – “mādisena saddhiṃ gacchantā imaṃ muṇḍakaṃ vandanti pasaṃsanti, añjaliñcassa paggaṇhantī”ti. So kupito hatthikkhandhato oruyha paccekabuddhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “laddhaṃ te, samaṇa, bhatta”nti vatvā “āma, kumārā”ti vutte tassa hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā saddhiṃ bhattena madditvā pādappahārena cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ akāsi. Paccekabuddho “naṭṭho vatāyaṃ satto”ti tassa mukhaṃ olokesi. Kumāro “ahaṃ, samaṇa, kitavāsarañño putto, nāmena duṭṭhakumāro nāma, tvaṃ me kuddho akkhīni ummīletvā olokento kiṃ karissasī”ti āha.

The prince thought, “While traveling with someone like me, these people bow to and praise this shaveling, raising their hands in reverence to him.” Angered, he descended from the elephant's back, approached the Paccekabuddha, and said, “Did you get alms, ascetic?” When the Paccekabuddha replied, “Yes, prince,” the prince snatched the bowl from his hand, threw it to the ground, crushed it along with the food, and shattered it into tiny pieces with a kick. The Paccekabuddha looked at his face and thought, “Alas, this being is ruined.” The prince said, “I, ascetic, am the son of King Kitavāsa, named Duṭṭhakumāra. What will you do, opening your eyes wide and looking at me angrily?”

Paccekabuddho [V 2.0163] chinnabhatto hutvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā uttarahimavante nandanamūlapabbhārameva gato. Kumārassāpi taṅkhaṇaññeva pāpakammaṃ paripacci. So “ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmī”ti samuggatasarīraḍāho tattheva pati. Tattha tattheva yattakaṃ pānīyaṃ, tattakaṃ pānīyaṃ sabbaṃ chijji, mātikā sussiṃsu, tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ [M 2.0179] patvā avīcimhi nibbatti. Rājā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā puttasokena abhibhūto cintesi – “ayaṃ me soko piyavatthuto uppajji, sace me sneho nābhavissa, soko na uppajjissa, ito dāni me paṭṭhāya saviññāṇake vā aviññāṇake vā kismiñci vatthusmiṃ sneho nāma mā uppajjatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi, tato paṭṭhāya sneho nāma natthi. Taṃ sandhāya “kitavāso nāmāha”nti gāthamāha.

The Paccekabuddha, having been deprived of his meal, rose into the air and went to the Nandanamūla mountain cave in the northern Himalayas. At that very moment, the prince's evil deed ripened. Crying, 'I am burning, I am burning!' as a burning sensation arose in his body, he fell right there. All the water that was there was cut off, the water channels dried up, and right there his life came to an end, and he was reborn in Avīci. The king, hearing of this event and overwhelmed by grief for his son, reflected: 'This sorrow of mine arose from a beloved object. If I had no affection, sorrow would not have arisen. From now on, may no affection whatsoever arise in me toward any object, whether conscious or unconscious.' He made this resolution, and from then on, he had no affection. Referring to this, he spoke the verse, 'I am called Kitavāsa.'

Tattha putto paccekabodhi me. Pattaṃ bhinditvā cavitoti mama putto paccekabodhipattaṃ bhinditvā cavitoti attho. Nisneho tassa kāraṇāti tadā uppannasnehavatthussa kāraṇā ahaṃ nisneho jātoti attho.

Therein, 'my son, a Paccekabodhi' and 'having broken the bowl, he passed away' means: my son, having broken the Paccekabuddha's bowl, passed away. 'Because of that, I am without affection' means: because of that object of affection which then arose, I became without affection.

Atha naṃ rājā “kiṃ pana, samma, ārammaṇaṃ disvā nikkodho jātosī”ti pucchi. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king asked him, "But, friend, having seen what object did you become free from anger?" Explaining that reason, he spoke this verse:

“Arako hutvā mettacittaṃ, satta vassāni bhāvayiṃ;

Satta kappe brahmaloke, tasmā akkodhano aha”nti.

"Having become Araka, I cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for seven years. For seven aeons, I was in the Brahma-world. Therefore, I am without anger."

Tassattho – ahaṃ, mahārāja, arako nāma tāpaso hutvā satta vassāni mettacittaṃ bhāvetvā satta saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe brahmaloke vasiṃ, tasmā ahaṃ dīgharattaṃ mettābhāvanāya āciṇṇapariciṇṇattā akkodhano jātoti.

The meaning is: "Great king, having become an ascetic named Araka and having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for seven years, I dwelt in the Brahma-world for seven aeons of world-contraction and expansion. Therefore, because I have long practiced and become familiar with the cultivation of loving-kindness, I have become free from anger."

Evaṃ chattapāṇinā attano catūsu aṅgesu kathitesu rājā parisāya iṅgitasaññaṃ adāsi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva amaccā ca brāhmaṇagahapatikādayo [P 2.0196] ca uṭṭhahitvā “are lañjakhādaka duṭṭhacora, tvaṃ lañjaṃ alabhitvā paṇḍitaṃ upavaditvā māretukāmo jāto”ti kāḷakaṃ senāpatiṃ hatthapādesu gahetvā rājanivesanā otāretvā gahitagahiteheva pāsāṇamuggarehi sīsaṃ bhinditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā pādesu gahetvā kaḍḍhantā saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍesuṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kārento yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, when Chattapāṇi had spoken of his four qualities, the king gave a signal to the assembly. Instantly, the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others rose up, saying, "You bribe-taker, you wicked thief! Not receiving a bribe, you disparaged a wise man and sought to kill him!" They seized General Kāḷaka by his hands and feet, dragged him down from the royal palace, and with whatever stones and hammers they could seize, they crushed his head, ending his life. Then, dragging him by the feet, they threw him onto a rubbish heap. From then on, the king ruled the kingdom righteously and passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 2.0164][M 2.0180] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kāḷakasenāpati devadatto ahosi, chattapāṇikappako sāriputto, sakko anuruddho, dhammadhajo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: "At that time, General Kāḷaka was Devadatta, Chattapāṇi the barber was Sāriputta, Sakka was Anuruddha, and Dhammadhaja was indeed myself."

Dhammadhajajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Dhammadhaja Jātaka, the tenth.

Bīraṇathambhavaggo sattamo.

The Bīraṇathambha Chapter, the seventh.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Somadattañca ucchiṭṭhaṃ, kuru puṇṇanadīpi ca;

Kacchapamacchaseggu ca, kūṭavāṇijagarahi;

Dhammadhajanti te dasa.

Somadatta and the Leftovers, Kuru and also Puṇṇanadī; The Turtle, the Fish, and Seggu, the Deceitful Merchant, Garahita; and Dhammadhaja—these are the ten.

8. Kāsāvavaggo

8. The Chapter on the Ochre Robe

[221] 1. Kāsāvajātakavaṇṇanā

[221] 1. The Commentary on the Kāsāva Jātaka

Anikkasāvo [V 2.0165] kāsāvanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana rājagahe samuṭṭhitaṃ. Ekasmiṃ samaye dhammasenāpati pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ veḷuvane viharati. Devadattopi attano anurūpāya dussīlaparisāya parivuto gayāsīse viharati. Tasmiṃ samaye rājagahavāsino chandakaṃ saṅgharitvā dānaṃ sajjayiṃsu. Atheko vohāratthāya āgatavāṇijo imaṃ sāṭakaṃ vissajjetvā “mampi pattikaṃ karothā”ti mahagghaṃ gandhakāsāvaṃ adāsi. Nāgarā mahādānaṃ pavattayiṃsu, sabbaṃ chandakena saṅkaḍḍhitaṃ kahāpaṇeheva niṭṭhāsi. So sāṭako atireko ahosi. Mahājano sannipatitvā “ayaṃ gandhakāsāvasāṭako atireko. Kassa naṃ dema, kiṃ sāriputtattherassa, udāhu devadattassā”ti mantayiṃsu.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this verse beginning "He who is not free from stain, yet wears the ochre robe," concerning Devadatta. The story, however, originated in Rājagaha. At one time, the General of the Dhamma was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove with five hundred monks. Devadatta, too, surrounded by his retinue of unvirtuous followers, was dwelling at Gayāsīsa. At that time, the residents of Rājagaha collected contributions and prepared an offering. Then a certain merchant who had come for trade gave a very expensive, fragrant ochre robe, saying, "Please make me a partaker in this merit." The citizens organized a great offering, and all the monetary contributions collected were spent. That robe was left over. The people gathered and deliberated: "This fragrant ochre robe is extra. To whom shall we give it? To the Elder Sāriputta, or to Devadatta?"

Tattheke “sāriputtattherassā”ti āhaṃsu. Apare “sāriputtatthero katipāhaṃ vasitvā yathāruci pakkamissati[P 2.0197], devadattatthero pana nibaddhaṃ amhākaṃ nagarameva upanissāya viharati, maṅgalāmaṅgalesu ayameva amhākaṃ [M 2.0181] avassayo, devadattassa dassāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Sambahulikaṃ karontesupi “devadattassa dassāmā”ti vattāro bahutarā ahesuṃ, atha naṃ devadattassa adaṃsu. Devadatto tassa dasā chindāpetvā ovaṭṭikaṃ sibbāpetvā rajāpetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭavaṇṇaṃ katvā pārupi. Tasmiṃ kāle tiṃsamattā bhikkhū rājagahā nikkhamitvā sāvatthiṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā katapaṭisanthārā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “evaṃ, bhante, attano ananucchavikaṃ arahaddhajaṃ pārupī”ti ārocesuṃ. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva attano ananurūpaṃ arahaddhajaṃ paridahati, pubbepi paridahiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Therein, some said, "To the Elder Sāriputta." Others said, "The Elder Sāriputta will stay for a few days and then depart as he pleases, but the Elder Devadatta constantly resides in dependence on our city. In both auspicious and inauspicious matters, he is our refuge. Let us give it to Devadatta." Although many opinions were expressed, those who said, "Let us give it to Devadatta," were the majority, and so they gave it to Devadatta. Devadatta had its fringes cut off, had its edges hemmed and sewn, had it dyed, and having made it the color of a golden plate, he wore it. At that time, about thirty monks departed from Rājagaha, went to Sāvatthi, paid homage to the Teacher, and after courteous greetings were exchanged, they reported the matter, saying, "Venerable sir, he is wearing the banner of an Arahant, which is unsuitable for him." The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta wears the banner of an Arahant that is unsuitable for him; he wore it in the past as well," and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese hatthikule nibbattitvā vayappatto asītisahassamattavāraṇaparivāro yūthapati hutvā araññāyatane vasati. Atheko duggatamanusso bārāṇasiyaṃ viharanto dantakāravīthiyaṃ dantakāre dantavalayādīni karonte disvā [V 2.0166] “hatthidante labhitvā gaṇhissathā”ti pucchi. Te “āma gaṇhissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. So āvudhaṃ ādāya kāsāvavatthavasano paccekabuddhavesaṃ gaṇhitvā paṭisīsakaṃ paṭimuñcitvā hatthivīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā āvudhena hatthiṃ māretvā dante ādāya bārāṇasiyaṃ vikkiṇanto jīvikaṃ kappesi. So aparabhāge bodhisattassa parivārahatthīnaṃ sabbapacchimaṃ hatthiṃ māretuṃ ārabhi. Hatthino devasikaṃ hatthīsu parihāyantesu “kena nu kho kāraṇena hatthino parihāyantī”ti bodhisattassa ārocesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into an elephant family in the Himalayan region. Having reached maturity, he became the leader of a herd of eighty thousand elephants and lived in a forest wilderness. At that time, a poor man living in Benares saw ivory carvers in the ivory-workers' street making ivory bracelets and other items, and asked them, "If I obtain elephant tusks, will you buy them?" They replied, "Yes, we will buy them." Taking a weapon, donning an ochre robe, and taking the guise of a Paccekabuddha, he covered his head and stood in the elephants' path. With his weapon, he would kill an elephant, take its tusks, and sell them in Benares, thus making his living. Later, he began to kill the very last elephant in the Bodhisatta's herd. As the elephants dwindled daily, the herd reported to the Bodhisatta, "For what reason are the elephants decreasing?"

Bodhisatto pariggaṇhanto “paccekabuddhavesaṃ gahetvā hatthivīthipariyante eko puriso tiṭṭhati, kacci nu kho so māreti, pariggaṇhissāmi na”nti ekadivasaṃ hatthī purato katvā sayaṃ [P 2.0198] pacchato ahosi. So bodhisattaṃ disvā āvudhaṃ ādāya pakkhandi. Bodhisatto nivattitvā ṭhito “bhūmiyaṃ pothetvā māressāmi na”nti soṇḍaṃ pasāretvā tena paridahitāni kāsāvāni disvā “imaṃ arahaddhajaṃ mayā garuṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti soṇḍaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā “ambho purisa, nanu esa arahaddhajo ananucchaviko tuyhaṃ, kasmā etaṃ paridahasī”ti imā gāthā avoca –

The Bodhisatta, investigating, thought, "A man stands alone at the end of the elephants' path, having taken the guise of a Paccekabuddha. Could it be that he is the one who kills them? I shall investigate him." One day, he put the other elephants in front and went last himself. Seeing the Bodhisatta, the man took up his weapon and rushed forward. The Bodhisatta turned and stood still, thinking, "I shall kill him by smashing him to the ground." But as he stretched out his trunk, he saw the ochre robes the man was wearing and thought, "It is proper for me to honor this banner of an Arahant." Withdrawing his trunk, he said, "Good man, is not this banner of an Arahant unsuitable for you? Why do you wear it?" Then he spoke these verses:

141.

141.

“Anikkasāvo kāsāvaṃ, yo vatthaṃ paridahissati;

Apeto damasaccena, na so kāsāvamarahati.

“One who is not free from defilements, yet wears the ochre robe, devoid of self-control and truth, is not worthy of the ochre robe.”

142.

142.

“Yo [M 2.0182] ca vantakasāvassa, sīlesu susamāhito;

Upeto damasaccena, sa ve kāsāvamarahatī”ti.

“But one who has disgorged defilements, is well established in virtue, and endowed with self-control and truth, truly deserves the ochre robe.”

Tattha anikkasāvoti kasāvo vuccati rāgo doso moho makkho paḷāso issā macchariyaṃ māyā sāṭheyyaṃ thambho sārambho māno atimāno mado pamādo, sabbe akusalā dhammā sabbe duccaritā sabbaṃ bhavagāmikammaṃ diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ, eso kasāvo nāma. So yassa puggalassa appahīno santānato anissaṭṭho anikkhanto, so anikkasāvo nāma. Kāsāvanti kasāyarasapītaṃ arahaddhajabhūtaṃ. Yo vatthaṃ paridahissatīti yo evarūpo hutvā evarūpaṃ vatthaṃ paridahissati nivāseti ceva pārupati ca. Apeto damasaccenāti indriyadamasaṅkhātena damena ca nibbānasaṅkhātena ca paramatthasaccena apeto parivajjito. Nissakkatthe vā karaṇavacanaṃ, etasmā damasaccā apetoti attho. “Sacca”nti cettha vacīsaccaṃ [V 2.0167] catusaccampi vaṭṭatiyeva. Na so kāsāvamarahatīti so puggalo anikkasāvattā arahaddhajaṃ kāsāvaṃ na arahati ananucchaviko etassa.

Herein, ‘not free from defilements’ (anikkasāvo): defilement is said to be lust, hatred, delusion, hypocrisy, spite, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, rivalry, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, heedlessness—all unwholesome states, all misconduct, all kamma leading to rebirth, the one and a half thousand defilements. This is called defilement. A person in whom this is not abandoned, not relinquished from their continuum, not expelled, is called ‘not free from defilements.’ ‘Ochre robe’ (kāsāva၁) refers to that which is dyed with ochre dye, the banner of the Arahants. ‘Who would wear the robe’ (yo vattha၁ paridahissatĦti) means one who, being of such a nature, would wear such a robe, both as a lower garment and as an upper garment. ‘Devoid of self-control and truth’ (apeto damasaccena) means devoid of and separated from self-control, known as the restraint of the senses, and truth, known as the ultimate truth of Nibbāna. Alternatively, the instrumental case is used in the sense of separation; hence, the meaning is ‘separated from this self-control and truth.’ Here, ‘truth’ (sacca၁) can refer to verbal truth or the Four Truths; it certainly applies. ‘Is not worthy of the ochre robe’ (na so kāsāvamarahatĦti) means that person, being not free from defilements, is not worthy of the ochre robe, the banner of the Arahants; it is not suitable for them.

Yo ca vantakasāvassāti yo pana puggalo yathāvuttasseva kasāvassa vantattā vantakasāvo assa. Sīlesu susamāhitoti maggasīlesu ceva phalasīlesu ca sammā āhito, ānetvā ṭhapito viya tesu patiṭṭhito. Tehi sīlehi samaṅgībhūtassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Upetoti samannāgato. Damasaccenāti vuttappakārena damena ca saccena ca. Sa ve kāsāvamarahatīti so evarūpo puggalo imaṃ arahaddhajaṃ kāsāvaṃ arahati.

‘But one who has disgorged defilements’ (Yo ca vantakasāvassa): a person who, by having disgorged the aforementioned defilements, would be one who has disgorged defilements. ‘Well established in virtue’ (sĦlesu susamāhito): rightly established in the path virtues and the fruition virtues, established in them as if brought and placed there. This is a designation for one who is endowed with those virtues. ‘Endowed’ (Upeto): possessed. ‘With self-control and truth’ (Damasaccena): with self-control and truth in the manner described. ‘Truly deserves the ochre robe’ (Sa ve kāsāvamarahati): such a person is indeed worthy of this banner of the Arahants, the ochre robe.

Evaṃ [P 2.0199] bodhisatto tassa purisassa imaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathetvā “ito paṭṭhāya mā idha āgami, āgacchasi ce, jīvitaṃ te natthī’”ti tajjetvā palāpesi.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having explained this reason to that man, threatened him, saying, ‘From now on, do not come here. If you do, your life will be forfeit,’ and chased him away.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā hatthimārakapuriso devadatto ahosi, yūthapati pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: ‘At that time, the elephant-killing man was Devadatta, but the herd leader was I myself.’

Kāsāvajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kāsāva Jātaka: The First.

[222] 2. Cūḷanandiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[222] 2. The Commentary on the Cũဳanandiya Jātaka

Idaṃ [M 2.0183] tadācariyavacoti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, devadatto nāma kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko sammāsambuddhe abhimāre payojesi, silaṃ pavijjhi, nāḷāgiriṃ payojesi, khantimettānuddayamattampissa tathāgate natthī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto kakkhaḷo pharuso nikkāruṇikoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘This is the Teacher’s instruction.’ The Teacher, while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove, spoke this concerning Devadatta. One day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Dhamma hall: ‘Friends, Devadatta is coarse, harsh, and reckless. He employed assassins against the Perfectly Enlightened One, hurled a rock, and unleashed the elephant Nāဳāgiri. Not even a trace of patience, loving-kindness, or compassion exists in him towards the Tathāgata.’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?’ When they replied, ‘This one,’ he said, ‘Not only now, monks, but in the past as well Devadatta was coarse, harsh, and without compassion.’ Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese mahānandiyo nāma vānaro ahosi, kaniṭṭhabhātiko panassa cūḷanandiyo nāma. Te ubhopi asītisahassavānaraparivārā himavantapadese andhamātaraṃ paṭijaggantā vāsaṃ kappesuṃ. Te mātaraṃ sayanagumbe ṭhapetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā madhurāni phalāphalāni mātuyā pesenti. Āharaṇakavānarā [V 2.0168] tassā na denti, sā khudāpīḷitā aṭṭhicammāvasesā kisā ahosi. Atha naṃ bodhisatto āha – “mayaṃ, amma, tumhākaṃ madhuraphalāphalāni pesema, tumhe kasmā milāyathā”ti. “Tāta, nāhaṃ labhāmī”ti. Bodhisatto cintesi [P 2.0200] – “mayi yūthaṃ pariharante mātā me nassissati, yūthaṃ pahāya mātaraṃyeva paṭijaggissāmī”ti. So cūḷanandiyaṃ pakkositvā “tāta, tvaṃ yūthaṃ parihara, ahaṃ mātaraṃ paṭijaggissāmī”ti āha. Sopi naṃ “bhātika, mayhaṃ yūthapariharaṇena kammaṃ natthi, ahampi mātarameva paṭijaggissāmī”ti āha. Iti te ubhopi ekacchandā hutvā yūthaṃ pahāya mātaraṃ gahetvā himavantā oruyha paccante nigrodharukkhe vāsaṃ kappetvā mātaraṃ paṭijaggiṃsu.
