In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārā၇asĦ, the Bodhisatta was a monkey named Mahānandiya in the Himalayan region, and his younger brother was named Cũဳanandiya. Both of them, with a retinue of eighty thousand monkeys, lived in the Himalayan region, attending to their blind mother. They would leave their mother in a sleeping-thicket, enter the forest, and send sweet fruits back to her. But the monkeys tasked with bringing the food did not give it to her, and so, tormented by hunger, she became emaciated, reduced to skin and bones. Then the Bodhisatta said to her, ‘Mother, we send you sweet fruits—why do you waste away?’ She replied, ‘My dear, I do not receive them.’ The Bodhisatta thought, ‘If I continue leading the troop, my mother will perish. I must abandon the troop and care for her myself.’ He summoned Cũဳanandiya and said, ‘Brother, you lead the troop; I will care for our mother.’ But Cũဳanandiya replied, ‘Brother, I have no business leading the troop. I too will care for our mother.’ Thus, both of them, being of one accord, abandoned the troop and, taking their mother, descended from the Himalayas. They settled in a banyan tree in a border region and cared for their mother.

Atheko bārāṇasivāsī brāhmaṇamāṇavo takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā “gamissāmī”ti ācariyaṃ āpucchi. Ācariyo aṅgavijjānubhāvena tassa kakkhaḷapharusasāhasikabhāvaṃ ñatvā “tāta, tvaṃ kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko, evarūpānaṃ na sabbakālaṃ ekasadisameva ijjhati, mahāvināsaṃ mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇissasi, mā tvaṃ kakkhaḷo hohi, pacchānutāpanakāraṇaṃ kammaṃ mā karī”ti [M 2.0184] ovaditvā uyyojesi. So ācariyaṃ vanditvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā gharāvāsaṃ gahetvā aññehi sippehi jīvikaṃ kappetuṃ asakkonto “dhanukoṭiṃ nissāya jīvissāmi, luddakammaṃ katvā jīvikaṃ kappessāmī”ti bārāṇasito nikkhamitvā paccantagāmake vasanto dhanukalāpasannaddho araññaṃ pavisitvā nānāmige māretvā maṃsavikkayena jīvikaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ araññe kiñci alabhitvā āgacchanto aṅgaṇapariyante ṭhitaṃ nigrodharukkhaṃ disvā “api nāmettha kiñci bhaveyyā”ti nigrodharukkhābhimukho pāyāsi.

Then a young Brahmin from Bārā၇asĦ, having learned all the arts from his world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā, asked permission of his teacher to leave, saying, ‘I will go.’ Knowing through his skill in physiognomy that the youth was coarse, harsh, and reckless, the teacher advised him, ‘Dear one, you are coarse, harsh, and reckless. For such people, success does not always come in the same way; you will meet with great ruin and suffering. Do not be coarse; do not perform actions that will cause regret later.’ Having given this advice, he sent him on his way. The youth paid respects to his teacher and went to Bārā၇asĦ, where he took up the household life. Unable to make a living with other skills, he thought, ‘I will live by relying on the tip of my bow; I will make a living by hunting.’ Leaving Bārā၇asĦ, he settled in a border village. Armed with bow and quiver, he entered the forest, killed various deer, and made a living by selling their meat. One day, having found nothing in the forest, he was returning when he saw a banyan tree standing at the edge of a clearing. Thinking, ‘Perhaps there is something here,’ he approached the banyan tree.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe ubhopi te bhātaro mātaraṃ phalāni khādāpetvā purato katvā viṭapabbhantare nisinnā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “kiṃ no mātaraṃ karissatī”ti sākhantare nilīyiṃsu. Sopi kho sāhasikapuriso rukkhamūlaṃ āgantvā taṃ tesaṃ mātaraṃ jarādubbalaṃ andhaṃ disvā cintesi – “kiṃ me tucchahatthagamanena imaṃ makkaṭiṃ vijjhitvā gahetvā gamissāmī”ti. So [P 2.0201] tassā vijjhanatthāya dhanuṃ gaṇhi. Taṃ disvā bodhisatto “tāta cūḷanandiya, eso me puriso mātaraṃ vijjhitukāmo, ahamassā jīvitadānaṃ dassāmi, tvaṃ mamaccayena mātaraṃ paṭijaggeyyāsī”ti vatvā sākhantarā nikkhamitvā “bho purisa, mā me mātaraṃ vijjhi, esā andhā jarādubbalā, ahamassā jīvitadānaṃ demi, tvaṃ etaṃ amāretvā maṃ mārehī”ti tassa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā sarassa āsannaṭṭhāne nisīdi. So nikkaruṇo bodhisattaṃ vijjhitvā pātetvā mātarampissa vijjhituṃ [V 2.0169] puna dhanuṃ sannayhi. Taṃ disvā cūḷanandiyo “ayaṃ me mātaraṃ vijjhitukāmo, ekadivasampi kho me mātā jīvamānā laddhajīvitāyeva nāma hoti, jīvitadānamassā dassāmī”ti sākhantarā nikkhamitvā “bho purisa, mā me mātaraṃ vijjhi, ahamassā jīvitadānaṃ dammi, tvaṃ maṃ vijjhitvā amhe dve bhātike gahetvā amhākaṃ mātu jīvitadānaṃ dehī”ti tassa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā sarassa āsannaṭṭhāne nisīdi. So tampi vijjhitvā pātetvā “ayaṃ makkaṭī ghare dārakānaṃ bhavissatī”ti mātarampi tesaṃ vijjhitvā pātetvā tayopi kājenādāya gehābhimukho pāyāsi.

At that moment, both monkey brothers, having fed their mother fruits and leading her, sat in a fork of a tree. Seeing him approaching, they thought, “What will he do to our mother?” and hid among the branches. That violent man came to the foot of the tree and, seeing their mother—old, weak, and blind—he thought, “What use is it for me to go empty-handed? I will shoot this monkey and take her.” So he took up his bow to shoot her. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta said to Cūḷanandiya, “Dear Cūḷanandiya, this man intends to shoot our mother. I will give her the gift of life. After my passing, you must care for her.” Having said this, he emerged from among the branches and said, “Sir, do not shoot my mother. She is blind, old, and weak. I offer my life for hers. Instead of killing her, kill me.” Having received his promise, he sat down in a place within range of the arrow. The merciless man shot the Bodhisatta, felling him, and then prepared his bow again to shoot the mother. Seeing this, Cūḷanandiya thought, “He intends to kill my mother. Even if my mother lives for just one more day, it is as if she has been given life. I will give her the gift of life.” Emerging from among the branches, he said, “Sir, do not shoot my mother. I offer my life for hers. Shoot me, take both of us brothers, and give our mother the gift of life.” Having received his promise, he sat down in a place within range of the arrow. The man shot him too, felling him, and thinking, “This monkey will be for the children at home,” he also shot their mother, felling her. Then, taking all three on a carrying pole, he set out towards his home.

Athassa pāpapurisassa gehe asani patitvā bhariyañca dve dārake ca geheneva saddhiṃ jhāpesi, piṭṭhivaṃsathūṇamattaṃ avasissi. Athassa naṃ gāmadvāreyeva eko puriso disvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. So puttadārasokena [M 2.0185] abhibhūto tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne maṃsakājañja dhanuñca chaḍḍetvā vatthaṃ pahāya naggo bāhā paggayha paridevamāno gantvā gharaṃ pāvisi. Athassa sā thūṇā bhijjitvā sīse patitvā sīsaṃ bhindi, pathavī vivaraṃ adāsi, avīcito jālā uṭṭhahi. So pathaviyā giliyamāno ācariyassa ovādaṃ saritvā “imaṃ vata [P 2.0202] kāraṇaṃ disvā pārāsariyabrāhmaṇo mayhaṃ ovādamadāsī”ti paridevamāno imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

Then lightning struck the house of that wicked man, burning his wife and two children along with the house; only the pillar supporting the roof-beam remained. Then a man saw him at the village gate and told him the news. Overwhelmed by grief for his wife and children, right there he discarded the carrying pole with the meat and his bow, threw off his clothes, and went naked, wailing with arms uplifted, until he entered his home. Then that pillar broke and fell on his head, splitting it open. The earth opened up, and flames from the Avīci hell rose up. As he was being swallowed by the earth, he remembered his teacher’s advice and lamented, “Indeed, seeing this very reason, the brahmin Pārāsariya gave me advice!” Then he uttered these two verses:

143.

143.

“Idaṃ tadācariyavaco, pārāsariyo yadabravi;

Māsu tvaṃ akari pāpaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ pacchā kataṃ tape.

“This was that word of the teacher, which Pārāsariya spoke: ‘Do not commit an evil deed, which, once done, would torment you later.’

144.

144.

“Yāni karoti puriso, tāni attani passati;

Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpakaṃ;

Yādisaṃ vapate bījaṃ, tādisaṃ harate phala”nti.

“Whatever deeds a person does, those they see in themselves. The doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil, evil. As the seed is sown, so is the fruit reaped.”

Tassattho – yaṃ pārāsariyo brāhmaṇo abravi – “māsu tvaṃ pāpaṃ akarī, yaṃ kataṃ pacchā tvaññeva tapeyyā”ti, idaṃ taṃ ācariyassa vacanaṃ. Yāni kāyavacīmanodvārehi kammāni puriso karoti, tesaṃ vipākaṃ paṭilabhanto tāniyeva attani passati. Kalyāṇakammakārī kalyāṇaṃ phalamanubhoti, pāpakārī ca pāpakameva hīnaṃ lāmakaṃ aniṭṭhaphalaṃ anubhoti. Lokasmimpi hi yādisaṃ vapate bījaṃ, tādisaṃ harate phalaṃ, bījānurūpaṃ bījānucchavikameva phalaṃ harati gaṇhāti anubhavatīti. Iti so paridevanto pathaviṃ pavisitvā avīcimahāniraye nibbatti.

The meaning is: What Pārāsariya the brahmin said—‘Do not commit an evil deed, which, once done, you yourself would later find tormenting’—this was the teacher's word. Whatever deeds a person performs through the doors of body, speech, and mind, in receiving the results of those deeds, they see those very deeds in themselves. The doer of good deeds experiences good fruit, while the doer of evil deeds experiences evil, inferior, wretched, and undesirable fruit. For in the world, as the seed is sown, so is the fruit reaped—one reaps, receives, and experiences fruit that is in accordance with the seed, fruit that is indeed suitable to the seed. Thus lamenting, he entered the earth and was reborn in the great Avīci hell.

Satthā [V 2.0170] “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva, pubbepi kakkhaḷo pharuso nikkāruṇikoyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā luddakapuriso devadatto ahosi, disāpāmokkho ācariyo sāriputto, cūḷanandiyo ānando, mātā mahāpajāpatigotamī, mahānandiyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having given this Dhamma discourse, said, “Monks, not only now is Devadatta harsh, cruel, and merciless; he was so in the past as well,” and he identified the birth: “At that time, the hunter was Devadatta, the world-renowned teacher was Sāriputta, Cūḷanandiya was Ānanda, the mother was Mahāpajāpati Gotamī, and Mahānandiya was none other than myself.”

Cūḷanandiyajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Explanation of the Cūḷanandiya Jātaka, the Second.

[223] 3. Puṭabhattajātakavaṇṇanā

[223] 3. The Explanation of the Puṭabhatta Jātaka

Name [M 2.0186] namantassa bhaje bhajantanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthinagaravāsī kireko kuṭumbiko ekena janapadakuṭumbikena saddhiṃ vohāraṃ akāsi. So [P 2.0203] attano bhariyaṃ ādāya tassa dhāraṇakassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Dhāraṇako “dātuṃ na sakkomī”ti na kiñci adāsi, itaro kujjhitvā bhattaṃ abhuñjitvāva nikkhami. Atha naṃ antarāmagge chātajjhattaṃ disvā maggapaṭipannā purisā “bhariyāyapi datvā bhuñjāhī”ti bhattapuṭaṃ adaṃsu. So taṃ gahetvā tassā adātukāmo hutvā “bhadde, idaṃ corānaṃ tiṭṭhanaṭṭhānaṃ, tvaṃ purato yāhī”ti uyyojetvā sabbaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā tucchapuṭaṃ dassetvā “bhadde, abhattakaṃ tucchapuṭameva adaṃsū”ti āha. Sā tena ekakeneva bhuttabhāvaṃ ñatvā domanassappattā ahosi. Te ubhopi jetavanapiṭṭhivihārena gacchantā “pānīyaṃ pivissāmā”ti jetavanaṃ pavisiṃsu.

“One should bow to one who bows, and associate with one who associates.” The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story concerning a certain householder. It is said that a householder living in Sāvatthi had a business transaction with a householder from the countryside. Taking his wife, he went to the debtor. The debtor, saying, “I am unable to give,” gave nothing. The other, becoming angry, left without eating a meal. Then, on the way, seeing him overcome by hunger, some men on the road gave him a packet of food, saying, “Give some to your wife as well, and then eat.” But he, taking it, was unwilling to give her any and said, “My dear, this is a place where thieves wait. You go on ahead.” Having sent her on, he ate all the food himself. Then, showing her the empty packet, he said, “My dear, they gave me only an empty packet with no food.” She, knowing that he had eaten it all by himself, became distressed. As the two of them were passing by the back of the Jetavana monastery, they entered Jetavana, thinking, “We will drink some water.”

Satthāpi tesaññeva āgamanaṃ olokento maggaṃ gahetvā ṭhitaluddako viya gandhakuṭichāyāya nisīdi, te satthāraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kiṃ, upāsike, ayaṃ te bhattā hitakāmo sasneho”ti pucchi. “Bhante, ahaṃ etassa sasnehā, ayaṃ pana mayhaṃ nisneho, tiṭṭhantu aññepi divasā, ajjevesa antarāmagge puṭabhattaṃ labhitvā mayhaṃ adatvā attanāva bhuñjī”ti. “Upāsike, niccakālampi tvaṃ etassa hitakāmā sasnehā, ayaṃ pana nisnehova. Yadā pana paṇḍite nissāya tava guṇe jānāti, tadā te sabbissariyaṃ niyyādetī”ti vatvā tāya yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, watching for their arrival, took his stand on the path like a hunter and sat in the shade of the Perfumed Chamber. Seeing the Teacher, they approached, paid homage, and sat down. The Teacher exchanged friendly greetings with them and asked, 'Laywoman, is this husband of yours well-wishing and affectionate?' 'Venerable sir, I am affectionate toward him, but he is without affection for me. Let alone other days, today on the way he received a packet of food and ate it all himself without giving me any.' 'Laywoman, you are always well-wishing and affectionate toward him, but he is indeed without affection. However, when, by relying on the wise, he comes to know your virtues, then he will hand over all authority to you.' Having said this, at her request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto amaccakule nibbattitvā vayappatto [V 2.0171] tassa atthadhammānusāsako ahosi. Atha rājā “padubbheyyāpi me aya”nti attano puttaṃ āsaṅkanto nīhari. So attano bhariyaṃ gahetvā nagarā nikkhamma ekasmiṃ kāsikagāmake vāsaṃ kappesi. So aparabhāge pitu kālakatabhāvaṃ [M 2.0187] sutvā “kulasantakaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti bārāṇasiṃ paccāgacchanto antarāmagge “bhariyāyapi datvā bhuñjāhī”ti bhattapuṭaṃ labhitvā tassā adatvā sayameva taṃ bhuñji. Sā “kakkhaḷo [P 2.0204] vatāyaṃ puriso”ti domanassappattā ahosi. So bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ gahetvā taṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā “ettakameva etissā ala”nti na aññaṃ sakkāraṃ vā sammānaṃ vā karoti, “kathaṃ yāpesī”tipi naṃ na pucchati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers and, having come of age, became his advisor in matters of welfare and righteousness. Then the king, suspecting his own son, thinking, 'This one might betray me,' banished him. Taking his wife, the prince left the city and lived in a certain village of farmers. Later, hearing of his father's death, he thought, 'I will take the ancestral kingdom,' and set out for Benares. On the way, he received a packet of food with the words, 'Eat this, having given some to your wife as well.' But he did not give her any and ate it all himself. She thought, 'How harsh this man is!' and became distressed. Having taken the throne in Benares, he placed her in the position of chief queen but, thinking, 'This much is enough for her,' he showed her no further honor or respect, nor did he even ask her, 'How are you faring?'

Bodhisatto cintesi – “ayaṃ devī rañño bahūpakārā sasnehā, rājā panetaṃ kismiñci na maññati, sakkārasammānamassā kāressāmī”ti taṃ upasaṅkamitvā upacāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā “kiṃ, tātā”ti vutte “kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetuṃ mayaṃ, devi, tumhe upaṭṭhahāma, kiṃ nāma mahallakānaṃ pitūnaṃ vatthakhaṇḍaṃ vā bhattapiṇḍaṃ vā dātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti āha. “Tāta, ahaṃ attanāva kiñci na labhāmi, tumhākaṃ kiṃ dassāmi, nanu labhanakāle adāsiṃ, idāni pana me rājā na kiñci deti. Tiṭṭhatu aññaṃ dānaṃ, rajjaṃ gaṇhituṃ āgacchanto antarāmagge bhattapuṭaṃ labhitvā bhattamattampi me adatvā attanāva bhuñjī”ti. “Kiṃ pana, amma, rañño santike evaṃ kathetuṃ sakkhissathā”ti? “Sakkhissāmi, tātā”ti. “Tena hi ajjeva mama rañño santike ṭhitakāle mayi pucchante evaṃ kathetha ajjeva vo guṇaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti evaṃ vatvā bodhisatto purimataraṃ gantvā rañño santike aṭṭhāsi. Sāpi gantvā rañño samīpe aṭṭhāsi.

The Bodhisatta thought: 'This queen has been very helpful to the king and is full of affection, yet the king does not care for her at all. I will cause honor and respect to be shown to her.' Approaching her, he showed her due respect and stood to one side. To start a conversation, when she asked, 'What is it, dear sir?' he replied, 'O queen, how may we serve you? Is it not proper to give even a piece of cloth or a morsel of food to one's elderly parents?' She said, 'Dear sir, I myself receive nothing. What can I give you? Did I not give when I was receiving things? But now the king gives me nothing. Let alone other gifts, when he was coming to take the kingdom, he received a packet of food on the way, yet without giving me even a mouthful of rice, he ate it all himself.' 'But, mother, would you be able to speak like this in the king’s presence?' 'I would, dear sir.' 'Then today, when I am standing in the king's presence and I ask you, speak thus. This very day I will make your virtues known.' Having said this, the Bodhisatta went ahead and stood near the king. She too went and stood near the king.

Atha naṃ bodhisatto “amma, tumhe ativiya kakkhaḷā, kiṃ nāma pitūnaṃ vatthakhaṇḍaṃ vā bhattapiṇḍamattaṃ vā dātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti āha. “Tāta, ahameva rañño santikā kiñci na labhāmi, tumhākaṃ kiṃ dassāmī”ti? “Nanu aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ te laddha”nti? “Tāta, kismiñci sammāne asati aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ kiṃ karissati, idāni me tumhākaṃ rājā kiṃ dassati, so antarāmagge bhattapuṭaṃ labhitvā tato kiñci adatvā [P 2.0205] sayameva bhuñjī”ti. Bodhisatto “evaṃ kira, mahārājā”ti pucchi. Rājā adhivāsesi. Bodhisatto tassa adhivāsanaṃ viditvā “tena hi, amma, rañño appiyakālato paṭṭhāya kiṃ tumhākaṃ idha vāsena. Lokasmiñhi appiyasampayogo ca dukkho, tumhākaṃ idha vāse sati rañño appiyasampayogova [V 2.0172] dukkhaṃ [M 2.0188] bhavissati, ime sattā nāma bhajante bhajanti, abhajanabhāvaṃ ñatvā aññattha gantabbaṃ, mahanto lokasannivāso”ti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –

Then the Bodhisatta said to her, 'Mother, you are exceedingly harsh. Why is it that you do not give even a piece of cloth or a mere morsel of food to your elders?' She replied, 'Dear sir, I myself receive nothing from the king. What can I give to you?' 'But surely you have obtained the position of chief queen?' 'Dear sir, when there is no respect, what will the position of chief queen do? What will your king give me now? He received a packet of food on the way and, without giving anything from it, he ate it all himself.' The Bodhisatta asked, 'Is this so, great king?' The king assented. Knowing his assent, the Bodhisatta said, 'Then, mother, since the king has no affection for you, what is the use of your living here? For in the world, association with the unloved is suffering. If you live here, your association with the king who has no affection for you will be suffering. Beings associate with those who associate with them; knowing they are no longer welcome, they should go elsewhere. The world of humans is vast.' And he spoke these verses:

145.

145.

“Name namantassa bhaje bhajantaṃ, kiccānukubbassa kareyya kiccaṃ;

Nānatthakāmassa kareyya atthaṃ, asambhajantampi na sambhajeyya.

One should bow to one who bows, associate with one who associates, and perform duties for one who helps with one's duties. One should not work for the benefit of one who does not desire one's welfare, nor should one associate with one who does not associate.

146.

146.

“Caje cajantaṃ vanathaṃ na kayirā, apetacittena na sambhajeyya;

Dijo dumaṃ khīṇaphalanti ñatvā, aññaṃ samekkheyya mahā hi loko”ti.

One should abandon one who abandons and not form an attachment; one should not associate with one whose heart has turned away. Knowing a tree to be devoid of fruit, a bird seeks another—for the world is vast.

Tattha name namantassa bhaje bhajantanti yo attano namati, tasseva paṭinameyya. Yo ca bhajati, tameva bhajeyya. Kiccānukubbassa kareyya kiccanti attano uppannakiccaṃ anukubbantasseva tassapi uppannakiccaṃ paṭikareyya. Caje cajantaṃ vanathaṃ na kayirāti attānaṃ jahantaṃ jaheyyeva, tasmiṃ taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ vanathaṃ na kareyya. Apetacittenāti vigatacittena vipallatthacittena. Na sambhajeyyāti tathārūpena saddhiṃ na samāgaccheyya. Dijo dumanti yathā sakuṇo pubbe phalitampi rukkhaṃ phale khīṇe “khīṇaphalo aya”nti ñatvā taṃ chaḍḍetvā aññaṃ samekkhati pariyesati, evaṃ aññaṃ samekkheyya. Mahā hi esa loko, atha tumhe sasnehaṃ ekaṃ purisaṃ labhissathāti.

Herein, 'one should bow to one who bows, associate with one who associates' means: to one who bows to oneself, one should bow in return; and with one who associates, with him only should one associate. 'Perform duties for one who helps with one's duties' means: for one who helps with a duty that has arisen for oneself, one should also perform a duty in return when it arises for him. 'One should abandon one who abandons and not form an attachment' means: one should indeed abandon one who leaves oneself, and should not form an attachment, known as craving, for that person. 'With one whose heart has turned away' means: with one whose mind has departed or whose mind is changed. 'One should not associate' means: one should not come together with such a person. 'A bird... a tree' means: just as a bird, knowing 'this tree is now fruitless' when the fruit of a tree that previously bore fruit is gone, abandons it and seeks another, so too should one seek another. For this world is vast, and you will surely find an affectionate man.

Taṃ sutvā bārāṇasirājā deviyā sabbissariyaṃ adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya samaggā sammodamānā vasiṃsu.

Hearing that, the king of Benares granted the queen all sovereignty. From then on, they lived together in harmony and joy.

Satthā [P 2.0206] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne dve jayampatikā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. “Tadā jayampatikā ime dve jayampatikā ahesuṃ, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher revealed the truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, the husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry. ‘At that time, the husband and wife were these two, and the wise minister was I myself.’

Puṭabhattajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Puṭabhatta Jātaka, the third.

[224] 4. Kumbhilajātakavaṇṇanā

[224] 4. The Commentary on the Kumbhila Jātaka

Yassete [V 2.0173][M 2.0189] caturo dhammāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi.

‘Whosoever has these four qualities...’ This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta.

147.

147.

“Yassete caturo dhammā, vānarinda yathā tava;

‘Whosoever has these four qualities, O king of monkeys, just as you do;’

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, diṭṭhaṃ so ativattati.

‘Truth, wisdom, steadfastness, and generosity—such a one overcomes his enemy.’

148.

148.

“Yassa cete na vijjanti, guṇā paramabhaddakā;

‘But one in whom these supreme and auspicious qualities are not found,’

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, diṭṭhaṃ so nātivattatī”ti.

‘Truth, wisdom, steadfastness, and generosity—such a one does not overcome his enemy.’

Tattha guṇā paramabhaddakāti yassa ete paramabhaddakā cattāro rāsaṭṭhena piṇḍaṭṭhena guṇā na vijjanti, so paccāmittaṃ atikkamituṃ na sakkotīti. Sesamettha sabbaṃ heṭṭhā kumbhilajātake vuttanayameva saddhiṃ samodhānenāti.

Herein, ‘supreme and auspicious qualities’ means one in whom these four supreme and auspicious qualities are not found, either in accumulation or in consolidation, is unable to overcome his enemy. The rest here is all in the same way as was told in the Kumbhila Jātaka previously, together with the connection.

Kumbhilajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Kumbhila Jātaka, the Fourth.

[225] 5. Khantivaṇṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[225] 5. The Commentary on the Khantivaṇṇa Jātaka

Atthi me puriso, devāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarājānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa kireko bahūpakāro amacco antepure padussi. Rājā “upakārako me”ti ñatvāpi adhivāsetvā satthu ārocesi. Satthā “porāṇakarājānopi, mahārāja, evaṃ adhivāsesuṃyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

‘I have a man, O king...’ This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the king of Kosala. It seems that one of his ministers, who had been of great service, had misconducted himself in the inner palace. The king, though knowing ‘He has been of great service to me,’ tolerated it and reported it to the Teacher. The Teacher said, ‘Great king, even the kings of old tolerated such things,’ and being requested by him, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente eko amacco tassa antepure padussi, amaccassāpi sevako tassa gehe padussi. So tassa aparādhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto taṃ ādāya rañño santikaṃ gantvā “deva, eko me upaṭṭhāko sabbakiccakārako[P 2.0207], so mayhaṃ gehe padussi, tassa kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, a minister misconducted himself in the king’s inner palace, and that minister’s servant also misconducted himself in the minister’s house. Unable to tolerate his servant’s offense, the minister took him to the king and, asking, ‘Your Majesty, I have an attendant who performs all my duties, but he has misconducted himself in my house. What is proper to be done with him?’ he spoke the first verse:

149.

149.

“Atthi me puriso deva, sabbakiccesu byāvaṭo;

Tassa cekoparādhatthi, tattha tvaṃ kinti maññasī”ti.

‘I have a man, O king, engaged in all duties; but he has committed a single offense. In that matter, what is your judgment?’

Tattha [V 2.0174][M 2.0190] tassa cekoparādhatthīti tassa ca purisassa eko aparādho atthi. Tattha tvaṃ kinti maññasīti tattha tassa purisassa aparādhe tvaṃ “kiṃ kātabba”nti maññasi, yathā te cittaṃ uppajjati, tadanurūpamassa daṇḍaṃ paṇehīti dīpeti.

Herein, ‘he has one offense’ means that this man has committed one offense of misconduct. ‘What do you think of this?’ means regarding that man’s offense, you should consider, ‘What is to be done?’; it indicates that you should impose a penalty corresponding to how it occurs to your mind.

Taṃ sutvā rājā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king spoke the second verse:

150.

150.

“Amhākampatthi puriso, ediso idha vijjati;

Dullabho aṅgasampanno, khantirasmāka ruccatī”ti.

“We too have such a man, he is found here;

A man endowed with good qualities is rare;

Forbearance is pleasing to us.”

Tassattho – amhākampi rājūnaṃ sataṃ ediso bahūpakāro agāre dussanakapuriso atthi, so ca kho idha vijjati, idānipi idheva saṃvijjati, mayaṃ rājānopi samānā tassa bahūpakārataṃ sandhāya adhivāsema, tuyhaṃ pana araññopi sato adhivāsanabhāro jāto. Aṅgasampanno hi sabbehi guṇakoṭṭhāsehi samannāgato puriso nāma dullabho, tena kāraṇena asmākaṃ evarūpesu ṭhānesu adhivāsanakhantiyeva ruccatīti.

The meaning is this: Even for us kings, there exists such a man—greatly helpful, yet a man of misconduct in the household—and he is found right here. Even though we are kings, we endure it, considering his great helpfulness. For you, however, even as a non-king, the burden of tolerance has arisen. A man endowed with all aspects of virtue is indeed rare; for that reason, in such cases, patient endurance is what is pleasing to us.

Amacco attānaṃ sandhāya rañño vuttabhāvaṃ ñatvā tato paṭṭhāya antepure padussituṃ na visahi, sopissa sevako rañño ārocitabhāvaṃ ñatvā tato paṭṭhāya taṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na visahi.

The minister, realizing the king’s words were spoken concerning himself, from then on did not dare to misconduct himself in the inner palace. That servant of his too, realizing it had been reported to the king, from then on did not dare to do that deed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ahameva bārāṇasirājā ahosi”nti. Sopi amacco rañño satthu kathitabhāvaṃ ñatvā tato paṭṭhāya taṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhīti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, I myself was the king of Benares.” And that minister, having learned that the Teacher had spoken to the king, was unable to do that deed from then on.

Khantivaṇṇajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Khantivaṇṇa Jātaka, the fifth.

[226] 6. Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[226] 6. The Commentary on the Kosiya Jātaka

Kāle [P 2.0208] nikkhamanā sādhūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarājānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kosalarājā paccantavūpasamanatthāya akāle nikkhami. Vatthu heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

“To depart at the right time is good”: this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the king of Kosala. The king of Kosala set out at an inopportune time to quell a border disturbance. The story is as told previously.

Satthā [V 2.0175] pana atītaṃ āharitvā āha – “mahārāja, atīte bārāṇasirājā akāle nikkhamitvā uyyāne khandhāvāraṃ nivesayi. Tasmiṃ kāle [M 2.0191] eko ulūkasakuṇo veḷugumbaṃ pavisitvā nilīyi. Kākasenā āgantvā ‘nikkhantameva taṃ gaṇhissāmā’”ti parivāresi. So sūriyatthaṅgamanaṃ anoloketvā akāleyeva nikkhamitvā palāyituṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ kākā parivāretvā tuṇḍehi koṭṭentā paripātesuṃ. Rājā bodhisattaṃ āmantetvā “kiṃ nu kho, paṇḍita, ime kākā kosiyaṃ paripātentī”ti pucchi. Bodhisatto “akāle, mahārāja, attano vasanaṭṭhānā nikkhamantā evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭilabhantiyeva, tasmā akāle attano vasanaṭṭhānā nikkhamituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsento imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

But the Teacher related a story of the past, saying: “Great king, in the past the king of Benares went out at an inopportune time and pitched his camp in a park. At that time, an owl entered a bamboo thicket and hid. An army of crows came and surrounded it, thinking, ‘We will seize him as soon as he comes out.’ Not waiting for sunset, the owl came out at the wrong time and tried to flee. Then the crows surrounded him, pecked him with their beaks, and struck him down. The king addressed the Bodhisatta and asked, ‘Wise sir, why are these crows striking down the owl?’ The Bodhisatta replied: ‘Great king, those who leave their dwelling place at the wrong time surely obtain such suffering. Therefore, one should not leave one’s dwelling place at the wrong time.’ To clarify this matter, he spoke these two verses:”

151.

151.

“Kāle nikkhamanā sādhu, nākāle sādhu nikkhamo;

Akālena hi nikkhamma, ekakampi bahujjano;

Na kiñci atthaṃ joteti, dhaṅkasenāva kosiyaṃ.

“To depart at the right time is good; departure at the wrong time is not good.

For by departing at the wrong time, whether alone or with many, one achieves no benefit,

just as the army of crows did to the owl.”

152.

152.

“Dhīro ca vidhividhānaññū, paresaṃ vivarānugū;

Sabbāmitte vasīkatvā, kosiyova sukhī siyā”ti.

“But the wise one, who knows the rules and their application,

and watches for the weak points of others,

having subdued all his enemies,

may be happy like the owl.”

Tattha kāle nikkhamanā sādhūti, mahārāja, nikkhamanā nāma nikkhamanaṃ vā parakkamanaṃ vā yuttapayuttakāle sādhu. Nākāle sādhu nikkhamoti akāle pana attano vasanaṭṭhānato aññattha gantuṃ nikkhamo nāma nikkhamanaṃ vā parakkamanaṃ vā na sādhu. “Akālena hī”tiādīsu catūsu padesu paṭhamena saddhiṃ tatiyaṃ, dutiyena catutthaṃ yojetvā evaṃ attho veditabbo. Attano vasanaṭṭhānato hi koci puriso akālena nikkhamitvā vā parakkamitvā vā na kiñci [P 2.0209] atthaṃ joteti, attano appamattakampi vuḍḍhiṃ uppādetuṃ na sakkoti, atha kho ekakampi bahujjano bahupi so paccatthikajano etaṃ akāle nikkhamantaṃ vā parakkamantaṃ vā ekakaṃ parivāretvā mahāvināsaṃ pāpeti. Tatrāyaṃ upamā – dhaṅkasenāva kosiyaṃ, yathā ayaṃ dhaṅkasenā imaṃ akāle nikkhamantañca parakkamantañca kosiyaṃ tuṇḍehi vitudanti mahāvināsaṃ pāpenti, tathā tasmā tiracchānagate ādiṃ katvā kenaci akāle attano vasanaṭṭhānato na nikkhamitabbaṃ na parakkamitabbanti.

Herein, O great king, 'departure at the right time is good' means that departure or striving at a proper time is good. 'Departure at the wrong time is not good' means that departing from one’s dwelling place to go elsewhere at an improper time, whether by departure or striving, is not good. In the four lines beginning with 'For by departing at the wrong time,' the meaning should be understood by connecting the first line with the third, and the second with the fourth. For by departing or striving from one’s dwelling place at the wrong time, a person accomplishes no purpose; they cannot bring about even the slightest growth for themselves. Rather, a hostile crowd—many hostile people—surrounds that single person who departs or strives at the wrong time and brings them to great ruin. The simile for this is: 'as an army of crows, the owl.' Just as this army of crows, pecking with their beaks, brings to great destruction this owl that departs and strives at the wrong time, so too, taking this case among animals as an example, no one should depart or strive from their dwelling place at the wrong time.

Dutiyagāthāya [M 2.0192] dhīroti paṇḍito. Vidhīti porāṇakapaṇḍitehi ṭhapitapaveṇī. Vidhānanti koṭṭhāso vā saṃvidahanaṃ vā. Vivarānugūti vivaraṃ anugacchanto jānanto. Sabbāmitteti [V 2.0176] sabbe amitte. Vasīkatvāti attano vase katvā. Kosiyovāti imamhā bālakosiyā añño paṇḍitakosiyo viya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo ca kho paṇḍito “imasmiṃ kāle nikkhamitabbaṃ parakkamitabbaṃ, imasmiṃ na nikkhamitabbaṃ na parakkamitabba”nti porāṇakapaṇḍitehi ṭhapitassa paveṇisaṅkhātassa vidhino koṭṭhāsasaṅkhātaṃ vidhānaṃ vā tassa vā vidhino vidhānaṃ saṃvidahanaṃ anuṭṭhānaṃ jānāti, so vidhividhānaññū paresaṃ attano paccāmittānaṃ vivaraṃ ñatvā yathā nāma paṇḍito kosiyo rattisaṅkhāte attano kāle nikkhamitvā ca parakkamitvā ca tattha tattha sayitānaññeva kākānaṃ sīsāni chindamāno te sabbe amitte vasīkatvā sukhī siyā, evaṃ dhīropi kāle nikkhamitvā parakkamitvā attano paccāmitte vasīkatvā sukhī niddukkho bhaveyyāti. Rājā bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā nivatti.

In the second verse, 'the wise one' means the sage. 'Tradition' (vidhī) means the custom established by the ancient sages. 'Arrangement' (vidhānaṃ) means a portion or a plan. 'Knowing the vulnerabilities' (vivarānugū) means one who follows and knows the weak points of others. 'All his enemies' means all foes. 'Having subdued' means having brought under his control. 'Like the owl' means like another, a wise owl, distinct from this foolish one. This is what is meant: A sage who knows when one should depart and strive and when one should not—that is, he knows the arrangement and execution of the tradition established by the ancient sages—such a one, knowing the procedures and the vulnerabilities of his adversaries, might be happy. Just as a wise owl, departing and striving at its own proper time, namely at night, and cutting off the heads of the crows sleeping here and there, becomes happy after subduing all its enemies, so too the wise person, by departing and striving at the right time and subduing his adversaries, might be happy and free from suffering. Hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, the king turned back.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, but the wise minister was I myself.”

Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The explanation of the Kosiya Jātaka, the sixth.

[227] 7. Gūthapāṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[227] 7. The explanation of the Gūthapāṇa Jātaka.

Sūro sūrena saṅgammāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiṃ kira kāle jetavanato tigāvutaḍḍhayojanamatte eko nigamagāmo, tattha bahūni salākabhattapakkhiyabhattāni atthi. Tatreko pañhapucchako koṇḍo vasati. So salākabhattapakkhiyabhattānaṃ atthāya āgate dahare ca [P 2.0210] sāmaṇere ca “ke khādanti, ke pivanti, ke bhuñjantī”ti pañhaṃ pucchitvā kathetuṃ asakkonte lajjāpesi. Te tassa bhayena salākabhattapakkhiyabhattatthāya taṃ gāmaṃ na gacchanti. Athekadivasaṃ eko bhikkhu salākaggaṃ gantvā “bhante, asukagāme salākabhattaṃ vā pakkhiyabhattaṃ vā atthī”ti pucchitvā [M 2.0193] “atthāvuso, tattha paneko koṇḍo pañhaṃ pucchati, taṃ kathetuṃ asakkonte akkosati paribhāsati, tassa bhayena koci gantuṃ na sakkotī”ti vutte “bhante, tattha bhattāni mayhaṃ pāpetha, ahaṃ taṃ dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā tato paṭṭhāya tumhe disvā palāyanakaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Bhikkhū “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tassa tattha bhattāni pāpesuṃ.

“A hero meeting with a hero”: this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk. It seems that at that time, there was a market town at a distance of three gāvutas and half a yojana from Jetavana, where there were many ticket-meals and fortnightly meals. A certain dullard who was a questioner lived there. When young monks and novices came for the ticket-meals and fortnightly meals, he would ask them the question, “Who eats? Who drinks? Who consumes?” and when they were unable to answer, he would shame them. Out of fear of him, they did not go to that village for the ticket-meals and fortnightly meals. Then one day, a monk went to the ticket-distribution hall and asked, “Venerable sir, is there a ticket-meal or a fortnightly meal in such-and-such village?” When he was told, “There is, friend, but a certain dullard there asks questions, and when they cannot answer, he reviles and abuses them. Out of fear of him, no one can go,” the monk said, “Venerable sirs, assign the meals there to me. I will tame him and humble him, and from then on I will make him run away at the sight of you.” The monks consented, saying, “Good,” and assigned the meals there to him.

So [V 2.0177] tattha gantvā gāmadvāre cīvaraṃ pārupi. Taṃ disvā koṇḍo caṇḍameṇḍako viya vegena upagantvā “pañhaṃ me, samaṇa, kathehī”ti āha. “Upāsaka, gāme caritvā yāguṃ ādāya āsanasālaṃ tāva me āgantuṃ dehī”ti. So yāguṃ ādāya āsanasālaṃ āgatepi tasmiṃ tatheva āha. Sopi naṃ bhikkhu “yāguṃ tāva me pātuṃ dehi, āsanasālaṃ tāva sammajjituṃ dehi, salākabhattaṃ tāva me āharituṃ dehī”ti vatvā salākabhattaṃ āharitvā tameva pattaṃ gāhāpetvā “ehi, pañhaṃ te kathessāmī”ti bahigāmaṃ netvā cīvaraṃ saṃharitvā aṃse ṭhapetvā tassa hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Tatrāpi naṃ so “samaṇa, pañhaṃ me kathehī”ti āha. Atha naṃ “kathemi te pañha”nti ekappahāreneva pātetvā aṭṭhīni saṃcuṇṇento viya pothetvā gūthaṃ mukhe pakkhipitvā “ito dāni paṭṭhāya imaṃ gāmaṃ āgataṃ kañci bhikkhuṃ pañhaṃ pucchitakāle jānissāmī”ti santajjetvā pakkāmi. So tato paṭṭhāya bhikkhū disvāva palāyati. Aparabhāge tassa bhikkhuno sā kiriyā bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭā jātā. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asukabhikkhu kira koṇḍassa mukhe gūthaṃ pakkhipitvā gato”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, so bhikkhu idāneva taṃ mīḷhena āsādeti, pubbepi āsādesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Having gone there, he put on his robe at the village gate. Seeing him, the cripple approached him swiftly like a fierce ram and said, ‘Recluse, answer my question!’ ‘Lay follower, first allow me to walk through the village for alms, get some gruel, and come to the refectory.’ Even when the monk came to the refectory with the gruel, the man said the same thing. The monk told him, ‘First let me drink the gruel, then let me sweep the refectory, then let me have the ticket-meal brought.’ Having brought the ticket-meal, he made the man hold the bowl himself and said, ‘Come, I will answer your question.’ He led him outside the village, folded his robe and placed it on his shoulder, took the bowl from the man’s hand, and stood still. Even then the man said to him, ‘Recluse, answer my question!’ Then the monk said, ‘I will answer your question,’ and with a single blow he knocked him down. He thrashed him as if grinding his bones to powder, stuffed excrement into his mouth, and threatened him, saying, ‘From now on, whenever you ask a question of any monk who comes to this village, I will deal with you!’ Then he departed. From then on, the man would run away as soon as he saw monks. Later on, that monk’s deed became known in the Saᅅgha. One day in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a discussion: ‘Friends, it is said that a certain monk stuffed excrement into the cripple’s mouth and went away.’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘For what discussion are you now gathered, monks?’ When they told him, he said, ‘Monks, it is not only now that this monk has assailed him with excrement; he assailed him in the past as well,’ and he related a story of the past.’

Atīte [P 2.0211] aṅgamagadhavāsino aññamaññassa raṭṭhaṃ gacchantā ekadivasaṃ dvinnaṃ raṭṭhānaṃ sīmantare ekaṃ saraṃ nissāya vasitvā suraṃ pivitvā macchamaṃsaṃ khāditvā pātova yānāni yojetvā pakkamiṃsu. Tesaṃ gatakāle eko gūthakhādako pāṇako gūthagandhena āgantvā tesaṃ pītaṭṭhāne chaḍḍitaṃ suraṃ disvā pipāsāya pivitvā matto hutvā gūthapuñjaṃ abhiruhi, allagūthaṃ [M 2.0194] tasmiṃ āruḷhe thokaṃ onami. So “pathavī maṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkotī”ti viravi. Tasmiññeva khaṇe eko mattavaravāraṇo taṃ padesaṃ patvā gūthagandhaṃ ghāyitvā jigucchanto paṭikkami. So taṃ disvā “esa mama bhayena palāyatī”ti saññī hutvā “iminā me saddhiṃ saṅgāmaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti taṃ avhayanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, the inhabitants of Aᅅga and Magadha, while traveling to each other’s country, one day stayed near a lake on the border between the two kingdoms. They drank liquor, ate fish and meat, and early in the morning, yoked their vehicles and departed. After they had left, a dung-eating creature, attracted by the smell of dung, came and saw the liquor they had discarded. Being thirsty, it drank and became intoxicated, then climbed onto a dung heap. As it climbed onto the wet dung, the heap sank slightly. It cried out, ‘The earth cannot support me!’ At that very moment, a splendid intoxicated elephant arrived at that spot. Smelling the dung, it was disgusted and turned back. Seeing this, the creature thought, ‘This one flees out of fear of me!’ and thinking, ‘It is fitting for me to do battle with him,’ he challenged him by reciting the first verse:

153.

153.

“Sūro sūrena saṅgamma, vikkantena pahārinā;

Ehi nāga nivattassu, kiṃ nu bhīto palāyasi;

Passantu aṅgamagadhā, mama tuyhañca vikkama”nti.

‘A hero has met with a hero, a valiant one with a striker; come, elephant, turn back! Why do you flee in fear? Let the people of Aᅅga and Magadha see the valor of both me and you.’

Tassattho [V 2.0178] – tvaṃ sūro mayā sūrena saddhiṃ samāgantvā vīriyavikkamena vikkantena pahāradānasamatthatāya pahārinā kiṃkāraṇā asaṅgāmetvāva gacchasi, nanu nāma ekasampahāropi dātabbo siyā, tasmā ehi nāga nivattassu, ettakeneva maraṇabhayatajjito hutvā kiṃ nu bhīto palāyasi, ime imaṃ sīmaṃ antaraṃ katvā vasantā passantu, aṅgamagadhā mama tuyhañca vikkamaṃ ubhinnampi amhākaṃ parakkamaṃ passantūti.

Its meaning is: You are a hero who has come together with me, a hero; you are valiant with heroic effort and a striker with the ability to deliver a blow. For what reason do you leave without fighting at all? Should not at least one blow be delivered? Therefore, come, elephant, turn back. Being so terrified by the fear of death, why do you flee in fear? Let those who dwell on either side of this border see; let the people of Aᅅga and Magadha see my valor and yours, the prowess of us both.

So hatthī kaṇṇaṃ datvā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā nivattitvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ apasādento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The elephant gave ear, listened to his words, turned back, approached him, and, scorning him, recited the second verse:

154.

154.

“Na taṃ pādā vadhissāmi, na dantehi na soṇḍiyā;

Mīḷhena taṃ vadhissāmi, pūti haññatu pūtinā”ti.

‘I will not slay you with my feet, nor with my tusks, nor with my trunk; with my dung I will slay you. Let the foul be slain by the foul!’

Tassattho [P 2.0212] – na taṃ pādādīhi vadhissāmi, tuyhaṃ pana anucchavikena mīḷhena taṃ vadhissāmīti.

Its meaning is: I will not slay you with my feet and so on, but I will slay you with dung, which is suitable for you.

Evañca pana vatvā “pūtigūthapāṇako pūtināva haññatū”ti tassa matthake mahantaṃ laṇḍaṃ pātetvā udakaṃ vissajjetvā tattheva taṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā koñcanādaṃ nadanto araññameva pāvisi.

And having said this, thinking, ‘Let the foul dung-creature be slain by what is foul!’ he dropped a large ball of dung on its head and discharged urine on it, thereby bringing it to its end right on that spot. Then, trumpeting like a crane, he entered the forest.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā gūthapāṇako koṇḍo ahosi, vāraṇo so bhikkhu, taṃ kāraṇaṃ paccakkhato disvā tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe nivutthadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: ‘At that time, the dung-creature was the cripple, the elephant was that monk, and the deity dwelling in that forest grove who witnessed the incident was I myself.’

Gūthapāṇajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Gũthapāᅅa Jātaka, the Seventh.

[228] 8. Kāmanītajātakavaṇṇanā

[228] 8. The Commentary on the Kāmanġta Jātaka

Tayo [M 2.0195] girinti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kāmanītabrāhmaṇaṃ nāma ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu paccuppannañca atītañca dvādasakanipāte kāmajātake (jā. 1.12.37 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Tesu pana dvīsu rājaputtesu jeṭṭhako āgantvā bārāṇasiyaṃ rājā ahosi, kaniṭṭho [V 2.0179] uparājā. Tesu rājā vatthukāmakilesakāmesu atitto dhanalolo ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto sakko devarājā hutvā jambudīpaṃ olokento tassa rañño dvīsupi kāmesu atittabhāvaṃ ñatvā “imaṃ rājānaṃ niggaṇhitvā lajjāpessāmī”ti brāhmaṇamāṇavavaṇṇena āgantvā rājānaṃ passi, raññā ca “kenatthena āgatosi māṇavā”ti vutte “ahaṃ, mahārāja, tīṇi nagarāni passāmi khemāni subhikkhāni pahūtahatthiassarathapattīni hiraññasuvaṇṇālaṅkārabharitāni, sakkā ca pana tāni appakeneva balena gaṇhituṃ, ahaṃ te tāni gahetvā dātuṃ āgato”ti āha. “Kadā gacchāma, māṇavā”ti vutte “sve mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi gaccha, pātova āgaccheyyāsī”ti. “Sādhu, mahārāja, vegena balaṃ sajjehī”ti vatvā sakko sakaṭṭhānameva [P 2.0213] gato.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher told this story concerning a brahmin named Kāmanīta, beginning with the words "Three mountains." The story, both present and past, will be made clear in the Kāma Jātaka in the Twelfth Book. Of those two princes, the elder returned and became king in Bārāṇasī, while the younger became viceroy. That king was insatiable in both objective and subjective sensual pleasures, and was greedy for wealth. At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, king of the devas. Surveying Jambudīpa and seeing the king's insatiability in both kinds of sensual pleasure, he thought, "I will humble this king and make him feel ashamed." Assuming the guise of a young brahmin, he approached the king. When the king asked, "For what purpose have you come, young man?" he replied, "Great king, I see three cities that are safe, prosperous, with abundant food, teeming with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and filled with gold, bullion, and ornaments. They can be taken with just a small force. I have come to take them and give them to you." When the king asked, "When shall we go, young man?" he replied, "Tomorrow, great king." "Then go, and come back early in the morning." "Very well, great king. Prepare your forces quickly," said Sakka, and returned to his own abode.

Rājā punadivase bheriṃ carāpetvā balasajjaṃ kāretvā amacce pakkosāpetvā hiyyo eko brāhmaṇamāṇavo “uttarapañcāle indapatte kekaketi imesu tīsu nagaresu rajjaṃ gahetvā dassāmī”ti āha, taṃ māṇavaṃ ādāya tīsu nagaresu rajjaṃ gaṇhissāma, vegena naṃ pakkosathāti. “Katthassa, deva, nivāso dāpito”ti? “Na me tassa nivāsagehaṃ dāpita”nti. “Nivāsaparibbayo pana dinno”ti? “Sopi na dinno”ti. Atha “kahaṃ naṃ passissāmā”ti? “Nagaravīthīsu olokethā”ti. Te olokentā adisvā “na passāma, mahārājā”ti āhaṃsu. Rañño māṇavaṃ apassantassa “evaṃ mahantā nāma issariyā parihīnomhī”ti mahāsoko udapādi, hadayavatthu uṇhaṃ ahosi, vatthulohitaṃ kuppi, lohitapakkhandikā udapādi, vejjā tikicchituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu.

The next day, the king had the drum beaten, the army prepared, and summoned his ministers. He said, "Yesterday a young brahmin came and said, 'I will take the sovereignty in these three cities—in Uttara Pañcāla, Indapatta, and Kekaka—and give it to you.' Taking that young man, we will seize the sovereignty in those three cities. Summon him quickly!" "Where, your majesty, was his lodging assigned?" "I did not assign him a dwelling." "Were expenses for his stay given?" "Those were not given either." "Then where shall we find him?" "Look for him in the city streets." They looked but did not see him, and reported, "We do not see him, great king." When the king could not see the young man, great sorrow arose in him, thinking, "I have been deprived of such great sovereignty!" The base of his heart became hot, his heart-blood was disturbed, and dysentery broke out. The physicians were unable to cure him.

Tato tīhacatūhaccayena sakko āvajjamāno tassa taṃ ābādhaṃ ñatvā “tikicchissāmi na”nti brāhmaṇavaṇṇena āgantvā dvāre ṭhatvā “vejjabrāhmaṇo [M 2.0196] tumhākaṃ tikicchanatthāya āgato”ti ārocāpesi. Rājā taṃ sutvā “mahantamahantā rājavejjā maṃ tikicchituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, paribbayamassa dāpetvā uyyojethā”ti āha. Sakko taṃ sutvā “mayhaṃ neva nivāsaparibbayena attho, vejjalābhampi na gaṇhissāmi, tikicchissāmi naṃ, puna rājā maṃ passatū”ti āha. Rājā taṃ sutvā “tena hi āgacchatū”ti āha. Sakko pavisitvā jayāpetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi, rājā “tvaṃ maṃ tikicchasī”ti āha. “Āma, devā”ti. “Tena hi tikicchassū”ti. “Sādhu, mahārāja, byādhino me lakkhaṇaṃ kathetha, kena kāraṇena uppanno, kiṃ khāditaṃ vā pītaṃ vā nissāya, udāhu diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā”ti? “Tāta, mayhaṃ byādhi sutaṃ nissāya uppanno”ti. “Kiṃ te suta”nti. “Tāta eko māṇavo [V 2.0180][P 2.0214] āgantvā mayhaṃ ‘tīsu nagaresu rajjaṃ gaṇhitvā dassāmī’ti āha, ahaṃ tassa nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ vā nivāsaparibbayaṃ vā na dāpesiṃ, so mayhaṃ kujjhitvā aññassa rañño santikaṃ gato bhavissati. Atha me ‘evaṃ mahantā nāma issariyā parihīnomhī’ti cintentassa ayaṃ byādhi uppanno. Sace sakkosi tvaṃ me kāmacittaṃ nissāya uppannaṃ byādhiṃ tikicchituṃ, tikicchāhī”ti etamatthaṃ pakāsento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, after three or four days had passed, Sakka, reflecting on the matter, became aware of the king's illness and thought, "I will cure him." He came in the guise of a brahmin, stood at the gate, and had it announced, "A physician-brahmin has come to treat you." Hearing this, the king said, "Great royal physicians have been unable to cure me. Give him expenses and send him away." Hearing this, Sakka said, "I have no need of lodging or expenses, nor will I accept a physician’s fee. I will cure him; let the king see me again." When the king heard this, he said, "Then let him come." Sakka entered, offered a salutation of victory, and stood to one side. The king asked, "Will you cure me?" "Yes, your majesty." "Then cure me." "Very well, great king. Tell me the symptoms of your illness. For what reason did it arise? Was it due to something eaten or drunk, or something seen or heard?" "Dear man, my illness arose because of something I heard." "What did you hear?" "Dear man, a young man came and told me, 'I will take the sovereignty in three cities and give it to you.' But I did not give him a place to stay or expenses. He must have become angry with me and gone to another king. Then, as I thought, 'I have been deprived of such great sovereignty,' this illness arose. If you are able to cure this illness of mine, which arose from a mind of sensual desire, then cure me." To explain this matter, he recited the first verse:

155.

155.

“Tayo giriṃ antaraṃ kāmayāmi, pañcālā kuruyo kekake ca;

Tatuttariṃ brāhmaṇa kāmayāmi, tikiccha maṃ brāhmaṇa kāmanīta”nti.

"I desire three mountains and the land between—the Pañcālas, Kurus, and the Kekakas. Beyond that, O brahmin, I still desire. Heal me, O brahmin, who am led on by desire!"

Tattha tayo girinti tayo girī, ayameva vā pāṭho. Yathā “sudassanassa girino, dvārañhetaṃ pakāsatī”ti ettha sudassanaṃ devanagaraṃ yujjhitvā duggaṇhatāya duccalanatāya “sudassanagirī”ti vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi tīṇi nagarāni “tayo giri”nti adhippetāni. Tasmā ayamettha attho – tīṇi ca nagarāni tesañca antaraṃ tividhampi raṭṭhaṃ kāmayāmi. “Pañcālā kuruyo kekake cā”ti imāni tesaṃ raṭṭhānaṃ nāmāni. Tesu pañcālāti uttarapañcālā, tattha kapilaṃ nāma nagaraṃ. Kuruyoti kururaṭṭhaṃ, tattha indapattaṃ nāma nagaraṃ. Kekake cāti paccatte upayogavacanaṃ, tena kekakaraṭṭhaṃ dasseti. Tattha kekakarājadhānīyeva nagaraṃ. Tatuttarinti taṃ [M 2.0197] ahaṃ ito paṭiladdhā bārāṇasirajjā tatuttariṃ tividhaṃ rajjaṃ kāmayāmi. Tikiccha maṃ, brāhmaṇa, kāmanītanti imehi vatthukāmehi ca kilesakāmehi ca nītaṃ hataṃ pahataṃ sace sakkosi, tikiccha maṃ brāhmaṇāti.

Herein, `tayo giriṃ` means 'three mountains' (`tayo girī`); or this latter is the reading. Just as in the line, “This gate of the Sudassana mountain is revealed,” the deva-city Sudassana is called “Sudassana mountain” because it is difficult to conquer and hard to shake, so here too three cities are intended by “three mountains.” Therefore, this is the meaning here: I desire the three cities and the land between them, the entire threefold realm. “Pañcālas, Kurus, and the Kekakas” are the names of those realms. Among them, “Pañcālas” refers to Uttara Pañcāla, where there is a city named Kapila. “Kurus” refers to the Kuru realm, where there is a city named Indapatta. The `ca` in “Kekakas” is a particle used in the sense of each one separately, thus indicating the Kekaka realm. There, the city is the capital of the Kekaka kingdom itself. “Beyond that” means: I, who have already obtained the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, desire that threefold kingdom beyond it. “Heal me, brahmin, one led on by desire” means: if you are able, heal me, brahmin, who have been led on, struck, and ruined by these sensual pleasures based on objects and sensual pleasures as defilements.

Atha naṃ sakko “mahārāja, tvaṃ mūlosadhādīhi atekiccho. Ñāṇosadheneva tikicchitabbo”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka said to him, "Great king, you cannot be cured by medicines such as roots and herbs. You must be cured only with the medicine of wisdom," and he recited the second verse:

156.

156.

“Kaṇhāhidaṭṭhassa [P 2.0215] karonti heke, amanussapaviṭṭhassa karonti paṇḍitā;

Na kāmanītassa karoti koci, okkantasukkassa hi kā tikicchā”ti.

"Some treat one bitten by a black snake; the wise treat one possessed by a non-human being. But no one treats one led on by desire; for what cure is there for one whose bright qualities have departed?"

Tattha kaṇhāhidaṭṭhassa karonti heketi ekacce hi tikicchakā ghoravisena kāḷasappena daṭṭhassa mantehi ceva osadhehi ca tikicchaṃ karonti. Amanussapaviṭṭhassa karonti paṇḍitāti apare paṇḍitā bhūtavejjā bhūtayakkhādīhi amanussehi paviṭṭhassa abhibhūtassa gahitassa balikammaparittakaraṇaosadhaparibhāvitādīhi tikicchaṃ karonti. Na kāmanītassa karoti kocīti [V 2.0181] kāmehi pana nītassa kāmavasikassa puggalassa aññatra paṇḍitehi añño koci tikicchaṃ na karoti, karontopi kātuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Okkantasukkassa hi kā tikicchāti, okkantasukkassa avakkantassa kusaladhammamariyādaṃ atikkantassa akusaladhamme patiṭṭhitassa puggalassa mantosadhādīhi kā nāma tikicchā, na sakkā osadhehi tikicchitunti.

Therein, "Some treat one bitten by a black snake" means that some physicians treat one bitten by a black snake of terrible venom with both mantras and medicinal herbs. "The wise treat one possessed by a non-human being" means that other wise men, exorcists, treat one who has been entered, overcome, or seized by non-human beings such as spirits and yakkhas, by means of offering rites, protective chants, and medicated applications. "But no one treats one led on by desire" means that for a person led on by sensual pleasures, under the sway of desire, no one other than the wise can provide a cure; even if they try, they are not able to do so. For what reason? "For what cure is there for one whose bright qualities have departed?"—for a person whose bright qualities have departed, who has transgressed the boundary of wholesome states and is established in unwholesome states, what cure could there be by means of mantras, medicines, and the like? It is not possible to cure them with such medicines.

Itissa mahāsatto imaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassetvā uttari evamāha – “mahārāja, sace tvaṃ tāni tīṇi rajjāni lacchasi, api nu kho imesu catūsu nagaresu rajjaṃ karonto ekappahāreneva cattāri sāṭakayugāni paridaheyyāsi, catūsu vā suvaṇṇapātīsu bhuñjeyyāsi, catūsu vā sayanesu sayeyyāsi, mahārāja, taṇhāvasikena nāma bhavituṃ na vaṭṭati, taṇhā hi nāmesā vipattimūlā. Sā vaḍḍhamānā yo taṃ vaḍḍheti, taṃ puggalaṃ aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu soḷasasu ussadanirayesu nānappakārabhedesu ca avasesesu apāyesu khipatī”ti. Evaṃ rājānaṃ nirayādibhayena tajjetvā mahāsatto dhammaṃ desesi. Rājāpissa dhammaṃ sutvā vigatasoko hutvā tāvadeva nibyādhitaṃ pāpuṇi[P 2.0216]. Sakkopissa ovādaṃ datvā [M 2.0198] sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā devalokameva gato. Sopi tato paṭṭhāya dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Then the Great Being, having pointed out this reason, said further: 'Great King, if you were to obtain those three kingdoms, could you, while ruling over these four cities, wear four pairs of garments at a single time, eat from four golden bowls at a single time, or sleep on four beds at a single time? Great King, it is not proper to be under the sway of craving, for this craving is the root of calamity. As it grows, it casts the person who fosters it into the eight great hells, the sixteen subsidiary hells, and into the remaining states of deprivation of various kinds.' Thus, having intimidated the king with the fear of hell and so on, the Great Being taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, the king became free from sorrow and immediately recovered from his illness. Sakka, having given him an exhortation and established him in the moral precepts, went back to the world of the devas. He too, from that time onwards, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā kāmanītabrāhmaṇo ahosi, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this discourse on the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths, made the connection with the birth story: “At that time, the king was the Kāmanīta brahmin, and Sakka was myself.”

Kāmanītajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kāmanīta Jātaka, the Eighth.

[229] 9. Palāyitajātakavaṇṇanā

[229] 9. The Commentary on the Palāyita Jātaka

Gajaggameghehīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto palāyitaparibbājakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira vādatthāya sakalajambudīpaṃ vicaritvā kañci paṭivādiṃ alabhitvā anupubbena sāvatthiṃ gantvā “atthi nu kho koci mayā saddhiṃ vādaṃ kātuṃ samattho”ti manusse pucchi. Manussā “tādisānaṃ sahassenapi saddhiṃ vādaṃ kātuṃ samattho sabbaññū dvipadānaṃ aggo mahāgotamo dhammissaro parappavādamaddano, sakalepi jambudīpe uppanno parappavādo taṃ bhagavantaṃ atikkamituṃ samattho nāma natthi. Velantaṃ patvā samuddaūmiyo viya hi sabbavādā tassa pādamūlaṃ patvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇā hontī”ti buddhaguṇe kathesuṃ. Paribbājako “kahaṃ [V 2.0182] pana so etarahī”ti pucchitvā “jetavane”ti sutvā “idānissa vādaṃ āropessāmī”ti mahājanaparivuto jetavanaṃ gacchanto jetena rājakumārena navakoṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā kāritaṃ jetavanadvārakoṭṭhakaṃ disvā “ayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa vasanapāsādo”ti pucchitvā “dvārakoṭṭhako aya”nti sutvā “dvārakoṭṭhako tāva evarūpo, vasanagehaṃ kīdisaṃ bhavissatī”ti vatvā “gandhakuṭi nāma appameyyā”ti vutte “evarūpena samaṇena saddhiṃ ko vādaṃ karissatī”ti tatova palāyi. Manussā unnādino hutvā jetavanaṃ pavisitvā satthārā “kiṃ akāle āgatatthā”ti vuttā taṃ pavattiṃ kathayiṃsu. Satthā “na kho upāsakā idāneva, pubbepesa mama vasanaṭṭhānassa dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ disvā palāyatevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

This story, which begins with the words “With clouds of foremost elephants,” the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain wanderer who fled. It is said that this wanderer, seeking a debate, traveled all over Jambudīpa but could not find any opponent. He came in due course to Sāvatthī and asked the people, “Is there anyone here capable of debating with me?” The people said: “There is the Omniscient One, the chief of bipeds, the great Gotama, the Lord of the Dhamma, the crusher of others' doctrines, who is able to debate with even a thousand such as you. Throughout all of Jambudīpa no opponent has arisen who is able to surpass the Blessed One. Just as the waves of the ocean are shattered to smithereens upon reaching the shore, so all doctrines are shattered to smithereens upon reaching his feet.” Thus they spoke of the Buddha's qualities. The wanderer asked, “Where is he now?” Hearing he was at Jetavana, he said, “I will challenge him to a debate right now!” Surrounded by a great crowd, he went to Jetavana. Seeing the gateway to Jetavana, which Prince Jeta had built by spending ninety million, he asked, “Is this the dwelling palace of the ascetic Gotama?” When he heard, “This is the gateway,” he said, “If the gateway is like this, what must his dwelling be like?” When he was told, “It is called the Perfumed Chamber, and it is peerless,” he thought, “Who could debate with such an ascetic?” and fled from that very spot. The people, making a great uproar, entered Jetavana. When the Teacher asked them, “Why have you come at an unseemly time?” they related the incident. The Teacher said: “Lay followers, it is not only now that he has fled. In the past, too, this one fled upon seeing the gateway to my dwelling.” And at their request, he related the past.

Atīte [P 2.0217][M 2.0199] gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilāyaṃ bodhisatto rajjaṃ kāresi, bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto. So “takkasilaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti mahantena balakāyena gantvā nagarato avidūre ṭhatvā “iminā niyāmena hatthī pesetha, iminā asse, iminā rathe, iminā pattī, evaṃ dhāvitvā āvudhehi paharatha, evaṃ ghanavassavalāhakā viya saravassaṃ vassathā”ti tenaṃ vicārento imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

In the past, when the Bodhisatta was ruling the kingdom in Takkasilā in the country of Gandhāra, Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī. The latter, thinking, “I will take Takkasilā,” went with a great army and, stationing it not far from the city, he gave his orders: “Send the elephants by this way, the horses by this way, the chariots by this way, and the foot soldiers by this way. Charging thus, strike with your weapons. Rain down a shower of arrows like a thick rain cloud.” While deploying them, he spoke this pair of verses:

157.

157.

“Gajaggameghehi hayaggamālibhi, rathūmijātehi sarābhivassebhi;

Tharuggahāvaṭṭadaḷhappahāribhi, parivāritā takkasilā samantato.

“With clouds of foremost elephants, with garlands of foremost horses, with waves of chariots that have arisen, with showers of arrows, with swordsmen who wield their hilts and strike hard as they wheel about—by these is Takkasilā surrounded on all sides.

158.

158.

“Abhidhāvatha cūpadhāvatha ca, vividhā vināditā vadantibhi;

Vattatajja tumulo ghoso yathā, vijjulatā jaladharassa gajjato”ti.

“Charge forward and rush upon them! Let your various sounds resound with the trumpeting elephants! Let a tumultuous roar arise today, like the lightning from a thundering cloud!”

Tattha gajaggameghehīti aggagajameghehi, koñcanādaṃ gajjantehi mattavaravāraṇavalāhakehīti attho. Hayaggamālibhīti aggahayamālīhi, varasindhavavalāhakakulehi assānīkehīti attho. Rathūmijātehīti sañjātaūmivegehi sāgarasalilehi viya sañjātarathūmīhi, rathānīkehīti attho. Sarābhivassebhīti tehiyeva rathānīkehi ghanavassamegho viya saravassaṃ vassantehi[P 2.0218]. Tharuggahāvaṭṭadaḷhappahāribhīti tharuggahehi āvaṭṭadaḷhappahārīhi, ito cito ca āvattitvā parivattitvā daḷhaṃ paharantehi gahitakhaggaratanatharudaṇḍehi pattiyodhehi cāti attho. Parivāritā takkasilā samantatoti yathā ayaṃ takkasilā parivāritā hoti, sīghaṃ tathā karothāti attho.

Herein, “With clouds of foremost elephants” means with clouds of the best elephants, that is, with clouds of excellent rutting elephants trumpeting with the cry of a curlew. “With garlands of foremost horses” means with lines of the best horses, that is, with squadrons of horses from the excellent breeds of Sindhava and the lineage of Valāhaka. “With waves of chariots that have arisen” means with waves of chariots that have arisen with the speed of ocean waves, that is, with squadrons of chariots. “With showers of arrows” means with those same squadrons of chariots raining down a shower of arrows like a thick rain cloud. “With swordsmen who wield their hilts and strike hard as they wheel about” means with foot soldiers who wield the hilts of their precious swords and staves, striking hard as they turn this way and that. “By these is Takkasilā surrounded on all sides” means: “Act swiftly so that Takkasilā is surrounded in this way.”

Abhidhāvatha [V 2.0183] cūpadhāvatha cāti vegena dhāvatha ceva upadhāvatha ca. Vividhā vināditā vadantibhīti varavāraṇehi saddhiṃ vividhā vinaditā bhavatha, selitagajjitavāditehi nānāviravā hothāti attho. Vattatajja tumulo ghosoti vattatu ajja tumulo mahanto asanisaddasadiso ghoso. Yathā vijjulatā jaladharassa gajjatoti yathā gajjantassa [M 2.0200] jaladharassa mukhato niggatā vijjulatā caranti, evaṃ vicarantā nagaraṃ parivāretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhathāti vadati.

“Charge forward and rush upon them!” means run swiftly and rush up to them. “Let your various sounds resound with the trumpeting elephants!” means: “Along with the excellent elephants, make various sounds resound; make diverse noises with war cries, roars, and thundering instruments.” “Let a tumultuous roar arise today” means let a great, tumultuous roar, like the sound of a thunderclap, arise today. “Like the lightning from a thundering cloud” means he is saying: “Just as lightning flashes from the mouth of a thundering cloud, so you should move about, surround the city, and seize the kingdom.”

Iti so rājā gajjitvā senaṃ vicāretvā nagaradvārasamīpaṃ gantvā dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ disvā “idaṃ rañño vasanageha”nti pucchitvā “ayaṃ nagaradvārakoṭṭhako”ti vutte “nagaradvārakoṭṭhako tāva evarūpo, rañño nivesanaṃ kīdisaṃ bhavissatī”ti vatvā “vejayantapāsādasadisa”nti sutvā “evaṃ yasasampannena raññā saddhiṃ yujjhituṃ na sakkhissāmā”ti dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ disvāva nivattitvā palāyitvā bārāṇasimeva agamāsi.

Thus that king, having roared and deployed his army, went near the city gate. Seeing the gatehouse, he asked, “Is this the king's dwelling?” When he was told, “This is the city gatehouse,” he said, “If the city gatehouse is like this, what must the king's palace be like?” Hearing that it was like the Vejayanta Palace, he thought, “We will not be able to fight with a king so endowed with glory.” And just from seeing the gatehouse, he turned back, fled, and went right back to Bārāṇasī.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasirājā palāyitaparibbājako ahosi, takkasilarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this discourse on the Dhamma, made the connection with the birth story: “At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī was the wanderer who fled, and the king of Takkasilā was myself.”

Palāyitajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Palāyita Jātaka is the ninth.

[230] 10. Dutiyapalāyitajātakavaṇṇanā

[230] 10. 10. Commentary on the Second Palāyita Jātaka

Dhajamaparimitanti [P 2.0219] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ palāyitaparibbājakameva ārabbha kathesi. Imasmiṃ pana vatthusmiṃ so paribbājako jetavanaṃ pāvisi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe satthā mahājanaparivuto alaṅkatadhammāsane nisinno manosilātale sīhanādaṃ nadanto sīhapotako viya dhammaṃ deseti. Paribbājako dasabalassa brahmasarīrapaṭibhāgaṃ rūpaṃ puṇṇacandasassirikaṃ mukhaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭasadisaṃ nalāṭañca disvā “ko evarūpaṃ purisuttamaṃ jinituṃ sakkhissatī”ti nivattitvā parisantaraṃ pavisitvā palāyi. Mahājano taṃ anubandhitvā nivattitvā satthussa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na so paribbājako idāneva, pubbepi mama suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ mukhaṃ disvā palātoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The flag is immeasurable”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain fleeing wanderer. In this story, that wanderer entered Jetavana. At that moment, the Teacher, surrounded by a great assembly and seated on a beautifully adorned Dhamma-seat, was teaching the Dhamma, roaring like a lion cub on a vermilion slab. The wanderer, seeing the Brahma-like form of the Ten-Powered One, his face glorious as the full moon, and his forehead like a golden plate, thought, “Who could conquer such a supreme person?” Turning back, he did not enter the midst of the crowd and fled. The great assembly pursued him, and upon returning, reported the incident to the Teacher. The Teacher said, “Not only now has that wanderer fled upon seeing my golden-hued face; he did so in the past as well,” and then he recounted a story of the past.

Atīte bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ kāresi, takkasilāyaṃ eko gandhārarājā. So “bārāṇasiṃ gahessāmī”ti caturaṅginiyā senāya āgantvā nagaraṃ parivāretvā nagaradvāre ṭhito attano [V 2.0184] balavāhanaṃ oloketvā “ko ettakaṃ balavāhanaṃ jinituṃ sakkhissatī”ti attano senaṃ saṃvaṇṇetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, the Bodhisatta reigned in Bārāṇasī. In Takkasilā, a certain king of Gandhāra reigned. Thinking, “I will seize Bārāṇasī,” he came with a fourfold army, besieged the city, and stood at the city gate. Surveying his own army, he wished to praise his forces, saying, “Who will be able to conquer such a great army as this?” and uttered the first verse:

159.

159.

“Dhajamaparimitaṃ [M 2.0201] anantapāraṃ, duppasahaṃ dhaṅkehi sāgaraṃva;

Girimiva anilena duppasayho, duppasaho ahamajja tādisenā”ti.

“My banner is immeasurable, boundless, hard to endure like the ocean by crows; like a mountain by the wind, hard to subdue—hard to subdue am I today by such a one as you.”

Tattha dhajamaparimitanti idaṃ tāva me rathesu morachade ṭhapetvā ussāpitadhajameva aparimitaṃ bahuṃ anekasatasaṅkhyaṃ. Anantapāranti balavāhanampi me “ettakā hatthī ettakā assā ettakā rathā ettakā pattī”ti gaṇanaparicchedarahitaṃ anantapāraṃ. Duppasahanti na sakkā paṭisattūhi sahituṃ abhibhavituṃ[P 2.0220]. Yathā kiṃ? Dhaṅkehi sāgaraṃva, yathā sāgaro bahūhi kākehi vegavikkhambhanavasena vā atikkamanavasena vā duppasaho, evaṃ duppasahaṃ. Girimiva anilena duppasayhoti apica me ayaṃ balakāyo yathā pabbato vātena akampanīyato duppasaho, tathā aññena balakāyena duppasaho. Duppasaho ahamajja tādisenāti svāhaṃ iminā balena samannāgato ajja tādisena duppasahoti aṭṭālake ṭhitaṃ bodhisattaṃ sandhāya vadati.

In that verse, ‘dhajamaparimitaṃ’ means: the many hundreds of banners raised upon my chariots and adorned with peacock feathers are themselves immeasurable and numerous. ‘Anantapāraṃ’ means: my army and transport—counting so many elephants, so many horses, so many chariots, and so many foot soldiers—are without limit or bound. ‘Duppasahaṃ’ means: it is not possible for enemies to withstand or overcome it. Like what? ‘Dhaṅkehi sāgaraṃva’—just as the ocean is hard for many crows to overcome by checking its force or by crossing it, so is my army. ‘Girimiva anilena duppasayho’ means: furthermore, this army of mine is hard to subdue, just as a mountain is hard for the wind to shake. ‘Duppasaho ahamajja tādisenā’ means: I, endowed with this force, am today hard to subdue by such a one as you—he says this with reference to the Bodhisatta standing on the watchtower.

Athassa so puṇṇacandasassirikaṃ attano mukhaṃ dassetvā “bāla, mā vippalapasi, idāni te balavāhanaṃ mattavāraṇo viya naḷavanaṃ viddhaṃsessāmī”ti santajjetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, displaying his own face, glorious as the full moon, threatened him, saying, “Fool, do not babble! Now I will scatter your army as a rutting elephant crushes a reed forest,” and spoke the second verse to complete the pair:

160.

160.

“Mā bāliyaṃ vilapi na hissa tādisaṃ, viḍayhase na hi labhase nisedhakaṃ;

Āsajjasi gajamiva ekacārinaṃ, yo taṃ padā naḷamiva pothayissatī”ti.

“Do not babble foolishly, for there is no such one; you are consumed with passion, yet find no one to restrain you. You assail one like a solitary elephant, who will crush you underfoot like a reed.”

Tattha mā bāliyaṃ vilapīti mā attano bālabhāvaṃ vippalapasi. Na hissa tādisanti na hi assa tādiso, ayameva vā pāṭho. Tādiso “anantapāraṃ me balavāhana”nti evarūpaṃ takkento rajjañca gahetuṃ samattho nāma na hi assa, na hotīti attho. Viḍayhaseti tvaṃ bāla, kevalaṃ rāgadosamohamānapariḷāhena viḍayhasiyeva. Na hi labhase nisedhakanti mādisaṃ pana pasayha abhibhavitvā nisedhakaṃ na tāva labhasi, ajja [M 2.0202] taṃ āgatamaggeneva palāpessāmi. Āsajjasīti upagacchasi. Gajamiva ekacārinanti ekacārinaṃ mattavaravāraṇaṃ viya. Yo taṃ padā naḷamiva pothayissatīti yo taṃ yathā nāma mattavaravāraṇo pādā naḷaṃ potheti saṃcuṇṇeti, evaṃ pothayissati, taṃ tvaṃ āsajjasīti attānaṃ sandhāyāha.

In that verse, ‘mā bāliyaṃ vilapi’ means: do not babble about your own foolishness. ‘Na hissa tādisaṃ’ means: for there is no such one. The meaning is: such a person who thinks “my army is boundless” and is capable of seizing the kingdom does not exist. ‘Viḍayhase’ means: you, fool, are simply consumed by the fever of greed, hatred, and the rest. ‘Na hi labhase nisedhakaṃ’ means: you will not find a restrainer like me who can forcibly overcome you. ‘Āsajjasi’ means: you approach. ‘Gajamiva ekacārinaṃ’ means: like a solitary, mighty, rutting elephant. ‘Yo taṃ padā naḷamiva pothayissatīti’ means: he who will crush you, just as a mighty elephant crushes a reed with its foot—referring to himself, he says, “you approach him.”

Evaṃ [V 2.0185] tajjentassa panassa kathaṃ sutvā gandhārarājā ullokento [P 2.0221] kañcanapaṭṭasadisaṃ mahānalāṭaṃ disvā attano gahaṇabhīto nivattitvā palāyanto sakanagarameva agamāsi.

Hearing the words of the Bodhisatta who was thus threatening him, the king of Gandhāra looked up and saw his great forehead, which was like a golden plaque. Fearing his own capture, he turned back and, fleeing, went to his own city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā gandhārarājā palāyitaparibbājako ahosi, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the king of Gandhāra was the fleeing wanderer, and the king of Bārāṇasī was myself.”

Dutiyapalāyitajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Second Palāyita Jātaka is the tenth.

Kāsāvavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Kāsāva Chapter, the Eighth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Kāsāvaṃ cūḷanandiyaṃ, puṭabhattañca kumbhilaṃ;

Khantivaṇṇaṃ kosiyañca, gūthapāṇaṃ kāmanītaṃ;

Palāyitadvayampi ca.

Kāsāva, Cūḷanandiya, Puṭabhatta, and Kumbhila; Khantivaṇṇa, Kosiya, Gūthapāṇa, Kāmanīta; and the two Palāyita Jātakas.

9. Upāhanavaggo

9. 9. The Chapter on Sandals

[231] 1. Upāhanajātakavaṇṇanā

[231] 1. 1. Commentary on the Upāhana Jātaka

Yathāpi [V 2.0186] kītāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dhammasabhāyañhi bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, devadatto ācariyaṃ paccakkhāya tathāgatassa paṭipakkho paṭisattu hutvā mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, devadatto [M 2.0203] idāneva ācariyaṃ paccakkhāya mama paṭipakkho hutvā mahāvināsaṃ patto, pubbepi pattoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher told this story beginning with 'Just as a bought one' while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Devadatta. For in the Hall of Dhamma, the monks raised a topic of discussion: 'Friends, Devadatta, having rejected his teacher and becoming an opponent and adversary of the Tathāgata, has come to great ruin.' The Teacher came and asked, 'For what discussion are you now gathered together, monks?' When they told him what it was, he said: 'Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has come to great ruin after rejecting his teacher and becoming my opponent; he came to it in the past as well.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto hatthācariyakule nibbattitvā vayappatto hatthisippe nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi. Atheko kāsigāmako māṇavako āgantvā tassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhi. Bodhisattā nāma sippaṃ vācentā ācariyamuṭṭhiṃ na karonti, attano jānananiyāmena niravasesaṃ sikkhāpenti. Tasmā so māṇavo bodhisattassa jānanasippaṃ niravasesamuggaṇhitvā bodhisattaṃ āha – “ācariya[P 2.0222], ahaṃ rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti. Bodhisatto “sādhu, tātā”ti gantvā rañño ārocesi – “mahārāja, mama antevāsiko tumhe upaṭṭhātuṃ icchatī”ti. “Sādhu, upaṭṭhātū”ti. “Tena hissa paribbayaṃ jānāthā”ti? “Tumhākaṃ antevāsiko tumhehi samakaṃ na lacchati, tumhesu sataṃ labhantesu paṇṇāsaṃ lacchati, dve labhantesu ekaṃ lacchatī”ti. So gehaṃ gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ antevāsikassa ārocesi. Antevāsiko “ahaṃ, ācariya, tumhehi samaṃ sippaṃ jānāmi. Sace samakaññeva paribbayaṃ labhissāmi, upaṭṭhahissāmi. No ce, na upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti āha. Bodhisatto taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā “sace so tumhehi samappakāro, tumhehi samakaññeva sippaṃ dassetuṃ sakkonto samakaṃ labhissatī”ti āha. Bodhisatto taṃ pavattiṃ tassa ārocetvā tena “sādhu dassessāmī”ti vutte rañño ārocesi. Rājā “tena hi sve sippaṃ dassethā”ti. “Sādhu, dassessāma, nagare bheriṃ carāpethā”ti. Rājā “sve kira ācariyo ca antevāsiko ca ubho hatthisippaṃ dassessanti, rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā daṭṭhukāmā passantū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of elephant trainers and, having come of age, became accomplished in the elephant craft. Then a young man from a village in Kāsi came and learned the craft from him. Bodhisattas, when teaching a craft, do not keep a 'teacher's fist' but teach everything without reservation according to their own knowledge. Therefore, that young man learned the Bodhisatta’s craft completely and said to the Bodhisatta, 'Teacher, I wish to serve the king.' The Bodhisatta said, 'Very well, my dear,' and went to inform the king: 'Great king, my pupil wishes to serve you.' 'Good, let him serve.' 'Then please determine his stipend.' 'Your pupil shall not receive the same as you. If you receive a hundred, he shall receive fifty; if you receive two, he shall receive one.' He returned home and told this to his pupil. The pupil said, 'Teacher, I know the craft as well as you. If I receive the same stipend, I will serve. If not, I will not.' The Bodhisatta reported this to the king. The king said, 'If he is of the same caliber as you and can demonstrate the craft as well as you, he shall receive the same.' The Bodhisatta informed his pupil of this, and when he said, 'Very well, I will demonstrate it,' he told the king. The king said, 'In that case, demonstrate the craft tomorrow.' 'Very well, we will demonstrate it. Have the drum beaten throughout the city.' The king had it proclaimed by beat of drum: 'Tomorrow, both the teacher and his pupil will demonstrate the elephant craft. Let those who wish to see gather in the royal courtyard and watch.'

Ācariyo [V 2.0187] “na me antevāsiko upāyakosallaṃ jānātī”ti ekaṃ hatthiṃ gahetvā ekaratteneva vilomaṃ sikkhāpesi. So taṃ “gacchā”ti vutte osakkituṃ, “osakkā”ti vutte gantuṃ, “tiṭṭhā”ti vutte nipajjituṃ, “nipajjā”ti vutte ṭhātuṃ, “gaṇhā”ti vutte ṭhapetuṃ, “ṭhapehī”ti vutte gaṇhituṃ sikkhāpetvā punadivase taṃ hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ agamāsi. Antevāsikopi ekaṃ manāpaṃ hatthiṃ abhiruhi. Mahājano sannipati. Ubhopi samakaṃ sippaṃ dassesuṃ. Puna bodhisatto attano hatthiṃ [M 2.0204] vilomaṃ kāresi, so “gacchā”ti [P 2.0223] vutte osakki, “osakkā”ti vutte purato dhāvi, “tiṭṭhā”ti vutte nipajji, “nipajjā”ti vutte aṭṭhāsi, “gaṇhā”ti vutte nikkhipi, “nikkhipā”ti vutte gaṇhi. Mahājano “are duṭṭhaantevāsika, tvaṃ ācariyena saddhiṃ sārambhaṃ karosi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsi, ‘ācariyena samakaṃ jānāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hosī”ti leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paharitvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi.
