The teacher, thinking, 'My pupil does not know mastery of strategy,' took an elephant and in a single night trained it in reverse. He taught it to retreat when told 'Go,' to go when told 'Retreat,' to lie down when told 'Stand,' to stand when told 'Lie down,' to release when told 'Take,' and to take when told 'Release.' The next day, he mounted that elephant and went to the royal courtyard. The pupil also mounted a fine elephant. A large crowd gathered. Both demonstrated the craft equally. Then the Bodhisatta made his elephant perform in reverse: when told 'Go,' it retreated; when told 'Retreat,' it ran forward; when told 'Stand,' it lay down; when told 'Lie down,' it stood up; when told 'Take,' it dropped it; when told 'Drop,' it took it. The crowd, shouting, 'You wicked pupil! You contend with your teacher! You do not know your own measure, thinking "I know the same as my teacher"!' struck him with clods, sticks, and the like, and brought his life to an end right there.

Bodhisatto hatthimhā oruyha rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mahārāja, sippaṃ nāma attano sukhatthāya gaṇhanti, ekaccassa pana gahitasippaṃ dukkaṭaupāhanā viya vināsameva āvahatī”ti vatvā idaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

The Bodhisatta, dismounting from the elephant and approaching the king, said: 'Great king, a craft is indeed acquired for one's own comfort, but for some, the acquired craft brings only ruin, like a badly made sandal.' Having said this, he spoke these two verses:

161.

161.

“Yathāpi kītā purisassupāhanā, sukhassa atthāya dukhaṃ udabbahe;

Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitā, tasseva pāde purisassa khādare.

'Just as a man's bought sandals, meant for comfort, might bring him pain; scorched by heat and pressed by the sole, they would bite that very man's feet.

162.

162.

“Evameva yo dukkulīno anariyo, tammāka vijjañca sutañca ādiya;

Tameva so tattha sutena khādati, anariyo vuccati pānadūpamo”ti.

'Just so, an ignoble person of low birth, having acquired knowledge and learning from us, bites that very one with that learning. Such an ignoble one is called "one like a sandal".'

Tattha udabbaheti udabbaheyya. Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitāti ghammena abhitattā pādatalena ca pīḷitā. Tassevāti yena tā sukhatthāya kiṇitvā pādesu paṭimukkā dukkaṭūpāhanā, tasseva. Khādareti vaṇaṃ karontā pāde khādanti.

Therein, 'udabbahe' means it would bring forth. 'Ghammābhitattā talasā papīḷitā' means scorched by heat and pressed by the sole of the foot. 'Tasseva' means of that very person who, having bought the badly made sandals for comfort, put them on his feet. 'Khādare' means they bite the feet, causing a wound.

Dukkulīnoti dujjātiko akulaputto. Anariyoti hirottappavajjito asappuriso. Tammāka vijjañca sutañca ādiyāti ettha taṃ taṃ manatīti “tammo”ti vattabbe tammāko, taṃ taṃ sippaṃ āsevati parivattetīti attho, ācariyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā tammākā, gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ [P 2.0224] panassa rassabhāvo kato. Vijjanti aṭṭhārasasu vijjāṭṭhānesu [M 2.0205] yaṃkiñci. Sutanti yaṃkiñci sutapariyatti. Ādiyātiādiyitvā. Tameva so tattha sutena khādatīti tamevāti [V 2.0188] attānameva. Soti yo dukkulīno anariyo ācariyamhā vijjañca sutañca ādiyati, so. Tattha sutena khādatīti tassa santike sutena so attānameva khādatīti attho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “teneva so tattha sutena khādatī”tipi pāṭho. Tassāpi so tena tattha sutena attānameva khādatīti ayameva attho. Anariyo vuccati pānadūpamoti iti anariyo dupāhanūpamo dukkaṭūpāhanūpamo vuccati. Yathā hi dukkaṭūpāhanā purisaṃ khādanti, evamesa sutena khādanto attanāva attānaṃ khādati. Atha vā pānāya dutoti pānadu, upāhanūpatāpitassa upāhanāya khāditapādassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā yo so attānaṃ sutena khādati, so tena sutena khāditattā “anariyo”ti vuccati pānadūpamo, upāhanūpatāpitapādasadisoti vuccatīti ayamettha attho. Rājā tuṭṭho bodhisattassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi.

Dukkulīno means of bad birth, a son of a low-class family. Anariyo means an ignoble person, one devoid of moral shame and dread of wrongdoing. In the phrase ‘tammāka vijjañca sutañca ādiyā’, tammāka is a term for a teacher; it is derived from ‘tammo’, one who esteems this and that, meaning one who pursues and practices various crafts. Thus, tammākā means ‘from a teacher’, with the vowel shortened for metrical ease. Vijjaṃ refers to any of the eighteen branches of knowledge. Sutaṃ refers to any learning or oral tradition. Ādiyā means having acquired. In the phrase ‘tameva so tattha sutena khādati’, tameva means ‘himself’. ‘So’ refers to that low-born, ignoble person who acquires knowledge and learning from a teacher. ‘Tattha sutena khādati’ means that through the learning acquired from that teacher, he destroys his very self. In the commentary, there is also the reading ‘teneva so tattha sutena khādati’, which bears the same meaning: he destroys himself with that very learning. ‘Anariyo vuccati pānadūpamo’ means the ignoble one is called ‘like a painful sandal’ (dupāhanūpamo), like a poorly-made sandal. For just as a poorly-made sandal bites the foot, so this person, through his learning, destroys his own self. Alternatively, ‘pānadu’ means one whose foot (pāna for pāda) is pained (dū); it is a name for one whose foot is tormented and bitten by a sandal. Therefore, one who ruins himself through his learning is called ‘ignoble’ because he is afflicted by that learning, and is described as ‘pānadūpamo’, similar to one with a foot tormented by a sandal. This is the meaning here. The king, being pleased, bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā antevāsiko devadatto ahosi, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: “At that time the pupil was Devadatta, and the teacher was I myself.”

Upāhanajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Upāhana Jātaka, the first.

[232] 2. Vīṇāthūṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[232] 2. The Commentary on the Vīṇāthūṇa Jātaka

Ekacintitoyamatthoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ kumārikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kirekā sāvatthiyaṃ seṭṭhidhītā attano gehe usabharājassa sakkāraṃ kayiramānaṃ disvā dhātiṃ pucchi – “amma, ko nāmesa evaṃ sakkāraṃ labhatī”ti. “Usabharājā nāma, ammā”ti. Puna sā ekadivasaṃ pāsāde ṭhatvā antaravīthiṃ olokentī ekaṃ khujjaṃ disvā cintesi – “gunnaṃ [P 2.0225] antare jeṭṭhakassa piṭṭhiyaṃ kakudhaṃ hoti, manussajeṭṭhakassapi tena bhavitabbaṃ, ayaṃ manussesu purisūsabho bhavissati, etassa mayā pādaparicārikāya bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sā dāsiṃ pesetvā [M 2.0206] “seṭṭhidhītā tayā saddhiṃ gantukāmā, asukaṭṭhānaṃ kira gantvā tiṭṭhā”ti tassa ārocetvā sārabhaṇḍakaṃ ādāya aññātakavesena pāsādā otaritvā tena saddhiṃ palāyi. Aparabhāge taṃ kammaṃ nagare ca bhikkhusaṅghe ca pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asukā kira seṭṭhidhītā khujjena saddhiṃ palātā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte satthā “na, bhikkhave, idānevesā khujjaṃ kāmeti, pubbepi kāmesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This matter was conceived by one.” This story the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain young girl. She was the daughter of a treasurer in Sāvatthī. Seeing the honor being paid to a bull-king in her own home, she asked her nurse, “Mother, who is this that receives such honor?” “It is the bull-king, my dear,” replied the nurse. One day, standing on the upper story of the palace and looking down into the street, she saw a hunchback and thought, “Among cattle, the chief one has a hump on its back; so it must be for the chief among humans too. This one must be a bull among men. It is fitting for me to be his attendant.” She sent a maidservant to tell him: “The treasurer’s daughter wishes to go with you. Go and wait at such-and-such a place.” Then, taking her valuables and disguising herself, she descended from the palace and fled with him. Later, this matter became known in the city and among the Saṅgha of monks. In the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised the topic: “Friends, it is said that such-and-such a treasurer’s daughter has run away with a hunchback.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?” When they told him, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that she has desired a hunchback; she desired one in the past as well.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 2.0189] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ nigamagāme seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā vayappatto gharāvāsaṃ vasanto puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhamāno attano puttassa bārāṇasīseṭṭhissa dhītaraṃ vāretvā divasaṃ ṭhapesi. Seṭṭhidhītā attano gehe usabhassa sakkārasammānaṃ disvā “ko nāmeso”ti dhātiṃ pucchitvā “usabho”ti sutvā antaravīthiyā gacchantaṃ ekaṃ khujjaṃ disvā “ayaṃ purisūsabho bhavissatī”ti sārabhaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā tena saddhiṃ palāyi. Bodhisattopi kho “seṭṭhidhītaraṃ gehaṃ ānessāmī”ti mahantena parivārena bārāṇasiṃ gacchanto tameva maggaṃ paṭipajji. Te ubhopi sabbarattiṃ maggaṃ agamaṃsu. Atha khujjassa sabbarattiṃ sītāsihatassa aruṇodaye sarīre vāto kuppi, mahantā vedanā vattanti. So maggā okkamma vedanāppatto hutvā vīṇādaṇḍako viya saṃkuṭito nipajji, seṭṭhidhītāpissa pādamūle nisīdi. Bodhisatto seṭṭhidhītaraṃ khujjassa pādamūle nisinnaṃ disvā sañjānitvā upasaṅkamitvā seṭṭhidhītāya saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a treasurer’s family in a market town. When he came of age, he lived the household life, and having raised sons and daughters, he arranged a marriage for his son with the daughter of the treasurer of Benares and fixed the wedding day. The treasurer’s daughter, seeing the honor and respect given to a bull in her home, asked her nurse, “What is this?” Hearing it was a bull, she later saw a hunchback passing along the street and thought, “This must be a bull among men!” Taking her valuables, she eloped with him. The Bodhisatta, thinking, “I will bring the treasurer’s daughter to my home,” set out for Benares with a large retinue and took the same path. The two of them traveled the whole night. At dawn, the hunchback, who had been chilled all night, suffered a disturbance of the bodily winds, and great pains arose. He went off the path and, overcome with pain, lay down curled up like the neck of a lute. The treasurer’s daughter sat at his feet. When the Bodhisatta saw her sitting at the hunchback’s feet, he recognized her. Approaching and conversing with her, he spoke the first verse:

163.

163.

“Ekacintitoyamattho[P 2.0226], bālo apariṇāyako;

Na hi khujjena vāmena, bhoti saṅgantumarahasī”ti.

“This matter was conceived by you alone; this fool is no leader. Surely, madam, you are not fit to associate with a deformed hunchback.”

Tattha ekacintitoyamatthoti amma, yaṃ tvaṃ atthaṃ cintetvā iminā khujjena saddhiṃ palātā, ayaṃ tayā ekikāya eva cintito bhavissati. Bālo apariṇāyakoti ayaṃ khujjo bālo, duppaññabhāvena mahallakopi bālova, aññasmiṃ gahetvā gacchante asati gantuṃ asamatthatāya apariṇāyako. Na hi khujjena vāmena, bhoti saṅgantumarahasīti [M 2.0207] iminā hi khujjena vāmanattā vāmena bhoti tvaṃ mahākule jātā abhirūpā dassanīyā saṅgantuṃ saha gantuṃ nārahasīti.

Herein, This matter was conceived by one alone means: my dear, this purpose you conceived when you eloped with this hunchback must have been thought up by you alone. This fool is no leader means: this hunchback is a fool; because of his lack of wisdom, though old in years, he is still a fool. He is no leader because he is unable to proceed unless someone else takes him along. Surely, madam, you are not fit to associate with a deformed hunchback means: you, madam, born into a great family, beautiful and lovely to see, are not fit to associate with or accompany this hunchback, who is deformed on account of being a dwarf.

Athassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā seṭṭhidhītā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having heard his words, the treasurer’s daughter spoke the second verse:

164.

164.

“Purisūsabhaṃ maññamānā, ahaṃ khujjamakāmayiṃ;

Soyaṃ saṃkuṭito seti, chinnatanti yathā thuṇā”ti.

“Thinking he was a bull among men, I desired the hunchback. But now he lies curled up, like a lute with broken strings.”

Tassattho – ahaṃ, ayya, ekaṃ usabhaṃ disvā “gunnaṃ jeṭṭhakassa piṭṭhiyaṃ kakudhaṃ hoti, imassapi taṃ atthi, imināpi purisūsabhena bhavitabba”nti evamahaṃ khujjaṃ purisūsabhaṃ maññamānā akāmayiṃ. Soyaṃ yathā nāma chinnatanti sadoṇiko vīṇādaṇḍako, evaṃ saṃkuṭito setīti.

The meaning is: ‘Venerable sir, having seen a bull, I thought: “The chief of the herd has a hump on its back, and this man has one too. He must be a bull among men.” Thus, thinking the hunchback was a bull among men, I desired him. But now he lies curled up just like the neck of a lute with its sound-box when the strings are broken.’

Bodhisatto [V 2.0190] tassā aññātakavesena nikkhantabhāvameva ñatvā taṃ nhāpetvā alaṅkaritvā rathaṃ āropetvā gehameva agamāsi.

The Bodhisatta, understanding that she had left her home in disguise, had her bathed and adorned, placed her in his chariot, and took her back to her home.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ayameva seṭṭhidhītā ahosi, bārāṇasīseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth, saying: “At that time, this very treasurer’s daughter was she, but the treasurer of Benares was I myself.”

Vīṇāthūṇajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Vīṇāthūṇa Jātaka, the second.

[233] 3. Vikaṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā

[233] 3. The Commentary on the Vikaṇṇaka Jātaka

Kāmaṃ [P 2.0227] yahiṃ icchasi tena gacchāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi dhammasabhaṃ ānīto “saccaṃ kira, tvaṃ bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhito”ti satthārā puṭṭho “sacca”nti vatvā “kasmā ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti vutte “kāmaguṇakāraṇā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “kāmaguṇā nāmete bhikkhu vikaṇṇakasallasadisā, sakiṃ hadaye patiṭṭhaṃ labhamānā vikaṇṇakaṃ viya viddhaṃ suṃsumāraṃ maraṇameva pāpentī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Go where you will…” This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a discontented bhikkhu. He was brought to the Hall of Dhamma and asked by the Teacher, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are discontented?” When he replied, “It is true,” he was asked, “Why are you discontented?” He said, “On account of sensual pleasures.” Then the Teacher said to him: “Bhikkhu, these sensual pleasures are like a barbless arrow. Once they find a place in the heart, they bring one to death, like a crocodile pierced by a barbless arrow.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ dhammena rajjaṃ kārento ekadivasaṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā pokkharaṇītīraṃ sampāpuṇi. Naccagītāsu kusalā naccagītāni [M 2.0208] payojesuṃ, pokkharaṇiyaṃ macchakacchapā gītasaddalolatāya sannipatitvā raññāva saddhiṃ gacchanti. Rājā tālakkhandhappamāṇaṃ macchaghaṭaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho ime macchā mayā saddhiṃyeva carantī”ti amacce pucchi. Amaccā “ete, deva, upaṭṭhahantī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā “ete kira maṃ upaṭṭhahantī”ti tussitvā tesaṃ niccabhattaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Devasikaṃ taṇḍulambaṇaṃ pācesi. Macchā bhattavelāya ekacce āgacchanti, ekacce nāgacchanti, bhattaṃ nassati. Rañño tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā “ito paṭṭhāya sattavelāya bheriṃ paharitvā bherisaññāya macchesu sannipatitesu bhattaṃ dethā”ti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya bhattakammiko bheriṃ paharāpetvā sannipatitānaṃ macchānaṃ bhattaṃ deti. Tepi bherisaññāya sannipatitvā bhuñjanti.

In the past, when the Bodhisatta was ruling righteously in Benares, he went one day to the park and came to the bank of a lotus pond. Those skilled in dance and song performed, and the fish and turtles in the pond, attracted by the sound of the music, gathered together and went along with the king. Seeing a shoal of fish the size of a palm trunk, the king asked his ministers, “Why ever do these fish travel along with me?” The ministers replied, “Your Majesty, they are attending on you.” The king was pleased that they were attending on him and established a regular food ration for them. Every day he had a measure of rice cooked. At mealtime some fish came and others did not, and the food was wasted. They reported the matter to the king. The king said, “Henceforth, beat a drum at the appointed time, and when the fish have gathered at the signal of the drum, give them the food.” From then on, the one in charge of the food had the drum beaten and gave the food to the fish that had gathered. And they would gather at the signal of the drum and eat.

Tesu evaṃ sannipatitvā bhuñjantesu eko suṃsumāro āgantvā macche khādi. Bhattakammiko rañño ārocesi. Rājā taṃ sutvā “suṃsumāraṃ macchānaṃ khādanakāle vikaṇṇakena [V 2.0191] vijjhitvā gaṇhā”ti āha[P 2.0228]. So “sādhū”ti gantvā nāvāya ṭhatvā macche khādituṃ āgataṃ suṃsumāraṃ vikaṇṇakena pahari, taṃ tassa antopiṭṭhiṃ pāvisi. So vedanāppatto hutvā taṃ gahetvāva palāyi. Bhattakammiko tassa viddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ ālapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

As they were thus gathering and eating, a crocodile came and ate the fish. The one in charge of the food reported this to the king. On hearing this, the king said, “When the crocodile is eating the fish, pierce it with a barbless arrow and catch it.” The man agreed, went and stood in a boat, and when the crocodile came to eat the fish, he struck it with the barbless arrow, which penetrated deep into its back. Overcome with pain, it fled, taking the arrow with it. The man in charge of the food, knowing it had been pierced, addressed it by reciting the first verse:

165.

165.

“Kāmaṃ yahiṃ icchasi tena gaccha, viddhosi mammamhi vikaṇṇakena;

Hatosi bhattena suvāditena, lolo ca macche anubandhamāno”ti.

“Go where you will, go where you please, for you are pierced in a vital spot by the barbless arrow. Pursuing the fish in your greed, you are slain by the well-sounded food.”

Tattha kāmanti ekaṃsena. Yahiṃ icchasi tena gacchāti yasmiṃ icchasi, tasmiṃ gaccha. Mammamhīti mammaṭṭhāne. Vikaṇṇakenāti vikaṇṇakasallena. Hatosi bhattena suvāditena, lolo ca macche anubandhamānoti tvaṃ bherivāditasaññāya bhatte dīyamāne lolo hutvā khādanatthāya macche anubandhamāno tena savāditena bhattena hato, gataṭṭhānepi te jīvitaṃ natthīti attho. So attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā jīvitakkhayaṃ patto.

Herein, kāmaṃ means for sure. Go where you wish means go to whatever place you desire. In a vital spot means in a vulnerable place. By the barbless arrow means by the barbless dart. Pursuing the fish in your greed, you are slain by the well-sounded food means: you became greedy when the food was being given at the signal of the drum being beaten, and while pursuing the fish to eat them, you were slain by that food announced by sound. The meaning is that even in the place you have reached, you have no life. It went to its dwelling place and met the end of its life.

Satthā [M 2.0209] imaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassetvā abhisambuddho hutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher showed this reason and, as the Fully Enlightened One, spoke the second verse:

166.

166.

“Evampi lokāmisaṃ opatanto, vihaññatī cittavasānuvattī;

So haññatī ñātisakhāna majjhe, macchānugo soriva suṃsumāro”ti.

“So too, one who follows the sway of his mind, swooping on the bait of the world, comes to grief. He is slain amidst his kinsmen and friends, like that crocodile that pursued the fish.”

Tattha lokāmisanti pañca kāmaguṇā. Te hi loko iṭṭhato kantato manāpato gaṇhāti, tasmā “lokāmisa”nti vuccati. Opatantoti taṃ lokāmisaṃ anupatanto kilesavasena cittavasānuvattī puggalo vihaññati kilamati, so haññatīti so evarūpo puggalo ñātīnañca sakhānañca majjhe so vikaṇṇakena viddho macchānugo suṃsumāro viya pañca kāmaguṇe manāpāti gahetvā haññati kilamati mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇātiyevāti.

Herein, the bait of the world means the five cords of sensual pleasure. Because the world takes them to be desirable, lovely, and pleasing, they are called ‘the bait of the world.’ Swooping on means pursuing that worldly bait. One who follows the sway of his mind by the power of the defilements comes to grief and grows weary. He is slain means: such a person, by grasping the five cords of sensual pleasure as pleasing, is slain and grows weary amidst his kinsmen and friends and certainly comes to great destruction, just like that crocodile pierced by the barbless arrow while it pursued the fish.

Evaṃ [P 2.0229] satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā suṃsumāro devadatto, macchā buddhaparisā, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and declared the Truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the talk on the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, the fish were the Buddha’s assembly, and the king of Bārāṇasī was I myself.”

Vikaṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Vikaṇṇaka Jātaka, the third.

[234] 4. Asitābhūjātakavaṇṇanā

[234] 4. The Commentary on the Asitābhū Jātaka

Tvameva [V 2.0192] dānimakarāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ kumārikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kirekasmiṃ dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ upaṭṭhākakule ekā kumārikā abhirūpā sobhaggappattā, sā vayappattā samānajātikaṃ kulaṃ agamāsi. Sāmiko taṃ kismiñci amaññamāno aññattha cittavasena carati. Sā tassa taṃ attani anādarataṃ agaṇetvā dve aggasāvake nimantetvā dānaṃ datvā dhammaṃ suṇantī sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya maggaphalasukhena vītināmayamānā “sāmikopi maṃ na icchati, gharāvāsena me kammaṃ natthi, pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā [M 2.0210] mātāpitūnaṃ ācikkhitvā pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tassā sā kiriyā bhikkhūsu pākaṭā jātā. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asukakulassa dhītā atthagavesikā sāmikassa anicchabhāvaṃ ñatvā aggasāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya puna mātāpitaro āpucchitvā pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pattā, evaṃ atthagavesikā, āvuso sā kumārikā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevesā kuladhītā atthagavesikā, pubbepi atthagavesikāyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"You yourself did it now..." The Teacher related this story while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain young girl. In Sāvatthī, it seems, in the family of a supporter of the two chief disciples, there was a beautiful and fortunate young girl. When she came of age, she went to a family of equal status. Her husband, holding her in no esteem, went about with his mind set on another. Disregarding his lack of respect for her, she invited the two chief disciples, gave them alms, and listened to the Dhamma, whereby she was established in the fruit of stream-entry. From then on, she passed her time in the bliss of the path and its fruit. She thought, "My husband does not desire me, and I have no business with the household life—I will go forth." Having informed her parents, she went forth and attained arahantship. Her action became well-known among the monks. One day, the monks raised a topic of discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, the daughter of such-and-such a family, a seeker of her own welfare, realizing her husband’s lack of desire for her, after hearing the Dhamma from the chief disciples, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, taking leave of her parents, she went forth and attained arahantship. Truly, friends, that young girl was a seeker of her own welfare." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered here?" When they told him, he said, "Not only now, monks, is this clanswoman a seeker of her own welfare; in the past, too, she was a seeker of her own welfare." And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā himavantapadese vāsaṃ kappesi. Tadā bārāṇasirājā attano puttassa brahmadattakumārassa parivārasampattiṃ disvā uppannāsaṅko puttaṃ raṭṭhā pabbājesi. So [P 2.0230] asitābhuṃ nāma attano deviṃ ādāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā macchamaṃsaphalāphalāni khādanto paṇṇasālāya nivāsaṃ kappesi. So ekaṃ kinnariṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto “imaṃ pajāpatiṃ karissāmī”ti asitābhuṃ agaṇetvā tassā anupadaṃ agamāsi. Sā taṃ kinnariṃ anubandhamānaṃ disvā “ayaṃ maṃ agaṇetvā kinnariṃ anubandhati, kiṃ me iminā”ti virattacittā hutvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā attano kasiṇaparikammaṃ kathāpetvā kasiṇaṃ olokentī abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā āgantvā attano paṇṇasālāya dvāre aṭṭhāsi. Brahmadattopi kinnariṃ anubandhanto vicaritvā tassā gatamaggampi adisvā chinnāso hutvā paṇṇasālābhimukhova āgato. Asitābhū taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā maṇivaṇṇe gaganatale ṭhitā “ayyaputta, taṃ nissāya mayā idaṃ jhānasukhaṃ laddha”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta went forth into the ascetic life. Having developed the direct knowledges and meditative attainments, he took up residence in the Himalayan region. At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī, seeing the great retinue of his son Prince Brahmadatta, became suspicious and banished his son from the kingdom. The prince, taking his queen named Asitābhū, entered the Himalayas. There, eating fish, meat, and various fruits, he lived in a leaf hut. One day, he saw a kinnarī and became infatuated. Thinking, 'I will make her my wife,' he disregarded Asitābhū and pursued the kinnarī. Asitābhū, seeing him chasing the kinnarī, thought, 'He disregards me and chases after a kinnarī. What use is he to me?' With a dispassionate mind, she approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and had the preliminary kasiṇa meditation explained to her. Focusing on the kasiṇa, she developed the direct knowledges and meditative attainments. Then, she paid homage to the Bodhisatta and returned to stand at the door of her leaf hut. Meanwhile, Brahmadatta, wandering in pursuit of the kinnarī and unable to find any trace of her, became hopeless and turned back toward the leaf hut. Asitābhū, seeing him approaching, rose into the air and stood in the jewel-colored sky. She said, 'Noble son, on account of you, I have attained this jhānic bliss,' and spoke this verse:

167.

167.

“Tvameva [V 2.0193] dānimakara, yaṃ kāmo byagamā tayi;

Soyaṃ appaṭisandhiko, kharachinnaṃva renuka”nti.

“You yourself have now brought it about that the desire I had for you has departed. That desire can no more be reconnected, like ivory cut by a saw.”

Tattha [M 2.0211] tvameva dānimakarāti, ayyaputta, maṃ pahāya kinnariṃ anubandhanto tvaññeva idāni idaṃ akara. Yaṃ kāmo byagamā tayīti yaṃ mama tayi kāmo vigato vikkhambhanappahānena pahīno, yassa pahīnattā ahaṃ imaṃ visesaṃ pattāti dīpeti. Soyaṃ appaṭisandhikoti so pana kāmo idāni appaṭisandhiko jāto, na sakkā paṭisandhituṃ. Kharachinnaṃva renukanti kharo vuccati kakaco, renukaṃ vuccati hatthidanto. Yathā kakacena chinno hatthidanto appaṭisandhiko hoti, na puna purimanayena allīyati, evaṃ puna mayhaṃ tayā saddhiṃ cittassa ghaṭanaṃ nāma natthīti vatvā tassa passantasseva uppatitvā aññattha agamāsi.

Herein, "You yourself have now brought it about" means: 'Noble son, by abandoning me and pursuing a kinnarī, you yourself have now done this (jhanic bliss).' "That the desire I had for you has departed" means: she indicates, 'That desire of mine for you has departed, abandoned by way of suppression, and because of its abandonment I have attained this special attainment.' "That desire can no more be reconnected" means: that desire has now become unable to be reconnected; it cannot be joined together again. "Like ivory cut by a saw" means: 'khara' is a saw, and 'renuka' is ivory. Just as ivory cut by a saw cannot be reconnected and does not adhere again as it was before, so too there can be no rejoining of my mind with you.' Having said this, she flew up and went elsewhere right before his eyes.

So tassā gatakāle paridevamāno dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

When she had departed, he lamented and spoke the second verse:

168.

168.

“Atricchaṃ atilobhena[P 2.0231], atilobhamadena ca;

Evaṃ hāyati atthamhā, ahaṃva asitābhuyā”ti.

“Through excessive desire and extreme greed, and through the intoxication of that greed, one thus falls away from one's welfare, just as I have from Asitābhū.”

Tattha atricchaṃ atilobhenāti atricchā vuccati atra atra icchāsaṅkhātā apariyantataṇhā, atilobho vuccati atikkamitvā pavattalobho. Atilobhamadena cāti purisamadaṃ uppādanato atilobhamado nāma jāyati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – atricchāvasena atricchamāno puggalo atilobhena ca atilobhamadena ca yathā ahaṃ asitābhuyā rājadhītāya parihīno, evaṃ atthā hāyatīti.

Herein, "Through excessive desire and extreme greed": 'atricchā' is called limitless craving, the insatiable thirst that arises for this and that; 'atilobha' is called greed that proceeds having transgressed its bounds. "And through the intoxication of extreme greed": the intoxication of extreme greed arises from producing manly conceit. This is the meaning: a person who is excessively desirous on account of excessive desire, through extreme greed and the intoxication of extreme greed, falls away from their welfare, just as I have been bereft of the princess Asitābhū.

Iti so imāya gāthāya paridevitvā araññe ekakova vasitvā pitu accayena gantvā rajjaṃ gaṇhi.

Thus, having lamented with this verse, he lived all alone in the forest. After his father’s passing, he went and took over the kingdom.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājaputto ca rājadhītā ca ime dve janā ahesuṃ, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having concluded this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher identified the birth: “At that time, the prince and the princess were these two people (of the current story), but the ascetic was I myself.”

Asitābhūjātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Asitābhū Jātaka, the Fourth.

[235] 5. Vacchanakhajātakavaṇṇanā

[235] 5. The Commentary on the Vacchanakha Jātaka

Sukhā [V 2.0194][M 2.0212] gharā vacchanakhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto rojamallaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kirāyasmato ānandassa gihisahāyo. So ekadivasaṃ āgamanatthāya therassa sāsanaṃ pāhesi, thero satthāraṃ āpucchitvā agamāsi. So theraṃ nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhojetvā ekamantaṃ nisinno therena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā theraṃ gihibhogehi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi nimantento “bhante ānanda, mama gehe pahūtaṃ saviññāṇakaaviññāṇakaratanaṃ, idaṃ majjhe bhinditvā tuyhaṃ dammi, ehi ubho agāraṃ ajjhāvasāmā”ti. Thero tassa kāmaguṇesu ādīnavaṃ kathetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ gantvā “diṭṭho te, ānanda, rojo”ti satthārā pucchito “āma, bhante”ti vatvā “kimassa kathesī”ti vutte “bhante, maṃ rojo gharāvāsena nimantesi, athassāhaṃ gharāvāse ceva kāmaguṇesu ca ādīnavaṃ kathesi”nti. Satthā “na kho, ānanda, rojo mallo idāneva pabbajite gharāvāsena nimantesi, pubbepi nimantesiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Pleasant are homes, Vacchanakha,” this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Roja the Malla. He was, it is said, a lay friend of the Venerable Ānanda. One day, he sent a message to the elder, asking him to come. The elder, having taken leave of the Teacher, went. Roja served the elder a meal with various choice flavors and, sitting to one side, exchanged friendly greetings with him. Then, inviting the elder with household possessions and the five cords of sensual pleasure, he said: “Venerable Ānanda, in my house there is abundant treasure, both animate and inanimate. I will split it down the middle and give half to you. Come, let us both dwell in the household life.” The elder explained to him the danger in sensual pleasures and then, rising from his seat, went to the monastery. When asked by the Teacher, “Ānanda, did you see Roja?” he replied, “Yes, venerable sir.” When asked, “What did he say?” he replied: “Venerable sir, Roja invited me to the household life, so I explained to him the danger in the household life and in sensual pleasures.” The Teacher said: “Ānanda, it is not only now that Roja the Malla has invited one who has gone forth to the household life; he invited one in the past as well.” And, being requested by the elder, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 2.0232] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto aññatarasmiṃ nigamagāme brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantapadese ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase bārāṇasiṃ pāvisi. Athassa bārāṇasiseṭṭhi ācāravihāre pasīditvā gehaṃ netvā bhojetvā uyyāne vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gahetvā taṃ paṭijagganto uyyāne vasāpesi. Te aññamaññaṃ uppannasinehā ahesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a certain market town. When he came of age, he went forth into the ascetic life. After dwelling for a long time in the Himalayan region, he came to Bārāṇasī to get salt and sour food. He stayed in the royal park and on the next day entered Bārāṇasī. The treasurer of Bārāṇasī, gaining confidence in his deportment, took him to his house, fed him, and, after getting his promise to stay, had him reside in the park while he looked after him. They developed affection for one another.

Athekadivasaṃ bārāṇasiseṭṭhi bodhisatte pemavissāsavasena evaṃ cintesi – “pabbajjā nāma dukkhā, mama sahāyaṃ vacchanakhaparibbājakaṃ uppabbājetvā sabbaṃ vibhavaṃ majjhe bhinditvā tassa datvā dvepi samaggavāsaṃ vasissāmā”ti. So ekadivasaṃ bhattakiccapariyosāne tena saddhiṃ madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā “bhante vacchanakha, pabbajjā nāma dukkhā, sukho gharāvāso, ehi ubho samaggā kāme paribhuñjantā vasāmā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then one day the treasurer of Bārāṇasī, out of affection and trust for the Bodhisatta, thought thus: “The ascetic life is painful. I will make my friend, the wanderer Vacchanakha, give up the going forth, split all my wealth in half and give it to him, and we will both live together in harmony.” So one day, at the conclusion of the meal, after exchanging pleasant greetings with him, he said: “Venerable Vacchanakha, the ascetic life is painful; the household life is pleasant. Come, let us both live together in harmony, enjoying sensual pleasures.” And he spoke the first verse:

169.

169.

“Sukhā [M 2.0213] gharā vacchanakha, sahiraññā sabhojanā;

Yattha bhutvā pivitvā ca, sayeyyātha anussuko”ti.

“Pleasant are homes, O Vacchanakha, with gold and with food, where, having eaten and drunk, you could lie down without a care.”

Tattha [V 2.0195] sahiraññāti sattaratanasampannā. Sabhojanāti bahukhādanīyabhojanīyā. Yattha bhutvā pivitvā cāti yesu sahiraññabhojanesu gharesu nānaggarasāni bhojanāni paribhuñjitvā nānāpānāni ca pivitvā. Sayeyyātha anussukoti yesu alaṅkatasirisayanapiṭṭhe anussuko hutvā sayeyyāsi, te gharā nāma ativiya sukhāti.

Herein, 'with gold' means endowed with the seven kinds of treasures. 'With food' means with abundant hard and soft food. 'Where, having eaten and drunk' means: in those homes with gold and food, having partaken of foods of various choice flavors and drunk various beverages. 'You could lie down without a care' means: you could lie down without longing on the surface of an adorned, splendid couch. Such homes are indeed very pleasant.

Athassa taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “mahāseṭṭhi, tvaṃ aññāṇatāya kāmagiddho hutvā gharāvāsassa guṇaṃ, pabbajjāya ca aguṇaṃ kathesi, gharāvāsassa te aguṇaṃ kathessāmi, suṇāhi dānī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said: “Great Treasurer, out of ignorance and greed for sensual pleasures you have spoken of the virtues of the household life and the faults of the renunciant life. I will now tell you the faults of the household life; listen now.” Then he spoke the second verse:

170.

170.

“Gharā [P 2.0233] nānīhamānassa, gharā nābhaṇato musā;

Gharā nādinnadaṇḍassa, paresaṃ anikubbato;

Evaṃ chiddaṃ durabhisambhavaṃ, ko gharaṃ paṭipajjatī”ti.

“The household is not for one who does not strive, nor for one who does not speak falsehoods; it is not for one who does not wield the rod, nor for one who does not oppress others. So flawed and hard to sustain, who would enter the household life?”

Tattha gharā nānīhamānassāti niccakālaṃ kasigorakkhādikaraṇena anīhamānassa avāyamantassa gharā nāma natthi, gharāvāso na patiṭṭhātīti attho. Gharā nābhaṇato musāti khettavatthuhiraññasuvaṇṇādīnaṃ atthāya amusābhaṇatopi gharā nāma natthi. Gharā nādinnadaṇḍassa, paresaṃ anikubbatoti nādinnadaṇḍassāti aggahitadaṇḍassa, nikkhittadaṇḍassa paresaṃ anikubbato gharā nāma natthi. Yo pana ādinnadaṇḍo hutvā paresaṃ dāsakammakarādīnaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ aparādhe aparādhānurūpaṃ vadhabandhanachedanatāḷanādivasena karoti, tasseva gharāvāso saṇṭhahatīti attho. Evaṃ chiddaṃ durabhisambhavaṃ, ko gharaṃ paṭipajjatīti taṃ dāni evaṃ etesaṃ īhanādīnaṃ akaraṇe sati tāya tāya parihāniyā chiddaṃ karaṇepi sati niccameva kātabbato durabhisambhavaṃ durārādhanīyaṃ, niccaṃ karontassapi vā durabhisambhavameva duppūraṃ gharāvāsaṃ “ahaṃ nipparitasso hutvā ajjhāvasissāmī”ti ko paṭipajjatīti.

Here, 'the household is not for one who does not strive' means: for one who does not constantly strive and exert himself in farming, cattle-herding, and so on, there is no such thing as a household; the household life is not established. 'Nor for one who does not speak falsehoods' means: for one who does not speak falsehoods for the sake of fields, property, gold, silver, and so on, there is no such thing as a household. 'It is not for one who does not wield the rod, nor for one who does not oppress others' means: for one who has not taken up the rod, who has laid down the rod, who does not oppress others, there is no such thing as a household. But for one who wields the rod and punishes his servants, workers, and so on for their various offenses in a manner corresponding to the offense—by means of killing, imprisonment, mutilation, or striking—only for such a one is the household life established. 'So flawed and hard to sustain, who would enter the household life?' means: since, when these actions like striving are not performed, flaws arise from that very neglect, and since they must always be performed, it is hard to manage and hard to satisfy. Or even for one who does them constantly, the household life is hard to manage and difficult to fulfill. Who would enter it thinking, 'I will dwell here without trouble'?

Evaṃ mahāsatto gharāvāsassa dosaṃ kathetvā uyyānameva agamāsi.

Thus the Great Being, having spoken of the faults of the household life, went to the park.

Satthā [M 2.0214] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasiseṭṭhi rojo mallo ahosi, vacchanakhaparibbājako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the birth: “At that time, the treasurer of Bārāṇasī was Roja the Mallian, and the wanderer Vacchanakha was I myself.”

Vacchanakhajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Vacchanakha Jātaka is finished.

[236] 6. Bakajātakavaṇṇanā

[236] 6. The Commentary on the Baka Jātaka

Bhaddako [V 2.0196] vatayaṃ pakkhīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā ānetvā dassitaṃ disvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa kuhakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This is a virtuous bird indeed.” This the Teacher said while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain deceitful bhikkhu. For when this bhikkhu was brought and shown, the Teacher saw him and said: “Bhikkhus, not only now is he deceitful; in the past, too, he was deceitful.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 2.0234] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese ekasmiṃ sare maccho hutvā mahāparivāro vasi. Atheko bako “macche khādissāmī”ti sarassa āsannaṭṭhāne sīsaṃ pātetvā pakkhe pasāretvā mandamando macche olokento aṭṭhāsi tesaṃ pamādaṃ āgamayamāno. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bodhisatto macchagaṇaparivuto gocaraṃ gaṇhanto taṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi. Macchagaṇo taṃ bakaṃ passitvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a fish in a lake in the Himalayan region and lived there with a large retinue. Then a certain crane, thinking, "I will eat the fish," stood near the lake, dropping its head and spreading its wings, looking at the fish very slowly, waiting for them to become heedless. At that moment the Bodhisatta, surrounded by a school of fish, came to that spot while searching for food. Seeing the crane, the school of fish spoke the first verse:

171.

171.

“Bhaddako vatayaṃ pakkhī, dijo kumudasannibho;

Vūpasantehi pakkhehi, mandamandova jhāyatī”ti.

“This is a virtuous bird indeed, a twice-born one like a white lily; with tranquil wings, it meditates ever so slowly.”

Tattha mandamandova jhāyatīti abalabalo viya hutvā kiñci ajānanto viya ekakova jhāyatīti.

Here, "it meditates ever so slowly" means: it meditates alone as if it were very weak and knew nothing.

Atha naṃ bodhisatto oloketvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, looking at it, spoke the second verse:

172.

172.

“Nāssa sīlaṃ vijānātha, anaññāya pasaṃsatha;

Amhe dijo na pāleti, tena pakkhī na phandatī”ti.

“You do not know its character; you praise it without understanding. This twice-born does not protect us; that is why the bird does not stir.”

Tattha anaññāyāti ajānitvā. Amhe dijo na pāletīti esa dijo amhe na rakkhati na gopāyati, “kataraṃ nu kho etesu kabaḷaṃ karissāmī”ti upadhāreti. Tena pakkhī na phandatīti tenāyaṃ sakuṇo na phandati [M 2.0215] na calatīti. Evaṃ vutte macchagaṇo udakaṃ khobhetvā bakaṃ palāpesi.

Herein, 'without understanding' means without knowing. 'This twice-born does not protect us' means: this twice-born one does not guard or protect us, but considers, “Which one of these shall I make into a morsel?” 'That is why the bird does not stir' means: for that reason this bird does not stir or move. When this was said, the school of fish churned up the water and made the crane flee.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bako kuhako bhikkhu ahosi, maccharājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the birth: “At that time, the crane was the deceitful bhikkhu, and the king of the fish was I myself.”

Bakajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Baka Jātaka, the sixth.

[237] 7. Sāketajātakavaṇṇanā

[237] 7. The Commentary on the Sāketa Jātaka

Ko [V 2.0197] nu kho bhagavā hetūti idaṃ satthā sāketaṃ upanissāya viharanto sāketaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu panettha atītampi paccuppannampi heṭṭhā ekakanipāte (jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.sāketajātakavaṇṇanā) kathitameva. Tathāgatassa [P 2.0235] pana vihāraṃ gatakāle bhikkhū “sineho nāmesa, bhante, kathaṃ patiṭṭhātī”ti pucchantā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

“What, O Blessed One, is the cause?” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling near Sāketa concerning the brahmin of Sāketa. The story here, both of the past and of the present, has already been told below in the Book of Ones in the commentary on the Sāketa Jātaka. When the Tathāgata had gone to his dwelling, the bhikkhus, asking, “Venerable sir, how is it that affection is established?” spoke the first verse:

173.

173.

“Ko nu kho bhagavā hetu, ekacce idha puggale;

Atīva hadayaṃ nibbāti, cittañcāpi pasīdatī”ti.

“What, O Blessed One, is the cause that, towards certain persons here, the heart is exceedingly soothed and the mind also grows serene?”

Tassattho – ko nu kho hetu, yena idhekacce puggale diṭṭhamatteyeva hadayaṃ ativiya nibbāti, suvāsitassa sītassa udakassa ghaṭasahassena parisittaṃ viya sītalaṃ hoti, ekacce na nibbāti. Ekacce diṭṭhamatteyeva cittaṃ pasīdati, mudu hoti, pemavasena allīyati, ekacce na allīyatīti.

The meaning is this: What is the cause, by which, on merely seeing certain persons here, the heart becomes exceedingly soothed—becoming cool as if sprinkled with a thousand pots of cool, fragrant water—while towards others it is not soothed? On merely seeing certain persons the mind becomes serene, grows soft, and cleaves to them out of affection, while towards others it does not cleave.

Atha nesaṃ satthā pemakāraṇaṃ dassento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Teacher, showing them the cause of affection, spoke the second verse:

174.

174.

“Pubbeva sannivāsena, paccuppannahitena vā;

Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃva yathodake”ti.

“Through past co-residence, or through a benefit in the present, thus is that affection born, like a lotus in the water.”

Tassattho – bhikkhave, pemaṃ nāmetaṃ dvīhi kāraṇehi jāyati, purimabhave mātā vā pitā vā putto vā dhītā vā bhātā vā bhaginī vā pati vā bhariyā vā sahāyo vā mitto vā hutvā yo yena saddhiṃ [M 2.0216] ekaṭṭhāne vutthapubbo, tassa iminā pubbeva sannivāsena bhavantarepi anubandhanto so sineho na vijahati. Imasmiṃ attabhāve katena paccuppannahitena vā evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi pemaṃ nāma jāyati. Yathā kiṃ? Uppalaṃva yathodaketi. Vā-kārassa rassattaṃ kataṃ. Samuccayatthe cesa vutto, tasmā uppalañca sesaṃ jalajapupphañca yathā udake jāyamānaṃ dve kāraṇāni nissāya jāyati udakañceva kalalañca, tathā etehi dvīhi kāraṇehi pemaṃ jāyatīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Its meaning is this: Bhikkhus, this thing called affection is born from two causes. When one has lived together with another in the same place in a former existence as a mother, father, son, daughter, brother, sister, husband, wife, companion, or friend, that affection, following one even into another existence because of this past co-residence, is not abandoned. Or affection is born from a benefit done in this present life. It is from these two causes that affection is born. How so? 'Like a lotus in the water.' The 'vā' has been shortened; it is used here in a conjunctive sense. Therefore, just as a lotus and other water-born flowers, being born in the water, arise depending on two causes—the water and the mud—so too affection arises from these two causes. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

Satthā [V 2.0198] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo ca brāhmaṇī ca ime dve janā ahesuṃ, putto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher identified the birth: “At that time, the brahmin and the brahmin woman were those two people, but the son was I myself.”

Sāketajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Sāketa Jātaka, the seventh.

[238] 8. Ekapadajātakavaṇṇanā

[238] 8. The Commentary on the Ekapada Jātaka

Iṅgha [P 2.0236] ekapadaṃ, tātāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthivāsī kiresa kuṭumbiko, athassa ekadivasaṃ aṅke nisinno putto atthassa dvāraṃ nāma pañhaṃ pucchi. So “buddhavisayo esa pañho, na taṃ añño kathetuṃ sakkhissatī”ti puttaṃ gahetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā “bhante, ayaṃ me dārako ūrumhi nisinno atthassa dvāraṃ nāma pañhaṃ pucchi, ahaṃ taṃ ajānanto idhāgato, kathetha, bhante, imaṃ pañha”nti. Satthā “na kho, upāsaka, ayaṃ dārako idāneva atthagavesako, pubbepi atthagavesakova hutvā imaṃ pañhaṃ paṇḍite pucchi, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpissa kathesuṃ, bhavasaṅkhepagatattā pana na sallakkhesī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Come, father, one word.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain householder. This householder, it seems, was a resident of Sāvatthī. One day, while his son was sitting on his lap, the boy asked him a question called “the door to what is beneficial.” The father thought, “This question is within the Buddha's range; no one else will be able to explain it.” Taking his son, he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and said: “Venerable sir, this boy of mine, while sitting on my thigh, asked me the question called ‘the door to what is beneficial.’ Not knowing it, I have come here. Please, venerable sir, explain this question.” The Teacher said: “Lay follower, it is not only now that this boy is a seeker of what is beneficial; in the past, too, he was a seeker of what is beneficial and asked this question of the wise. The wise ones of old also explained it to him, but because of the interval of another existence, he did not remember it.” And being requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā vayappatto pitu accayena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhi. Athassa putto daharo kumāro ūrumhi nisīditvā “tāta, mayhaṃ ekapadaṃ anekatthanissitaṃ ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathethā”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the family of a treasurer. When he came of age, upon his father’s passing, he received the position of treasurer. Then his young son, sitting on his thigh, asked, “Father, tell me one principle, a single word that relies on many meanings,” and in asking, he spoke the first verse:

175.

175.

“Iṅgha [M 2.0217] ekapadaṃ tāta, anekatthapadassitaṃ;

Kiñci saṅgāhikaṃ brūsi, yenatthe sādhayemase”ti.

“Come, father, tell me one word that is based on many meanings, something comprehensive by which we might achieve our aims.”

Tattha iṅghāti yācanatthe codanatthe vā nipāto. Ekapadanti ekaṃ kāraṇapadaṃ, ekaṃ kāraṇūpasañhitaṃ vā byañjanapadaṃ. Anekatthapadassitanti anekāni atthapadāni kāraṇapadāni nissitaṃ. Kiñci saṅgāhikaṃ brūsīti kiñci ekapadaṃ bahūnaṃ padānaṃ saṅgāhikaṃ brūhi, ayameva vā pāṭho. Yenatthe sādhayemaseti yena ekena padena anekatthanissitena mayaṃ attano vuḍḍhiṃ sādheyyāma, taṃ me kathehīti pucchi.

Herein, 'iṅgha' is a particle used in the sense of requesting or urging. 'One word' means one word of principle, or a verbal expression connected to a principle. 'Based on many meanings' means relying on many meaningful words or words of principle. 'Something comprehensive' means: tell me one word that is comprehensive of many words; or this is simply the reading. 'By which we might achieve our aims' means: he asked, 'Tell me that one word, relying on its many meanings, by which we may achieve our own prosperity.'

Athassa pitā kathento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then his father, speaking, uttered the second verse:

176.

176.

“Dakkheyyekapadaṃ [V 2.0199] tāta, anekatthapadassitaṃ;

Tañca sīlena saññuttaṃ, khantiyā upapāditaṃ;

Alaṃ mitte sukhāpetuṃ, amittānaṃ dukhāya cā”ti.

“My son, a single word of skill, based on many grounds of meaning, conjoined with virtue and endowed with patience, is sufficient to make friends happy and to bring sorrow to enemies.”

Tattha [P 2.0237] dakkheyyekapadanti dakkheyyaṃ ekapadaṃ. Dakkheyyaṃ nāma lābhuppādakassa chekassa kusalassa ñāṇasampayuttaṃ vīriyaṃ. Anekatthapadassitanti evaṃ vuttappakāraṃ vīriyaṃ anekehi atthapadehi nissitaṃ. Katarehīti? Sīlādīhi. Teneva “tañca sīlena saññutta”ntiādimāha. Tassattho – tañca panetaṃ vīriyaṃ ācārasīlasampayuttaṃ adhivāsanakhantiyā upetaṃ mitte sukhāpetuṃ amittānañca dukkhāya alaṃ samatthaṃ. Ko hi nāma lābhuppādakañāṇasampayuttakusalavīriyasamannāgato ācārakhantisampanno mitte sukhāpetuṃ, amitte vā dukkhāpetuṃ na sakkotīti.

Herein, 'a single word of skill' means a skilled word. Skill (dakkheyya) is the energy associated with knowledge that is clever, wholesome, and productive of gain. 'Based on many grounds of meaning' means that this kind of energy just mentioned is based upon many grounds of meaning. Which ones? Virtue and so on. For that reason he said, ‘and that conjoined with virtue,’ and so on. Its meaning is this: and this energy, conjoined with virtuous conduct, endowed with the patience of endurance, is able and competent to make friends happy and for the sorrow of enemies. For who indeed, possessed of wholesome energy associated with knowledge productive of gain, accomplished in conduct and patience, would not be able to make friends happy or to make enemies sorrowful?

Evaṃ bodhisatto puttassa pañhaṃ kathesi. Sopi pitu kathitanayeneva attano atthaṃ sādhetvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus the Bodhisatta answered the question for his son. He too, having achieved his own purpose in the manner explained by his father, fared according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne pitāputtā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā. “Tadā putto ayameva putto ahosi, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, proclaimed the truths and made the connection in the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, the father and son were established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the son was this very son, but the treasurer of Bārāṇasī was I myself.”

Ekapadajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the One-Word Jātaka, the eighth.

[239] 9. Haritamaṇḍūkajātakavaṇṇanā

[239] 9. The Commentary on the Green Frog Jātaka

Āsīvisampi [M 2.0218] maṃ santanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ajātasattuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kosalarājassa hi pitā mahākosalo bimbisārarañño dhītaraṃ dadamāno dhītu nhānamūlaṃ kāsigāmakaṃ nāma adāsi. Sā ajātasattunā pitughātakakamme kate rañño sinehena nacirasseva kālamakāsi. Ajātasattu mātari kālakatāyapi taṃ gāmaṃ bhuñjateva. Kosalarājā “pitughātakassa corassa mama kulasantakaṃ gāmaṃ na dassāmī”ti tena saddhiṃ yujjhati. Kadāci mātulassa jayo hoti, kadāci bhāgineyyassa. Yadā pana [V 2.0200] ajātasattu jināti, tadā somanassappatto rathe dhajaṃ ussāpetvā mahantena yasena nagaraṃ pavisati. Yadā pana parājayati, tadā domanassappatto kañci ajānāpetvāva pavisati. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, ajātasattu mātulaṃ jinitvā tussati, parājito domanassappatto hotī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi [P 2.0238] kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa jinitvā tussati, parājito domanassappatto hotī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Though I am a serpent…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove concerning Ajātasattu. For the Kosalan king’s father, Mahākosala, when giving his daughter to King Bimbisāra, gave a village in Kāsī as her bath-money. When Ajātasattu committed the act of patricide, she, out of love for the king, died not long after. Even after his mother had died, Ajātasattu continued to enjoy that village. The Kosalan king declared, “I will not give a village belonging to my clan to a patricidal thief,” and he waged war with him. Sometimes the maternal uncle was victorious, sometimes the nephew. When Ajātasattu won, he was filled with joy, and hoisting a banner on his chariot, he would enter the city with great splendor. But when he was defeated, he was filled with sorrow and would enter without letting anyone know. Then one day in the hall of Dhamma, the bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion: “Venerable sirs, Ajātasattu rejoices when he defeats his maternal uncle, but when he is defeated, he becomes sorrowful.” The Teacher came and asked, “For what discussion are you now gathered here, bhikkhus?” When they told him, “For this one,” he said: “Not only now, bhikkhus, but in the past, too, he rejoiced when he won and became sorrowful when he was defeated,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto nīlamaṇḍūkayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Tadā manussā nadīkandarādīsu tattha tattha macche gahaṇatthāya kumīnāni oḍḍesuṃ. Ekasmiṃ kumīne bahū macchā pavisiṃsu. Atheko udakāsīviso macche khādanto taṃ kumīnaṃ pāvisi, bahū macchā ekato hutvā taṃ khādantā ekalohitaṃ akaṃsu. So paṭisaraṇaṃ apassanto maraṇabhayatajjito kumīnamukhena nikkhamitvā vedanāppatto udakapariyante nipajji. Nīlamaṇḍūkopi tasmiṃ khaṇe uppatitvā kumīnasūlamatthake nipanno hoti. Āsīviso vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ alabhanto tattha nipannaṃ taṃ disvā “samma nīlamaṇḍūka, imesaṃ macchānaṃ kiriyā ruccati tuyha”nti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a green frog. At that time, people set up fish-traps here and there in rivers, ravines, and so on, in order to catch fish. Many fish entered one fish-trap. Then a water serpent, while eating fish, entered that trap. Many fish gathered together and, while devouring it, made it all bloody. Seeing no refuge and terrified by the fear of death, it escaped through the mouth of the trap and lay on the water’s edge, afflicted by pain. At that moment, the green frog also leaped up and lay on top of the fish-trap’s stake. The serpent, not finding a place of rest, saw him lying there and, asking, “Friend green frog, do you approve of this action of the fish?” he uttered the first verse:

177.

177.

“Āsīvisampi maṃ santaṃ, paviṭṭhaṃ kumināmukhaṃ;

Ruccate haritāmātā, yaṃ maṃ khādanti macchakā”ti.

“Though I am a serpent who has entered the fish-trap’s mouth, does it please you, mother of the green one, that the little fish are eating me?”

Tattha [M 2.0219] āsīvisampi maṃ santanti maṃ āgatavisaṃ samānaṃ. Ruccate haritāmātā, yaṃ maṃ khādanti macchakāti etaṃ tava ruccati haritamaṇḍūkaputtāti vadati.

Herein, 'āsīvisampi maṃ santaṃ' means: me, being a venomous one. As for 'ruccate haritāmātā, yaṃ maṃ khādanti macchakā', he is saying: ‘Does this please you, son of the green frog?’

Atha naṃ haritamaṇḍūko “āma, samma, ruccatī”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Sace tvampi tava padesaṃ āgate macche khādasi, macchāpi attano [P 2.0239] padesaṃ āgataṃ taṃ khādanti, attano visaye padese gocarabhūmiyaṃ abalavā nāma natthī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the green frog said to him: “Yes, friend, it pleases me.” “For what reason?” “If you eat fish that have come into your domain, the fish also eat you when you have come into their domain. In one's own sphere, domain, and feeding ground, no one is weak.” Having said this, he uttered the second verse:

178.

178.

“Vilumpateva puriso, yāvassa upakappati;

Yadā caññe vilumpanti, so vilutto vilumpatī”ti.

“A person plunders only so long as it serves his turn; but when others plunder him, the plunderer is plundered in turn.”

Tattha vilumpateva puriso, yāvassa upakappatīti yāva assa purisassa issariyaṃ upakappati ijjhati pavattati, tāva so aññaṃ vilumpatiyeva. “Yāva so upakappatī”tipi pāṭho[V 2.0201], yattakaṃ kālaṃ so puriso sakkoti vilumpitunti attho. Yadā caññe vilumpantīti yadā ca aññe issarā hutvā vilumpanti. So vilutto vilumpatīti atha so vilumpako aññehi vilumpati. “Vilumpate”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. “Vilumpana”ntipi paṭhanti, tassattho na sameti. Evaṃ “vilumpako puna vilumpaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti bodhisattena aḍḍe vinicchite udakāsīvisassa dubbalabhāvaṃ ñatvā “paccāmittaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti macchagaṇā kumīnamukhā nikkhamitvā tattheva naṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā pakkamuṃ.

Herein, 'vilumpateva puriso, yāvassa upakappati' means: as long as that person’s sovereignty is possible, succeeds, and continues, for so long does he plunder another. There is also the reading 'yāva so upakappati', which means: for as long a time as that person is able to plunder. 'Yadā caññe vilumpanti' means: and when others, having become sovereign, plunder. 'So vilutto vilumpati' means: then that plunderer is plundered by others. There is also the reading 'vilumpate'; this has the same meaning. Some also read 'vilumpanaṃ', but its meaning does not fit. Thus, when the matter was judged by the Bodhisatta with the words, ‘The plunderer again meets with plundering,’ the shoal of fish, recognizing the weakness of the water serpent and thinking, ‘We will seize our enemy,’ came out from the mouth of the fish-trap and right there brought him to the end of his life and departed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā udakāsīviso ajātasattu ahosi, nīlamaṇḍūko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the Jātaka: “At that time, the water serpent was Ajātasattu, but the green frog was myself.”

Haritamaṇḍūkajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Green Frog Jātaka, the ninth.

[240] 10. Mahāpiṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā

[240] 10. The Commentary on the Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka

Sabbo janoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadatte satthari āghātaṃ bandhitvā navamāsaccayena jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake pathaviyaṃ nimugge jetavanavāsino ca sakalaraṭṭhavāsino ca “buddhapaṭikaṇṭako devadatto pathaviyā gilito, nihatapaccāmitto dāni [M 2.0220] sammāsambuddho jāto”ti tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā [P 2.0240] ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā paramparaghosena sakalajambudīpavāsino yakkhabhūtadevagaṇā ca tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā eva ahesuṃ. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, devadatte pathaviyaṃ nimugge ‘buddhapaṭikaṇṭako devadatto pathaviyā gilito’ti mahājano attamano jāto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatte mate mahājano tussati ceva hasati ca, pubbepi tussi ceva hasi cā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“All the people,” this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Devadatta. When Devadatta, having conceived a grudge against the Teacher, sank into the earth at the gatehouse of Jetavana at the end of nine months, the residents of Jetavana and the inhabitants of the entire country were pleased and delighted, saying: “Devadatta, the adversary of the Buddha, has been swallowed by the earth! Now the Perfectly Enlightened One has his enemy defeated!” Hearing their talk, which spread by successive reports, all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa and the hosts of yakkhas, spirits, and devas were also pleased and delighted. Then one day, the bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion in the hall of Dhamma: “Friends, when Devadatta sank into the earth, the great populace was pleased, saying, ‘Devadatta, the adversary of the Buddha, has been swallowed by the earth!’” The Teacher came and asked, “For what discussion are you now gathered here, bhikkhus?” When they told him, “For this one,” he said: “Not only now, bhikkhus, does the great populace rejoice and laugh when Devadatta dies; in the past, too, they rejoiced and laughed,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ mahāpiṅgalo nāma rājā adhammena visamena rajjaṃ kāresi, chandādivasena pāpakammāni karonto daṇḍabalijaṅghakahāpaṇādiggahaṇena ucchuyante ucchuṃ viya mahājanaṃ pīḷesi kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko, paresu anuddayāmattampi nāmassa natthi, gehe itthīnampi puttadhītānampi amaccabrāhmaṇagahapatikādīnampi appiyo amanāpo, akkhimhi patitarajaṃ viya, bhattapiṇḍe sakkharā viya, paṇhiṃ vijjhitvā paviṭṭhakaṇṭako viya ca ahosi[V 2.0202]. Tadā bodhisatto mahāpiṅgalassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Mahāpiṅgalo dīgharattaṃ rajjaṃ kāretvā kālamakāsi. Tasmiṃ kālakate sakalabārāṇasivāsino haṭṭhatuṭṭhā mahāhasitaṃ hasitvā dārūnaṃ sakaṭasahassena mahāpiṅgalaṃ jhāpetvā anekehi ghaṭasahassehi āḷāhanaṃ nibbāpetvā bodhisattaṃ rajje abhisiñcitvā “dhammiko no rājā laddho”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā nagare ussavabheriṃ carāpetvā samussitadhajapaṭākaṃ nagaraṃ alaṅkaritvā dvāre dvāre maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā vippakiṇṇalājakusumamaṇḍitatalesu alaṅkatamaṇḍapesu nisīditvā khādiṃsu ceva piviṃsu ca.

In the past in Bārāṇasī, a king named Mahāpiṅgala ruled the kingdom unrighteously and unfairly. Acting through favoritism and the like, he committed evil deeds, oppressing the great populace like sugarcane in a sugar-mill by exacting fines, taxes, forced labor, and money. He was rough, harsh, and violent; there was not even a trace of compassion in him for others. He was unloved and disagreeable to the women in his house, to his sons and daughters, and to his ministers, brahmins, and householders. He was like dust fallen in the eye, like a pebble in a lump of rice, and like a thorn that has pierced the heel. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born as Mahāpiṅgala’s son. After ruling for a long time, Mahāpiṅgala died. When he died, all the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, pleased and delighted, laughed a great laugh. They cremated Mahāpiṅgala with a thousand cartloads of wood and extinguished the funeral pyre with many thousands of pots of water. Then they consecrated the Bodhisatta as king and, pleased and delighted, said: “We have obtained a righteous king!” They had festival drums beaten through the city, adorned the city with hoisted banners and flags, and built pavilions at every gate. Sitting in the decorated pavilions on floors strewn with parched grain and flowers, they ate and drank.

Bodhisattopi alaṅkate mahātale samussitasetacchattassa pallaṅkavarassa [P 2.0241] majjhe mahāyasaṃ anubhavanto nisīdi. Amaccā ca brāhmaṇagahapatiraṭṭhikadovārikādayo ca rājānaṃ parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Atheko dovāriko nātidūre ṭhatvā assasanto passasanto parodi. Bodhisatto taṃ disvā “samma dovārika, mama pitari kālakate sabbe tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhā ussavaṃ kīḷantā vicaranti, tvaṃ pana rodamāno ṭhito[M 2.0221], kiṃ nu kho mama pitā taveva piyo ahosi manāpo”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta also sat, enjoying great glory, in the middle of a noble throne under a raised white parasol on a decorated dais. Ministers, brahmins, householders, district officers, gatekeepers, and others stood surrounding the king. Then a certain gatekeeper, standing not far away, wept, sighing heavily. Seeing him, the Bodhisatta, wondering: “Good gatekeeper, when my father died, everyone was pleased and delighted, celebrating and going about; but you stand here weeping. Was my father dear and pleasing only to you?” asked him by reciting the first verse:

179.

179.

“Sabbo jano hiṃsito piṅgalena, tasmiṃ mate paccayā vedayanti;

Piyo nu te āsi akaṇhanetto, kasmā nu tvaṃ rodasi dvārapālā”ti.

“All the people were oppressed by Piṅgala; now that he is dead, they experience joy. Was he dear to you, the one with the tawny eyes? Why then do you weep, O gatekeeper?”

Tattha hiṃsitoti nānappakārehi daṇḍabaliādīhi pīḷito. Piṅgalenāti piṅgalakkhena. Tassa kira dvepi akkhīni nibbiddhapiṅgalāni biḷārakkhivaṇṇāni ahesuṃ, tenevassa “piṅgalo”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Paccayā vedayantīti pītiyo pavedayanti. Akaṇhanettoti piṅgalanetto. Kasmā nu tvanti kena nu kāraṇena tvaṃ rodasi. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “kasmā tuva”nti pāṭho.

Herein, harmed means oppressed in various ways, with punishments, taxes, and so on. By Piṅgala means by the one with tawny eyes. For it is said that both his eyes were of a piercing tawny color, like a cat’s eyes, and for that reason they gave him the name “Piṅgala.” They feel delight means they express their joy. One with not-black eyes means one with tawny eyes. Why then do you means for what reason do you weep. In the commentary, however, the reading is kasmā tuvaṃ.

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “nāhaṃ, mahārāja, ‘mahāpiṅgalo mato’ti sokena rodāmi, sīsassa me sukhaṃ jātaṃ. Piṅgalarājā hi pāsādā otaranto ca ārohanto ca kammāramuṭṭhikāya paharanto viya mayhaṃ sīse aṭṭhaṭṭha khaṭake deti, so paralokaṃ gantvāpi mama sīse dadamāno viya nirayapālānampi yamassapi sīle khaṭake dassati, atha naṃ te ‘ativiya ayaṃ amhe bādhatī’ti puna idheva ānetvā vissajjeyyuṃ, atha me so punapi sīse khaṭake dadeyyāti bhayenāhaṃ rodāmī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, the gatekeeper said: “Great king, I do not weep out of sorrow because ‘Great Piṅgala is dead’; a sense of relief has come to my head. For King Piṅgala, whenever he descended from or ascended the palace, would give me eight knocks on my head, as if striking with a blacksmith’s hammer. Even though he has gone to the next world, he will give knocks on the heads of the hell-guardians and even Yama, just as he did to mine. Then they, thinking, ‘This one harasses us too much,’ might bring him back here and release him. Then he would give me knocks on my head once more. I weep out of fear of this.” Explaining this, he spoke the second verse:

180.

180.

“Na [V 2.0203][P 2.0242] me piyo āsi akaṇhanetto, bhāyāmi paccāgamanāya tassa;

Ito gato hiṃseyya maccurājaṃ, so hiṃsito āneyya puna idhā”ti.

“The one with tawny eyes was not dear to me; I fear his return. Having gone from here, he might harass the King of Death; and he, being harassed, might bring him back here again.”

Atha naṃ bodhisatto “so rājā dārūnaṃ vāhasahassena daḍḍho udakaghaṭasatehi sitto, sāpissa āḷāhanabhūmi samantato khatā, pakatiyāpi ca paralokaṃ gatā nāma aññattha gativasā puna teneva sarīrena nāgacchanti, mā tvaṃ bhāyī”ti taṃ samassāsento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, reassuring him, said: “That king was burned with a thousand cartloads of wood and sprinkled with hundreds of pots of water. Moreover, the ground of his cremation site has been dug up all around. In the course of nature, those who have gone to the next world, being established in another existence, do not return in that same body. Do not be afraid.” Reassuring him thus, he spoke this verse:

181.

181.

“Daḍḍho [M 2.0222] vāhasahassehi, sitto ghaṭasatehi so;

Parikkhatā ca sā bhūmi, mā bhāyi nāgamissatī”ti.

“He was burned with a thousand cartloads, sprinkled with hundreds of pots; and the ground has been dug up all around. Fear not, he will not return.”

Tato paṭṭhāya dovāriko assāsaṃ paṭilabhi. Bodhisatto dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

From that time on, the gatekeeper found relief. The Bodhisatta ruled the kingdom righteously, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and passed away according to his deeds.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mahāpiṅgalo devadatto ahosi, putto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, Mahāpiṅgala was Devadatta, but the son was I myself.”

Mahāpiṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka is finished.

Upāhanavaggo navamo.

The Upāhana Chapter, the ninth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Upāhanaṃ vīṇāthūṇaṃ, vikaṇṇakaṃ asitābhu;

Vacchanakhaṃ bakañceva, sāketañca ekapadaṃ;

Haritamātu piṅgalaṃ.

Upāhana, Vīṇāthūṇa, Vikaṇṇaka, Asitābhu; Vacchanakha and Baka, Sāketa and Ekapada; Haritamātu, Piṅgala.

10. Siṅgālavaggo

10. 10. The Jackal Chapter

[241] 1. Sabbadāṭhajātakavaṇṇanā

[241] 1. 1. The Sabbadāṭha Jātaka

Siṅgālo [V 2.0204] mānatthaddhoti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadatto ajātasattuṃ pasādetvā uppāditaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ ciraṭṭhitikaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi, nāḷāgiripayojane pāṭihāriyassa diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya tassa so lābhasakkāro [P 2.0243] antaradhāyi. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, devadatto lābhasakkāraṃ uppādetvā ciraṭṭhitikaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva attano uppannaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ antaradhāpeti, pubbepi antaradhāpesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“A jackal stiff with conceit….” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta. Devadatta, having won the confidence of Ajātasattu, was unable to make the gain and honor that arose for him long-lasting. From the time the miracle was seen in the incident of the elephant Nāḷāgiri, that gain and honor of his disappeared. Then one day, the bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: “Friends, Devadatta generated gain and honor but was unable to make it long-lasting.” The Teacher came and asked, “For what discussion are you now sitting together, bhikkhus?” When they told him what it was, he said: “Not only now, bhikkhus, does Devadatta cause the gain and honor that has arisen for him to disappear; he caused it to disappear in the past as well,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 2.0223] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa purohito ahosi tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ aṭṭhārasannañca sippānaṃ pāraṃ gato. So pathavījayamantaṃ nāma jānāti. Pathavījayamantoti āvaṭṭanamanto vuccati. Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto “taṃ mantaṃ sajjhāyissāmī”ti ekasmiṃ aṅgaṇaṭṭhāne piṭṭhipāsāṇe nisīditvā sajjhāyamakāsi. Taṃ kira mantaṃ aññavihitaṃ dhitivirahitaṃ sāvetuṃ na sakkā, tasmā naṃ so tathārūpe ṭhāne sajjhāyati. Athassa sajjhāyanakāle eko siṅgālo ekasmiṃ bile nipanno taṃ mantaṃ sutvāva paguṇamakāsi. So kira anantarātīte attabhāve paguṇapathavījayamanto eko brāhmaṇo ahosi. Bodhisatto sajjhāyaṃ katvā uṭṭhāya “paguṇo vata me ayaṃ manto”ti āha. Siṅgālo bilā nikkhamitvā “ambho brāhmaṇa, ayaṃ manto tayāpi mameva paguṇataro”ti vatvā palāyi. Bodhisatto “ayaṃ siṅgālo mahantaṃ akusalaṃ karissatī”ti “gaṇhatha gaṇhathā”ti thokaṃ anubandhi. Siṅgālo palāyitvā araññaṃ pāvisi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his chaplain, one who had mastered the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge. He knew a spell called the Earth-Conquering Spell. The Earth-Conquering Spell is called a spell of subjugation. One day the Bodhisatta thought, “I will recite that spell,” and sitting on a stone slab in a courtyard, he recited it. It is said that this spell should not be made heard by one who is distracted or lacking in steadiness; therefore, he recited it in such a place. Now at the time of his recitation, a jackal lying in a certain hole heard the spell and mastered it. It seems that in his immediately preceding existence, this jackal had been a brahmin who was proficient in the Earth-Conquering Spell. When the Bodhisatta had finished his recitation, he got up and said, “Indeed, this spell has become proficient for me.” The jackal came out of his hole, said, “Hey, brahmin, this spell is even more proficient for me than for you,” and ran away. The Bodhisatta thought, “This jackal will do much evil,” and pursued him for a short distance, shouting, “Catch him! Catch him!” But the jackal escaped and entered the forest.

So gantvā ekaṃ siṅgāliṃ thokaṃ sarīre ḍaṃsi, “kiṃ, sāmī”ti ca vutte “mayhaṃ jānāsi na jānāsī”ti āha. Sā “āma, jānāmī”ti sampaṭicchi. So pathavījayamantaṃ parivattetvā [V 2.0205] anekāni siṅgālasatāni āṇāpetvā sabbepi hatthiassasīhabyagghasūkaramigādayo catuppade attano santike [P 2.0244] akāsi. Katvā ca pana sabbadāṭho nāma rājā hutvā ekaṃ siṅgāliṃ aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Dvinnaṃ hatthīnaṃ piṭṭhe sīho tiṭṭhati, sīhapiṭṭhe sabbadāṭho siṅgālo rājā siṅgāliyā aggamahesiyā saddhiṃ nisīdati, mahanto yaso ahosi. So yasamahantena pamajjitvā mānaṃ uppādetvā “bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti sabbacatuppadaparivuto bārāṇasiyā avidūraṭṭhānaṃ sampāpuṇi, parisā dvādasayojanā ahosi. So avidūre ṭhitoyeva “rajjaṃ vā detu, yuddhaṃ vā”ti rañño sāsanaṃ pesesi. Bārāṇasivāsino bhītatasitā nagaradvārāni pidahitvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

He went and bit a she-jackal lightly on her body. When she asked, “What is it, master?” he said, “Do you know me or not?” She replied, “Yes, I know you,” and submitted. He then recited the Earth-Conquering Spell and commanded many hundreds of jackals, and brought all the quadrupeds—elephants, horses, lions, tigers, boars, deer, and so on—under his control. Having done so, he became a king named Sabbadāṭha and made a certain she-jackal his chief queen. A lion stood on the backs of two elephants, and on the lion’s back sat Sabbadāṭha the jackal king together with his chief queen, the she-jackal. His glory was great. Heedless because of his great glory, he became conceited and thought, “I will seize the kingdom of Bārāṇasī.” Surrounded by all the quadrupeds, he reached a place not far from Bārāṇasī; his retinue extended for twelve yojanas. Stationing himself not far away, he sent a message to the king: “Either give up the kingdom or give battle.” The inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, frightened and terrified, closed the city gates and remained inside.

Bodhisatto rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, sabbadāṭhasiṅgālena saddhiṃ yuddhaṃ mama bhāro, ṭhapetvā maṃ añño tena saddhiṃ yujjhituṃ [M 2.0224] samattho nāma natthī”ti rājānañca nāgare ca samassāsetvā “kinti katvā nu kho sabbadāṭho rajjaṃ gahessati, pucchissāmi tāva na”nti dvāraṭṭālakaṃ abhiruhitvā “samma sabbadāṭha, kinti katvā imaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhissasī”ti pucchi. “Sīhanādaṃ nadāpetvā mahājanaṃ saddena santāsetvā gaṇhissāmī”ti. Bodhisatto “attheta”nti ñatvā aṭṭālakā oruyha “sakaladvādasayojanikabārāṇasinagaravāsino kaṇṇacchiddāni māsapiṭṭhena lañjantū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Mahājano bheriyā āṇaṃ sutvā antamaso biḷāle upādāya sabbacatuppadānañceva attano ca kaṇṇacchiddāni yathā parassa saddaṃ sotuṃ na sakkā, evaṃ māsapiṭṭhena lañji.

The Bodhisatta approached the king and said: “Do not fear, great king. The battle with the jackal Sabbadāṭha is my responsibility; apart from me, there is no one else capable of fighting with him.” Having thus reassured the king and the citizens, he thought, “Now, how will Sabbadāṭha take the kingdom? I will first ask him.” He climbed a gate tower and asked, “Friend Sabbadāṭha, how will you take this kingdom?” “By making the lions roar and terrifying the populace with the sound, I will take it.” The Bodhisatta, knowing that that was the case, descended from the tower and had a drum beaten with the proclamation: “Let all the inhabitants of the twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī stop up their ear-holes with bean-flour paste!” Hearing the command of the drum, the great populace stopped up their own ear-holes and those of all quadrupeds, even down to the cats, with bean-flour paste, so that they could not hear another’s sound.

Atha bodhisatto puna aṭṭālakaṃ abhiruhitvā “sabbadāṭhā”ti āha. “Kiṃ, brāhmaṇā”ti? “Imaṃ rajjaṃ kinti katvā gaṇhissasī”ti? “Sīhanādaṃ nadāpetvā manusse tāsetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā gaṇhissāmī”ti. “Sīhanādaṃ nadāpetuṃ na sakkhissasi. Jātisampannā hi surattahatthapādā kesarasīharājāno tādisassa jarasiṅgālassa āṇaṃ na karissantī”ti. Siṅgālo mānatthaddho hutvā [P 2.0245] “aññe tāva sīhā tiṭṭhantu, yassāhaṃ piṭṭhe nisinno, taññeva nadāpessāmī”ti āha. “Tena hi nadāpehi, yadi sakkosī”ti. So yasmiṃ sīhe nisinno, tassa “nadāhī”ti pādena saññaṃ adāsi. Sīho hatthikumbhe mukhaṃ uppīḷetvā tikkhattuṃ appaṭivattiyaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadi. Hatthī santāsappattā hutvā siṅgālaṃ pādamūle pātetvā pādenassa sīsaṃ akkamitvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ akaṃsu, sabbadāṭho tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patto. Tepi hatthī sīhanādaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayatajjitā aññamaññaṃ ovijjhitvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, ṭhapetvā sīhe sesāpi migasūkarādayo sasabiḷārapariyosānā sabbe [V 2.0206] catuppādā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Sīhā palāyitvā araññaṃ pavisiṃsu, dvādasayojaniko maṃsarāsi ahosi. Bodhisatto aṭṭālakā otaritvā nagaradvārāni vivarāpetvā “sabbe attano kaṇṇesu māsapiṭṭhaṃ apanetvā maṃsatthikā maṃsaṃ āharantū”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpesi. Manussā allamaṃsaṃ khāditvā sesaṃ sukkhāpetvā vallūramakaṃsu. Tasmiṃ kira kāle vallūrakaraṇaṃ udapādīti vadanti.

Then the Bodhisatta climbed the watchtower again and said, “Sabbadāṭha.” “What is it, brahmin?” “How will you take this kingdom?” “I will make the lions roar, terrify the people, cause them to perish, and take it.” “You will not be able to make the lions roar. For lion kings of noble birth, with reddish paws and feet, will not obey the command of such an old jackal.” Stiff with pride, the jackal said: “Let the other lions be. I will make the very one on whose back I am sitting roar.” “Then make him roar, if you can.” He then gave a signal with his foot to the lion on which he was sitting to roar. The lion pressed its mouth against an elephant’s temple and roared the unrivaled lion’s roar three times. The elephants, struck with terror, threw the jackal down at their feet, trampled on his head with their feet, and crushed him to powder. Sabbadāṭha met his end right there. Those elephants too, hearing the lion’s roar and menaced by the fear of death, collided with one another and perished on the spot. Except for the lions, all the other four-footed creatures—deer, boars, and so on, down to the hares and cats—also met their end right there. The lions fled into the forest. There was a heap of meat twelve leagues in extent. The Bodhisatta descended from the watchtower, had the city gates opened, and had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: “Let all who want meat remove the bean flour from their ears and fetch meat.” The people ate the fresh meat and dried the rest, making it into cured meat. They say that the practice of making cured meat originated at that time.

Satthā [M 2.0225] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā imā abhisambuddhagāthā vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi –

The Teacher, having related this Dhamma discourse and spoken these verses of the Enlightened One, made the connection to the birth story:
