182.

182.

“Siṅgālo mānatthaddho ca, parivārena atthiko;

Pāpuṇi mahatiṃ bhūmiṃ, rājāsi sabbadāṭhinaṃ.

“The jackal, stiff with pride and wanting a retinue, attained a great position, becoming the king of all beasts of prey.”

183.

183.

“Evameva manussesu, yo hoti parivāravā;

So hi tattha mahā hoti, siṅgālo viya dāṭhina”nti.

“So too among human beings, one who has a retinue becomes great in their midst, like the jackal among the beasts of prey.”

Tattha mānatthaddhoti parivāraṃ nissāya uppannena mānena thaddho. Parivārena atthikoti uttarimpi parivārena atthiko hutvā. Mahatiṃ bhūminti mahantaṃ sampattiṃ. Rājāsi sabbadāṭhinanti sabbesaṃ dāṭhīnaṃ [P 2.0246] rājā āsi. So hi tattha mahā hotīti so parivārasampanno puriso tesu parivāresu mahā nāma hoti. Siṅgālo viya dāṭhinanti yathā siṅgālo dāṭhīnaṃ mahā ahosi, evaṃ mahā hoti, atha so siṅgālo viya pamādaṃ āpajjitvā taṃ parivāraṃ nissāya vināsaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

Herein, ‘stiff with pride’ means stiff with the pride that arose by relying on his retinue. ‘Wanting a retinue’ means being desirous of an even larger retinue. ‘A great position’ means great prosperity. ‘King of all with fangs’ means he was king of all the fanged creatures. ‘Becomes great in its midst’ means that a person endowed with a retinue is called great among that retinue. ‘Like the jackal among the fanged’ means that just as the jackal was great among the fanged creatures, so he becomes great; but then, like that jackal, he becomes heedless and, by relying on that retinue, he meets with destruction.

“Tadā siṅgālo devadatto ahosi, rājā sāriputto, purohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

“At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, the king was Sāriputta, but the royal chaplain was I myself.”

Sabbadāṭhajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first is the Commentary on the Sabbadāṭha Jātaka.

[242] 2. Sunakhajātakavaṇṇanā

[242] 2. The Commentary on the Sunakha Jātaka

Bālo vatāyaṃ sunakhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ambaṇakoṭṭhake āsanasālāya bhattabhuñjanasunakhaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ kira jātakālato paṭṭhāya pānīyahārakā gahetvā tattha posesuṃ. So aparabhāge tattha bhattaṃ bhuñjanto thūlasarīro ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ eko gāmavāsī [V 2.0207] puriso taṃ ṭhānaṃ patto sunakhaṃ disvā pānīyahārakānaṃ uttarisāṭakañca kahāpaṇañca datvā gaddūlena bandhitvā taṃ ādāya pakkāmi. So gahetvā nīyamāno na vassi, dinnaṃ dinnaṃ khādanto pacchato pacchato agamāsi. Atha so puriso “ayaṃ idāni maṃ piyāyatī”ti gaddūlaṃ mocesi, so vissaṭṭhamatto ekavegena [M 2.0226] āsanasālameva gato. Bhikkhū taṃ disvā tena gatakāraṇaṃ jānitvā sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, āsanasālāya sunakho bandhanamokkhakusalo vissaṭṭhamattova puna āgato”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, so sunakho idāneva bandhanamokkhakusalo, pubbepi kusaloyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This dog is truly a fool…” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a dog that ate its food in a trough in the assembly hall. It seems that from the time of its birth, the water-carriers had raised it there. In time, eating its food there, it grew fat. Then one day a certain villager who came to that place saw the dog. He gave the water-carriers an upper robe and a kahāpaṇa, tied the dog with a leash, and went off with it. While being led away, it did not bark; eating whatever was given to it, it followed along behind. Then the man thought, “Now it has grown fond of me,” and he untied the leash. As soon as it was released, it ran back in a single dash to the assembly hall. When the bhikkhus saw it and learned why it had gone, in the evening they raised a topic of discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: “Friends, the dog in the assembly hall is skilled in getting free from its bonds. As soon as it was released, it came back again.” The Teacher came and asked, “For what topic of discussion are you now gathered here, bhikkhus?” When they told him, he said: “Not only now, bhikkhus, is this dog skilled in getting free from its bonds; it was skilled in the past as well.” And he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ mahābhogakule nibbattitvā vayappatto gharāvāsaṃ aggahesi. Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ ekassa manussassa sunakho ahosi, so piṇḍibhattaṃ labhanto thūlasarīro [P 2.0247] jāto. Atheko gāmavāsī bārāṇasiṃ āgato taṃ sunakhaṃ disvā tassa manussassa uttarisāṭakañca kahāpaṇañca datvā sunakhaṃ gahetvā cammayottena bandhitvā yottakoṭiyaṃ gahetvā gacchanto aṭavimukhe ekaṃ sālaṃ pavisitvā sunakhaṃ bandhitvā phalake nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkami. Tasmiṃ kāle bodhisatto kenacideva karaṇīyena aṭaviṃ paṭipanno taṃ sunakhaṃ yottena bandhitvā ṭhapitaṃ disvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth in the Kāsī country. When he came of age, he settled down to a household life. At that time, a certain man in Bārāṇasī had a dog, which grew fat on the balls of rice it received. Then a villager who had come to Bārāṇasī saw the dog. He gave the man an upper robe and a kahāpaṇa, took the dog, tied it with a leather leash, and, holding the end of the leash, he departed. At the entrance to a forest, he entered a rest house, tied up the dog, lay down on a plank, and fell asleep. At that time the Bodhisatta, who had entered the forest on some business, saw the dog tied up with the leash and spoke the first verse:

184.

184.

“Bālo vatāyaṃ sunakho, yo varattaṃ na khādati;

Bandhanā ca pamuñceyya, asito ca gharaṃ vaje”ti.

“This dog is truly a fool, not to chew through the leather strap. He could be free from his bonds and go home satisfied.”

Tattha pamuñceyyāti pamoceyya, ayameva vā pāṭho. Asito ca gharaṃ vajeti asito suhito hutvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gaccheyya.

Herein, ‘he could be free from his bonds’ means he could free himself; or this is the reading itself. ‘And go home satisfied’ means that, having become well-fed, he could go to his own dwelling place.

Taṃ sutvā sunakho dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the dog spoke the second verse:

185.

185.

“Aṭṭhitaṃ me manasmiṃ me, atho me hadaye kataṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, yāva passupatū jano”ti.

“It is resolved within my mind, and also set within my heart. I await the time until the people fall asleep.”

Tattha aṭṭhitaṃ me manasmiṃ meti yaṃ tumhe kathetha, taṃ mayā adhiṭṭhitameva, manasmiṃyeva me etaṃ. Atho me hadaye katanti atha ca pana me tumhākaṃ vacanaṃ hadaye katameva. Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmīti [V 2.0208] kālaṃ paṭimānemi. Yāva passupatū janoti yāvāyaṃ mahājano pasupatu niddaṃ okkamatu, tāvāhaṃ kālaṃ paṭimānemi[M 2.0227]. Itarathā hi “ayaṃ sunakho palāyatī”ti ravo uppajjeyya, tasmā rattibhāge sabbesaṃ suttakāle cammayottaṃ khāditvā palāyissāmīti. So evaṃ vatvā mahājane niddaṃ okkante yottaṃ khāditvā suhito hutvā palāyitvā attano sāmikānaṃ gharameva gato.

Herein, ‘It is resolved within my mind’ means: what you say has already been resolved by me; it is already in my mind. ‘And also set within my heart’ means: and furthermore, your words are indeed set within my heart. ‘I await the time’ means: I am awaiting the right moment. ‘Until the people fall asleep’ means: I am waiting for the time until all these people fall asleep and sink into slumber. For otherwise, a cry would be raised, ‘This dog is running away!’ Therefore, at night when everyone is asleep, I will gnaw through the leather strap and escape.” Having said this, when the people had fallen asleep, the dog gnawed through the strap and, being well-fed, ran away and went straight to his own masters’ house.

Satthā [P 2.0248] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sunakhova etarahi sunakho, paṇḍitapuriso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time the dog was the present dog, and the wise man was I myself.”

Sunakhajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Sunakha Jātaka, the second.

[243] 3. Guttilajātakavaṇṇanā

[243] 3. The Commentary on the Guttila Jātaka

Sattatantiṃ sumadhuranti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi kāle bhikkhū devadattaṃ āhaṃsu – “āvuso devadatta, sammāsambuddho tuyhaṃ ācariyo, tvaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ nissāya tīṇi piṭakāni uggaṇhi, cattāri jhānāni uppādesi, ācariyassa nāma paṭisattunā bhavituṃ na yutta”nti. Devadatto “kiṃ pana me, āvuso, samaṇo gotamo ācariyo, nanu mayā attano baleneva tīṇi piṭakāni uggahitāni, cattāri jhānāni uppāditānī”ti ācariyaṃ paccakkhāsi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto ācariyaṃ paccakkhāya sammāsambuddhassa paṭisattu hutvā mahāvināsaṃ patto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva ācariyaṃ paccakkhāya mama paṭisattu hutvā vināsaṃ pāpuṇāti, pubbepi pattoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The seven-stringed, so very sweet…” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove concerning Devadatta. At that time the bhikkhus said to Devadatta: “Friend Devadatta, the Perfectly Enlightened One is your teacher. It was by relying on the Perfectly Enlightened One that you learned the three Piṭakas and produced the four jhānas. It is not proper to become a rival to one’s teacher.” Devadatta replied: “But friends, how is the ascetic Gotama my teacher? Was it not by my own power that I learned the three Piṭakas and produced the four jhānas?” Thus he repudiated his teacher. The bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: “Friends, having repudiated his teacher and become a rival to the Perfectly Enlightened One, Devadatta has come to great ruin.” The Teacher came and asked, “For what topic of discussion are you now gathered here, bhikkhus?” When they told him, he said: “Not only now, bhikkhus, does Devadatta come to ruin after repudiating his teacher and becoming my rival; he came to ruin in the past as well.” And he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gandhabbakule nibbatti, “guttilakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto gandhabbasippe nipphattiṃ patvā guttilagandhabbo nāma sakalajambudīpe aggagandhabbo ahosi. So dārābharaṇaṃ akatvā andhe mātāpitaro posesi. Tadā bārāṇasivāsino vāṇijā vaṇijjāya ujjeninagaraṃ gantvā [M 2.0228] ussave ghuṭṭhe chandakaṃ saṃharitvā bahuṃ mālāgandhavilepanañca khajjabhojjādīni ca ādāya kīḷanaṭṭhāne sannipatitvā “vetanaṃ datvā ekaṃ gandhabbaṃ ānethā”ti āhaṃsu. Tena ca samayena [V 2.0209] ujjeniyaṃ mūsilo nāma jeṭṭhagandhabbo [P 2.0249] hoti, te taṃ pakkosāpetvā attano gandhabbaṃ kāresuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a family of musicians, and they named him the boy Guttila. When he came of age, he attained proficiency in the art of music and became known as Guttila the Musician, the foremost musician in all of Jambudīpa. Without taking a wife, he supported his blind mother and father. At that time, merchants from Bārāṇasī went to the city of Ujjenī on business. When a festival was proclaimed there, they collected contributions and, taking many garlands, perfumes, and ointments, as well as various kinds of food, hard and soft, they assembled at a pleasure ground and said: “Pay the fee and bring a musician.” Now at that time in Ujjenī there was a chief musician named Mūsila. They had him summoned and made him give his musical performance.

Mūsilo vīṇaṃ vādanto vīṇaṃ uttamamucchanāya mucchitvā vādesi. Tesaṃ guttilagandhabbassa gandhabbe jātaparicayānaṃ tassa gandhabbaṃ kilañjakaṇḍūvanaṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhāsi, ekopi pahaṭṭhākāraṃ na dassesi. Mūsilo tesu tuṭṭhākāraṃ adassentesu “atikharaṃ katvā vādemi maññe”ti majjhimamucchanāya mucchitvā majjhimasarena vādesi, te tatthapi majjhattāva ahesuṃ. Atha so “ime na kiñci jānanti maññe”ti sayampi ajānanako viya hutvā tantiyo sithile vādesi, te tatthapi na kiñci āhaṃsu. Atha ne mūsilo “ambho vāṇijā, kiṃ nu kho mayi vīṇaṃ vādente tumhe na tussathā”ti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ vīṇaṃ vādesi, mayañhi ‘ayaṃ vīṇaṃ mucchetī’ti saññaṃ akarimhā”ti. “Kiṃ pana tumhe mayā uttaritaraṃ ācariyaṃ jānātha, udāhu attano ajānanabhāvena na tussathā”ti. Vāṇijā “bārāṇasiyaṃ guttilagandhabbassa vīṇāsaddaṃ sutapubbānaṃ tava vīṇāsaddo itthīnaṃ dārake tosāpanasaddo viya hotī”ti āhaṃsu. “Tena hi, handa, tumhehi dinnaparibbayaṃ paṭiggaṇhatha, na mayhaṃ etenattho, apica kho pana bārāṇasiṃ gacchantā maṃ gaṇhitvā gaccheyyāthā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā gamanakāle taṃ ādāya bārāṇasiṃ gantvā tassa “etaṃ guttilassa vasanaṭṭhāna”nti ācikkhitvā sakasakanivesanaṃ agamiṃsu.

Mūsila tuned his lute to the highest pitch and played. To those merchants, who were familiar with the music of Guttila the Musician, his performance sounded like the scratching of a mat, and not one of them showed any sign of delight. When Mūsila saw they showed no sign of pleasure, he thought, “I must be playing too harshly,” so he tuned his lute to the middle pitch and played in a medium tone. But they remained indifferent to that as well. Then he thought, “These people must know nothing,” and, as if he himself were ignorant, he played with loose strings. Still they said nothing. Then Mūsila asked them: “Sirs, you merchants, why are you not pleased when I play the lute?” “Were you really playing the lute? We thought you were just tuning it.” “Do you know a teacher superior to me, or is it because of your own ignorance that you are not pleased?” The merchants replied: “For us who have previously heard the sound of the lute of Guttila the Musician in Bārāṇasī, the sound of your lute is like the noise made by women to soothe children.” “In that case, please take back the payment you gave me; I have no use for it. However, when you go to Bārāṇasī, please take me with you.” They agreed, saying, “Very well,” and when it was time to leave, they took him with them to Bārāṇasī. After pointing out to him, “This is Guttila’s residence,” they went to their own respective homes.

Mūsilo bodhisattassa gehaṃ pavisitvā laggetvā ṭhapitaṃ bodhisattassa jātivīṇaṃ disvā gahetvā vādesi, atha bodhisattassa mātāpitaro andhabhāvena taṃ apassantā [P 2.0250] “mūsikā maññe vīṇaṃ khādantī”ti saññāya “susū”ti āhaṃsu. Tasmiṃ kāle mūsilo vīṇaṃ ṭhapetvā bodhisattassa mātāpitaro vanditvā “kuto āgatosī”ti vutte “ācariyassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhituṃ ujjenito āgatomhī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti vutte “kahaṃ ācariyo”ti pucchitvā “vippavuttho, tāta, ajja āgamissatī”ti sutvā tattheva nisīditvā bodhisattaṃ āgataṃ disvā [M 2.0229] tena katapaṭisanthāro attano āgatakāraṇaṃ ārocesi. Bodhisatto aṅgavijjāpāṭhako, so tassa asappurisabhāvaṃ ñatvā “gaccha tāta, natthi tava sippa”nti paṭikkhipi. So bodhisattassa mātāpitūnaṃ pāde gahetvā upakāraṃ karonto te ārādhetvā “sippaṃ me dāpethā”ti yāci. Bodhisatto mātāpitūhi punappunaṃ vuccamāno te atikkamituṃ asakkonto sippaṃ adāsi. So bodhisatteneva saddhiṃ rājanivesanaṃ gacchati. Rājā taṃ disvā “ko esa, ācariyā”ti pucchi. “Mayhaṃ antevāsiko, mahārājā”ti. So anukkamena [V 2.0210] rañño vissāsiko ahosi. Bodhisatto ācariyamuṭṭhiṃ akatvā attano jānananiyāmena sabbaṃ sippaṃ sikkhāpetvā “niṭṭhitaṃ te, tāta, sippa”nti āha.

Mūsila entered the Bodhisatta’s house and, seeing the Bodhisatta’s heirloom lute hanging there, he took it and played it. Then the Bodhisatta’s parents, being blind and unable to see him, thought, "Mice, I suppose, are gnawing the lute," and cried out, "Shoo, shoo!" At that, Mūsila put down the lute and paid homage to the Bodhisatta’s parents. When they asked, "Where have you come from?" he replied, "I have come from Ujjenī to learn the art from the master." When they said, "Very well," he asked, "Where is the master?" Hearing, "He is away, my dear, but he will return today," he sat down right there. When the Bodhisatta arrived and saw him, they exchanged friendly greetings, and Mūsila told him the reason for his visit. The Bodhisatta was an expert in physiognomy and, recognizing Mūsila's ignoble character, he rejected him, saying, "Go, my dear, there is no art for you." Mūsila then grasped the feet of the Bodhisatta’s parents and, by rendering them service, won them over and pleaded, "Please have him give me the art." Being told again and again by his parents, the Bodhisatta was unable to go against them and gave him the art. Mūsila then went with the Bodhisatta to the royal palace. The king saw him and asked, "Who is this, master?" "He is my pupil, great king," he replied. In due course, Mūsila became a confidant of the king. The Bodhisatta, without a 'teacher's fist,' taught him the entire art according to his own method of knowledge and said, "Your art is perfected, my dear."

So cintesi – “mayhaṃ sippaṃ paguṇaṃ, idañca bārāṇasinagaraṃ sakalajambudīpe agganagaraṃ, ācariyopi mahallako, idheva mayā vasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So ācariyaṃ āha – “ācariya ahaṃ rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti. Ācariyo “sādhu, tāta, rañño ārocessāmī”ti gantvā “amhākaṃ antevāsiko devaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ icchati, deyyadhammamassa jānāthā”ti rañño ārocetvā raññā “tumhākaṃ deyyadhammato upaḍḍhaṃ labhissatī”ti vutte taṃ pavattiṃ mūsilassa ārocesi. Mūsilo “ahaṃ tumhehi samakaññeva labhanto upaṭṭhahissāmi, na alabhanto”ti āha[P 2.0251]. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Nanu ahaṃ tumhākaṃ jānanasippaṃ sabbaṃ jānāmī”ti? “Āma, jānāsī”ti. “Evaṃ sante kasmā mayhaṃ upaḍḍhaṃ detī”ti? Bodhisatto rañño ārocesi. Rājā “yadi evaṃ tumhehi samakaṃ sippaṃ dassetuṃ sakkonto samakaṃ labhissatī”ti āha. Bodhisatto rañño vacanaṃ tassa ārocetvā tena “sādhu dassessāmī”ti vutte rañño taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “sādhu dassetu, kataradivasaṃ sākacchā hotū”ti vutte “ito sattame divase hotu, mahārājā”ti āha.

He thought: 'My art is proficient, and this city of Bārāṇasī is the chief city in all of Jambudīpa. My teacher, too, is old. It is fitting for me to live right here.' He said to his teacher: 'Master, I will serve the king.' The teacher replied: 'Good, my dear, I will inform the king.' He went and told the king: 'Our pupil wishes to serve Your Majesty. Please determine his stipend.' When the king said, 'He shall receive half of your stipend,' the teacher reported this to Mūsila. Mūsila said: 'I will serve only if I receive the same reward as you, not if I receive less.' 'For what reason?' 'Do I not know all the art that you know?' 'Yes, you do.' 'That being so, why does he give me only half?' The Bodhisatta reported this to the king. The king said: 'If that is so, if he is able to display art equal to yours, he shall receive an equal reward.' The Bodhisatta reported the king's words to him. When Mūsila said, 'Good, I will display it,' the Bodhisatta reported this to the king. When the king said, 'Very well, let him display it. On which day should the contest take place?' he replied, 'Let it be on the seventh day from now, great king.'

Rājā mūsilaṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ ācariyena saddhiṃ sākacchaṃ karissasī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, devā”ti vutte “ācariyena saddhiṃ viggaho nāma na vaṭṭati, mā karī”ti vāriyamānopi “alaṃ, mahārāja, hotuyeva me ācariyena saddhiṃ sattame divase sākacchā, katarassa [M 2.0230] jānibhāvaṃ jānissāmā”ti āha. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “ito kira sattame divase ācariyaguttilo ca antevāsikamūsilo ca rājadvāre aññamaññaṃ sākacchaṃ katvā sippaṃ dassessanti, nāgarā sannipatitvā sippaṃ passantū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi.

The king had Mūsila summoned and asked, 'Is it true that you will have a contest with your master?' When he replied, 'It is true, Your Majesty,' the king tried to prevent him, saying, 'A conflict with one's master is not proper. Do not do it.' But even though he was being prevented, Mūsila said: 'Enough, great king! Let there be a contest between me and my master on the seventh day. We shall then know which of the two is more skilled.' The king agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: 'On the seventh day from now, the master Guttila and his pupil Mūsila will contest with one another at the palace gate and display their art. Let the townspeople assemble and watch the display.'

Bodhisatto cintesi – “ayaṃ mūsilo daharo taruṇo, ahaṃ mahallako parihīnathāmo, mahallakassa kiriyā nāma na sampajjati. Antevāsike nāma parājitepi viseso natthi, antevāsikassa pana jaye sati pattabbalajjato araññaṃ pavisitvā maraṇaṃ varatara”nti. So araññaṃ pavisitvā maraṇabhayena nivattati, lajjābhayena gacchati. Evamassa gamanāgamanaṃ karontasseva cha divasā atikkantā, tiṇāni matāni, jaṅghamaggo nibbatti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko āvajjamāno taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “guttilagandhabbo antevāsikassa [V 2.0211] bhayena araññe mahādukkhaṃ anubhoti[P 2.0252], etassa mayā avassayena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vegena gantvā bodhisattassa purato ṭhatvā “ācariya, kasmā araññaṃ paviṭṭhosī”ti pucchitvā “kosi tva”nti vutte “sakkohamasmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “ahaṃ kho, devarāja, antevāsikato parājayabhayena araññaṃ paviṭṭho”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta thought: 'This Mūsila is young and fresh, while I am old and my strength has waned. The performance of an old man is never perfect. Even if a pupil is defeated, there is nothing unusual; but if a pupil wins, it is better to enter the forest and die than to face the shame that must be borne.' So he entered the forest, but turned back from fear of death, then went forward again from fear of shame. As he was thus going back and forth, six days passed. The grass was worn away and a footpath was formed. At that moment, Sakka's throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting and discerning the reason, thought: 'Guttila the musician is experiencing great suffering in the forest out of fear of his pupil. I must be a support for him.' He went there swiftly, stood before the Bodhisatta, and asked: 'Master, why have you entered the forest?' When the Bodhisatta asked, 'Who are you?' he replied, 'I am Sakka.' Then the Bodhisatta, saying, 'O king of the gods, I have entered the forest from fear of being defeated by my pupil,' spoke the first verse:

186.

186.

“Sattatantiṃ sumadhuraṃ, rāmaṇeyyaṃ avācayiṃ;

So maṃ raṅgamhi avheti, saraṇaṃ me hoti kosiyā”ti.

"The seven-stringed lute, so sweet and delightful, I taught him how to play; he challenges me in the arena—be my refuge, O Kosiya!"

Tassattho – ahaṃ, devarāja, mūsilaṃ nāma antevāsikaṃ sattatantiṃ sumadhuraṃ rāmaṇeyyaṃ vīṇaṃ attano jānananiyāmena sikkhāpesiṃ, so maṃ idāni raṅgamaṇḍale pakkosati, tassa me tvaṃ, kosiyagotta, saraṇaṃ hohīti.

Its meaning is: O king of the gods, I taught my pupil named Mūsila the seven-stringed lute, so sweet and delightful, according to my own method of knowledge. Now he challenges me in the midst of the festival arena. For that reason, you, O Kosiya, be my refuge.

Sakko tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “mā bhāyi, ahaṃ te tāṇañca leṇañcā”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard his words, Sakka said, "Do not fear. I will be your protection and your shelter," and he spoke the second verse:

187.

187.

“Ahaṃ taṃ saraṇaṃ samma, ahamācariyapūjako;

Na taṃ jayissati sisso, sissamācariya jessasī”ti.

"I am your refuge, my friend, for I am one who honors teachers. The pupil will not defeat you; you, the master, will defeat the pupil."

Tattha [M 2.0231] ahaṃ taṃ saraṇanti ahaṃ saraṇaṃ avassayo patiṭṭhā hutvā taṃ tāyissāmi. Sammāti piyavacanametaṃ. Sissamācariya, jessasīti, ācariya, tvaṃ vīṇaṃ vādayamāno sissaṃ jinissasi. Apica tvaṃ vīṇaṃ vādento ekaṃ tantiṃ chinditvā cha vādeyyāsi, vīṇāya te pakatisaddo bhavissati. Mūsilopi tantiṃ chindissati, athassa vīṇāya saddo na bhavissati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe so parājayaṃ pāpuṇissati. Athassa parājayabhāvaṃ ñatvā dutiyampi tatiyampi catutthampi pañcamampi sattamampi tantiṃ chinditvā suddhadaṇḍakameva vādeyyāsi, chinnatantikoṭīhi saro nikkhamitvā sakalaṃ dvādasayojanikaṃ bārāṇasinagaraṃ [P 2.0253] chādetvā ṭhassatīti.

Therein, 'I am your refuge' means: having become a refuge, a resort, and a support for you, I will protect you. 'Samma' is a term of endearment. 'O master, you will defeat the pupil' means: O master, while playing the vīṇā you will defeat the pupil. Moreover, while you are playing the vīṇā, you should cut one string and play on the remaining six; your vīṇā will retain its natural sound. Mūsila too will cut a string, but then his vīṇā will make no sound. At that moment he will meet with defeat. Then, knowing he is defeated, you should cut a second, a third, a fourth, a fifth, and even the seventh string, and play on just the bare frame. A sound will issue from the ends of the cut strings, and it will cover the entire twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī and remain there.

Evaṃ vatvā sakko bodhisattassa tisso pāsakaghaṭikā datvā evamāha – “vīṇāsaddeneva pana sakalanagare chādite ito ekaṃ pāsakaghaṭikaṃ ākāse khipeyyāsi, atha te purato otaritvā tīṇi accharāsatāni naccissanti. Tāsaṃ naccanakāle ca dutiyaṃ khipeyyāsi, athāparānipi tīṇi satāni otaritvā tava vīṇādhure naccissanti. Tato tatiyaṃ khipeyyāsi, athāparāni tīṇi satāni otaritvā raṅgamaṇḍale naccissanti. Ahampi te santikaṃ [V 2.0212] āgamissāmi, gaccha mā bhāyī”ti bodhisattaṃ assāsesi. Bodhisatto pubbaṇhasamaye gehaṃ agamāsi. Nāgarā rājadvārasamīpe maṇḍapaṃ katvā rañño āsanaṃ paññapesuṃ. Rājā pāsādā otaritvā alaṅkatamaṇḍape pallaṅkamajjhe nisīdi, dvādasasahassā alaṅkatitthiyo amaccabrāhmaṇagahapatikādayo ca rājānaṃ parivārayiṃsu, sabbe nāgarā sannipatiṃsu, rājaṅgaṇe cakkāticakke mañcātimañce bandhiṃsu.

Having said this, Sakka gave the Bodhisatta three dice and said: 'When the entire city is covered with the sound of the vīṇā, you should throw one die into the air. Then three hundred celestial nymphs will descend before you and dance. While they are dancing, you should throw the second, and another three hundred will descend and dance at the head of your vīṇā. Then throw the third, and another three hundred will descend and dance in the arena. I too will come to you. Go, do not be afraid.' Thus Sakka encouraged the Bodhisatta. In the forenoon, the Bodhisatta went home. The townspeople built a pavilion near the king’s gate and prepared a seat for the king. The king descended from his palace and sat on a couch in the middle of the decorated pavilion. Twelve thousand adorned women, along with ministers, brahmins, householders, and others, surrounded the king. All the townspeople assembled. In the royal courtyard, they set up circular tiers and platforms row upon row.

Bodhisattopi nhātānulitto nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā vīṇaṃ gāhāpetvā attano paññattāsane nisīdi. Sakko adissamānakāyena āgantvā ākāse aṭṭhāsi, bodhisattoyeva naṃ passati. Mūsilopi āgantvā attano āsane nisīdi. Mahājano parivāresi, āditova dvepi samasamaṃ vādayiṃsu. Mahājano dvinnampi vāditena tuṭṭho ukkuṭṭhisahassāni pavattesi. Sakko ākāse ṭhatvā bodhisattaññeva sāvento “ekaṃ tantiṃ chindā”ti āha. Bodhisatto tantiṃ chindi, sā chinnāpi chinnakoṭiyā saraṃ muñcateva, devagandhabbaṃ viya vattati. Mūsilopi tantiṃ chindi, tato saddo na nikkhami. Ācariyo dutiyampi chindi [M 2.0232] …pe… sattamampi chindi. Suddhadaṇḍakaṃ vādentassa saddo nagaraṃ chādetvā aṭṭhāsi. Celukkhepasahassāni ceva ukkuṭṭhisahassāni [P 2.0254] ca pavattayiṃsu. Bodhisatto ekaṃ pāsakaṃ ākāse khipi, tīṇi accharāsatāni otaritvā nacciṃsu. Evaṃ dutiye ca tatiye ca khitte tīṇi tīṇi accharāsatāni otaritvā vuttanayeneva nacciṃsu.

The Bodhisatta, having bathed and anointed himself, ate a meal with various choice flavors, had his vīṇā brought, and sat on the seat prepared for him. Sakka, having become invisible, came and stood in the sky; only the Bodhisatta saw him. Mūsila also came and sat on his own seat. The great crowd surrounded them. From the very beginning, both played equally well. The great crowd, delighted by the playing of both, raised thousands of cheers. Standing in the sky and making only the Bodhisatta hear, Sakka said, “Cut one string.” The Bodhisatta cut a string, and though it was cut, a sound still issued from the cut end, sounding like the music of celestial gandhabbas. Mūsila also cut a string, but then no sound came forth. The teacher cut a second... and so on... up to the seventh. When he played on just the bare frame, the sound covered the city and remained. Thousands of cloths were waved and thousands of cheers were raised. The Bodhisatta threw one die into the sky, and three hundred celestial nymphs descended and danced. Similarly, when the second and third dice were thrown, three hundred celestial nymphs descended each time and danced in the manner described.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā mahājanassa iṅgitasaññaṃ adāsi, mahājano uṭṭhāya “tvaṃ ācariyena saddhiṃ virujjhitvā ‘samakāraṃ karomī’ti vāyamasi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī”ti mūsilaṃ tajjetvā gahitagahiteheva pāsāṇadaṇḍādīhi saṃcuṇṇetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā pāde gahetvā saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍesi. Rājā tuṭṭhacitto ghanavassaṃ vassāpento viya bodhisattassa bahuṃ dhanaṃ adāsi, tathā nāgarā. Sakko bodhisattena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “ahaṃ te, paṇḍita, sahassayuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ gāhāpetvā pacchā mātaliṃ pesessāmi, tvaṃ sahassayuttaṃ vejayantarathavaraṃ abhiruyha devalokaṃ āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

At that moment, the king gave a signal to the great crowd. The crowd rose up and rebuked Mūsila, saying: “Having opposed your teacher, you try to claim, ‘I can perform equally well,’ but you do not know your own measure!” Then, with whatever stones and clubs they had grabbed, they beat him to a pulp, brought about his death, seized him by the feet, and threw him on a rubbish heap. The king, with a pleased mind, gave much wealth to the Bodhisatta as if letting loose a great shower of rain, and the townspeople did likewise. Sakka, after exchanging friendly greetings with the Bodhisatta, said: “Wise one, I will have the chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbreds prepared and will later send Mātali. You should mount the excellent Vejayanta chariot yoked with a thousand steeds and come to the world of the devas.” Having said this, he departed.

Atha naṃ gantvā paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ nisinnaṃ “kahaṃ gatāttha, mahārājā”ti devadhītaro pucchiṃsu. Sakko tāsaṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ vitthārena kathetvā bodhisattassa sīlañca guṇañca vaṇṇesi. Devadhītaro “mahārāja, mayampi ācariyaṃ daṭṭhukāmā, idha naṃ ānehī”ti āhaṃsu. Sakko mātaliṃ āmantetvā “tāta, devaccharā guttilagandhabbaṃ daṭṭhukāmā, gaccha naṃ vejayantarathe nisīdāpetvā [V 2.0213] ānehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti gantvā bodhisattaṃ ānesi. Sakko bodhisattena saddhiṃ sammoditvā “devakaññā kira te, ācariya, gandhabbaṃ sotukāmā”ti āha. “Mayaṃ mahārāja, gandhabbā nāma sippaṃ nissāya jīvāma, mūlaṃ labhantā vādeyyāmā”ti. “Vādehi, ahaṃ te mūlaṃ dassāmī”ti. “Na mayhaṃ aññena mūlenattho, imā pana devadhītaro attano attano kalyāṇakammaṃ kathentu, evāhaṃ vādessāmī”ti[P 2.0255]. Atha naṃ devadhītaro āhaṃsu – “amhehi kataṃ kalyāṇakammaṃ pacchā tumhākaṃ kathessāma, gandhabbaṃ karohi ācariyā”ti. Bodhisatto sattāhaṃ devatānaṃ gandhabbaṃ akāsi, taṃ dibbagandhabbaṃ abhibhavitvā pavatti. Sattame divase ādito paṭṭhāya devadhītānaṃ kalyāṇakammaṃ pucchi. Ekaṃ kassapasammāsambuddhakāle ekassa bhikkhuno uttamavatthaṃ [M 2.0233] datvā sakkassa paricārikā hutvā nibbattaṃ accharāsahassaparivāraṃ uttamavatthadevakaññaṃ “tvaṃ purimabhave kiṃ kammaṃ katvā nibbattā”ti pucchi. Tassa pucchanākāro ca vissajjanā ca vimānavatthumhi āgatameva. Vuttañhi tattha –

Then the deva daughters asked Sakka, who had gone and sat upon the Paṇḍukambala stone, "Great king, where have you been?" Sakka explained the matter to them in detail and praised the virtue and merit of the Bodhisatta. The deva daughters said, "Great king, we too wish to see the teacher; please bring him here." Sakka summoned Mātali and said, "Dear Mātali, the celestial nymphs wish to see Guttila the musician. Go, seat him in the Vejayanta chariot and bring him here." He replied, "Very well," and went and brought the Bodhisatta. Sakka exchanged pleasantries with the Bodhisatta and said, "Teacher, it seems the deva maidens wish to hear your music." "Great king," he replied, "we musicians live by our art. If we receive a fee, we will play." "Play, I will give you a fee." "I have no need of any other fee. But let these deva daughters each speak of their own meritorious deeds; then I will play." Then the deva daughters said to him, "We will tell you of our meritorious deeds later. Please play your music, teacher." The Bodhisatta played for the devas for seven days, and it surpassed even the divine music. On the seventh day, beginning from the first, he asked the deva daughters about their meritorious deeds. He asked one deva maiden—who wore an excellent robe and was attended by a thousand nymphs, having been reborn as an attendant of Sakka because she had given an excellent robe to a monk in the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—"What deed did you perform in your previous life to be reborn thus?" The manner of his questioning and her answering is found in the Vimānavatthu. For it is said there:

“Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, yā tvaṃ tiṭṭhasi devate;

Obhāsentī disā sabbā, osadhī viya tārakā.

“With surpassing beauty, O deity, you stand illuminating all directions, like the morning star.

“Kena tetādiso vaṇṇo, kena te idha mijjhati;

Uppajjanti ca te bhogā, ye keci manaso piyā.

“By what is your beauty such? Through what do you prosper here? And why do all these enjoyments that are dear to your mind arise for you?

“Pucchāmi taṃ devi mahānubhāve, manussabhūtā kimakāsi puññaṃ;

Kenāsi evaṃ jalitānubhāvā, vaṇṇo ca te sabbadisā pabhāsatī”ti.

“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty, what meritorious deed did you perform when you were a human being? By what do you possess such blazing power, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?”

“Vatthuttamadāyikā nārī, pavarā hoti naresu nārīsu;

Evaṃ piyarūpadāyikā manāpaṃ, dibbaṃ sā labhate upecca ṭhānaṃ.

“A woman who is a giver of excellent cloth is foremost among men and women. Thus, a giver of a pleasing gift obtains a delightful divine state upon passing away and reaching that place.

“Tassā me passa vimānaṃ, accharā kāmavaṇṇinīhamasmi;

“Behold the celestial mansion of mine; I am a celestial nymph of lovely form.

Accharāsahassassāhaṃ, pavarā passa puññānaṃ vipākaṃ.

“I am the foremost among a thousand celestial nymphs; behold the result of my meritorious deeds.

“Tena metādiso vaṇṇo, tena me idha mijjhati;

Uppajjanti ca me bhogā, ye keci manaso piyā.

“By that meritorious deed my beauty is such; by that I prosper here; and for me arise enjoyments, whatever are dear to my mind.

“Tenamhi [V 2.0214] evaṃ jalitānubhāvā;

Vaṇṇo ca me sabbadisā pabhāsatī”ti. (vi. va. 329-331, 333-336);

“By that I am of such blazing power, and my beauty illuminates all directions.”

Aparā [P 2.0256] piṇḍāya caramānassa bhikkhuno pūjanatthāya pupphāni adāsi, aparā “cetiye gandhapañcaṅgulikaṃ dethā”ti gandhe adāsi, aparā madhurāni phalāphalāni adāsi, aparā ucchurasaṃ adāsi, aparā kassapadasabalassa cetiye gandhapañcaṅgulikaṃ adāsi, aparā maggapaṭipannānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnañca kulagehe vāsaṃ upagatānaṃ santike dhammaṃ assosi, aparā nāvāya upakaṭṭhāya velāya bhuttassa bhikkhuno udake ṭhatvā udakaṃ adāsi, aparā agāramajjhe vasamānā akkodhanā hutvā sassusasuravattaṃ akāsi, aparā attano laddhakoṭṭhāsatopi saṃvibhāgaṃ katvāva [M 2.0234] paribhuñji, sīlavatī ca ahosi, aparā paragehe dāsī hutvā nikkodhanā nimmānā attano laddhakoṭṭhāsato saṃvibhāgaṃ katvā devarañño paricārikā hutvā nibbattā (vi. va. aṭṭha. 328-336). Evaṃ sabbāpi guttilavimānavatthusmiṃ āgatā chattiṃsa devadhītā yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ katvā tattha nibbattā, sabbaṃ bodhisatto pucchi. Tāpissa attano katakammaṃ gāthāhiyeva kathesuṃ. Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me, svāhaṃ idhāgantvā appamattakenapi kammena paṭiladdhadibbasampattiyo assosiṃ. Ito dāni paṭṭhāya manussalokaṃ gantvā dānādīni kusalakammāneva karissāmī”ti vatvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Another gave flowers to a monk on his alms round to honor him. Another gave perfumes, saying, "Make a five-fingered scented mark at the shrine." Another gave sweet fruits. Another gave sugarcane juice. Another made five-fingered scented marks at the shrine of Kassapa of the Ten Powers. Another listened to the Dhamma in the presence of traveling monks and nuns who had come for a stay in her family's house. Another, standing in the water, gave water to a monk who had eaten on the bank near a boat. Another, living in a household, being free from anger, performed her duties toward her mother-in-law and father-in-law. Another shared even her own portion and ate only after giving to a virtuous person. Another, being a maidservant in another's house, was free from anger and pride, shared from her own portion, and was reborn as an attendant of the king of the gods. In this way, the Bodhisatta asked all thirty-six deva daughters mentioned in the Guttila Vimāna Story what deeds they had done to be reborn there. They too related their own deeds to him in verses. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta exclaimed: "What a gain for me! What a wonderful thing I have obtained! For having come here, I have heard of the divine fortunes obtained through even a small deed. From now on, having returned to the human world, I will perform only wholesome deeds such as giving!" Then he uttered this inspired utterance:

“Svāgataṃ vata me ajja, suppabhātaṃ suhuṭṭhitaṃ;

Yaṃ addasāmi devatāyo, accharākāmavaṇṇiyo.

“Truly, today is a welcome arrival for me, a good dawn, a good rising; for I have seen these goddesses, celestial nymphs of lovely form.

“Imāsāhaṃ [P 2.0257] dhammaṃ sutvā, kāhāmi kusalaṃ bahuṃ;

Dānena samacariyāya, saṃyamena damena ca;

Svāhaṃ tattha gamissāmi, yattha gantvā na socare”ti. (vi. va. 617-618);

“Having heard the Dhamma from them, I will perform much merit—through giving, through righteous living, through restraint, and through self-control. I shall go to that place where, having gone, they do not grieve.”

Atha naṃ sattāhaccayena devarājā mātalisaṅgāhakaṃ āṇāpetvā rathe nisīdāpetvā bārāṇasimeva pesesi. So bārāṇasiṃ gantvā devaloke attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃ manussānaṃ ācikkhi. Tato paṭṭhāya manussā saussāhā puññāni kātuṃ maññiṃsu.

Then, at the end of seven days, the king of the gods commanded Mātali the charioteer, had him seat the Bodhisatta in the chariot, and sent him back to Bārāṇasī. Having reached Bārāṇasī, he told the people about what he had seen in the world of the gods. From then on, people became diligent and intended to perform meritorious deeds.

Satthā [V 2.0215] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mūsilo devadatto ahosi, sakko anuruddho, rājā ānando, guttilagandhabbo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, identified the Birth: 'At that time, Mūsila was Devadatta, Sakka was Anuruddha, the king was Ānanda, and Guttila the musician was indeed I myself.'

Guttilajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The explanation of the Guttila Jātaka: Third.

[244] 4. Vigaticchajātakavaṇṇanā

[244] 4. The explanation of the Vigaticcha Jātaka.

Yaṃ [M 2.0235] passati na taṃ icchatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ palāyikaṃ paribbājakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sakalajambudīpe paṭivādaṃ alabhitvā sāvatthiṃ āgantvā “ko mayā saddhiṃ vādaṃ kātuṃ samattho”ti pucchitvā “sammāsambuddho”ti sutvā mahājanaparivuto jetavanaṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ catuparisamajjhe dhammaṃ desentaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Athassa satthā taṃ vissajjetvā “ekaṃ nāma ki”nti pañhaṃ pucchi, so taṃ kathetuṃ asakkonto uṭṭhāya palāyi. Nisinnaparisā “ekapadeneva vo, bhante, paribbājako niggahito”ti āhaṃsu. Satthā “nāhaṃ, upāsakā, idānevetaṃ ekapadeneva niggaṇhāmi, pubbepi niggaṇhiṃyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘What one sees, one does not desire’: this the Teacher said while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain fugitive wanderer. It seems that this wanderer, unable to find a rival debater in all of Jambudīpa, came to Sāvatthī and asked, ‘Who is able to debate with me?’ Hearing it was the Perfectly Enlightened One, he went to Jetavana surrounded by a great crowd and asked a question of the Blessed One, who was teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly. The Teacher answered it and then asked him a question: ‘What is the one?’ Unable to explain it, he got up and fled. The seated assembly said: ‘Venerable sir, the wanderer has been refuted by you with a single word.’ The Teacher said: ‘Lay followers, it is not only now that I have refuted him with a single word; I refuted him in the past as well,’ and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā dīgharattaṃ himavante [P 2.0258] vasi. So pabbatā oruyha ekaṃ nigamagāmaṃ nissāya gaṅgānivattane paṇṇasālāyaṃ vāsaṃ kappesi. Atheko paribbājako sakalajambudīpe paṭivādaṃ alabhitvā taṃ nigamaṃ patvā “atthi nu kho koci mayā saddhiṃ vādaṃ kātuṃ samattho”ti pucchitvā “atthī”ti bodhisattassa ānubhāvaṃ sutvā mahājanaparivuto tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “vaṇṇagandhaparibhāvitaṃ gaṅgāpānīyaṃ pivissatī”ti pucchi. Paribbājako vādena ottharanto “kā gaṅgā, vālukā gaṅgā, udakaṃ gaṅgā, orimatīraṃ gaṅgā, pārimatīraṃ gaṅgā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “tvaṃ pana, paribbājaka, ṭhapetvā udakaṃ vālukaṃ orimatīraṃ pārimatīrañca kahaṃ gaṅgaṃ labhissasī”ti āha. Paribbājako appaṭibhāno hutvā uṭṭhāya palāyi. Tasmiṃ palāte bodhisatto nisinnaparisāya dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kāsī country. Having come of age, he renounced sensual pleasures, went forth into the ascetic life, and lived for a long time in the Himalayas. Descending from the mountains, he took up residence in a leaf-hut near a market town at a bend of the Ganges. Then a certain wanderer, unable to find a rival debater in all of Jambudīpa, reached that market town. Asking, ‘Is there anyone able to debate with me?’ and hearing of the Bodhisatta's power, he went to his dwelling place surrounded by a great crowd and, after exchanging friendly greetings, sat down. The Bodhisatta then asked him, ‘Will you drink this Ganges water, imbued with color and scent?’ The wanderer, seeking to overwhelm him with debate, said: ‘What is the Ganges? Is the sand the Ganges? Is the water the Ganges? Is the near bank the Ganges? Is the far bank the Ganges?’ The Bodhisatta said: ‘But, wanderer, setting aside the water, the sand, the near bank, and the far bank, where will you find the Ganges?’ The wanderer, at a loss for a reply, got up and fled. When he had fled, the Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma to the seated assembly and spoke these verses:

188.

188.

“Yaṃ passati na taṃ icchati, yañca na passati taṃ kiricchati;

Maññāmi ciraṃ carissati, na hi taṃ lacchati yaṃ sa icchati.

‘What he sees, he does not want; and what he does not see, for that he longs. I think he will wander for a long time, for he will not get what he wants.’

189.

189.

“Yaṃ [V 2.0216] labhati na tena tussati, yañca pattheti laddhaṃ hīḷeti;

Icchā hi anantagocarā, vigaticchāna namo karomase”ti.

‘He is not satisfied with what he gets; and having gained what he aspired for, he despises it. For desire has an endless range; homage we pay to those free from desire.’

Tattha [M 2.0236] yaṃ passatīti yaṃ udakādiṃ passati, taṃ gaṅgāti na icchati. Yañca na passatīti yañca udakādivinimuttaṃ gaṅgaṃ na passati, taṃ kiricchati. Maññāmi ciraṃ carissatīti ahaṃ evaṃ maññāmi – ayaṃ paribbājako evarūpaṃ gaṅgaṃ pariyesanto ciraṃ carissati. Yathā vā udakādivinimuttaṃ gaṅgaṃ, evaṃ rūpādivinimuttaṃ attānampi pariyesanto saṃsāre ciraṃ [P 2.0259] carissati. Na hi taṃ lacchatīti ciraṃ carantopi yaṃ taṃ evarūpaṃ gaṅgaṃ vā attānaṃ vā icchati, taṃ na lacchati. Yaṃ labhatīti yaṃ udakaṃ vā rūpādiṃ vā labhati, tena na tussati. Yañca pattheti laddhaṃ hīḷetīti evaṃ laddhena atussanto yaṃ yaṃ sampattiṃ pattheti, taṃ taṃ labhitvā “kiṃ etāyā”ti hīḷeti avamaññati. Icchā hi anantagocarāti laddhaṃ hīḷetvā aññamaññaṃ ārammaṇaṃ icchanato ayaṃ icchā nāma taṇhā anantagocarā. Vigaticchāna namo karomaseti tasmā ye vigaticchā buddhādayo, tesaṃ mayaṃ namakkāraṃ karomāti.

Herein, ‘what he sees’ means whatever water and so on he sees, he does not want that as the Ganges. ‘And what he does not see’ means whatever Ganges apart from water and so on he does not see, for that he longs. ‘I think he will wander for a long time’ means I think thus: this wanderer, seeking such a Ganges, will wander for a long time. Just as he seeks a Ganges apart from water and so on, so too, seeking a self apart from form and so on, he will wander for a long time in saṃsāra. ‘For he will not get it’ means even wandering for a long time, he will not get that which he wants—that is, such a Ganges or a self. ‘With what he gets’ means with whatever water or form and so on he gets, he is not satisfied. ‘And having gained what he aspired for, he despises it’ means thus, being unsatisfied with what has been gained, whatever attainment he aspires to, having gained it, he despises and scorns it, thinking, ‘What is this to me?’ ‘For desire has an endless range’ means because, despising what has been gained and wanting one object after another, this desire, that is, craving, has an endless range. ‘Homage we pay to those free from desire’ means therefore, we pay homage to those who are free from desire, the Buddhas and others.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paribbājako etarahi paribbājako ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having related this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth: ‘At that time, the wanderer was the wanderer of the present day, but the ascetic was myself.’

Vigaticchajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Vigaticcha Jātaka: Fourth.

[245] 5. Mūlapariyāyajātakavaṇṇanā

[245] 5. The Commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Jātaka

Kālo ghasati bhūtānīti idaṃ satthā ukkaṭṭhaṃ nissāya subhagavane viharanto mūlapariyāyasuttantaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā kira pañcasatā brāhmaṇā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū sāsane pabbajitvā tīṇi piṭakāni uggaṇhitvā mānamadamattā hutvā “sammāsambuddhopi tīṇeva piṭakāni jānāti, mayampi tāni jānāma, evaṃ sante kiṃ tassa amhehi nānākaraṇa”nti buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ na gacchanti, paṭipakkhā hutvā caranti.

‘Time devours beings’: this the Teacher said while dwelling in the Subhagavana near Ukkaṭṭhā, concerning the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. It seems that at that time, five hundred brahmins who were masters of the three Vedas had gone forth in the Dispensation. Having learned the three Piṭakas, they became intoxicated with conceit and pride, thinking, ‘The Perfectly Enlightened One also knows the three Piṭakas, and we too know them. This being so, what is the difference between him and us?’ Thus they did not go to attend on the Buddha but went about as his opponents.

Athekadivasaṃ satthā tesu āgantvā attano santike nisinnesu aṭṭhahi bhūmīhi paṭimaṇḍetvā mūlapariyāyasuttantaṃ kathesi, te na kiñci sallakkhesuṃ. Atha nesaṃ etadahosi – “mayaṃ [V 2.0217] amhehi sadisā paṇḍitā natthī’ti [M 2.0237] mānaṃ karoma, idāni pana na kiñci jānāma, buddhehi sadiso paṇḍito nāma natthi, aho buddhaguṇā nāmā”ti. Te tato paṭṭhāya nihatamānā hutvā uddhaṭadāṭhā viya sappā nibbisevanā jātā. Satthā ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā vesāliṃ gantvā gotamakacetiye gotamakasuttantaṃ nāma kathesi, dasasahassilokadhātu kampi, taṃ sutvā te bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Mūlapariyāyasuttantapariyosāne pana satthari ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharanteyeva bhikkhū [P 2.0260] dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, aho buddhānaṃ ānubhāvo, te nāma brāhmaṇapabbajitā tathā mānamadamattā bhagavatā mūlapariyāyadesanāya nihatamānā katā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepāhaṃ ime evaṃ mānapaggahitasire vicarante nihatamāne akāsiṃyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day the Teacher came to them and, while they were seated near him, he delivered the discourse on the root of all things, adorning it with eight grounds, but they did not grasp any of it. Then it occurred to them: “We hold the conceit, ‘There are no pandits like us,’ but now we do not understand anything. Truly, there is no pandit like the Buddhas. Ah, the qualities of a Buddha!” From then on, their pride was crushed, and they became like snakes with their fangs removed, rendered harmless. The Teacher, after dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā for as long as he wished, went to Vesālī and at the Gotamaka Shrine delivered the Gotamaka Sutta. The ten-thousandfold world-system quaked. Hearing it, those bhikkhus attained arahantship. Now, after the conclusion of the discourse on the root of all things, while the Teacher was still dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā, the bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion in the hall of the Dhamma: “Friends, ah, the spiritual power of the Buddhas! Those brahmin ascetics, so intoxicated with pride and conceit, were humbled by the Blessed One’s teaching on the root of all things.” The Teacher came and asked: “For what discussion are you now gathered here, bhikkhus?” When they told him, he said: “Not only now, bhikkhus, but in the past, too, I humbled these same ones who were wandering about with their heads held high in pride.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañca māṇavakasatāni mante vācesi. Te pañcasatāpi niṭṭhitasippā sippe anuyogaṃ datvā “yattakaṃ mayaṃ jānāma, ācariyopi tattakameva, viseso natthī”ti mānatthaddhā hutvā ācariyassa santikaṃ na gacchanti, vattapaṭivattaṃ na karonti. Te ekadivasaṃ ācariye badarirukkhamūle nisinne taṃ vambhetukāmā badarirukkhaṃ nakhena ākoṭetvā “nissārovāyaṃ rukkho”ti āhaṃsu. Bodhisatto attano vambhanabhāvaṃ ñatvā antevāsike “ekaṃ vo pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti āha. Te haṭṭhatuṭṭhā “vadetha, kathessāmā”ti. Ācariyo pañhaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family. When he came of age, he became a world-renowned teacher, a master of the three Vedas, and he taught the sacred texts to five hundred young brahmins. When these five hundred had completed their training and applied themselves to their craft, they became stiff with pride and thought, “Our teacher knows only as much as we know; there is no difference.” They no longer went to their teacher or performed their duties and services for him. One day, as the teacher was sitting at the foot of a jujube tree, wishing to belittle him, they tapped the jujube tree with their fingernails and said, “This tree is pithless!” The Bodhisatta, knowing they meant to belittle him, said to his pupils, “I will ask you one question.” Overjoyed, they said, “Ask it, sir, we will answer.” The teacher, posing the question, spoke the first stanza:

190.

190.

“Kālo ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā;

Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto, sa bhūtapacaniṃ pacī”ti.

“Time devours all beings, and itself as well; but the being who is a devourer of time, he cooks the cooker of all beings.”

Tattha kāloti purebhattakālopi pacchābhattakālopīti evamādi. Bhūtānīti sattādhivacanametaṃ, na kālo bhūtānaṃ cammamaṃsādīni luñcitvā khādati, apica kho nesaṃ āyuvaṇṇabalāni khepento yobbaññaṃ [M 2.0238] maddanto ārogyaṃ vināsento ghasati khādatīti vuccati. Evaṃ ghasanto ca na kiñci vajjeti, sabbāneva ghasati. Na kevalañca bhūtāneva, apica kho sahattanā attānampi ghasati, purebhattakālo pacchābhattakālaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Esa nayo pacchābhattakālādīsu. Yo ca kālaghaso bhūtoti khīṇāsavassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ[P 2.0261]. So hi ariyamaggena āyatiṃ paṭisandhikālaṃ khepetvā khāditvā ṭhitattā “kālaghaso bhūto”ti vuccati[V 2.0218]. Sa bhūtapacaniṃ pacīti so yāyaṃ taṇhā apāyesu bhūte pacati, taṃ ñāṇagginā paci dahi bhasmamakāsi, tena “bhūtapacaniṃ pacī”ti vuccati. “Pajani”ntipi pāṭho, janikaṃ nibbattakinti attho.

Herein, ‘time’ means the forenoon, the afternoon, and so on. ‘Beings’ is a term for living beings; time does not tear off and eat their skin, flesh, and so on. Rather, it is said to devour and consume them by depleting their lifespan, complexion, and strength, by crushing their youth, and by destroying their health. And in so devouring, it spares nothing; it devours all. Not only does it devour beings, but with itself it devours itself: the forenoon does not reach the afternoon. The same principle applies to the afternoon and so on. ‘The being who is a devourer of time’ is a term for one whose taints are destroyed. For since he has, by means of the noble path, exhausted and consumed the time for future rebirth-linking, he is called ‘a being who is a devourer of time.’ ‘He cooks the cooker of all beings’: this means that craving which cooks beings in the planes of misery—that craving he has cooked with the fire of knowledge, burned it, and reduced it to ashes. Therefore it is said, ‘he cooks the cooker of all beings.’ There is also the reading ‘pajaniṃ,’ which means ‘the generator,’ that which brings into being.

Imaṃ pañhaṃ sutvā māṇavesu ekopi jānituṃ samattho nāma nāhosi. Atha ne bodhisatto “mā kho tumhe ‘ayaṃ pañho tīsu vedesu atthī’ti saññaṃ akattha, tumhe ‘yamahaṃ jānāmi, taṃ sabbaṃ jānāmā’ti maññamānā maṃ badarirukkhasadisaṃ karotha, mama tumhehi aññātassa bahuno jānanabhāvaṃ na jānātha, gacchatha sattame divase kālaṃ dammi, ettakena kālena imaṃ pañhaṃ cintethā”ti. Te bodhisattaṃ vanditvā attano attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā sattāhaṃ cintetvāpi pañhassa neva antaṃ, na koṭiṃ passiṃsu. Te sattamadivase ācariyassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisīditvā “kiṃ, bhadramukhā, jānittha pañha”nti vutte “na jānāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Atha bodhisatto te garahamāno dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

When they heard this question, not a single one of the young brahmins was able to understand it. Then the Bodhisatta said to them: “Do not suppose that this question is to be found in the three Vedas. Thinking, ‘All that I know, we know,’ you treat me like a pithless jujube tree. You do not know that I know much that is unknown to you. Go. I give you until the seventh day; in that time, ponder this question.” They paid homage to the Bodhisatta and went to their own dwellings. Though they pondered for seven days, they could see neither the beginning nor the end of the question. On the seventh day, they went to the teacher, paid homage, and sat down. When he asked, “Well, good sirs, have you understood the question?” they replied, “We have not.” Then the Bodhisatta, rebuking them, spoke a second stanza:

191.

191.

“Bahūni narasīsāni, lomasāni brahāni ca;

Gīvāsu paṭimukkāni, kocidevettha kaṇṇavā”ti.

“Many are the heads of men, hairy and large, fastened upon their necks; but scarcely one among them here has ears.”

Tassattho – bahūni narānaṃ sīsāni dissanti, sabbāni ca tāni lomasāni, sabbāni mahantāni gīvāsuyeva ṭhapitāni, na tālaphalaṃ viya hatthena gahitāni, natthi tesaṃ imehi dhammehi nānākaraṇaṃ. Ettha pana kocideva kaṇṇavāti attānaṃ sandhāyāha. Kaṇṇavāti paññavā, kaṇṇachiddaṃ pana na kassaci natthi. Iti te māṇavake “kaṇṇachiddamattameva tumhākaṃ bālānaṃ atthi, na paññā”ti garahitvā pañhaṃ vissajjesi. Te sutvā [P 2.0262] – “aho [M 2.0239] ācariyā nāma mahantā”ti khamāpetvā nihatamānā bodhisattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu.

Its meaning is this: many heads of men are seen; they are all hairy and large, and are all set upon necks, not held in the hand like a palm-fruit. In these respects, there is no difference between them. But here ‘scarcely one has ears’ was said with reference to himself. ‘Having ears’ means being wise; for no one lacks ear-holes. Thus, having rebuked those young brahmins by saying, “You fools have only ear-holes, but no wisdom,” he explained the question. When they heard it, they thought, “Ah, great indeed is our teacher!” and they begged his forgiveness. With their pride crushed, they attended upon the Bodhisatta.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā pañcasatā māṇavakā ime bhikkhū ahesuṃ, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth: “At that time, the five hundred young brahmins were these bhikkhus, and the teacher was myself.”

Mūlapariyāyajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Jātaka, the Fifth.

[246] 6. Bālovādajātakavaṇṇanā

[246] 6. The Commentary on the Bālovāda Jātaka

Hantvā [V 2.0219] chetvā vadhitvā cāti idaṃ satthā vesāliṃ upanissāya kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ viharanto sīhasenāpatiṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gantvā nimantetvā punadivase samaṃsakabhattaṃ adāsi. Nigaṇṭhā taṃ sutvā kupitā anattamanā tathāgataṃ viheṭhetukāmā “samaṇo gotamo jānaṃ uddissakataṃ maṃsaṃ bhuñjatī”ti akkosiṃsu. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto ‘samaṇo gotamo jānaṃ uddissakataṃ maṃsaṃ bhuñjatī’ti saddhiṃ parisāya akkosanto āhiṇḍatī”ti. Taṃ sutvā satthā “na, bhikkhave, nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto idāneva maṃ uddissakatamaṃsakhādanena garahati, pubbepi garahiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Having killed, cut, and slain...” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Gabled Hall near Vesālī, concerning General Sīha. For he had gone for refuge to the Blessed One, invited him, and on the next day offered him a meal that included meat. Hearing this, the Nigaṇṭhas became angry and displeased. Wishing to harass the Tathāgata, they reviled him, saying, “The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared on purpose for him.” The bhikkhus raised this topic in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, together with his following, is going about reviling the Teacher, saying, ‘The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat prepared on purpose for him.’” Hearing this, the Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta reviles me for eating meat prepared on purpose for me; he reviled me in the past as well.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya himavantato bārāṇasiṃ gantvā punadivase nagaraṃ bhikkhāya pāvisi. Atheko kuṭumbiko “tāpasaṃ viheṭhessāmī”ti gharaṃ pavesetvā paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā macchamaṃsena parivisitvā bhattakiccāvasāne ekamantaṃ nisīditvā “imaṃ maṃsaṃ tumheyeva uddissa pāṇe māretvā kataṃ, idaṃ akusalaṃ mā amhākameva, tumhākampi hotū”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family. When he came of age, he went forth into the ascetic life of a seer. In order to get salt and vinegar, he traveled from the Himalayas to Bārāṇasī, and on the next day he entered the city for alms. A certain householder, thinking, “I will harass this ascetic,” invited him into his house, had him sit on a prepared seat, and served him with fish and meat. When the meal was over, he sat to one side and said: “This meat was prepared by killing living beings just for you. Let this demerit not be ours alone, but yours as well!” And he spoke the first stanza:

192.

192.

“Hantvā chetvā vadhitvā ca, deti dānaṃ asaññato;

Edisaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjamāno, sa pāpena upalippatī”ti.

“Having killed, cut, and slain the living, an unrestrained man gives a gift; one who eats such a meal as this is thereby smeared with evil.”

Tattha [P 2.0263][M 2.0240] hantvāti paharitvā. Chetvāti kilametvā. Vadhitvāti māretvā. Deti dānaṃ asaññatoti asaññato dussīlo evaṃ katvā dānaṃ deti. Edisaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjamāno, sa pāpena upalippatīti edisaṃ uddissakatabhattaṃ bhuñjamāno so samaṇopi pāpena upalippati saṃyujjatiyevāti.

Herein, ‘having killed’ means having struck. ‘Having cut’ means having tormented. ‘Having slain’ means having killed. ‘An unrestrained man gives a gift’ means an unrestrained, immoral person gives a gift after having done so. ‘One who eats such a meal is smeared with evil’ means that even an ascetic who eats such a meal prepared on purpose for him is smeared and yoked with evil.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second stanza:

193.

193.

“Puttadārampi ce hantvā, deti dānaṃ asaññato;

Bhuñjamānopi sappañño, na pāpena upalippatī”ti.

“Though having killed his child and wife, an unrestrained man gives a gift; a wise one, though he eats of it, is not thereby smeared with evil.”

Tattha [V 2.0220] bhuñjamānopi sappaññoti tiṭṭhatu aññaṃ maṃsaṃ, puttadāraṃ vadhitvāpi dussīlena dinnaṃ sappañño khantimettādiguṇasampanno taṃ bhuñjamānopi pāpena na upalippatīti. Evamassa bodhisatto dhammaṃ kathetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi.

Herein, ‘a wise one, though he eats of it’ means this: let alone other meat, even if an immoral person gives something after having killed his own child and wife, a wise person endowed with such qualities as patience and loving-kindness is not smeared with evil even when eating it. Having thus taught the Dhamma to the householder, the Bodhisatta rose from his seat and departed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kuṭumbiko nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time the householder was Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, and the ascetic was I myself.”

Bālovādajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Bālovāda Jātaka, the Sixth.

[247] 7. Pādañjalijātakavaṇṇanā

[247] 7. The Commentary on the Pādañjali Jātaka

Addhā pādañjalī sabbeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lāḷudāyītheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi divase dve aggasāvakā pañhaṃ vinicchinanti, bhikkhū pañhaṃ suṇantā there pasaṃsanti. Lāḷudāyīthero pana parisantare nisinno “ete amhehi samaṃ kiṃ jānantī”ti oṭṭhaṃ bhañji. Taṃ disvā therā uṭṭhāya pakkamiṃsu, parisā bhijji. Dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso lāḷudāyī, dve aggasāvake garahitvā oṭṭhaṃ bhañjī”ti. Taṃ sutvā satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi lāḷudāyī ṭhapetvā oṭṭhabhañjanaṃ tato uttari aññaṃ na jānātī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Indeed, Pādañjali surpasses all...” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana in connection with the Elder Lāḷudāyī. For one day, the two chief disciples were deciding a question, and the monks, hearing the matter, praised the elders. But the Elder Lāḷudāyī, sitting in the midst of the assembly, twisted his lip, thinking, “What do these know compared to me?” Seeing this, the elders rose and left, and the assembly broke up. In the Hall of Dhamma, the monks raised a topic of discussion: “Friend, Lāḷudāyī disparaged the two chief disciples and twisted his lip.” Hearing this, the Teacher said: “Not only now, monks, but in the past too, Lāḷudāyī knew nothing beyond twisting his lip,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 2.0264][M 2.0241] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako amacco ahosi. Rañño pādañjalī nāma putto lālo dandhaparisakkano ahosi. Aparabhāge rājā kālamakāsi. Amaccā rañño matakiccāni katvā “taṃ rajje abhisiñcissāmā”ti mantayamānā rājaputtaṃ pādañjaliṃ āhaṃsu. Bodhisatto pana “ayaṃ kumāro lālo dandhaparisakkano, pariggahetvā naṃ abhisiñcissāmā”ti āha. Amaccā vinicchayaṃ sajjetvā kumāraṃ samīpe nisīdāpetvā aḍḍaṃ vinicchinantā na sammā vinicchiniṃsu. Te assāmikaṃ sāmikaṃ katvā kumāraṃ pucchiṃsu – “kīdisaṃ, kumāra, suṭṭhu aḍḍaṃ vinicchinimhā”ti. So oṭṭhaṃ bhañji. Bodhisatto “paṇḍito vata maññe kumāro, asammāvinicchitabhāvo tena ñāto bhavissatī”ti maññamāno paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister who instructed him in things temporal and spiritual. The king had a son named Pādañjali, who was a dullard and slow-witted. In the course of time, the king passed away. The ministers, having performed the funeral rites for the king, were conferring, “We will consecrate him to the kingship.” They then addressed Prince Pādañjali. But the Bodhisatta said: “This prince is a dullard and slow-witted. Let us test him and then consecrate him.” The ministers set up a legal case, and having seated the prince nearby, they judged the case, but did not judge it correctly. They declared the non-owner to be the owner and asked the prince: “Prince, how is it? Have we judged the case well?” He twisted his lip. The Bodhisatta, thinking, “The prince must be wise; he must have known that it was judged incorrectly,” spoke the first stanza:

194.

194.

“Addhā [V 2.0221] pādañjalī sabbe, paññāya atirocati;

Tathā hi oṭṭhaṃ bhañjati, uttariṃ nūna passatī”ti.

“Indeed, Pādañjali surpasses all in wisdom; for he twists his lip. Surely he sees something further.”

Tassattho – ekaṃsena pādañjalikumāro sabbe amhe paññāya atirocati. Tathā hi oṭṭhaṃ bhañjati, nūna uttariṃ aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ passatīti.

The meaning is: Prince Pādañjali certainly surpasses all of us in wisdom. For he twists his lip; surely he sees some further reason.

Te aparasmimpi divase vinicchayaṃ sajjetvā aññaṃ aḍḍaṃ suṭṭhu vinicchinitvā “kīdisaṃ, deva, suṭṭhu vinicchinita”nti pucchiṃsu. So punapi oṭṭhameva bhañji. Athassa andhabālabhāvaṃ ñatvā bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

On another day, they set up a legal case, and having judged another case correctly, they asked: “Your Majesty, how is it? Has it been judged well?” Again, he just twisted his lip. Then, realizing his blind foolishness, the Bodhisatta spoke the second stanza:

195.

195.

“Nāyaṃ dhammaṃ adhammaṃ vā, atthānatthañca bujjhati;

Aññatra oṭṭhanibbhogā, nāyaṃ jānāti kiñcana”nti.

“This one understands neither right nor wrong, nor benefit and harm; apart from twisting his lip, he knows nothing at all.”

Amaccā pādañjalikumārassa lālabhāvaṃ ñatvā bodhisattaṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu.

The ministers, realizing Prince Pādañjali’s foolishness, consecrated the Bodhisatta to the kingship.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā pādañjalī lāḷudāyī ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, Prince Pādañjali was Lāḷudāyī, but the wise minister was I myself.”

Pādañjalijātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Explanation of the Pādañjali Jātaka, the Seventh.

[248] 8. Kiṃsukopamajātakavaṇṇanā

[248] 8. The Explanation of the Kiṃsukopama Jātaka

Sabbehi [P 2.0265][M 2.0242] kiṃsuko diṭṭhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kiṃsukopamasuttantaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Cattāro hi bhikkhū tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ yāciṃsu, satthā tesaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Te kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā attano rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni agamiṃsu. Tesu eko cha phassāyatanāni pariggaṇhitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, eko pañcakkhandhe, eko cattāro mahābhūte, eko aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo. Te attano attano adhigatavisesaṃ satthu ārocesuṃ. Athekassa bhikkhuno parivitakko udapādi – “imesaṃ kammaṭṭhānāni nānā, nibbānaṃ ekaṃ, kathaṃ sabbehi arahattaṃ patta”nti. So satthāraṃ pucchi. Satthā “kiṃ te, bhikkhu, kiṃsukadiṭṭhabhātikehi nānatta”nti vatvā “idaṃ no, bhante, kāraṇaṃ kathethā”ti bhikkhūhi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“The kiṃsuka tree has been seen by all…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana in connection with the Kiṃsukopama Sutta. Four monks approached the Tathāgata and requested a meditation subject. The Teacher gave them a meditation subject. Having taken the meditation subject, they went to their respective places for the day and for the night. Among them, one attained arahantship by comprehending the six sense bases, one the five aggregates, one the four great elements, and one the eighteen elements. They each reported their special attainment to the Teacher. Then a reflection arose in one monk: “Their meditation subjects are different, but Nibbāna is one. How is it that all have attained arahantship?” He asked the Teacher. The Teacher said: “Monk, how does your case differ from the brothers who saw the kiṃsuka tree?” Then, requested by the monks, “Venerable sir, please tell us this story,” he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 2.0222] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa cattāro puttā ahesuṃ. Te ekadivasaṃ sārathiṃ pakkosetvā “mayaṃ, samma, kiṃsukaṃ daṭṭhukāmā, kiṃsukarukkhaṃ no dassehī”ti āhaṃsu. Sārathi “sādhu, dassessāmī”ti vatvā catunnampi ekato adassetvā jeṭṭharājaputtaṃ tāva rathe nisīdāpetvā araññaṃ netvā “ayaṃ kiṃsuko”ti khāṇukakāle kiṃsukaṃ dassesi. Aparassa bahalapalāsakāle, aparassa pupphitakāle, aparassa phalitakāle. Aparabhāge cattāropi bhātaro ekato nisinnā “kiṃsuko nāma kīdiso”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Tato eko “seyyāthāpi jhāmathūṇo”ti āha. Dutiyo “seyyathāpi nigrodharukkho”ti, tatiyo “seyyathāpi maṃsapesī”ti, catuttho “seyyathāpi sirīso”ti. Te aññamaññassa kathāya aparituṭṭhā pitu santikaṃ gantvā “deva, kiṃsuko nāma kīdiso”ti pucchitvā “tumhehi kiṃ kathita”nti vutte attanā kathitanīhāraṃ rañño kathesuṃ. Rājā “catūhipi tumhehi kiṃsuko diṭṭho, kevalaṃ vo kiṃsukassa dassento sārathi ‘imasmiṃ kāle kiṃsuko kīdiso[P 2.0266], imasmiṃ kīdiso’ti vibhajitvā na pucchito, tena vo kaṅkhā uppannā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, he had four sons. One day they called their charioteer and said: “Friend, we want to see a kiṃsuka tree. Show us a kiṃsuka tree.” The charioteer said, “Very well, I will show you,” but without showing it to all four at once, he first had the eldest prince sit in the chariot, took him to the forest, and showed him the kiṃsuka tree at a time when it was a bare stump, saying, “This is a kiṃsuka tree.” To the second he showed it when it had thick foliage, to the third when it was in flower, and to the fourth when it was bearing fruit. Later, when the four brothers were sitting together, they raised the question: “What is a kiṃsuka tree like?” One said: “It is like a charred stump.” The second said: “It is like a banyan tree.” The third said: “It is like a piece of meat.” The fourth said: “It is like an acacia tree.” Dissatisfied with one another’s accounts, they went to their father and asked: “Your Majesty, what is a kiṃsuka tree like?” When he asked what they had said, they related their accounts to the king. The king said: “All four of you have seen the kiṃsuka tree. It is just that when the charioteer was showing it to you, you did not ask him, making the distinction: ‘What is the kiṃsuka like at this time, and what is it like at that time?’ That is why doubt has arisen in you.” And he spoke the first stanza:

196.

196.

“Sabbehi [M 2.0243] kiṃsuko diṭṭho, kiṃ nvettha vicikicchatha;

Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu, sārathī paripucchito”ti.

“The kiṃsuka tree has been seen by all of you, so why do you doubt about it? For the charioteer was not questioned about it in all its states.”

Tattha na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu, sārathī paripucchitoti sabbehi vo kiṃsuko diṭṭho, kiṃ nu tumhe ettha vicikicchatha, sabbesu ṭhānesu kiṃsukoveso, tumhehi pana na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu sārathi paripucchito, tena vo kaṅkhā uppannāti.

Herein, the line “For the charioteer was not questioned about it in all its states” means: the kiṃsuka tree was seen by all of you, so why do you doubt it? In all its states, it is indeed that very kiṃsuka tree. But you did not question the charioteer about it in all its states, and for that reason doubt has arisen in you.

Satthā imaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassetvā “yathā, bhikkhu, te cattāro bhātikā vibhāgaṃ katvā apucchitattā kiṃsuke kaṅkhaṃ uppādesuṃ, evaṃ tvampi imasmiṃ dhamme kaṅkhaṃ uppādesī”ti vatvā abhisambuddho hutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having shown this reason, the Teacher said: “Monk, just as those four brothers, because they did not ask about its different states, gave rise to doubt about the kiṃsuka tree, so you too give rise to doubt about this Dhamma.” Then, as the Fully Enlightened One, he spoke the second stanza:

197.

197.

“Evaṃ sabbehi ñāṇehi, yesaṃ dhammā ajānitā;

Te ve dhammesu kaṅkhanti, kiṃsukasmiṃva bhātaro”ti.

“So too, those who have not known the teachings with all the modes of knowledge, they indeed doubt the teachings, just like the brothers with the kiṃsuka tree.”

Tassattho – yathā te bhātaro sabbesu ṭhānesu kiṃsukassa adiṭṭhattā kaṅkhiṃsu, evaṃ sabbehi vipassanāñāṇehi yesaṃ sabbe chaphassāyatanakhandhabhūtadhātubhedā dhammā ajānitā, sotāpattimaggassa [V 2.0223] anadhigatattā appaṭividdhā, te ve tesu phassāyatanādidhammesu kaṅkhanti yathā ekasmiṃyeva kiṃsukasmiṃ cattāro bhātaroti.

The meaning is: Just as those brothers were doubtful because they had not seen the kiṃsuka tree in all its states, so too, those by whom the phenomena—divided into the six sense bases, the aggregates, the great elements, and the other elements—are not known with all the insight knowledges, because the path of stream-entry has not been attained and penetrated, they indeed doubt those phenomena such as the sense bases, just as the four brothers doubted the single kiṃsuka tree.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasirājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī was I myself.”

Kiṃsukopamajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Explanation of the Kiṃsukopama Jātaka, the Eighth.

[249] 9. Sālakajātakavaṇṇanā

[249] 9. The Explanation of the Sālaka Jātaka

Ekaputtako bhavissasīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ mahātheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kirekaṃ kumārakaṃ pabbājetvā pīḷento tattha viharati. Sāmaṇero pīḷaṃ sahituṃ asakkonto uppabbaji. Thero gantvā taṃ upalāpeti “kumāra, tava cīvaraṃ [P 2.0267] taveva bhavissati pattopi, mama santakaṃ pattacīvarampi taveva bhavissati, ehi pabbajāhī”ti. So “nāhaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti vatvāpi punappunaṃ vuccamāno pabbaji[M 2.0244]. Atha naṃ pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya puna thero viheṭhesi. So pīḷaṃ asahanto puna uppabbajitvā anekavāraṃ yācantepi tasmiṃ “tvaṃ neva maṃ sahasi, na vinā vattituṃ sakkosi, gaccha na pabbajissāmī”ti na pabbaji. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, suhadayo vata so dārako mahātherassa āsayaṃ ñatvā na pabbajī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa suhadayo, pubbepi suhadayova, ekavāraṃ etassa dosaṃ disvā na puna upagacchī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“You will be an only son.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain great elder. It seems that after ordaining a young boy, he harassed him while staying there. The novice, unable to endure the harassment, disrobed. The elder went and coaxed him, saying, “Dear boy, your robe will be yours, and your bowl too. My own bowl and robe will also be yours. Come, go forth.” Though he said, “I will not go forth,” being repeatedly urged, he did go forth. Then, from the day of his ordination, the elder harassed him again. Unable to endure the harassment, he disrobed once more. Though begged many times by the elder, he said, “You neither tolerate me nor can you live without me. Go, I will not go forth,” and did not re-ordain. The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, indeed that boy is wise. Knowing the elder’s disposition, he did not go forth.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?” When told, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, not only now is he wise. In the past too, he was wise. Seeing his fault once, he did not approach him again.” And he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kuṭumbikakule nibbattitvā vayappatto dhaññavikkayena jīvikaṃ kappesi. Aññataropi ahituṇḍiko ekaṃ makkaṭaṃ sikkhāpetvā osadhaṃ gāhāpetvā tena sappaṃ kīḷāpento jīvikaṃ kappesi. So bārāṇasiyaṃ ussave ghuṭṭhe ussavaṃ kīḷitukāmo “imaṃ mā pamajjī”ti taṃ makkaṭaṃ tassa dhaññavāṇijassa hatthe ṭhapetvā ussavaṃ kīḷitvā sattame divase tassa santikaṃ gantvā “kahaṃ makkaṭo”ti pucchi. Makkaṭo sāmikassa saddaṃ sutvāva dhaññāpaṇato vegena nikkhami. Atha naṃ so veḷupesikāya piṭṭhiyaṃ pothetvā ādāya uyyānaṃ gantvā ekamante bandhitvā niddaṃ okkami. Makkaṭo tassa niddāyanabhāvaṃ ñatvā attano bandhanaṃ mocetvā palāyitvā ambarukkhaṃ āruyha ambapakkaṃ khāditvā aṭṭhiṃ ahituṇḍikassa sarīre pātesi. So pabujjhitvā ullokento taṃ disvā [V 2.0224] “madhuravacanena naṃ vañcetvā rukkhā otāretvā gaṇhissāmī”ti taṃ upalāpento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder's family and, when he came of age, made a living by selling grain. A certain snake charmer trained a monkey and earned his livelihood by making it handle herbs and play with a snake. When a festival was proclaimed in Benares, wanting to enjoy the festival, he placed the monkey in the hands of that grain merchant, saying, "Do not be heedless of this one." After enjoying the festival, on the seventh day he went to the merchant and asked, "Where is the monkey?" Hearing its master’s voice, the monkey quickly rushed out from the grain shop. Then the snake charmer struck it on the back with a piece of bamboo, took it away, went to a park, tied it up in a secluded spot, and fell asleep. Knowing that the man was asleep, the monkey freed itself from its bonds, escaped, climbed a mango tree, ate a ripe mango, and dropped the pit on the snake charmer’s body. Waking up and looking up, the man saw it and thought, "I will deceive it with sweet words, lure it down from the tree, and catch it." So he coaxed it, reciting the first verse:

198.

198.

“Ekaputtako bhavissasi, tvañca no hessasi issaro kule;

Oroha [P 2.0268] dumasmā sālaka, ehi dāni gharakaṃ vajemase”ti.

"You will be an only son, and you will be lord in our family; come down from the tree, Sālaka, come now, let us go home."

Tassattho – tvaṃ mayhaṃ ekaputtako bhavissasi, kule ca me bhogānaṃ issaro, etamhā rukkhā otara, ehi amhākaṃ gharaṃ gamissāma. Sālakāti nāmena ālapanto āha.

The meaning is this: You will be my only son and the master of the wealth in my family. Come down from this tree; come, we will go to our home. He spoke, addressing him by the name "Sālaka."

Taṃ [M 2.0245] sutvā makkaṭo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the monkey recited the second verse:

199.

199.

“Nanu maṃ suhadayoti maññasi, yañca maṃ hanasi veḷuyaṭṭhiyā;

Pakkambavane ramāmase, gaccha tvaṃ gharakaṃ yathāsukha”nti.

"Surely you consider me a friend, that you strike me with a bamboo stick? We shall enjoy ourselves in the ripe mango grove; you go home as you please."

Tattha nanu maṃ suhadayoti maññasīti nanu tvaṃ maṃ “suhadayo”ti maññasi, “suhadayo aya”nti maññasīti attho. Yañca maṃ hanasi veḷuyaṭṭhiyāti yaṃ maṃ evaṃ atimaññasi, yañca veḷupesikāya hanasi, tenāhaṃ nāgacchāmīti dīpeti. Atha naṃ “mayaṃ imasmiṃ pakkambavane ramāmase, gaccha tvaṃ gharakaṃ yathāsukha”nti vatvā uppatitvā vanaṃ pāvisi. Ahituṇḍikopi anattamano attano gehaṃ agamāsi.

Therein, 'Surely you consider me a friend' means: 'Surely you think of me as a friend?' 'Surely you think, "This one is a friend"?' is the meaning. 'That you strike me with a bamboo stick' indicates: 'Because you so despise me, and because you strike me with a piece of bamboo, for that reason I will not come.' Then, saying, "We shall enjoy ourselves in this ripe mango grove; you go home as you please," it leaped up and entered the forest. The snake charmer, dejected, went to his own home.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā makkaṭo sāmaṇero ahosi, ahituṇḍiko mahāthero, dhaññavāṇijo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, the monkey was the novice, the snake charmer was the great elder, and the grain merchant was I myself.”

Sālakajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Sālaka Jātaka, the Ninth.

[250] 10. Kapijātakavaṇṇanā

[250] 10. The Commentary on the Kapi Jātaka

Ayaṃ isī upasamasaṃyame ratoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa hi kuhakabhāvo bhikkhūsu pākaṭo jāto. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko bhikkhu niyyānike buddhasāsane pabbajitvā kuhakavattaṃ pūretī”ti. Satthā āgantvā [V 2.0225] “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave[P 2.0269], etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, esa bhikkhu idāneva, pubbepi kuhakoyeva, aggimattassa kāraṇā makkaṭo hutvā kohaññamakāsī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.
