“This ascetic delights in peace and restraint.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain deceitful monk. His deceitful nature had become well-known among the monks. The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, a certain monk, having gone forth in the Buddha’s dispensation which leads to liberation, fulfills the practice of a deceiver.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?” When they replied, “This one,” he said, “Monks, this monk is not deceitful only now—he was deceitful in the past as well. For the sake of fire, he became a monkey and practiced deceit.” Having said this, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto puttassa ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle brāhmaṇiyā matāya puttaṃ aṅkenādāya himavantaṃ [M 2.0246] pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tampi puttaṃ tāpasakumārakaṃ katvā paṇṇasālāya vāsaṃ kappesi. Vassārattasamaye acchinnadhāre deve vassante eko makkaṭo sītapīḷito dante khādanto kampanto vicarati. Bodhisatto mahante dārukkhandhe āharitvā aggiṃ katvā mañcake nipajji, puttakopissa pāde parimajjamāno nisīdi. So makkaṭo ekassa matatāpasassa santakāni vakkalāni nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca ajinacammaṃ aṃse katvā kājakamaṇḍaluṃ ādāya isivesenāgantvā paṇṇasāladvāre aggissa kāraṇā kuhakakammaṃ katvā aṭṭhāsi. Tāpasakumārako taṃ disvā “tāta, tāpaso eko sītapīḷito kampamāno tiṭṭhati, idha naṃ pakkosatha, visibbessatī”ti pitaraṃ āyācanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kasi country. When he came of age, at the time his son was old enough to run about, his brahmin wife died. Taking his son on his hip, he entered the Himalayas, went forth as an ascetic, and also made his son a young ascetic, and they took up residence in a leaf hut. During the rainy season, as the heavens rained down in an unbroken stream, a certain monkey, afflicted by the cold, wandered about shivering, its teeth chattering. The Bodhisatta brought large logs, made a fire, and lay down on a cot, while his son sat massaging his feet. That monkey, having put on and wrapped himself in the bark garments belonging to a dead ascetic, slung a deer hide over his shoulder, took a carrying-pole and a water pot, and approached in the guise of an ascetic. He stood at the door of the leaf hut, practicing deceit for the sake of the fire. The young ascetic, seeing him, pleaded with his father, saying, “Father, an ascetic stands there, shivering, afflicted by the cold. Call him in here, he will warm himself,” and he recited the first verse:

200.

200.

“Ayaṃ isī upasamasaṃyame rato, sa tiṭṭhati sisirabhayena aṭṭito;

Handa ayaṃ pavisatumaṃ agārakaṃ, vinetu sītaṃ darathañca kevala”nti.

“This sage delights in peace and self-restraint; he stands there, afflicted by the fear of the cold. Pray, let him enter this dwelling, to dispel the cold and all his distress.”

Tattha upasamasaṃyame ratoti rāgādikilesaupasame ca sīlasaṃyame ca rato. Sa tiṭṭhatīti so tiṭṭhati. Sisirabhayenāti vātavuṭṭhijanitassa sisirassa bhayena. Aṭṭitoti pīḷito. Pavisatumanti pavisatu imaṃ. Kevalanti sakalaṃ anavasesaṃ.

Therein, 'delights in peace and self-restraint' means delighting in the calming of defilements such as lust and in moral restraint. 'He stands there' means so he stands. 'By the fear of the cold' means by fear of the cold produced by wind and rain. 'Afflicted' means oppressed. 'Let him enter this' is the meaning of 'pavisatumaṃ'. 'All' means the whole, without remainder.

Bodhisatto puttassa vacanaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāya olokento makkaṭabhāvaṃ ñatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his son’s words, the Bodhisatta rose, and looking, he realized it was a monkey and recited the second verse:

201.

201.

“Nāyaṃ [P 2.0270] isī upasamasaṃyame rato, kapī ayaṃ dumavarasākhagocaro;

So dūsako rosako cāpi jammo, sace vajemampi dūseyyagāra”nti.

“This is no sage delighting in peace and restraint; this is a monkey, whose domain is the branches of excellent trees. He is a defiler, a vexer, and a wretch; if we let him in, he would defile the dwelling.”

Tattha dumavarasākhagocaroti dumavarānaṃ sākhagocaro. So dūsako rosako cāpi jammoti so evaṃ gatagataṭṭhānassa dūsanato dūsako, ghaṭṭanatāya rosako, lāmakabhāvena jammo. Sace vajeti [V 2.0226] yadi imaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ vaje paviseyya, sabbaṃ uccārapassāvakaraṇena ca aggidānena ca dūseyyāti.

There, “whose range is the finest branches of trees” means whose range is the branches of excellent trees. “A defiler, an irritator, and a wretch” means it is a defiler because it defiles the places it goes to, an irritator because of its harassing nature, and a wretch because of its inferior nature. “If it were to enter” means if it were to enter this leaf-hut, it would defile everything by urinating and defecating and by setting it on fire.

Evañca [M 2.0247] pana vatvā bodhisatto ummukaṃ gahetvā taṃ santāsetvā palāpesi. So uppatitvā vanaṃ pakkhanto tathā pakkhantova ahosi, na puna taṃ ṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Bodhisatto abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā tāpasakumārassa kasiṇaparikammaṃ ācikkhi, sopi abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca uppādesi. Te ubhopi aparihīnajjhānā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta took a firebrand and frightened the monkey, causing him to flee. He jumped up and fled into the forest, and having thus fled, he remained there, never returning to that place again. The Bodhisatta then attained the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and taught the ascetic youth the preliminary exercise for the meditation device. He too developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments. Both of them, without declining in their meditative states, were destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, porāṇato paṭṭhāyapesa kuhakoyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. Saccapariyosāne keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino keci arahanto ahesuṃ. “Tadā makkaṭo kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, putto rāhulo, pitā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, “Monks, not only now, but from ancient times this one has been a deceiver.” Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths, and connected the Jātaka, at the conclusion of the Truths some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some arahants. “At that time, the monkey was the deceitful monk, the son was Rāhula, and the father was I myself.”

Kapijātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Kapijātaka, the Tenth.

Siṅgālavaggo dasamo.

The Chapter of the Jackal, the tenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Sabbadāṭhī ca sunakho, guttilo vigaticchā ca;

Mūlapariyāyaṃ bālovādaṃ, pādañjali kiṃ sukopamaṃ;

Sālakaṃ kapi te dasa.

Sabbadāṭhī and the Dog, Guttila and the Absence of Desire; The Root Exposition, Foolish Instruction; Pādañjali, Kiṃsukopama; Sālaka and the Monkey—these ten.

Atha vagguddānaṃ –

Then, the chapter summary:

Daḷhavaggo ca santhavo, kalyāṇadhammāsadiso;

Rūhako daḷhavaggo ca, bīraṇathambhakāsāvo;

Upāhano siṅgālo ca, dasavaggā duke siyuṃ.

The Daḷha Chapter and the Santhava Chapter, the Kalyāṇadhamma Chapter and the Asadisa Chapter; The Rūhaka Chapter and the Nataṃdaḷha Chapter, the Bīraṇathambha Chapter and the Kāsāva Chapter; The Upāhana Chapter and the Siṅgāla Chapter—these are the ten chapters in the Book of the Twos.

Dukanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dukanipāta is completed.

3. Tikanipāto

3. The Book of the Threes

1. Saṅkappavaggo

1. The Chapter on Conceptions

[251] 1. Saṅkapparāgajātakavaṇṇanā

[251] 1. Commentary on the Saṅkapparāga Jātaka

Saṅkapparāgadhotenāti [V 2.0227][P 2.0271][M 2.0248] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthinagaravāsī kireko kulaputto sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajitvā ekadivasaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caranto ekaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ itthiṃ disvā uppannakāmarāgo anabhirato vicari. Tamenaṃ ācariyupajjhāyādayo disvā anabhiratikāraṇaṃ pucchitvā vibbhamitukāmabhāvamassa ñatvā “āvuso, satthā nāma kāmarāgādikilesapīḷitānaṃ kilese hāretvā saccāni pakāsetvā sotāpattiphalādīni deti, ehi taṃ satthu santikaṃ nessāmā”ti ādāya agamaṃsu. Satthārā ca “kiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, anicchamānakaññeva bhikkhuṃ gahetvā āgatatthā”ti vutte tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhito”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kiṃkāraṇā”ti pucchi. So tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ satthā “itthiyo nāmetā, bhikkhu, pubbe jhānabalena vikkhambhitakilesānaṃ visuddhasattānampi saṃkilesaṃ uppādesuṃ, tādisaṃ tucchapuggalaṃ kiṃkāraṇā na saṃkilesissanti, visuddhāpi sattā saṃkilissanti, uttamayasasamaṅginopi āyasakyaṃ pāpuṇanti, pageva aparisuddhā. Sinerukampanakavāto purāṇapaṇṇakasaṭaṃ kiṃ [P 2.0272] na kampessati, bodhitale nisīditvā abhisambujjhanakasattaṃ ayaṃ kileso āloḷesi, tādisaṃ kiṃ na āloḷessatī”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Saṅkapparāgadhotenāti”: The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who was dissatisfied. It is said that a certain son of a good family, a resident of Sāvatthī, having dedicated his life to the Dispensation, went forth. One day, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a woman beautifully adorned. Lust arose in him, and he lived in discontent. His teachers and preceptors, noticing this and asking the reason for his discontent, realized his desire to return to the lay life and said, “Friend, the Teacher is known to remove the defilements of those oppressed by lust and other passions, reveal the Truths, and grant the fruits such as stream-entry. Come, let us take you to the Teacher.” And they took him there. When the Teacher asked, “Monks, why have you brought this monk even though he is unwilling?” they explained the matter. The Teacher asked, “Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?” and when he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” the Teacher asked, “For what reason?” He then explained the matter. Then the Teacher said to him, “Monk, in the past, these women have caused even pure beings whose defilements were suppressed by the power of jhāna to become defiled. Why would they not defile a void person like you? Even pure beings become defiled; even those endowed with the highest fame fall into disgrace, let alone the impure. How could the wind that shakes Mount Sineru not shake a heap of dry leaves? This defilement agitated even the Great Being who was sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree to attain full awakening; why would it not agitate one such as you?” Having said this, at their request, he told a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhave brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasiṃ paccāgantvā katadārapariggaho mātāpitūnaṃ accayena tesaṃ matakiccāni katvā hiraññolokanakammaṃ karonto “idaṃ dhanaṃ paññāyati, yehi panetaṃ sambhataṃ, te [M 2.0249] na paññāyantī”ti [V 2.0228] āvajjento saṃvegappatto ahosi, sarīrā sedā mucciṃsu. So gharāvāse ciraṃ vasanto mahādānaṃ datvā kāme pahāya assumukhaṃ ñātisaṅghaṃ pariccajitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā ramaṇīye padese paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā uñchācariyāya vanamūlaphalādīhi yāpento nacirasseva abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto ciraṃ vasitvā cintesi – “manussapathaṃ gantvā loṇambilaṃ upasevissāmi, evaṃ me sarīrañceva thiraṃ bhavissati, jaṅghavihāro ca kato bhavissati, ye ca mādisassa sīlasampannassa bhikkhaṃ vā dassanti, abhivādanādīni vā karissanti, te saggapuraṃ pūressantī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a great brahmin family possessing eighty crores of wealth. Upon reaching maturity, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and returned to Benares to lead a householder's life. After his parents passed away, he performed their funeral rites. While inspecting his treasure, he reflected, “This wealth is visible, but those who accumulated it are no longer seen.” Struck with a sense of urgency, sweat poured from his body. Having lived long in the household life, he gave a great donation, renounced sensual pleasures, and leaving behind his tearful relatives, he entered the Himalayas and took up the life of an ascetic. In a delightful spot, he built a leaf-hut, sustained himself on forest roots and fruits through gleaning, and soon attained the higher knowledges and meditative attainments. Living long in the joy of meditation, he thought: “I will go to human habitations to consume salt and sour seasonings. In this way, my body will become firm and I will practice wandering on foot. And those who give alms or show reverence to a virtuous monk like me will fill the heavenly city.”

So himavantā otaritvā anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno bārāṇasiṃ patvā sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ olokento rājuyyānaṃ disvā “idaṃ paṭisallānasāruppaṃ, ettha vasissāme”ti uyyānaṃ pavisitvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinno jhānasukhena rattiṃ khepetvā punadivase katasarīrapaṭijaggano pubbaṇhasamaye jaṭājinavakkalāni saṇṭhapetvā bhikkhābhājanaṃ ādāya santindriyo santamānaso iriyāpathasampanno yugamattadassano hutvā sabbākārasampannāya attano rūpasiriyā lokassa [P 2.0273] locanāni ākaḍḍhento nagaraṃ pavisitvā bhikkhāya caranto rañño nivesanadvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Rājā mahātale caṅkamanto vātapānantarena bodhisattaṃ disvā iriyāpathasmiññeva pasīditvā “sace santadhammo nāma atthi, imassa tena abbhantare bhavitabba”nti cintetvā “gaccha, taṃ tāpasaṃ ānehī”ti ekaṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi. So gantvā vanditvā bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā “rājā, bhante, taṃ pakkosatī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “mahāpuñña, amhe rājā na jānātī”ti āha. “Tena hi, bhante, yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva idheva hothā”ti gantvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā “amhākaṃ kulūpakatāpaso natthi, gaccha, naṃ ānehī”ti sayampi vātapānena hatthaṃ pasāretvā vandanto “ito etha, bhante”ti āha. Bodhisatto amaccassa hatthe bhikkhābhājanaṃ datvā mahātalaṃ abhiruhi.

Descending from the Himalayas and wandering in stages, he reached Benares. As the sun was setting, he looked for a place to stay and, seeing the royal park, thought, 'This is a suitable place for seclusion; I shall stay here.' He entered the park and, sitting at the foot of a certain tree, spent the night in the bliss of meditation. On the following day, having performed his bodily duties, he arranged his matted hair, antelope skin, and bark garments in the morning. Taking his alms bowl, with calmed senses, a peaceful mind, and perfect deportment, looking only a yoke's length ahead, he entered the city, drawing the eyes of the people with the splendor of his form, which was perfect in every way. While walking for alms, he arrived at the gate of the king's residence. The king, walking on the upper terrace, saw the Bodhisatta through a window and, being pleased with his deportment alone, thought, 'If there is such a thing as the nature of peace, it must be within him.' He then ordered a minister, 'Go, bring that ascetic here.' The minister went, paid respects, took the alms bowl, and said, 'Venerable sir, the king summons you.' The Bodhisatta said, 'O meritorious one, the king does not know us.' The minister replied, 'In that case, venerable sir, please stay right here until I return,' and went to inform the king. The king said, 'We have no regular supported ascetic. Go, bring him here.' The king himself also stretched out his hand from the window in greeting and said, 'Come here, venerable sir.' The Bodhisatta handed his alms bowl to the minister and ascended to the upper terrace.

Atha naṃ rājā vanditvā rājapallaṅke nisīdāpetvā attano sampāditehi yāgukhajjakabhattehi parivisitvā katabhattakiccaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Pañhabyākaraṇena bhiyyosomattāya pasīditvā vanditvā “bhante, tumhe katthavāsikā[M 2.0250], kuto āgatatthā”ti pucchitvā “himavantavāsikā mayaṃ, mahārāja, himavantato āgatā”ti vutte puna “kiṃkāraṇā”ti pucchitvā “vassārattakāle, mahārāja, nibaddhavāso nāma laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte “tena hi, bhante, rājuyyāne vasatha, tumhe ca catūhi paccayehi na kilamissatha, ahañca saggasaṃvattanikaṃ puññaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā bhuttapātarāso bodhisattena saddhiṃ [V 2.0229] uyyānaṃ gantvā paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā caṅkamaṃ māpetvā sesānipi rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīni sampādetvā pabbajitaparikkhāre paṭiyādetvā “sukhena vasatha, bhante”ti uyyānapālaṃ sampaṭicchāpesi. Bodhisatto tato paṭṭhāya dvādasa [P 2.0274] saṃvaccharāni tattheva vasi.

Then the king, having paid homage to him, seated him on the royal couch, served him with the rice-gruel, hard food, and rice prepared for himself, and after the meal was finished, asked him a question. Pleased even more by his answer to the question, the king paid homage again and asked, 'Venerable sir, where do you reside? From where have you come?' When told, 'Great king, we reside in the Himalayas; we have come from the Himalayas,' he asked further, 'For what reason?' And when told, 'Great king, during the rainy season, it is proper to obtain a fixed residence,' the king said, 'In that case, venerable sir, dwell in the royal park. You will not be troubled for the four requisites, and I will gain merit leading to heaven.' Having obtained his consent, the king, after his morning meal, went to the park with the Bodhisatta. There he had a leaf-hut built, a walking path prepared, and other necessities for night and day dwelling arranged, and provided the requisites for a renunciant. Saying, 'Dwell at ease, venerable sir,' he entrusted him to the park keeper. From then on, the Bodhisatta dwelt there for twelve years.

Athekadivasaṃ rañño paccanto kupito. So tassa vūpasamanatthāya gantukāmo deviṃ āmantetvā “bhadde, tayā nagare ohīyituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. “Kiṃ nissāya kathetha, devā”ti. “Sīlavantaṃ tāpasaṃ, bhadde”ti. “Deva, nāhaṃ tasmiṃ pamajjissāmi, amhākaṃ ayyassa paṭijagganaṃ mama bhāro, tumhe nirāsaṅkā gacchathā”ti. Rājā nikkhamitvā gato, devīpi bodhisattaṃ tatheva sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Bodhisatto pana rañño gatakāle nibaddhavelāyaṃ āgantvā attano rucitāya velāya rājanivesanaṃ gantvā bhattakiccaṃ karoti.

Now one day, the border region of the king's territory was in revolt. Wishing to go and pacify it, he addressed the queen: 'My dear, you should remain in the city.' 'Based on what grounds do you say this, lord?' 'My dear, because of the virtuous ascetic.' 'Lord, I will not be remiss in this. Attendance on our master is my responsibility. You may go without anxiety.' The king departed, and the queen attended upon the Bodhisatta with the same respect. However, during the king's absence, the Bodhisatta, though coming at the regular time, would go to the royal residence at whatever time he pleased to take his meal.

Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatte aticirāyante devī sabbaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādetvā nhatvā alaṅkaritvā nīcamañcakaṃ paññāpetvā bodhisattassa āgamanaṃ olokayamānā maṭṭhasāṭakaṃ sithilaṃ katvā nivāsetvā nipajji. Bodhisattopi velaṃ sallakkhetvā bhikkhābhājanaṃ ādāya ākāsenāgantvā mahāvātapānadvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Tassa vakkalasaddaṃ sutvā sahasā uṭṭhahamānāya deviyā sarīrā maṭṭhasāṭako bhassittha, bodhisatto visabhāgārammaṇaṃ disvā indriyāni bhinditvā subhavasena olokesi. Athassa jhānabalena sannisinnopi kileso karaṇḍake pakkhittaāsīviso viya phaṇaṃ katvā uṭṭhahi, khīrarukkhassa vāsiyā ākoṭitakālo viya ahosi. Kilesuppādanena saheva jhānaṅgāni parihāyiṃsu, indriyāni aparipuṇṇāni ahesuṃ, sayaṃ pakkhacchinnakāko viya ahosi. So pubbe viya nisīditvā bhattakiccaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi[M 2.0251], nisīdāpiyamānopi na nisīdi. Athassa devī sabbaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ bhikkhābhājaneyeva [P 2.0275] pakkhipi. Yathā ca pubbe bhattakiccaṃ katvā sīhapañjarena nikkhamitvā ākāseneva gacchati, evaṃ taṃ divasaṃ gantuṃ nāsakkhi. Bhattaṃ pana gahetvā mahānisseṇiyā otaritvā uyyānaṃ agamāsi. Devīpi assa attani paṭibaddhacittataṃ aññāsi. So uyyānaṃ gantvā bhattaṃ abhuñjitvāva heṭṭhāmañcake nikkhipitvā “deviyā evarūpā hatthasobhā pādasobhā, evarūpaṃ kaṭipariyosānaṃ, evarūpaṃ ūrulakkhaṇa”ntiādīni vippalapanto sattāhaṃ nipajji, bhattaṃ pūtikaṃ ahosi nīlamakkhikāparipuṇṇaṃ.

Then one day, as the Bodhisatta delayed for a long time, the queen prepared all kinds of food and drink, bathed, adorned herself, set up a low couch, and while awaiting the Bodhisatta’s arrival, she dressed herself loosely in a smooth cloth and lay down. The Bodhisatta, observing the time, took his alms bowl and arrived through the air, reaching the great window. Hearing the rustling sound of his bark garments, the queen rose up suddenly, and as she did so, her smooth cloth slipped off her body. Seeing this inappropriate object, the Bodhisatta’s self-control was broken, and he gazed at her with the notion of beauty. Then, although his defilements had been suppressed by the power of meditation, they arose like a hooded cobra rearing up from a basket. It was like a milk-sap tree being struck with an axe. Together with the arising of defilements, his meditative factors vanished, his faculties became impaired, and he became like a crow with clipped wings. He was unable to sit and take his meal as before; even when invited to sit, he did not sit. Then the queen placed all the food and drink into his alms bowl. Though he had previously taken his meal and left through the lion-window, flying through the air, on that day he could not do so. Instead, he took the food and descended by the great staircase to the garden. The queen understood that his mind was attached to her. He went to the garden but did not eat the food. Placing it under the couch, he lay there for seven days, lamenting: 'The queen has such beautiful hands, such beautiful feet, such a beautiful waist, such beautiful thighs,' and so on. The food rotted and became full of blueflies.

Atha rājā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā paccāgato alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rājanivesanaṃ agantvāva “bodhisattaṃ passissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā uklāpaṃ assamapadaṃ disvā [V 2.0230] “pakkanto bhavissatī”ti paṇṇasālāya dvāraṃ vivaritvā antopaviṭṭho taṃ nipannakaṃ disvā “kenaci aphāsukena bhavitabba”nti pūtibhattaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā paṇṇasālaṃ paṭijaggāpetvā “bhante, kiṃ te aphāsuka”nti pucchi. “Viddhosmi, mahārājā”ti. Rājā “mama paccāmittehi mayi okāsaṃ alabhantehi ‘mamāyanaṭṭhānamassa dubbalaṃ karissāmā’ti āgantvā esa viddho bhavissati maññe”ti sarīraṃ parivattetvā viddhaṭṭhānaṃ olokento viddhaṭṭhānaṃ adisvā “kattha viddhosi, bhante”ti pucchi. Bodhisatto “nāhaṃ, mahārāja, aññena viddho, ahaṃ pana attanāva attānaṃ hadaye vijjhi”nti vatvā uṭṭhāya nisīditvā imā gāthā avoca –

Then the king, having pacified the border region and returned, circled the adorned and prepared city. Without even entering the royal residence, thinking, 'I shall see the Bodhisatta,' he went to the park. Seeing the squalid hermitage, he thought, 'He must have departed.' Upon opening the door of the leaf-hut and entering, he saw him lying there. Thinking, 'He must be suffering from some ailment,' he had the spoiled food discarded and the leaf-hut cleaned. Then he asked, 'Venerable sir, what troubles you?' 'I am wounded, great king,' he replied. The king thought, 'My enemies, unable to find an opportunity against me, must have come here thinking, "We will weaken his place of refuge," and thus he has been wounded.' He turned the body over, searching for the wound, but not finding it, he asked, 'Where are you wounded, venerable sir?' The Bodhisatta replied, 'I am not wounded by another, great king, but I have pierced my own heart.' Then he rose and sat down, reciting these verses:

1.

1.

“Saṅkapparāgadhotena, vitakkanisitena ca;

Nālaṅkatena bhadrena, usukārākatena ca.

Washed with the lust of intention, and sharpened by thought; neither adorned nor beautiful, and not made by an arrow-maker.

2.

2.

“Na kaṇṇāyatamuttena, nāpi morūpasevinā;

Tenamhi hadaye viddho, sabbaṅgaparidāhinā.

Not shot having been drawn to the ear, nor fletched with peacock feathers; by that I am pierced in the heart—by that which sets all my limbs ablaze.

3.

3.

“Āvedhañca [P 2.0276] na passāmi, yato ruhiramassave;

Yāva ayoniso cittaṃ, sayaṃ me dukkhamābhata”nti.

I see no wound from which blood might flow; to such an extent was the mind unwisely directed, that I myself have brought this suffering upon me.

Tattha [M 2.0252] saṅkapparāgadhotenāti kāmavitakkasampayuttarāgadhotena. Vitakkanisitena cāti teneva rāgodakena vitakkapāsāṇe nisitena. Nālaṅkatena bhadrenāti neva alaṅkatena bhadrena, analaṅkatena bībhacchenāti attho. Usukārākatena cāti usukārehipi akatena. Na kaṇṇāyatamuttenāti yāva dakkhiṇakaṇṇacūḷakaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā amuttakena. Nāpi morūpasevināti morapattagijjhapattādīhi akatūpasevanena. Tenamhi hadaye viddhoti tena kilesakaṇḍenāhaṃ hadaye viddho amhi. Sabbaṅgaparidāhināti sabbāni aṅgāni paridahanasamatthena. Mahārāja, tena hi kilesakaṇḍena hadaye viddhakālato paṭṭhāya mama aggi padittāniva sabbāni aṅgāni ḍayhantīti dasseti.

In those verses: 'Washed with the lust of intention' means washed with the lust associated with thoughts of sensual desire. 'And sharpened by thought' means sharpened on the whetstone of thought with that very water of lust. 'Neither adorned nor beautiful' means not adorned and beautiful, but rather unadorned and repulsive—this is the meaning. 'And not made by an arrow-maker' means not crafted by arrow-makers. 'Not shot having been drawn to the ear' means not released after being drawn as far as the tip of the right ear. 'Nor fletched with peacock feathers' means not fletched with peacock feathers, vulture feathers, and so on. 'By that I am pierced in the heart' means 'I am pierced in the heart by that arrow of defilement.' 'Sets all my limbs ablaze' means capable of consuming all limbs. He shows: 'Great king, from the moment my heart was pierced by that arrow of defilement, all my limbs have been burning as if set on fire.'

Āvedhañca na passāmīti viddhaṭṭhāne vaṇañca na passāmi. Yato ruhiramassaveti yato me āvedhato lohitaṃ pagghareyya, taṃ na passāmīti attho. Yāva ayoniso cittanti ettha yāvāti daḷhatthe nipāto, ativiya daḷhaṃ katvā ayoniso cittaṃ vaḍḍhitanti attho. Sayaṃ me dukkhamābhatanti attanāva mayā attano dukkhaṃ ānītanti.

'I see no wound' means I do not see a wound at the point of entry. 'From which blood might flow' means 'from which piercing blood might flow, that I do not see'—this is the meaning. Here, in the phrase 'the mind was so unwisely directed,' the word 'yāva' is an intensive particle, meaning 'the mind has been developed unwisely to a very great extent.' 'I myself have brought this suffering' means 'I myself have brought this suffering upon myself.'

Evaṃ [V 2.0231] bodhisatto imāhi tīhi gāthāhi rañño dhammaṃ desetvā rājānaṃ paṇṇasālato bahi katvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā naṭṭhaṃ jhānaṃ uppādetvā paṇṇasālāya nikkhamitvā ākāse nisinno rājānaṃ ovaditvā “mahārāja, ahaṃ himavantameva gamissāmī”ti vatvā “na sakkā, bhante, gantu”nti vuccamānopi “mahārāja, mayā idha vasantena evarūpo vippakāro patto, idāni na sakkā idha vasitu”nti rañño yācantasseva ākāse uppatitvā himavantaṃ gantvā tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus, the Bodhisatta taught the king the Dhamma with these three verses. He then asked the king to step outside the leaf-hut, performed the kasiṇa preliminary exercises, restored his lost jhāna, and emerged from the leaf-hut. Seated in the sky, he advised the king, saying, 'Great king, I shall return to the Himalayas.' Though the king pleaded, 'Venerable sir, you should not go,' he replied, 'Great king, by staying here I have come to such a state of ruin; it is no longer proper for me to live here.' Even as the king was pleading, he rose into the air and returned to the Himalayas, where he remained for the rest of his life and was reborn in the Brahma-realm.

Satthā [P 2.0277] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhahi. Keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahanto ahesuṃ. “Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of Arahantship. Some became Stream-enterers, some Once-returners, some Non-returners, and some became Arahants. He identified the Jātaka thus: 'At that time, the king of Benares was Ānanda, and the ascetic was I myself.'

Saṅkapparāgajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The explanation of the Saṅkapparāga Jātaka, the first.

[252] 2. Tilamuṭṭhijātakavaṇṇanā

[252] 2. The Explanation of the Tilamuṭṭhi Jātaka

Ajjāpi [M 2.0253] me taṃ manasīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ kodhanaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Aññataro kira, bhikkhu, kodhano ahosi upāyāsabahulo, appampi vutto samāno kuppi abhisajji, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātvākāsi. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu kodhano upāyāsabahulo uddhane pakkhittaloṇaṃ viya taṭataṭāyanto vicarati, evarūpe nikkodhane buddhasāsane pabbajito samāno kodhamattampi niggaṇhituṃ na sakkotī”ti. Satthā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ pesetvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, kodhano”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ayaṃ kodhano ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Even now, that is in my mind'—this the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana, concerning a certain irritable monk. It is said that a certain monk was prone to anger and full of vexation; even when spoken to slightly, he would become angry and abusive, displaying wrath, hatred, and discontent. One day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, so-and-so monk is angry and full of vexation, going about crackling and sputtering like salt thrown into a furnace. Having gone forth in the Buddha's dispensation, which is free from anger, he cannot even restrain a little anger.' Hearing their talk, the Teacher sent a monk to summon him and asked, 'Is it true, monk, that you are irritable?' When he replied, 'Yes, venerable sir,' the Teacher said, 'Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he was irritable,' and he recounted the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa putto brahmadattakumāro nāma ahosi. Porāṇakarājāno ca attano putte “evaṃ ete nihatamānadappā sītuṇhakkhamā lokacārittaññū ca bhavissantī”ti attano nagare disāpāmokkhaācariye vijjamānepi sippuggahaṇatthāya dūre tiroraṭṭhaṃ pesenti, tasmā sopi rājā soḷasavassuddesikaṃ puttaṃ pakkosāpetvā ekapaṭalikaupāhanā [V 2.0232] ca paṇṇacchattañca kahāpaṇasahassañca datvā “tāta, takkasilaṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggaṇhā”ti [P 2.0278] pesesi. So “sādhū”ti mātāpitaro vanditvā nikkhamitvā anupubbena takkasilaṃ patvā ācariyassa gehaṃ pucchitvā ācariye māṇavakānaṃ sippaṃ vācetvā uṭṭhāya gharadvāre caṅkamante gehaṃ gantvā yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhito ācariyaṃ addasa, tattheva upāhanā omuñcitvā chattañca apanetvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. So tassa kilantabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgantukasaṅgahaṃ kāresi. Kumāro bhuttabhojano thokaṃ vissamitvā ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi, “kuto āgatosi, tātā”ti ca vutte “bārāṇasito”ti āha. “Kassa puttosī”ti? “Bārāṇasirañño”ti. “Kenatthenāgatosī”ti? “Sippaṃ uggaṇhatthāyā”ti. “Kiṃ te ācariyabhāgo ābhato, udāhu dhammantevāsiko hotukāmosī”ti? So “ācariyabhāgo me [M 2.0254] ābhato”ti vatvā ācariyassa pādamūle sahassatthavikaṃ ṭhapetvā vandi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, he had a son named Prince Brahmadatta. The ancient kings, thinking, ‘In this way they will have their pride and arrogance subdued, will become patient in heat and cold, and will know the ways of the world,’ would send their sons to a distant foreign land for the purpose of learning the arts, even though there were world-renowned teachers in their own city. Therefore, that king summoned his sixteen-year-old son, gave him a pair of single-soled sandals, a leaf umbrella, and a thousand coins, and sent him, saying, ‘Dear son, go to Takkasilā and learn the arts.’ Saying, ‘Very well,’ he paid homage to his parents and departed. In due course, he reached Takkasilā, inquired about the teacher’s house, and went there. At that time, the teacher, having taught the arts to his pupils, had risen and was walking up and down at the door of his house. The prince went and stood at the place where he saw the teacher. There, he removed his sandals, set aside his umbrella, paid homage to the teacher, and stood. Recognizing that he was weary, the teacher extended hospitality to the guest. After the prince had eaten and rested a little, he approached the teacher, paid homage, and stood there. When asked, ‘Where have you come from, dear boy?’ he replied, ‘From Benares.’ ‘Whose son are you?’ ‘The son of the king of Benares.’ ‘For what purpose have you come?’ ‘To learn the arts.’ ‘Have you brought the teacher’s fee, or do you wish to be a resident pupil?’ He said, ‘I have brought the teacher’s fee,’ and having placed the purse containing a thousand coins at the teacher’s feet, he paid homage and sat in a suitable place.

Dhammantevāsikā divā ācariyassa kammaṃ katvā rattiṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhanti, ācariyabhāgadāyakā gehe jeṭṭhaputtā viya hutvā sippameva uggaṇhanti. Tasmā sopi ācariyo sallahukena subhanakkhattena kumārassa sippaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Kumāropi sippaṃ uggaṇhanto ekadivasaṃ ācariyena saddhiṃ nhāyituṃ agamāsi. Athekā mahallikā itthī tilāni sete katvā pattharitvā rakkhamānā nisīdi. Kumāro setatile disvā khāditukāmo hutvā ekaṃ tilamuṭṭhiṃ gahetvā khādi, mahallikā “taṇhāluko eso”ti kiñci avatvā tuṇhī ahosi. So punadivasepi tāya velāya tatheva akāsi, sāpi naṃ na kiñci āha. Itaro tatiyadivasepi tathevākāsi, tadā mahallikā “disāpāmokkho ācariyo attano antevāsikehi maṃ vilumpāpetī”ti bāhā paggayha kandi. Ācariyo nivattitvā “kiṃ etaṃ[P 2.0279], ammā”ti pucchi. “Sāmi, antevāsiko te mayā katānaṃ setatilānaṃ ajjekaṃ muṭṭhiṃ khādi, hiyyo ekaṃ, pare ekaṃ, nanu evaṃ khādanto mama santakaṃ sabbaṃ nāsessatī”ti. “Amma, mā rodi, mūlaṃ te dāpessāmī”ti. “Na me, sāmi, mūlenattho, yathā panesa kumāro puna evaṃ na karoti, tathā taṃ sikkhāpehī”ti. Ācariyo “tena hi passa, ammā”ti dvīhi māṇavehi taṃ kumāraṃ dvīsu hatthesu gāhāpetvā veḷupesikaṃ gahetvā “puna evarūpaṃ mā akāsī”ti tikkhattuṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ pahari. Kumāro ācariyassa kujjhitvā rattāni akkhīni katvā pādapiṭṭhito yāva kesamatthakā olokesi. Sopissa kujjhitvā olokitabhāvaṃ aññāsi. Kumāro sippaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā “anuyogaṃ datvā mārāpetabbo esa mayā”ti tena katadosaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā gamanakāle ācariyaṃ vanditvā “yadāhaṃ, ācariya, bārāṇasirajjaṃ patvā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pesessāmi, tadā tumhe āgaccheyyāthā”ti sasineho viya paṭiññaṃ gahetvā pakkāmi.

Resident pupils perform tasks for the teacher during the day and learn the arts at night, while those who pay the teacher’s fee live like the eldest sons in the house and only learn the arts. Therefore, that teacher, on an easy and auspicious day, began teaching the arts to the prince. While learning the arts, one day the prince went to bathe with the teacher. Then an old woman sat guarding some sesame seeds that she had cleaned and spread out. Seeing the white sesame seeds and desiring to eat them, the prince took a handful and ate. The old woman, thinking, ‘This one is greedy,’ said nothing and remained silent. On the next day, at the same time, he did the same. She also said nothing to him. On the third day, he did the same. Then the old woman cried out, raising her arms, ‘The world-renowned teacher is letting his pupils rob me!’ The teacher turned back and asked, ‘What is it, mother?’ ‘Master, your pupil ate a handful of my cleaned sesame seeds today, one yesterday, and one the day before. Surely, if he eats like this, he will destroy all my property!’ ‘Mother, do not cry, I will have the price paid to you.’ ‘Master, I do not need the price; but teach this prince so that he does not do this again.’ The teacher said, ‘Then watch, mother,’ and having two young men hold the prince by his two hands and taking a bamboo slip, he struck him three times on the back, saying, ‘Do not do such a thing again.’ The prince, angry at the teacher, with his eyes turned red, glared at him from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair. The teacher also knew that he was looking at him with anger. After finishing his studies, the prince thought, ‘I must have him killed after finding some fault,’ and keeping the offense committed by the teacher in his heart, he paid homage to the teacher when departing and said, ‘Teacher, when I have attained the kingship of Benares and send for you, please come.’ Having obtained a promise as if with affection, he departed.

So [V 2.0233] bārāṇasiṃ patvā mātāpitaro vanditvā sippaṃ dassesi. Rājā “jīvamānena me putto diṭṭho, jīvamānovassa rajjasiriṃ passāmī”ti puttaṃ rajje patiṭṭhāpesi. So rajjasiriṃ anubhavamāno ācariyena katadosaṃ [M 2.0255] saritvā uppannakodho “mārāpessāmi na”nti pakkosanatthāya ācariyassa dūtaṃ pāhesi. Ācariyo “taruṇakāle naṃ saññāpetuṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti agantvā tassa rañño majjhimavayakāle “idāni naṃ saññāpetuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti gantvā rājadvāre ṭhatvā “takkasilācariyo āgato”ti ārocāpesi. Rājā tuṭṭho brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpetvā taṃ attano santikaṃ āgataṃ disvāva kodhaṃ uppādetvā rattāni akkhīni katvā amacce āmantetvā “bho, ajjāpi me ācariyena pahaṭaṭṭhānaṃ rujjati, ācariyo nalāṭena maccuṃ ādāya ‘marissāmī’ti [P 2.0280] āgato, ajjassa jīvitaṃ natthī”ti vatvā purimā dve gāthā avoca –

Arriving at Benares, he paid homage to his parents and demonstrated his skills. The king, thinking, ‘I have seen my son while I am alive, let me see his royal glory while I am alive,’ established his son in the kingdom. While enjoying royal glory, the prince remembered the offense committed by the teacher and, becoming angry, sent a messenger to the teacher with gifts to summon him, thinking, ‘I will have him killed.’ The teacher, thinking, ‘I will not be able to reason with him in his youth,’ did not go. In the king’s middle age, thinking, ‘Now I will be able to reason with him,’ he went and, standing at the palace gate, had it announced, ‘The teacher from Takkasilā has arrived.’ The king, pleased, had the brahmin summoned. As soon as he saw the brahmin approaching him, he became enraged, and with eyes turned red, he addressed his ministers, ‘Bho! Even today the spot where the teacher struck me aches. Today the teacher has come with death on his forehead, thinking, “I shall die.” Today his life is at an end.’ Saying this, he spoke these verses:

4.

4.

“Ajjāpi me taṃ manasi, yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ tilamuṭṭhiyā;

Bāhāya maṃ gahetvāna, laṭṭhiyā anutāḷayi.

“Even today it is in my mind, how you, on account of a handful of sesame seeds, seized me by the arm and struck me with a stick.”

5.

5.

“Nanu jīvite na ramasi, yenāsi brāhmaṇāgato;

Yaṃ maṃ bāhā gahetvāna, tikkhattuṃ anutāḷayī”ti.

“Surely you do not delight in life, O brahmin, that you have come here—you who, having seized me by the arms, struck me three times!”

Tattha yaṃ maṃ bāhāya manti dvīsu padesu upayogavacanaṃ anutāḷanagahaṇāpekkhaṃ. Yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ tilamuṭṭhiyā kāraṇā anutāḷayi, anutāḷento ca maṃ bāhāya gahetvā anutāḷayi, taṃ anutāḷanaṃ ajjāpi me manasīti ayañhettha attho. Nanu jīvite na ramasīti maññe tvaṃ attano jīvitamhi nābhiramasi. Yenāsi brāhmaṇāgatoti yasmā brāhmaṇa idha mama santikaṃ āgatosi. Yaṃ maṃ bāhā gahetvānāti yaṃ mama bāhā gahetvā, yaṃ maṃ bāhāya gahetvātipi attho. Tikkhattuṃ anutāḷayīti tayo vāre veḷulaṭṭhiyā tāḷesi, ajja dāni tassa phalaṃ vindāhīti naṃ maraṇena santajjento evamāha.

Here, in the two phrases 'yaṃ maṃ' and 'bāhāya', the word 'maṃ' is in the accusative case, depending on the actions of striking and seizing. 'The fact that you struck me because of a handful of sesame seeds, and while striking, you seized me by the arm and struck me—that striking is in my mind even today'; this is the meaning here. 'Surely you do not delight in life?' means 'I think you do not delight in your own life.' 'By which you have come, O brahmin' means 'because you, O brahmin, have come here to my presence.' 'In that you grabbed my arm' means 'having grabbed my arm'; 'having grabbed me by the arm' is also the meaning. 'Struck three times' means 'he struck three times with a bamboo stick.' Threatening him with death, he said: 'Now, today, experience the fruit of that!'

Taṃ sutvā ācariyo tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the teacher spoke the third verse:

6.

6.

“Ariyo anariyaṃ kubbantaṃ, yo daṇḍena nisedhati;

Sāsanaṃ taṃ na taṃ veraṃ, iti naṃ paṇḍitā vidū”ti.

"A noble one who restrains with punishment one who acts ignobly: that is discipline, not enmity—so the wise understand it."

Tattha [V 2.0234][M 2.0256] ariyoti sundarādhivacanametaṃ. So pana ariyo catubbidho hoti ācāraariyo dassanaariyo liṅgaariyo paṭivedhaariyoti. Tattha manusso vā hotu tiracchāno vā, ariyācāre ṭhito ācāraariyo nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Here, 'noble' (ariya) is a term for excellence. That noble one is of four kinds: noble by conduct, noble by vision, noble by appearance, and noble by penetration. Among these, whether a human or an animal, one established in noble conduct is called 'noble by conduct.' And this has been said:

“Ariyavattasi vakkaṅga, yo piṇḍamapacāyati;

Cajāmi te taṃ bhattāraṃ, gacchathūbho yathāsukha”nti. (jā. 2.21.106);

"You are of noble conduct, O crooked-limbed one, who honors with almsfood; I renounce that husband of yours; go, both of you, as you please."

Rūpena pana iriyāpathena ca pāsādikena dassanīyena samannāgato dassanaariyo nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

One endowed with a pleasing and admirable form and deportment is called 'noble by vision.' And this was said:

“Ariyāvakāsosi [P 2.0281] pasannanetto, maññe bhavaṃ pabbajito kulamhā;

Kathaṃ nu cittāni pahāya bhoge, pabbaji nikkhamma gharā sapaññā”ti. (jā. 2.17.143);

"You have the bearing of a noble one, with serene eyes; I think, sir, you have gone forth from a good family. How, having abandoned thoughts of sensual pleasures, did you wisely go forth, leaving home?"

Nivāsanapārupanaliṅgaggahaṇena pana samaṇasadiso hutvā vicaranto dussīlopi liṅgaariyo nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

But even an immoral person, wandering about like an ascetic by adopting the sign of wearing robes, is called 'noble by sign'. In reference to this, it was said:

“Chadanaṃ katvāna subbatānaṃ, pakkhandī kuladūsako pagabbho;

Māyāvī asaññato palāpo, patirūpena caraṃ sa maggadūsī”ti.

"Making a cloak of the virtuous, he plunges in, a defiler of families, insolent; deceitful, unrestrained, a prattler, he walks in disguise, a defiler of the Path."

Buddhādayo pana paṭivedhaariyā nāma. Tena vuttaṃ – “ariyā vuccanti buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca buddhasāvakā cā”ti. Tesu idha ācāraariyova adhippeto.

But the Buddhas and others are called 'noble by penetration'. Therefore it is said: "The noble ones are called the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Buddha's disciples." Among these, it is 'noble by conduct' that is intended here.

Anariyanti dussīlaṃ pāpadhammaṃ. Kubbantanti pāṇātipātādikaṃ pañcavidhadussīlyakammaṃ karontaṃ, ekameva vā etaṃ atthapadaṃ, anariyaṃ hīnaṃ lāmakaṃ pañcaverabhayakammaṃ karontaṃ puggalaṃ. Yoti khattiyādīsu yo koci. Daṇḍenāti yena kenaci paharaṇakena. Nisedhatīti “mā puna evarūpaṃ karī”ti paharanto nivāreti. Sāsanaṃ taṃ na taṃ veranti taṃ, mahārāja, akattabbaṃ karonte puttadhītaro vā antevāsike vā evaṃ paharitvā nisedhanaṃ nāma imasmiṃ loke sāsanaṃ anusiṭṭhi ovādo, na veraṃ. Iti naṃ paṇḍitā [M 2.0257] vidūti evametaṃ paṇḍitā jānanti. Tasmā, mahārāja, tvampi evaṃ jāna, na evarūpe ṭhāne veraṃ kātuṃ arahasi. Sace hi [V 2.0235] tvaṃ, mahārāja, mayā evaṃ sikkhāpito nābhavissa, atha gacchante kāle pūvasakkhaliādīni ceva phalāphalādīni ca haranto corakammesu paluddho anupubbena sandhicchedanapanthadūhanagāmaghātakādīni katvā “rājāparādhiko coro”ti sahoḍḍhaṃ gahetvā rañño dassito “gacchathassa dosānurūpaṃ daṇḍaṃ upanethā”ti daṇḍabhayaṃ pāpuṇissa, kuto te evarūpā sampatti abhavissa, nanu maṃ nissāya idaṃ issariyaṃ tayā laddhanti evaṃ ācariyo rājānaṃ saññāpesi[P 2.0282]. Parivāretvā ṭhitā amaccāpissa kathaṃ sutvā “saccaṃ, deva, idaṃ issariyaṃ tumhākaṃ ācariyasseva santaka”nti āhaṃsu.

'Anariya' means an immoral person, one of evil nature. 'Kubbanta' means a person performing the five kinds of immoral action such as killing living beings; or this is a single phrase: a person performing ignoble, low, base actions that lead to the five kinds of enmity and fear. 'Yo' means anyone among the khattiyas and others. 'Daṇḍena' means by any kind of striking instrument. 'Nisedhati' means one restrains by striking, saying, 'Do not do such a thing again.' 'That is discipline, not enmity' means: that restraint, O great king, by striking one's sons, daughters, or pupils who are doing what should not be done, is called in this world discipline, instruction, and admonishment; it is not enmity. 'So the wise understand it' means the wise know it in this way. Therefore, O great king, you too should understand this; you should not harbor enmity in such a situation. For if you, O great king, had not been trained by me in this way, then, as time passed, you would have become addicted to stealing things like bean-cakes, sesame-fried snacks, fruits, and produce. Gradually, you would have progressed to housebreaking, highway robbery, and looting villages; and having been caught red-handed as a thief who had offended the king, you would have been shown to the king, who would say, 'Go, inflict upon him a punishment fitting his crime.' Thus, you would have faced the fear of punishment. How then could such prosperity have come to you? Is it not through reliance on me that this sovereignty was obtained by you? In this way, the teacher convinced the king. The ministers standing around, having heard his words, said, 'Truly, Your Majesty, this sovereignty of yours belongs to your teacher alone.'

Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā ācariyassa guṇaṃ sallakkhetvā “sabbissariyaṃ te, ācariya, dammi, rajjaṃ paṭicchā”ti āha. Ācariyo “na me, mahārāja, rajjenattho”ti paṭikkhipi. Rājā takkasilaṃ pesetvā ācariyassa puttadāraṃ āharāpetvā mahantaṃ issariyaṃ datvā tameva purohitaṃ katvā pituṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā tassovāde ṭhito dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi.

At that moment, the king, recognizing the teacher’s virtues, said, 'Teacher, I give you all sovereignty; accept the kingdom.' The teacher declined, saying, 'O great king, I have no need for a kingdom.' The king then sent to Takkasilā and had the teacher’s wife and children brought, bestowed great sovereignty upon him, appointed him as his royal chaplain, established him in the position of a father, and, abiding by his advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and was destined for heaven.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kodhano bhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi, bahū janā sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmino ahesuṃ. “Tadā rājā kodhano bhikkhu ahosi, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and declared the Truths, identified the birth story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the angry monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning, and many people became Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners. “At that time, the angry monk was the king, and I myself was the teacher.”

Tilamuṭṭhijātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Tilamuṭṭhi Jātaka is the second.

[253] 3. Maṇikaṇṭhajātakavaṇṇanā

[253] 3. The Commentary on the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka

Mamannapānanti idaṃ satthā āḷaviṃ nissāya aggāḷave cetiye viharanto kuṭikārasikkhāpadaṃ (pārā. 342) ārabbha kathesi. Āḷavakā hi bhikkhū saññācikāya kuṭiyo kārayamānā yācanabahulā viññattibahulā vihariṃsu “purisaṃ detha, purisatthakaraṃ dethā”tiādīni vadantā. Manussā [M 2.0258] upaddutā yācanāya upaddutā viññattiyā bhikkhū disvā ubbijjiṃsupi uttasiṃsupi palāyiṃsupi. Athāyasmā mahākassapo āḷaviṃ upasaṅkamitvā piṇḍāya pāvisi, manussā therampi disvā tatheva paṭipajjiṃsu. So pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto bhikkhū āmantetvā “pubbāyaṃ, āvuso, āḷavī sulabhapiṇḍā, idāni kasmā [V 2.0236] dullabhapiṇḍā jātā”ti pucchitvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā bhagavati āḷaviṃ āgantvā aggāḷavacetiye viharante bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā etasmiṃ kāraṇe bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā āḷavake bhikkhū paṭipucchi [P 2.0283] – “saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, saññācikāya kuṭiyo kārethā”ti. “Saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte te bhikkhū garahitvā “bhikkhave, yācanā nāmesā sattaratanaparipuṇṇe nāgabhavane vasantānaṃ nāgānampi amanāpā, pageva manussānaṃ, yesaṃ ekaṃ kahāpaṇakaṃ uppādentānaṃ pāsāṇato maṃsaṃ uppāṭanakālo viya hotī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Regarding the verse 'My food and drink', the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at the Aggāḷava Shrine near Āḷavī, concerning the training rule on building huts. For the monks of Āḷavī, while having huts built by asking for materials, lived with excessive begging and excessive soliciting, saying, 'Give a man, give a worker,' and so on. People, harassed by the begging and harassed by the soliciting, would get agitated, terrified, and flee upon seeing the monks. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa came to Āḷavī and entered for alms. Even seeing the Elder, the people behaved in the same way. After the meal, having returned from his almsround, he addressed the monks: 'Friends, formerly in this Āḷavī, alms were easy to get; why are they now difficult to get?' Hearing that reason, when the Blessed One had come to Āḷavī and was dwelling at the Aggāḷava Shrine, he approached the Blessed One and reported this matter. The Teacher, on account of this matter, had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks of Āḷavī: 'Is it true, monks, that you are having huts built by asking for materials?' 'It is true, Venerable Sir,' they replied. Rebuking those monks, he said: 'Monks, this begging is unpleasant even to the nāgas living in the nāga realm which is full of the seven treasures, much more so to humans, for whom producing even a single kahāpaṇa is like the time of tearing a piece of stone from a rock.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mahāvibhave brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Tassa ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle aññopi puññavā satto tassa mātu kucchismiṃ nibbatti. Te ubhopi bhātaro vayappattā mātāpitūnaṃ kālakiriyāya saṃviggahadayā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā gaṅgātīre paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā vasiṃsu. Tesu jeṭṭhassa uparigaṅgāya paṇṇasālā ahosi, kaniṭṭhassa adhogaṅgāya. Athekadivasaṃ maṇikaṇṭho nāma nāgarājā nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā gaṅgātīre māṇavakavesena vicaranto kaniṭṭhassa assamaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi, te aññamaññaṃ sammodanīyakathaṃ kathetvā vissāsikā ahesuṃ, vinā vattituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Maṇikaṇṭho abhiṇhaṃ kaniṭṭhatāpasassa santikaṃ āgantvā kathāsallāpena nisīditvā gamanakāle tāpase sinehena attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā bhogehi tāpasaṃ parikkhipanto parissajitvā uparimuddhani mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ dhāretvā thokaṃ vasitvā taṃ sinehaṃ vinodetvā sarīraṃ viniveṭhetvā tāpasaṃ vanditvā sakaṭṭhānameva gacchati. Tāpaso tassa bhayena kiso ahosi lūkho dubbaṇṇo uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto dhamanisanthatagatto.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family of great wealth. During the time when he was able to run and wander about, another virtuous being was conceived in his mother's womb. Both brothers, when they reached of age, their hearts stirred by the death of their parents, went forth as ascetics. They built leaf huts on the banks of the Ganges and lived there. Of these, the elder brother's leaf hut was upstream on the Ganges, while the younger brother's was downstream. One day, a nāga king named Maṇikaṇṭha left the nāga abode and, wandering along the bank of the Ganges in the guise of a young man, went to the younger ascetic's hermitage, paid homage, and sat to one side. They exchanged friendly greetings and became intimate, unable to live apart from each other. Maṇikaṇṭha frequently visited the younger ascetic, sat chatting with him, and when it was time to leave, out of affection for the ascetic, he would abandon his human form, envelop the ascetic with his coils, embrace him, and spread a large hood over his head. After staying for a short while, he would satisfy his affection, uncoil his body, pay homage to the ascetic, and return to his own place. The ascetic, out of fear of the nāga, became thin, haggard, discolored, pale and yellowish, with his veins standing out over his body.

So [M 2.0259] ekadivasaṃ bhātu santikaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ so pucchi – “kissa, tvaṃ bho, kiso lūkho dubbaṇṇo uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto dhamanisanthatagatto”ti. So tassa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “kiṃ pana, tvaṃ bho, tassa nāgarājassa āgamanaṃ [P 2.0284] icchasi, na icchasī”ti puṭṭho “na icchāmī”ti vatvā “so pana nāgarājā tava santikaṃ āgacchanto kiṃ piḷandhanaṃ piḷandhitvā āgacchatī”ti vutte “maṇiratana”nti āha. Tena hi tvaṃ tasmiṃ nāgarāje tava santikaṃ āgantvā anisinneyeva “maṇiṃ me dehī”ti yāca, evaṃ so nāgo taṃ bhogehi aparikkhipitvāva gamissati. Punadivase assamapadadvāre ṭhatvā āgacchantameva naṃ yāceyyāsi, tatiyadivase gaṅgātīre ṭhatvā udakā ummujjantameva naṃ yāceyyāsi, evaṃ so tava santikaṃ puna na āgamissatīti.

One day, that younger ascetic went to his brother. Then the elder ascetic asked him, “Friend, why are you so thin, haggard, discolored, pale and yellowish, with your veins standing out over your body?” He told him the situation, and when asked, “Do you, friend, desire the coming of that nāga king, or not?” he replied, “I do not.” When asked, “When that nāga king comes to you, what ornament does he wear?” he answered, “A precious jewel.” “In that case, when that nāga king comes to you, before he even sits down, ask him for the jewel. In this way, the nāga will leave without enveloping you in his coils. The next day, stand at the door of your hermitage and ask him for the jewel as he arrives. On the third day, stand on the bank of the Ganges and ask him for the jewel as he emerges from the water. If you ask in this way, the nāga will not come to you again.”

Tāpaso [V 2.0237] “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā attano paṇṇasālaṃ gantvā punadivase nāgarājānaṃ āgantvā ṭhitamattameva “etaṃ attano piḷandhanamaṇiṃ me dehī”ti yāci, so anisīditvāva palāyi. Atha naṃ dutiyadivase assamapadadvāre ṭhatvā āgacchantameva “hiyyo me maṇiratanaṃ nādāsi, ajja dānaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Nāgo assamapadaṃ apavisitvāva palāyi. Tatiyadivase udakato ummujjantameva naṃ “ajja me tatiyo divaso yācantassa, dehi dāni me etaṃ maṇiratana”nti āha. Nāgarājā udake ṭhatvāva tāpasaṃ paṭikkhipanto dve gāthā āha –

The ascetic, agreeing with “Very well,” went to his own leaf hut. The next day, as soon as the nāga king arrived and stood there, he asked, “Give me that ornament-jewel of yours.” The nāga fled without even sitting down. Then, on the second day, standing at the entrance of the hermitage, as the nāga was arriving, he said, “Yesterday you did not give me the precious jewel; today it is right that I should receive it.” The nāga fled without entering the hermitage grounds. On the third day, as the nāga was emerging from the water, he said, “Today is the third day of my asking; now give me this precious jewel.” The nāga king, standing in the water, rejecting the ascetic's request, spoke these two verses:

7.

7.

“Mamannapānaṃ vipulaṃ uḷāraṃ, uppajjatīmassa maṇissa hetu;

Taṃ te na dassaṃ atiyācakosi, na cāpi te assamamāgamissaṃ.

“My abundant and excellent food and drink arise because of this jewel. I will not give it to you, for you are an excessive beggar, nor will I come to your hermitage again.

8.

8.

“Susū yathā sakkharadhotapāṇī, tāsesimaṃ selaṃ yācamāno;

Taṃ te na dassaṃ atiyācakosi, na cāpi te assamamāgamissa”nti.

“Like a youth with a whetted sword in his hand, you terrify me by asking for this jewel. I will not give it to you, for you are an excessive beggar, nor will I come to your hermitage again.”

Tattha [P 2.0285] mamannapānanti mama yāgubhattādidibbabhojanaṃ aṭṭhapānakabhedañca dibbapānaṃ. Vipulanti bahu. Uḷāranti seṭṭhaṃ paṇītaṃ. Taṃ teti taṃ maṇiṃ tuyhaṃ. Atiyācakosīti [M 2.0260] kālañca pamāṇañca atikkamitvā ajja tīṇi divasāni mayhaṃ piyaṃ manāpaṃ maṇiratanaṃ yācamāno atikkamma yācakosi. Na cāpi teti na kevalaṃ na dassaṃ, assamampi te nāgamissaṃ. Susū yathāti yathā nāma yuvā taruṇamanusso. Sakkharadhotapāṇīti sakkharāya dhotapāṇi, telena pāsāṇe dhotaasihattho. Tāsesimaṃ selaṃ yācamānoti imaṃ maṇiṃ yācanto tvaṃ kañcanatharukhaggaṃ abbāhitvā “sīsaṃ te chindāmī”ti vadanto taruṇapuriso viya maṃ tāsesi.

Therein, 'my food and drink' refers to my divine food, such as gruel and cooked rice, and divine drink, consisting of the eight kinds of beverages. 'Abundant' means much. 'Excellent' means supreme and exquisite. Regarding 'that to you': this means 'that jewel to you'. 'You are an excessive beggar' means that, having transgressed the proper time and measure by asking for my beloved and delightful precious jewel for three days now, you have become an excessive beggar. 'Nor will I come to your hermitage' means not only will I not give it, but I will not even come to your hermitage. 'Just as a youth' means just as a youthful, vigorous person. 'Hand washed with gravel' means a hand washed with gravel, or a hand holding a sword polished with oil on a stone. 'You threaten me, begging for this jewel' means 'begging for this jewel, you threaten me just like a young man who, having drawn a golden-hilted sword, says, “I will cut off your head.”'

Evaṃ vatvā so nāgarājā udake nimujjitvā attano nāgabhavanameva gantvā na paccāgañchi. Atha so tāpaso tassa dassanīyassa nāgarājassa adassanena bhiyyosomattāya kiso ahosi lūkho dubbaṇṇo uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto dhamanisanthatagatto. Atha jeṭṭhatāpaso “kaniṭṭhassa pavattiṃ jānissāmī”ti tassa santikaṃ āgantvā taṃ bhiyyosomattāya paṇḍuroginaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho, bho, tvaṃ bhiyyosomattāya paṇḍurogī jāto”ti vatvā “tassa dassanīyassa nāgarājassa adassanenā”ti sutvā “ayaṃ tāpaso nāgarājānaṃ vinā vattituṃ na sakkotī”ti sallakkhetvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, the nāga king plunged into the water and went to his own nāga abode, never to return. Then that ascetic, through not seeing the beautiful nāga king, became exceedingly thin, haggard, discolored, pale and yellowish, with his veins standing out over his body. Then the elder ascetic, wishing to find out about his younger brother, came to him and, seeing him even more afflicted with pallor, said, “Why, friend, have you become so exceedingly pale?” Hearing that it was through not seeing the beautiful nāga king, he realized, “This ascetic cannot live without the nāga king,” and spoke the third verse:

9.

9.

“Na [V 2.0238] taṃ yāce yassa piyaṃ jigīse, desso hoti atiyācanāya;

Nāgo maṇiṃ yācito brāhmaṇena, adassanaṃyeva tadajjhagamā”ti.

“One should not ask for what one knows is dear to another; one becomes hateful through excessive begging. The nāga, asked for his jewel by the brahmin, went away and was never seen again.”

Tattha na taṃ yāceti taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ na yāceyya. Yassa piyaṃ jigīseti yaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ assa puggalassa piyanti jāneyya. Desso hotīti appiyo hoti. Atiyācanāyāti pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvā varabhaṇḍaṃ yācanto tāya atiyācanāya. Adassanaṃyeva tadajjhagamāti tato paṭṭhāya adassanameva gatoti.

Herein, 'one should not beg from him' means one should not beg for that item. 'Whose dear possession one desires' means one knows that the item is dear to that person. 'He becomes hateful' means he becomes disliked. 'Through excessive begging' means asking for a choice item by transgressing the limit, through that excessive begging. 'He simply went out of sight' means from that moment onward, he was simply gone from sight.

Evaṃ pana taṃ vatvā “ito dāni paṭṭhāya mā socī”ti samassāsetvā jeṭṭhabhātā attano assamameva gato. Athāparabhāge te [P 2.0286] dvepi bhātaro abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Having spoken thus to the younger ascetic and consoled him, saying, "From now on, do not grieve," the elder brother went to his own hermitage. Later, both brothers developed the supernormal powers and meditative attainments, and were reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā [M 2.0261] “evaṃ, bhikkhave, sattaratanaparipuṇṇe nāgabhavane vasantānaṃ nāgānampi yācanā nāma amanāpā, kimaṅgaṃ pana manussāna”nti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kaniṭṭho ānando ahosi, jeṭṭho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even for nāgas dwelling in nāga abodes replete with the seven treasures, begging is unpleasant—how much more so for humans?" Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he identified the birth: "At that time, the younger brother was Ānanda, and the elder brother was I myself."

Maṇikaṇṭhajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka is finished.

[254] 4. Kuṇḍakakucchisindhavajātakavaṇṇanā

[254] 4. The Commentary on the Kuṇḍakakucchi-Sindhava Jātaka

Bhutvā tiṇaparighāsanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāriputtattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye sammāsambuddhe sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ vasitvā cārikaṃ caritvā puna paccāgate manussā “āgantukasakkāraṃ karissāmā”ti buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ dadanti. Vihāre ekaṃ dhammaghosakabhikkhuṃ ṭhapesuṃ, so ye ye āgantvā yattake bhikkhū icchanti, tesaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhū vicāretvā deti.

'Having eaten grass and fodder'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Sāriputta. Once, when the Perfectly Enlightened One, having spent the rains retreat in Sāvatthī, went forth on tour and returned, the people, saying, 'We will make a welcome offering to the newcomers,' gave a great donation to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. They appointed a certain monk as a distributor in the monastery. He would inquire of those who arrived how many monks they desired and would assign the monks to each accordingly.

Athekā duggatamahallikā itthī ekameva paṭivīsaṃ sajjetvā tesaṃ tesaṃ manussānaṃ bhikkhūsu vicāretvā dinnesu ussūre dhammaghosakassa santikaṃ āgantvā “mayhaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ dethā”ti āha. So “mayā sabbe bhikkhū vicāretvā dinnā, sāriputtatthero pana vihāreyeva, tvaṃ tassa bhikkhaṃ dehī”ti āha. Sā “sādhū”ti tuṭṭhacittā jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake ṭhatvā therassa āgatakāle [V 2.0239] vanditvā hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā gharaṃ netvā nisīdāpesi. “Ekāya kira mahallikāya dhammasenāpati attano ghare nisīdāpito”ti bahūni saddhāni kulāni assosuṃ. Tesu rājā passenadī kosalo taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā tassā sāṭakena ceva sahassatthavikāya ca saddhiṃ bhattabhājanāni pahiṇi “mayhaṃ ayyaṃ parivisamānā imaṃ sāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā ime kahāpaṇe vaḷañjetvā theraṃ parivisatū”ti. Yathā ca rājā, evaṃ anāthapiṇḍiko [P 2.0287] cūḷaanāthapiṇḍiko visākhā ca mahāupāsikā pahiṇi. Aññānipi pana kulāni ekasatadvisatādivasena attano attano balānurūpena kahāpaṇe pahiṇiṃsu. Evaṃ ekāheneva sā mahallikā satasahassamattaṃ labhi. Thero pana tāya dinnayāgumeva pivitvā [M 2.0262] tāya katakhajjakameva pakkabhattameva ca paribhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ katvā taṃ mahallikaṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā vihārameva agamāsi.

Then a certain poor old woman, having prepared only a single portion of almsfood, came to the distributor monk late in the day after the monks had been assigned to various people and said, 'Give me one monk.' He replied, 'I have already assigned all the monks, but the Elder Sāriputta is still in the monastery; give your alms to him.' Pleased at heart, she said, 'Very well,' and stood at the gate-tower of Jetavana. When the elder arrived, she paid homage, took the bowl from his hand, led him to her house, and invited him to sit. 'It is said that a certain old woman has invited the General of the Dhamma to sit in her house,' many faithful families heard. Among them, King Pasenadi of Kosala, hearing that news, sent her a robe and a purse of a thousand coins together with vessels of fine food, saying, 'While serving my lord, let her wear this robe, use these coins, and serve the elder.' Just as the king did, so also did Anāthapiṇḍika, Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, and Visākhā the great female lay devotee send gifts. Other families also sent coins in amounts of one hundred or two hundred and so on, each according to their means. Thus, in a single day, that old woman received about one hundred thousand. The elder, however, drank only the gruel she offered and ate only the snacks and the cooked rice she had prepared. After expressing appreciation and establishing that old woman in the fruit of stream-entry, he returned to the monastery.

Dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū therassa guṇakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, dhammasenāpati mahallikagahapatāniṃ duggatabhāvato mocesi, patiṭṭhā ahosi. Tāya dinnamāhāraṃ ajigucchanto paribhuñjī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, sāriputto idāneva etissā mahallikāya avassayo jāto, na ca idāneva tāya dinnaṃ āhāraṃ ajigucchanto paribhuñjati, pubbepi paribhuñjiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

In the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a discussion about the elder's virtues: 'Friends, the General of the Dhamma has freed the poor elderly lady from her state of poverty and has become her support. He partook of the food she offered without any loathing.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now seated together?' When they replied, 'For this one,' the Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta has become a refuge for this old woman, nor is it only now that he eats the food she gives without loathing; he has eaten it in the past as well.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto uttarāpathe assavāṇijakule nibbatti. Uttarāpathajanapadato pañcasatā assavāṇijā asse bārāṇasiṃ ānetvā vikkiṇanti. Aññataropi assavāṇijo pañcaassasatāni ādāya bārāṇasimaggaṃ paṭipajji. Antarāmagge ca bārāṇasito avidūre eko nigamagāmo atthi, tattha pubbe mahāvibhavo seṭṭhi ahosi. Tassa mahantaṃ nivesanaṃ, taṃ pana kulaṃ anukkamena parikkhayaṃ gataṃ, ekāva mahallikā avasiṭṭhā, sā tasmiṃ nivesane vasati. Atha so assavāṇijo taṃ nigamagāmaṃ patvā “vetanaṃ dassāmī”ti tassā nivesane nivāsaṃ gaṇhitvā asse ekamante ṭhapesi. Taṃdivasamevassa ekissā ājānīyāvaḷavāya gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. So dve tayo divase vasitvā asse balaṃ gāhāpetvā “rājānaṃ passissāmī”ti asse ādāya pāyāsi. Atha naṃ mahallikā “gehavetanaṃ dehī”ti vatvā “sādhu, amma, demī”ti [P 2.0288] vutte “tāta, vetanaṃ me dadamāno imampi assapotakaṃ vetanato khaṇḍetvā dehī”ti āha. Vāṇijo tathā katvā [V 2.0240] pakkāmi. Sā tasmiṃ assapotake puttasinehaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā avassāvanajhāmakabhattavighāsatiṇāni datvā taṃ paṭijaggi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of horse traders in the Northern Country. Five hundred horse traders from the Northern Country used to bring horses to Benares to sell. A certain horse trader, taking five hundred horses, set out on the road to Benares. On the way, not far from Benares, there was a market town where a very wealthy merchant had formerly lived. He had a large residence, but that family had gradually fallen into ruin, and only one old woman remained, who lived in that residence. Then the horse trader, reaching that market town, said, 'I will pay rent,' took lodging in her house, and kept the horses to one side. On that very day, one of his thoroughbred mares gave birth. After staying for two or three days and letting the horses regain their strength, he set out with the horses, thinking, 'I will see the king.' Then the old woman said to him, 'Give me the rent for the house.' When he replied, 'Very well, mother, I will give it,' she said, 'My dear, when giving me the rent, please deduct this foal from the rent and give it to me.' The trader did so and departed. She, developing a mother's affection for that foal, cared for it, giving it rice-scum, scorched rice-crusts, scraps, and grass.

Athāparabhāge bodhisatto pañca assasatāni ādāya āgacchanto tasmiṃ gehe nivāsaṃ gaṇhi. Kuṇḍakakhādakassa sindhavapotakassa ṭhitaṭṭhānato gandhaṃ ghāyitvā ekaassopi gehaṃ pavisituṃ nāsakkhi. Bodhisatto mahallikaṃ pucchi – “amma, kacci imasmiṃ gehe asso atthī”ti[M 2.0263]. “Tāta, añño asso nāma natthi, ahaṃ pana puttaṃ katvā ekaṃ assapotakaṃ paṭijaggāmi, so ettha atthī”ti. “Kahaṃ so, ammā”ti? “Carituṃ gato, tātā”ti. “Kāya velāya āgamissati, ammā”ti? “Sāyanhe, tātā”ti. Bodhisatto tassa āgamanaṃ paṭimānento asse bahi ṭhapetvāva nisīdi. Sindhavapotakopi vicaritvā kāleyeva āgami. Bodhisatto kuṇḍakakucchisindhavapotakaṃ disvā lakkhaṇāni samānetvā “ayaṃ sindhavo anaggho, mahallikāya mūlaṃ datvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintesi. Sindhavapotakopi gehaṃ pavisitvā attano vasanaṭṭhāneyeva ṭhito. Tasmiṃ khaṇe te assā gehaṃ pavisituṃ sakkhiṃsu.

Later, the Bodhisatta, arriving with five hundred horses, took lodging in that house. Smelling the scent from the spot where the Sindh foal, the Bran-Eater, had stood, not a single horse dared to enter the house. The Bodhisatta asked the old woman, 'Mother, is there a horse in this house?' 'My dear, there is no other horse, but I am rearing one foal as my son; he is here.' 'Where is he, mother?' 'He has gone to graze, my dear.' 'At what time will he return, mother?' 'In the evening, my dear.' The Bodhisatta, awaiting his arrival, sat down, keeping his horses outside. The Sindh foal, having roamed about, returned in the evening. The Bodhisatta, seeing the Sindh foal of the Bran-Belly, examined its marks and thought, 'This Sindh horse is priceless; it is proper to give the old woman a price and take it.' The Sindh foal entered the house and stood in its own place. At that moment, those other horses were able to enter the house.

Bodhisatto dvīhatīhaṃ vasitvā asse santappetvā gacchanto “amma, imaṃ assapotakaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvā mayhaṃ dehī”ti āha. “Kiṃ vadesi, tāta, puttaṃ vikkiṇantā nāma atthī”ti. “Amma, tvaṃ etaṃ kiṃ khādāpetvā paṭijaggasī”ti? “Odanakañjikañca jhāmakabhattañca vighāsatiṇañca khādāpetvā kuṇḍakayāguñca pāyetvā paṭijaggāmi, tātā”ti. “Amma, ahaṃ etaṃ labhitvā piṇḍarasabhojanaṃ bhojessāmi, ṭhitaṭṭhāne [P 2.0289] celavitānaṃ pasāretvā attharaṇapiṭṭhe ṭhapessāmī”ti. “Tāta, evaṃ sante mama putto ca sukhaṃ anubhavatu, taṃ gahetvā gacchā”ti. Atha bodhisatto tassa catunnaṃ pādānaṃ naṅguṭṭhassa mukhassa ca mūlaṃ ekekaṃ katvā cha sahassatthavikāyo ṭhapetvā mahallikaṃ navavatthaṃ nivāsāpetvā sindhavapotakassa purato ṭhapesi. So akkhīni ummīletvā mātaraṃ oloketvā assūni pavattesi. Sāpi tassa piṭṭhiṃ parimajjitvā āha – “mayā puttaposāvanikaṃ laddhaṃ, tvaṃ, tāta, gacchāhī”ti, tadā so agamāsi.

The Bodhisatta, having stayed there for two or three days and having fed the horses, as he was leaving, said, “Mother, take the price for this young horse and give him to me.” “What are you saying, dear? Is there such a person who sells their own child?” “Mother, what have you been feeding and nurturing him with?” “I nurture him by feeding him rice gruel, burnt rice, and leftover grass, and by giving him bran-gruel to drink, dear.” “Mother, if I obtain him, I will feed him choice food; I will spread a cloth canopy where he stands and place him on a cushioned floor.” “Dear, if that is so, may my son enjoy happiness. Take him and go.” Then the Bodhisatta, assigning a value to each of his four feet, his tail, and his mouth, placed six bags of a thousand coins each, dressed the old woman in new clothes, and placed her before the Sindhu colt. The colt opened his eyes, looked at his mother, and shed tears. She stroked his back and said, “I have gained the reward for raising a son. You, dear, may go.” Then he departed.

Bodhisatto punadivase assapotakassa piṇḍarasabhojanaṃ sajjetvā “vīmaṃsissāmi tāva naṃ, jānāti nu kho attano balaṃ, udāhu na jānātī”ti doṇiyaṃ kuṇḍakayāguṃ ākirāpetvā dāpesi. So “nāhaṃ imaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjissāmī”ti taṃ yāguṃ pāyituṃ na icchi. Bodhisatto tassa vīmaṃsanavasena paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The next day, the Bodhisatta prepared choice food for the young horse, thinking, “I will test him first to see if he knows his own strength or not.” He had bran-gruel poured into a trough and given to him. The colt thought, “I will not eat this food; I do not wish to drink the gruel.” The Bodhisatta, for the purpose of testing him, spoke the first verse:

10.

10.

“Bhutvā [V 2.0241] tiṇaparighāsaṃ, bhutvā ācāmakuṇḍakaṃ;

Etaṃ te bhojanaṃ āsi, kasmā dāni na bhuñjasī”ti.

“Having eaten leftover fodder, having eaten leftover rice and bran; this was your food, why do you not eat it now?”

Tattha [M 2.0264] bhutvā tiṇaparighāsanti tvaṃ pubbe mahallikāya dinnaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ khāditāvasesaṃ vighāsatiṇasaṅkhātaṃ parighāsaṃ bhuñjitvā vaḍḍhito. Bhutvā ācāmakuṇḍakanti ettha ācāmo vuccati odanāvasesaṃ. Kuṇḍakanti kuṇḍakameva. Etañca bhuñjitvā vaḍḍhitosīti dīpeti. Etaṃ teti etaṃ tava pubbe bhojanaṃ āsi. Kasmā dāni na bhuñjasīti mayāpi te tameva dinnaṃ, tvaṃ taṃ kasmā idāni na bhuñjasīti.

In this verse, 'having eaten leftover fodder' means you grew up eating the leftovers of others, consisting of grass, given to you by the old woman previously. 'Having eaten leftover rice and bran': here 'leftover rice' refers to what remains of the cooked rice, and 'bran' means just bran. It indicates that you grew up eating this. 'This was your food' means this was your food previously. 'Why do you not eat it now?' means, 'I have given you the very same; why do you not eat it now?'

Taṃ sutvā sindhavapotako itarā dve gāthā avoca –

Hearing this, the Sindhu colt spoke the other two verses:

11.

11.

“Yattha posaṃ na jānanti, jātiyā vinayena vā;

Bahu tattha mahābrahme, api ācāmakuṇḍakaṃ.

“Where they do not know a person, whether by birth or by conduct, there, O Great Brahma, even leftover rice and bran is plenty.

12.

12.

“Tvañca khomaṃ pajānāsi, yādisāyaṃ hayuttamo;

Jānanto jānamāgamma, na te bhakkhāmi kuṇḍaka”nti.

“But you indeed know me, what kind of excellent horse this is. Knowing my own strength, and having come to one who knows it, I will not eat your bran.”

Tattha [P 2.0290] yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne. Posanti sattaṃ. Jātiyā vinayena vāti “jātisampanno vā eso, na vā, ācārayutto vā, na vā”ti evaṃ na jānanti. Mahābrahmeti garukālapanena ālapanto āha. Yādisāyanti yādiso ayaṃ, attānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Jānanto jānamāgammāti ahaṃ attano balaṃ jānanto jānantameva taṃ āgamma paṭicca tava santike kuṇḍakaṃ kiṃ bhuñjissāmi. Na hi tvaṃ kuṇḍakaṃ bhojāpetukāmatāya cha sahassāni datvā maṃ gaṇhīti.

In these verses, 'where' means in which place. 'Person' means a being. 'By birth or by conduct' means they do not know: 'Is this one endowed with noble birth or not? Is he possessed of good conduct or not?' 'O Great Brahma' is an address used with great respect. 'What kind of' means of what sort this is; he speaks referring to himself. 'Knowing, and having come to one who knows' means, 'I, knowing my own strength, having come to you who also know, why should I eat bran in your presence? For surely, you did not acquire me by giving six thousand coins with the intention of feeding me bran.'

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “taṃ vīmaṃsanatthāya taṃ mayā kataṃ, mā kujjhī”ti taṃ samassāsetvā subhojanaṃ bhojetvā ādāya rājaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ passe pañca assasatāni ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ passe vicittasāṇiṃ parikkhipitvā heṭṭhā attharaṇaṃ pattharitvā upari celavitānaṃ bandhitvā sindhavapotakaṃ ṭhapesi.

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said, “I did that only to test you, do not be angry.” Having consoled him and fed him excellent food, he took him to the royal courtyard. There, on one side, he placed five hundred horses; on another side, he surrounded an area with colorful screens. He spread a covering below and fastened a cloth canopy above, then placed the Sindhu colt there.

Rājā āgantvā asse olokento “ayaṃ asso kasmā visuṃ ṭhapito”ti pucchitvā “mahārāja[V 2.0242], ayaṃ sindhavo ime asse visuṃ akato mocessatī”ti sutvā “sobhano, bho, sindhavo”ti pucchi. Bodhisatto “āma, mahārājā”ti vatvā “tena hissa javaṃ passissāmī”ti [M 2.0265] vutte taṃ assaṃ kappetvā abhiruhitvā “passa, mahārājā”ti manusse ussāretvā rājaṅgaṇe assaṃ pāhesi. Sabbaṃ rājaṅgaṇaṃ nirantaraṃ assapantīhi parikkhittamivāhosi. Puna bodhisatto “passa, mahārāja, sindhavapotakassa vega”nti vissajjesi, ekapurisopi naṃ na addasa. Puna ratthapaṭaṃ udare parikkhipitvā vissajjesi, rattapaṭameva passiṃsu. Atha naṃ antonagare ekissā uyyānapokkharaṇiyā udakapiṭṭhe vissajjesi, tatthassa udakapiṭṭhe dhāvato khuraggānipi na temiṃsu. Punavāraṃ paduminipattānaṃ upari [P 2.0291] dhāvanto ekapaṇṇampi na udake osīdāpesi. Evamassa javasampannaṃ dassetvā oruyha pāṇiṃ paharitvā hatthatalaṃ upanāmesi, asso upagantvā cattāro pāde ekato katvā hatthatale aṭṭhāsi. Atha mahāsatto rājānaṃ āha – “mahārāja, imassa assapotakassa sabbākārena vege dassiyamāne samuddapariyanto nappahotī”ti. Rājā tussitvā mahāsattassa upaḍḍharajjaṃ adāsi. Sindhavapotakampi abhisiñcitvā maṅgalaassaṃ akāsi.

The king arrived and, looking at the horses, asked, “Why is this horse kept separate?” Hearing, “Great king, this is a Sindhu horse; he is superior among these horses,” he inquired, “Is this Sindhu horse excellent, sir?” The Bodhisatta replied, “Yes, great king.” When the king said, “Then I shall see its speed,” he saddled the horse, mounted it, and saying, “Watch, great king,” he moved the people aside and sent the horse racing through the royal courtyard. The entire royal courtyard seemed as if encircled by continuous lines of horses. Again, the Bodhisatta said, “See, great king, the speed of the Sindhu colt,” and released it—not a single person could see it. Once more, he wrapped a red cloth around its belly and released it; they saw only the red cloth. Then, within the inner city, he released it on the surface of a garden pond, and as it ran across the water’s surface, not even the tips of its hooves got wet. When it ran over lotus leaves, it did not cause a single leaf to sink into the water. Having thus displayed its supreme speed, he dismounted, clapped his hands, and held out his palm. The horse approached, gathered all four feet together, and stood on his palm. Then the Great Being said to the king, “Great king, were this colt’s speed to be displayed in every way, the region bounded by the ocean would not be enough to contain its speed.” Pleased, the king granted the Great Being half his kingdom. He also anointed the Sindhu colt and made it his auspicious royal horse.

So rañño piyo ahosi manāpo, sakkāropissa mahā ahosi. Tassa hi vasanaṭṭhānaṃ rañño alaṅkatapaṭiyatto vāsagharagabbho viya ahosi, catujātigandhehi bhūmilepanaṃ akaṃsu, gandhadāmamālādāmāni osārayiṃsu, upari suvaṇṇatārakakhacitaṃ celavitānaṃ ahosi, samantato citrasāṇi parikkhittā ahosi, niccaṃ gandhatelapadīpā jhāyiṃsu, uccārapassāvaṭṭhānepissa suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu, niccaṃ rājārahabhojanameva bhuñji. Tassa pana āgatakālato paṭṭhāya rañño sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ hatthagatameva ahosi. Rājā bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi.

He was dear and beloved to the king, and great honors were bestowed upon him. Indeed, his dwelling place was like the king’s decorated and well-prepared private chamber; they plastered the floor with four kinds of fragrant substances, hung fragrant garlands and festoons of flowers, and above was a canopy adorned with golden stars. All around were colorful screens, and lamps of fragrant oil were constantly burning. Even for his place of excrement and urine they placed a golden vessel. He always ate only food worthy of a king. Moreover, from the time of his arrival, the king's rule over the entire Jambudīpa was as if in his grasp. The king, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, performed meritorious deeds such as generosity and was destined for heaven.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū sotāpannā sakadāgāmino anāgāmino arahanto ca ahesuṃ. “Tadā mahallikā ayameva mahallikā ahosi, sindhavo sāriputto, rājā ānando, assavāṇijjo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher revealed the Truths and made the connection in the birth story.
