At the conclusion of the Truths, many became stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants. “At that time, the old woman was this same old woman, the Sindhu horse was Sāriputta, the king was Ānanda, and the horse trader was indeed I myself.”

Kuṇḍakakucchisindhavajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Kuṇḍakakucchisindhava Jātaka, the fourth.

[255] 5. Sukajātakavaṇṇanā

[255] 5. The Commentary on the Suka Jātaka

Yāva [V 2.0243][M 2.0266] so mattamaññāsīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ atibahuṃ bhuñjitvā ajīraṇena kālakataṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha [P 2.0292] kathesi. Tasmiṃ kira evaṃ kālakate dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū tassa aguṇakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu attano kucchippamāṇaṃ ajānitvā atibahuṃ bhuñjitvā jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto kālakato”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa atibhojanapaccayeneva mato”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“As long as he knew moderation…” This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who had died from indigestion after eating too much. When that monk had died, the monks in the Dhamma hall started a discussion about his faults: “Friends, the monk named so-and-so, not knowing the measure of his stomach, ate too much and, unable to digest it, died.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “For what discussion are you gathered here now, monks?” When they told him, he said, “Not just now, monks, but also in the past he died due to overeating,” and he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese sukayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā anekānaṃ sukasahassānaṃ samuddānugate himavantapadese vasantānaṃ rājā ahosi. Tasseko putto ahosi, tasmiṃ balappatte bodhisatto dubbalacakkhuko ahosi. Sukānaṃ kira sīgho vego hoti, tena tesaṃ mahallakakāle paṭhamaṃ cakkhumeva dubbalaṃ hoti. Bodhisattassa putto mātāpitaro kulāvake ṭhapetvā gocaraṃ āharitvā posesi. So ekadivasaṃ gocarabhūmiṃ gantvā pabbatamatthake ṭhito samuddaṃ olokento ekaṃ dīpakaṃ passi. Tasmiṃ pana suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ madhuraphalaṃ ambavanaṃ atthi. So punadivase gocaravelāya uppatitvā tasmiṃ ambavane otaritvā ambarasaṃ pivitvā ambapakkaṃ ādāya āgantvā mātāpitūnaṃ adāsi. Bodhisatto taṃ khādanto rasaṃ sañjānitvā “tāta, nanu imaṃ asukadīpake ambapakka”nti vatvā “āma, tātā”ti vutte “tāta, etaṃ dīpakaṃ gacchantā nāma sukā dīghamāyuṃ pālentā nāma natthi, mā kho tvaṃ puna taṃ dīpakaṃ agamāsī”ti āha. So tassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā agamāsiyeva.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Himalayan region into a parrot family and became the king of many thousands of parrots living in the Himalayan region bordering the sea. He had one son, and when that son reached full strength, the Bodhisatta's eyes became weak. It is said that parrots have great speed, so in their old age, their eyesight is the first thing to weaken. The Bodhisatta's son, leaving his parents in the nest, would bring back food and nourish them. One day, while in a foraging area, he stood on a mountaintop and, looking out at the sea, saw an island. On it was a mango grove with golden-colored, delicious fruit. The next day, at foraging time, he flew to that mango grove, drank the mango juice, took a ripe mango, and came back and gave it to his parents. The Bodhisatta, eating it, recognized the taste and said, “My child, is this not a ripe mango from such-and-such island?” When his son replied, “Yes, father,” the Bodhisatta said, “My child, parrots who go to that island do not live a long life. Do not go to that island again.” But he did not heed his words and went anyway.

Athekadivasaṃ bahuṃ ambarasaṃ pivitvā mātāpitūnaṃ atthāya ambapakkaṃ ādāya samuddamatthakenāgacchanto [P 2.0293] atidhātatāya kilantakāyo niddāyābhibhūto, so niddāyantopi āgacchateva, tuṇḍena panassa gahitaṃ ambapakkaṃ pati. So anukkamena āgamanavīthiṃ jahitvā osīdanto udakapiṭṭheneva āgacchanto udake pati. Atha naṃ eko maccho gahetvā [M 2.0267] khādi. Bodhisatto tasmiṃ āgamanavelāya anāgacchanteyeva “samudde patitvā mato bhavissatī”ti aññāsi. Athassa mātāpitaropi āhāraṃ alabhamānā sussitvā mariṃsu.

Then one day, after drinking much mango juice, taking a ripe mango for his parents, and flying over the sea, his body grew weary from being over-satiated and he was overcome by sleep. Even as he slept, he kept flying, but the ripe mango he held in his beak fell. Gradually straying from his flight path, sinking, and flying just at the water's surface, he fell into the water. Then a fish seized and devoured him. The Bodhisatta, when his son did not return at the usual time, knew, “He must have fallen into the sea and died.” Then his parents, receiving no food, withered away and died.

Satthā [V 2.0244] imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

The Teacher, having related this past story, then as the Fully Enlightened One, spoke these verses:

13.

13.

“Yāva so mattamaññāsi, bhojanasmiṃ vihaṅgamo;

Tāva addhānamāpādi, mātarañca aposayi.

“As long as that bird knew moderation in food, he lived a long life and supported his mother.”

14.

14.

“Yato ca kho bahutaraṃ, bhojanaṃ ajjhavāhari;

Tato tattheva saṃsīdi, amattaññū hi so ahu.

“But when he consumed much more food, he sank right there, for he was one who knew no moderation.”

15.

15.

“Tasmā mattaññutā sādhu, bhojanasmiṃ agiddhatā;

Amattaññū hi sīdanti, mattaññū ca na sīdare”ti.

“Therefore, knowing moderation in food is good, as is non-greediness. Those who know no moderation sink down, while those who know moderation do not.”

Tattha yāva soti yāva so vihaṅgamo bhojane mattamaññāsi. Tāva addhānamāpādīti tatthakaṃ kālaṃ jīvitaaddhānaṃ āpādi, āyuṃ vindi. Mātarañcāti desanāsīsametaṃ, mātāpitaro ca aposayīti attho. Yato ca khoti yasmiñca kho kāle. Bhojanaṃ ajjhavāharīti ambarasaṃ ajjhohari. Tatoti tasmiṃ kāle. Tattheva saṃsīdīti tasmiṃ samuddeyeva osīdi nimujji, macchabhojanataṃ āpajji.

Therein, ‘As long as he’ means: as long as that bird knew moderation in food. ‘For so long he lived a long life’ means: for that long he completed the journey of his life, he attained his lifespan. ‘And his mother’: this is the heading of the teaching; the meaning is that he supported his parents. ‘And when’ means: at which time. ‘He consumed food’ means: he devoured the mango juice. ‘Then’ means: at that time. ‘He sank right there’ means: right there in the ocean he sank down, was submerged, and became food for the fish.

Tasmā mattaññutā sādhūti yasmā bhojane amattaññū suko samudde osīditvā mato, tasmā bhojanasmiṃ agiddhitāsaṅkhāto mattaññubhāvo sādhu, pamāṇajānanaṃ sundaranti attho. Atha vā “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāreti, neva davāya na madāya…pe… phāsuvihāro cā”ti.

‘Therefore, knowing moderation is good’: since the parrot, not knowing moderation in food, sank in the ocean and died, therefore the state of knowing moderation, which is called non-greediness in food, is good; the meaning is that knowing the proper measure is excellent. Alternatively: “Reflecting wisely, one consumes food not for amusement, not for intoxication... but for the comfortable abiding.”

“Allaṃ sukkhañca bhuñjanto, na bāḷhaṃ suhito siyā;

Ūnudaro mitāhāro, sato bhikkhu paribbaje.

“Eating both fresh and dry food, one should not be overly full; with stomach not quite full, moderate in eating, a mindful monk should wander.”

“Cattāro [P 2.0294] pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno. (theragā. 982-983);

“Leaving four or five morsels uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the comfortable abiding of a resolute monk.”

“Manujassa [V 2.0245][M 2.0268] sadā satīmato, mattaṃ jānato laddhabhojane;

Tanū tassa bhavanti vedanā, saṇikaṃ jīrati āyuṃ pālaya”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.124) –

“For a person who is ever mindful, who knows moderation in the food obtained, his pains become slight; he ages slowly, protecting his life.”

Evaṃ vaṇṇitā mattaññutāpi sādhu.

Thus, knowing moderation, praised in this way, is also good.

“Kantāre puttamaṃsaṃva, akkhassabbhañjanaṃ yathā;

Evaṃ āhari āharaṃ, yāpanatthamamucchito”ti. (visuddhi. 1.19) –

“As with a son's flesh in the wilderness, and as with grease for an axle, so one should consume food, uninfatuated, for sustenance alone.”

Evaṃ vaṇṇitā agiddhitāpi sādhu. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “agiddhimā”ti likhitaṃ, tato ayaṃ aṭṭhakathāpāṭhova sundarataro. Amattaññū hi sīdantīti bhojane pamāṇaṃ ajānantā hi rasataṇhāvasena pāpakammaṃ katvā catūsu apāyesu sīdanti. Mattaññū ca na sīdareti ye pana bhojane pamāṇaṃ jānanti, te diṭṭhadhammepi samparāyepi na sīdantīti.

Thus, non-greediness, praised in this way, is also good. In the Pāli, however, it is written as ‘agiddhimā’ (one who is not greedy), so this reading from the commentary is more excellent. ‘Those who know no moderation sink down’: for those who do not know the measure in food, driven by craving for taste, perform evil deeds and sink into the four woeful states. ‘While those who know moderation do not sink’: but those who know the measure in food do not sink either in this present life or in the life to come.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū sotāpannāpi sakadāgāminopi anāgāminopi arahantopi ahesuṃ. “Tadā sukarājaputto bhojane amattaññū bhikkhu ahosi, sukarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, many became stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, or arahants. “At that time, the parrot prince was the monk who knew no moderation in food, but the parrot king was I myself.”

Sukajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Suka Jātaka, the Fifth.

[256] 6. Jarūdapānajātakavaṇṇanā

[256] 6. The Commentary on the Jarūdapāna Jātaka

Jarūdapānaṃ khaṇamānāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāvatthivāsino vāṇije ārabbha kathesi. Te kira sāvatthiyaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā sakaṭāni pūretvā vohāratthāya gamanakāle tathāgataṃ nimantetvā saraṇāni gahetvā sīlesu patiṭṭhāya satthāraṃ vanditvā “mayaṃ, bhante, vohāratthāya dīghamaggaṃ gamissāma, bhaṇḍaṃ vissajjetvā siddhippattā sotthinā paccāgantvā pana tumhe vandissāmā”ti vatvā maggaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu. Te kantāramagge purāṇaudapānaṃ disvā “imasmiṃ udapāne pānīyaṃ natthi, mayañca pipāsitā, khaṇissāma na”nti khaṇantā paṭipāṭiyā bahuṃ [P 2.0295] ayaṃ…pe… veḷuriyaṃ labhiṃsu. Te teneva santuṭṭhā hutvā tesaṃ ratanānaṃ sakaṭāni [M 2.0269] pūretvā sotthinā [V 2.0246] sāvatthiṃ paccāgamiṃsu. Te ābhataṃ dhanaṃ paṭisāmetvā mayaṃ “siddhippattā bhattaṃ dassāmā”ti tathāgataṃ nimantetvā dānaṃ datvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinnā attano dhanassa laddhākāraṃ satthu ārocesuṃ. Satthā “tumhe kho upāsakā tena dhanena santuṭṭhā hutvā pamāṇaññutāya dhanañca jīvitañca alabhittha, porāṇakā pana asantuṭṭhā amattaññuno paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā jīvikkhayaṃ pattā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

While the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, he told this story concerning some merchants who were residents of Sāvatthī. It is said that these merchants, having gathered goods in Sāvatthī and loaded their carts, intending to travel for trade, invited the Tathāgata, took the refuges, established themselves in the precepts, paid homage to the Teacher, and said, 'Venerable sir, we are going on a long journey for trade. After selling our goods and achieving success, we will return safely and pay homage to you again.' Having said this, they set out on their journey. On a wilderness path, they saw an old well and thought, 'There is no water in this well, and we are thirsty. Shall we not dig?' As they dug in succession, they found much iron... and so on... and obtained beryl. Satisfied with just that, they filled their carts with those gems and returned safely to Sāvatthī. After storing away the wealth they had brought back, they thought, 'Having achieved success, we will offer a meal.' They invited the Tathāgata, gave alms, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Then they reported to the Teacher how they had obtained their wealth. The Teacher said, 'You, lay followers, being content with that wealth and knowing moderation, have obtained both wealth and life. But in the past, those who were discontented, immoderate, and did not heed the words of the wise perished.' Being requested by them, he then related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ vāṇijakule nibbattitvā vayappatto satthavāhajeṭṭhako ahosi. So bārāṇasiyaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā sakaṭāni pūretvā bahū vāṇije ādāya tameva kantāraṃ paṭipanno tameva udapānaṃ addasa. Tattha te vāṇijā “pānīyaṃ pivissāmā”ti taṃ udapānaṃ khaṇantā paṭipāṭiyā bahūni ayādīni labhiṃsu. Te bahumpi ratanaṃ labhitvā tena asantuṭṭhā “aññampi ettha ito sundarataraṃ bhavissatī”ti bhiyyosomattāya taṃ khaṇiṃsuyeva. Atha bodhisatto te āha – “bho vāṇijā, lobho nāmesa vināsamūlaṃ, amhehi bahu dhanaṃ laddhaṃ, ettakeneva santuṭṭhā hotha, mā atikhaṇathā”ti. Te tena nivāriyamānāpi khaṇiṃsuyeva. So ca udapāno nāgapariggahito, athassa heṭṭhā vasanakanāgarājā attano vimāne bhijjante leḍḍūsū ca paṃsūsu ca patamānesu kuddho ṭhapetvā bodhisattaṃ avasese sabbepi nāsikavātena paharitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ [P 2.0296] pāpetvā nāgabhavanā nikkhamma sakaṭāni yojetvā sabbaratanānaṃ pūretvā bodhisattaṃ sukhayānake nisīdāpetvā nāgamāṇavakehi saddhiṃ sakaṭāni yojāpento bodhisattaṃ bārāṇasiṃ netvā gharaṃ pavesetvā taṃ paṭisāmetvā attano nāgabhavanameva gato. Bodhisatto taṃ dhanaṃ vissajjetvā sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā jīvitapariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūresi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family in Bārāṇasī and, having come of age, became the leader of a caravan. Taking goods from Bārāṇasī, he filled his carts and set out on that same wilderness road with many merchants, where they saw that same well. There, the merchants, thinking, 'We will drink water,' dug that well and in succession found many things, beginning with iron. Though they obtained much treasure, they were unsatisfied and thought, 'There must be something even more beautiful here,' and dug ever more eagerly. Then the Bodhisatta said to them: 'Sirs, greed is indeed the root of destruction. We have obtained much wealth; be content with this much, do not dig excessively.' Though he tried to restrain them, they kept digging. Now, that well was possessed by a nāga, and the nāga king dwelling below, enraged as his palace was being broken and clods of earth and dust were falling upon it, spared only the Bodhisatta. Striking all the others with the breath from his nostrils, he brought them to the destruction of their lives. Then, emerging from the nāga abode, he yoked the carts, filled them with all the treasures, seated the Bodhisatta on a comfortable vehicle, and having the nāga youths drive the carts, he led the Bodhisatta to Bārāṇasī and into his home. After settling him there, the nāga king returned to his own nāga abode. The Bodhisatta distributed that wealth, making the whole of Jambudīpa a place where ploughs were laid aside, gave alms, undertook the moral precepts, kept the Uposatha observance, and at the end of his life, went to fill the heavenly city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, now as the Fully Enlightened One, spoke these verses:

16.

16.

“Jarūdapānaṃ [M 2.0270] khaṇamānā, vāṇijā udakatthikā;

Ajjhagamuṃ ayasaṃ lohaṃ, tipusīsañca vāṇijā;

Rajataṃ jātarūpañca, muttā veḷuriyā bahū.

“Merchants desiring water, digging an old well, came upon iron and copper; the merchants found tin and lead, silver and gold, many pearls and beryl.”

17.

17.

“Te ca tena asantuṭṭhā, bhiyyo bhiyyo akhāṇisuṃ;

Te tatthāsīviso ghoro, tejassī tejasā hani.

“But they, discontent with that, dug ever more and more; there a terrible, venomous serpent, full of fiery energy, struck them down with its power.”

18.

18.

“Tasmā [V 2.0247] khaṇe nātikhaṇe, atikhātañhi pāpakaṃ;

Khātena ca dhanaṃ laddhaṃ, atikhātena nāsita”nti.

“Therefore, one should dig, but not dig too much; for digging too much is evil. By digging, wealth was obtained; by digging too much, it was destroyed.”

Tattha ayasanti kāḷalohaṃ. Lohanti tambalohaṃ. Muttāti muttāyo. Te ca tena asantuṭṭhāti te ca vāṇijā tena dhanena asantuṭṭhā. Te tatthāti te vāṇijā tasmiṃ udapāne. Tejassīti visatejena samannāgato. Tejasā hanīti visatejena ghātesi. Atikhātena nāsitanti atikhaṇena tañca dhanaṃ jīvitañca nāsitaṃ.

Therein, ayasam means black iron. Loham means copper. Muttā means pearls. Te ca tena asantuṭṭhā means: and those merchants were discontent with that wealth. Te tattha means: those merchants in that well. Tejassī means: endowed with the power of venom. Tejasā hani means: he killed them with the power of his venom. Atikhātena nāsitam means: by excessive digging, both that wealth and their lives were destroyed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā nāgarājā sāriputto ahosi, satthavāhajeṭṭhako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story, saying: 'At that time, the Nāga king was Sāriputta, and the caravan leader was myself.'

Jarūdapānajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Jarūdapāna Jātaka, the Sixth.

[257] 7. Gāmaṇicandajātakavaṇṇanā

[257] 7. The Commentary on the Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka

Nāyaṃ [P 2.0297] gharānaṃ kusaloti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paññāpasaṃsanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dhammasabhāyañhi bhikkhū dasabalassa paññaṃ pasaṃsantā nisīdiṃsu – “āvuso, tathāgato mahāpañño puthupañño hāsapañño javanapañño tikkhapañño nibbedhikapañño sadevakaṃ lokaṃ paññāya atikkamatī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato paññavāyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This one is not skilled regarding houses...” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the praise of wisdom. For in the Hall of Dhamma, the monks sat praising the wisdom of the one of Ten Powers, saying: 'Friends, the Tathāgata is of great wisdom, extensive wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom; he surpasses the world with its gods through his wisdom.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When they replied, 'For this one,' he said, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past too, the Tathāgata was wise,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ janasandho nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Tassa mukhaṃ suparimajjitakañcanādāsatalaṃ [M 2.0271] viya parisuddhaṃ ahosi atisobhaggappattaṃ, tenassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “ādāsamukhamāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ sattavassabbhantareyeva pana pitā tayo vede ca sabbañca loke kattabbākattabbaṃ sikkhāpetvā tassa sattavassikakāle kālamakāsi. Amaccā mahantena sakkārena rañño sarīrakiccaṃ katvā matakadānaṃ datvā sattame divase rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā “kumāro atidaharo, na sakkā rajje abhisiñcituṃ, vīmaṃsitvā naṃ abhisiñcissāmā”ti ekadivasaṃ nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0248] sajjetvā pallaṅkaṃ paññapetvā kumārassa santikaṃ gantvā “vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ, deva, gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āhaṃsu. Kumāro “sādhū”ti mahantena parivārena gantvā pallaṅke nisīdi.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Janasandha reigned. The Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of his chief queen. His face was as pure as the surface of a well-polished golden mirror, having attained supreme beauty; therefore, on his naming day, they gave him the name 'Prince Ādāsamukha.' Within seven years, his father had him instructed in the three Vedas and in all that should and should not be done in the world. When the prince was seven years old, his father passed away. The ministers performed the king's funeral rites with great ceremony, gave offerings for the dead, and on the seventh day, they gathered in the royal courtyard, saying, 'The prince is very young; it is not possible to consecrate him as king. We will test him and then consecrate him.' One day, having had the city decorated, they prepared the hall of judgment, set up a throne, and went to the prince, saying, 'Your Majesty, it is fitting to go to the hall of judgment.' The prince replied, 'Very well,' and went with a great retinue to sit upon the throne.

Tassa nisinnakāle amaccā ekaṃ dvīhi pādehi vicaraṇamakkaṭaṃ vatthuvijjācariyavesaṃ gāhāpetvā vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ netvā “deva, ayaṃ puriso pitu mahārājassa kāle vatthuvijjācariyo paguṇavijjo antobhūmiyaṃ sattaratanaṭṭhāne [P 2.0298] guṇadosaṃ passati, eteneva gahitaṃ rājakulānaṃ gehaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, imaṃ devo saṅgaṇhitvā ṭhānantare ṭhapetū”ti āhaṃsu. Kumāro taṃ heṭṭhā ca uparica oloketvā “nāyaṃ manusso, makkaṭo eso”ti ñatvā “makkaṭā nāma kataṃ kataṃ viddhaṃsetuṃ jānanti, akataṃ pana kātuṃ vā vicāretuṃ vā na jānantī”ti cintetvā amaccānaṃ paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

As he was seated, the ministers took a monkey that walked on two feet, dressed it in the guise of a master of building science, and brought it to the hall of judgment. They said, 'Your Majesty, this man was a master of building science in the time of your father the great king, skilled in his science. He perceives the qualities and faults of a site even at a depth of seven cubits within the earth. It is by him alone that the site for the dwellings of royal families is chosen. May Your Majesty accept him and establish him in high office.' The prince, looking at it from bottom to top, realized, 'This is not a human being, it is a monkey.' Thinking, 'Monkeys know how to destroy whatever has been made, but they do not know how to make or to plan what has not yet been made,' he spoke the first verse to the ministers:

19.

19.

“Nāyaṃ gharānaṃ kusalo, lolo ayaṃ valīmukho;

Kataṃ kataṃ kho dūseyya, evaṃ dhammamidaṃ kula”nti.

“He is not skilled in houses; this fickle one is a wrinkled-faced monkey. He would spoil whatever is done; such is the nature of this clan.”

Tattha nāyaṃ gharānaṃ kusaloti ayaṃ satto na gharānaṃ kusalo, gharāni vicāretuṃ vā kātuṃ vā cheko na hoti. Loloti lolajātiko. Valīmukhoti valiyo mukhe assāti valīmukho. Evaṃ dhammamidaṃkulanti idaṃ makkaṭakulaṃ nāma kataṃ kataṃ dūsetabbaṃ vināsetabbanti evaṃ sabhāvanti.

In the verse, ‘He is not skilled in houses’ means this being is not skilled in the science of houses; he is not clever at planning or building houses. ‘Fickle’ means of a fickle nature. ‘Wrinkled-faced’ means one who has wrinkles on his face. ‘Such is the nature of this clan’ means this monkey clan is by nature inclined to spoil and destroy whatever has been done.

Athāmaccā “evaṃ bhavissati, devā”ti taṃ apanetvā ekāhadvīhaccayena puna tameva alaṅkaritvā vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ ānetvā “ayaṃ, deva, pitu mahārājassa kāle vinicchayāmacco, vinicchayasuttamassa supavattitaṃ, imaṃ [M 2.0272] saṅgaṇhitvā vinicchayakammaṃ kāretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āhaṃsu. Kumāro taṃ oloketvā “cittavato manussassa lomaṃ nāma evarūpaṃ na hoti, ayaṃ nicittako vānaro vinicchayakammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissatī”ti ñatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the ministers said, “So be it, Your Majesty,” and took him away. After a day or two, they adorned that same monkey again and brought him to the hall of judgment, saying, “Your Majesty, this was a minister of justice in the time of your father the great king. The principles of judgment are well-mastered by him. It would be fitting to accept him and have him perform the duty of judgment.” The prince, observing him, realized, “The hair of a human with a thoughtful mind is not of such a nature. This is a mindless monkey; he will not be capable of judicial work.” Knowing this, he spoke the second verse:

20.

20.

“Nayidaṃ cittavato lomaṃ, nāyaṃ assāsiko migo;

Siṭṭhaṃ me janasandhena, nāyaṃ kiñci vijānatī”ti.

“This is not the hair of one with a thoughtful mind, nor is this a creature that can provide reassurance. This was taught to me by Janasandha; he knows nothing at all.”

Tattha nayidaṃ cittavato lomanti yaṃ idaṃ etassa sarīre pharusalomaṃ, idaṃ vicāraṇapaññāya sampayuttacittavato na hoti. Pākatikacittena pana acittako nāma tiracchānagato natthi. Nāyaṃ [V 2.0249] assāsikoti ayaṃ avassayo vā hutvā anusāsaniṃ vā datvā aññaṃ assāsetuṃ asamatthatāya na assāsiko. Migoti [P 2.0299] makkaṭaṃ āha. Siṭṭhaṃ me janasandhenāti mayhaṃ pitarā janasandhena etaṃ siṭṭhaṃ kathitaṃ, “makkaṭo nāma kāraṇākāraṇaṃ na jānātī”ti evaṃ anusāsanī dinnāti dīpeti. Nāyaṃ kiñci vijānatīti tasmā ayaṃ vānaro na kiñci jānātīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “nāyaṃ kiñci na dūsaye”ti likhitaṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi.

In the verse, ‘this is not the hair of one with a thoughtful mind’ means that this coarse hair on his body does not belong to one whose mind is associated with reflective wisdom. In terms of ordinary mind, however, there is no animal that is truly mindless. ‘He is not a provider of reassurance’ means that, being unable to console another by serving as a refuge or by giving instruction, he is not one who provides reassurance. ‘Creature’ refers to the monkey. ‘This was taught to me by Janasandha’ means: this was spoken by my father, Janasandha, indicating that this instruction was given: ‘A monkey does not know right from wrong.’ ‘He knows nothing’ means the conclusion to be reached here is that this monkey knows nothing. In the Pāḷi text, however, it is written, ‘There is nothing he would not spoil,’ but that is not found in the commentary.

Amaccā imampi gāthaṃ sutvā “evaṃ bhavissati, devā”ti taṃ apanetvā punapi ekadivasaṃ tameva alaṅkaritvā vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ ānetvā “ayaṃ, deva, puriso pitu mahārājassa kāle mātāpituupaṭṭhānakārako, kulejeṭṭhāpacāyikakammakārako, imaṃ saṅgaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āhaṃsu. Kumāro taṃ oloketvā “makkaṭā nāma calacittā, evarūpaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na samatthā”ti cintetvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The ministers, having heard this verse as well, said, “So be it, Your Majesty,” and took him away. Then, one day, having adorned that same monkey again, they brought him to the hall of judgment and said, “Your Majesty, this man, during your father the great king’s time, was one who attended to his parents and one who performed the duty of revering family elders. It is fitting to accept him.” The prince, observing him, thought, “Monkeys are fickle-minded and incapable of performing such deeds,” and spoke the third verse:

21.

21.

“Na mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā, bhātaraṃ bhaginiṃ sakaṃ;

Bhareyya tādiso poso, siṭṭhaṃ dasarathena me”ti.

“Neither mother nor father, nor his own brother or sister—such a person would not support them. This was taught to me by Dasaratha.”

Tattha bhātaraṃ bhaginiṃ sakanti attano bhātaraṃ vā bhaginiṃ vā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “sakha”nti likhitaṃ, taṃ pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sakanti vutte sakabhātikabhaginiyo labbhanti, sakhanti vutte sahāyako labbhatī”ti vicāritameva. Bhareyyāti poseyya. Tādiso posoti yādiso esa dissati, tādiso makkaṭajātiko satto na bhareyya. Siṭṭhaṃ dasarathena meti [M 2.0273] evaṃ me pitarā anusiṭṭhaṃ. Pitā hissa janaṃ catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi sandahanato “janasandho”ti vuccati, dasahi rathehi kattabbākattabbaṃ attano ekeneva rathena karaṇato “dasaratho”ti. Tassa santikā evarūpassa ovādassa sutattā evamāha.

In the verse, ‘his own brother or sister’ means one's own brother or sister. In the Pāḷi text, however, it is written as ‘sakhaṃ’ (friend), but this is discussed in the commentary: ‘When “sakaṃ” is said, one's own brothers and sisters are understood; when “sakhaṃ” is said, a companion is understood.’ ‘Bhareyya’ means ‘would support.’ ‘Such a person’ means a being of the monkey kind, such as this one seen here, would not support them. ‘Taught to me by Dasaratha’ means: thus was I instructed by my father. His father was called ‘Janasandha’ because he bound people together with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), and he was called ‘Dasaratha’ because he accomplished with his own single chariot what usually requires ten chariots. Having heard such advice from him, the prince spoke thus.

Amaccā “evaṃ bhavissati, devā”ti makkaṭaṃ apanetvā “paṇḍito kumāro, sakkhissati rajjaṃ kāretu”nti bodhisattaṃ rajje [P 2.0300] abhisiñcitvā “ādāsamukharañño āṇā”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpesuṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya bodhisatto dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi, paṇḍitabhāvopissa sakalajambudīpaṃ pattharitvā gato.

The ministers, saying, 'So be it, O King,' took the monkey away and, thinking, 'The prince is wise; he will be able to rule,' they consecrated the Bodhisatta as king and had a drum beaten throughout the city to proclaim, 'This is the command of King Ādāsamukha.' From then on, the Bodhisatta ruled righteously, and his reputation for wisdom spread throughout all of Jambudīpa.

Paṇḍitabhāvadīpanatthaṃ panassa imāni cuddasa vatthūni ābhatāni –

Now, to illustrate his wisdom, these fourteen cases have been brought forward:

“Goṇo [V 2.0250] putto hayo ceva, naḷakāro gāmabhojako;

Gaṇikā taruṇī sappo, migo tittiradevatā;

Nāgo tapassino ceva, atho brāhmaṇamāṇavo”ti.

The ox, the son, the horse, the basket-maker, the village headman; the courtesan, the young woman, the snake, the deer, the partridge, the deity; the elephant, the ascetics, and the young brahmin.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbīkathā – bodhisattasmiñhi rajje abhisiñcite eko janasandharañño pādamūliko nāmena gāmaṇicando nāma evaṃ cintesi – “idaṃ rajjaṃ nāma samānavayehi saddhiṃ sobhati, ahañca mahallako, daharaṃ kumāraṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ na sakkhissāmi, janapade kasikammaṃ katvā jīvissāmī”ti, so nagarato tiyojanamattaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ gāmake vāsaṃ kappesi. Kasikammatthāya panassa goṇāpi natthi, so deve vuṭṭhe ekaṃ sahāyakaṃ dve goṇe yācitvā sabbadivasaṃ kasitvā tiṇaṃ khādāpetvā goṇe sāmikassa niyyādetuṃ gehaṃ agamāsi. So tasmiṃ khaṇe bhariyāya saddhiṃ gehamajjhe nisīditvā bhattaṃ bhuñjati. Goṇāpi paricayena gehaṃ pavisiṃsu, tesu pavisantesu sāmiko thālakaṃ ukkhipi, bhariyā thālakaṃ apanesi. Gāmaṇicando “bhattena maṃ nimanteyyu”nti olokento goṇe aniyyādetvāva gato. Corā rattiṃ vajaṃ bhinditvā teyeva goṇe hariṃsu. Goṇasāmiko pātova vajaṃ paviṭṭho te goṇe adisvā corehi haṭabhāvaṃ jānantopi “gāmaṇicandassa gīvaṃ karissāmī”ti taṃ upasaṅkamitvā [P 2.0301] “bho goṇe, me dehī”ti āha. “Nanu goṇā gehaṃ paviṭṭhā”ti. “Kiṃ pana te mayhaṃ niyyāditā”ti? “Na niyyāditā”ti. “Tena hi ayaṃ te rājadūto, ehī”ti [M 2.0274] āha. Tesu hi janapadesu yaṃkiñci sakkharaṃ vā kapālakhaṇḍaṃ vā ukkhipitvā “ayaṃ te rājadūto, ehī”ti vutte yo na gacchati, tassa rājāṇaṃ karoti, tasmā so “rājadūto”ti sutvāva nikkhami.

Here is the sequential account: When the Bodhisatta was consecrated as king, a former courtier of King Janasandha named Gāmaṇicanda thought, 'This kingship is suited for those of the same age, but I am old. I will not be able to serve the young prince. I will live by farming in the countryside.' He went about three leagues from the city and lived in a small village. However, he had no oxen for farming. When it rained, he borrowed two oxen from a friend and, after plowing all day and letting them graze, he went to the owner's house to return them. At that moment, the owner was sitting in the middle of the house with his wife, eating. The oxen, out of habit, entered the house. As they entered, the owner lifted his bowl and his wife removed hers. Gāmaṇicanda, waiting to be invited to eat, did not formally hand over the oxen and left. That night, thieves broke into the pen and stole those very oxen. Early next morning, the owner went to the pen and, not seeing the oxen, though he knew they were stolen, he thought, 'I will hold Gāmaṇicanda responsible.' He approached him and said, 'Friend, give me my oxen.' Gāmaṇicanda said, 'Did the oxen not enter your house?' 'But did you hand them over to me?' 'No, I did not.' 'Then here is the king’s messenger for you—come!' he said. For in those regions, if one threw a pebble or a potsherd and said, 'This is the king’s messenger—come!' anyone who did not go was considered to have violated the king’s command. Therefore, upon hearing the words 'king’s messenger,' he set out.

So tena saddhiṃ rājakulaṃ gacchanto ekaṃ sahāyakassa vasanagāmaṃ patvā “bho, atichātomhi, yāva gāmaṃ pavisitvā āhārakiccaṃ katvā āgacchāmi, tāva idheva hohī”ti vatvā sahāyagehaṃ pāvisi. Sahāyo panassa gehe natthi, sahāyikā disvā “sāmi, pakkāhāro natthi, muhuttaṃ adhivāsehi, idāneva pacitvā dassāmī”ti nisseṇiyā vegena taṇḍulakoṭṭhakaṃ abhiruhantī bhūmiyaṃ pati, taṅkhaṇaññeva tassā sattamāsiko gabbho patito. Tasmiṃ khaṇe tassā sāmiko āgantvā taṃ disvā “tvaṃ me bhariyaṃ paharitvā gabbhaṃ pātesi, ayaṃ te rājadūto, ehī”ti taṃ gahetvā nikkhami. Tato paṭṭhāya dve janā gāmaṇiṃ majjhe katvā gacchanti.

As he was going with him to the palace, he reached a village where a friend lived and, being very hungry, said, 'Friend, I am famished. Wait here while I go into the village to get some food and come back.' He entered his friend's house, but the friend was away. Seeing him, the friend's wife said, 'Sir, there is no cooked food. Wait a moment; I will cook some for you right away.' As she was hurriedly climbing a ladder to the rice granary, she fell to the ground, and at that moment, she miscarried her seven-month-old fetus. Just then, her husband arrived and, seeing this, said, 'You struck my wife and caused her to miscarry! Here is the king’s messenger for you—come!' He seized him and set out. From then on, the two men proceeded with Gāmaṇicanda between them.

Athekasmiṃ gāmadvāre eko assagopako assaṃ nivattetuṃ na sakkoti, assopi tesaṃ santikena [V 2.0251] gacchati. Assagopako gāmaṇicandaṃ disvā “mātula gāmaṇicanda, etaṃ tāva assaṃ kenacideva paharitvā nivattehī”ti āha. So ekaṃ pāsāṇaṃ gahetvā khipi, pāsāṇo assassa pāde paharitvā eraṇḍadaṇḍakaṃ viya bhindi. Atha naṃ assagopako “tayā me assassa pādo bhinno, ayaṃ te rājadūto”ti vatvā gaṇhi.

Then, at a certain village gate, a horse herder was unable to turn a horse back, and the horse was running towards them. Seeing Gāmaṇicanda, the horse herder said, 'Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, throw something at that horse to turn it back.' He picked up a stone and threw it; the stone struck the horse's leg and broke it like a castor-oil stalk. Then the horse herder said, 'You have broken my horse's leg; here is the king’s messenger for you,' and seized him.

So tīhi janehi nīyamāno cintesi – “ime maṃ rañño dassessanti, ahaṃ goṇamūlampi [P 2.0302] dātuṃ na sakkomi, pageva gabbhapātanadaṇḍaṃ, assamūlaṃ pana kuto labhissāmi, mataṃ me seyyo”ti. So gacchanto antarāmagge aṭaviyaṃ maggasamīpeyeva ekaṃ ekato papātaṃ pabbataṃ addasa, tassa chāyāya dve pitāputtā naḷakārā ekato kilañjaṃ cinanti. Gāmaṇicando “bho, sarīrakiccaṃ kātukāmomhi, thokaṃ idheva hotha, yāva āgacchāmī”ti vatvā pabbataṃ abhiruhitvā papātapasse patamāno pitunaḷakārassa piṭṭhiyaṃ pati, naḷakāro ekappahāreneva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Gāmaṇi uṭṭhāya aṭṭhāsi. Naḷakāraputto “tvaṃ me pitughātakacoro, ayaṃ te rājadūto”ti vatvā taṃ hatthe gahetvā gumbato nikkhami[M 2.0275], “kiṃ eta”nti ca vutte “pitughātakacoro me”ti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya gāmaṇiṃ majjhe katvā cattāro janā parivāretvā nayiṃsu.

Being led by the three men, he thought, 'These people will bring me before the king. I cannot pay for the oxen, let alone the penalty for the miscarriage; and where will I get the money for the horse? Death is better for me.' As he was going along, he saw a mountain with a sheer cliff on one side near the forest road. In its shade, two basket-makers, a father and son, were weaving mats. Gāmaṇicanda said, 'Sirs, I wish to relieve myself. Wait here a moment until I return.' He climbed the mountain and, jumping off the cliff, fell onto the back of the father basket-maker. The basket-maker died instantly. Gāmaṇicanda stood up. The son said, 'You are the murderer of my father! Here is the king’s messenger for you!' He seized him by the hand and led him out of the thicket. When asked what happened, he said, 'He is the murderer of my father.' From then on, the four men surrounded Gāmaṇicanda and led him away.

Athāparasmiṃ gāmadvāre eko gāmabhojako gāmaṇicandaṃ disvā “mātula gāmaṇicanda, kahaṃ gacchasī”ti vatvā “rājānaṃ passitu”nti vutte “addhā tvaṃ rājānaṃ passissasi, ahaṃ rañño sāsanaṃ dātukāmo, harissasī”ti āha. “Āma, harissāmī”ti. “Ahaṃ pakatiyā abhirūpo dhanavā yasasampanno arogo, idāni panamhi duggato ceva paṇḍurogī ca, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ puccha, rājā kira paṇḍito, so te kathessati, tassa sāsanaṃ puna mayhaṃ katheyyāsī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

Then, at another village gate, a village headman saw Gāmaṇicanda and said, 'Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?' When he replied, 'To see the king,' the headman said, 'Surely you will see the king. I wish to send a message to the king; will you carry it?' 'Yes, I will,' he replied. 'By nature, I was handsome, wealthy, famous, and healthy. But now I am both destitute and afflicted with jaundice. Ask the king what the cause of this is. The king, they say, is wise; he will tell you. Then you must report his message back to me.' He agreed, saying, 'Very well.'

Atha naṃ purato aññatarasmiṃ gāmadvāre ekā gaṇikā disvā “mātula gāmaṇicanda, kahaṃ gacchasī”ti vatvā “rājānaṃ passitu”nti vutte “rājā kira paṇḍito, mama sāsanaṃ harā”ti [P 2.0303] vatvā evamāha – “pubbe ahaṃ bahuṃ bhatiṃ labhāmi, idāni pana tambulamattampi na labhāmi, koci me santikaṃ āgato nāma natthi, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ pucchitvā paccāgantvā mayhaṃ katheyyāsī”ti.

Then, at a certain village gate ahead, a courtesan saw him and said, 'Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?' When he replied, 'To see the king,' she said, 'The king is said to be wise; carry my message.' She continued, 'Before, I received much payment, but now I do not receive even the price of a betel leaf. No one at all comes to me. Ask the king what the cause of this is and, upon returning, tell me.'

Atha naṃ purato aññatarasmiṃ gāmadvāre ekā taruṇitthī disvā tatheva pucchitvā “ahaṃ neva [V 2.0252] sāmikassa gehe vasituṃ sakkomi, na kulagehe, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ pucchitvā paccāgantvā mayhaṃ katheyyāsī”ti āha.

Then, at another village gate ahead, a young woman saw him and, after asking as before, said, 'I can neither stay in my husband's house nor in my family's home. Ask the king what the cause of this is and, upon returning, tell me.'

Atha naṃ tato parabhāge mahāmaggasamīpe ekasmiṃ vammike vasanto sappo disvā “gāmaṇicanda, kahaṃ yāsī”ti pucchitvā “rājānaṃ passitu”nti vutte “rājā kira paṇḍito, sāsanaṃ me harā”ti vatvā “ahaṃ gocaratthāya gamanakāle chātajjhatto milātasarīro vammikato nikkhamanto sarīrena bilaṃ pūretvā sarīraṃ kaḍḍhento kicchena nikkhamāmi, gocaraṃ caritvā āgato pana suhito thūlasarīro hutvā pavisanto bilapassāni aphusanto sahasāva pavisāmi, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ pucchitvā mayhaṃ katheyyāsī”ti āha.

Then, further on, near the main road, a snake living in an anthill saw him and asked, 'Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?' When he replied, 'To see the king,' it said, 'The king is said to be wise; carry my message.' It continued, 'When I leave to forage, I am overcome by hunger and my body is withered. Emerging from the anthill, I fill the hole with my body and drag myself out with difficulty. But when I return well-fed and with a plump body, I enter swiftly without even brushing against the sides of the hole. Ask the king what the cause of this is and tell me.'

Atha [M 2.0276] naṃ purato eko migo disvā tatheva pucchitvā “ahaṃ aññattha tiṇaṃ khādituṃ na sakkomi, ekasmiṃyeva rukkhamūle sakkomi, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ puccheyyāsī”ti āha.

Then a deer saw him ahead and, having asked him in the same way, said, 'I am unable to eat grass elsewhere; I can only do so at the foot of a single tree. You should ask the king what the cause of this is.'

Atha naṃ tato parabhāge eko tittiro disvā tatheva pucchitvā “ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva vammikapāde nisīditvā vassanto manāpaṃ karitvā vassituṃ sakkomi, sesaṭṭhānesu nisinno na sakkomi, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ puccheyyāsī”ti āha.

Then, further on, a partridge saw him and, having asked in the same way, said, 'I am able to call pleasantly only when perched on the base of a particular anthill, but I am unable to do so when sitting in other places. You should ask the king what the cause of this is.'

Atha naṃ purato ekā [P 2.0304] rukkhadevatā disvā “canda, kahaṃ yāsī”ti pucchitvā “rañño santika”nti vutte “rājā kira paṇḍito, ahaṃ pubbe sakkārappatto ahosiṃ, idāni pana pallavamuṭṭhimattampi na labhāmi, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ puccheyyāsī”ti āha.

Then a tree-deity, seeing him ahead, asked, 'Canda, where are you going?' When he replied, 'To the king's presence,' she said, 'The king is said to be wise. Formerly, I received offerings, but now I do not receive even a handful of sprouts. You should ask the king what the cause of this is.'

Tato aparabhāge eko nāgarājā taṃ disvā tatheva pucchitvā “rājā kira paṇḍito, pubbe imasmiṃ sare udakaṃ pasannaṃ maṇivaṇṇaṃ, idāni āvilaṃ paṇṇakasevālapariyonaddhaṃ, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ puccheyyāsī”ti āha.

Later, a nāga king saw him and, having asked in the same way, said, 'The king is said to be wise. Before, the water in this lake was clear and jewel-colored, but now it is turbid and overgrown with water-plants and algae. You should ask the king what the cause of this is.'

Atha naṃ purato nagarassa āsannaṭṭhāne ekasmiṃ ārāme vasantā tāpasā disvā tatheva pucchitvā “rājā kira paṇḍito, pubbe imasmiṃ ārāme phalāphalāni madhurāni ahesuṃ, idāni nirojāni kasaṭāni jātāni, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ puccheyyāsī”ti āhaṃsu.

Then, at a place near the city, some ascetics living in a grove saw him and, having asked in the same way, said, 'The king is said to be wise. Before, the fruits in this grove were sweet, but now they have become tasteless and astringent. You should ask the king what the cause of this is.'

Tato [V 2.0253] naṃ purato gantvā nagaradvārasamīpe ekissaṃ sālāyaṃ brāhmaṇamāṇavakā disvā “kahaṃ, bho canda, gacchasī”ti vatvā “rañño santika”nti vutte “tena hi no sāsanaṃ gahetvā gaccha, amhākañhi pubbe gahitagahitaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ ahosi, idāni pana chiddaghaṭe udakaṃ viya na saṇṭhāti na paññāyati, andhakāro viya hoti, tattha kiṃ kāraṇanti rājānaṃ puccheyyāsī”ti āhaṃsu.

Then, proceeding onward, near the city gate, some brahmin youths in a hall saw him and said, 'Where are you going, friend Canda?' When he replied, 'To the king's presence,' they said, 'In that case, take our message. For us, previously, whatever lessons we learned became clear. But now, like water in a leaky pot, it does not remain nor is it understood; it is like darkness. You should ask the king what the cause of this is.'

Gāmaṇicando imāni dasa sāsanāni gahetvā rañño santikaṃ agamāsi. Rājā vinicchayaṭṭhāne nisinno ahosi. Goṇasāmiko gāmaṇicandaṃ gahetvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkami. Rājā gāmaṇicandaṃ disvā sañjānitvā [M 2.0277] “ayaṃ amhākaṃ pitu upaṭṭhāko, amhe ukkhipitvā parihari, kahaṃ nu kho ettakaṃ kālaṃ vasī”ti [P 2.0305] cintetvā “ambho gāmaṇicanda, kahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ vasasi, cirakālato paṭṭhāya na paññāyasi, kenatthena āgatosī”ti āha. “Āma, deva, amhākaṃ devassa saggagatakālato paṭṭhāya janapadaṃ gantvā kasikammaṃ katvā jīvāmi, tato maṃ ayaṃ puriso goṇaaḍḍakāraṇā rājadūtaṃ dassetvā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ ākaḍḍhī”ti. “Anākaḍḍhiyamāno nāgaccheyyāsi”, “ākaḍḍhitabhāvoyeva sobhano, idāni taṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhāmi, kahaṃ so puriso”ti? “Ayaṃ, devā”ti. “Saccaṃ kira, bho, amhākaṃ candassa dūtaṃ dassesī”ti? “Saccaṃ, devā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Ayaṃ me deva dve goṇe na detī”ti. “Saccaṃ kira, candā”ti. “Tena hi, deva, mayhampi vacanaṃ suṇāthā”ti sabbaṃ pavattiṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā goṇasāmikaṃ pucchi – “kiṃ, bho, tava gehaṃ pavisante goṇe addasā”ti. “Nāddasaṃ, devā”ti. “Kiṃ, bho, maṃ ‘ādāsamukharājā nāmā’ti kathentānaṃ na sutapubbaṃ tayā, vissattho kathehī”ti? “Addasaṃ, devā”ti. “Bho canda, goṇānaṃ aniyyāditattā goṇā tava gīvā, ayaṃ pana puriso disvāva ‘na passāmī’ti sampajānamusāvādaṃ bhaṇi, tasmā tvaññeva kammiko hutvā imassa ca purisassa pajāpatiyāya cassa akkhīni uppāṭetvā sayaṃ goṇamūlaṃ catuvīsati kahāpaṇe dehī”ti. Evaṃ vutte goṇasāmikaṃ bahi kariṃsu. So “akkhīsu uppāṭitesu catuvīsatikahāpaṇehi kiṃ karissāmī”ti gāmaṇicandassa pādesu patitvā “sāmi canda, goṇamūlakahāpaṇā tuyheva hontu, ime ca gaṇhāhī”ti aññepi kahāpaṇe datvā palāyi.

Gāmaṇicanda took these ten messages and went to the king. The king was seated in the hall of justice. The ox-owner seized Gāmaṇicanda and approached the king. Seeing Gāmaṇicanda and recognizing him, the king thought, 'This was our father’s attendant; he carried us and cared for us. I wonder where he has lived all this time?' Then he said, 'Friend Gāmaṇicanda, where have you been all this time? You have not been seen for a long time. For what reason have you come?' 'Indeed, Your Majesty, ever since our lord went to heaven, I went to the countryside and lived by farming. Then this man, on account of a dispute over oxen, treated me as a royal messenger and dragged me into your presence.' 'If you were not dragged, would you not have come?' 'The fact of being dragged was indeed good, for now I get to see you. Where is that man?' 'Here he is, Your Majesty.' 'Is it true, sir, that you showed a summons to our Canda?' 'It is true, Your Majesty.' 'For what reason?' 'Your Majesty, this man does not give me my two oxen.' 'Is it true, Canda?' 'In that case, Your Majesty, please listen to my words also.' And he related the entire event. Having heard this, the king questioned the ox-owner: 'Sir, did you see the oxen entering your house?' 'I did not see them, Your Majesty.' 'Sir, have you never heard of me, that I am called King Ādāsamukha? Speak truthfully.' 'I did see them, Your Majesty.' 'Friend Canda, because the oxen were not returned, you are liable for them. This man, however, having seen them, told a deliberate lie, saying, "I did not see them." Therefore, you yourself shall act as the officer: pluck out the eyes of this man and his wife, and then you yourself give him twenty-four kahāpaṇas as the price of the oxen.' When this was said, they took the ox-owner outside. He thought, 'If my eyes are plucked out, what will I do with twenty-four kahāpaṇas?' Falling at Gāmaṇicanda’s feet, he said, 'Master Canda, let the kahāpaṇas for the oxen be yours alone, and take these as well.' Giving him even more kahāpaṇas, he fled.

Tato dutiyo āha – “ayaṃ, deva, mama pajāpatiṃ paharitvā [P 2.0306] gabbhaṃ pātesī”ti. “Saccaṃ candā”ti? “Suṇohi mahārājā”ti cando sabbaṃ vitthāretvā kathesi. Atha naṃ rājā “kiṃ pana tvaṃ etassa pajāpatiṃ paharitvā gabbhaṃ pātesī”ti pucchi. “Na pātemi, devā”ti[V 2.0254]. “Ambho sakkhissasi tvaṃ iminā gabbhassa pātitabhāvaṃ sādhetu”nti? “Na sakkomi, devā”ti. “Idāni kiṃ karosī”ti? “Deva, puttaṃ me laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Tena hi, ambho canda, tvaṃ etassa pajāpatiṃ tava gehe karitvā yadā puttavijātā [M 2.0278] hoti, tadā naṃ netvā etasseva dehī”ti. Sopi gāmaṇicandassa pādesu patitvā “mā me, sāmi, gehaṃ, bhindī”ti kahāpaṇe datvā palāyi.

Then the second litigant said, 'Your Majesty, this man struck my wife and caused a miscarriage.' 'Is that true, Canda?' 'Listen, Great King,' said Canda, and related everything in detail. Then the king asked him, 'Did you then strike this man's wife and cause a miscarriage?' 'I did not cause it, Your Majesty.' The king then asked the accuser, 'Friend, will you be able to prove that the miscarriage was caused by this man?' 'I cannot, Your Majesty.' 'What do you want now?' 'Your Majesty, it is right that I should receive a son.' 'In that case, friend Canda, take this man's wife into your house, and when she has given birth to a son, then take her and give her back to this very man.' That man also fell at Gāmaṇicanda’s feet and said, 'Master, do not break up my home!' and giving him kahāpaṇas, he fled.

Atha tatiyo āgantvā “iminā me, deva, paharitvā assassa pādo bhinno”ti āha. “Saccaṃ candā”ti. “Suṇohi, mahārājā”ti cando taṃ pavattiṃ vitthārena kathesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā assagopakaṃ āha – “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ ‘assaṃ paharitvā nivattehī’ti kathesī”ti. “Na kathemi, devā”ti. So punavāre pucchito “āma, kathemī”ti āha. Rājā candaṃ āmantetvā “ambho canda, ayaṃ kathetvāva ‘na kathemī’ti musāvādaṃ vadati, tvaṃ etassa jivhaṃ chinditvā assamūlaṃ amhākaṃ santikā gahetvā sahassaṃ dehī”ti āha. Assagopako aparepi kahāpaṇe datvā palāyi.

Then the third man came and said, 'Your Majesty, this man struck my horse and its leg was broken.' 'Is that true, Canda?' 'Listen, Great King,' said Canda, and related the matter in detail. Having heard this, the king said to the horse-keeper, 'Is it true that you said, "Strike the horse and turn it back"?' 'I did not say so, Your Majesty.' When questioned a second time, he said, 'Yes, I said it.' The king addressed Canda and said, 'Friend Canda, this man, although he said it, speaks a falsehood saying "I did not say it." You cut off his tongue, and taking a thousand kahāpaṇas from our presence as the price for the horse, give it to him.' The horse-keeper gave still more kahāpaṇas and fled.

Tato naḷakāraputto “ayaṃ me, deva, pitughātakacoro”ti āha. “Saccaṃ kira, candā”ti. “Suṇohi, devā”ti cando tampi kāraṇaṃ vitthāretvā kathesi. Atha rājā naḷakāraṃ āmantetvā “idāni kiṃ karosī”ti pucchi. “Deva [P 2.0307] me pitaraṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Ambho canda, imassa kira pitaraṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, matakaṃ pana na sakkā puna ānetuṃ, tvaṃ imassa mātaraṃ ānetvā tava gehe katvā etassa pitā hohī”ti. Naḷakāraputto “mā me, sāmi, matassa pitu gehaṃ bhindī”ti gāmaṇicandassa kahāpaṇe datvā palāyi.

Then the reed-worker’s son said, 'Your Majesty, this is the thief who killed my father.' 'Is that true, Canda?' 'Listen, Your Majesty,' said Canda, and explained that matter also in detail. Then the king addressed the reed-worker’s son and asked, 'What do you want now?' 'Your Majesty, it is right that I should get my father back.' 'Friend Canda, it seems it is right for this man to get his father back, but a dead man cannot be brought back again. You are to bring this man’s mother to your house and become a father to him.' The reed-worker’s son said, 'Master, do not break up the home of my dead father!' and giving kahāpaṇas to Gāmaṇicanda, he fled.

Gāmaṇicando aḍḍe jayaṃ patvā tuṭṭhacitto rājānaṃ āha – “atthi, deva, tumhākaṃ kehici sāsanaṃ pahitaṃ, taṃ vo kathemī”ti. “Kathehi, candā”ti. Cando brāhmaṇamāṇavakānaṃ sāsanaṃ ādiṃ katvā paṭilomakkamena ekekaṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Rājā paṭipāṭiyā vissajjesi.

Gāmaṇicanda, having won the lawsuits and being pleased in mind, said to the king, 'Your Majesty, some persons have sent messages to you; I shall relate them.' 'Relate them, Canda.' Beginning with the message of the brahmin youths, Canda recounted each matter in reverse order. The king resolved them in sequence.

Kathaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ tāva sāsanaṃ sutvā “pubbe tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne velaṃ jānitvā vassanakukkuṭo ahosi, tesaṃ tena saddena uṭṭhāya mante gahetvā sajjhāyaṃ karontānaññeva aruṇo uggacchati, tena tesaṃ gahitagahitaṃ na nassati. Idāni pana nesaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne avelāya vassanakakukkuṭo atthi, so atirattiṃ vā vassati atipabhāte vā, atirattiṃ vassantassa tassa saddena uṭṭhāya mante gahetvā niddābhibhūtā [M 2.0279] sajjhāyaṃ akatvāva puna sayanti[V 2.0255], atipabhāte vassantassa saddena uṭṭhāya sajjhāyituṃ na labhanti, tena tesaṃ gahitagahitaṃ na paññāyatī”ti āha.

How is it? First, having heard the message, he said: 'In the past, at their dwelling place, there was a cock that crowed, knowing the proper time. Rising at its sound, they would take up their texts and recite, and the dawn would break while they were still reciting. Thus, what they had learned was not lost. But now, in their dwelling place, there is a cock that crows at the wrong time. It crows either in the middle of the night or when it is already bright. When it crows in the middle of the night, they rise at its sound and take up their texts, but being overcome by sleep, they lie down again without reciting. When it crows when it is already bright, they rise at its sound but do not get a chance to recite. Thus, what they have learned is not retained.'

Dutiyaṃ sutvā “te pubbe samaṇadhammaṃ karontā kasiṇaparikamme yuttapayuttā ahesuṃ. Idāni pana samaṇadhammaṃ vissajjetvā akattabbesu yuttapayuttā ārāme uppannāni phalāphalāni upaṭṭhākānaṃ datvā piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍakena micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappenti, tena nesaṃ phalāphalāni na madhurāni [P 2.0308] jātāni. Sace pana te pubbe viya puna samaṇadhamme yuttapayuttā bhavissanti, puna tesaṃ phalāphalāni madhurāni bhavissanti. Te tāpasā rājakulānaṃ paṇḍitabhāvaṃ na jānanti, samaṇadhammaṃ tesaṃ kātuṃ vadehī”ti āha.

Second, having heard, he said: 'In the past, while performing the duties of a recluse, they were diligent and devoted to the preliminary kasiṇa meditation. But now, having abandoned the duties of a recluse, they are diligent and devoted to what ought not to be done. They give the various fruits grown in the monastery to their supporters and maintain themselves by wrong livelihood through an exchange of alms-food. For that reason, their various fruits have not become sweet. But if they again become diligent and devoted to the duties of a recluse as before, their various fruits will again become sweet. Those ascetics do not understand the wisdom of the royal house. Tell them to perform the duties of a recluse.'

Tatiyaṃ sutvā “te nāgarājāno aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ karonti, tena taṃ udakaṃ āvilaṃ jātaṃ. Sace te pubbe viya samaggā bhavissanti, puna pasannaṃ bhavissatī”ti āha.

Third, having heard, he said: 'Those nāga kings are quarreling with one another; for that reason, the water has become turbid. If they become harmonious as they were before, it will become clear again.'

Catutthaṃ sutvā “sā rukkhadevatā pubbe aṭaviyaṃ paṭipanne manusse rakkhati, tasmā nānappakāraṃ balikammaṃ labhati. Idāni pana ārakkhaṃ na karoti, tasmā balikammaṃ na labhati. Sace pubbe viya ārakkhaṃ karissati, puna lābhaggappattā bhavissati. Sā rājūnaṃ atthibhāvaṃ na jānāti, tasmā aṭaviāruḷhamanussānaṃ ārakkhaṃ kātuṃ vadehī”ti āha.

Having heard the fourth, he said: 'That tree-deity formerly protected people traveling in the forest, and thus received various offerings. But now, she provides no protection, and thus receives no offerings. If she provides protection as before, she will again attain the highest gain. She does not know of the existence of kings. Tell her to protect the people traveling in the forest.'

Pañcamaṃ sutvā “yasmiṃ vammikapāde nisīditvā so tittiro manāpaṃ vassati, tassa heṭṭhā mahantī nidhikumbhi atthi, taṃ uddharitvā tvaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha.

Having heard the fifth, he said: 'At the foot of the anthill where that partridge sits and utters pleasant sounds, there is a large treasure pot beneath. Dig it up and take it.'

Chaṭṭhaṃ sutvā “yassa rukkhassa mūle so migo tiṇāni khādituṃ sakkoti, tassa rukkhassa upari mahantaṃ bhamaramadhu atthi, so madhumakkhitesu tiṇesu paluddho aññāni khādituṃ na sakkoti, tvaṃ taṃ madhupaṭalaṃ haritvā aggamadhuṃ amhākaṃ pahiṇa, sesaṃ attanā paribhuñjā”ti āha.

Having heard the sixth, he said: 'At the foot of the tree where that deer is able to eat grass, there is a large honeycomb above. Allured by the honey-smeared grass, that deer cannot eat any other grass. You take that honeycomb, send the choicest honey to us, and enjoy the rest yourself.'

Sattamaṃ sutvā “yasmiṃ vammike so sappo vasati, tassa heṭṭhā mahantī nidhikumbhi atthi, so taṃ rakkhamāno vasanto nikkhamanakāle dhanalobhena sarīraṃ sithilaṃ katvā lagganto nikkhamati, gocaraṃ gahetvā [M 2.0280] dhanasinehena alagganto vegena sahasā pavisati. Taṃ nidhikumbhiṃ uddharitvā tvaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha.

Having heard the seventh, he said: 'In that anthill where the serpent dwells, there is a large treasure pot beneath. Guarding it, he stays there, but when leaving, out of greed for wealth, he makes his body loose and exits slowly, scraping along. After getting his food, out of attachment to wealth, he enters swiftly and suddenly without scraping. You must dig up that treasure pot and take it.'

Aṭṭhamaṃ [V 2.0256] sutvā “tassā taruṇitthiyā sāmikassa ca mātāpitūnañca vasanagāmānaṃ [P 2.0309] antare ekasmiṃ gāmake jāro atthi. Sā taṃ saritvā tasmiṃ sinehena sāmikassa gehe vasituṃ asakkontī ‘mātāpitaro passissāmī’ti jārassa gehe katipāhaṃ vasitvā mātāpitūnaṃ gehaṃ gacchati, tattha katipāhaṃ vasitvā puna jāraṃ saritvā ‘sāmikassa gehaṃ gamissāmī’ti puna jārasseva gehaṃ gacchati. Tassā itthiyā rājūnaṃ atthibhāvaṃ ācikkhitvā ‘sāmikasseva kira gehe vasatu. Sace taṃ rājā gaṇhāpeti, jīvitaṃ te natthi, appamādaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti tassā kathehī”ti āha.

Having heard the eighth, he said: 'Between the villages where that young woman’s husband and her parents live, there is a lover in a certain small village. Remembering him, and unable to stay in her husband’s house due to affection for him, she says, “I will visit my parents,” but stays a few days at the lover’s house, then goes to her parents’ home. After staying there a few days, remembering the lover again, she says, “I will return to my husband’s house,” but goes back to the lover’s house instead. Having informed her of the existence of kings, say to her: “Let her stay only in her husband’s house. If the king has you seized, your life will be forfeit; it is fitting to be heedful.”'

Navamaṃ sutvā “sā gaṇikā pubbe ekassa hatthato bhatiṃ gahetvā taṃ ajīrāpetvā aññassa hatthato na gaṇhāti, tenassā pubbe bahuṃ uppajji. Idāni pana attano dhammataṃ vissajjetvā ekassa hatthato gahitaṃ ajīrāpetvāva aññassa hatthato gaṇhāti, purimassa okāsaṃ akatvā pacchimassa karoti, tenassā bhati na uppajjati, na keci naṃ upasaṅkamanti. Sace attano dhamme ṭhassati, pubbasadisāva bhavissati. Attano dhamme ṭhātumassā kathehī”ti āha.

Having heard the ninth, he said: 'That courtesan formerly took a fee from one man and would not take from another until the first was exhausted. Thus, she prospered greatly in the past. But now, abandoning her own principle, she takes from another without the fee from the first being exhausted, giving opportunity to the later one without having given it to the former. Hence, her fee does not arise, and no one approaches her. If she abides by her own principle, she will be just as before. Tell her to abide by her own principle.'

Dasamaṃ sutvā “so gāmabhojako pubbe dhammena samena aḍḍaṃ vinicchini, tena manussānaṃ piyo ahosi manāpo, sampiyāyamānā cassa manussā bahupaṇṇākāraṃ āhariṃsu, tena abhirūpo dhanavā yasasampanno ahosi. Idāni pana lañjavittako hutvā adhammena aḍḍaṃ vinicchinati, tena duggato kapaṇo hutvā paṇḍurogena abhibhūto. Sace pubbe viya dhammena aḍḍaṃ vinicchinissati, puna pubbasadiso bhavissati. So rañño atthibhāvaṃ na jānāti, dhammena aḍḍaṃ vinicchinitumassa kathehī”ti āha.

Having heard the tenth, he said: 'That village headman formerly judged disputes righteously and impartially, so he was beloved and dear to the people. Being cherished, the people brought him many gifts, and thus he was handsome, wealthy, and renowned. But now, having become a bribe-taker, he judges disputes unrighteously, and so he is poor, miserable, and afflicted by jaundice. If he judges disputes righteously as before, he will again become like before. He does not know of the king's existence; tell him to judge disputes righteously.'

Iti so gāmaṇicando imāni ettakāni sāsanāni rañño ārocesi, rājā attano paññāya sabbānipi tāni sabbaññubuddho [P 2.0310] viya byākaritvā gāmaṇicandassa bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā tassa vasanagāmaṃ brahmadeyyaṃ katvā tasseva datvā uyyojesi. So nagarā nikkhamitvā bodhisattena dinnasāsanaṃ [M 2.0281] brāhmaṇamāṇavakānañca tāpasānañca nāgarājassa ca rukkhadevatāya ca ārocetvā tittirassa vasanaṭṭhānato nidhiṃ gahetvā migassa tiṇakhādanaṭṭhāne rukkhato bhamaramadhuṃ gahetvā rañño madhuṃ pesetvā sappassa vasanaṭṭhāne vammikaṃ khaṇitvā nidhiṃ gahetvā taruṇitthiyā ca gaṇikāya ca gāmabhojakassa ca rañño kathitaniyāmeneva sāsanaṃ ārocetvā mahantena yasena [V 2.0257] attano gāmakaṃ gantvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gato. Ādāsamukharājāpi dānādīni puññāni katvā jīvitapariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūrento gato.

Thus Gāmaṇicanda reported all these messages to the king. The king, by his own wisdom, explained them all just like an omniscient Buddha. He then gave Gāmaṇicanda much wealth, made his dwelling village a tax-free grant, and after giving it to him, sent him away. Leaving the city, he conveyed the messages given by the Bodhisatta to the brahmin youths, the ascetics, the nāga king, and the tree-deity. He took the treasure from the partridge’s dwelling place, took the honeycomb from the tree at the place where the deer ate grass, and sent the honey to the king. Digging up the anthill at the serpent’s dwelling place, he took the treasure. He also delivered the messages to the young woman, the courtesan, and the village headman, exactly in the manner spoken by the king. With great retinue, he went to his own village, lived there for the rest of his life, and passed away according to his deeds. King Ādāsamukha also performed meritorious deeds such as generosity and, at the end of his life, went to populate the heavenly city.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva mahāpañño, pubbepi mahāpaññoyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmiarahanto ahesuṃ. “Tadā gāmaṇicando ānando ahosi, ādāsamukharājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Monks, the Tathāgata is not of great wisdom only now; in the past also he was of great wisdom." Having said this, he brought forth this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths, and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many became stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants. "At that time, Gāmaṇicanda was Ānanda, and King Ādāsamukha was none other than myself."

Gāmaṇicandajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Seventh: The Explanation of the Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka.

[258] 8. Mandhātujātakavaṇṇanā

[258] 8. The Explanation of the Mandhātu Jātaka

Yāvatā candimasūriyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya caramāno ekaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ itthiṃ disvā ukkaṇṭhi. Atha naṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhaṃ ānetvā “ayaṃ, bhante, bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhito”ti satthu dassesuṃ. Satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhito”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kadā tvaṃ[P 2.0311], bhikkhu, agāraṃ ajjhāvasamāno taṇhaṃ pūretuṃ sakkhissasi, kāmataṇhā hi nāmesā samuddo viya duppūrā, porāṇakarājāno dvisahassaparittadīpaparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu cakkavattirajjaṃ kāretvā manussaparihāreneva cātumahārājikadevaloke rajjaṃ kāretvā tāvatiṃsadevaloke chattiṃsāya sakkānañca vasanaṭṭhāne devarajjaṃ kāretvāpi attano kāmataṇhaṃ pūretuṃ asakkontāva kālamakaṃsu, tvaṃ panetaṃ taṇhaṃ kadā pūretuṃ sakkhissasī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"As far as the moon and sun..." This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a discontented monk. It is said that while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a well-adorned and dressed woman and became discontented. Then the monks brought him to the Dhamma hall and presented him to the Teacher, saying, "Venerable sir, this monk is discontented." The Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?" When he replied, "It is true, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Monk, when will you ever be able to satisfy your craving while living as a householder? For this craving for sensual pleasures is like the ocean—impossible to fill. Ancient kings, having exercised universal sovereignty over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand lesser islands, having exercised kingship in the heaven of the Four Great Kings with only a human retinue, and even having exercised divine kingship in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the abode of thirty-six Sakkas, still died unable to satisfy their craving for sensual pleasures. When, then, will you ever be able to satisfy this craving?" Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte paṭhamakappikesu mahāsammato nāma rājā ahosi. Tassa putto rojo nāma, tassa putto vararojo nāma, tassa putto kalyāṇo nāma, tassa putto [M 2.0282] varakalyāṇo nāma, tassa putto uposatho nāma, tassa putto mandhātu nāma ahosi. So sattahi ratanehi catūhi ca iddhīhi samannāgato cakkavattirajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa vāmahatthaṃ samañjitvā dakkhiṇahatthena apphoṭitakāle ākāsā dibbamegho viya jāṇuppamāṇaṃ sattaratanavassaṃ vassati, evarūpo acchariyamanusso ahosi. So caturāsīti vassasahassāni kumārakīḷaṃ kīḷi. Caturāsīti vassasahassāni [V 2.0258] oparajjaṃ kāresi, caturāsīti vassasahassāni cakkavattirajjaṃ kāresi, āyuppamāṇaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ ahosi.

In the past, among the people of the first aeon, there was a king named Mahāsammata. His son was named Roja; his son was Vararoja; his son was Kalyāṇa; his son was Varakalyāṇa; his son was Uposatha; and his son was Mandhātu. Endowed with the seven treasures and the four powers, he reigned as a wheel-turning monarch. When he clenched his left hand and snapped the fingers of his right hand, a rain of the seven treasures, knee-deep, would fall from the sky like a divine cloud—such a marvelous human being was he. He spent eighty-four thousand years in princely play, eighty-four thousand years as viceroy, and eighty-four thousand years as a wheel-turning monarch. His lifespan was an incalculable period.

So ekadivasaṃ kāmataṇhaṃ pūretuṃ asakkonto ukkaṇṭhitākāraṃ dassesi. Athāmaccā “kiṃ nu kho, deva, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Mayhaṃ puññabale olokiyamāne idaṃ rajjaṃ kiṃ karissati, kataraṃ nu kho ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīya”nti? “Devaloko, mahārājā”ti. So cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkiritvā saddhiṃ parisāya cātumahārājikadevalokaṃ [P 2.0312] agamāsi. Athassa cattāro mahārājāno dibbamālāgandhahatthā devagaṇaparivutā paccuggamanaṃ katvā taṃ ādāya cātumahārājikadevalokaṃ gantvā devarajjaṃ adaṃsu. Tassa sakaparisāya parivāritasseva tasmiṃ rajjaṃ kārentassa dīgho addhā vītivatto.

One day, unable to satisfy his craving for sensual pleasures, he showed signs of discontent. Then his ministers asked, "Why, lord, are you discontented?" "When the power of my merit is considered, what is this kingdom? What place is truly delightful?" "The world of the devas, great king," they replied. He then sprinkled the wheel-treasure with water and, together with his retinue, went to the heaven of the Four Great Kings. There, the Four Great Kings, with divine garlands and perfumes in their hands and surrounded by a host of devas, came to meet him. Taking him with them, they went to the heaven of the Four Great Kings and gave him the divine kingship. While he ruled there, surrounded only by his own retinue, a long time passed.

So tatthāpi taṇhaṃ pūretuṃ asakkonto ukkaṇṭhitākāraṃ dassesi, cattāro mahārājāno “kiṃ nu kho, deva, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Imamhā devalokā kataraṃ ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīya”nti. “Mayaṃ, deva, paresaṃ upaṭṭhākaparisā, tāvatiṃsadevaloko ramaṇīyo”ti. Mandhātā cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkiritvā attano parisāya parivuto tāvatiṃsābhimukho pāyāsi. Athassa sakko devarājā dibbamālāgandhahattho devagaṇaparivuto paccuggamanaṃ katvā taṃ hatthe gahetvā “ito ehi, mahārājā”ti āha. Rañño devagaṇaparivutassa gamanakāle pariṇāyakaratanaṃ cakkaratanaṃ ādāya saddhiṃ parisāya manussapathaṃ otaritvā attano nagarameva pāvisi. Sakko mandhātuṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ netvā devatā dve koṭṭhāse katvā attano devarajjaṃ majjhe bhinditvā adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya dve rājāno rajjaṃ kāresuṃ. Evaṃ kāle gacchante sakko saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassāni tisso ca vassakoṭiyo āyuṃ khepetvā cavi, añño sakko nibbatti. Sopi devarajjaṃ [M 2.0283] kāretvā āyukkhayena cavi. Etenūpāyena chattiṃsa sakkā caviṃsu, mandhātā pana manussaparihārena devarajjaṃ kāresiyeva.

There too, unable to satisfy his craving, he showed signs of discontent. The Four Great Kings asked him, 'Why, lord, are you discontented?' 'What place is more delightful than this world of the devas?' he inquired. 'We, lord, are an attendant retinue for others; the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is delightful,' they replied. Mandhātā, having sprinkled the wheel-treasure with water, surrounded by his retinue, set out toward Tāvatiṃsa. Then Sakka, king of the devas, with divine garlands and perfumes in hand, surrounded by a host of devas, came forth to welcome him. Taking him by the hand, he said, 'Come here, great king.' As the king, surrounded by the host of devas, proceeded, the counsellor-treasure, taking the wheel-treasure, descended with the retinue to the human world and entered his own city. Sakka led Mandhātā to the Tāvatiṃsa palace and, dividing the devas into two groups, split his own kingdom of the devas in the middle and gave it to him. From then on, two kings ruled. As time passed, Sakka, having exhausted his lifespan of thirty-six million years, passed away, and another Sakka arose. He too ruled the kingdom of the devas and passed away at the end of his life. In this way, thirty-six Sakkas passed away, but Mandhātā, with his human form, continued to rule the kingdom of the devas.

Tassa evaṃ kāle gacchante bhiyyosomattāya kāmataṇhā uppajji, so “kiṃ me upaḍḍharajjena, sakkaṃ māretvā ekarajjameva karissāmī”ti cintesi. Sakkaṃ māretuṃ nāma na sakkā, taṇhā nāmesā vipattimūlā, tenassa āyusaṅkhāro parihāyi, jarā sarīraṃ pahari. Manussasarīrañca [P 2.0313] nāma devaloke na bhijjati, atha so devalokā bhassitvā uyyāne otari. Uyyānapālo tassa āgatabhāvaṃ rājakule nivedesi. Rājakulaṃ āgantvā uyyāneyeva sayanaṃ paññapesi. Rājā anuṭṭhānaseyyāya nipajji. Amaccā “deva, tumhākaṃ parato [V 2.0259] kinti kathemā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Mama parato tumhe imaṃ sāsanaṃ mahājanassa katheyyātha – ‘mandhātumahārājā dvisahassaparittadīpaparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu cakkavattirajjaṃ kāretvā dīgharattaṃ cātumahārājikesu rajjaṃ kāretvā chattiṃsāya sakkānaṃ āyuppamāṇena devaloke rajjaṃ kāretvā taṇhaṃ apūretvā kālamakāsī’”ti. So evaṃ vatvā kālaṃ katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

As time passed in this way, his craving for sensual pleasures arose all the more. He thought, 'What use is half a kingdom to me? I will kill Sakka and rule as the sole monarch.' It is, however, impossible to kill Sakka; for craving is the root of ruin. Because of it, his life-force diminished, and old age struck his body. A human body does not disintegrate in the world of the devas, so he fell from the world of the devas and descended into a park. The park-keeper informed the royal family of his arrival. The royal family came and prepared a couch for him right there in the park. The king lay down on his deathbed. His ministers asked, 'Lord, what shall we say after you are gone?' 'After I am gone, you should proclaim this message to the populace: “King Mandhātā, having reigned as a wheel-turning monarch over the four great continents with their two thousand surrounding islands, having reigned for a long time in the heaven of the Four Great Kings, and having reigned in the world of the devas for the lifespan of thirty-six Sakkas, died without having fulfilled his craving.”' Having spoken thus, he passed away and went according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

The Teacher, having related this story of the past, as the Fully Enlightened One, spoke these verses:

22.

22.

“Yāvatā candimasūriyā, pariharanti disā bhanti virocanā;

Sabbeva dāsā mandhātu, ye pāṇā pathavissitā.

As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the directions, all beings who dwell upon the earth are vassals of Mandhātā.

23.

23.

“Na kahāpaṇavassena, titti kāmesu vijjati;

Appassādā dukhā kāmā, iti viññāya paṇḍito.

Not by a rain of coins is satisfaction in sensual pleasures found; sensual pleasures are of little enjoyment, are suffering—this a wise person understands.

24.

24.

“Api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati;

Taṇhakkhayarato hoti, sammāsambuddhasāvako”ti.

Even in divine sensual pleasures, he finds no delight. A disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One delights in the destruction of craving.

Tattha yāvatāti paricchedavacanaṃ. Pariharantīti yattakena paricchedena sineruṃ pariharanti. Disā bhantīti dasasu disāsu bhāsanti pabhāsanti. Virocanāti ālokakaraṇatāya virocanasabhāvā. Sabbeva dāsā mandhātu, ye pāṇā pathavissitāti ettake padese ye pathavinissitā [M 2.0284] pāṇā janapadavāsino manussā, sabbeva te “dāsā mayaṃ rañño mandhātussa, ayyako no rājā mandhātā”ti evaṃ upagatattā bhujissāpi samānā dāsāyeva.

Herein, 'as far as' is a word indicating extent. 'Revolve' means they revolve around Sineru within that extent. 'Illuminating the directions' means they shine and illuminate in the ten directions. 'Shining brightly' means their nature is to shine because they produce light. 'All beings who dwell upon the earth are vassals of Mandhātā' means that in that region, all beings who dwell on the earth, the people inhabiting the country, all of them, though they are free men, are indeed vassals, because they have submitted themselves, saying, 'We are the vassals of King Mandhātā, our lord is King Mandhātā.'

Na kahāpaṇavassenāti tesaṃ dāsabhūtānaṃ manussānaṃ anuggahāya yaṃ mandhātā apphoṭetvā [P 2.0314] sattaratanavassaṃ vassāpeti, taṃ idha “kahāpaṇavassa”nti vuttaṃ. Titti kāmesūti tenāpi kahāpaṇavassena vatthukāmakilesakāmesu titti nāma natthi, evaṃ duppūrā esā taṇhā. Appassādā dukhā kāmāti supinakūpamattā kāmā nāma appassādā parittasukhā, dukkhameva panettha bahutaraṃ. Taṃ dukkhakkhandhasuttapariyāyena dīpetabbaṃ. Iti viññāyāti evaṃ jānitvā.

‘Not by a rain of coins’: that rain of the seven treasures which Mandhātā, by snapping his fingers, caused to fall for the benefit of those humans who had become his vassals, is here called a 'rain of coins.' 'Satisfaction in sensual pleasures': even with that rain of coins, there is no satisfaction in sensual pleasures, whether of the object or of the defilement. So hard to fill is this craving. 'Sensual pleasures are of little enjoyment, are suffering': sensual pleasures are of little enjoyment, like a dream or a pit, with limited happiness; suffering is far greater therein. This should be explained by way of the Discourse on the Mass of Suffering. 'Having understood this' means having known this.

Dibbesūti devatānaṃ paribhogesu rūpādīsu. Ratiṃ soti so vipassako bhikkhu dibbehi kāmehi [V 2.0260] nimantiyamānopi tesu ratiṃ nādhigacchati āyasmā samiddhi viya. Taṇhakkhayaratoti nibbānarato. Nibbānañhi āgamma taṇhā khīyati, tasmā taṃ “taṇhakkhayo”ti vuccati. Tattha rato hoti abhirato. Sammāsambuddhasāvakoti buddhassa savanante jāto bahussuto yogāvacarapuggalo.

‘In divine (pleasures)’ means in the forms and so on which are the devas' objects of enjoyment. 'He finds no delight': that insight-meditating monk, even when invited with divine sensual pleasures, finds no delight in them, like the Venerable Samiddhi. 'Delights in the destruction of craving' means delighting in Nibbāna. For it is on account of Nibbāna that craving is destroyed; therefore, it is called 'the destruction of craving.' Therein he is delighted, greatly pleased. 'A disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One' means a learned person, a practitioner of the meditative discipline, who is born upon hearing the Buddha's teaching.

Evaṃ satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, aññe pana bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu. “Tadā mandhāturājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the explanation of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and many others attained the fruits of stream-entry and so on. 'At that time, I myself was King Mandhātā.'

Mandhātujātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Mandhātu Jātaka, the Eighth.

[259] 9. Tirīṭavacchajātakavaṇṇanā

[259] 9. The Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka.

Nayimassa vijjāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto āyasmato ānandassa kosalarañño mātugāmānaṃ hatthato pañcasatāni, rañño hatthato pañcasatānīti dussasahassapaṭilābhavatthuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā dukanipāte guṇajātake (jā. aṭṭha. 2.2.guṇajātakavaṇṇanā) vitthāritameva.

"He has no knowledge": this story the Teacher told while dwelling in Jetavana concerning the matter of the Venerable Ānanda's receiving a thousand cloths: five hundred from the queens of the king of Kosala, and five hundred from the king himself. The story is elaborated below in the Guṇajātaka of the Dukanipāta.

Atīte [M 2.0285] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā nāmaggahaṇadivase tirīṭavacchakumāroti katanāmo anupubbena vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā agāraṃ ajjhāvasanto mātāpitūnaṃ kālakiriyāya saṃviggahadayo hutvā nikkhamitvā isipabbajjaṃ [P 2.0315] pabbajitvā araññāyatane vanamūlaphalāhāro hutvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Tasmiṃ tattha vasante bārāṇasirañño paccanto kupi, so tattha gantvā yuddhe parājito maraṇabhayabhīto hatthikkhandhagato ekena passena palāyitvā araññe vicaranto pubbaṇhasamaye tirīṭavacchassa phalāphalatthāya gatakāle tassa assamapadaṃ pāvisi. So “tāpasānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāna”nti hatthito otaritvā vātātapena kilanto pipāsito pānīyaghaṭaṃ olokento katthaci adisvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ udapānaṃ addasa. Udakaussiñcanatthāya pana rajjughaṭaṃ adisvā pipāsaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto hatthissa kucchiyaṃ baddhayottaṃ gahetvā hatthiṃ udapānataṭe ṭhapetvā tassa pāde yottaṃ bandhitvā yottena udapānaṃ otaritvā yotte apāpuṇante uttaritvā uttarasāṭakaṃ yottakoṭiyā saṅghāṭetvā puna otari, tathāpi nappahosiyeva. So aggapādehi [V 2.0261] udakaṃ phusitvā atipipāsito “pipāsaṃ vinodetvā maraṇampi sumaraṇa”nti cintetvā udapāne patitvā yāvadatthaṃ pivitvā paccuttarituṃ asakkonto tattheva aṭṭhāsi. Hatthīpi susikkhitattā aññattha agantvā rājānaṃ olokento tattheva aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto sāyanhasamaye phalāphalaṃ āharitvā hatthiṃ disvā “rājā āgato bhavissati, vammitahatthīyeva pana paññāyati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti so hatthisamīpaṃ upasaṅkami. Hatthīpi tassa upasaṅkamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto udapānataṭaṃ gantvā rājānaṃ disvā “mā bhāyi, mahārājā”ti samassāsetvā nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā rājānaṃ uttāretvā kāyamassa sambāhitvā telena makkhetvā nhāpetvā phalāphalāni khādāpetvā [P 2.0316] hatthissa sannāhaṃ mocesi. Rājā dvīhatīhaṃ vissamitvā bodhisattassa attano santikaṃ āgamanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gahetvā pakkāmi. Rājabalakāyo nagarassa avidūre khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā ṭhito. Rājānaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā parivāresi, rājā nagaraṃ pāvisi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kasi country. On the naming day, he was given the name Tirīṭavaccha Kumāra. In due course, having reached maturity, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā. While living at home, his parents passed away, and with a heart agitated by a sense of spiritual urgency, he renounced the household life, went forth as an ascetic, and dwelling in a forest hermitage, he sustained himself on forest roots and fruits. While he was living there, a border revolt arose in the kingdom of Benares. The king went there, was defeated in battle, and fearing for his life, mounted his elephant and fled alone into the forest. Wandering in the wilderness, in the early morning, while Tirīṭavaccha was away gathering fruits, the king entered his hermitage. Thinking, 'This is a dwelling place for ascetics,' he dismounted from his elephant. Exhausted by the wind and sun, and parched with thirst, he looked around for a water pot but found none. Then, at the edge of the walking path, he spotted a well. However, seeing no rope or bucket to draw water, and unable to endure his thirst, he took the harness tied around the elephant’s belly, placed the elephant at the edge of the well, tied the harness to its foot, and descended into the well using the harness. But when the harness did not reach the water, he climbed out, tied his upper garment to the end of the harness, and descended again, yet still it was not enough. He touched the water with his toes, and being extremely thirsty, he thought, 'Having quenched my thirst, even death will be a good death.'
