So he plunged into the well, drank to his satisfaction, but could not climb back out and remained there. The elephant, being well-trained, did not go elsewhere but stood right there, watching the king. In the evening, the Bodhisatta returned with fruits and saw the elephant. 'The king must have come,' he thought, 'but this appears to be an armored elephant. What could be the reason?' So he approached the elephant, which, knowing his approach, stood aside. The Bodhisatta went to the edge of the well and, seeing the king, reassured him, 'Do not fear, great king.' He fashioned a ladder, helped the king climb out, massaged his body, anointed him with oil, bathed him, fed him fruits, and then released the elephant’s armor. After resting for two or three days, the king took leave, having received a promise from the Bodhisatta to visit him. The royal army had encamped not far from the city; seeing the king return, they surrounded him, and the king entered the city.

Bodhisattopi [M 2.0286] aḍḍhamāsaccayena bārāṇasiṃ patvā uyyāne vasitvā punadivase bhikkhaṃ caramāno rājadvāraṃ gato. Rājā mahāvātapānaṃ ugghāṭetvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ olokayamāno bodhisattaṃ disvā sañjānitvā pāsādā oruyha vanditvā mahātalaṃ āropetvā samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisīdāpetvā attano paṭiyāditaṃ āhāraṃ bhojetvā sayampi bhuñjitvā uyyānaṃ netvā tatthassa caṅkamanādiparivāraṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kāretvā sabbe pabbajitaparikkhāre datvā uyyānapālaṃ paṭicchāpetvā vanditvā pakkāmi. Tato paṭṭhāya bodhisatto rājanivesaneyeva paribhuñji, mahāsakkārasammāno ahosi.

The Bodhisatta, after half a month, reached Benares and stayed in a park. The next day, while going for alms, he went to the palace gate. The king, having opened a large window and looking out over the royal courtyard, saw the Bodhisatta. Recognizing him, he descended from the palace, paid homage, led him up to the palace, seated him on a royal throne under a raised white parasol, and fed him with the food prepared for himself, after which he also ate. Then he took him to the park, had a dwelling place prepared for him there with walking paths and other amenities, gave him all the requisites for an ascetic, entrusted him to the park keeper, paid homage, and departed. From then on, the Bodhisatta took his meals in the royal palace itself and was held in great honor and respect.

Taṃ asahamānā amaccā “evarūpaṃ sakkāraṃ ekopi yodho labhamāno kiṃ nāma na kareyyā”ti vatvā uparājānaṃ upagantvā “deva, amhākaṃ rājā ekaṃ tāpasaṃ ativiya mamāyati, kiṃ nāma tena tasmiṃ diṭṭhaṃ, tumhepi tāva raññā saddhiṃ mantethā”ti āhaṃsu. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā amaccehi saddhiṃ rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Unable to bear this, the ministers said, 'If even a single warrior received such honor, what task would he not perform?' They approached the viceroy and said, 'Your Highness, our king is excessively fond of an ascetic. What indeed has the king seen in him? You should discuss this with the king.' The viceroy agreed, and together with the ministers, he approached the king and spoke the first verse:

25.

25.

“Nayimassa vijjāmayamatthi kiñci, na bandhavo no pana te sahāyo;

Atha kena vaṇṇena tirīṭavaccho, tedaṇḍiko bhuñjati aggapiṇḍa”nti.

"He has no knowledge or skill whatsoever, he is not a relative, nor is he your friend. Then for what reason does Tirīṭavaccha, the three-staffed ascetic, eat the best alms-food?"

Tattha nayimassa vijjāmayamatthi kiñcīti imassa tāpasassa vijjāmayaṃ kiñci kammaṃ natthi. Na bandhavo tiputtabandhavasippabandhavagottabandhavañātibandhavesu [P 2.0317] aññataropi na hoti[V 2.0262]. No pana te sahāyoti sahapaṃsukīḷiko sahāyakopi te na hoti. Kena vaṇṇenāti kena kāraṇena. Tirīṭavacchoti tassa nāmaṃ. Tedaṇḍikoti kuṇḍikaṭhapanatthāya tidaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā caranto. Aggapiṇḍanti rasasampannaṃ rājārahaṃ aggabhojanaṃ.

Herein, 'He has no knowledge whatsoever' means: this ascetic has no work whatsoever that consists of specialized knowledge. 'Not a relative' means: he is not any kind of relative, such as by marriage, by craft, by clan, or by blood. 'Nor is he your friend' means: he is not even a companion who played with you in the dust. 'For what reason' (kena vaṇṇena) means for what cause. 'Tirīṭavaccha' is his name. 'The three-staffed one' means: one who wanders carrying a three-legged stand to place his water pot on. 'The best alms-food' means: the finest food, rich in flavor and fit for a king.

Taṃ sutvā rājā puttaṃ āmantetvā “tāta, mama paccantaṃ gantvā yuddhaparājitassa dvīhatīhaṃ anāgatabhāvaṃ sarasī”ti vatvā “sarāmī”ti vutte “tadā mayā imaṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ laddha”nti sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā “tāta[M 2.0287], mayhaṃ jīvitadāyake mama santikaṃ āgate rajjaṃ dadantopi ahaṃ neva etena kataguṇānurūpaṃ kātuṃ sakkomī”ti vatvā itarā dve gāthā avoca –

Hearing this, the king addressed his son, 'Dear son, do you remember that after I went to the border region and was defeated in battle, I did not return for two or three days?' When he replied, 'I remember,' the king said, 'At that time, my life was saved because of this man.' He then explained the whole incident and said, 'Dear son, when the giver of my life has come to me, even if I were to give him the kingdom, I would not be able to do enough to match the gratitude for the service he performed.' Then he spoke the other two verses:

26.

26.

“Āpāsu me yuddhaparājitassa, ekassa katvā vivanasmi ghore;

Pasārayī kicchagatassa pāṇiṃ, tenūdatāriṃ dukhasampareto.

“When I was in distress, defeated in battle and alone in the dreadful wilderness, he showed compassion and stretched out his hand to me in my hardship; through him, though overcome by suffering, I was rescued.”

27.

27.

“Etassa kiccena idhānupatto, vesāyino visayā jīvaloke;

Lābhāraho tāta tirīṭavaccho, dethassa bhogaṃ yajathañca yañña”nti.

“By his deed I have arrived here in the world of the living, from the domain of Death. Worthy of reward, dear son, is Tirīṭavaccha; give him wealth and make offerings to him.”

Tattha āpāsūti āpadāsu. Ekassāti adutiyassa. Katvāti anukampaṃ karitvā pemaṃ uppādetvā. Vivanasminti pānīyarahite araññe. Ghoreti dāruṇe. Pasārayī kicchagatassa pāṇinti nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā kūpaṃ otāretvā dukkhagatassa mayhaṃ uttāraṇatthāya vīriyapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ hatthaṃ pasāresi. Tenūdatāriṃ dukhasamparetoti tena kāraṇenamhi dukkhaparivāritopi tamhā kūpā uttiṇṇo.

Herein, āpāsu means in calamities. Ekassa means of one who is alone, without a companion. Katvā means having shown compassion, having generated affection. Vivanasmiṃ means in a waterless forest. Ghore means terrible. Pasārayī kicchagatassa pāṇiṃ means: by constructing a ladder and lowering it into the well, he stretched out his hand, endowed with effort, to lift me out, who was in a state of suffering. Tenūdatāriṃ dukhasampareto means: for that reason, although surrounded by suffering, I came out of that well.

Etassa kiccena idhānupattoti ahaṃ etassa tāpasassa kiccena, etena katassa kiccassānubhāvena idhānuppatto[P 2.0318]. Vesāyino visayāti vesāyī vuccati yamo, tassa visayā. Jīvaloketi manussaloke. Ahañhi imasmiṃ jīvaloke ṭhito yamavisayaṃ maccuvisayaṃ paralokaṃ gato nāma ahosiṃ, somhi etassa kāraṇā tato puna idhāgatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Lābhārahoti lābhaṃ araho catupaccayalābhassa anucchaviko. Dethassa bhoganti etena paribhuñjitabbaṃ catupaccayasamaṇaparikkhārasaṅkhātaṃ bhogaṃ etassa detha. Yajathañca yaññanti tvañca amaccā ca nāgarā cāti sabbepi tumhe etassa bhogañca detha, yaññañca yajatha. Tassa hi dīyamāno deyyadhammo [V 2.0263] tena bhuñjitabbattā bhogo hoti, itaresaṃ dānayaññattā yañño. Tenāha “dethassa bhogaṃ yajathañca yañña”nti.

“By his deed I have come here” means: I have come here by the deed of that ascetic, through the power of the deed he performed. “To the realm of Vesāyī” means the domain of Yama, who is called Vesāyī. “In the world of the living” means in the human world. For I, while established in this world of the living, had gone to Yama’s domain, the domain of death, the other world, but on his account, I have returned here. “Worthy of gain” means deserving of gain, fitting to receive the four requisites. “Give him possessions” means give him the wealth that is to be used by him, consisting of the four requisites and the monastic equipment of an ascetic. “And perform a sacrifice” means you, the ministers, and the townsfolk—all of you—should give him possessions and offer a sacrifice. For what is given to him is possessions (bhoga), as it is to be used by him, and for others, it is a sacrifice, as it is a sacrificial offering. Thus it is said, “Give him possessions and offer a sacrifice.”

Evaṃ [M 2.0288] raññā gaganatale puṇṇacandaṃ uṭṭhāpentena viya bodhisattassa guṇe pakāsite tassa guṇo sabbatthameva pākaṭo jāto, atirekataro tassa lābhasakkāro udapādi. Tato paṭṭhāya uparājā vā amaccā vā añño vā koci kiñci rājānaṃ vattuṃ na visahi. Rājā bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggapuraṃ pūresi. Bodhisattopi abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, when the king proclaimed the Bodhisatta's virtues, as if raising the full moon in the sky, his virtue became manifest everywhere, and his gain and honor increased greatly. From then on, neither the viceroy, nor the ministers, nor anyone else dared to say anything to the king. The king, abiding in the Bodhisatta’s advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and filled the city of heaven. The Bodhisatta, too, having developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā “porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi upakāravasena kariṃsū”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher brought forth this Dhamma discourse, saying, “The wise ones of old also acted out of gratitude,” and connected the Jātaka, concluding: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the ascetic was indeed myself.”

Tirīṭavacchajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The ninth, the commentary on the Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka, is finished.

[260] 10. Dūtajātakavaṇṇanā

[260] 10. The Commentary on the Dūta Jātaka (The Messenger)

Yassatthā dūramāyantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu navakanipāte cakkavākajātake (jā. 1.9.69 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantetvā [P 2.0319] “na kho, bhikkhu, idāneva, pubbepi tvaṃ lolo, lolyakāraṇeneva pana asinā sīsacchedanaṃ labhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“For whose sake they come from afar”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a greedy monk. The story will be made clear in the Cakkavāka Jātaka in the Book of the Nines. The Teacher, having addressed that monk, said, “Not only now, monk, but in the past as well you were greedy; and on account of that greed you once had your head cut off with a sword, but you found relief through a wise king,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa putto hutvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya bhojanasuddhiko ahosi, tenassa bhojanasuddhikarājātveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ. So kira tathārūpena vidhānena bhattaṃ bhuñjati, yathāssa ekissā bhattapātiyā satasahassaṃ vayaṃ gacchati. Bhuñjanto pana antogehe na bhuñjati, attano bhojanavidhānaṃ olokentaṃ mahājanaṃ puññaṃ kāretukāmatāya rājadvāre ratanamaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā bhojanavelāya taṃ alaṅkarāpetvā kañcanamaye samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisīditvā khattiyakaññāhi parivuto [M 2.0289] satasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇapātiyā sabbarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjati. Atheko lolapuriso tassa bhojanavidhānaṃ oloketvā taṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjitukāmo [V 2.0264] hutvā pipāsaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto “attheko upāyo”ti gāḷhaṃ nivāsetvā hatthe ukkhipitvā “bho, ahaṃ dūto, dūto”ti uccāsaddaṃ karonto rājānaṃ upasaṅkami. Tena ca samayena tasmiṃ janapade “dūtomhī”ti vadantaṃ na vārenti, tasmā mahājano dvidhā bhijjitvā okāsaṃ adāsi. So vegena gantvā rañño pātiyā ekaṃ bhattapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā mukhe pakkhipi, athassa “sīsaṃ chindissāmī”ti asigāho asiṃ abbāhesi, rājā “mā paharī”ti nivāresi, “mā bhāyi, bhuñjassū”ti hatthaṃ dhovitvā nisīdi. Bhojanapariyosāne [P 2.0320] cassa attano pivanapānīyañceva tambūlañca dāpetvā “bho purisa, tvaṃ ‘dūtomhī’ti vadasi, kassa dūtosī”ti pucchi. “Mahārāja ahaṃ taṇhādūto, udaradūto, taṇhā maṃ āṇāpetvā ‘tvaṃ gacchāhī’ti dūtaṃ katvā pesesī”ti vatvā purimā dve gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as his son. When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and, after his father’s passing, was established on the throne. He was pure in his eating habits, for which reason his name became King Bhojanasuddhika. It is said that he ate his meal with such ceremony that the expense for a single bowl of food was a hundred thousand. He did not eat inside the house, but, desiring to let the great crowd make merit by watching his dining ceremony, he had a jeweled pavilion built at the palace gate. At mealtime, he had it decorated, and sitting on a royal throne of gold under a raised white parasol, surrounded by khattiya maidens, he ate a meal with all flavors from a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand. Then a certain greedy man, seeing his dining ceremony and desiring to eat that food, was unable to restrain his craving. Thinking, “There is a way,” he dressed himself tightly, raised his hands, and approached the king, shouting loudly, “Ho, I am a messenger, a messenger!” In that country at that time, they did not stop one who said, “I am a messenger,” so the people parted and gave him passage. He went quickly, took a morsel of rice from the king's bowl, and placed it in his mouth. Then the sword-bearer drew his sword, thinking, “I will cut off his head.” The king stopped him, saying, “Do not strike!” He washed his hands and sat down, saying, “Do not be afraid, eat.” At the end of the meal, having had his own drinking water and betel given to him, the king asked, “Good man, you say, ‘I am a messenger.’ Whose messenger are you?” “Great king, I am a messenger of craving, a messenger of the belly. Craving commanded me, saying, ‘You, go!’ and sent me as a messenger.” Having said this, he spoke these two verses:

28.

28.

“Yassatthā dūramāyanti, amittamapi yācituṃ;

Tassūdarassahaṃ dūto, mā me kujjha rathesabha.

“For whose sake beings come from afar, to beg even from an enemy; I am a messenger of that belly, be not angry with me, O bull among charioteers.”

29.

29.

“Yassa divā ca ratto ca, vasamāyanti māṇavā;

Tassūdarassahaṃ dūto, mā me kujjha rathesabhā”ti.

“He under whose power, by day and by night, beings come; I am a messenger of that belly, be not angry with me, O bull among charioteers.”

Tattha yassatthā dūramāyantīti yassa atthāya ime sattā taṇhāvasikā hutvā dūrampi gacchanti. Rathesabhāti rathayodhajeṭṭhaka.

Therein, “for whose sake they come from afar” means: for whose sake these beings, having come under the sway of craving, go even to a distant place. “Bull among charioteers” means the chief among chariot warriors.

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “saccametaṃ, ime sattā udaradūtā taṇhāvasena vicaranti, taṇhāva ime satte vicāreti, yāva manāpaṃ vata iminā kathita”nti tassa purisassa tussitvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, having heard his words, thought, “This is true. These beings wander as messengers of the belly under the sway of craving; craving alone makes these beings wander. How very pleasing is what has been said by this man!” And being pleased with the man, he spoke the third verse:

30.

30.

“Dadāmi te brāhmaṇa rohiṇīnaṃ, gavaṃ sahassaṃ saha puṅgavena;

Dūto hi dūtassa kathaṃ na dajjaṃ, mayampi tasseva bhavāma dūtā”ti.

“I give you, Brahmin, a thousand red cows, together with a bull. For how should I, a messenger, not give to a messenger? We too are messengers of that very same one.”

Tattha [M 2.0290] brāhmaṇāti ālapanamattametaṃ. Rohiṇīnanti rattavaṇṇānaṃ. Saha puṅgavenāti yūthapariṇāyakena upaddavarakkhakena usabhena saddhiṃ. Mayampīti ahañca avasesā ca sabbe sattā tasseva udarassa dūtā bhavāma, tasmā ahaṃ udaradūto samāno udaradūtassa tuyhaṃ kasmā na [V 2.0265] dajjanti. Evañca pana vatvā “iminā vata purisena assutapubbaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathita”nti tuṭṭhacitto tassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi.

Therein, “brahmin” is merely a form of address. “Of red cows” means of red color. “Together with a bull” means together with a bull that leads the herd and protects from danger. “We too” means: I and all remaining beings are messengers of that very belly; therefore, being a messenger of the belly myself, why should I not give to you, who are also a messenger of the belly? Having spoken thus, with a delighted mind, thinking, “Indeed, this man has stated a reason unheard before,” he granted him great wealth.

Satthā [P 2.0321] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so lolabhikkhu sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi, aññepi bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. “Tadā lolapuriso etarahi lolabhikkhu ahosi, bhojanasuddhikarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and proclaimed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that greedy monk was established in the fruit of once-returning, and many others attained stream-entry and the like. “At that time, the greedy man was the present greedy monk, but the king who was pure in his food was I myself.”

Dūtajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The tenth, the commentary on the Dūta Jātaka.

Saṅkappavaggo paṭhamo.

The Saṅkappa Chapter, the first.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Saṅkappa tilamuṭṭhi ca, maṇi ca sindhavāsukaṃ;

Jarūdapānaṃ gāmaṇi, mandhātā tirīṭadūtanti.

Saṅkappa, Tilamuṭṭhi, Maṇi, and Sindhavāsuka; Jarūdapāna, Gāmaṇi, Mandhātā, Tirīṭa, and Dūta.

2. Padumavaggo

2. The Paduma Chapter

[261] 1. Padumajātakavaṇṇanā

[261] 1. The Commentary on the Paduma Jātaka.

Yathā [V 2.0266] kesā ca massū cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ānandabodhimhi mālāpūjakārake bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu kāliṅgabodhijātake āvibhavissati. So pana ānandattherena ropitattā “ānandabodhī”ti jāto. Therena hi jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake bodhissa ropitabhāvo sakalajambudīpe patthari. Athekacce janapadavāsino bhikkhū “ānandabodhimhi mālāpūjaṃ karissāmā”ti jetavanaṃ [M 2.0291] āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā punadivase sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā uppalavīthiṃ gantvā mālaṃ alabhitvā āgantvā ānandattherassa ārocesuṃ – “āvuso, mayaṃ ‘bodhimhi mālāpūjaṃ karissāmā’ti uppalavīthiṃ gantvā ekamālampi na labhimhā”ti. Thero “ahaṃ vo, āvuso, āharissāmī”ti uppalavīthiṃ gantvā bahū nīluppalakalāpe ukkhipāpetvā āgamma tesaṃ dāpesi, te tāni gahetvā bodhissa pūjaṃ kariṃsu. Taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū therassa guṇakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, jānapadā bhikkhū appapuññā uppalavīthiṃ gantvā mālaṃ na labhiṃsu, thero pana gantvāva āharāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva [P 2.0322] vattuchekā kathākusalā mālaṃ labhanti, pubbepi labhiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Just as hair and beard—this the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning the monks who were making flower offerings at the Ānanda Bodhi tree. The story will be explained in the Kāliṅga Bodhi Jātaka. That tree, because it was planted by the Elder Ānanda, became known as the “Ānanda Bodhi.” Indeed, the fact that the Bodhi tree was planted by the Elder at the gatehouse of Jetavana spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Then, some monks from the countryside, thinking, “We will make a flower offering at the Ānanda Bodhi tree,” came to Jetavana. After paying homage to the Teacher, the next day they entered Sāvatthī and went to the lotus market, but could not obtain any flowers. Returning, they reported to Elder Ānanda: “Friend, we went to the lotus market intending to make a flower offering at the Bodhi tree, but we could not obtain even a single flower.” The Elder said, “Friends, I will bring them for you.” He went to the lotus market, had many bundles of blue lotuses gathered, and upon returning, gave them to the monks. They took them and made offerings to the Bodhi tree. Hearing of this event, the monks in the Dhamma hall began praising the Elder’s virtues: “Friends, the monks from the countryside, lacking merit, went to the lotus market but could not obtain flowers, whereas the Elder went and had them brought.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you engaged in at present?” When they replied, “This one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that those clever in speech and skilled in discussion obtain flowers—they obtained them in the past as well.” And he related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhiputto ahosi. Antonagare ca ekasmiṃ sare padumāni pupphanti. Eko chinnanāso puriso taṃ saraṃ rakkhati. Athekadivasaṃ bārāṇasiyaṃ ussave ghuṭṭhe mālaṃ piḷandhitvā ussavaṃ kīḷitukāmā tayo seṭṭhiputtā “nāsacchinnassa abhūtena vaṇṇaṃ vatvā mālaṃ yācissāmā”ti tassa padumāni bhañjanakāle sarassa santikaṃ gantvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was the son of a wealthy merchant. In the inner city, there was a pond where lotuses bloomed. A man with a severed nose guarded that pond. One day, when a festival was announced in Benares, three sons of wealthy merchants, wishing to play at the festival after adorning themselves with garlands, thought, “We will falsely praise the noseless one and ask for flowers.” While he was plucking lotuses, they approached the pond and stood to one side.

Tesu eko taṃ āmantetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Among them, one addressed him and spoke the first verse:

31.

31.

“Yathā [V 2.0267] kesā ca massū ca, chinnaṃ chinnaṃ virūhati;

Evaṃ ruhatu te nāsā, padumaṃ dehi yācito”ti.

“Just as hair and beard, when cut, grow again and again, so may your nose grow; give me a lotus, as you are asked.”

So tassa kujjhitvā padumaṃ na adāsi.

He was angered by that and did not give him a lotus.

Athassa dutiyo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the second one spoke the second verse to him:

32.

32.

“Yathā sāradikaṃ bījaṃ, khette vuttaṃ virūhati;

Evaṃ ruhatu te nāsā, padumaṃ dehi yācito”ti.

“Just as a seed sown in a field in autumn sprouts, so may your nose grow; give me a lotus, as you are asked.”

Tattha sāradikanti saradasamaye gahetvā nikkhittaṃ sārasampannaṃ bījaṃ. So tassapi kujjhitvā padumaṃ na adāsi.

There, ‘sāradika’ means a seed full of vigor, taken and stored during the autumn season. Becoming angry with him also, he did not give a lotus.

Athassa tatiyo tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the third one spoke the third verse to him:

33.

33.

“Ubhopi [M 2.0292] palapantete, api padmāni dassati;

Vajjuṃ vā te na vā vajjuṃ, natthi nāsāya rūhanā;

Dehi samma padumāni, ahaṃ yācāmi yācito”ti.

“These two are both babbling, hoping he might give them lotuses. Whether they speak it or not, there is no regrowth for a nose. Give me the lotuses, friend; I am the one asking you.”

Tattha ubhopi palapanteteti ete dvepi musā vadanti. Api padmānīti “api nāma no padumāni dassatī”ti cintetvā evaṃ vadanti. Vajjuṃ vā [P 2.0323] te na vā vajjunti “tava nāsā ruhatū”ti evaṃ vadeyyuṃ vā na vā vadeyyuṃ, etesaṃ vacanaṃ appamāṇaṃ, sabbatthāpi natthi nāsāya ruhanā, ahaṃ pana te nāsaṃ paṭicca na kiñci vadāmi, kevalaṃ yācāmi, tassa me dehi, samma, padumāni yācitoti.

Here, ‘These two are both babbling’ means these two are speaking falsely. ‘Hoping for lotuses’ means they think, ‘Perhaps he will give us the lotuses,’ and thus they speak. ‘Whether they speak or not’ means whether they might say, ‘May your nose grow,’ or not. Their words are unreliable; in any case, there is no regrowth for a nose. But I, regarding your nose, say nothing; I simply ask. Therefore, friend, give the lotuses to me who asks.”

Taṃ sutvā padumasaragopako “imehi dvīhi musāvādo kathito, tumhehi sabhāvo kathito, tumhākaṃ anucchavikāni padumānī”ti mahantaṃ padumakalāpaṃ ādāya tassa datvā attano padumasarameva gato.

Hearing this, the lotus pond keeper thought, “These two have spoken lies, but you have spoken the truth; these lotuses are suitable for you.” He took a large bundle of lotuses, gave it to him, and went back to his own lotus pond.

Satthā [V 2.0268] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā padumalābhī seṭṭhiputto ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth story: “At that time, the merchant's son who obtained the lotuses was I myself.”

Padumajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first, the commentary on the Paduma Jātaka.

[262] 2. Mudupāṇijātakavaṇṇanā

[262] 2. The Commentary on the Mudupāṇi Jātaka.

Pāṇi ce muduko cassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā dhammasabhaṃ ānītaṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu, itthiyo nāmetā kilesavasena gamanato arakkhiyā, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi attano dhītaraṃ rakkhituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, pitarā hatthe gahetvā ṭhitāva pitaraṃ ajānāpetvā kilesavasena purisena saddhiṃ palāyī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"If his hand were soft..."—this the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke concerning a discontented monk. The Teacher, having brought him to the Dhamma hall, asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?" When the monk replied, "Yes, Lord," the Teacher said, "Monk, women are indeed hard to guard due to their being led by defilements. Even the wise men of old could not protect their own daughters. One, even while held by the hand by her father, fled with a man, led by defilement, without her father's knowledge." Having said this, he related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. So [M 2.0293] dhītarañca bhāgineyyañca dvepi antonivesane posento ekadivasaṃ amaccehi saddhiṃ nisinno “mamaccayena mayhaṃ bhāgineyyo rājā [P 2.0324] bhavissati, dhītāpi me tassa aggamahesī bhavissatī”ti vatvā aparabhāge bhāgineyyassa vayappattakāle puna amaccehi saddhiṃ nisinno “mayhaṃ bhāgineyyassa aññassa rañño dhītaraṃ ānessāma, mayhaṃ dhītarampi aññasmiṃ rājakule dassāma, evaṃ no ñātakā bahutarā bhavissantī”ti āha. Amaccā sampaṭicchiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of his chief queen. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā and, after his father's death, was established in the kingdom and ruled righteously. He raised both his daughter and his nephew in the inner palace. One day, while sitting with his ministers, he said, "After my death, my nephew will become king, and my daughter will be his chief queen." Later, when his nephew came of age, he sat again with his ministers and said, "We will bring the daughter of another king for my nephew, and we will give my daughter to another royal family. Thus, our relatives will increase." The ministers agreed.

Atha rājā bhāgineyyassa bahigehaṃ dāpesi, anto pavesanaṃ nivāresi. Te pana aññamaññaṃ paṭibaddhacittā ahesuṃ. Kumāro “kena nu kho upāyena rājadhītaraṃ bahi nīharāpeyya”nti cintento “atthi upāyo”ti dhātiyā lañjaṃ datvā “kiṃ, ayyaputta, kicca”nti vutte “amma, kathaṃ nu kho rājadhītaraṃ bahi kātuṃ okāsaṃ labheyyāmā”ti āha. “Rājadhītāya saddhiṃ kathetvā jānissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, ammā”ti. Sā gantvā “ehi, amma, sīse te ūkā gaṇhissāmī”ti taṃ nīcapīṭhake nisīdāpetvā sayaṃ ucce nisīditvā tassā sīsaṃ attano ūrūsu ṭhapetvā ūkā gaṇhayamānā rājadhītāya sīsaṃ nakhehi vijjhi[V 2.0269]. Rājadhītā “nāyaṃ attano nakhehi vijjhati, pitucchāputtassa me kumārassa nakhehi vijjhatī”ti ñatvā “amma, tvaṃ kumārassa santikaṃ agamāsī”ti pucchi. “Āma, ammā”ti. “Kiṃ tena sāsanaṃ kathita”nti? “Tava bahikaraṇūpāyaṃ pucchati, ammā”ti. Rājadhītā “paṇḍito honto jānissatī”ti paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ bandhitvā “amma, imaṃ uggahetvā kumārassa kathehī”ti āha.

Then the king had a separate house built for his nephew outside the inner palace and prevented him from entering it. Yet, their hearts remained bound to each other. The prince thought, "By what means can I bring the princess outside?" Reflecting, he decided, "There is a way." He gave a bribe to a nurse and when she asked, "What is your purpose, young master?" he replied, "Nurse, how can I get an opportunity to bring the princess outside?" She said, "I will speak with the princess and find out." "Very well, nurse," he said. She went and said, "Come, my lady, let me pick lice from your head." She made the princess sit on a low stool while she herself sat on a higher one. Placing the princess’s head on her thighs, she pretended to pick lice but scratched the princess’s head with her nails. The princess realized, "These are not her own nails scratching me—these are the nails of my paternal aunt’s son, the prince." Knowing this, she asked, "Nurse, have you been to the prince?" "Yes, my lady," she replied. "What message did he give?" "He asks for a way to bring you outside, my lady." The princess, thinking, "If he is wise, he will understand," composed the first verse and said, "Nurse, memorize this and recite it to the prince."

34.

34.

“Pāṇi ce muduko cassa, nāgo cassa sukārito;

Andhakāro ca vasseyya, atha nūna tadā siyā”ti.

"If his hand were soft and pliable, and the elephant well-trained, and if darkness were to pour down, then indeed that might be."

Sā taṃ uggaṇhitvā kumārassa santikaṃ gantvā “amma, rājadhītā kimāhā”ti vutte “ayyaputta, aññaṃ kiñci avatvā imaṃ gāthaṃ [P 2.0325] pahiṇī”ti taṃ gāthaṃ udāhāsi. Kumāro ca tassatthaṃ ñatvā “gaccha, ammā”ti taṃ uyyojesi.

She took it and went to the prince. When asked, "Mother, what did the princess say?" she replied, "My dear son, without saying anything else, she sent this verse," and recited that verse. The prince, understanding its meaning, said, "Go, mother," and sent her away.

Gāthāyattho – sace te ekissā cūḷupaṭṭhākāya mama hattho viya hattho mudu assa, yadi ca te āneñjakāraṇaṃ sukārito eko hatthī assa, yadi ca taṃ divasaṃ caturaṅgasamannāgato ativiya bahalo andhakāro assa, devo ca vasseyya. Atha nūna tadā siyāti [M 2.0294] tādise kāle ime cattāro paccaye āgamma ekaṃsena te manorathassa matthakagamanaṃ siyāti.

The meaning of the verse is this: If your hand were as soft as the hand of a young serving-maid, and if you had a well-trained elephant that remained imperturbable, and if on that day there were an exceedingly dense darkness endowed with four factors, and if it were to rain. Then, at such a time, relying on these four conditions, your heart's desire would certainly reach its peak.

Kumāro etamatthaṃ tathato ñatvā ekaṃ abhirūpaṃ muduhatthaṃ cūḷupaṭṭhākaṃ sajjaṃ katvā maṅgalahatthigopakassa lañjaṃ datvā hatthiṃ āneñjakāraṇaṃ kāretvā kālaṃ āgamento acchi.

The prince, understanding this matter as it truly was, prepared a handsome, soft-handed young attendant, gave a bribe to the keeper of the state elephant, had the elephant trained to remain imperturbable, and waited for the right time.

Athekasmiṃ kāḷapakkhuposathadivase majjhimayāmasamanantare ghanakāḷamegho vassi. So “ayaṃ dāni rājadhītāya vuttadivaso”ti vāraṇaṃ abhiruhitvā muduhatthakaṃ cūḷupaṭṭhākaṃ hatthipiṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā gantvā rājanivesanassa ākāsaṅgaṇābhimukhe ṭhāne hatthiṃ mahābhittiyaṃ allīyāpetvā vātapānasamīpe temento aṭṭhāsi. Rājāpi dhītaraṃ rakkhanto aññattha sayituṃ na deti, attano santike cūḷasayane sayāpeti. Sāpi “ajja kumāro āgamissatī”ti ñatvā niddaṃ anokkamitvāva nipannā “tāta nhāyitukāmāmhī”ti āha. Rājā “ehi, ammā”ti taṃ hatthe gahetvā vātapānasamīpaṃ netvā “nhāyāhi, ammā”ti ukkhipitvā vātapānassa bahipasse pamukhe ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ hatthe gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Sā nhāyamānāva kumārassa hatthaṃ pasāresi, so tassā hatthato ābharaṇāni omuñcitvā upaṭṭhākāya hatthe piḷandhitvā [V 2.0270] taṃ ukkhipitvā rājadhītaraṃ nissāya pamukhe ṭhapesi[P 2.0326]. Sā tassā hatthaṃ gahetvā pitu hatthe ṭhapesi, so tassā hatthaṃ gahetvā dhītu hatthaṃ muñci, sā itarasmāpi hatthā ābharaṇāni omuñcitvā tassā dutiyahatthe piḷandhitvā pitu hatthe ṭhapetvā kumārena saddhiṃ agamāsi. Rājā “dhītāyeva me”ti saññāya taṃ dārikaṃ nhānapariyosāne sirigabbhe sayāpetvā dvāraṃ pidhāya lañchetvā ārakkhaṃ datvā attano sayanaṃ gantvā nipajji.

On a certain Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, just after the middle watch, a dense black cloud rained down. He, thinking, "Now is the day appointed by the princess," mounted an elephant, seated a soft-handed young attendant on its back, and went. Having made the elephant lean against a great wall at a place facing the open courtyard of the royal palace, he stood near the window, getting wet. The king, guarding his daughter, did not allow her to sleep elsewhere but had her sleep on a small bed near him. She, knowing, "Today the prince will come," lay down without falling asleep and said, "Father, I wish to bathe." The king said, "Come, dear," and taking her by the hand, led her near the window. "Bathe, dear," he said, lifting her and placing her on the projection outside the window, holding her with one hand. As she bathed, she stretched out her hand toward the prince. He removed the ornaments from her hand, fastened them on the attendant's hand, lifted the attendant up, and placed her on the projection in place of the princess. She (the princess) took her (the attendant's) hand and placed it in her father’s hand. He (the king), holding her (the attendant's) hand, released his daughter’s hand. She (the princess) then removed the ornaments from her other hand, fastened them on the attendant's second hand, placed that hand in her father's hand, and went away with the prince. The king, thinking, "This is indeed my daughter," had the girl sleep in the royal chamber at the end of her bath, then closed the door, sealed it, set a guard, and went to his own bed to lie down.

So pabhātāya rattiyā dvāraṃ vivaritvā taṃ dārikaṃ disvā “kimeta”nti pucchi. Sā tassā kumārena saddhiṃ gatabhāvaṃ kathesi. Rājā vippaṭisārī hutvā “hatthe gahetvā carantenapi mātugāmaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkā, evaṃ arakkhiyā nāmitthiyo”ti cintetvā itarā dve gāthā avoca –

At the break of day, he opened the door and, seeing the girl, asked, "What is this?" She told him that the princess had gone with the prince. The king, filled with regret, thought, "Even when held by the hand, it is impossible to guard a woman; thus, women are indeed unguardable." Then he spoke these two verses:

35.

35.

“Analā mudusambhāsā, duppūrā tā nadīsamā;

Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna, ārakā parivajjaye.

Insatiable and soft-spoken, hard to fill like a river; knowing they cause one to sink into hell, the wise should avoid them from afar.

36.

36.

“Yaṃ [M 2.0295] etā upasevanti, chandasā vā dhanena vā;

Jātavedova saṃ ṭhānaṃ, khippaṃ anudahanti na”nti.

Whomever they associate with, whether through desire or for wealth, they quickly burn him up, just as fire burns its own place.

Tattha analā mudusambhāsāti muduvacanenapi asakkuṇeyyā, neva sakkā saṇhavācāya saṅgaṇhitunti attho. Purisehi vā etāsaṃ na alanti analā. Mudusambhāsāti hadaye thaddhepi sambhāsāva mudu etāsanti mudusambhāsā. Duppūrā tā nadīsamāti yathā nadī āgatāgatassa udakassa sandanato udakena duppūrā, evaṃ anubhūtānubhūtehi methunādīhi aparitussanato duppūrā. Tena vuttaṃ –

Therein, 'analā' means they cannot be won over even with gentle speech, nor can they be restrained by soft words—that is the meaning. Or, 'analā' means men are not sufficient for them. 'Mudusambhāsā' means though their hearts are hard, their speech is soft; thus, they are called 'mudusambhāsā.' 'Duppūrā tā nadīsamā' means like a river which is difficult to fill with the continuous flow of water, so too are they hard to fill, never satisfied by repeated indulgence in sexual acts and the like. Therefore, it is said—

“Tiṇṇaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ atitto appaṭivāno mātugāmo kālaṃ karoti. Katamesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ? Methunasamāpattiyā ca vijāyanassa ca alaṅkārassa ca. Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ atitto appaṭivāno mātugāmo kālaṃ karotī”ti.

"Monks, a woman dies unsatisfied, insatiable in three things. Which three? In sexual union, in giving birth, and in ornamentation. Monks, a woman dies unsatisfied, insatiable in these three things."

Sīdantīti aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu soḷasasu ussadanirayesu nimujjanti. Nanti nipātamattaṃ[P 2.0327]. Viditvānāti evaṃ jānitvā. Ārakā parivajjayeti “etā itthiyo nāma methunadhammādīhi atittā kālaṃ katvā etesu nirayesu sīdanti, etā evaṃ attanā sīdamānā kassaññassa [V 2.0271] sukhāya bhavissantī”ti evaṃ ñatvā paṇḍito puriso dūratova tā parivajjayeti dīpeti. Chandasā vā dhanena vāti attano vā chandena ruciyā pemena, bhativasena laddhadhanena vā yaṃ purisaṃ etā itthiyo upasevanti bhajanti. Jātavedoti aggi. So hi jātamattova vediyati, vidito pākaṭo hotīti jātavedo. So yathā attano ṭhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ okāsaṃ anudahati, evametāpi yaṃ upasevanti, taṃ purisaṃ dhanayasasīlapaññāsamannāgatampi tesaṃ sabbesaṃ dhanādīnaṃ vināsanato puna tāya sampattiyā abhabbuppattikaṃ kurumānā khippaṃ anudahanti jhāpenti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

"They sink" means they submerge in the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells. "Naṃ" is merely a particle. "Having known" means having understood thus. "One should avoid them from afar" means: knowing that these women, unsatisfied with sexual pleasures and the like, die and sink into these hells, and that they, sinking thus by themselves, will not bring happiness to anyone else, the wise man avoids them from afar—this is what is shown. "Through desire or wealth" means either through their own desire, liking, or affection, or through wealth obtained as payment, these women associate with or attend to a man. "Jātaveda" means fire. For it is known, or evident, as soon as it is born, hence it is called "jātaveda." Just as fire burns up its own place, cause, and base, so too these women, whomever they associate with—even if he is endowed with wealth, fame, virtue, and wisdom—they quickly burn him up by destroying all his wealth and such, making him incapable of regaining that prosperity. And this has been said:

“Balavanto dubbalā honti, thāmavantopi hāyare;

Cakkhumā andhakā honti, mātugāmavasaṃ gatā.

The strong become weak, the powerful also decline; those with sight become blind, having come under the power of women.

“Guṇavanto [M 2.0296] nigguṇā honti, paññavantopi hāyare;

Pamattā bandhane senti, mātugāmavasaṃ gatā.

The virtuous become devoid of virtue, and the wise also decline; the heedless fall into bondage, having come under the power of women.

“Ajjhenañca tapaṃ sīlaṃ, saccaṃ cāgaṃ satiṃ matiṃ;

Acchindanti pamattassa, panthadūbhīva takkarā.

They snatch away the study, austerity, virtue, truth, generosity, mindfulness, and wisdom of the heedless one, like bandits on a road.

“Yasaṃ kittiṃ dhitiṃ sūraṃ, bāhusaccaṃ pajānanaṃ;

Khepayanti pamattassa, kaṭṭhapuñjaṃva pāvako”ti.

Fame, renown, resolve, heroism, great learning, and understanding—they destroy these for the heedless one, like a fire a pile of wood.

Evaṃ vatvā mahāsatto “bhāgineyyopi mayāva posetabbo”ti mahantena sakkārena dhītaraṃ tasseva datvā taṃ oparajje patiṭṭhapesi. Sopi mātulassa accayena rajje patiṭṭhahi.

Having said this, the Great Being, thinking, "My nephew also must be supported by me," gave his daughter to him with great honor and established him in the position of viceroy. He too, upon the death of his uncle, was established in the kingship.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesenaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā rājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, made the connection in the Jātaka. At the end of the exposition of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the king was I myself."

Mudupāṇijātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The second, the commentary on the Mudupāṇi Jātaka.

[263] 3. Cūḷapalobhanajātakavaṇṇanā

[263] 3. The Commentary on the Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka

Abhijjamāne [V 2.0272][P 2.0328] vārisminti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhumeva ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā dhammasabhaṃ ānītaṃ “saccaṃ kira, tvaṃ bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu, itthiyo nāmetā porāṇake suddhasattepi saṃkilesesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Abhijjamāne vārismiṃ": the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, told this story concerning a certain discontented monk. For the Teacher, having brought him to the Dhamma hall, asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?" When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Monk, these women defile even pure beings of old," and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto rājā aputtako hutvā attano itthiyo “puttapatthanaṃ karothā”ti āha. Tā putte patthenti. Evaṃ addhāne gate bodhisatto brahmalokā cavitvā aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbatti. Taṃ jātamattaṃ nhāpetvā thaññapāyanatthāya dhātiyā adaṃsu. So pāyamāno rodati, atha naṃ aññissā adaṃsu. Mātugāmahatthagato neva tuṇhī hoti. Atha naṃ ekassa pādamūlikassa adaṃsu, tena gahitamattoyeva tuṇhī ahosi. Tato paṭṭhāya purisāva [M 2.0297] taṃ gahetvā caranti. Thaññaṃ pāyentā duhitvā vā pāyenti, sāṇiantarena vā thanaṃ mukhe ṭhapenti. Tenassa anitthigandhakumāroti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa aparāparaṃ vaddhamānassapi mātugāmaṃ nāma dassetuṃ na sakkā. Tenassa rājā visuṃyeva nisajjādiṭṭhānāni jhānāgārañca kāresi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, being childless, he told his wives, "Make a prayer for a son." They made the prayer. After some time had passed, the Bodhisatta passed away from the Brahma world and was conceived in the womb of the chief queen. As soon as he was born, they bathed him and gave him to a nurse to be suckled. While being suckled, he cried; then they gave him to another. When he came into the hands of a woman, he would not be quiet. Then they gave him to a male attendant; as soon as he was held by him, he became quiet. From then on, only men carried him. When giving him milk, they either expressed it first or placed the breast in his mouth through a curtain. Therefore they gave him the name Prince Anitthigandha. Even as he grew up, it was impossible for him to see a woman. Therefore the king had separate places built for his sitting and so on, as well as a meditation chamber.

So tassa soḷasavassikakāle cintesi – “mayhaṃ añño putto natthi, ayaṃ pana kumāro kāme na paribhuñjati, rajjampi na icchissati, dulladdho vata me putto”ti. Atha naṃ ekā naccagītavāditakusalā purise paricaritvā attano vase kātuṃ paṭibalā taruṇanāṭakitthī upasaṅkamitvā “deva, kiṃ nu cintesī”ti āha, rājā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhi. “Hotu, deva[P 2.0329], ahaṃ taṃ palobhetvā kāmarasaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti. “Sace me puttaṃ anitthigandhakumāraṃ palobhetuṃ sakkissasi, so rājā bhavissati, tvaṃ aggamahesī”ti. Sā “mameso bhāro, tumhe mā cintayitthā”ti vatvā ārakkhamanusse upasaṅkamitvā āha – “ahaṃ paccūsasamaye āgantvā ayyaputtassa sayanaṭṭhāne bahijhānāgāre ṭhatvā gāyissāmi. Sace so kujjhati, mayhaṃ katheyyātha, ahaṃ apagacchissāmi. Sace suṇāti, vaṇṇaṃ me katheyyāthā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu.

When he was sixteen years old, the king thought: "I have no other son. This prince does not enjoy sensual pleasures and will not desire the kingdom; truly, my son is a lost cause to me." Then a certain young dancing girl, skilled in dancing, singing, and music, who was capable of bringing men under her control by serving them, approached the king and asked, "Great King, what are you thinking about?" The king told her the reason. "Let it be, Great King, I will entice him and make him know the taste of sensual pleasure." "If you can entice my son, Prince Anitthigandha, he shall be king and you shall be his chief queen." She said, "This is my task; do not worry." Then she went to the guards and said, "I will come at dawn and stand outside the meditation chamber near the prince’s sleeping place and sing. If he gets angry, tell me and I will leave. If he listens, praise me to him." They agreed, saying, "Very well."

Sāpi paccūsakāle tasmiṃ padese ṭhatvā tantissarena gītassaraṃ, gītassarena tantissaraṃ anatikkamitvā madhurena saddena gāyi, kumāro suṇantova nipajji, punadivase ca āsannaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā [V 2.0273] gāyituṃ āṇāpesi, punadivase jhānāgāre ṭhatvā gāyituṃ āṇāpesi, punadivase attano samīpe ṭhatvāti evaṃ anukkameneva taṇhaṃ uppādetvā lokadhammaṃ sevitvā kāmarasaṃ ñatvā “mātugāmaṃ nāma aññesaṃ na dassāmī”ti asiṃ gahetvā antaravīthiṃ otaritvā purise anubandhanto vicari. Atha naṃ rājā gāhāpetvā tāya kumārikāya saddhiṃ nagarā nīharāpesi. Ubhopi araññaṃ pavisitvā adhogaṅgaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ passe gaṅgaṃ, ekasmiṃ samuddaṃ katvā ubhinnamantare assamapadaṃ māpetvā vāsaṃ kappayiṃsu. Kumārikā paṇṇasālāyaṃ nisīditvā kandamūlādīni pacati, bodhisatto araññato phalāphalaṃ āharati.

At dawn, she stood in that place and sang with a sweet voice, her song not exceeding the lute's melody, nor the lute's melody her song. The prince lay listening. The next day, he commanded her to stand nearby and sing. The day after, he ordered her to stand in the meditation hall and sing. The day after that, he had her stand close to him. Thus, gradually arousing craving, he indulged in worldly ways, and having known the taste of sensual pleasure, he thought, “I will not give this woman to others.” Taking up his sword, he went down into the inner streets, chasing men. Then the king had him seized and expelled from the city along with the young woman. Both entered the forest, went down the Ganges, and with the river on one side and the ocean on the other, they built a hermitage between the two and settled there. The young woman would sit in the leaf hut and cook roots and tubers, while the Bodhisatta brought fruits from the forest.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 2.0298] tasmiṃ phalāphalatthāya gate samuddadīpakā eko tāpaso bhikkhācāratthāya ākāsena gacchanto dhūmaṃ disvā assamapade otari. Atha naṃ sā “nisīda, yāva paccatī”ti nisīdāpetvā itthikuttena palobhetvā jhānā cāvetvā brahmacariyamassa antaradhāpesi. So pakkhacchinnakāko viya hutvā [P 2.0330] taṃ jahituṃ asakkonto sabbadivasaṃ tattheva ṭhatvā bodhisattaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā vegena samuddābhimukho palāyi. Atha naṃ so “paccāmitto me ayaṃ bhavissatī”ti asiṃ gahetvā anubandhi. Tāpaso ākāse uppatanākāraṃ dassetvā samudde pati. Bodhisatto “esa tāpaso ākāsenāgato bhavissati, jhānassa parihīnattā samudde patito, mayā dānissa avassayena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā velante ṭhatvā imā gāthā avoca –

Then one day, when the Bodhisatta had gone for fruits, an ascetic from a sea-island, traveling through the sky for alms, saw the smoke and descended at the hermitage. Then she, saying, “Sit down until this is cooked,” had him sit down. Seducing him with feminine wiles, she made him fall from his meditative absorption and caused his holy life to disappear. Like a crow with clipped wings, unable to leave her, he stayed there the whole day. Seeing the Bodhisatta approaching, he quickly fled toward the sea. Then the Bodhisatta, thinking, “This one will become my rival,” took his sword and pursued him. The ascetic, making a show of flying up into the sky, fell into the sea. The Bodhisatta reflected: “This ascetic must have come through the sky; because he has lost his meditative absorption, he has fallen into the sea. It is now right that I should be his refuge.” Standing on the shore, he spoke these verses:

37.

37.

“Abhijjamāne vārismiṃ, sayaṃ āgamma iddhiyā;

Missībhāvitthiyā gantvā, saṃsīdasi mahaṇṇave.

“Though the water was unparted, you came yourself by psychic power; but having mingled with a woman, you now sink in the great ocean.

38.

38.

“Āvaṭṭanī mahāmāyā, brahmacariyavikopanā;

Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna, ārakā parivajjaye.

“They are whirlpools, great illusions, destroyers of the holy life; [men] sink [through them]. Knowing this, one should avoid them from afar.

39.

39.

“Yaṃ etā upasevanti, chandasā vā dhanena vā;

Jātavedova saṃ ṭhānaṃ, khippaṃ anudahanti na”nti.

“Whomever these women associate with, whether out of desire or for wealth, they quickly burn him up, just as fire burns its own dwelling.”

Tattha abhijjamāne vārisminti imasmiṃ udake acalamāne akampamāne udakaṃ anāmasitvā sayaṃ ākāseneva iddhiyā āgantvā. Missībhāvitthiyāti lokadhammavasena itthiyā [V 2.0274] saddhiṃ missībhāvaṃ. Āvaṭṭanī mahāmāyāti itthiyo nāmetā kāmāvaṭṭena āvaṭṭanato āvaṭṭanī, anantāhi itthimāyāhi samannāgatattā mahāmāyā nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Herein, 'though the water was unparted' means: in this still and unshaken water, without touching the water, having come himself through the sky by psychic power. 'Having mingled with a woman' means: having become intimate with a woman due to worldly states. 'Whirlpools, great illusions' means: women are called ‘whirlpools’ because they draw one in with the whirlpool of sensual pleasure; they are called ‘of great illusion’ because they are endowed with endless feminine wiles. For it is said:

“Māyā cetā marīcī ca, soko rogo cupaddavo;

Kharā ca bandhanā cetā, maccupāso guhāsayo;

Tāsu yo vissase poso, so naresu narādhamo”ti. (jā. 2.21.118);

“They are illusion and a mirage, sorrow, disease, and calamity; they are harsh and a bond, the snare of Death, a lair in a cave. The man who trusts in them is the lowest of men.”

Brahmacariyavikopanāti [M 2.0299] seṭṭhacariyassa methunaviratibrahmacariyassa vikopanā. Sīdantīti itthiyo nāmetā isīnaṃ brahmacariyavikopanena apāyesu sīdanti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ.

‘Destroyer of the holy life’ means: the destroyer of the noble conduct, that is, the holy life which is abstinence from sexual intercourse. ‘They sink’ means: these women, by destroying the holy life of the seers, cause them to sink into the planes of misery. The rest should be understood in the same way as before.

Etaṃ pana bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā tāpaso samuddamajjhe ṭhitoyeva naṭṭhajjhānaṃ puna uppādetvā ākāsena attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gato. Bodhisatto cintesi – “ayaṃ tāpaso evaṃ bhāriko samāno simbalitūlaṃ viya ākāsena gato, mayāpi iminā [P 2.0331] viya jhānaṃ uppādetvā ākāsena carituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So assamaṃ gantvā taṃ itthiṃ manussapathaṃ netvā “gaccha, tva”nti uyyojetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā manuññe bhūmibhāge assamaṃ māpetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having heard these words of the Bodhisatta, the ascetic, while still standing in the middle of the ocean, redeveloped his lost meditative absorption and went through the sky back to his own dwelling. The Bodhisatta thought: “This ascetic, despite his heavy body, went through the sky like a silk-cotton tuft. It is fitting that I too should develop meditative absorption like him and travel through the sky.” So he went to the hermitage, led the woman to a human path, and sending her away with the words, “You may go,” he entered the forest. There, in a delightful spot, he built a hermitage, went forth into the ascetic life, practiced the kasina meditation, and developed the direct knowledges and meditative attainments. He became one destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā anitthigandhakumāro ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, explained the Truths and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, I myself was Prince Anitthigandha.”

Cūḷapalobhanajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The third, the Commentary on the Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka.

[264] 4. Mahāpanādajātakavaṇṇanā

[264] 4. 4. The Commentary on the Mahāpanāda Jātaka

Panādo nāma so rājāti idaṃ satthā gaṅgātīre nisinno bhaddajittherassānubhāvaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye satthā sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ vasitvā “bhaddajikumārassa saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto cārikaṃ caramāno bhaddiyanagaraṃ patvā jātiyāvane tayo māse [V 2.0275] vasi kumārassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno. Bhaddajikumāro mahāyaso asītikoṭivibhavassa bhaddiyaseṭṭhino ekaputtako. Tassa tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavikā tayo pāsādā ahesuṃ. Ekekasmiṃ cattāro cattāro māse vasati. Ekasmiṃ vasitvā nāṭakaparivuto mahantena yasena aññaṃ pāsādaṃ gacchati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe “kumārassa yasaṃ passissāmā”ti sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi, pāsādantare cakkāticakkāni mañcātimañcāni bandhanti.

“That king named Panāda.” This the Teacher spoke while seated on the bank of the Ganges River in connection with the spiritual power of the Elder Bhaddaji. For on one occasion, the Teacher, having spent the rains residence in Sāvatthī, set out on tour surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, thinking, ‘I will give my support to the young Bhaddaji.’ Arriving at the city of Bhaddiya, he stayed for three months in the Jātiyā Grove, awaiting the maturing of the young man's knowledge. The young Bhaddaji, of great fame, was the only son of the millionaire Bhaddiya, who possessed eighty crores of wealth. He had three mansions suitable for the three seasons, and he would dwell in each for four months. After dwelling in one, surrounded by entertainers and with great splendor, he would go to another mansion. At that moment, the entire city would be stirred up, eager to witness the young man's glory. Between the mansions they would set up carts upon carts and couches upon couches.

Satthā [M 2.0300] tayo māse vasitvā “mayaṃ gacchāmā”ti nagaravāsīnaṃ ārocesi. Nāgarā “bhante, sve gamissathā”ti satthāraṃ nimantetvā dutiyadivase buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ sajjetvā nagaramajjhe maṇḍapaṃ katvā alaṅkaritvā āsanāni paññapetvā kālaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto tattha gantvā nisīdi, manussā mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Satthā niṭṭhitabhattakicco madhurassarena anumodanaṃ ārabhi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bhaddajikumāropi pāsādato pāsādaṃ gacchati[P 2.0332], tassa sampattidassanatthāya taṃ divasaṃ na koci agamāsi, attano manussāva parivāresuṃ. So manusse pucchi – “aññasmiṃ kāle mayi pāsādato pāsādaṃ gacchante sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhati, cakkāticakkāni mañcātimañcāni bandhanti, ajja pana ṭhapetvā mayhaṃ manusse añño koci natthi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti. “Sāmi, sammāsambuddho imaṃ bhaddiyanagaraṃ upanissāya tayo māse vasitvā ajjeva gamissati, so bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā mahājanassa dhammaṃ deseti, sakalanagaravāsinopi tassa dhammakathaṃ suṇantī”ti. So “tena hi etha, mayampi suṇissāmā”ti sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitova mahantena parivārena upasaṅkamitvā parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ suṇanto ṭhitova sabbakilese khepetvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The Teacher, having stayed for three months, announced to the city dwellers, ‘We shall depart.’ The citizens invited the Teacher, saying, ‘Venerable sir, please stay for tomorrow.’ The next day, they prepared a great offering for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head, built and decorated a pavilion in the middle of the city, arranged seats, and announced the time. The Teacher, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went there and sat down, and the people gave the great offering. When the meal was finished, the Teacher began the thanksgiving discourse with his sweet voice. At that moment, the young Bhaddaji was also moving from one mansion to another. That day, no one went to see his wealth; only his own people surrounded him. He asked them: ‘At other times, when I move from mansion to mansion, the whole city is in an uproar, and they stack carts upon carts and couches upon couches. But today, apart from my own people, there is no one else. What is the reason?’ ‘Master, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having stayed near the city of Bhaddiya for three months, is departing today. Having finished his meal, he is teaching the Dhamma to the great assembly, and all the city’s inhabitants are listening to his Dhamma talk.’ ‘Well then, come, let us also listen,’ he said. Adorned with all his ornaments and surrounded by a large retinue, he approached and stood at the edge of the assembly. While standing there listening to the Dhamma, he eradicated all defilements and attained arahantship, the supreme fruit.

Satthā bhaddiyaseṭṭhiṃ āmantetvā “mahāseṭṭhi, putto te alaṅkatapaṭiyattova dhammakathaṃ suṇanto arahatte patiṭṭhito, tenassa ajjeva pabbajituṃ vā vaṭṭati parinibbāyituṃ vā”ti āha. “Bhante, mayhaṃ puttassa parinibbānena kiccaṃ natthi, pabbājetha naṃ, pabbājetvā ca pana naṃ gahetvā sve amhākaṃ gehaṃ upasaṅkamathā”ti. Bhagavā nimantanaṃ adhivāsetvā kulaputtaṃ ādāya vihāraṃ gantvā pabbājetvā upasampadaṃ dāpesi. Tassa mātāpitaro sattāhaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ kariṃsu. Satthā sattāhaṃ vasitvā kulaputtamādāya cārikaṃ caranto koṭigāmaṃ pāpuṇi. Koṭigāmavāsino manussā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Satthā bhattakiccāvasāne anumodanaṃ ārabhi. Kulaputto anumodanakaraṇakāle bahigāmaṃ gantvā “satthu āgatakāleyeva uṭṭhahissāmī”ti gaṅgātitthasamīpe ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi[V 2.0276]. Mahallakattheresu āgacchantesupi anuṭṭhahitvā satthu āgatakāleyeva uṭṭhahi. Puthujjanā bhikkhū “ayaṃ pure viya pabbajitvā mahāthere āgacchantepi disvā na uṭṭhahatī”ti kujjhiṃsu.

The Teacher addressed the treasurer of Bhaddiya: ‘Great treasurer, your son, while still adorned and arrayed, has become established in arahantship while listening to the Dhamma talk. Therefore, he must either go forth or attain parinibbāna this very day.’ ‘Venerable sir, my son has no need to attain parinibbāna. Please let him go forth. After ordaining him, please take him and come to our house tomorrow.’ The Blessed One accepted the invitation. He took the young man of good family to the monastery, ordained him, and conferred the higher ordination. His parents performed a great ceremony of honor for seven days. After staying for seven days, the Teacher took the young man and, while wandering on tour, arrived at the village of Koṭigāma. The people of Koṭigāma gave a great offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher began the thanksgiving discourse. During the thanksgiving, the young man went outside the village and, thinking, ‘I will rise only when the Teacher arrives,’ he sat down at the foot of a tree near a ford of the Ganges and entered meditative absorption. He did not rise even when the senior elders arrived, but rose only when the Teacher arrived. The worldling bhikkhus became angry, saying: ‘This one, though having gone forth, does not rise even when he sees the senior elders coming, just as he was before!’

Koṭigāmavāsino [M 2.0301] manussā nāvāsaṅghāte bandhiṃsu. Satthā nāvāsaṅghāte ṭhatvā “kahaṃ[P 2.0333], bhaddajī”ti pucchi. “Esa, bhante, idhevā”ti. “Ehi, bhaddaji, amhehi saddhiṃ ekanāvaṃ abhiruhā”ti. Theropi uppatitvā ekanāvāya aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ gaṅgāya majjhaṃ gatakāle satthā āha – “bhaddaji, tayā mahāpanādarājakāle ajjhāvutthapāsādo kaha”nti. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne nimuggo, bhanteti. Puthujjanā bhikkhū “bhaddajitthero aññaṃ byākarotī”ti āhaṃsu. Satthā “tena hi, bhaddaji, sabrahmacārīnaṃ kaṅkhaṃ chindā”ti āha. Tasmiṃ khaṇe thero satthāraṃ vanditvā iddhibalena gantvā pāsādathūpikaṃ pādaṅguliyā gahetvā pañcavīsatiyojanaṃ pāsādaṃ gahetvā ākāse uppati. Uppatito ca pana heṭṭhāpāsāde ṭhitānaṃ pāsādaṃ bhinditvā paññāyi. So ekayojanaṃ dviyojanaṃ tiyojananti yāva vīsatiyojanā udakato pāsādaṃ ukkhipi. Athassa purimabhave ñātakā pāsādalobhena macchakacchapanāgamaṇḍūkā hutvā tasmiṃyeva pāsāde nibbattā pāsāde uṭṭhahante parivattitvā parivattitvā udakeyeva patiṃsu. Satthā te patante disvā “ñātakā te, bhaddaji, kilamantī”ti āha. Thero satthu vacanaṃ sutvā pāsādaṃ vissajjesi, pāsādo yathāṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhahi, satthā pāragaṅgaṃ gato. Athassa gaṅgātīreyeva āsanaṃ paññāpayiṃsu, so paññatte varabuddhāsane taruṇasūriyo viya rasmiyo muñcanto nisīdi. Atha naṃ bhikkhū “kasmiṃ kāle, bhante, ayaṃ pāsādo bhaddajittherena ajjhāvuttho”ti pucchiṃsu. Satthā “mahāpanādarājakāle”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The people of Koṭigāma fastened together a raft of boats. The Teacher stood on the raft of boats and asked, “Where is Bhaddaji?” “Here he is, venerable sir,” they replied. “Come, Bhaddaji, board the same boat with us.” The elder leaped up and stood on the same boat. When they reached the middle of the Ganges, the Teacher said, “Bhaddaji, where is the palace you lived in during the time of King Mahāpanāda?” “It is submerged here, venerable sir,” he replied. The worldling monks said, “The Venerable Bhaddaji is declaring something false.” The Teacher then said, “Well then, Bhaddaji, dispel the doubt of your companions in the holy life.” At that moment, the elder paid homage to the Teacher and, by his psychic power, went and took hold of the palace's pinnacle with his toe, lifted the twenty-five-yojana palace, and rose into the air. As he rose, he was visible to those standing below the palace as if he had broken through it. He lifted the palace from the water by one yojana, two yojanas, three yojanas, and up to twenty yojanas. Then his relatives from a previous existence, who had been reborn in that very palace as fish, turtles, nāgas, and frogs because of their attachment to the palace, tumbled about as the palace rose and fell back into the water. Seeing them falling, the Teacher said, “Bhaddaji, your relatives are being troubled.” Hearing the Teacher's words, the elder released the palace, and it settled back in its original place. The Teacher then went to the far shore of the Ganges. There they prepared a seat for him right on the riverbank, and he sat down on the prepared excellent Buddha-seat, emitting rays like the morning sun. Then the monks asked him: “Venerable Sir, at what time did the Venerable Bhaddaji live in this palace?” The Teacher replied, “During the time of King Mahāpanāda,” and he related the story of the past.

Atīte videharaṭṭhe mithilāyaṃ suruci nāma rājā ahosi, puttopi tassa suruciyeva, tassa pana putto mahāpanādo nāma ahosi, te imaṃ pāsādaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Paṭilābhatthāya panassa idaṃ pubbakammaṃ – dve pitāputtā naḷehi ca udumbaradārūhi ca paccekabuddhassa vasanapaṇṇasālaṃ kariṃsu. Imasmiṃ jātake sabbaṃ atītavatthu pakiṇṇakanipāte surucijātake (jā. 1.14.102 ādayo) āvibhavissati.

In the past, in the Videha kingdom, at Mithilā, there was a king named Suruci. His son was also named Suruci, and his son was named Mahāpanāda. They obtained this palace. Now, this was the past deed for its acquisition: a father and son made a leaf-hut for a paccekabuddha to dwell in, using reeds and udumbara wood. The entire story of the past for this Jātaka will be made clear in the Suruci Jātaka of the Pakiṇṇaka Nipāta.

Satthā [P 2.0334] imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā sammāsambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

Having related this story of the past, the Teacher, now the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, spoke these verses:

40.

40.

“Panādo [M 2.0302] nāma so rājā, yassa yūpo suvaṇṇayo;

Tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedho, uddhamāhu sahassadhā.

“That king was named Panāda, whose palace was made of gold; sixteen arrow-flights wide, it rose a thousandfold high, they say.”

41.

41.

“Sahassakaṇḍo [V 2.0277] satageṇḍu, dhajālu haritāmayo;

Anaccuṃ tattha gandhabbā, cha sahassāni sattadhā.

“With a thousand sections and a hundred tiers, adorned with banners, made of emerald; there six thousand gandhabbas danced in seven groups.”

42.

42.

“Evametaṃ tadā āsi, yathā bhāsasi bhaddaji;

Sakko ahaṃ tadā āsiṃ, veyyāvaccakaro tavā”ti.

“It was exactly as you say, Bhaddaji; I was Sakka at that time, your attendant.”

Tattha yūpoti pāsādo. Tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedhoti vitthārato soḷasakaṇḍapātavitthāro ahosi. Uddhamāhu sahassadhāti ubbedhena sahassakaṇḍagamanamattaṃ ucco ahu, sahassakaṇḍagamanagaṇanāya pañcavīsatiyojanappamāṇaṃ hoti. Vitthāro panassa aṭṭhayojanamatto.

Herein, yūpo means a palace. Tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedho means that in breadth it was sixteen arrow-flights wide. Uddhamāhu sahassadhā means that in height it was as high as a thousand arrow-flights; by the calculation of a thousand arrow-flights, it measures twenty-five yojanas. Its width, however, was eight yojanas.

Sahassakaṇḍo satageṇḍūti so panesa sahassakaṇḍubbedho pāsādo satabhūmiko ahosi. Dhajālūti dhajasampanno. Haritāmayoti haritamaṇiparikkhitto. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “samāluharitāmayo”ti pāṭho, haritamaṇimayehi dvārakavāṭavātapānehi samannāgatoti attho. Samālūti kira dvārakavāṭavātapānānaṃ nāmaṃ. Gandhabbāti naṭā, cha sahassāni sattadhāti cha gandhabbasahassāni sattadhā hutvā tassa pāsādassa sattasu ṭhānesu rañño ratijananatthāya nacciṃsūti attho. Te evaṃ naccantāpi rājānaṃ hāsetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, atha sakko devarājā devanaṭaṃ pesetvā samajjaṃ kāresi, tadā mahāpanādo hasi.

Sahassakaṇḍo satageṇḍu: this palace, a thousand arrow-flights high, had a hundred stories. Dhajālu means endowed with banners. Haritāmayo means inlaid with emeralds. In the commentary, however, the reading is samāluharitāmayo, which means furnished with doors, door-panels, and windows made of emerald; for samālu, it is said, is a name for doors, door-panels, and windows. Gandhabbā means dancers. Cha sahassāni sattadhā means that six thousand gandhabbas, forming seven groups, danced in seven places in that palace to delight the king. But even though they danced in this way, they were unable to make the king laugh. Then Sakka, king of the devas, sent a celestial dancer and held a festival; then Mahāpanāda laughed.

Yathā bhāsasi, bhaddajīti bhaddajittherena hi “bhaddaji, tayā mahāpanādarājakāle ajjhāvutthapāsādo kaha”nti vutte “imasmiṃ ṭhāne nimuggo, bhante”ti vadantena tasmiṃ kāle attano atthāya tassa pāsādassa nibbattabhāvo ca mahāpanādarājabhāvo ca bhāsito hoti. Taṃ gahetvā satthā “yathā tvaṃ, bhaddaji, bhāsasi, tadā etaṃ tatheva ahosi, ahaṃ tadā tava kāyaveyyāvaccakaro sakko devānamindo ahosi”nti āha. Tasmiṃ [P 2.0335] khaṇe puthujjanabhikkhū nikkaṅkhā ahesuṃ.

Yathā bhāsasi, bhaddaji: For when the Venerable Bhaddaji was asked, “Bhaddaji, where is the palace you lived in during the time of King Mahāpanāda?” and he replied, “It is submerged in this place, Bhante,” he was thereby stating that the palace had come into being for his sake at that time and that he himself had been King Mahāpanāda. Taking this up, the Teacher said: “Just as you say, Bhaddaji, so it was then. At that time I was Sakka, lord of the devas, who performed services for you.” At that moment the worldling monks became free from doubt.

Satthā [M 2.0303] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mahāpanādo rājā bhaddaji ahosi, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, King Mahāpanāda was Bhaddaji, and Sakka was I myself.”

Mahāpanādajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Mahāpanāda Jātaka, the Fourth.

[265] 5. Khurappajātakavaṇṇanā

[265] 5. 5. Khurappa Jātaka (The Story of the Razor-Arrow)

Disvā [V 2.0278] khurappeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ossaṭṭhavīriyo”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu, kasmā evaṃ tvaṃ niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā vīriyaṃ ossaji, porāṇakapaṇḍitā aniyyānikaṭṭhānepi vīriyaṃ kariṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Seeing the razor-arrows…” This the Teacher told while staying at Jetavana, concerning a monk who had given up his effort. The Teacher asked him, “Is it true, monk, that you have given up your effort?” When he replied, “It is true, Bhante,” the Teacher said: “Monk, why have you given up your effort after having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation? The wise of old put forth effort even in a situation that did not lead to liberation.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ aṭaviārakkhakakule nibbattitvā vayappatto pañcapurisasataparivāro aṭaviārakkhakesu sabbajeṭṭhako hutvā aṭavimukhe ekasmiṃ gāme vāsaṃ kappesi. So bhatiṃ gahetvā manusse aṭaviṃ atikkāmeti. Athekasmiṃ divase bārāṇaseyyako satthavāhaputto pañcahi sakaṭasatehi taṃ gāmaṃ patvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “samma, sahassaṃ gahetvā maṃ aṭaviṃ atikkāmehī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti tassa hatthato sahassaṃ gaṇhi, bhatiṃ gaṇhantoyeva tassa jīvitaṃ pariccaji. So taṃ ādāya aṭaviṃ pāvisi, aṭavimajjhe pañcasatā corā uṭṭhahiṃsu, core disvāva sesapurisā urena nipajjiṃsu, ārakkhakajeṭṭhako ekova nadanto vagganto paharitvā pañcasatepi core palāpetvā satthavāhaputtaṃ sotthinā kantāraṃ tāresi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of forest guards. When he grew up, he became the chief of five hundred forest guards and lived in a village at the edge of the forest. He would take a fee to guide people through the forest. One day, the son of a caravan leader from Bārāṇasī arrived at that village with five hundred carts. He summoned the Bodhisatta and said, “Friend, take a thousand pieces of money and guide me through the forest.” He agreed, took the thousand from him, and at the very moment of taking the fee, he sacrificed his life for the caravan leader. Taking him along, he entered the forest. In the middle of the forest, five hundred robbers appeared. As soon as they saw the robbers, the other men lay down on their bellies. But the chief guard, alone, shouting and leaping about, attacked and drove off all five hundred robbers, and led the caravan leader's son safely across the wilderness.

Satthavāhaputto parakantāre satthaṃ nivesetvā [P 2.0336] ārakkhakajeṭṭhakaṃ nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhojetvā sayampi bhuttapātarāso sukhanisinno tena saddhiṃ sallapanto “samma, tathādāruṇānaṃ corānaṃ āvudhāni gahetvā avattharaṇakāle kena nu kho te kāraṇena cittutrāsamattampi na uppanna”nti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The caravan leader's son, having halted the caravan on the other side of the wilderness, provided the chief guard with food of various excellent flavors. After he had eaten his own breakfast, he sat down comfortably and, while conversing with him, asked: “Friend, for what reason did not even a slight tremor of fear arise in your mind when those fierce robbers took up their weapons and attacked?” And asking this, he spoke the first verse:

43.

43.

“Disvā [M 2.0304] khurappe dhanuveganunne, khagge gahīte tikhiṇe teladhote;

Tasmiṃ bhayasmiṃ maraṇe viyūḷhe, kasmā nu te nāhu chambhitatta”nti.

“Seeing the razor-arrows sped by the bow's force, and the sharp, oil-polished swords being grasped; in that terrifying moment, with death imminent, why was there no trembling in you?”

Tattha dhanuveganunneti dhanuvegena vissaṭṭhe. Khagge gahīteti tharudaṇḍehi sugahite khagge. Maraṇe viyūḷheti maraṇe paccupaṭṭhite. Kasmā nu te nāhūti kena nu kho kāraṇena nāhosi. Chambhitattanti sarīracalanaṃ.

Herein, dhanuveganunne means released by the force of the bow. Khagge gahīte means swords firmly grasped by their hilts. Maraṇe viyūḷhe means when death was imminent. Kasmā nu te nāhu means for what reason was there not? Chambhitattaṃ means trembling of the body.

Taṃ sutvā ārakkhakajeṭṭhako itarā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the chief guard spoke the remaining two verses:

44.

44.

“Disvā [V 2.0279] khurappe dhanuveganunne, khagge gahīte tikhiṇe teladhote;

Tasmiṃ bhayasmiṃ maraṇe viyūḷhe, vedaṃ alatthaṃ vipulaṃ uḷāraṃ.

“Seeing the razor-arrows sped by the bow's force, and the sharp, oil-polished swords being grasped; in that terrifying moment, with death imminent, I felt a vast and sublime joy.”

45.

45.

“So vedajāto ajjhabhaviṃ amitte, pubbeva me jīvitamāsi cattaṃ;

Na hi jīvite ālayaṃ kubbamāno, sūro kayirā sūrakiccaṃ kadācī”ti.

“With that joy arisen, I overcame my enemies, for my life had already been sacrificed. For a hero who clings to life can never perform a hero's duty.”

Tattha vedaṃ alatthanti tuṭṭhiñceva somanassañca paṭilabhiṃ. Vipulanti bahuṃ. Uḷāranti uttamaṃ. Ajjhabhavinti jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā abhibhaviṃ. Pubbeva me jīvitamāsi cattanti mayā pubbeva tava hatthato bhatiṃ gaṇhanteneva jīvitaṃ cattamāsi. Na hi jīvite ālayaṃ kubbamānoti jīvitasmiñhi nikantiṃ kurumāno purisakiccaṃ kadācipi na karoti.

Herein, vedaṃ alatthaṃ means I obtained both satisfaction and joy. Vipulaṃ means abundant. Uḷāraṃ means sublime. Ajjhabhaviṃ means: having given up my life, I overcame [them]. Pubbeva me jīvitamāsi cattaṃ means: my life had already been given up by me before, at the very moment of taking the fee from your hand. Na hi jīvite ālayaṃ kubbamāno means: for one who has an attachment to life never performs a heroic duty.

Evaṃ [P 2.0337] so saravasse vassante jīvitanikantiyā vissaṭṭhattā attanā sūrakiccassa katabhāvaṃ ñāpetvā satthavāhaputtaṃ uyyojetvā sakagāmameva paccāgantvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, having made known that he had performed a hero's duty by abandoning his attachment to life while the rain of arrows was falling, he sent off the caravan leader's son, returned to his own village, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and went according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā ārakkhakajeṭṭhako ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse and revealed the truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, the monk who had relaxed his effort was established in arahantship. "At that time, I myself was the chief guard," he said, thus connecting the Jātaka.

Khurappajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Khurappa Jātaka, the fifth.

[266] 6. Vātaggasindhavajātakavaṇṇanā

[266] 6. The Commentary on the Vātaggasindhava Jātaka

Yenāsi [M 2.0305] kisiyā paṇḍūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāvatthiyaṃ aññataraṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kirekā abhirūpā itthī ekaṃ abhirūpaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ disvā paṭibaddhacittā ahosi, sakalasarīraṃ jhāyamāno viyassā abbhantare kilesaggi uppajji. Sā neva kāyassādaṃ labhi, na cittassādaṃ, bhattampissā na rucci, kevalaṃ mañcakaaṭaniṃ gahetvā nipajji. Atha naṃ upaṭṭhāyikā ca sahāyikā ca pucchiṃsu – “kiṃ nu kho tvaṃ kampamānacittā aṭaniṃ gahetvā nipannā, kiṃ te aphāsuka”nti. Sā ekaṃ dve vāre akathetvā punappunaṃ vuccamānā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ tā samassāsetvā “tvaṃ mā cintayi, mayaṃ taṃ [V 2.0280] ānessāmā”ti vatvā gantvā kuṭumbikena saddhiṃ mantesuṃ, so paṭikkhipitvā punappunaṃ vuccamāno adhivāsesi. Tā “asukadivase asukavelāyaṃ āgacchā”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā gantvā tassā ārocesuṃ. Sā attano sayanagabbhaṃ sajjetvā attānaṃ alaṅkaritvā sayanapiṭṭhe nisinnā tasmiṃ āgantvā sayanekadese nisinne cintesi – “sacāhaṃ imassa [P 2.0338] garukaṃ akatvā idāneva okāsaṃ karissāmi, issariyaṃ me parihāyissati, āgatadivaseyeva okāsakaraṇaṃ nāma akāraṇaṃ, ajja na maṅkuṃ katvā aññasmiṃ divase okāsaṃ karissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ hatthagahaṇādivasena keḷiṃ kātuṃ āraddhaṃ hatthe gahetvā “apehi apehi, na me tayā attho”ti nibbhacchesi. So osakkitvā lajjito uṭṭhāya attano gehameva gato.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jeta's Grove, told this story beginning with the words, "By which you are thin and pale," concerning a certain householder in Sāvatthī. It is said that in Sāvatthī a beautiful woman saw a handsome householder and became infatuated with him. The fire of defilement arose within her as if her whole body were burning. She found no pleasure in body or mind, nor did food appeal to her; she just lay down, clutching the frame of the bed. Then her attendants and friends asked her, "Why are you lying there, clutching the bed-frame with a trembling heart? What is wrong with you?" After not speaking once or twice, being asked again and again, she told them the matter. Then they comforted her, saying, "Do not worry, we will bring him to you," and went and spoke with the householder. He refused, but being asked again and again, he consented. Having obtained his promise, "Come on such-and-such a day at such-and-such a time," they went and told her. She prepared her bedchamber, adorned herself, and sat on the bed. When he came and sat on a part of the bed, she thought, "If I give him an opportunity now without treating him with gravity, my mastery over him will diminish. To give an opportunity on the very day he comes is groundless. Today, having made him dejected, I will give him an opportunity on another day." Then, when he began to dally with her by taking her hand and so on, she seized his hand and rebuked him, saying, "Go away, go away! I have no use for you!" He, ashamed, got up, withdrew, and went to his own home.

Itarā itthiyo tāya tathā katabhāvaṃ ñatvā kuṭumbike nikkhante taṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – “tvaṃ etasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā āhāraṃ paṭikkhipitvā nipajji, atha naṃ mayaṃ punappunaṃ yācitvā ānayimha, tassa kasmā okāsaṃ na akāsī”ti. Sā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Itarā “tena hi paññāyissasī”ti vatvā pakkamiṃsu. Kuṭumbiko puna nivattitvāpi na olokesi. Sā taṃ alabhamānā nirāhārā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Kuṭumbiko tassā matabhāvaṃ ñatvā bahuṃ mālāgandhavilepanaṃ ādāya jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā satthārā ca “kiṃ nu kho, upāsaka, na paññāyasī”ti pucchite tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “svāhaṃ, bhante, ettakaṃ kālaṃ lajjāya buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ nāgato”ti āha. Satthā “na[M 2.0306], upāsaka, idānevesā kilesavasena taṃ pakkosāpetvā āgatakāle taṃ okāsaṃ akatvā lajjāpesi, pubbepi pana paṇḍitesu paṭibaddhacittā hutvā pakkosāpetvā āgatakāle okāsaṃ akatvā kilametvāva uyyojesī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The other women, knowing what she had done, approached her after the householder had left and said, "You were so infatuated with him that you refused food and lay down. Then we, having begged him again and again, brought him here. Why did you not give him an opportunity?" She explained the matter to them. The others said, "In that case, you will see for yourself!" and departed. The householder did not even look back again. Unable to get him, she went without food and right there came to the end of her life. The householder, learning of her death, took many garlands, perfumes, and ointments, went to Jeta's Grove, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side. When the Teacher asked, "Why is it, lay follower, that you have not been seen?" he told him the matter and said, "Venerable sir, for so long, out of shame, I have not come to attend upon the Buddha." The Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not only now that she, through the power of defilement, had you summoned and, when you came, did not give you an opportunity and shamed you. In the past, too, having become infatuated with wise men, she had them summoned and, when they came, did not give them an opportunity, but tormented them and sent them away." At his request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sindhavakule nibbattitvā vātaggasindhavo nāma hutvā tassa maṅgalaasso ahosi. Assagopakā taṃ netvā gaṅgāyaṃ nhāpenti. Atha naṃ bhaddalī nāma gadrabhī disvā paṭibaddhacittā hutvā kilesavasena kampamānā neva tiṇaṃ khādi[P 2.0339], na udakaṃ pivi, parisussitvā kisā aṭṭhicammamattā ahosi. Atha naṃ putto gadrabhapotako mātaraṃ parisussamānaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho tvaṃ, amma, neva tiṇaṃ khādasi, na udakaṃ pivasi, parisussitvā tattha tattha kampamānā nipajjasi, kiṃ te aphāsuka”nti pucchi. Sā akathetvā punappunaṃ vuccamānā tamatthaṃ kathesi. Atha naṃ putto samassāsetvā “amma, mā cintayi, ahaṃ taṃ ānessāmī”ti vatvā vātaggasindhavassa nhāyituṃ [V 2.0281] āgatakāle taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tāta, mayhaṃ mātā tumhesu paṭibaddhacittā nirāhārā sussitvā marissati, jīvitadānamassā dethā”ti āha. “Sādhu, tāta, dassāmi, assagopakā maṃ nhāpetvā thokaṃ gaṅgātīre vicaraṇatthāya vissajjenti, tvaṃ mātaraṃ gahetvā taṃ padesaṃ ehī”ti. So gantvā mātaraṃ ānetvā tasmiṃ padese vissajjetvā ekamantaṃ paṭicchanno aṭṭhāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in a family of Sindh horses and became the king's state horse, named Vātaggasindhava. The grooms would take him and bathe him in the Ganges. Then a she-donkey named Bhaddalī saw him and became infatuated. Trembling with the power of defilement, she neither ate grass nor drank water, but withered away until she was just skin and bones.
