Then her son, a young donkey, seeing his mother withering away, asked, "Mother, why do you neither eat grass nor drink water? You are withering away, trembling and lying down here and there. What is wrong with you?" After not speaking, being asked again and again, she told him the matter. Then her son comforted her, saying, "Mother, do not worry, I will bring him to you." When Vātaggasindhava came to bathe, he approached him and said, "Sir, my mother is infatuated with you. Without food, she is withering away and will die. Please grant her the gift of life." "Very well, my dear," he replied, "I will grant it. The grooms, after bathing me, release me for a little while to roam on the bank of the Ganges. You bring your mother to that place." He went, brought his mother, left her in that place, and stood hidden to one side.

Assagopakāpi vātaggasindhavaṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne vissajjesuṃ. So taṃ gadrabhiṃ oloketvā upasaṅkami. Atha sā gadrabhī tasmiṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano sarīraṃ upasiṅghamāne “sacāhaṃ garuṃ akatvā āgatakkhaṇeyevassa okāsaṃ karissāmi, evaṃ me yaso ca issariyañca parihāyissati, anicchamānā viya bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā sindhavassa heṭṭhāhanuke pādena paharitvā palāyi, dantamūlamassa bhijjitvā gatakālo viya ahosi. Vātaggasindhavo “ko me etāya attho”ti [P 2.0340] lajjito tatova palāyi. Sā vippaṭisārinī hutvā tattheva patitvā socamānā nipajji.

The grooms released the Vātagga Sindh horse in that place. He saw the she-donkey and approached her. Then, as he approached and was sniffing her body, the she-donkey thought, 'If I give him an opportunity the moment he arrives without making myself seem important, my reputation and authority will diminish. It is proper to act as if unwilling.' Having so thought, she kicked the Sindh horse on the lower jaw with her foot and fled. The root of his tooth was broken, and it was as if his time had come. The Vātagga Sindh horse, ashamed, thought, 'What use is she to me?' and fled from there. She, becoming remorseful, fell down right there and lay grieving.

Atha [M 2.0307] naṃ putto upasaṅkamitvā pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then her son approached her and, wishing to question her, spoke the first verse:

46.

46.

“Yenāsi kisiyā paṇḍu, yena bhattaṃ na ruccati;

Ayaṃ so āgato bhattā, kasmā dāni palāyasī”ti.

“On account of whom you are thin and pale,

on whose account your food has no appeal;

that very husband has now come for you,

so why is it that you now flee?”

Tattha yenāti tasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittatāya yena kāraṇabhūtena.

Herein, 'on account of whom' (yena) means: by that which is the cause, namely, because your heart is attached to him. 'Thin' (kisiyā) means emaciated. 'Pale' (paṇḍu) means having a yellowish complexion. 'On whose account your food has no appeal' means because of your attachment to that Sindh horse, you do not enjoy your food. 'That very husband' (ayaṃ so bhattā) refers to that Sindh horse. 'Why do you now flee' means why do you now make him flee?

Puttassa vacanaṃ sutvā gadrabhī dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing her son's words, the she-donkey spoke the second verse:

47.

47.

“Sace panādikeneva, santhavo nāma jāyati;

Yaso hāyati itthīnaṃ, tasmā tāta palāyaha”nti.

“If intimacy should arise

right at the very start,

the reputation of women declines;

therefore, my dear, I make him flee.”

Tattha ādikenevātiāditova paṭhamameva. Santhavoti methunadhammasaṃyogavasena mittasanthavo. Yaso hāyati itthīnanti, tāta, itthīnañhi garukaṃ akatvā āditova santhavaṃ kurumānānaṃ yaso hāyati, issariyagabbitabhāvo parihāyatīti. Evaṃ sā itthīnaṃ sabhāvaṃ puttassa kathesi.

Herein, 'right at the very start' (ādikeneva) means from the very beginning. 'Intimacy' (santhavo) means friendly intimacy by way of sexual connection. 'The reputation of women declines' means: my dear, for women who establish intimacy right from the start without making themselves seem important, their reputation declines, and their proud sense of authority diminishes. Thus she explained the nature of women to her son.

Tatiyagāthaṃ [V 2.0282] pana satthā abhisambuddho hutvā āha –

But the Teacher, having become perfectly enlightened, spoke the third verse:

48.

48.

“Yasassinaṃ kule jātaṃ, āgataṃ yā na icchati;

Socati cirarattāya, vātaggamiva bhaddalī”ti.

“She who does not want the one of high reputation,

born in a good family, who has come to her,

grieves for a very long time,

just as Bhaddalī grieves for Vātagga.”

Tattha yasassinanti yasasampannaṃ. Yā na icchatīti yā itthī tathārūpaṃ purisaṃ na icchati. Cirarattāyāti cirarattaṃ, dīghamaddhānanti attho.

Herein, 'of high reputation' (yasassinaṃ) means endowed with wealth and glory. 'She who does not want' means a woman who does not desire such a man. 'For a very long time' (cirarattāya) means for a long duration. 'Like Bhaddalī for Vātagga' means just as the she-donkey named Bhaddalī grieves on account of the Vātagga Sindh horse.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kuṭumbiko sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā gadrabhī sā itthī ahosi, vātaggasindhavo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. 'At that time, the she-donkey was that woman, and the Vātagga Sindh horse was I myself.'

Vātaggasindhavajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Vātaggasindhava Jātaka, the sixth.

[267] 7. Kakkaṭakajātakavaṇṇanā

[267] 7. The Commentary on the Kakkaṭaka Jātaka

Siṅgī [P 2.0341][M 2.0308] migoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ itthiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kireko kuṭumbiko attano bhariyaṃ gahetvā uddhārasodhanatthāya janapadaṃ gantvā uddhāraṃ sodhetvā āgacchanto antarāmagge corehi gahito. Bhariyā panassa abhirūpā pāsādikā dassanīyā, corajeṭṭhako tassā sinehena kuṭumbikaṃ māretuṃ ārabhi. Sā pana itthī sīlavatī ācārasampannā patidevatā, sā corajeṭṭhakassa pādesu nipatitvā “sāmi, sace mayi sineho atthi, mā mayhaṃ sāmikaṃ mārehi. Sace māresi, ahampi visaṃ vā khāditvā nāsavātaṃ vā sannirumbhitvā marissāmi, tayā pana saddhiṃ na gamissāmi, mā me akāraṇena sāmikaṃ mārehī”ti yācitvā taṃ vissajjāpesi. Te ubhopi sotthinā sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavanapiṭṭhivihārena gacchantā “vihāraṃ pavisitvā satthāraṃ vandissāmā”ti gandhakuṭipariveṇaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Te satthārā “kahaṃ gatattha, upāsakā”ti puṭṭhā “uddhārasodhanatthāyā”ti āhaṃsu. “Antarāmagge pana ārogyena āgatatthā”ti vutte kuṭumbiko āha – “antarāmagge no, bhante, corā gaṇhiṃsu, tatresā maṃ māriyamānaṃ corajeṭṭhakaṃ yācitvā mocesi, imaṃ nissāya mayā jīvitaṃ laddha”nti. Satthā “na, upāsaka, idānevetāya [V 2.0283] evaṃ tuyhaṃ jīvitaṃ dinnaṃ, pubbepi paṇḍitānampi jīvitaṃ adāsiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“The horned animal,” etc. The Teacher told this story while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain woman. It is said that at Sāvatthī, a certain householder took his wife and went to the countryside to settle a debt. Having settled the debt, while he was returning, he was captured by robbers on the way. His wife was beautiful, graceful, and lovely to behold. The robber chief, out of desire for her, prepared to kill the householder. But that woman was virtuous, of good conduct, and devoted to her husband. She fell at the feet of the robber chief and pleaded, “Master, if you have affection for me, do not kill my husband. If you kill him, I will either swallow poison or die by holding my breath; I will not go with you. Do not kill my husband without cause.” Having thus pleaded, she secured his release. Both of them reached Sāvatthī safely. As they were passing by the back of the Jetavana monastery, they thought, “Let us enter the monastery and pay homage to the Teacher.” They went to the precincts of the Fragrant Chamber, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down at one side. The Teacher asked them, “Where have you been, lay followers?” They replied, “To settle a debt, venerable sir.” When asked, “Did you return safely along the way?” the householder said, “On the way, venerable sir, robbers captured us. When I was about to be killed, this woman pleaded with the robber chief and set me free. It is on account of her that my life was saved.” The Teacher said, “Lay follower, it is not only now that she has given you your life; in the past, too, she gave life to the wise.” And, at his request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente himavante mahāudakarahado, tattha mahāsuvaṇṇakakkaṭako ahosi. So tassa nivāsabhāvena “kuḷīradaho”ti paññāyittha. Kakkaṭako mahā ahosi khalamaṇḍalappamāṇo, hatthī gahetvā vadhitvā khādati. Hatthī tassa bhayena tattha otaritvā gocaraṃ [P 2.0342] gaṇhituṃ na sakkonti. Tadā bodhisatto kuḷīradahaṃ upanissāya vasamānaṃ hatthiyūthajeṭṭhakaṃ paṭicca kareṇuyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Athassa mātā “gabbhaṃ rakkhissāmī”ti aññaṃ pabbatappadesaṃ gantvā gabbhaṃ rakkhitvā puttaṃ vijāyi. So anukkamena viññutaṃ patto [M 2.0309] mahāsarīro thāmasampanno sobhaggappatto añjanapabbato viya ahosi. So ekāya kareṇuyā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappetvā “kakkaṭakaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti attano bhariyañca mātarañca ādāya taṃ hatthiyūthaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pitaraṃ passitvā “tāta, ahaṃ kakkaṭakaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ pitā “na sakkhissasi, tātā”ti vāretvā punappunaṃ vadantaṃ “tvaññeva jānissasī”ti āha.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a great lake in the Himalayas where a huge golden crab lived. Because it was its dwelling place, the lake became known as 'Crab Lake.' The crab was as large as a threshing floor; it would seize elephants, kill them, and eat them. Out of fear of it, the elephants could not descend into the lake to feed. At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of a she-elephant by the leader of an elephant herd that lived in dependence on Crab Lake. His mother, thinking, 'I will protect my womb,' went to another mountain region, protected her womb, and gave birth to a son. In due course, he attained maturity, grew large-bodied, was endowed with strength, and possessed great beauty, appearing like a mountain of collyrium. He took a certain she-elephant as his mate and, thinking, 'I will catch the crab,' he took his wife and mother, approached that elephant herd, and seeing his father, said, 'Father, I will catch the crab.' His father tried to stop him, saying, 'You will not be able to, my son,' but when he insisted again and again, his father said, 'You yourself will know.'

So kuḷīradahaṃ upanissāya vasante sabbavāraṇe sannipātetvā sabbehi saddhiṃ dahasamīpaṃ gantvā “kiṃ so kakkaṭako otaraṇakāle gaṇhāti, udāhu gocaraṃ gaṇhanakāle, udāhu uttaraṇakāle”ti pucchitvā “uttaraṇakāle”ti sutvā “tena hi tumhe kuḷīradahaṃ otaritvā yāvadatthaṃ gocaraṃ gahetvā paṭhamaṃ uttaratha, ahaṃ pacchato bhavissāmī”ti āha. Vāraṇā tathā kariṃsu. Kuḷīro pacchato uttarantaṃ bodhisattaṃ mahāsaṇḍāsena kammāro lohasalākaṃ viya aḷadvayena pāde daḷhaṃ gaṇhi, kareṇukā bodhisattaṃ avijahitvā samīpeyeva aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto ākaḍḍhanto kuḷīraṃ cāletuṃ nāsakkhi, kuḷīro pana taṃ ākaḍḍhanto attano abhimukhaṃ karoti. So maraṇabhayatajjito baddharavaṃ ravi, sabbe vāraṇā maraṇabhayatajjitā koñcanādaṃ katvā muttakarīsaṃ cajamānā palāyiṃsu, kareṇukāpissa saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontī palāyituṃ ārabhi.

He assembled all the elephants living in dependence on Crab Lake and, going with all of them to the vicinity of the lake, he asked: “Does that crab seize one at the time of descending, or while feeding, or at the time of ascending?” Hearing that it was at the time of ascending, he said: “In that case, you all descend into Crab Lake, feed as you wish, and ascend first. I will be last.” The elephants did so. As the Bodhisatta was ascending last, the crab seized his feet firmly with its two great claws, like a blacksmith gripping an iron rod with tongs. The she-elephant, not abandoning the Bodhisatta, stood right nearby. Though the Bodhisatta pulled, he could not move the crab, but the crab, pulling him, drew him towards itself. Terrified by the fear of death, he let out a loud roar. All the elephants, terrified by the fear of death, trumpeted and fled, discharging urine and dung. Even his she-elephant, unable to stand her ground, began to flee.

Atha naṃ [P 2.0343] so attano baddhabhāvaṃ saññāpetvā tassā apalāyanatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, to make her aware of his captive state and to prevent her from fleeing, he spoke the first verse:

49. Tattha [V 2.0284] siṅgī migoti siṅgī suvaṇṇavaṇṇo migo. Dvīhi aḷehi siṅgakiccaṃ sādhentehi yuttatāya siṅgīti attho. Migoti pana sabbapāṇasaṅgāhakavasena idha kuḷīro vutto. Āyatacakkhunettoti ettha dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu, nayanaṭṭhena nettaṃ, āyatāni cakkhusaṅkhātāni nettāni [M 2.0310] assāti āyatacakkhunetto, dīghaakkhīti attho. Aṭṭhimevassa tacakiccaṃ sādhetīti aṭṭhittaco. Tenābhibhūtoti tena migena abhibhūto ajjhotthato niccalaṃ gahito hutvā. Kapaṇaṃ rudāmīti kāruññappatto hutvā rudāmi viravāmi. Mā heva manti maṃ evarūpaṃ byasanappattaṃ attano pāṇasamaṃ piyasāmikaṃ tvaṃ mā heva jahīti.

49. Herein, a horned creature: a creature of golden color. The meaning is ‘horned one’ (siṅgī) because it is endowed with two claws that perform the function of horns. Creature (migo), however, is said here of the crab in the sense of including all living beings. With long eyes: here cakkhu is in the sense of seeing, and netta in the sense of leading; one for whom the eyes (netta), designated as cakkhu, are long is one with long eyes (āyatacakkhunetto); the meaning is long-eyed. Its shell serves as its skin, thus it is ‘shell-skinned’ (aṭṭhittaco). Overpowered by it: overpowered by that creature, overwhelmed, seized and held motionless. I cry wretchedly: having become pitiable, I cry, I wail. Do not abandon me: you should not abandon me, your beloved husband who is as dear as your own life and has met with such a disaster.

Atha sā kareṇukā nivattitvā taṃ assāsayamānā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then that she-elephant, turning back and reassuring him, spoke the second verse:

50.

50.

“Ayya na taṃ jahissāmi, kuñjaraṃ saṭṭhihāyanaṃ;

Pathabyā cāturantāya, suppiyo hosi me tuva”nti.

“My lord, I will not abandon you, the elephant of sixty years; on the earth bounded by the four oceans, you are very dear to me.”

Tattha saṭṭhihāyananti jātiyā saṭṭhivassakālasmiñhi kuñjarā thāmena parihāyanti, sā ahaṃ evaṃ thāmahīnaṃ imaṃ byasanaṃ pattaṃ taṃ na jahissāmi, mā bhāyi, imissā hi catūsu disāsu samuddaṃ patvā ṭhitāya cāturantāya pathaviyā tvaṃ mayhaṃ suṭṭhu piyoti.

Herein, of sixty years: for at the age of sixty years from birth, elephants decline in strength. She says: “I will not abandon you who have thus lost your strength and met with this disaster. Do not be afraid. For on this earth bounded by the four oceans, you are very dear to me.”

Atha naṃ santhambhetvā “ayya, idāni taṃ kuḷīrena saddhiṃ thokaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ labhamānā vissajjāpessāmī”ti vatvā kuḷīraṃ yācamānā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having encouraged him, she said, “My lord, now I will secure your release by having a little talk with the crab.” And pleading with the crab, she spoke the third verse:

51.

51.

“Ye [P 2.0344] kuḷīrā samuddasmiṃ, gaṅgāya yamunāya ca;

Tesaṃ tvaṃ vārijo seṭṭho, muñca rodantiyā pati”nti.

“Of the crabs in the ocean, and in the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, you, O water-born, are the best. Release the husband of her who weeps!”

Tassattho – ye samudde vā gaṅgāya vā yamunāya vā kuḷīrā, sabbesaṃ vaṇṇasampattiyā ca mahantattena ca tvameva seṭṭho uttamo. Tena taṃ yācāmi, mayhaṃ rodamānāya sāmikaṃ muñcāti.

Its meaning is: Of whatever crabs there are in the ocean, or in the Gaṅgā, or in the Yamunā, you are the best and most excellent of them all in perfection of color and in greatness. Therefore I plead with you: release the husband of me who is weeping.

Kuḷīro tassā kathayamānāya itthisadde nimittaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhiyamānaso hutvā vāraṇassa pādato aḷe viniveṭhento “ayaṃ vissaṭṭho idaṃ nāma karissatī”ti na kiñci aññāsi. Atha naṃ vāraṇo pādaṃ ukkhipitvā piṭṭhiyaṃ akkami, tāvadeva aṭṭhīni bhijjiṃsu. Vāraṇo tuṭṭharavaṃ [V 2.0285] ravi, sabbe vāraṇā sannipatitvā kuḷīraṃ nīharitvā mahītale ṭhapetvā maddantā cuṇṇavicuṇṇamakaṃsu. Tassa dve aḷā sarīrato bhijjitvā ekamante patiṃsu. So ca kuḷīradaho gaṅgāya ekābaddho[M 2.0311], gaṅgāya pūraṇakāle gaṅgodakena pūrati, udake mandībhūte dahato udakaṃ gaṅgaṃ otarati. Atha dvepi te aḷā uplavitvā gaṅgāya vuyhiṃsu. Tesu eko samuddaṃ pāvisi, ekaṃ dasabhātikarājāno udake kīḷamānā labhitvā āḷiṅgaṃ nāma mudiṅgaṃ akaṃsu. Samuddaṃ pana paviṭṭhaṃ asurā gahetvā ālambaraṃ nāma bheriṃ kāresuṃ. Te aparabhāge sakkena saṅgāme parājitā taṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyiṃsu, atha naṃ sakko attano atthāya gaṇhāpesi. “Ālambaramegho viya thanatī”ti taṃ sandhāya vadanti.

The crab, captivated by the sound of her female voice, began to loosen its claws from the elephant's feet, not knowing at all what the elephant would do once released. Then the elephant lifted its foot and stepped on its back, and instantly its bones were crushed. The elephant roared with delight. All the elephants gathered, dragged the crab out, placed it on the ground, and trampled it until it was completely pulverized. Its two claws broke off from its body and fell to one side. That Crab Lake was connected to the Gaṅgā; when the Gaṅgā was full, it was filled with water from the Gaṅgā, and when the water subsided, water from the lake flowed into the Gaṅgā. Then both those claws floated up and were carried away by the Gaṅgā. One of them entered the ocean; the other was found by the ten brother kings while they were playing in the water, and they made it into a tabor called the Āḷiṅga. The one that entered the ocean was seized by the asuras, who made it into a war-drum called the Ālambara. Later, when they were defeated in battle by Sakka, they abandoned it and fled. Then Sakka had it taken for his own use. It is in reference to this that they say, “It thunders like the Ālambara cloud.”

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ubho jayampatikā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu[P 2.0345]. “Tadā kareṇukā ayaṃ upāsikā ahosi, vāraṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the truths and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the truths, both husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the she-elephant was this laywoman, and the elephant was myself.”

Kakkaṭakajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Kakkaṭaka Jātaka, the Seventh.

[268] 8. Ārāmadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā

[268] 8. The Commentary on the Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka

Yo ve sabbasametānanti idaṃ satthā dakkhiṇāgirijanapade aññataraṃ uyyānapālaputtaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Satthā kira vutthavasso jetavanā nikkhamitvā dakkhiṇāgirijanapade cārikaṃ cari. Atheko upāsako buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā uyyāne nisīdāpetvā yāgukhajjakehi santappetvā “ayyā, uyyānacārikaṃ caritukāmā iminā uyyānapālena saddhiṃ carantū”ti vatvā “ayyānaṃ phalāphalāni dadeyyāsī”ti uyyānapālaṃ āṇāpesi. Bhikkhū caramānā ekaṃ chiddaṭṭhānaṃ disvā “idaṃ ṭhānaṃ chiddaṃ viraḷarukkhaṃ, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti pucchiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ uyyānapālo ācikkhi – “eko kira uyyānapālaputto uparopakesu udakaṃ āsiñcanto ‘mūlappamāṇena āsiñcissāmī’ti uppāṭetvā mūlappamāṇena udakaṃ āsiñci, tena taṃ ṭhānaṃ chiddaṃ jāta”nti. Bhikkhū satthu santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva pubbepi so kumārako ārāmadūsakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“He who was esteemed the best…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the region of Dakkhiṇāgiri, concerning a certain park-keeper’s son. It seems that after completing the rains-residence, the Teacher left Jetavana and went on tour in the region of Dakkhiṇāgiri. Then a certain lay follower invited the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at its head, seated them in his park, and satisfied them with rice gruel and solid food. He then said, “Venerable sirs, if you wish to walk about in the park, please do so with this park-keeper,” and he instructed the park-keeper, “You should give fruits to the venerable sirs.” As the monks were walking about, they saw a certain spot that was bare and had sparse trees. They asked, “This place is bare and has sparse trees—what is the reason?” Then the park-keeper explained to them: “It is said that a certain park-keeper’s son, while watering the saplings, thought, ‘I will water them according to the size of their roots.’ So he uprooted them and watered them according to the size of their roots. Because of that, that spot became bare.” The monks went to the Teacher and reported the matter. The Teacher said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, that boy was a destroyer of parks.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 2.0312] bārāṇasiyaṃ vissasene nāma raññe rajjaṃ kārente ussave ghuṭṭhe uyyānapālo “ussavaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti uyyānavāsino makkaṭe āha – “idaṃ uyyānaṃ tumhākaṃ bahūpakāraṃ[V 2.0286], ahaṃ sattāhaṃ ussavaṃ kīḷissāmi, tumhe satta divase uparopakesu udakaṃ āsiñcathā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu. So tesaṃ cammaghaṭake datvā pakkāmi. Makkaṭā udakaṃ āsiñcantā uparopakesu āsiñciṃsu. Atha ne makkaṭajeṭṭhako āha – “āgametha tāva, udakaṃ nāma sabbakālaṃ dullabhaṃ, taṃ rakkhitabbaṃ, uparopake uppāṭetvā mūlappamāṇaṃ [P 2.0346] ñatvā dīghamūlakesu bahuṃ, rassamūlakesu appaṃ udakaṃ siñcituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Te “sādhū”ti vatvā ekacce uparopake uppāṭetvā gacchanti, ekacce te ropetvā udakaṃ siñcanti.

In the past, when King Vissasena was reigning in Benares and a festival was proclaimed, the park-keeper thought, “I will enjoy the festival.” He said to the monkeys dwelling in the park: “This park is of great service to you. I will enjoy the festival for seven days. During these seven days, you must water the saplings.” They agreed, saying, “Very well.” He gave them leather water pots and departed. The monkeys started watering the saplings. Then the monkey chief said to them: “Wait a bit, water is always scarce and should be conserved. It is fitting to pull up the saplings, ascertain the size of their roots, and then water them—much water for those with long roots, and little for those with short roots.” They agreed, saying, “Very well.” So some went about uprooting the saplings, while others replanted and watered them.

Tasmiṃ kāle bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ ekassa kulassa putto ahosi, so kenacideva karaṇīyena uyyānaṃ gantvā te makkaṭe tathā karonte disvā “ko tumhe evaṃ kāretī”ti pucchitvā “vānarajeṭṭhako”ti vutte “jeṭṭhakassa tāva vo ayaṃ paññā, tumhākaṃ pana kīdisī bhavissatī”ti tamatthaṃ pakāsento imaṃ paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, the Bodhisatta was the son of a certain family in Benares. Having gone to the park on some business, he saw those monkeys acting in that way and asked, “Who makes you do this?” When they replied, “Our chief,” he said, “If this is the wisdom of your chief, what must yours be like?” And clarifying the matter, he spoke this first verse:

52.

52.

“Yo ve sabbasametānaṃ, ahuvā seṭṭhasammato;

Tassāyaṃ edisī paññā, kimeva itarā pajā”ti.

“Of all assembled here, he was esteemed the best; if such is the wisdom that he possessed, what can be said about the rest?”

Tattha sabbasametānanti imesaṃ sabbesaṃ samānajātīnaṃ. Ahuvāti ahosi. Kimeva itarā pajāti yā itarā etesu lāmikā pajā, kīdisā nu kho tassā paññāti.

Herein, 'of all assembled' means of all these of the same species. 'Ahuvā' means 'ahosi' (he was). 'What can be said about the rest?' means: as for the other, inferior folk among them, what kind of wisdom might they have?

Tassa kathaṃ sutvā vānarā dutiyaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Having heard his words, the monkeys spoke the second verse:

53.

53.

“Evameva tuvaṃ brahme, anaññāya vinindasi;

Kathaṃ mūlaṃ adisvāna, rukkhaṃ jaññā patiṭṭhita”nti.

“Thus, O brahmin, you censure through ignorance; without having seen the root, how could one know if a tree is firmly established?”

Tattha brahmeti ālapanamattaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – tvaṃ, bho purisa, kāraṇākāraṇaṃ ajānitvā evameva amhe vinindasi, rukkhaṃ nāma “gambhīre patiṭṭhito vā esa, na vā”ti mūlaṃ anuppāṭetvā kathaṃ ñātuṃ sakkā, tena mayaṃ uppāṭetvā mūlappamāṇena udakaṃ āsiñcāmāti.

Herein, 'brahmin' is just a term of address. This is the concise meaning: ‘You, good sir, censure us without knowing the reason. How is it possible to know whether a tree is established deep down or not without pulling up its root? That is why we pull them up and water them according to the size of their roots.’”

Taṃ [M 2.0313] sutvā bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:

54.

54.

“Nāhaṃ [V 2.0287] tumhe vinindāmi, ye caññe vānarā vane;

Vissasenova gārayho, yassatthā rukkharopakā”ti.

“I do not censure you, nor the other monkeys in the forest; Vissasena alone is to be blamed, he for whose sake you became the tree-planters.”

Tattha vissasenova gārayhoti bārāṇasirājā vissasenoyeva ettha garahitabbo. Yassatthā rukkharopakāti yassatthāya tumhādisā rukkharopakā jātāti.

Herein, 'Vissasena alone is to be blamed' means that King Vissasena of Benares is the one to be censured here. 'He for whose sake you became the tree-planters' means for whose benefit those like you have become tree-planters.

Satthā [P 2.0347] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vānarajeṭṭhako ārāmadūsakakumāro ahosi, paṇḍitapuriso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, the monkey chief was the park-destroying boy, but the wise man was myself.”

Ārāmadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka, the Eighth.

[269] 9. Sujātajātakavaṇṇanā

[269] 9. The Commentary on the Sujāta Jātaka

Na hi vaṇṇena sampannāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikassa suṇisaṃ dhanañcayaseṭṭhidhītaraṃ visākhāya kaniṭṭhabhaginiṃ sujātaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kira mahantena yasena anāthapiṇḍikassa gharaṃ pūrayamānā pāvisi, “mahākulassa dhītā aha”nti mānathaddhā ahosi kodhanā caṇḍī pharusā, sassusasurasāmikavattāni na karoti, gehajanaṃ tajjentī paharantī carati. Athekadivasaṃ satthā pañcahi bhikkhusatehi parivuto anāthapiṇḍikassa gehaṃ gantvā nisīdi. Mahāseṭṭhi dhammaṃ suṇantova bhagavantaṃ upanisīdi, tasmiṃ khaṇe sujātā dāsakammakarehi saddhiṃ kalahaṃ karoti. Satthā dhammakathaṃ ṭhapetvā “kiṃ saddo eso”ti āha. Esā, bhante, kulasuṇhā agāravā, nevassā sassusasurasāmikavattaṃ atthi, assaddhā appasannā ahorattaṃ kalahaṃ kurumānā vicaratīti. Tena hi naṃ pakkosathāti. Sā āgantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

“Not by beauty endowed…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning Sujātā, the daughter-in-law of Anāthapiṇḍika, who was the daughter of the treasurer Dhanañjaya and the younger sister of Visākhā. It is said that she entered Anāthapiṇḍika’s house with a great retinue. Thinking, “I am the daughter of a great family,” she became proud and stubborn, irascible, fierce, and harsh. She did not perform her duties to her mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband, but went about threatening and beating the household members. One day the Teacher, surrounded by five hundred monks, went to Anāthapiṇḍika’s house and sat down. The great treasurer sat near the Blessed One, listening to the Dhamma. At that moment, Sujātā was quarreling with the servants and workers. The Teacher paused his Dhamma talk and asked, “What is that noise?” “Venerable sir, it is my daughter-in-law. She is disrespectful, has no sense of duty toward her mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband. She is faithless, without confidence, and goes about quarreling day and night.” “Then summon her.” She came, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood to one side.

Atha naṃ satthā “sattimā, sujāte, purisassa bhariyā, tāsaṃ tvaṃ katarā”ti pucchi. “Bhante, nāhaṃ saṃkhittena kathitassa atthaṃ ājānāmi, vitthārena me kathethā”ti. Satthā “tena hi ohitasotā suṇohī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Teacher asked her: “Sujātā, there are these seven kinds of wives a man may have. Which of them are you?” “Venerable sir, I do not understand the meaning of what is said in brief. Please explain it to me in detail.” The Teacher said, “Then listen with an attentive ear,” and he spoke these verses:

“Paduṭṭhacittā [V 2.0288][M 2.0314] ahitānukampinī, aññesu rattā atimaññate patiṃ,

Dhanena kītassa vadhāya ussukā; Yā evarūpā purisassa bhariyā,

Vadhakā ca bhariyāti ca sā pavuccati. [1]

“She who has a corrupt mind, wishing for his harm, infatuated with other men, and despises her husband; she is intent on the murder of him who was bought with wealth. A wife of such a kind is called a slayer-wife.

“Yaṃ itthiyā vindati sāmiko dhanaṃ, sippaṃ vaṇijjañca kasiṃ adhiṭṭhahaṃ,

Appampi [P 2.0348] tassa apahātumicchati; Yā evarūpā purisassa bhariyā,

Corī ca bhariyāti ca sā pavuccati. [2]

“Whatever wealth her husband gains through craft, trade, or agriculture, she desires to pilfer even a little of it. A wife of such a kind is called a robber-wife.

“Akammakāmā alasā mahagghasā, pharusā ca caṇḍī ca duruttavādinī,

Uṭṭhāyakānaṃ abhibhuyya vattati; Yā evarūpā purisassa bhariyā,

Ayyā ca bhariyāti ca sā pavuccati. [3]

“Unwilling to work, lazy, gluttonous, harsh, fierce, and rude in speech, she lives by overpowering those who are industrious. A wife of such a kind is called a mistress-wife.

“Yā sabbadā hoti hitānukampinī, mātāva puttaṃ anurakkhate patiṃ,

Tato dhanaṃ sambhatamassa rakkhati; Yā evarūpā purisassa bhariyā,

Mātā ca bhariyāti ca sā pavuccati. [4]

“She who is always compassionate and desires his welfare, who protects her husband as a mother protects her son, and who guards the wealth he has acquired—a wife of such a kind is called a mother-wife.

“Yathāpi jeṭṭhā bhaginī kaniṭṭhakā, sagāravā hoti sakamhi sādhike,

Hirīmanā bhattu vasānuvattinī; Yā evarūpā purisassa bhariyā,

Bhaginī ca bhariyāti ca sā pavuccati. [5]

“She who respects her husband as a younger sister respects her elder brother, who is modest and complies with her husband’s wishes—a wife of such a kind is called a sister-wife.

“Yācīdha disvāna patiṃ pamodati, sakhī sakhāraṃva cirassamāgataṃ,

Koleyyakā sīlavatī patibbatā; Yā evarūpā purisassa bhariyā,

Sakhī ca bhariyāti ca sā pavuccati. [6]

“She who rejoices when she sees her husband, as a friend rejoices to see a friend returned after a long absence; who is of noble birth, virtuous, and devoted to her husband—a wife of such a kind is called a friend-wife.

“Akkuddhasantā [M 2.0315] vadhadaṇḍatajjitā, aduṭṭhacittā patino titikkhati,

Akkodhanā bhattu vasānuvattinī; Yā evarūpā purisassa bhariyā,

Dāsī ca bhariyāti ca sā pavuccati”. (a. ni. 7.63); [7]

“Remaining calm even when threatened with violence and punishment, with a mind free from hate she endures her husband. Not given to anger, she complies with her husband’s wishes. A wife of such a kind is called a slave-wife.”

Imā [P 2.0349] kho, sujāte, purisassa satta bhariyā. Tāsu vadhakasamā corīsamā ayyasamāti imā tisso niraye nibbattanti, itarā catasso nimmānaratidevaloke.

“These, Sujātā, are the seven kinds of wives a man may have. Among them, these three—the slayer-wife, the robber-wife, and the mistress-wife—are reborn in hell. The other four are reborn in the Nimmānaratī heaven.”

“Yācīdha [V 2.0289] bhariyā vadhakāti vuccati, corīti ayyāti ca yā pavuccati;

Dussīlarūpā pharusā anādarā, kāyassa bhedā nirayaṃ vajanti tā.

“The wives who are called slayers, robbers, or tyrants—immoral, harsh, and disrespectful—at the breakup of the body, go to hell.

“Yācīdha mātā bhaginī sakhīti ca, dāsīti bhariyāti ca yā pavuccati;

Sīle ṭhitattā cirarattasaṃvutā, kāyassa bhedā sugatiṃ vajanti tā”ti. (a. ni. 7.63);

“The wives who are called mother, sister, friend, or slave-wife—established in virtue, long restrained—at the breakup of the body, go to a good destination.”

Evaṃ satthari imā satta bhariyā dassenteyeva sujātā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Sujāte, tvaṃ imāsaṃ sattannaṃ bhariyānaṃ katarā”ti vutte “dāsisamā ahaṃ, bhante”ti vatvā tathāgataṃ vanditvā khamāpesi. Iti satthā sujātaṃ gharasuṇhaṃ ekovādeneva dametvā katabhattakicco jetavanaṃ gantvā bhikkhusaṅghena vatte dassite gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Dhammasabhāyampi kho, bhikkhū, satthu guṇakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, ekovādeneva satthā sujātaṃ gharasuṇhaṃ dametvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi mayā sujātā ekovādeneva damitā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Thus, while the Teacher was showing these seven kinds of wives, Sujātā was established in the fruit of stream-entry. When asked, “Sujātā, which of these seven wives are you?” she replied, “I am like a slave-wife, venerable sir,” and after paying homage to the Tathāgata, she asked for his forgiveness. In this way, the Teacher tamed Sujātā, the daughter-in-law of the house, with a single exhortation. After finishing his meal, he went to Jetavana, and after the bhikkhus had performed their duties, he entered the Perfumed Chamber. In the Hall of Dhamma, the bhikkhus started a discussion on the Teacher’s virtues: “Friends, with a single exhortation the Teacher tamed Sujātā, the daughter-in-law, and established her in the fruit of stream-entry.” The Teacher came and asked, “For what discussion, bhikkhus, are you now assembled?” When they replied, “About this matter,” he said: “Not only now, bhikkhus, but in the past, too, I tamed Sujātā with a single exhortation,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni [M 2.0316] uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa mātā kodhanā ahosi caṇḍā pharusā akkosikā paribhāsikā. So mātu ovādaṃ dātukāmopi “avatthukaṃ kathetuṃ na yutta”nti tassā anusāsanatthaṃ ekaṃ upamaṃ olokento carati. Athekadivasaṃ uyyānaṃ agamāsi, mātāpi puttena saddhiṃyeva agamāsi[P 2.0350]. Atha antarāmagge kikī sakuṇo viravi, bodhisattaparisā taṃ saddaṃ sutvā kaṇṇe pidahitvā “ambho, caṇḍavāce pharusavāce mā saddamakāsī”ti āha. Bodhisatte pana nāṭakaparivārite mātarā saddhiṃ uyyāne vicarante ekasmiṃ supupphitasālarukkhe nilīnā ekā kokilā madhurena sarena vassi. Mahājano tassā saddena sammatto hutvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā “saṇhavāce sakhilavāce muduvāce vassa vassā”ti gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā ohitasoto olokento aṭṭhāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. Having come of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā and, after his father’s passing, he ascended the throne and ruled the kingdom righteously and impartially. His mother, however, was wrathful, fierce, harsh, abusive, and given to scolding. Although he wished to advise her, he thought, “It is not proper to speak without a reason,” and he went about looking for a suitable parable with which to instruct her. One day, he went to the park, and his mother accompanied him. Along the way, a lapwing (kikī bird) cried out. Hearing its sound, the Bodhisatta’s attendants covered their ears and said, “Oh, you of harsh voice, you of rough voice, do not make a sound!” Later, while the Bodhisatta, surrounded by his retinue of entertainers, was walking in the park with his mother, a cuckoo hidden in a fully blossomed sāl tree sang with a sweet voice. The great crowd, enchanted by its song, raised their joined hands in reverence and, craning their necks, stood listening intently, saying, “O gentle-voiced one, O friendly-voiced one, O soft-voiced one, sing, sing!”

Atha mahāsatto tāni dve kāraṇāni disvā “idāni mātaraṃ saññāpetuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti cintetvā “amma, antarāmagge kikīsaddaṃ sutvā mahājano ‘mā saddamakāsi[V 2.0290], mā saddamakāsī’ti kaṇṇe pidahi, pharusavācā nāma na kassaci piyā”ti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –

Then the Great Being, seeing these two incidents, thought, “Now I will be able to make my mother understand.” He said: “Mother, on the way here the people heard the cry of the lapwing and covered their ears, saying, ‘Don’t make a sound! Don’t make a sound!’ Harsh speech is truly dear to no one.” Then he spoke these verses:

55.

55.

“Na hi vaṇṇena sampannā, mañjukā piyadassanā;

Kharavācā piyā honti, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.

“Not indeed by beauty, though lovely and pleasing to see, are the harsh-spoken beloved, in this world or in the next.

56.

56.

“Nanu passasimaṃ kāḷiṃ, dubbaṇṇaṃ tilakāhataṃ;

Kokilaṃ saṇhabhāṇena, bahūnaṃ pāṇinaṃ piyaṃ.

“Do you not see this black cuckoo, of ugly complexion and marked with spots? Yet it is beloved by many beings for its gentle voice.

57.

57.

“Tasmā sakhilavācassa, mantabhāṇī anuddhato;

Atthaṃ dhammañca dīpeti, madhuraṃ tassa bhāsita”nti.

“Therefore, of one who is friendly in speech, who speaks with wisdom and is not arrogant, the speech is sweet; they illuminate both the meaning and the Dhamma.”

Tāsaṃ ayamattho – amma, ime sattā piyaṅgusāmādinā sarīravaṇṇena samannāgatā kathānigghosassa madhuratāya mañjukā, abhirūpatāya piyadassanā samānāpi antamaso mātāpitaropi akkosaparibhāsādivasena pavattāya kharavācāya samannāgatattā kharavācā imasmiñca parasmiñca loke piyā nāma na honti antarāmagge kharavācā kikī viya, saṇhabhāṇino [M 2.0317] pana maṭṭhāya madhurāya vācāya samannāgatā virūpāpi piyā honti. Tena taṃ vadāmi – nanu passasi tvaṃ imaṃ kāḷiṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ sarīravaṇṇatopi kāḷatarehi tilakehi [P 2.0351] āhataṃ kokilaṃ, yā evaṃ dubbaṇṇā samānāpi saṇhabhāsanena bahūnaṃ piyā jātā. Iti yasmā kharavāco satto loke mātāpitūnampi appiyo, tasmā bahujanassa piyabhāvaṃ icchanto poso sakhilavāco saṇhamaṭṭhamuduvāco assa. Paññāsaṅkhātāya mantāya paricchinditvā vacanato mantabhāṇī, vinā uddhaccena pamāṇayuttasseva kathanato anuddhato. Yo hi evarūpo puggalo pāḷiñca atthañca dīpeti, tassa bhāsitaṃ kāraṇasannissitaṃ katvā paraṃ anakkosetvā kathitatāya madhuranti.

This is their meaning: Mother, though some beings are endowed with a body color like the priyangu creeper, are charming with a sweet-sounding voice, and are pleasing to see because of their beauty, if they are harsh-spoken—being given to abuse and scolding—they are not dear to anyone in this world or the next, not even to their own parents, just like the harsh-voiced kikī bird on the path. But those with gentle speech, endowed with a polished and sweet voice, are dear even if they are unattractive. Therefore I say to you: Do you not see this black cuckoo, of an ugly complexion, marked with spots even blacker than its body color? Though it is so ugly, it has become dear to many because of its gentle voice. Thus, since a harsh-spoken person is unloved in the world even by their parents, a person who wishes to be dear to many people should have friendly speech, a voice that is gentle, polished, and soft. ‘Who speaks wisely’ (mantabhāṇī) means one who speaks after having discerned with the wisdom called ‘mantā.’ ‘Not arrogant’ (anuddhato) means one is not puffed up because one speaks with moderation and without conceit. When such a person illuminates the text and its meaning, their speech is sweet because it is based on reason and spoken without reviling others.

Evaṃ bodhisatto imāhi tīhi gāthāhi mātu dhammaṃ desetvā mātaraṃ saññāpesi, sā tato paṭṭhāya ācārasampannā ahosi. Bodhisattopi mātaraṃ ekovādena nibbisevanaṃ katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus the Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma to his mother with these three verses and made her understand. From then on, she became accomplished in conduct. The Bodhisatta, having humbled his mother with this single admonition and freed her from pride, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 2.0291] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasirañño mātā sujātā ahosi, rājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: 'At that time, the mother of the king of Benares was Sujātā, and the king was myself.'

Sujātajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Sujāta Jātaka is concluded.

[270] 10. Ulūkajātakavaṇṇanā

[270] 10. 10. Ulūka Jātaka

Sabbehi kira ñātīhīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kākolūkakalahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi kāle kākā divā ulūke khādanti, ulūkā sūriyatthaṅgamanato paṭṭhāya tattha tattha sayitānaṃ kākānaṃ sīsāni chinditvā te jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpenti. Athekassa bhikkhuno jetavanapaccante ekasmiṃ pariveṇe vasantassa sammajjanakāle rukkhato patitāni sattaṭṭhanāḷimattānipi bahutarānipi kākasīsāni chaḍḍetabbāni honti. So tamatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, amukassa kira bhikkhuno vasanaṭṭhāne [M 2.0318] divase divase ettakāni [P 2.0352] nāma kākasīsāni chaḍḍetabbāni hontī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchi, bhikkhū “imāya nāmā”ti vatvā “kadā paṭṭhāya pana, bhante, kākānañca ulūkānañca aññamaññaṃ veraṃ uppanna”nti pucchiṃsu, satthā “paṭhamakappikakālato paṭṭhāyā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher told this story, which begins with 'By all the kinsmen, it is said,' while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a quarrel between crows and owls. At that time, crows would attack owls by day, while owls, from sunset onwards, would cut off the heads of crows sleeping here and there, thus putting an end to their lives. Now a certain bhikkhu was dwelling in a monastic cell on the outskirts of Jetavana. When sweeping, he would have to discard seven or eight measures of crow heads that had fallen from a tree and were covered in blood. He reported this matter to the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: 'Friends, they say that in the dwelling place of such-and-such a bhikkhu, this many crow heads have to be discarded every day.' The Teacher came and asked, 'For what discussion, bhikkhus, are you now assembled?' They replied, 'About this matter,' and then asked, 'But, venerable sir, since when has this enmity between crows and owls arisen?' The Teacher said, 'Since the time of the first eon,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte paṭhamakappikā manussā sannipatitvā ekaṃ abhirūpaṃ sobhaggappattaṃ ācārasampannaṃ sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ purisaṃ gahetvā rājānaṃ kariṃsu, catuppadāpi sannipatitvā ekaṃ sīhaṃ rājānaṃ akaṃsu, mahāsamudde macchā ānandaṃ nāma macchaṃ rājānaṃ akaṃsu. Tato sakuṇagaṇā himavantapadese ekasmiṃ piṭṭhipāsāṇe sannipatitvā “manussesu rājā paññāyati, tathā catuppadesu ceva macchesu ca. Amhākaṃ panantare rājā nāma natthi, appatissavāso nāma na vaṭṭati, amhākampi rājānaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, ekaṃ rājaṭṭhāne ṭhapetabbayuttakaṃ jānāthā”ti. Te tādisaṃ sakuṇaṃ olokayamānā ekaṃ ulūkaṃ rocetvā “ayaṃ no ruccatī”ti āhaṃsu. Atheko sakuṇo sabbesaṃ ajjhāsayaggahaṇatthaṃ tikkhattuṃ sāvesi. Tassa sāventassa dve sāvanā adhivāsetvā tatiyasāvanāya eko kāko uṭṭhāya “tiṭṭha tāvetassa imasmiṃ rājābhisekakāle evarūpaṃ mukhaṃ bhavati, kuddhassa kīdisaṃ bhavissati, iminā hi kuddhena olokitā mayaṃ tattakapāle pakkhittaloṇaṃ viya tattha tattheva bhijjissāma, imaṃ rājānaṃ kātuṃ mayhaṃ na ruccatī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsetuṃ paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, the people of the first eon assembled and made a man who was handsome, majestic, accomplished in conduct, and perfect in all respects their king. The quadrupeds also assembled and made a lion their king. The fish in the great ocean made a fish named Ānanda their king. Then the flocks of birds gathered on a great flat rock in the Himalayan region and said: 'A king is known among humans, and also among the quadrupeds and the fish. But among us there is no king. It is not right to live without a leader. We too should appoint a king. Choose one who is suitable to be established in the kingship.' As they were looking for such a bird, they chose an owl and said, 'This one pleases us.' Then one bird, in order to gain the consent of all, made the announcement three times. After two announcements had been heard in silence, upon the third announcement, a crow rose up and said: 'Hold on! If this is what his face looks like at his coronation, what will it be like when he is angry? If he were to look at us in anger, we would shatter on the spot like salt thrown on a hot pan. I do not approve of making him king.' To make this point, he spoke the first verse:

58.

58.

“Sabbehi [V 2.0292][P 2.0353] kira ñātīhi, kosiyo issaro kato;

Sace ñātīhanuññāto, bhaṇeyyāhaṃ ekavācika”nti.

“By all the kinsmen, it is said, the owl has been made the lord. If I am permitted by my kinsmen, I would like to say one thing.”

Tassattho – yā esā sāvanā vattati, taṃ sutvā vadāmi. Sabbehi kira imehi samāgatehi ñātīhi ayaṃ kosiyo rājā kato. Sace panāhaṃ ñātīhi anuññāto bhaveyyaṃ, ettha vattabbaṃ ekavācikaṃ kiñci bhaṇeyyanti.

Its meaning is this: I speak having heard the announcement that is being made. By all these assembled kinsmen, it is said, this owl has been made king. If I were to be permitted by my kinsmen, I would say a certain single thing that ought to be said here.

Atha [M 2.0319] naṃ anujānantā sakuṇā dutiyaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Then, giving the crow permission, the birds spoke the second verse:

59.

59.

“Bhaṇa samma anuññāto, atthaṃ dhammañca kevalaṃ;

Santi hi daharā pakkhī, paññavanto jutindharā”ti.

“Speak, friend, you have our permission; speak only what is meaningful and right. For there are young birds here who are wise and endowed with brilliance.”

Tattha bhaṇa, samma, anuññātoti, samma, vāyasa tvaṃ amhehi sabbehi anuññāto, yaṃ te bhaṇitabbaṃ, taṃ bhaṇa. Atthaṃ dhammañca kevalanti bhaṇanto ca kāraṇañceva paveṇiāgatañca vacanaṃ amuñcitvā bhaṇa. Paññavanto jutindharāti paññāsampannā ceva ñāṇobhāsadharā ca daharāpi pakkhino atthiyeva.

Herein, ‘Speak, friend, you have our permission’ means: Friend crow, you are permitted by all of us; speak whatever you have to say. ‘Speak only what is meaningful and right’ means: when you speak, speak without omitting what is logical and what is traditional. ‘Wise and endowed with brilliance’ means: there are indeed young birds here who are endowed with wisdom and who bear the light of knowledge.

So evaṃ anuññāto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus permitted, the crow spoke the third verse:

60.

60.

“Na me ruccati bhaddaṃ vo, ulūkassābhisecanaṃ;

Akkuddhassa mukhaṃ passa, kathaṃ kuddho karissatī”ti.

“I do not approve of anointing the owl; good luck to you! Look at the face of one who is not angry; how will he act when he is angry?”

Tassattho – bhaddaṃ tumhākaṃ hotu, yaṃ panetaṃ tikkhattuṃ sāvanavācāya ulūkassa abhisecanaṃ karīyati, etaṃ mayhaṃ na ruccati. Etassa hi idāni tuṭṭhacittassa akkuddhassa mukhaṃ passatha, kuddho panāyaṃ kathaṃ karissatīti na jānāmi, sabbathāpi etaṃ mayhaṃ na ruccatīti.

The meaning is: May good fortune be yours, but this anointing of the owl by a threefold proclamation does not please me. Look now at the face of this one, content and not angry—I do not know how he will act when angry; in every way, this does not please me.

So evaṃ vatvā “mayhaṃ na ruccati, mayhaṃ na ruccatī”ti viravanto ākāse uppati, ulūkopi naṃ uṭṭhāya anubandhi. Tato paṭṭhāya te aññamaññaṃ veraṃ bandhiṃsu. Sakuṇā suvaṇṇahaṃsaṃ rājānaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu.

Having spoken thus, crying out, “It does not please me, it does not please me!” he flew up into the sky. The owl, rising up, pursued him. From that time onward, they bound themselves in mutual enmity. The birds, having made the golden swan their king, departed.

Satthā [V 2.0293][P 2.0354] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. “Tadā rajje abhisittahaṃsapoto ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, many attained stream-entry and the other fruits. “At that time, the young swan anointed king was I myself.”

Ulūkajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Ulūka Jātaka, the Tenth.

Padumavaggo dutiyo.

The Paduma Chapter, the Second.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Padumaṃ mudupāṇī ca, palobhanaṃ panādakaṃ;

Khurappaṃ sindhavañceva, kakkaṭā, rāmadūsakaṃ;

Sujātaṃ ulūkaṃ dasa.

Paduma, Mudupāṇi, Palobhana, Panādaka, Khurappa, Sindhava, Kakkaṭa, Rāmadūsaka, Sujāta, and Ulūka—these ten.

3. Udapānavaggo

3. The Well Chapter

[271] 1. Udapānadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā

[271] 1. 1. The Commentary on the Udapānadūsaka Jātaka

Āraññikassa [V 2.0294][M 2.0320] isinoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ udapānadūsakasiṅgālaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira siṅgālo bhikkhusaṅghassa pānīyaudapānaṃ uccārapassāvakaraṇena dūsetvā pakkāmi. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ udapānasamīpaṃ āgataṃ sāmaṇerā leḍḍūhi paharitvā kilamesuṃ, so tato paṭṭhāya taṃ ṭhānaṃ puna nivattitvāpi na olokesi. Bhikkhū taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, udapānadūsakasiṅgālo kira sāmaṇerehi kilamitakālato paṭṭhāya puna nivattitvāpi na olokesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa siṅgālo udapānadūsakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Of the forest-dwelling sage…”: this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a jackal that polluted a well. It is said that a certain jackal defiled the drinking well of the Sangha of bhikkhus by defecating and urinating in it, and then departed. Then one day, when it came near the well, the novices struck it with clods of earth and tormented it. From that time on, it never returned to that place nor even glanced at it. The bhikkhus, having learned of this incident, raised a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: “Friends, it is said that from the time it was tormented by the novices, the jackal that polluted the well has never even looked back at this place.” The Teacher came and asked, “For what discussion, bhikkhus, are you now sitting together?” When they said, “Concerning this,” he said, “Not only now, bhikkhus, in the past too this jackal was a polluter of wells,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ idameva isipatanaṃ ayameva udapāno ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ kulaghare nibbattitvā vayappatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā isigaṇaparivuto isipatane vāsaṃ kappesi. Tadā eko siṅgālo idameva udapānaṃ dūsetvā pakkamati. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ tāpasā parivāretvā ṭhitā ekenupāyena gahetvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ ānayiṃsu. Bodhisatto siṅgālena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, this very Isipatana and this very well existed. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a good family in Bārāṇasī. When he came of age, he went forth into the ascetic life and, surrounded by a company of ascetics, took up residence at Isipatana. At that time, a jackal would defile this very well and depart. Then one day, the ascetics surrounded it and, using a stratagem, captured it and brought it to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, conversing with the jackal, spoke the first stanza:

61.

61.

“Āraññikassa isino, cirarattatapassino;

Kicchākataṃ udapānaṃ, kathaṃ samma avāhayī”ti.

“Of the forest-dwelling sage, long practicing austerities, the well made with difficulty—how, friend, did you pollute it?”

Tassattho [P 2.0355] – araññe vasanatāya āraññikassa, esitaguṇattā isino, cirarattaṃ tapaṃ nissāya vutthattā cirarattatapassino kicchākataṃ kicchena dukkhena nipphāditaṃ udapānaṃ kathaṃ kimatthāya samma siṅgāla, tvaṃ avāhayi muttakarīsena ajjhotthari dūsesi, taṃ vā muttakarīsaṃ ettha avāhayi pātesīti.

The meaning is: ‘forest-dweller’ because of dwelling in the forest; ‘sage’ because of possessing sought-after qualities; ‘long-practicing ascetic’ because of having lived in reliance on long-term austerity. ‘The well made with difficulty’ means accomplished with hardship and trouble. ‘How,’ for what reason, friend jackal, did you ‘pollute’ it—that is, cover and defile it with urine and feces? Or did you bring that urine and feces here and drop it in?

Taṃ [V 2.0295] sutvā siṅgālo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, the jackal spoke the second stanza:

62.

62.

“Esa dhammo siṅgālānaṃ, yaṃ pitvā ohadāmase;

Pitupitāmahaṃ dhammo, na taṃ ujjhātumarahasī”ti.

“This is the nature of jackals: that after drinking, we defecate there. It is the custom of our fathers and grandfathers; you should not condemn it.”

Tattha [M 2.0321] esa dhammoti esa sabhāvo. Yaṃ pitvā ohadāmaseti, samma, yaṃ mayaṃ yattha pānīyaṃ pivāma, tameva ūhadāmapi omuttemapi, esa amhākaṃ siṅgālānaṃ dhammoti dasseti. Pitupitāmahanti pitūnañca pitāmahānañca no esa dhammo. Na taṃ ujjhātumarahasīti taṃ amhākaṃ paveṇiāgataṃ dhammaṃ sabhāvaṃ tvaṃ ujjhātuṃ na arahasi, na yuttaṃ te ettha kujjhitunti.

Herein, ‘this is the nature’ means this is our innate disposition. ‘That after drinking, we defecate there’: friend, wherever we drink water, we also defecate and urinate there; this shows the nature of us jackals. ‘Of our fathers and grandfathers’ means this is the custom of our fathers and our grandfathers. ‘You should not condemn it’ means: you are not right to condemn this nature of ours that has come down by lineage; it is not proper for you to be angry about this.

Athassa bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke a third stanza to him:

63.

63.

“Yesaṃ vo ediso dhammo, adhammo pana kīdiso;

Mā vo dhammaṃ adhammaṃ vā, addasāma kudācana”nti.

“If this is the nature for you, what then would be your non-nature? May we never again see your ‘nature’ or your ‘non-nature’!”

Tattha mā voti tumhākaṃ dhammaṃ vā adhammaṃ vā na mayaṃ kadāci addasāmāti.

Therein, the meaning is: May we never see your nature or your non-nature.

Evaṃ bodhisatto tassa ovādaṃ datvā “mā puna āgacchā”ti āha. So tato paṭṭhāya puna nivattitvāpi na olokesi.

Thus the Bodhisatta gave it this admonition, saying, “Do not come here again.” From that time on, it did not even turn back to look.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā udapānadūsako ayameva siṅgālo ahosi, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the well-polluter was this very jackal, but the teacher of the group was I myself.”

Udapānadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Udapānadūsaka Jātaka, the First.

[272] 2. Byagghajātakavaṇṇanā

[272] 2. The Commentary on the Byaggha Jātaka

Yena [P 2.0356] mittena saṃsaggāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kokālikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kokālikavatthu terasakanipāte takkāriyajātake (jā. 1.13.104 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Kokāliko pana “sāriputtamoggallāne gahetvā āgamissāmī”ti kokālikaraṭṭhato [V 2.0296] jetavanaṃ āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā there upasaṅkamitvā “āvuso, kokālikaraṭṭhavāsino manussā tumhe pakkosanti, etha gacchāmā”ti āha. “Gaccha tvaṃ, āvuso, na mayaṃ āgacchāmā”ti. So therehi paṭikkhitto sayameva agamāsi. Atha bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, kokāliko sāriputtamoggallānehi sahāpi [M 2.0322] vināpi vattituṃ na sakkoti, saṃyogampi na sahati, viyogampi na sahatī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi kokāliko sāriputtamoggallānehi neva saha, na vinā vattituṃ sakkotī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“By the friend with whom one associates…”: this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Kokālika. The story of Kokālika will appear in the Takkāriya Jātaka in the Book of Thirteen. Now, Kokālika came from the Kokālikan country to Jetavana with the thought, “I will take Sāriputta and Moggallāna and return.” Having paid homage to the Teacher, he approached the Elders and said: “Friends, the people of the Kokālikan country summon you. Come, let us go.” “You go, friend; we are not coming.” Having been rejected by the Elders, he went alone. Then the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: “Friends, Kokālika cannot live either with or without Sāriputta and Moggallāna; he cannot bear connection, nor can he bear separation.” The Teacher came and asked, “For what discussion, bhikkhus, are you now sitting together?” When they told him, he said, “Not only now, bhikkhus, but in the past too Kokālika could not live either with or without Sāriputta and Moggallāna,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto aññatarasmiṃ araññāyatane rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tassa vimānato avidūre aññatarasmiṃ vanappatijeṭṭhake aññā rukkhadevatā vasati. Tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe sīho ca byaggho ca vasanti. Tesaṃ bhayena koci tattha na khettaṃ karoti, na rukkhaṃ chindati, nivattitvā oloketuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Te pana sīhabyagghā nānappakāre mige vadhitvā khādanti, khāditāvasesaṃ tattheva pahāya gacchanti. Tena so vanasaṇḍo asucikuṇapagandho hoti. Atha itarā rukkhadevatā andhabālā kāraṇākāraṇaṃ ajānamānā ekadivasaṃ bodhisattaṃ āha – “samma, ete no sīhabyagghe nissāya vanasaṇḍo asucikuṇapagandho jāto, ahaṃ ete palāpemī”ti. Bodhisatto “samma, ime dve nissāya amhākaṃ vimānāni [P 2.0357] rakkhiyanti, etesu palāyantesu vimānāni no vinassissanti, sīhabyagghānaṃ padaṃ apassantā manussā sabbaṃ vanaṃ chinditvā ekaṅgaṇaṃ katvā khettāni karissanti, mā te evaṃ ruccī”ti vatvā purimā dve gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree-deity in a certain forest. Not far from his celestial mansion, another tree-deity dwelt in a great forest tree. In that same forest grove, a lion and a tiger lived. Out of fear of them, no one would cultivate a field there or cut down a tree; no one was even able to turn and look back. That lion and tiger would kill and eat various kinds of animals, and leaving the remains right there, they would depart. Because of this, that forest grove became foul with the stench of impure corpses. Then the other tree-deity, who was blind and foolish and did not know cause and reason, one day said to the Bodhisatta: “Friend, because of this lion and tiger, our forest grove has become foul with the stench of corpses. I will drive them away!” The Bodhisatta replied: “Friend, it is by relying on these two that our mansions are protected. If they flee, our mansions will be destroyed. Not seeing the tracks of the lion and tiger, people will cut down the entire forest, make it a single clearing, and cultivate fields. Do not let this please you!” Having said this, he spoke the first two stanzas:

64.

64.

“Yena mittena saṃsaggā, yogakkhemo vihiyyati;

Pubbevajjhābhavaṃ tassa, rakkhe akkhīva paṇḍito.

“The friend by association with whom one’s security from bondage is lost—a wise person should guard against being overcome by him beforehand, as he would his own eye.”

65.

65.

“Yena mittena saṃsaggā, yogakkhemo pavaḍḍhati;

Kareyyattasamaṃ vuttiṃ, sabbakiccesu paṇḍito”ti.

“The friend by association with whom one’s security from bondage increases—a wise person should maintain a conduct equal to himself in all matters.”

Tattha yena mittena saṃsaggāti yena pāpamittena saddhiṃ saṃsaggahetu saṃsaggakāraṇā, yena saddhiṃ dassanasaṃsaggo savanasaṃsaggo kāyasaṃsaggo samullapanasaṃsaggo paribhogasaṃsaggoti imassa pañcavidhassa saṃsaggassa katattāti attho. Yogakkhemoti kāyacittasukhaṃ. Tañhi [M 2.0323] dukkhayogato khemattā [V 2.0297] idha yogakkhemoti adhippetaṃ. Vihiyyatīti parihāyati. Pubbevajjhābhavaṃ tassa, rakkhe akkhīva paṇḍitoti tassa pāpamittassa ajjhābhavaṃ tena abhibhavitabbaṃ attano lābhayasajīvitaṃ, yathā naṃ so na ajjhābhavati, tathā paṭhamatarameva attano akkhī viya paṇḍito puriso rakkheyya.

Therein, ‘by association with which friend’ means: because of association with an evil friend; because of having engaged in the five kinds of association, namely, association by sight, by hearing, by bodily contact, by conversation, and by shared use. ‘Security from bondage’ means bodily and mental happiness; for here it is intended as ‘security from bondage’ because it is security from the yoke of suffering. ‘Is lost’ means it diminishes. ‘A wise person should guard against being overcome by him beforehand, as he would his own eye’: a wise person should guard his own gain, fame, and life, which could be overcome by that evil friend, so that he is not overcome by him; he should guard it from the very beginning just like his own eye.

Dutiyagāthāya yenāti yena kalyāṇamittena saha saṃsaggakāraṇā. Yogakkhemo pavaḍḍhatīti kāyacittasukhaṃ vaḍḍhati. Kareyyattasamaṃ vuttinti tassa kalyāṇamittassa sabbakiccesu paṇḍito puriso yathā attano jīvitavuttiñca upabhogaparibhogavuttiñca karoti, evametaṃ sabbaṃ kareyya, adhikampi kareyya, hīnaṃ pana na kareyyāti.

In the second verse, ‘by which’ means: because of association with a good friend. ‘Security from bondage increases’ means: happiness of body and mind grows. ‘Maintain a conduct equal to himself’ means: in all duties for that good friend, a wise person should act just as they would for their own livelihood and for their own use and enjoyment. Thus, they should do all this, and even more, but should not do less.

Evaṃ bodhisattena kāraṇe kathitepi sā bāladevatā anupadhāretvā ekadivasaṃ bheravarūpārammaṇaṃ dassetvā te sīhabyagghe palāpesi. Manussā tesaṃ padavalañjaṃ adisvā “sīhabyagghā aññaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ gatā”ti ñatvā vanasaṇḍassa ekapassaṃ chindiṃsu. Devatā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā [P 2.0358] “ahaṃ, samma, tava vacanaṃ akatvā te palāpesiṃ, idāni tesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā manussā vanasaṇḍaṃ chindanti, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti vatvā “idāni te asukavanasaṇḍe nāma vasanti, gantvā te ānehī”ti vuttā tattha gantvā tesaṃ purato ṭhatvā añjaliṃ paggayha tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Even though the Bodhisatta had explained the reason, that foolish deity paid it no heed. One day, she manifested a terrifying form and drove away those lions and tigers. When the people saw no trace of their footprints, they knew, “The lions and tigers have gone to another forest grove,” and they began to clear one side of the grove. The deity approached the Bodhisatta and said: “Friend, I did not follow your words and drove them away. Now that the people know they have gone, they are clearing the forest grove. What is to be done?” When she was told, “They are now living in such-and-such a forest grove; go and bring them back,” she went there, stood before them, raised her hands in respectful salutation, and spoke the third verse:

66.

66.

“Etha byagghā nivattavho, paccupetha mahāvanaṃ;

Mā vanaṃ chindi nibyagghaṃ, byagghā māhesu nibbanā”ti.

“Come, tigers, turn back; return to the great forest. Let them not cut down the tigerless forest; may the tigers not be without their forest.”

Tattha byagghāti ubhopi te byagghanāmenevālapantī āha. Nivattavhoti nivattatha. Paccupetha mahāvananti taṃ mahāvanaṃ paccupetha puna upagacchatha, ayameva vā pāṭho. Mā vanaṃ chindi nibyagghanti amhākaṃ vasanakavanasaṇḍaṃ idāni tumhākaṃ abhāvena nibyagghaṃ manussā mā chindiṃsu. Byagghā māhesu nibbanāti tumhādisā ca byaggharājāno attano vasanaṭṭhānā palāyitattā nibbanā vasanaṭṭhānabhūtena vanena virahitā mā ahesuṃ. Te evaṃ tāya devatāya yāciyamānāpi “gaccha tvaṃ, na mayaṃ āgamissāmā”ti paṭikkhipiṃsuyeva. Devatā ekikāva vanasaṇḍaṃ paccāgañchi. Manussāpi katipāheneva sabbaṃ vanaṃ chinditvā khettāni karitvā kasikammaṃ kariṃsu.

Here, 'tigers': she spoke addressing both of them by the name ‘tiger.’ 'Turn back' means: you turn back. 'Return to the great forest' means: return to that great forest, go back again; this is an alternative reading. 'Let them not cut down the tigerless forest' means: may the people not cut down our dwelling-grove, now tigerless because of your absence. 'May the tigers not be without their forest' means: and may tiger-kings like you, having fled from your dwelling place, not be 'without a forest' (nibbanā), that is, deprived of the forest that was your home. Though they were thus entreated by the deity, they rejected her, saying, “You go! We will not come back.” The deity returned to the forest grove alone. In a few days, the people cut down the entire forest, made fields, and took up farming.

Satthā [V 2.0298][M 2.0324] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā apaṇḍitā devatā kokāliko ahosi, sīho sāriputto, byaggho moggallāno, paṇḍitadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths, and identified the birth, saying: “At that time, the foolish deity was Kokālika, the lion was Sāriputta, the tiger was Moggallāna, but the wise deity was myself.”

Byagghajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Vyaggha Jātaka, the Second.

[273] 3. Kacchapajātakavaṇṇanā

[273] 3. The Commentary on the Kacchapa Jātaka

Ko [P 2.0359] nu uddhitabhattovāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarājassa dvinnaṃ mahāmattānaṃ kalahavūpasamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu dukanipāte kathitameva.

“Who now, like one with food served up...?” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the settling of a quarrel between two great ministers of the king of Kosala. The story of the present has already been told in the Book of Twos (Duka Nipāta).

Atīte pana bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantapadese gaṅgātīre assamapadaṃ māpetvā tattha abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto vāsaṃ kappesi. Imasmiṃ kira jātake bodhisatto paramamajjhatto ahosi, upekkhāpāramiṃ pūresi. Tassa paṇṇasāladvāre nisinnassa eko pagabbho dussīlo makkaṭo āgantvā kaṇṇasotesu aṅgajātena salākapavesanakammaṃ karoti, bodhisatto avāretvā majjhatto hutvā nisīdatiyeva. Athekadivasaṃ eko kacchapo udakā uttaritvā gaṅgātīre mukhaṃ vivaritvā ātapaṃ tappanto niddāyati. Taṃ disvā so lolavānaro tassa mukhe salākapavesanakammaṃ akāsi. Athassa kacchapo pabujjhitvā aṅgajātaṃ samugge pakkhipanto viya ḍaṃsi, balavavedanā uppajji. Vedanaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto “ko nu kho maṃ imamhā dukkhā moceyya, kassa santikaṃ gacchāmī”ti cintetvā “añño maṃ imamhā dukkhā mocetuṃ samattho natthi aññatra tāpasena, tasseva santikaṃ mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kacchapaṃ dvīhi hatthehi ukkhipitvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Bodhisatto tena dussīlamakkaṭena saddhiṃ davaṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kāsī country. Having come of age, he learned all the crafts at Takkasilā, then renounced sensual pleasures and went forth into the ascetic life. He had a hermitage built on the bank of the Ganges in the Himalayan region, and there he developed the supernormal powers and meditative attainments and dwelt enjoying the bliss of jhāna. In this birth, it is said, the Bodhisatta was supremely impartial, fulfilling the perfection of equanimity (upekkhāpāramī). As he was sitting at the door of his leaf-hut, a shameless, immoral monkey came and inserted his penis into the Bodhisatta’s ear-holes. The Bodhisatta did not stop him but sat on, remaining impartial. Then one day a tortoise came out of the water, opened its mouth, and fell asleep on the bank of the Ganges while basking in the sun. Seeing it, that lustful monkey inserted his penis into its mouth. Then the tortoise woke up and bit down on his penis as if shutting it in a casket. A strong, painful feeling arose in him. Unable to endure the pain, he thought, “Who can free me from this suffering? To whom shall I go? No one else is able to free me from this suffering except the ascetic. I should go to him.” Lifting the tortoise with both hands, he went to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, teasing that immoral monkey, spoke the first verse:

67.

67.

“Ko [P 2.0360][M 2.0325] nu uddhitabhattova, pūrahatthova brāhmaṇo;

Kahaṃ nu bhikkhaṃ acari, kaṃ saddhaṃ upasaṅkamī”ti.

“Who now, like one with food served up, a brahmin with his hands full? Where did you wander for alms? What faithful person did you approach?”

Tattha ko nu uddhitabhattovāti ko nu esa vaḍḍhitabhatto viya, ekaṃ vaḍḍhitabhattaṃ bhattapūrapātiṃ [V 2.0299] hatthehi gahetvā viya ko nu eso āgacchatīti attho. Pūrahatthova brāhmaṇoti kattikamāse vācanakaṃ labhitvā pūrahattho brāhmaṇo viya ca ko nu kho esoti vānaraṃ sandhāya vadati. Kahaṃ nu bhikkhaṃ acarīti, bho vānara, kasmiṃ padese ajja tvaṃ bhikkhaṃ acari. Kaṃ saddhaṃ upasaṅkamīti kataraṃ nāma pubbapete uddissa kataṃ saddhabhattaṃ, kataraṃ vā saddhaṃ puggalaṃ tvaṃ upasaṅkami, kuto te ayaṃ deyyadhammo laddhoti dīpeti.

Here, 'Who now, like one with food served up?' means: Who is this coming along as if with food served up, as if holding a bowl full of food in his hands? 'A brahmin with his hands full' means: And who is this like a brahmin with full hands, who has received a fee for recitation in the month of Kattika? He says this with reference to the monkey. 'Where did you wander for alms?' means: Hey, monkey, in what region did you wander for alms today? 'What faithful person did you approach?' means: What meal given in faith for the departed ancestors, or what faithful person did you approach? From where did you obtain this gift? This is what he points out.

Taṃ sutvā dussīlavānaro dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the immoral monkey spoke the second verse:

68.

68.

“Ahaṃ kapismi dummedho, anāmāsāni āmasiṃ;

Tvaṃ maṃ mocaya bhaddaṃ te, mutto gaccheyya pabbata”nti.

“I am a witless monkey; I touched what should not be touched. You release me, bless you! Freed, I would go to the mountain.”

Tattha ahaṃ kapismi dummedhoti bhaddaṃ te ahaṃ asmi dummedho capalacitto makkaṭo. Anāmāsāni āmasinti anāmasitabbaṭṭhānāni āmasiṃ. Tvaṃ maṃ mocaya bhaddaṃ teti tvaṃ dayālu anukampako maṃ imamhā dukkhā mocehi, bhaddaṃ te hotu. Mutto gaccheyya pabbatanti sohaṃ tavānubhāvena imamhā byasanā mutto pabbatameva gaccheyyaṃ, na te puna cakkhupathe attānaṃ dasseyyanti.

Here, 'I am a witless monkey' means: Bless you, I am a witless, fickle-minded monkey. 'I touched what should not be touched' means: I touched places that should not be touched. 'You release me, bless you' means: You, who are kind and compassionate, release me from this suffering; may it be well with you. 'Freed, I would go to the mountain' means: Freed from this calamity by your power, I would go to the mountain and never again show myself within your sight.

Bodhisatto tasmiṃ kāruññena kacchapena saddhiṃ sallapanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, out of compassion for him, conversing with the tortoise, spoke the third verse:

69.

69.

“Kacchapā kassapā honti, koṇḍaññā honti makkaṭā;

Muñca kassapa koṇḍaññaṃ, kataṃ methunakaṃ tayā”ti.

“Tortoises are of the Kassapa clan, and monkeys are of the Koṇḍañña clan. Release, Kassapa, the Koṇḍañña; a union has been made by you.”

Tassattho [P 2.0361] – kacchapā nāma kassapagottā honti, makkaṭā koṇḍaññagottā, kassapakoṇḍaññānañca aññamaññaṃ āvāhavivāhasambandho atthi. Addhā tayidaṃ lolena dussīlamakkaṭena tayā saddhiṃ, tayā ca dussīlena iminā makkaṭena saddhiṃ gottasadisatāsaṅkhātassa methunadhammassa [M 2.0326] anucchavikaṃ dussīlyakammasaṅkhātampi methunakaṃ kataṃ, tasmā muñca, kassapa, koṇḍaññanti.

Its meaning is: Tortoises are of the Kassapa clan, and monkeys are of the Koṇḍañña clan, and between the Kassapas and Koṇḍaññas there is a relationship of intermarriage. Surely, by this lustful, immoral monkey with you, and by you with this immoral monkey, a union has been made. This immoral act is even [ironically] fitting, given the 'union' characterized by the similarity of your clans. Therefore, release, Kassapa, the Koṇḍañña.

Kacchapo bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā kāraṇena pasanno vānarassa aṅgajātaṃ muñci. Makkaṭo muttamattova bodhisattaṃ vanditvā palāto, puna taṃ ṭhānaṃ nivattitvāpi na olokesi. Kacchapopi [V 2.0300] bodhisattaṃ vanditvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Bodhisattopi aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, the tortoise was pleased with his reasoning and released the monkey’s penis. As soon as he was freed, the monkey paid homage to the Bodhisatta and fled; he did not even look back at that place again. The tortoise also paid homage to the Bodhisatta and went back to his own place. The Bodhisatta, without having lost his jhāna, was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kacchapavānarā dve mahāmattā ahesuṃ, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths, and identified the birth, saying: “At that time, the tortoise and the monkey were the two great ministers, but the ascetic was myself.”

Kacchapajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Tortoise Jātaka, the Third.

[274] 4. Lolajātakavaṇṇanā

[274] 4. The Commentary on the Lola Jātaka

Kāyaṃ balākā sikhinīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi dhammasabhaṃ ānītaṃ satthā “na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva lolo, pubbepi loloyeva, lolatāyeva ca jīvitakkhayaṃ patto, taṃ nissāya porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi attano vasanaṭṭhānā paribāhirā ahesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Who is this crested crane…?” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a greedy monk. When he was brought to the Dhamma hall, the Teacher said: “Not only now, bhikkhu, are you greedy; in the past, too, you were greedy, and because of your greed you met with the destruction of your life. On your account, even the wise ones of the past were driven out from their dwelling place.” So saying, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasiseṭṭhino mahānase bhattakārako puññatthāya nīḷapacchiṃ ṭhapesi. Tadā bodhisatto pārāvatayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā tattha vāsaṃ kappesi. Atheko lolakāko mahānasamatthakena gacchanto nānappakāraṃ macchamaṃsavikatiṃ disvā pipāsābhibhūto “kaṃ nu kho nissāya sakkā bhaveyyaṃ okāsaṃ [P 2.0362] laddhu”nti cintetvā bodhisattaṃ disvā “imaṃ nissāya sakkā”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā tassa gocarāya araññagamanakāle piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhi. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “mayaṃ kho, kāka, aññagocarā, tvampi aññagocaro, kiṃ nu kho maṃ anubandhasī”ti āha. “Tumhākaṃ, sāmi, kiriyā mayhaṃ ruccati, ahampi tumhehi samānagocaro hutvā tumhe upaṭṭhātuṃ [M 2.0327] icchāmī”ti. Bodhisatto sampaṭicchi. So tena saddhiṃ gocarabhūmiyaṃ ekagocaraṃ caranto viya osakkitvā gomayarāsiṃ viddhaṃsetvā pāṇake khāditvā kucchipūraṃ katvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tumhe ettakaṃ kālaṃ caratheva, nanu bhojane nāma pamāṇaṃ ñātuṃ vaṭṭati, etha nātisāyameva gacchāmā”ti āha. Bodhisatto taṃ ādāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Bhattakārako “amhākaṃ pārāvato sahāyaṃ gahetvā āgato”ti kākassāpi ekaṃ thusapacchiṃ ṭhapesi. Kākopi catūhapañcāhaṃ teneva nīhārena vasi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the cook in the kitchen of the treasurer of Benares set up a nest-basket out of a desire to make merit. At that time, the Bodhisatta had been reborn as a pigeon and was dwelling there. Then a greedy crow, passing over the kitchen, saw various preparations of fish and meat and, overcome by craving, he thought, 'By relying on whom might I get an opportunity?' Seeing the Bodhisatta, he decided, 'It is possible by relying on him.' So when the Bodhisatta went to the forest for food, the crow followed close behind. The Bodhisatta asked him: 'Crow, we have different feeding grounds, and you have a different one. Why do you follow me?' The crow replied: 'Master, your conduct pleases me. I wish to share your feeding ground and to attend on you.' The Bodhisatta consented. While pretending to forage in the same area with him, the crow would slip away, break apart a pile of cow dung, eat the insects, and fill his belly. Then he would approach the Bodhisatta and say: 'You forage for such a long time. Surely one should know moderation in eating. Come, let us not go too late in the evening.' The Bodhisatta then took him back to their dwelling. The cook, thinking, 'Our pigeon has brought a companion,' also set up a basket of husks for the crow. The crow lived in this way for four or five days.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 2.0301] seṭṭhino bahumacchamaṃsaṃ āhariyittha, kāko taṃ disvā lobhābhibhūto paccūsakālato paṭṭhāya nitthunanto nipajji. Atha naṃ punadivase bodhisatto “ehi, samma, gocarāya pakkamissāmā”ti āha. “Tumhe gacchatha, mayhaṃ ajiṇṇāsaṅkā atthī”ti. “Samma, kākānaṃ ajīrako nāma natthi, dīpavaṭṭimattameva hi tumhākaṃ kucchiyaṃ thokaṃ tiṭṭhati, sesaṃ ajjhohaṭamattameva jīrati, mama vacanaṃ karohi, mā etaṃ [P 2.0363] macchamaṃsaṃ disvā evamakāsī”ti. “Sāmi, kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathetha, ajiṇṇāsaṅkāva mayha”nti. “Tena hi appamatto hohī”ti taṃ ovaditvā bodhisatto pakkāmi.

Then one day, a large quantity of fish and meat was brought for the treasurer. Seeing this, the crow, overcome by greed, lay groaning from dawn onwards. The next day, the Bodhisatta said to him: 'Come, friend, let us set out for food.' 'You go. I suspect I have indigestion.' 'Friend, there is no such thing as indigestion for crows. Indeed, only a little, the size of a lamp-wick, remains in your belly; the rest is digested as soon as it is swallowed. Follow my advice; do not act this way just because you have seen this fish and meat.' 'Master, what is this you say? I really do suspect I have indigestion.' 'In that case, be heedful.' Having thus advised him, the Bodhisatta departed.

Bhattakārakopi nānāmacchamaṃsavikatiyo sampādetvā sarīrato sedaṃ apanento mahānasadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Kāko “ayaṃ idāni kālo maṃsaṃ khāditu”nti gantvā rasakaroṭimatthake nisīdi. Bhattakārako “kirī”ti saddaṃ sutvā nivattitvā olokento kākaṃ disvā pavisitvā taṃ gahetvā sakalasarīralomaṃ luñcitvā matthake cūḷaṃ ṭhapetvā siṅgīveramaricādīni pisitvā takkena āloḷetvā “tvaṃ amhākaṃ seṭṭhino macchamaṃsaṃ ucchiṭṭhakaṃ karosī”ti sakalasarīramassa makkhetvā khipitvā nīḷapacchiyaṃ pātesi, balavavedanā uppajji. Bodhisatto gocarabhūmito āgantvā taṃ nitthunantaṃ disvā davaṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The cook, having prepared various dishes of fish and meat, stood at the kitchen door wiping sweat from his body. The crow, thinking, 'Now is the time to eat meat,' went and perched on a pot of savory liquid. The cook heard a 'kirī' sound, and turning and looking, he saw the crow. He went inside, seized it, and plucked all the feathers from its body, leaving a top-knot on its head. He then ground up ginger, pepper, and other spices, mixed them with buttermilk, and smeared the crow's entire body with the mixture, saying, 'You defile our treasurer's fish and meat!' He then threw it and dropped it into its nest-basket, where a severe pain arose in it. The Bodhisatta, returning from his feeding ground, saw it groaning and, teasing it, spoke the first verse:

70.

70.

“Kāyaṃ balākā sikhinī, corī laṅghipitāmahā;

Oraṃ balāke āgaccha, caṇḍo me vāyaso sakhā”ti.

“Who is this crested crane, this thief,

Granddaughter of the sky-leaper?

Come here, O crane,

For my friend the crow is fierce.”

Tattha [M 2.0328] kāyaṃ balākā sikhinīti taṃ kākaṃ tassa bahalatakkena makkhitasarīrasetavaṇṇattā matthake ca sikhāya ṭhapitattā “kā esā balākā sikhinī”ti pucchanto ālapati. Corīti kulassa ananuññāya kulagharaṃ, kākassa vā aruciyā pacchiṃ paviṭṭhattā “corī”ti vadati. Laṅghipitāmahāti laṅghī vuccati ākāse laṅghanato megho, balākā ca nāma meghasaddena gabbhaṃ gaṇhantīti meghasaddo balākānaṃ pitā, megho pitāmaho hoti. Tenāha “laṅghipitāmahā”ti. Oraṃ balāke āgacchāti, ambho balāke, ito ehi. Caṇḍo me vā yaso sakhāti mayhaṃ sakhā pacchisāmiko vāyaso caṇḍo pharuso[P 2.0364], so āgato taṃ disvā kaṇayasadisena tuṇḍena koṭṭetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpeyya, tasmā yāva vāyaso nāgacchati, tāva pacchito otaritvā ito ehi, sīghaṃ palāyassūti vadati.

Herein, Who is this crested crane?: he addresses the crow, asking this because its body was white from being smeared with thick buttermilk and because a crest had been left on its head. Thief: this is said because it entered the family home without the family's permission, or because it entered the basket against the wish of the crow. Granddaughter of the sky-leaper: the cloud is called the 'leaper' because it leaps in the sky.
