Since cranes are said to conceive at the sound of a cloud, the sound of the cloud is the father of cranes, and the cloud is their grandfather. Thus he says, 'granddaughter of the sky-leaper.' Come here, O crane: this means, 'Ho, crane, come here.' For my friend the crow is fierce: this means: 'My friend, the crow who owns this basket, is fierce and harsh. When he returns and sees you, he will peck you with his spear-like beak and put an end to your life. Therefore, before that crow arrives, get down from the basket, come here, and flee quickly!'

Taṃ sutvā kāko dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the crow spoke the second verse:

71.

71.

“Nāhaṃ [V 2.0302] balākā sikhinī, ahaṃ lolosmi vāyaso;

Akatvā vacanaṃ tuyhaṃ, passa lūnosmi āgato”ti.

“I am no crested crane, I am a greedy crow. Not having heeded your words, see me plucked, now that you have returned.”

Tattha āgatoti tvaṃ idāni gocarabhūmito āgato, maṃ lūnaṃ passāti attho.

Herein, 'returned' refers to: 'You have now returned from the feeding ground; see me plucked' is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:

72.

72.

“Punapāpajjasī samma, sīlañhi tava tādisaṃ;

Na hi mānusakā bhogā, subhuñjā honti pakkhinā”ti.

“Again you will come to ruin, friend, for such is your character. Indeed, the enjoyments of humans are not easily enjoyed by a bird.”

Tattha punapāpajjasī sammāti samma vāyasa, punapi tvaṃ evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭilabhissaseva, natthi te ettakena mokkho. Kiṃkāraṇā? Sīlañhi tava tādisaṃ pāpakaṃ, yasmā tava ācārasīlaṃ tādisaṃ dukkhādhigamasseva anurūpaṃ. Na hi mānusakāti manussā nāma mahāpuññā, tiracchānagatānaṃ tathārūpaṃ puññaṃ natthi, tasmā mānusakā bhogā tiracchānagatena pakkhinā na bhuñjīyantīti.

Herein, 'Again you will come to ruin, friend': friend crow, you will certainly experience such suffering again; there is no escape for you with just this. For what reason? 'For such is your character': because your character is so evil, your habitual conduct being suitable only for the acquisition of suffering. 'Indeed, the enjoyments of humans': humans are those of great merit, but those born as animals do not have such merit. Therefore, the enjoyments of humans are not to be enjoyed by a bird, an animal.

Evañca [M 2.0329] pana vatvā bodhisatto “ito dāni paṭṭhāya mayā ettha vasituṃ na sakkā”ti uppatitvā aññattha agamāsi. Kākopi nitthunanto tattheva kālamakāsi.

And having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta thought, 'From now on it is not possible for me to live here,' and he flew up and went elsewhere. The crow, still groaning, died right there.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne lolabhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā lolakāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, pārāvato pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the exposition of the truths, the greedy bhikkhu was established in the fruit of non-returning. 'At that time the greedy crow was the greedy bhikkhu, but the pigeon was I myself.'

Lolajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Lola Jātaka: The Fourth.

[275] 5. Rucirajātakavaṇṇanā

[275] 5. The Commentary on the Rucira Jātaka

Kāyaṃ [P 2.0365] balākā rucirāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dvepi vatthūni purimasadisāneva gāthāpi.

“Who is this beautiful crane?”—This the Teacher said while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain greedy bhikkhu. Both the stories and the verses are similar to the preceding ones.

73.

73.

“Kāyaṃ [V 2.0303] balākā rucirā, kākanīḷasmimacchati;

Caṇḍo kāko sakhā mayhaṃ, yassa cetaṃ kulāvakaṃ.

“Who is this beautiful crane that stays in a crow’s nest? Fierce is the crow, my friend, to whom this little nest belongs.”

74.

74.

“Nanu maṃ samma jānāsi, dija sāmākabhojana;

Akatvā vacanaṃ tuyhaṃ, passa lūnosmi āgato.

“Surely, friend, you know me, O twice-born who eats millet. Not having heeded your words, see me plucked, now that you have returned.”

75.

75.

“Punapāpajjasī samma, sīlañhi tava tādisaṃ;

Na hi mānusakā bhogā, subhuñjā honti pakkhinā”ti. –

“Again you will come to ruin, friend, for such is your character. Indeed, the enjoyments of humans are not easily enjoyed by a bird.”

Gāthā hi ekantarikāyeva.

The verses are simply alternating.

Tattha “rucirā”ti takkamakkhitasarīratāya setavaṇṇataṃ sandhāya vadati. Rucirā piyadassanā, paṇḍarāti attho. Kākanīḷasminti kākakulāvake. “Kākaniḍḍhasmi”ntipi pāṭho. Dijāti kāko pārevataṃ ālapati. Sāmākabhojanāti tiṇabījabhojana. Sāmākaggahaṇena hettha sabbampi tiṇabījaṃ gahitaṃ. Idhāpi bodhisatto “na idāni sakkā ito paṭṭhāya mayā ettha vasitu”nti uppatitvā aññattha gato.

Herein, 'beautiful': this is said with reference to its white color due to its body being smeared with buttermilk. 'Beautiful' means 'pleasing to see,' that is, 'white.' 'In a crow’s nest' means in a crow's nest. There is also the reading 'kākaniḍḍhasmiṃ'. 'Twice-born': the crow addresses the pigeon. 'Who eats millet': one who eats grass seeds. By the mention of 'millet,' all kinds of grass seeds are included here. Here too, the Bodhisatta thought, 'From now on it is not possible for me to live here,' and he flew up and went elsewhere.

Satthā [M 2.0330] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne lolabhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā lolakāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, pārāvato pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the exposition of the truths, the greedy bhikkhu was established in the fruit of non-returning. 'At that time the greedy crow was the greedy bhikkhu, but the pigeon was I myself.'

Rucirajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Rucira Jātaka: The Fifth.

[276] 6. Kurudhammajātakavaṇṇanā

[276] 6. The Commentary on the Kurudhamma Jātaka

Tava saddhañca sīlañcāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ haṃsaghātakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthivāsino [P 2.0366] dve sahāyakā bhikkhū pabbajitvā laddhūpasampadā yebhuyyena ekato vicaranti. Te ekadivasaṃ aciravatiṃ gantvā nhatvā vālukapuline ātapaṃ tappamānā sāraṇīyakathaṃ kathentā aṭṭhaṃsu, tasmiṃ khaṇe dve haṃsā ākāsena gacchanti. Atheko daharabhikkhu sakkharaṃ gahetvā “ekassa haṃsapotakassa akkhiṃ paharissāmī”ti āha, itaro “na sakkhissasī”ti [V 2.0304] āha. “Tiṭṭhatu imasmiṃ passe akkhi, parapasse akkhiṃ paharissāmī”ti. “Idampi na sakkhissasiyevā”ti. “Tena hi upadhārehī”ti tiyaṃsaṃ sakkharaṃ gahetvā haṃsassa pacchābhāge khipi. Haṃso sakkharasaddaṃ sutvā nivattitvā olokesi, atha naṃ itaro vaṭṭasakkharaṃ gahetvā parapasse akkhimhi paharitvā orimakkhinā nikkhamāpesi. Haṃso viravanto parivattitvā tesaṃ pādamūleyeva pati. Tattha tattha ṭhitā bhikkhū disvā āgantvā “āvuso, evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā ananucchavikaṃ vo kataṃ pāṇātipātaṃ karontehī”ti vatvā te ādāya tathāgatassa dassesuṃ. Satthā “saccaṃ, kira tayā bhikkhu pāṇātipāto kato”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu, kasmā evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā evamakāsi, porāṇakapaṇḍitā anuppanne buddhe agāramajjhe saṃkiliṭṭhavāsaṃ vasamānā appamattakesupi ṭhānesu kukkuccaṃ kariṃsu, tvaṃ pana evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā kukkuccamattampi na akāsi, nanu nāma bhikkhunā kāyavācācittehi saññatena bhavitabba”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Your faith and virtue…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a monk who killed a goose. Two friends, residents of Sāvatthī, went forth and received the full ordination, and they generally traveled together. One day, they went to the Aciravatī River, bathed, and stood on the sandy bank warming themselves in the sun while engaged in cordial talk. At that moment, two geese were flying through the sky. Then one young monk picked up a pebble and said, “I will strike the eye of one of the young geese.” The other replied, “You will not be able to.” “Never mind the eye on this side; I will strike the eye on the other side.” “You will not be able to do that either.” “Well then, watch!” Taking a three-cornered pebble, he threw it at the goose’s rear. Hearing the sound of the pebble, the goose turned and looked. Then the other monk took a round pebble and struck it in the eye on the far side, making it come out through the eye on the near side. The goose cried out, tumbled about, and fell right at their feet. Monks standing here and there saw this, came over, and said, “Friends, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, you have done an unsuitable thing by committing the destruction of life.” They took the two of them and showed them to the Tathāgata. The Teacher asked, “Is it true, monk, that you committed the destruction of life?” When he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” the Teacher said: “Monk, why, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, did you do such a thing? The wise of old, living the sullied life in the household before a Buddha had arisen, felt scrupulousness even in minor matters. But you, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, did not feel even a trifle of scrupulousness. Should not a monk be restrained in body, speech, and mind?” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 2.0331] kururaṭṭhe indapatthanagare dhanañcaye korabye rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā anupubbena viññutaṃ patto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā pitarā oparajje patiṭṭhāpito aparabhāge [P 2.0367] pitu accayena rajjaṃ patvā dasa rājadhamme akopento kurudhamme vattittha. Kurudhammo nāma pañca sīlāni, tāni bodhisatto parisuddhāni katvā rakkhi. Yathā ca bodhisatto, evamassa mātā aggamahesī kaniṭṭhabhātā uparājā purohito brāhmaṇo rajjugāhako amacco sārathi seṭṭhi doṇamāpako mahāmatto dovāriko nagarasobhinī vaṇṇadāsīti evamete.

In the past, when Dhanañjaya Korabya was ruling in the city of Indapatta in the Kuru kingdom, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of his chief queen. Having gradually come of age and learned all the arts at Takkasilā, he was appointed viceroy by his father. Later, on his father’s demise, he succeeded to the kingdom and reigned without transgressing the ten royal duties, while observing the Kuru-dhamma. The Kuru-dhamma consists of the five precepts, and the Bodhisatta observed them in their purity. Just as the Bodhisatta did, so too did his mother, his chief queen, his younger brother the viceroy, the brahmin chaplain, the minister who was the surveyor, the charioteer, the treasurer, the great minister who was the grain-measurer, the gatekeeper, and the courtesan who was the city’s beauty.

“Rājā mātā mahesī ca, uparājā purohito;

Rajjuko sārathi seṭṭhi, doṇo dovāriko tathā;

Gaṇikekādasa janā, kurudhamme patiṭṭhitā”ti.

“The king, the mother, the chief queen, the viceroy, the chaplain, the assessor, the charioteer, the treasurer, the grain-measurer, the gatekeeper, and the courtesan—these eleven people are established in the Kuru principles.”

Iti ime sabbepi parisuddhāni katvā pañca sīlāni rakkhiṃsu. Rājā catūsu nagaradvāresu ca nagaramajjhe ca nivesanadvāre cāti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassaṃ dhanaṃ vissajjento sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā dānaṃ adāsi, tassa pana dānajjhāsayatā dānābhiratatā sakalajambudīpaṃ ajjhotthari. Tasmiṃ kāle kāliṅgaraṭṭhe dantapuranagare kāliṅgarājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa raṭṭhe devo na vassi, tasmiṃ avassante sakalaraṭṭhe [V 2.0305] chātakaṃ jātaṃ, āhāravipattiyā ca manussānaṃ rogo udapādi, dubbuṭṭhibhayaṃ chātakabhayaṃ rogabhayanti tīṇi bhayāni uppajjiṃsu. Manussā niggahaṇā dārake hatthesu gahetvā tattha tattha vicaranti.

Thus all these people observed the five precepts in their purity. The king had six alms halls built—at the four city gates, in the city center, and at his own palace gate—and he would daily distribute six hundred thousand pieces of money, giving alms and making the whole of Jambudīpa cease from plowing. His inclination to give and his delight in charity pervaded the whole of Jambudīpa. At that time, in the city of Dantapura in the Kāliṅga country, a king of Kāliṅga was reigning. In his kingdom the god did not send rain, and because it did not rain, a famine arose in the entire country. Due to the failure of food, disease arose among the people. Three fears arose: the fear of drought, the fear of famine, and the fear of disease. Deprived of support, people wandered about here and there, taking their children by the hand.

Sakalaraṭṭhavāsino ekato hutvā dantapuraṃ gantvā rājadvāre ukkuṭṭhimakaṃsu. Rājā vātapānaṃ nissāya ṭhito taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ kāraṇā ete viravantī”ti pucchi. “Mahārāja[P 2.0368], sakalaraṭṭhe tīṇi bhayāni uppannāni, devo na vassati, sassāni na vipannāni, chātakaṃ jātaṃ. Manussā dubbhojanā rogābhibhūtā niggahaṇā putte hatthesu gahetvā vicaranti, devaṃ vassāpehi mahārājā”ti. “Porāṇakarājāno deve avassante kiṃ karontī”ti? “Porāṇakarājāno, mahārāja, deve avassante dānaṃ datvā [M 2.0332] uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya samādinnasīlā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā dabbasanthare sattāhaṃ nipajjanti, tadā devo vassatī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tathā akāsi. Evaṃ santepi devo na vassi.

All the inhabitants of the country gathered, went to Dantapura, and raised a cry at the king’s gate. The king, who was standing leaning against a window, heard the noise and asked, “Why are these people crying out?” “Great king, three fears have arisen in the entire country: the god does not send rain, the crops fail to ripen, and a famine has occurred. The people, suffering from poor food and overcome by disease, wander about helplessly, taking their children by the hand. Make the god send rain, great king!” “What did the kings of old do when the god did not send rain?” “Great king, when the god did not send rain, the kings of old would give alms, undertake the observance day, take upon themselves the precepts, enter the auspicious chamber, and lie down on a spread of grass for seven days. Then the god would send rain.” The king agreed, saying, “Good,” and did so. But even so, the god did not send rain.

Rājā amacce pucchi – “ahaṃ kattabbakiccaṃ akāsiṃ, devo na vassati, kinti karomā”ti? “Mahārāja, indapatthanagare dhanañcayassa korabyarañño añjanavaṇṇo nāma maṅgalahatthī atthi, taṃ ānessāma, evaṃ sante devo vassatī”ti. “So rājā balavāhanasampanno duppasaho, kathamassa hatthiṃ ānessāmā”ti? “Mahārāja, tena saddhiṃ yuddhakiccaṃ natthi, dānajjhāsayo rājā dānābhirato yācito samāno alaṅkatasīsampi chinditvā pasādasampannāni akkhīnipi uppāṭetvā sakalarajjampi niyyādetvā dadeyya, hatthimhi vattabbameva natthi, avassaṃ yācito dassatī”ti. “Ke pana taṃ yācituṃ samatthā”ti? “Brāhmaṇā, mahārājā”ti. Rājā brāhmaṇagāmato aṭṭha brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā sakkārasammānaṃ katvā hatthiṃ yācanatthāya pesesi. Te paribbayaṃ ādāya addhikavesaṃ gahetvā sabbattha ekarattivāsena turitagamanaṃ gantvā katipāhaṃ nagaradvāre dānasālāsu bhuñjitvā sarīraṃ santappetvā “kadā rājā dānaggaṃ āgacchissatī”ti pucchiṃsu. Manussā “pakkhassa tayo divase [P 2.0369] cātuddase pannarase aṭṭhamiyañca āgacchati, sve pana puṇṇamī, tasmā sve āgacchissatī”ti vadiṃsu.

The king asked his ministers: “I have done what ought to be done, but the god does not rain. What shall we do?” “Great king, in the city of Indapatta, King Dhanañjaya Korabya has an auspicious state elephant named Añjanavaṇṇa. We should bring it here. If this is done, the god will rain.” “But that king is endowed with a powerful army and is difficult to assail. How shall we get his elephant?” “Great king, there is no need to do battle with him. The king is disposed to giving, devoted to charity. If asked, he would cut off his own adorned head, or pluck out his serene eyes, or hand over his entire kingdom and give it away. What need is there to speak of the elephant? When asked, he will certainly give it.” “But who is able to ask him for it?” “Brahmins, great king.” The king had eight brahmins summoned from a brahmin village, paid them honor and respect, and sent them to ask for the elephant. Taking their travel expenses and adopting the guise of travelers, they traveled with haste, staying only one night in any place. After some days, having eaten in the alms halls at the city gate and refreshed their bodies, they asked, “When will the king come to the alms hall?” The people replied: “He comes on three days of the lunar fortnight: the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth. Tomorrow is the full moon, so he will come tomorrow.”

Brāhmaṇā punadivase pātova gantvā pācīnadvāre aṭṭhaṃsu. Bodhisatto pātova nhatvā gattānulitto sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito alaṅkatahatthikkhandhavaragato mahantena parivārena pācīnadvārena dānasālaṃ gantvā otaritvā sattaṭṭhajanānaṃ sahatthā bhattaṃ datvā “imināva nīhārena [V 2.0306] dethā”ti vatvā hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā dakkhiṇadvāraṃ agamāsi. Brāhmaṇā pācīnadvāre ārakkhassa balavatāya okāsaṃ alabhitvā dakkhiṇadvārameva gantvā rājānaṃ āgacchantaṃ olokayamānā dvārato nātidūre unnataṭṭhāne ṭhitā sampattaṃ rājānaṃ hatthe ukkhipitvā “jayatu bhavaṃ, mahārājā”ti jayāpesuṃ. Rājā vajiraṅkusena vāraṇaṃ nivattetvā tesaṃ santikaṃ [M 2.0333] gantvā “bho brāhmaṇā, kiṃ icchathā”ti pucchi. Brāhmaṇā bodhisattassa guṇaṃ vaṇṇentā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

The next day the brahmins went early in the morning and stood at the eastern gate. The Bodhisatta also rose early, bathed, anointed his body, decked himself with all his ornaments, and mounting his splendidly adorned state elephant, he went with a great retinue through the eastern gate to the alms hall. He dismounted and with his own hand gave food to seven or eight people. Then, saying, “Give in this same manner,” he mounted his elephant and went toward the southern gate. The brahmins, being unable to get an opportunity at the eastern gate because of the strong guard, went to the southern gate. Watching for the king’s arrival, they stood on high ground not far from the gate. When the king arrived, they raised their hands and acclaimed him, crying: “Victory to your majesty, great king!” The king turned the elephant back with his diamond goad, went up to them, and asked: “Good brahmins, what do you wish for?” The brahmins, praising the Bodhisatta’s virtues, recited the first verse:

76.

76.

“Tava saddhañca sīlañca, viditvāna janādhipa;

Vaṇṇaṃ añjanavaṇṇena, kāliṅgasmiṃ nimimhase”ti.

“O lord of men, having known of your faith and virtue, we would barter for the one of noble appearance, the Antimony-Colored one, for the sake of Kalinga.”

Tattha saddhanti kammaphalānaṃ saddahanavasena okappaniyasaddhaṃ. Sīlanti saṃvarasīlaṃ avītikkamasīlaṃ. Vaṇṇanti tadā tasmiṃ dese suvaṇṇaṃ vuccati, desanāsīsameva cetaṃ. Iminā pana padena sabbampi hiraññasuvaṇṇādidhanadhaññaṃ saṅgahitaṃ. Añjanavaṇṇenāti añjanapuñjasamānavaṇṇena iminā tava nāgena, kāliṅgasminti kāliṅgarañño santike. Nimimhaseti vinimayavasena gaṇhimha, paribhogavasena vā udare pakkhipimhāti attho. Seti nipātamattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mayañhi, janādhipa, tava saddhañca sīlañca viditvāna “addhā no evaṃ saddhāsīlasampanno [P 2.0370] rājā yācito añjanavaṇṇaṃ nāgaṃ dassatī”ti iminā attano santakena viya añjanavaṇṇena kāliṅgarañño santike nāgaṃ vo āharissāmāti vatvā bahudhanadhaññaṃ nimimhase parivattayimha ceva udare ca pakkhipimha. Evaṃ taṃ mayaṃ dhārayamānā idhāgatā. Tattha kattabbaṃ devo jānātūti.

Here, 'faith' (saddhaṃ) refers to the faith of conviction by way of believing in the fruits of kamma. 'Virtue' (sīlaṃ) means the virtue of restraint, the virtue of non-transgression. 'Gold' (vaṇṇaṃ) refers to what was called gold in that region at that time, and this is simply the heading of the discourse. By this term, however, all wealth and grain, such as bullion and gold, is included. 'Of the color of collyrium' means with this elephant of yours, which is of a color like a heap of collyrium. 'In Kalinga' means in the presence of the king of Kalinga. 'We have bartered' (nimimhase) means we have acquired it by way of exchange, or the meaning is that we have 'put it into our bellies' by way of consumption. The syllable 'se' is a mere particle. This is what is meant: 'O lord of men, having come to know your faith and virtue, we thought: "Surely a king so endowed with faith and virtue will give the elephant of collyrium color when asked." Thus, in the presence of the king of Kalinga, speaking of this elephant of collyrium color as if it were our own, we said we would bring it to him, and for much wealth and grain, we bartered it—both exchanging it and consuming the proceeds. Thus, bearing that obligation, we have come here. In this matter, let your majesty know what should be done.'

Aparo nayo – tava saddhañca sīlaguṇasaṅkhātaṃ vaṇṇañca sutvā “uḷāraguṇo rājā jīvitampi yācito dadeyya, pageva tiracchānagataṃ nāga”nti evaṃ kāliṅgassa santike iminā añjanavaṇṇena tava vaṇṇaṃ nimimhase nimimha tulayimha, tenamhā idhāgatāti.

Another way: Having heard of your faith and your renown (vaṇṇaṃ), which is known as the quality of your virtue, we thought: 'A king of such lofty qualities would give even his life if asked, how much more so an animal like an elephant.' Thus, in the presence of the king of Kalinga, with this elephant of collyrium color, we appraised your renown—we weighed and measured it. For that reason, we have come here.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “sace, vo brāhmaṇā, imaṃ nāgaṃ parivattetvā dhanaṃ khāditaṃ sukhāditaṃ mā cintayittha, yathālaṅkatameva vo nāgaṃ dassāmī”ti samassāsetvā itarā dve gāthā avoca –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta consoled them, saying: 'Brahmins, if you have exchanged this elephant for wealth and have consumed it—well-consumed!—do not worry. I will give you the elephant just as it is adorned.' Then he spoke the other two verses:

77.

77.

“Annabhaccā cabhaccā ca, yodha uddissa gacchati;

Sabbe te appaṭikkhippā, pubbācariyavaco idaṃ.

“Those supported by food and those who are not, whoever approaches another here with an aim—none of them should be rejected. This is the word of the ancient teachers.”

78.

78.

“Dadāmi [V 2.0307][M 2.0334] vo brāhmaṇā nāgametaṃ, rājārahaṃ rājabhoggaṃ yasassinaṃ;

Alaṅkataṃ hemajālābhichannaṃ, sasārathiṃ gacchatha yenakāma”nti.

“I give you this elephant, brahmins, worthy of a king, fit for a king's use, glorious, adorned, covered with a golden net, with its driver. Go wherever you wish.”

Tattha annabhaccā cabhaccā cāti purisaṃ upanissāya jīvamānā yāgubhattādinā annena bharitabbāti annabhaccā, itare tathā abharitabbattā abhaccā. Sandhivasena panettha akāralopo veditabbo. Ettāvatā attānaṃ upanissāya ca anupanissāya ca jīvamānavasena sabbepi sattā dve koṭṭhāse katvā dassitā honti. Yodha uddissa gacchatīti tesu sattesu idha jīvaloke yo satto yaṃ purisaṃ kāyacideva paccāsīsanāya uddissa gacchati. Sabbe te appaṭikkhippāti tathā uddissa gacchantā sacepi bahū honti, tathāpi tena purisena sabbe te appaṭikkhippā, “apetha, na vo dassāmī”ti evaṃ na paṭikkhipitabbāti attho. Pubbācariyavaco idanti pubbācariyā vuccanti mātāpitaro, idaṃ tesaṃ vacanaṃ. Evamahaṃ mātāpitūhi sikkhāpitoti dīpeti.

Here, 'those supported by food and those who are not' (annabhaccā ca abhaccā ca): those who live in dependence on a person and are to be supported with food such as rice gruel and meals are called 'supported by food' (annabhaccā); others, not being supported in that way, are 'not supported' (abhaccā). The elision of the 'a' here should be understood as due to euphonic combination. By this, all beings are shown to be divided into two categories: those who live in dependence on oneself and those who do not. 'Whoever approaches with an aim' (yodha uddissa gacchati): among beings in this living world, whoever approaches a person with some hope or other. 'None of them should be rejected' (sabbe te appaṭikkhippā): even if many approach in this way, that person should not reject any of them; that is, they should not be turned away with the words, 'Go away, I will not give to you.' 'This is the word of the ancient teachers' (pubbācariyavaco idaṃ): the ancient teachers refer to one's mother and father; this is their instruction. This indicates: 'Thus I was taught by my parents.'

Dadāmi vo brāhmaṇā nāgametanti yasmā [P 2.0371] idaṃ amhākaṃ pubbācariyavaco, tasmāhaṃ brāhmaṇā tumhākaṃ imaṃ nāgaṃ dadāmi. Rājārahanti rañño anucchavikaṃ. Rājabhogganti rājaparibhogaṃ. Yasassinanti parivārasampannaṃ, taṃ kira hatthiṃ nissāya hatthigopakahatthivejjādīni pañca kulasatāni jīvanti, tehi saddhiññeva vo dadāmīti attho. Alaṅkatanti nānāvidhehi hatthialaṅkārehi alaṅkataṃ. Hemajālābhichannanti suvaṇṇajālena abhicchannaṃ. Sasārathinti yo panassa sārathi hatthigopako ācariyo, tena saddhiṃyeva dadāmi, tasmā sasārathi hutvā tumhe saparivāraṃ imaṃ nāgaṃ gahetvā yenakāmaṃ gacchathāti.

'I give to you, brahmins, this elephant': Since this is the word of our ancient teachers, therefore I give this elephant to you, brahmins. 'Worthy of a king' means suitable for a king. 'For a king's use' means for the king's enjoyment. 'Glorious' (yasassinaṃ) means endowed with a retinue. It is said that five hundred families—such as elephant keepers and elephant doctors—make their living in dependence on this elephant; the meaning is, 'I give it to you along with them.' 'Adorned' means decorated with various elephant ornaments. 'Covered with a golden net' means covered over with a net of gold. 'With its driver' means that its driver, the elephant keeper and trainer, is given along with it. Therefore, 'Take this elephant with its driver and retinue, and go wherever you wish.'

Evaṃ hatthikkhandhavaragatova mahāsatto vācāya datvā puna hatthikkhandhā oruyha “sace analaṅkataṭṭhānaṃ atthi, alaṅkaritvā dassāmī”ti vatvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto upadhāretvā analaṅkataṭṭhānaṃ adisvā tassa soṇḍaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ hatthesu ṭhapetvā suvaṇṇabhiṅkārena pupphagandhavāsitaṃ udakaṃ pātetvā adāsi. Brāhmaṇā saparivāraṃ nāgaṃ sampaṭicchitvā [M 2.0335] hatthipiṭṭhe nisinnā dantapuraṃ gantvā hatthiṃ rañño adaṃsu, hatthimhi āgatepi devo na vassateva. Rājā “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti uttariṃ pucchanto “dhanañcayakorabyarājā kurudhammaṃ rakkhati, tenassa raṭṭhe anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ anudasāhaṃ devo vassati, rañño guṇānubhāvo cesa, imassa pana tiracchānagatassa guṇā hontāpi kittakā bhaveyyu”nti sutvā “tena hi yathālaṅkatameva saparivāraṃ hatthiṃ patinetvā rañño datvā yaṃ so kurudhammaṃ rakkhati, taṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhitvā ānethā”ti [V 2.0308] brāhmaṇe ca amacce ca pesesi. Te gantvā rañño hatthiṃ niyyādetvā “deva, imasmiṃ hatthimhi gatepi amhākaṃ raṭṭhe [P 2.0372] devo na vassati, tumhe kira kurudhammaṃ nāma rakkhatha, amhākampi rājā taṃ rakkhitukāmo imasmiṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhitvā ānethā”ti pesesi. “Detha no kurudhamma”nti. “Tātā, saccāhaṃ etaṃ kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, idāni pana me tattha kukkuccaṃ atthi, na me so kurudhammo cittaṃ ārādheti, tasmā tumhākaṃ dātuṃ na sakkā”ti.

Thus the Great Being, while remaining on the back of the noble elephant, gave it with his word. Then, descending from the elephant’s back, he said, “If there is any unadorned spot, I will give it after adorning it.” After circumambulating it three times and inspecting it, seeing no unadorned spot, he placed its trunk in the hands of the brahmins and, pouring water scented with flowers and fragrances from a golden pitcher, he gave it. The brahmins accepted the noble elephant with its retinue and, sitting on its back, went to Dantapura and gave the elephant to the king. Even when the elephant had arrived, the god did not rain. The king, inquiring further, “What indeed is the reason?” heard: “King Dhanafjaya Korabya protects the Kurudhamma. Because of that, the god rains in his kingdom every half-month and every ten days; this is the power of the king’s virtue. But as for this animal, even if it has virtues, how great could they be?” Hearing this, the king sent the brahmins and ministers, saying: “In that case, lead the elephant back with its retinue just as it is adorned and give it to the king. Having written on a golden plate the Kurudhamma that he protects, bring it back.” They went, handed over the elephant to the king, and said: “Your Majesty, even when this elephant arrived, the god does not rain in our kingdom. It is said that you protect the Kurudhamma. Our king also wishes to protect it; he has sent us with the instruction, ‘Having written it on this golden plate, bring it back.’ Give us the Kurudhamma.” “Bitters, it is true that I protect this Kurudhamma, but now I have a scruple about it. That Kurudhamma does not satisfy my mind, therefore I cannot give it to you.”

Kasmā pana taṃ sīlaṃ rājānaṃ na ārādhetīti? Tadā kira rājūnaṃ tatiye tatiye saṃvacchare kattikamāse pavatto chaṇo nāma hoti, taṃ chaṇaṃ kīḷantā rājāno sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā devavesaṃ gahetvā cittarājassa nāma yakkhassa santike ṭhatvā catuddisā pupphapaṭimaṇḍite cittasare khipanti. Ayampi rājā taṃ khaṇaṃ kīḷanto ekissā taḷākapāḷiyā cittarājassa yakkhassa santike ṭhatvā catuddisā cittasare khipitvā tesu sesadisāgate tayo sare disvā udakapiṭṭhe khittasaraṃ na addasa. Rañño “kacci nu kho mayā khitto saro macchasarīre patito”ti kukkuccaṃ ahosi pāṇātipātakammena sīlabhedaṃ ārabbha, tasmā sīlaṃ na ārādheti. So evamāha – “tātā, mayhaṃ kurudhamme kukkuccaṃ atthi, mātā pana me surakkhitaṃ rakkhati, tassā santike gaṇhathā”ti. “Mahārāja, tumhākaṃ ‘pāṇaṃ vadhissāmī’ti cetanā natthi, taṃ vinā pāṇātipāto nāma na hoti, detha no attanā rakkhitaṃ kurudhamma”nti. “Tena hi likhathā”ti suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhāpesi – “pāṇo na hantabbo, adinnaṃ nādātabbaṃ[P 2.0373], kāmesu micchā na caritabbaṃ, musā na bhaṇitabbaṃ[M 2.0336], majjaṃ na pātabba”nti likhāpetvā ca pana “evaṃ santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, mātu me santike gaṇhathā”ti āha.

Now, why did that virtue not satisfy the king? At that time, it is said, every third year in the month of Kattika, there was a festival. While celebrating that festival, the kings, adorned with all ornaments, assumed the form of devas and, standing near a yakkha named Cittarāja, shot variegated arrows adorned with flowers in the four directions. This king also, while celebrating that festival, stood near the yakkha Cittarāja on the bank of a pond and shot variegated arrows in the four directions. Among them, seeing three arrows that went in the other directions, he did not see the arrow shot onto the surface of the water. A scruple arose in the king concerning a breach of virtue through the act of killing, thinking: ‘Could the arrow I shot have fallen on the body of a fish?’ Therefore, the virtue did not satisfy him. He said: ‘Sirs, I have a scruple concerning the Kurudhamma, but my mother protects it well; take it from her.’ ‘Great king, you had no intention saying, “It is my intention to kill a living being.” Without that intention, there is no act of killing. Give us the Kurudhamma protected by yourself.’ ‘In that case, write it,’ he said, and had it written on a golden plate: ‘A living being is not to be killed; what is not given is not to be taken; one must not misbehave in sensual pleasures; falsehood must not be spoken; intoxicants must not be drunk.’ Having had it written, he said: ‘Even though it is so, it does not satisfy me. Take it from my mother.’

Dūtā rājānaṃ vanditvā tassā santikaṃ gantvā “devi, tumhe kira kurudhammaṃ rakkhatha, taṃ no dethā”ti vadiṃsu. “Tātā, saccāhaṃ kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, idāni pana me tattha kukkuccaṃ uppannaṃ, na me so kurudhammo ārādheti tena vo dātuṃ na sakkā”ti. Tassā kira dve puttā jeṭṭho rājā, kaniṭṭho uparājā. Atheko rājā bodhisattassa satasahassagghanakaṃ candanasāraṃ sahassagghanakaṃ kañcanamālaṃ pesesi. So “mātaraṃ pūjessāmī”ti taṃ sabbaṃ mātu pesesi. Sā cintesi – “ahaṃ neva candanaṃ vilimpāmi, na mālaṃ dhāremi, suṇisānaṃ dassāmī”ti. Athassā etadahosi – “jeṭṭhasuṇisā me issarā, aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhitā, tassā suvaṇṇamālaṃ dassāmi. Kaniṭṭhasuṇisā pana duggatā, tassā candanasāraṃ dassāmī”ti. Sā rañño deviyā suvaṇṇamālaṃ datvā uparājabhariyāya candanasāraṃ adāsi, datvā ca panassā “ahaṃ [V 2.0309] kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, etāsaṃ duggatāduggatabhāvo mayhaṃ appamāṇaṃ, jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammameva pana kātuṃ mayhaṃ anurūpaṃ, kacci nu kho me tassa akatattā sīlaṃ bhinna”nti kukkuccaṃ ahosi, tasmā evamāha. Atha naṃ dūtā “attano santakaṃ nāma yathāruciyā dīyati, tumhe ettakenapi kukkuccaṃ kurumānā kiṃ aññaṃ pāpaṃ karissatha, sīlaṃ nāma evarūpena na [P 2.0374] bhijjati, detha no kurudhamma”nti vatvā tassāpi santike gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

The messengers paid homage to the king and went to her, saying: “Queen, it is said that you protect the Kurudhamma; give it to us.” “My dears, it is true that I protect the Kurudhamma, but now a scruple has arisen in me regarding it. That Kurudhamma does not satisfy me, so I cannot give it to you.” She had two sons: the elder was the king, the younger was the viceroy. Then another king sent to the Bodhisatta sandalwood core worth a hundred thousand and a golden wreath worth a thousand. He sent all that to his mother, thinking: “In order to honor my mother.” She thought: ‘I neither anoint myself with sandalwood nor wear a wreath; I will give them to my daughters-in-law.’ Then it occurred to her: ‘My elder daughter-in-law is a lady of rank, established in the position of chief queen; I will give her the golden wreath. My younger daughter-in-law is poor; I will give her the sandalwood core.’ After giving the golden wreath to the king’s queen and the sandalwood core to the viceroy’s wife, a scruple arose in her: ‘I protect the Kurudhamma. The wealth or poverty of these women is no measure for me. It is proper for me only to perform an act of respect for the elder. I wonder if my virtue is broken because I did not do that?’ Therefore she spoke thus. Then the messengers said to her: ‘One’s own property is given as one pleases. If you feel scruples even for this much, what other evil would you do? Virtue is not broken by such a thing. Give us the Kurudhamma.’ Having spoken thus, they received it from her also and wrote it on a golden plate.

“Tātā, evaṃ santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, suṇisā pana me suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassā santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana aggamahesiṃ upasaṅkamitvā purimanayeneva kurudhammaṃ yāciṃsu. Sāpi purimanayeneva vatvā “idāni maṃ sīlaṃ nārādheti, tena vo dātuṃ na sakkā”ti āha. Sā kira ekadivasaṃ sīhapañjare ṭhitā rañño nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karontassa pacchato hatthipiṭṭhe nisinnaṃ uparājaṃ disvā lobhaṃ uppādetvā “sacāhaṃ iminā saddhiṃ santhavaṃ kareyyaṃ, bhātu accayena rajje patiṭṭhito maṃ esa saṅgaṇheyyā”ti cintesi. Athassā “ahaṃ kurudhammaṃ rakkhamānā sasāmikā hutvā kilesavasena aññaṃ purisaṃ olokesiṃ, sīlena me bhinnena bhavitabba”nti [V 2.0310] kukkuccaṃ ahosi, tasmā evamāha. Atha naṃ dūtā “aticāro nāma ayye cittuppādamattena [M 2.0337] na hoti, tumhe ettakenapi kukkuccaṃ kurumānā vītikkamaṃ kiṃkarissatha, na ettakena sīlaṃ bhijjati, detha no kurudhamma”nti vatvā tassāpi santike gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

“My dears, even so, it does not satisfy me. But my daughter-in-law observes it well; get it from her.” Being told this, they approached the chief queen and asked for the Kurudhamma in the same way as before. She too, speaking as before, said: “Now my virtue does not satisfy me, so I cannot give it to you.” It seems that one day, while standing at a lion-window, she saw the viceroy seated on an elephant’s back behind the king as he was circumambulating the city. Lust arose in her, and she thought: ‘If I were to become intimate with him, then after his brother’s death, when he is established in the kingdom, he would take me as his own.’ Then a scruple arose in her: ‘Though I am observing the Kurudhamma and have a husband, out of defilement I have looked upon another man. My virtue must be broken.’ That is why she spoke as she did. Then the messengers said: ‘Noble lady, a transgression does not occur by the mere arising of a thought. If you are scrupulous about even this, how would you commit a transgression? Virtue is not broken by so little. Give us the Kurudhamma.’ Having spoken thus, they received it from her as well and inscribed it on a golden plate.

“Tātā, evaṃ santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, uparājā pana suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassa santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana uparājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā purimanayeneva kurudhammaṃ yāciṃsu. So pana sāyaṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto ratheneva rājaṅgaṇaṃ patvā sace rañño santike bhuñjitvā tattheva sayitukāmo hoti, rasmiyo ca patodañca antodhure chaḍḍeti. Tāya saññāya jano pakkamitvā punadivase pātova gantvā tassa nikkhamanaṃ olokentova tiṭṭhati. Sārathipi rathaṃ gopayitvā [P 2.0375] punadivase pātova taṃ ādāya rājadvāre tiṭṭhati. Sace taṅkhaṇaññeva nikkhantukāmo hoti, rasmiyo ca patodañca antoratheyeva ṭhapetvā rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati. Mahājano tāya saññāya “idāneva nikkhamissatī”ti rājadvāreyeva tiṭṭhati. So ekadivasaṃ evaṃ katvā rājanivesanaṃ pāvisi, paviṭṭhamattassayevassa devo pāvassi. Rājā “devo vassatī”ti tassa nikkhantuṃ nādāsi, so tattheva bhuñjitvā sayi. Mahājano “idāni nikkhamissatī”ti sabbarattiṃ temento aṭṭhāsi. Uparājā dutiyadivase nikkhamitvā temetvā ṭhitaṃ mahājanaṃ disvā “ahaṃ kurudhammaṃ rakkhanto ettakaṃ janaṃ kilamesiṃ, sīlena me bhinnena bhavitabba”nti kukkuccaṃ ahosi, tena tesaṃ dūtānaṃ “saccāhaṃ kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, idāni pana me kukkuccaṃ atthi, tena vo na sakkā dātu”nti vatvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ dūtā “tumhākaṃ, deva, ‘ete kilamantū’ti cittaṃ natthi, acetanakaṃ kammaṃ na hoti, ettakenapi kukkuccaṃ karontānaṃ kathaṃ tumhākaṃ vītikkamo bhavissatī”ti vatvā tassapi santike sīlaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

“My dears, even so, it does not satisfy me. But the viceroy observes it well; get it from him.” Being told this, they approached the viceroy and asked for the Kurudhamma in the same way as before. Now, when he went to attend on the king in the evening, he would arrive at the royal courtyard by chariot. If he intended to eat there and sleep there, he would leave the reins and goad at the front of the pole. Taking this as a sign, the people would depart and, returning early the next day, would stand watching for his departure. The charioteer, too, after tending to the chariot, would bring it early the next day and stand with it at the palace gate. If he intended to leave right away, he would place the reins and goad inside the chariot itself and go to attend on the king. The great crowd, taking this as a sign, would stand right at the palace gate, thinking, ‘He will come out now.’ One day, having done the former, he entered the royal palace. Just as he entered, it began to rain. The king, saying, ‘It is raining,’ did not allow him to leave, so he ate and slept right there. The great crowd, thinking, ‘He will come out now,’ stood all night getting drenched. On the next day, the viceroy came out and saw the people standing there drenched, and a scruple arose in him: ‘While observing the Kurudhamma, I have caused so many people to be troubled. My virtue must be broken.’ Therefore, he told those messengers: ‘It is true that I observe the Kurudhamma, but now I have a scruple, so I cannot give it to you,’ and he explained the matter. Then the messengers said: ‘Your Majesty, you had no intention, “Let these people be troubled.” There is no kamma without intention. If you are scrupulous about even this, how could you commit a transgression?’ Having spoken thus, they also received the virtue from him and inscribed it on a golden plate.

“Evaṃ santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, purohito pana suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassa santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana purohitaṃ upasaṅkamitvā yāciṃsu. Sopi ekadivasaṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto ekena raññā tassa rañño pesitaṃ taruṇaravivaṇṇaṃ rathaṃ antarāmagge disvā “kassāyaṃ ratho”ti pucchitvā “rañño ābhato”ti sutvā “ahaṃ [M 2.0338] mahallako, sace me rājā imaṃ rathaṃ dadeyya, sukhaṃ imaṃ āruyha vicareyya”nti cintetvā rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gato. Tassa jayāpetvā ṭhitakāle rañño rathaṃ [P 2.0376] dassesuṃ. Rājā disvā “ati viya sundaro ayaṃ ratho, ācariyassa naṃ dethā”ti āha. Purohito na icchi, punappunaṃ vuccamānopi na icchiyeva. Kiṃkāraṇā? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ahaṃ kurudhammaṃ rakkhantova parasantake lobhaṃ akāsiṃ, bhinnena me sīlena bhavitabba”nti. So etamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā “tātā, kurudhamme me kukkuccaṃ atthi, na maṃ so dhammo ārādheti, tasmā na sakkā dātu”nti āha. Atha naṃ dūtā “ayya, lobhuppādamattena na sīlaṃ bhijjati, tumhe ettakenapi kukkuccaṃ karontā kiṃ vītikkamaṃ karissathā”ti vatvā tassapi santike sīlaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

“Even so, it does not satisfy me. But the chaplain observes it well; get it from him.” Being told this, they approached the chaplain and made their request. He too, one day, while going to attend on the king, saw on the way a chariot the color of the young sun, sent by one king to that king. He asked, ‘Whose chariot is this?’ Hearing it was ‘brought for the king,’ he thought: ‘I am an old man. If the king would give me this chariot, I could ride about comfortably in it,’ and went to attend on the king. While he was standing there after paying his respects, they showed the chariot to the king. The king saw it and said: ‘This chariot is exceedingly beautiful. Give it to the teacher.’ The chaplain did not want it. Even when told again and again, he still did not want it. For what reason? It seems this occurred to him: ‘While observing the Kurudhamma, I have been greedy for another’s property. My virtue must be broken.’ Explaining this matter, he said: ‘My dears, I have a scruple concerning the Kurudhamma. That Dhamma does not satisfy me, so I cannot give it.’ Then the messengers told him: ‘Venerable sir, virtue is not broken by the mere arising of greed. If you are scrupulous about even this, how could you commit a transgression?’ Having spoken thus, they also received the virtue from him and inscribed it on a golden plate.

“Evaṃ santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, rajjugāhako amacco pana suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassa santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana tampi upasaṅkamitvā yāciṃsu. Sopi ekadivasaṃ janapade khettaṃ minanto rajjuṃ daṇḍake bandhitvā ekaṃ koṭiṃ khettasāmikena gaṇhāpetvā ekaṃ attanā aggahesi, tena gahitarajjukoṭiyā baddhadaṇḍako ekassa kakkaṭakassa bilamajjhaṃ pāpuṇi. So cintesi – “sace daṇḍakaṃ bile otāressāmi, antobile kakkaṭako nassissati. Sace pana parato karissāmi, rañño santakaṃ nassissati. Sace orato karissāmi, kuṭumbikassa santakaṃ nassissati, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti? Athassa etadahosi – “bile kakkaṭakena bhavitabbaṃ, sace bhaveyya, paññāyeyya, ettheva naṃ otāressāmī”ti bile daṇḍakaṃ otāresi, kakkaṭako “kirī”ti saddamakāsi. Athassa etadahosi – “daṇḍako kakkaṭakapiṭṭhe otiṇṇo bhavissati, kakkaṭako mato bhavissati, ahañca kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, tena me sīlena bhinnena bhavitabba”nti[P 2.0377]. So etamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā “iminā me [V 2.0311] kāraṇena kurudhamme kukkuccaṃ atthi, tena vo na sakkā dātu”nti āha. Atha naṃ dūtā “tumhākaṃ ‘kakkaṭako maratū’ti cittaṃ natthi, acetanakaṃ kammaṃ nāma na hoti. Tumhe ettakenapi kukkuccaṃ karontā kiṃ vītikkamaṃ karissathā”ti vatvā tassapi santike sīlaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

“Even though it is given in this way, it does not satisfy me. But the minister who holds the measuring rope observes it well; get it from him.” Being told this, they approached him too and made their request. He too, one day, while measuring a field in the countryside, tied the measuring rope to a stick, had the owner of the field take one end, and took the other himself. The stick tied to the end of the rope he held came right over the middle of a crab’s hole. He thought: “If I lower the stick into the hole, the crab inside will perish. If I place it beyond, the king’s property will be lost. If I place it on this side, the householder’s property will be lost. What is to be done?” Then it occurred to him: “There should not be a crab in the hole; if there were, it would be apparent. I will lower the stick right here.” He lowered the stick into the hole, and the crab made a ‘kiri’ sound. Then it occurred to him: “The stick must have landed on the crab’s back. The crab must be dead. And I am observing the Kurudhamma! My virtue must be broken by this.” Explaining this matter, he said: “For this reason, I have a scruple concerning the Kurudhamma, so I cannot give it to you.” Then the messengers said: “You had no intention, ‘Let the crab die.’ An unintentional act is not kamma. If you are scrupulous about such a thing, what transgression would you commit?” Having spoken thus, they also received the precepts from him and inscribed them on a golden plate.

“Evaṃ [M 2.0339] santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, sārathi pana suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassa santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana tampi upasaṅkamitvā yāciṃsu. So ekadivasaṃ rājānaṃ rathena uyyānaṃ nesi. Rājā tattha divā kīḷitvā sāyaṃ nikkhamitvā rathaṃ abhiruhi, tassa nagaraṃ asampattasseva sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāya megho uṭṭhahi. Sārathi rañño temanabhayena sindhavānaṃ patodasaññamadāsi. Sindhavā javena pakkhandiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya ca pana te uyyānaṃ gacchantāpi tato āgacchantāpi taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā javena gacchanti āgacchanti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Tesaṃ kira etadahosi – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne parissayena bhavitabbaṃ, tena no sārathi tadā patodasaññaṃ adāsī”ti. Sārathissapi etadahosi – “rañño temane vā atemane vā mayhaṃ doso natthi, ahaṃ pana aṭṭhāne susikkhitasindhavānaṃ patodasaññaṃ adāsiṃ, tena ime idāni aparāparaṃ javantā kilamanti, ahañca kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, tena me bhinnena sīlena bhavitabba”nti. So etamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā “iminā kāraṇena kurudhamme kukkuccaṃ atthi, tena vo na sakkā dātu”nti āha. Atha naṃ dūtā “tumhākaṃ ‘sindhavā kilamantū’ti cittaṃ natthi, acetanakaṃ kammaṃ nāma na hoti, ettakenapi ca tumhe kukkuccaṃ karontā kiṃ vītikkamaṃ karissathā”ti vatvā tassa santike sīlaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe [P 2.0378] likhiṃsu.

“Even so, it [my virtue] does not satisfy me, but the charioteer guards [his virtue] well. Take it from him.” Having been told this, they approached him as well and requested it. One day, he took the king to the park in his chariot. The king played there during the day, and in the evening, he departed and mounted the chariot. Before he had even reached the city, at the time of sunset, a storm cloud arose. Fearing the king would get wet, the charioteer gave a signal with the goad to the thoroughbred horses. The thoroughbreds rushed forward with speed. From then on, whether they were going to the park or coming from it, upon reaching that spot, they would go and come with speed. What was the reason? It occurred to them, it seems: “There must be some danger in this place; that is why the charioteer gave us the signal with the goad then.” It also occurred to the charioteer: “Whether the king gets wet or not, there is no fault in me; but I gave the signal with the goad to the well-trained thoroughbreds at an improper place. Because of this, they now tire from repeatedly running fast. And I observe the Kuru Dhamma; therefore, my virtue must be broken.” He explained this matter and said: “For this reason, I have a scruple concerning the Kuru Dhamma; therefore, I cannot give it to you.” Then the messengers said to him: “You had no intention for the thoroughbreds to be tired. There is no such thing as kamma without intention. Since you have scruples even over such a small matter, what transgression would you ever commit?” Having said this, they took the precepts from him and inscribed them on a golden plate.

“Evaṃ santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, seṭṭhi pana suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassa santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana tampi upasaṅkamitvā yāciṃsu. Sopi ekadivasaṃ gabbhato nikkhantasālisīsaṃ attano sālikhettaṃ gantvā paccavekkhitvā nivattamāno “vīhimālaṃ bandhāpessāmī”ti ekaṃ sālisīsamuṭṭhiṃ gāhāpetvā thūṇāya bandhāpesi. Athassa etadahosi – “imamhā kedārā mayā rañño bhāgo dātabbo, adinnabhāgatoyeva me kedārato sālisīsamuṭṭhi gāhāpito, ahañca kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, tena me bhinnena sīlena bhavitabba”nti. So etamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā “iminā me kāraṇena kurudhamme kukkuccaṃ atthi, tena vo na sakkā dātu”nti āha. Atha naṃ dūtā “tumhākaṃ theyyacittaṃ natthi, tena vinā adinnādānaṃ nāma paññāpetuṃ na sakkā, ettakenapi kukkuccaṃ karontā tumhe parasantakaṃ nāma [M 2.0340] kiṃ gaṇhissathā”ti vatvā tassapi santike sīlaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

“Even so, it does not satisfy me, but the merchant guards it well. Take it from him.” Having been told this, they approached him too and requested it. One day, he went to his rice field, where the ears of rice were emerging from their sheaths, and after inspecting it, on his way back he thought, “I will have a garland of paddy tied.” He had a handful of rice ears taken and tied to his topknot. Then it occurred to him: “From this field, the king’s share must be given by me. But a handful of rice ears has been taken from my field from which the share has not yet been given. And I am one who observes the Kuru Dhamma; therefore, my virtue must have been broken.” He explained this matter and said: “For this reason, I have a scruple concerning the Kuru Dhamma, so I cannot give it to you.” Then the messengers said to him: “You had no thievish intent. Without that, taking what is not given cannot be established. Since you have such a scruple even over this much, how would you ever take what belongs to another?” Having said this, they also received the precepts from him and inscribed them on a golden plate.

“Evaṃ [V 2.0312] santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, doṇamāpako pana mahāmatto suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassa santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana tampi upasaṅkamitvā yāciṃsu. So kira ekadivasaṃ koṭṭhāgāradvāre nisīditvā rājabhāge vīhiṃ mināpento amitavīhirāsito vīhiṃ gahetvā lakkhaṃ ṭhapesi, tasmiṃ khaṇe devo pāvassi. Mahāmatto lakkhāni gaṇetvā “mitavīhī ettakā nāma hontī”ti vatvā lakkhavīhiṃ saṃkaḍḍhitvā mitarāsimhi pakkhipitvā vegena gantvā dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhatvā cintesi – “kiṃ nu kho mayā lakkhavīhī mitavīhirāsimhi pakkhittā, udāhu amitarāsimhī”ti. Athassa etadahosi – “sace me [P 2.0379] mitavīhirāsimhi pakkhittā akāraṇeneva rañño santakaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ, gahapatikānaṃ santakaṃ nāsitaṃ, ahañca kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, tena me bhinnena sīlena bhavitabba”nti. So etamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā “iminā me kāraṇena kurudhamme kukkuccaṃ atthi, tena vo na sakkā dātu”nti āha. Atha naṃ dūtā “tumhākaṃ theyyacittaṃ natthi, tena vinā adinnādānaṃ nāma paññāpetuṃ na sakkā, ettakenapi kukkuccaṃ karontā kiṃ tumhe parassa santakaṃ gaṇhissathā”ti vatvā tassapi santike sīlaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

“Even so, it does not satisfy me, but the grain-measuring minister guards it well. Take it from him.” Having been told this, they approached him too and requested it. It is said that one day, while sitting at the door of the granary and having the king’s share of paddy measured, he took some paddy from the unmeasured heap and set it as a marker. At that moment, it rained heavily. The minister, having counted the markers, said, “The measured paddy is this much,” and, sweeping up the marker paddy, he threw it onto the measured heap. Then he went quickly and stood in the gateway, where he thought: “Now, did I throw the marker paddy onto the measured heap or onto the unmeasured heap?” Then it occurred to him: “If I threw it onto the measured heap, the king’s property has been increased without reason, and the householders’ property has been diminished. And I observe the Kuru Dhamma; therefore, my virtue must have been broken.” He explained this matter and said: “For this reason, I have a scruple concerning the Kuru Dhamma; therefore, I cannot give it to you.” Then the messengers said to him: “You had no thievish intent. Without that, it is not possible to define it as taking what is not given. If you have such scruples, how would you ever take what belongs to another?” Having said this, they also received the virtue from him and inscribed it on a golden plate.

“Evaṃ santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, dovāriko pana suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassa santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana tampi upasaṅkamitvā yāciṃsu. Sopi ekadivasaṃ nagaradvāraṃ pidhānavelāya tikkhattuṃ saddamanussāvesi. Atheko daliddamanusso attano kaniṭṭhabhaginiyā saddhiṃ dārupaṇṇatthāya araññaṃ gantvā nivattanto tassa saddaṃ sutvā bhaginiṃ ādāya vegena dvāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Atha naṃ dovāriko “tvaṃ nagare rañño atthibhāvaṃ kiṃ na jānāsi, ‘sakalasseva imassa nagarassa dvāraṃ pidhīyatī’ti na jānāsi, attano mātugāmaṃ gahetvā araññe kāmaratikīḷaṃ kīḷanto divasaṃ vicarasī”ti āha. Athassa itarena “na me, sāmi, bhariyā, bhaginī me esā”ti vutte etadahosi – “akāraṇaṃ vata me kataṃ bhaginiṃ bhariyāti kathentena, ahañca kurudhammaṃ rakkhāmi, tena me bhinnena sīlena bhavitabba”nti. So etamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā “iminā me kāraṇena kurudhamme kukkuccaṃ [M 2.0341] atthi, tena vo na sakkā dātu”nti āha. Atha naṃ dūtā “etaṃ tumhehi tathāsaññāya kathitaṃ, ettha [P 2.0380] vo sīlabhedo natthi, ettakenapi ca tumhe kukkuccāyantā kurudhamme sampajānamusāvādaṃ nāma kiṃ karissathā”ti vatvā tassapi santike sīlaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

“Even so, it does not satisfy me, but the gatekeeper guards it well. Take it from him.” Having been told this, they approached him too and requested it. One day, at the time for closing the city gate, he made an announcement three times. A poor man, who had gone to the forest with his younger sister for firewood and leaves, heard the sound on his way back and, taking his sister, hurried to the gate. The gatekeeper said to him: “Do you not know there is a king in this city? Do you not know that the gates of this entire city are being closed? Taking your woman and playing the game of sensual delight, you spend the day wandering in the forest.” When the other replied, “Sir, she is not my wife; she is my sister,” it occurred to the gatekeeper: “Alas, I have done something groundless by speaking of his sister as his wife. And I observe the Kuru Dhamma; therefore, my virtue must have been broken.” He explained this matter and said: “For this reason, I have a scruple concerning the Kuru Dhamma; therefore, I cannot give it to you.” Then the messengers said to him: “You spoke based on such a perception; there is no breach of virtue in this. If you are scrupulous about even this much, how could you ever tell a deliberate lie?” Having said this, they also received the virtue from him and inscribed it on a golden plate.

“Evaṃ santepi neva maṃ ārādheti, vaṇṇadāsī pana suṭṭhu rakkhati, tassa santike gaṇhathā”ti vuttā ca pana tampi upasaṅkamitvā yāciṃsu. Sā purimanayeneva paṭikkhipi. Kiṃkāraṇā[V 2.0313]? Sakko kira devānamindo “tassā sīlaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti māṇavakavaṇṇena āgantvā “ahaṃ āgamissāmī”ti vatvā sahassaṃ datvā devalokameva gantvā tīṇi saṃvaccharāni nāgacchi. Sā attano sīlabhedabhayena tīṇi saṃvaccharāni aññassa purisassa hatthato tambūlamattampi na gaṇhi, sā anukkamena duggatā hutvā cintesi – “mayhaṃ sahassaṃ datvā gatapurisassa tīṇi saṃvaccharāni anāgacchantassa duggatā jātā, jīvitavuttiṃ ghaṭetuṃ na sakkomi, ito dāni paṭṭhāya mayā vinicchayamahāmattānaṃ ārocetvā paribbayaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sā vinicchayaṃ gantvā “sāmi, paribbayaṃ datvā gatapurisassa me tīṇi saṃvaccharāni, matabhāvampissa na jānāmi, jīvitaṃ ghaṭetuṃ na sakkomi, kiṃ karomi, sāmī”ti āha. Tīṇi saṃvaccharāni anāgacchante kiṃ karissasi, ito paṭṭhāya paribbayaṃ gaṇhāti. Tassā laddhavinicchayāya vinicchayato nikkhamamānāya eva eko puriso sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ upanāmesi.

“Even so, it does not satisfy me, but the courtesan guards it well. Take it from her.” Having been told this, they approached her too and requested it. She refused in the same way as before. For what reason? It is said that Sakka, king of the devas, wishing to test her virtue, had come in the guise of a young man. Saying, “I will come,” he gave her a thousand and went to the deva world, and did not return for three years. Fearing a breach of her virtue, for three years she did not accept so much as a betel leaf from the hand of another man. Gradually she became poor and thought: “The man who gave me a thousand and left has not returned for three years, and I have become poor. I cannot manage to make a living. From now on, it is proper for me to inform the ministers of justice and accept a fee.” She went to the court of justice and said: “Sirs, it has been three years since the man who gave me my fee left. I do not know if he is dead. I cannot manage my life. What should I do, sirs?” “If he does not return for three years, what can you do? From now on, take a fee.” As she was leaving the court, having received the verdict, a man offered her a bag of a thousand.

Tassa gahaṇatthāya hatthaṃ pasāraṇakāle sakko attānaṃ dassesi. Sā disvāva “mayhaṃ saṃvaccharattayamatthake sahassadāyako puriso āgato, tāta, natthi me tava kahāpaṇehi attho”ti hatthaṃ samiñjesi. Sakko attano sarīraññeva abhinimminitvā taruṇasūriyo viya jalanto ākāse aṭṭhāsi, sakalanagaraṃ sannipati. Sakko mahājanamajjhe “ahaṃ [P 2.0381] etissā vīmaṃsanavasena saṃvaccharattayamatthake sahassaṃ adāsiṃ, sīlaṃ rakkhantā nāma evarūpā hutvā rakkhathā”ti ovādaṃ datvā tassā nivesanaṃ sattaratanehi pūretvā “ito paṭṭhāya appamattā hohī”ti taṃ anusāsitvā devalokameva agamāsi. Iminā kāraṇena sā “ahaṃ gahitabhatiṃ ajīrāpetvāva aññena dīyamānāya bhatiyā hatthaṃ pasāresiṃ, iminā kāraṇena [M 2.0342] maṃ sīlaṃ nārādheti, tena vo dātuṃ na sakkā”ti paṭikkhipi. Atha naṃ dūtā “hatthappasāraṇamattena sīlabhedo natthi, sīlaṃ nāma etaṃ paramavisuddhi hotī”ti vatvā tassāpi santike sīlaṃ gahetvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhiṃsu.

As she was extending her hand to take it, Sakka revealed himself. Upon seeing him, she withdrew her hand, saying: 'The man who gave me a thousand three years ago has come. Sir, I have no need for your coins.' Sakka then manifested his own form and stood in the sky, blazing like the morning sun, and the whole city assembled. In the midst of the great crowd, Sakka gave this counsel: 'I gave her a thousand three years ago for the purpose of testing her. Those who protect their virtue should protect it by being like this.' After giving this advice, he filled her house with the seven kinds of treasures and, having admonished her, 'From now on, be diligent,' he returned to the world of the devas. For this reason, she had refused them, saying: 'Without having fulfilled my obligation for the payment I had already received, I stretched out my hand for another payment that was being offered. For this reason, my virtue does not satisfy me, so it cannot be given to you.' Then the messengers said to her: 'Virtue is not broken merely by extending the hand; this virtue of yours is of supreme purity.' Then, having received the precepts from her as well, they inscribed them on a golden plate.

Iti imesaṃ ekādasannaṃ janānaṃ rakkhaṇasīlaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhitvā dantapuraṃ gantvā kāliṅgarañño suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ datvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā tasmiṃ kurudhamme vattamāno pañca sīlāni pūresi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakalakāliṅgaraṭṭhe devo vassi, tīṇi bhayāni vūpasantāni, raṭṭhaṃ khemaṃ subhikkhaṃ ahosi. Bodhisatto yāvajīvaṃ dānādīni puññāni katvā saparivāro saggapuraṃ pūresi.

Thus, having inscribed the virtue observed by these eleven people on a golden plate, they went to Dantapura and, giving the golden plate to the king of Kāliṅga, informed him of the matter. The king, abiding by the Kurudhamma, fulfilled the five precepts. At that very moment, rain fell throughout the entire kingdom of Kāliṅga, the three fears subsided, and the land became secure and prosperous. The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds such as generosity throughout his life, along with his retinue, filled the celestial city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. “Saccapariyosāne [V 2.0314] keci sotāpannā ahesuṃ, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahanto”ti. Jātakasamodhāne pana –

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some arahants. Now, in connecting the Jātaka:

“Gaṇikā uppalavaṇṇā, puṇṇo dovāriko tadā;

Rajjugāho kaccāyano, moggallāno doṇamāpako.

The courtesan was Uppalavaṇṇā; Puṇṇa was the doorkeeper then; Kaccāyana was the rope-holder; Moggallāna was the grain-measurer.

“Sāriputto tadā seṭṭhi, anuruddho ca sārathi;

Brāhmaṇo kassapo thero, uparājā nandapaṇḍito.

Sāriputta was the merchant then, and Anuruddha the charioteer; the brahmin was the Elder Kassapa, and the viceroy was the wise Nanda.

“Mahesī rāhulamātā, māyādevī janettiyā;

Kururājā bodhisatto, evaṃ dhāretha jātaka”nti.

The chief queen was Rāhula's mother, Māyādevī was the mother; the king of the Kurus was the Bodhisatta—thus should you remember the Jātaka.

Kurudhammajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Explanation of the Kurudhamma Jātaka, the Sixth.

[277] 7. Romakajātakavaṇṇanā

[277] 7. 7. The Explanation of the Romaka Jātaka

Vassāni [P 2.0382] paññāsa samādhikānīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto bhagavato vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu uttānameva.

'Fifty years and more': this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove with reference to the attempt to murder the Blessed One. The story of the present is self-evident.

Atīte pana bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto pārāvato hutvā bahupārāvataparivuto araññe pabbataguhāyaṃ vāsaṃ kappesi. Aññataropi kho tāpaso sīlasampanno tesaṃ pārāvatānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānato [M 2.0343] avidūre ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ upanissāya assamapadaṃ māpetvā pabbataguhāyaṃ vāsaṃ kappesi. Bodhisatto antarantarā tassa santikaṃ āgantvā sotabbayuttakaṃ suṇāti. Tāpaso tattha ciraṃ vasitvā pakkāmi, athañño kūṭajaṭilo āgantvā tattha vāsaṃ kappesi. Bodhisatto pārāvataparivuto taṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā assamapade vicaritvā girikandarasamīpe gocaraṃ gahetvā sāyaṃ attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati. Kūṭatāpaso tattha atirekapaṇṇāsavassāni vasi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta had been born as a pigeon and, surrounded by a large flock of pigeons, made his dwelling in a mountain cave in the forest. Now a certain ascetic endowed with virtue, relying on a frontier village not far from the pigeons' dwelling place, built a hermitage and took up residence in a mountain cave. From time to time, the Bodhisatta would visit him and listen to the Dhamma. After that ascetic had lived there for a long time, he departed. Then another, a fraudulent matted-hair ascetic, came and took up residence there. The Bodhisatta, surrounded by his flock of pigeons, would approach him, pay homage, exchange friendly greetings, wander about the hermitage grounds, forage for food near the mountain cleft, and in the evening return to his own dwelling. The fraudulent ascetic lived there for more than fifty years.

Athassa ekadivasaṃ paccantagāmavāsino manussā pārāvatamaṃsaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā adaṃsu. So tattha rasataṇhāya bajjhitvā “kiṃ maṃsaṃ nāmeta”nti pucchitvā “pārāvatamaṃsa”nti sutvā cintesi [V 2.0315] – “mayhaṃ assamapadaṃ bahū pārāvatā āgacchanti, te māretvā maṃsaṃ khādituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So taṇḍulasappidadhikhīramaricādīni āharitvā ekamante ṭhapetvā muggaraṃ cīvarakaṇṇena paṭicchādetvā pārāvatānaṃ āgamanaṃ olokento paṇṇasāladvāre nisīdi. Bodhisatto pārāvataparivuto āgantvā tassa kūṭajaṭilassa duṭṭhakiriyaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ duṭṭhatāpaso aññenākārena nisinno, kacci nu kho amhākaṃ samānajātīnaṃ maṃsaṃ khādi, parigaṇhissāmi na”nti anuvāte ṭhatvā tassa sarīragandhaṃ [P 2.0383] ghāyitvā “ayaṃ amhe māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditukāmo, na tassa santikaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pārāvate ādāya paṭikkamitvā cari. Tāpaso taṃ anāgacchantaṃ disvā “madhurakathaṃ tehi saddhiṃ kathetvā vissāsena upagate māretvā maṃsaṃ khādituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā purimā dve gāthā avoca –

Then one day the people dwelling in the frontier village prepared pigeon meat and gave it to him. Becoming enslaved by craving for the taste, he asked, 'What meat is this?' When he heard it was pigeon meat, he thought: 'Many pigeons come to my hermitage. It is proper to kill them and eat their flesh.' He brought rice, ghee, curd, milk, pepper, and other things and set them aside. Then, covering a club with a corner of his robe, he sat at the door of his leaf-hut, watching for the pigeons' arrival. The Bodhisatta arrived with his flock of pigeons and, observing the wicked ascetic's demeanor, he thought: 'This wicked ascetic is sitting in a different manner. I wonder if he has eaten the flesh of our own kind. I will investigate him.' Standing downwind, he smelled the scent of pigeon meat from the ascetic's body and realized: 'He wants to kill us and eat our flesh. It is not proper to go near him.' Taking the pigeons with him, he turned back and left. When the ascetic saw that he did not approach, he thought: 'It is proper to speak sweet words to them, and when they approach trustingly, to kill them and eat their flesh.' Then he spoke the first two verses:

79.

79.

“Vassāni paññāsa samādhikāni, vasimha selassa guhāya romaka;

Asaṅkamānā abhinibbutattā, hatthattamāyanti mamaṇḍajā pure.

For fifty years and more, O Romaka, I have dwelt in this mountain cave; without suspicion, their minds at peace, the birds would formerly come to my hand.

80.

80.

“Tedāni vakkaṅga kimatthamussukā, bhajanti aññaṃ girikandaraṃ dijā;

Na nūna maññanti mamaṃ yathā pure, cirappavutthā atha vā na te ime”ti.

Now, O Crooked-neck, why are they so eager to resort to another mountain cleft? Surely they do not regard me as they did before. Or have they been away long, or are these not the same birds?

Tattha [M 2.0344] samādhikānīti samaadhikāni. Romakāti rumāya uppanna, sudhotapavāḷena samānavaṇṇanettapādatāya bodhisattaṃ pārāvataṃ ālapati. Asaṅkamānāti evaṃ atirekapaññāsavassāni imissā pabbataguhāya vasantesu amhesu ete aṇḍajā ekadivasampi mayi āsaṅkaṃ akatvā abhinibbutacittāva hutvā pubbe mama hatthattaṃ hatthappasāraṇokāsaṃ āgacchantīti attho.

Herein, 'samādhikāni' means 'and more.' 'Romaka': he addresses the Bodhisatta, the pigeon, by this name, meaning 'the downy one' (from 'ruma', down), because its eyes and feet were the color of well-washed coral. 'Asaṅkamānā' means: 'Although we have been living in this mountain cave for more than fifty years, these egg-born ones, without having any suspicion of me even for a single day, with minds at peace, formerly came into my hand, that is, to a place where I could stretch out my hand.' This is the meaning.

Tedānīti te idāni. Vakkaṅgāti bodhisattaṃ ālapati, sabbepi pana pakkhino uppatanakāle gīvaṃ vakkaṃ katvā uppatanato “vakkaṅgā”ti vuccanti. Kimatthanti kiṃkāraṇaṃ sampassamānā? Ussukāti ukkaṇṭhitarūpā hutvā. Girikandaranti girito aññaṃ pabbatakandaraṃ. Yathā pureti yathā pubbe ete pakkhino maṃ garuṃ katvā piyaṃ katvā maññanti, tathā idāni na nūna maññanti, pubbe idha nivutthatāpaso añño, ayaṃ añño, evaṃ maññe ete maṃ maññantīti dīpeti. Cirappavutthā atha vā na te imeti kiṃ nu kho ime ciraṃ vippavasitvā dīghassa addhuno accayena āgatattā maṃ “soyeva [P 2.0384] aya”nti na sañjānanti, udāhu ye amhesu abhinibbutacittā, na te ime, aññeva āgantukapakkhino, ime kena maṃ na upasaṅkamantīti pucchati.

'Tedāni' means 'they now.' 'Vakkaṅga': he addresses the Bodhisatta. Indeed, all birds are called 'crooked-necks' because when they fly up, they do so making their necks crooked. 'Kimattham' means: seeing what reason? 'Ussukā' means: having become anxious. 'Girikandaraṃ' means a mountain cleft other than this one. 'Yathā pure': he explains, 'Just as these birds formerly regarded me with respect and affection, surely they do not regard me so now. I think they must regard me thus: "The ascetic who lived here before was another; this one is another."' 'Cirappavutthā atha vā na te ime': he asks, 'I wonder, having been away for a long time and returned after a long interval, do they not recognize me as "this is that same one"? Or is it that those who had peaceful minds toward me are not these birds, but are other, newly arrived ones? For what reason do they not approach me?'

Taṃ [V 2.0316] sutvā bodhisatto pakkamitvā ṭhitova tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard this, the Bodhisatta, who had stepped back and was standing there, spoke the third verse:

81.

81.

“Jānāma taṃ na mayaṃ sampamūḷhā, soyeva tvaṃ te mayamasma nāññe;

Cittañca te asmiṃ jane paduṭṭhaṃ, ājīvikā tena tamuttasāmā”ti.

“We know you; we are not confused. You are that very one; we are those same ones, not others. But your mind toward these beings is corrupt, O ascetic, and for that reason we fear you.”

Tattha na mayaṃ sampamūḷhāti mayaṃ mūḷhā pamattā na homa. Cittañca te asmiṃ jane paduṭṭhanti tvaṃ, soyeva mayampi teyeva, na taṃ sañjānāma, apica kho pana tava cittaṃ asmiṃ jane paduṭṭhaṃ amhe māretuṃ uppannaṃ. Ājīvikāti ājīvahetu pabbajita paduṭṭhatāpasa. Tena tamuttasāmāti tena kāraṇena taṃ uttasāma bhāyāma na upasaṅkamāma.

Herein, 'na mayaṃ sampamūḷhā' means: we are not bewildered or heedless. 'Cittañca te asmiṃ jane paduṭṭhaṃ' means: you are that same one, and we are those same ones; it is not that we do not recognize you. But your mind toward these beings is corrupt, having arisen with the intent to kill us. 'Ājīvika': a corrupt ascetic who has gone forth for the sake of a livelihood. 'Tena tamuttasāma' means: for that reason we are afraid of you, we fear you, and we do not approach you.

Kūṭatāpaso [M 2.0345] “ñāto ahaṃ imehī”ti muggaraṃ khipitvā virajjhitvā “gaccha tāva tvaṃ viraddhomhī”ti āha. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “maṃ tāva viraddhosi, cattāro pana apāye na virajjhasi. Sace idha vasissasi, gāmavāsīnaṃ ‘coro aya’nti ācikkhitvā taṃ gāhāpessāmi sīghaṃ palāyassū”ti taṃ tajjetvā pakkāmi. Kūṭajaṭilo tattha vasituṃ nāsakkhi, aññattha agamāsi.

The fraudulent ascetic, thinking, 'I have been found out by them,' threw his club but missed, and said: 'Go now! I have missed you.' Then the Bodhisatta said to him: 'You have missed me, but you will not fail to reach the four planes of misery. If you stay here, I will inform the villagers, "This is a thief," and have you seized. Flee quickly!' Having threatened him thus, he departed. The fraudulent matted-hair ascetic was unable to remain there and went elsewhere.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kūṭatāpaso devadatto ahosi, purimo sīlavantatāpaso sāriputto, pārāvatajeṭṭhako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the fraudulent ascetic was Devadatta, the former virtuous ascetic was Sāriputta, and the chief of the pigeons was I myself.'

Romakajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Explanation of the Romaka Jātaka, the Seventh.

[278] 8. Mahiṃsarājajātakavaṇṇanā

[278] 8. The Commentary on the Buffalo King Jātaka

Kimatthamabhisandhāyāti [P 2.0385] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolamakkaṭaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira ekasmiṃ kule eko posāvaniyalolamakkaṭo hatthisālaṃ gantvā ekassa sīlavantassa hatthissa piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīditvā uccārapassāvaṃ karoti, piṭṭhiyaṃ caṅkamati. Hatthī attano sīlavantatāya khantisampadāya na kiñci karoti. Athekadivasaṃ tassa hatthissa ṭhāne añño duṭṭhahatthipoto aṭṭhāsi. Makkaṭo “soyeva aya”nti saññāya duṭṭhahatthissa piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhi. Atha naṃ so soṇḍāya gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā pādena akkamitvā sañcuṇṇesi. Sā [V 2.0317] pavatti bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭā jātā. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, lolamakkaṭo kira sīlavantahatthisaññāya duṭṭhahatthipiṭṭhiṃ abhiruhi, atha naṃ so jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa, lolamakkaṭo evaṃsīlo, porāṇato paṭṭhāya evaṃsīloyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“For what reason...”: The Teacher told this story while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a certain mischievous monkey. In Sāvatthī, it seems, there was a mischievous pet monkey in a certain family. It went to the elephant stable and, sitting on the back of a virtuous elephant, would defecate and urinate, and walk about on its back. The elephant, because of its virtuous nature and endowment with patience, did nothing. Then one day, a young, ill-tempered elephant stood in that elephant's place. The monkey, thinking, “This is the same one,” climbed onto the back of the ill-tempered elephant. Then that elephant grabbed it with its trunk, placed it on the ground, stepped on it with its foot, and crushed it. This incident became known among the community of bhikkhus. Then one day, the bhikkhus started a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: “Friends, it seems a mischievous monkey, mistaking an ill-tempered elephant for a virtuous one, climbed on its back, and the elephant caused its death.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you sitting together here now?” When they told him, “For this one,” he said, “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this mischievous monkey has been of such a nature; from ancient times he has been of such a nature.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese mahiṃsayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto thāmasampanno mahāsarīro [M 2.0346] pabbatapādapabbhāragiriduggavanaghaṭesu vicaranto ekaṃ phāsukaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ disvā gocaraṃ gahetvā divā tasmiṃ rukkhamūle aṭṭhāsi. Atheko lolamakkaṭo rukkhā otaritvā tassa piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhitvā uccārapassāvaṃ katvā siṅge gaṇhitvā olambanto naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā dolāyantova kīḷi. Bodhisatto khantimettānuddayasampadāya taṃ tassa anācāraṃ na manasākāsi, makkaṭo punappunaṃ tatheva kari. Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā rukkhakkhandhe ṭhatvā naṃ “mahiṃsarāja [P 2.0386] kasmā imassa duṭṭhamakkaṭassa avamānaṃ sahasi, nisedhehi na”nti vatvā etamatthaṃ pakāsentī purimā dve gāthā avoca –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a buffalo in the Himalayan region. Having reached maturity, he was endowed with strength and had a large body. He roamed among the foothills, mountain slopes, impassable mountain terrain, and forest thickets. Seeing a pleasant spot at the foot of a tree, after grazing he stood there during the day. Then a mischievous monkey descended from the tree, climbed onto his back, defecated and urinated, grabbed his horns and hung down, and played, grabbing his tail and swinging on it as if on a swing. The Bodhisatta, endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, paid no mind to the monkey’s misbehavior. The monkey did the same thing again and again. Then one day, the deity dwelling in that tree stood on the tree trunk and said to him, “O king of buffaloes, why do you endure the insults of this wicked monkey? Stop him!” To make this matter clear, she spoke the first two verses:

82.

82.

“Kimatthamabhisandhāya, lahucittassa dubbhino;

Sabbakāmadadasseva, imaṃ dukkhaṃ titikkhasi.

“For what reason do you tolerate this suffering from this fickle-minded and treacherous one, you who are as patient as the earth that grants all desires?”

83.

83.

“Siṅgena nihanāhetaṃ, padasā ca adhiṭṭhaha;

Bhiyyo bālā pakujjheyyuṃ, no cassa paṭisedhako”ti.

“Strike him down with your horn, and trample him with your foot. Fools will misbehave even more if there is no one to restrain them.”

Tattha kimatthamabhisandhāyāti kiṃ nu kho kāraṇaṃ paṭicca kiṃ sampassamāno. Dubbhinoti mittadubbhissa. Sabbakāmadadassevāti sabbakāmadadassa sāmikassa iva. Titikkhasīti adhivāsesi. Padasā ca adhiṭṭhahāti pādena ca naṃ tiṇhakhuraggena yathā ettheva marati, evaṃ akkama. Bhiyyo bālāti sace hi paṭisedhako na bhaveyya, bālā aññāṇasattā punappunaṃ kujjheyyuṃ ghaṭṭeyyuṃ viheṭheyyuṃ evāti dīpeti.

Herein, 'For what reason' means for what reason, based on what cause, seeing what? 'Of the treacherous one' means of one who betrays friends. 'Like a giver of all desires' means like a master who gives all desires. 'You tolerate' means you endure. 'And trample with your foot' means trample him with your sharp-hoofed foot so that he dies right there, thus step on him. 'Fools even more'—this shows that if there were no one to restrain them, foolish, ignorant beings would repeatedly become angry, strike, and harass.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “rukkhadevate, sacāhaṃ iminā jātigottabalādīhi adhiko samāno imassa dosaṃ na sahissāmi, kathaṃ me manoratho nipphattiṃ gamissati. Ayaṃ pana maṃ viya aññampi maññamāno evaṃ anācāraṃ karissati, tato yesaṃ caṇḍamahiṃsānaṃ esa evaṃ karissati[V 2.0318], eteyeva etaṃ vadhissanti. Sā tassa aññehi māraṇā mayhaṃ dukkhato ca pāṇātipātato ca vimutti bhavissatī”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said: ‘O tree deity, if I, being superior to him in birth, lineage, strength, and so on, do not endure his offense, how will my heart's desire be fulfilled? This monkey, thinking another is also like me, will misbehave in the same way. Then those fierce buffaloes to whom he does this will themselves kill him. That killing by others will be a release for me from suffering and from the taking of life.’ Having said this, he spoke the third verse:

84.

84.

“Mamevāyaṃ maññamāno, aññepevaṃ karissati;

Te naṃ tattha vadhissanti, sā me mutti bhavissatī”ti.

‘Thinking another is just like me, he will act in the same way; they will kill him there, and that will be my release.’

Katipāhaccayena [M 2.0347] pana bodhisatto aññattha gato. Añño caṇḍamahiṃso tattha āgantvā aṭṭhāsi. Duṭṭhamakkaṭo “soyeva [P 2.0387] aya”nti saññāya tassa piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhitvā tatheva anācāraṃ cari. Atha naṃ so vidhunanto bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā siṅgena hadaye vijjhitvā pādehi madditvā sañcuṇṇesi.

After a few days had passed, the Bodhisatta went elsewhere. Another fierce buffalo came and stood there. The wicked monkey, thinking, ‘This is the same one,’ climbed onto its back and misbehaved in the same manner. Then that buffalo, shaking him off, threw him to the ground, pierced his heart with its horn, trampled him with its feet, and crushed him to pieces.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā duṭṭhamahiṃso ayaṃ duṭṭhahatthī ahosi, duṭṭhamakkaṭo etarahi ayaṃ makkaṭo, sīlavā mahiṃsarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse to a conclusion and revealed the Truths, identified the birth: ‘At that time, the fierce buffalo was this fierce elephant, the wicked monkey was this present monkey, but the virtuous buffalo-king was I myself.’

Mahiṃsarājajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Eighth, the Commentary on the Buffalo King Jātaka, is finished.

[279] 9. Satapattajātakavaṇṇanā

[279] 9. 9. The Commentary on the Satapatta Jātaka (Mistaking an enemy for a friend)

Yathā māṇavako pantheti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paṇḍukalohitake ārabbha kathesi. Chabbaggiyānañhi dve janā mettiyabhūmajakā rājagahaṃ upanissāya vihariṃsu, dve assajipunabbasukā kīṭāgiriṃ upanissāya vihariṃsu, paṇḍukalohitakā ime pana dve sāvatthiṃ upanissāya jetavane vihariṃsu. Te dhammena nīhaṭaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ ukkoṭenti. Yepi tesaṃ sandiṭṭhasambhattā honti, tesaṃ upatthambhā hutvā “na, āvuso, tumhe etehi jātiyā vā gottena vā sīlena vā nihīnatarā. Sace tumhe attano gāhaṃ vissajjetha, suṭṭhutaraṃ vo ete adhibhavissantī”tiādīni vatvā gāhaṃ vissajjetuṃ na denti. Tena bhaṇḍanāni ceva kalahaviggahavivādā ca pavattanti. Bhikkhū etamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Atha bhagavā etasmiṃ nidāne etasmiṃ pakaraṇe bhikkhū sannipātāpetvā paṇḍukalohitake pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, attanāpi adhikaraṇaṃ ukkoṭetha, aññesampi gāhaṃ vissajjetuṃ na dethā”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “evaṃ sante, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ kiriyā satapattamāṇavassa kiriyā viya hotī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘Just as the young man on the path...’: The Teacher told this story while dwelling in Jetavana concerning the monks Paᅇᄉuka and Lohitaka. Of the group-of-six monks, two, Mettiya and Bhũmajaka, lived depending on Rājagaha; two, Assaji and Punabbasuka, lived depending on Kĩᅡᄁiri; and these two, Paᅇᄉuka and Lohitaka, lived depending on Sāvatthĩ in Jetavana. They would reopen a legal case that had been settled in accordance with the Dhamma. Those who were their friends and companions would support them, saying: ‘Friends, you are not inferior to them in birth, clan, or virtue. If you abandon your view, they will completely overpower you,’ and so on, not allowing them to abandon their view. Because of this, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, and contentions arose.
