The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this context, had the community of monks assembled, summoned Paᅇᄉuka and Lohitaka, and asked: ‘Is it true, monks, that you yourselves reopen legal cases and do not allow others to abandon their view?’ When they replied, ‘It is true, Venerable Sir,’ he said, ‘In that case, monks, your action is like the action of the woodpecker and the young man.’ And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 2.0319][M 2.0348] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto aññatarasmiṃ kāsigāmake ekasmiṃ kule nibbattitvā vayappatto kasivaṇijjādīhi jīvikaṃ akappetvā pañcasatamatte [P 2.0388] core gahetvā tesaṃ jeṭṭhako hutvā panthadūhanasandhicchedādīni karonto jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ eko kuṭumbiko ekassa jānapadassa kahāpaṇasahassaṃ datvā puna aggahetvāva kālamakāsi. Athassa bhariyā aparabhāge gilānā maraṇamañce nipannā puttaṃ āmantetvā “tāta, pitā te ekassa sahassaṃ datvā anāharāpetvāva mato, sace ahampi marissāmi, na so tuyhaṃ dassati, gaccha naṃ mayi jīvantiyā āharāpetvā gaṇhā”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tattha gantvā kahāpaṇe labhi. Athassa mātā kālakiriyaṃ katvā puttasinehena tassa āgamanamagge opapātikasiṅgālī hutvā nibbati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāᅇasĩ, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a certain family in a village of the Kāsi country. When he came of age, not making a living by farming, trade, and so on, he gathered about five hundred robbers, became their chief, and made his living by committing highway robbery, housebreaking, and the like. At that time in Bārāᅇasĩ, a certain householder had given a thousand kahāpaᅇas to a country-dweller but died without having collected it. Later his wife, having fallen ill and lying on her deathbed, addressed her son: ‘Dear son, your father gave someone a thousand kahāpaᅇas and died without having it collected. If I too die, that person will not give it to you. Go and have it collected and take it while I am still alive.’ He agreed, saying, ‘Very well,’ went there, and received the kahāpaᅇas. Then his mother died and, out of affection for her son, was reborn as a spontaneously arisen she-jackal on the path of his return.

Tadā so corajeṭṭhako maggapaṭipanne vilumpamāno sapariso tasmiṃ magge aṭṭhāsi. Atha sā siṅgālī putte aṭavīmukhaṃ sampatte “tāta, mā aṭaviṃ abhiruhi, corā ettha ṭhitā, te taṃ māretvā kahāpaṇe gaṇhissantī”ti punappunaṃ maggaṃ occhindamānā nivāreti. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ ajānanto “ayaṃ kāḷakaṇṇī siṅgālī mayhaṃ maggaṃ occhindatī”ti leḍḍudaṇḍaṃ gahetvā mātaraṃ palāpetvā aṭaviṃ paṭipajji. Atheko satapattasakuṇo “imassa purisassa hatthe kahāpaṇasahassaṃ atthi, imaṃ māretvā taṃ kahāpaṇaṃ gaṇhathā”ti viravanto corābhimukho pakkhandi. Māṇavo tena katakāraṇaṃ ajānanto “ayaṃ maṅgalasakuṇo, idāni me sotthi bhavissatī”ti cintetvā “vassa, sāmi, vassa, sāmī”ti vatvā añjaliṃ paggaṇhi.

At that time the robber chief, plundering travelers on the road, stood on that path with his retinue. Then the she-jackal, when her son reached the entrance to the wilderness, repeatedly blocked his path to stop him, thinking: ‘Dear son, do not enter the wilderness. Robbers are standing here; they will kill you and take the kahāpaᅇas.’ Not knowing the reason, he thought, ‘This unlucky jackal is blocking my path!’ and taking a clod and a stick, he drove his mother away and entered the wilderness. Then a woodpecker, crying out, ‘This man has a thousand kahāpaᅇas in his hand! Kill him and take the kahāpaᅇas!’ flew towards the robbers. The young man, not knowing the reason for its action, thought, ‘This is an auspicious bird; now I will have good fortune!’ and raising his hands in reverence, he said, ‘Cry, master, cry, master!’

Bodhisatto sabbarutaññū tesaṃ dvinnaṃ kiriyaṃ disvā cintesi – imāya siṅgāliyā etassa mātarā bhavitabbaṃ, tena sā “imaṃ māretvā kahāpaṇe gaṇhantī”ti bhayena vāreti. Iminā pana satapattena paccāmittena bhavitabbaṃ, tena so “imaṃ māretvā kahāpaṇe gaṇhathā”ti amhākaṃ ārocesi. Ayaṃ pana etamatthaṃ ajānanto atthakāmaṃ [P 2.0389] mātaraṃ tajjetvā palāpesi, anatthakāmassa satapattassa “atthakāmo me”ti saññāya añjaliṃ paggaṇhāti, aho vatāyaṃ bāloti[M 2.0349]. Bodhisattānañhi evaṃ mahāpurisānampi sataṃ parasantakaggahaṇaṃ visamapaṭisandhiggahaṇavasena hoti, “nakkhattadosenā”tipi vadanti.

The Bodhisatta, who knew all sounds, saw the actions of those two and reflected: "This she-jackal must be his mother; therefore, out of fear that he would be killed and his coins taken, she is trying to stop him. But this woodpecker must be his enemy; therefore, he informed us, saying, 'Kill this one and take the coins.' Yet this fool, not understanding the matter, scolds and drives away his mother who wishes him well, and with the perception that the ill-wishing woodpecker 'wishes me well,' he raises his hands in reverence to it. Alas, how foolish he is!" For even in the case of such great beings as Bodhisattas, the taking of what belongs to another occurs by way of an irregular rebirth and so forth; it is also said to be due to a defect in the constellations.

Māṇavo āgantvā corānaṃ sīmantaraṃ pāpuṇi. Bodhisatto taṃ gāhāpetvā “kattha vāsikosī”ti pucchi. “Bārāṇasivāsikomhī”ti. “Kahaṃ agamāsī”ti? “Ekasmiṃ gāmake sahassaṃ laddhabbaṃ atthi, tattha agamāsi”nti. “Laddhaṃ pana te”ti? “Āma, laddha”nti[V 2.0320]. “Kena tvaṃ pesitosī”ti? “Sāmi, pitā me mato, mātāpi me gilānā, sā ‘mayi matāya esa na labhissatī’ti maññamānā maṃ pesesī”ti. “Idāni tava mātu pavattiṃ jānāsī”ti? “Na jānāmi, sāmī”ti. “Mātā te tayi nikkhante kālaṃ katvā puttasinehena siṅgālī hutvā tava maraṇabhayabhītā maggaṃ te occhinditvā taṃ vāresi, taṃ tvaṃ tajjetvā palāpesi, satapattasakuṇo pana te paccāmitto. So ‘imaṃ māretvā kahāpaṇe gaṇhathā’ti amhākaṃ ācikkhi, tvaṃ attano bālatāya atthakāmaṃ mātaraṃ ‘anatthakāmā me’ti maññasi, anatthakāmaṃ satapattaṃ ‘atthakāmo me’ti. Tassa tumhākaṃ kataguṇo nāma natthi, mātā pana te mahāguṇā, kahāpaṇe gahetvā gacchā”ti vissajjesi.

The young man arrived and entered the thieves' territory. The Bodhisatta had him seized and asked, "Where do you live?" "I am from Bārāṇasī." "Where did you go?" "There is a village where a thousand coins were to be had, so I went there." "And did you get them?" "Yes, I got them." "Who sent you?" "Master, my father is dead and my mother is ill. Thinking, 'If I die, he will not get this,' she sent me." "Do you know what has happened to your mother now?" "I do not know, master." "After you left, your mother died out of love for her son. She became a she-jackal and, terrified by the fear of your death, she blocked your path to stop you. But you scolded her and drove her away. The woodpecker, however, was your enemy. He told us, 'Kill this one and take the coins.' Because of your foolishness, you think your well-wishing mother is an ill-wisher, and the ill-wishing woodpecker is a well-wisher. He has done you no good at all, but your mother has been of great good to you. Take the coins and go." And he let him go.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā avoca –

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse and, as the Perfectly Enlightened One, spoke these verses:

85.

85.

“Yathā māṇavako panthe, siṅgāliṃ vanagocariṃ;

Atthakāmaṃ pavedentiṃ, anatthakāmāti maññati;

Anatthakāmaṃ satapattaṃ, atthakāmoti maññati.

"Just as the young man on the path regarded the she-jackal roaming the woods, who was showing her good will, as an ill-wisher, and regarded the ill-wishing woodpecker as a well-wisher."

86.

86.

“Evameva idhekacco, puggalo hoti tādiso;

Hitehi vacanaṃ vutto, paṭiggaṇhāti vāmato.

"Even so, in this world, a certain person is of such a kind: when spoken to by his well-wishers, he takes their words wrongly."

87.

87.

“Ye [P 2.0390] ca kho naṃ pasaṃsanti, bhayā ukkaṃsayanti vā;

Tañhi so maññate mittaṃ, satapattaṃva māṇavo”ti.

"But those who praise him, or exalt him out of fear, he considers them his friends, just as the young man did the woodpecker."

Tattha hitehīti hitaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ icchamānehi. Vacanaṃ vuttoti hitasukhāvahaṃ ovādānusāsanaṃ vutto. Paṭiggaṇhāti vāmatoti ovādaṃ agaṇhanto “ayaṃ me na atthāvaho hoti, anatthāvaho me aya”nti gaṇhanto vāmato paṭiggaṇhāti nāma.

Herein, by his well-wishers means by those who desire his welfare and growth. When told a word means when he is given advice and instruction that brings welfare and happiness. He takes it wrongly means that, not accepting the advice, he takes it perversely, thinking, "This person is not beneficial to me, he is harmful to me."

Ye [M 2.0350] ca kho nanti ye ca kho taṃ attano gāhaṃ gahetvā ṭhitapuggalaṃ “adhikaraṇaṃ gahetvā ṭhitehi nāma tumhādisehi bhavitabba”nti vaṇṇenti. Bhayā ukkaṃsayanti vāti imassa gāhassa vissaṭṭhapaccayā tumhākaṃ idañcidañca bhayaṃ uppajjissati, mā vissajjayittha, na ete bāhusaccakulaparivārādīhi tumhe sampāpuṇantīti evaṃ vissajjanapaccayā bhayaṃ dassetvā ukkhipanti. Tañhi so maññate mittanti ye evarūpā honti, tesu yaṃkiñci so ekacco bālapuggalo [V 2.0321] attano bālatāya mittaṃ maññati, “ayaṃ me atthakāmo mitto”ti maññati. Satapattaṃva māṇavoti yathā anatthakāmaññeva satapattaṃ so māṇavo attano bālatāya “atthakāmo me”ti maññati, paṇḍito pana evarūpaṃ “anuppiyabhāṇī mitto”ti agahetvā dūratova naṃ vivajjeti. Tena vuttaṃ –

But those who means those who praise that person who stands holding to his own view, saying, "People like you should indeed be ones who stand holding to a cause." Or exalt him out of fear means they exalt him by showing the fear that is a condition for abandoning, saying: "Because of abandoning this view, this and that fear will arise for you. Do not abandon it! Those others cannot match you in extensive learning, family, retinue, and so on." He considers them his friends means that foolish person, out of his own foolishness, considers any of those who are of such a kind to be a friend, thinking, "This is my well-wishing friend." Just as the young man did the woodpecker means: just as that young man, out of his own foolishness, considered the woodpecker, who was in fact an ill-wisher, to be his well-wisher. A wise person, however, does not regard such a person as a "friend who speaks agreeably" but avoids him from afar. Therefore it is said:

“Aññadatthuharo mitto, yo ca mitto vacīparo;

Anuppiyañca yo āha, apāyesu ca yo sakhā.

"The friend who is a mere taker, the friend who pays lip service, the one who flatters, and the companion in ruin—

“Ete amitte cattāro, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, maggaṃ paṭibhayaṃ yathā”ti. (dī. ni. 3.259);

these four are foes. Having thus discerned, the wise person should avoid them from afar, as one would a perilous path."

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā corajeṭṭhako ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth, saying: "At that time, the chief of the thieves was I myself."

Satapattajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Satapatta Jātaka, the ninth.

[280] 10. Puṭadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā

[280] 10. 10. The Commentary on the Puṭadūsaka Jātaka

Addhā hi nūna migarājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ puṭadūsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kireko amacco buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā uyyāne nisīdāpetvā [P 2.0391] dānaṃ dadamāno “antarābhatte uyyāne caritukāmā carantū”ti āha. Bhikkhū uyyānacārikaṃ cariṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe uyyānapālo pattasampannaṃ rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā mahantamahantāni paṇṇāni gahetvā “ayaṃ pupphānaṃ bhavissati, ayaṃ phalāna”nti puṭe katvā rukkhamūle pāteti. Tassa putto dārako pātitapātitaṃ puṭaṃ viddhaṃseti. Bhikkhū tamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Satthā [M 2.0351] “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa puṭadūsakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Surely now, the king of beasts.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a spoiler of leaf-containers. It seems that in Sāvatthī, a certain minister invited the Bhikkhu Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head, had them seated in a park, and while giving alms said, “In the interval before the meal, let those who wish to walk about in the park do so.” The bhikkhus went for a walk in the park. At that moment, the park keeper climbed a tree rich in leaves, and taking very large leaves, he made them into containers, thinking, “This one will be for flowers, this one for fruit,” and dropped them at the foot of the tree. His young son would destroy each container as it was dropped. The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, not only now is he a spoiler of leaf-containers; he was one in the past as well,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ ekasmiṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto agāraṃ ajjhāvasamāno ekadivasaṃ kenacideva karaṇīyena uyyānaṃ agamāsi. Tattha bahū vānarā vasanti. Uyyānapālo imināva niyāmena pattapuṭe pāteti, jeṭṭhavānaro pātitapātite viddhaṃseti. Bodhisatto taṃ āmantetvā “uyyānapālena pātitapātitaṃ puṭaṃ viddhaṃsetvā manāpataraṃ kātukāmo maññe”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family in Bārāṇasī. Having come of age and living the household life, one day he went to a park on some business. Many monkeys lived there. The park keeper, in just this way, was dropping leaf-containers, and the chief monkey was destroying each one as it was dropped. The Bodhisatta addressed him and said, “I suppose you are destroying each leaf-container dropped by the park keeper because you wish to make a more pleasing one,” and he spoke the first verse:

88.

88.

“Addhā [V 2.0322] hi nūna migarājā, puṭakammassa kovido;

Tathā hi puṭaṃ dūseti, aññaṃ nūna karissatī”ti.

“Surely the king of beasts is skilled in making leaf-containers; for he spoils the container thus, surely he will make another.”

Tattha migarājāti makkaṭaṃ vaṇṇento vadati. Puṭakammassāti mālāpuṭakaraṇassa. Kovidoti cheko. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – ayaṃ migarājā ekaṃsena puṭakammassa kovido maññe, tathā hi pātitapātitaṃ puṭaṃ dūseti, aññaṃ nūna tato manāpataraṃ karissatīti.

Herein, “king of beasts”: he says this describing the monkey. “Of making leaf-containers” means of making leaf-containers for garlands. “Skilled” means clever. This is the concise meaning here: “This king of beasts, I think, is certainly skilled in making leaf-containers, for he spoils each container as it is dropped; surely he will make another more pleasing than that.”

Taṃ sutvā makkaṭo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the monkey spoke the second verse:

89.

89.

“Na me mātā vā pitā vā, puṭakammassa kovido;

Kataṃ kataṃ kho dūsema, evaṃ dhammamidaṃ kula”nti.

“Neither my mother nor my father is skilled in making leaf-containers. We spoil whatever has been made; such is the nature of this clan.”

Taṃ [P 2.0392] sutvā bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:

90.

90.

“Yesaṃ vo ediso dhammo, adhammo pana kīdiso;

Mā vo dhammaṃ adhammaṃ vā, addasāma kudācana”nti.

“If such is your nature, then what is your bad conduct like? May we never, at any time, see either your nature or your bad conduct!”

Evaṃ vatvā ca pana vānaragaṇaṃ garahitvā pakkāmi.

And having spoken thus and rebuked the troop of monkeys, he departed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vānaro puṭadūsakadārako ahosi, paṇḍitapuriso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, identified the birth: “At that time, the monkey was the leaf-container-spoiling boy, but the wise man was I myself.”

Puṭadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Puṭadūsaka Jātaka, the tenth.

Udapānavaggo tatiyo.

The Udapāna Chapter, the third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Udapānavaraṃ [M 2.0352] vanabyaggha kapi, sikhinī ca balāka ruciravaro;

Sujanādhipa romaka dūsa puna, satapattavaro puṭakamma dasāti.

Excellent Udapāna, Forest Tiger, Monkey, Peahen and Crane, excellent Rucira; Lord of Good Men, Romaka, Dūsa again, excellent Satapatta, and Puṭakamma make ten.

4. Abbhantaravaggo

4. The Abbhantara Chapter

[281] 1. Abbhantarajātakavaṇṇanā

[281] 1. The Commentary on the Abbhantara Jātaka

Abbhantaro [V 2.0323] nāma dumoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāriputtattherassa bimbādevītheriyā ambarasadānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sammāsambuddhe hi pavattitavaradhammacakke vesāliyaṃ kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ viharante mahāpajāpatī gotamī pañca sākiyasatāni ādāya gantvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajjañceva upasampadañca labhi. Aparabhāge tā pañcasatā bhikkhuniyo nandakovādaṃ (ma. ni. 3.398 ādayo) sutvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Satthari pana sāvatthiṃ upanissāya viharante rāhulamātā bimbādevī “sāmiko me pabbajitvā sabbaññutaṃ patto, puttopi me pabbajitvā tasseva santike vasati, ahaṃ agāramajjhe kiṃkarissāmi, ahampi pabbajitvā sāvatthiṃ gantvā sammāsambuddhañca puttañca nibaddhaṃ passamānā viharissāmī”ti cintetvā bhikkhunupassayaṃ gantvā pabbajitvā ācariyupajjhāyāhi saddhiṃ sāvatthiṃ gantvā satthārañca piyaputtañca passamānā ekasmiṃ bhikkhunupassaye vāsaṃ kappesi. Rāhulasāmaṇero āgantvā mātaraṃ passati.

“Abbhantara is the name of a tree”—this the Teacher told while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the gift of mango juice by the Elder Sāriputta to the Therī Bimbādevī. For when the Perfectly Enlightened One had set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma and was dwelling in the Peaked Hall at Vesālī, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, taking five hundred Sakyan women with her, went and requested ordination, and received both the going forth and the higher ordination. Later, those five hundred nuns attained Arahantship after listening to the Nandakovāda Sutta. But when the Teacher was dwelling near Sāvatthī, Rāhula’s mother, Bimbādevī, thought: “My husband has gone forth and attained omniscience, and my son too has gone forth and lives in his presence. What shall I do in the household? I too will go forth, go to Sāvatthī, and dwell there, constantly seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One and my dear son.” Having thus reflected, she went to the nunnery, went forth, and traveled to Sāvatthī with her teachers and preceptors. There, seeing the Teacher and her dear son, she took up residence in a certain nunnery. The novice Rāhula came to see his mother.

Athekadivasaṃ theriyā udaravāto [P 2.0393] kuppi. Sā putte daṭṭhuṃ āgate tassa dassanatthāya nikkhamituṃ nāsakkhi, aññāva āgantvā aphāsukabhāvaṃ kathayiṃsu. So mātu santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ te laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pucchi. “Tāta, agāramajjhe me sakkharayojite ambarase pīte udaravāto vūpasammati, idāni piṇḍāya caritvā jīvikaṃ kappema, kuto taṃ labhissāmā”ti. Sāmaṇero “labhanto āharissāmī”ti vatvā nikkhami. Tassa [M 2.0353] panāyasmato upajjhāyo dhammasenāpati, ācariyo mahāmoggallāno, cūḷapitā ānandatthero, pitā sammāsambuddhoti mahāsampatti. Evaṃ santepi aññassa santikaṃ agantvā upajjhāyassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā dummukhākāro hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ thero “kiṃ nu kho, rāhula, dummukho viyāsī”ti āha. “Mātu me, bhante, theriyā udaravāto kupito”ti. “Kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Sakkharayojitena kira ambarasena phāsu hotī”ti. “Hotu labhissāmi, mā cintayī”ti.

Then one day, the Therī’s stomach wind was disturbed. When her son came to see her, she was unable to go out to meet him; others who came told of her discomfort. He went to his mother and asked, “What should you obtain?” “Dear son, when I lived in the household, my stomach wind would subside when I drank mango juice mixed with sugar. Now we live by walking for alms; where will we get that?” The novice said, “If I can get it, I will bring it,” and departed. Now, that venerable one's preceptor was the General of the Dhamma, his teacher was Mahāmoggallāna, his uncle was the Elder Ānanda, and his father was the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha—such was his great prosperity. Even so, without going to anyone else, he went to his preceptor, paid homage, and stood there with a dejected expression. Then the Elder said to him, “Why, Rāhula, do you stand as if dejected?” “Venerable sir, my mother the Therī’s stomach wind is disturbed.” “What should she obtain?” “It is said that mango juice mixed with sugar would be beneficial.” “Let it be, I will get it; do not worry,” the Elder said.

So [V 2.0324] punadivase taṃ ādāya sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā sāmaṇeraṃ āsanasālāyaṃ nisīdāpetvā rājadvāraṃ agamāsi. Kosalarājā theraṃ disvā nisīdāpesi, taṅkhaṇaññeva uyyānapālo piṇḍipakkānaṃ madhuraambānaṃ ekaṃ puṭaṃ āhari. Rājā ambānaṃ tacaṃ apanetvā sakkharaṃ pakkhipitvā sayameva madditvā therassa pattaṃ pūretvā adāsi. Thero rājanivesanā nikkhamitvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā sāmaṇerassa adāsi “haritvā mātu te dehī”ti. So haritvā adāsi, theriyā paribhuttamatteva udaravāto vūpasami. Rājāpi manussaṃ pesesi – “thero idha nisīditvā ambarasaṃ na paribhuñji, gaccha kassaci dinnabhāvaṃ jānāhī”ti. So therena saddhiṃyeva gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā āgantvā rañño kathesi. Rājā cintesi – “sace satthā agāraṃ ajjhāvasissa, cakkavattirājā abhavissa, rāhulasāmaṇero pariṇāyakaratanaṃ, therī itthiratanaṃ, sakalacakkavāḷarajjaṃ etesaññeva abhavissa. Amhehi ete upaṭṭhahantehi caritabbaṃ assa, idāni pabbajitvā amhe upanissāya vasantesu etesu na yuttaṃ amhākaṃ pamajjitu”nti. So tato paṭṭhāya theriyā nibaddhaṃ ambarasaṃ dāpesi. Therena bimbādevītheriyā ambarasassa dinnabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo jāto. Athekadivasaṃ [P 2.0394] bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, sāriputtatthero kira bimbādevītheriṃ ambarasena santappesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva rāhulamātā sāriputtena ambarasena santappitā, pubbepesa etaṃ santappesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

On the following day, taking him along, he entered Sāvatthī, had the novice sit in the alms-hall, and went to the king’s gate. The King of Kosala, seeing the Elder, had him seated. At that very moment, a park keeper brought a basket of sweet, tree-ripened mangoes. The king peeled the mangoes, added sugar, mashed them with his own hands, filled the Elder’s bowl, and gave it to him. Leaving the king’s palace, the Elder went to the alms-hall and gave it to the novice, saying, “Take this and give it to your mother.” He took it and gave it to her, and as soon as the Therī had consumed it, her stomach wind subsided. The king also sent a man, saying, “The Elder sat here but did not consume the mango juice. Go and find out to whom it was given.” The man went along with the Elder, learned what had happened, returned, and told the king. The king reflected: “If the Teacher had remained in the household life, he would have been a wheel-turning monarch, the novice Rāhula would have been the counselor-treasure, and the Therī the woman-treasure; the sovereignty over the entire world-system would have been theirs. We would have had to attend on them. Now that they have gone forth and live depending on us, it is not right for us to be negligent.” From then on, he had mango juice regularly given to the Therī. The Elder’s gift of mango juice to the Therī Bimbādevī became known in the Saṅgha of monks. One day, the monks raised a topic of discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, it seems the Elder Sāriputta satisfied the Therī Bimbādevī with mango juice.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “For what reason, monks, are you now gathered here talking?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Rāhula’s mother has been satisfied by Sāriputta with mango juice. In the past, too, he satisfied her.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 2.0354] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsigāmake brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā saṇṭhapitagharāvāso mātāpitūnaṃ accayena isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantapadese abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā isigaṇaparivuto gaṇasatthā hutvā dīghassa addhuno accayena loṇambilasevanatthāya pabbatapādā otaritvā cārikaṃ caramāno bārāṇasiṃ patvā uyyāne vāsaṃ kappesi. Athassa isigaṇassa sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Sakko āvajjamāno taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “imesaṃ tāpasānaṃ avāsāya parisakkissāmi, atha te bhinnāvāsā upaddutā caramānā cittekaggataṃ na labhissanti, evaṃ me phāsukaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā “ko nu kho upāyo”ti vīmaṃsanto imaṃ upāyaṃ addasa – majjhimayāmasamanantare rañño aggamahesiyā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā ākāse ṭhatvā “bhadde, sace tvaṃ abbhantaraambapakkaṃ khādeyyāsi, puttaṃ labhissasi, so cakkavattirājā bhavissatī”ti ācikkhissāmi. Rājā deviyā kathaṃ sutvā ambapakkatthāya uyyānaṃ pesessati, athāhaṃ ambāni antaradhāpessāmi, rañño uyyāne ambānaṃ abhāvaṃ ārocessanti[V 2.0325], “ke te khādantī”ti vutte “tāpasā khādantī”ti vakkhanti, taṃ sutvā rājā tāpase pothetvā nīharāpessati, evaṃ te upaddutā bhavissantīti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a village in the Kāsi country. Having come of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, and after establishing a household, he went forth as a seer after his parents passed away. Dwelling in the Himalayan region, he developed the supernormal powers and meditative attainments. Surrounded by a company of seers, he became their teacher. After a long time had passed, he descended from the foothills of the mountains in order to seek salt and sour seasonings. Wandering on tour, he reached Bārāṇasī and stayed in a park. Then, by the power of the virtue of that company of seers, Sakka’s mansion trembled. Reflecting on the cause, Sakka understood and thought: “I will try to make the residence of these ascetics uninhabitable. Then, with their residence broken up, afflicted and wandering, they will not attain one-pointedness of mind. Thus it will be comfortable for me.” Considering what stratagem to use, he saw this one: “Just after the middle watch of the night, I will enter the chief queen’s private chamber, stand in the air, and declare: ‘Good lady, if you eat a ripe Abbhantara mango, you will bear a son who will become a wheel-turning monarch.’ Hearing the queen’s words, the king will send men to the park for a ripe mango. Then I will make the mangoes disappear. They will report to the king that there are no mangoes in the park. When asked, ‘Who is eating them?’ they will say, ‘The ascetics are eating them.’ Hearing this, the king will have the ascetics beaten and driven out. Thus they will be afflicted.”

So majjhimayāmasamanantare sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā ākāse ṭhito attano devarājabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā tāya saddhiṃ sallapanto purimā dve gāthā avoca –

So, just after the middle watch of the night, he entered the royal chamber and stood in the air. Making known his status as the king of the devas, he conversed with her and spoke the first two stanzas:

91.

91.

“Abbhantaro [P 2.0395] nāma dumo, yassa dibyamidaṃ phalaṃ;

Bhutvā dohaḷinī nārī, cakkavattiṃ vijāyati.

“There is a tree named Abbhantara, which has this divine fruit. A woman with a pregnancy craving, after eating it, gives birth to a wheel-turning monarch.

92.

92.

“Tvampi bhadde mahesīsi, sā cāpi patino piyā;

Āharissati te rājā, idaṃ abbhantaraṃ phala”nti.

“You too, good lady, are the chief queen, and you are dear to your husband. The king will have this Abbhantara fruit brought for you.”

Tattha abbhantaro nāma dumoti iminā tāva gāmanigamajanapadapabbatādīnaṃ asukassa abbhantaroti avatvā kevalaṃ ekaṃ abbhantaraṃ ambarukkhaṃ [M 2.0355] kathesi. Yassa dibyamidaṃ phalanti yassa ambarukkhassa devatānaṃ paribhogārahaṃ dibyaṃ phalaṃ. Idanti pana nipātamattameva. Dohaḷinīti sañjātadohaḷā. Tvampi, bhadde, mahesīsīti tvaṃ, sobhane mahesī, asi. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “mahesī cā”tipi pāṭho. Sā cāpi patino piyāti soḷasannaṃ devīsahassānaṃ abbhantare aggamahesī cāpi patino cāpi piyāti attho. Āharissati te rājā, idaṃ abbhantaraṃ phalanti tassā te piyāya aggamahesiyā idaṃ mayā vuttappakāraṃ phalaṃ rājā āharāpessati, sā tvaṃ taṃ paribhuñjitvā cakkavattigabbhaṃ labhissasīti.

Therein, regarding ‘There is a tree named Abbhantara’: by this, without specifying ‘the interior of such-and-such village, town, country, or mountain,’ he spoke of just a single mango tree named Abbhantara. ‘Whose fruit is this divine one’ means the divine fruit of that mango tree, fit to be enjoyed by deities. The word ‘idaṃ’ (this) is merely a particle. ‘Dohaḷinī’ means one in whom a pregnancy craving has arisen. ‘You too, good lady, are the chief queen’ means: ‘You, O beautiful one, are the chief queen.’ In the commentary, there is also the reading ‘mahesī ca.’ ‘And you are dear to your husband’ means that even among the sixteen thousand queens, she, the chief queen, is dear to her husband. ‘The king will have this Abbhantara fruit brought for you’ means: for you, his beloved chief queen, the king will have this fruit of the kind described brought. Then you, having partaken of it, will conceive a wheel-turning monarch.”

Evaṃ sakko deviyā imā dve gāthā vatvā “tvaṃ appamattā hohi, mā papañcaṃ akāsi, sve rañño āroceyyāsī”ti taṃ anusāsitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gato. Sā punadivase gilānālayaṃ dassetvā paricārikānaṃ saññaṃ datvā nipajji. Rājā samussitasetacchatte sīhāsane nisinno nāṭakāni passanto deviṃ adisvā “kahaṃ, devī”ti paricārike pucchi. “Gilānā, devā”ti. So tassā santikaṃ gantvā sayanapasse nisīditvā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjanto “kiṃ te, bhadde, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. “Mahārāja aññaṃ aphāsukaṃ nāma natthi, dohaḷo me uppanno”ti. “Kiṃ icchasi, bhadde”ti? “Abbhantaraambaphalaṃ devā”ti. “Abbhantaraambo nāma kahaṃ atthī”ti? “Nāhaṃ, deva, abbhantaraambaṃ jānāmi, tassa pana me phalaṃ labhamānāya jīvitaṃ atthi, alabhamānāya natthī”ti. “Tena hi āharāpessāmi[V 2.0326], mā cintayī”ti rājā deviṃ assāsetvā uṭṭhāya gantvā rājapallaṅke nisinno amacce pakkosāpetvā “deviyā [P 2.0396] abbhantaraambe nāma dohaḷo uppanno, kiṃ kātabba”nti pucchi. “Deva dvinnaṃ ambānaṃ antare ṭhito ambo abbhantaraambo nāma, uyyānaṃ pesetvā abbhantare ṭhitaambato phalaṃ āharāpetvā deviyā dāpethā”ti.

Having thus spoken these two verses to the queen, Sakka advised her, “Be heedful, do not delay; inform the king tomorrow,” and then returned to his own dwelling. The next day, feigning illness and giving a sign to her attendants, she lay down. The king, seated on his lion-throne under a raised white parasol watching the dancers, did not see the queen and asked the attendants, “Where is the queen?” “She is ill, your majesty.” He went to her, sat down by her bedside, and while stroking her back asked, “What ails you, dear lady?” “Great king, I have no other ailment, but a pregnancy craving has arisen in me.” “What do you desire, dear lady?” “The fruit of an inner mango, your majesty.” “Where is this so-called inner mango?” “I do not know, your majesty, where the inner mango is, but if I obtain its fruit, I shall live; if I do not obtain it, I shall die.” “Then I will have it brought; do not worry.” The king consoled the queen, rose, went and sat on the royal throne, summoned his ministers, and asked: “The queen has conceived a pregnancy craving for an inner mango. What is to be done?” “Your majesty, a mango tree that stands between two other mango trees is called an ‘inner mango.’ Send someone to the park, have the fruit from the mango tree standing in between brought, and give it to the queen.”

Rājā “sādhu, evarūpaṃ ambaṃ āharathā”ti uyyānaṃ pesesi. Sakko attano ānubhāvena uyyāne ambāni khāditasadisāni katvā antaradhāpesi. Ambatthāya gatā manussā sakalauyyānaṃ vicarantā ekaṃ ambampi alabhitvā gantvā uyyāne ambānaṃ abhāvaṃ rañño kathayiṃsu. “Ke [M 2.0356] ambāni khādantī”ti? “Tāpasā, devā”ti. “Tāpase uyyānato pothetvā nīharathā”ti. Manussā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā nīhariṃsu. Sakkassa manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇi. Devī ambaphalatthāya nibaddhaṃ katvā nipajjiyeva. Rājā kattabbakiccaṃ apassanto amacce ca brāhmaṇe ca sannipātāpetvā “abbhantaraambassa atthibhāvaṃ jānāthā”ti pucchi. Brāhmaṇā āhaṃsu – “deva, abbhantaraambo nāma devatānaṃ paribhogo, ‘himavante kañcanaguhāya anto atthī’ti ayaṃ no paramparāgato anussavo”ti. “Ko pana tato ambaṃ āharituṃ sakkhissatī”ti? “Na sakkā tattha manussabhūtena gantuṃ, ekaṃ suvapotakaṃ pesetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

The king said, “Very well, bring such a mango,” and sent men to the park. Sakka, by his power, made the mangoes in the park look as if they had been eaten and then made them disappear. The men who went for the mangoes searched the entire park, but not finding even a single mango, they went and reported to the king the absence of mangoes in the park. “Who is eating the mangoes?” the king asked. “The ascetics, Sire,” they replied. “Beat the ascetics and drive them out of the park!” the king said. The men assented, saying, “Very well,” and drove them out. Sakka’s wish was thus fulfilled. The queen, making a persistent demand for the mango fruit, just lay there. The king, seeing no way out, had his ministers and brahmins assemble and asked, “Do you know of the existence of the inner mango?” The brahmins said: “Sire, the so-called inner mango is for the enjoyment of the gods. We have an oral tradition passed down to us that it exists inside a golden cave in the Himalayas.” “Who then will be able to bring a mango from there?” the king asked. “It is not possible for a human being to go there. A young parrot should be sent.”

Tena ca samayena rājakule eko suvapotako mahāsarīro kumārakānaṃ yānakacakkanābhimatto thāmasampanno paññavā upāyakusalo. Rājā taṃ āharāpetvā “tāta suvapotaka, ahaṃ tava bahūpakāro, kañcanapañjare vasasi, suvaṇṇataṭṭake madhulāje khādasi, sakkharapānakaṃ pivasi, tayāpi amhākaṃ ekaṃ kiccaṃ nittharituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. “Kiṃ, devā”ti. “Tāta deviyā abbhantaraambe dohaḷo uppanno, so ca ambo himavante kañcanapabbatantare atthi devatānaṃ paribhogo, na sakkā [P 2.0397] manussabhūtena tattha gantuṃ, tayā tato ambaphalaṃ āharituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Sādhu, deva, āharissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ rājā suvaṇṇataṭṭake madhulāje khādāpetvā sakkharapānakaṃ pāyetvā satapākatelena tassa pakkhantarāni makkhetvā ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā sīhapañjare ṭhatvā ākāse vissajjesi. Sopi rañño nipaccakāraṃ dassetvā ākāse pakkhandanto manussapathaṃ atikkamma himavante paṭhame pabbatantare vasantānaṃ sukānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā abbhantaraambo nāma kattha atthi, kathetha me taṃ ṭhāna”nti pucchi. “Mayaṃ na jānāma, dutiye pabbatantare sukā jānissantī”ti.

At that time, there was in the royal household a young parrot with a large body, the size of the hub of a children’s chariot wheel, endowed with strength and wisdom, and skilled in means. The king had him brought and said: “My dear young parrot, I have been of great service to you. You live in a golden cage, eat honey-parched grain from a golden dish, and drink sugar-syrup. You too should now accomplish a task for us.” “What task is it, Sire?” he asked. “My dear, a craving for an inner mango has arisen in the queen. That mango is between the golden mountains in the Himalayas and is for the enjoyment of the gods. It is not possible for a human being to go there; you should bring the mango fruit from there.” “Very well, Sire, I will bring it,” he replied. Then the king had him eat honey-parched grain from a golden dish and drink sugar-syrup, anointed the spaces between his wings with oil refined a hundred times, and, holding him with both hands, stood at the lion-window and released him into the sky. Showing his respect to the king, the parrot soared into the sky, and passing beyond the path of humans, he went to the parrots dwelling in the first mountain range of the Himalayas and asked: “Where is the so-called inner mango? Tell me that place.” They replied: “We do not know. The parrots in the second mountain range will know.”

So tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā tato uppatitvā dutiyaṃ pabbatantaraṃ agamāsi, tathā tatiyaṃ, catutthaṃ[V 2.0327], pañcamaṃ, chaṭṭhaṃ agamāsi. Tatthapi naṃ sukā “na mayaṃ jānāma, sattamapabbatantare sukā jānissantī”ti āhaṃsu. So tatthapi gantvā “abbhantaraambo nāma kattha atthī”ti pucchi. “Asukaṭṭhāne nāma kañcanapabbatantare”ti āhaṃsu. “Ahaṃ tassa phalatthāya āgato, maṃ tattha netvā tato me phalaṃ dāpethā”ti. Sukagaṇā [M 2.0357] āhaṃsu – “samma, so vessavaṇamahārājassa paribhogo, na sakkā upasaṅkamituṃ, sakalarukkho mūlato paṭṭhāya sattahi lohajālehi parikkhitto, sahassakumbhaṇḍarakkhasā rakkhanti, tehi diṭṭhassa jīvitaṃ nāma natthi, kappuṭṭhānaggiavīcimahānirayasadisaṭṭhānaṃ, mā tattha patthanaṃ karī”ti. “Sace tumhe na gacchatha, mayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ ācikkhathā”ti. “Tena hi asukena ca asukena ca ṭhānena yāhī”ti. So tehi ācikkhitavaseneva suṭṭhu maggaṃ upadhāretvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā divā attānaṃ adassetvā majjhimayāmasamanantare rakkhasānaṃ niddokkamanasamaye abbhantaraambassa santikaṃ gantvā ekena mūlantarena saṇikaṃ abhiruhituṃ ārabhi. Lohajālaṃ “kirī”ti saddamakāsi[P 2.0398].

Hearing their words, he flew up from there and went to the second mountain valley, and likewise to the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth. There too the parrots said to him, 'We do not know; the parrots in the seventh mountain valley will know.' He went there as well and asked, 'Where is the mango tree named Abbhantara?' They said, 'In such and such a place, in a golden mountain valley.' 'I have come for the sake of its fruit; lead me there and give me fruit from that tree.' The flock of parrots said, 'Friend, that Abbhantara mango is for the use of the Great King Vessavaṇa; it is impossible to approach. The entire tree, from its roots, is enveloped in seven layers of iron nets. A thousand Kumbhaṇḍa demons guard it; for any creature seen by them, there is no life. The place is like the fire at the end of an aeon, like the great Avīci hell. Do not desire to go there.' 'If you will not go, then tell me the way,' he said. The parrots replied, 'In that case, go by such and such a place.' Following the path exactly as they had described, he reached that place. Not showing himself by day, just after the middle watch when the demons had fallen into sleep, he went to the Abbhantara mango tree and began to climb up slowly through a gap in the roots. The iron net made a 'kirī' sound.

Rakkhasā pabujjhitvā sukapotakaṃ disvā “ambacoroya”nti gahetvā kammakaraṇaṃ saṃvidahiṃsu. Eko “mukhe pakkhipitvā gilissāmi na”nti āha, aparo “hatthehi madditvā puñjitvā vippakirissāmi na”nti, aparo “dvedhā phāletvā aṅgāresu pacitvā khādissāmī”ti. So tesaṃ kammakaraṇasaṃvidhānaṃ sutvāpi asantasitvāva te rakkhase āmantetvā “ambho rakkhasā, tumhe kassa manussā”ti āha. “Vessavaṇamahārājassā”ti. “Ambho, tumhepi ekassa raññova manussā, ahampi raññova manusso, bārāṇasirājā maṃ abbhantaraambaphalatthāya pesesi, svāhaṃ tattheva attano rañño jīvitaṃ datvā āgato. Yo hi attano mātāpitūnañceva sāmikassa ca atthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajati, so devalokeyeva nibbattati, tasmā ahampi imamhā tiracchānayoniyā cavitvā devaloke nibbattissāmī”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The rakkhasas awoke and, seeing the young parrot, they seized him, saying, 'This is a mango thief!' and prepared an arrangement for his punishment. One said, 'I will put him in my mouth and swallow him!' Another said, 'I will crush him with my hands, crumble him, and scatter him!' Another said, 'I will split him in two, roast him on the coals, and eat him!' Hearing their preparation for punishment, the parrot, without any fear, addressed those rakkhasas, saying, 'Sirs, rakkhasas, whose men are you?' 'We belong to the Great King Vessavaṇa.' 'Sirs, you are the men of one king, and I too am the man of a king. The king of Bārāṇasī sent me for the sake of the inner mango fruit. I have come here, having given my life for my king in that very place. For whoever gives up his life for the sake of his parents and his master is reborn in the world of the gods. Therefore, I too, having passed away from this animal birth, will be reborn in the world of the gods.' Having said this, he spoke the third verse:

93.

93.

“Bhatturatthe parakkanto, yaṃ ṭhānamadhigacchati;

Sūro attapariccāgī, labhamāno bhavāmaha”nti.

Whatever state a self-sacrificing hero who strives for his master’s welfare attains, I am one who obtains that state.

Tattha bhatturattheti bhattā vuccanti bhattādīhi bharaṇaposakā pitā mātā sāmiko ca, iti tividhassapetassa bhattu atthāya. Parakkantoti parakkamaṃ karonto vāyamanto. Yaṃ ṭhānamadhigacchatīti yaṃ sukhakāraṇaṃ yasaṃ vā lābhaṃ vā saggaṃ vā adhigacchati. Sūroti abhīru vikkamasampanno. Attapariccāgīti [M 2.0358] kāye ca jīvite ca nirapekkho hutvā tassa tividhassapi bhattu atthāya attānaṃ pariccajanto. Labhamāno bhavāmahanti yaṃ so evarūpo sūro devasampattiṃ vā [V 2.0328] manussasampattiṃ vā labhati, ahampi taṃ labhamāno bhavāmi, tasmā hāsova me ettha, na tāso, kiṃ maṃ tumhe tāsethāti.

Herein, for his master’s welfare: a master is one who supports and nourishes with food and so on, namely, one’s father, mother, and lord; thus it means for the welfare of this threefold master. Striving: making an effort, exerting oneself. Whatever state he attains: whatever cause of happiness, or fame, or gain, or heaven he attains. Hero: fearless, endowed with courage. Self-sacrificing: being unconcerned with body and life, one gives up oneself for the welfare of that threefold master. May I be one who obtains it: whatever divine or human fortune such a hero obtains, I too shall be one who obtains it. Therefore, for me there is only joy in this, not terror. Why do you try to frighten me?

Evaṃ so imāya gāthāya tesaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. Te tassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā pasannacittā “dhammiko esa, na sakkā māretuṃ, vissajjema na”nti vatvā sukapotakaṃ vissajjetvā ‘ambho sukapotaka, muttosi, amhākaṃ hatthato sotthinā gacchā”ti [P 2.0399] āhaṃsu. “Mayhaṃ āgamanaṃ mā tucchaṃ karotha, detha me ekaṃ ambaphala”nti. “Sukapotaka, tuyhaṃ ekaṃ ambaphalaṃ dātuṃ nāma na bhāro, imasmiṃ pana rukkhe ambāni aṅketvā gahitāni, ekasmiṃ phale asamente amhākaṃ jīvitaṃ natthi. Vessavaṇena hi kujjhitvā sakiṃ olokite tattakapāle pakkhittatilā viya kumbhaṇḍasahassaṃ bhijjitvā vippakirīyati, tena te dātuṃ na sakkoma, labhanaṭṭhānaṃ pana ācikkhissāmā”ti. “Yo koci detu, phaleneva me attho, labhanaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhathā”ti. “Etassa kañcanapabbatassa antare jotiraso nāma tāpaso aggiṃ juhamāno kañcanapattiyā nāma paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasati vessavaṇassa kulūpako, vessavaṇo tassa nibaddhaṃ cattāri ambaphalāni peseti, tassa santikaṃ gacchā”ti.

Thus, with this verse, he taught them the Dhamma. Hearing his Dhamma talk, their minds were satisfied, and they said, 'This one is righteous; he cannot be killed. Let us release him.' So they released the young parrot and said, 'O young parrot, you are free. Go safely from our hands.' 'Do not make my coming here in vain. Give me one mango fruit.' 'Young parrot, it is no burden to give you one mango fruit. However, the mangoes on this tree have been marked and recorded. If even one fruit is missing, we will lose our lives. For if Vessavaṇa is angry and looks but once, a thousand kumbhaṇḍas would be broken and scattered like sesame seeds thrown on a hot pan. Therefore, we do not dare to give it to you. But we will tell you where it can be obtained.' 'Let anyone give it; I only need the fruit. Tell me where to get it.' 'Between this golden mountain, an ascetic named Jotirasa lives in a leaf-hut called Kañcanapatti, tending the sacred fire. He is the teacher of Vessavaṇa. Vessavaṇa regularly sends him four mango fruits. Go to him.'

So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tāpasassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ tāpaso “kuto āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Bārāṇasirañño santikā”ti. “Kimatthāya āgatosī”ti? “Sāmi, amhākaṃ rañño deviyā abbhantaraambapakke dohaḷo uppanno, tadatthaṃ āgatomhi, rakkhasā pana me sayaṃ ambapakkaṃ adatvā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pesesu”nti. “Tena hi nisīda, labhissasī”ti. Athassa vessavaṇo cattāri phalāni pesesi. Tāpaso tato dve paribhuñji, ekaṃ suvapotakassa khādanatthāya adāsi. Tena tasmiṃ khādite ekaṃ phalaṃ sikkāya pakkhipitvā suvapotakassa gīvāya paṭimuñcitvā “idāni gacchā”ti sukapotakaṃ vissajjesi[M 2.0359]. So taṃ āharitvā deviyā adāsi. Sā taṃ khāditvā dohaḷaṃ paṭippassambhesi, tatonidānaṃ panassā putto nāhosi.

He agreed, saying 'Very well,' went to the ascetic, paid homage, and sat down at one side. Then the ascetic asked him, 'Where have you come from?' 'From the presence of the king of Bārāṇasī.' 'For what purpose have you come?' 'Sir, our king's queen has a pregnancy craving for an inner mango fruit. I have come for that. But the rakkhasas, not giving the fruit themselves, sent me to you.' 'In that case, you shall have it,' said the ascetic. Then Vessavaṇa sent four fruits to the ascetic. The ascetic consumed two of those four fruits and gave one to the young parrot to eat. When it was eaten, he placed one fruit in a basket-net, tied it around the young parrot's neck, and released him, saying, 'Now go.' The young parrot took that fruit and gave it to the queen. She ate the fruit and her craving was satisfied. However, because of eating that mango, she did not conceive a son.

Satthā [P 2.0400] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā devī rāhulamātā ahosi, suko ānando, ambapakkadāyako tāpaso sāriputto, uyyāne nivutthatāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher identified the birth, saying: 'At that time, the queen was Rāhula's mother, the parrot was Ānanda, the ascetic who gave the ripe mango was Sāriputta, and the ascetic dwelling in the park was myself.'

Abbhantarajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Abbhantara Jātaka, the First.

[282] 2. Seyyajātakavaṇṇanā

[282] 2. The Commentary on the Seyya Jātaka

Seyyaṃso [V 2.0329] seyyaso hotīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kosalarañño amaccaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira rañño bahūpakāro sabbakiccanipphādako ahosi. Rājā “bahūpakāro me aya”nti tassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi. Taṃ asahamānā aññe rañño pesuññaṃ upasaṃharitvā taṃ paribhindiṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ vacanaṃ saddahitvā dosaṃ anupaparikkhitvāva taṃ sīlavantaṃ niddosaṃ saṅkhalikabandhanena bandhāpetvā bandhanāgāre pakkhipāpesi. So tattha ekako vasanto sīlasampattiṃ nissāya cittekaggataṃ labhitvā ekaggacitto saṅkhāre sammasitvā sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. Athassa rājā aparabhāge niddosabhāvaṃ ñatvā saṅkhalikabandhanaṃ bhindāpetvā purimayasato mahantataraṃ yasaṃ adāsi. So “satthāraṃ vandissāmī”ti bahūni mālāgandhādīni ādāya vihāraṃ gantvā tathāgataṃ pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto “anattho kira te uppannoti assumhā”ti āha. “Āma, bhante, uppanno, ahaṃ pana tena anatthena atthaṃ akāsiṃ, bandhanāgāre nisīditvā sotāpattiphalaṃ nibbattesi”nti. Satthā “na kho, upāsaka, tvaññeva anatthena atthaṃ āhari, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi attano anatthena atthaṃ āhariṃ suyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this story concerning a minister of the king of Kosala. It is said that this minister was of great service to the king and accomplished all his tasks. The king, thinking, 'This man is of great service to me,' bestowed great honor upon him. Others, unable to bear this, slandered him to the king and brought about his ruin. The king, believing their words without investigating the offense, had that virtuous and faultless minister bound in chains and thrown into prison. While dwelling there alone, relying on his perfection of virtue, he attained one-pointedness of mind and, contemplating the conditioned formations, attained the fruit of stream-entry. Later, the king, having realized his innocence, had his chains broken and bestowed upon him even greater honor than before. The minister, thinking, 'I will pay homage to the Teacher,' took many flowers, perfumes, and so on, went to the monastery, honored the Tathāgata, paid homage, and sat down at one side. The Teacher, exchanging friendly greetings with him, said, 'We have heard that a misfortune befell you.' 'Yes, venerable sir, it did. But I turned that misfortune into a benefit; while sitting in prison, I realized the fruit of stream-entry.' The Teacher said, 'Lay follower, it is not only you who has turned misfortune into benefit. The wise of old also brought benefit out of their own misfortune.' And being requested, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni [M 2.0360] uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya dasa rājadhamme akopetvā dānaṃ deti, pañca sīlāni rakkhati[P 2.0401], uposathakammaṃ karoti. Athasseko amacco antepure padussi. Pādamūlikādayo ñatvā “asukaamacco antepure paduṭṭho”ti rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā pariggaṇhanto yathāsabhāvato ñatvā pakkosāpetvā “mā maṃ ito paṭṭhāya upaṭṭhāhī”ti nibbisayaṃ akāsi. So gantvā aññataraṃ sāmantarājānaṃ upaṭṭhahīti sabbaṃ vatthu heṭṭhā mahāsīlavajātake (jā. 1.1.51) kathitasadisameva. Idhāpi so rājā tikkhattuṃ vīmaṃsitvā tassa amaccassa vacanaṃ saddahitvā “bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti mahantena parivārena rajjasīmaṃ pāpuṇi. Bārāṇasirañño sattasatamattā mahāyodhā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “deva, asuko nāma kira rājā bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti janapadaṃ bhindanto āgacchati, ettheva naṃ gantvā gaṇhissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. “Mayhaṃ paravihiṃsāya laddhena rajjena kiccaṃ natthi, mā kiñci karitthā”ti?

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā. After his father’s death, he was established on the throne and reigned righteously, upholding the ten royal duties without violation. He gave alms, observed the five precepts, and performed the uposatha observance. Now, one of his ministers committed an offense in the inner palace. The personal attendants and others came to know of it and reported to the king: "Such-and-such a minister has committed an offense in the inner palace." The king investigated the matter, and having learned the truth of it, he summoned the minister and banished him from the kingdom, saying: "From now on, do not attend upon me." The minister left and went to serve a neighboring king. The entire story is just as it was told below in the Mahāsīlava Jātaka. Here too, that king, after investigating the matter three times, trusted the minister’s word and, thinking, "I will seize the kingdom of Benares," reached the border of the kingdom with a large army. When the seven hundred great warriors of the king of Benares heard the news, they said: "Your Majesty, a certain king, it is said, is coming to seize the kingdom of Benares, laying waste to the countryside. Let us go and capture him right there." But the king replied: "I have no need for a kingdom obtained by harming others. Do nothing."

Corarājā [V 2.0330] āgantvā nagaraṃ parikkhipi, puna amaccā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, mā evaṃ karittha, gaṇhissāma na”nti āhaṃsu. Rājā “na labbhā kiñci kātuṃ, nagaradvārāni vivarathā”ti vatvā sayaṃ amaccagaṇaparivuto mahātale rājapallaṅke nisīdi. Corarājā catūsu dvāresu manusse pothento nagaraṃ pavisitvā pāsādaṃ abhiruyha amaccaparivutaṃ rājānaṃ gāhāpetvā saṅkhalikāhi bandhāpetvā bandhanāgāre pakkhipāpesi. Rājā bandhanāgāre nisinnova corarājānaṃ mettāyanto mettajjhānaṃ uppādesi. Tassa mettānubhāvena corarañño kāye ḍāho uppajji, sakalasarīraṃ yamakaukkāhi jhāpiyamānaṃ viya jātaṃ. So mahādukkhābhitunno “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti pucchi. “Tumhe sīlavantaṃ rājānaṃ bandhanāgāre pakkhipetha, tena vo idaṃ dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ bhavissatī”ti. So gantvā bodhisattaṃ khamāpetvā “tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ tumhākameva hotū”ti rajjaṃ tasseva [P 2.0402] niyyādetvā “ito paṭṭhāya tumhākaṃ paccatthiko me bhāro hotū”ti vatvā paduṭṭhāmaccassa rājāṇaṃ kāretvā attano nagarameva gato.

The robber king came and besieged the city. Again the ministers approached the king and said: "Your Majesty, do not act thus. We will capture him." The king replied: "Nothing can be done. Open the city gates." Then, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, he himself sat on the royal throne on the great terrace. The robber king entered the city, beating people at the four gates, ascended the palace, and had the king, who was surrounded by his ministers, seized, bound with chains, and thrown into prison. While sitting in prison, the king suffused the robber king with loving-kindness and developed the meditation on loving-kindness. Through the power of his loving-kindness, a burning sensation arose in the robber king's body; his entire body felt as if it were being scorched by twin torches. Overcome by great pain, he asked: "What can be the reason for this?" The attendants replied: "You have thrown a virtuous king into prison; that is why this suffering has arisen for you." He went and begged the Bodhisatta’s forgiveness. Saying, "Let your kingdom be yours alone," he handed the kingdom back to him. He then declared, "From now on, the responsibility for your enemies is mine," and having had the treacherous minister punished according to royal decree, he returned to his own city.

Bodhisatto alaṅkatamahātale samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisinno amaccehi saddhiṃ sallapanto purimā dvegāthā avoca –

The Bodhisatta, seated on the royal throne under a raised white parasol on the adorned great terrace, conversing with his ministers, spoke the first two verses:

94.

94.

“Seyyaṃso [M 2.0361] seyyaso hoti, yo seyyamupasevati;

Ekena sandhiṃ katvāna, sataṃ vajjhe amocayiṃ.

“One who associates with the superior becomes superior still; by making peace with one, I freed a hundred who were condemned to death.

95.

95.

“Tasmā sabbena lokena, sandhiṃ katvāna ekato;

Pecca saggaṃ nigaccheyya, idaṃ suṇātha kāsiyā”ti.

“Therefore, by making peace with all the world as one, on passing away one would go to heaven—hear this, O people of Kāsī!”

Tattha seyyaṃso seyyaso hoti, yo seyyamupasevatīti anavajjauttamadhammasaṅkhāto seyyo aṃso koṭṭhāso assāti seyyaṃso, kusaladhammanissitapuggalo. Yo punappunaṃ taṃ seyyaṃ kusaladhammabhāvanaṃ kusalābhirataṃ vā uttamapuggalamupasevati, so seyyaso hoti pāsaṃsataro ceva uttaritaro ca hoti. Ekena sandhiṃ katvāna, sataṃ vajjhe amocayinti tadamināpi cetaṃ veditabbaṃ – ahañhi seyyaṃ mettābhāvanaṃ upasevanto tāya mettābhāvanāya ekena coraraññā sandhiṃ santhavaṃ katvā mettābhāvanaṃ bhāvetvā tumhe satajane vajjhe amocayiṃ.

Herein, 'seyyaṃso seyyaso hoti, yo seyyamupasevati' means: 'seyyaṃso' is one who possesses a superior part ('seyyo aṃso'), that is, a person who relies on wholesome qualities; this superior part is defined as the blameless and supreme Dhamma. One who repeatedly associates with that which is superior—the cultivation of wholesome qualities or an excellent person who delights in the wholesome—becomes superior still ('seyyaso'), that is, more praiseworthy and more sublime. 'Ekena sandhiṃ katvāna, sataṃ vajjhe amocayiṃ' should be understood thus: I, by practicing the superior cultivation of loving-kindness, made a friendly connection with the one robber king through that very cultivation. Having thus developed loving-kindness, I freed you hundred men who were to be killed.

Dutiyagāthāya attho – yasmā ahaṃ ekena saddhiṃ ekato mettābhāvanāya sandhiṃ katvā tumhe vajjhappatte satajane mocayiṃ, tasmā veditabbamevetaṃ, tasmā sabbena lokena saddhiṃ mettābhāvanāya [V 2.0331] sandhiṃ katvā ekato puggalo pecca paraloke saggaṃ nigaccheyya. Mettāya hi upacāraṃ kāmāvacare paṭisandhiṃ deti, appanā brahmaloke. Idaṃ mama vacanaṃ sabbepi tumhe kāsiraṭṭhavāsino suṇāthāti.

The meaning of the second verse is: Since I, by making an alliance with one person through the development of loving-kindness, freed you, a hundred men subject to execution, it should be understood that a person who makes an alliance with the entire world through the development of loving-kindness will, after death, go to a heavenly world. For loving-kindness as access concentration gives rebirth in the sense-sphere realm, while as absorption it gives rebirth in the Brahma-world. Let all of you inhabitants of the Kāsī country hear this word of mine.

Evaṃ mahāsatto mahājanassa mettābhāvanāya guṇaṃ vaṇṇetvā dvādasayojanike bārāṇasinagare setacchattaṃ pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Satthā [P 2.0403] sammāsambuddho hutvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus the Great Being, having extolled to the great multitude the virtue of developing loving-kindness, renounced the white parasol in the twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī, entered the Himalayas, and went forth into the ascetic life. The Teacher, having become a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, spoke the third verse:

96.

96.

“Idaṃ vatvā mahārājā, kaṃso bārāṇasiggaho;

Dhanuṃ kaṇḍañca nikkhippa, saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamī”ti.

“Having said this, the great king, Kaṃsa, seizer of Bārāṇasī, laid aside his bow and arrow and undertook self-restraint.”

Tattha mahanto rājāti mahārājā. Kaṃsoti tassa nāmaṃ. Bārāṇasiṃ gahetvā ajjhāvasanato bārāṇasiggaho. So rājā idaṃ vacanaṃ vatvā dhanuñca sarasaṅkhātaṃ kaṇḍañca nikkhippa ohāya chaḍḍetvā sīlasaṃyamaṃ [M 2.0362] upagato pabbajito, pabbajitvā ca pana jhānaṃ uppādetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke uppannoti.

Herein, 'mahārājā' means a great king. Kaṃsa is his name. He is the seizer of Bārāṇasī because he seized Bārāṇasī and dwelt there. Having spoken this word, that king laid aside, left, and abandoned his bow and arrows, undertook moral restraint, and went forth. And having gone forth, he developed the jhānas, and without having fallen away from jhāna, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā corarājā ānando ahosi, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story: “At that time the king of the bandits was Ānanda, but the king of Bārāṇasī was I myself.”

Seyyajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary to the Seyya Jātaka, the Second.

[283] 3. Vaḍḍhakīsūkarajātakavaṇṇanā

[283] 3. The Commentary to the Jātaka of the Carpenter’s Boar

Varaṃ varaṃ tvanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dhanuggahatissattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Pasenadirañño pitā mahākosalo bimbisārarañño dhītaraṃ vedehiṃ nāma kosaladeviṃ dadamāno tassā nhānacuṇṇamūlaṃ satasahassuṭṭhānaṃ kāsigāmaṃ adāsi. Ajātasattunā pana pitari mārite kosaladevīpi sokābhibhūtā kālamakāsi. Tato pasenadi kosalarājā cintesi – “ajātasattunā pitā mārito, bhaginīpi me sāmike kālakate tena sokena kālakatā, pitughātakassa corassa kāsigāmaṃ na dassāmī”ti. So taṃ ajātasattussa na adāsi. Taṃ gāmaṃ nissāya tesaṃ dvinnampi kālena kālaṃ yuddhaṃ hoti, ajātasattu taruṇo samattho, pasenadi [V 2.0332] mahallakoyeva. So abhikkhaṇaṃ parajjati, mahākosalassāpi manussā yebhuyyena parājitā. Atha rājā “mayaṃ abhiṇhaṃ parajjāma, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti amacce pucchi. “Deva, ayyā nāma mantacchekā honti, jetavanavihāre bhikkhūnaṃ kathaṃ sotuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Rājā “tena hi tāyaṃ velāyaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ suṇāthā”ti carapurise āṇāpesi. Te tato paṭṭhāya tathā akaṃsu.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this story beginning with "Varaṃ varaṃ tvaṃ" concerning the Elder Dhanuggahatissa. King Mahākosala, the father of King Pasenadi, when giving his daughter, the Kosalan princess named Vedehī, to King Bimbisāra, gave her a village in Kāsī that yielded a hundred thousand for the cost of her bath powder. But when Ajātasattu killed his father, Queen Kosaladevī, overwhelmed with grief, also passed away. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala thought: "Ajātasattu has killed his father, and my sister too has died from grief over her husband’s death. I will not give the Kāsī village to that patricide and thief!" So he did not give it to Ajātasattu. On account of that village, war arose between the two of them from time to time. Ajātasattu was young and capable, while Pasenadi was quite old, so he was repeatedly defeated, and the Kosalan men were for the most part defeated as well. Then the king asked his ministers: "We are constantly being defeated. What should be done?" They replied: "Your Majesty, the noble ones are skilled in counsel. It would be good to listen to the talk of the bhikkhus in the Jetavana monastery." The king then commanded his spies: "Well then, listen to the conversation of the bhikkhus at that time." From then on, they did so.

Tasmiṃ pana kāle dve mahallakattherā vihārapaccante paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasanti dattatthero ca dhanuggahatissatthero [P 2.0404] ca. Tesu dhanuggahatissatthero paṭhamayāmepi majjhimayāmepi niddāyitvā pacchimayāme pabujjhitvā ummukkāni sodhetvā [M 2.0363] aggiṃ jāletvā nisinnako āha – “bhante, dattattherā”ti. “Kiṃ, bhante, tissattherā”ti? “Kiṃ niddāyasi no tva”nti. “Aniddāyantā kiṃ karissāmā”ti? “Uṭṭhāya tāva nisīdathā”ti. So uṭṭhāya nisinno taṃ dattattheraṃ āha – “bhante dattatthera, ayaṃ te lolo mahodarakosalo cāṭimattaṃ bhattameva pūtiṃ karoti, yuddhavicāraṇaṃ pana kiñci na jānāti, parājito parājitotveva vadāpetī”ti. “Kiṃ pana kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? Tasmiṃ khaṇe te carapurisā tesaṃ kathaṃ suṇantā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Now at that time, two elderly elders, the Elder Datta and the Elder Dhanuggahatissa, were dwelling in a leaf-hut on the outskirts of the monastery. Of the two, the Elder Dhanuggahatissa, having slept through the first and middle watches of the night, would awaken in the last watch, clean the firebrands, light a fire, and while seated would say: "Venerable Datta!" "What is it, Venerable Tissa?" "Why are you sleeping?" "If we don’t sleep, what are we to do?" "Just get up and sit." So he got up and sat down. Then he said to the Elder Datta: "Venerable Datta, this greedy, big-bellied Kosalan just lets a pot of rice go bad and knows nothing about military strategy; he just lets it be announced, 'Defeated! Defeated!'" "But what should be done?" At that moment the spies stood there listening to their conversation.

Dhanuggahatissatthero yuddhaṃ vicāresi – “bhante, yuddho nāma tividho – padumabyūho, cakkabyūho, sakaṭabyūhoti. Ajātasattuṃ gaṇhitukāmena asuke nāma pabbatakucchismiṃ dvīsu pabbatabhittīsu manusse ṭhapetvā purato dubbalabalaṃ dassetvā pabbatantaraṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ jānitvā paviṭṭhamaggaṃ occhinditvā purato ca pacchato ca ubhosu pabbatabhittīsu vaggitvā unnaditvā khipe patitamacchaṃ viya antomuṭṭhiyaṃ vaṭṭapotakaṃ viya ca katvā sakkā assa taṃ gahetu”nti. Carapurisā taṃ sāsanaṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Taṃ sutvā rājā saṅgāmabheriṃ carāpetvā gantvā sakaṭabyūhaṃ katvā ajātasattuṃ jīvaggāhaṃ gāhāpetvā attano dhītaraṃ vajirakumāriṃ bhāgineyyassa datvā kāsigāmaṃ tassā nhānamūlaṃ katvā datvā uyyojesi. Sā pavatti bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭā jātā. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, kosalarājā kira dhanuggahatissattherassa vicāraṇāya ajātasattuṃ jinī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi dhanuggahatisso yuddhavicāraṇāya chekoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Elder Dhanuggahatissa explained the strategy: "Venerable sir, there are three kinds of battle formation: the lotus formation, the wheel formation, and the cart formation. One who wishes to capture Ajātasattu should station men in a certain mountain gorge between two mountain walls, show a weak force in front, and when it is known that the enemy has entered the mountain pass, he should cut off their path of entry. Then, by raising a cry and attacking from both mountain walls, they can make him like a fish that has fallen into a net or like a quail chick in one’s fist. In this way it would be possible to capture him." The spies reported this message to the king. Having heard it, the king had the war drum beaten, went forth, set up the cart formation, and had Ajātasattu captured alive. He then gave his daughter, Princess Vajirā, to his nephew, gave the Kāsī village as the cost for her bath, and sent him off. This matter became well known in the Sangha of bhikkhus. Then one day, the bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion in the hall of Dhamma: "Friends, it is said that the king of Kosala defeated Ajātasattu by means of the Elder Dhanuggahatissa’s strategy." The Teacher came and asked: "For what discussion are you now gathered here, bhikkhus?" When they told him, "For this one," he said: "Not only now, bhikkhus, but in the past too Dhanuggahatissa was an expert in military strategy," and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 2.0405] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññe rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti[V 2.0333]. Tadā bārāṇasiṃ nissāya nivutthavaḍḍhakigāmakā eko vaḍḍhakī thambhatthāya araññaṃ gantvā āvāṭe patitaṃ sūkarapotakaṃ disvā taṃ gharaṃ netvā paṭijaggi. So vuḍḍhippatto mahāsarīro vaṅkadāṭho [M 2.0364] ācārasampanno ahosi, vaḍḍhakinā positattā pana “vaḍḍhakīsūkaro”tveva paññāyi. Vaḍḍhakissa rukkhatacchanakāle tuṇḍena rukkhaṃ parivatteti, mukhena ḍaṃsitvā vāsipharasunikhādanamuggare āharati, kālasuttakoṭiyaṃ gaṇhāti. Atha so vaḍḍhakī “kocideva, naṃ khādeyyā”ti bhayena netvā araññe vissajjesi. Sopi araññaṃ pavisitvā khemaṃ phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ olokento ekaṃ pabbatantare mahantaṃ girikandaraṃ addasa sampannakandamūlaphalaṃ phāsukaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ anekasatasūkarasamākiṇṇaṃ. Te sūkarā taṃ disvā tassa santikaṃ āgamaṃsu. Sopi te āha – “ahaṃ tumheva olokento vicarāmi, apica vo mayā diṭṭhā, idañca ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ, ahampi idāni idheva vasissāmī”ti. “Saccaṃ idaṃ ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ, parissayo panettha atthī”ti. “Ahampi tumhe disvā etaṃ aññāsiṃ, evaṃ gocarasampanne ṭhāne vasantānaṃ vo sarīresu maṃsalohitaṃ natthi, kiṃ pana vo ettha bhaya”nti? “Eko byaggho pātova āgantvā diṭṭhadiṭṭhaṃyeva gahetvā gacchatī”ti. “Kiṃ pana so nibaddhaṃ gaṇhāti, udāhu antarantarā”ti? “Nibaddhaṃ gaṇhātī”ti. “Kati pana te byagghā”ti? “Ekoyevā”ti. “Ettakā tumhe ekassa yujjhituṃ na sakkothā”ti? “Āma, na sakkomā”ti. “Ahaṃ taṃ gaṇhissāmi, kevalaṃ tumhe mama vacanaṃ karotha, so byaggho kahaṃ vasatī”ti? “Etasmiṃ pabbate”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree-deity in a forest. At that time, a carpenter from a carpenters’ village near Bārāṇasī went to the forest for timber. Seeing a young boar that had fallen into a pit, he took it home and raised it. When it grew up, it became large-bodied, with curved tusks, and was well-behaved. Because it was raised by the carpenter, it became known as ‘the carpenter’s boar.’ When the carpenter was dressing timber, the boar would turn over the logs with its snout, and would fetch the adze, axe, chisel, and hammer, holding them in its mouth. It would also hold the end of the measuring line. Then the carpenter, fearing that someone might eat it, took it and released it in the forest. The boar entered the forest and, looking for a safe and comfortable place, saw a large mountain gorge in a mountain range. It was a pleasant place to live, endowed with yams, roots, and fruits, and teeming with many hundreds of boars. When those boars saw it, they approached it. It said to them: ‘I have been wandering looking for you, and now I have seen you. This place is delightful, and I will now live right here.’ ‘It is true this place is delightful, but there is a danger here.’ ‘I knew that when I saw you. Though you live in a place so rich in food, there is no flesh and blood on your bodies. What is your fear here?’ ‘A tiger comes early in the morning and seizes and carries off whichever one it sees.’ ‘Does it seize one regularly, or only from time to time?’ ‘It seizes one regularly.’ ‘How many tigers are there?’ ‘Only one.’ ‘Are all of you unable to fight one?’ ‘Yes, we are unable.’ ‘I will capture it. You just do as I say. Where does that tiger live?’ ‘On this mountain.’

So rattiññeva sūkare carāpetvā yuddhaṃ vicārento “yuddhaṃ nāma [P 2.0406] padumabyūhacakkabyūhasakaṭabyūhavasena tividhaṃ hotī”ti vatvā padumabyūhavasena vicāresi. So hi bhūmisīsaṃ jānāti. Tasmā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne yuddhaṃ vicāretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sūkarapillake mātaro ca tesaṃ majjhaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. So tā āvijjhitvā majjhimasūkariyo, tā āvijjhitvā potakasūkare, te āvijjhitvā jarasūkare, te āvijjhitvā dīghadāṭhasūkare, te āvijjhitvā yuddhasamatthe balavatarasūkare dasa vīsa tiṃsa jane tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne balagumbaṃ katvā ṭhapesi. Attano ṭhitaṭṭhānassa purato ekaṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇāpesi, pacchato ekaṃ suppasaṇṭhānaṃ anupubbaninnaṃ pabbhārasadisaṃ. Tassa saṭṭhisattatimatte yodhasūkare ādāya tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne “mā bhāyitthā”ti kammaṃ vicārato aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahi.

That very night, he had the boars move about and planned the battle. Saying, ‘A battle is of three kinds: the lotus formation, the wheel formation, and the cart formation,’ he arranged it in the lotus formation. For he knew the strategic points of the ground. Therefore, thinking, ‘It is suitable to arrange the battle in this place,’ he placed the youngest piglets and their mothers in the center. Around them, he placed the middle-aged sows; around those, the young boars; around those, the old boars; around those, the long-tusked boars; and around those, he placed the strongest boars fit for battle, forming troops of ten, twenty, or thirty in various places. In front of his own position, he had a circular pit dug, and behind it, a well-formed pit, gradually sloping down like a cavernous hollow. Taking about sixty or seventy warrior boars, he stationed them in various places, saying, ‘Do not be afraid,’ and as he was arranging the operation, dawn broke.

Byaggho [M 2.0365] uṭṭhāya “kālo”ti ñatvā gantvā tesaṃ sammukhā ṭhite pabbatatale ṭhatvā akkhīni ummīletvā sūkare olokesi. Vaḍḍhakīsūkaro “paṭioloketha na”nti sūkarānaṃ saññaṃ [V 2.0334] adāsi, te paṭiolokesuṃ. Byaggho mukhaṃ ugghāṭetvā assosi, sūkarāpi tathā kariṃsu. Byaggho muttaṃ chaḍḍesi, sūkarāpi chaḍḍayiṃsu. Iti yaṃ yaṃ so karoti, taṃ taṃ te paṭikariṃsu. So cintesi – “pubbe sūkarā mayā olokitakāle palāyantā palāyitumpi na sakkonti, ajja apalāyitvā mama paṭisattu hutvā mayā katameva paṭikaronti. Etasmiṃ bhūmisīse ṭhito eko tesaṃ saṃvidhāyakopi atthi, ajja mayhaṃ gatassa jayo na paññāyatī”ti. So nivattitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Tena pana gahitamaṃsakhādako eko kūṭajaṭilo atthi, so taṃ tucchahatthameva āgacchantaṃ disvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The tiger got up, and knowing it was time, he went and stood on a mountain slope before them. He opened his eyes wide and looked at the boars. The carpenter’s boar gave the boars the signal, ‘Look back at him,’ and they looked back. The tiger opened his mouth and listened, and the boars did likewise. The tiger urinated, and the boars also urinated. Thus, whatever he did, they did in return. He thought: ‘Previously, when I looked at these boars, they would flee, unable even to run away. But today, instead of fleeing, they have become my adversaries and do back to me exactly what I do. There must be some organizer for them standing on this strategic ground; for me, if I go, victory is not in sight today.’ So he turned back and went to his own dwelling place. Now, there was a certain fraudulent matted-hair ascetic who ate the meat brought by the tiger. Seeing the tiger returning empty-handed, he conversed with him and spoke the first verse:

97.

97.

“Varaṃ [P 2.0407] varaṃ tvaṃ nihanaṃ pure cari,

Asmiṃ padese abhibhuyya sūkare;

Sodāni eko byapagamma jhāyasi,

Balaṃ nu te byaggha na cajja vijjatī”ti.

“Formerly you roamed, killing the very best,

Having overpowered the boars in this region;

But now you have gone off alone and are brooding.

Do you then have no strength today, O tiger?”

Tattha varaṃ varaṃ tvaṃ nihanaṃ pure cari, asmiṃ padese abhibhuyya sūkareti ambho byaggha, tvaṃ pubbe imasmiṃ padese sabbasūkare abhibhavitvā imesu sūkaresu varaṃ varaṃ tvaṃ uttamuttamaṃ sūkaraṃ nihananto vicari. Sodāni eko byapagamma jhāyasīti so tvaṃ idāni aññataraṃ sūkaraṃ aggahetvā ekakova apagantvā jhāyasi pajjhāyasi. Balaṃ nu te byaggha na cajja vijjatīti kiṃ nu te, ambho byaggha, ajja kāyabalaṃ natthīti.

Herein, ‘Formerly you roamed, killing the very best, having overpowered the boars in this region’ means: ‘Friend tiger, formerly in this region, having overpowered all the boars, you roamed about killing the very best—the most excellent—boars among them.’ ‘But now you have gone off alone and are brooding’ means: ‘You, now, without having caught a single boar, have gone off all alone and are brooding and moping.’ ‘Do you then have no strength today, O tiger?’ means: ‘What, friend tiger, do you have no bodily strength today?’”

Taṃ sutvā byaggho dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the tiger spoke the second verse:

98.

98.

“Ime sudaṃ yanti disodisaṃ pure, bhayaṭṭitā leṇagavesino puthū;

Te dāni saṅgamma vasanti ekato, yatthaṭṭhitā duppasahajjame mayā”ti.

“These who formerly went in all directions,

Afflicted by fear, separately seeking refuge;

They now have come together and dwell as one,

And where they stand, they are hard for me to overcome today.”

Tattha [M 2.0366] sudanti nipāto. Ayaṃ pana saṅkhepattho – ime sūkarā pubbe maṃ disvā bhayena aṭṭitā pīḷitā attano leṇagavesino puthū visuṃ visuṃ hutvā disodisaṃ yanti, taṃ taṃ disaṃ abhimukhā palāyanti, te dāni sabbepi samāgantvā ekato vasanti tiṭṭhanti, tañca bhūmisīsaṃ upagatā, yattha ṭhitā duppasahā dummaddayā ajja ime mayāti.

Herein, ‘sudaṃ’ is a particle. This is the meaning in brief: Formerly, on seeing me, these boars were afflicted and oppressed by fear. Seeking refuge for themselves, they would go separately in all directions, fleeing toward whatever direction they faced. But now they have all come together and dwell and stand as one. They have occupied that high ground, where, standing, they are hard for me to withstand, hard for me to crush today.

Athassa [V 2.0335] ussāhaṃ janento kūṭajaṭilo “mā bhāyi, gaccha tayi naditvā pakkhandante sabbepi bhītā bhijjitvā palāyissantī”ti āha. Byaggho tasmiṃ ussāhaṃ janente sūro hutvā puna gantvā pabbatatale aṭṭhāsi. Vaḍḍhakīsūkaro dvinnaṃ āvāṭānaṃ antare aṭṭhāsi. Sūkarā “sāmi, mahācoro punāgato”ti āhaṃsu. “Mā bhāyittha, idāni taṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti. Byaggho naditvā vaḍḍhakīsūkarassa upari patati, sūkaro tassa attano upari patanakāle [P 2.0408] parivattitvā vegena ujukaṃ khataāvāṭe pati. Byaggho vegaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto uparibhāgena gantvā suppamukhassa tiriyaṃ khataāvāṭassa atisambādhe mukhaṭṭhāne patitvā puñjakato viya ahosi. Sūkaro āvāṭā uttaritvā asanivegena gantvā byagghaṃ antarasatthimhi dāṭhāya paharitvā yāva vakkapadesā phāletvā pañcamadhuramaṃsaṃ dāṭhāya paliveṭhetvā byagghassa matthake āvijjhitvā “gaṇhatha tumhākaṃ paccāmitta”nti ukkhipitvā bahiāvāṭe chaḍḍesi. Paṭhamaṃ āgatā byagghamaṃsaṃ labhiṃsu, pacchā āgatā “byagghamaṃsaṃ kīdisaṃ hotī”ti tesaṃ mukhaṃ upasiṅghantā vicariṃsu.

Then the fraudulent matted-hair ascetic, rousings his courage, said: 'Do not be afraid. Go! When you roar and charge, they will all become frightened, break ranks, and flee.' When he roused his courage, the tiger became brave, went back, and stood on the mountain plateau. The carpenter boar stood between the two trenches. The boars said, 'Master, the great thief has come again!' 'Do not be afraid,' he said, 'I will catch him now.' The tiger roared and leaped upon the carpenter boar. But as the tiger was falling upon him, the boar swerved and the tiger fell with force into the straight-dug trench. Unable to check his momentum, the tiger went over the top and fell into the very narrow opening of the crosswise-dug trench, becoming huddled like a heap. The boar, climbing out of the trench, went with the speed of a thunderbolt, struck the tiger between the thighs with his tusk, and ripped him open up to the kidneys. Wrapping the choicest flesh on his tusk, he gored the tiger's head, lifted him up, and shouting, 'Take your enemy!', threw him outside the trench. Those who came first got the tiger's meat; those who came later went about sniffing the mouths of those who had eaten, asking, 'What does tiger meat taste like?'

Sūkarā na tāva tussanti. Vaḍḍhakīsūkaro tesaṃ iṅghitaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho tumhe na tussathā”ti āha. “Sāmi, kiṃ etena byagghena ghātitena, añño pana byagghaāṇāpanasamattho kūṭajaṭilo atthiyevā”ti. “Ko nāmeso”ti? “Eko dussīlatāpaso”ti. “Byagghopi mayā ghātito, so me kiṃ pahoti, etha gaṇhissāma na”nti sūkaraghaṭāya saddhiṃ pāyāsi. Kūṭatāpasopi byagghe cirāyante “kiṃ nu kho sūkarā byagghaṃ gaṇhiṃsū”ti paṭipathaṃ gacchanto te sūkare āgacchante disvā attano parikkhāraṃ ādāya palāyanto tehi anubandhito parikkhāraṃ chaḍḍetvā vegena udumbararukkhaṃ abhiruhi. Sūkarā “idānimha, sāmi, naṭṭhā, tāpaso palāyitvā [M 2.0367] rukkhaṃ abhiruhī”ti āhaṃsu. “Kiṃ rukkhaṃ nāmā”ti? “Udumbararukkha”nti. So “sūkariyo udakaṃ āharantu, sūkarapotakā pathaviṃ khaṇantu, dīghadāṭhā sūkarā mūlāni chindantu, sesā parivāretvā ārakkhantū”ti saṃvidahitvā tesu tathā karontesu sayaṃ udumbarassa ujukaṃ thūlamūlaṃ [P 2.0409] pharasunā paharanto viya ekappahārameva katvā udumbararukkhaṃ pātesi. Parivāretvā ṭhitasūkarā kūṭajaṭilaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ katvā yāva aṭṭhito khāditvā vaḍḍhakīsūkaraṃ udumbarakhandheyeva nisīdāpetvā kūṭajaṭilassa paribhogasaṅkhena udakaṃ āharitvā abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ kariṃsu, ekañca taruṇasūkariṃ tassa aggamahesiṃ akaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya kira yāvajjatanā rājāno udumbarabhaddapīṭhe nisīdāpetvā tīhi saṅkhehi abhisiñcanti.

The boars were still not satisfied. The carpenter boar, seeing their intention, asked, 'Why are you not satisfied?' 'Master, what is the use of this tiger being killed? There is still another, the fraudulent matted-hair ascetic who is capable of commanding the tiger.' 'Who is that?' 'A certain immoral ascetic.' 'The tiger was killed by me; what can he do to me? Come, let us catch him!' And he set out with the troop of boars. Meanwhile, as the tiger was delayed, the fraudulent ascetic wondered, 'Can it be that the boars have caught the tiger?' Going back along the path, he saw the boars approaching. Taking his requisites, he fled. Pursued by them, he dropped his requisites and quickly climbed an udumbara tree. The boars said, 'Master, now he has escaped! The ascetic has fled and climbed a tree!' 'What kind of tree?' 'An udumbara tree.' He commanded: 'Let the sows bring water, let the piglets dig the earth, let the long-tusked boars sever the roots, and let the rest surround and guard it.' When they had done so, he himself, as if striking the straight, thick root of the udumbara with an axe, felled the tree with a single blow. The boars that stood surrounding it knocked the fraudulent ascetic to the ground, tore him to pieces, and devoured him down to the bones. Then, seating the carpenter boar on the very trunk of the udumbara tree, they brought water in the fraudulent ascetic's used conch and consecrated him as king. And they made a young sow his chief queen. It is said that from that time right up to the present day, kings are seated on a throne of udumbara wood and consecrated with three conches.

Tasmiṃ [V 2.0336] vanasaṇḍe adhivatthā devatā taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā ekasmiṃ viṭapantare sūkarānaṃ abhimukhā hutvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The deity dwelling in that forest grove, seeing this marvel, stood amidst the branches facing the boars and spoke the third verse:

99.

99.

“Namatthu saṅghāna samāgatānaṃ, disvā sayaṃ sakhya vadāmi abbhutaṃ;

Byagghaṃ migā yattha jiniṃsu dāṭhino, sāmaggiyā dāṭhabalesu muccare”ti.

“Homage to the assembly of those come together! Having seen for myself this wonderful friendship, I speak. Where indeed the tusked beasts have conquered a tiger; through unity, those whose strength is their tusks are freed.”

Tattha namatthu saṅghānanti ayaṃ mama namakkāro samāgatānaṃ sūkarasaṅghānaṃ atthu. Disvā sayaṃ sakhya vadāmi abbhutanti idaṃ pubbe abhūtapubbaṃ abbhutaṃ sakhyaṃ mittabhāvaṃ sayaṃ disvā vadāmi. Byagghaṃ migā yattha jiniṃsu dāṭhinoti yatra hi nāma dāṭhino sūkaramigā byagghaṃ jiniṃsu, ayameva vā pāṭho. Sāmaggiyā dāṭhabalesu muccareti yā sā dāṭhabalesu sūkaresu sāmaggī ekajjhāsayatā, tāya tesu sāmaggiyā te dāṭhabalā paccāmittaṃ gahetvā ajja maraṇabhayā muttāti attho.

Herein, 'Homage to the assembly' means: 'May this homage of mine be for the assembled multitude of boars.' 'Having seen for myself this wonderful friendship, I speak' means: 'I speak having myself seen this unprecedented, wonderful friendship and camaraderie.' 'Where the tusked beasts have conquered a tiger' means: 'Where indeed the tusked beasts, the boars, conquered the tiger'; or this is also a reading.
