'Through unity, the tusk-strong are freed' means: 'That unity, that single-mindedness, among the boars whose strength is their tusks—by that unity among them, those tusk-strong ones, having seized the enemy, are today freed from the fear of death.' This is the meaning.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dhanuggahatisso vaḍḍhakīsūkaro ahosi, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka thus: “At that time, Tissa the archer was the carpenter boar, but the tree deity was myself.”

Vaḍḍhakīsūkarajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Carpenter Boar Jātaka, the Third.

[284] 4. Sirijātakavaṇṇanā

[284] 4. 4. Commentary on the Siri Jātaka

Yaṃ [M 2.0368] ussukā saṅgharantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ siricorabrāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Imasmiṃ jātake [P 2.0410] paccuppannavatthu heṭṭhā khadiraṅgārajātake (jā. 1.1.40) vitthāritameva. Idhāpi pana sā anāthapiṇḍikassa ghare catutthe dvārakoṭṭhake vasanakā micchādiṭṭhidevatā daṇḍakammaṃ karontī catupaññāsahiraññakoṭiyo āharitvā koṭṭhe pūretvā seṭṭhinā saddhiṃ sahāyikā ahosi. Atha naṃ so ādāya satthu santikaṃ nesi. Satthā tassā dhammaṃ desesi, sā dhammaṃ sutvā sotāpannā ahosi. Tato paṭṭhāya seṭṭhino yaso yathāporāṇova jāto. Atheko sāvatthivāsī sirilakkhaṇaññū brāhmaṇo cintesi – “anāthapiṇḍiko duggato hutvā puna issaro jāto, yaṃnūnāhaṃ taṃ daṭṭhukāmo viya gatvā tassa gharato siriṃ thenetvā āgaccheyya”nti. So tassa gharaṃ gantvā tena katasakkārasammāno sāraṇīyakathāya vattamānāya “kimatthaṃ āgatosī”ti vutte “kattha nu kho sirī patiṭṭhitā”ti olokesi. Seṭṭhino ca sabbaseto [V 2.0337] dhotasaṅkhapaṭibhāgo kukkuṭo suvaṇṇapañjare pakkhipitvā ṭhapito atthi, tassa cūḷāya sirī patiṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇo olokayamāno siriyā tattha patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā āha – “ahaṃ, mahāseṭṭhi, pañcasate māṇave mante vācemi, akālaraviṃ ekaṃ kukkuṭaṃ nissāya te ca mayañca kilamāma, ayañca kira kukkuṭo kālaravī, imassatthāya āgatomhi, dehi me etaṃ kukkuṭa”nti. “Gaṇha, brāhmaṇa, demi te kukkuṭa”nti. “Demī”ti ca vuttakkhaṇeyeva sirī tassa cūḷato apagantvā ussīsake ṭhapite maṇikkhandhe patiṭṭhāsi.

‘Those who are diligent amass wealth’—this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain brahmin who was a fortune-thief. The story of the present in this Jātaka has been explained in detail previously in the Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka. Here, however, a certain deity of wrong view dwelling in the fourth gatehouse of Anāthapiṇḍika's house, as an act of penance, brought fifty-four crores of gold and filled the granaries, and she became a friend to the merchant. Then he took her to the Teacher. The Teacher taught her the Dhamma, and having heard the Dhamma, she became a stream-enterer. From then on, the merchant's fortune became just as it was before. Now, a certain brahmin living in Sāvatthī who knew the marks of fortune thought: ‘Anāthapiṇḍika, having become poor, has become a lord again. What if I were to go as if wishing to see him and steal the fortune from his house?’ He went to his house, and while being honored and engaged in friendly conversation, when asked ‘For what purpose have you come?’, he looked around, thinking ‘Where indeed is the fortune established?’ The merchant had an all-white rooster, like a polished conch shell, kept in a golden cage; the fortune was established on its crest. The brahmin, observing and knowing the fact of the fortune being established there, said: ‘Great merchant, I teach the mantras to five hundred young students. Because of a rooster that crows at the wrong time, they and I are exhausted. This rooster, it is said, crows at the right time. I have come for this rooster. Give me this rooster.’ ‘Take it, brahmin, I give it to you.’ At the very moment he said ‘I give,’ the fortune departed from its crest and established itself on a gem-stone placed at the head-rest.

Brāhmaṇo siriyā maṇimhi patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā maṇimpi yāci. “Maṇimpi demī”ti vuttakkhaṇeyeva sirī maṇito apagantvā ussīsake ṭhapitaārakkhayaṭṭhiyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇo siriyā tattha patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā tampi yāci. “Gahetvā gacchāhī”ti vuttakkhaṇeyeva sirī yaṭṭhito apagantvā puññalakkhaṇadeviyā nāma seṭṭhino aggamahesiyā sīse patiṭṭhāsi. Siricorabrāhmaṇo tattha patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “avissajjiyabhaṇḍaṃ etaṃ, yācitumpi na sakkā”ti cintetvā seṭṭhiṃ etadavoca – “mahāseṭṭhi, ahaṃ [M 2.0369] tumhākaṃ gehe ‘siriṃ thenetvā gamissāmī’ti āgacchiṃ, sirī pana te kukkuṭassa cūḷāyaṃ patiṭṭhitā ahosi, tasmiṃ mama dinne tato apagantvā maṇimhi patiṭṭhahi, maṇimhi dinne ārakkhayaṭṭhiyaṃ patiṭṭhahi, ārakkhayaṭṭhiyā dinnāya tato apagantvā puññalakkhaṇadeviyā [P 2.0411] sīse patiṭṭhahi, ‘idaṃ kho pana avissajjiyabhaṇḍa’nti imampi me na gahitaṃ, na sakkā tava siriṃ thenetuṃ, tava santakaṃ taveva hotū”ti uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Anāthapiṇḍiko “imaṃ kāraṇaṃ satthu kathessāmī”ti vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno sabbaṃ tathāgatassa ārocesi. Satthā taṃ sutvā “na kho, gahapati, idāneva aññesaṃ sirī aññattha gacchati, pubbepi appapuññehi uppāditasirī pana puññavantānaṃyeva pādamūlaṃ gatā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The brahmin, knowing the fact of the fortune being established on the gem, asked for the gem as well. At the very moment he said ‘I give the gem too,’ the fortune departed from the gem and established itself on a protective staff placed at the head-rest. The brahmin, knowing the fact of the fortune being established there, asked for that too. At the very moment he said ‘Take it and go,’ the fortune departed from the staff and established itself on the head of the merchant's chief consort, named Puññalakkhaṇādevī. The fortune-thief brahmin, knowing its presence there, thought, ‘This is an inalienable possession; it is impossible even to ask for it,’ and said to the merchant: ‘Great merchant, I came to your house thinking “I will steal your fortune and go,” but your fortune was established on your rooster's crest. When that was given to me, it departed from there and settled on the gem. When the gem was given, it settled on the protective staff. When the protective staff was given, it departed from there and settled on the head of Puññalakkhaṇādevī. Thinking, “This is indeed an inalienable possession,” I have not taken this. It is impossible to steal your fortune. Let what is yours remain yours alone.’ He rose from his seat and departed. Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking ‘I will report this matter to the Teacher,’ went to the monastery, worshipped and paid homage to the Teacher, and sitting to one side, reported everything to the Tathāgata. The Teacher, having heard it, said, ‘Householder, it is not only now that the fortune of some goes elsewhere; in the past, too, the fortune produced by those of little merit went to the very feet of the meritorious.’ Being requested by him, he brought forth the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā agāraṃ ajjhāvasanto mātāpitūnaṃ kālakiriyāya saṃviggo nikkhamitvā himavantapadese isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā dīghassa addhuno accayena loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadaṃ gantvā bārāṇasirañño uyyāne vasitvā punadivase bhikkhaṃ caramāno hatthācariyassa gharadvāraṃ agamāsi. So tassa ācāravihāre pasanno bhikkhaṃ datvā uyyāne vasāpetvā niccaṃ paṭijaggi. Tasmiṃ kāle eko kaṭṭhahārako araññato dārūni āharanto velāya nagaradvāraṃ pāpuṇituṃ [V 2.0338] nāsakkhi. Sāyaṃ ekasmiṃ devakule dārukalāpaṃ ussīsake katvā nipajji, devakule vissaṭṭhā bahū kukkuṭā tassa avidūre ekasmiṃ rukkhe sayiṃsu. Tesu uparisayitakukkuṭo paccūsakāle vaccaṃ pātento heṭṭhāsayitakukkuṭassa sarīre pātesi. “Kena me sarīre vaccaṃ pātita”nti ca vutte “mayā”ti āha. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti ca vutte “anupadhāretvā”ti vatvā punapi pātesi. Tato ubhopi aññamaññaṃ kuddhā “kiṃ te balaṃ, kiṃ te bala”nti kalahaṃ kariṃsu. Atha heṭṭhāsayitakukkuṭo āha – “maṃ māretvā aṅgāre pakkamaṃsaṃ khādanto pātova kahāpaṇasahassaṃ [P 2.0412] labhatī”ti. Uparisayitakukkuṭo āha – “ambho, mā tvaṃ ettakena gajji, mama thūlamaṃsaṃ khādanto rājā hoti, bahimaṃsaṃ [M 2.0370] khādanto puriso ce, senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ, itthī ce, aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ labhati. Aṭṭhimaṃsaṃ pana me khādanto gihī ce, bhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhānaṃ, pabbajito ce, rājakulūpakabhāvaṃ labhatī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. Having come of age, he learned the arts at Takkasilā. While living the household life, he felt a sense of spiritual urgency at the death of his parents, went forth from home, and undertook the ascetic life of a seer in the Himalayan region. He developed the five direct knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. After a long time, needing to obtain salt and vinegar, he went to an inhabited region and dwelt in the park of the king of Bārāṇasī. The next day, while wandering for alms, he came to the door of the elephant trainer's house. Pleased with his deportment, the trainer gave him alms, had him take up residence in the park, and regularly attended to him. At that time, a woodcutter bringing firewood from the forest was unable to reach the city gate in time. In the evening, he lay down in a shrine to a deity, making his bundle of wood a pillow. Many roosters that had been set free at the shrine were sleeping on a tree nearby. At dawn, the rooster perched above dropped its excrement, and it fell on the body of the rooster below. When the latter asked, 'Who dropped excrement on my body?' the one above replied, 'I did.' When asked, 'For what reason?' he said, 'Carelessly,' and dropped some again. Then both, angry with each other, started a quarrel, saying, 'What is your power? What is your power?' Then the rooster below said: 'One who kills me and eats my meat roasted on embers will get a thousand kahāpaṇas in the morning.' The rooster above said: 'Hey, do not boast about just that! One who eats my thick meat becomes king. If a man eats the outer meat, he obtains the position of commander-in-chief; if a woman, she obtains the position of chief queen. But one who eats the meat on my bones, if a layman, obtains the position of treasurer; if one gone forth, he becomes the spiritual advisor to the royal family.'

Kaṭṭhahārako tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “rajje patte sahassena kiccaṃ natthī”ti saṇikaṃ abhiruhitvā uparisayitakukkuṭaṃ gahetvā māretvā ucchaṅge katvā “rājā bhavissāmī”ti gantvā vivaṭadvāreneva nagaraṃ pavisitvā kukkuṭaṃ nittacaṃ katvā udaraṃ sodhetvā “idaṃ kukkuṭamaṃsaṃ sādhukaṃ sampādehī”ti pajāpatiyā adāsi. Sā kukkuṭamaṃsañca bhattañca sampādetvā “bhuñja, sāmī”ti tassa upanāmesi. “Bhadde, etaṃ maṃsaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ, etaṃ khāditvā ahaṃ rājā bhavissāmi, tvaṃ aggamahesī bhavissasi, taṃ bhattañca maṃsañca ādāya gaṅgātīraṃ gantvā nhāyitvā bhuñjissāmā”ti bhattabhājanaṃ tīre ṭhapetvā nhānatthāya otariṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe vātena khubhitaṃ udakaṃ āgantvā bhattabhājanaṃ ādāya agamāsi. Taṃ nadīsotena vuyhamānaṃ heṭṭhānadiyaṃ hatthiṃ nhāpento eko hatthācariyo mahāmatto disvā ukkhipāpetvā vivarāpetvā “kimetthā”ti pucchi. “Bhattañceva kukkuṭamaṃsañca sāmī”ti. So taṃ pidahāpetvā lañchāpetvā “yāva mayaṃ āgacchāma, tāvimaṃ bhattaṃ mā vivarā”ti bhariyāya pesesi. Sopi kho kaṭṭhahārako mukhato paviṭṭhena vālukodakena uddhumātaudaro palāyi.

The woodcutter, hearing their words, thought, 'When kingship is attained, what need is there for a thousand?' Quietly climbing up, he caught the rooster perched above, killed it, placed it in the fold of his garment, and thinking, 'I will become king,' he went and entered the city by the already open gate. He plucked and cleaned the rooster and gave it to his wife, saying, 'Prepare this rooster meat well.' She prepared the rooster meat and rice and brought it to him, saying, 'Eat, master.' He said: 'Good lady, this meat is of great power. Having eaten it, I will become king, and you will become the chief queen. Taking this rice and meat, let us go to the bank of the Ganges, bathe, and eat.' They placed the rice-basket on the bank and went down to bathe. At that moment, a wave stirred up by the wind came and carried the rice-basket away. As it was being carried away by the river's current, a certain great minister, an elephant trainer, who was bathing an elephant downstream, saw it. He had it retrieved and opened, and asked, 'What is in here?' 'Rice and rooster meat, master.' He had it closed and sealed, and sent it to his wife with the message: 'Do not open this food until we arrive.' And that woodcutter, his belly bloated with the sandy water that had entered his mouth, fled.

Atheko tassa hatthācariyassa kulūpako dibbacakkhukatāpaso “mayhaṃ upaṭṭhāko hatthiṭṭhānaṃ na vijahati, kadā nu kho sampattiṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti dibbacakkhunā upadhārento taṃ purisaṃ disvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā puretaraṃ gantvā hatthācariyassa nivesane nisīdi. Hatthācariyo āgantvā taṃ vanditvā [P 2.0413] ekamantaṃ nisinno taṃ bhattabhājanaṃ āharāpetvā “tāpasaṃ maṃsodanena parivisathā”ti āha. Tāpaso bhattaṃ gahetvā maṃse dīyamāne aggahetvā “imaṃ maṃsaṃ ahaṃ vicāremī”ti vatvā “vicāretha[V 2.0339], bhante”ti vutte thūlamaṃsādīni ekekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ kāretvā thūlamaṃsaṃ hatthācariyassa dāpesi, bahimaṃsaṃ tassa bhariyāya, aṭṭhimaṃsaṃ attanā paribhuñji. So bhattakiccāvasāne gacchanto “tvaṃ ito tatiyadivase rājā bhavissasi, appamatto hohī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Tatiyadivase eko sāmantarājā āgantvā bārāṇasiṃ parivāresi. Bārāṇasirājā [M 2.0371] hatthācariyaṃ rājavesaṃ gāhāpetvā “hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā yujjhā”ti āṇāpetvā sayaṃ aññātakavesena senāya vicārento ekena mahāvegena sarena viddho taṅkhaṇaññeva mari. Tassa matabhāvaṃ ñatvā hatthācariyo bahū kahāpaṇe nīharāpetvā “dhanatthikā purato hutvā yujjhantū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Balakāyo muhutteneva sāmantarājānaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Amaccā rañño sarīrakiccaṃ katvā “kaṃ rājānaṃ karomā”ti mantayamānā “amhākaṃ rājā jīvamāno attano vesaṃ hatthācariyassa adāsi, ayameva yuddhaṃ katvā rajjaṃ gaṇhi, etasseva rajjaṃ dassāmā”ti taṃ rajjena abhisiñciṃsu, bhariyampissa aggamahesiṃ akaṃsu. Bodhisatto rājakulūpako ahosi.

Then a certain ascetic possessing the divine eye, who was a regular visitor to that elephant trainer's family, thought: 'My attendant does not leave the elephant post; when, I wonder, will he attain prosperity?' Observing that man with his divine eye and understanding the reason, he went on ahead and sat down in the elephant trainer's residence. When the elephant trainer arrived, he paid homage to the ascetic and sat down to one side. He had the basket of food brought and said, 'Serve the ascetic with rice and meat.' The ascetic took the rice, but when the meat was being offered, he did not accept it, saying, 'I will divide this meat.' When he was told, 'Divide it, venerable sir,' he had the meat divided into portions. He had the thick meat given to the elephant trainer, the outer meat to his wife, and he himself consumed the meat on the bones. At the conclusion of the meal, as he was leaving, he said, 'On the third day from today you will become king. Be heedful!' and he departed. On the third day, a neighboring king came and besieged Bārāṇasī. The king of Bārāṇasī had the elephant trainer dress in the royal regalia and commanded him, 'Mount the elephant and fight!' While the king himself was moving about the army in disguise, he was struck by a very swift arrow and died on the spot. Learning that the king was dead, the elephant trainer had many kahāpaṇas brought out and had a drum beaten with the proclamation: 'Let those who desire wealth come forward and fight!' In a moment, the army brought the neighboring king to his life's end. The ministers performed the funeral rites for the king and deliberated, 'Whom should we make king?' They concluded: 'While he was alive, our king gave his own regalia to the elephant trainer. It was he who fought the battle and won the kingdom. We will give the kingdom to him.' They then anointed him king and made his wife the chief queen. The Bodhisatta became the spiritual advisor to the royal family.

Satthā atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imā dve gāthā abhāsi –

The Teacher related this story of the past, and then, as the Perfectly Enlightened One, he spoke these two stanzas:

100.

100.

“Yaṃ ussukā saṅgharanti, alakkhikā bahuṃ dhanaṃ;

Sippavanto asippā ca, lakkhivā tāni bhuñjati.

‘‘The luckless, whether skilled or unskilled, eagerly amass much wealth; but the one with good fortune enjoys it.

101.

101.

“Sabbattha katapuññassa, aticcaññeva pāṇino;

Uppajjanti bahū bhogā, appanāyatanesupī”ti.

‘‘For one who has made merit, surpassing other beings in every way; abundant treasures arise even in places that are not their source.’’

Tattha yaṃ ussukāti yaṃ dhanasaṅgharaṇe ussukkamāpannā chandajātā kicchena bahuṃ dhanaṃ saṅgharanti.“Ye ussukā”tipi pāṭho, ye purisā [P 2.0414] dhanasaṃharaṇe ussukā hatthisippādivasena sippavanto asippā ca antamaso vetanena kammaṃ katvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ saṅgharantīti attho. Lakkhivā tāni bhuñjatīti tāni “bahuṃ dhana”nti vuttāni dhanāni puññavā puriso attano puññaphalaṃ paribhuñjanto kiñci kammaṃ akatvāpi paribhuñjati.

In those verses, ‘yaṃ ussukā’ means those who, having become eager and full of desire for amassing wealth, gather much wealth with difficulty. There is also a reading ‘ye ussukā,’ meaning those men who are eager to amass wealth—whether they are skilled in arts such as elephant training or are unskilled, and even those working for wages—gather much wealth. ‘Lakkhivā tāni bhuñjati’ means a person of merit, enjoying the fruit of his own merit, enjoys that wealth spoken of as ‘much wealth’ even without performing any work himself.

Aticcaññeva pāṇinoti aticca aññe eva pāṇino. Eva-kāro purimapadena yojetabbo, sabbattheva katapuññassa aññe akatapuññe satte atikkamitvāti attho. Appanāyatanesupīti api anāyatanesupi aratanākaresu ratanāni asuvaṇṇāyatanādīsu suvaṇṇādīni ahatthāyatanādīsu hatthiādayoti saviññāṇakaaviññāṇakā bahū bhogā uppajjanti[V 2.0340]. Tattha muttāmaṇiādīnaṃ anākare uppattiyaṃ duṭṭhagāmaṇiabhayamahārājassa vatthu kathetabbaṃ.

‘Aticcaññeva pāṇino’ means having indeed surpassed other beings. The particle ‘eva’ should be connected with the preceding word, meaning that one who has made merit in every way surpasses other beings who have not made merit. ‘Appanāyatanesupī’ means even in unsuitable places, such as places that are not sources of jewels, or non-sources of gold, or non-habitats for elephants, many treasures—both animate and inanimate—arise. In this connection, regarding the arising of pearls, gems, and so on from a non-source, the story of the Great King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya should be related.

Satthā [M 2.0372] pana imā gāthā vatvā “gahapati, imesaṃ sattānaṃ puññasadisaṃ aññaṃ āyatanaṃ nāma natthi, puññavantānañhi anākaresu ratanāni uppajjantiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammaṃ desesi –

The Teacher, having spoken these stanzas, said: ‘Householder, for these beings there is no other foundation like merit. For those with merit, treasures indeed arise even from non-sources.’ Having said this, he taught this Dhamma:

“Esa devamanussānaṃ, sabbakāmadado nidhi;

Yaṃ yadevābhipatthenti, sabbametena labbhati.

‘‘This is a treasure for gods and humans, a giver of all desired things; whatever they may long for, all is obtained by means of this.

“Suvaṇṇatā susaratā, susaṇṭhānā surūpatā;

Ādhipaccaparivāro, sabbametena labbhati.

‘‘A fine complexion, a sweet voice, a graceful figure, a beautiful form, sovereignty, and a retinue—all this is obtained by means of this.

“Padesarajjaṃ issariyaṃ, cakkavattisukhaṃ piyaṃ;

Devarajjampi dibbesu, sabbametena labbhati.

‘‘Regional kingship, sovereignty, the beloved happiness of a wheel-turning monarch, even divine kingship among the gods—all this is obtained by means of this.

“Mānussikā ca sampatti, devaloke ca yā rati;

Yā ca nibbānasampatti, sabbametena labbhati.

‘‘Human accomplishment, whatever delight is in the world of the gods, and the accomplishment of Nibbāna—all this is obtained by means of this.

“Mittasampadamāgamma, yonisova payuñjato;

Vijjāvimuttivasībhāvo, sabbametena labbhati.

‘‘Relying on the blessing of good friends, for one who strives in the right way, mastery over knowledge, liberation, and the powers—all this is obtained by means of this.

“Paṭisambhidā vimokkhā ca, yā ca sāvakapāramī;

Paccekabodhi buddhabhūmi, sabbametena labbhati.

‘‘The analytical knowledges, the liberations, the perfections of a disciple, the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, and the stage of Buddhahood—all this is obtained by means of this.

“Evaṃ mahatthikā esā, yadidaṃ puññasampadā;

Tasmā dhīrā pasaṃsanti, paṇḍitā katapuññata”nti. (khu. pā. 8.10-16);

‘‘Thus the attainment of merit is of such great benefit. Therefore the wise, the sagacious, praise the state of having made merit.’’

Idāni [P 2.0415] yesu anāthapiṇḍikassa sirī patiṭṭhitā, tāni ratanāni dassetuṃ “kukkuṭo”tiādimāha.

Now, to show those treasures in which Anāthapiṇḍika's good fortune resided, he spoke the verse beginning, ‘A cock...’

102.

102.

“Kukkuṭo [V 2.0341] maṇayo daṇḍo, thiyo ca puññalakkhaṇā;

Uppajjanti apāpassa, katapuññassa jantuno”ti.

‘‘A cock, gems, a staff, and women with the marks of merit; these arise for a person who is without evil and who has made merit.’’

Tattha daṇḍoti ārakkhayaṭṭhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, thiyoti seṭṭhibhariyaṃ puññalakkhaṇadeviṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Gāthaṃ vatvā ca pana jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, kulūpakatāpaso pana ahameva sammāsambuddho ahosi”nti.

Therein, ‘daṇḍo’ refers to a protective staff; ‘thiyo’ refers to the treasurer's wife, Puññalakkhaṇā Devī. The rest here is clear. Having spoken the stanza, he then made the connection of the Jātaka: ‘At that time the king was Ānanda, but the family-advisor ascetic was I myself, the Perfectly Enlightened One.’

Sirijātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Fourth, the Sirijātaka Commentary.

[285] 5. Maṇisūkarajātakavaṇṇanā

[285] 5. The Maṇisūkarajātaka Commentary

Dariyā [M 2.0373] satta vassānīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sundarīmāraṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukatoti vatthu udāne (udā. 38) āgatameva. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – bhagavato kira bhikkhusaṅghassa ca pañcannaṃ mahānadīnaṃ mahoghasadise lābhasakkāre uppanne hatalābhasakkārā aññatitthiyā sūriyuggamanakāle khajjopanakā viya nippabhā hutvā ekato sannipatitvā mantayiṃsu – “mayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya hatalābhasakkārā, na koci amhākaṃ atthibhāvampi jānāti, kena nu kho saddhiṃ ekato hutvā samaṇassa gotamassa avaṇṇaṃ uppādetvā lābhasakkāramassa antaradhāpeyyāmā”ti. Atha nesaṃ etadahosi – “sundariyā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā sakkuṇissāmā”ti.

‘For seven years the cave...’—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story concerning the murder of Sundarī. The background story, ‘At that time the Blessed One was honored and revered,’ is found in the Udāna. This is the summary: When gain and honor accrued to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus like the great flood of the five great rivers, the adherents of other sects lost their own gain and honor and became as lustreless as fireflies at sunrise. Gathering together, they conferred: ‘From the time the ascetic Gotama arose, we have lost our gain and honor. No one even knows that we exist. With whom can we conspire to spread dispraise of the ascetic Gotama and make his gain and honor disappear?’ Then it occurred to them: ‘We can do it by conspiring with Sundarī.’

Te ekadivasaṃ sundariṃ titthiyārāmaṃ pavisitvā vanditvā ṭhitaṃ nālapiṃsu. Sā punappunaṃ sallapantīpi paṭivacanaṃ alabhitvā “api nu, ayyā, tumhe kenaci viheṭhitātthā”ti pucchi. “Kiṃ, bhagini, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ amhe viheṭhetvā hatalābhasakkāre katvā vicarantaṃ na passasī”ti. Sā evamāha – “mayā ettha kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? Tvaṃ khosi, bhagini, abhirūpā sobhaggappattā, samaṇassa gotamassa ayasaṃ āropetvā mahājanaṃ tava kathaṃ [P 2.0416] gāhāpetvā hatalābhasakkāraṃ karohī”ti? Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā vanditvā pakkantā. Tato paṭṭhāya mālāgandhavilepanakappūrakaṭukaphalādīni gahetvā sāyaṃ mahājanassa satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nagaraṃ pavisanakāle jetavanābhimukhī gacchati. “Kahaṃ gacchasī”ti ca puṭṭhā “samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ, ahañhi tena saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasāmī”ti vatvā aññatarasmiṃ [V 2.0342] titthiyārāme vasitvā pātova jetavanamaggaṃ otaritvā nagarābhimukhī gacchati. “Kiṃ, sundari, kahaṃ gatāsī”ti ca puṭṭhā “samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasitvā taṃ kilesaratiyā ramāpetvā āgatāmhī”ti vadati.

One day, when the sectarians did not speak to Sundarī as she entered their park, paid them homage, and stood there. Although she tried to speak with them repeatedly, she received no reply and asked, 'Sirs, has someone vexed you?' They replied, 'Sister, do you not see the ascetic Gotama going about, having vexed us and destroyed our gain and honor?' She said, 'What can I do about this?' They said, 'Sister, you are beautiful and have attained the height of charm. Impute infamy to the ascetic Gotama, make the people believe your words, and cause his gain and honor to be destroyed.' Agreeing with 'Very well,' she paid them homage and departed. From then on, taking garlands, perfumes, ointments, camphor, and pungent fruits, she would head toward Jetavana in the evening at the time when the great crowd, having listened to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, was entering the city. When asked, 'Where are you going?' she would say, 'To the ascetic Gotama; I live with him in the same perfumed chamber.' Then, after staying in a certain sectarian park, she would come down the road from Jetavana early in the morning and head toward the city. When asked, 'Sundarī, where have you been?' she would say, 'I have come from staying with the ascetic Gotama in the same perfumed chamber, having delighted him with sensual pleasure.'

Atha naṃ katipāhaccayena dhuttānaṃ kahāpaṇe datvā “gacchatha sundariṃ māretvā samaṇassa gotamassa gandhakuṭiyā samīpe mālākacavarantare nikkhipitvā [M 2.0374] ethā”ti vadiṃsu, te tathā akaṃsu. Tato titthiyā “sundariṃ na passāmā”ti kolāhalaṃ katvā rañño ārocetvā “kahaṃ vo āsaṅkā”ti vuttā “imesu divasesu jetavane vasati, tatrassā pavattiṃ na jānāmā”ti vatvā “tena hi gacchatha, naṃ vicinathā”ti raññā anuññātā attano upaṭṭhāke gahetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā vicinantā mālākacavarantare disvā mañcakaṃ āropetvā nagaraṃ pavesetvā “samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā ‘satthārā katapāpakammaṃ paṭicchādessāmā’ti sundariṃ māretvā mālākacavarantare nikkhipiṃsū”ti rañño ārocesuṃ, rājā “tena hi gacchatha, nagaraṃ āhiṇḍathā”ti āha. Te nagaravīthīsu “passatha samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ kamma”ntiādīni viravitvā puna rañño nivesanadvāraṃ agamaṃsu.

Then, after a few days had passed, the sectarians gave coins to some scoundrels and said, 'Go, kill Sundarī, and having thrown her into the refuse of flowers near the ascetic Gotama’s perfumed chamber, come back.' They did as they were told. Then the sectarians, making an uproar that they could not find Sundarī, reported it to the king. When asked, 'Where do you have suspicion?' they said, 'In these days she has been staying in Jeta’s Grove, but we do not know her condition there.' The king permitted them, saying, 'Well then, go and search for her.' They took their own attendants, went to Jeta’s Grove, and while searching, they found her in the flower refuse. Placing her on a bier and bringing her into the city, they reported to the king: 'The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, wishing to conceal the evil deed done by their Teacher, killed Sundarī and threw her into the flower refuse.' The king said, 'Well then, go and parade through the city.' They went through the city streets shouting, 'Behold the deed of the Sakyan ascetics!' and so on, and then returned to the gate of the king’s palace.

Rājā sundariyā sarīraṃ āmakasusāne aṭṭakaṃ āropetvā rakkhāpesi. Sāvatthivāsino ṭhapetvā ariyasāvake sesā yebhuyyena “passatha samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ kamma”ntiādīni vatvā antonagare ca bahinagare ca bhikkhū akkosantā paribhāsantā vicaranti. Bhikkhū taṃ pavattiṃ tathāgatassa ārocesuṃ. Satthā “tena hi tumhepi te manusse evaṃ paṭicodethā”ti –

The king had Sundarī’s body placed on a platform in the charnel ground and had it guarded. Except for the noble disciples, the inhabitants of Sāvatthī for the most part went about reviling and abusing the bhikkhus both inside and outside the city, saying: 'Behold the deed of the Sakyan ascetics!' and so on. The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Teacher said: 'Well then, bhikkhus, you should reprove those people thus:'

“Abhūtavādī nirayaṃ upeti, yo vāpi katvā na karomi cāha;

Ubhopi [P 2.0417] te pecca samā bhavanti, nihīnakammā manujā paratthā”ti. (udā. 38) –

'One who speaks what is not true goes to hell, as does one who, having done a deed, says, "I did not do it." Both of them, being people of base actions, become equal in the world beyond.'

Imaṃ gāthamāha.

He spoke this verse.

Rājā “sundariyā aññehi māritabhāvaṃ jānāthā”ti purise pesesi. Tepi kho dhuttā tehi kahāpaṇehi suraṃ pivantā aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ karonti. Tattheko evamāha – “tvaṃ sundariṃ ekappahāreneva māretvā mālākacavarantare nikkhipitvā tato laddhakahāpaṇehi suraṃ pivasi, hotu hotū”ti. Rājapurisā te dhutte gahetvā rañño dassesuṃ. Atha te rājā “tumhehi [V 2.0343] māritā”ti pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Kehi mārāpitā”ti? “Aññatitthiyehi, devā”ti. Rājā [M 2.0375] titthiye pakkosāpetvā sundariṃ ukkhipāpetvā “gacchatha tumhe, evaṃ vadantā nagaraṃ āhiṇḍatha ‘ayaṃ sundarī samaṇassa gotamassa avaṇṇaṃ āropetukāmehi amhehi mārāpitā, neva samaṇassa gotamassa, na gotamasāvakānaṃ doso atthi, amhākaṃyeva doso’”ti āṇāpesi. Te tathā akaṃsu. Bālamahājano tadā saddahi, titthiyāpi purisavadhadaṇḍena palibuddhā. Tato paṭṭhāya buddhānaṃ mahantataro lābhasakkāro ahosi.

The king sent men, saying, 'Find out if Sundarī was killed by others.' Those scoundrels, drinking liquor with the coins they had received, were quarreling with one another. One of them said: 'You killed Sundarī with a single blow, threw her into the flower refuse, and now you drink liquor with the coins obtained from that. What kind of people are you?' The king’s men seized those scoundrels and presented them to the king. The king then asked them, 'Did you kill Sundarī?' They replied, 'Yes, Your Majesty.' 'Who had you kill her?' the king asked. 'The sectarians from outside the Dispensation had us kill her,' they said. The king summoned the sectarians and commanded them to carry Sundarī on a bier and parade through the city, saying: 'This Sundarī was killed by us, who wished to impute infamy to the ascetic Gotama. There is no fault on the part of the ascetic Gotama's disciples; the fault is ours alone.' They did as the king commanded. The foolish populace then believed the truth. The sectarians were also punished with the penalty for murder. From then on, even greater gain and honor arose for the Buddhas.

Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, titthiyā ‘buddhānaṃ kāḷakabhāvaṃ uppādessāmā’ti sayaṃ kāḷakā jātā, buddhānaṃ pana mahantataro lābhasakkāro udapādī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, sakkā buddhānaṃ saṃkilesaṃ uppādetuṃ, buddhānaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhabhāvakaraṇaṃ nāma jātimaṇino kiliṭṭhabhāvakaraṇasadisaṃ, pubbe jātimaṇiṃ ‘kiliṭṭhaṃ karissāmā’ti vāyamantāpi nāsakkhiṃsu kiliṭṭhaṃ kātu”nti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: 'Friends, the sectarians, intending to create a stain for the Buddhas, have themselves become stained, while even greater gain and honor have arisen for the Buddhas.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'For what discussion are you now gathered, bhikkhus?' When they told him, he said: 'Bhikkhus, it is not possible to create a defilement for the Buddhas. Attempting to defile a Buddha is like trying to stain a genuine gem. In the past, people made efforts to stain a genuine ruby, but they were unable to do so.' Then, at the request of the bhikkhus, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ gāmake brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā nikkhamitvā himavantapadese tisso pabbatarājiyo atikkamitvā tāpaso hutvā paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasi. Tassā avidūre maṇiguhā ahosi, tattha tiṃsamattā sūkarā vasanti, guhāya avidūre eko sīho carati, tassa maṇimhi [P 2.0418] chāyā paññāyati. Sūkarā sīhacchāyaṃ disvā bhītā utrastā appamaṃsalohitā ahesuṃ. Te “imassa maṇino vippasannattā ayaṃ chāyā paññāyati, imaṃ maṇiṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ vivaṇṇaṃ karomā”ti cintetvā avidūre ekaṃ saraṃ gantvā kalale pavaṭṭetvā āgantvā taṃ maṇiṃ ghaṃsanti. So sūkaralomehi ghaṃsiyamāno vippasannataro ahosi. Sūkarā upāyaṃ apassantā “imassa maṇino vivaṇṇakaraṇūpāyaṃ tāpasaṃ pucchissāmā”ti bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā purimā dve gāthā udāhariṃsu –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a small village. When he came of age, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, he went forth from home. Crossing three mountain ranges in the Himalayan region, he became an ascetic and dwelt in a leaf-hut. Not far from it there was a jewel-cave where about thirty boars lived. Not far from the cave a lion used to roam, and its reflection would appear in the jewel. Seeing the lion’s reflection, the boars were frightened and terrified, and they grew lean and wasted away. They thought: “It is because this jewel is so clear that this reflection appears. Let us make this jewel stained and discolored.” They went to a nearby lake, rolled in the mud, came back, and rubbed the jewel. But as it was rubbed with the boars’ bristles, it became even more radiant. Unable to find a means to succeed, the boars thought: “We will ask the ascetic for a way to discolor this jewel.” They approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage to him, stood to one side, and recited the first two verses:

103.

103.

“Dariyā satta vassāni, tiṃsamattā vasāmase;

Haññāma maṇino ābhaṃ, iti no mantaraṃ ahu.

“For seven years in this cave

we thirty boars have dwelt.

‘Let’s destroy the jewel’s sheen!’—

such was the plan we made.

104.

104.

“Yāvatā [V 2.0344][M 2.0376] maṇiṃ ghaṃsāma, bhiyyo vodāyate maṇi;

Idañcadāni pucchāma, kiṃ kiccaṃ idha maññasī”ti.

“But the more we rub the jewel,

the brighter does it shine.

So now we come to ask you:

What do you think we should do?”

Tattha dariyāti maṇiguhāyaṃ. Vasāmaseti vasāma. Haññāmāti hanissāma, mayampi vivaṇṇaṃ karissāma. Idañcadāni pucchāmāti idāni mayaṃ “kena kāraṇena ayaṃ maṇi kilissamāno vodāyate”ti idaṃ taṃ pucchāma. “Kiṃ kiccaṃ ‘idha maññasī’ti imasmiṃ atthe tvaṃ imaṃ kiccaṃ kinti maññasī”ti.

Therein, ‘in this cave’ means in the jewel-cave. ‘We have dwelt’ means we dwell. ‘Let’s destroy’ means we will destroy, we will make it discolored. ‘So now we come to ask you’ means: now we ask you this, “For what reason does this jewel become purer even when being soiled?” ‘What do you think we should do?’ means: in this matter, what do you think should be done?

Atha nesaṃ ācikkhanto bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, explaining it to them, spoke the third verse:

105.

105.

“Ayaṃ maṇi veḷuriyo, akāco vimalo subho;

Nāssa sakkā siriṃ hantuṃ, apakkamatha sūkarā”ti.

“This jewel is beryl, flawless, stainless, pure, and bright. Its splendor cannot be destroyed. Go away from here, you boars!”

Tattha akācoti akakkaso. Subhoti sobhano. Sirinti pabhaṃ. Apakkamathāti imassa maṇissa pabhā nāsetuṃ na sakkā, tumhe pana imaṃ maṇiguhaṃ pahāya aññattha gacchathāti.

Therein, ‘flawless’ means not coarse. ‘Bright’ means beautiful. ‘Splendor’ means radiance. ‘Go away from here’ means: the radiance of this jewel cannot be destroyed; you should abandon this jewel-cave and go elsewhere.

Te tassa kathaṃ sutvā tathā akaṃsu. Bodhisatto jhānaṃ uppādetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having heard his words, they did so. The Bodhisatta developed the jhānas and was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā tāpaso ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher identified the birth: “At that time, I myself was the ascetic.”

Maṇisūkarajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary to the Maṇisūkara Jātaka, the Fifth.

[286] 6. Sālūkajātakavaṇṇanā

[286] 6. The Commentary to the Sālūka Jātaka

Mā [P 2.0419] sālūkassa pihayīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto thullakumārikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ cūḷanāradakassapajātake (jā. 1.13.40 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Taṃ pana bhikkhuṃ satthā pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, bhikkhu, ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchi. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti. “Ko taṃ ukkaṇṭhāpetī”ti? “Thullakumārikā, bhante”ti. Satthā “esā te bhikkhu [V 2.0345] anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ etissā vivāhatthāya āgataparisāya uttaribhaṅgo ahosī”ti vatvā bhikkhūhi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Do not envy Sālūka.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the luring of a bhikkhu by a stout young woman. The full story will be told in the Cūḷanārada-Kassapa Jātaka. The Teacher had that bhikkhu summoned and asked: “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are discontented?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.” “What has made you discontented?” “A stout young woman, Venerable Sir.” The Teacher said: “Bhikkhu, she is a cause of harm for you. In the past, too, on her account you were made into a special dish for the guests who had come for her wedding.” Then, at the request of the bhikkhus, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 2.0377] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mahālohitagoṇo nāma ahosi, kaniṭṭhabhātā panassa cūḷalohito nāma. Ubhopi goṇā gāmake ekasmiṃ kule kammaṃ karonti. Tassa kulassa ekā vayappattā kumārikā atthi, taṃ aññakulaṃ vāresi. Atha naṃ kulaṃ “vivāhakāle uttaribhaṅgo bhavissatī”ti sālūkaṃ nāma sūkaraṃ yāgubhattena paṭijaggi, so heṭṭhāmañce sayati. Athekadivasaṃ cūḷalohito bhātaraṃ āha – “bhātika, mayaṃ imasmiṃ kule kammaṃ karoma, amhe nissāya imaṃ kulaṃ jīvati, atha ca panime manussā amhākaṃ tiṇapalālamattaṃ denti, imaṃ sūkaraṃ yāgubhattena posenti, heṭṭhāmañce sayāpenti, kiṃ nāmesa etesaṃ karissatī”ti. Mahālohito “tāta, mā tvaṃ etassa yāgubhattaṃ patthaya, etissā kumārikāya vivāhadivase etaṃ uttaribhaṅgaṃ kātukāmā ete maṃsassa thūlabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ posenti, katipāhaccayena taṃ passissasi heṭṭhāmañcato nikkhāmetvā vadhitvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā āgantukabhattaṃ kariyamāna”nti vatvā purimā dve gāthā samuṭṭhāpesi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a great red ox named Mahālohita, and his younger brother was named Cūḷalohita. Both oxen worked for a family in a small village. That family had a daughter who had come of age, and another family sought her in marriage. Then the family, thinking, “At the wedding there will be a special dish,” took care of a boar named Sālūka, feeding it with gruel and rice. It slept under the bed. One day Cūḷalohita said to his brother: “Brother, we do all the work in this family; this family lives because of us. Yet these people give us only grass and straw, while they nourish this boar with gruel and rice and let it sleep under the bed. What work will it do for them?” Mahālohita replied: “My dear, do not envy its gruel and rice. They are nourishing it to fatten its flesh because they want to make it into a special dish on the day of the daughter’s wedding. In a few days you will see it being dragged out from under the bed, killed, cut into pieces, and made into a meal for the guests.” Having said this, he recited the first two verses:

106.

106.

“Mā [P 2.0420] sālūkassa pihayi, āturannāni bhuñjati;

Appossukko bhusaṃ khāda, etaṃ dīghāyulakkhaṇaṃ.

“Do not envy Sālūka, for he eats the food of the afflicted. Be unconcerned and eat chaff; this is a mark of long life.

107.

107.

“Idāni so idhāgantvā, atithī yuttasevako;

Atha dakkhasi sālūkaṃ, sayantaṃ musaluttara”nti.

“Now the guest has come here, attended by his retinue. Then you will see Sālūka lying dead, with his pestle-like snout.”

Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – tāta, tvaṃ mā sālūkasūkarabhāvaṃ patthayi, ayañhi āturannāni maraṇabhojanāni bhuñjati, yāni bhuñjitvā nacirasseva maraṇaṃ pāpuṇissati, tvaṃ pana appossukko nirālayo hutvā attanā laddhaṃ imaṃ palālamissakaṃ bhusaṃ khāda, etaṃ dīghāyubhāvassa lakkhaṇaṃ sañjānananimittaṃ. Idāni katipāhasseva so vevāhikapuriso mahatiyā parisāya yutto yuttasevako idha atithi hutvā āgato bhavissati, athetaṃ sālūkaṃ musalasadisena uttaroṭṭhena samannāgatattā musaluttaraṃ māritaṃ sayantaṃ dakkhasīti.

Here is the concise meaning: ‘Dear, do not aspire to the state of the pig Sālūka. For he eats food that brings affliction—food for the dying; having eaten it, he will soon meet his death. But you, being without anxiety and without attachment, eat this chaff mixed with straw that you have obtained—this is a mark and a sign of a long life. Now, in just a few days, that bridegroom, accompanied by a great crowd and attended by servants, will arrive here as a guest. Then you will see this Sālūka killed and lying dead, who is called ‘pestle-snout’ on account of having an upper lip like a pestle.’

Tato katipāhasseva vevāhikesu āgatesu sālūkaṃ māretvā uttaribhaṅgamakaṃsu. Ubho goṇā [V 2.0346] taṃ tassa vipattiṃ disvā “amhākaṃ [M 2.0378] bhusameva vara”nti cintayiṃsu. Satthā abhisambuddho hutvā tadatthajotikaṃ tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, after only a few days, when the relatives of the bride had arrived, they killed Sālūka and made him into a side dish. Both oxen, seeing his misfortune, thought, 'Our own food of chaff is indeed better.' The Teacher, having attained perfect enlightenment, spoke the third verse to illustrate the meaning:

108.

108.

“Vikantaṃ sūkaraṃ disvā, sayantaṃ musaluttaraṃ;

Jaraggavā vicintesuṃ, varamhākaṃ bhusāmivā”ti.

“Seeing the slaughtered pig lying dead, with its pestle-like snout, the old oxen thought, ‘Our chaff is indeed better!’”

Tattha bhusāmivāti bhusameva amhākaṃ varaṃ uttamanti attho.

Here, 'bhusāmivā' means our chaff alone is better, is excellent.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā kumārikā etarahi thullakumārikā ahosi, sālūko ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, cūḷalohito ānando, mahālohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, revealed the truths, and connected the Jātaka, the Teacher concluded the birth-story. At the conclusion of the truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the young woman was this stout woman, Sālūka was the discontented monk, Cūḷalohita was Ānanda, and Mahālohita was none other than myself.”

Sālūkajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Sālūka Jātaka, the sixth.

[287] 7. Lābhagarahajātakavaṇṇanā

[287] 7. The Commentary on the Lābhagaraha Jātaka

Nānummattoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāriputtattherassa saddhivihārikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Therassa kira saddhivihāriko [P 2.0421] theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno “lābhuppattipaṭipadaṃ me, bhante, kathetha, kiṃ karonto cīvarādīnaṃ lābhī hotī”ti pucchi. Athassa thero “āvuso, catūhaṅgehi samannāgatassa lābhasakkāro uppajjati, attano abbhantare hirottappaṃ bhinditvā sāmaññaṃ pahāya anummatteneva ummattena viya bhavitabbaṃ, pisuṇavācā vattabbā, naṭasadisena bhavitabbaṃ, vikiṇṇavācena kutūhalena bhavitabba”nti imaṃ lābhuppattipaṭipadaṃ kathesi. So taṃ paṭipadaṃ garahitvā uṭṭhāya pakkanto. Thero satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Satthā “neso, sāriputta, bhikkhu idāneva lābhaṃ garahati, pubbepesa garahiyevā”ti vatvā therena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Not mad”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the co-resident of the Elder Sāriputta. It seems the Elder's co-resident approached the Elder, paid homage, sat to one side, and asked, “Venerable sir, please tell me the practice for the arising of gain. By doing what does one become a recipient of robes and other requisites?” Then the Elder said to him, “Friend, gain and honor arise for one endowed with four qualities: one must break one’s inner sense of shame and dread, abandon the state of a recluse, and behave like a madman though not mad; one must speak divisive words; one must be like an actor; and one must be a busybody with scattered talk.” Thus he explained the practice for the arising of gain. Disapproving of that practice, the monk rose and left. The Elder approached the Teacher, paid homage, and reported the matter. The Teacher said, “Sāriputta, this monk does not only now reproach gain; in the past also he reproached it.” Having been requested by the Elder, he related the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto soḷasavassikakāleyeva tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ aṭṭhārasannañca sippānaṃ pariyosānaṃ patvā disāpāmokkho ācariyo [M 2.0379] hutvā pañca māṇavakasatāni sippaṃ vācesi. Tatreko māṇavo sīlācārasampanno ekadivasaṃ ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kathaṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ lābho uppajjatī”ti [V 2.0347] lābhuppattipaṭipadaṃ pucchi. Ācariyo “tāta, imesaṃ sattānaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi lābho uppajjatī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. Having come of age, by the time he was sixteen years old, he had reached the limit of the three Vedas and the eighteen arts. Becoming a world-renowned teacher, he taught the arts to five hundred students. Among them, one student, accomplished in virtue and conduct, approached the teacher one day and asked, “How does gain arise for these beings?” The teacher replied, “Dear one, gain arises for these beings through four causes,” and then recited the first verse:

109.

109.

“Nānummatto nāpisuṇo, nānaṭo nākutūhalo;

Mūḷhesu labhate lābhaṃ, esā te anusāsanī”ti.

“One who acts mad, a slanderer, an actor, and a busybody—among the deluded, such a one obtains gain. This is the instruction for you.”

Tattha nānummattoti na anummatto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā ummattako nāma itthipurisadārikadārake disvā tesaṃ vatthālaṅkārādīni vilumpati, tato tato macchamaṃsapūvādīni balakkārena gahetvā khādati, evameva yo gihibhūto ajjhattabahiddhasamuṭṭhānaṃ hirottappaṃ pahāya kusalākusalaṃ agaṇetvā nirayabhayaṃ abhāyanto lobhābhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto kāmesu pamatto sandhicchedādīni sāhasikakammāni karoti, pabbajitopi hirottappaṃ pahāya kusalākusalaṃ agaṇetvā nirayabhayaṃ abhāyanto satthārā paññattaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ maddanto lobhena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto cīvarādimattaṃ nissāya attano sāmaññaṃ vijahitvā pamatto vejjakammadūtakammādīni karoti, veḷudānādīni nissāya jīvikaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ anummattopi ummattasadisattā ummatto nāma[P 2.0422], evarūpassa khippaṃ lābho uppajjati. Yo pana evaṃ anummatto lajjī kukkuccako, esa mūḷhesu apaṇḍitesu purisesu lābhaṃ na labhati, tasmā lābhatthikena ummattakena viya bhavitabbanti.

Herein, 'nānummatto' means one who is not not-mad [i.e., one who acts mad]. This is what is meant: Just as a madman, upon seeing men, women, boys, or girls, snatches their clothes and ornaments, and then forcibly seizes and eats fish, meat, cakes, and so on; even so, a householder who, abandoning the shame and dread arising from within and without, disregarding good and evil, not fearing hell, is overwhelmed by greed, with a mind completely seized, and being heedless in sensual pleasures, commits violent acts like housebreaking; and also a monk who, abandoning shame and dread, disregarding good and evil, not fearing hell, violating the training rules laid down by the Teacher, is overwhelmed by greed, with a mind completely seized, and for the sake of a mere robe and so on, abandons his state as a recluse and heedlessly engages in medical practices, messenger work, and the like, or makes a living by means of giving bamboo and so on—this one, though not mad, is called 'mad' because of being like a madman. For such a person, gain quickly arises. But one who is truly not mad, being modest and scrupulous, does not obtain gain among foolish, unwise people. Therefore, one who desires gain should act like a madman.

Nāpisuṇoti etthāpi yo pisuṇo hoti, “asukena idaṃ nāma kata”nti rājakule pesuññaṃ upasaṃharati, so aññesaṃ yasaṃ acchinditvā attano gaṇhāti. Rājānopi naṃ “ayaṃ amhesu sasasneho”ti ucce ṭhāne ṭhapenti, amaccādayopissa “ayaṃ no rājakule paribhindeyyā”ti bhayena dātabbaṃ maññanti, evaṃ etarahi pisuṇassa lābho uppajjati. Yo pana apisuṇo, so mūḷhesu lābhaṃ na labhatīti evamattho veditabbo.

Regarding 'nāpisuṇo': one who acts as a backbiter, saying, “So-and-so did such a thing,” carries tales to the royal court, and thus, by taking away the honor of others, takes it for himself. Kings too, thinking, “This one is fond of us,” place him in high positions, while ministers and others, fearing, “This one might cause division for us in the royal court,” think they ought to give to him. Thus, gain arises for a backbiter. But one who is not a backbiter does not obtain gain among the foolish—this is how the meaning should be understood.

Nānaṭoti lābhaṃ uppādentena naṭena viya bhavitabbaṃ. Yathā naṭo hirottappaṃ pahāya naccagītavāditehi kīḷaṃ katvā dhanaṃ saṃharati, evameva lābhatthikena [M 2.0380] hirottappaṃ bhinditvā itthipurisadārikadārakānaṃ soṇḍasahāyena viya nānappakāraṃ keḷiṃ karontena vicaritabbaṃ. Yo evaṃ anaṭo, so mūḷhesu lābhaṃ na labhati.

Regarding 'nānaṭo': to produce gain, one should be like an actor. Just as an actor, abandoning shame and dread, collects wealth by making sport with dances, songs, and music, even so, one seeking gain should break through shame and dread and wander about behaving like a boon companion to women, men, girls, and boys, engaging in various kinds of sport. Whoever is thus not an actor does not obtain gain among the foolish.

Nākutūhaloti [V 2.0348] kutūhalo nāma vippakiṇṇavāco. Rājāno hi amacce pucchanti – “asukaṭṭhāne kira ‘manusso mārito, gharaṃ viluttaṃ, paresaṃ dārā padhaṃsitā’ti suyyati, kesaṃ nu kho idaṃ kamma”nti. Tattha sesesu akathentesuyeva yo uṭṭhahitvā “asuko ca asuko ca nāmā”ti vadati, ayaṃ kutūhalo nāma. Rājāno tassa vacanena te purise pariyesitvā nisedhetvā “imaṃ nissāya no nagaraṃ niccoraṃ jāta”nti tassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ denti, sesāpi janā “ayaṃ no rājapurisehi puṭṭho suyuttaduyuttaṃ katheyyā”ti bhayena tasseva dhanaṃ denti, evaṃ kutūhalassa lābho uppajjati. Yo pana akutūhalo, esa na mūḷhesu labhati lābhaṃ. Esā te anusāsanīti esā amhākaṃ santikā tuyhaṃ lābhānusiṭṭhīti.

Regarding 'not a gossip': a gossip is one of scattered speech. For kings ask their ministers: 'In such and such a place, it is heard that "a man was killed, a house was robbed, the wives of others were violated." Whose deed is this?' There, while the others remain silent, the one who stands up and says, 'So-and-so and so-and-so by name,' is called a gossip. Based on his words, the kings search for those men, restrain them, and thinking, 'Because of him, our city has become free of thieves,' they grant him great honor. Other people too, fearing, 'If questioned by the king's men, he might speak of what is proper or improper,' give him wealth. Thus, gain arises for the gossip. But one who is not a gossip does not obtain gain among the foolish. 'This is the instruction for you' means this is the instruction regarding gain given to you from our presence.

Antevāsiko ācariyassa kathaṃ sutvā lābhaṃ garahanto –

The student, having heard the teacher’s words, reproaching gain, said:

110.

110.

“Dhiratthu taṃ yasalābhaṃ, dhanalābhañca brāhmaṇa;

Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena vā.

“Shame on that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O Brahmin; whatever livelihood exists through self-ruin or through unrighteous conduct.

111.

111.

“Api ce pattamādāya, anagāro paribbaje;

Esāva jīvikā seyyo, yā cādhammena esanā”ti. – gāthādvayamāha;

“Even if one, taking a bowl, should wander homeless, this livelihood is indeed better than that seeking which is through unrighteousness.” — thus he spoke these two verses.

Tattha yā vuttīti yā jīvitavutti. Vinipātenāti attano vinipātena. Adhammacaraṇenāti adhammakiriyāya visamakiriyāya vadhabandhanagarahādīhi attānaṃ vinipātetvā adhammaṃ caritvā yā vutti, tañca yasadhanalābhañca [P 2.0423] sabbaṃ dhiratthu nindāmi garahāmi, na me etenatthoti adhippāyo. Pattamādāyāti bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā. Anagāro paribbajeti ageho pabbajito hutvā careyya, na ca sappuriso kāyaduccaritādivasena adhammacariyaṃ careyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Esāva jīvikā seyyo. Yā cādhammena esanāti, yā [M 2.0381] esā adhammena jīvikapariyesanā, tato esā pattahatthassa parakulesu bhikkhācariyāva seyyo, sataguṇena sahassaguṇena sundarataroti dasseti.

In this context, 'whatever livelihood' means any means of sustaining life. 'Through ruin' means through one’s own ruin. 'Through unrighteous conduct' means through unrighteous action or through improper action; having brought about one's own ruin through killing, imprisonment, reproach, and so on, and having practiced unrighteousness, whatever livelihood exists, along with the gain of fame and wealth—'Shame on it all, I despise and reproach it, for I have no need of it'—this is the intention. 'Taking a bowl' means taking an alms bowl. 'Should wander homeless' means having become a homeless renunciant, one should wander; and a good man should not practice unrighteous conduct by way of bodily misconduct and so on. For what reason? 'This livelihood is indeed better.' Regarding 'the seeking which is through unrighteousness': than that seeking of a livelihood through unrighteousness, this wandering for alms among families by one with bowl in hand is indeed better, showing it to be a hundred times, a thousand times more excellent.

Evaṃ māṇavo pabbajjāya guṇaṃ vaṇṇetvā nikkhamitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā dhammena bhikkhaṃ pariyesanto abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus the young man, having praised the virtue of renunciation, went forth and undertook the ascetic life of a sage. Seeking alms righteously, he developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and became destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā [V 2.0349] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā māṇavo lābhagarahī bhikkhu ahosi, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the young man was the monk who reproached gain; the teacher, however, was I myself.'

Lābhagarahajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Lābhagaraha Jātaka, the seventh.

[288] 8. Macchuddānajātakavaṇṇanā

[288] 8. The Commentary on the Macchuddāna Jātaka

Agghanti macchāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kūṭavāṇijaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā kathitameva.

“The fish are worth much” — this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a fraudulent merchant. The story has been related before.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kuṭumbikakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapesi. Kaniṭṭhabhātāpissa atthi, tesaṃ aparabhāge pitā kālakato. Te ekadivasaṃ “pitu santakaṃ vohāraṃ sādhessāmā”ti ekaṃ gāmaṃ gantvā kahāpaṇasahassaṃ labhitvā āgacchantā nadītitthe nāvaṃ paṭimānentā puṭabhattaṃ bhuñjiṃsu. Bodhisatto atirekabhattaṃ gaṅgāya macchānaṃ datvā nadīdevatāya pattiṃ adāsi. Devatā pattiṃ anumoditvāyeva dibbena yasena vaḍḍhitvā attano yasavuḍḍhiṃ āvajjamānā taṃ kāraṇaṃ aññāsi. Bodhisattopi vālikāyaṃ [P 2.0424] uttarāsaṅgaṃ pattharitvā nipanno niddaṃ okkami, kaniṭṭhabhātā panassa thokaṃ corapakatiko. So te kahāpaṇe bodhisattassa adatvā sayameva gaṇhitukāmatāya kahāpaṇabhaṇḍikasadisaṃ ekaṃ sakkharabhaṇḍikaṃ katvā dvepi bhaṇḍikā ekatova ṭhapesi. Tesaṃ nāvaṃ abhiruhitvā gaṅgāmajjhagatānaṃ kaniṭṭho nāvaṃ khobhetvā “sakkharabhaṇḍikaṃ udake [M 2.0382] khipissāmī”ti sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ khipitvā “bhātika, sahassabhaṇḍikā udake patitā, kinti karomā”ti āha. “Udake patitāya kiṃ karissāma, mā cintayī”ti. Nadīdevatā cintesi – “ahaṃ iminā dinnapattiṃ anumoditvā dibbayasena vaḍḍhitvā etassa santakaṃ rakkhissāmī”ti attano ānubhāvena taṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ ekaṃ mahāmacchaṃ gilāpetvā sayaṃ ārakkhaṃ gaṇhi. Sopi coro gehaṃ gantvā “bhātā me vañcito”ti bhaṇḍikaṃ mocento sakkharā passitvā hadayena sussantena mañcassa aṭaniṃ upagūhitvā nipajji.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of householders. Having reached the age of discretion, he established the family estate. He also had a younger brother, and in time, their father passed away. One day, thinking, 'Let us settle our father’s business,' they went to a village where they obtained a thousand coins. On their return, while waiting for a boat at the river crossing, they ate their packed meal. The Bodhisatta gave the leftover food to the fish in the Ganges and shared the merit with the river deity. The deity, rejoicing in the shared merit, increased in divine glory; reflecting on her increase in glory, she understood the cause. The Bodhisatta spread his upper robe on the sand, lay down, and fell asleep. His younger brother, however, was of a somewhat thievish nature. Wishing to take the coins for himself without giving them to the Bodhisatta, he fashioned a bag of gravel resembling the bag of coins and placed both bags together. When they had boarded the boat and reached the middle of the Ganges, the younger brother rocked the boat and, intending to throw the gravel bag into the water, threw the bag of a thousand coins instead, exclaiming, 'Brother, the bag of a thousand coins has fallen into the water! What shall we do?' The Bodhisatta replied, 'What can we do if it has fallen into the water? Do not worry.' The river deity thought, 'Having rejoiced in the merit shared by him and increased in divine glory, I shall protect his property.' By her power, she made a large fish swallow the bag and took it under her own protection. That thief, returning home and thinking, 'I have deceived my brother,' opened the bag and saw only gravel. With a withering heart, he lay down, clutching the frame of his bed.

Tadā kevaṭṭā macchagahaṇatthāya jālaṃ khipiṃsu. So maccho devatānubhāvena jālaṃ pāvisi. Kevaṭṭā taṃ gahetvā vikkiṇituṃ nagaraṃ paviṭṭhā. Manussā mahāmacchaṃ disvā mūlaṃ pucchanti. Kevaṭṭā “kahāpaṇasahassañca satta ca māsake datvā gaṇhathā”ti vadanti. Manussā “sahassagghanakamacchopi [V 2.0350] no diṭṭho”ti parihāsaṃ karonti. Kevaṭṭā macchaṃ gahetvā bodhisattassa gharadvāraṃ gantvā “imaṃ macchaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āhaṃsu. “Kimassa mūla”nti? “Satta māsake datvā gaṇhathā”ti. “Aññesaṃ dadamānā kathaṃ dethā”ti? “Aññesaṃ sahassena ca sattahi ca māsakehi dema, tumhe pana satta māsake datvā gaṇhathā”ti. So tesaṃ satta māsake datvā macchaṃ bhariyāya pesesi. Sā macchassa kucchiṃ phālayamānā sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ disvā bodhisattassa [P 2.0425] ārocesi. Bodhisatto taṃ oloketvā attano lañchaṃ disvā sakasantakabhāvaṃ ñatvā “idāni ime kevaṭṭā imaṃ macchaṃ aññesaṃ dadamānā sahassena ceva sattahi ca māsakehi denti, amhe pana patvā sahassassa amhākaṃ santakattā satteva māsake gahetvā adaṃsu, idaṃ antaraṃ ajānantaṃ na sakkā kañci saddahāpetu”nti cintetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, fishermen cast their nets to catch fish. By the power of a deity, that fish entered the net. The fishermen caught it and entered the city to sell it. People saw the great fish and asked the price. The fishermen said, "Give a thousand kahapanas and seven masakas and take it." The people mocked them, saying, "We have never seen a fish worth a thousand." The fishermen took the fish, went to the Bodhisatta’s house door, and said, "Buy this fish." "What is its price?" "Give seven masakas and take it." "When giving it to others, for how much do you sell it?" "To others, we sell it for a thousand and seven masakas, but you may take it for seven masakas." He gave them seven masakas and sent the fish to his wife. While cutting open the fish’s belly, she saw a purse of a thousand coins and told the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta examined it, saw his own seal, and knew it was his property. He thought, "Now, these fishermen, when offering this fish to others, ask for a thousand and seven masakas, but having come to us, they took only seven masakas and gave it. Since the thousand was our property, it is impossible to convince anyone who does not know this circumstance," and he spoke the first verse:

112.

112.

“Agghanti macchā adhikaṃ sahassaṃ, na so atthi yo imaṃ saddaheyya;

Mayhañca assu idha satta māsā, ahampi taṃ macchuddānaṃ kiṇeyya”nti.

“The fish are worth more than a thousand, but there is no one who would believe this. And if I had seven masakas here, I too would buy that haul of fish.”

Tattha adhikanti aññehi pucchitā kevaṭṭā “sattamāsādhikaṃ sahassaṃ agghantī”ti vadanti. Na so atthi yo imaṃ saddaheyyāti so puriso na [M 2.0383] atthi, yo imaṃ kāraṇaṃ paccakkhato ajānanto mama vacanena saddaheyya, ettakaṃ vā macchā agghantīti yo imaṃ saddaheyya, so natthi, tasmāyeva te aññehi na gahitātipi attho. Mayhañca assūti mayhaṃ pana satta māsakā ahesuṃ. Macchuddānanti macchavaggaṃ. Tena hi macchena saddhiṃ aññepi macchā ekato baddhā taṃ sakalampi macchuddānaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiṇeyyanti kiṇiṃ, satteva māsake datvā ettakaṃ macchavaggaṃ gaṇhinti attho.

Herein, 'adhikaṃ' means that when asked by others, the fishermen say, "They are worth a thousand plus seven masakas." 'Na so atthi yo imaṃ saddaheyya' means there is no person who, not knowing this reason firsthand, would believe my words; or, there is no one who would believe that the fish are worth so much, and that is why they were not bought by others. 'Mayhañca assu' means 'but seven masakas were mine.' 'Macchuddānaṃ' means a group of fish. Since other fish were tied together with that fish, this was said in reference to the entire haul. 'Kiṇeyyaṃ' means 'I bought'; the meaning is, 'having given only seven masakas, I took such a group of fish.'

Evañca pana vatvā idaṃ cintesi – “kiṃ nu kho nissāya mayā ete kahāpaṇā laddhā”ti? Tasmiṃ khaṇe nadīdevatā ākāse dissamānarūpena ṭhatvā “ahaṃ, gaṅgādevatā, tayā macchānaṃ atirekabhattaṃ datvā mayhaṃ patti dinnā, tenāhaṃ tava santakaṃ rakkhantī āgatā”ti dīpayamānā gāthamāha –

And having said this, he reflected: "By what means have I obtained these coins?" At that moment, the river deity, standing in the sky in a visible form, revealed: "I am the river deity. Because you gave the excess food to the fish and shared the merit with me, I have come, guarding your property." Explaining this, she spoke this verse:

113.

113.

“Macchānaṃ bhojanaṃ datvā, mama dakkhiṇamādisi;

Taṃ dakkhiṇaṃ sarantiyā, kataṃ apacitiṃ tayā”ti.

“Having given food to the fish, you shared the merit with me; remembering that merit and the honor shown by you.”

Tattha [V 2.0351][P 2.0426] dakkhiṇanti imasmiṃ ṭhāne pattidānaṃ dakkhiṇā nāma. Sarantiyā kataṃ apacitiṃ tayāti taṃ tayā mayhaṃ kataṃ apacitiṃ sarantiyā mayā idaṃ tava dhanaṃ rakkhitanti attho.

In this context, 'dakkhiṇā' means the sharing of merit (pattidāna). 'Sarantiyā kataṃ apacitiṃ tayā' means: "Remembering that honor done by you to me, I have protected this wealth of yours."

Idaṃ vatvā ca pana sā devatā tassa kaniṭṭhena katakūṭakammaṃ sabbaṃ kathetvā “eso idāni hadayena sussantena nipanno, duṭṭhacittassa vuḍḍhi nāma natthi, ahaṃ pana ‘tava santakaṃ mā nassī’ti dhanaṃ te āharitvā adāsiṃ, idaṃ kaniṭṭhacorassa adatvā sabbaṃ tvaññeva gaṇhā”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, the deity told him all the deceitful acts committed by his younger brother and said: "Now, he lies here with a parched heart. There is no prosperity for one with a corrupt mind. But I, thinking, 'Let not what belongs to you be lost,' brought the wealth and gave it to you. Without giving it to the thieving younger brother, take it all yourself." Then she spoke the third verse:

114.

114.

“Paduṭṭhacittassa na phāti hoti, na cāpi taṃ devatā pūjayanti;

Yo bhātaraṃ pettikaṃ sāpateyyaṃ, avañcayī dukkaṭakammakārī”ti.

“There is no prosperity for one with a corrupt mind, nor do the deities honor him—the evil-doer who has defrauded his brother of his paternal inheritance.”

Tattha na phāti hotīti evarūpassa puggalassa idhaloke vā paraloke vā vuḍḍhi nāma na hoti. Na cāpi tanti taṃ puggalaṃ tassa santakaṃ rakkhamānā devatā na pūjayanti.

Here, 'na phāti hoti' means for such a person there is no progress, either in this world or the next. 'Na cāpi taṃ' means the deities who guard property do not honor such a person.

Iti [M 2.0384] devatā mittadubbhicorassa kahāpaṇe adātukāmā evamāha. Bodhisatto pana “na sakkā evaṃ kātu”nti tassapi pañca kahāpaṇasatāni pesesiyeva.

Thus the deity, not wishing to give the coins to the treacherous thief, spoke in this way. The Bodhisatta, however, thinking, "It is not possible to act thus," sent five hundred coins to his brother anyway.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne vāṇijo sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā kaniṭṭhabhātā idāni kūṭavāṇijo, jeṭṭhabhātā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the merchant was established in the fruit of stream-entry. "At that time, the younger brother was the deceitful merchant, and the elder brother was I myself."

Macchuddānajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Macchuddāna Jātaka, the eighth.

[289] 9. Nānāchandajātakavaṇṇanā

[289] 9. The Commentary on the Nānāchanda Jātaka

Nānāchandā, mahārājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto āyasmato ānandassa aṭṭhavaralābhaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu ekādasakanipāte juṇhajātake (jā. 1.11.13 ādayo) āvibhavissati.

“Nānāchandā, O great king”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the eight boons received by the Venerable Ānanda. The story will appear in the Juṇha Jātaka in the Eleventh Nipāta.

Atīte [P 2.0427] pana bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi [V 2.0352] nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggahetvā pitu accayena rajjaṃ pāpuṇi. Tassa ṭhānato apanīto pitu purohito atthi. So duggato hutvā ekasmiṃ jaragehe vasati. Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto aññātakavesena rattibhāge nagaraṃ pariggaṇhanto vicarati. Tamenaṃ katakammacorā ekasmiṃ surāpāne suraṃ pivitvā aparampi ghaṭenādāya attano gehaṃ gacchantā antaravīthiyaṃ disvā “are kosi tva”nti vatvā paharitvā uttarisāṭakaṃ gahetvā ghaṭaṃ ukkhipāpetvā tāsentā gacchiṃsu. Sopi kho brāhmaṇo tasmiṃ khaṇe nikkhamitvā antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhito nakkhattaṃ olokento rañño amittānaṃ hatthagatabhāvaṃ ñatvā brāhmaṇiṃ āmantesi. Sā “kiṃ, ayyā”ti vatvā vegena tassa santikaṃ āgatā. Atha naṃ so āha – “bhoti amhākaṃ rājā amittānaṃ vasaṃ gato”ti. “Ayya, kiṃ te rañño santike pavattiyā, brāhmaṇā jānissantī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and, upon his father's death, attained the throne. There was a chaplain of his father who had been removed from his position. This chaplain, having fallen into poverty, lived in a dilapidated house. Then one day, the Bodhisatta, in disguise, was wandering through the city at night to inspect it. Some thieves, who had already committed a robbery, were drinking liquor at a tavern. As they were going to their own home carrying another pot of liquor, they saw him in the street. They struck him, saying, "Hey, who are you?" Then they took his upper garment, made him carry the pot, and went off threatening him. At that very moment, the brahmin came out and stood in the street. Observing the constellations, he realized that the king had fallen into the hands of his enemies and called to his wife. She asked, "What is it, my lord?" and quickly came to him. Then he said to her, "Madam, our king has fallen into the power of his enemies." She replied, "My lord, what concern are the king's affairs to you? The brahmins who receive wealth from the king will know."

Rājā [M 2.0385] brāhmaṇassa saddaṃ sutvā thokaṃ gantvā dhutte āha – “duggatomhi, sāmi, uttarāsaṅgaṃ gahetvā vissajjetha ma”nti. Te punappunaṃ kathentaṃ kāruññena vissajjesuṃ. So tesaṃ vasanagehaṃ sallakkhetvā nivatti. Atha porāṇakapurohito brāhmaṇopi “bhoti, amhākaṃ rājā amittahatthato mutto”ti āha. Rājā tampi sutvā tampi gehaṃ sallakkhetvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. So vibhātāya rattiyā brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā “kiṃ ācariyā rattiṃ nakkhattaṃ olokayitthā”ti pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Kiṃ sobhana”nti? “Sobhanaṃ, devā”ti. “Koci gāho natthī”ti. “Natthi, devā”ti. Rājā “asukagehato brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosathā”ti porāṇakapurohitaṃ pakkosāpetvā “kiṃ, ācariya, rattiṃ te nakkhattaṃ [P 2.0428] diṭṭha”nti pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Atthi koci gāho”ti. “Āma, mahārāja, ajja rattiṃ tumhe amittavasaṃ gantvā muhutteneva muttā”ti. Rājā “nakkhattajānanakena nāma evarūpena bhavitabba”nti sesabrāhmaṇe nikkaḍḍhāpetvā “brāhmaṇa, pasannosmi te, varaṃ tvaṃ gaṇhā”ti āha. “Mahārāja, puttadārena saddhiṃ mantetvā gaṇhissāmī”ti. “Gaccha mantetvā ehī”ti.

The king, hearing the brahmin's voice, followed for a short distance and said to the rogues, "Sirs, I am a poor man; take my upper garment and release me." As he pleaded repeatedly, they released him out of compassion. He noted their dwelling place and then turned back. Then the brahmin, the former chaplain, said, "Madam, our king has been freed from the hands of the enemy." Hearing this as well, the king noted that house and ascended to the palace. When the night had turned to dawn, he summoned the brahmins and asked, "Teachers, did you observe the stars last night?" "Yes, great king," they replied. "Was it auspicious?" the king asked. "It was auspicious, great king," they said. He asked, "Was there no danger or adversity?" and they replied, "There was none, great king." The king then said, "Summon the brahmin from such-and-such house," and had the former chaplain summoned. He asked, "Teacher, did you observe the stars last night?" "Yes, great king," he replied. "Was there any danger?" He answered, "Yes, great king; last night you fell into the power of your enemies but were freed in just a moment." The king said, "One who knows the stars must indeed be such a person as this." He then had the other brahmins expelled from the city and said, "Brahmin, I am pleased with you; choose a boon." The brahmin replied, "Great king, I will consult with my wife and children and then choose." "Go, consult them and return," said the king.

So gantvā brāhmaṇiñca puttañca suṇisañca dāsiñca pakkositvā “rājā me varaṃ dadāti, kiṃ gaṇhāmā”ti pucchi. Brāhmaṇī “mayhaṃ dhenusataṃ ānehī”ti āha, putto chattamāṇavo nāma “mayhaṃ kumudavaṇṇehi catūhi sindhavehi yuttaṃ ājaññaratha”nti, suṇisā “mayhaṃ maṇikuṇḍalaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbālaṅkāra”nti, puṇṇā nāma dāsī “mayhaṃ udukkhalamusalañceva suppañcā”ti. Brāhmaṇo pana gāmavaraṃ gahetukāmo rañño santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ[V 2.0353], brāhmaṇa, pucchito te puttadāro”ti puṭṭho “āma, deva, pucchito, anekacchando”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

The brahmin went and summoned his wife, son, daughter-in-law, and slave girl, and asked, "The king is granting me a boon; what shall we choose?" The brahmin woman said, "Bring me a hundred milch cows." The son, named Chattamāṇava, said, "For me, a chariot yoked with four Sindh horses of the color of white lotuses." The daughter-in-law said, "Bring me all kinds of ornaments, beginning with jeweled earrings." The slave girl named Puṇṇā said, "For me, a mortar, a pestle, and a winnowing basket." But the brahmin desired to have an excellent village. The brahmin went to the king and, when asked, "Brahmin, have you consulted your wife and children?" he replied, "Yes, great king, I have consulted them, and they have diverse desires." He then spoke these two verses:

115.

115.

“Nānāchandā mahārāja, ekāgāre vasāmase;

Ahaṃ gāmavaraṃ icche, brāhmaṇī ca gavaṃ sataṃ.

"Great king, we live in one house, yet our desires are diverse. I wish for an excellent village, and the brahmin woman for a hundred cows.

116.

116.

“Putto ca ājaññarathaṃ, kaññā ca maṇikuṇḍalaṃ;

Yā cesā puṇṇikā jammī, udukkhalaṃbhikaṅkhatī”ti.

"My son wishes for a chariot yoked with thoroughbreds, the maiden for jeweled earrings; and this wretched Puṇṇikā desires a mortar."

Tattha [M 2.0386] iccheti icchāmi. Gavaṃ satanti dhenūnaṃ gunnaṃ sataṃ. Kaññāti suṇisā. Yā cesāti yā esā amhākaṃ ghare puṇṇikā nāma dāsī, sā jammī lāmikā suppamusalehi saddhiṃ udukkhalaṃ abhikaṅkhati icchatīti.

In those verses, 'icche' means 'I desire.' 'Gavaṃ sataṃ' means a hundred milch cows. 'Kaññā' refers to the daughter-in-law. 'Yā cesā' means 'this Puṇṇikā, the slave girl in our house; she, being lowly, desires a mortar along with a winnowing basket and pestles.'

Rājā “sabbesaṃ icchiticchitaṃ dethā”ti āṇāpento –

The king, wishing to give to all whatever they desired, spoke this verse:

117.

117.

“Brāhmaṇassa [P 2.0429] gāmavaraṃ, brāhmaṇiyā gavaṃ sataṃ;

Puttassa ājaññarathaṃ, kaññāya maṇikuṇḍalaṃ;

Yañcetaṃ puṇṇikaṃ jammiṃ, paṭipādethudukkhala”nti. – gāthamāha;

"Give the brahmin an excellent village, the brahmin woman a hundred cows; the son a chariot yoked with thoroughbreds, the maiden jeweled earrings; and as for this wretched Puṇṇikā, provide her with a mortar."

Tattha yañcetanti yañca etaṃ puṇṇikanti vadati, taṃ jammiṃ udukkhalaṃ paṭipādetha sampaṭicchāpethāti.

In that verse, 'yañcetaṃ puṇṇikaṃ' refers to the one called Puṇṇikā; 'provide that lowly one with a mortar, a winnowing basket, and a pestle.'

Iti rājā brāhmaṇena patthitañca aññañca mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā “ito paṭṭhāya amhākaṃ kattabbakiccesu ussukkaṃ āpajjā”ti vatvā brāhmaṇaṃ attano santike akāsi.

In this way, the king gave the brahmin his desired boon and much other great wealth, saying, "From this day forward, be diligent in our affairs," and kept the brahmin in his presence.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo ānando ahosi, rājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, and the king was I myself."

Nānāchandajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Ninth, the Nānāchanda Jātaka.

[290] 10. Sīlavīmaṃsakajātakavaṇṇanā

[290] 10. Commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka

Sīlaṃ [V 2.0354] kireva kalyāṇanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ sīlavīmaṃsakabrāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana paccuppannampi atītampi heṭṭhā ekakanipāte sīlavīmaṃsakajātake (jā. 1.1.86) vitthāritameva. Idha pana bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa purohito sīlasampanno “attano sīlaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti heraññikaphalakato dve divase ekekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ gaṇhi. Atha naṃ tatiyadivase “coro”ti gahetvā rañño santikaṃ nayiṃsu. So antarāmagge ahituṇḍike sappaṃ kīḷāpente addasa. Atha naṃ rājā disvā “kasmā evarūpaṃ akāsī”ti pucchi[M 2.0387]. Brāhmaṇo “attano sīlaṃ vīmaṃsitukāmatāyā”ti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –

"Virtue, they say, is truly good." The Teacher said this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a brahmin who investigated virtue. The story, both present and past, has already been detailed in the Ekakanipāta in the Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka (Jātaka 1.1.86). Here, however, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, his chaplain, who was endowed with virtue, thought, 'I will investigate my own virtue,' and for two days took one kahāpana each from a money-changer's counter. Then, on the third day, they seized him, calling him a thief, and brought him before the king. On the way, he saw a snake charmer making a snake play. Then the king, seeing him, asked, 'Why did you do such a thing?' The brahmin replied, 'Because I wished to investigate my own virtue,' and spoke these verses:

118.

118.

“Sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇaṃ, sīlaṃ loke anuttaraṃ;

Passa ghoraviso nāgo, sīlavāti na haññati.

"Virtue, it is said, is truly good; virtue is supreme in the world. Behold the fierce venomous serpent: because it is said to have virtue, it is not harmed."

119.

119.

“Sohaṃ [P 2.0430] sīlaṃ samādissaṃ, loke anumataṃ sivaṃ;

Ariyavuttisamācāro, yena vuccati sīlavā.

"I shall therefore undertake virtue, which is approved in the world as auspicious; the practice of noble conduct, by which one is called virtuous."

120.

120.

“Ñātīnañca piyo hoti, mittesu ca virocati;

Kāyassa bhedā sugatiṃ, upapajjati sīlavā”ti.

"He is dear to his relatives, and he shines among his friends; at the breaking up of the body, the virtuous one is reborn in a happy realm."

Tattha sīlanti ācāro. Kirāti anussavatthe nipāto. Kalyāṇanti sobhanaṃ, “sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇa”nti evaṃ paṇḍitā vadantīti attho. Passāti attānameva vadati. Na haññatīti parampi na viheṭheti, parehipi na viheṭhīyati. Samādissanti samādiyissāmi. Anumataṃ sivanti “khemaṃ nibbhaya”nti evaṃ paṇḍitehi sampaṭicchitaṃ. Yena vuccatīti yena sīlena sīlavā puriso ariyānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ paṭipattiṃ samācaranto “ariyavuttisamācāro”ti vuccati, tamahaṃ samādiyissāmīti attho. Virocatīti pabbatamatthake aggikkhandho viya virocati.

Here, 'sīla' means conduct. 'Kira' is a particle indicating hearsay. 'Kalyāṇa' means beautiful; the meaning is that the wise say, 'virtue is indeed good.' 'Passa' (see) refers to the speaker himself. 'Na haññati' means one does not harm others, nor is one harmed by others. 'Samādissaṃ' means 'I will undertake.' 'Anumataṃ sivaṃ' means that which is accepted by the wise as 'safe and free from fear.' 'Yena vuccati' means: that virtue by which a virtuous person, practicing the path of the noble ones such as the Buddhas, is called 'one of noble conduct and behavior'—'that I will undertake' is the meaning. 'Virocati' means he shines like a mass of fire on a mountaintop.

Evaṃ bodhisatto tīhi gāthāhi sīlassa vaṇṇaṃ pakāsento rañño dhammaṃ desetvā “mahārāja, mama gehe pitu santakaṃ mātu santakaṃ attanā uppāditaṃ tayā dinnañca bahu dhanaṃ atthi[V 2.0355], pariyanto nāma na paññāyati, ahaṃ pana sīlaṃ vīmaṃsanto heraññikaphalakato kahāpaṇe gaṇhiṃ. Idāni mayā imasmiṃ loke jātigottakulapadesānaṃ lāmakabhāvo, sīlasseva ca jeṭṭhakabhāvo ñāto, ahaṃ pabbajissāmi, pabbajjaṃ me anujānāhī”ti anujānāpetvā raññā punappunaṃ yāciyamānopi nikkhamma himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus the Bodhisatta, extolling the virtues of morality in three verses, taught the Dhamma to the king and said: 'Great king, in my home there is much wealth inherited from my parents, earned by myself, and given by you—the end of it is not seen. But I, wishing to investigate my virtue, took kahāpanas from the money-changer's counter. Now, I have realized the lowliness of birth, lineage, and family status in this world, and the supremacy of virtue alone. I will go forth; grant me permission to go forth.' Having obtained permission, though repeatedly entreated by the king, he departed and entered the Himalayas. There, he embraced the life of an ascetic, developed higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and was destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā [M 2.0388] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sīlavīmaṃsako purohito brāhmaṇo ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the chaplain, the brahmin who investigated virtue, was none other than myself.'

Sīlavīmaṃsakajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka is finished.

Abbhantaravaggo catuttho.

The Abbhantara Vagga, the Fourth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Duma kaṃsavaruttamabyagghamigā, maṇayo maṇi sālukamavhayano;

Anusāsaniyopi ca macchavaro, maṇikuṇḍalakena kirena dasāti.

The Tree, the Excellent Bronze Bowl, the Tiger and Deer, the Jewels, the Gem, the Lotus Root, the Invitation, the Instruction, and the Excellent Fish; with the Gem Earring and 'Indeed', these are ten.

5. Kumbhavaggo

5. 5. The Kumbha Group

[291] 1. Surāghaṭajātakavaṇṇanā

[291] 1. 1. The Surāghaṭa Jātaka

Sabbakāmadadaṃ [V 2.0356][P 2.0431] kumbhanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikassa bhāgineyyaṃ ārabbha kathesi.
