So kira mātāpitūnaṃ santakā cattālīsa hiraññakoṭiyo pānabyasanena nāsetvā seṭṭhino santikaṃ agamāsi. Sopissa “vohāraṃ karohī”ti sahassaṃ adāsi, tampi nāsetvā puna agamāsi. Punassa pañca satāni dāpesi, tānipi nāsetvā puna āgatassa dve thūlasāṭake dāpesi. Tepi nāsetvā puna āgataṃ gīvāyaṃ gāhāpetvā nīharāpesi. So anātho hutvā parakuṭṭaṃ nissāya kālamakāsi, tamenaṃ kaḍḍhitvā bahi chaḍḍesuṃ. Anāthapiṇḍiko vihāraṃ gantvā sabbaṃ taṃ bhāgineyyassa pavattiṃ tathāgatassa ārocesi. Satthā “tvaṃ etaṃ kathaṃ santappessasi, yamahaṃ pubbe sabbakāmadadaṃ kumbhaṃ datvāpi santappetuṃ nāsakkhi”nti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"The pot that grants all desires." The Teacher said this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika. It is said that he squandered forty crores of gold inherited from his parents through addiction to drinking and then went to the merchant. The merchant gave him a thousand coins, saying, 'Engage in trade,' but he squandered those too and returned. Again, the merchant gave him five hundred, which he also squandered. When he returned once more, the merchant gave him two thick garments. Having squandered those as well, when he returned yet again, the merchant had him seized by the neck and driven out. Finding no refuge, he died leaning against the wall of another's house, and they dragged him away and discarded him outside. Anāthapiṇḍika went to the monastery and reported the whole story of his nephew to the Tathāgata. The Teacher said, 'Merchant, how could you satisfy him? In the past, even when I gave him a pot that granted all desires, I could not satisfy him.' And being requested by the merchant, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā pitu accayena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhi. Tassa gehe bhūmigatameva [M 2.0389] cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ ahosi, putto panassa ekoyeva. Bodhisatto dānādīni puññāni katvā kālakato sakko devarājā hutvā nibbatti. Athassa putto vīthiṃ āvaritvā maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā mahājanaparivuto nisīditvā suraṃ pātuṃ ārabhi. So laṅghanadhāvananaccagītādīni karontānaṃ sahassaṃ sahassaṃ dadamāno itthisoṇḍasurāsoṇḍamaṃsasoṇḍādibhāvaṃ āpajjitvā “kva gītaṃ, kva naccaṃ, kva vādita”nti samajjatthiko pamatto hutvā āhiṇḍanto nacirasseva cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ upabhogaparibhogūpakaraṇāni [P 2.0432] ca vināsetvā duggato kapaṇo pilotikaṃ nivāsetvā vicari. Sakko āvajjento tassa duggatabhāvaṃ ñatvā puttapemena āgantvā sabbakāmadadaṃ kumbhaṃ datvā “tāta, yathā ayaṃ kumbho na bhijjati, tathā naṃ rakkha, imasmiṃ te sati dhanassa paricchedo nāma na bhavissati, appamatto hohī”ti ovaditvā devalokameva gato. Tato paṭṭhāya suraṃ pivanto vicari. Athekadivasaṃ matto taṃ kumbhaṃ ākāse khipitvā sampaṭicchanto ekavāraṃ virajjhi[V 2.0357], kumbho bhūmiyaṃ patitvā bhijji. Tato paṭṭhāya puna daliddo hutvā pilotikaṃ nivāsetvā kapālahattho bhikkhaṃ caranto parakuṭṭaṃ nissāya kālamakāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a merchant's family. After his father's passing, he received the position of merchant. In his house, there was a treasure of forty crores buried underground, and he had only one son. The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, died and was reborn as Sakka, the king of the gods. Then his son, having blocked the street and erected a pavilion, sat surrounded by a large crowd and began to drink liquor. Giving thousands to those who leaped, ran, danced, and sang, he became addicted to women, drink, and meat. Asking, 'Where is the song? Where is the dance? Where is the music?' he became heedless and fond of revelry, and wandering about, he soon squandered the forty crores of wealth and all his belongings. Becoming destitute and miserable, he wandered about clad in a rag. Sakka, reflecting, perceived his wretched state and, moved by paternal love, came to him. He gave him a pot that grants all desires, saying, 'Dear son, guard this pot so that it does not break. As long as you have this, there will be no limit to your wealth. Be heedful!' Having advised him thus, he returned to the heavenly realm. From then on, he wandered about drinking liquor. One day, while intoxicated, he tossed the pot into the air and, in trying to catch it, he missed. The pot fell to the ground and shattered. From that moment, he became poor again, clad in a rag, and with a bowl in hand, he went begging. Leaning against another's wall, he passed away.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā –

The Teacher, having recounted this story of the past, said:

121.

121.

“Sabbakāmadadaṃ kumbhaṃ, kuṭaṃ laddhāna dhuttako;

Yāva naṃ anupāleti, tāva so sukhamedhati.

"A profligate, obtaining a pot that grants all desires, a jar, thrives in happiness so long as he guards it.

122.

122.

“Yadā matto ca ditto ca, pamādā kumbhamabbhidā;

Tadā naggo ca pottho ca, pacchā bālo vihaññati.

"When intoxicated and arrogant, through heedlessness he broke the pot; then naked and in rags, the fool later suffers.

123.

123.

“Evameva yo dhanaṃ laddhā, pamatto paribhuñjati;

Pacchā tappati dummedho, kuṭaṃ bhitvāva dhuttako”ti. –

"Just so, one who gains wealth and heedlessly consumes it; later the fool grieves, like the profligate who broke the pot."

Imā abhisambuddhagāthā vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi.

Having spoken these verses of perfect enlightenment, he identified the Jātaka.

Tattha sabbakāmadadanti sabbe vatthukāme dātuṃ samatthaṃ kumbhaṃ. Kuṭanti kumbhavevacanaṃ. Yāvāti yattakaṃ kālaṃ. Anupāletīti yo koci evarūpaṃ labhitvā yāva rakkhati, tāva so sukhamedhatīti attho. Matto [M 2.0390] ca ditto cāti surāmadena matto dappena ditto. Pamādā kumbhamabbhidāti pamādena kumbhaṃ bhindi. Naggo ca pottho cāti kadāci naggo, kadāci potthakapilotikāya nivatthattā pottho. Evamevāti evaṃ eva. Pamattoti pamādena. Tappatīti socati.

There, 'sabbakāmadadaṃ' means a pot capable of giving all objects of desire. 'Kuṭaṃ' is a synonym for pot. 'Yāva' means for as long as. 'Anupāleti' means: whoever obtains such a thing and protects it, for as long as he does so, he thrives in happiness—that is the meaning. 'Matto ca ditto ca' means intoxicated by the intoxication of liquor and proud with conceit. 'Pamādā kumbhamabbhidā' means through heedlessness, he broke the pot. 'Naggo ca pottho ca' means sometimes naked, and sometimes 'pottho' because of being clad in a rag made of coarse cloth. 'Evameva' means just so. 'Pamatto' means through heedlessness. 'Tappati' means he grieves.

“Tadā surāghaṭabhedako dhutto seṭṭhibhāgineyyo ahosi, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

"At that time, the profligate who broke the liquor jar was the merchant's nephew, but Sakka was I myself."

Surāghaṭajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The explanation of the Surāghaṭa Jātaka, the first.

[292] 2. Supattajātakavaṇṇanā

[292] 2. The Explanation of the Supatta Jātaka

Bārāṇasyaṃ[V 2.0358][P 2.0433], mahārājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto bimbādeviyā sāriputtattherena dinnaṃ rohitamaccharasaṃ navasappimissakaṃ sālibhattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā kathitaabbhantarajātake (jā. 1.3.91-93) vatthusadisameva. Tadāpi hi theriyā udaravāto kuppi, rāhulabhaddo therassa ācikkhi. Thero taṃ āsanasālāyaṃ nisīdāpetvā kosalarañño nivesanaṃ gantvā rohitamaccharasaṃ navasappimissakaṃ sālibhattaṃ āharitvā tassa adāsi. So āharitvā mātu theriyā adāsi, tassā bhuttamattāya udaravāto paṭippassambhi. Rājā purise pesetvā pariggaṇhāpetvā tato paṭṭhāya theriyā tathārūpaṃ bhattaṃ adāsi. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso dhammasenāpati, theriṃ evarūpena nāma bhojanena santappesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva sāriputto rāhulamātāya patthitaṃ deti, pubbepi adāsiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"In Benares, O great king"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the meal of fine rice with red-fish sauce and fresh ghee given by the Elder Sāriputta to Bimbādevī. The story is similar to the one told in the Abbhantara Jātaka. At that time too, the elder nun's stomach wind was disturbed, and the fortunate Rāhula informed the Elder. The Elder had him [Rāhula] sit in the assembly hall, went to the residence of the King of Kosala, and brought back a meal of fine rice with red-fish sauce mixed with fresh ghee and gave it to him. He brought it and gave it to his mother, the elder nun. As soon as she had eaten it, her stomach wind subsided. The King sent men to investigate, and from then on provided such food to the elder nun. One day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: 'Friends, the Captain of the Dhamma has satisfied the elder nun with such food!' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you sitting here now?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta gives what Rāhula’s mother desires; he gave it in the past too.' Having said this, he recounted the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kākayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto asītiyā kākasahassānaṃ jeṭṭhako supatto nāma kākarājā ahosi, aggamahesī panassa suphassā nāma kākī ahosi, senāpati sumukho nāma. So asītiyā kākasahassehi parivuto bārāṇasiṃ upanissāya vasi. So [M 2.0391] ekadivasaṃ suphassaṃ ādāya gocaraṃ pariyesanto bārāṇasirañño mahānasamatthakena agamāsi. Sūdo rañño nānāmacchamaṃsavikatiparivāraṃ bhojanaṃ sampādetvā thokaṃ bhājanāni vivaritvā usumaṃ palāpento aṭṭhāsi. Suphassā macchamaṃsagandhaṃ ghāyitvā rājabhojanaṃ bhuñjitukāmā hutvā taṃ divasaṃ akathetvā dutiyadivase “ehi, bhadde, gocarāya gamissāmā”ti vuttā “tumhe gacchatha, mayhaṃ eko dohaḷo atthī”ti vatvā “kīdiso dohaḷo”ti vutte “bārāṇasirañño bhojanaṃ bhuñjitukāmāmhi, na kho pana sakkā [P 2.0434] mayā taṃ laddhuṃ, tasmā jīvitaṃ pariccajissāmi, devā”ti āha. Bodhisatto cintayamāno nisīdi. Sumukho āgantvā “kiṃ, mahārāja, anattamanosī”ti pucchi, rājā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Senāpati “mā cintayi, mahārājā”ti te ubhopi assāsetvā “ajja tumhe idheva hotha, mayaṃ bhattaṃ āharissāmā”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the form of a crow and, having reached maturity, became the chief of eighty thousand crows, the crow-king named Supatta. His chief queen was a crow named Suphassā, and his general was named Sumukha. Surrounded by eighty thousand crows, he lived near Benares. One day, while searching for food with Suphassā, he passed over the roof of the great kitchen of the king of Benares. The cook, having prepared food for the king with various kinds of fish and meat, stood letting the steam escape, having left the vessels slightly open. Suphassā, smelling the aroma of fish and meat, became desirous of eating the king’s food. That day, she said nothing, but on the second day, when told, 'Come, my dear, let us go for food,' she replied, 'You go, I have a craving.' When asked, 'What kind of craving?' she said, 'I wish to eat the food of the king of Benares, but I cannot obtain it; therefore I will give up my life, my lord.' The Bodhisatta sat pondering. Sumukha arrived and asked, 'Why, great king, are you disheartened?' The king explained the matter. The general reassured them both, saying, 'Do not worry, great king. You both stay here today; we will bring the food.' With that, he departed.

So kāke sannipātetvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ kathetvā “etha bhattaṃ āharissāmā”ti kākehi saddhiṃ bārāṇasiṃ pavisitvā mahānasassa avidūre kāke vagge vagge katvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne [V 2.0359] ārakkhatthāya ṭhapetvā sayaṃ aṭṭhahi kākayodhehi saddhiṃ mahānasachadane nisīdi rañño bhattaharaṇakālaṃ olokayamāno. Te ca kāke āha – “ahaṃ rañño bhatte hariyamāne bhājanāni pātessāmi, bhājanesu patitesu mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ natthi, tumhesu cattāro janā mukhapūraṃ bhattaṃ, cattāro macchamaṃsaṃ gahetvā netvā supattaṃ sapajāpatikaṃ kākarājānaṃ bhojetha, ‘kahaṃ senāpatī’ti vutte ‘pacchato ehitī’ti vadeyyāthā”ti. Atha sūdo rañño bhojanavikatiṃ sampādetvā kājena gahetvā rājakulaṃ pāyāsi. Tassa rājaṅgaṇaṃ gatakāle kākasenāpati kākānaṃ saññaṃ datvā sayaṃ uppatitvā bhattahārakassa ure nisīditvā nakhapañjarena paharitvā kaṇayaggasadisena tuṇḍena nāsaggamassa abhihantvā uṭṭhāya dvīhi pakkhehi mukhamassa pidahi. Rājā mahātale caṅkamanto mahāvātapānena oloketvā taṃ kākassa kiriyaṃ disvā bhattahārakassa saddaṃ datvā “bho bhattakāraka, bhājanāni chaḍḍetvā kākameva gaṇhā”ti āha. So bhājanāni chaḍḍetvā kākaṃ daḷhaṃ gaṇhi. Rājāpi naṃ “ito ehī”ti āha.

He gathered the crows, explained the situation to them, and said, 'Come, we will fetch the food.' Then, entering Benares with the crows, he arranged them in groups near the royal kitchen, stationing them in various places to stand guard. He himself sat on the roof of the kitchen with eight crow warriors, watching for the time when the king’s meal would be carried out. He then instructed the crows: 'When the king’s food is being carried, I will knock over the dishes. When the dishes fall, my life will be over. Four of you should take a beakful of rice, and the other four should take fish and meat, then go and feed the crow-king Supatta and his queen. If asked, "Where is the general?" you should say, "He is coming later."' Then the cook, having prepared the king’s various dishes, took them with a carrying pole and set out for the palace. As he entered the royal courtyard, the crow general gave the signal to the crows. He himself flew up, landed on the food-bearer’s chest, struck him with his talons, and pecked the tip of his nose with his beak, which was like the point of an iron dart. Then, rising up, he covered the man’s face with both wings. The king, walking to and fro on the upper terrace, looked through a large window and saw the crow’s actions. He called out to the food-bearer, 'Ho, food-bearer, drop the dishes and catch only that crow!' The man dropped the dishes and firmly seized the crow. The king then said, 'Bring him here.'

Tasmiṃ [M 2.0392] khaṇe kākā āgantvā attano pahonakaṃ bhuñjitvā [P 2.0435] sesaṃ vuttaniyāmeneva gahetvā agamiṃsu. Tato sesā āgantvā sesaṃ bhuñjiṃsu. Tepi aṭṭha janā gantvā rājānaṃ sapajāpatikaṃ bhojesuṃ, suphassāya dohaḷo vūpasami. Bhattahārako kākaṃ rañño upanesi. Atha naṃ rājā pucchi – “bho kāka, tvaṃ mamañca na lajji, bhattahārakassa ca nāsaṃ khaṇḍesi, bhattabhājanāni ca bhindi, attano ca jīvitaṃ na rakkhi, kasmā evarūpaṃ kammamakāsī”ti? Kāko “mahārāja, amhākaṃ rājā bārāṇasiṃ upanissāya vasati, ahamassa senāpati, tassa suphassā nāma bhariyā dohaḷinī tumhākaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjitukāmā, rājā tassā dohaḷaṃ mayhaṃ ācikkhi. Ahaṃ tattheva mama jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā āgato, idāni me tassā bhojanaṃ pesitaṃ, mayhaṃ manoratho matthakaṃ patto, iminā kāraṇena mayā evarūpaṃ kammaṃ kata”nti dīpento imā gāthā āha.

At that moment, the crows came, ate their fill, and took the rest in the manner instructed and departed. Then the remaining crows came and ate what was left. Those eight crows went and fed the king and his consort, and Suphassā’s craving was pacified. The food-bearer brought the crow general to the king. Then the king asked him, 'Ho, crow, you were not ashamed before me, you cut the food-bearer's nose, you broke the food vessels, and you did not protect your own life—why did you commit such an act?' The crow replied, 'Great king, our king lives near Benares. I am his general. His wife, named Suphassā, has a craving and desires to eat your food. The king told me of her craving. I came here, having already forsaken my life in the presence of the king. Now the food for her has been sent, and my wish has been fulfilled. For this reason, I acted in such a way.' Explaining this, he spoke these verses:

124.

124.

“Bārāṇasyaṃ mahārāja, kākarājā nivāsako;

Asītiyā sahassehi, supatto parivārito.

“O great king, in Benares dwells the crow-king, Supatta, surrounded by eighty thousand crows.

125.

125.

“Tassa dohaḷinī bhariyā, suphassā bhakkhitumicchati;

Rañño mahānase pakkaṃ, paccagghaṃ rājabhojanaṃ.

“His wife, Suphassā, has a craving and desires to eat the royal food, prepared in the king’s kitchen, fresh and costly.

126.

126.

“Tesāhaṃ [V 2.0360] pahito dūto, rañño camhi idhāgato;

Bhattu apacitiṃ kummi, nāsāyamakaraṃ vaṇa”nti.

“I was sent as their messenger; I have come here from the king. I performed an act of honor for my master; I made a wound upon the nose.”

Tattha bārāṇasyanti bārāṇasiyaṃ. Nivāsakoti nibaddhavasanako. Pakkanti nānappakārena sampāditaṃ. Keci “siddha”nti sajjhāyanti. Paccagghanti abbhuṇhaṃ apārivāsikaṃ, macchamaṃsavikatīsu vā paccekaṃ mahagghaṃ etthāti paccagghaṃ. Tesāhaṃ pahito dūto, rañño camhi idhāgatoti tesaṃ ubhinnampi ahaṃ dūto āṇattikaro rañño ca amhi pahito, tasmā idha āgatoti attho. Bhattu apacitiṃ kummīti svāhaṃ evaṃ āgato attano bhattu apacitiṃ sakkārasammānaṃ karomi. Nāsāyamakaraṃ vaṇanti, mahārāja, iminā kāraṇena tumhe ca attano [M 2.0393] ca jīvitaṃ agaṇetvā bhattabhājanaṃ pātāpetuṃ bhattahārakassa nāsāya mukhatuṇḍakena vaṇaṃ akāsiṃ, mayā attano rañño apaciti katā, idāni tumhe yaṃ icchatha, taṃ daṇḍaṃ karothāti.

Here, 'Bārāṇasyaṃ' means in Benares. 'Nivāsako' means one who has a permanent residence. 'Pakkaṃ' means prepared in various ways; some recite it as 'siddhaṃ'. 'Paccagghaṃ' means piping hot and not stale, or that each of the various fish and meat dishes is of great value. 'Tesāhaṃ pahito dūto, rañño camhi idhāgato' means: 'I am a messenger, an agent for both of them, and I was sent by the king; therefore I have come here.' 'Bhattu apacitiṃ kummi' means: 'I, having come thus, perform an act of honor, respect, and reverence for my master.' Regarding 'Nāsāyamakaraṃ vaṇaṃ': 'O great king, for this reason, disregarding both you and my own life, I made a wound on the food-bearer’s nose with my beak in order to make the food vessels fall. I have thus performed an act of honor for my king; now you may inflict whatever punishment you wish.'

Rājā [P 2.0436] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “mayaṃ tāva manussabhūtānaṃ mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā amhākaṃ suhajje kātuṃ na sakkoma, gāmādīni dadamānāpi amhākaṃ jīvitadāyakaṃ na labhāma, ayaṃ kāko samāno attano rañño jīvitaṃ pariccajati, ativiya sappuriso madhurassaro dhammakathiko”ti guṇesu pasīditvā taṃ setacchattena pūjesi. So attanā laddhena setacchattena rājānameva pūjetvā bodhisattassa guṇe kathesi. Rājā naṃ pakkosāpetvā dhammaṃ sutvā ubhinnampi tesaṃ attano bhojananiyāmena bhattaṃ paṭṭhapesi, sesakākānaṃ devasikaṃ ekaṃ taṇḍulambaṇaṃ pacāpesi, sayañca bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā sabbasattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā pañca sīlāni rakkhi. Supattakākovādo pana satta vassasatāni pavatti.

Hearing the commander's words, the king thought, 'We, though being human, cannot make our friends so devoted even by giving them great honor, nor can we find one who would give their life for us even by giving them villages and the like. This one, though being a crow, sacrifices his life for his king; he is indeed exceedingly virtuous, sweet-voiced, and a preacher of the Dhamma.' Delighted by these virtues, he honored the commander with a white parasol. The crow, having received the white parasol, honored the king with it in return and spoke of the virtues of the Bodhisatta. The king had the Bodhisatta summoned, listened to the Dhamma, and established a regular meal for both the crow-commander and the crow-king from his own royal provisions. For the remaining crows, he ordered a daily ambaṇa measure of rice to be cooked. He himself, abiding by the Bodhisatta's advice, granted safety to all beings and observed the five precepts. The teaching of Supatta the crow-king continued for seven hundred years.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, sumukho senāpati sāriputto, suphassā rāhulamātā, supatto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka thus: 'At that time, the king was Ānanda, Sumukha the commander was Sāriputta, Suphassā the crow-queen was Rāhula's mother, and Supatta the crow-king was I myself.'

Supattajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Supatta Jātaka, the second.

[293] 3. Kāyanibbindajātakavaṇṇanā

[293] 3. The Commentary on the Kāyanibbinda Jātaka

Phuṭṭhassa meti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ purisaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kireko puriso paṇḍurogena aṭṭito vejjehi paṭikkhitto. Puttadāropissa “ko imaṃ paṭijaggituṃ [V 2.0361] sakkotī”ti cintesi. Tassa etadahosi – “sacāhaṃ imamhā rogā vuṭṭhahissāmi, pabbajissāmī”ti. So katipāheneva kiñci sappāyaṃ labhitvā arogo hutvā jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci. So satthu santike pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko nāma paṇḍurogī [P 2.0437] ‘imamhā rogā vuṭṭhito pabbajissāmī’ti cintetvā pabbajito ceva arahattañca patto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti[M 2.0394]. Pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāni ayameva; pubbe paṇḍitāpi evaṃ vatvā rogā vuṭṭhāya pabbajitvā attano vuḍḍhimakaṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this Jātaka beginning with 'Phuṭṭhassa me,' concerning a certain man. In Sāvatthī, it seems, a certain man was afflicted with jaundice and had been given up by the physicians. His wife and children also thought, 'Who is capable of nursing him?' He reflected, 'If I recover from this illness, I will go forth.' After two or three days, having obtained some suitable remedy, he became well, went to Jetavana, and asked the Teacher for the going forth. Having received both the going forth and the higher ordination in the Teacher's presence, he soon attained arahantship. Then one day, the monks started a discussion in the hall of Dhamma: 'Friends, a certain man with jaundice, having thought, "If I recover from this illness, I will go forth," has indeed gone forth and attained arahantship.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When they told him, he said, 'Not only now, monks, has this one done so; in the past, the wise also spoke thus, recovered from illness, went forth, and achieved their own welfare.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanto paṇḍurogī ahosi. Vejjāpi paṭijaggituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, puttadāropissa vippaṭisārī ahosi. So “imamhā rogā vuṭṭhito pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā kiñcideva sappāyaṃ labhitvā arogo hutvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā jhānasukhena viharanto “ettakaṃ kālaṃ evarūpaṃ sukhaṃ nāma nālattha”nti udānaṃ udānento imā gāthā āha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he came of age and established his household, he became afflicted with jaundice. Even physicians could not cure him, and his wife and children were distressed. Thinking, 'Once I recover from this illness, I will go forth,' he found some suitable remedy and, having regained his health, entered the Himalayas. There, he embraced the ascetic life of a sage, developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and dwelt in the bliss of jhāna. Exclaiming in joy, 'For so long, I have never attained such happiness as this,' he uttered these verses:

127.

127.

“Phuṭṭhassa me aññatarena byādhinā, rogena bāḷhaṃ dukhitassa ruppato;

Parisussati khippamidaṃ kaḷevaraṃ, pupphaṃ yathā paṃsuni ātape kataṃ.

“Afflicted by a certain malady, suffering greatly from disease, being oppressed by pain, this body of mine quickly withers, like a delicate flower placed on hot sand in the sun.”

128.

128.

“Ajaññaṃ jaññasaṅkhātaṃ, asuciṃ sucisammataṃ;

Nānākuṇapaparipūraṃ, jaññarūpaṃ apassato.

“Ignoble, yet known as noble; impure, yet regarded as pure; full of various corpses—it appears as a delightful form to one who does not see.”

129.

129.

“Dhiratthumaṃ āturaṃ pūtikāyaṃ, jegucchiyaṃ assuciṃ byādhidhammaṃ;

Yatthappamattā adhimucchitā pajā, hāpenti maggaṃ sugatūpapattiyā”ti.

“Fie on this frail, putrid body, repulsive, impure, and subject to disease, in which heedless and deeply infatuated beings abandon the path to a good rebirth.”

Tattha aññatarenāti aṭṭhanavutiyā rogesu ekena paṇḍurogabyādhinā. Rogenāti rujjanasabhāvattā evaṃladdhanāmena. Ruppatoti ghaṭṭiyamānassa pīḷiyamānassa. Paṃsuni ātape katanti yathā ātape tattavālikāya ṭhapitaṃ sukhumapupphaṃ parisusseyya, evaṃ parisussatīti attho.

Therein, 'by a certain' means by one of the ninety-eight diseases, specifically the malady of jaundice. 'By disease' refers to that which has the nature of causing pain. 'Being oppressed' means being struck and pained. 'Placed on hot sand in the sun' means: just as a delicate flower placed on sand heated by the sun would wither, so does this body wither—this is the meaning.

Ajaññaṃ jaññasaṅkhātanti paṭikūlaṃ amanāpameva bālānaṃ manāpanti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Nānākuṇapaparipūranti [V 2.0362] kesādīhi dvattiṃsāya kuṇapehi paripuṇṇaṃ[M 2.0395]. Jaññarūpaṃ apassatoti apassantassa andhabālaputhujjanassa [P 2.0438] manāpaṃ sādhurūpaṃ paribhogasabhāvaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, “akkhimhā akkhigūthako”tiādinā nayena pakāsito asubhasabhāvo bālānaṃ na upaṭṭhāti.

'Ignoble, yet known as noble' means that which is repulsive and unpleasant is considered pleasant by fools. 'Full of various corpses' means it is filled with the thirty-two impurities, such as hair of the head. 'It appears as a delightful form to one who does not see' means that to the blind, foolish worldling who does not see, it appears as a pleasant, fine form, suitable for enjoyment. The impure nature, revealed by the method beginning with 'from the eye, eye-excrement,' does not appear to fools.

Āturanti niccagilānaṃ. Adhimucchitāti kilesamucchāya ativiya mucchitā. Pajāti andhabālaputhujjanā. Hāpenti maggaṃ sugatūpapattiyāti imasmiṃ pūtikāye laggā laggitā hutvā apāyamaggaṃ pūrentā devamanussabhedāya sugatiupapattiyā maggaṃ parihāpenti.

'Frail' means constantly ill. 'Deeply infatuated' means extremely infatuated with the intoxication of defilements. 'Beings' refers to blind, foolish worldlings. 'They abandon the path to a good rebirth' means that, being attached and clinging to this putrid body and thus filling the path to the states of misery, they abandon the path to a good rebirth among gods and humans.

Iti mahāsatto nānappakārena asucibhāvañca niccāturabhāvañca pariggaṇhanto kāye nibbinditvā yāvajīvaṃ cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, the Great Being, comprehending in various ways the impure nature and constant frailty of the body, became disenchanted with it. Cultivating the four divine abidings for the rest of his life, he was destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahujanā sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu. “Tadā tāpaso ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, made the connection in the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many people attained the fruit of stream-entry and so forth. 'At that time, I myself was the ascetic.'

Kāyanibbindajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Kāyanibbinda Jātaka, the third.

[294] 4. Jambukhādakajātakavaṇṇanā

[294] 4. The Commentary on the Jambukhādaka Jātaka

Koyaṃ bindussaro vaggūti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattakokālike ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi devadatte parihīnalābhasakkāre kokāliko kulāni upasaṅkamitvā “devadattatthero nāma mahāsammatapaveṇiyā okkākarājavaṃse jāto asambhinnakhattiyavaṃse vaḍḍhito tipiṭakadharo jhānalābhī madhurakatho dhammakathiko, detha karotha therassā”ti devadattassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Devadattopi “kokāliko udiccabrāhmaṇakulā nikkhamitvā pabbajito bahussuto dhammakathiko, detha karotha kokālikassā”ti kokālikassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Iti te aññamaññassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitvā kulagharesu bhuñjantā vicaranti. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū [M 2.0396] kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso devadattakokālikā, aññamaññassa abhūtaguṇakathaṃ kathetvā bhuñjantā vicarantī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva te aññamaññassa abhūtaguṇakathaṃ kathetvā bhuñjanti, pubbepevaṃ bhuñjiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Who is this with a sweet, melodious voice?”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove concerning Devadatta and Kokālika. At that time, when Devadatta’s gains and honor had declined, Kokālika would approach families and say, “The Elder Devadatta is born in the royal lineage of Okkāka, from the line of the Greatly Elect; he was raised in an unbroken warrior lineage, is a master of the Tipiṭaka, an attainer of jhāna, a sweet speaker, and a preacher of the Dhamma. Give to the Elder, serve the Elder.” Thus he would speak in praise of Devadatta. Devadatta, too, would speak in praise of Kokālika, saying, “Kokālika went forth from an aristocratic brahmin family; he is very learned and a preacher of the Dhamma. Give to Kokālika, serve Kokālika.” In this way, speaking in praise of each other, they went about eating in the homes of families. Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a topic of discussion: “Venerable sirs, Devadatta and Kokālika go about eating after speaking of each other’s non-existent qualities.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?” When they told him, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that they eat after speaking of each other’s non-existent qualities; they ate in the same way in the past.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 2.0363] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto aññatarasmiṃ jambuvanasaṇḍe rukkhadevatā hutvā [P 2.0439] nibbatti. Tatreko kāko jambusākhāya nisinno jambupakkāni khādati. Atheko siṅgālo āgantvā uddhaṃ olokento kākaṃ disvā “yaṃnūnāhaṃ imassa abhūtaguṇakathaṃ kathetvā jambūni khādeyya”nti tassa vaṇṇaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a certain rose-apple grove. There, a crow, sitting on a rose-apple branch, was eating ripe rose-apples. Then a jackal came, and looking up, he saw the crow and thought, “What if I were to speak of his non-existent qualities and get to eat some rose-apples?” Speaking in praise of him, he uttered this verse:

130.

130.

“Koyaṃ bindussaro vaggu, saravantānamuttamo;

“Who is this with a sweet, melodious voice, the finest among those with a voice,

Accuto jambusākhāya, moracchāpova kūjatī”ti.

perched securely on the rose-apple branch, cooing like a young peacock?”

Tattha bindussaroti bindunā avisārena piṇḍitena sarena samannāgato. Vaggūti madhurasaddo. Accutoti na cuto sannisinno. Moracchāpova kūjatīti taruṇamorova manāpena saddena “ko nāmeso kūjatī”ti vadati.

Therein, 'melodious voice' (bindussaro) means endowed with a voice that is compact, unscattered, and rounded. 'Sweet' (vaggu) means a pleasant sound. 'Securely' (accuto) means not fallen, well-seated. 'Cooing like a young peacock' means he speaks like a young peacock with a pleasing sound, as if to say, “Who is this cooing?”

Atha naṃ kāko paṭipasaṃsanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the crow, praising him in return, spoke the second verse:

131.

131.

“Kulaputtova jānāti, kulaputtaṃ pasaṃsituṃ;

Byagghacchāpasarīvaṇṇa, bhuñja samma dadāmi te”ti.

“A man of good family knows how to praise another of good family. O you with the complexion of a tiger cub, eat, my friend, I give to you.”

Tattha byagghacchāpasarīvaṇṇāti tvaṃ amhākaṃ byagghapotakasamānavaṇṇova khāyasi, tena taṃ vadāmi ambho byagghacchāpasarīvaṇṇa. Bhuñja, samma, dadāmi teti vayassa yāvadatthaṃ jambupakkāni khāda, ahaṃ te dadāmīti.

Therein, ‘you with the complexion of a tiger cub’ means: ‘You appear to us with a color like that of a tiger cub, therefore I address you as, “O one with the complexion of a tiger cub.”’ ‘Eat, my friend, I give to you’ means: ‘Friend, eat as many ripe rose-apples as you wish; I give them to you.’”

Evañca pana vatvā jambusākhaṃ cāletvā phalāni pātesi. Atha tasmiṃ jamburukkhe adhivatthā devatā te ubhopi abhūtaguṇakathaṃ kathetvā jambūni khādante disvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

And having said this, he shook the rose-apple branch and made the fruits fall. Then the deity dwelling in that rose-apple tree, seeing both of them eating the rose-apples after speaking of each other's non-existent qualities, spoke the third verse:

132.

132.

“Cirassaṃ [M 2.0397] vata passāmi, musāvādī samāgate;

Vantādaṃ kuṇapādañca, aññamaññaṃ pasaṃsake”ti.

“After a long time, indeed, I see liars come together: a vomit-eater and a carrion-eater, praising one another.”

Tattha vantādanti paresaṃ vantabhattakhādakaṃ kākaṃ. Kuṇapādañcāti kuṇapakhādakaṃ siṅgālañca.

Therein, 'vomit-eater' refers to the crow, an eater of others' vomited food. 'Carrion-eater' refers to the jackal, an eater of corpses.

Imañca pana gāthaṃ vatvā sā devatā bheravarūpārammaṇaṃ dassetvā te tato palāpesi.

And having spoken this verse, that deity showed them a terrifying form and made them flee from that rose-apple tree.

Satthā [V 2.0364][P 2.0440] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo devadatto ahosi, kāko kokāliko, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the Jātaka: “At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, the crow was Kokālika, and the tree deity was myself.”

Jambukhādakajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Jambukhādaka Jātaka, the Fourth.

[295] 5. Antajātakavaṇṇanā

[295] 5. The Commentary on the Anta Jātaka

Usabhasseva te khandhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto teyeva dve jane ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu purimasadisameva.

“Your shoulders are like a bull’s”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning those same two individuals. The present story is just like the previous one.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ gāmūpacāre eraṇḍarukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tadā ekasmiṃ gāmake mataṃ jaraggavaṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā gāmadvāre eraṇḍavane chaḍḍesuṃ. Eko siṅgālo āgantvā tassa maṃsaṃ khādi. Eko kāko āgantvā eraṇḍe nilīno taṃ disvā “yaṃnūnāhaṃ etassa abhūtaguṇakathaṃ kathetvā maṃsaṃ khādeyya”nti cintetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the deity of a castor-oil tree in the vicinity of a village. At that time, in a certain small village, an old ox having died, they dragged it out and discarded it near the village gate in a wood of castor-oil trees. A jackal came and ate its flesh. A crow came and, perched in a castor-oil tree, saw this and thought, 'Suppose I were to speak of his non-existent virtues and then eat some flesh,' and so he spoke the first verse:

133.

133.

“Usabhasseva te khandho, sīhasseva vijambhitaṃ;

Migarāja namo tyatthu, api kiñci labhāmase”ti.

“Your shoulders are like a bull's, your majestic bearing is like a lion's; homage be to you, O king of beasts, might we obtain something?”

Tattha namo tyatthūti namo te atthu.

Therein, 'namo tyatthu' means 'homage be to you.'

Taṃ sutvā siṅgālo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the jackal spoke the second verse:

134.

134.

“Kulaputtova jānāti, kulaputtaṃ pasaṃsituṃ;

Mayūragīvasaṅkāsa, ito pariyāhi vāyasā”ti.

“A son of good family knows how to praise a son of good family; O you whose neck is like a peacock's, come down from there, O crow!”

Tattha [M 2.0398] ito pariyāhīti eraṇḍato otaritvā ito yenāhaṃ, tenāgantvā maṃsaṃ khādāti vadati.

Therein, 'ito pariyāhi' means 'descend from the castor-oil tree and come here to where I am, and eat the flesh,' he says.

Taṃ tesaṃ kiriyaṃ disvā rukkhadevatā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing their interaction, the tree deity spoke the third verse:

135.

135.

“Migānaṃ [V 2.0365] siṅgālo anto, pakkhīnaṃ pana vāyaso;

Eraṇḍo anto rukkhānaṃ, tayo antā samāgatā”ti.

“Among beasts, the jackal is the lowest; among birds, the crow; among trees, the castor-oil tree is the lowest—the three lowest have come together.”

Tattha antoti hīno lāmako.

Therein, 'anta' means inferior and wretched.

Satthā [P 2.0441] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo devadatto ahosi, kāko kokāliko, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the birth story: “At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, the crow was Kokālika, and the tree deity was I myself.”

Antajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Anta Jātaka, the fifth.

[296] 6. Samuddajātakavaṇṇanā

[296] 6. Commentary on the Samudda Jātaka

Ko nāyanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto upanandattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi mahagghaso mahātaṇho ahosi, sakaṭapūrehi paccayehipi santappetuṃ na sakkā. Vassūpanāyikakāle dvīsu tīsu vihāresu vassaṃ upagantvā ekasmiṃ upāhane ṭhapeti, ekasmiṃ kattarayaṭṭhiṃ, ekasmiṃ udakatumbaṃ. Ekasmiṃ sayaṃ vasati, janapadavihāraṃ gantvā paṇītaparikkhāre bhikkhū disvā ariyavaṃsakathaṃ kathetvā tesaṃ paṃsukūlāni gāhāpetvā tesaṃ cīvarāni gaṇhāti, mattikāpatte gāhāpetvā manāpamanāpe patte thālakāni ca gahetvā yānakaṃ pūretvā jetavanaṃ āgacchati. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, upanando sakyaputto mahagghaso mahiccho aññesaṃ paṭipattiṃ kathetvā samaṇaparikkhārena yānakaṃ pūretvā āgacchatī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “ayuttaṃ, bhikkhave, upanandena kataṃ paresaṃ ariyavaṃsakathaṃ kathentena, paṭhamatarañhi attanā appicchena hutvā pacchā paresaṃ ariyavaṃsaṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this, which begins with 'Ko nāyaṃ,' concerning the Elder Upananda. For he was of great appetite and great craving; he could not be satisfied even with cartloads of provisions. At the time of the rains retreat, he would approach two or three monasteries to spend the rains, leaving a sandal in one, a walking stick in another, and a water pot in a third. He himself would stay in one, then go to a monastery in the countryside. Seeing the monks with fine requisites, he would speak to them about the noble traditions, and having persuaded them to take up rag-robes, he would take their robes. Having persuaded them to take up clay bowls, he would take their pleasing bowls and vessels, fill a cart, and return to Jetavana. Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: 'Friends, Upananda the Sakyan is of great appetite and many desires. He speaks to others about the practice, then fills a cart with a monk's requisites and returns.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When it was told, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, what Upananda has done is improper, speaking to others about the noble traditions. For one should first be of few wishes oneself, and only then is it proper to speak to others about the noble traditions.'

“Attānameva [M 2.0399] paṭhamaṃ, patirūpe nivesaye;

Athaññamanusāseyya, na kilisseyya paṇḍito”ti. (dha. pa. 158) –

“First one should establish oneself in what is proper; then one may instruct another. The wise one should not be troubled.”

Imaṃ dhammapade gāthaṃ desetvā upanandaṃ garahitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva upanando mahiccho, pubbe mahāsamuddepi udakaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ maññī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Having taught this verse from the Dhammapada and rebuked Upananda, he said, “Monks, not only now is Upananda of many desires; in the past, too, he thought the water of the great ocean should be guarded.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 2.0366] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto samuddadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Atheko kāko samuddassa uparibhāge vicaranto “samudde udakaṃ pamāṇena pivatha, rakkhantā pivathā”ti macchasaṅghasakuṇasaṅghe [P 2.0442] vārento vārento carati. Taṃ disvā samuddadevatā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a sea deity. Then a certain crow, wandering over the surface of the sea, went about preventing the schools of fish and flocks of birds, saying, “Drink the water of the sea in measure; drink while protecting it.” Seeing this, the sea deity spoke the first verse:

136.

136.

“Ko nāyaṃ loṇatoyasmiṃ, samantā paridhāvati;

Macche makare ca vāreti, ūmīsu ca vihaññatī”ti.

“Who is this that runs all about in the salt water, keeping away fish and sea monsters, and is afflicted by the waves?”

Tattha ko nāyanti ko nu ayaṃ.

In this verse, 'ko nāyaṃ' means 'who indeed is this?'

Taṃ sutvā samuddakāko dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the sea-crow spoke the second verse:

137.

137.

“Anantapāyī sakuṇo, atittoti disāsuto;

Samuddaṃ pātumicchāmi, sāgaraṃ saritaṃpati”nti.

“A bird that drinks from the infinite, insatiable—so it is known in all directions. I wish to drink the ocean, the sea, the lord of rivers.”

Tassattho – ahaṃ anantasāgaraṃ pātumicchāmi, tenamhi anantapāyī nāma sakuṇo mahatiyāpi apūraṇiyā taṇhāya samannāgatattā atittotipi ahaṃ disāsu suto vissuto pākaṭo, svāhaṃ imaṃ sakalasamuddaṃ sundarānaṃ ratanānaṃ ākarattā sāgarena vā khatattā sāgaraṃ saritānaṃ patibhāvena saritaṃpatiṃ pātumicchāmīti.

The meaning is: I wish to drink the endless ocean; therefore, I am a bird named 'endless-drinker.' Because I am possessed of a great and unfillable craving, I am 'insatiable.' I am heard of, renowned, and famous in all directions. I wish to drink this entire ocean—called 'sāgara' because it is a mine of beautiful gems or was dug out by the sons of Sagara, and 'saritaṃpati' because it is the lord of rivers.

Taṃ sutvā samuddadevatā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the sea deity spoke the third verse:

138.

138.

“So ayaṃ hāyati ceva, pūrate ca mahodadhi;

Nāssa nāyati pītanto, apeyyo kira sāgaro”ti.

“This great ocean both ebbs and flows; its limit is not known by drinking; the sea, it seems, is undrinkable.”

Tattha [M 2.0400] so ayaṃ hāyati cevāti udakassa osakkanavelāya hāyati, nikkhamanavelāya pūrati. Nāssa nāyatīti assa mahāsamuddassa sacepi naṃ sakalaloko piveyya, tathāpi “ito ettakaṃ nāma udakaṃ pīta”nti pariyanto na paññāyati. Apeyyo kirāti eso kira sāgaro na sakkā kenaci udakaṃ khepetvā pātunti.

Here, 'so ayaṃ hāyati ceva' means it diminishes at the time of the water's receding, and it fills at the time of its flowing. 'Nāssa nāyati' means that even if the whole world were to drink the water of this great ocean, its limit—'this much water has been drunk from here'—would not be perceived. 'Apeyyo kira' means this sea, it seems, cannot be drunk by anyone to the point of exhaustion.

Evañca pana vatvā sā bheravarūpārammaṇaṃ dassetvā samuddakākaṃ palāpesi.

And having spoken thus, the deity, manifesting a terrifying form, made the sea-crow flee.

Satthā [V 2.0367] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā samuddakāko upanando ahosi, devatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the birth story: “At that time, the sea-crow was Upananda, and the deity was I myself.”

Samuddajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The commentary on the Samudda Jātaka, the sixth.

[297] 7. Kāmavilāpajātakavaṇṇanā

[297] 7. Commentary on the Kāmavilāpa Jātaka

Ucce [P 2.0443] sakuṇa ḍemānāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu puppharattajātake (jā. 1.1.147) kathitaṃ, atītavatthu indriyajātake (jā. 1.8.60 ādayo) āvibhavissati. Taṃ pana purisaṃ jīvantaṃ sūle uttāsesuṃ. So tattha nisinno ākāsena gacchantaṃ ekaṃ kākaṃ disvā tāvakharampi taṃ vedanaṃ agaṇetvā piyabhariyāya sāsanaṃ pesetuṃ kākaṃ āmantento imā gāthā āha –

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this, which begins 'Ucce sakuṇa ḍemāna,' concerning the luring of a former wife. The story of the present is told in the Puppharatta Jātaka; the story of the past will become clear in the Indriya Jātaka. They impaled that man on a stake while he was alive. As he sat there, he saw a crow flying through the sky, and disregarding even that intense pain, he addressed the crow to send a message to his beloved wife, and spoke these verses:

139.

139.

“Ucce sakuṇa ḍemāna, pattayāna vihaṅgama;

Vajjāsi kho tvaṃ vāmūruṃ, ciraṃ kho sā karissati.

“O bird flying high, winged sky-goer, tell her with the beautiful thighs that she will long wonder [at my delay].”

140.

140.

“Idaṃ kho sā na jānāti, asiṃ sattiñca oḍḍitaṃ;

Sā caṇḍī kāhati kodhaṃ, taṃ me tapati no idaṃ.

“She does not know this, that the sword and spear are set up; she, being fierce, will become angry; that torments me, not this stake.”

141.

141.

“Esa uppalasannāho, nikkhañcussīsakohitaṃ;

Kāsikañca muduṃ vatthaṃ, tappetu dhanikā piyā”ti.

“This wreath of blue lotuses, the golden ornament placed by the pillow, and the soft cloth of Kāsī—let my dear mistress be satisfied with these.”

Tattha [M 2.0401] ḍemānāti gacchamāna caramāna. Pattayānāti tamevālapati, tathā vihaṅgamāti. So hi pattehi yānaṃ katvā gamanato pattayāno, ākāse gamanato vihaṅgamo. Vajjāsīti vadeyyāsi. Vāmūrunti kadalikkhandhasamānaūruṃ, mama sūle nisinnabhāvaṃ vadeyyāsi. Ciraṃ kho sā karissatīti sā imaṃ pavattiṃ ajānamānā mama āgamanaṃ ciraṃ karissati, “ciraṃ me gatassa piyassa na ca āgacchatī”ti evaṃ cintessatīti attho.

Here, 'ḍemāna' means going or moving. 'Pattayāna' is an address to the bird, as is 'vihaṅgama.' For it is called 'pattayāna' from going by means of wings, and 'vihaṅgama' from moving through the sky. 'Vajjāsi' means 'you should say.' 'Vāmūru' refers to one with thighs resembling a banana trunk; you should tell her that I am seated on a stake. 'Ciraṃ kho sā karissatī' means that she, not knowing this news, will long wonder at my coming, thinking, 'It has been long since my beloved left and he does not return'—this is the meaning.

Asiṃ sattiñcāti asisamānatāya sattisamānatāya ca sūlameva sandhāya vadati. Tañhi [P 2.0444] tassa uttāsanatthāya oḍḍitaṃ ṭhapitaṃ. Caṇḍīti kodhanā. Kāhati kodhanti “aticirāyatī”ti [V 2.0368] mayi kodhaṃ karissati. Taṃ me tapatīti taṃ tassā kujjhanaṃ maṃ tapati. No idanti idha pana idaṃ sūlaṃ maṃ na tapatīti dīpeti.

'Asiṃ sattiñca' refers to the stake, due to its resemblance to a sword and a spear. For it was set up there to frighten him. 'Caṇḍī' means wrathful. 'Kāhati kodhaṃ' means she will be angry with me, thinking, 'He is taking too long.' 'Taṃ me tapati' means that her anger torments me. 'No idaṃ' means, 'But here this stake does not torment me'—this is what he explains.

“Esa uppalasannāho”tiādīhi ghare ussīsake ṭhapitaṃ attano bhaṇḍaṃ ācikkhati. Tattha uppalasannāhoti uppalo ca sannāho ca uppalasannāho, uppalasadiso kaṇayo ca sannāhako cāti attho. Nikkhañcāti pañcahi suvaṇṇehi kataṃ aṅgulimuddikaṃ. Kāsikañca mudu vatthanti muduṃ kāsikasāṭakayugaṃ sandhāyāha. Ettakaṃ kira tena ussīsake nikkhittaṃ. Tappetu dhanikā piyāti etaṃ sabbaṃ gahetvā sā mama piyā dhanatthikā iminā dhanena tappetu pūretu, santuṭṭhā hotūti.

With the words 'Esa uppalasannāho' and so on, he indicates his belongings placed at the headrest in the house. Here, 'uppalasannāho' is a compound of 'uppala' (lotus) and 'sannāha' (armor); the meaning is a lotus-like spear and armor. 'Nikkhañca' refers to a finger-ring made with five suvaṇṇas of gold. 'Kāsikañca mudu vatthanti' refers to a pair of soft Kāsī cloths. This much was placed by him at the headrest. 'Tappetu dhanikā piyā' means: having taken all this, may my dear wife, who desires wealth, be satisfied and fulfilled; may she be content with this wealth.

Evaṃ so paridevamānova kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbatti.

Thus, lamenting in this way, he passed away and was reborn in hell.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā bhariyā etarahi bhariyā ahosi, yena pana devaputtena taṃ kāraṇaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, so ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the end of the enunciation of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruition of stream-entry. 'At that time, the wife was the wife now, but the devaputta who witnessed that event was none other than I myself.'

Kāmavilāpajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The commentary on the Kāmavilāpa Jātaka, the seventh.

[298] 8. Udumbarajātakavaṇṇanā

[298] 8. The Commentary on the Udumbara Jātaka

Udumbarā [M 2.0402] cime pakkāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira aññatarasmiṃ paccantagāmake vihāraṃ kāretvā vasati. Ramaṇīyo vihāro piṭṭhipāsāṇe niviṭṭho, mandaṃ sammajjanaṭṭhānaṃ udakaphāsukaṃ, gocaragāmo nātidūre nāccāsanne, sampiyāyamānā manussā bhikkhaṃ denti. Atheko bhikkhu cārikaṃ caramāno taṃ vihāraṃ pāpuṇi. Nevāsiko tassa āgantukavattaṃ katvā punadivase taṃ ādāya gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Manussā paṇītaṃ bhikkhaṃ datvā svātanāya nimantayiṃsu. Āgantuko katipāhaṃ bhuñjitvā cintesi – “ekenupāyena imaṃ bhikkhuṃ vañcetvā [P 2.0445] nikkaḍḍhitvā imaṃ vihāraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ therūpaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ pucchi – “kiṃ, āvuso, buddhūpaṭṭhānaṃ nākāsī”ti? “Bhante, imaṃ vihāraṃ paṭijagganto natthi, tenamhi na gatapubbo”ti. “Yāva tvaṃ [V 2.0369] buddhūpaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā āgacchasi, tāvāhaṃ paṭijaggissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti nevāsiko “yāva mamāgamanā there mā pamajjitthā”ti manussānaṃ vatvā pakkāmi.

“These udumbara figs are ripe…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk. It seems he had a monastery built in a certain border village and was living there. The monastery was delightful, situated at the foot of a rock slab, with a small area to sweep, convenient water, and the alms village was neither too far nor too near. The people were very fond of him and offered alms. Then a certain wandering monk arrived at that monastery. The resident monk performed the duties of hospitality for the guest, and the next day took him along to the village for alms. The people gave excellent alms and invited them for the following day. After eating for a few days, the guest thought, “By some means, I will deceive this monk, drive him out, and take this monastery for myself.” Then, when the resident monk came to attend upon the elder, the guest asked him, “Why, friend, have you not paid homage to the Buddha?” The resident replied, “Venerable sir, there is no one to look after this monastery; therefore, I have not gone.” The guest said, “Until you go to pay homage to the Buddha and return, I will look after it.” The resident monk said, “Very well, venerable sir,” and after saying to the people, “Until my return, do not neglect the elder,” he departed.

Tato paṭṭhāya āgantuko “tassa nevāsikassa ayañca ayañca doso”ti te manusse paribhindi. Itaropi satthāraṃ vanditvā punāgato, athassa so senāsanaṃ na adāsi. So ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasitvā punadivase piṇḍāya gāmaṃ pāvisi, manussā sāmīcimattampi na kariṃsu. So vippaṭisārī hutvā puna jetavanaṃ gantvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesi. Te bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko kira bhikkhu asukaṃ bhikkhuṃ vihārā nikkaḍḍhitvā sayaṃ tattha vasī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi so imaṃ vasanaṭṭhānā nikkaḍḍhiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

From then on, the visitor slandered the resident monk to the people, saying, “This and that is the fault of that resident monk.” The other monk, having paid homage to the Teacher, returned, but the visitor did not give him back his lodging. He stayed in a certain place and the next day entered the village for alms, but the people did not show him even the slightest respect. Filled with displeasure, he went back to Jetavana and reported the matter to the monks. The monks raised the topic in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, it seems that such-and-such a monk has driven such-and-such a monk from his monastery and lives there himself.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?” When they told him, he said, “Not just now, monks, but in the past too he drove him from his dwelling place,” and he related a past incident.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññe rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tattha vassāne sattasattāhaṃ devo vassi. Atheko rattamukhakhuddakamakkaṭo ekissā anovassikāya pāsāṇadariyā vasamāno ekadivasaṃ daridvāre atemanaṭṭhāne sukhena [M 2.0403] nisīdi. Tattha eko kāḷamukhamahāmakkaṭo tinto sītena pīḷiyamāno vicaranto taṃ tathānisinnaṃ disvā “upāyena naṃ nīharitvā ettha vasissāmī”ti cintetvā kucchiṃ olambetvā suhitākāraṃ dassetvā tassa purato ṭhatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in the forest. There, during the rainy season, it rained for seven times seven days. At that time, a small, red-faced monkey, who lived in a rocky cave where it did not rain, sat comfortably one day at the cave's entrance in a dry place. Then, a large, black-faced monkey, drenched and suffering from the cold, wandered about and saw him sitting there. Thinking, “By some means, I will drive him out and live here,” he let his belly hang down, showing the appearance of being full, stood before him, and spoke the first verse:

142.

142.

“Udumbarā cime pakkā, nigrodhā ca kapitthanā;

Ehi nikkhama bhuñjassu, kiṃ jighacchāya miyyasī”ti.

“These udumbara fruits are ripe, and so are the nigrodha and kapitthana. Come out and eat; why do you die of hunger?”

Tattha [P 2.0446] kapitthanāti pilakkhā. Ehi nikkhamāti ete udumbarādayo phalabhāranamitā, ahampi khāditvā suhito āgatosmi, tvampi gaccha bhuñjassūti.

Here, ‘kapitthana’ means pilakkha trees. ‘Come out and eat’ means: these udumbara and other trees are bent down with the weight of their fruit. I too have eaten and returned full; you also go and eat.

Sopi tassa vacanaṃ sutvā saddahitvā phalāni khāditukāmo nikkhamitvā tattha tattha vicaritvā kiñci alabhanto punāgantvā taṃ antopāsāṇadariyaṃ pavisitvā nisinnaṃ disvā “vañcessāmi na”nti tassa purato ṭhatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

He too, having heard his words and believing them, went out, desiring to eat the fruits. After wandering here and there and finding nothing, he returned and saw the other monkey sitting inside the rock cave, which he had entered. Thinking, “I will deceive him,” that monkey stood before him and spoke the second verse:

143.

143.

“Evaṃ [V 2.0370] so suhito hoti, yo vuḍḍhamapacāyati;

Yathāhamajja suhito, dumapakkāni māsito”ti.

“Thus is one happy, who shows respect to the aged; just as I am happy today, having eaten ripened fruits from the tree.”

Tattha dumapakkāni māsitoti udumbarādīni rukkhaphalāni khāditvā asito dhāto suhito.

Here, ‘having eaten ripened fruits from the tree’ means having eaten tree fruits such as udumbara, he is not hungry, nourished, and satisfied.

Taṃ sutvā mahāmakkaṭo tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the great monkey uttered the third verse:

144.

144.

“Yaṃ vanejo vanejassa, vañceyya kapino kapi;

Daharo kapi saddheyya, na hi jiṇṇo jarākapī”ti.

“That a forest-dweller might deceive a forest-dweller, a monkey another monkey, a young monkey might believe, but not an old, aged monkey.”

Tassattho – yaṃ vane jāto kapi vane jātassa kapino vañcanaṃ kareyya, taṃ tayā sadiso daharo vānaro saddaheyya, mādiso pana jiṇṇo jarākapi mahallakamakkaṭo na hi saddaheyya, satakkhattumpi bhaṇantassa tumhādisassa na saddahati. Imasmiñhi himavantapadese sabbaṃ phalāphalaṃ [M 2.0404] vassena kilinnaṃ patitaṃ, puna tava idaṃ ṭhānaṃ natthi, gacchāti. So tatova pakkāmi.

The meaning is this: If a monkey born in the forest were to deceive another monkey born in the forest, a young monkey like you might believe it. But an old monkey like me, an aged, decrepit, great monkey, would not believe it; he would not believe someone like you even if you spoke a hundred times. For in this Himalayan region, all fruits, ripe and unripe, have been made wet by the rain and have fallen. There is no longer a place for you here—go! With that, he departed from there.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā khuddakamakkaṭo nevāsiko ahosi, kāḷamahāmakkaṭo āgantuko, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the little monkey was the resident monk, the great black monkey was the newcomer, and the tree deity was indeed myself.'

Udumbarajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Udumbara Jātaka, the Eighth.

[299] 9. Komāraputtajātakavaṇṇanā

[299] 9. The Commentary on the Komāraputta Jātaka.

Pure [P 2.0447] tuvanti idaṃ satthā pubbārāme viharanto keḷisīle bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Te kira bhikkhū satthari uparipāsāde viharante heṭṭhāpāsāde diṭṭhasutādīni kathentā kalahañca paribhāsañca karontā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā mahāmoggallānaṃ āmantetvā “ete bhikkhū saṃvejehī”ti āha. Thero ākāse uppatitvā pādaṅguṭṭhakena pāsādathupikaṃ paharitvā yāva udakapariyantā pāsādaṃ kampesi. Te bhikkhū maraṇabhayabhītā nikkhamitvā bahi aṭṭhaṃsū. Tesaṃ so keḷisīlabhāvo bhikkhūsu pākaṭo jāto. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ [V 2.0371] – “āvuso, ekacce bhikkhū evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā keḷisīlā hutvā vicaranti, ‘aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā’ti vipassanāya kammaṃ na karontī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepete keḷisīlakāyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at the Eastern Park, spoke this regarding some playful monks. It is said that while the Teacher was staying in the upper palace, those monks sat in the lower palace discussing what they had seen and heard, engaging in quarrels and derision. The Teacher called Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and said, 'Go and strike terror into these monks.' The Elder rose into the air and, striking the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe, shook the palace down to its very foundations. Terrified by the fear of death, those monks fled outside and stood there. Their playful nature became well-known among the monks. Then one day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: 'Friends, some monks, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, live with playful habits, not performing the work of insight on "impermanence, suffering, and non-self."' When the Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?' and they replied, 'For this,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that they are playful; they were playful in the past as well,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ gāmake brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, “komāraputto”ti naṃ sañjāniṃsu. So aparabhāge nikkhamitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantapadese vasi. Athaññe keḷisīlā tāpasā himavantapadese assamaṃ māpetvā vasiṃsu, kasiṇaparikammamattampi nesaṃ natthi, araññato phalāphalāni āharitvā khāditvā hasamānā nānappakārāya keḷiyā vītināmenti. Tesaṃ santike eko makkaṭo atthi, sopi keḷisīlakova [M 2.0405] mukhavikārādīni karonto tāpasānaṃ nānāvidhaṃ keḷiṃ dasseti. Tāpasā tattha ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya manussapathaṃ agamaṃsu. Tesaṃ gatakālato paṭṭhāya bodhisatto taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā vāsaṃ kappesi, makkaṭo tesaṃ viya tassapi keḷiṃ dassesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain village. They named him 'Komāraputta.' Later, he renounced the world, took up the ascetic life, and lived in the Himalayan region. Meanwhile, some other playful ascetics built a hermitage in the Himalayan region and lived there. They had no practice of meditation or kasiṇa exercises; instead, they gathered fruits from the forest, ate them, and spent their time laughing and engaging in various kinds of play. With them was a monkey, who, being just as playful, made faces and performed various antics for the ascetics. After living there for a long time, the ascetics went to human settlements to obtain salt and sour things. From the time of their departure, the Bodhisatta came to that place and took up residence. The monkey performed his antics for him just as he had done for the others.

Bodhisatto accharaṃ paharitvā “susikkhitapabbajitānaṃ santike vasantena nāma ācārasampannena [P 2.0448] kāyādīhi susaññatena jhānesu yuttena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tassa ovādaṃ adāsi. So tato paṭṭhāya sīlavā ācārasampanno ahosi, bodhisattopi tato aññattha agamāsi. Atha te tāpasā loṇambilaṃ sevitvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. Makkaṭo pubbe viya tesaṃ keḷiṃ na dassesi. Atha naṃ tāpasā “pubbe, tvaṃ āvuso, amhākaṃ purato keḷiṃ akāsi, idāni na karosi, kiṃkāraṇā”ti pucchantā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

The Bodhisatta, snapping his fingers, gave him this advice: 'One who dwells near well-trained ascetics should be accomplished in conduct, well-restrained in body and so forth, and devoted to jhāna.' From then on, the monkey became virtuous and accomplished in conduct. The Bodhisatta then went elsewhere. Then those ascetics, having partaken of salt and sour things, returned to that place. The monkey no longer performed his antics for them as before. Then the ascetics, asking him, 'Friend, you used to play before us, but now you do not. What is the reason?' spoke the first verse:

145.

145.

“Pure tuvaṃ sīlavataṃ sakāse, okkantikaṃ kīḷasi assamamhi;

Karohare makkaṭiyāni makkaṭa, na taṃ mayaṃ sīlavataṃ ramāmā”ti.

“Formerly, in the presence of us 'virtuous' ones, you played by leaping about in the hermitage. Perform your monkey-tricks, O monkey! We do not delight in that habit of yours.”

Tattha sīlavataṃ sakāseti keḷisīlānaṃ amhākaṃ santike. Okkantikanti migo viya okkantitvā kīḷasi. Karohareti ettha areti ālapanaṃ. Makkaṭiyānīti mukhamakkaṭikakīḷāsaṅkhātāni mukhavikārāni. Na taṃ mayaṃ sīlavataṃ ramāmāti yaṃ pubbe tava keḷisīlaṃ keḷivataṃ, taṃ mayaṃ etarahi na ramāma, tvampi no na ramāpesi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇanti.

Herein, 'in the presence of the virtuous' means in the presence of us who are of playful habit. 'Okkantikaṃ' means playing by leaping like a deer. In 'Karohare,' 'are' is a term of address. 'Makkaṭiyāni' refers to the facial distortions known as monkey-tricks. 'We do not delight in that habit of yours' means: we no longer take pleasure in your former playful conduct and playful habit, nor do you please us now. What is the reason?

Taṃ [V 2.0372] sutvā makkaṭo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the monkey spoke the second verse:

146.

146.

“Sutā hi mayhaṃ paramā visuddhi, komāraputtassa bahussutassa;

Mā dāni maṃ maññi tuvaṃ yathā pure, jhānānuyutto viharāmi āvuso”ti.

“For I have heard of the supreme purity from the learned Komāraputta. Do not now think of me as you did before; I dwell devoted to jhāna, O friend.”

Tattha [M 2.0406] mayhanti karaṇatthe sampadānaṃ. Visuddhīti jhānavisuddhi. Bahussutassāti bahūnaṃ kasiṇaparikammānaṃ aṭṭhannañca samāpattīnaṃ sutattā ceva paṭividdhattā ca bahussutassa. Tuvanti tesu ekaṃ tāpasaṃ ālapanto idāni mā maṃ tvaṃ pure viya sañjāni, nāhaṃ purimasadiso, ācariyo me laddhoti dīpeti.

Herein, 'mayhaṃ' is the dative case used in the sense of the instrumental ('by me'). 'Visuddhi' refers to the purity of jhāna. 'Bahussutassa' means of one who is learned because of having heard and realized many kasiṇa preliminary practices and the eight attainments. 'Tuvaṃ' addresses one ascetic among them, clarifying: 'Do not regard me as before; I am not as I was, for I have found a teacher.'

Taṃ [P 2.0449] sutvā tāpasā tatiyaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Hearing that, the ascetics spoke the third verse:

147.

147.

“Sacepi selasmi vapeyya bījaṃ, devo ca vasse na hi taṃ virūḷhe;

Sutā hi te sā paramā visuddhi, ārā tuvaṃ makkaṭa jhānabhūmiyā”ti.

“Even if one were to sow seeds on a rock, and the rain god were to pour down rain, they would not grow. So too, though you have heard of the highest purity, far are you, O monkey, from the ground of jhāna.”

Tassattho – sacepi pāsāṇapiṭṭhe pañcavidhaṃ bījaṃ vapeyya, devo ca sammā vasseyya, akhettatāya taṃ na virūḷheyya, evameva tayā paramā jhānavisuddhi sutā, tvaṃ pana tiracchānayonikattā ārā jhānabhūmiyā dūre ṭhito, na sakkā tayā jhānaṃ nibbattetunti makkaṭaṃ garahiṃsu.

The meaning is this: Even if one were to sow the five kinds of seeds on a stone slab, and the rain god were to pour down rain properly, those seeds would not sprout because it is not a suitable field. In the same way, though you have heard about the supreme purity of jhāna, you are far from the ground of jhāna because you belong to the animal realm. It is not possible for you to produce jhāna—thus they rebuked the monkey.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā keḷisīlā tāpasā ime bhikkhū ahesuṃ, komāraputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the Jātaka: ‘At that time, the ascetics of playful habit were these monks, but Komāraputta was none other than myself.’

Komāraputtajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Komāraputta Jātaka, the Ninth.

[300] 10. Vakajātakavaṇṇanā

[300] 10. The Commentary on the Vaka Jātaka.

Parapāṇarodhā jīvantoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇasanthataṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu vinaye (pārā. 565 ādayo) vitthārato āgatameva. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – āyasmā upaseno duvassiko ekavassikena saddhivihārikena saddhiṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā satthārā garahito [V 2.0373] vanditvā pakkanto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattappatto appicchatādiguṇayutto terasa dhutaṅgāni samādāya parisampi terasadhutaṅgadharaṃ katvā bhagavati temāsaṃ paṭisallīne sapariso satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā parisaṃ nissāya paṭhamaṃ garahaṃ labhitvā adhammikāya katikāya ananuvattane dutiyaṃ sādhukāraṃ labhitvā “ito paṭṭhāya dhutaṅgadharā bhikkhū yathāsukhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā maṃ passantū”ti satthārā katānuggaho nikkhamitvā bhikkhūnaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Tato pabhuti bhikkhū dhutaṅgadharā hutvā satthāraṃ [M 2.0407] dassanāya upasaṅkamitvā satthari paṭisallānā vuṭṭhite tattha tattha paṃsukūlāni chaḍḍetvā attano pattacīvarāneva gaṇhiṃsu. Satthā sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ senāsanacārikaṃ caranto [P 2.0450] tattha tattha patitāni paṃsukūlāni disvā pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “bhikkhave, imesaṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ dhutaṅgasamādānaṃ na ciraṭṭhitikaṃ vakassa uposathakammasadisaṃ ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this in reference to an old felt rug. The incident is fully recounted in the Vinaya (Pārā. 565ff.). Here is the summary: The Venerable Upasena, who had spent two years, along with his fellow monk who had spent one year, approached the Teacher. Having been reproached by the Teacher, he paid homage and departed. He then developed insight and attained arahantship, endowed with such qualities as contentment. He undertook the thirteen ascetic practices and also made his community undertake the thirteen ascetic practices. When the Blessed One had spent three months in seclusion, Upasena and his community approached the Teacher. Relying on his community, he first received reproach and then praise for not complying with an unrighteous agreement. The Teacher granted him a favor, saying, 'From now on, monks who observe the ascetic practices may visit me at their convenience.' Upasena then left and informed the monks of this matter. Thereafter, monks observing the ascetic practices would visit the Teacher. When the Teacher emerged from seclusion, they would discard their rag-robes here and there, taking only their own bowls and robes. The Teacher, walking around the dwellings with many monks, noticed the discarded rag-robes scattered about. Upon inquiring and hearing the reason, he said, 'Monks, the undertaking of the ascetic practices by these monks was not long-lasting; it was like a wolf’s observance of the Uposatha.' Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakko devarājā ahosi. Atheko vako gaṅgātīre pāsāṇapiṭṭhe vasati, atha gaṅgāya mahodakaṃ āgantvā taṃ pāsāṇaṃ parikkhipi. Vako abhiruhitvā pāsāṇapiṭṭhe nipajji, nevassa gocaro atthi, na gocarāya gamanamaggo, udakampi vaḍḍhateva. So cintesi – “mayhaṃ neva gocaro atthi, na gocarāya gamanamaggo, nikkammassa pana nipajjanato uposathakammaṃ vara”nti manasāva uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya sīlāni samādiyitvā nipajji. Tadā sakko devarājā āvajjamāno tassa taṃ dubbalasamādānaṃ ñatvā “etaṃ vakaṃ viheṭhessāmī”ti eḷakarūpena āgantvā tassa avidūre ṭhatvā attānaṃ dassesi. Vako taṃ disvā “aññasmiṃ divase uposathakammaṃ jānissāmī”ti uṭṭhāya taṃ gaṇhituṃ pakkhandi. Eḷakopi ito cito ca pakkhanditvā attānaṃ gahetuṃ nādāsi. Vako taṃ gahetuṃ asakkonto nivattitvā āgamma “uposathakammaṃ tāva me na bhijjatī”ti tattheva puna nipajji. Sakko sakkattabhāveneva ākāse ṭhatvā “tādisassa dubbalajjhāsayassa kiṃ uposathakammena, tvaṃ mama sakkabhāvaṃ ajānanto eḷakamaṃsaṃ khāditukāmo ahosī”ti taṃ viheṭhetvā garahitvā devalokameva gato.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, king of the gods. At that time, a wolf lived on a rock surface on the bank of the Ganges. Then a great flood came to the Ganges and surrounded that rock. The wolf climbed up and lay down on the rock surface. There was no feeding ground for him, nor any path to go for food, and the water kept rising. He thought, 'I have no feeding ground, nor any path to go for food. For one who is inactive, the observance of the Uposatha is better than merely lying down.' Resolving in his mind to observe the Uposatha and undertaking the precepts, he lay down. At that time, Sakka, king of the gods, reflecting and knowing the wolf’s weak undertaking, thought, 'I will harass this wolf.' Taking the form of a ram, he approached and stood not far from him, revealing himself. Seeing him, the wolf thought, 'I will see to the Uposatha observance another day,' and rising up, he rushed to seize him. The ram darted here and there, not letting himself be caught. Unable to catch him, the wolf turned back and thought, 'At least my Uposatha observance is not broken,' and lay down again in the same place. Sakka, standing in the air in his true form as Sakka, said, 'What use is the Uposatha observance for one with such a weak disposition? Not knowing my state as Sakka, you desired to eat the flesh of a ram.' Having harassed and rebuked him, he went to the world of the gods.

148.

148.

“Parapāṇarodhā jīvanto, maṃsalohitabhojano;

Vako vataṃ samādāya, upapajji uposathaṃ.

Living by taking the lives of others, a feeder on flesh and blood, the wolf undertook a vow and entered upon the Uposatha.

149.

149.

“Tassa [M 2.0408] sakko vataññāya, ajarūpenupāgami;

Vītatapo ajjhappatto, bhañji lohitapo tapaṃ.

Then Sakka, knowing his vow, approached in the form of a goat; his austerity gone, the blood-drinker drew near and broke his ascetic practice.

150.

150.

“Evameva [V 2.0374][P 2.0451] idhekacce, samādānamhi dubbalā;

Lahuṃ karonti attānaṃ, vakova ajakāraṇā”ti. –

Just so, some here are weak in their undertaking; they make light of themselves, like the wolf on account of the goat.

Tissopi abhisambuddhagāthāva.

All three are verses of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Tattha upapajji uposathanti uposathavāsaṃ upagato. Vataññāyāti tassa dubbalavataṃ aññāya. Vītatapo ajjhappattoti vigatatapo hutvā upagato, taṃ khādituṃ pakkhandīti attho. Lohitapoti lohitapāyī. Tapanti taṃ attano samādānatapaṃ bhindi.

There, 'he entered upon the Uposatha' means he entered upon the Uposatha observance. 'Knowing his vow' means knowing his weak vow. 'His austerity gone, he approached' means he approached having lost his ascetic resolve, intending to devour him—that is the meaning. 'Blood-drinker' means one who drinks blood. 'Ascetic practice' means he broke his own undertaken ascetic practice.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sakko ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, I myself was Sakka.'

Vakajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Vaka Jātaka, the Tenth.

Kumbhavaggo pañcamo.

The Pot Chapter, the Fifth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Varakumbha supatta sirivhayano, sucisammata bindusaro cusabho;

Saritaṃpati caṇḍi jarākapinā, atha makkaṭiyā vakakena dasāti.

The Excellent Pot, the Well-Winged, the Auspiciously-Named, the Pure and Esteemed, the Drop-Lake, and the Bull; The Lord of Rivers, the Fierce, the Old Monkey, then the She-Monkey and the Wolf—thus are the ten.

Atha vagguddānaṃ –

Then, the summary of the chapters:

Saṅkappo padumo ceva, udapānena tatiyaṃ;

Abbhantaraṃ ghaṭabhedaṃ, tikanipātamhilaṅkatanti.

The Intention, and the Lotus, the third with the Well; The Inner, the Breaking of the Pot—thus is the Tikanipāta adorned.

Tikanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Tikanipāta is concluded.

(Dutiyo bhāgo niṭṭhito.)

(The second part is concluded.)
